Representative Hakeem Jeffries, expected to be the next House speaker, said his party would focus on affordability after seizing control of Congress. President Trump focused on his renovation projects as Republicans grasped for answers.

Jess Bidgood and Catie Edmondson

A new political era opened in Washington on Wednesday, as Democrats vowed to use their sweeping majority to check President Trump’s power, while prominent Republicans blamed their midterm wipeout on his agenda and party leadership.

Democrats were on track to secure at least a 50-seat majority in the House and solid control of the Senate after notching seismic victories around the country, in deep red House districts and long-Republican Senate seats. Vice President JD Vance blamed the rout on Mr. Trump’s decision to start a war with Iran, a remarkable break from a president who, for much of the past decade, has demanded total fealty from his party.

“Everyone knows why we lost,” Mr. Vance said on social media. For his part, Mr. Trump said Mr. Vance’s assessment was “largely true.” He added, “If I had to do it again, I’d have to do it again.”

Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the minority leader who is expected to become the first Black speaker of the House, predicted Democrats would win at least 255 of the 435 seats in the chamber, comparing the scope of his party’s romp to an “American tsunami.” Democrats picked off Republicans who had not expected competitive races in conservative-leaning seats from Indiana to Missouri to Alabama, putting themselves on pace to make generational gains similar to those of the Republican wave of 1994 — only in reverse.

After two years of Republican control of Congress that reduced the House’s role to that of mere bystander, Mr. Jeffries promised to reassert the chamber’s power by undertaking aggressive investigations with oversight.

“The days of the House of Representatives functioning like a wholly owned subsidiary of the Trump administration are over,” Mr. Jeffries promised.

Republicans lost Senate seats in Maine, Iowa, Kansas, Ohio, North Carolina, South Carolina and even Texas, according to The Associated Press. Two other tight Senate contests haven’t been called: Ballots were still being counted in Alaska’s contentious Senate race and in the unlikely battleground of Mississippi, where roughly 1,100 votes separated the two candidates as of Wednesday evening.

The decisive control of the Senate is a “generational remake,” Senator Chuck Schumer of New York, the Democratic leader, told reporters in Washington.

Voters across every major demographic group — race, age, gender and education — made a drastic swing left in Tuesday’s election, reversing the gains Mr. Trump had made with them in 2024.

Mr. Trump seemed to brush off the sweeping repudiation. He used his first public appearance on Wednesday to tour the site of the ballroom he is building on the White House grounds. There, he defended what he considered to be his legacy-defining projects. “It’s going to be not only one of the biggest, but it’ll be the most beautiful ballroom, I think, anywhere in the world,” he said.

The shock waves from the election reverberated more resoundingly among other Republicans, who had feared widespread losses but had not anticipated such a renunciation of their party.

Speaker Mike Johnson of Louisiana told aides that he would not seek to lead the House G.O.P. conference in the minority, setting off a scramble among ambitious Republicans to succeed him. Representative Jim Jordan of Ohio announced he would seek the role, arguing that Republicans needed to take a combative approach toward the Democratic majority next year.

“In these next two years, our job cannot be merely to spotlight how radical this new Democrat party is,” he said. “Offense, not defense, wins elections.”

Representative Steve Scalise of Louisiana also jumped into the contest, arguing that Republicans must act with more unity.

Gov. Ron DeSantis of Florida said his fellow Republicans in Washington should have voted to release the Epstein files earlier and banned congressional stock trading. He called the election as “close to an extinction-level event for Republicans in many parts of the country as we have seen probably in the last 100 years.”

Mr. Trump told The New York Times in an interview late Tuesday night that he was “absolutely willing to accept” the midterm results and was prepared to work with Democrats — despite his repeated efforts to sow doubts about voter fraud and to have the Justice Department intervene in elections.

Here’s what else we’re covering:

Democratic landslide: The Democrats’ landslide did not just reach the federal races but also state and local governments. The party notched firsts in governors’ races and won down-ballot races like those for state treasurer, secretary of state and state legislature. Democrats are set to be in the majority in a dozen statehouse chambers where they had been the minority party.

G.O.P. bright spots: Republicans fended off a significant challenge in a Senate race in Florida, with Senator Ashley Moody defeating Angie Nixon, a progressive Democrat. Byron Donalds, a staunch Trump supporter, was elected Florida’s first Black governor, keeping the Republicans’ hold on that office.

Ballot measures: Voters across the country also weighed in on a range of statewide issues, including abortion, how future elections would be run and how their own votes would be counted. Read more ›

Shawn HublerJill Cowan and Orlando Mayorquín

Reporting from Los Angeles

Nithya Raman, a 45-year-old democratic socialist who tapped into a widespread frustration with the quality of life in the nation’s second-largest city, will become the new mayor of Los Angeles, The Associated Press reported Thursday.

Her victory over Karen Bass, the 73-year-old incumbent, is a sweeping success for a new generation of progressive leaders and the arrival of younger Angelenos as a political force in the sprawling metropolis.

A Harvard-educated policy expert who served six years on the City Council, Ms. Raman turned the page on a liberal bastion whose leaders had been consumed with big-picture battles with the Trump administration. Instead, she zoomed in on the nuts-and-bolts distress of young voters who increasingly found themselves priced out of the famously expensive city. Polls consistently showed her ahead by a wide margin with voters under 35.

The vote also revealed a broad appetite for change among the four million residents of the city — an echo of calls for a fresh perspective that on Tuesday night propelled a Democratic wave from Maine to California. In Los Angeles, which is already deep blue, it also suggested a widespread openness to the Democratic Socialists of America, the leftist movement that helped elect New York’s mayor, Zohran Mamdani.

By Thursday, Ms. Raman was leading with 52 percent of the vote and D.S.A.-backed candidates had won races for city attorney and Congress. Members of the movement already hold three seats on the 15-member City Council. Ms. Bass called Ms. Raman, her one-time ally, to concede on Thursday morning as the ongoing vote count showed a widening lead for Ms. Raman.

“I have committed to ensuring a smooth and seamless transition,” the mayor said in a statement. “Moving this city forward is what Los Angeles needs from all of us.”

On Thursday evening, Ms. Raman, who until recently was little known outside of progressive political circles, spoke to reporters at a farmers market in the Fairfax District, surrounded by throngs of news cameras, supporters and onlooking shoppers. She wore a blood-orange leather jacket and seemed to pause in front of the microphones, as if taking in her first moments before the public as mayor-elect.

“The key priorities that we’ve heard across this entire city are homelessness, housing costs and public safety,” Ms. Raman said, adding, “These will have to be the priorities that I take on in the city.”

She sought to reassure those who voted for her opponent or opted to not participate in the election. “I think that’s a sign of the deep distrust and cynicism that has taken hold here in the city of Los Angeles,” she said. “My goal is to earn your trust.”

Ms. Raman, an immigrant from India with a screenwriter husband and two children, said her story of becoming mayor was emblematic of the opportunity the city represented to the rest of the world. “This city has opened its arms to people to come and build their dreams here,” she said. “And the idea that Angelenos voted for an immigrant to be their next mayor, at this moment in American history, is so deeply moving to me.”

Preliminary election results showed that Ms. Raman had amassed support on the city’s gentrifying Eastside and in neighborhoods dense with young people, newcomers and renters. Ms. Bass drew from homeowners on the city’s Westside and in the San Fernando Valley and historically Black neighborhoods in South Los Angeles.

In one largely Latino neighborhood — Boyle Heights — where a cold storage warehouse fire burned for days in June, filling the air with the stench of rotten meat and seafood, voters who had backed Ms. Bass during the primary election flipped and supported Ms. Raman by large margins in the general election vote.

In interviews this week, voters said they welcomed Ms. Raman’s return to basics. Anthony Nabea, 36, said that he liked her focus on city services and potholes. Marisol Medina, 52, disapproved of the money Ms. Bass had spent on the police, whose union was among her primary supporters.

Zanisha Butler, 33, said she was simply ready for a new face in the mayor’s office. “I feel like Karen Bass has run her course to be honest,” Ms. Butler said.

Others expressed concern over the loss by Ms. Bass, whom they viewed as a steady hand compared to the relatively untested Ms. Raman. Daquan Houston, 42, a truck driver in the South Los Angeles of Vermont Square, said the mayor deserved a chance to finish the work she had started.

“If you get someone new,” he said, “then they’re going to be starting from scratch.”

Overall, however, Zev Yaroslavsky, the director of the Los Angeles Initiative at the University of California, Los Angeles, and a longtime civic leader, said Ms. Raman’s victory was “a reflection of an electorate that feels the city is on the wrong track.”

An annual survey conducted early this year by the Luskin School of Public Affairs at U.C.L.A., found that residents across the county were less satisfied with their quality of life than at any point in more than a decade.

Few members of the civic establishment publicly backed Ms. Raman. But those who did cited pragmatic motives.

George Kieffer, a former chair of the University of California board of regents and a principal coauthor of the Los Angeles City Charter, said that at 78, he had decided that only a major political shake-up would wake the city bureaucracy out of its lethargy.

“My party’s establishment is caught in its own bubble,” he said. “Nithya sees it. When she jumped, I did.”

A physician assistant and native Angeleno who organized in South Los Angeles against the crack epidemic in the 1980s, Ms. Bass rose politically as a progressive outside the city’s establishment circles. When she was elected mayor in 2022 , as the city strained to emerge from the Covid-19 pandemic, she defeated Rick Caruso, a billionaire real estate developer and civic leader who spent $100 million of his own money on the campaign.

But her fortunes turned in January 2025. Traveling to Africa at the behest of the Biden administration, she was out of the country when devastating wildfires erupted.

The disaster all but leveled the star-studded Los Angeles enclave of Pacific Palisades, and many survivors never forgave her for being absent during a time of crisis. Her campaign for re-election was an uphill battle from then on.

Six months after the fire, a violent crackdown on immigrants in Los Angeles by the Trump administration set off protests that the White House then seized upon to deploy some 4,000 National Guard troops and 700 U.S. Marines into Southern California. Throughout the occupation, which lasted until the end of the year, the Republican president and his allies clashed with Ms. Bass.

The partisan tension shored up her support, but not enough to fend off a serious challenge. After Austin Beutner, a civic leader from Pacific Palisades, entered the race and then withdrew in the wake of a family tragedy, Ms. Raman jumped in.

Ms. Raman, a specialist in urban planning who had been elected to the City Council in 2020 during the Black Lives Matter movement, channeled both Mr. Mamdani and San Francisco’s more centrist mayor, Daniel Lurie. Los Angeles was “broken,” she charged, and Mayor Bass had fallen short on ensuring a basic quality of life.

Although Ms. Raman at times stumbled on camera, and had to scramble to clarify her missteps, her campaign also shrewdly deployed social media videos designed to reach younger voters. Following in the footsteps of Mr. Mamdani, she gamely appeared in spoofs of microdramas made by real Hollywood production crews and election-themed skits with D.S.A.-aligned actors and influencers. In one video, she talked about creating more shade in the urban sprawl of Los Angeles, while pretending to be burned by hot surfaces — a car door, a picnic bench.

She also distanced herself in some ways from the D.S.A., supporting changes to a local “mansion tax,” for instance, that would have benefited one of the D.S.A.’s usual targets: apartment owners. But she pledged to replace the police chief, whose aggressive crowd-control tactics during immigration protests were denounced by the D.S.A. The group also accused the Police Department of protecting federal agents.

Ms. Bass seized on Ms. Raman’s promise, calling it reckless with the Olympics coming to Los Angeles in 2028, and charged that her challenger was “untested” and “not ready for prime time.” Ms. Bass’s 2022 opponent, Mr. Caruso, came to her aid, urging voters to reject Ms. Raman and the D.S.A. Every member of the City Council expressed support of Ms. Bass, except for Ms. Raman.

None of it was enough. After a hedge fund manager and advocate for increased bicycle use in the car-crazy city, backed Ms. Raman, becoming the race’s largest donor, Ms. Raman began airing ads on Dodger games and national news shows.

As her victory became clear, lobbyists, unions, downtown businesses, nonprofits and other entrenched civic interests were already preparing for a realignment. The pressure will be on the mayor-elect, according to Mr. Yaroslavsky at U.C.L.A.

Ms. Raman, he said, “now must face the challenge of erecting a new administration and beginning to fulfill her promise to fix the city she will lead in six short weeks.”

Vik Jolly contributed reporting.

JoAnna Mendoza, a Democrat and retired Marine, ousted Representative Juan Ciscomani, a two-term Republican, in a competitive southeastern Arizona district, according to The Associated Press on Thursday, handing her party a crucial seat to expand its House majority.

Mr. Ciscomani, elected to Congress in 2022, had been one of House Republicans’ top recruits. He highlighted a personal narrative grounded in a belief in the American dream, recalling how he and his father, who immigrated from Mexico, used to wash expensive cars to help make ends meet.

But Mr. Ciscomani was ultimately unable to overcome a brutal national landscape of voter discontent with rising prices driven by President Trump’s policies, including the war with Iran and tariffs. And Ms. Mendoza hammered him relentlessly for his vote for Republicans’ marquee tax and spending cut legislation that included slashing Medicaid and a nutrition assistance program for low-income people.

In the closing days of the campaign, Mr. Ciscomani had insisted in a direct-to-camera advertisement that he was “not a rubber stamp for anyone.” But he had done little to distance himself from Mr. Trump, repeatedly voting against efforts to end the war in Iran or cancel tariffs against Canada and Mexico, and supporting the so-called One Big Beautiful Bill.

Republicans had hoped that voters would reward them for enacting that measure, which limited taxes on tips and overtime. But with costs soaring, even those benefits had appeared to fall flat with some voters who said they still had trouble making ends meet.

Mr. Ciscomani’s pitch that Ms. Mendoza would raise taxes, citing her work as the executive director of a group advocating a more progressive tax policy in Arizona, failed to win over voters amid broader concerns about the price of gasoline and food.

Ms. Mendoza, in turn, weaponized Mr. Ciscomani’s voting record against him. She also leaned heavily into her own unique biography: Ms. Mendoza is a single mother who grew up in rural poverty and relied on food stamps, served two tours in Iraq and Afghanistan, survived two sexual assaults and struggled with substance abuse.

“We can start lowering costs by actually reversing all of the tax cuts to billionaires that my opponent voted for,” Ms. Mendoza said during a debate in September. “We reinstate programs like SNAP, programs that I used as a young child growing up.”

Democrats had targeted Mr. Ciscomani’s seat ever since he won it in 2022, flipping a seat that had been vacated by a Democrat. He won re-election in 2024 in a rematch by just three points.

It wasn’t long after Democrats claimed victory across huge swaths of the nation on Tuesday night that Republicans started pointing fingers at one another. Meanwhile, Democrats, riding high on the promise of a congressional majority, started pointing to their work.

Pete Buttigieg, the former transportation secretary, posted more than 30 photos of himself campaigning with winning candidates as their race calls rolled in. Senator Mark Kelly of Arizona and Gov. Andy Beshear of Kentucky each posted a dozen such photos.

The biggest names in Democratic politics had helped midterm candidates raise money, court voters and generate buzz, in some cases spending months traveling the country to campaign. Now they want to share in the victory lap, even if they themselves weren’t on the ballot.

Their efforts weren’t always purely altruistic: Many of this cycle’s busiest campaign surrogates are mulling 2028 presidential runs, and hitting the trail can be a prime opportunity to road-test ideas and build a national brand. And picking winners, of course, is generally a good look.

Here are some of the Democratic heavyweights who made big bets that paid off this midterm season.

Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, the democratic socialist from the Bronx, focused much of her campaigning this year on New York, but there was a major exception: Michigan.

One of the party’s top fund-raisers, Ms. Ocasio-Cortez endorsed Abdul El-Sayed for Senate in Michigan, then campaigned with him and transferred $1 million to an account to help him get elected — a huge sum for a House member to devote to a Senate contest.

Ms. Ocasio-Cortez, who is considering a run for president in 2028, made clear that she saw Mr. El-Sayed’s race as a test of the broader progressive movement’s electoral appeal. During a private fund-raiser, she said that “if Abdul can win in Michigan, anybody can win anywhere.” This week, he did just that.

Former President Barack Obama has considerable sway in a Democratic Party without an obvious standard-bearer. So it was notable when, in May, he showed up at a taco joint in Austin, Texas, with Gina Hinojosa and James Talarico.

“Do you know our outstanding next governor and senator?” Mr. Obama asked as he went from table to table. His wishful question proved prophetic: Both candidates won their elections.

Aside from a late blitz in a handful of battlegrounds, the former president was very selective about showing support for candidates. But he used those occasional interventions to cultivate a new generation of Democratic leaders who, like him, aim to build bridges across party lines.

His record this cycle was strong: Mr. Obama made one of his first formal endorsements in July by filming a video in which he shot hoops with Josh Turek, a centrist state lawmaker and Paralympian running for Senate. Mr. Turek won, becoming Iowa’s first Democratic senator in a decade.

The Rev. Raphael Warnock, a Democratic senator from Georgia, has been one of the loudest voices calling on Democrats to invest more resources in the South.

Mr. Warnock, who may be eyeing a 2028 presidential bid, focused his own midterm efforts there and urged others to do the same: “As goes the South, so goes the nation,” he said while campaigning in North Carolina.

And this week, Democrats delivered some of their most stunning electoral performances in the region in races that Mr. Warnock had prioritized earlier and more heavily than many other Democrats had.

He campaigned in South Carolina with Annie Andrews, a pediatrician who defied expectations by flipping a Senate seat in one of the country’s most conservative states; in North Carolina with Roy Cooper, a former governor who flipped another Senate seat; and in Mississippi with Scott Colom, a prosecutor who remains locked in a close Senate race against a Republican incumbent.

“We can win in Mississippi, but even if we don’t, it would be foolhardy for Democrats not to lean into that state,” Mr. Warnock told The New York Times before the election.

Mr. Buttigieg was one of the cycle’s most prolific campaigners.

He endorsed more than 100 candidates and appeared at events in more than 30 states. He focused his efforts on Democrats running to flip Republican-held House seats, and those candidates scored victories across the country.

Mr. Buttigieg campaigned with 29 candidates running to flip seats this year; at least 20 of them pulled it off.

He was the only national surrogate to campaign in North Carolina with Jamie Ager, a farmer who won a House district that President Trump had carried by 10 points, according to Grayson Barnette, Mr. Ager’s campaign manager. And Mr. Buttigieg was early to endorse Mr. Turek during a competitive primary in which some polls had shown him trailing.

Teresa Benitez-Thompson, a Democrat and former state legislator, defeated David Flippo, an Air Force veteran and financial adviser, according to The Associated Press, to win the open seat in Nevada’s open Second Congressional District, a conservative region in the northern part of the state.

The district has never been represented by a Democrat, but Flippo was plagued by a series of scandals related to his finances and accusations of stolen military valor, with even the district’s retiring Republican incumbent, Representative Mark Amodei, saying he would not vote for him.

Washington State voters have approved a ballot measure restricting transgender girls from participating in girls’ sports, The Associated Press reported. The measure has been widely viewed as a test of efforts to enact similar bans beyond the 27 Republican-led states where they are already in place.

In the race to replace Representative Nancy Pelosi in California’s 11th Congressional District, Connie Chan, a San Francisco supervisor, conceded to State Senator Scott Wiener on Wednesday after she fell further behind in the latest vote count. Both Wiener and Chan are liberal Democrats, but they split on housing and transit policy. Chan thanked Pelosi for her support and congratulated Wiener. The Associated Press has not yet called the race.

Nithya Raman widened her lead slightly over Mayor Karen Bass on Wednesday, as California’s notoriously slow vote count continued in the Los Angeles mayor’s race. Raman, a democratic socialist and former Bass ally on the City Council, was ahead 52-48 percent with a little more than two-thirds of the expected vote in.

President Trump used to gloat about his near-perfect endorsement record, reveling in the control he exerted over the Republican nomination process during this year’s primary season. Voters overwhelmingly rewarded the candidates he backed and punished those who displeased him, muscling numerous less loyal candidates out of contention.

“If you pushed back” on Mr. Trump, said Justin Evans, a Republican strategist in South Carolina, “you’d get your head chopped off.”

Mr. Trump has little to brag about this week. Senate candidates he had helped elevate, including Darline Graham in South Carolina, Michael Whatley in North Carolina and Ken Paxton in Texas, lost by margins previously unimagined by even the most optimistic Democrats. Those high-profile defeats contributed to what Gov. Ron DeSantis of Florida, a one-time Trump rival for the presidential nomination, called as “close to an extinction-level event for Republicans” as the country has seen in a century.

“The people who did the best last night were the people who distanced themselves from the president,” Mr. Evans said, calling the results “a universal repudiation of the bullying that’s been taking place during this primary” by Mr. Trump.

Here’s a look at what happened to some of the candidates who tied their fortunes most closely to Mr. Trump.

After Senator Lindsey Graham, a Republican, died in July, Mr. Trump threw his weight behind Mr. Graham’s sister, Darline Graham, in a snap primary election. While many Republican insiders objected, primary voters listened, narrowly nominating Ms. Graham over Representative Ralph Norman, despite her self-described lack of experience or policy expertise.

On Tuesday, the wider South Carolina electorate rejected Ms. Graham, choosing to send a Democrat to Washington for the first time in nearly 30 years.

“It wasn’t that voters rebuked Trump,” Mr. Evans said, noting that the Republican nominee for governor had earned at least 90,000 more votes than Ms. Graham. “It was that the entire Washington machine pushed this woman on South Carolina, and South Carolina resoundingly pushed back.”

Senate Republicans begged Mr. Trump to endorse Senator John Cornyn over Ken Paxton, the Texas attorney general, in the state’s Republican Senate primary. Many argued that Mr. Paxton’s scandal-ridden past would make it significantly more difficult, and more costly, to win in a general election. They also said a contentious intraparty battle would waste resources needed in more competitive states. Mr. Trump ignored them, waiting until days before a May primary runoff to back Mr. Paxton.

On Tuesday, despite dramatically outspending Democrats, Republicans lost the Senate seat, the governor’s mansion, and every other statewide race in Texas, breaking a more than three-decade-long streak of G.O.P. dominance.

Some Texas Republicans speculated that Mr. Paxton would have won the primary regardless of Mr. Trump’s choice. It is also not clear that Mr. Cornyn could have defied the tsunami of voter anger that propelled Democrats to victory up and down the ballot. But some blamed Mr. Paxton, and Mr. Trump, for the extent of the losses.

“You stand by Trump at your own peril at this point,” said Dade Phelan, the former Republican speaker of the State House. He recalled how Mr. Trump asked voters in Texas and elsewhere to “pretend I’m on the ballot.”

“Well, voters imagined he was on the ballot,” Mr. Phelan said. “And it was an absolute apocalypse for Republicans.”

Mr. Trump’s fingerprints were all over North Carolina’s Senate race. First, Senator Thom Tillis, a Republican who has served in North Carolina for more than a decade, announced he would retire rather than run for re-election after the president threatened to back a primary opponent against him.

Then, Mr. Trump handpicked Michael Whatley, a former Republican National Committee chairman, and Mr. Whatley spent millions touting Mr. Trump’s endorsement ahead of his victory in the Republican Senate primary. On Tuesday night, Mr. Whatley fell to former North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper, a Democrat, by around 20 points, a stunning leftward shift for a state that Mr. Trump won in 2024.

Meghan McMichael, 33, a voter in Canton, N.C., said on Tuesday that she had voted for Mr. Cooper and other Democrats in order to hold the Trump administration accountable for its treatment of immigrants, and the state of the economy.

“I’m just hopeful that certain people will be held accountable for things that have happened over the last two years,” she said.

Senator Jon Husted, Ohio’s Republican Senate nominee and a former college football player, was little known nationally until President Trump started talking about his rear end while on the campaign trail. Mr. Husted also joined Mr. Trump at several Ohio rallies in the final weeks of the campaign, tying himself to the president.

Mr. Husted lost to former Senator Sherrod Brown on Tuesday, making Ohio one of seven states that Democrats had flipped as of Wednesday evening.

The president’s comments about Mr. Husted’s backside may also have backfired, with voters across the country telling The New York Times they had disapproved of his remarks that Mr. Husted had a “great ass” and a “pile of muscle.”

In Lincoln, Neb., on Tuesday, Deondre Webster, 36, said he didn’t believe Mr. Trump is a good role model for his three daughters.

“We don’t want to see the leader of the country talking about male behinds or stuff like that onstage,” he said. “When he’s supposed to be the leader, and that’s not what we’re teaching our kids.”

Mark Barrett in North Carolina and Justin Diep in Nebraska contributed reporting.

An earlier version of this article incorrectly stated that Senator Jon Husted of Ohio is a former professional football player. Mr. Husted is a former college football player but never played professionally.

“It’s so dark outside,” President Trump just wrote on social media. He wasn’t talking about the midterms, but a failed legislative effort to make daylight saving time permanent, which would have ended the semiannual time change that shortens winter days.

Continuing his effort to shrug off an overwhelming Republican defeat in Tuesday’s elections, Trump complained that the Senate had not passed the measure by Election Day, and that the clock change back to standard time had moved the sunset in Washington today to 5:06 p.m.

“Just a few days ago it was so nice and sunny at this same time,” Trump said in a post at 6:33 p.m., adding that “I didn’t want to make a big deal out of this prior to the Election because I didn’t want to have certain Senators lose their Race, in a landslide, but it is too bad they can’t get it done.”

He conceded that the country has “far bigger priorities” than making daylight saving time permanent, but added, “I will keep fighting for this!”

Many Republicans tied their fates to President Trump, only to suffer a rude awakening on Tuesday night. That included Mayes Middleton, the Republican nominee for Texas attorney general, who spent millions from his personal fortune to brand himself as “MAGA Mayes” during a Republican primary he ultimately won over Representative Chip Roy, an established Republican and former assistant attorney general, whom he branded as anti-Trump.

But Middleton lost soundly to a Democrat, Nathan Johnson, on Tuesday despite outspending him by more than six to one. In an interview, Johnson said he was “delighted when Mayes Middleton nicknamed himself ‘MAGA Mayes,’ because I saw this coming.”

Mississippi’s secretary of state, Michael Watson, has mapped out the wait ahead for votes to be counted in the tight contest between Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith and Scott Colom, her Democratic challenger, who leads by 1,138 votes. There’s about 3,600 absentee-by-mail ballots that have to be received within five business days, plus an “unknown number of affidavit ballots.” Counties have until Nov. 13 to submit certified results to the state.

Caroline Soler and Christine Zhang

Control of the U.S. Senate has already been determined, with 33 of the 35 contests being called within hours of polls closing. In Alaska and Mississippi, however, no race calls have been made for the Senate and it could be quite some time until either contest is decided, even as some additional vote totals trickle out in the coming days.

In both cases, the Democratic nominee is clinging to a slim lead, but the reasons for the lack of a call are far different.

Alaska’s Senate race could take days or weeks to be called. Mary Peltola, the Democratic nominee, had a lead of fewer than 1,000 votes as of Wednesday afternoon, but nearly a quarter of the expected votes remain uncounted.

The bulk of the remaining vote is in the form of mail-in ballots. Some were cast close to Election Day, while others were postmarked by Election Day and will be received in the days after. A smaller chunk of early in-person ballots are also outstanding.

The deadline to tabulate all ballots, including provisional ballots, is Nov. 18. That is also the date that ranked-choice tabulation will begin, should neither Ms. Peltola nor Senator Daniel S. Sullivan, the Republican incumbent, cross the 50 percent threshold needed to win the election in the first round.

While the late mail vote typically leans toward Democrats, multiple factors could undercut Ms. Peltola’s possible advantage, including how many ballots will be received and how many are from voters who did not rank additional candidates beyond their first choice. There is also the potentially confounding presence of the other two candidates on the ballot, Gerald L. Heikes and Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.

A New York Times analysis of the available ranked-choice data pulled from each voter’s ballot shows that more than a third of voters who ranked Mr. Heikes or Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. as their first choice did not rank another candidate. That means these ballots would not count toward either Ms. Peltola or Senator Sullivan in subsequent rounds of the ranked-choice tabulation.

As of Wednesday evening, Scott Colom, the Democratic nominee in Mississippi, had a lead of roughly 1,000 votes over Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, the Republican incumbent. Because the margin is so tight, The Associated Press may not be able to make a race call until the state certifies a winner.

Mississippi is somewhat of an outlier in that it does not have a mechanism for automatic recounts, and has no method for a candidate to contest the election, so a court order would be required to initiate a recount.

Nearly all of the votes have been counted in the race, but a smattering of provisional ballots — which are ballots given to those with questions about their eligibility to vote — are still waiting to be counted, as are some late-arriving mail ballots. According to Mississippi's secretary of state, there are approximately 3,600 outstanding mail ballots that could arrive in time to be counted.

Mississippi’s Supreme Court ruled in June that the state must accept mail-in ballots that arrive by the Tuesday after Election Day — this year, Nov. 10. And provisional ballots in the state must be tallied by that day as well. For a provisional ballot to be accepted, the voter is required to provide proper identification to elections officials, obtain a state voter ID card, or submit a religious exemption.

Some counties in the state have said they hope to begin releasing some results of provisional ballots on Wednesday. It is currently unknown how many ballots remain uncounted statewide. Adding a layer of complexity, ballot processing and counting, which includes ruling on provisional ballots, is conducted by each county’s five-person elections commission rather than a single elections official.

In 2024, the state had just under 15,000 provisional ballots, of which 70 percent were accepted. In 2022, the state had about 5,700 provisional ballots, of which 75 percent were accepted.

Evan Peng contributed reporting.

Reporting from Washington

A group that champions electing conservative women to public office issued a blunt warning to Republicans on Wednesday after the Democratic sweep of Congress, calling the defeats of a large number of G.O.P. women an emergency that must be addressed.

“We are once again facing a crisis-level decline in Republican women in Congress,” Danielle Barrow, the president of Winning For Women Action Fund, an outside group dedicated to electing Republican women, said in a statement.

Ms. Barrow sounded the alarm as Democrats were celebrating their own milestone of electing more than 100 women to the House for the first time in history.

Republicans already have far less gender diversity in their ranks in the House, where there are currently 32 G.O.P. women (including two nonvoting delegates) — around 15 percent of their members.

With the landslide Democratic victories that are projected to win them the largest House majority in decades, that number could potentially dip to below 20 next year, after all races are called.

In 2018, when Republicans lost 40 seats and elected just one new G.O.P. woman to Congress, the party made a commitment to recruit and invest in female candidates, Ms. Barrow said. It worked: Two years later, 11 of the 15 seats Republicans flipped were by women.

“But that commitment to recruiting women faded when the urgency did,” she said. “Republicans cannot only make this investment after a wipeout election and abandon it when things improve. It is time for party leaders to treat this as a permanent strategy, not a crisis response.”

Reporting from Washington

Democrats in Congress are poised to ramp up investigations into Trump administration efforts to limit renewable energy development, promote fossil fuels and mining, and open up public lands to commercial interests.

Before the elections, House Democrats had already announced probes into some of those actions, including a $1 billion payout to cancel offshore wind farms, cuts to renewable energy investments in Puerto Rico and the shrinking of two national monuments in Utah. In other cases, they have raised allegations of corruption against officials overseeing public lands, fisheries and offshore energy development.

But with a majority in Congress next year, they can deepen those inquiries, said Representative Jared Huffman, Democrat of California, who stands to be chairman of the House Natural Resources Committee as its current ranking member. In January, Democrats will gain power to convene hearings, call witnesses to testify under oath and go to court to compel cooperation by the executive branch. Under Republican control, Congress has not used those powers to look into the Trump administration.

Just in the hours since the scope of the Democratic gains became clear, outside groups also began clamoring for new inquiries into steps by the administration to limit enforcement of pollution regulations and reduce the flow of federal disaster aid.

Senator Sheldon Whitehouse, Democrat of Rhode Island, said such investigations could help deliver on his party’s campaign promises to promote affordability. The Trump administration’s efforts to purge the government of any focus on climate change have contributed to rising property insurance premiums and energy costs, Mr. Whitehouse said.

“Democrats will work every angle to lower consumers’ energy costs, and we will demand accountability for the massive corruption wrought by Trump’s fossil-fuel donors through their climate denial fraud and corrupting dark money influence,” Mr. Whitehouse said in a statement.

The Environmental Protection Network, a nonpartisan group of hundreds of former Environmental Protection Agency officials, called for investigations into Trump administration pollution-limit rollbacks and rule exemptions. The group said the administration has ignored scientific evidence and its own experts to put industry above public health.

Samantha Montano, a professor of emergency management at the Massachusetts Maritime Academy who has criticized the Trump administration’s disaster management policy, said Democrats should investigate staffing cuts at the Federal Emergency Management Agency, as well as the agency’s distribution of key preparedness grants and recovery funding. Analyses have shown a partisan bias in President Trump’s approval of federal disaster declarations, which unlock FEMA aid for communities.

As Susan Collins campaigned in York County, Maine, recently, a woman approached to inform the Republican senator that she had always supported her and “absolutely” loved her. But she wasn’t going to vote for her this time.

“She said it was the only way she could send a message to Trump,” Ms. Collins recounted in an interview on Wednesday, a day after she lost to the Democrat Troy Jackson in her attempt to win a sixth term.

That was the story of the election for Ms. Collins, the chairwoman of the Appropriations Committee and a force in the Senate for three decades.

“I was caught up in the Trump tsunami that swept away many incumbent Republican senators who have served their states well for many years and really care about our country,” she said.

The five-term Republican senator had long seemed invulnerable to the ordinary laws of politics because of her singular political brand as a New England centrist with a gift for constituent service and an ability to steer federal dollars back home. In 2008, she triumphed in Maine while Barack Obama was romping and other Republicans were falling. In 2020, it seemed like her number might be up when polls had her down against a well-funded state lawmaker, but she again won easily.

Democrats saluted ruefully in respect.

But 2026 turned out to be a different case entirely as Ms. Collins was brought down by a combination of factors, most of which were attributable to President Trump and the war with Iran. There were soaring fuel prices in a state reliant on home heating oil. The punishing tariffs the president imposed on neighboring Canada. An immigration crackdown that resulted in a fatal shooting by federal agents in one Maine community. And always the perception that she wasn’t doing enough to stand up to the president, even when she was one of the few Republicans to occasionally break with him.

“Everybody ignores the fact that I voted to convict him in the second impeachment trial,” Ms. Collins said. “What bigger break could there be? It is never enough. I want results and they want angry rhetoric.”

On top of dissatisfaction that she hadn’t distanced herself sufficiently from the president, some voters harbored resentment about her vote in 2018 to confirm Justice Brett M. Kavanaugh to the Supreme Court, given his later role in overturning Roe v. Wade.

The coming result was evident from talking to voters on Tuesday as they exited the central polling place in Bangor — home turf for Ms. Collins. Several of them said they had repeatedly marked their ballots for “our senator,” as her ubiquitous yard signs proclaimed, but they would not do so this time.

“This time,” said Deborah Hanson of Bangor, “I’ve got to try something new. Susan Collins has voted with Trump on so many things.”

“To me, it is a close thing,” said Bob Kelly, another longtime Bangor voter. “But I can’t support anybody that supports Trump.”

In rejecting Ms. Collins, Maine voters gave up a tremendous amount of influence over federal spending by turning out the woman at the helm of the influential committee that controls federal spending. It is unusual but not unheard-of for voters to reject senior leaders.

Voters in Washington State dumped Representative Tom Foley, a Democrat, when he was speaker of the House in 1994. Senator Tom Daschle, the Democratic leader, lost his re-election bid to Senator John Thune, now the majority leader, in South Dakota in 2004.

Ms. Collins leaned heavily on her role in spending as she campaigned around the state, visiting the fire stations, community projects and infrastructure improvements for which she had secured funding, noting that if she were no longer in office, that money might dry up.

“I wanted to make sure people know what their choice was,” she said.

The man who defeated her, Mr. Jackson, will be a junior member of the Senate with little ability to steer to the state anywhere near the kind of financial aid that Ms. Collins had helped win.

“What she has been able to do over the last six years is extraordinary,” said Steve Abbott, her campaign manager and longtime senior aide. “Every town you go to, you see a project that was funded and work that needed to be done. That’s an opportunity that the state has walked away from.”

Up until the end, Ms. Collins and her team had hoped they could pull out a win as they watched from a hotel suite in Bangor. They had been cheered by the “rock star” reception they received around the state, an outpouring they said was better than during some of her winning races in the past.

“We went all over the state and I’ve got to tell you, the crowds were huge, the reception was warm and the response could not have been better,” Ms. Collins said as she addressed and thanked supporters in Bangor before the results were known.

But results from the Democratic stronghold of Portland overwhelmed her.

The race was chaotic, and Ms. Collins and her advisers like to note that they basically had to run against three opponents: Gov. Janet Mills, who initially appeared to be the likely challenger before she dropped out; the oyster farmer Graham Platner, who won the Democratic primary but dropped out after sexual abuse allegations; and Mr. Jackson, who had lost the state’s Democratic primary for governor but was then selected to replace Mr. Platner on the ballot.

Democrats have been frustrated for years both by Ms. Collins herself and their inability to defeat her. They poured huge amounts of money into the campaign, trying to highlight her ties to Mr. Trump and her votes for his policies. Ms. Collins pushed back, noting her own differences with the president on the Iran war, tariffs, the immigration crackdown and safety net cuts.

Over the course of her career, Ms. Collins was at the center of many major legislative negotiations on such tough issues as gun safety, health care and, following the Jan. 6, 2021, assault at the Capitol, a bill overhauling how electoral votes were counted. Her absence in the Senate will be felt on big legislative fights. She has not missed a vote in her Senate tenure.

Her political career was inspired in part by Margaret Chase Smith, the Maine Republican who served in the Senate from 1949 to 1972. Ms. Collins once met Ms. Smith, who had delivered a famous denunciation of Joseph McCarthy, and noted that some constituents encouraged her to have a Smith-like moment of conscience when it came to Mr. Trump.

“I would argue that I have, like Margaret Chase Smith, taken a lot of tough votes and stood up for what I believe in,” she said. “But I think the best comparison is we each lost our last race for the Senate.

“I have now had my Margaret Chase Smith moment.”

About a half-dozen Democrats who flipped Republican congressional seats are doctors and nurses, many of whom made health policy and their opposition to Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s agenda central to their campaigns.

Senator-elect Annie Andrews of South Carolina, a pediatrician, repeatedly called out Mr. Kennedy as her “archnemesis.” She and Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan appear to be the first Democrats with medical degrees elected to the Senate in about 60 years.

In California, Representative-elect Richard Pan, a pediatrician and a former state legislator who worked to tighten vaccine exemptions, beat the incumbent, Kevin Kiley, a former Republican who this year ran as an independent.

“This election cycle, R.F.K. Jr. was hands down our No. 1 recruitment and fund-raising tool,” said Erik Polyak, executive director of 314 Action, an organization that spent $30 million to support Democratic scientists and health care professionals.

Other successful health care candidates who flipped House districts include Kristina Knickerbocker, an oncology nurse practitioner in Ohio, and Mitchell Berman, a former Veterans Affairs nurse in Wisconsin. Amish Shah, an emergency room physician, appears to be on track to win in a competitive Arizona district, and Adam Hamawy, a plastic surgeon, won a safe Democratic seat in New Jersey.

Their success reflects, in part, the overall momentum of Democrats in Tuesday’s election. “It was a good thing to be a Democrat last night,” said Kristoffer Shields, director of the Eagleton Science and Politics Program at Rutgers-New Brunswick. Still, they ran, at least in part, on their credibility as medical professionals, “and it clearly seems to have worked,” he said.

They will join several Democratic medical professionals who have been elected since 2018, when a smaller wave of doctors and scientists ran in opposition to President Trump’s first administration.

“You could see a doctors’ caucus here in the Democratic Party,” Dr. Shields said. Just as the candidates were credible on health care to voters, “they’re going to be credible to other senators, or other representatives, once they get into Congress,” he said. He expects that among their top priorities will be making health care through the Affordable Care Act more affordable, perhaps by reinstating the subsidies that expired last year, and streamlining insurance processes to benefit patients.

I talked exclusively to Senator Susan Collins in the wake of her defeat, and she said she had been swept away in the anti-Trump wave. The Maine Republican has long defied political gravity, but voters in the state who had backed her repeatedly said they couldn’t do it this time — not because of Collins, but because of Trump.

She also compared herself to Margaret Chase Smith, the Maine senator who inspired her career and is known for having delivered a sharp denunciation of Joseph McCarthy. Collins said that she, too, had “taken a lot of tough votes and stood up for what I believe in.” But the best comparison, she noted, was that they both ultimately lost their last Senate race.

For Texas Democrats, the hits just keep on coming.

After routing Republicans in every statewide race and overturning a generation of conservative, one-party rule, the Democrats have also taken control of the Texas House of Representatives. The last time they held the majority in either legislative chamber was 2003.

Republicans will keep their majority in the Texas Senate. But the lieutenant governor, who, as the president of that chamber, is arguably the single most powerful force in lawmaking, will also be a Democrat: Vikki Goodwin. So is the governor-elect, Gina Hinojosa.

For the first time in about 25 years, Texas Democrats will have a real chance to govern. “Democrats have to deliver,” Gene Wu, the chairman of the Texas House Democratic Caucus, said from his home in Houston on Wednesday morning. “No excuses, no whining, no crying.”

Mr. Wu was wasting no time. He planned to drive to the state capital, Austin, on Wednesday to prepare for the next legislative session in January.

The Texas Legislature meets only once every two years, making the pressure especially high on Democrats to deliver real policymaking wins — and quickly. They’ve promised to focus their attention on pocketbook issues like taxes and education funding.

For a dozen years, Republicans forced Texas further to the right. Conservative legislators outlawed abortion, banned diversity offices in colleges, legalized the open carrying of firearms on their campuses, and stripped rights from the state’s gay community. They targeted big cities, all run by Democrats, by restricting local control.

Gov. Greg Abbott and Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick led those efforts. Both men lost their re-election bids.

Mr. Wu said his party’s wins were a rebuke to big government policies that he said have come to define the modern Republican Party.

“We’re going to let cities decide if they want to have rainbow sidewalks again,” Mr. Wu said, referencing recent Republican-enforced bans on such displays.

Senfronia Thompson, a Houston Democrat first elected before women could easily have credit cards, is the early favorite for House speaker. She would be the first Black Texan and the first woman in the role.

Tom Oliverson, the chairman of the House Republican Caucus, said the future for his party looked brighter than the present.

“When you kind of hit the bottom,” he said, “you can only go up from there, right?”

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/07/nx-s1-603.title: Homelessness in the U.S. saw its largest drop in more than a decade last year
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/07/nx-s1-603.author: Jennifer Ludden
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/07/nx-s1-603.text:
People line up along temporary tents to partake in a free Thanksgiving meal provided by the Union Rescue Mission as the Los Angeles Skid Row district annual feast hosts thousands of homeless and others in need, in downtown Los Angeles on Nov. 24, 2022.

After years of increasing to record-high levels, the homeless population in the U.S. dropped more than 6% in 2025. That amounts to roughly 49,000 fewer people without housing. It's the second year in a row that homelessness has declined, with a smaller drop in 2024.

"President Trump's actions to secure the border, get criminal illegals off our streets, and restore safety to our communities drove a historic decrease in homelessness," Housing and Urban Development Secretary Scott Turner said in a press release announcing the results of an annual count in communities around the country. The agency had not yet posted a detailed report.

A second independent analysis based on the same count, but commissioned by the advocacy group National Alliance to End Homelessness, found a similar decline but credited different reasons for it.

"It's good news that more people are getting housed, and that the programs that are funded by Congress are working," said CEO Ann Oliva.

Both analyses find there's still nearly 700,000 people in the U.S. living in shelters or on the streets, significantly more than before the COVID-19 pandemic.

The Trump administration cited its changes in immigration policy as a key factor in the decline. During the Biden administration, New York, Chicago, Boston and Denver all saw a surge in asylum seekers who turned up at homeless shelters. "That's also the four cities that have driven half of the drop most recently," said Devon Kurtz, Public Safety Policy Director at the Cicero Institute, an administration ally on homelessness policy.

Kurtz also pointed to declines in cities like San Francisco, which is moving to support more sober-living options, housing that bans drugs and alcohol. But critics say that can send more people back to the street if they relapse, which is common.

The Trump administration argues that the requirement to be drug-free would help more people achieve recovery, and wants to expand such programs. In fact, the administration wants to overhaul several billion dollars in homelessness spending and shift it toward short-term housing with mandated addiction and mental health treatment. So far that's been blocked by courts.

Manny Sarria, of the Miami-Dade County Homeless Trust, left, walks past people sleeping on the street during the annual Point-in-Time count of people experiencing homelessness Friday, Jan. 24, 2025, in Miami.

The administration says longstanding federal policy of getting people into permanent housing first, then offering voluntary treatment, has failed, and is to blame for the pandemic spike in homelessness. But Oliva, with the homelessness alliance, said programs that get people off the street without preconditions were a big part of the latest declines, especially among veterans.

"Investments in programs like that are much closer to the scale of need for veterans than for any other population experiencing homelessness," she said. Homelessness among U.S. veterans was down more than 7% last year, and has declined nearly 60% since 2010.

By contrast, Oliva said more permanent housing is needed for people who are chronically homeless, and more likely to suffer from mental health problems and addiction. Unlike other groups that saw a decline last year, there was a small uptick in people who've been homeless for a long time.

HUD also credited a crackdown on homeless encampments after the Supreme Court in 2024 said cities can ban people from sleeping and camping in public places. Oliva said the analysis her group commissioned showed that cities with such bans "actually did worse than the national average."

Oliva noted last year's decline in homelessness was broad and likely due to a number of factors, including softening rental markets in some places. Even though rents are still high they're down from record peaks during the pandemic, and that could stem the flow of newly unhoused people.

There were also declines in places that saw major weather disasters, like western North Carolina and Hawaii. When HUD and other groups move in to help those displaced, unhoused people also get assistance they did not have before.

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/07/nx-s1-603.title: The surprising and often forgotten history of economic populism in Texas
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/07/nx-s1-603.author: Michelle Aslam
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/07/nx-s1-603.text:
NPR's Rob Schmitz speaks with Austin-based political commentator David Griscom. He authored a book titled The Myth of Red Texas which tells the story of economic populism in Texas.

As the votes came in on election night Tuesday, some of the most shocking results were in Texas. The blue wave did not stop at the border of the Lone Star State. Democrats swept the top races in Texas with James Talarico winning a Senate seat and Gina Hinojosa winning the race for governor.

Austin-based political commentator David Griscom was perhaps not as surprised to see his state flip. Earlier this year, he published a book titled "The Myth Of Red Texas: Cowboys, Populism, And Class War In The Radical South." He joins us now. Welcome.

DAVID GRISCOM: Thank you so much for having me. It's been a really wonderful past few days.

SCHMITZ: What great timing, with a book title like that. Texas, obviously, as you've written, has a reputation for being a reliably red state, but as we've seen, it's a lot more complicated than that. How did Texas Democrats pull this off?

GRISCOM: Well, I think in a lot of ways, you saw Texas Democrats returning to our roots here. You know, many people forget this, but Texas was once the hotbed of kind of left-wing, pro-working-class politics. Going all the way back to the 1890s, we were the heart of the populist movement, and it's no accident that James Talarico, Clayton Tucker and Gina Hinojosa all call themselves populists.

Using this kind of rhetoric, I think, really focuses on the billionaires and the folks who are harming our democracy. And I think that gave a lot of people who might have been waiting for an excuse to maybe buck the Republican Party, which has dominated state politics here for so long, the opportunity to do so.

SCHMITZ: Let's go back in history a little. You know, Texas politics are often associated, you know, with oil billionaires, conservative evangelical voters and the Republican establishment. You know, your book, "The Myth Of Red Texas," tells the story of, you know, working-class, populist tradition that oftentimes goes overlooked. Tell us a little bit about that.

GRISCOM: So there's multiple phases of this. It's an entire kind of generation or tradition in Texas politics that has been forgotten. My book opens up talking about barbed wire, which we all associate with Texas. But when barbed wire first comes to Texas, it was fiercely resisted. There was an episode called The Fence Cutting War, and this happened all across the state, where working-class cowboys got together and they started cutting down these new barbed wire fences because they saw these as a tool that was being used to dispossess them.

This then flows into the populist movement, which was born right here in Texas in Lampasas, where a bunch of farmers got together and they started asking themselves why those who work most get least and those who work least get most. And they started to look around and realize that it was the monopoly powers, the power of the banks, and it was the corruption of the politicians.

SCHMITZ: I want to dig in a little bit on that and the populism aspect of this. Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa has embraced the populist label with open arms. You know, I want to play a clip here from an interview that she did before the election with The New York Times.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

GINA HINOJOSA: Populism is about economic power. We see that things are so stacked against working people in this country. Fighting culture wars at this time is not a winnable fight, and that is not the fight of 2026.

SCHMITZ: And that's really interesting. I mean, she's separating her and Talarico's style of politics from Democrats elsewhere, who have sort of engaged more in identity politics. Is there something uniquely Texan about Hinojosa's or Talarico's approach as Democrats?

GRISCOM: Absolutely. So again, you know, Texas has had major swings before where everyday working people - cotton farmers, Black and white - they were able to unite working people, the vast majority of people, on messages about the ways that they can improve their life. And that's what Gina and James were able to do. They didn't run a partisan message, and that is a long tradition that has existed in this state.

I'd also add, if I could, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez - after 2024, she made a very strong point about how effective some of the anti-trans ads that the Trump administration put out were - you know, they are for they/them, Trump is for you. And AOC said, like, this was a problem with Democrats. When a lot of people were feeling economic pain, they felt that the things that Democrats were interested in weren't immediately important to their lives.

And in this election, the table was kind of reversed because all of the ads in Texas were about anti-LGBTQ things, anti-trans. And when somebody's talking about that - in this case being Republicans - when you're really struggling to get by, it does really show that these folks are out of touch with your economic needs, and that really helped Gina and James, for sure.

SCHMITZ: That is David Griscom, author of "The Myth Of Red Texas." David, thank you.

GRISCOM: Thank you so much.

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/07/g-s1-1525.title: Israel's president taps opposition candidate, not Netanyahu, to form a government
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/07/g-s1-1525.author: Tara Neill
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/07/g-s1-1525.text:
Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar ("Straight") party, waves an Israeli flag onstage last month
in Tel Aviv following the release of the first exit poll results in Israel's general election.

Israel's president has tapped Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's main political rival, Gadi Eisenkot, to try to form the next government. It's a setback for Netanyahu, whose party won the most seats but failed to secure a parliamentary majority.

Netanyahu's Likud party won 27 seats in last month's election, six more than Eisenkot's Yashar party. But neither secured enough support to command a majority in Israel's 120-seat parliament.

President Isaac Herzog will formally give Eisenkot the mandate at 5 p.m. local time on Sunday.

Eisenkot is a former chief of staff of the Israel Defense Forces, serving as the country's top military commander from 2015 to 2019. A veteran of several military campaigns, he later joined Netanyahu's emergency war cabinet following the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attacks on Israel, but left the following year, accusing Netanyahu of failing to make progress toward ending the Gaza war and securing the release of hostages. Eisenkot lost his son, Gal, a reservist killed in Gaza, as well as two nephews during the war.

Eisenkot leads the centrist Yashar party, which he founded on an anti-corruption and government reform platform. He will now have 28 days to put together a coalition government, with a possible 14-day extension.

That gives him up to six weeks to negotiate with rival parties and secure the 61 seats needed for a parliamentary majority.

If Eisenkot fails, Herzog can give another lawmaker a chance to form a government. If those efforts also fail, Israel could face another election. Netanyahu would remain caretaker prime minister in the meantime.

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/07/g-s1-1525.title: Polish gunman who killed 6 people in Krakow has 'ultranationalistic' views, authorities say
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/07/g-s1-1525.author: The Associated Press
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/07/g-s1-1525.text:
Police cars are parked in a cordoned off area after a shooter opened fire in a market square in Krakow, Poland, Saturday, Nov. 7, 2026,

KRAKOW, Poland (AP) — A Polish man with far-right views drove into a busy central square in Krakow on Saturday and opened fire, killing six people and injuring 15 others before police shot and wounded him, authorities said.

The attack, which Poland's defense minister described as an "act of terror," happened in Main Square, which is in the heart of Krakow's Old Town and is a major tourist hub in the country's second-largest city.

The 25-year-old attacker drove to multiple spots in the square and opened fire at each stop with an automatic weapon, authorities said. Although they didn't release his name, Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said the man holds "very radical" and "ultranationalistic" views.

"Everything indicates that he was fascinated by far-right ideologies," Kierwiński said at a news conference.

Hours after the attack, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said authorities found the bodies of three of the suspect's close family members — two women and a man — inside of his home in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, a city about 150 kilometers (93 miles) northeast of Krakow.

"We have the next acts of this tragedy," Tusk told reporters.

Four women and two men were killed in the Krakow attack. At least three of the women were Polish, and one of the dead was a U.K. citizen, authorities said. Police were still trying to identify the other two people who were killed.

A total of 13 people were hospitalized in serious condition, authorities said, though that figure may include the gunman, who underwent surgery after the attack.

Armed police officers secure a cordoned off area after a shooter opened fire in a market square in Krakow, Poland, Saturday, Nov. 7, 2026, leaving people dead and injured, according to authorities.

It's unclear how many of the injured were shot. Two of them were treated and released within hours of the mass shooting. Two police officers were seriously injured, Kierwiński said. Five non-Poles were also injured, police commander Marek Boroń said.

People were wounded at several locations

The attacker wore military-style fatigues and a bulletproof vest, and used a military-type long gun, Krakow police spokesperson Katarzyna Cisło said. Police found other weapons and ammunition in his car. He kept firing at the police even after being shot himself, she said.

The attacker engaged in a "wild ride" around Main Square, which is why people were wounded at several locations, said Cisło, adding that the gunman appears to have acted alone.

Krakow mayor Łukasz Gibała said the city will be in official mourning until Wednesday. He vowed that Krakow will remain open to visitors despite the tragedy.

"The square will belong to us again," Gibała said in a video posted on X.

Mass shootings are rare in Poland

Videos posted on social media by witnesses show people running away from the square to take cover on small streets nearby, as well as first responders trying to resuscitate victims. In one video, a police officer is seen repeatedly shooting the attacker, who is lying on the street, only to later slowly collapse himself to the ground.

Photos showed a Polish Medical Air Rescue helicopter after it landed in the square.

It wasn't immediately clear whether the gun used in the attack or those found in the attacker's car are legal. Around 411,000 people hold gun permits in Poland, which has a population of 37 million, and interest in gun ownership has been rising.

Mass shootings are uncommon in Poland. However, in mid-October three attacks at schools in the central province of Mazovia took place within four days, leaving one person dead and many wounded, including children.

The Krakow attacker's military gear, guns and overall look were similar to those of other "extreme right lone actors" committing attacks around Europe, said Kacper Rekawek, a senior researcher at the International Center for Counterterrorism in The Hague. "We have had attempts before, but now we can say that these kinds of attacks have become successful in Poland."

Warsaw mayor Rafał Trzaskowski announced increased security measures, including road barriers, along main streets in the old town in the Polish capital in the aftermath of the Krakow attack.

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/07/nx-s1-603.title: Ousted Paraguayan president appears before prosecutors
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/07/nx-s1-603.author: Ava Berger
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/07/nx-s1-603.text:
Paraguay's President Santiago Peña waves after a meeting with Venezuela's interim President Delcy Rodriguez at the Miraflores Presidential Palace in Caracas, on September 19, 2026.

Paraguayan President Santiago Peña was impeached and placed under house arrest Friday after the collapse of a prominent U.S.-owned bank with ties to Paraguay's government. The fallout has left millions across the country without access to their money.

Peña is one of Washington's closest allies in the region and was a shareholder in Ueno Bank, a digital lender that served about 3 million customers — more than half of the country's adult population.

He was known as a pro-market leader focused on making it easier to do business in the country, but legislators said he jeopardized state assets and benefitted himself through his connection to the bank.

Ueno Bank previously said more than a million people opened bank accounts for the first time using its services, which included generous cash back offers on groceries.

A trial has proceeded against Peña, and he appeared before prosecutors Saturday morning. The last president ousted from office was Fernando Lugo in 2012.

Peña has denied any wrongdoing but on Thursday he announced his resignation. Lawmakers refused to accept that resignation, and instead moved forward with the country's impeachment process.

At proceedings inside the country's Senate Friday, legislators unanimously found Peña guilty of malfeasance in office, according to the Senate's website.

Prosecutors then accused him of a breach of trust, among other charges, before placing him under house arrest.

"I want to apologize to the Paraguayan people if I have failed you," Peña said in a speech posted to social media.

Demonstrators burn an image depicting Paraguay's President Santiago Pena, during a protest over the banking crisis and his resignation, at the main square in the surroundings of the National Congress in Asuncion, on November 5, 2026.

Pedro Alliana, the country's vice president, was sworn in as president to serve out the rest of Peña's term until August 2028. In a speech on Friday, he announced he would take action to compensate people whose money was lost in the bank's collapse.

Paraguay's central bank said it seized control of Ueno Bank on Tuesday because its solvency ratio, an assessment of a company's long-term financial viability, no longer met legal standards.

Protests erupted across Asunción, the country's capital city, following the seizure.

NPR's John Otis and Catherine Osborn contributed reporting to this story.

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/07/nx-s1-602.title: A promising new medicine against heart disease fails unexpectedly
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/07/nx-s1-602.author: Rob Stein
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/07/nx-s1-602.text:
For stories on the science of healthy living, subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.

An experimental drug doctors hoped would be the next big advance in preventing heart attacks and strokes failed a crucial test, researchers reported Saturday.

The medicine, which reduces levels of a particle in the blood associated with heart attacks and strokes, didn't protect volunteers in a closely watched study.

"I was shocked. I had high hopes for success," says Steven Nissen, a cardiologist at the Cleveland Clinic who led the study. "Cardiovascular disease is still the leading cause of death in developed countries. And so we really were hoping to find additional therapies that would reduce risk."

The research aimed to help people who seem to do everything right. They keep their cholesterol and blood pressure low, eat well, maintain a healthy weight, and exercise regularly. But many still suffer heart attacks and strokes.

"That sort of patient we see very frequently, and we were really doing our best to try to find a way to help those patients," Nissen says.

Many of these patients have elevated blood levels of a cholesterol-carrying protein called lipoprotein(a) or Lp(a), which has long been thought to increase the risk for heart disease.

"About 20% of the global population have elevated levels. And that's about a billion people. So it's a common disorder," Nissen says.

Until recently, doctors didn't have any drugs that could lower Lp(a) levels. But several drug companies have developed experimental new medications in recent years that can slash elevated Lp(a).

So Nissen and his colleagues gave 8,350 adults who already had heart disease either a placebo or a drug called pelacarsen, which cuts Lp(a).

The drug did suppress Lp(a) levels by about 78%, the researchers showed. But after five years, that drop didn't translate into saving people from suffering cardiovascular complications.

"Very disappointing, terribly disappointing," says Nissen, who presented the first details about the study at an American Heart Association meeting in Chicago Saturday and published more specifics in the New England Journal of Medicine and the NEJM Evidence.

Drugmaker Novartis, which sponsored the study, announced last month that the study results hadn't met its goals but without releasing specifics.

In a statement, Novartis said the study "provides meaningful evidence" about the relationship between Lp(a) and heart disease and may "help inform future approaches to cardiovascular management." "Progress in science depends on pursuing challenging questions and studies [like the pelacarsen study] play a crucial role in moving the field forward, even if the results are not what we had hoped for," the company said.

The failure of the drug to help patients is stunning because so many scientists, doctors and drug companies hoped Lp(a)-lowering drugs would provide the next major weapon in the fight against cardiovascular disease, which kills more than 900,000 Americans each year.

"I think it's a big deal because the expectation was so high that this would end up being positive," says Harlan Krumholz, a Yale University cardiologist. "And so it was really jarring to see this."

Researchers are scratching their heads about what went wrong.

It could turn out that high Lp(a) doesn't actually cause heart attacks and strokes, but instead is a marker for something else that increases the risk.

There could be other reasons for why the study failed.

"Maybe you need to treat longer. You may need to treat earlier, before people have advanced hardening of the arteries," says Roger Blumenthal, a cardiologist at Johns Hopkins University.

Another possibility is that Lp(a)-lowering drugs may only help people with higher Lp(a) levels.

"Maybe a higher Lp(a) should have been required for entry into the trial," says David Maron, a Stanford University cardiologist who serves as the president of the American Society for Preventive Cardiology.

The pelacarsen study could also have failed because Lp(a)-lowering drugs may only benefit people whose blood pressure and bad cholesterol weren't as well controlled, several experts said.

Another explanation could be that there's something about pelacarsen, the experimental drug, that doesn't produce a benefit.

It's possible other Lp(a)-lowering drugs might.

Several other drugmakers, including Amgen and Eli Lilly, are testing other experimental Lp(a)-lowering drugs. The results of those trials are expected to become available over the next few years.

"The take-home message is the story's not over," says Karol Watson, a cardiologist at the University of California, Los Angeles. "It's kind of just starting."
