https://www.npr.org/2026/11/07/nx-s1-602.title: Democrats plan to widen their probes of fatal ICE shootings
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/07/nx-s1-602.author: Meg Anderson
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/07/nx-s1-602.text:
Community members placed "I voted" stickers on a pole next to the memorial for Alex Pretti, who was shot and killed by Border Patrol agents during the federal immigration enforcement surge in Minneapolis last January.

The morning after Tuesday's midterms was gloomy and rainy in Minneapolis, but people still gathered at the place where Border Patrol agents shot and killed Alex Pretti, a VA nurse and U.S. citizen, last January. All week, community members have come here to place their "I Voted" stickers at the memorial.

Nicki Adams, who dated Pretti and was his close friend for nearly 17 years, watched quietly as a woman added her sticker to a street lamp completely covered in the red decals.

"I wanted to see all the stickers. I just wanted to be here," she says. "It just means a lot to me. I think it would mean a lot to Alex, too."

A few blocks away, people left their stickers where an ICE officer killed Renee Good, a mom of three and a U.S. citizen, just a few weeks before Pretti's death. In Houston, they left them where an ICE officer killed Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a father of three and a Mexican immigrant, in July.

Adams says these stickers, and the election results this week, send a clear message to Congress: "You work for us, and please carry on these values that we care about … We want to be seen and heard and taken care of and have our neighbors taken care of."

The deaths of Pretti and Good during the ICE surge in Minneapolis marked a pivotal moment for the country, sparking intense public backlash to President Trump's aggressive deportation efforts. But federal law enforcement officials have given little indication they're progressing in investigating their deaths, or the deaths of at least seven other people killed by federal immigration agents since Trump took office again last year. DHS did not respond to an NPR request for the status of those investigations.

Now, after Democrats' sweeping wins this week, their deaths at the hands of immigration agents will likely be the targets of renewed investigations. With a majority in Congress, Democrats can issue subpoenas to the major players in Trump's mass deportation plan, compelling them to testify under oath before the legislature.

That could include White House Border Czar Tom Homan, former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, former Border Patrol Commander Gregory Bovino, and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, among others.

Congress can also demand internal documents like use-of-force reports.

"They can dissect these individual shootings, and really unravel the story of what happened," says Naureen Shah, who leads the ACLU's immigration policy work.

Democrats have already held shadow hearings on the ICE shootings, during which they've called in family members and witnesses to testify.

But Shah says now Congress can ask key questions of top decision makers: What orders were given to immigration officers in the field? What was training like for these officers?

Who made the decision to paint Good and Pretti as threats, including calling Pretti a "would-be assassin" and a domestic terrorist, when video showed otherwise?

"It's like we can turn the faucet on and actually find out so much more," Shah says. "There's an aspect of this that is really about a kind of reckoning with how it's possible that things that seemed unthinkable could happen on American streets. How do you have that reckoning if you don't actually have the ability to force people to explain themselves?"

Democratic leaders have already said that's the plan.

Maryland Democratic Rep. Jamie Raskin, who is expected to lead the House Judiciary Committee, told NPR in a statement that Congress will use "every tool" at its disposal to investigate ICE and that it is time for the agency to "start answering to the American people."

California Democratic Rep. Robert Garcia, expected to lead the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, vowed to take on DHS and ICE abuses in a two-word statement: "Lawyer Up."

Mississippi Democratic Rep. Bennie Thompson, expected to lead the House Committee on Homeland Security, sent a letter on Wednesday to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, demanding the agency "comply with all document preservation requirements."

Illinois Democratic Rep. Delia Ramirez wrote on social media that Noem, Miller, Homan, Bovino and Mullin should "clear" their schedules.

In response to that, DHS general counsel James Percival said Democrats are "more interested in political shenanigans than in governing" but said the agency is prepared to "deal with this nonsense."

There are key limitations to what Democrats in Congress can do with their majority when it comes to ICE accountability, says Rachel Moran, a professor at the University of St. Thomas School of Law.

Major changes, like clawing back funding for the agency, would require a veto-proof majority, something the Democrats don't have.

"You still have a president who has shown a complete lack of interest in accountability for federal agents and in fact, a great deal of knee jerk defensiveness about their conduct," Moran says.

In a statement, a White House spokesperson told NPR "if Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people."

Democrats, the statement added, "should be reminded that we still control the federal government and all of its powers."

But that's not true. Congress has its own powers, one of them being the ability to compel testimony. Moran says a deeper probe into the shootings could still serve important purposes, like making evidence available for states to use in their own criminal investigations.

Minnesota officials, for instance, have been fighting with the federal government to get evidence related to the Pretti and Good killings.

Brent Ganger, Renee Good's brother, says learning more information about his sister's death will be hard to hear, "but I think it's also super important for us to understand what happened that day. I don't want history to keep repeating itself."

It was painful, he says, to watch immigration agents kill more people after his sister. He thought her death would be a turning point. In a way, it might have been the start of one. After the surge in Minneapolis, most Americans said ICE had gone too far.

Ganger, who considers himself a moderate, was happy to see the Blue Wave this week. On election night, he was scrolling Instagram when he saw a photo of his sister's memorial site, with all the "I Voted" stickers.

"I was very grateful to see the repudiation of this administration from the country. It felt very supportive of my entire family," he says.

The next morning, in his home in Colorado, he got up and made biscuits and gravy, his sister's favorite breakfast.

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/07/nx-s1-602.title: Perspective: Simon Winchester was here to tell a story
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/07/nx-s1-602.author: Scott Simon
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/07/nx-s1-602.text:
Author and journalist Simon Winchester with his 1914 Royal typewriter at his home in Sandisfield, Massachusetts in 2006.

I met Simon Winchester decades ago, covering a big story in a small town. The Menominee Warrior Society had seized an abandoned Catholic monastery in Gresham, Wisconsin, and other indigenous rights activists - including the actor Marlon Brando - came to join them.

I was a young reporter who had traveled up from Chicago. Simon Winchester was there for The Guardian newspaper, wearing a Sherlock Holmes-style hat and a tweed cape. We wound up in the same local rooming house, and I would creep onto the stairs at midnight to hear Simon, on a payphone, read his elegant copy to an editor in London between quaffs of brandy.

"Analysis is just so much gabble," I remember him remonstrating to an editor one night. "I'm here to tell a story."

Simon Winchester, who died this week at the age of 82, told so many stories. He covered Bloody Sunday in Derry, Northern Ireland; the Watergate scandal in Washington DC; and the Falklands war - during which Argentine authorities accused him of spying for the British government and threw him in jail for three months.

"Who on earth would make me a spy?," he used to ask in re-telling the story. "As if I could keep a secret!"

Simon Winchester went on to author dozens of bestsellers that ranged around the world, and humanity. He wrote about earthquakes and cities, explorers on open seas, mountains, and in laboratories, the English language, and the human mind and soul.

"It was a brave man," Simon wrote in his book about the Atlantic Ocean, "who ate the first oyster."

This week, as exit polls show so much human anxiety over Artificial Intelligence, I wondered if Simon Winchester might want people to hear some of the final, surprisingly buoyant thoughts from his 2024 book, Knowing What We Know.

"An existential intellectual crisis looms," he wrote. "If machines will acquire all our knowledge for us and do our thinking for us, then what, pray, is the need for us to be?...

"But what if the opposite is true?" asked Simon Winchester. "What if mental leisure gives us the time and space to suppose, ponder, ruminate, consider, assess, wonder, contemplate, imagine, dream?...

"And by doing so perhaps come to know not simply what we do know, but what we should know, in order to be fully human."

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/07/g-s1-1522.title: This teen boy set out to get people talking about periods. He's now a Diana honoree
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/07/g-s1-1522.author: Kamala Thiagarajan
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/07/g-s1-1522.text:
Aadvik Jain (third from right) has won a Princess Diana award for starting Team Period to counter menstrual stigma. He's standing with other members of this activist group and teacher Sonia Rao (center, in green sari). "Our work would not be possible without her guidance and support," he says.

Can a teenage boy change the way people think about menstruation?

At just 14, Aadvik Jain, studying in India's capital city, Delhi, set out to do exactly that. It all began when he had to watch a close friend struggle with debilitating menstrual pain that wasn't being taken seriously.

This year, he's among the 198 young people from 44 countries who were honored with the Diana Award, an international recognition for young changemakers working to improve lives in their communities. The awardees were announced on November 4 at a virtual ceremony streamed internationally.

Established in memory of Diana, Princess of Wales, the international award recognizes young people ages 16 to 25 for their social action and humanitarian efforts. This year, India accounted for nearly a quarter of the recipients, with 49 honorees.

Among them are Shiv Mandlik, who invented a bendable pole to help construction workers avoid working at dangerous heights and who developed an app to detect falls; Krish Aggarwal, who created an inexpensive filter that can be fitted onto ordinary fans to reduce indoor air pollution; and Kushal Sachdeva, who at age 11 began feeding a starving street dog. His organization, Protect Paws, has reportedly helped more than 1,500 stray dogs by arranging for medical treatment, vaccinations and reflective collars.

And then there's Jain. Now 18, he leads Team Period, an initiative he started in 2024 with three close friends. Together, they are challenging menstrual stigma through workshops, street performances, awareness campaigns and efforts to improve access to menstrual pads and products. He's also set to start studying medicine and public health at the University of Bologna in Italy in February.

Aadvik Jain, founder of Team Period, plans to study medicine and public health in Italy next year.

NPR spoke to Jain through a video call about the experiences that inspired him, the challenge of persuading boys and men to join the conversation on periods and what he has learned about changing deeply entrenched attitudes.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

You were just 14 when you became concerned about menstrual health. What happened to make you realize that something needed to change?

It started with something that happened to a very close friend of mine in 2023, when we were in the tenth grade. We had been friends since the fifth grade. She used to call me her brother and would tie a rakhi every year [a sacred thread that girls tie around the wrist of a brother or brother-like figure, as a symbol of their bond, during the Indian festival of Raksha Bandhan].

During our midterm examinations, I noticed that she was struggling. She was in so much pain. I could not put a finger on it. What's happening? Does she have a fever? What's going on? So I checked in on her, and she said "I'm on my period, and I'm having really bad cramps." And then she just started crying. We took her to the medical room, where she was given a painkiller, and her parents were called to take her home. In India, menstruation is something that is very concealed. It's a very hush-hush topic. Not a lot of people talk about it openly in their families.

She had been experiencing severe cramps for six to eight months, and before that, her periods had been very irregular. But the next day, she was back in school, with the same pain. Her parents thought she was trying to get out of her examinations.

She is such a bright person, but for one or two weeks every month, she would become like a wilted rose. She couldn't concentrate in class or do well in her tests.

I went home and asked my mother what we could do. My mother spoke to our teacher, who contacted my friend's parents and encouraged them to take her to a doctor.

She was subsequently diagnosed with PCOS [now referred to as PMOS, or polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome], and doctors were also investigating the possibility of endometriosis. She received treatment, made changes to her lifestyle and gradually improved. She's so much better now, because of her own efforts, and because she got the help she needed at the right time.

That experience really stayed with me.

Why did her experience affect you so deeply?

I remember once breaking my little toe against the edge of my bed. My father left his office, which was two hours away, came home and took me to the emergency room. I had an X-ray, and my foot was bandaged.

I thought, what if we responded to menstrual pain with the same concern?

What if a girl could simply tell her father, "Dad, I'm having really bad cramps, and I can't go to school today," and he would say, "Okay, let me get you a heating pad"?

But because menstruation is such a hush-hush topic, especially around the men in a family, that kind of conversation often doesn't happen.

And sometimes, even the women in a family aren't able to support other women in the way they deserve.

I realized that this was something that needed attention.

How did that concern and empathy develop into Team Period?

I studied at Amity International School, and our school runs a program called Youth Power through its student newspaper, The Global Times. [the only registered school newspaper in India].

Schools form teams of four students, choose a social cause and spend several months working to create change in their communities. Then the schools compete with each other [to see who has the best ideas]. Our team consisted of me, Shivansh Arora, Aaratrika Jha Anand and Navya Manglik — so we're two boys and two girls.

Initially, Team Period began like any other school competition. We spent about six months working on the issue. But when the competition ended, I didn't want the work to end.

There is a certain feeling you get when you're talking to people, knowing that what you are saying matters, and maybe one day it could even change someone's life. But it wasn't just about that feeling. It was about the change we were creating at the grassroots level.

I have always been interested in public health, and I hope to work with an organization like the WHO or the United Nations one day. But as a 16- or 17-year-old, you can't just show up at the WHO and say you want to change things.

You have to start somewhere.

As a teenage boy, did you encounter resistance when you began talking about menstruation? Did girls ever accuse you of mansplaining?

Of course, people were surprised that a 15-year-old boy wanted to tackle menstrual shame.

But our friends were very supportive because we never approached the issue as experts. We approached it as learners. I never thought that I could explain what happens to a woman's body better than a woman herself.

At times, I was the face of the campaign. I was the spokesperson delivering speeches and talking to young women about menstruation. But it never came from a place of thinking that I knew more than they did. It came from a place of wanting to help solve a problem.

Everything we did was approached with empathy, sensitivity and respect. One girl might be completely comfortable talking about her periods in front of a classroom, while another might be deeply embarrassed.

Our goal is to end that shame, but we don't want to do it by shaming the person herself.

Were there moments when you realized that it might be harder than you thought to include boys in this conversation?

Yes. There was a workshop we organized at a school where the boys were asked to leave the room, so the girls could discuss these issues freely.

Initially, I was very upset because the whole point of our project was that boys should learn about menstruation, too.

But once the boys left, I saw girls who had been completely silent suddenly asking questions, laughing and speaking openly.

That was a learning experience for me.

Sometimes, girls need their own space to talk about these things. You can't force everyone to be comfortable immediately. We later held a separate session for the boys and eventually brought everyone together for a discussion. So at the end of the day, boys and girls were able to talk about it openly. I learned that creating an open environment is a process.

Can you describe an experience that convinced you your work was making a difference? Anything that really surprised you?

We once held an activity with middle-school students where we taught them to make simple heating pads using socks filled with lentils or chickpeas.

There was a boy, about 12 years old, who was very disruptive. He kept interrupting us and asking why he needed to learn about periods. His attitude was essentially that this had nothing to do with him. The teacher wanted to send him to another classroom, but we said no. We wanted him to stay and participate. About a year later, after I had finished school, I returned to visit my teachers and met that boy again.

He told me that his younger sister, who was barely 9 years old, had got her first period when they were alone at home. She was terrified. She had gone to the bathroom, seen the blood and started crying and screaming for help. But because of our workshop, he knew what was happening. He called his mother and asked where she kept the sanitary pads. He reassured his sister, helped her get cleaned up, made her a heating pad and even ordered chocolates for her.

By the time his mother returned, his sister was feeling much better.

He came up to me and thanked me. He said that when we first held the workshop, he couldn't understand why he needed to know any of this.

But when his sister needed help, he knew what to do. The fulfillment I felt in that moment was incomparable. To know that you've touched even one life is such a big honor.

You have used some unusual ways to get people talking about menstruation, including dance performances and flash mobs. How did those work?

We wanted to tackle menstrual shame from different directions, including through culture and performance.

One of our productions was a dance drama set during Durga Puja [a major Hindu festival honoring Goddess Durga's victory over a demon].

In the story, a young girl is performing the aarti [a Hindu ritual where a lamp is lit and prayers are offered] when her grandmother notices a menstrual stain on her clothes. The grandmother immediately excludes her from the prayers.

But Durga [the goddess] sees what has happened. She appears, comforts the girl and brings her back. I came up with the story, but the whole school helped put it together — the dance teachers, art teachers, costume designers, students and everyone involved in the production.

We performed it before an audience of more than 500 people in April 2025, and we've since performed or screened it at other events.

We also organized a flash mob at a mall and held activities at our school's winter carnival, where students, parents and grandparents participated in games about menstrual health.

One game involved picking colored chits containing questions about menstruation. People had only a short time to respond, which encouraged spontaneous answers instead of rehearsed ones. Sometimes a young boy would play, pick up a question and ask, all confused, "What is PCOS?"

We would stop the game and spend 10 minutes explaining it.

Our goal was to spark conversations.

You conducted surveys. Did this give you an insight into the way people think about menstruation?

We have been conducting surveys among students, parents and the wider community. At this point, we have collected around 4,000 responses.

One response that really struck us came from an eighth-grade girl.

She was angry that nobody cared if someone got a vegetable stain or ketchup on their clothes, but if a girl had a red menstrual stain on the back of her uniform, it became a huge issue.

Until then, our approach had been to teach boys to be sensitive — if a girl had a stain, you could quietly tell her or offer her your jacket.

But her response made us question that approach. Why should a menstrual stain be so embarrassing in the first place?

So we decided to normalize it.

We began wearing red stains on our uniforms. Some were stitched from red cloth, while others were stickers. At first, everyone laughed at us. Even the school objected because we were ruining the look of our uniforms with these big red patches.

But over the course of a week, more and more students joined in.

By the end, there was a sea of students wearing red stains. Some wore them on their backs, others on their shirts or identification cards.

When we conducted another survey months later, many students said they no longer felt that it was such a shame to spot or have a red stain.

We can't change attitudes across all of India immediately, but we were able to change something in our school.

In addition to changing attitudes and addressing stigma, what other aspects of menstrual care are you looking into?

There are several aspects to our work.

One is cultural — breaking down taboos and stigma. Another is logistical. How do you ensure that girls and women have access to menstrual products without feeling ashamed to ask for them? We installed a sanitary pad dispenser at our school.

Now we're talking to companies about how we could make dispensers available to other schools at a nominal cost. We are also exploring the possibility of developing our own design.

Disposal is another major issue. Used sanitary pads are often wrapped in newspaper and thrown into the garbage. But think about the people who sort that waste. How are they supposed to know what is inside the newspaper?

We're exploring a disposal system in which used pads can be sealed in specially designed bags, with clear warnings and illustrations in different languages. We want to think not just about the people using menstrual products but also those who handle the waste.

Your work has largely been concentrated in Delhi. Any plans to expand?

Until now, we've worked in government schools, orphanages, underserved neighborhoods and our own school in Delhi. We've also organized health camps.

But we were students, and our budgets were limited. We couldn't simply fly to Chennai or another city to replicate everything.

Now we want to decentralize Team Period and create local chapters.

Our team members are already spreading out to different cities and countries for their studies.

We'd like to bring in volunteers who speak different regional languages so that we can communicate more effectively with communities.

What does winning the Diana Award mean to you? Does it provide funding to help expand Team Period?

The Diana Award doesn't come with prize money.

But I think what it gives us is something equally valuable: recognition that our work matters.

When you're young and approaching potential sponsors or partners, people naturally have questions. They want to know whether you're legitimate and whether your work is making a difference. An international recognition like the Diana Award helps establish that credibility.

It gives us a platform to take our work to a larger audience.

For me, personally, it's deeply meaningful because we've faced moments when people questioned why boys were talking about menstruation. We've received strange looks from older people and even people of our own generation.

But this recognition tells us to keep showing up, even when things are difficult.

For stories about life in our changing world, subscribe to NPR's Global Health newsletter.

Kamala Thiagarajan is a freelance journalist based in Madurai, South India. She reports on global health, science and development and has been published in The New York Times , The British Medical Journal , the BBC, The Guardian  and other outlets. You can find her on X: @Kamal_t.

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/07/nx-s1-600.title: An unexpected activist emerged to help block a $5 billion data center in Maryland
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/07/nx-s1-600.author: Jenny Abamu
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/07/nx-s1-600.text:
Taylor Frazier McCollum has been active in the opposition to the possible data center at the site of the demolished Landover Mall in Prince George's County, less than a mile from where she lived. If the project is built, the development could occupy more than 80 acres.

The overgrown grass and weeds seem to stretch into the horizon on nearly 90 acres of empty land in Landover, Md. It used to be Landover Mall, but that closed in 2002, and the site has been mostly vacant since.

In 2024, the developer that built the mall won approval from county planners for a $5 billion data center campus, and word began spreading through the largely Black community nearby.

"I was like, 'Oh, hell no,'" said Taylor Frazier McCollum, describing the moment she learned about the project. She lived less than a mile away from it. "Why would you want to bring water-polluting, diesel-generating data centers right down the street from where people live, work, play? It just didn't make sense to me."

Frazier McCollum is one of a number of Americans whose political awakening was triggered by data center development. Across the country, community members have taken to local council hearings to voice their opposition. They've prompted — though estimates vary — about 500 moratoriums on data centers nationwide.

Unlike a lot of land-use activists trying to protect their homes from threats in their backyards, Frazier McCollum does not own a home. In 2024, she and her young daughter were evicted from their apartment. She was working at a waxing center that cut wages, and she could no longer cover her rent.

"It was difficult," Frazier McCollum recalled. "Because I created the ideal life paying for us to live in this apartment and have our own space ... and then to have it taken away ... It felt like something that wasn't ever going to end."

They've moved around and were living in her grandfather's home when she learned about the proposed project less than a mile away.

Taylor Frazier McCollum in front of her grandfather's home, where she lived when she heard about the proposed data center site less than a mile away in Landover, Md.

She created a petition that gathered over 25,000 signatures, leading to widely attended protests and culminating in multiple local moratoriums imposed on data centers throughout the county. It blocked the $5 billion project that was set to break ground between 2026 and 2027.

The fight pushed Frazier McCollum to the forefront of local politics. She went to county meetings, testified before Maryland legislators and endorsed political candidates. She found herself in a coalition of socialists, environmentalists, people angry about their electric bills and neighbors new to organizing.

Local media interviewed her, and people in data center circles called her "the Landover girl."

Staci Hartwell, a longtime local environmental activist, says she spent years struggling to get traction on the data center issue before Frazier McCollum came along.

"This is something that was happening in her neighborhood, and it was really like her awakening," Hartwell said.

But with data centers paused, some in Prince George's County worry about declining tax revenue. Last year, a local Six Flags closed. The NFL's Washington Commanders announced plans to return to neighboring Washington, D.C. Thousands of federal workers have lost their jobs. The county faces a budget deficit.

The possible data center site, which was once the Landover Mall, in Prince George's County. If the project is built, the development will occupy more than 80 acres.

In September, Frazier McCollum appeared at a county council meeting to advocate for a fund for roof repairs, something her grandfather's home needs. Council member Wanika Fisher, who supports moving some data center projects forward, reminded her that the county needs development.

"Our county has an economic future that we have to grapple with," said Fisher, addressing the request. "I don't see where the money is coming from. I think we have to have a real conversation. And I'm not saying that a data center is the answer, but I'm saying it's worth the hard discussion."

With the Landover project on hold, Frazier McCollum now wants a full ban on that and other data center projects. And with grants Hartwell and others have found, Frazier McCollum has taken her message to Black communities fighting data center growth in Atlanta, Memphis and even across the globe in Zambia.

"I feel like so many people are depending on this fight to be successful," Frazier McCollum explained. "Not just for myself, but even across the country, to set precedent for other people that are fighting against hyperscale data centers."

She's lost out on work to attend public meetings or knock on doors, and she's relied on family for rides and childcare.

Her father, Lacy McCollum Jr., sees the data center fight as rooted in civil rights.

"We're talking about the right to water, the right to clean air, the right to a place to live. That's everybody's fight, right?" Lacy McCollum Jr. said. "While I'm afraid for her, we need those people. We needed the Medgar Everses. We needed the Martin Luther Kings. We needed the Malcolm X's. People like Taylor, they jump out here so the people behind them get to make progress."

Some urge her to run for office. She says she wants to pay off her debt and traffic tickets and find a home first.

"I didn't want to have to focus on housing and the campaign and doing everything else," explained Frazier McCollum. "Now is not maybe the moment for it, but I do have aspirations to run for something."

In the meantime, she's pitching plans to turn the old Landover site into a sports complex or affordable housing, or to use some of it to support heritage tourism in the county. But none of those ideas, she acknowledges, would be as lucrative as a data center campus.

Jenny Abamu is a reporter for WAMU.

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/07/nx-s1-603.title: Texas's 'Blue Tsunami' has former Texas congressman Beto O'Rourke 'over the moon'
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/07/nx-s1-603.author: Michelle Aslam
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/07/nx-s1-603.text:
NPR's Rob Schmitz speaks with former Texas congressman Beto O'Rourke about how past efforts by him and other Democrats helped the party win big in Texas in the midterms.

While Texas' populist roots may have laid the foundation for Democratic victories in the state, they weren't the only factor that helped Texas Democrats win on Tuesday. Former Texas congressman and presidential candidate Beto O'Rourke has helped pave the way for Democrat victories in the Lone Star State. You might remember his 2018 bid to unseat longstanding Republican Senator Ted Cruz. Ultimately, he lost by just a few percentage points. In 2022, he ran against Governor Greg Abbott and again lost, that time by only a slightly larger margin. Beto O'Rourke joins us now. Welcome.

BETO O'ROURKE: It's good to be with you.

SCHMITZ: So I feel like you have been out of the national spotlight for a while, but perhaps that's because you've been hard at work on the ground there in Texas mobilizing voters. Tell us about that.

O'ROURKE: After the Senate race, we asked ourselves, what would it take to win in Texas? And from that, we started a group called Powered By People, and it's thousands of folks - many of whom volunteered on that Senate race - who get trained as volunteer deputy registrars, meet young people in person, get them registered and then, importantly, stay in touch with them and help them overcome the obstacles in a state that makes it harder than any other in the nation for young people to register and to vote, to help them participate in our politics.

SCHMITZ: Young folks showed up big time for Democrats this cycle. An NBC exit poll shows that 79% of voters under the age of 30 voted for Talarico. What do you think appealed to that demographic?

O'ROURKE: I think, first and foremost, James Talarico, who described this contest as not between a Democrat and a Republican or right versus left, but top versus bottom. When I spend time on these college campuses or at (inaudible) or clubs with young people as we help them to get registered and I ask them what's important to them, they are absolutely disgusted with the concentration of wealth and privilege and power in this country. They ask me about the Epstein files and say, you know, how can the wealthiest, most powerful men rape and traffic girls and women with complete impunity? How is it that we're at war again in the Middle East? Why are we complicit in this genocide in Gaza? Why is no one doing anything about these things?

And then at home in Texas, the minimum wage is 7.25. It's the hardest state in the nation in which to see a doctor, and schoolteachers are working two or three jobs to make ends meet. These aren't Republican or Democrat issues. They're issues of basic justice, and I think that young people have the most acute sense of what is right or wrong. They are impatient with excuses or equivocation or blaming it on one party or another. They want solutions, and they want people to deliver.

SCHMITZ: That's interesting. I mean, this is something that we spoke with our previous guest, David Griscom - he's an author in Texas - about, that economic populism was one of the reasons that James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa won both the Senate and gubernatorial election. Is there anything that Democrats can learn from how this played out and what really matters to Texans?

O'ROURKE: I think the takeaway is it is incredibly important for Democrats now in power to deliver for the people they represent in ways that they can feel immediately. So raising the minimum wage - if you're working for $7.25 an hour, you're probably working two or three of those jobs to make ends meet. Raising that minimum wage will be felt immediately.

You know, if you can't afford to see a doctor right now, and you're suffering as a result of that, being able to, through Medicaid expansion, see a provider - that's going to change your life immediately. And the follow-on effects of being able to afford tuition or down payment on a home or an automobile, these are significant material differences in people's lives.

And so we have high expectations for Gina and James. And really, as you probably know, every single statewide office was won by a Democrat. The Democrats also picked a majority in the state House. They now have the opportunity to deliver for people. And so while we're excited and we're celebrating their victories, we're also understanding there's accountability, responsibility, and the clock is ticking.

SCHMITZ: You obviously had a lot to do with this popularity of Democrats that we are seeing right now. I mean, you, of course, ran for Senate. You ran for governor. You lost time and time again for both of those races. But a lot in the background was gained. How is this feeling for you right now, seeing these wins?

O'ROURKE: I'm over the moon. I mean, you know, my wife, Amy, and I, in 2016, when Trump won - I happened to be in Congress at the time - we looked at each other and we said, we have got to do something more. What we've been doing so far serving in Congress is insufficient to the task at hand, this threat of authoritarianism and fascism and the rise of this oligarchy in America. We needed to do something.

And from that was born this crazy snowball's-chance-in-Texas idea of running for Senate in a state that last elected a Democrat to the Senate in 1988. And I was joined by hundreds of thousands - and by the end, millions - of my fellow Texans who believed in that dream. And so it wasn't so much, you know, should Beto O'Rourke serve in the Senate or, you know, my name on an office or on the ballot. It is, can we change this state? And by extension, given the outsized importance of Texas, can we change this country?

SCHMITZ: Well, Beto O'Rourke, since I've got you here, I should ask you whether you have plans to run for president in 2028.

O'ROURKE: No, I don't, but I am going to be involved one way or another. This extraordinary experiment 250 years in the making that is the product of so much service and sacrifice and struggle - all of us must do all that we can to keep it going. So that's my mission. That's what I'm going to be focused on. And wherever I can be useful or helpful, that's where you'll find me.

SCHMITZ: That is former Texas Congressman Beto O'Rourke. Thanks so much for joining us.

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/07/nx-s1-602.title: President of The Heritage Foundation looks ahead to the future of the GOP
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/07/nx-s1-602.author: Henry Larson
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/07/nx-s1-602.text:
Kevin Roberts, the president of the conservative think tank The Heritage Foundation, talks about the organization's priorities and hopes for the future of the Republican Party and its policies.

After the midterms this week, Republicans are asking, where do we go from here? The conservative think tank The Heritage Foundation has long provided answers to that question ever since it wrote the mandate for leadership for President Reagan in 1981. The foundation has informed many of the Trump administration's priorities through the policy blueprint known as Project 2025.

Kevin Roberts is a political strategist and was a key architect of Project 2025. He's led The Heritage Foundation as its president since 2021. He joins us now to talk about the path forward for Republicans. Welcome.

KEVIN ROBERTS: Thanks, Rob, for having me. It's a pleasure.

SCHMITZ: So before we get to the midterm results, we had news yesterday. Susie Wiles is out as President Trump's chief of staff. Stephen Miller is in. What does this tell us about the path forward for the Trump administration?

ROBERTS: Well, it's a great promotion of a great patriot, Stephen Miller, because what it signals to not just the radical-left majority coming into Congress, but for all of us on the political right, is that President Trump and his administration are not rolling over. I know that people who are on the political left disagree maybe with Stephen Miller with everything. They probably disagree with me and Heritage with everything. He's an extremely competent, politically conservative, very intellectual policymaker, and for those of us on the political right who are charting the way forward after this week's major defeat, I think Stephen's a perfect choice.

SCHMITZ: Why the change?

ROBERTS: I think what the president is signaling is that it is a new era, and he needs Stephen's acumen, particularly his ability to be on offense even with a large Democrat majority in the House and Senate.

SCHMITZ: So I think it's safe to say here that the midterms did not go the way that the president hoped. How do these results shape the plans that you and The Heritage Foundation are making for Republicans going forward?

ROBERTS: Yeah, even for people who were more pessimistic than I am, I actually thought the midterms would be OK. Obviously, I was wrong about that. But the people who were more pessimistic did not think that it would be a defeat on the scale. And so the first thing that we have to do is just to read reality truthfully. You acknowledge that, at least in terms of messaging, the message from the political right, from the administration, was insufficient.

I happen to think that the Iran war was a major problem even though I'm supportive of the Iran war, I've been saying since April and May that the administration needs to find a way to declare victory because the economic consequences that have aggravated existing inflationary concerns that Trump inherited were a real problem.

And so moving forward, what the administration needs to do is not just handle some of the lawfare and what I'm sure will be some nonsense coming from the Democrat majorities, but articulate a policy vision that gets back to that domestic policy, especially kitchen-table economics issues.

SCHMITZ: So on election night - you know, talking about Iran here - you told my colleague Mary Louise Kelly that larger-scale Republican defeats are not a wholesale rejection of President Trump's agenda but instead a, quote, "complaint by voters about the economic consequences of the Iran conflict." You just mentioned that. What needs to change when it comes to the U.S. war in Iran?

ROBERTS: Well, I've been saying since May or June, along with my colleagues - national security colleagues at Heritage, that No. 1, we're supportive of the war. No. 2, the president could have declared victory given the military achievements as early as May or June. And had he done that, I think we would have been able to see the diminished economic disadvantages that have come from the war in time to affect - in a positive way, from our vantage point - the election. It's really important that the president and the administration make that declaration soon because it will take, according to my economist colleagues at Heritage, several months for the inflationary pressure brought on by energy prices, energy inflation to come down.

I think that what you do - to cut to the chase here, Rob - is you obviously leave some naval and air superiority in Iran, maybe not to the extent of the deployment now. And when the Iranians misbehave, you can zing them with cruise missile attacks, and you also pair that with what has been a really good economic strangulation campaign by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.

SCHMITZ: The election's been largely understood as a referendum on the economy and the cost of living for average Americans. Gas prices - because of the war with Iran and also because of President Trump's tariffs, which you were initially against before you embraced them - have been a problem. Would you embrace a pivot away from tariffs at this point?

ROBERTS: No, I'm very supportive. We at Heritage are very supportive of a true reciprocal tariff regime. And, you know, if we were building the tariff policy - and we said this going back to the so-called Liberation Day - that we would focus on the 5 to 10 worst transgressors of, quote-unquote, "free trade." And had the administration focused on that, I think the American people, maybe even a bipartisan way, would have really embraced that. I think there's still a future for that policy, but it's going to have to be, you know, more circumscribed than it's been.

SCHMITZ: You know, when we're talking about the economy and the problems of the economy right now, you have sort of boiled it down to Iran. Are there any other problems in the economy that you see?

ROBERTS: Oh, yeah. The point about Iran - so thanks for the opportunity to follow up on that - is not that it, in and of itself, has caused all of our economic difficulties or worries. It's that it's aggravated some long-standing existing problems. It's just objectively true, to put respective politics off to the side, that the Trump administration inherited very high inflation from the previous administration, and all of those economic measures were improving the week before the war in Iran. In fact, our chief economist at Heritage, Dr. E.J. Antoni, has predicted that there would have been a Trump economic boom had he not started the war in Iran. The point is that Iran, especially by increasing energy prices, aggravated those inflationary pressures.

SCHMITZ: You know, another question I have for you has to do with corruption. You know, corruption was also at the top of voters' concerns going into these midterm I was in Hungary earlier this year, where corruption also played a big part in Viktor Orbán's routing there. People see the president and his family benefiting from cryptocurrency, other investments. You know, what is your reaction to how this has damaged Republicans at the polls?

ROBERTS: Well, just looking at the exit polls, it's - American voters are saying, obviously, this is a concern, and you draw a very accurate parallel, Rob, with Hungary. I think, as you know, the Orbán government's policies were very good, but, you know, they had been in power for 16 years, and there clearly was corruption that was a problem.

And so it's really important moving forward - not just for the administration, not just for Republican allies in Congress, but also for the incoming Democrat majority in the House and Senate - to remember that this has been a very anti-power election. The American people are saying, we're tired of this. It isn't just a problem on the right. It isn't just a problem on the left. Thank goodness, Americans are paying attention, and they want leaders who are not engaged.

SCHMITZ: The agenda for the right used to be really clear - you know, smaller government, lower taxes, free trade. Project 2025 was a huge effort to define this new post-Reagan conservative movement. But you've had challenges, I think, keeping everyone aligned. It seems there's, like, sort of a generational civil war happening in the party with influencers and other right-wing think tanks all trying to define the party. Looking ahead to 2028, what is Heritage's core vision? How do you see regaining voter trust here?

ROBERTS: Yeah, you're definitely right about tensions on the right. And to state the obvious, President Trump will be leaving the stage in early 2029, and so all of us who are conservative policy leaders are trying to articulate a vision for the future. For us at Heritage, Rob, we want to do two things. No. 1, we want to focus on those economic matters. We want to actually provide the policy solutions for Americans' legitimate worries about affordability.

And secondly, we are gratified that still a slight majority of Americans think that socialist policies are bad. But we're worried that somewhere between 40- and 45% of Americans are willing to try those policies. We have to go explain why those policies of socialists - legitimate socialists - are problematic rather than just, as has been customary of conservative elected officials this cycle, pointing to socialists, pointing to neo-Marxists and just labeling them as that. The American people actually want answers.

And so that's a way of saying, to give you the bottom line here, that at Heritage, we're trying to keep things simple. We're trying to address the kitchen-table issues. We will continue to preach for a more restrained national security posture, which, until the Iran War, this Trump administration has done a very good job of.

SCHMITZ: So are you going to put a stake in the ground here and say whether you'll support Marco Rubio or JD Vance for 2028?

ROBERTS: (Laughter) Nice try, but that's not something we do or can do at Heritage. We don't get into endorsements. What we can say is, if - whoever the conservative standard bearer is in 2028, whoever the conservative officials are running for office in 2028, we want them to be talking about these issues that address these affordability and economic concerns.

SCHMITZ: That is Kevin Roberts, president of the conservative think tank The Heritage Foundation. Thank you.

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/06/nx-s1-603.title: Health intel-sharing group warns industry in wake of cyberattack on French blood bank
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/06/nx-s1-603.author: Jenna McLaughlin
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/06/nx-s1-603.text:
A close up of the hands of a nurse from the French Blood Establishment checking the identification and traceability of blood samples beside a donor during a mobile blood donation session in Paimpol Cotes d Armor Brittany France on July 23, 2026.

In a new security bulletin, the information sharing and analysis center devoted to the healthcare industry, Health ISAC, alerted members to a recent wave of cyberattacks targeting refrigeration controllers — including one incident that affected a major French blood bank.

"This alert is issued for situational awareness, highlighting how recent operational technology (OT) attacks against specific refrigeration brands directly intersect with emerging threats to the health sector," reads the bulletin seen by NPR. Operational technology refers to the machines that control physical processes in the real world, from cooling systems to water pumps.

Cyberattacks on grocery stores and food processing plants everywhere from Europe and Israel to U.S. military bases have drawn headlines in recent months, particularly as attacks have resulted in spoiled food, fires, broken machinery, and major business disruptions. Attackers are clearly aware of the vulnerability of these systems and are taking advantage.

However, until news broke that the French blood bank, known as the French Blood Establishment, had also been targeted, there was less public attention focused on the potential consequences of refrigeration controllers failing in other industries, particularly healthcare, where lifesaving implements like blood and vaccines often require finely tuned temperature-controlled environments to remain viable.

"This incident underscores a stark operational reality: cybersecurity in healthcare is fundamentally about patient safety," wrote Errol Weiss, the chief security officer at Health ISAC in an email to NPR. "When threat actors manipulate operational technology like cold-chain storage and refrigeration units holding donor blood, plasma, or critical therapies, they aren't merely stealing data or locking down administrative files, they are directly endangering the physical resources required to sustain human life."

On Thursday, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, the FBI, the Department of Health and Human Services, and the U.S. Department of Agriculture published their own fact sheet about threats to industrial refrigeration and cold chain monitoring systems, tools they identify as critical to multiple industries from healthcare to chemical production, food and agriculture, and transportation.

The FBI Cyber Branch Operations director, Brett Leatherman, said the bureau is tracking bad actors targeting these systems "across critical infrastructure sectors globally, putting inventory and equipment at risk."

"Industrial refrigeration and cold-chain monitoring systems protect food, medicine, and other temperature-sensitive products, making them attractive targets for malicious cyber actors," Leatherman said.

The French blood bank confirmed in a press release Tuesday that one of its vendors used in cold storage rooms was targeted by malicious cyber activity, resulting in the defrost and temperature thresholds being raised dangerously high. The French Blood Establishment ultimately managed to detect the suspicious activity in time to rescue blood samples.

It remains unclear who is responsible for the global attacks on refrigeration controllers, and whether it's multiple actors or groups.

Iran has been linked to at least one incident in Israel earlier in the spring, though that breach involved a lot more sophistication and malicious activity. Investigators probing the disruptions at U.S. military bases are also considering Iran as the potential culprit.

Meanwhile, two pro-Russian hacking groups, NoName057(16) and Z-Pentest Alliance, belatedly released videos and posted on Telegram claiming responsibility for the attacks across Europe, publishing a sample of alleged hacked credentials that would've allowed them to access equipment including machines made by the Danish company Danfoss and the American company Copeland. Those machines can monitor and control temperature and other functions. The hacking groups have some history of targeting refrigeration controllers and other operational technology. However, it's unclear if the recent wave of attacks on refrigerators and freezers across Europe even required stolen credentials to execute, a factor that has led some cybersecurity experts to be skeptical of their claims.

Even so, it will require more evidence like access logs, configuration changes, and connections between maintenance accounts on the controllers to make any clear assessments, explained Tom Hegel, who leads threat intelligence research at cybersecurity firm SentinelOne.

"Russian-aligned actors are a credible hypothesis because there is a credible precedent, including the refrigeration-related attack DOJ attributed to CyberArmyofRussia_Reborn and NoName's history of politically motivated disruption. But that is only the context, not the missing evidentiary link to these European incidents," Hegel told NPR.

"It's important to note that such Russian threat actors often seek attention and claim to cause incidents even when false," he continued.

Regardless of who's responsible, the incident highlights how these nearly ubiquitous tools used to remotely manage critical systems are vulnerable to attack in several different ways.

For one, thousands of the refrigeration controllers in France alone were exposed to the open internet with almost no protection put in place before unidentified hackers went after them in October. Afterward, experts were still tracking hundreds of devices left unprotected. That's just a fraction of the tens of thousands of exposed operational devices online, many of them embedded in critical infrastructure.

Additionally, many of the major remote management systems used in refrigerators and freezers have security vulnerabilities. After alerting the companies to the problems, cybersecurity firm Claroty published research on vulnerabilities in multiple major refrigeration controllers, including those made by both the American manufacturer Copeland and by Danfoss.

While some of those vulnerabilities have been discovered and the vendors have designed patches to seal the hole, the problems don't stop there.

Experts warn it's difficult to patch operational technology because doing so often requires shutting systems down. In industries like healthcare, even minutes of downtime create extreme risk for patient safety. And for some aging models, it's impossible to patch, because the vendor is no longer offering updates — and companies can't afford to spring for a new model.

Sometimes, executives don't even know what machines are on their networks.

Additionally, for many companies, vendors that work with them demand remote access to systems like refrigeration controllers to regularly service them. It's often a requirement in the contract companies sign.

"Industrial chillers operate under vendor contracts that mandate persistent remote access," explained Nic Adams, CEO of 0rcus, a U.S. offensive security firm. "These commercial agreements leave national food and medical supplies defenseless against basic credential abuse."

Finally, hackers are now using AI to find these vulnerabilities faster than ever, and AI is also helping them to better understand the complex machines and the processes they control. Bad actors a world away no longer need to understand individual languages or industries, or even the physics involved to disrupt operations. In recent weeks, cyber incident responders tell NPR they're seeing a massive spike in attacks that are at least in part carried out by AI agents.

The good news is that a lot of these attacks, even if they incorporate AI, are not particularly sophisticated, novel, or stealthy.

Weiss of Health ISAC tells NPR there are basic steps the healthcare industry can take to prevent being a victim of these opportunistic attacks.

That process "begins" by "eliminating public internet exposure," wrote Weiss, then "enforcing strict network segmentation" in order to isolate refrigeration systems "from standard enterprise and guest networks" and finally adding on safeguards "that software overrides cannot bypass" like "hard-wired mechanical cutoffs" and "independent thermal alarms."

In the Health ISAC alert, the industry is urged to separate not just refrigeration controllers from hospital IT systems, but also medical gas monitors, for one, and train staff onsite on how to take physical manual control of machines in an emergency.

Finally, the alert urges hospitals to have offline backups of their systems.

Sharing intelligence about these kinds of cyberattacks can help other potential victims avoid disaster.

While Estonian grocery stores were targeted in the most recent wave of attacks, many of those store managers were on high alert thanks to warnings issued by Estonia's Information Systems Authority, RIA. "When one Selver store was attacked on 2 November, the attackers managed to change the refrigeration system's temperature setting to +50°C. However, the service provider reacted quickly and prevented significant damage," said Annika Müür, a spokesperson for RIA. "So while we can't say that Estonia managed to prevent the attacks entirely, I think this case is a good example of the importance of monitoring threats internationally, acting on early warnings and working closely with businesses to minimise the impact."

Weiss of Health ISAC also urged companies across sectors that are being targeted by this recent wave of attacks to share information to help others defend themselves.

"The attack highlights why timely, trusted information sharing across borders and sectors is our strongest collective defense," he wrote.

"Rapid intelligence sharing allows hospitals and health facilities globally to recognize emerging attack patterns, verify vendor exposure, and harden critical infrastructure before threat actors can cause physical harm."

Elon Musk gave more than $445 million to Republican candidates, political action committees and outside groups, according to federal election filings but most of the candidates he backed on Tuesday lost.

Elon Musk wasn't on Tuesday's ballot, but he stands to lose a lot from Democrats' sweeping midterm victories in the House and Senate. In no state was this more acutely felt than in Texas, home to the headquarters of Musk's companies and where he spent more than $200 million, according to federal filings, in a mission to sway the Senate race in the Republican candidate's favor.

With a Democratic majority in Congress, the billionaire, who controls Tesla and SpaceX, will likely face investigations into the billions of dollars of government contracts his companies have been awarded since President Trump returned to office and his role leading the Department of Government Efficiency at the beginning of Trump's second term.

Musk gave more than $445 million to Republican candidates, political action committees and outside groups, according to federal election filings analyzed by OpenSecrets, a nonprofit that tracks campaign spending. That makes him the top donor in the midterms and among the very largest political donors in American history.

The central question Democratic lawmakers say they want answered is whether Musk used his influence inside the Trump administration to benefit his own businesses, and whether taxpayer money, government data and public institutions were put at risk in the process.

During the four months Musk led DOGE, he received at least $6.3 billion in government contracts. Since then, he has gained at least another $10 billion in government contracts, according to the Democracy Defenders Fund, a legal advocacy nonprofit.

"The DOGE chickens are coming home to roost. Elon Musk waved a chainsaw on stage and laughed while firing public servants and gutting the services Americans rely on. Then he lied to the American people about the savings. He must answer for it under oath," Rep. James Walkinshaw (D-Va.) wrote on X.

Musk's foreign dealings are also under scrutiny. Democratic Sen. Chris Coons of Delaware posted on X that Musk's links to Russia's President Vladimir Putin are "One more thing to add to the list of questions for Musk when I subpoena him."

U.S. Rep. Mike Levin of California highlighted that Musk restricted Ukraine's use of his Starlink satellite internet service days after Trump eased sanctions on Russia and began buying Russian diesel in October. Starlink and its military-grade counterpart, Starshield, are vital for Ukraine's civilian infrastructure, frontline communications and drone operations in its war against Russia.

"How on earth did we get to this point? How is it possible that Musk can disrupt an American ally's military operations whenever he chooses, maintain a clear line to the Kremlin, and face zero accountability to the American people or the U.S. government?" Levin wrote on X.

Musk did not respond to a request for comment from NPR.

While leading DOGE, Musk was a part-time special government employee, and as such was subject to a federal law prohibiting covered executive branch and related personnel from participating in official matters affecting their personal financial interests, said Richard Painter, former chief White House ethics lawyer in the George W. Bush administration.

"SpaceX is a big contractor and gets a lot of money from NASA and the Department of Defense. If [Musk] touched anything that he knew would have an impact on SpaceX, he would've committed a crime," Painter said.

Texas in particular has become a big focus of Musk's efforts to exert political power, as he has made the state the nerve center of his sprawling business empire. Tesla's corporate headquarters and a major vehicle manufacturing facility are in Austin. X, formerly Twitter, is based outside of Austin. SpaceX, which makes rockets and satellites, is based in southern Texas. Musk's Neuralink and The Boring Company are also headquartered in the state.

Much of Musk's estimated wealth is tied up in his ownership stakes in his companies. Even as markets rose Wednesday after Democrats' midterm wins, SpaceX shares fell nearly 4% and Tesla dropped 3%.

SpaceX is reportedly exploring several possible Texas sites for large data centers. Tesla owns and operates its massive Giga Texas data center in Austin. In August, plans for a $16.8 billion SpaceXAI semiconductor fabrication project in Texas were announced.

Musk directed at least $225 million of his midterm spending to Texas, according to OpenSecrets, including supporting Republican Ken Paxton's bid for U.S. Senate and Gov. Greg Abbott's reelection campaign.

But Paxton and Abbott both lost, suggesting Musk's money wasn't enough to overcome a wave of enthusiasm that saw Democrats capture every statewide office in Texas.

"Elon Musk wants our land. He wants our water. He wants our tax dollars. He wants his very own personal United States senator. He is trying to buy Texas," said James Talarico, who defeated Paxton in the Senate race, at a campaign rally in Lubbock last month.

Elon Musk's own posts on X about Talarico were often personal and incendiary. "Talarico will vote to trans your kids," he wrote on Nov. 1.

Talarico addressed Musk in his victory speech on Tuesday.

"We just sent a message to every billionaire mega-donor, every trillionaire mega-donor, every corrupt defender of this broken political system in this state, in this country. Power belongs to the people," Talarico said. "The real fight in this country is not right versus left; it is top versus bottom."

As results came in on Tuesday night, Musk wrote on X, "Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn't work this time," followed by a shrug emoji.

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/04/nx-s1-602.title: Review: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake is superb, streamlined and safe
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/04/nx-s1-602.author: James Perkins Mastromarino
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/04/nx-s1-602.text:
James Perkins Mastromarino

Link, the Hero of Time, grown-up and newly awoken from a magical seven-year slumber.

With its tale of an idyllic world despoiled by the lust for power, The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time feels as relevant today as it did in 1998. Nintendo's new remake, out Thursday on the Switch 2, enshrines its place in the gaming canon for generations to come. But despite its stupendous production values and painstaking details, the game left me feeling oddly bereft.

Perhaps I should have expected as much. Ocarina of Time weaponizes nostalgia even within its narrative, as the protagonist Link ventures to save his post-apocalyptic world as an adult after first working through it as a kid. You'll uncover old characters enduring new catastrophes. You'll try to rescue everyone you meet. You'll strive to bring things back to how they were before — no, better than they were before.

Seven years stretch between Link's childhood and adult adventures. 28 years yawn between the remake and the original's release. Both in and out of the game, Ocarina of Time makes us yearn for an idealized past.

Decent remakes evoke how you remember a game rather than re-create dated controls and chunky graphics. In myriad small ways, Nintendo has brought Ocarina of Time up to contemporary standards while (mostly) preserving its soul.

In one of the game's most poignant scenes, kid Link answers to the call to adventure, leaving his friend Saria and the Kokiri Forest they called home.

I miss the thoughtfully-composed camera angles from the original, but quickly got used to the over-the-shoulder camera the remake employs (though I was irked that it abandoned the top-down view when you sneak into Hyrule Castle). The new jump and sprint buttons made navigating the world feel more natural. Combat's smoother too, though it's still not easy to switch between targeted enemies (unlike modern third-person games like Elden Ring, where you can toggle between foes by simply flicking the right stick).

You can, thankfully, swap between items in a quick menu — the same system introduced to the series in 2023's Tears of the Kingdom and continued in 2024's Echoes of Wisdom. It's still not as fast as I'd wish (I'd have preferred a customizable wheel), but I vastly prefer it to constantly pausing to access my equipment. It made it easy to change my strategy on the fly. I'd often cast Naryu's Love and deploy Bombchus, for example, where before I'd mostly stick to the Longshot and Bow.

The villain Ganondorf, on the precipice of his initial triumph over Princess Zelda, Link, and the whole of Hyrule.

If you get stuck, a new "Threads of Time" quest log can point you in the right direction (though you'll likely still need to look up a guide for the convoluted Biggoron Sword quest!). And yes, the notoriously frustrating Water Temple is much more tolerable this time around. But mind your rupees! Inflation's hit Hyrule. While wallets can now carry double the cash that they used to, Great Fairy upgrades are no longer free. They can cost up to 500 rupees!

It's the remake's aesthetic changes that stand out most. The game's astonishingly ornate textures can jar with its cartoony proportions. Ninety-eight percent of the time the translation is a clear upgrade, but other times it leads straight into the uncanny valley (Nabooru looks bizarrely yassified with huge red lips and golden eye-shadow, for example).

Gerudo thief Nabooru, flanked by the malicious witches Kotake and Koume.

The animations are much more extensive — so much so that the new cutscenes, particularly in the game's opening hours, can drag down the pacing. The game also fleshes out unspoken implications and flattens rough edges. Mido, the jerk who blocks your progress in Kokiri Forest, has been subtly rewritten from bully to overbearing but well-intentioned boss. Kaepora Gaebora, the talking owl who guides your path, won't repeat himself at the slightest provocation. Navi, your fairy companion, no longer chimes in with an incessant "Hey! Listen!"

Such changes risk eroding the game's character. Still, it ultimately stands as one of the most faithful adaptations I've seen — less than the Demon's Souls remake but far more than the Final Fantasy 7 Remake trilogy or even the Resident Evil 4 remake. It gives me hope that Ocarina of Time's surreal sequel, Majora's Mask, could receive such treatment in the future.

Sheik, Link's ally in the fight against Ganondorf, demonstrates one of the many songs you'll play by pressing buttons or humming directly into the Switch 2's microphone.

Yet this remake will never eclipse my memories of the first Ocarina of Time. Of course it couldn't — that game helped launch a new 3D era and defined the childhoods of a whole generation. Where once it innovated, now it represents the safest of safe bets.

But by lavishing such attention on an all-time classic — ahead of a Zelda movie next year — Nintendo has ensured it won't go out of style for at least another few decades. I look forward to sharing it with my nephews and, eventually, my own toddling son. As much as I detest how media giants can't seem to move past the hits of yesteryear, some harmonies are worth turning back time for.

Editor's note: This story initially and inadvertently published 24 hours before its embargo lifted.
Nov. 4, 2026

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/02/nx-s1-602.title: How former Yahoo CEO Marissa Mayer sees AI assistants fitting into busy women's lives
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/02/nx-s1-602.author: Juana Summers
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/02/nx-s1-602.text:
NPR's Juana Summers talks with former Yahoo CEO Marissa Mayer about AI assistants and lightening the load of emotional labor.

Former Yahoo CEO Marissa Mayer wants more women to use AI, so she created an AI assistant that centered on women's experiences to help lighten the mental load of parenting as a working mom. But she also touched off a heated debate about the role artificial intelligence should have in parenting and gender expectations. And we wanted to talk directly with the person who sparked this discussion. Marissa Mayer joins us now. Welcome to ALL THINGS CONSIDERED.

MARISSA MAYER: Thank you very much for having me.

SUMMERS: OK, let's just start at the beginning here because last week, the New York Times ran the super buzzy profile of you. It opened with a story where you used your AI assistant Dazzle to come up with a list of three bullet points about your daughter. And that anecdote just sparked a ton of backlash. It was all over my social media feeds last week. Were you surprised by the reaction?

MAYER: I was because I think there was some context that was missing, which is I shared that anecdote because it was from back when we were first building the product. I was testing the technology. And what happened was basically all my engineers were really excited. From our photos, we could tell their pet's name. From their photos, we could tell, you know, their mother's birth date. And I wondered what it could tell.

And I got this assignment from the school to prepare a slide for my twins birthday, and I put it in. And I have to say, I didn't have high hopes because most facial recognition can't tell my twins apart. They're identical. And then, much to my surprise, Dazzle came back and described them pretty perfectly and also pulled up examples from kindergarten projects they had done five years before where these traits were evident.

So it's just kind of a fun anecdote, not necessarily how people use the product. There's lots of different ways to use Dazzle, and we're delighted with however people do. But this is really more about the power of what's in our photos, and when you give that to an AI assistant, how that can help you.

SUMMERS: Why do you think women need their own tailored AI assistant or something that perhaps functions differently and more specially for us?

MAYER: Well, first of all, Dazzle isn't just for women. It's for everyone. So, you know, it's not necessarily tailored for that experience. I do think, because busy women have a lot on their plates, this is a great thing, where you can actually delegate some of what you have to do, be it buying, fixing things around the house, booking things, calendaring.

SUMMERS: But as I think about this, I wonder, instead of an AI tool to help us outsource emotional labor, those long to do lists that I think every woman in my life, including myself, has, why not an AI tool to help men pitch in? The implication is that, you know, women need to do more work. We're not really talking about the fact that, like, we carry this huge emotional load.

MAYER: Yeah, and I think that for the emotional piece, I will say that's one of the things where I think that's something that my example wasn't perfect for on the birthday slide...

MAYER: ...Because that's something that - you know, you want a deep connection with your child, and I have them with mine.

MAYER: And I think what you want to do is take some of the things that are less personal, less emotional and outsource those to AI. And as I said, it doesn't have to be just women.

MAYER: I just feel that at the current moment, from what we're seeing, women might need a little bit more of a nudge to use it and also ideas and examples for how to get the best out of it.

SUMMERS: I can't help thinking about the dynamic between emotional labor versus emotional connection. One might argue that labor is what gives our connections value. Do you worry at all that these types of tools could devalue the actual relationships we have?

MAYER: Well, again, I - here I wasn't outsourcing my relationship with my daughter.

MAYER: I was going to have to write the slide one way or the other. What I would outsource is, you know, being able to add all the, you know, calendar dates of, you know, an upcoming trivia night at school or, you know, a dance studio closure.

MAYER: So this is less about the emotional piece, which is where I think AI frees us up. What Dazzle is trying to do is give people the gift of time. Like, I think that with it you can decide how you want to use Dazzle, and you can also decide, with the time that you're given back, how to spend it. And I think it would be great. I know, for me, as a parent, I've used that time to have more quality time with my kids.

SUMMERS: We've been speaking with former Yahoo CEO Marissa Mayer. Thank you so much for joining us.

MAYER: Thank you for having me.
