https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: FAA announces first US digital air traffic control towers in Florida and Alaska
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Marina Dunbar
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Systems provide 360-degree view of airport operations, but concerns have been raised about the technology

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has announced that the first digital air traffic control towers in the US are officially operational, bringing new technology first to smaller airports in Florida and Alaska as the Trump administration presses ahead with updating the country’s ageing aviation infrastructure.

The systems are now online at the Bartow executive airport (KBOW) in Florida and the Kenai municipal airport (PAEN) in Alaska, with five additional regional airports slated to receive the technology next.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

The digital towers use advanced camera systems and digital displays to give air traffic controllers a continuous, 360-degree view of airport operations, including runways, taxiways and surrounding airspace, according to the agency.

The FAA maintains that the technology is not intended to replace human controllers. Instead, the systems are designed to provide greater visibility and additional information to help controllers perform their existing duties.

“Our air traffic controllers continue to do the critical job of keeping aircraft safely separated, and we’re giving them better technology to do that,” said the FAA’s administrator, Bryan Bedford, in a statement.

“Digital towers provide controllers with greater visibility of airport activity and more information to make critical decisions,” he added.

Bedford is scheduled to appear before the House transportation and infrastructure committee next week, where he will face questions about the progress and challenges surrounding the administration’s ongoing $12.5bn modernization initiative.

The effort aims to replace decades-old equipment still used throughout the aviation system, including copper telecommunications lines, floppy disks and paper strips used to track aircraft.

Congress approved $12.5bn over five years in June 2025 to support air traffic control reforms, but the Trump administration is seeking another $30bn from the legislative branch to fund additional improvements.

Concerns about the types of technology being implemented within air traffic control have been gaining traction alongside the increasing unease about artificial intelligence as a whole. In September, the FAA rolled out a new AI software tool called the Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories (Smart).

Trump has been heavily criticized for his response to a national shortage of air traffic controllers following last year’s government shutdown.

Staffing levels in control towers and many related aspects of US air traffic safety systems have been under especially close scrutiny since a midair collision between a passenger jet and a military helicopter on the outskirts of Washington DC in 2025 that killed 67 people. It was the deadliest crash in the US for more than 20 years and the authorities later deemed it “100% preventable”.
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: The first digital air traffic control towers in the US are officially operational. The systems are now online at the Bartow executive airport in Florida and the Kenai municipal airport in Alaska. The FAA maintains that the technology is not intended to replace human controllers.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Stephen Miller, Trump’s incoming chief of staff, pledges ‘total devotion’ to the president
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Adam Gabbatt in New York
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Hardline aide offers ‘unwavering commitment’ to president amid fears White House will double down on far-right immigration agenda

Stephen Miller, Donald Trump’s most controversial aide and the architect of his sweeping immigration crackdown, has lavished praise on the president after his appointment as White House chief of staff.

In his first public remarks since the move was announced, Miller – who begins the role on Monday – pledged “total devotion” to Trump amid concern the administration is now poised to double down on its far-right, nativist immigration agenda.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

“If it wasn’t for President Trump the United States of America would not exist right now,” Miller, standing alongside his boss, declared at an event on Friday evening. “This man saved America. He saved our military from collapse. He saved our economy from destruction. He saved our border from annihilation. He saved our country from threats at home and abroad which would have been the end of the American dream for ever.”

His appointment was unveiled after Americans punished Trump’s Republican party in this week’s US midterm elections, unleashing a blue wave that swept through parts of the country where Democrats have not won in decades.

As of Saturday morning, Republicans have lost seven seats in the Senate, and Democrats hold narrow leads in the two races – Alaska and Mississippi – that have yet to be called. Republicans have also lost 42 seats in the House of Representatives, and five governor races.

Despite this extraordinary array of losses nationwide – which senior Republicans including JD Vance have blamed on the Iran war and tariffs, key pillars of Trump’s agenda – Miller praised the president on Friday for having “saved the Republican party from the ash heap of history and has made it stronger, more popular and more resilient than ever before”.

Miller added: “It is the honor of my life to be President Trump’s chief of staff, and I swear to you, and I pledge to you, Mr President, my absolute loyalty, my unwavering commitment, and my total devotion to your success and the success of this country.”

The speech will likely add to concerns that the Trump administration is set to continue pursuing its hardline immigration agenda, which Miller had been leading in his previous role as deputy chief of staff.

Republicans including longtime Trump ally and adviser Roger Stone and party operative Caroline Wren described Miller as the president’s “wartime consigliere”, drawing a sharp line under Trump’s vague suggestions in recent days that he could seek to work with Democrats after they won back control of the US Congress.

Miller’s appointment has been met with dismay by Democrats and some Republicans, with Marlin Stutzman, the Republican congressman from Indiana, describing the move as a “horrible decision” in comments to Politico.

Don Bacon, the outgoing Republican congressman from Nebraska, predicted that Miller will “have an antagonistic relationship with many”, telling CNN: “He cost us seats in Texas and Arizona by alienating many Hispanic voters who voted for Trump in 2024.”

Sign up to This Week in Trumpland

A deep dive into the policies, controversies and oddities surrounding the Trump administration

after newsletter promotion

Miller’s appointment was announced as Trump said he expects to make “a few changes” to his team.

“I love my cabinet. I think they’re good. But I’ll do – be doing maybe a few changes. I don’t want to mention who,” Trump told 60 Minutes, in an interview due to air on Sunday.

Asked if he has confidence in his defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, who has faced questions over his future in the role as the scale of the Republicans’ midterm losses became clear, Trump said “I do”, but notably stopped short of crediting him for what the president said were military successes.

Last month, after reports he might replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff, Trump was unequivocal: there is “zero chance” that will happen, he told reporters.
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: Stephen Miller has lavished praise on the president after his appointment as White House chief of staff. He pledged ‘total devotion’ to Trump amid fears White House will double down on immigration agenda. Miller was Donald Trump’s most controversial aide and architect of his sweeping immigration crackdown.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: LA’s newer, bluer wave: Nithya Raman leads way as city’s progressives make their mark
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Dani Anguiano in Los Angeles
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Democratic socialists won the mayorship, a US House seat and powerful positions in Los Angeles – and a large network of volunteers helped them do it

As a blue tsunami overtook US politics this week, Los Angeles saw a major shake-up of its own with a wave of democratic socialists elected to key offices.

Most notably, Nithya Raman, the first democratic socialist to serve on the Los Angeles city council, prevailed over incumbent Karen Bass to become the next mayor. Even in the deep blue city, Raman’s victory was hardly a given, and marked a stunning win for the progressive wing of the party. With her election, America’s two largest cities will now be run by democratic socialist mayors.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

The wins for the organization didn’t stop there.

Los Angeles voters backed numerous DSA-LA-endorsed candidates, including Marissa Roy for city attorney, and Angela Gonzales-Torres, who defeated the incumbent Jimmy Gomez for a US House seat. Other members won seats on school boards and the Burbank city council, meaning Burbank has the first socialist-majority city council on the west coast, DSA-LA said.

The organization saw its largest-ever slate of candidate victories after an election season in which volunteers knocked on more than 110,000 doors.

“These results show us what we’ve known for a long time: Angelenos are looking for an alternative to politicians beholden to billionaires and corporate interests,” Anna Gross, a DSA-LA steering member, said in a statement.

“With representation across LA county, in the most powerful positions in city hall and for the first time in US Congress [Gonzales-Torres], we look forward to showing Angelenos what Democratic Socialist leadership can deliver.”

DSA support was significant for Raman, and meant that a large network of volunteers canvassed for her across the city in the lead up to the election. But her campaign was also helped by the fact that Karen Bass was deeply unpopular. Polling has long shown that Angelenos are frustrated about the state of the city, and resentment over Bass’s handling of the Palisades fire damaged her.

“If there hadn’t been the Palisades fire in January of last year, I don’t think Nithya would have run. And I don’t think Karen Bass would have been defeated,” said Zev Yaroslavsky, the director of the Los Angeles initiative at the Luskin School of Public Affairs at the University of California, Los Angeles.

“The majority of the people of the city, a significant majority, think that the city is on the wrong track. And the Palisades fire was really the poster child for all that people are unhappy about.”

This week’s victories have boosted DSA-LA, which had more than 6,000 members as of last month, and has seen another 2,000 people join this week alone, the chapter said.

The organization has significantly expanded its power and reach in recent years. Raman, who joined DSA in 2019, was the first elected to city council in 2020 in a stunning victory that saw her defeat an incumbent Democrat backed by Nancy Pelosi and Hillary Clinton. Yaroslavsky said at the time that her election marked a “a significant shift in the architecture of Los Angeles politics”, he recalled.

In the years since, the city has voted in three other DSA candidates to serve on its 14-member council.

“The DSA organization has made an impact on LA city politics since 2020 when they supported Nithya Raman the first time,” Yaroslavsky said. “They’re pretty sophisticated in the way they target their resources, [which] are human resources – they have a lot of campaign workers and precinct walkers.”

In an interview with the Guardian in September, DSA member Patrick Padilla said the organization’s platform has broad appeal – including among many people who don’t identify as democratic socialists. The group focuses on an array of issues, including affordable housing and tenant rights, immigrant rights, Medicare for All and the Green New Deal, among others, according to its website.

“We’re coming to find that the status quo has not been serving everyday working Americans. And when I’m on the doors, I’m talking to people. People are just focused on how they can get by day to day,” Padilla said.

Several candidates of the slate endorsed by the chapter this year won by huge margins this week. In the city attorney race, Roy won with 67.39% of the vote, according to the latest data available. Roy has pledged to make the city attorney’s office into the “largest public interest law office in the city” and to use “the law to fight for working people, immigrants, renters, consumers”.

Gonzalez-Torres won with 60.6% of the vote to Gomez’s 39.4%, according to the most recently available figures. Gomez had served in Congress for nearly a decade and was endorsed by Aipac, which spent $2.7m in support of his candidacy. He stood in sharp contrast to Gonzalez-Torres who described the war in Gaza as a genocide that the “Israeli military is only able to commit with the financial and political support of the US government”.

While Raman’s victory is undoubtedly a win for the chapter, the endorsement was complicated.

Raman entered the race at the last minute after DSA-affiliated colleagues had already backed Bass, and another candidate was in the running. DSA member Rae Huang also ran in the mayoral primary and the chapter opted not to support any candidate.

The organization censured Raman in 2024 for pursuing an endorsement from a Democrats for Israel group, and its decision to back her in this election came after internal debate. (And while the chapter endorsed her, the other DSA-affiliated council members stood by Bass.)

Shortly before the election, the organization’s national leaders considered rescinding the chapter’s support until Raman stated her position on the boycott, divestment and sanctions movement. A vote on the matter ultimately failed.

The chapter has been outspoke in its support of her, writing in a social media post: “YUP, that’s our Mayor!!!”

While its the start of a new era in Los Angeles politics, the job of the mayor is the same. Once in office, Raman will have to build trust in communities that didn’t vote for her, Yaroslavsky said, which the mayor-elect has acknowledged.

“To every voter out there who voted for Mayor Bass or who chose not to vote in this election at all, please know this, I am going to city hall to work every single day to earn your trust and to earn your trust in this city again,” Raman said.

“That works starts now so that we can build housing people can afford, parks for our children, a transit system that can get people where they need to go, a city that is safe for its working people and its families, and a city government that is actually capable of delivering on its promises.”
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: Nithya Raman, the first democratic socialist to serve on the Los Angeles city council, prevailed over incumbent Karen Bass to become the next mayor. Raman's victory was hardly a given, and marked a stunning win for the progressive wing of the party.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Trump’s elevation of Stephen Miller a middle finger to millions of voters
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: David Smith in Washington
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Architect of Trump’s far-right immigration agenda is now most powerful unelected figure in government – it suggests White House is moving to a war footing

Donald Trump just gave the middle finger to millions of American voters.

Any other president who suffered the kind of drubbing at the polls that Trump did this week might have felt at least a sliver of humility – and perhaps even an obligation to work with the new opposition in Congress.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

But not for the first time in his political career, Trump veered in the opposite direction. On Friday he made Stephen Miller, condemned by Democrats and civil rights groups as a white nationalist, one of the most powerful unelected officials in Washington by naming him White House chief of staff.

Miller is the architect of Trump’s far-right, nativist immigration agenda. He is, therefore, arguably the architect of the blue wave that engulfed Republicans in Tuesday’s midterm elections as voters – including many Latinos – expressed their disgust. Yet instead of firing Miller, Trump promoted him.

It was a declaration of war. Miller, 41, is a longtime proponent of the presidential authority that Trump has spent the past two years expanding at the expense of Congress. In 2017 he declared: “The powers of the president to protect our country are very substantial and will not be questioned.”

Now Republicans’ catastrophic defeat is likely to leave Trump more reliant on unilateral executive action than ever to advance his domestic agenda.

“In a lot of ways Stephen Miller has been the id to Trump’s authoritarian impulses and machinations,” Kurt Bardella, an adviser to Democrats in Texas, said. “I have to imagine that anointing this person chief of staff – the most powerful non-elected position in all of government – is a signal that they intend to double down on that authoritarianism.

“You’re going to see a lot of executive orders, unilateral action and stress testing of the checks and balances system continue for the final two years of his presidency.”

Trump’s second term has presented a concerted effort to dismantle those checks and balances that have traditionally constrained the occupant of the White House. He has signed 292 executive orders in less than two years, more than in his entire first term and a record pace for a modern presidency.

He has bypassed Congress on military action and tariffs, withheld congressionally approved spending, deployed the National Guard against the will of state authorities, politicised the justice department, punished critics and challenged judicial independence. Congress, dominated by Republicans reluctant to confront him, offered little resistance.

But this week’s landslide, the biggest in a midterm election since Watergate, puts Democrats back in charge of the House of Representatives and Senate. That the elections were free and fair, and that Trump did not dispute the result, was itself a victory for democracy.

Democrats will now seek to rein in the president and block his legislative agenda, bringing them into direct conflict with Miller, who was already a hugely powerful deputy chief of staff at the White House and now takes over from Susie Wiles.

Miller has been a champion of the Iran war and prominent voice on many of the president’s other priorities, including countering diversity initiatives and targeting transgender rights. He is reportedly one of a small group of White House staffers who approve all executive orders.

He is best known for driving the ‌immigration crackdown in Trump’s second term, setting ‌a target of 3,000 arrests per day – far above levels under previous administrations. He has pushed Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) to target anybody in ‌the country illegally, not just those with criminal records.

There are limits on what Democrats can do to stop the immigration drive since the One Big Beautiful Bill Act included major increases for Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) that will keep it funded for the rest of Trump’s term.

Even so, they will now chair House committees with the ability to launch investigations, issue subpoenas and hold high profile hearings. Along with ICE, they might scrutinise Jeffrey Epstein files and the department of government efficiency (Doge). They have also vowed to look at how Trump and his family have become wealthier since he returned to office.

The appointment of the pugnacious Miller as Trump’s consigliere suggests that the White House is moving to a war footing. He is likely to marshal a team of lawyers and attack Democrats by accusing them of weaponising the deep state against the president. As a frequent guest on the conservative Fox News network, he will also wage war in the court of public opinion.

“Trump’s decision to elevate Stephen Miller means that he’s spoiling for a fight with Democrats and they’re going to just rely on executive action to try and push their agenda through,” said David Cohen, a political science professor at the University of Akron in Ohio, who studies the American presidency and White House staffing.

Cohen added: “It’s a White House that doesn’t seek out cooperation with Congress. It’s their way or the highway, essentially, and it’s possible Stephen Miller is relishing this because he’s a believer in the unitary presidency and executive presidential action and he views this as a way where he can expand the powers of the presidency.”

Trump is not the first president to seek to consolidate authority. Arthur Schlesinger Jr’s 1973 book The Imperial Presidency warned that an accumulation of presidential power threatened the constitutional separation of powers.

In 1989 the American Enterprise Institute thinktank published The Fettered Presidency, a counterpoint arguing that legal and congressional constraints had unduly weakened the executive. It helped inspire a modern conservative drive to expand presidential authority, which accelerated under George W Bush and was subsequently exploited by Barack Obama as congressional gridlock made legislating increasingly difficult.

The combination of Trump and Miller, however, takes the concept of an American Caesar to a new extreme – and flies in the face of the verdict delivered by the electorate on Tuesday.

“It’s a step that I find hard to fathom except as the president giving the middle finger to the American public,” said Bill Galston, a senior fellow in governance studies at the Brookings Institution thinktank in Washington.

“In the same way that he ransacked the state of Texas for the very worst senatorial nominee imaginable, now he’s done the same thing with the chief of staff position. This is simply outrageous.”
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: Stephen Miller is the architect of Trump’s far-right immigration agenda. Miller is a believer in the unitary presidency and executive presidential action.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Trump says he asked Dana White, UFC boss, to be his new White House press secretary
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Robert Mackey
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
White says he has meeting with Trump in Washington DC on Monday, without saying whether he will accept the job

Donald Trump has offered the job of White House press secretary to Dana White, the chief executive of the Ultimate Fighting Championship, the president said in a social media post on Saturday.

Trump described White, who staged a cage-fighting spectacle at the White House to mark the president’s 80th birthday in June, as “a violent Fighter and Warrior”, credentials unlike any ever used to describe previous press secretaries.

Trump added that he asked White, a vocal supporter who campaigned for him in 2024, to bring six UFC fighters with him to serve as press aides. “We need these people to defend us against the Lunatic Left,” Trump wrote. “Dana, please take the job!”

It was initially unclear whether the job offer was part of an actual plan, or an attention-grabbing stunt from a president desperate to change the subject from the huge losses suffered by his party in elections this week.

There was no immediate response from White, who, some observers noted, might hesitate to leave a lucrative role running the UFC, which has earned him a fortune estimated to be in excess of $600m, for a job in government service that pays $195,000 a year.

Later on Saturday, after CNN reported that White had declined the offer and that one aide to the president had described it as a joke, White posted an Instagram story with an image of himself in the White House briefing room above the caption: “On to the next chapter.”

The UFC boss was then asked about the president’s post at a news conference after a boxing match in London on Saturday night. “I’m flying to Washington DC right now” to meet with Trump, White replied, without saying whether he would accept the job. “I’m going to meet with him, we have a meeting on Monday, so I’m sure I’ll have more to talk about after that,” he added.

The president’s Truth Social post was illustrated by seven images, including what appeared to be an AI-generated image of White behind the presidential seal in a press room, and photographs of the six UFC fighters whom Trump fantasizes about deploying to deal with reporters who ask him awkward questions: Islam Makhachev and Khabib Nurmagomedov (who are both from a Muslim-majority region of Russia), Justin Gaethje, Daniel Cormier, Amanda Nunes and Kayla Harrison – whose last name was mistakenly rendered as “Harris” by the president.

In his post, Trump acknowledged that two of his dream hires, Makhachev and Nurmagomedov, are not Americans, but he did not mention that Nurmagomedov is reportedly close to the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, or that Makhachev has spoken out in defense of Palestinian civilians killed by Israel in Gaza. In 2023, Makhachev also celebrated a victory in one fight by saying, “Alhamdulillah,” the Arabic phrase for “praise be to God” used by Muslims. Democrat Abdul El-Sayed was criticized in the rightwing media for using that same Arabic phrase in his victory speech this week.

The first in a series of taxpayer-funded pro-Trump ads broadcast by the White House in the run-up to the recent midterms closed with images of the UFC fight on Trump’s birthday and remarks about him from White, who could be heard saying: “He is the toughest, most resilient human being I have ever met in my life.” White used that formulation to describe Trump multiple times during the 2024 presidential election campaign, most notably to sing Trump’s praises at the Republican national convention.

The role of White House press secretary has been vacant for three weeks, since Trump’s previous pick, far-right commentator Katie Zacharia, was forced to resign after trying, and failing, to dodge questions about why she described herself as an attorney despite having failed the bar exam.

Henry Smith contributed reporting
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: Trump says he has met with Dana White, the chief executive of the Ultimate Fighting Championship, on Monday. White has been a vocal supporter of the president since 2024. The UFC boss has been in the White House for three weeks.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Wisconsin state patrol trooper detained by ICE released from custody
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Uwa Ede-Osifo
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Carel Aaron Van Der Merwe immigrated to US at 14 and has been waiting seven years for asylum case to be heard

A Wisconsin state patrol trooper, whom federal immigration agents detained on Thursday at an airport, has been released from their custody.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents approached Carel Aaron Van Der Merwe, a South African national, as he waited to board a domestic flight, according to his law firm Christopher & De León.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

Van Der Merwe, who immigrated to the US when he was 14, has been waiting seven years for his asylum case to be heard, his attorneys said in social media posts. In the meantime, he received work authorization, valid through 2030, to serve in Wisconsin’s law enforcement.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) defended Van Der Merwe’s detention in a statement this week, saying he had overstayed a 2019 visa. “Work authorization or a pending application do not confer legal status in the US,” an agency spokesperson told the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel.

Van Der Merwe’s lawyers rejected that claim, noting that another DHS agency, US Citizenship and Immigration Services, “authorized him to work”.

“We don’t think ICE even believes its own statement,” the law firm added.

The agency did not immediately respond to an inquiry about what prompted the state trooper’s release.

In a social media update on Friday, Van Der Merwe’s law firm shared that their client would be released, but subject to electronic monitoring and regular check-ins with immigration authorities.

“His release is welcome news. But our fight is not over. Carel will still have to defend his immigration case before an immigration judge,” the attorneys wrote.

“USCIS, an agency within DHS, authorized Carel to work. He used that authorization to serve and protect Wisconsin communities. ICE, another agency within DHS, then detained him. DHS owes this family more than silence,” they continued.

Video of Van Der Merwe’s graduation ceremony last year showed that his badge was pinned on by his father in front of Wisconsin’s governor.

Van Der Merwe’s family of white South Africans arrived during Donald Trump’s first term, but they had good reason to expect that they would be granted asylum after Trump returned to office last year and signed an executive order saying the US would “promote the resettlement of Afrikaner refugees”, based on the false claim that they would be “escaping government-sponsored race-based discrimination” at home.

In addition to a series of highly public, contentious and in some cases deadly ICE raids across several US cities, the Trump administration’s mass deportation agenda has played out more furtively at domestic and international airports. Travelers with visas, green-card holders and pending asylum cases have been detained in what some experts say is an effort to meet arrest quotas imposed on the agency by the White House.

Van Der Merwe’s law firm advised noncitizens with unresolved immigration paperwork to consult immigration attorneys before traveling by air.

“Even if you have flown without problems before, do not assume the same will happen now,” they said.
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: Carel Aaron Van Der Merwe, a South African national, was detained by ICE agents on Thursday. He was released from custody after his lawyers said he had been waiting seven years for his asylum case to be heard. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) defended his detention in a statement this week.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: ‘People are active, they are fed up’: young voters fueled the Democratic wave
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Lex McMenamin
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
After helping Trump to victory in 2024, young voters swung decisively toward Democrats, helping deliver a wave of midterm victories

The 2026 blue tsunami owes a lot to the youth vote.

According to data from Tufts University’s Center for Information & Research on Civic Learning and Engagement (Circle), which monitors youth civic engagement, early estimates show the second-highest youth turnout in a midterm election in 30 years, second only to 2018, when an estimated 31% of young voters turned out during Donald Trump’s first presidency.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

While voters over 45 were roughly split between parties, voters ages 18-29 went for congressional Democrats at a 35-point edge, across race, gender, ethnicity, and education levels. Latino youth went for Trump by slim majorities in 2024; this year, they voted Democrat by margins of +10 to +15. 63% of young white men went for Trump in 2024; this cycle, 54% voted Dem. White young women also switched allegiance from 2024 by +15. Rural voters went from 50% voting for Trump in 2024 to 60% supporting Democratic candidates.

This is something of a return to form for the youth vote, which leaned Democratic by double digits in elections between 2018 and 2022. Indeed, the +35 lean for voters 18-35 parallels that in the 2018 blue wave which elected populist Democrats like Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, said Leela Strong, the director of Circle.

“It was such a soundbite for 2024, about the shift of young white men specifically, and folks without formal college experience,” said Strong. “Now, even though we’re comparing a midterm to a presidential, we’re seeing shifts among those demographic groups switching back to Democrats, overwhelmingly so.”

According to Strong, the data even suggests that 15% of young people who voted for Trump in 2024 voted for a Democratic House candidate this cycle. The outcome has been so decisive that Republicans are openly fretting over heavily Blue youth vote turnout in states like Florida, Georgia and South Carolina.

In battleground states – Florida, Georgia, Iowa, Maine, Michigan, Minnesota, North Carolina, Nebraska, New Hampshire, Nevada, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Texas, and Wisconsin – the estimated youth turnout was, in aggregate, 30%.

“I voted because in my working-class, immigrant neighborhood, families are afraid to go outside, drive to work or pick up their kid from school,” said Motyko Morales, 26, an artist in Miami, who says her family members have experienced “real physical and psychological impact” over attacks on legal routes to citizenship and the threat of third-country deportations. She’s “cautiously optimistic” that congressional Democrats will “hold ICE accountable and reverse course on harmful legislation”.

“For the first time in my life, I got to see a candidate that looked [like] and represented the same values of the Rio Grande Valley that I have,” said Amanda Chapa, 22, a recent college graduate and community organizer from Rio Grande City, Texas, of Gina Hinojosa. The governor-elect won 77% of voters 18-29, based on exit polling analysis from NBC News. In 2024, Trump flipped Starr county on the Texas-Mexico border – where Rio Grande City is located – by over 70 points; this year, despite navigating barriers to the polls, voters flipped it back by over 70 points.

Just over half of young voters ranked the economy and jobs as their top priority, followed by healthcare, Iran, immigration, education and the climate. Chapa’s top issues were reinstating cut funding to Medicaid and fighting ICE and the “brutalization of our community members”.

Sarah John, 26, a law student from Los Angeles, said she’s critical of Democrats, but having witnessed the impacts of Trump’s ICE raids in LA (still being felt), she strongly believed her vote against Republicans would make a difference. On Thursday, Los Angeles elected its first democratic socialist mayor, Nithya Raman – making two of the country’s three biggest cities now run by democratic socialists.

The enthusiasm even reached states without competitive federal races. Patrick Schranck, 27, who manages an independent movie theater in Portland, “identif[ies] more as an independent these days” and is active in his local Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) chapter. He spent Tuesday night at Portland DSA’s election night party celebrating the re-election of their three city councilmembers.

Schranck remains skeptical of congressional Democrats’ ability to “fix everything” with their newfound majorities, but, he said: “I’m just glad to see the Republicans lose and see more socialists and progressives get elected nationally.”

For Jordan Korgood, 24, of Boston, voting in this election was especially personal. The Massachusetts sexual health educator feels so passionately about civic engagement that she filed to run for a state board seat overseeing judicial appointments. But another candidate in the primary had Korgood tossed from the race on a technicality: Because she was homeless for a few months while in college in 2023, her opponent argued she could not meet the five-year residency requirement.

“Voting was the most immediate and direct way I could still engage with electoral politics in a meaningful way,” said Korgood, whose biggest issues were protecting the first amendment and trans rights. Regardless of who was up for re-election in Massachusetts, she said it felt necessary “at a time when fascists who seek to limit or repress my rights as a trans woman are seated in office in both red states and blue states alike”.

Young people were credited in part with powering Trump’s 2024 win, though just under half of eligible young voters turned out, not hitting the 50% turnout achieved in 2020. Plenty chose to sit out the election over US funding for Israel’s assault in Gaza, as well as the decision by both schools and elected officials to criminalize students in the thousands for protesting it. They also felt that the Democratic party had failed to offer a strong counter to what Republicans had on offer, instead tacking to the center.

In a sign of things to come, a year later, 75% of New York City voters 18-29 chose democratic socialist Zohran Mamdani as the city’s mayor, forming “his strongest supporter [bloc] out of all age groups” in the election tally, according to Circle. Political commentators and national party leaders argued a DSA campaign like his could only win in New York City.

Twenty-six-year-old Elise Joshi runs the progressive campus program More Perfect University and has spent the last several months hosting many of the progressive candidates that won big Tuesday at “Students vs. Billionaires Town Halls” on college campuses across the country. When the program launched this spring, Joshi told the New York Times that it was intended in part as a progressive counterpoint to Turning Point USA, whose existing campus presence has expanded in the year since Charlie Kirk’s killing. She argued that TPUSA “refus[es] to champion working-class issues”, and that youth voters were desperate for candidates who would.

Candidates like Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed – whose campaign slogan was “get money out of politics, put money in your pocket, and pass Medicare for All,” and who refused to compromise on trans girls in sports – are at the forefront of what Joshi and others are calling a blue tsunami.

“We’ve been in Florida, Maine, North Carolina, and I’ve seen the youth enthusiasm every single time – and not just enthusiasm for a specific candidate: Students who are very inquisitive about the issues and the solutions to those issues they’re dealing with, [from] from healthcare to economic issues to trans rights,” said Joshi. “Young people are active, they are fed up with corporate greed and corruption from Washington, and are ready to be really engaged in politics in all the ways you can be.”

More than a few of the successful candidates promising change, regardless of location, are young people themselves, like Melat Kiros, 29, the newly elected Colorado congresswoman who defeated a 15-term incumbent; many are DSA candidates. This week, Providence, Rhode Island, elected its youngest-ever mayor: 28-year-old David Morales, a democratic socialist. That same day, the city became the largest in the United States to vote in support of divesting from “companies complicit in genocide”, organized by the Providence for Palestine campaign.

In a period of global youth uprising against government corruption and seizing power in elections, it’s a partial answer to anyone questioning when America might see its youth in revolt. It’s also a rebuke to a tremendous amount of Republican campaign spending. Elon Musk alone spent nearly half a billion dollars backing Republicans and attacking candidates like Texas’s James Talarico, especially on trans issues. Talarico went on to win voters ages 18-29 by nearly 50 points.

“With the price of gas what it is alongside a hiring freeze, the only solution offered by the Republican party was to blind yourself with bigotry and pick a God and pray – except it has to be the Christian one, or else,” said model Vivian Wilson, 22, who has been financially independent from Musk, her father, since she came out as trans as a teenager. “Spending hundreds of millions of dollars on ‘trans kids boogieman’ ads makes voters feel like they’re being talked down to or ignored – which they were – rather than focusing on any actual tangible policy for change.”

She sees youth turnout for Democrats as only logical amid economic crisis, war on Iran, military support for Israel, ICE raids, and “the known sexual misconduct of Republican candidates”.

Wilson added: “There have been so many nails placed in this coffin that it’s turning into a Theseus’ ship kind of situation.”

“We feel fantastic,” said Kidus Girma, campaigns director for the Sunrise Movement, the youth climate organization that burst on to the scene in 2018 with a sit-in for the Green New Deal in then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi’s office alongside newly elected Ocasio-Cortez. This week, one of the movement’s cofounders, Will Lawrence, 36, won his race in Michigan, with Sunrise’s support.

Joshi and Girma are clear: It’s not “vote blue, no matter who.” There are plenty of power players still in the party who organizers feel didn’t listen to them outside election years, when they need them to power youth turnout.

Up next: Holding these new electeds – and the Democratic party – accountable. On Thursday, Wilson posted to her Instagram account backing a rising call from the US young left to reject Senator Chuck Schumer and congressman Hakeem Jeffries for leadership positions in the new Congress. By Saturday, a Change.org petition calling for Jeffries’ leadership ouster had attracted more than a million signatures.

This article was amended on 7 November 2026. An earlier version said Jordan Korgood’s bid for a state board seat in Massachusetts ended after an intervention by the 41-year-old incumbent. In fact, it was another candidate who intervened.
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: The data suggests that 15% of young people who voted for Trump in 2024 voted for a Democratic House candidate. The Democratic party failed to offer a strong counter to what Republicans had on offer. 75% of New York City voters 18-29 chose democratic socialist Zohran Mamdani as the city’s mayor.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Did the Bay Area just save its transit system from the brink of certain death?
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Isabeau Doucet in San Francisco
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Voters approved two measures to save the region’s financially distressed public transit agencies

V
oters in the San Francisco Bay Area overwhelmingly approved two transit measures this week that advocates hope will save the region’s financially distressed public transit agencies from a potential death spiral that could have had massive repercussions for the area’s residents and its economy.

The Regional Transit Measure (RTM), a 0.5% sales tax across four Bay Area counties and a 1% sales tax in San Francisco, will generate approximately $1bn annually to fund the region’s four largest transit operators. It received a strong 62.2% support across all five counties that voted on the measure, winning with a landslide of 78.6% in San Francisco.

Sign in now (it takes 30 seconds) to carry on reading

Not signed in before? Create a free account

In San Francisco, 73.6% of voters also approved a parcel tax to fund Muni, the first publicly owned and operated transit agency in a major US city.

Had the measures not passed, Bay Area Rapid Transit (Bart) would be forced to close as many as 15 stations as soon as early next year, dramatically reducing frequency of service and increasing the cost of rides and parking. Caltrain, a commuter rail that connects San Francisco with the South Bay region, would have closed 10 stations and ended weekend service. And Muni, the city of San Francisco’s main transit system, would have been forced to reduce a third of its service, eliminate 20 bus lines and suspend its iconic streetcars and cable cars. All agencies would have had to end evening services.

Less frequent service and fewer stations would have meant less fare revenue, fewer commuters and a downward cascade of financial austerity, creating a transit doom spiral that would have left Bay Area residents without reliable, affordable ways to get around the sprawling metropolis. The potential impacts were enormous in a region formed around a large body of water, where the freeways and bridges are notoriously jammed with traffic.

A recent report authored by Laura Tolkoff, transportation policy director for the San Francisco Bay Area Planning and Urban Research Association, estimated traffic delays on the San Francisco-Oakland Bay Bridge, which sees roughly 3.5m crossings a month, and other chokepoints around the region would have more than doubled during peak hours.

Bay Area transit agencies were left uniquely exposed to the low ridership during the pandemic given their dependence on fares for operating revenue and the region’s nation-leading shift to remote and hybrid work. As pandemic relief funds were set to expire and the fiscal cliff came into view, transit advocates shifted gears into action.

In 2023, Connect Bay Area organizer Lian Chang got involved with the fight to save public transit when she made coffins and replicas of local trains and buses out of cardboard for a mock funeral procession in front of city hall. Those cardboard replicas have done considerable mileage since, some needing new paint jobs as they circulated from press conferences to campaign events and rallies, Chang said.

She had no experience campaigning then, but has since helped rally volunteers in painting many banker boxes into buses and trains to carry the signatures that got the measures on the ballot, adding a playful and visually striking element to the campaign.

The biggest challenge, Chang found, was finding ways to get transit riders to self-identify and organize themselves into a constituency. To create a sense of pride among transit riders, who tend to be immigrants, children, seniors and lower-income people, she worked with local designers to make buttons to hand out on specific bus lines slated for cuts. This also helped recruit more volunteer signature-gatherers.

In the end, thousands of volunteers collected 77,000 of the 305,000 signatures that qualified the measure for the ballot, which, according to the Connect Bay Area campaign, is the highest number in recent memory. “We don’t know of any larger signature-gathering mobilization in the Bay Area,” said Chang.

The measures could still face legal challenges from anti-tax groups, as past transit initatives have faced, tying up the funds in escrow accounts for years.

“The Public Transit Revenue Measure District is prepared to vigorously defend the will of the voters and the validity of the measure,” said Rebecca Long of the Metropolitan Transportation Commission, the agency in charge of administering the RTM funds.

Jeff Cretan, spokesperson for Connect Bay Area, the coalition that backed the two initiatives, wants to keep the momentum high so voters aren’t facing another transit catastrophe when the measures expire in about 15 years.

“This is an opportunity for us to go to the state and say, we need to change how we do this, not just here, but in other parts of the state,” said Cretan.

Compared with other world-class regions in the United States and beyond, California has historically underinvested in the public transit of its urban centers, despite priding itself on robust climate policies.

A 2022 report from the California Air Resources Board said for the state to meet its own climate goals, existing public transit networks would need to double their capacity and service frequency by 2030. Bart, AC Transit, Caltrain and Muni make up 30% of the state’s transit ridership. Yet, only 5% of Bart’s operating revenue comes from the state.

Tuesday’s election also brought a wave of new leadership to the state. Transit advocates already see an ally in state senator Scott Wiener, who co-authored the transit measures and won his bid to succeed Nancy Pelosi in Congress.

But they are also hopeful governor-elect Xavier Becerra will prioritize public transit after seeing strong support from Bay Area voters, despite not making it a central issue of his gubernatorial campaign. (Becerra’s campaign did not return the Guardian’s request for comment.)

“I hope that Governor Becerra and elected representatives take note of the messages voters just sent: transit is not controversial – it’s essential and it’s incredibly popular,” said Tolkoff.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: The Trump administration wants underwater datacenters. One Great Lakes non-profit is already preparing
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Stephen Starr
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Tech companies like the idea, as they largely eliminate community opposition, and could cut down on utility costs

While Elon Musk has often touted putting datacenters in space, reports suggest that another geographic area may soon become a widespread target: our lakes and oceans.

Two underwater datacenters are already in operation off the coast of China, and recent reports suggest that the Trump administration is considering plans for four proposed underwater, sealed-pod datacenters to be built off the shores of Maine and Alaska.

Sign in now (it takes 30 seconds) to carry on reading

Not signed in before? Create a free account

At a campaign rally in Ohio last month, Donald Trump said of datacenters: “There’s so much money to be made for Ohio … they’ll go to China … we want them.”

Underwater iterations are particularly attractive to tech companies as they largely eliminate community opposition and controversy around datacenters in residential areas on land. In theory, underwater datacenters could also significantly cut down on utility costs, another issue that’s currently riling communities across the country.

A Microsoft project set up off the coast of northern Scotland in 2018 found that after two years, server failures were reduced by 87% compared with on-land datacenter equivalents. Microsoft executives saw the project, which ended after two years, as an unmitigated success.

That makes the cool, salt-free waters of the Great Lakes, home to 30 million people in major cities such as Chicago, Toronto and Detroit, potentially attractive to datacenter companies.

A spokesperson for the federal Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) said: “The EPA supports development of data center infrastructure that is essential to remaining the world leader in Super Intelligence while using its statutory authorities to protect water quality.”

But the environmental consequences of any similar project in the freshwater Great Lakes, which those tens of millions of people depend on for drinking water every day, could be significant. Local environmental activists are already worried and sounding the alarm – even though no underwater datacenter projects are currently proposed for the region.

For them, they think it is better to be prepared than surprised, given the high stakes of the ecologically sensitive ecosystem.

“We are concerned because if you think about what a datacenter does, it throws off a lot of heat. Lake Erie already has an issue with harmful algal blooms, and they develop because of heat, not only because of fertilizers and agricultural runoff,” said John Lipaj of the Lake Erie Foundation, a non-profit based in Ohio.

The floor of Lake Erie on the US side falls under the jurisdiction of the state of Ohio. In the past, its state government, where Republicans hold a supermajority, proposed a law making it easier for datacenter companies to discharge wastewater into public waterways. That measure was denied by the state’s EPA last July following a public outcry. Of the eight US Great Lakes states, only New York currently has a temporary state-wide moratorium on datacenter construction. That ends in mid-2027.

“We’re also concerned about the possibility of contamination and leaks. These have not been around a long time,” said Lipaj.

“We are concerned about the types of fluid contained in a datacenter, the batteries and electrical equipment. These are all things that could lead to a catastrophic failure that we don’t want happening in the Great Lakes.”

Lake Erie is home or close to major cities such as Cleveland, Detroit and Buffalo and is already by far the warmest of the five Great Lakes during summer months. It also ranks as one of the most polluted large lakes in the country in large part due to agricultural runoff in its western basin. A number of fish species are under threat due to the lake’s warming trend.

“Warm water can impact aquatic life and ecosystems in a number of ways. One immediate effect is what is known as a thermal shock,” said Helena Volzer of the Alliance for the Great Lakes, an environmental group based in Chicago.

“Aquatic organisms are highly sensitive to temperature changes, and even a small, rapid increase of just 2-5F can be dramatic for the aquatic ecosystem. When a facility releases warm water, it can alter metabolism and increase oxygen demand, reduce dissolved oxygen availability, disrupt food webs [and] force fish to move away from preferred habitats.”

On 3 November, residents of Conneaut, a Lake Erie community of about 12,000 people an hour’s drive north-east of Cleveland, voted in favor of a charter amendment to prohibit the construction of large datacenters in its area.

But the idea of offshore underwater datacenters is not a popular one here.

“Being one of the largest freshwater sources in the world, I would be very much for protecting that resource,” said Mariana Branch, a Conneaut council member who lives a short distance from the Lake Erie shoreline. Branch said she hadn’t previously been aware of the idea of datacenters operating underwater.

“Technology is moving so quickly, it’s difficult for cities to keep up with,” she said.

Still, some suggest that following Microsoft’s lead in Scotland may have some merit considering the public opposition to on-land equivalents; and, unlike the open ocean, there are no large fauna in the Great Lakes ecosystems.

“They require a lot of energy for cooling … one of the biggest advantages of these underwater datacenters is the low cooling cost [associated]. They don’t have to spend a lot to cool the servers,” said Nir Kshetri, a professor of emerging technologies at the University of North Carolina Greensboro.

“Datacenters have been a big issue for communities and in the recent elections. Also, datacenters don’t have to worry about any latency problems because they can be located close to large population centers where they are needed. A lake is a great place to do a datacenter. Cold water is even better.”

However, the Great Lakes are not without significant challenges to any such project.

Last winter saw one of the most extensive Great Lakes freeze-ups in decades, with almost all of Lake Erie and up to half of the four other lakes freezing over up to several feet deep. Experts say it isn’t clear to what extent ice cover could affect underwater projects.

What’s more, a Microsoft spokesperson said: “We have no plans to deploy an underwater datacenter in any location at this time,” and: “Our focus today is on building and operating datacenters responsibly on land.”

A spokesperson for Ohio’s EPA said it had not yet received any applications to permit an underwater datacenter in its part of Lake Erie.

For its part, Lipaj says the Lake Erie Foundation has contacted state representatives and state senators in New York, Ohio and Michigan to discuss the issue.

“Whether or not they happen, [we’re saying] let’s propose to state legislatures in Great Lakes states that they consider that this may be coming down the line and let’s get some regulations in place before the datacenter developers make their proposals and then state legislators are scrambling. That’s what we’re trying to avoid. We’re exercising an abundance of caution,” he said.

“The Great Lakes states should take some leadership in this, get the regulations written so that nothing is forced on them.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Guardian staff and agency
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Ana Reyes wants to know whether federal officials lied about extent of renovation plans at East Potomac golf course

A federal judge said on Saturday that she intended to appoint an ex-top federal prosecutor who served during Donald Trump’s first term to investigate whether she was purposely misled by lawyers and administration officials over changes to a historic public golf course in Washington DC.

Jessie Liu, a former US attorney for the District of Columbia, would examine whether officials with the interior department and the National Park Service and attorneys with the Department of Justice violated ethics or misled US district judge Ana Reyes during the course of the civil case that was initiated with a lawsuit in February by the DC Preservation League and two golfers.

Sign in now (it takes 30 seconds) to carry on reading

Not signed in before? Create a free account

The lawsuit challenges one of the US president’s flurry of construction projects around the nation’s capital – in this case, the renovation of a public golf facility along the Potomac River, which is less high-profile that some of his other plans but had still riled many.

The Republican administration plans to close the East Potomac golf course and park on 15 November with the intention of constructing what it has called a “World Class, championship-level golf course that is capable of hosting major events”.

An injunction issued by Reyes last month temporarily bars the government from removing or damaging any additional trees on the course and ordered the administration to give 10 days’ notice in writing before making any “irreparable modification” to any “forms or features” of the course while the lawsuit is active.

Reyes is now giving each side a chance to be heard on her plan to name Liu as special master in the case. They must do so in writing by Friday, when the next court hearing in the dispute is scheduled.

Reyes, who was nominated by Joe Biden during his term, wants to know whether federal officials lied about the extent of renovation plans during prior months of hearings.

She also demands to know whether they were truthful about various steps they took, including cutting down hundreds of trees early last month.

Reyes announced during a hearing on 30 October that she was starting a formal investigation into the government’s conduct. Earlier in the case, she had rejected numerous motions from the plaintiffs to step in, saying she trusted the government attorneys.

As the city’s then chief federal prosecutor, Liu oversaw some of the matters referred to her office by then-special counsel Robert Mueller during his investigation into alleged ties between Trump’s 2016 election campaign and Russia.

Trump later nominated her to be associate attorney general, the third-highest-ranking justice department job. Liu withdrew from consideration after running into opposition on the Republican-led Senate judiciary committee because of her past membership in a lawyers’ group that had supported abortion rights.

David Super, a law professor at the Georgetown University law center, said the initiation of a formal investigation by a judge to look into the conduct of a trial’s participants “can be a precursor to holding someone in contempt of court”.

Super said it also is a reflection “of the difficulty she had in determining who initiated the tree-cutting in defiance of the assurances DoJ provided. She doesn’t have the time to keep holding long, complex hearings and so wants a special master to narrow the issues.”

Meanwhile, on Saturday afternoon, Trump posted a long and outlandish message on his social media platform declaring that he was “ordering” the justice department immediately to “look into” Democrats whom he said were “threatening” people in his administration with impeachment, referring to such suggested conduct as a “criminal act”.

The garbled post also accused Democrats of threatening Republican donors and called out the Michigan US senator Elissa Slotkin, a Democrat, saying she was “going after” young people who “give even the slightest inclination to be a Republican” and that this amounted to extortion. The US president did not present further detail or explanation of his claims.

The Associated Press contributed reporting

Reyes is now giving each side a chance to be heard on her plan to name Jessie Liu as special master

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Trump faces criticism for ‘dangerous’ Stephen Miller appointment as White House chief of staff
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Ariana Baio in Washington
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Democrats and Republicans blast promotion of ‘xenophobe’ who led administration’s immigration crackdown in wake of US midterm elections

Democratic lawmakers decried Stephen Miller as a “hatemonger”, a “xenophobe” and “vile” after Donald Trump appointed his most trusted adviser as White House chief of staff.

On Friday afternoon, the US president abruptly announced via his Truth Social platform that Miller – the architect of his sweeping immigration crackdown – would replace Susie Wiles, whom he confirmed had been ousted.

Sign in now (it takes 30 seconds) to carry on reading

Not signed in before? Create a free account

The announcement came just days after voters overwhelmingly elected Democrats in the US midterm elections, a sharp rebuke of Trump’s agenda that ended his Republican party’s control of US Congress.

“For Trump to promote this hatemonger shows he has learned nothing,” Dick Durbin, a Democratic senator from Illinois, wrote on X. Chuck Schumer, who is expected to become Senate majority leader, said Trump “learned nothing from his historic defeat” and “couldn’t have made a worse choice” in elevating Miller.

Hakeem Jeffries, the top Democrat in the House of Representatives, who is widely expected to become the chamber’s first Black speaker, called Miller “a dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist who has American blood on his hands”, and demanded he be fired.

Chris Van Hollen, a Democratic senator from Maryland, called Trump’s decision to elevate Miller “another kick in the teeth to the American people” and “a sign of Trump’s contempt for the voters”.

Miller, who has been serving as Trump’s deputy chief of staff, has become one of the most controversial figures in the administration. An author of the rightwing Project 2025 manifesto, Miller often makes TV appearances to attack Trump’s opponents or bolster policies such as ending birthright citizenship and suggesting the US could invade Greenland.

As a policy adviser, Miller is credited as the architect of Trump’s mass deportation agenda, which Democrats pointed to in denouncing his promotion.

Gavin Newsom, the outgoing California governor, called Miller “one of the most vile thugs to ever slither into the Oval Office” and said the move was “an insult to every American who voted for change” on Tuesday.

But Trump’s Republican allies and aides celebrated the announcement. Steven Cheung, the White House communications director, called Miller a “Trump OG”, and said: “There is no bigger advocate for the Trump agenda than Stephen.”

Mike Lee, a senator from Utah, said Miller had been “a staunch defender of law and order against illegal invasions and leftist lawlessness”. Eric Schmitt, a senator from Missouri, insisted Miller was exactly what the country needed. “Our country is at a pivotal point and Stephen Miller understands exactly what is at stake,” Schmitt wrote on X.

Cabinet members including JD Vance, defense secretary Pete Hegseth, health secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr and secretary of state Marco Rubio also praised Miller’s record.

Not all Republicans were pleased by the appointment, however.

Congressman Marlin Stutzman, an Indiana Republican who held his seat, argued Miller “should be fired” earlier this week amid anger over the administration’s deportation drive. Asked on Friday what he made of Trump’s choice to promote Miller instead, Stutzman told Semafor it was a “horrible decision”.

Miles Taylor, who served as chief of staff at the Department of Homeland Security during Trump’s first term, and later joined the ranks of anti-Trump Republicans, said: “I spent two years working with Stephen Miller. His appointment as White House chief of staff is among the most dangerous personnel decisions in the history of our republic. I say that without reservation.”

Asked about such criticism on Friday, the White House hailed Miller as a “key player” delivering Trump’s agenda. “He has spearheaded the administration’s crime crackdown including in DC and Memphis, record setting deregulation, unleashed American energy, dismantled drug cartels, and secured our border,” it said in a statement. “In his new role, he will continue to deliver historic successes for the American people.”

Accepting his new role, Miller thanked Trump and said he was “honored beyond words” to serve. “The mission now is more clear than ever: Fight with all of our soul to support our President and defend this magnificent Republic,” Miller wrote on X.

He was the architect of the immigration crackdown and was appointed by President Trump. Democrats decried him as a ‘hatemonger’ and a “xenophobe’ who has American blood on his hands’s hands”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Stephen Miller, architect of Trump’s immigration crackdown, to become White House chief of staff
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: David Smith in Washington
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
US president confirms Susie Wiles, current chief of staff and first woman to serve in the role, will step down

Stephen Miller, Donald Trump’s most controversial aide and the architect of his sweeping immigration crackdown, will become his new White House chief of staff days after Republicans lost control of the US Congress in US midterm elections.

The president announced the extraordinary appointment on Friday, confirming that Susie Wiles – his current chief of staff, and the first woman to serve in the role – had been ousted.

Sign in now (it takes 30 seconds) to carry on reading

Not signed in before? Create a free account

In a social media ‌post, Trump called Miller, 41, “one of ​my most trusted advisors” and praised Wiles for doing “an ⁠outstanding job”. Miller will begin on Monday.

Wiles, 69, reportedly handed in her resignation on Thursday night and said in a social media post that serving Trump “has been the honor of a lifetime”.

Holding an umbrella, Trump emerged from the White House South Portico on Friday for a trip to Florida. “I wanted to make a change,” he said. “I think Susie’s done a very good job ... Stephen’s been great, and we’ve got to make moves.”

“Stephen’s been with me from the beginning. He gets it,” the president said. “Very good politically and he’s a very good man. He’ll do a great job. Great manager.”

Trump then boarded the Marine One helicopter, followed by Miller, secretary of state Marco Rubio and close aide Natalie Harp.

In a statement, Wiles added: “I’m so proud to have been a part of what we’ve accomplished together from securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America First.”

She said her commitment to “the President and the mission” will not change.

Miller posted on X that he was “honored beyond words” to serve as Trump’s chief of staff. He added: “The mission now is more clear than ever: Fight with all of our soul to support our President and defend this magnificent Republic.”

But a growing chorus of Democrats condemned the appointment.

Hakeem Jeffries, who is poised to become the first Black speaker of the House, posted: “Stephen Miller is a dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist who has American blood on his hands. His presence in government should be eradicated like a malignant tumor. Fire him today.”

Chuck Schumer, likely to be the next majority leader of the Senate, wrote: “Donald Trump learned nothing from his historic defeat. Stephen Miller is the architect of the most barbaric, inhumane policies of this administration. Trump couldn’t have made a worse choice. Our Democratic majorities will fight him every step of the way.”

Miller’s appointment is the first sign of a shake-up at the White House following Republicans’ catastrophic defeat in the midterms. His record as a far-right firebrand implies that Trump is preparing for an aggressive fight against congressional Democrats’ oversight and investigations.

Chris Whipple, author of The Gatekeepers: How the White House Chiefs of Staff Define Every Presidency, told CNN: “It’s almost a declaration of war by Trump … He [Miller] only knows one gear and that’s full-throttle, full steam ahead over the cliff.”

David Axelrod, a veteran Democratic strategist, added on X: “For those who hoped the @POTUS might pivot to work with the incoming Congress, the appointment of Miller is a bucket of ICE cold water.”

Miller is one of the most polarising figures in the administration and one of Trump’s closest and longest-serving advisers, having joined his 2016 presidential campaign as a speechwriter. He is a former aide to the former senator Jeff Sessions of Alabama, who would go on to serve as Trump’s first attorney general.

In Trump’s first term, Miller was the driving force behind policies such as family separation and a travel ban on Muslim-majority countries. More than a hundred Democrats in Congress signed a letter to Trump calling Miller a “documented white nationalist” and demanding his removal.

A biography of Miller, written by journalist Jean Guerrero in 2020, was entitled Hatemonger.

Sign up to Breaking News US

Get the most important news as it breaks

after newsletter promotion

Miller has served as deputy chief of staff since Trump’s return to the presidency in January 2025. He had been hugely influential in hardline immigration policies and demanding an end to birthright citizenship. He is also one Trump’s most ardent, outspoken and pugnacious defenders.

Appearing on Sean Hannity’s Fox News show on Monday, just before the midterms, Miller said of the president: “He saved America from a corrupt political class. He saved America from open borders. He saved America from countries that want the American way of life to end, from foreign adversaries, from domestic adversaries.”

Miller added: “President Trump took a bullet for you, he bled for you, he faced life in prison for you. And what he needs from you tomorrow is your vote.”

Wiles is the longest-serving White House chief of staff for Trump, who cycled through four of them during his first four-year term.

Wiles led Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign to victory and was credited with bringing discipline to a chaotic effort and clamping down on leaks from his second administration.

The Florida operative generally shunned the limelight. At Trump’s 2024 election night victory party, she repeatedly shook her head and avoided the microphone as Trump tried to coax her to speak to the crowd.

But Wiles made headlines last year when Vanity Fair magazine published a series of interviews with her and other top Trump administration officials. Her comments stood out for their candour, including her observation that Trump has an “alcoholic’s personality”.

Her departure came months after she indicated she no longer showed evidence of breast cancer after she underwent months of treatment for the disease. She went public with the diagnosis in March.

Critics said Miller’s appointment showed that Trump had learned the wrong lessons from Tuesday’s electoral reckoning.

Becca Balint, a Democratic congresswoman from Vermont, posted on X: “On Tuesday, the American people rose up and overwhelmingly voted in opposition to the disgusting and inhumane policies of this second Trump administration. What does Trump do? He promotes Stephen Miller – the architect of some of this administration’s worst decisions. Sickening.”

Anthony Scaramucci, who had a brief spell as White House communications director during Trump’s first term, tweeted: “Trump saw the midterm results and decided elevating Stephen Miller is the answer. 🤣 He is even more delusional than I thought. Or maybe he actually wants to finish destroying the @GOP? 🤔”
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: Susie Wiles, 69, will step down as White House chief of staff. Miller is Donald Trump's most controversial aide and architect of his immigration crackdown.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Wiles thanks president for ‘honor of a lifetime’ as departure leaves behind overwhelmingly male leadership team

US politics live – latest updates

Donald Trump on Friday said Susie Wiles, the first woman to serve as White House chief of staff, will leave her post, a major shake-up of his inner circle that comes amid a steady exodus of senior female officials from his administration.

The president announced her ouster – and her replacement, by the immigration hardliner Stephen Miller – in a post on Truth Social, days after a sweeping blue wave gave Democrats control of both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections. Wiles’s departure leaves behind an overwhelmingly male leadership team.

Sign in now (it takes 30 seconds) to carry on reading

Not signed in before? Create a free account

“I wanted to make a change,” he told reporters on Friday. “I think Susie’s done a very good job … Stephen’s been great and we’ve got to make moves.”

Wiles, who reportedly handed in her resignation on Thursday night, said her role as chief of staff “has been the honor of a lifetime,” adding: “I’m so proud to have been a part of what we’ve accomplished together, from securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America first.”

Wiles’s exit follows a string of high-profile resignations and dismissals of women in the Trump administration. In recent months, White House press secretary Katie Zacharia was ousted just five days after taking up the role, while former homeland security secretary Kristi Noem and former attorney general Pam Bondi were also dismissed.

Former national intelligence director Tulsi Gabbard reportedly resigned under pressure, while Kimberly Guilfoyle, the former US ambassador to Greece, has also departed her post.

As high-ranking women left the administration, Wiles, diagnosed with breast cancer, stayed put, with Trump even claiming at one point: “She’s going to be here for a long time”. Wiles announced in September that she was cancer-free.

Just a day before Trump’s announcement of Wiles’s ouster, Harmeet Dhillon, a staunch Trump ally and controversial head of the justice department’s civil rights division, also resigned, marking yet another high-profile woman’s departure from the Trump administration.

Dhillon’s resignation comes amid expectations Democrats will use their majority in Congress to investigate federal agencies under Trump, including the US justice department, which has repeatedly been accused of being weaponized by the administration to pursue Trump’s own political enemies.

Other justice department officials have also since resigned amid the major post-midterm personnel shakeup, including John Eisenberg, the assistant attorney general for national security, as well as Jason Reding Quiñones, a key attorney that led inquiries into Trump’s rivals.

Only a handful of women remain in Trump’s cabinet, including agriculture secretary Brooke Rollins and Kelly Loeffler, head of the Small Business Administration.

Natalie Harp, the 35-year-old political aide, remains a frequent presence by the president’s side at public events. Harp has previously written letters to the president in which she described him as “my guardian and protector”.
