https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
The ‘secretary of war’ and his shameful history are facing bipartisan scrutiny

Can you smell the schadenfreude in the air?

Watching some of the worst people in the world get their comeuppance this week has been deeply satisfying. And the show isn’t over yet. While the midterms have wrapped up, the blame game is only just getting started, with Republicans desperate to find scapegoats for their shellacking.

Sign in now (it takes 30 seconds) to carry on reading

Not signed in before? Create a free account

He may be a big, strong, testosterone-obsessed warrior, but I suspect Pete Hegseth is panicking right now. When it comes to scapegoats, the defence secretary (or “war secretary” as he prefers to identify as) is an obvious choice. The disastrous US-Israeli war on Iran played a key role in the midterm upset, as even JD Vance has admitted, and Hegseth was one of its main architects.

The Democrats have already declared war on the former Fox News personality. “In the majority, one of the first things we’re going to do is run Pete Hegseth out of town,” Hakeem Jeffries announced at a campaign rally before the midterms.

It’s not just the Democrats; many of Hegseth’s peers are eager to give him the boot.

The outgoing Republican senator Thom Tillis told CBS News on Tuesday night that Hegseth has a “reckoning” coming. Meanwhile, the (also outgoing) Republican congressman Thomas Massie told Bloomberg News he will “definitely” reintroduce articles of impeachment against Hegseth next week. (Massie has already tried to impeach Hegseth for starting the war in Iran without congressional approval.)

In a Wednesday post on Twitter/X, Massie wrote: “There is one contingency in which I won’t reintroduce the articles of impeachment: Hegseth resigns.”

There is little chance that Hegseth will unilaterally decide to make a dignified exit. On Thursday, the defense secretary posted a longwinded video in which, after rambling about DEI and trans people, he asserted that he wasn’t going anywhere.

“A disgruntled, defeated congressman [aka Massie], along with all his Democrat allies, has also dropped sham articles of impeachment against yours truly, just like they tried against President Trump twice,” Hegseth said. “Didn’t work against President Trump, and it won’t work with me. You can rest assured of that.”

This little performance did not quieten his critics.

“@PeteHegseth, cabinet secretaries shouldn’t be wasting taxpayer dollars on campaign style videos,” Tillis wrote on social media in response. “This is about you: the incompetence you’ve displayed, the bad advice you’ve given to president, and your shameful and embarrassing episodes from firing our top generals to texting war plans to reporters.”

There have been rather a lot of shameful and embarrassing episodes in Hegseth’s career, haven’t there?

There are all the allegations about his previous drunk and disorderly conduct, for example. And the settlement he paid to a woman who accused him of raping her in 2017. And the time his own mother called him an “abuser of women”. (He’s denied any wrongdoing.) And the New Yorker’s report that, in 2015, Hegseth was accused of drunkenly chanting “Kill All Muslims! Kill All Muslims!” (Hegseth’s lawyer told the New Yorker that they weren’t going to comment on these “outlandish claims”.) And the time he accidentally sent top secret war plans in a Signal group chat that included a reporter from the Atlantic. And then, of course, there are all the alleged war crimes he’s responsible for.

Hegseth loves to rail against “DEI hires”, but imagine for a moment if a woman was texting classified information to the wrong people and battling scandal after scandal. There’s no way she’d still be heading up the Pentagon. As has been widely observed, Trump seems to like getting rid of his high-level female officials when they embarrass him, while holding on to his mediocre men.

Indeed, while the secretary of war may be on the defensive now, there’s always the depressing possibility that his sex – and his sycophancy towards the president – may end up saving him. Particularly as Trump is publicly standing by his man for the moment.

When asked on Wednesday if he was considering replacing Hegseth, Trump told reporters: “No, I think ⁠he’s doing a very good job.” Behind the scenes, of course, it could be a different story. NBC News reported on Wednesday that Trump has told some of his allies that he’s considering replacing the defense secretary.

But even if Hegseth is able to cling on to the sinking ship until it finally goes down, I take solace in the fact that he must be feeling very uncomfortable right now. And I am clinging on to hope that he will have a very public downfall.

This is, let’s not forget, a man who wanted to livestream an execution via firing squad. While that thankfully never happened, perhaps we’ll all get to watch a live stream of Hegseth getting fired.

Nancy Lacore was in the navy for 35 years before the three-star admiral was ousted by Hegseth without cause amid a broader purge. In response, she mounted a bid for Congress that made Hegseth’s incompetence a key talking point. At the time of writing, the race hasn’t been officially called, but it looks like she’s managed to flip a traditionally Republican seat. Wouldn’t it be poetic if she plays a part in firing Pete?

Sign up to The Week in Patriarchy

Get Arwa Mahdawi’s weekly recap of the most important stories on feminism and sexism and those fighting for equality

after newsletter promotion

“Eighteen- to 29-year-old young white men with no college degrees swung 40 points to the Democrats, and I don’t think it’s all because they’re socialists,” the podcaster Tim Pool told Fox News. “I think it’s because many of them want to burn the Republican party down.” Go ahead, guys!

Part of Brand’s defence was the claim: “Not one of [the victims] resisted or screamed or even tried to leave.” Speaking after the trial, the victims’ commissioner for England and Wales, Claire Waxman, emphasized how dangerous these sorts of misconceptions about sexual assault are. “The idea that rape victims must scream, physically resist or immediately report an offence is a well-established rape myth, rooted in outdated and harmful assumptions about how victims are expected to behave,” she said. “Justice must be grounded in evidence, not misconceptions.”

Just when you think the US is getting a smidgen more sane, you see something like this.

Israeli militants killed five teenage students at al-Mughayyir school in the West Bank last academic year, one at the school gates. In response to parents being afraid to send their kids back to the classroom, the school has had to build bigger fences. Meanwhile, “settlers” continue their violent pogroms on the village, and far too many US politicians continue to excuse and enable this violence.

A Guardian investigation has found that groups such as Crunchy Moms (which has more than 490,000 members) are hives of anti-vaccine content and medical misinformation. Most alarmingly: Meta “appears to have helped spread such ideas by promoting Crunchy Moms into users’ feeds, even when they do not seek it out”.

While the midterms were on everyone’s mind this week, an alligator in North Carolina was just thinking about brunch. Surveillance cameras caught the creature strolling into the back of a bagel shop, startling the customers. The police were called and the gator was removed. The gator insists he did nothing wrong and is the victim of a schmear campaign.

Arwa Mahadwi is a Guardian columnist

The victims’ commissioner for English and Wales, Claire Waxman, emphasized how dangerous these sorts of misconceptions about sexual assault are.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Flip voters discovered that Trump’s racism and xenophobia are expensive
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Saida Grundy
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Maga’s regret voters were all-in for Trump’s racism. Then they found out they couldn’t afford it

F
or the first time in a decade, election predictions far exceeded public expectations. What pollsters anticipated as a blue wave billowed into a blue tsunami. Wins that held ground for already blue seats eased nerves, and the flips of swing states like Michigan, Georgia, North Carolina and Ohio energized the blue base. But red-belt-busting wins in Republican strongholds like Texas, South Carolina and Kansas alongside pending races in Alaska and Mississippi left mouths agape. The explanation was that Democrats turned out far more supporters than their regulars, and that the “regret voter” (both swing voters and partisan Republicans) expanded the wave across districts Trump previously won. Elation and sighs of relief rolled over consistently Democratic voters who suffered multiple sucker punches from recent years of Republican upsets. Regret voters, who run the gamut from gen Z men to Latinos, farmers and the white working class, hope a different party can deliver on the economy Trump promised them.

Blue voters look at the dismantling of democracy, multiple wars, mass deportations and Trump’s unchecked power in these last two years and see how it all could have been avoided. Regret voters, however, either co-signed or conceded to Trump’s naked racism and brutish bullying of marginalized people, but switched their votes as soon as the consequences hit their pockets. While some of the president’s backers may have been turned away by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) gunning down American citizens, the final straw for most wasn’t ICE’s brutality, but rather the price of eggs. Some may have been upset by the Tomahawk missile assault that killed 120 schoolgirls in Iran, but most fumed at the rocketing costs at the gas pump that followed. Few demanded answers for the nearly 60 deaths of innocent people detained in DHS detention centers since the start of 2024, but many felt scorned by lost immigrant labor that cut into owners’ profit margins. Maga’s regret voters were all-in for Trump’s racism. Then they found out they couldn’t afford it.

Sign in now (it takes 30 seconds) to carry on reading

Not signed in before? Create a free account

Since Trump’s arrival in 2016, political discourse has been dominated by a narrative that the president galvanized particularly white voters whose economic anxiety went ignored by the left and much of the elite political establishment. It wasn’t completely true. Researchers found that status threat anxiety derived from an increasing majority-minority demographic shift also anchored their voting choices. In the 2026 Maga exodus, however, brass-tacks items like affordability, tariffs and rising inflation are consistently top of mind over other concerns.

Through focus groups across hundreds of Trump’s supporters, political consultant and former Republican Sarah Longwell spotted the immediate trend. “The first thing we do is ask people: how do you think things are going in the country?” Longwell said. “And every focus group, every single time, doesn’t matter – whether left, right or center – right now, people say: bad. And then they immediately start talking about the prices of something.” Underlying economic angst even determined the degree of attention and priority regret voters gave to other issues like the Trump family’s corruption. “Everything comes back to people’s relationship to the economy,” Longwell said. “Trump voters and more low-information voters would probably let Trump get away with corruption. In fact, we know they would – he was doing a lot of corrupt things in his first term.”

Maga voters looked past unchecked government corruption and abuses of power until it affected them financially. While voters were magnetized by Trump’s campaign promises to lower prices, the effects of his economic plans worsened affordability for moderate- to low-income Americans and cut $1tn from essential social safety net services like Snap. He simultaneously pushed a unilateral increase in tariffs, which policy wonks and economists insisted had “no basis in economic reality” and would drastically increase the cost of goods.

His pitches to his base two years ago sounded an awful lot like he murmured “lower prices” and barked his priorities to mass-deport immigrants, gut research and diversity initiatives, and wage an all-out war against gender-nonconforming Americans, including children. Trump’s rhetoric that immigrants take American jobs, access social services such as healthcare for free, and are a drag on the economy are tried-and-tested conservative dog-whistle tactics that mask deliberate xenophobia and anti-immigrant violence as a commonsense protection of Americans’ bottom lines. That dog-whistling further conditions those who embrace Maga ideologies to mark racialized groups as threats to the economic resources to which they feel entitled.

At an ICE job fair in Arlington, Texas, on 2 September 2025, an IT specialist named Aaron Ely told a Washington Post reporter that his private-sector career stalled because the job market was crowded with cheaper and higher-skilled south Asian candidates. Maga and ICE’s racial profiling, surveillance and harassment of immigrants provided an easy solution for eliminating the competition. “I keep seeing these memes where Indians are bragging about taking our tech jobs,” said Ely, 36, while explaining his motivations for joining the agency. “Well, I’m going to work with guys that are going to arrest you, slam your face on the pavement, and send you home.” It wasn’t the price of milk, but a chance to milk state-sanctioned racial violence for his personal advantage that drew Ely to Trump’s policies.

But regret voters’ financial motives also provide Democrats a valuable lesson, one that the most successful social movements against the most ironclad regimes learned long ago: economic exigencies transfer power from governments to everyday people. When the anti-apartheid movement strategized their first boycotts in 1959, Black South Africans knew that the white Boer regime that occupied and brutalized them was first and foremost a capitalist enterprise. The human-rights atrocities of apartheid were meaningless to its profit motives. Over the course of 35 years, Black South Africans organized the “Apartheid Kills – Look at the Label” campaign, in which everyday consumers and vendors were asked to boycott products and goods from South Africa. After a union of Black longshoremen in California refused to offload South African cargo in 1984, the boycott electrified globally and turned the Boers into bad business, bringing apartheid to its knees a decade later.

The economic motive behind millions of regret voters’ actions on Tuesday should remind us that what hits their pockets will hit the polls. Targeting the economics behind the politics is echoed in movements today, even those that seem daunting and impossible to win. “I don’t believe that our people power comes from moral arguments,” said Randa Abdel-Fattah, an Australian lawyer and Palestinian human rights advocate. “Black people have proven that to us … It’s about making genocide unprofitable.”

Millions of Americans are fired up by the blue tsunami. It’s the largest and perhaps only comprehensive, nationwide gain many of our collective populist movements for social justice, civil liberties and human-rights causes have seen in a decade that has been a reign of terrorfor us, and just a financial setback for others. Racism, “wokeness” and Islamophobia alone never changed their hearts and minds, nor are they even the main reason they regret their votes. “Hearts and minds” don’t shift balances of power, but power always shifts when it no longer pays.

The economic motives behind the politics are echoed in movements today, even those that seem daunting and impossible to win.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Israel took a beating in the US midterms | Judith Levine
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Judith Levine
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
In a reversal of longstanding assumptions, strong criticism of Israel’s actions may have helped put candidates over the top

“Y
ou took a chance on the unlikeliest of candidates,” Abdul El-Sayed told a Detroit crowd on Wednesday, declaring victory in Michigan’s hard-fought, often ugly, Senate race. In what was predicted to be a squeaker, the Democrat beat his Republican opponent, Mike Rogers, by a healthy seven points.

In some ways, El-Sayed was an unlikely candidate. At 34, in his first run for elected office, he set his sights almost cockily on a US Senate seat. He ran on what has become an uncontroversial affordability platform but also championed the socialist-adjacent Medicare for All.

Sign in now (it takes 30 seconds) to carry on reading

Not signed in before? Create a free account

But what was generally believed to qualify him as an unlikely candidate – and an even unlikelier winner – was his uncompromising criticism of Israel’s policies toward Palestine and Palestinians.

The assumption that El-Sayed’s Israel politics would doom his chances shaped the campaigns of his pro-Zionist Democratic primary rival, Haley Stevens, and the pro-Israel Rogers. It was certainly the wager that the rightwing American Israel Public Affairs Committee, or Aipac, placed when it wasted nearly $30m – its biggest investment ever in a single race – trying to defeat El-Sayed.

We don’t know yet, but his strong criticism of Israel may have put El-Sayed, and other Democrats, over the top. And like the Republicans, Israel and its prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, took a beating in the US midterms.

Six candidates endorsed by the Democratic Socialists of America, a prominent antagonist to rightwing Zionism, won Congressional races in part by foregrounding their primary opponents’ links to Aipac and their own refusal to take its funds. They all were running in bright-blue districts where the winner of the Democratic primary is the winner of the general election.

In Colorado, Melat Kiros, a 29-year-old lawyer, handily beat primary rival Diana DeGette, the 15-term incumbent backed by a Super Pac with Aipac links. In a New York district comprising portions of upper Manhattan and the Bronx, Darializa Avila Chevalier took down the once invincible Adriano Espaillat, who also had help from a Super Pac with ties to the group. The publication City and State New York predicted that Chevalier, a graduate student leader in Columbia University’s anti-Gaza war encampments, would be “the most pro-Palestine member of Congress”.

Where there was no sunlight between the candidates on the Israel question, some candidates used artificial light. In Brooklyn’s “commie corridor”, the victory of former state assembly member and artist Claire Valdez over the principled progressive Antonio Reynoso was tainted by her unsubstantiated charges that a mysterious Pac supporting him was funded by Aipac. It was in fact funded by one of New York’s teachers’ unions.

The Times of Israel noted pointedly that Pennsylvania’s Chris Rabb had the endorsement of the “far-left online streamer Hasan Piker”, whose support plagued El-Sayed in Michigan. But Rabb’s support did not come only from the extremes. Along with the DSA, the Maryland representative Jaimie Raskin, a Jew, endorsed Rabb, as did the respectable, radical Jewish Voice for Peace.

Rabb won without pulling any political punches. Last week he posted on X: “The Nakba never ended,” referring to the 1948 expulsion of Palestinians to establish a Jewish state on their land. In Michigan, Donavan McKinney defiantly labeled the last section of his plank “Palestine”.

More nuanced Israel politics also were in play. In Ohio, both Democrat Sherrod Brown, the winner, and Republican John Husted got help from pro-Israel organizations, but with different politics. The liberal Zionist J Street, which backed Brown, is critical of Israeli government policies and supports a two-state solution. Aipac stood with Husted.

In Georgia, the Jewish Democratic senator Jon Ossoff mapped a position that must have nettled voters on both sides. Expressing a commitment to Israel’s security and also to valuing “the lives of innocent Palestinians”, he voted in the Senate for some US military aid to Israel while opposing certain weapons transfers. That said, the choice was probably uncomplicated for Georgia’s Jews. Mike Collins, the Republican whom Ossoff trounced 59% to 41%, has ties to promoters of white nationalism and antisemitism.

Brad Lander, a lifer in New York City left-Democratic politics, has maintained his Jewish and progressive bona fides by displaying sympathy for both Israeli Jews and Palestinians. But he is not a slave to any official progressive stance.

He launched his primary campaign by vowing he would not be “doing Aipac’s bidding” and challenging the incumbent Dan Goldman, an unwavering Zionist and recipient of Aipac funds, to do what he had refused to do: call the Gaza war genocide and support the Block the Bombs Act, which would limit arms sales to Israel. Still, Lander quit the DSA after 30 years of membership when it publicized a patently pro-Hamas rally the day after the Hamas-led massacre of Israeli civilians on 7 October 2023. He picked up the endorsement of the Working Families party.

Their politics run from radical to liberal. But what all these winners have in common is their rejection of Israel’s wars and occupation and their support of Palestinian self-determination.

In many places, Israel probably had little effect on the elections. While its military continues to commit what the UN calls crimes against humanity in the occupied territories, Israel is off the front pages of US newspapers. Voters in poll after poll placed foreign policy way down their lists of concerns. Trump may be wrong that “people agree with what [he’s] doing in Iran”, but he might be right that it’s the consequent high gas prices that trouble them most.

In the president’s cold heart, Israel still has a place, and he believes the feeling is mutual. “I’m at 99% approval rating in Israel – can you believe it?” he mused on Fox & Friends. (Actually, no. Pew found his numbers were not even close.) Then Trump dreamed out loud: “If people get tired of me in the US, I’ll move to Israel and become prime minister.”

He’s certainly lost patience with the prime minister that country has now. Before election day, Trump said he’d cease sending $4bn annually in aid to Israel. While Maga’s ship is foundering, maybe its captain hopes to ride the ripple of the blue wave that’s cooling Americans’ sentiment toward Israel.

Judith Levine is a frequent contributor to the Guardian. Her Substack is Today in Fascism

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: The Guardian view on the AI backlash: American voters want a say in their future | Editorial
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Editorial
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Tech stocks have lost trillions while voters have rejected the industry’s political champions. The billionaire-led boom is facing a democratic reckoning

T
his week’s midterms showed that the political bill for the AI boom is falling due. The Democratic sweep intensified fears over runaway spending, mounting debt and resistance to datacentres, sending tech shares tumbling. On Thursday Wall Street suffered its worst day since the pandemic as $3.2tn was wiped from markets. Anthropic, developer of the Claude chatbot, is hoping to float within the next fortnight for $1.5tn (£1.1tn), but it may not now get even a trillion dollars. The dominant AI chipmaker Nvidia saw its value crash by more than $400bn. The world’s richest man, Elon Musk, lost $113bn in two days.

While a few very rich people may be a little less wealthy, the sell-off may not be a bad thing. It brings a needed dose of reality to an industry whose spending plans and valuations depend on heroic expectations of future profits. That is a view held by many influential figures – from Goldman Sachs’ research boss to Nobel laureate Daron Acemoğlu. AI may transform the economy. That does not guarantee investors will earn back the sums being poured into it.

Sign in now (it takes 30 seconds) to carry on reading

Not signed in before? Create a free account

Donald Trump is the other big loser. He rejected concerns about AI and the need to impose stricter rules despite most Americans wanting more safeguards. He called concerns about the potential dangers of AI development a “hoax”. Republicans paid a price for his refusal to listen. Mr Trump argued computing capacity was a national asset that needed to expand rapidly, while dismissing resistance to the infrastructure and the companies building it. The US president was deaf to voter frustration over electricity prices, water demand and disruption. Democrats could campaign against those costs falling on residents while the gains went to tech billionaires and their companies, which donated money to Mr Trump’s favoured causes.

Mr Musk’s SpaceX, a combined space, satellite-connectivity and AI group, warned in its June 2026 prospectus that new regulations could derail its growth plans. He spent $200m in Texas for Republicans as Democrats took aim at AI datacentres in a state where there was rising voter discontent over the industry’s rapid expansion. Mr Musk could not buy this election. Democrats won a US senate seat, the state governorship and wiped out every other statewide Republican office, taking the Texas house with a comfortable margin. Across the US, the blue wave saw wins for Democrats who have been critical of datacentre construction and pledged to slow or pause their rollout.

Democrats say they intend to make AI companies answerable for the environmental and societal costs of their infrastructure buildup as well as the harm their products cause. The new Congress is likely to be much more ready to shield voters from rising prices caused by datacentre expansion, ensure independent safety testing for advanced AI and clarify liability for possible harms. Democrats’ willingness to take public fears about AI seriously is welcome. People need confidence that elected governments can protect their livelihoods and communities.

Whatever happens to tech stocks, the genie of AI won’t be put back into its lamp. This year alone the technology was given as the reason 120,000 Americans lost their jobs. Politicians ought to strengthen workers’ bargaining power and ensure that productivity gains are fairly shared. Just letting the markets decide will only deepen the economic insecurity and political distrust that is corroding democracy.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: The most diverse, anti-establishment Congress in history is cause for optimism
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Ankita Rao
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
After years of outrage or numbness being the main options for dealing with politics, Tuesday’s results were permission to be optimistic

This was originally published in the Stakes 2026, a newsletter about the midterm elections. Sign up to get it in your inbox

We shed some tears this midterm cycle.

US politics always makes people emotional, but I heard from friends and colleagues many times this year that speeches, campaigns and underdog success stories moved people in unexpected ways, whether it was this ad of Michigan senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed doing bedtime, a photo of newly elected Texas Democrats James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa at a Whataburger, or Georgia’s Keisha Lance Bottoms becoming the first Black female governor in the entire country.

Sign in now (it takes 30 seconds) to carry on reading

Not signed in before? Create a free account

While you might reduce this to Democrats being happy about historically defeating the Republican party and Trumpism, there’s something much deeper to be seen and felt in Tuesday’s election results. A broad coalition of Americans, including Republicans, independents and those who had never voted before, decided to elect the most diverse, anti-establishment Congress in history.

People saw themselves reflected in the candidates, some first rejected by party leaders. In Maine, Troy Jackson, who entered the race at the last minute after the spectacular collapse of Graham Platner’s campaign, has bona fide blue collar credentials. El-Sayed is a son of Michigan, reflecting communities that have long resided in the state but never been represented in the Senate. Annie Andrews in South Carolina came from a true grassroots effort to elect pro-science candidates at a time when children are dying from measles.

Along with that came a repudiation of some of the racist, xenophobic, transphobic and other rhetoric that has escalated in recent years. Bo French, the Texas politician who had posted a racist diatribe about south Asian students at a football game, lost his election, along with Vivek Ramaswamy and his abhorrent attack ad, Ken Paxton with his transphobic AI ads, and Mike Collins and his multiple associations with neo-Nazis. At a time when the Trump administration itself peddles racist tropes on its X account and at rallies, there were tears of relief and cautious hope of an era of decency.

When people told me in recent months that something made them cry they seemed almost embarrassed. But I see it as a very good sign. After years of outrage or numbness – fight or flight – being the main options for dealing with political news and the impacts of those in power, this kind of catharsis and joy feels like permission to be human and to be optimistic.

This is not to say voters in the US have any illusions that the newly elected public servants will immediately resolve political gridlock and restore normalcy to the country. Trump is unlikely to go quietly into the night his final two years in office, and Democrats have a track record of bungling opportunities to make big, bold progress. But seeing engagement and investment in the future take the place of the nihilism that has characterized the Trump era has been refreshing.

It’s a feeling that some are comparing to Barack Obama’s first election. As congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez herself said in a video to young voters who helped power the massive political shift: “If you want to understand millennial cringe … this earnestness, imagine all the seats we flipped last night plus on top of it electing the first Black president ever, and on top of that you did it the first time you voted.”

after newsletter promotion

In an election that did what has recently seemed impossible: turning Texas blue, dumping Trump’s handpicked candidates, openly rejecting bigotry, the tears and the cringe are just history being made.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: What is this strange, post-election feeling? Oh right – it’s utter joy | Dave Schilling
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Dave Schilling
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
A decade of political misery does terrible things to the mind. Tuesday’s wins came with a sense of unreality

Late on Tuesday night, the comedian Alex Edelman asked a poignant question on social media: “I know we’ve never had to ask this before tonight, but what’s the opposite of doomscrolling?”

I don’t have a definitive answer to that, though I did offer the term “boomscrolling”, accompanied by a gif of the social media sensation and Costco enthusiast Big Boom AJ.

Sign in now (it takes 30 seconds) to carry on reading

Not signed in before? Create a free account

AJ and his son became famous for yelling “Boom!” after biting down on revolting, sodium-infused food from Costco’s food court while flexing meaty biceps.

It strikes me as an apt illustration of how we all felt as election day unspooled before us. After every miraculous call, I couldn’t help but flex my muscles and let out a howl to the heavens. How is this real? Boom, indeed.

Those of us who consider ourselves liberal or left or progressive or whatever buzzword my media colleagues want to ascribe to general human decency were left somewhat incapable of making literal sense of what we were witnessing on Tuesday night. Texas and Iowa and Kansas? Mississippi and Alaska in play?

It’s like a democracy simulation game spit up an outcome so improbable that you start to wonder if it’s glitching out. The soaring, optimistic oration from Jon Ossoff and James Talarico had us crying. At least I was. I’m a large baby-man who cries when a bonus curly fry accidentally lands in my takeout bag.

Abdul El-Sayed’s righteous anger at the Trump administration had me ready to run through a brick wall. And the thousand-yard death stares of conservative pundits on the various cable news channels delivered the schadenfreude my life has sorely lacked.

The feelings were potent, but deeply unfamiliar. It was not all progressive triumph – anti-trans bills passed in numerous states and California’s one-time billionaire tax seems destined to fail – but the macro-message sent by voters was clear. Maybe this Trump thing didn’t work out quite like his people hoped.

It’s been over a decade since Donald Trump announced his candidacy for president. In that decade, I’ve aged 20 years. A steady dearth of good news does terrible things to the body and the mind.

No wonder people are tweeting about not having a name for how they feel. Happiness and optimism are as foreign to the people of 2026 as a Samsung Galaxy would be to a Victorian-era eel merchant. Good cheer is an invading antigen to modern Americans, but one I welcome with open arms. There’s no cure for what I have, and thank God for that.

Tuesday was like the intermission in the middle of The Brutalist – a chance to go outside and breathe fresh air before a third act where things could potentially get worse. I famously don’t watch cable news, but I stayed up past midnight with the glee of a child on Christmas Eve. I was as elated and giggly as Rachel Maddow throwing away a statement from President Trump live on the air. I chortled at the thought of John Fetterman – the Democratic senator some feared would turn Republican – losing his remaining shred of relevance in the Senate and returning to his old job, carrying Krang from the Ninja Turtles around in his stomach.

But, despite my numerous suggestions to the LA mayor-elect, Nithya Raman, we can’t have an election every day. This euphoria will fade, and then we’re stuck with the drudgery of actual day-to-day governance by the Democratic congressional majority.

What will the priorities be? Abolishing the electoral college? Impeachment? Medicare-for-all? Ending funding for the Iran war? Crazy hat day on the Senate floor? Coca-Cola Freestyle machines at every bus stop?

I think part of the dizziness that is afflicting the liberal American populace is that, in some ways, anything is possible. If the electorate speaks with such a clear voice, what’s stopping us from accomplishing something remarkable?

Some people will understandably point to the limited ambition and moderate rhetoric from Democratic leadership. They’ll roll their eyes and point to the countless times the Democrats controlled Congress, bungled it and handed it back to the Republicans.

I get that impulse. The worst thing we on the left can do is to cheer for an electoral victory and then take a two-year nap until the presidential election. But I fully support “libbing out” and enjoying the open road, the possibilities, and the potential.

For the first time in years, the Democratic bench is full of superstar politicians. The wind is at our backs, and the mood of the country matches our thirst for change.

For the next two months, I’m going to huff these fumes. I’m periodically going to tune into Fox News to see Jesse Watters fumble for his words while he silently dreams of getting a Russian passport.

It’s the holiday season, after all. Before Thanksgiving, before Christmas and New Year’s, I’m going to treat the glorious halo of this election like its own holiday. A holiday away from fear, panic and self-loathing. A respite from doomscrolling. A time for boomscrolling. I’m going to flex on the haters. I’ll be living my life on the tenets of Shakira law.

On 3 January, when the new Congress is sworn in, I’ll put my hard-hat on and go back to being a lovable curmudgeon. But that day is not today.

Dave Schilling is a Los Angeles-based writer and humorist

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Democrats finally decided to take rural America seriously – and won big | Anthony Flaccavento and Erica Etelson
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Anthony Flaccavento and Erica Etelson
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Democrats won over rural voters from Maga in the midterms by focusing more on working people and less on culture wars

Long before Jamie Ager entered politics, he was making a name for himself in a very different place: the meat counter of a grocery store in Boone, North Carolina.

It was the early 2000s, and Ager owned and operated Hickory Nut Gap, a regenerative farm near Asheville. Over the next 20 years, he helped build a regional food system that delivered healthier food to thousands of people, improved land stewardship and made farming a bit more profitable.

Sign in now (it takes 30 seconds) to carry on reading

Not signed in before? Create a free account

We’ve long believed that American politics would be a whole lot better if people like him – working folks who care for the land and their communities so well – were representing us.

And now he is. On Tuesday night, Ager won the House race for North Carolina’s 11th congressional district, resoundingly flipping a Republican seat that Donald Trump won handily in 2024.

He wasn’t alone. Democrats tore into Republicans’ rural vote margins, wiping out almost half of Trump’s colossal 40-point advantage in 2024. Of the 21 most rural-populated states that held elections for US Senate, Democrats won in 10 of them, including states like Kansas, Mississippi and Iowa, all long surrendered to the Republican juggernaut.

Rural voters still favor Republicans – but by a whole lot less. They swung 15 points toward Democratic US Senate candidates, compared to their 2024 presidential vote choice. (Nationwide, Republican turnout was down, so we don’t yet know what percentage of the swing was toward Democrats versus the couch).

Non-college voters swung hard as well. For the first time since 2012, a majority (51%) of non-college voters voted for a Democrat for the US House of Representatives, a stunning 17-point improvement over 2024.

The campaign platforms of winning (or leading) candidates in red and purple states demonstrate a clear pattern: concrete economic issues of working and rural people were central.

In Kansas, Adam Hamilton’s “prairie populism” railed against the crushing costs of farming inputs, something Iowa’s Josh Turek also stressed. In Mississippi, Scott Colom emphasized the loss of labor and delivery departments in rural communities. Texas’s Gina Hinojosa and James Talarico both spoke out for rural schools against defunding and voucher programs. Keisha Lance Bottoms spoke openly about the rural-urban divide and her own roots in the Georgia countryside.

In South Carolina, Annie Andrews focused on kitchen table economics, rural healthcare and farmland preservation. And Sam Forstag, the first Democrat Montana has sent to the US House since 1994, emphasized the protection of public lands that Montanans rely on for recreation and sustenance.

All nine of the Senate candidates who flipped (or are projected to flip) their seats focused unrelentingly on easing voters’ pocketbook pain, reining in corruption, putting the brakes on AI datacenters, and supporting workers, farmers, veterans and small businesses. With the exception of Troy Jackson and Andrews, you’d be hard pressed to find more than a glancing mention of a single culture war issue on any campaign website.

The same goes for the five Democrats who flipped governorships. Hinojosa, Texas’s governor-elect, told the New York Times: “I have no interest in fighting culture wars. There is just one fight [against tech giants], and we are so caught up fighting each other … over the ways we disagree about social issues … I’m not going to perpetuate that any more.”

That stance earned her an eight-point Democratic shift in Texas’s 17 rural counties.

It’s taken Democrats several painful cycles to learn the benefits of sitting down at the kitchen table and staying there, a strategy that will serve them well for the foreseeable future.

Having learned the hard way that ignoring rural and factory town voters is the road to ruin, House and Senate candidates flocked to small towns. Abdul El-Sayed showed up at barns, union halls and fairgrounds in Michigan’s Upper Peninsula. Colom visited almost every county in Mississippi, held 60 townhalls and even showed up at a small town Maga rally to talk to Trump supporters.

Rob Sand undertook a 100-stop tour across Iowa, including all of its rural counties. Ohio governor-elect Amy Acton met with local agricultural extension districts to advocate for rural broadband and 4-H. Jake Johnson, who flipped Minnesota’s first congressional district, had teams of volunteers fan out across the district for one-on-one conversations with voters, contributing to a six-point swing in their rural county.

For the first time ever, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee fielded a rural engagement program that included local organizing in rural districts, mobilizing volunteers and assisting with ad buys and mailers. Grassroots organizations, like Every State Blue, Dirt Road Organizing and many others fought for every vote, mobilizing the base while also reaching out to swing voters and disaffected Trump supporters.

The combined effect of all of these rural outreach efforts was gamechanging: When Democrats play ball in rural areas, they can win or, at least, begin to make significant inroads in those districts.

Democrats won big on Tuesday, most noticeably in rural regions and red states. The actions they take next will determine whether this is a short-lived repudiation of Trump or the start of a movement that finally, truly takes on elite power in service of working people everywhere.

As Corbin Trent, a media strategist and former communications director for congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, put it, the Democrats “have been given the keys by the American people. It’s time to drive the car to a better place.”

Anthony Flaccavento and Erica Etelson are co-founders of the Rural Urban Bridge Initiative. Read more in this series

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: After the midterms, the global right is reeling. But the danger of Trumpism will never be gone | Jonathan Freedland
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Jonathan Freedland
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Yes, the Republicans suffered humiliating defeat. But the fact that a Trump presidency was even possible means something like it could happen again

H
e’s down, but not quite out. Barring divine or other intervention, Donald Trump will remain in the Oval Office for a further two years and 10 weeks. Or, as the White House put it in a plaintive social media post brimming with neediness: “PSA [Public Service Announcement]: Trump is still your president.” But that’s not the only reason why the global celebrations that greeted the Democratic tidal wave that swept Republicans out of even their deepest heartlands should be tempered, if only a tad.

Don’t get me wrong, the results of Tuesday’s midterm elections are cause for genuine international jubilation. The defeats of Trump allies in Serbia and Brazil were delicious appetisers, but this was the feast. No mere electoral setback in line with midterm tradition, this was a thorough repudiation of the second Trump presidency and of Trumpism. The 16% swing to Democrats in the popular vote for the House of Representatives was greater even than the 11.2% swing recorded in the Watergate midterms of November 1974, following the resignation in disgrace of Richard Nixon. Trump had worked hard for many months to undermine these elections, either by gerrymandering districts in his favour or preparing the ground for a later claim the vote was rigged, but to no avail: the democratic system proved too resilient, and the American public too determined to have their say. And have it they did, in a voice loud and clear.

Sign in now (it takes 30 seconds) to carry on reading

Not signed in before? Create a free account

Beyond the US, the temptation will be strong to see this as the moment the wheels came off the authoritarian, nationalist populist bandwagon that has rolled through so much of our politics this past decade. Viktor Orbán’s fall in April was pivotal, but the humiliation of Trump was always going to matter more. Thanks to the sheer might of the US, Trump has for a decade been the engine of the illiberal international. And now it is sputtering.

All that is cause for delight. But the risk is that those who have fought nationalist populism will take Tuesday’s success as their cue to relax. That would be to repeat the mistake made by Trump himself – and too many others – in November 2024, when he interpreted his win over Kamala Harris not as the cry of a public fed up with rising grocery bills and petrol prices, but as a permanent “vibe shift” in the culture and a mandate to turn the US into an autocracy, take a chainsaw to US government agencies, have masked men abduct and shoot American citizens on the streets, launch a doomed and disastrous war, and fill the US capital with monuments to his own vanity, all while lining his pockets and those of his inner circle.

The equivalent error this time, whether it’s made inside or outside the US, would be to read these midterm results as the end of the Trump threat and as proof that normal service will resume shortly. The danger of Trumpism, sadly, will never be gone. Because if something can happen once, it can happen again. Trump was possible – which means another Trump is possible.

That is the lesson the US’s traditional allies, in Britain, the EU or elsewhere, need to internalise. Even if Capitol Hill will soon be in saner hands, even if Trump’s eventual successor is a good internationalist who believes in a rules-based order, the reliability of the US as an ally can never again be taken for granted. After Trump, the US’s status as a guarantor of western security is anything but guaranteed, contingent instead on this or that election result. Which means that the rest of the west must still plan for its own protection and defence.

Sure, nationalist populism is now badly damaged, marked as the cause of losers. What’s more, Trump may well have demonstrated that nationalist movements whose sole currency is grievance will ultimately always fail – thereby deterring voters in France and Germany tempted to vote for Marine Le Pen or the AfD.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

But, again, it’s hard to rely on that. Did Trump fail because politicians of his ilk always will? Or was it because he made stupid and, crucially, avoidable decisions, such as attacking Iran – which not only broke his core pledge, so cherished by Maga voters, to end wars rather than start them, but also drove up the very inflation he was elected to curb? Either way, it’s hard to speak of inevitable failure when describing a man who, despite all the havoc he wreaked the first time around – including the violent insurrection of 6 January 2021 – was elected to a fresh term less than four years later. He disgraced himself, but was rewarded with victory.

Besides, it’s too soon to speak of Trump in the past tense. True, he’s lost the doormat House and the rubber-stamp Senate that enabled him to act without restraint. But a weakened Trump is not necessarily a tamed Trump. I think of the seasoned Washington hand who told me Trump in defeat could become “a cornered animal”. When it comes to the world stage, he still has the power to act – foreign policy is largely the preserve of the president – and a double motive to do so. First, he will want a legacy to offset this week’s historic drubbing and, second and even more elementally, he craves the attention. The notion of ceding the spotlight to Democrats, or in fact anyone, will appal him.

Maybe he will bow to the demands lodged by JD Vance - in a statement on X that saw the vice president all but break from his boss – and move to end the war with Iran, even if that means capitulation. Or he might double down and push for the toppling of the Tehran regime that he likely believes would give him the place in history he deserves.

Until 20 January 2029 those decisions will be Trump’s. He still has the power to shape world events, even if that power has diminished. Take as just one example, the US relationship with Israel. That country had elections of its own last week that, though far from delivering the repudiation of Benjamin Netanyahu many Israelis sought, did wipe out his parliamentary majority. Coalition horsetrading is now under way, and the US midterms are already playing a part. Israeli opposition leaders argue that what Netanyahu long claimed as an asset – his closeness to Trump – is, after Tuesday, a liability, rendering Israel’s prime minister “toxic” among the Democrats who will soon wield power on Capitol Hill. If that argument prevails, the blue tsunami will have claimed not only Kansas and Texas, but the man once dubbed the Republican senator from Jerusalem.

On the morning of election day, Trump announced the termination of military aid to Israel, perhaps in a last-ditch attempt to win over Tucker Carlson Republicans who are hostile to the country. He could continue on that path, especially if he seeks to punish Netanyahu for his role in the joint US-Israeli war on Tehran that broke his presidency or, alternatively, he could defy Vance and hug the Israeli PM close.

The point is, these fateful choices still rest with Trump. Democrats will soon have the power to investigate allegations of corruption and hold him to account. America’s allies in Europe and elsewhere will soon find in Washington people who talk like partners, rather than enemies. Both prospects come as a great relief. But that does not alter two key facts: Trump happened – and he’s still there.

Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnist
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.summary: Donald Trump was possible to break from his boss, but not quite out of the spotlight. The danger of Trumpism, sadly, will never be gone, says David Frum.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: There is a showdown looming in the Democratic party over support for Israel | Moustafa Bayoumi
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Moustafa Bayoumi
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Even Donald Trump has acknowledged that support for Israel is increasingly a political liability in US politics. Will the Democratic leadership listen?

A
bdul El-Sayed’s victorious path to the US Senate must become a wake-up call to the Democratic party. It shows us, yet again, that Democratic voters care about Gaza, that Palestinian demands for freedom are increasingly connected to American demands for freedom, and that the old smears and accusations against Palestinians and their supporters are fast losing potency.

Even Donald Trump has acknowledged that support for Israel is increasingly a political liability in American politics. Will Chuck Schumer and the rest of the Democratic leadership listen?

Sign in now (it takes 30 seconds) to carry on reading

Not signed in before? Create a free account

El-Sayed ran a hard-fought and disciplined campaign that focused on issues which spoke to Michiganders. “Money out of politics, money in your pocket, Medicare for all” was the campaign’s signature slogan. But from the outset, the vilest Islamophobic and racist attacks, some of the worst that that we’ve seen in years, were constantly pelted at the candidate, in large part because of his outspoken support for Palestinians.

Over the last few months, Trump obsessively called him a jihadist and a terrorist sympathizer while mocking his name or referring to him by his middle name of Mohamed. “I will be Senator Mohamed to you, bro,” El-Sayed clapped back.

During the final televised debate between Michigan’s Senate candidates, Republican Mike Rogers asked El-Sayed: “Are you for America, or are you for these terrorist groups overseas?”

After calling the question “shameful”, which it absolutely was, El-Sayed responded with: “I’m proud of our constitution that guarantees all of us the right to pray as we choose to pray.” Roger’s TV ads were even worse.

Behind all of it was an eye-watering amount of money spent against El-Sayed, more than $150m, according to the nonpartisan organization OpenSecrets, which tracks money in politics. Pro-Israel groups, including Aipac, were behind much of it.

Back in August, Rogers was said to have asked Aipac not to advertise for him, and in October Aipac itself said it would no longer make endorsements or fund campaigns. Aipac and Israel-supporting politicians seem all too aware of the toxic associations the organization’s name now brings to political races. But the group is not dropping out of politics. It’s rebranding. The lobby is still channeling its money into races through other means, such as its super Pac, United Democracy Project, according to the Intercept. United Democracy Project donated heavily against El-Sayed.

But do you know who has been one of Aipac’s biggest recipients going back years? The man who will now almost certainly become the first Black speaker of the House in US history, Hakeem Jeffries. (Who can forget when the radio host Charlamagne Tha God called him “Aipac Shakur.”) And Chuck Schumer, the incoming Senate majority leader, said “my job is to keep the left pro-Israel” in a conversation with the New York Times last year.

Is there a showdown coming? The pro-Israel positions of the old guard are diametrically opposed to the values of the new members of their party. And there are many incoming progressives beyond the new senator from Michigan.

The number of Democrats who won their elections while proclaiming support to Palestine include New Jersey’s Adam Hamawy, a doctor who joined a medical mission to Gaza in 2024; New York’s Darializa Avila Chevalier, a doctoral student active in campus politics supporting Palestinian rights; California’s Randy Villegas, who has called Israel’s actions in Gaza a genocide and took no money from corporate or pro-Israel groups; and many more, including down-ballot winners such as Aber Kawas, the first Palestinian American to be elected to the New York state senate.

Sign up to Breaking News US

Get the most important news as it breaks

after newsletter promotion

Palestine matters because, while the US government continues to walk in lockstep with Israel, Americans are increasingly critical of Israel and its policies (six in 10 American now hold unfavorable views of Israel, according to the Pew Research Center; with Democrats, it’s eight in 10). And Palestine matters because US support for Israel continues to disrupt and distort American politics and life.

JD Vance realizes this. The vice-president wrote on social media that “the real reason we [Republicans] lost is the war” in Iran, a war begun and carried out in partnership with Israel. And Donald Trump seems ready to loosen the public association of Israel with his administration. Just before the election, he announced that he would end military aid to Israel by the end of the year.

“We were giving them $4bn,” he said of Israel’s military aid. “But it gets cut off at the end of the year.” Experts have said such moves won’t change the deeply integrated military relationship between the two countries, but Trump is making the announcement anyway. The reason? “Why should we suffer the slings from lunatics like El-Sayed when they don’t need it?” Trump said. “It’s a bad talking point.”

For Trump, support for Israel is now about poor optics, not about destructive and inhumane policies. The Democrats, on the other hand, have an obligation. They must listen to their constituents, understand why they were elected and take a stand out of principle.

Since Congress controls government expenditures, the Democrats will soon have a very significant role to play. “We don’t want our money sent to do apartheid or genocide or war,” El-Sayed said on Tuesday night in his victory speech, to raucous applause. Hakeem Jeffries and Chuck Schumer better be listening.

Moustafa Bayoumi is the author of the award-winning books How Does It Feel to Be a Problem?: Being Young and Arab in America and This Muslim American Life: Dispatches from the War on Terror. He is a professor of English at Brooklyn College, City University of New York

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.title: Another No 1 falls as Notre Dame hold off Miami to shake up college football playoff race
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.author: Agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.text:
Carr throws for 319 yards and three TDs in 31-24 win

No 4 Irish avenge loss that cost them playoff berth

Miami comeback falls short after disputed late call

CJ Carr threw for 319 yards and three touchdowns as No 4 Notre Dame avenged their most damaging loss of last season, racing to a 21-point lead before holding on to beat top-ranked Miami 31-24 on Saturday night.

Micah Gilbert caught two of Carr’s touchdown passes, Jordan Faison had the other and Nolan James Jr added a rushing score for Notre Dame (8-1, No 11 College Football Playoff), who entered the game knowing another defeat to Miami could derail their national championship hopes.

Sign in now (it takes 30 seconds) to carry on reading

Not signed in before? Create a free account

The Hurricanes (8-1, No 1 CFP) started slowly on offense in their first game without injured wide receiver and Heisman Trophy hopeful Malachi Toney. Notre Dame, whose 27-24 loss to Miami last season ultimately kept them out of the playoff, never trailed.

“I’m happy for this university,” Notre Dame coach Marcus Freeman said in a televised on-field interview. “I’m happy for our players. There’s a lot of support from Notre Dame Nation and this is special moment for them. ... They’re a dang good football team and they beat a dang good football team.”

Darian Mensah threw three touchdown passes for Miami, twice bringing the Hurricanes within seven points after they had trailed 24-3 early in the third quarter. Cooper Barkate caught two of those passes, while Elija Lofton had the other.

Lofton nearly hauled in another touchdown that would have made it 31-30 – the same score as the teams’ famous 1988 meeting – with 3:36 remaining. He appeared to make a fourth-down catch in the end zone and get both feet down, but Notre Dame’s Luke Talich, who had intercepted Mensah in the third quarter, knocked the ball away.

Officials ruled that Lofton had not completed the catch. Notre Dame took over on downs, ran the clock down to about a minute and held on for the victory.

Miami coach Mario Cristobal said he was “beyond upset” that Lofton’s apparent catch had not been ruled a touchdown.

“Obviously, a tough loss to take,” Cristobal said. “Proud of our players for the resilience. ... Don’t leave it in the hands of the officials. Play better. Coach better. Find a way to win.”

Miami’s defeat left just two unbeaten teams in the Football Bowl Subdivision: Utah and UCLA, who both improved to 9-0 with victories on Saturday. It marked the first time since 2003 that only two teams had made it through their first nine games unbeaten, when TCU and Oklahoma achieved the feat.

A capacity crowd packed Notre Dame Stadium on a bitterly cold night, with temperatures falling from 40F at kickoff into the mid-30s. Forty-three NFL scouts were also in attendance as the Irish delivered their biggest victory of the season.

Miami had a chance to cut into Notre Dame’s lead in the second quarter after reaching first-and-goal at the Irish one-yard line. But three rushing attempts – one by Mark Fletcher Jr and two quarterback keepers by Mensah – went nowhere, forcing the Hurricanes to settle for a field goal.

Miami trailed 17-3 at halftime, having scored at least 14 first-half points and averaged 27 before the break in their first eight games.

Notre Dame also pulled out all the stops for the occasion, honoring a host of former stars including Joe Montana, Jerome Bettis Sr, Tony Rice, Chris Zorich, Ricky Watters and Ron Powlus. NBA president of basketball operations Byron Spruell was among those recognized, along with Pat Murphy, manager of the World Series champion Milwaukee Brewers and a former Notre Dame baseball coach.

The victory carried historical echoes of Notre Dame’s famous 31-30 upset of top-ranked Miami in the 1988 “Catholics vs Convicts” game. The Hurricanes fell to 44-7 all-time when ranked No 1 in the AP Top 25, including an 0-2 record against the Irish.

Notre Dame improved to 10-17-1 against No 1 teams, claiming their first such victory in exactly six years. Their previous win came against top-ranked Clemson on 7 November 2020, when the Tigers were without star quarterback Trevor Lawrence.

The Irish host Boston College next Saturday, while Miami return home to face Duke.

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: Messi claims second straight Golden Boot as Nashville sets points record on MLS Decision Day
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
Messi first to win consecutive MLS Golden Boots

Inter Miami surrender 3-0 lead in dramatic draw

Nashville set new league record with 77 points

Lionel Messi won his second consecutive MLS Golden Boot award on Saturday, but Inter Miami squandered a three-goal lead in a 3-3 draw with Charlotte on the final day of the regular season.

The Argentine superstar failed to score but set up Miami’s first two goals from corners at Nu Stadium as the defending champions secured second place in the Eastern Conference and home-field advantage for the first two rounds of the playoffs.

Sign in now (it takes 30 seconds) to carry on reading

Not signed in before? Create a free account

Messi’s 26 goals made him the first player to win back-to-back MLS Golden Boot awards. Dallas forward Petar Musa finished second with 22 after failing to score in his team’s 3-1 home victory over Colorado.

Ian Fray, Luis Suárez and Rodrigo De Paul scored first-half goals for Miami before Liel Abada struck twice shortly after the break to spark a Charlotte comeback, completed by Rodolfo Aloko’s 90th-minute equalizer.

Nashville broke the MLS single-season points record with a 2-0 victory over Cincinnati, finishing with 77 points to surpass the previous mark of 74 set by Miami in 2024.

Nashville finished atop the Eastern Conference with 23 wins, three defeats and eight draws, while Miami took second place with 60 points. Third-place New England missed a chance to overtake Miami after suffering a surprise 1-0 defeat at Orlando, leaving them on 58 points.

Miami will face Columbus in the opening round of the playoffs. Elsewhere in the East, New England will meet Philadelphia, Charlotte will take on Chicago and top-seeded Nashville will face the winner of the wild-card matchup between Orlando and Cincinnati.

Columbus secured seventh place and avoided the wild-card round with a 4-3 victory at Chicago.

At Nu Stadium, Messi’s 14th-minute corner fell unexpectedly to Charlotte’s Luca de la Torre, whose attempted clearance popped up for Fray to open the scoring.

Another Messi corner in the 33rd minute found Suárez unmarked at the near post, where the Uruguayan glanced a header into the net to double Miami’s advantage.

De Paul made it 3-0 before half-time, but Abada pulled one back for Charlotte shortly after the restart and struck again in the 55th minute.

Aloko completed the comeback in the 90th minute, reacting quickest after Smalls’s shot rebounded off the post.

A visibly frustrated Messi struck the woodwork in stoppage time before Aloko came within inches of an improbable winner with a thunderous shot into the side-netting.

Western Conference champions Vancouver defeated Canadian rivals Montreal 2-0 to finish second in the overall standings, securing home-field advantage should the Whitecaps face Inter Miami in a rematch of last year’s MLS Cup final.

Six teams entered Decision Day fighting for the final three Western Conference playoff places, with all 30 MLS clubs in action.

Portland, Colorado and the LA Galaxy each needed only a victory to secure a playoff berth, but only the Timbers delivered, winning 2-0 at Austin.

Real Salt Lake defeated the Galaxy 2-1, while Colorado fell 3-1 at Dallas, allowing Salt Lake to claim a postseason place.

Seattle secured the other remaining berth with a 2-1 home victory over Los Angeles FC. Albert Rusnák scored in the opening minute and set up Sebastián Gómez’s 31st-minute goal before Eddie Segura pulled one back for LAFC in the 82nd minute.

Minnesota defeated visiting San Jose 3-1 but, like the Galaxy, finished a point behind Real Salt Lake and missed the playoffs.

The opening Western Conference playoff matchups pit Vancouver against the winner of the wild-card meeting between Seattle and Real Salt Lake, Dallas against Portland, LAFC against St Louis and Houston against San Jose.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.title: Golden State Warriors’ Kristaps Porziņģis steps away from basketball over undisclosed health issue
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.author: Agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.text:
Warriors center, 31, announces decision on social media

Latvian big man does not disclose nature of health issue

Porziņģis leaves door open to return after long absence

Golden State Warriors center Kristaps Porziņģis announced he is stepping away from basketball to prioritize his health due to an undisclosed matter in a social media post on Friday.

Porziņģis did not reveal the nature of the issue in a message posted on his X account, and the 31-year-old did not make clear whether he will resume playing.

Sign in now (it takes 30 seconds) to carry on reading

Not signed in before? Create a free account

“I was really looking forward to running it with this group, but as I ramped up, my body didn’t respond the way I anticipated,” Porziņģis wrote.

“I’m doing good, but I know what it takes, and I’m not where I want to be to perform at the level I expect from myself,” he added. “At this point, I’ve made the decision to prioritize my health and step away from the game I love.”

Selected fourth overall by the New York Knicks in the 2015 draft, Porziņģis was on his sixth team in 11 seasons.

The issue appears to date to last season, when the Latvian missed significant time after being acquired by Golden State in a trade with Atlanta. The Warriors, however, fully anticipated Porziņģis would be ready for this season after signing him to a two-year, $40m contract in late June.

Porziņģis’ status has been uncertain since late September, when the Warriors announced he would be out indefinitely with a health issue and would not travel with the team to Hawaii for training camp.

On 14 October, the team said Porziņģis would spend time with staff and teammates in some capacity while still out indefinitely after he met with general manager Mike Dunleavy and vice-president of player health and performance Dr Rick Celebrini a day earlier.

A week later, the Warriors reversed course, saying Porziņģis would not be with the team for “the immediate future”, with coach Steve Kerr providing no further insight ahead of the team’s season opener at the Los Angeles Lakers.

In his message, Porziņģis said he intends to work with the Warriors to “find a solution that makes sense”.

He closed his message by writing: “I’m thankful to my family and close ones for always being there. Much appreciation to all of you for the support. Onwards and upwards.”

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.title: Bad blood? Knicks defend Taylor Swift after players accuse her of being ‘fake fan’
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.author: Guardian sport
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.text:
Kolek calls singer’s courtside appearances ‘performative’

McBride agrees as teammates question celebrity fandom

Knicks give statement saying Swift is longtime supporter

Taylor Swift’s love story with the New York Knicks caught an unexpected stray after two players from last season’s NBA champions accused the singer of being a fair-weather fan.

The Knicks released a statement on Friday defending Swift after Tyler Kolek and Miles McBride questioned whether the pop superstar was a genuine supporter of the team.

Sign in now (it takes 30 seconds) to carry on reading

Not signed in before? Create a free account

The reserve guards were asked during an NBA 2K livestream on Thursday to name the least authentic celebrity fan they had seen courtside at an NBA game.

“At the Knicks games, I would say it’s very performative because like they just want to be seen at the game,” Kolek said. “They’re not necessarily fans. Probably Taylor Swift.”

McBride agreed with the assessment, while Kolek acknowledged that his comments could provoke a backlash from Swift’s supporters.

“I’m going to get some hate from the Swifties,” Kolek said. “I guess she’s got a lot going on, so she can’t come all the time, but ... it’s a little performative.”

McBride identified actor Ben Stiller and comedian Tracy Morgan as more committed Knicks supporters, describing both as “solid” fans.

The Knicks found themselves in the delicate position of defending one of their most famous fans against their own players, moving quickly on Friday to head off any bad blood with Swift.

“Taylor Swift has been a Knicks fan for many years, has a long history with Madison Square Garden, and we are incredibly appreciative of her support of the organization,” a team spokesperson said.

Swift, 36, has attended several high-profile Knicks games, including Game 4 of this year’s NBA finals, when she sat courtside alongside actor Mariska Hargitay and musicians Alana and Este Haim. Wearing a royal blue “Stevie Knicks” T-shirt with orange lettering that quickly went viral and inspired a wave of copycat merchandise, she watched OG Anunoby score a last-second tip-in to secure a famous New York victory.

She also attended Game 3 of the Eastern Conference finals in Cleveland with her husband, Kansas City Chiefs tight end Travis Kelce, a longtime Cleveland sports fan.

Swift knows Madison Square Garden all too well, having first performed there as a 13-year-old in 2003 during a Knicks half-time talent contest. She and Kelce married at the arena in July.

Kolek and McBride are both eligible for contract extensions, although the Knicks said in October they were not holding extension talks with players. The team hold a $2.5m option on Kolek for the 2026-27 season.
