https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.title: Trump may have lost but don’t bet Democrats can fix the economy
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.author: Eduardo Porter
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.text:
There’s not much they can do over the next couple of years to alleviate angry voters’ stress over prices

It was the economy, again. Although Donald Trump largely ignored it, voters’ acute concerns over the rising cost of living fuelled a political upheaval for the ages that is likely to deliver the biggest swing toward Democrats since Watergate, granting them the largest House majority in nearly four decades alongside their biggest edge in the Senate since 2008.

Still, having come to power promising to restore affordability, the new crop of Democrats are soon to discover that there is not much they can do over the next couple of years to alleviate angry voters’ stress over pricey gas and groceries, exorbitant mortgages and unaffordable healthcare.

Sign in now (it takes 30 seconds) to carry on reading

Not signed in before? Create a free account

Democrats would do well to recall that the affordability strains that helped deliver them to power are not dissimilar to those that delivered the presidency to Trump two years ago. And they could again quickly become their enemy.

“First, Americans want Washington to bring down the cost of living,” said Chuck Schumer, Senate majority leader-in-waiting. Likely House speaker Hakeem Jeffries added that “we’ve promised to fight for an affordable America, and that’s exactly what we will do”. They will soon discover the limits to their power to undo Trump’s economic blunders and steer an economy that is largely driven by forces outside their control.

Take gas prices, the single most powerful motivation for voters’ rebellion against the Republicans enabling Trump’s policy choices. Reining them in will require reaching an understanding with Iran that reopens the strait of Hormuz. Schumer thinks Democrats can achieve that. “We are going to end the war,” he said.

Trump may disagree, however. And while it is true that Congress is legally entitled to end wars – it is the only branch of government entitled to start one – it is unclear what such legal niceties might mean in practice. Republicans have controlled Congress since Trump went to war. Still, he has pursued it without asking for their approval. Democrats could now try to cut war funding, but they do not have the requisite 60 Senate votes to prevent a filibuster.

Trump’s trade war has similar characteristics. When the supreme court struck down Trump’s “national security” tariffs because they exceeded presidential authority, the administration reimposed many of them under a different statute, deploying a new, also spurious rationale. There is also little that Democrats can do to stop Trump’s war on immigration. It is fully funded and can carry on unimpeded, further disrupting construction and other immigrant-reliant industries.

Even the low-hanging fruit hangs rather high. While it may seem easy to reinstate federal subsidies for health insurance programs under the Affordable Care Act, or undo or postpone cuts to Medicaid and food stamps in Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Democrats will be hard-pressed to find the money, given a budget deficit that is already running at a whopping 6% of the nation’s gross domestic product.

Just preventing further damage will be an uphill battle. A lame duck Trump who no longer feels the need to please voters is likely to give free rein to his most destructive urges. While Democrats will be able to block Trump’s new legislative proposals, they don’t have the votes to overcome presidential vetoes.

Optimists may believe that after Tuesday’s shellacking, sufficient Republicans in Congress could be convinced to buck their president’s wishes. But most of those who survived the bloodbath come from the most faithful Maga districts and states and are the least likely to abandon their leader.

The economy itself – driven almost exclusively by a frenzied artificial intelligence investment boom – is unlikely to help Democrats achieve their goal of easing voters’ economic strains.

Wall Street is already doubting that the massive investments to build data-processing centers to train powerful AI models will pay off in time to justify the money. The tech-heavy Nasdaq stock index has fallen by more than 10% in the last month.

Goldman Sachs estimates that the large AI hyperscalers have raised almost $200bn in bond markets so far this year, almost twice as much as in all of 2025. Altogether, the bank added, AI-related firms have raised nearly $500bn in debt so far in 2026.

Were this bubble to pop and the funding to stop, it would likely deliver an economic downfall to beat even the Great Recession sparked by the housing bubble in 2008. When the time comes, a government hamstrung by $40tn in debt and interest rates hovering near 20-year highs will have little fiscal space to soften the blow.

Can voters’ newfound love for Democrats survive the likely turbulence ahead? Justin Wolfers, an economist at the University of Michigan who runs Platypus Economics, observes that neither the unemployment rate nor inflation are bad enough to justify Americans’ extreme pessimism about the economy. So what’s driving the sour mood? A collapse in confidence in economic leadership.

Tuesday’s Republican bloodbath might, on its own, improve Americans’ spirits. Limited though their powers may be, Democrats will at least offer some resistance to Trump’s most destructive impulses. But the economy will likely pose a greater challenge for the new Democratic Congress than it has to the Republicans currently in charge. In two years’ time, Democrats might be facing anger over an economic scenario that has gotten palpably worse.

They might then come to embrace the limits of their power and hope voters blame the president – not Congress – for their economic unhappiness.

Eduardo Porter is a journalist focused on economics and politics. He writes the newsletter Being There on Substack
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.summary: Democrats will soon discover the limits to their power to undo Trump's economic blunders and steer an economy that is largely driven by forces outside their control. The economy is driven almost exclusively by a frenzied artificial intelligence investment boom.

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: US tech stock rout: is the AI bubble bursting?
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Richard Partington Senior economics correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
After Thursday’s share price plunge on Wall Street, could the volatility be the start of a huge market meltdown?

Global financial markets have been thrown into a tailspin as investors bet on an AI slowdown after the US midterm elections.

This is not the first time stock markets have wobbled in recent months due to concerns over a tech bubble. But could this volatility be the start of a huge market meltdown?

Sign in now (it takes 30 seconds) to carry on reading

Not signed in before? Create a free account

Shares on Wall Street plunged on Thursday, in a rout driven by AI and technology stocks that extended to Asia and Europe on Friday. US markets rebounded after trading reopened in New York, but failed to recover all of the lost ground amid lingering concerns of a relapse in selling pressure.

More than $3.2tn (£2.4tn) was wiped from the value of the US stock market on Thursday – bigger than the annual output of the Canadian economy – after the tech-heavy Nasdaq fell by 5.5% and the blue-chip S&P 500 fell by 4.4%.

After months of warnings over the valuations of AI companies – amid fears of tinderbox conditions in the world economy fuelled by the Iran war and concerns that the tech bubble could burst – the trigger for the sell-off has been attributed to the Democrats’ sweeping US midterm election victory.

Investors are predicting that a Democrat-controlled Congress could lead to tighter control of AI and datacentre construction – slowing development in one of the engines of global economic growth and corporate earnings on the stock market.

Challenging billionaire power and calling out Wall Street and big tech were the rallying cries of many Democrats in the midterm elections. Moratoriums on datacentre construction were effectively on the ballot in several states amid growing public opposition to the building of vast, resource-hungry facilities.

Highlighting the stakes, the SpaceX and Tesla CEO, Elon Musk, set a record for election spending after pouring nearly half a billion dollars into backing Republicans – and moved his personal residence to Texas, the leading state for datacentre construction. After the midterms shares in both his companies fell sharply.

Fears of an AI bubble have been growing for some time, given the astronomical rise in tech company valuations, which some analysts said had become increasingly detached from reality.

One measure of whether a market is overvalued, the cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings (Cape) ratio, had risen to its highest level since 2000, showing that the US stock market was unusually highly valued relative to profits.

Highlighting the disconnect, shares in Alphabet, the Google parent company, plunged last week after it reported lower than expected profits, wiping more than $500bn from its value.

Some form of a check on progress was also likely, amid a groundswell of public opposition to datacentre construction and worries over AI safety. Opinion polls show most Americans are opposed to US datacentre construction, while governments around the world have encouraged citizens to stockpile for multiple eventualities including cyber-attacks.

Ben Barringer, the head of technology research at Quilter Cheviot, said: “It is too easy to say that the Democrats will be bad for datacentres.

“Yes, there will be a pause in the buildout and delay in approvals, but if you go off the words of the new Texas governor-elect, Gina Hinojosa, they are likely to be more pragmatic and ensure resources are more fairly allocated.”

What happens to the share prices of the US tech giants has enormous consequences for savers worldwide.

The “magnificent seven” tech stocks – Nvidia, Apple, Google, Microsoft, Meta, Amazon and Tesla – account for more than a third of the S&P 500, meaning that funds that track this index are directly tied to their performance.

AI has been a big growth driver, with the tech boom helping to soften the hit to the world economy from the war in the Middle East.

The prospect of a sustained tech sell-off could prove a big setback, in a blow to countries that have pinned their hopes on the AI revolution creating jobs and generating a productivity boost to overcome years of relative economic stagnation.

In response to the inflation shock from the Iran war, central banks around the world have been raising interest rates. However, an economic slowdown could force a rethink amid the risk of stagflation, when weak growth is accompanied by fast-rising consumer prices.

Financial markets are prone to volatile swings and investors are divided about whether things will get worse from here. Many were, however, worried a big crash was overdue – and when investors begin to lose confidence, it can become self-reinforcing.

Barringer said: “A virtuous circle could quickly turn into a vicious one, and they [investors] must now ride it out until the direction of travel becomes clearer.”

For some, the latest tech rout represents a reset rather than a lasting downturn. Demand for AI and semiconductors will not vanish overnight: new tools will continue to be launched, and datacentres will be built.

Mark Haefele, the chief investment officer at UBS Global Wealth Management, said the AI investment cycle should remain intact, despite the latest “market indigestion”.

“We do not think fundamentals justify a prolonged downturn,” he added.

More than $3.2tn (£2.4tn) wiped from the value of the US stock market on Thursday. Fears of an AI bubble have been growing for some time, given the astronomical rise in tech company valuations

https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.title: US job growth exceeds expectations in October despite economic uncertainty
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.author: Lauren Aratani in New York
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.text:
‘Low-hire, low-fire’ labor market shows sluggish growth but few layoffs, with an interest rate hike expected in December

The US added 165,000 jobs to the economy in October, a sign of resilience in the labor market amid ongoing war in the Middle East and inflation, according to new data released on Friday.

Economists had said the labor market has been stuck in a “low-hire, low-fire” state, in which job growth is sluggish but layoffs also remain low, but October’s data surpassed economist expectations. The unemployment rate went down slightly to 4.1%, the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) reported.

Sign in now (it takes 30 seconds) to carry on reading

Not signed in before? Create a free account

Average hourly earnings increased at an annual rate of 3.1%, slightly higher than last month. Inflation over the last few months has largely outpaced the growth in wages – what often leads people to feel they are spending even more to buy essentials. In September, the annualized inflation rate was 3.7%.

Initial figures for August and September were also revised up by a total of 84,000 jobs. Job growth was seen in healthcare, transportation, warehousing and manufacturing.

Other data released earlier this week showed employment has been steady. Layoffs in September fell to their lowest level in a year and a half, according to the bureau, while outplacement firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas tracked just under 44,000 layoffs in October – a 71% decrease compared with last October.

The new data comes after a seismic midterm election that solidified Democrats’ control of Congress for the next two years. Multiple polls had shown Americans were most frustrated about the state of the economy, especially higher gas and grocery prices.

“Americans delivered a clear verdict in the midterm elections that the current economy is squeezing people financially and making it hard to get by, let alone get ahead,” said Heather Long, chief economist at the Navy Federal Credit Union, in a statement before Friday’s report. “The labor market is a good example of why people are frustrated.”

But it’s unclear when Americans will get relief. Gas prices are on average $1 a gallon higher than they were a year ago because of the war in Iran. The price of diesel, which is used throughout the supply chain to power large vehicles, is 60% higher compared with prewar levels.

In times of stubborn inflation, the US Federal Reserve usually intervenes by raising interest rates, which slows price increases. In September, the Fed hiked interest rates for the first time since 2023, bringing them up to a range of 3.75%-4%, citing inflation. Though officials kept rates steady at their last meeting in October, held the week before the election, economists are expecting one more rate hikes at the next central bank meeting in December.

Meanwhile, markets over the last week have been shaken as investors appeared worried about AI spending. After reaching correction territory, when an index drops 10% below its most recent peak, the tech-heavy Nasdaq index briefly made a recovery on Wednesday before diving back into correction territory on Thursday.

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: TikTok accused of helping to promote sex industry to girls
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Amelia Gentleman
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
Researchers say popular performers covertly market OnlyFans content and tell followers about wealthy lifestyle

TikTok is helping to promote and normalise the sex industry, allowing “sexfluencers” to post videos aimed at marketing pornographic content they have uploaded elsewhere on sites such as OnlyFans, a report indicates.

After studying non-explicit content posted on TikTok over the course of a year by some of OnlyFans’ most popular young female performers, researchers said the women buried coded references to pornography in “girly lifestyle content” that showed them shopping, playing with their pets, baking or offering skincare advice.

While mentioning OnlyFans or directly linking to OnlyFans from TikTok accounts is prohibited, euphemisms, emojis and crude gestures are used to indicate that performers’ adult content is available for sale on other platforms. TikTok prohibits sexual solicitation, including invitations to share explicit images, but the platform distributes so-called safe-for-work material produced by popular OnlyFans performers.

The report analyses how hints about adult content are hidden in widely shared TikToks that show OnlyFans stars filming their hair and makeup routine for “get ready with me” posts – known by the acronym GRWM. Performers may use the word “corn” instead of the word “porn”, or add the corn emoji next to a star emoji, to avoid the content being blocked.

The “TikTok to OnlyFans pipeline” study was conducted by researchers from the campaigning organisations Cease (Centre to End All Sexual Exploitation) in the UK and Collective Shout in Australia. Researchers spent months scrolling through posts from a number of key “sexfluencers” and then following recommendations offered up by TikTok’s algorithm.

In viral posts, OnlyFans performers told their followers on TikTok about the money they had earned from selling sexual content. “One of the most pervasive messages across these posts is that selling sexual services on OnlyFans gives you a fabulous life – a life filled with freedom, fun, friendship and lots of money,” the report states.

Many posts promoted this message with images of cash, big houses, private jets and expensive cars, beneath headlines such as “how it feels knowing I own all of this at 23 thanks to 250,000 men”.

In some posts, OnlyFans was presented as the answer to poverty and unemployment by performers who described rag-to-riches stories. Opening an OnlyFans account was marketed as a solution, “rescuing women and girls from bleak, underprivileged lives, gifting them with the nice, luxury items that they – and their struggling families – have always deserved”, the report says.

OnlyFans’ own data indicates that its top 5,000 creators have made more than $1m each on the site since the platform launched in 2016. But the average earnings of the site’s 5 million registered performers are estimated to be about $1,000 a year, the report states.

Melinda Tankard Reist, of Collective Shout, condemned TikTok as “an industrial-scale digital pimp funnelling girls into the sex industry”. She said: “It is our view that young women and girls deserve to be protected from a predatory industry grooming them to be producers of explicit content.”

Tankard Reist said the research was commissioned in response to an awareness that OnlyFans stars such as Sophie Rain and Ari Kytsya had a huge following on TikTok among teenage girls, and concern that they were using the site to promote benefits of creating pornography.

Rain became famous with content filmed in the “Bop House”, a luxury pornography production house in Miami, which is home to a rotating group of women who sell sexual content on OnlyFans. Auditions to join the Bop House are shared on TikTok and would-be recruits respond by posting sexually suggestive dances tagging Bop House recruitment.

OnlyFans performers rely on building up their followers on TikTok and other social media platforms, so they have become adept at finding ways to make subtle nods to the presence of explicit content that is for sale elsewhere. The report focuses on the ties between TikTok and OnlyFans because TikTok has such a high proportion of young users and because it is where the careers of many on OnlyFans start out.

Many OnlyFans stars do brand promotion alongside their lifestyle content on TikTok, advertising household items such as pet food, burgers and pineapple juice, as well as sex toys and condoms. The global cosmetics brand L’Oréal last year appointed Kytsya – who refers to herself as a “mattress actress” – as a brand ambassador for Urban Decay, a makeup brand popular with teenagers and sold globally. In these advertisements, viewed millions of times on TikTok, she calls for makeup that performs well on mattresses.

The report’s authors have called for an extension of the ban that exists in many countries on showing explicitly pornographic content to under-18s so that it also includes posts that promote or are related to the sex industry.

A TikTok spokesperson said: “TikTok strictly prohibits the sharing or showing of sexual content and we use advanced technologies to enforce our community guidelines. In addition, our systems are designed to prevent age-inappropriate content from reaching teens.”

An OnlyFans spokesperson said: “OnlyFans is a platform for people aged 18 and over and we have strict onboarding processes to prevent minors accessing the platform.”

https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.title: Reform UK councillor promoted collapsed $1.9bn ‘Ponzi scheme’ HyperVerse that left victims suicidal
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.author: Ben Quinn and Sarah Martin
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.text:
Susan Lawrence, elected to Wolverhampton city council, sits on committee overseeing financial reporting of multimillion-pound budget

A woman who promoted a notorious cryptocurrency scam has been elected as a Reform UK councillor and now sits on the audit and risk committee of a major city council.

Susan Lawrence was one of the main UK promoters of the HyperVerse cryptocurrency scheme, which was named in US court documents as an alleged “pyramid and Ponzi scheme” that cheated investors worldwide out of a “staggering” $1.89bn (£1.41bn).

The HyperVerse scheme spread through the US and the UK from 2020 to 2022, and also targeted investors in developing countries across Asia, Africa and the Pacific before its eventual collapse left many people unable to access funds.

In some cases, people who took out bank loans to buy packages in the scheme said they felt suicidal when they were unable to withdraw their money, with some cases of self-harm.

Lawrence is now a Reform councillor on Wolverhampton city council and sits on the authority’s audit and risk committee, which independently reviews governance and risk management and oversees the financial reporting relating to a multimillion-pound budget.

Lawrence, who has not personally been accused of wrongdoing by authorities, promoted the HyperVerse scheme, or later variations of it, even after the UK’s Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) issued a consumer warning that the firm may have been promoting financial services or products without the regulator’s permission.

“You should avoid dealing with this firm and beware of scams,” the FCA said in a 2021 warning.

In a 2022 presentation, Lawrence addressed members of the HyperVerse community who were concerned they could no longer access their invested funds.

Lawrence, who worked with a fraudster whose company was later forcibly shut down by the UK high court, participated in lengthy promotional videos and webinars to market the project to the public and recruit new participants.

after newsletter promotion

She is also linked to various other cryptocurrency schemes that were promoted by HyperVerse’s alleged co-founder Sam Lee, an Australian bitcoin entrepreneur who moved to Dubai in 2021.

Lee was charged in the US in 2024 with both civil and criminal offences for his role in the HyperVerse schemes. He has denied all charges.

Lawrence travelled to Dubai to meet Lee, and was filmed promoting two other related investment schemes. She was also referred to as a “super leader” for one of Lee’s investment platforms called “Vidilook”. The status of a group participant is usually based on how many other people they recruit into the scheme.

Lawrence continued to promote iterations of the same network, including one that was later subject to a cease and desist order by US federal authorities which described it as a “fraudulent pyramid and Ponzi scheme”. US authorities said: “It does not sell or purport to sell any actual product and has no apparent source of revenue other than funds received from investors.”

She promoted the Ponzi schemes alongside Desmond Amey, the scams’ key UK-based promoter. The UK’s high court acted to shut down the company used by him to funnel millions of pounds into the platforms.

Lawrence did not respond when approached by the Guardian. A spokesperson for Reform UK said: “Cllr Lawrence was one of many victims of this scam, losing her pension and tens of thousands of pounds on a scheme she believed was genuine.

“She later became involved with HyperNation in an attempt to recoup the money she had lost.

“She was not employed by Des Amey and has not been questioned by any authority over her links. Cllr Lawrence has no current involvement in any of these companies or any similar schemes.”

Reform, which has been under renewed pressure over its vetting processes amid new allegations about the conduct of councillors and candidates, did not respond to a question about whether its vetting team had picked up on Lawrence’s background.

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/n.title: Standing in the way of slop bowls: the woman blocking food delivery robots
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/n.author: Arwa Mahdawi with visuals by Kriston Jae Bethel
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/n.text:
Semi-retired professor Carolyn Marvin became a local celebrity facing down Philadelphia’s growing robot delivery army: ‘It’s my first amendment right to protest’

“One of you needs to be on the lookout for cops, while I block the robot, OK?”

It is a crisp fall morning in Philadelphia. Tucked away in a dingy alley, opposite a garage called Patriot Parking, 78-year-old Carolyn Marvin is laying out some ground rules for a robot-disrupting expedition. Once a suitable target is identified, we will follow it to a busy sidewalk and Marvin will stand in front of the robot, blocking its way. The photographer and I will take turns ensuring we’re not all carted off by the police.

If Marvin sounds like she’s done this before, it’s because she has. Many, many times. The semi-retired University of Pennsylvania (UPenn) communications professor has become something of a local celebrity after taking it upon herself to block the UberEats food delivery robots which have become a ubiquitous presence in the city’s downtown. She doesn’t do this every day – “I have a life” – but whenever a robot crosses her path she’ll stare it down as a protest against their incursion into public spaces.

Her antics have gone viral: so much so that some Philadelphians dressed up as Marvin and the robot for Halloween. But while she may have supporters, her protesting isn’t universally admired: a few weeks ago it got her in trouble with the law.

“I was coming back from my flu shot and I saw a robot,” she recounts. “Since I had some time, I stayed in front of it as it was a very highly trafficked area.” A crowd amassed and a spirited debate occurred. Some people agreed with Marvin’s argument that, along with taking people’s jobs, the delivery robots pose a hazard to people with mobility issues. Others were concerned that she was stopping someone from getting the food they’d ordered and paid for. Eventually the cops were called about “criminal mischief” involving a delivery robot and three officers showed up.

“They asked me to move and I said ‘no, it’s my first amendment to protest against corporations in the same public space the robots are occupying.’ So I don’t see any reason to stop that.” The police officers, presumably a bit befuddled by the small but serious professor, who was dressed in her trademark blue visor, continued to try to get her to move along. Marvin just kept staring at the robot.

“So then they came up from behind me, took the food I was holding out of my hands, handcuffed me and hustled me over to a police car,” says Marvin. “I tried to make it hard for them but there were three of them and one of me. But I kept arguing with them. I think they weren’t sure what they could arrest me for because it’s all brand new stuff. And they hesitated a long time because I think the first amendment argument probably made some sense to them.”

The police ended up writing Marvin a ticket for disorderly conduct, with the rationale that she was blocking a business. She is still waiting for her court hearing date, but intends to contest the charges vigorously. “The wheels of justice grind slow, but I’ll go make my arguments,” she says. And one imagines these arguments will be convincing. Marvin has written a celebrated book, When Old Technologies Were New: Thinking About Electric Communication in the Late Nineteenth Century, about the social impact of electronic media. She is a formidable thinker who, in 1985, became the first woman to receive tenure at UPenn’s Annenberg School and now has an endowed chair named after at the Ivy League university.

A pending court date has not slowed Marvin down. Which is why she agreed to allow me to shadow her today, while she goes about her robot-disrupting business. I’ve picked our rendezvous spot because I’ve noticed that a number of the delivery machines congregate here while waiting for orders. We can trail them the moment they set off on their mission.

It’s unclear exactly how many food delivery robots there are in Philadelphia. Avride, the Texas-based company behind the machines, would only tell me that the number fluctuates according to demand. But there are only two in the alley when we arrive around brunch time. One of them is flashing Halloween graphics on the screen that operates as its “face” and another has little zzz on it, indicating that it’s sleeping. I’ve got to admit, they look cute. And, of course, that’s by design. “Humanizing the robots is important, because they are a completely new entity,” a spokesperson for Avride told me when I called them for an interview a couple of days earlier. “We want people to feel comfortable around the robots and not to feel scared about some weird box travelling down the sidewalk.”

The humanization didn’t fool Marvin, but it seems to have worked on other people. Avride, which operates almost 1,000 food delivery machines on more than 25 different college campuses and a growing number of urban locations including Jersey City and Austin, says it used to get concerned emails from people who’d see a robot in hibernation mode and assume it was lost or broken. Avride then added the zzz visuals to communicate the robot was waiting for an order, and now the emails have stopped. I ask the Avride spokespeople if they have they heard about Carolyn Marvin? There is a little pause. “We are all well aware of this lady, yes.”

As we wait for the robots to get moving, I start to wonder if the professor’s notoriety might have prompted Avride to install Marvin-mode software which disables the machines if they detect her presence. We’ve been hanging around for about 40 minutes and nothing is happening. Eventually, I hear a beeping noise and one of the robots whirs into an action. Someone had put an order in and robot 1617 was going from its holding pen to a nearby restaurant to pick up the food and deliver it.

While it may be equipped with all sorts of sophisticated cameras, sensors, and AI-powered software, the poor robot didn’t have the instincts to realize its mission was about to be thwarted. We chase it down the alley and, as soon as 1617 turns on to Walnut Street, a main thoroughfare, Marvin blocks its pathway and stares it down.

For the first few minutes people politely ignore the professor-robot standoff, although I do notice one woman rolling her eyes as she passes. But then the compliments and questions start rolling in. One elderly woman thanks Marvin profusely. A middle-aged man dressed in a nice suit cheers her on and says “someone’s got to do it!” Another man says he appreciates the efforts and “the gig economy sucks for everyone.”

“OMG,” a young passerby called Cadence says as she recognizes Marvin and her trademark blue visor. “It’s the queen! I feel like I met a celebrity!” Cadence, a 22-year-old recent graduate, is on board with the professor’s protest. “AI and robotics are supposed to make life easier for us and help us do the things we enjoy, not take the jobs of other people,” she effuses. “I will support any small business that doesn’t use AI. I appreciate what is made by humans.”

Passing kids, meanwhile, seem less concerned about the gig economy, and more interested in the robots’ cute faces. Every toddler who goes by points at them with delight. A couple of kids who pass have a heated discussion about whether the robot looks like a dog or a cat. (It looks like neither.) The only child we come across who isn’t enthralled looks around seven years old and yells “clanker!” at it. “I’ve watched enough movies to know that these things are going to hunt us down!” he says.

The people cheering Marvin on aren’t outliers: these protests have struck a chord with people because of a growing distrust around AI and automation. According to a recent study by Pew Research, a majority of Americans are deeply skeptical of AI; more adults are expecting it to have a negative impact than a positive one. And while I’m not sure if other people are blocking food delivery robots, we’re certainly seeing a rise in protests against datacenters and other symbols of automation. A few weeks ago in Philadelphia I passed a woman standing in front of a Waymo self-driving taxi (which is being tested in the city with human safety drivers) blocking its path and yelling “LAME-O”.

Despite this antipathy, robots are gradually being normalized. Pennsylvania legalized delivery robots via Act 106 of 2020, defining them as “pedestrians” and they’re slowly becoming part of the landscape. When Avride’s robots first appeared in Philadelphia back in March people would gawk at them and take selfies. Now most people just ignore them. And this same phenomenon is happening all across the world. While it isn’t clear exactly how many food delivery robots are in operation there are a number of companies besides Avride which operate these machines in the US, including Serve Robotics, which is one of the biggest players, with a fleet of 2,000 deployed robots.

While the automation industry has big plans to grow their fleets of robots, Marvin stages these protests because she wants to remind people that they have a say in all of this. They have a right to weigh in on whether private robots should be allowed on public streets.

“I’m very supportive of the kinds of things that AI is doing in terms of medical breakthroughs,” Marvin says. “And I think robots are fine on factory floors, but they don’t belong in public space. I take the position that this isn’t inevitable. But you have to have the will to do something. In Toronto they banned delivery robots from sidewalks in 2021. And I think, you know, the question is: who is public infrastructure designed to serve?”

The robot in front of Marvin isn’t (yet) smart enough to answer to this question. But it does seem to have clocked that it’s not going to be able to get to the restaurant to pick up its food today. After repeatedly trying to get around the professor it seems to have gone into hibernation mode. Eventually Marvin, who has to go to campus and prepare for a class, steps aside. The robot powers back up and trundles home to its garage. I know it’s only a computer with wheels, but I could swear it looked dejected. Marvin, on the other hand, looks triumphant.
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/n.summary: Carolyn Marvin, 78, is a professor who has been accused of blocking food delivery robots. She has been arrested for disorderly conduct after she was arrested for blocking a business. Marvin says she is protesting against the delivery robots, which are a hazard to people with mobility issues.

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: The datacentre arms race hits pause in south-east Asia
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Arundhati Hazra
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
Power and water constraints are pressuring what seemed like a juggernaut of growth for the region just months ago

I
n early 2026, Thailand’s datacentre industry was on a roll. The country’s board of investment had recently announced approval of datacentre projects from Tiktok, a UAE-based Skyline datacentre and Singapore’s Bridge datacentres, totalling a planned investment of $27bn.

As the year has passed, however, what once seemed like a new industrial juggernaut has ground to a halt. Thailand paused construction on 49 projects and approval decisions on 117 more in September 2026, amidst growing concern about the lack of sufficient details for regulation and monitoring. It is not alone in reconsidering datacentre projects. In neighbouring Indonesia, the governor of the country’s most populous province of West Java halted construction on a datacentre due to lack of permits and an incomplete environmental assessment process.

With the global rise of AI usage driving an increased demand for datacentres, south-east Asia has emerged as a surprise centre of growth in the Asia Pacific region. While China has the largest operational datacentre capacity in the region, a 2026 report by real estate firm Cushman and Wakefield shows that south-east Asia has the largest share of under-construction datacentre capacity in Asia Pacific, about 50% of the total. Malaysia and Thailand comprise a large portion of that capacity.

Through the 2010s, Singapore was south-east Asia’s leading datacentre hub, with companies like Alibaba and Facebook opening facilities there. However, the city-state implemented a moratorium on new datacentres from 2019 to 2022 because they were “intensive users of water and electricity”, as described in a press release from the Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry. Since then, approval has been selective amidst land constraints and sustainability requirements, with just 95MW of operational capacity added between 2023 and 2026, per Cushman and Wakefield.

With the advent of LLMs and rise in usage of AI, associated datacentre demand has surged in the last half decade, and desperate companies looked beyond Singapore to build datacentres. Malaysia has been a major beneficiary, with operational capacity in the southern state of Johor growing more than tenfold from 94MW in 2023 to 1110MW in 2026, with 3088MW additional under construction or planned. Johor has become the largest datacentre hub in south-east Asia, attracting $40bn of datacentre investment as of 2026, according to Menteri Besar Onn Hafiz Ghazi, the head of the state government. Key operators include Microsoft, which announced a $2.2bn investment for cloud and AI infrastructure across Kuala Lumpur and Johor in 2024, and Australian datacentre company AirTrunk, which said it plans to invest $3bn to double its datacentres in Johor from two to four.

Other countries in south-east Asia are catching up. Indonesia has a datacentre development pipeline of 1699MW in greater Jakarta, and is developing the island of Batam as a secondary hub. Microsoft is building five datacentres as part of a$1.7bn investment in the country, and Singapore-based datacentre operators Princeton Digital Group and Digital Edge are also expanding. In Thailand, Bangkok’s development pipeline stands at 2084MW, while secondary markets like Manila and Ho Chi Minh City are ramping up operations, based on Cushman and Wakefield’s analysis.

While the rush to build more datacentres is attracting big investments across the region, it is putting a strain on each country’s resources. Energy consultancy Wood Mackenzie estimates that datacentres in Johor already account for 24% of the state’s total power consumption today, which could grow to 40% by 2035.

“The rapid growth of datacentre developments in Johor has the potential to create localized grid connection bottlenecks and increase the need for transmission network upgrades as well as new power supply capacity,” says Alvin Tan, research analyst at Wood Mackenzie.

Thailand’s energy minister, Akanat Promphan, has said that datacentres require large amounts of power generated from expensive imported gas, and called for a new electricity user category with higher tariffs to reflect the demand.

Datacentres’ water-guzzling tendencies are also a major cause of concern for officials in the region. Johor is prone to droughts, and the current operational datacentres are estimated to need about 675m cubic meters of water per day. In Indonesia, a report by research firm Tenggara Strategics shows that many datacentres are water-cooled and situated in hot and humid lowland environments, resulting in elevated water consumption in comparison to facilities in more favourable temperatures.

In Thailand, datacentre projects in the country’s Eastern Economic Corridor have residents concerned about the pressure on their already depleted water reservoirs.

“The Khlong Luang Reservoir in Chonburi (in eastern Thailand) is a primary flashpoint,” says Somnuck Jongmeewasin, research director of research and advocacy group EEC Watch. “Despite the reservoir being shallow and under strain, authorities are piping its water to industrial estates,” he adds.

A weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our lives

after newsletter promotion

Local communities are waking up to the changes. In February, Johor saw its first public protest against datacentre construction, with demonstrators picketing a project by China’s ZData Technologies. Protesters expressed concern about the dust pollution caused by construction of the site near a residential location and the potential impact on water supply.

“While datacentres may create substantial investment and construction activity, they generally generate fewer long-term jobs than many other industries requiring comparable amounts of land, electricity and water,” says Jie-Sheng Tan-Soo, an assistant professor at Singapore’s Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy. “Communities may therefore reasonably ask whether they are receiving a proportionate share of the benefits while bearing the environmental and infrastructure costs.”

South-east Asia’s datacentre operators claim they are working toward making their facilities more resource efficient. Bridge datacentres, among Malaysia’s top datacentre operators, built a water reclamation plant and pipe network in Johor to cool its upcoming datacentre, expected to come online next year, while AirTrunk, among the largest datacentre platforms in Asia-Pacific, announced a partnership with sewage treatment operator Johor Special Water in April to recycle unused wastewater for the operational needs of its data centres. An AirTrunk representative said that its “campuses are designed to operate significantly more efficiently than conventional datacentres and incorporate advanced technologies to optimise energy performance,” but did not respond to detailed queries regarding data on efficiency and energy optimization.

Sustainability challenges remain. Microsoft has said that it is looking at south-east Asian clean energy projects to fuel its datacentres, but its published data on Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE), an industry metric measuring the energy efficiency of a datacentre, shows that its Asia-Pacific facilities are the least energy efficient globally.

Resource pressures have forced countries to become more circumspect about approving new datacentres. After Singapore’s moratorium ended, approval for new datacentres in the country has been strictly tied to a number of factors including power efficiency and carbon emissions. Malaysia has established a datacentre taskforce to review new projects with an eye on energy and water security, and Johor announced that it would no longer approve Tier 1 and Tier 2 datacentres, which used up to 50m litres of water per day, equivalent to the daily drinking water needs of 25 million people. Thailand announced an approval framework for new datacentre projects that considers energy and water use, along with power guarantee requirements and higher tariffs for datacentre operators.

To promote resource efficiency by datacentres, Tan-Soo advocates for integrated policy frameworks from national governments that have datacentre operators face the full social opportunity cost of the resources they consume.

“South-east Asia is increasingly aware but only partially prepared,” he says, and preparedness for environmental impacts needs to keep pace with the speed of investment.

The country’s board of investment had recently announced approval of datacentre projects from Tiktok, a UAE-based Skyline datacentres and Singapore’S Bridge datacentrres.

https://www.theguardian.com/money/2026/n.title: Can AI really save you money on your heating bill? I spent two years testing to find out
https://www.theguardian.com/money/2026/n.author: Samuel Gibbs Consumer technology editor
https://www.theguardian.com/money/2026/n.text:
Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

Samuel Gibbs doubted he could cut costs and still keep warm by putting tech in control. The results surprised him

C
an smart thermostats and AI reduce your heating bills? Every manufacturer claims the answer is yes, quoting average savings in the 25%, or £180 a year range. But all of these promises are heavily caveated and, with energy costs changing regularly, it can be very difficult to tell what is having an impact.

To find out if technology can really help, I spent the last two years comparing my miserly manual control and basic heating schedule to an AI-governed system. The results surprised me.

I used my 1930s solid-brick house with a recent, insulated loft conversion as the test bed.

In the winter of 2024 my heating system consisted of a 10-year-old Worcester Bosch combination gas boiler set to a medium heat, a Hive thermostat in a central hallway with its smart features disabled and 13 radiators equipped with standard thermostatic radiator valves (TRVs).

To maximise energy savings, I set a basic schedule to turn the heating on for a couple of hours in the morning and evening, turned off the TRVs in rooms we did not use and manually adjusted those in other rooms when we did not need them to be heated. I also manually turned the heating off when leaving the house.

It was laborious and not all that comfortable at times. I frequently found myself being glared at by other members of the family who were shivering under blankets in the living room while watching The Traitors. Or being called a traitor after denying yet another request to turn up the heating. But it kept bills low throughout the winter and money in my pocket.

After controlling for hot water usage by using recordings from when the heating was not used during the summer months of 2025 to create a daily average, my manual control consumed 14,316.7 kilowatt hours of gas across 213 days from November to May. This was about 10 to 15% lower than in previous years when I had not been quite so controlling and miserly.

In the summer of 2025 I replaced the Hive thermostat with a full Tado X system connected to the existing combi boiler. This system consisted of 13 smart radiator thermostats to replace the standard TRVs, a wireless thermostat in each of the two largest rooms, and a programmer wired to the boiler.

Instead of a central thermostat and a schedule with just one temperature for the whole house, heating is managed room by room. Each smart TRV can control the temperature of an individual room by commanding the boiler to turn on and then adjusting the hot water flow into the radiator. The TRVs in rooms that don’t need heating turn the radiators off, which maximises the efficiency of the boiler as it has to burn less gas to maintain the same water temperature.

If your boiler supports the OpenTherm protocol – check your boiler’s documentation or contact the manufacturer to find out – it can also tell the boiler to turn down its flow temperature to reduce energy consumption. My boiler does not.

Tado’s smartphone app controls the lot and allows you to quickly mirror schedules across multiple rooms or get as fine-grained for each room as you like.

The system is not cheap. It costs about £930 for the full setup I tested – I was lent the equipment by Tado. It can be easily DIY installed apart from the part wired into your boiler, which costs about £80 in labour by a heating engineer.

By default, it uses push notifications to remind you to turn the heating off when you leave or if it detects an open window in a room. But for the AI-powered smarts I tested, a subscription is required, costing £3.99 a month or £29.99 a year.

This promises to further improve the system’s efficiency through automation and numerous additional features. The monthly subscription can be paused if you are not using the heating.

The AI is built by Tado using anonymised data collected from more than 1m homes, which it does not sell to third parties. It learns how quickly a room heats up and cools down and uses that information to more precisely control the temperature and energy consumption.

It also performs automatic hydronic balancing to increase efficiency, taking the guesswork out of balancing your radiators. It automatically turns off the radiators in a room when it detects an open window, turns off the heating when the last person with the Tado app on their phone leaves home and preheats your home for when it predicts you will step back in the door.

The subscription records 13 months of logs of your heating activity, rather than just the last month, and enables Tado’s energy IQ system, which shows you the overall cost of your heating down to the cost for individual rooms, helping to spot any potential for improvements in any part of your house.

Tado is the biggest manufacturer of smart heating controls in Europe, but there are alternatives with similar per-radiator control, including Hive, Drayton and Honeywell. Google’s Nest, which offered smart-learning thermostats, pulled out of Europe in 2025.

I set a schedule for when the heating would run in each room. I turned on all the AI features and recorded monthly meter readings throughout the winter of 2025 and into 2026.

In the first week, the energy IQ feature highlighted that one of my radiators consumed a lot of energy heating an uninsulated porch. Since you are barely in the porch for any time before closing the front door, it seemed a waste, so I quickly adjusted the schedule to turn it off most of the time.

After that the system quietly ran in the background without interference from me. Letting go was hard initially. Compared with under my miserly manual control regime, it seemed like the boiler was on more often, rooms heated up faster and the house was generally warmer and more comfortable. It was much more pleasant so I was convinced that we must be using more energy compared with the previous winter. But to avoid the irresistible urge to adjust things, which would bias the test, I took the “head in the sand” approach and did not run the numbers as I went.

When the final numbers were in, to my surprise we had used 18% less gas.

Across the same 213 days from November-May with relatively similar outside temperatures, and after adjusting for hot water usage, the AI-controlled heating used 11,735.7 kWh of energy, which was 2,581 kWh less than my manual control despite us being more comfortable. At the current energy price cap, ending on 31 December, that equates to a saving of £205.70.

After two years of testing, I concluded that AI can save you money on your heating bill. We reduced our usage by 18%, but you could save much more if you are less frugal in the first place or lead a less predictable home schedule.

It also has multiple side-benefits beyond efficiency. The ability to control rooms individually made it very easy to have a warm living room in the evening without overheating the bedroom for the night. I could heat up a bathroom before an evening shower, increase the temperature of just a child’s room at night or heat the porch to dry out wet coats and boots in the depth of winter.

Each of the temperature sensors and smart thermostats also measures humidity, which made it easy to see when the dehumidifier needed to be put on, or rooms needed to be ventilated to improve the air quality.

And it can do all this while significantly increasing your comfort level, taking the stress out of managing your heating and your relationship with other family members.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: Activists break into building site of Microsoft datacentre in Amsterdam
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Ajit Niranjan
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
Separate actions also take place outside fence and across Europe in backlash against impact of AI boom

Activists have stormed the site of a Microsoft datacentre being built in Amsterdam, as the backlash to the social and environmental harms of the AI boom spreads across Europe.

Protesters from Geef Tegengas, a Dutch direct action group, clashed with police while breaking into a construction site at Westpoort, Amsterdam, where some members climbed a crane, lit flares and tied helium balloons to equipment.

Not signed in before? Continue with Google

The action comes amid Europe-wide resistance to the rapid expansion of energy-hungry AI, with more than 100 groups involved in a two-day series of protests to demand moratoria on the construction of new datacentres.

The break-in at the Dutch site, where protesters hung banners objecting to Microsoft’s services to the Israeli military and US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), was separate from the pan-European “Stop Dirty Data Centres” campaign, which targeted the same site but whose affiliated members stayed outside the perimeter fence.

Police said in a statement to NOS, a Dutch public broadcaster: “The police attempted to prevent [the occupation] and arrest protesters, but were unable to prevent it and force was used.

“An officer was slightly injured during the protest.”

Protesters from both groups said police used force and teargas to dispel the activists trying to enter the construction site. Organisers and local media reported hundreds of protesters on each side of the fence.

Smaller protests took place in the centre of Bristol, in the UK, at a datacentre in Berlin, Germany, outside the Polish parliament in Warsaw and at the main square in Zagreb, Croatia. Further protests are expected on Saturday.

Stop Dirty Data Centres, a coalition of independent groups that include national branches of Greenpeace and Friends of the Earth, said it had not coordinated or promoted the direct action that took place in the Netherlands, but that is was “understandable” communities would turn to a range of tactics when they were unable to meaningfully participate in decision-making.

“Big tech and government are racing ahead with large-scale datacentre development despite significant public concern about the impacts on local communities, natural resources and other industries,” said Owen Espley, campaign coordinator. “Many datacentre developments are planned with limited transparency or scrutiny, while communities across Europe are being shut out of decisions that will shape their local environments and futures.”

The ecological fallout of the datacentre boom has alarmed some climate scientists, while growing frustration with AI’s societal impact – from energy bills and job losses to the role of tech companies in undermining democracy – has increased public anger. In the US midterm elections this week, nearly every proposed moratorium on datacentres on the ballot was approved.

after newsletter promotion

Roos Molenaar, an activist from Geef Tegengas, said the struggle against big tech was inseparable from the fight against oppression and fascism. “We won’t accept Amsterdam being used for the creation of AI slop and the facilitation of genocide,” said Molenaar. “This datacentre is gulping up our drinking water to make the rich even richer.”

A spokesperson for Microsoft said it was aware of the demonstration and that its first concern was the wellbeing of everyone at and around the site. “We understand that people feel strongly about the project, and we respect their right to express those views peacefully. However, we do not condone any actions that are unlawful or that put people’s safety at risk.”

A spokesperson for Pure Data Centres, the site owner, said it respected the right to peaceful protest but that entering a live construction site was unlawful and dangerous.

“Our immediate priority is everyone’s safety, and we respectfully ask those on site to leave safely and engage with us in dialogue about the development and any concerns they may have,” a Pure DC spokesperson said.

Governments across Europe have supported the building of AI datacentres to boost tax revenues and catch up with the breakneck deployment of computing power in the US and China, with some framing the AI race as a matter of national security.

But datacentres have emerged as a flashpoint for public anger over issues from environment and energy to human rights and democracy. Last week, an investigation by the Guardian and Investigate Europe found evidence of dangerous conditions for some of the workers building them.

More than 100 groups involved in two-day series of protests to demand moratoria on construction of new datacentres.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Freezer meltdowns and airline hoaxes are a taste of things to come. Hoping for the best is no longer an option | Elisabeth Braw
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Elisabeth Braw
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Acts of greyzone aggression aim to spread panic. Europe has to show the saboteurs that we are resilient

I
t was as though a ghostly hand had switched the settings on supermarket freezers across Europe from “freeze” to “defrost”. From Finland to Ireland, they suddenly began heating up, many reaching 50C and food worth millions of euros had to be thrown away. But no actual hand was needed to cause the meltdown. This was a cyber-attack, or rather a chain of attacks. Like pretty much everything else in 2026, supermarket freezers are digitally enabled. That makes them smarter and more efficient, but like everything else that is connected to the internet, it also makes them more vulnerable.

Russian hacktivists claimed they were behind some of the supermarket sabotage, but no one knows for sure. It could also be Iran, Iranian proxies, North Korea – or unaffiliated bedroom hackers. When Transport for London suffered a devastating hack two years ago, the culprits turned out to be two British teenagers. Governments regularly warn retailers and other companies about cyber-attacks and even provide cyber-defence training to businesses. The lessons of costly ransomware and cyber-attacks also mean many big organisations and retailers have become much better at keeping their payments and logistics systems safe.

We're committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight in to your preferences, you're helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all

Not signed in before? Continue with Google

But freezers present a new vulnerability. In Sweden, for example, some of the stores that were attacked this week hadn’t connected their freezers to national retailers’ systems, which have centralised protection. Now they’ve learned their lesson the hard way.

Hybrid warfare – or, to use the defence term, greyzone aggression – refers to an array of hostile acts by a country’s adversaries that fall short of full-on military conflict. Cyber-hackers also this week attempted to meddle with fridges at French blood banks, while hoax bomb threats forced commercial airliners across Europe to divert, make emergency landings or require fighter jet escort to safety.

This comes after at least two years of sporadic Kremlin-suspected arson attacks on factories, explosives-laden drones flown into airports and drone incursions into countries’ airspace. There is constant GPS interference in the skies around the Baltic Sea, highly suspicious damage to subsea cables and pipelines, disinformation spread by bot farms and repeated acts of cyber-aggression.

Saboteurs and hackers usually have two aims: the first is to disrupt, but they also want to psychologically destabilise the target societies by spreading fear. It is fortunate then that the aviation hoaxes and freezer incidents coincide with a renewed conversation across Europe about resilience. It is as if the hackers wanted to showcase the need for preparedness projects such as the UK government’s new Be Ready campaign, which launched last month.

The British campaign, which instructs people on such things as stockpiling for emergencies whether caused by climate change or state-sponsored terrorism, had been in the works for months. Ministers hesitated however, fearing that citizens would respond with cynicism or ridicule, or just wouldn’t follow the advice.

Such campaigns are commonplace elsewhere. Earthquake zones such as Tokyo and San Francisco have had them for decades. “Make a Plan. Gather Supplies. Get Connected. Get Trained,” are the San Francisco city government’s pillars of instruction.

The newest version of Sweden’s official booklet In Case of Crisis or War, distributed to every home since 2018, is even more comprehensive, with clear language about everything from civil defence duties, how to volunteer (give blood or team up with neighbours for mutual support), to what items always to have at home, and how to find out if a crisis is real or a fake warning by bots.

For several years, I have been calling on the UK to follow Sweden’s lead and send a similar instruction leaflet to UK households, only to be told by officials that doing so would cause too much panic and frighten people. A House of Lords committee heard from the chair of the UK National Preparedness Commission in March that “the bulk of the UK population is blissfully unaware” of some of the risks they face.

It turns out that British people are less cynical than their leaders had assumed. Perhaps a few minds were also changed by Covid-19, which dramatically illustrated how vulnerable globalised and open societies are to all manner of threats.

Sign up to This is Europe

The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment

after newsletter promotion

Either way, within a week of the Be Ready campaign launching, the retailer Robert Dyas reported that weekly sales of radios had shot up by 160%. Maplin reported that sales of radios had nearly doubled and sales of power banks had more than doubled, while torch sales had soared to nearly four times the usual figure.

The puddles of defrosted ice in the supermarket aisles and stress for air travellers this week show that we need to be prepared for a very wide range of threats including power and water outages. We have already seen what happens to our complex food supply chains when global shipping lanes are suddenly disrupted. Iran’s obstruction of the strait of Hormuz following US airstrikes has given us painful food inflation and costly global oil and fertiliser shortages.

But what if the ships importing the food we eat can no longer make it to our ports? No industrialised nation grows all the food it consumes. What if the internet goes down? It’s not impossible. Even companies with the best cyber defence could fall victim to sabotage of the subsea data cables that transmit nearly all our connectivity.

This week has been a nasty preview of what could happen in future with alarming regularity. Severe disruption will come our way so simply hoping for the best is not an option. The good news is that by accepting that we need to prepare, and demonstrating that we remain strong in times of crisis, we can signal to Vladimir Putin and other rogue actors that disrupting our services is unwelcome, but ultimately it is futile.

Elisabeth Braw is a Swedish security expert and the author of The Undersea War: The International Battle for Supremacy at the Bottom of the World

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.author: Aisha Down
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text:
DataVita has revised plan for Chapelhall development to be wholly powered by 1GW of renewable energy

A datacentre company that said it would power a massive AI development near Glasgow with renewable energy has admitted that the scheme will be entirely served by the National Grid.

It's still free to read - this is not a paywall

Not signed in before? Continue with Google

DataVita, a key plank of the UK’s AI strategy, had promised that the Lanarkshire project would draw 1GW – the equivalent output of a small nuclear reactor, or Britain’s largest windfarm – from green sources. But when the Guardian raised questions about the pledge, it said the arrangement was “subject to final commercial agreements, planning, grid and consenting processes”.

Now, the company, which says its proposals would transform the economy of the village of Chapelhall, outside Airdrie, has quietly revised the plan. It now says the datacentres will be “fully grid served” with the possibility that solar and windfarms “could connect in the future”.

DataVita says the power it draws from the grid will be largely renewable energy. The company remains in receipt of £202m of public money in the form of wealth guarantees from Britain’s national wealth fund.

While the shift may appear to have been inevitable given the implausibility of the claimed renewables provision, it could present a problem for both DataVita and Britain’s AI strategy.

Under the former prime minister Keir Starmer, Britain’s AI strategy was to build massive datacentres in zones across the country. Their developers would get incentives – including, potentially, discounts on energy and expedited planning approvals. DataVita was to build one of the key developments associated with this strategy, an “AI growth zone” in Lanarkshire.

But this strategy began to founder just over a year after it was announced, when the Guardian’s investigations demonstrated that there was little solidity behind many announced plans.

AI datacentres are some of the most energy-intensive structures humanity has ever built, and energy costs are higher in Britain than in most of Europe. There is a years-long wait for the UK developments to connect to the grid.

Two key UK AI investments – announced with great fanfare by Starmer’s government – are on shaky ground after questions emerged over their ability to power themselves, or pay the high energy costs necessary to realise their stated ambitions. Now DataVita, which was supposed to bring 3,400 jobs to Lanarkshire by building a 500MW datacentre, also appears to be backtracking on its energy plans.

In a response to the Guardian, the company said it had not misrepresented its intention to supply renewables to the site earlier this year. “Our commitment to renewable energy is unchanged,” said a spokesperson. However, they added: “Our datacentres are being designed to be grid served … Our grid supply will be through a renewable power purchase agreement.”

This appears to contradict an earlier announcement, in which the company said: “More than 1GW of renewable energy capacity, including wind, solar, and battery storage, will be delivered through private wire connections directly linked to the datacentres.”

DataVita left open the possibility that its datacentres would connect to renewable energy in the future, through a wind and solar park it proposes to build in North Lanarkshire.

Kat Jones, the director of the Edinburgh-based charity Action to Protect Rural Scotland, said DataVita’s apparent change in direction was “emblematic of the hyperbolic claims being made by datacentre developers in Scotland”.

“Hyperscale AI datacentres simply cannot run on renewable power alone, they absolutely need a highly reliable source of grid power,” she said. “It is not surprising that the goalposts have now changed.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Three men charged in US with using AI to impersonate CEOs and steal millions
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Johana Bhuiyan
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Men allegedly impersonated voices and images of executives to convince employees to send large payments

Three foreign nationals were arrested and charged with using AI to allegedly impersonate corporate CEOs and attorneys to steal over $100m, according to an indictment that was newly unsealed by the US Department of Justice.

According to a press release from the United States attorney’s office for the southern district of New York, three men – Jacob Soall, Sharon Hazan, and Guy Sheetrit – were arrested for using AI to alter and impersonate the voices and images of executives and attorneys at various companies in order to convince employees to send over large payments. Soall and Hazan were arrested in Spain over the summer, while Sheetrit was arrested in the United Kingdom in September. The alleged fraud took place between 2024 and 2026.

It's still free to read - this is not a paywall

We're committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight in to your preferences, you're helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all

Not signed in before? Continue with Google

With the help of AI, the men allegedly acted as a corporate executive, targeting employees of various companies and telling them they needed their help with sensitive financial transactions. They would then instruct the employees to get in touch with lawyers at a large international law firm. The men would then impersonate a lawyer at these firms and have the employees wire a large amount of money.

The men ultimately stole more than $129m from companies all over the world including in the US, according to the DoJ. The men allegedly stole nearly $5m from a hospital system headquartered in Missouri; about $2.7m from a Rhode Island bank, about $3m from a California hospital system, over $4.6m from a mutual fund headquartered in Massachusetts and about $5m from a pet food company in Florida. The men also stole over $11m from a UK tech company.

The men would direct employees to wire money to bank accounts all over the world including in the United States, Spain, Portugal, Greece, the United Arab Emirates, Singapore, Austria, Slovakia and China. After the money had been wired, the men would covert the money into cryptocurrency “in an attempt to conceal the source, ownership, and control of the stolen proceeds and distributed it amongst themselves and their co-conspirators”, according to the DoJ press release. Soall and Hazan went by several aliases: Soal’s nicknames included “Seba Clarke” and “Rocky Balboa,” while Hazan went by “Superman Cash,” “Fat Boy,” and “Ron.”

In a statement, Jamie McDonald, a US attorney, said artificial intelligence had great potential but that the public should recognize that some may seek to use the technology to pursue criminal goals.

“The alleged scheme orchestrated by Soall, Hazan, and Sheetrit demonstrates how the use of advanced technology can be exploited to commit large-scale fraud,” said James C Barnacle Jr, the FBI assistant director in charge, in a statement. “As criminals continue to weaponize emerging technologies, the FBI remains committed to rapidly adapting our capabilities to identify, investigate, and disrupt those who seek to harm New Yorkers and businesses operating in our communities.”

The men have been charged with conspiracy to commit wire fraud, various counts of money-laundering conspiracy and aggravated identity theft.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Several Democrats renew calls for datacenter pauses after blue wave
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Nick Robins-Early
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Tech industry fears delays to its multi-trillion dollar infrastructure buildout meant to power artificial intelligence

Several newly elected Democrats and Senator Bernie Sanders have renewed calls for datacenter moratoriums in the days after the US midterm elections. The sweeping Democratic victory, which was buoyed in part by backlash to the tech industry, has added momentum to efforts to slow down the multi-trillion-dollar buildout of the controversial facilities.

On the social media platform X, Sanders posted a call for an immediate national datacenter moratorium this week. “Americans don’t want Big Tech oligarchs wrecking the environment, gutting jobs and threatening humanity’s future,” Sanders said on Wednesday.

Sanders was joined by several Democrats, including Representative Yassamin Ansari of Arizona – a state where Elon Musk’s SpaceX has proposed a datacenter project that would span more than 700 acres.

“Top of the Democratic agenda on day 1 needs to be a pause on advanced AI development, regulation of this out of control industry, and a ban on artificial superintelligence,” Ansari posted Wednesday on X. Musk mocked her post in a retweet, and the two sparred, with Ansari forecasting congressional hearings, telling the centi-billionaire: “See you soon.”

The pushback to the buildout of datacenters, which tech companies need to power the AI products that have become central to their businesses, was one of the most visible issues of the midterms. Opposition to datacenters figured heavily in campaigns across the US, while voters passed dozens of local ballot measures aimed at restricting datacenter projects in their states.

The outcome of the midterm elections has so far alarmed tech investors and executives, with Meta platforms president Dina Powell McCormick telling the Wall Street Journal that it is “going to be harder” to build datacenters following the vote. After Elon Musk spent nearly half a billion dollars backing Republican candidates and attacking Democrats on his social media platform, he jokingly posted on election night that “datacenters in space looking pretty appealing right now.”

Post-midterms anxiety also helped fuel a massive selloff of AI stocks this week, as tech investors worried about new regulation such as datacenter pauses. White House National Economic Council director Kevin Hassett was confident that the construction of datacenters would continue, however, arguing to CNBC that the ballot initiatives largely wouldn’t affect existing projects.

Datacenters and AI opposition featured in numerous Democratic victory speeches after midterms, as newly elected representatives vowed to curb the power of Big Tech. In New Hampshire, Senator-elect Chris Pappas praised his constituents for “opposing big data centers that harm our communities”. New Mexico congressman Gabe Vasquez meanwhile proclaimed “the time is now to stop the AI billionaire class from forcing datacenters in our community.”

Several victorious Democratic candidates also promised that they would hand local communities the decision-making power over AI and data centers.

“I do not work for data centers,” Ohio Senator-elect Sherrod Brown said to applause. “I work for you. I work for Ohio.”

Newly elected governors in several states key to the datacenter buildout, including Texas and Georgia, have also called for moratoriums on datacenters. Incoming Texas Governor Gina Hinojosa, whose state has become a hotspot for datacenter construction, pledged to halt new datacenter projects until new protections are in place.

“There are no rules and laws to protect Texans, and Texans are being taken advantage of,” Hinojosa said this week on CNN. “We need to stop what we are doing with data centers until we have those protections.”

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: A ‘customer success story’: leaked documents show Cisco doubled down on Israeli military deals during Gaza war
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Alice Speri
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
Tech giant leaped to shore up relationship even as company was roiled by worker protest over its role in the war

A
year into the war in Gaza, the networks of Israel’s military intelligence community were plagued with technical problems. There were major, multi-hour outages to their systems, and repeated crashes. Built-in debugging mechanisms failed.

The problems, which started as intelligence operations were undergoing updates to digital infrastructure, became so persistent as to undermine the “confidence” of Israeli intelligence agencies in one of their top network providers: the multinational tech conglomerate Cisco.

It's still free to read - this is not a paywall
