Not signed in before? Continue with Google

“This series of events happened during the period of war, deeply impacting customer sentiment,” warned a confidential memo drafted by Cisco and obtained by the Guardian. “During a period of national conflict, these repeated outages severely impacted critical operations.”

The September 2025 draft memo was part of a trove of internal documents leaked by Cisco workers furious with the company’s ties to Israel’s military three years into the war, which has killed more than 70,000 Palestinians.

Cisco, one of the largest tech companies in the world and at one point the single most valuable, is often described as selling the “plumbing” of the internet. It provides the routers, servers and communications systems that move data for companies, governments and militaries around the globe. While its business ties to the Israeli military have received less scrutiny than those of other tech giants, the company has worked with the Israeli security state for years. Israel’s military intelligence contracts alone generated about $67m in business in three years, according to a 2025 document reviewed by the Guardian.

While Cisco’s involvement with Israel’s military before and since 2023 has been documented before, the leaked documents obtained by the Guardian reveal the lengths the company went to in order to preserve and expand the relationship as the war in Gaza dragged on. They also show that earlier this year, Splunk – a Cisco subsidiary platform that can process and analyze massive volumes of machine-generated data – made a pitch to join the controversial cloud computing contract between the Israeli government, Google and Amazon known as Project Nimbus.

Cisco pursued these opportunities as the mass killing of civilians in Gaza was amply documented, international organizations and governments began to refer to Israel’s actions in Gaza as genocide, and the company itself was roiled by internal turmoil over its own role in the war.

Cisco did not respond to a request for comment. A spokesperson for the Israeli military wrote in a statement to the Guardian: “The [Israel Defense Forces] is assisted by services provided by a range of companies to meet its ongoing needs and objectives. The IDF does not intend to comment on matters relating to contracts or services provided by other entities.”

Members of Bridge to Humanity, a group of current and former Cisco workers who have objected to the company’s role in the Gaza war, called the company’s work with Israeli intelligence a “shocking and complete contradiction of values Cisco sells to us employees and externally to its customers, investors, and the public”. They said the company, which pitches itself internally and to the public as an ethics-driven company, had become “an instrument of genocide”.

“Cisco has been able to skate under the radar because they sell hardware and software,” the group wrote in a statement to the Guardian, adding that its business with Israeli intelligence made it “no different to an arms company that is supplying the bombs and fighter jets”.

Earlier this year, the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) found reasonable cause to believe that, following the 7 October 2023 Hamas attacks on southern Israel, and Israel’s subsequent war in Gaza, Cisco oversaw a hostile work environment rife with racist rhetoric that violated the rights of Palestinian, Arab and Muslim employees. Cisco previously told the Guardian that it disagreed with the EEOC’s findings and that it is committed to being an equal opportunity employer.

The Bridge to Humanity members alleged that the treatment they endured was linked directly to Cisco’s business interests.

“While Cisco leadership was constantly dismissing our concerns about how it was enabling the horrors we were witnessing,” they wrote, “they were behind the scenes going above and beyond to actively continue to expand their business relationship with the Israeli military and ensure they did not lose a cent of business.”

When repeated technical failures presented a “risk to operations” during the war, Israeli intelligence leaders threatened to cancel their business.

Cisco went into crisis mode.

In the documents obtained by the Guardian, Cisco referred to its client as the Israel Intelligence Force, or IIF, a body it described as responsible for “delivering critical network infrastructure for various intelligence departments within the Israeli Ministry of Defense”. Several branches of Israel’s government and military are dedicated to intelligence operations, but the IIF appears to be a reference to the IDF’s military intelligence directorate, known as Aman in Israel.

According to Cisco workers familiar with the technical issues, the outages and blackouts endangered intelligence forces’ access to military data.

The leaked documents also reveal that the company activated senior staff in an effort to salvage what it described as a “critical” account, and that it mobilized multiple internal teams over several months to fix the bugs. Cisco also sent staff to meet on site with a secretive Israeli military unit, known as Sapir, which since the 7 October attacks has reportedly been responsible for moving Israel’s intelligence apparatus underground. According to the Cisco documents, fixing the technical issues and training the customer “required site visits by Cisco under extreme security due to ongoing war”.

Cisco’s goal, according to the documents, was to restore “customer confidence” and reverse “negative sentiment”. After fixing the technical issues and helping Sapir return to “business as usual”, between 2024 and the summer of 2025, Cisco noted the client was satisfied and billed the damage control effort as a “customer success story” in an internal presentation.

The leaked documents detail dozens of deals Cisco worked on in 2026 with different Israeli government clients, including the intelligence community, air force and navy, many of which were tagged as “AI” deals. They include evidence that executives for the Cisco-owned Splunk platform sought to join Project Nimbus, though it is not clear whether the deal went through.

Watchdogs that document the private sector’s involvement in Israel’s occupation have found that Cisco has long provided Israel with technological support for its surveillance of Palestinians. Earlier this year, Drop Site News cited Cisco documents which noted that investment in technology had become as important to the military “as the focus on aircrafts, tanks, and any other essential military tools”. It also reported on a company presentation featuring the quote: “Never let a good crisis go to waste.”

Cisco is only the latest tech giant to face the anger of its employees over work with Israel’s military. Since October 2023, tech workers across the sector have denounced what they view as their employers’ complicity in Israeli crimes enabled by the tech products they develop and sell.

“At the same time, we’ve seen more and more reporting coming out showing that a lot of these companies have increased their revenue streams through larger military contracts with the Israeli military,” said Eric Sype, a US-based organizer with the Palestinian digital rights non-profit 7amleh, which has documented several companies’ repressive response to workers’ activism. “The tech sector is moving more and more aggressively into military contracting, and these companies are becoming weapons manufacturing companies.”

Cisco in particular has come under increasing public pressure over its role in the war. A group of investors has called on the company to commission an independent human rights assessment of its business with the Israeli military, and shareholders are expected to vote on a proposal requiring the company to do so at its upcoming general meeting this month.

While Microsoft, Google and Amazon have faced far more scrutiny and backlash over their business with Israel’s military, those companies’ contracts “would mean nothing without the physical hardware and infrastructure that Cisco provides”, Sype said.

“Cisco is at the foundational level facilitating all of these atrocity crimes that are happening and should be talked about and referenced in the same way.”

https://www.theguardian.com/thefilter-us.title: The nine best personalized gift ideas: customized for the person you love
https://www.theguardian.com/thefilter-us.author: Marissa Miller
https://www.theguardian.com/thefilter-us.text:
Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

Monogramming or customizing takes gifts to the next level – and shows recipients that you know what they like and who they are

The best beauty Advent calendars of 2026 in the US

Sign up for the Filter US newsletter, your weekly guide to buying fewer, better things

A
personalized gift is a special thing that says that you not only know what the recipient likes, but that you also know who they are. “Gift math” suggests you score extra points for offering a personalized gift, and it’s not hard to see why: monogramming or engraving, which takes time and effort, may feel more meaningful than, say, a last-minute grocery store bouquet of carnations.

When shopping for a loved one (or even the colleague on the other side of your cubicle), a personalized gift suggests foresight and consideration that is incredibly thoughtful without coming on too strong. To get you started on your quest for shopping for that perfect personalized gift this holiday season, we have sourced from ideas we’ve given, received and truly, truly love.

I’ve been a longtime devotee of Shutterfly’s handsome selection of customizable goodies, from wedding stationery (yes, my menus and processional cards were beautiful enough to take home as keepsakes) to mugs with my mug on it. As a proponent of the handwritten thank-you note, the brand’s notecards get the most compliments, and they’re entirely customizable, from text to trim and color to cardstock. Though I opted for the cheapest cardstock for these personalized note cards, they still feel incredibly luxe and durable. A gift of personalized stationery is also the gift of time because your recipient will no longer need to rush to the convenience store for a card each time a thank you or a congratulations are in order.

When my friend FaceTimed me from Pottery Barn Kids so I could pick out the color and text on this baby blanket the week before my son was born, my initial thought was: “This kid is about to have a nursery so aesthetic it will become my entire online personality.” The impossibly plush patchwork blanket has the comforting appeal of something grandma may have knitted, with the aesthetic construction and motifs only Pottery Barn Kids could pull off. It is almost too pretty to use, what with the near-constant looming threat of spit-up dribbles, but it serves as an unbelievably soft and warm layer as the late fall chill sets in. Kids really get a kick out of seeing their name on something, making it an ideal gift even for literate school-age children.

Not entirely sure what to give the person who has everything, or someone you don’t know particularly well? Chances are they drink water, or can benefit from more of it. Bingo: a personalized Nalgene water bottle that may actually get them excited about hitting their eight glasses a day. First, pick a wide- or narrow-mouth bottle in a color of your choosing, then your text or design. Easy as that. I personalized a wide-mouthed bottle for my perpetually parched husband years ago with the text “4ever thirsty 4 u”, which you are welcome to steal should your recipient be someone with whom you are well acquainted.

Money can’t buy happiness, but it can buy a personalized video from a niche D-list reality TV star sitting on their living room couch, if your recipient is into that sort of thing. The beauty about Cameo videos is that they become a gift for all who are present to watch the giftee press play, especially when the video hits on special moments or inside jokes the whole crew can enjoy. Simply select your talent, share details about the occasion or your relationship to the recipient, and give them up to seven days to cook up a bespoke message. Out of more than 50,000 stars – from recognizable to off-the-beaten path across everything from comedians to musicians – there is bound to be someone on Cameo’s platform that would send them into a starstruck frenzy.

Everyone can benefit from a catch-all organizer that helps consolidate the chaos. When I got one of these keepsake boxes for my daughter two years ago, it became a dedicated spot to safely stash all the documents I received from the hospital where she was born, plus sentimental cards full of well wishes on her birth. There are removable dividers to accommodate a range of items, from small trinkets to photos, and the box looks beautiful perched on a display shelf. Add a customizable name in your choice of font to the custom-dyed box for a gift that’s at once pretty and practical.

Whether you’re trying to look in-the-know, or genuinely need to take everything but the kitchen sink with you on your commute, LL Bean totes are a study in utilitarian fashion. Instead of gifting them something everyone and their cousin already has, opt for this proven favorite with a personalized twist. Hit “add monogram”, add to cart, then, depending on the size of your bag, choose up to 10 characters (or a single letter or initials) in your choice of color. The durable cotton canvas handles are reinforced with nylon thread, so your gift will hold up to years of toting – and as its name suggests, maybe even boating.

This heavy-duty leakproof Yeti water bottle with double-wall vacuum insulation will survive an apocalypse, and I can attest to that after seeing it withstand the wrath of my daughter’s mean backhand. But beyond its indestructible build, it keeps drinks ice-cold for several hours, and it makes for a pretty gift. I got one with my daughter’s name on it so she doesn’t lose it at daycare, but I bet it would make a recipient of any age feel special. Simply pick your text, choose your decal that represents them best, and watch the waterworks roll in (they will be well hydrated, after all).

A pair of wireless earbuds of any stripe is a pretty sweet gift, and Apple’s latest version, with their impressive sound and noise-cancelling properties, is something anyone would be happy with. But customizing their case (and for free!) is an unbeatable offer. While customizing AirPods may sound like a luxury, there is actually a practical reason for it. My friend calls this “the best gift to myself ever” because with her name engraved on the case, she’s no longer mixing her earbuds up with her partner’s. (And if ear hygiene is your thing, it may just keep the peace in your home too.)

If the wine fanatic in your life has more wine than they know what to do with (like a whole cellar of vintages spanning decades), a gift that’s a little more creative may be in order. My friend gave her wine-obsessed husband this five-piece, bespoke wine kit with his name on it, which he displays proudly atop his bar. It comes with everything your loved one needs to get the holiday party started, from a solid and sturdy-looking corkscrew to a drip ring that will protect the label (or your tablecloth) from errant dribbles. The fun part for you is choosing the finish and engraving style for a gift they wouldn’t even think of regifting (and couldn’t even get away with if they tried).

From Polaroid cameras to skincare, loungewear to gaming accessories, here are the presents teenage boys and girls told us they rate for 2026

Homemade Christmas gifts anyone can make

B
ecause there is no doubt your teen thinks they know better than you, we took them at their word and asked what they think makes the perfect gift for Christmas (or other religious festival they celebrate).

To ensure the selection was truly tried and tested, we asked them only about presents they have already received, love and use constantly. We also made sure to ask a broad range of teens – from book lovers to tech fiends and plenty in between – to try to represent the myriad tastes of this age group.

Lego retro roller skate

Lego keeps you entertained for a long time. You can keep coming back to it, take it apart and rebuild it, and it’s really good to collect. Anon, 14

Lego Technic Lamborghini Huracán

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: Measles, mumps and misinformation: how Crunchy Moms became ‘the most dangerous’ group on Facebook
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Michelle R Smith
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
Exclusive: Meta says it removes content that could cause imminent physical harm – but nearly half a million members have joined a group that regularly promotes misinformation

A
s a measles outbreak spread through Lancaster county, Pennsylvania, in August, a parent turned to a massive public Facebook group, Crunchy Moms, for advice. They were considering getting their three-year-old vaccinated, in part to protect their six-month-old.

“I’m nervous for my baby,” the parent wrote.

“First of all your children cannot die of measles. It is literally impossible,” one member responded. “Do not do it,” advised another. Others said the vaccine would spread measles or that it would be like “injecting poison”.

At the end of the post, Facebook’s AI system – run by its parent company, Meta – summarized the 589 responses, writing in part that commenters “claim the vaccine is unnecessary or even harmful”.

None of those claims are true. Pennsylvania has reported six measles-associated deaths this year, including two babies in Lancaster county. The measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine is safe and effective. Health officials say it is the best defense against measles spreading and injuring or killing people.

Scientists, doctors and advocates for health and children’s safety told the Guardian that what they saw in Crunchy Moms and similar groups was alarming. They worried that children could be getting hurt and that mothers were getting pulled into an online community that rejected science and fact-based medicine. One scientist who spends her free time monitoring the platform to highlight harmful health misinformation calls Crunchy Moms “the most dangerous group on Facebook”.

Meta did not comment on that characterization.

The spread of misinformation on Facebook has been a problem for years, but in the past, the company took steps to curb it. During the Covid-19 pandemic, for example, Facebook recognized it had a problem and changed its policies to “prioritize connecting people with accurate health information”.

But last year, shortly before the inauguration of Donald Trump, Mark Zuckerberg, Facebook’s billionaire founder, said there was “too much censorship” on Meta’s platforms.

Meta changed course; it eliminated factcheckers in the US and dialed down active moderation of anything but the most severe or illegal content. The company still maintains a policy that prohibits harmful health misinformation, but it is not known how Meta enforces it, and how its new permissive approach affects users at a time when measles and other infectious diseases are making a comeback.

In response to questions from the Guardian, Meta claimed nothing had changed in the policy or how it was enforced since 2023.

A Guardian investigation has found that dangerous medical misinformation is flowing freely on Facebook in groups like Crunchy Moms – now more than 490,000 members strong. What’s more, the company appears to have helped spread such ideas by promoting Crunchy Moms into users’ feeds, even when they do not seek it out.

Zuckerberg previously suggested that waiting for users to report “bad stuff” – rather than having automated systems catch them – would strike a better balance between what he termed censorship and free expression. But the Guardian found that Zuckerberg’s suggested approach appears to have little to no discernible effect on false information that circulates on Crunchy Moms.

Facebook took no action on more than 50 posts and comments a Guardian journalist reported to the platform from her own Facebook account. The posts appeared to violate Meta’s own standards, including that vaccines caused autism, that measles is not deadly, or that “miracle cures” like the caustic agent black salve that destroys skin tissue can treat cancer. Facebook did not acknowledge or respond to a single one of the Guardian’s reports, made in May, July and September.

In a response, Meta said its misinformation policies allow people to discuss personal experiences and scientific research. It said it removed misinformation when it was likely to directly contribute to the risk of imminent physical harm. But Meta did not respond to detailed questions about Crunchy Moms or experts’ assessment that such misinformation is commonplace in the group.

Meta’s revenue last year exceeded $200bn.

Doctors, researchers, former employees and public health advocates said the Guardian’s findings show that the pendulum at Meta has swung back to a time when there was little moderation of false health information.

“We were documenting Facebook recommending anti-vaccine groups to parents almost a decade ago,” said Renée DiResta, a professor at Georgetown University who studies online manipulation.

She and others have shown how that approach harmed children. Back then, there were stories of children being hurt or dying after their parents turned to Facebook groups for health advice.

“I’m afraid that we’re going to see that same kind of dynamic all over again,” DiResta said.

A Guardian journalist was scrolling on her phone in March when something caught her eye. Her Facebook feed recommended she join a group called Crunchy Moms: Natural Living & Clean Products.

The group was created in March 2025, less than three months after Zuckerberg announced Meta’s new hands-off approach.

Crunchy Moms’ administrators describe it as “a supportive space for moms who want to raise their families using toxin-free products, low-tox alternatives, and clean ingredient solutions”. But a quick check of the group revealed, and experts confirmed, it was a hotbed of false medical information that could hurt people – especially children and their mothers, who turn to the group for community, advice and affirmation.

The group focuses largely on health, though some posters also come to seek parenting tips, product recommendations and other non-medical questions. Many posters appear to take it as a given that group members are – or should be – against vaccinating their children. They frequently describe vaccines and their ingredients as deadly, toxic or poisonous.

“We don’t vaccinate in this group. It’s the foundation of becoming a crunchy mom,” one anonymous member explained last month, in response to a question about the vaccine for RSV, a respiratory virus. A group administrator responded to a different post that “As a crunchy community we are generally against v@cs” – a code for “vaccines”.

Crunchy Moms has more than doubled in size since January, and receives hundreds of posts a day, and thousands of comments and replies.

Sara Rupe launched the group in March 2025. It was less than three months after Zuckerberg announced Meta’s new hands-off approach. The Connecticut mom said in an interview that her intention in creating the group was to share product recommendations for things like personal care products and makeup, but it turned into something bigger.

At least part of Crunchy Moms’ success, she said, was because it does not block “free speech”.

“Everybody has a right to say what they want to say as long as it’s within community standards of Facebook,” Rupe said. “I don’t censor things.”

Rupe added: “If somebody wants to say something, then I usually let them. But I mean, within reason, if I really think it’s going to hurt somebody, I don’t. But I also think letting some information get out there could be good.”

Crunchy Moms is the largest group in a network of groups that collectively has more than 1 million members. Rupe runs them with the help of several administrators and moderators, including her husband, who is a registered nurse; a pastor and wife couple in upstate New York; and a woman whose Meta-verified account describes her as a doctor of holistic health.

They post often with links to supplements and other products for sale on an Amazon store, with links to another administrator’s skincare line, or with affiliate links to products that provide a cut of sales to the person sharing it.

Rupe said she and another administrator use multiple accounts to run the group, which lets them maintain access to it if Facebook restricts her account. Her daughter was in seventh grade last year when Rupe used her account to post a listing of more than three dozen products, including herbal remedy bundles that run over $100, non-fluoride toothpaste, $25 tallow balm and red light therapy panels that cost $200 or more.

A second administrator, Dawn Mannion, said she didn’t make any money from the group, though others made a small commission that was “not even minimum wage”. She said she frequently recommended that members seek medical attention from holistic or other qualified healthcare professionals. She added: “We do not discourage people from seeking medical care. We encourage it.”

Other administrators and moderators contacted by the Guardian did not respond to Facebook messages and texts seeking comment.

Many Crunchy Moms members were already into “natural living” and questioning vaccines when they come to the group, and group leaders don’t try to sway anyone’s mind, Rupe said.

Rupe has a child with autism that she now believes is connected to vaccination, and said many others in the group believed their children were injured by vaccines.

“We don’t want anybody to be hurt at all,” she said. “We want everybody to be as happy and healthy as possible.”

While Crunchy Moms posters often vehemently counsel against vaccines and modern medicine, Rupe said she did not think the group was harming anyone. Instead, she said it was helping people make their own decisions.

Some members say vaccines are so dangerous that it is safer to get a deadly or life-altering vaccine-preventable disease than it is to get immunized. They tell other members that catching a disease like measles or chicken pox “naturally” can be more healthy than getting vaccinated. Others repeat the US health secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr’s unproven claims that Tylenol is linked to autism. One recent comment said that catching measles makes your body stronger, trains your immune system and results in a lower risk of cardiovascular disease and cancer.

Many posts spread the false assertion that vaccines cause autism and sudden infant death syndrome (Sids) – even though Meta specifies in its own policies that posts saying so violate its terms.

New or soon-to-be mothers looking for help and advice are frequent posters, and targets for swarms of comments telling them not to follow science-backed health recommendations for their children, like giving their newborns a vitamin K shot that can prevent brain bleeds.

One woman asked about a link between vaccination and Sids, suggesting she feared she was putting her baby at risk of death if she followed the recommended vaccine schedule. She said she was considering spacing out her infant’s vaccines to lessen the risk. She ended her post: “I’m terrified.”

“Delaying poison won’t do anything beneficial. Injecting poison WILL increase the likelihood of SIDS,” one woman replied. Another, labeled an “All-Star contributor” by Facebook, weighed in: “SIDS is vaccine death. SIDS was invented to cover up the fact that vaccines kill infants.”

Scrolling through a post asking whether vaccines cause autism, readers will find comment after comment saying that they do. In one post, a frequent commenter offered a false statistic that 79% of autism cases were caused by vaccines. She replied to a person who said they were neurodiverse: “Your parents caused this with their vaccines. I am sorry.”

The same commenter later counseled the Lancaster county parent who was worried about their community’s measles outbreak that “it is not worth risking death or a disabling lifelong neurodegenerative condition, such as autism, for a vaccine that is ineffective, at best, at preventing measles”.

The group includes a mix of views. Some commenters will offer encouragement to seek medical care and to vaccinate their children. The Guardian spoke to people who became members of Crunchy Moms to try to provide a counterweight to the false information shared there.

Mannion said they did not endorse every statement made by individual members.

One of the Crunchy Moms rules that is supposed to govern the group is that the information shared is not medical advice, and that members should consult a healthcare provider before making any health or medical decisions. But in the many posts from parents asking for advice or sharing what their doctors told them, commenters often urge them not to follow what the doctor suggests, or say there is no need to speak to a doctor at all.

Rupe said she believes many of the comments are from “trolls” trying to get the group in trouble, and that people are simply posting their opinions.

Dr Alok Patel, a pediatrician who reviewed the group at the Guardian’s request, pointed to those kinds of comments as particularly concerning. It is a time-honored tradition for mothers to turn to fellow mothers for advice, and Patel believes it is important for people to use social media to find connection.

“But when people are outright dismissing modern medicine and putting their foot down and saying don’t get vaccines, don’t get the vitamin K shot, don’t see a doctor, and instead promoting a product – that is outright misinformation and potentially dangerous,” he said.

Patel has built up his own following on Meta’s Instagram platform to deliver science-based medical information to people. Social media companies, he said, should show it is more important to provide quality information than it is to keep people on their apps.

“Prove to us that you are prioritizing public health as much as you prioritize profits for your investors,” Patel said.

Research has shown that health misinformation shared on Facebook can have a real-world impact on people’s decisions.

Jennifer Allen, a professor at NYU Stern who worked at Facebook from 2016 to 2018, has researched the effect of misinformation and vaccine-skeptical content on Facebook. She and her colleagues have estimated that exposure to vaccine-skeptical content on the platform during the Covid-19 pandemic reduced people’s intention to get vaccinated. Without that exposure, they estimated 5 million more Americans would have been vaccinated, saving approximately 21,000 lives.

While people should be able to express themselves, Allen said, there was evidence that the kinds of expression she saw in Crunchy Moms could be dangerous.

“The fact that this group seems to exist and is being recommended to people, and there is so much clear misinformation in it, it seems to me that that means that there’s a failure along the way of Facebook,” Allen said.

During the pandemic, she said Facebook got pretty good at identifying and taking down egregiously false information and also not recommending it to people. She said she was surprised to now see such explicit misinformation being shared in a public group, and Facebook recommending it to users.

One scientist who spends her free time trawling Facebook to highlight the harmful information she sees there spoke to the Guardian on condition of anonymity because she has received harassment and threats. She said Crunchy Moms stood out among the worst, but was far from the only group where these problems were happening.

“Meta, and specifically Facebook, is allowing for these things to continue,” she said. She cited posts she has seen that counsel mothers not to get the vitamin K shot for their newborns and others that sell unregulated supplements. She said she believed it was more dangerous than any other groups she monitored.

“Everybody should have the freedom to talk about what they want to talk about,” Rupe said when given the opportunity to respond to that criticism.

Given the volume of the posts, Rupe said she and other administrators couldn’t vet every single post.

“I’m assuming that if Meta sees that it doesn’t agree that it will just take it down. So I don’t really worry about that part,” she said.

In 2019, Facebook announced it would stop recommending groups that spread misinformation about vaccinations, saying it was “fully committed to the safety of our community”. DiResta said the company responded to public pressure as it became clear anti-vaccine activists were using Facebook to undermine public health in places like Samoa, where a 2019 measles outbreak killed 83 people, mostly children under age five. Facebook’s regional policy director said at the time that its teams were “proactively scanning for any health-related misinformation and are taking action to prevent its spread on our platforms”.

Later that year, Zuckerberg was pressed on the issue by a Republican congressman who complained that Facebook was censoring users’ speech about vaccine risks and injuries. Zuckerberg, whose wife, Priscilla Chan, is a pediatrician and who donated $75m to a major San Francisco hospital which now bears their name, acknowledged the concern. But he said “we also hear consistently from our community that people want us to stop the spread of misinformation” and that he understood “scientific consensus is that it is important that people get their vaccines”. While users would be allowed to post anti-vaccine content or join such groups, Zuckerberg said Facebook would not “recommend or go out of our way to show people content that would encourage people to join those groups”.

After Covid hit in 2020, Facebook stopped recommending health groups altogether, explaining that “it’s crucial that people get their health information from authoritative sources”.

Anti-vaccine activists complained of censorship and joined with Republican politicians and others who took issue with Facebook’s response to false information about elections and other civic matters. Then Trump was elected to a second term. His pick to lead the nation’s health department was Kennedy, a longtime leader in the anti-vaccine movement who has accused Facebook of censoring him and the group he used to run, and sued over it. The case was dismissed.

Shortly before Trump was sworn into office, Zuckerberg and Meta announced the end to third-party factchecking in the US as well as rollbacks to moderation. A few weeks later, Zuckerberg and tech CEOs attended Trump’s inauguration.

Still, Meta retained a misinformation policy.

The current policy says it removes what it calls harmful health misinformation that is “likely to directly contribute to imminent harm to public health and safety”. It lists several specific examples of what it does not allow – much of it about vaccines. Among those are claims that vaccines cause autism or Sids; that vaccine ingredients are deadly, toxic, poisonous, harmful or dangerous; that vaccines are not effective; and that measles is not deadly. Meta’s policy also says it bars promoting or advocating for harmful miracle cures, including black salve, which is peddled online as a skin cancer treatment without evidence that it works, and it has disfigured people or left their cancer to grow.

Though Facebook issued a report on how it has enforced its community standards this year, it did not discuss how or whether it has enforced its standards that govern misinformation on health.

The Guardian spoke to several people who had reported Crunchy Moms posts to Facebook or who had tried to report posts outside the group that similarly contained dangerous health misinformation. They said they had little success.

“My own personal post reports have universally been ignored by Facebook,” said Dr Frank Han, a pediatric cardiologist in Connecticut.

“While Facebook claims that they moderate, the practical effect is that medical misinformation propagates much faster than medically correct information,” Han said.

Another Crunchy Moms member, Emily Loving-Rodriguez, said she had made dozens of reports to Facebook, and possibly hundreds, since she joined earlier this year. The Idaho resident has a personal interest in child welfare and misinformation, and noted a post she had seen recently in Crunchy Moms in which someone said herpes could be cured with the dietary supplement zeolite. She said her reports rarely had any effect.

Kasey Kramps, another member, said she had made reports to Facebook in the past for medical misinformation but said she could no longer find a way to report it.

“Their health misinformation rules are very explicit. They’re still up there,” said DiResta, who reviewed the group at the Guardian’s request. “They have a policy and they actively choose – at this point – it does not seem that they are enforcing it.”

To test how Facebook enforces its harmful medical misinformation policy, the Guardian reported 55 Crunchy Moms posts, comments and replies and one video reel to Facebook that appeared to violate the policy.

It is the approach that Zuckerberg endorsed when he announced Meta’s changes in January 2025.

“We used to have filters that scanned for any policy violation,” Zuckerberg said then. “Now we’re going to focus those filters on tackling illegal and high severity violations. And for lower severity violations, we’re going to rely on someone reporting an issue before we take action.”

The Guardian’s reports spanned a range of content. One post stated in part that scientific research shows “vaccines cause autism”. A comment said: “The MMR vaccine CAUSES measles.” Another: “Vaccines are extremely toxic and unnecessary as well as NOT safe or effective. They all poison.”

In a video shared in the group that downplayed the dangers of tetanus and urged against vaccines, a caption included the line “High-dose vitamin C led to 100% survival in tetanus-infected children and reduced death rates in adults.” Meta’s policy prohibits saying vitamin C is as effective as a vaccine.

On a post asking: “What are we using to get rid of skin cancer?” the Guardian reported several replies suggesting black salve. It also reported a post asking for a brand of black salve to use on a “questionable mole/mark”, as well as the reply from a group administrator providing an affiliate link to purchase a black salve product, as well as to another administrator’s Amazon store.

The Guardian also reported the entire Crunchy Moms group on 1 October, given that similar content is commonplace within it.

There is no way to report content specifically as harmful health misinformation. Instead, the user making a report must first select a broad category: “scam, fraud or false information”. Then, content can be reported under the heading “Sharing false information”.

The Guardian did not receive a single confirmation from Facebook to any of its reports, even though the company says it alerts users to the outcomes of their reports. Loving-Rodriguez said when she reported comments for hate or Nazi content in other Facebook communities, she received a message from Facebook confirming her report. But not when she flagged content that seemed to violate Facebook’s rules in Crunchy Moms.

Nearly all of the content the Guardian reported to Facebook was still up when Meta was approached for comment.

While the repeated reports of policy violations by the Guardian didn’t receive any responses, Facebook invited the journalist to join the platform’s community notes program. The program replaced third-party factcheckers in the United States after the 2025 rollbacks. Meta has said it was already testing the program in several countries and planned to roll it out and eliminate factcheckers once it was confident it was working well.

The Guardian this week provided Meta with examples of content found on the group. Meta said it was reviewing those links and would take action on posts that violate its policies.

Recommendations have become an important source of content on Facebook, now representing 36% to 39% of what users see in their news feed, according to the company’s most recent reports. That content comes from sources they are not connected to but which Facebook determines might interest them. By contrast, content from friends makes up only about 20% of users’ feeds.

Facebook says it makes such personalized recommendations to help people “discover new communities and content”.

When Facebook chose to promote a group, DiResta claimed, it was using its editorial discretion, exercising its speech and making a value judgment. In the past, she said, Facebook had acknowledged that recommendations created a different level of responsibility from simply allowing people to speak.

The Guardian found several people who encountered Crunchy Moms in their feed as a result of Facebook’s curation choices.

“It came across my feed, and I engaged,” said Kramps, who joined the group about six months ago. “I did not seek it out.”

“It was offered to me organically in my feed,” said Dr Casey Husser, an anesthesiologist in Sioux Falls, South Dakota. “I didn’t look for Crunchy Moms.”

A Minneapolis mother of two children, ages two and five, told the Guardian that Crunchy Moms showed up in her feed for months, even though she was not part of the group and did not seek it out.

Meta told the Guardian its approach to misinformation was to create an environment that reduced its distribution. It did not address specific questions about why it was recommending Crunchy Moms to users’ feeds.

Facebook also has taken the step of adding titles or comment summaries to some posts. Generated by Meta’s AI tool, they are meant to “help people catch up” on conversations on the platform. The comment summaries it offered on some posts conflicted with good science, critics said.

For example, Meta’s AI entitled one post: “What vaccines are recommended or skipped during pregnancy and infancy?” It summarized the comments by stating: “Hepatitis B and flu vaccines are commonly suggested to skip, while some recommend delaying or picking and choosing vaccines.”

That conflicts with recommendations from doctors’ groups in the US, which recommend universal hepatitis B vaccination for all infants at birth, as well as flu vaccine for children six months and older and for pregnant women during influenza season.

On the Lancaster measles post, which asked for ways to “detox” from the MMR vaccine, Meta’s AI summarized the discussion as: “No detox needed, some commenters cite vitamin A deficiency as a measles risk factor, while others claim the vaccine is unnecessary or even harmful.”

Meta’s AI system could be adding context to that post to clarify that a vaccine detox was not a scientifically valid idea, DiResta said.

“It’s very easy for an AI to do that,” she said, pointing out that Meta uses AI for some notes on Threads. “But it seems, again, that they’re choosing not to do that.”

Meta told the Guardian on Wednesday evening it had gotten rid of AI summaries of discussions in September. But the Guardian took screenshots of more than 10 such summaries in October, some going back as far as December 2025.

Meta did not respond to specific questions on the issues the Guardian raised about the substance of the AI-generated content.

Husser said he made it a habit to pay attention to bad medical information circulating online so he wouldn’t be surprised at work if patients asked him about it.

“[Facebook is] way more permissive,” Husser said. “Since 2025, it’s become a totally different environment.”

Crunchy Moms’ administrator Rupe said she has noticed a change as well. In the past, she remembered getting Facebook strikes or removals for mentioning the word “vaccines”.

“It seems like we’re not getting in trouble for a lot of things like we used to,” Rupe said.

In the past, she recalled that Facebook would flag posts it deemed as containing misinformation before they were approved, and said she usually would not approve them if she saw such a message. But she didn’t remember getting any this year. Rupe said Facebook only took down about one post per month from Crunchy Moms.

Meta’s AI would alert her when someone uses a swear word, or a variation of one, in the group. But Rupe said it didn’t give her any alerts about what some might call medical misinformation.

DiResta said the fact that Facebook was recommending this group to people was significant.

“Meta is pushing this thing unsolicited into the feeds of particularly new parents” who naturally have concerns and fears about their children’s health, DiResta said. “They want to feel that they’re doing the best for their kids.”

The group focuses largely on health, though some posters also come to seek parenting tips, product recommendations and other non-medical questions. Facebook has been criticized for its policy on health and safety.

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: Tech barons cozied up to Trump. What will they do in newly blue America?
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Blake Montgomery
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
Democrats’ success was helped by popular anger over tech, AI and the super rich – life for billionaires could become much more difficult

The photo of Silicon Valley centibillionaires at Donald Trump’s inauguration – Musk, Bezos and Zuckerberg, front row and side by side – now looks like a hitlist for a blue Congress hellbent on making life difficult for billionaires.

The picture symbolized at the time the bending of the knee by the richest men in the world to its most powerful, a symbiosis of the ultra-rich. Already unfathomably wealthy, Silicon Valley tycoons believed a Maga-sized public shift to the right would enrich them even more. It did. For several years, while Trump seemed an everlasting kingmaker and AI’s expansion seemed unstoppable, their fortunes ballooned to values beyond comprehension. Elon Musk’s surpassed $1tn.

In the harsh blue light of Tuesday’s midterms, though, going all-in on Maga seems an unwisely unhedged bet. Democrats took decisive control of the US Congress, flipping seats right and left that in previous years seemed like given wins for Republicans. Governors’ mansions across the country likewise lit up blue as Democrats ascended even in the reddest of states, such as Texas.

Voters concerned about corruption expressed their displeasure at oligarchs’ blatant attempts to create a political environment to their liking. Voting against technocrats drove people into the hands of Democrats and away from Republicans. Tech oligarchs themselves, along with anger over the AI boom, datacenters and Flock surveillance cameras, shifted the tides.

“Voters rejected Republicans in part because they were bought and paid for by AI billionaires. Democrats must hold them accountable instead of cashing their checks,” wrote the Texas Democratic representative Greg Casar.

The Georgia Democrat Jon Ossoff, who won re-election to the Senate, summed up the prevailing attitude towards the tech industry in his victory speech.

“The titans of Silicon Valley dig bunkers for themselves and warn that the artificial intelligence they’re creating risks human extinction,” he said. He pledged to bring “big tech to heel”.

Others were more bellicose. Ed Markey, a Democratic senator from Massachusetts, tweeted late on Tuesday: “They are going to need to plant new forests for all of the subpoenas we’ll be printing.”

Democrats have both promised congressional investigations into tech companies and moratoriums on datacenters, which may hamstring compute-hungry AI companies.

In the past year, the major AI firms have been competing in a fierce race to buy or build massive, noisy, resource-intensive facilities full of semiconductor chips that will supply their growing needs for computing power. Americans hate them. Democrats stand firmly in the way of that arms race. Democrats took governors’ mansions by promising to institute moratoriums on hyperscale datacenter construction.

Gina Hinojosa of Texas, Amy Acton of Ohio and Keisha Lance Bottoms of Georgia have all pledged pauses.

Then there are the promised investigations. Letters to preserve records for future investigations have already gone out to Nvidia and Amazon. Tech was the villain of the midterms. Angry constituents want to see it penalized. Elon Musk presents a meaty target as the billionaire most closely allied with the Trump administration and the richest man in the world. Investigating his conduct with the “department of government efficiency”, which laid waste to the humanitarian agency USAID and wide swaths of the US government, will be a political lay-up for Democrats newly in control and desiring a public spectacle.

Musk had the worst night of anyone but Trump on Tuesday. The world’s richest man gave $450m in support of Republican candidates, most of all to Ken Paxton in Texas, but he reaped little, if any, reward. Paxton lost by a major margin. Musk remained silent for about eight hours as results poured in, each piece of news more disastrous for his rightwing project than the last. In what seemed like capitulation, he deleted a Tuesday tweet that read: “Vote red today!”

after newsletter promotion

By Wednesday morning, the SpaceX CEO wanted off the planet. “Datacenters in space are looking pretty good right now,” he wrote.

He may not get the chance to set up his orbital computers. Democrats may likewise investigate or attempt to unwind the multibillion-dollar merger of SpaceX and Musk’s AI company, xAI, which makes the Nazi-friendly nudification bot Grok. xAI has a $200m contract with the US military, which likewise seems like an easy win for Democrats to meddle with.

Mark Zuckerberg may feel deja vu when he finds himself sitting across the table from an inquisition, as he repeatedly did at the end of the 2010s. The Meta CEO made a nakedly political pivot under Trump 2.0 with his shift to the right. He appeared at Mar-a-Lago to show off Meta’s camera-equipped glasses to Trump and axed his company’s vaunted diversity, equity and inclusion program as the president waged war on DEI.

Already the most disliked man in America, Zuckerberg will show with his next era whether he believes in anything as much as he does power. Was his interest in jiu-jitsu mixed martial arts authentic or a way to ingratiate himself with the manosphere’s podcast hosts? We may know by the time he faces his first inquest. Perhaps he’ll return to the liberal roots of his former public image like founding a pro-immigration non-profit, as he did a decade ago.

Meanwhile, OpenAI’s CEO, Sam Altman, himself seen at Mar-a-Lago, appears in damage control mode on Tuesday. His tweet on Tuesday night read like a Bernie Sanders talking point: “People should not cede control of the future to superintelligence, and that requirement should ultimately constrain AI progress.” Inviting human-first regulation, Altman appeared to be trying to distance himself from Trump’s free-for-all stance, and the president’s recent efforts to rebrand AI as “superintelligence”.

But the billionaires of Silicon Valley seem unlikely to rehabilitate their public images overnight after years of pandering only to power brokers. They have little to say on the issues of the day: affordability and corruption. The majority of Americans see them as avatars of extreme wealth inequality and cynical, pay-to-play politics. What can a billionaire offer a populace angry about prices?

Was Elon Musk the US midterms’ biggest loser?

Datacenters were on the ballot. US voters rejected them

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: Elon Musk’s nearly half a billion dollars in midterms spending was a flop
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Nick Robins-Early
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
The tech billionaire set spending record as he poured $446m into campaigns for failed Republican candidates

Elon Musk set a record for election spending this year after pouring nearly half a billion dollars into backing Republicans in the US midterm elections. It turned out to be a poor investment.

The SpaceX and Tesla CEO contributed at least $446m to Republican-aligned Super Pacs and groups over the course of the elections, specifically targeting several key Senate races in an effort to help the Trump administration retain Republican control of Congress. He outdid his own 2024 spending of nearly $290m. Yet as Democrats swept to power across the country on Tuesday night, it became clear that Musk would get nearly nothing in return for his hundreds of millions in spending.

Democrats won every one of the five Senate races where Musk’s America Pac spent the most money backing Republican candidates. In Texas, where Musk’s empire is based and where he directed most of his political efforts, Republicans lost the Senate race, governor’s office and are expected to relinquish control of the state house.

After months of Musk posting attacks on Democrats and amplifying election conspiracy theories on X, the tech mogul was unusually quiet on election night. He jokingly posted “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” but the top Republican mega-donor was otherwise largely silent on the results.

Musk’s losses from midterms go beyond the enormous sums that he dumped into failed campaigns, however, potentially ending an era of lax regulation and cozy relations with state officials that has benefited his companies. The world’s richest person will soon face a House, Senate and Texas government filled with Democrats that have vowed to take a tougher stance on tech and specifically scrutinize his operations in particular.

Altogether, Musk’s political spending this midterms flowed into at least eight Republican-aligned Super Pacs that targeted races across the country, with the largest donation of at least $216m going into his own America Pac. He also gave $168m to the Senate Leadership Fund, which backed a series of candidates that included the Texas Republican Ken Paxton.

Out of all of Musk’s political activity in midterms, the contest where he put the most money and focus was the Senate race in Texas between Paxton and Democrat James Talarico. America Pac spent at least $28m on anti-Talarico ad buys and messaging alone, while Musk repeatedly posted attacks on X, his social media platform, such as “Talarico wants to trans your kids and destroy the border.”

After Talarico achieved a commanding win on Tuesday night, the Democratic senator-elect referenced Musk in his victory speech.

“We just proved that all the money in the world is no match for the people of Texas,” Talarico said. “We just sent a message to every billionaire mega-donor, every trillionaire mega-donor.”

Senate races in Michigan, Maine, Ohio and Iowa similarly went for Democratic candidates after America Pac spent tens of millions supporting Republican campaigns. The Pac’s money had gone into attack ads that focused on transgender rights or accused Democrats of being radical socialists.

after newsletter promotion

Even if Musk’s spending was not successful, it doesn’t mean it wasn’t impactful. Musk and the Super Pacs’ expenditures created several of the most expensive races in US history and set a potential precedent for how much spending will take place in the 2028 presidential election. It will also probably spur months of analysis around the limits of what money can buy in politics.

Musk’s businesses have benefited greatly from lucrative contracts with the Trump administration, as well as Trump’s hands-off approach to regulating artificial intelligence. In Texas, the state legislature and Governor Greg Abbott have provided him a friendly environment to do business while passing laws backed by the billionaire’s lobbyists.

Gina Hinojosa, the incoming Democratic governor in Texas, will probably take a more critical stance towards Musk and his businesses. Hinojosa has called for a datacenter moratorium and has been in a legal battle in recent months to gain access to unredacted emails between Abbott’s office and Musk. Meanwhile, House Democrats have called for launching investigations into Musk’s conduct while he was leader of the so-called “department of government efficiency” last year and vowed to scrutinize federal funding for his companies.

https://www.theguardian.com/games/2026/n.title: Gotta buy ’em all: how Pokémon card collecting became race against scalpers
https://www.theguardian.com/games/2026/n.author: Zoe Wood

Fans trying to access latest releases are being priced out in a cut-throat market driven by crypto-like hype

T
he runaway demand for Pokemon cards is because they are being hyped “like crypto”, according to one young fan who had spent the night queueing outside a London store to make sure he did not miss out on the latest card release.

Before its 10am opening on Friday, the line outside the pop culture store Forbidden Planet in central London snaked past five others and, despite its strict sales policy, was probably “50/50” fans and resellers, said Kai, who had been there since 3am.

The 25-year-old has loved Pokémon since he was a child but the immense rise in reselling and scalping in recent years means fans like him are being priced out. “The cards used to be cheap but they have ballooned in price,” he says.

Kai blames the fact that “people in the crypto space have got into Pokémon” for fuelling the now rabid interest in buying cards for profit, and even gambling, with fans targeted by livestreams to bid on cards.

The signs on the door of Forbidden Planet spell out the rules. Like other stores, it limits high-demand products – in this case the £49.99 Delta Reign “elite trainer” box – to one a customer. (The set will be selling with big markups on eBay by the end of the day.)

It also has what it calls a “supplier-requested unsealing policy”. This approach deters some resellers because an opened product cannot be sold on as brand new.

“It’s calmer here,” said Kai of the queue of more than 120 people. “The people and workers are nice here.”

Like others in the queue he has (Pokémon) war stories of fights and overwhelmed security staff.

The clamour for cards has the most determined buyers zooming from store to store by e-bike. Others reportedly get around purchase limits by changing clothes or paying cash for other people’s hauls.

The traders were identifiable by their multiple shopping bags, said Kai, who added that “as a collector there is no reason to have that many”.

Some stores, such as Argos, only sell the trading cards online. On Amazon, high-demand lines are sold by an “invite-only” process designed to combat scalper bots.

With tattoos of his favourite Pokémon, Gengar and Dragonite ,on his leg and arm, Anthony, 26, started collecting when he was five. He secured the third queue spot after coming straight from his waiting shift at 1am.

He admits to doing “everything” – buying, selling and exchanging cards – and using the sale proceeds to subsidise his collection.

Like Luke, second in the queue, and Hiep, who secured first place at 11pm, he wanted to buy the expensive elite trainer sets. Luke, 30, said nostalgia around Pokémon’s 30th anniversary this year was the “straw that broke me”.

He had a binder with placeholders for missing cards. It was an “expensive” hobby with scalpers being the reason “people like us turn up so early”.

Frustrated parents are increasingly found lurking in Reddit threads and Facebook groups looking for advice on how to buy cards for their children.

Even though Pokémon produces about 10bn cards a year, Calvin Innes, a fandom and pop culture strategist, said the demand had “outrun the machines, so everything else – bots, scalpers, queues etc – sits on the fact that there is a hard supply limit”.

“It’s not impossible for kids to get cards but the buying experience has gotten really ugly,” said Innes, author of Fandom Power: Marketing in the Age of Nerd Culture. “As a father of three kids who are all into Pokémon, it sucks.”

While elite trainer and booster box sets, plus Pokémon Center exclusives, were the hardest products to get, Innes said single packs and blisters were more accessible, although smaller high street retailers sold out quickly.

He also advised parents to buy singles from a UK card shop, singles marketplace, such as Cardmarket, or top-rated sellers on eBay UK.

Another option for parents was to go to a prerelease or league event at a game shop. Innes said they typically cost £25-£30 and the child usually got guaranteed cards, and the opportunity to play the game.

Daniel Garnett, who owns the Hull Pops Gaming Centre in Hessle, East Yorkshire, runs a free kids club and said he tries to keep product back for regular players. “We teach kids all about the Pokémon game, about the cards and how to play. We also have a qualified Pokémon judge that helps out.

“Sadly, however, about a month ago, we had lots of parents bring their kids in purely to buy product, and had no intention of playing or staying for the session.”

https://www.theguardian.com/games/2026/n.title: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time has revived the midnight game launch – but was it worth the wait?
https://www.theguardian.com/games/2026/n.author: Tom Regan
https://www.theguardian.com/games/2026/n.text:
When our writer found himself among the hundreds on Oxford Street hoping to get their hands on early copies and collectibles, it was a heartwarming reminder of the shared experience of fandom

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time review – a dream come true

I
t is Thursday night and I am sat blurry-eyed and runny nosed outside the Argos on Oxford Street. Incredibly, I am far from alone. This is not some strange protest against the popular retailer. When the clock strikes midnight, the lavish 4K Switch 2 remake of beloved N64 classic The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time will be released, and I have joined a lengthy queue of about 500 fans desperate to snag early copies. There are similar events taking place across the world, from Melbourne to Mexico City; at key locations, Nintendo has senior executives waiting at the tills.

These days, of course, most video games are bought as digital copies that download straight to your PC or console on the day of release. You don’t even have to get out of bed to start playing. But in a bygone era, when we used to go to shops to buy games, midnight launches offered a space for likeminded enthusiasts to gather and celebrate their fandom. Every Call of Duty, Halo or Grand Theft Auto release would have fans queueing outside branches of Game or Electronics Boutique, many dressed as favourite characters.

As one of the few Brits deluded enough to spend six hours queueing at the Wii U’s midnight launch, I have a certain fondness for the game launch as a cultural event rather than just a weird display of performative consumerism. There was something heartwarming about seeing the video game hype cycle transformed into a shared experience.

In our age of downloads and streaming services, however, you might wonder why anyone would bother queueing for hours in the November chill. Well, myself and hundreds of others have made the pilgrimage for one infuriatingly irresistible reason: those attending the launch would not only get a copy of the game but also a limited ocarina-shaped keyring and an exclusive replica of the original 1998 N64 box. To you, perhaps, a worthless piece of cardboard – but to us, a highly collectible, nostalgia-soaked … piece of cardboard.

Arriving at the queue for 22:45, bottle of water in hand, it’s not long before I realise I may have already blown it. With midnight launch events now few and far between, I had no idea whether people would still show up. Yet London’s Zelda fans had answered the Ocarina’s hymn and assembled en masse – snaking all the way around the corner.

Thankfully, we’re soon informed by staff that everyone will be receiving a precious exclusive box regardless. Even if the stock runs out tonight, they say, we will all be posted one. Cue the Zelda treasure chest fanfare. I befriend a popcorn-munching man behind me who regales me with tales of the GameCube launch, as confused gen Z queuers regard us elderly Nintendo fanatics with disdain. The throng shuffles ever closer from the sidestreet into the back street, but when the clock strikes midnight, the shop is still a world away. A parade of men with cameraphones clutched to their chests circles the snaking queue, recording our suffering for future generations.

At 2am, progress halts and frustration grows. Reluctantly, I scout to the front to investigate. It transpires that the store will soon shut, and the hundreds of queuers that remain will need to leave their details to receive the feted box by post. By the time I scrawl my name and address, I have been queueing for four hours.

As I wait for my taxi, questioning my life choices, I see a fellow cardboard enthusiast peering into the shuttered window, wistfully admiring the Zelda display. He tells me that his partner attended the Paris midnight launch where the queues were similarly enormous. Not only did she walk away with nothing, but Nintendo France were not taking details or promising to post boxes out to unlucky queuers. As my lift pulls up, the nostalgic appeal of the midnight launch has all but dissipated. I take small comfort in knowing one thing – at least we’re better off than the French.

https://www.theguardian.com/games/2026/n.author: Keith Stuart
https://www.theguardian.com/games/2026/n.text:
As GTA 6 looms, we look at the films that have influenced Rockstar’s creatives, from Heat to Bonnie and Clyde, via Boyz n the Hood and Speed

G
rand Theft Auto is arguably the most cinematic video game series ever made. Over the past three decades, the games have studied and stolen the themes, conventions and visual dynamism of great gangster and action movies, applying them to open worlds filled with low-life characters and grand set-piece possibilities. Here then are the movies (and TV show) that have shaped the GTA experience, from the 1996 original to this year’s inescapable instalment.

Not signed in before? Continue with Google

Really? Jan de Bont’s ludicrous bus bomb action flick? Well yes, according to Paul Farley, a game designer who worked on the original GTA, Speed was a huge influence, no doubt due to its fast pace, quip-filled dialogue and wanton vehicular destruction. Farley and his co-designers also took inspiration from 1980s Saturday afternoon TV classics Knight Rider and The A-Team. Basically, anything with a lot of car chases and things exploding.

A Coney Island street gang must make it back to their own territory after a midnight summit in the Bronx, facing multiple attacks from rival crews en route. Directed by Walter Hill, the revered 1979 cult classic remains a stylish depiction of a city in crisis – and a major influence on Rockstar. “This was one of our favourites during the making of GTA 2,” Sam Houser told Official PlayStation Magazine during the making of GTA 3. “It was a great inspiration when creating the various street gangs, and it’s also good for reference on how to construct really seedy, run-down urban areas.” Rockstar loved it so much they made a criminally overlooked adaptation.

Brian De Palma’s explosive, neon-splattered examination of life and bloody death in the Miami drug underworld set the bar for sleaze, style and anarchy that every GTA instalment has aimed at. Seductive and unstoppable, Tony Montana is the ultimate action protagonist, while the film’s footsoldier-to-king narrative – a staple of the Hollywood gangster picture – is fundamental to Rockstar’s series. The film’s synth-laden soundtrack was also hugely influential on the sound of the games. Five of its songs were featured in GTA 3.

The ultra stylish 1980s TV crime series kickstarted the career of its producer Michael Mann, while capturing the glitz, glamour and simmering drug-fuelled violence of the city. It was a major tonal reference for GTA Vice City, and no doubt a lingering inspiration on GTA 6. “Michael Mann’s use of colour and light is wonderful,” Sam Houser told Edge in 2012. “Miami is such a beautiful place anyway, so the light is gorgeous, but his use of night lighting made it so glossy and sexy. He’s also an expert in the use of weapons, and we met all of the weapons experts who worked on Miami Vice. We got into the details in a hardcore way.”

The energy of Martin Scorsese’s movies absolutely fills the GTA series – not just all the violence and chaos, but also the emphasis on the immigrant experience in America and on the connected themes of male identity, brotherhood and betrayal. Goodfellas is so seminal to the series, Rockstar even employed Ray Liotta to voice Tommy Vercetti, the main character in GTA: Vice City. Like Scorsese, Rockstar is also obsessed with the importance of popular music as a structural element of its worlds, cramming the games with hundreds of licensed tracks selected to provide an appropriate aural backdrop to the carnage. Taxi Driver and Mean Streets were also clear influences on the Liberty City-based games.

For GTA: San Andreas, Rockstar transferred the action to 1990s Los Santos, a pastiche of Los Angeles with its mix of skyscrapers, glitzy mansions and sprawling poverty-stricken neighbourhoods. The model for hero Carl “CJ” Johnson was undoubtedly Tre Styles from John Singleton’s 1991 drama Boyz n the Hood, a young kid desperate to escape the local gang culture, but equally seduced by it. The game’s woozy orange patina, its hip-hop soundtrack and its cast list of rappers, gang leaders and corrupt cops drew heavily from this film, and also contemporaries such as Menace II Society and Colors, as well as cult 80s classic To Live and Die in LA.

For GTA 4, Rockstar wanted to explore a different kind of criminal narrative, with a darker, more sombre tone. Its protagonist, ex-soldier Niko Bellic, is an eastern European immigrant who comes to Liberty City to live the American dream, but instead finds an abyss of crime and violence that has already swallowed his cousin, Roman. Dan Houser has said the game has no major movie inspirations, but there are certainly echoes of Russian neo-noir film Brother, about a de-mobbed soldier who becomes entangled in his brother’s violent gangland empire.

De Palma again, with another staple narrative of gangster cinema: the return of the veteran. Al Pacino’s career criminal Carlito Brigante is freed from prison and wants to retire, but is inevitably pulled back into a quagmire of drugs and violence. Rockstar art director Aaron Garbut has cited this film’s nuanced underworld characters as an influence on Vice City, but it is there too in the dark, inescapable fate of GTA 4’s Niko Bellic.

Robert De Niro’s world-weary professional bank robber was surely the template for Michael De Santa, the lead character in GTA 5, a game structured around the sorts of epic heists that made Heat so gripping and visually mesmerising. That film’s crazed antagonist Waingro is also present in the game as co-lead Trevor, a similarly murderous, torturing psychopath. The way Michael Mann shot Los Angeles also feeds into the Los Santos of GTA 5, a slick, soulless megalopolis baking beneath a pitiless sun. People have also seen the hyper-stylised, hyper-violent LA of Drive in the game, though that film’s director Nicolas Winding Refn was himself clearly inspired by the GTA series – a self-reflexive closing of the circle of influence that perfectly encapsulates Rockstar’s culturally carnivorous series.

The 1967 movie that ushered in the new Hollywood of the 70s also provides the modern blueprint of the “romantic-couple-on-the-run” narrative. Warren Beatty and Faye Dunaway are beautifully watchable in their lead roles and director Arthur Penn doesn’t shy away from the sort of graphic, stylised violence that GTA 6 will no doubt revel in. It will be fascinating to see how layered the central relationship in the game is and whether it will stray into the more gritty, sexy, adrenaline-fuelled style of Sam Peckinpah’s The Getaway.

Titanium Court is a bizarre world of 8-bit fairies, Shakespeare and surprise songs – its magic lies in never knowing what on earth is going on

Don’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up here

E
arlier this year, I was stuck in hospital for several days, fuzzy on pain medication and bored out of my mind, with nothing but a Steam Deck for company. In the middle of one of those long nights, unable to sleep, I played a game called Titanium Court. It’s a strange creation that looks like it was made for the ZX Spectrum and reads like a postmodern Shakespeare adaptation – a compelling mix of strategy game and match-3 where you rearrange battlefields by matching tiles, before sending tiny lo-fi fairy armies to their deaths.

At the end of this late-night run, I met a boss I’d defeated before – a comically hungry dragon – and the game asked if I would like to skip the boss fight and enjoy a musical performance instead. A game has never asked me this before. Of course, I accepted. And then, instead of the familiar tiled battlefield, I was looking at a pixellated singer-songwriter, who launched into an extremely long preamble about the mating habits of the Pacific salmon before saying, “This is a song for anyone else who ever got so horny they could die,” and launching into a soulful acoustic guitar number accompanied by crude images of leaping fish. I began to wonder if my meds were making me hallucinate.

That pixellated singer-songwriter is AP Thomson, the game’s 36-year-old almost-solo developer. When I interviewed him, he told me he learned to play the guitar with the express intention of making music for Titanium Court, and went to open mic nights every week for over a year, workshopping songs to replace the boss fights – songs that are, I must emphasise, entirely optional for the player. He also made all the warped, chill, shoegazey music that accompanies the rest of this singularly weird game, which started out as a side project while he was helping to make the (also brilliant) Consume Me with designer Jenny Jiao Hsia.

It was a Covid project in the beginning, and indeed it does have a distinct flavour of “do you think a depressed person could make this?” about it. I get the impression that Thomson put pretty much every thought and idea he has ever had in there, somewhere, spiralling out from a deceptively simple matching game.

Titanium Court is one of my games of the year because even after 30 years of playing video games, I genuinely had no idea what was going to happen every time I loaded it up. It begins as you walk through the woods and are magically transported to a fairy castle, where you are suddenly expected to take up the crown and lead the fairies in a never-ending war. It is woozy and surreal and verbose: in between the battles, you wander the castle and its secret passages, talking to the fairies and trying to figure out what the hell is going on. There are obvious echoes of A Midsummer Night’s Dream; the screen is framed by curtains, and the game is framed as a play within a play within a game. Sometimes the fairies talk about her – that is, you, the player, looking down on them from on high – in hushed, terrified tones.

“Fairies are a really good avenue for exploring weird ideas about the world,” Thomson told me. “As a narrative plot device, it let me do whatever I wanted, which was great for a side project where I was throwing all sorts of stuff into the mix.” In 2019 he read Spinning Silver by Naomi Novik, “which is a really good fantasy novel in the mode of a fairytale, and I thought, we should be doing this more. I got a little sick of the Tolkien-style fantasy. It’s interesting that Shakespeare isn’t as common a touchpoint in game development as Marvel and Tolkien.”

I’ve been a game critic for a very long time, so I really enjoy it when I struggle to describe a game, and what’s good about it. It’s an interesting creative challenge. But I am not going to say much more about how Titanium Court works or what happens within it, because discovering that is the entire point of the game. Fairies allow for a kind of unreality and double meaning, for things to not really make sense in the moment or indeed at all. I experienced many moments that seemed so specific and serendipitous that I felt as if I must surely be the only player to have ever seen them.

“For a lot of it, I did wonder if anybody is actually going to see this particular thing or combination,” Thomson says. During testing, his girlfriend came across a scene that he didn’t even remember writing.

The sense of unreality is heightened by Titanium Court’s very odd 8-bit-style pixel art and extremely pink colour palette: it’s very 80s core, and the fairies around the castle are mostly power-dressed in suits and skirts. This visual character was inspired by stock photos, Thomson says. “Stock photos do feel otherworldly, right? They feel like they are representations of common parts of human experience, but they’re also caricatures of those things … there’s an uncanniness to the stock photo.”

In the game fiction there is a spell keeping you inside Titanium Court’s castle – but I didn’t need any magic to keep me obsessed with this game long after I left hospital. I think I’ve seen almost everything it has to offer, but I can’t possibly be sure. Over time you come to understand its warped logic and its sense of humour; you know when it’s about to screw you over, and you anticipate the laugh. It’s now out on consoles and smartphones, so you no longer need a Steam Deck or PC to play it. Give it a go – you will never forget it.

Speaking of games of the year: I have spent the past couple of weeks playing through one of the most pivotal games of my childhood in newly remade form, and I am happy to report that The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time on Switch 2 is a dream come true. It’s always a risk returning to games this important (and this old), but in contrast to the light-touch remaster that came out on the Nintendo 3DS in 2011, this is a full-on reinvention that brings out the best of what was already there, while elegantly addressing whatever needed updating. It is a melancholy story, rather than a whimsical one – there is a central tragedy to child Link awakening in the Temple of Time as a grown man, with the weight of saving the world on his shoulders. But there are so many moments of pure delight that I fail to see how anyone could be unmoved by it. What a time to be into video games!
