https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.title: As cancer treatments become more effective, we must ask: what is life like for the people who receive them? | Ranjana Srivastava
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.author: Ranjana Srivastava
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text:
Many treatments are now extending lives but the measure of progress should not end with a scan or a survival curve

T
wo decades ago, a dear friend called me in a trembling voice. Was there hope for his young nephew, whose cancer had spread to the brain? Sadly, “no”, I said. But today, for such patients, there are options that were unimaginable back then.

Recently, researchers at the European Society For Medical Oncology presented the latest chapter results from a randomised controlled trial of a bespoke cancer vaccine for patients with high-risk melanoma. The trial involved 1,137 patients whose melanoma had been surgically removed but remained at high recurrence risk. They received either pembrolizumab, an established immunotherapy, or pembrolizumab combined with an experimental mRNA vaccine, designed to help the immune system recognise and attack targets unique to the patient’s tumour.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

At two years, 82.2% of those who received the combination were alive without their cancer returning, compared with 70% of those given pembrolizumab alone – a difference of about 12 percentage points. The combination also reduced the relative risk of distant metastasis or death by 38%.

These results raise the prospect that personalised vaccines could become an important addition to cancer treatment. Whether they will deliver similar benefits in other cancers remains to be established.

Overall survival data are not yet mature, so we don’t know whether the combination helps people live longer. Fever, injection-site pain and fatigue were common with the vaccine combination. Rates of severe treatment-related adverse events were similar between the groups; quality-of-life data is not yet available.

The standing ovation for the researchers was deserved, as was praise for the pharmaceutical companies that backed an idea that was once a pipe dream. Yet as cancer treatments become more effective, another question gains importance: what is life like for the people who receive them?

Treatment can delay a cancer’s return but can impose a considerable burden. Side-effects, fatigue, impaired mobility, psychological trauma, financial strain and the disruption of family and career all shape the experience.

In my work, I am often sobered by the juxtaposition of scans showing no cancer with a patient who cannot sleep, work or enjoy what others take for granted.

Recently, a retired academic approaching 90 told me: “My dear, the best thing you could do for me is get me safely home.” For this patient, their priority was clear; pursuing intervention would have caused a serious decline in their quality of life.

That does not mean some people should automatically be offered less treatment, or that the value of treatment depends on age alone. But it does mean oncologists must understand what each person hopes treatment will achieve, and explain what they may have to endure to get there.

My experience with elderly patients has made me more conscious of my other patients who are mid-career, raising children or caring for relatives.

The parent whose persistent nausea makes school drop-offs impossible.

The hairdresser who can’t work due to neuropathy.

The executive dismayed by cognitive fog.

A treatment that offers a cure or extra months of survival may be worthwhile to one person, even with significant toxicity. Others may place greater value on earning an income, caring for a child or living independently. These are not competing definitions of success: they are individual priorities that good medicine should respect.

Yet quality of life is often reported less rigorously than response, recurrence and survival. Less than a third of trials report quality-of-life measures in the primary publication, which most professionals read, and just half publish them at all.

Patient-centred care demands that information about quality of life should appear alongside the main findings, not years later in a separate publication, or not at all. When patients ask, “Doctor, how will this treatment affect my life?”, the information gap can become an indirect permission for oncologists to skim over the granular details.

A recent paper in The Lancet Oncology urges better reporting of health-related quality of life in trials of adjuvant treatments (treatments given after surgery to reduce the risk of recurrence). The researchers argue that average scores conceal important differences between patients: trials should instead report how many people experience a clinically meaningful deterioration, how long it lasts, and whether and when they recover.

Collecting quality-of-life data is not simple but, when data is missing, we should know why. Questionnaires are burdensome for sick patients and doctors have a different notion of quality of life from their patients. Of course, for a patient facing a life-threatening diagnosis, a chance at cure may reasonably outweigh significant toxicity concerns, but imperfect measurement is a reason to improve the status quo, not to look away.

From where I sit, I see immense gratitude for modern therapies but not inconsiderable decisional regret: “If only I had known.” We should empower patients to ask and be ready to tell them not only how likely a treatment is to work but also what it may cost them in daily life. Far too often, they find out later that treatment can bring months, years or even a lifetime of adverse effects.

None of this downplays scientific progress. Many treatments are now extending lives and personalised medicine may bring further gains. But the measure of progress should not end with a scan or a survival curve. Researchers must collect quality of life outcomes diligently, clinicians should discuss them openly and health systems should treat them as central, not optional, to care.

While writing this column, my thoughts returned to the young man and his family, whose happiness for today’s melanoma patients is tinged with regret for their own loss. Today’s advance stands on the shoulders of the patients who generously volunteered to a take part in a study not knowing if they would themselves benefit. They deserve our gratitude.

Our ambition should be not only to keep people alive but to protect the lives they want to live, and to recognise that the true cost of treatment is measured in more than money.

Ranjana Srivastava is an Australian oncologist, award-winning author and Fulbright scholar. Her latest book is Every Word Matters: Writing to Engage the Public

When the water in Flint, Michigan, became contaminated with dangerous levels of lead, Dr Siddhartha Roy, then a third year PhD student, was part of the team of scientists who publicly contradicted state and federal claims that it was safe. He became a local hero until a new piece of research challenged the idea that children in Flint had been left permanently brain damaged by the crisis. https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.title: From gold rush to cosmic questions: a South Dakota mine and the search for the secrets of the universe
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.author: Ian Sample Science editor
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.text:
A mile beneath the Black Hills, scientists are building giant detectors to analyse neutrino particles – and possibly find the answer to existence

F
or more than a century, the mining town of Lead, in the Black Hills of South Dakota, attracted workers with a taste for gold. Now, a flagship experiment being built in the old mine is drawing scientists in search of more intriguing riches: answers to the deepest mysteries of the universe.

Construction of the Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (Dune) in the former Homestake mine is due to start on Monday. Engineers will begin assembling four giant detectors inside caverns blasted from rock a mile underground.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

Once switched on, the detectors will quietly spark and flicker as ghostly particles called neutrinos hurtle through them. Some will arrive from the sun and distant supernovae, others in an intense beam sent through 800 miles (1,300km) of rock from a government laboratory near Chicago, Illinois.

Observing the neutrinos could uncover entirely new science and shed light on cosmic spectacles, such as the death of stars and the birth of black holes. Scientists are particularly hopeful of solving one of the most enduring puzzles in nature: why everything around us is made from matter and not its “evil twin”, antimatter. In other words, why we, and why anything, is here at all.

“It’s a super exciting time to be working on this,” said Dr Kate Shaw, an experimental particle physicist on Dune from the University of Sussex. “Neutrinos do not make sense yet and they could open a door to new physics.”

Neutrinos are the most abundant matter particles in the universe, outnumbered only by photons, the massless particles of light that illuminate the universe. They are produced in natural nuclear reactions, such as those that power the sun, in radioactive decay and in particle accelerators.

Even by physicists’ standards, neutrinos are oddballs. The chargeless particles barely interact with other matter: about a trillion pass unnoticed through your body each second. Neutrinos come in three varieties, all with minuscule but different masses. Weirdly, they change from one variety to another, a process called oscillation, as they travel. “It’s a very strange behaviour,” said Shaw. “It’s like me throwing you an apple and it turns into a banana.”

Lead has a history with these peculiar particles. In the 1960s, the physicist Ray Davis followed miners down the shaft and built a detector from a 100,000-gallon tank filled with dry-cleaning fluid. Shielded so deep beneath the ground, the detector became the first to record neutrinos from the sun as they struck chlorine atoms in the fluid and turned them into argon.

The mine closed in 2001 and transitioned, thanks to visionary forethought, into a dedicated subterranean laboratory, the Sanford Underground Research Facility (Surf). It is already home to the Lux-Zeplin (LZ) experiment which last month reported the first potential detection of dark matter.

“We’ve gone from mining the Earth to helping scientists explore the universe,” said Robin Lucero, Lead’s city administrator, whose family has lived locally for generations. “We’re incredibly proud and lucky that Dune is happening here, and Surf, which has other experiments like LZ. Having world-class science brings new opportunities, new people and new possibilities for our local businesses and especially our young people.”

Unlike Davis’s apparatus, the Dune experiment is enormous. Made from more than 4,000 tonnes of steel, the detectors will stand up to five-storeys high and hold a combined 70,000 tonnes of liquid argon that must be chilled to -200C. Assembling the detectors should take nearly three years. Filling them with liquid argon, another year.

“This is a heavy duty engineering operation,” and a partnership with the skilled local workforce, said Prof David Newbold, of the UK’s Science and Technology Facilities Council and a Dune spokesperson. “It’s like building a ship underground.” The UK is the largest international partner in the US-led experiment and is making core detector components, critical computing to reconstruct events in the detectors, and the graphite target needed to generate neutrinos at Femilab, a particle physics facility in Illinois.

Once operational, Dune will study an intense beam of neutrinos sent from Fermilab through 800 miles of the Earth’s crust and mantle. Most neutrinos will shoot straight through, but every so often one will strike an argon atom, creating a flicker of light and a pulse of electric charge. Analysing these will reveal intimate details about the mysterious particles.

One big question surrounds the masses of different neutrinos. Which is lightest and which heaviest? The answer could reveal fundamental new forces of nature. And in an attempt to answer the matter v antimatter question, Dune will look for subtle differences between neutrinos and their antimatter twins, antineutrinos.

Beyond the beams of particles sent from Fermilab, Dune will also study neutrinos arriving from space, carrying with them fresh information on stellar explosions and the formation of black holes.

Earlier this month, the Nobel prize for physics honoured the Belgian researcher Francis Halzen, who used a cubic kilometre of Antarctica to detect high-energy neutrinos from deep space. But detection is far from the end of the story. “This really is going to be a golden era,” Newbold said. “There’s a lot more of that to come.”

https://www.theguardian.com/science/ng-i.title: Ukraine’s new frontier: how space has become critical to balance of the war
https://www.theguardian.com/science/ng-i.author: Peter Beaumont Senior international correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/science/ng-i.text:
In a war driven by drones and battlefield sensors, access to space is essential. After Starlink speed restrictions and Russian Oreshnik missile strikes, Kyiv is racing to develop its own space capabilities

For people in the Russian industrial city of Samara on the banks of the Volga, the first they knew of the Ukrainian attack were detonations that sent a column of smoke into the air.

If the Kremlin was vague about the target, video footage on social media soon made it clear what had been hit in the early hours of 15 August: the Progress Rocket and Space Centre, manufacturer of Russia’s Soyuz-2 rockets.

Two Flamingo missiles had slammed into a pair of buildings, including a facility known as 106A, a “clean room” where motherboards for the Soyuz launch systems were assembled.

In the midst of other Ukrainian strikes against Russian refineries and industry, the Samara attack stood out, providing evidence of a spreading war, the geographical impact of which – already felt across Europe via hybrid attacks, and assaults on civilian shipping in the Black Sea – has crept into the domain of space.

In a conflict that is redefining warfare through the heavy use of drones and battlefield sensors, access to space and the satellites that power those systems – as well as the ability to disrupt enemy operations there – has become ever more critical.

The attack on Samara was a case in point, hitting the rockets that deliver Russia’s new Rassvet satellite system, which is being rapidly deployed as a replacement for Elon Musk’s Starlink, from which Russia was shut out earlier this year.

In addition, Ukraine has attacked other sites belonging to Roscosmos this year, including Korolyov, a large complex north of Moscow, and a Ukrainian-built radio telescope captured by Russia in Crimea.

Russia’s attempts to rapidly deploy its Rassvet network are not the only challenge from space that Ukraine faces. Moscow has also used Oreshnik ballistic missiles on at least three occasions – a system that launches into near space, then deploys multiple independently targetable warheads initially designed for nuclear weapons.

All of this has prompted Kyiv to intensify efforts to diversify its own access to space-based systems away from the US and Starlink, which was controversially choked in recent weeks, and to develop new space countermeasures against threats such as the Oreshnik.

Ukraine has conducted at least three tests of near-space interceptions as it has sought to launch its own sovereign satellites, joining a rapidly expanding number of countries working towards a foothold in space.

That became a reality last month when Ukraine and Denmark’s GomSpace announced they had successfully launched the Obria Nano, the first test satellite for a future independent Ukrainian communications network, reportedly envisaging about 245 satellites.

The increasing incursion of the Ukraine conflict into space, say experts, is only the latest evidence of the rapid militarisation of a domain the treaties for which remain ill defined, outdated and difficult to enforce.

In September the US air force secretary, Troy Meink, admitted for the first time that Washington had deployed “on-orbit space control weapons” amid reports that Russia had regularly flown its satellites close to US and other countries’ assets in space.

As if to underline that point, a few weeks later a Russian satellite, Kosmos 2612, was observed aggressively manoeuvring towards a commercial radar satellite operated by the Finnish group Iceye that provides three-dimensional terrain imaging to the Ukrainian military, in what experts described as an act of deliberate harassment.

“[Space warfare] has been talked about as the future,” says Dr Elena Grossfeld, an expert on space and security at the Swedish Defence University. “But we’re already in that future.”

For Russia, Grossfeld argues, space has become essential to military success, with Moscow treating offensive operations there as a precursor to broader conflict in a new reality where war is inseparable from satellite-based intelligence and targeting.

“This started before the war in Ukraine,” Grossfield said. “The US Space Force [then second in command, Gen David Thompson] said in 2021 that the US was seeing daily attacks [by Russia and China] on US satellites.

“They are not necessarily kinetic [attacks], but now with the war and with everyone’s dependency on space for intelligence and communications, it has become front and centre.”

While Grossfield said Russia’s intention in the recent “bullying” of the Iceye satellite was not clear, one possibility was to force it to use fuel to change course and in doing so shorten its lifespan.

That is not the only tactic that has been seen. Russia has also used signal jamming, laser-dazzling of satellites, and placed “inspector” spy satellites near foreign space assets.

Complicating what is happening in space, experts say, is that treaties on governance in space, and deployment of weapons, have in recent years been overtaken.

Victoria Samson, the head of the space security and stability programme at the Secure World Foundation, which advocates for space safety and sustainability, noted a rapid increase in the number of countries operating in space, in tandem with the expansion of commercial activities by companies such as Elon Musk’s SpaceX and Jeff Bezos’s Blue Origin.

But while many countries have opted to use SpaceX for its satellite launches, Musk’s recent actions towards Ukraine, cutting Starlink data speeds, have forced a rapid rethink of whether to rely on unreliable and sometimes ideologically led commercial ventures.

“The big shift in the past decade,” said Samson, “has been towards commercial space operations and that has been an issue in the current conflict [in Ukraine].”

Like Grossfeld, Samson sees frictions in space becoming more overt. “It’s all part of strategic competition,” she said, describing the recent Russian satellite-bullying incident. She added that with more escalation, there had been “more openness on the US side to talk about what they are doing [in relation to weapons in space] while Russia and China are working on a lot of the same stuff.

“Then there is the issue of space being used in an active military conflict. We have already seen Russia jamming GPS, which has resulted in aviation being disrupted over the Baltics. But it has been particularly visible in the issue of Starlink and in pauses by the US to sharing satellite intelligence with Ukraine [that warns] of incoming ballistic missiles.”

If there has been a consequence of Musk’s and the Trump administration’s unreliability, Samson believes, it has been to push countries to seek alternatives. “Like the Russians with [the] Rassvet network, everyone now wants their own versions of Starlink, including the Europeans.”

For Ukraine, said Fedir Venislavskyi, the head of the state security subcommittee of its parliamentary defence committee, that meant a “sovereign” Ukrainian presence in space, now achieved via the Obria Nano satellite.

“Since the war the space domain has been crucial for Ukrainian forces and that has been underlined by recent events – whether at the instigation of the US government or from SpaceX – where we saw communications drop and jeopardise our military’s command-and-control systems.

“Now we need to raise it to another level, not least because the enemy is already threatening Ukrainian territory from international space via Oreshnik missiles. It’s essential we’re not shortsighted about this risk.”

With Russian launch sites now beyond the range of Ukraine’s longest-range missiles, Ukraine has instead conducted three tests on exo-atmospheric kill systems to intercept launches in near space, including launches of weapons piggybacked on very high-flying aircraft.

“It is a priority,” said Venislavskyi. “We’ve already demonstrated launches of exo-atmospheric systems and we are working to see if we can get that in production.” However, he admitted, given the huge demands of the war, funding would be a significant issue.

In the meantime, the new race for space continues.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: New ‘high safety’ chemicals in plastic food packaging linked to lower birth weight, study finds
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Tom Perkins
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Dinch, an allegedly ‘safe’ alternative, used in the EU and US also found to cause fetal development complications

Exposure to a new generation of allegedly “safe” plasticizers is linked to lower birth weight and fetal development complications, which could cause serious health problems later in life, a new peer-reviewed study found.

As the health risks in exposure to common phthalate plasticizers became clear over the last few decades, industry began switching to a new type of chemical, called Dinch, that it claimed was a “high safety”, nontoxic alternative. It is widely used in soft plastic food packaging in the United States and European Union, and is found in children’s toys, medical devices, some textiles, flooring and other consumer goods.

But it may not be as safe as industry has claimed, the New York University Langone Health analysis of federal US health data suggests. There is a dearth of research into Dinch health risks, though what exists points toward the chemicals being hormone disruptors that can impact kids’ development.

The new paper is the first to link Dinch to lower birth weights and birth lengths. Fetal growth problems can raise the risk for heart disease, learning difficulties, obesity and other issues that can echo into adolescence and adulthood, the authors wrote.

“Chemicals should be properly tested for their safety before they become a widespread exposure for unwitting people in the general public,” said Leonardo Trasande, a lead author on the NYU paper.

The chemical is formally named 1,2-cyclohexane dicarboxylic acid diisononyl ester. It is used to make plastic more flexible and durable, and is found in common kitchen products such as cling film and plastic wine corks.

Researchers looked at data for over 6,600 pregnancies collected as part of the National Institutes of Health Environmental influences on Child Health Outcomes (Echo) Program. Up to 70% of women showed Dinch in their urine, and higher levels increased the risk of the child being classified as “small for gestational age”, or below the 10th percentile for babies born at the same stage of pregnancy.

Each tenfold increase in Dinch exposure resulted in a 27-gram reduction in newborn birth weight. An average newborn weighs about 3,400 grams (about 7.5lbs). Hispanic mothers or those with lower education levels were more likely to have children affected by Dinch, the study found.

Previous research on animals and human cells has found that Dinch by-products can interfere with the hormones in a pregnant woman that guide fetal development, and may trigger inflammation that affects how nutrients and oxygen reach the baby, NYU’s authors wrote.

The paper appears to expose yet another classic example of industry replacing one dangerous chemical with a compound that has similar health effects. This resets the regulatory and research process, even though the new chemical is very similar in structure or has the same health risks.

After the US and EU regulators began taking action in the aughts over toxic phthalates such as DEHP, industry began increasing the use of Dinch. German chemical giant BASF is among Dinch’s major producers and overall global production volume jumped from 25,000 tons in 2002 to 400,000 tons in 2024.

This process is called “regrettable substitution”, and is common. For example, many chemical companies and goods producers replaced the most dangerous Pfas “forever chemicals”, such as Pfoa, with GenX compounds. But after years of research, the latter have been found to be more toxic.

Researchers with the Switzerland-based Food Packaging Forum said they are concerned about Dinch and the lack of health information around it. But there is evidence that it migrates from food packaging into food, and levels in the EU population have been increasing across recent decades. The Food Packaging Forum is currently conducting health research on DINCH.

The NYU findings “raise pretty serious concerns about regrettable substitution”, Trasande said.

“These results underscore the need for stronger oversight of chemicals used in food packaging and other household products by requiring they be tested before they are introduced to the market, instead of after they are connected to health concerns,” Trasande said, noting that the plastics treaty under negotiation at the United Nations is an opportunity to establish better policies.

Women can protect themselves and their children by buying plastic-free products as much as possible, including clothing and toys. Look for food at the grocery store that comes in glass packaging, and use glass or wood storage and utensils in the kitchen.
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: Study finds Dinch, an allegedly ‘safe’ alternative, used in the EU and US, is linked to lower birth weight and fetal development complications. The study is the first to link Dinch to lower baby birth weights and birth lengths.

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: Famous New Mexico rock formation destroyed after torrential El Niño rains
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Lois Beckett
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
Officials expected to investigate whether super El Niño storms in US south-west damaged the Alien Throne spires

Undulating, gravity-defying rock spires are one of the most magical parts of the landscape of the US south-west.

But after torrential rainstorms linked to the super El Niño season, at least one famous rock formation in north-west New Mexico has been found in pieces.

And as local communities in the Four Corners region struggle with the aftermath of flooding, washed-out roads and damaged homes, more damage to the region’s natural wonders may still be discovered.

Kialo Winters was leading a tour of the Valley of Dreams trail in New Mexico, near the Ah-Shi-Sle-Pah Wilderness, on 30 October when he discovered that one of the area’s most famous spires, or “hoodoos”, had been destroyed.

“We turned the corner, and my heart just dropped,” he said. “The highlight feature that everyone wants to see is the Alien Throne.”

The majestic formation, which is featured prominently on a local tourism website, had broken into pieces. Winters said he immediately assumed that the heavy rains and the super El Niño season were to blame.

A week before, rainstorms and flooding had hit north-west New Mexico hard, forcing evacuations and hundreds of water rescues of stranded residents. In Farmington, the nearest town to the Valley of Dreams area, some families spent the night on rooftops watching the river flood their homes before they were rescued, officials said.

Winters has been guiding visitors to the region for 13 years as part of Navajo Tours USA, a company he founded. The rock spires, which are on Navajo Nation land, are beloved by visitors and photographers, but they also have a deeper significance to the region’s Indigenous residents, he said.

“They are traditional waypoints in our Indigenous history that have guided our people across the land for many generations,” Winters said.

And it was not just the Alien Throne that had tumbled down, Winters said. Another nearby formation, the King of Wings, what Winters called “the unicorn of hoodoos”, has also been damaged in recent weeks. Multiple user posts on AllTrails, a hiking website, suggested the formation had broken sometime before 9 October, before intense rains hit the region.

“Those are heavy losses for us,” Winters said. But, he added: “The land is alive, and we understand it changes. The same erosion that made them also brings them down, that is what our elders tell us.”

Winters called for visitors to the damaged spires to “let that site rest,” and not to climb what’s left of the formations, or take stones home for relics. “It’s illegal to do that,” he said, adding: “It’s disrespectful to the community as a whole.”

While his assumption is that the Alien Throne broke because of “natural causes”, Winters said, the Navajo Nation and the Bureau of Land Management are expected to examine the site and confirm the cause.

It’s not yet clear how much damage may have been done to other rock spires across the Four Corners region of Utah, Colorado, Arizona and New Mexico during the past weeks of heavy rain and flooding. Park rangers at the Chiricahua, Goblin Valley, Gold Butte and Cathedral Gorge state and national parks with extensive “hoodoo” formations, told SFGate that they had not yet documented any damage.

In a super El Niño year of ongoing intense storms in the Pacific, famous rock formations across time zones are showing damage. Earlier in October, Hawaii’s centuries-old Hōlei sea arch collapsed into the Pacific.

“We’ll keep honoring those sentinels and waypoints through story and photographs and art installations,” Winters said of the lost formations on Navajo Nation land. “Their legacies live on.”
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.summary: The Alien Throne spires are one of the most magical parts of the US south-west. But after torrential rainstorms linked to the super El Niño season, at least one famous rock formation in north-west New Mexico has been found in pieces.

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: In Alaska’s capital, food comes by water, air or, most often, community sharing
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Stephanie Gravalese
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
Juneau has little arable land, a short growing season and few farmers – and deep traditions of residents and the land feeding each other

Forty miles north-west of Alaska’s capital, the highway just ends.

At Glacier Highway’s most northern point, the pavement turns to gravel, the gravel widens into a turnaround and the tire tracks curve back the way they came. At the far end, the woods begin, a narrow hiking trail slipping toward the southern end of Berners Bay.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Locals call this stretch “out the road”. It is the only road that reaches Juneau, population 35,000, and that means virtually everything arriving in Alaska’s capital comes by water or air.

Meghan Stangeland meets vehicles coming off the Alaska Marine Highway ferry to offload boxes of cabbage. As south-east food systems manager at Ecotrust, a non-profit based in Portland, Oregon, working from California to Alaska, she runs its Salt and Soil program, part online farmers’ market, part food hub. In a state capital that has no weekly farmers’ market, the farmers and processors in its network get each order to Juneau however it works for them: often by barge, sometimes by seaplane and even by air.

One figure follows Alaska food coverage everywhere. The US Department of Agriculture (USDA) cites it. So do journalists, policy researchers and anyone making the case that Alaska is vulnerable to supply chain disruption. When the state created an office of food security in 2022, the governor’s announcement led with it, even though, as KTOO reported, no one has ever traced the number to a verifiable source. “Alaska imports 95% of the product that it purchases,” Stangeland says, repeating the often-used number.

“I always caveat that with: that is the product that we purchase. We share so much food, there’s so much subsistence. So it’s not 95% of the food that Alaskans are consuming. There’s so much food economy in the state of Alaska that is not economically transacted.”

That figure cannot measure how Juneau feeds itself, sharing and harvesting from the land. Alaskans took in roughly 46m pounds of wild food in 2014, the state’s most recent comprehensive estimate; in rural areas, that works out to about 275lbs per person per year.

Ricardo Worl recalls about the villages of south-east Alaska: if one person is going hungry, so are their relatives, because everyone shares. Worl, who is Tlingit and from Juneau, is the senior communications officer at Sealaska Heritage Institute, and he describes a regional economy that the import figure only partly captures. About 14 communities dot the region, reachable only by boat or plane. A village of a few hundred people supports only a handful of formal jobs, Worl said, and in the mixed economy that results, cash serves the subsistence harvest, not the other way around.

“Subsistence harvesting in the rural areas is not just culture,” he said. “It’s survival. When we harvest, even if it’s only a couple of fish, we’ll share the best parts, like the heads and the bellies, with grandparents or elders. It’s never just for ourselves.”

Inside Juneau, however, not everyone holds what Stangeland calls the privilege of a boat and a freezer, the space and equipment that processing that volume demands. Worl said that if there is an informal processing center in a community, “it’s going to be in some auntie’s kitchen”.

A family processing food here isn’t just stocking their own pantry for the winter. The food that moves through these networks is hunted, fished, gathered and shared. Growing it commercially in Juneau is a different problem.

The drive to Joe Orsi’s property heads “out the road”, past the Auke Bay neighborhood north-west of downtown. His steep driveway curves up a hillside through a thick wall of evergreens, revealing how scarce flat agricultural space is in Juneau.

Orsi, a 67-year-old retired research fishery biologist for the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, is one of the few farmers supplying Juneau residents and restaurants with locally grown produce. He cultivates a third of an acre with terraced garden beds, endless rows of rhubarb and a large hoop house up the slope behind his home.

It’s a challenging environment for farming. Finding flat, non-marshy land is rare here, and the naturally acidic soil requires improvement. At the height of summer, south-east Alaska gets up to 18 hours of daylight, but the growing season runs only from May through September. Orsi has spent years working out what garlic can actually do in this specific environment. Over time, he tried roughly 45 varieties, paying close attention to what could withstand these soil conditions and that short window.

On paper, the farm provides a modest living, but that is not the point for him. “I may make $20,000 a year. That’s it, not much for all the work I do,” he said. “But I just feel blessed to be able to work the land.”

Some of Orsi’s harvest ends up at Juneau Greens, a hydroponic operation and retail storefront run by John Krapek. Krapek started the business in 2017 with 18 grow beds. Today, he operates 100 in his own retail space. Competing with cheap California produce proved impossible, and wholesale demand from restaurants swung week to week. “When you’re at our scale, we really have to sell every piece of lettuce to make it work,” Krapek said.

His workaround was a weekly subscription model, now 425 residents strong, which stabilized demand enough to open a storefront in 2024. He stocks produce from Orsi and other local vendors alongside his own greens. Krapek said scaling up was never the goal. “It’s really nice to actually know your customer, know the chefs who we deal with,” he said. When subscribers picked up orders at a separate location, the communication was mostly over email. The storefront changed that, he said: “That’s what has been so cool is, like, actually getting to work for this.”

Operations like Krapek’s and Orsi’s can’t feed a community on their own. Stangeland has spent years watching what works in this unique space: a deeply embedded culture of mutual provisioning.

Asked whether that sharing had shifted with rising grocery prices, Stangeland said that’s just always been the way of life: “It’s always been the water that south-east Alaskans have swam in.” She pointed to practices that predate any marketplace, like the first harvest going to elders. “There’s still so much of that that happens in our communities,” she said. “It’s the way it’s always been and continues to be.”

For Worl, the harvest is never individual. “We’re members of a clan, we’re members of a specific community, extended families,” he said. “It’s not going to be: ‘OK, I’m going to process all of this jam, but I’m going to put it on the shelf. Maybe I’ll give some away at Christmas.’ We’re always thinking: ‘Oh boy, there’s a ku.éex [ceremony],’ there’s a payoff party coming, and we better set a case aside, or two aside, to share with them, so there’s that community, the sharing, the responsibility beyond yourself.”

Back at Salt and Soil, Stangeland runs into a different structural gap: federal nutrition programs are designed for farmers selling their own product or stores that buy and resell. A consignment marketplace like Salt and Soil fits neither definition. In 2019, the non-profit created its own program, Healthy Foods = Healthy Families. “We don’t have to jump through the bureaucratic hoops,” Stangeland said. “It’s a much more streamlined initiative to get local food to those who wouldn’t otherwise be able to access or afford it.”

In Sealaska Heritage Institute’s traditional foods and medicine kitchen, students and employees had spent the past few days vacuum-sealing halibut. The Indigenous Science Building, which houses the kitchen, has been open for less than two years, said Anya Nelson, the institute’s Indigenous science and higher education director. Stainless steel counters line one side of the room; a commercial kitchen built for volume processing lines the other. Along the far wall is a hydroponic grow setup.

For Nelson, the space recognizes the deep methodology of traditional survival. The classes also teach the western science behind those methods, the work of generations who “observed and [were] able to create systems and methods that beautifully held salmon and preserved it for months without things like refrigeration”, she said. “There’s so much science in that.”

Joel Bos runs a school garden program through Discovery Southeast that produces 1,300lbs of food a year across two elementary schools. Students follow the harvest through the whole season, from rolling out carrot seed tape in March to cooking soup in October. “A shareable harvest is what creates the buy-in,” Bos said. “They take pride and ownership.”

Ecotrust also operates Moby, a mobile greenhouse that travels between communities on the Alaska Marine Highway. It returned to Juneau this fall at the Dzantik’i Héeni campus for school programming. Almost every community Moby has visited, Stangeland said, now has a permanent greenhouse or high tunnel of its own.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: ‘An abomination’: Idaho hunters earned thousands of dollars to kill newborn wolf pups, records reveal
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Roque Planas
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Wildlife advocates incensed as documents show state paid out $2,000 per kill in effort to shrink state’s wolf population

Idaho officials paid hunters thousands of dollars for killing a dozen newborn wolf pups this spring, including what appears to be at least one full litter killed in or near its den, according to state records shared with the Guardian and Public Domain.

The wolf pup killings have incensed wildlife advocates in Idaho, where state wildlife officials have been ordered to take extraordinary measures to shrink the state’s re-introduced wolf population amid complaints from the livestock industry and big game hunting outfitters.

A law passed five years ago by the Republican-dominated state legislature loosened restrictions on hunting seasons, removed restrictions on killing methods and allowed people to contract third parties to kill wolves. Individual hunters and trappers are able to buy an unlimited number of permits to kill wolves, which cost $14 each for state residents and $32 for non-residents.

In 2021, Idaho game officials also entered into an agreement with the Foundation for Wildlife Management, a non-profit devoted to reducing wolves to help boost deer and elk numbers, to reimburse expenses to any hunter and trapper who provides proof of killing a wolf. The program pays for a wide range of expenses, including truck payments, fuel, ammunition and outdoor clothing.

The reimbursement program paid $2,000 per wolf kill through the hunting season that ended in June, including the 12 pups, records from the state’s fish and game agency show. The program is funded with a mix of taxpayer money, hunting license sales and contributions from the Foundation for Wildlife Management. .

“It’s an abomination,” said Brooks Fahy, director of the advocacy group Predator Defense. “I think most people, even in Idaho, if they actually understood the depth of this, the fact that taxpayer dollars are paying for this – they would be appalled.”

“Let’s call this what it is – it’s a goddamned bounty,” Fahy said. “What kind of receipts are you going to show for 12 pups who weigh 12lbs? It’s ridiculous on its face and the state of Idaho should be ashamed.”

Neither the foundation nor the Idaho wolf depredation control board, a government entity that oversees payments for third-party wolf killings, responded to requests for comment.

Gray wolves were all but wiped off the map in the continental United States by the mid-20th century through government extermination programs, but the population has rebounded in Idaho since being reintroduced by the US Fish and Wildlife Service in 1995. That has reignited tensions with ranchers and big game outfitters whose livelihoods are affected by the animals.

Three separate hunters used rifles to kill a total of 12 wolf pups in Idaho’s northern panhandle region on April 25, the records show – though in at least two instances the records also include a contradictory statement saying that “no weapon” was used. The pups were likely between one and three weeks old by that date. Wolves give birth once a year in the spring.

Hunters and trappers must present a skull and hide with proof of sex attached to a wildlife officer for every wolf killed in the state. The officer normally takes a tooth sample, which allows state biologists to estimate the animal’s age and genetic information.

Officers did not take teeth samples from the 12 pups, however – likely because their teeth had yet to grow in or were too small to extract, according to Idaho fish and game biologist Cory Mosby.

Mosby confirmed that the 12 wolves documented in the records were pups. No state regulation bars the killing of pups, he said. Wildlife officials would normally restrict killing pups by closing the hunting and trapping seasons during the spring, when wolves typically give birth.

But the state management plan, adopted in 2023, mandates culling wolves to about 650 animals in spring, when wolf numbers typically peak. The state’s permissive hunting and trapping regulations, including the yearlong season, are designed to tamp wolf numbers down to that target and will likely become more restrictive as the population dwindles, Mosby said.

That day remains a long way away. Idaho wildlife authorities estimate that the population peaked at about 1,600 wolves in spring back in 2019. That figure for this year still stood at more than 1,100 wolves, despite aggressive hunting and trapping and state-backed payments to incentivize wolf killings. Mosby said that hitting the target would require consistently killing more than a third of the wolf population annually.

“They’re an incredibly impressive and resilient species,” Mosby said. “It takes sustained, high levels of harvest to get into what you call ‘additive’ mortality – where you’re actually removing animals.”

The records state that all 12 wolf pups were killed by “still stalk” – a method in which hunters spot an animal and then sneak up on it to take a shot.

But wolf experts said that the hunters responsible had more likely located the dens, monitored them until the mothers had given birth, then pulled the pups out to kill them.

The tactic of fishing wild canine pups from dens has a long history in the American west, where livestock interests have historically clashed with wolves and coyotes. Modern trail cameras with cellular technology make it far easier to watch over dens, said Carter Niemeyer, who spent nearly three decades working at the US Department of Agriculture’s wildlife services, an agency charged with lethal removal of animals that prey on livestock.

“Killing six wolves or 12 wolves total all on the same day by stalking – that doesn’t happen,” Niemeyer said. “Never heard of it.”

“It would be easy to determine when a female had her pups by her physical appearance going in and out of her den,” Niemeyer added. “I think the public should be outraged by it and sportsmen should be outraged by it too. I’m a sportsman and that’s stooping pretty low – collecting bounties on wolf pups.”

Doug Smith, a biologist who oversaw the wolf program at Yellowstone national park, said he has pulled wolf pups out of dens for research purposes. The parents don’t usually protect their young. Instead, they scurry off about 50 yards away and bark.

“It’s easy to do,” Smith said. “If you can’t reach them, you dig them out with a shovel.”

Smith raised concerns about killing whole litters, however. Wolves travel more independently in the summer and use the den to regroup later in the year. Killing a whole litter could fracture a pack or dissolve it entirely, he said.

“Wolves breed once a year, so the birth of the pups is a very important thing,” Smith said. “The pack’s life hinges on those pups. They’re the glue that holds the pack together.”

Gray wolves remain protected by the Endangered Species Act in most of the continental United States. But the northern Rocky states of Idaho, Montana and Wyoming have all secured state management of wolves since their reintroduction to the region in the 1990s. All three states have pursued aggressive tactics to beat their numbers back.

Idaho hunters and trappers have targeted wolf pups in the past. Hunters killed three pups with rifle shots in the same region two years ago, according to a report from the Idaho Statesman. Federal wildlife control officers killed eight wolf pups from Idaho’s Timberline pack outside Boise back in 2021 to avoid conflict with a rancher, drawing condemnation from wolf advocates, environmental groups and local students who had adopted the pack as their high school mascot.

But advocates view the continuing trend as more worrisome in light of Donald Trump’s recent moves against wolves. In September, Trump signed an executive order encouraging the interior department to consider stripping gray wolves of their Endangered Species Act (ESA) protections across the continental United States – despite the fact that ESA protections for gray wolves remain tied up in federal litigation.

At the signing ceremony, Trump appeared to ask an Arizona rancher whether his new order allowed people to kill Mexican gray wolves, a sub-species in the south-west that is also federally protected.

“You can shoot them as of today?” Trump asked.

The crowd laughed. US agriculture secretary Brooke Rollins responded that interior secretary Doug Burgum “has to do a little magic, but yes” – despite the fact that Mexican gray wolves remain ESA-protected and have not come close to meeting de-listing requirements.

Another rancher at the ceremony told Trump about his struggles with wolves in the state of Washington.

“You’re allowed to go and take care of it,” Trump said.

“If you say so, sir,” the rancher responded.

“We have no choice,” Trump said. “I’ve been hearing about it for a long time.”

“Trump says you can go out and kill wolves now – how many people took him at his word?” said Fahy, the wolf advocate. “These are sentient creatures. They’re basically dogs. They form family bonds. They mate for life, pretty much. They have a pack structure that is very similar to our social structure. How could we be so wantonly cruel to something that is so similar to us?”

This article was co-published with Public Domain, an investigative newsroom covering public lands, the interior department and wildlife

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: How Democrats used the midterms to turn affordability concerns into ‘green populism’
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Hilary Beaumont
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
From energy prices to datacenters, climate became a cost-of-living issue – and a winning one

Q&A: Ask your questions about Democrats’ win in the midterms

C
limate-forward Democrats swept into power on Tuesday night as a blue tsunami flipped the Senate, House and several governor’s races. Voters were laser-focused on affordability, and experts said Democrats succeeded in linking cost-of-living concerns with rising energy prices, datacenters and, to some extent, the climate crisis. They may have even created a path for a “new climate politics”.

The results delivered a sharp rebuke of Donald Trump, who started a war with Iran that raised gas pump prices across the country and exposed the fragility of fossil fuels, all while the US oil industry earned $130bn in profits since the war began. Household energy costs soared, driven by various factors including constraints on renewables, climate disasters and a datacenter boom.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

But how to articulate this before the election was a matter of debate among Democrats known for “climate forward” views: should they talk about the worsening climate crisis directly or keep messaging tight on affordability? Some senior figures including Gavin Newsom warned about “climate hushing”.

In the end, as one analysis on Wednesday put it, the results showed “candidates can win on green economic populism”.

Successful candidates “made connections between the cost of living crisis and the climate crisis, and how the same bad actors – such as utilities, oil companies, corporate landlords, and data center developers – are driving both”, said the analysis, by the thinktank Climate and Community Institute (CCI).

It found the candidates with the “strongest alignment with green economic populism won 39 of 56 (70 percent) of federal races for House and Senate in which they ran, including 6 of 7 in the Senate and 33 of 49 (67 percent) in the House”. The results show that “voters want leaders who will make life affordable and stand up for working people against elites, and climate is a critical part of that equation,” said Johanna Bozuwa, the CCI’s executive director.

While climate was not at the heart of this election, voters were focused on intersecting issues, said environmentalist and author Bill McKibben. “Energy prices played a significant role, and so did the war in Iran, and those are linked,” he said. “Those are both about the president’s strategy of oil dominance, which people are realizing is expensive folly … [The blue wave] was a rejection of this focus on oil as the way to power the future.”

Datacenters became a key focus of voters’ ire, he added: “There’s no question it was the biggest crossover issue to get Republicans, Democrats and independents going in the same direction.”

The debate about how to talk about the climate in elections will continue – but attention will shift to how Democrats use their success when the new Congress forms.

Holding power in the House and Senate will give Democrats the ability to launch investigations and subpoena witnesses and documents. The representative Jared Huffman, the top Democrat on the House natural resources committee, has vowed to investigate big oil’s skyrocketing profits amid the war in Iran.

Climate-forward Democrats now have several avenues to push their agenda. Trump must compromise with Democrats to pass budgets, giving them the power to add climate provisions. Controlling the Senate means Democrats can prevent the appointments of anti-climate federal judges, cabinet officers and sub-cabinet positions.

The election results may shake up negotiations in a controversial permitting reform bill that would clear the way for both clean energy and fossil fuel projects. However, McKibben noted, as newly elected candidates won’t take their seats until January, the permitting bill could be pushed through at a 9 November Senate vote.

McKibben called on Democrats to use their leverage over the budget to restore funding to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration and other agencies that have faced dire cuts to climate science. And, he said, big oil companies are pushing for legislation that would give them immunity from climate damages, and Democrats should “raise holy hell and do everything they can to stop it”.

A handful of climate advocates won House seats Tuesday night. In a tight race in Arizona’s sixth congressional district, Democrat JoAnna Mendoza declared victory against Republican congressman Juan Ciscomani. The incumbent Republican voted to phase out Biden-era clean energy tax credits, while Mendoza campaigned on investing in clean energy to save money for ratepayers. She also advocated for water security, including protecting groundwater and cleaning up Pfas ‘“forever chemicals” in drinking water.

In another close race in the Central valley, Democrat Randy Villegas, a 31-year-old college professor, declared victory in California’s 22nd congressional district against Republican incumbent David Valadao. Villegas campaigned on an “all of the above” approach to energy, supporting oil and gas jobs while calling for more jobs in solar, geothermal and battery storage. The son of Mexican immigrants, Villegas supports stronger heat protections for farm workers as temperatures increase each year. When Trump entered office, he halted federal heat protections for outdoor workers.

Democrat Brad Lander, who has also pushed for heat protections for outdoor workers, won New York’s 10th congressional district, a reliably blue district. He opposed the controversial Northeast Supply Enhancement methane gas pipeline that the New York governor, Kathy Hochul, revived under Trump.

Will Lawrence, a 36-year-old climate activist and co-founder of the youth-led environmental group the Sunrise Movement, declared victory in a purple congressional seat in Michigan after campaigning for state and federal moratoriums against hyperscale datacenters. However, he has recently expressed skepticism of large-scale clean energy projects, too. As Grist reported, his politics have shifted away from the Green New Deal, which advocated for a massive clean energy build-out, and toward a politics of community control over projects.

McKibben, who door-knocked for Lawrence all election, said it was “really remarkable” to see him come up through the climate movement and overcome $4m in Trump Pac-funded attack ads to win.

“Voters sent a clear message across the country: we are tired of politicians putting corporations over people,” Lawrence wrote in a statement. “We are going to stand up to the Trump administration that hands favors to polluters and big tech while rolling back climate protections. Voters are looking for leaders who will fight to protect our land, air and water, and push clean energy that lowers bills and protects ratepayers. It’s the work I built my career on, and I’m ready to legislate on it in Congress.”

On Wednesday morning, Democrat Cait Conley was declared the winner in the race for New York’s 17th district, a suburban battleground. Conley has called climate change a “national security crisis”, and has vowed to fight for federal investments in solar, wind and geothermal, and to pressure the Trump administration to rejoin the Paris climate agreement.

The blue wave brought climate advocates into Senate seats, too. In one of the fiercest battleground races in the country, Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed defeated Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan. El-Sayed supported the Green New Deal and has advocated moving toward 100% renewable energy. He expressed support for state and local datacenter moratoriums, and ran on a platform of affordability and taking money out of politics. He criticized his opponent for accepting past donations from big oil companies and DTE Energy, an unpopular investor-owned utility that has increased energy bills in Michigan.

In Ohio, Democrat Sherrod Brown won his Senate race against Republican Jon Husted. Brown’s campaign focused on the expansion of datacenters across the state, which has the fourth-highest number of proposed and operational datacenters of any state. As Ohio’s lieutenant governor, Husted helped attract datacenters to the state with tax breaks. Brown ran ads calling Husted the “face of datacenters”, connecting his support for the industry to rising electric bills, which have gone up by 34% in Ohio since 2022. In a leaked memo in August, Republicans acknowledged: “More than any other thing in this race, datacenters are the anchor hanging around Husted’s neck.”

James Talarico won Democrats their first Texas Senate seat in decades against Republican Ken Paxton. Once an outspoken climate advocate, Talarico has since moderated his position in the face of Republican attacks that claimed he was against the oil and gas industry. In 2022, Talarico said “fossil fuels are destroying the planet”, and in 2021, he introduced the Texas Climate Action act, which didn’t pass but would have established greenhouse gas reduction targets. Now he’s proposing an “all of the above” approach to energy that protects the fossil fuel industry while investing in renewables.

In North Carolina, Roy Cooper defeated former oil and gas lobbyist Michael Whatley to gain yet another Senate seat for the Democrats. When he was governor of the state, Cooper pushed for climate policies despite a Republican-controlled legislature that resisted his goals. This election cycle, Cooper tied Whatley to cost-of-living concerns by calling out his investments in Duke Energy, an investor-owned utility that had asked the North Carolina Utilities Commission to approve a rate hike before the election.

Democrat Ed Markey, co-author of the Green New Deal, won his Senate race in Massachusetts. The incumbent, who was favored to win, was one of the few national politicians to explicitly campaign on federal clean energy investments, green union job creation and climate accountability.

Meanwhile, the midterms were an expensive and unsuccessful excursion for Elon Musk, and for big oil and gas, as Emily Atkins of Heated reported, with the industry spending at least $182m to try to get Republicans elected.

Democrats swept a handful of governor’s races, giving them the chance to introduce climate policies at the state level. One of the fiercest climate advocates of the bunch, Deb Haaland, won the New Mexico governor’s race, becoming the country’s first female Native American governor. As interior secretary under Joe Biden, she integrated climate science and Indigenous knowledge into department policies and established a climate taskforce to accelerate renewable energy development on public lands. She was a supporter of the Green New Deal and opponent of the Keystone XL pipeline.

In a big upset, Gina Hinojosa won the Texas governor’s race, replacing Republican Greg Abbott, the incumbent since 2015. After hundreds of people died in the 2021 polar vortex, Hinojosa advocated for a Texas climate plan that would reduce emissions and prevent climate disasters in the state, which has the most carbon emissions in the country.

In Georgia, Keisha Lance Bottoms won the governor’s race, becoming the first Black female governor in the country, after campaigning on slowing down and reassessing datacenter expansion to ease utility bills. As mayor of Atlanta, she testified before Congress about the climate crisis and committed her city to achieving 100% clean energy by 2035.

Democrat Amy Acton won the Ohio governor’s race after a battle over datacenters and utility bills. Acton promised to place a conditional moratorium on datacenters, and to appoint Ohio public utilities commissioners who would focus on lowering consumer costs. In a purple state, she campaigned on an “all of the above” approach to energy, including nuclear, fossil fuels and solar, although she faces constraints to solar expansion due to the state’s restrictive law SB52.

Electricity bills were a major issue during this election amid broader affordability concerns, and nine states held elections for state utility commissioners, who oversee energy bills and datacenters. Perhaps the most closely watched of these races was the Georgia public service commission, which flipped from Republican to Democratic control on Tuesday night. Since 2022, the average Georgia residential power bill has gone up by $43 per month, or $516 per year, partly driven by datacenter growth.

Several climate-related ballot measures passed on Tuesday night. Voters in Eugene, Oregon, passed a measure called the Eugene Clean Energy Fund that places a 2% fee on corporations like Amazon and Walmart and allocates those funds toward supporting renewable energy and clean energy jobs training. The measure is expected to generate at least $15m annually beginning no later than 2030. It was based on the 2018 Portland Clean Energy Fund, which has invested $1.7bn in climate and clean energy in that Oregon city.

In Michigan, a ballot measure supported by El-Sayed passed, prohibiting state-regulated electric and gas utilities like DTE Energy from making campaign contributions to candidates for office who oversee them. However, another ballot measure that aimed to replace investor-owned DTE with a public utility was narrowly defeated. The measure was part of a broader “public power” movement that aims to lower utility bills by replacing investor-owned utilities with public utilities.
