https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: The Iran war is deepening the US energy crisis. A bad winter is ahead | Mark Wolfe
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Mark Wolfe
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Congress must act to ensure that families are able to heat their homes before the start of the season

H
eating oil may be the clearest warning yet of how the war in Iran is deepening the US’s energy affordability crisis. Families who heat their homes with oil are facing bills that could be 50% higher this winter, adding nearly $900 to the cost of keeping their homes warm. These families were already struggling before the war began.

As the Guardian recently reported, research by my organization found that electricity shutoffs in 10 states had increased 28% over the past two years. Millions of Americans were already falling behind on their utility bills, forced to choose between paying for energy, food, medicine and rent. Now they face another round of increases in gasoline, electricity and home heating costs.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

The war didn’t create America’s energy affordability crisis. But it is making a bad situation much worse.

For families living on social security, minimum-wage workers and others with little room in their budgets, higher energy prices are taking an especially heavy toll. Even middle-class families are struggling to absorb another $100 or $150 a month for gasoline, groceries and home heating.

Heating oil is the canary in the coalmine for the broader affordability crisis.

Heating oil and diesel are essentially the same petroleum product, and both have been hit hard by the disruption to global energy markets. Higher diesel prices increase the cost of moving food, delivering goods and operating farms and construction equipment. Those costs eventually find their way into the prices families pay.

But for the millions of households that rely on heating oil, the impact is much more immediate. Unlike gasoline, which families can sometimes conserve by driving less, heating oil is essential for keeping homes warm. Families cannot simply stop filling their tanks when prices rise.

Trump described higher oil prices resulting from the war as “a very small price to pay for USA, and world, safety and peace”. But there is nothing small about an additional $878 in heating costs for a family living on social security or working for minimum wage. The president has also said that fuel prices will fall “like a rock” when the war ends. I hope he is right.

Even if the war ended tomorrow, energy prices would not necessarily return to their previous levels. Damaged refineries need repairs, shipping routes must reopen, and depleted petroleum inventories need to be replenished. That could take months. Families cannot postpone paying their heating bills while the oil market recovers.

Congress needs to act when it returns after the midterm elections and before winter arrives. We are calling on lawmakers to add $3bn to the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program (Liheap), which helps low-income families pay their heating bills.

This would allow states to provide families with supplemental assistance to cover rising heating oil and electricity prices before the start of the winter heating season.

The problem extends beyond the poorest families. Many working families earn too much to qualify for assistance but still struggle to pay their energy bills. Congress should consider temporarily expanding eligibility for Liheap to struggling middle-class families, with additional funding to ensure that assistance to the lowest-income households is not reduced.

A recent survey conducted by Consumer Reports found that more than a quarter of all families reported reduced the heating and cooling in their homes to uncomfortable levels to save money and 19% cutback on groceries or switched to less expensive food options.

Without additional energy assistance, families will fall further behind, and some will face the possibility of losing heat during the coldest months of the year.

But Congress also needs to address the larger problem. For too long, we’ve measured America’s energy security by how much oil and natural gas we produce. Yet producing more energy at home hasn’t protected the US families from price shocks caused by wars overseas.

We need to think about energy security differently. That means expanding energy sources, including wind and solar, whose fuel costs cannot be driven up by a war. There is no strait of Hormuz for solar power.

That is the longer-term challenge. Right now, millions of families are heading into winter facing energy bills they cannot afford.

At some point, the war in Iran will end, but the affordability crisis will not end with it. Washington needs to help families get through this winter and make sure the next war thousands of miles away doesn’t once again determine whether they can afford to heat their homes.

Mark Wolfe is an energy economist and serves as the executive director of the National Energy Assistance Directors Association (Neada) representing the state directors of the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program and the co-director of the Center on Energy Poverty and Climate (CEPC). He also serves as an adjunct professor at the George Washington University public policy school

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: Tesla to wind down Cybertruck production as Elon Musk focuses on robotics and AI
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Jasper Jolly
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
Decision made in order for factory in Texas to be used for Cybercab, the carmaker’s self-driving taxi

Elon Musk has announced that Tesla will wind down production of its Cybertruck, marking the end of a failed effort to take a chunk of the lucrative market for pickups in the US.

The billionaire chief executive said production of the car would stop in about the middle of next year at the company’s factory in Texas in order to use the plant for the Cybercab, its self-driving taxi.

Musk did not say whether Tesla had plans to produce the vehicle in another factory, although that would probably require significant investment for the specialised tooling needed to make it.

Musk has pinned hopes for Tesla on robotics, artificial intelligence and an autonomous driving fleet rather than following the traditional carmakers’ approach of developing a steady stream of new models to entice private buyers.

It caps a tricky week for the world’s richest person, after Republican candidates he had backed with $446m (£332m) in donations lost in the US midterm elections. The paper value of Musk’s fortune fell by $113bn after the extent of the rout became clear, as stock market investors questioned whether a Democrat-led Congress could slow the pace of the AI boom.

Tesla shares fell by 11% on Thursday, while his AI and rocket launch company, SpaceX, dropped by 9%.

Tesla started deliveries of the Cybertruck in late 2023, after several long delays as the company tried to cope with the technical challenges of producing such an unusual vehicle – and particularly its steel shell.

The Cybertruck never made it on sale in Europe because it did not reach the required safety standards.

Even before sales began, Musk acknowledged how difficult it would be to make it a success. In a 2023 earnings call, he said: “We dug our own grave with Cybertruck,” and noted “enormous challenges” in increasing production and earning money from it.

Musk had said the company aimed to sell 200,000 Cybertrucks each year but it never approached that target. Tesla does not report sales of the trucks separately but in the third quarter of 2026 it delivered only 8,300 “other models”, which include the Cybertruck. The vast majority of its sales were the Model 3 saloon and the Model Y SUV, with 478,000 combined deliveries during the quarter.

Tesla also this year stopped production of its Model S and Model X, its premium saloon and SUV, amid declining sales for ageing products.

Tesla’s automotive focus has shifted to the Cybercab. Tesla has started offering paid trips in the car, which has space for two passengers and no steering wheel, in limited parts of Austin, Texas. However, it is unclear how quickly the company will be able to roll out the taxi service around the US or further afield amid close regulatory scrutiny of driverless car technology.

As well as the Cybercab, Tesla is still ramping up production of its long-delayed Semi electric lorry. Musk is also aiming to produce one other new model: the Roadster sportscar, which Musk revealed with a demonstration of a “flying car” version that used thrusters developed by SpaceX to drive up a curved ramp before flipping and landing. Tesla is aiming to start production of a road-bound version in 2028. Analysts do not expect the Roadster to make a large difference to Tesla’s future profits.

Beyond vehicles, the Texas factory will also be used to build Tesla’s Optimus humanoid robot.

Musk posted on X, the social network he owns: “Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production.”

https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.title: Rural voters were feeling left behind before the midterms, poll shows
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.author: Lauren Aratani
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.text:
Polling done for the Guardian shows plummeting support from a former key constituency of Donald Trump’s base

Q&A: Ask your questions about Democrats’ win in the midterms

Polling conducted by the Harris Poll for the Guardian before the election shows just how angry voters were and points to one key reason Republicans lost so badly: plummeting support from rural voters, once a key constituency of Donald Trump’s base.

Over the summer, 95% of Americans indicated they believed there was an affordability crisis, particularly because of steep gas and grocery prices. By October, 61% of voters believed the country was experiencing a recession, even though technically it wasn’t.

It’s hard to ignore the impact inflation has had on this election. Key voters had expressed for months deep discontent with what had become the status quo. Loggers in Maine said that tariffs against Canada were hurting their already-battered industry. Drivers in Texas facing three-hour commutes to work were spending $400 a month on gas. Farmers across the midwest said diesel prices were exacerbating a growing season beleaguered by drought.

Recent data showed the flip wasn’t just seen among Democrats and independents, who have held pessimistic views on the economy since Trump returned to office, but among some Republicans, too.

In February, right before the war in Iran began, 49% of Republicans said the economy was getting better. By October, that number would drop to just 28%.

The pain seemed especially acute for rural voters, long considered a core base for Trump.

The president had gained many of his supporters by angling himself as a successful businessman who would be an outsider in Washington. But soaring gas and diesel prices have been a major pain point in parts of the country where driving long distances is an everyday part of life.

Rural voters were much more likely to say that gas prices were hurting their finances and that they were in economic “survival mode”, or that one surprise bill could sink them, compared with their urban and suburban counterparts. They were also slightly more likely to say that Republicans had a bigger problem with corruption, or elected officials using their position for personal financial gain, than Democrats.

In the month before the midterms, the number of rural Americans who said the economy was getting worse climbed 17% since Trump took office, compared with a 5% increase for those in the suburbs and a 3% jump among urban voters.

Yet on the eve of the midterm elections, Trump was trying to speak a different reality into existence, one where gas prices were going down, wages were rising and the US’s trade with other countries had never been stronger.

“I’ve traveled all across the country, spoken at all of these rallies I’ve done over the last two and a half weeks, and America is ready to go. They’re ready to vote,” Trump said in front of the Lincoln Memorial’s Reflecting Pool on Monday. “I hope they’re ready to do the right thing.”

But the reality that Americans have been facing is vastly different, and Americans responded accordingly. Republicans in key races from Maine to Texas lost their toss-up races on Tuesday, and Democrats will have control of Congress for the next two years.

Democrats have promised they will be busy trying to address the issues that were at the forefront of the election: the Trump administration’s brutal immigration crackdown, corruption in the White House, rising healthcare costs and the economy, specifically higher prices.

Republicans are just starting to take stock of the role prices had on the election outcome. JD Vance on Wednesday said the loss was the “cost to pay” for the Iran war. “Any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there,” Vance said.

As much as the midterms were a “blue-nami” for Democrats, pre-midterm polls showed voters were still unsure about the party’s ability to deal with affordability. When asked which party had the solution to the affordability crisis a month before the election, 34% said that neither party had a solution. Democrats (27%) slightly edged out Republicans (24%), but many voters seemed unsure whether any party could deal with these pocketbook issues.

Similar polling conducted before the 2024 presidential election showed that key independent voters were feeling just as pessimistic about the economy. Inflation had reached a generational high in 2022, and many Americans felt that Biden and Democrats weren’t doing enough.

Price increases under Trump, particularly after the Iran war, have only gotten worse. But many voters are dealing with years of economic burnout and will expect results in the coming years.

https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.author: Joanna Partridge
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.text:
Government bond yields fall while initial fears ease over impact of election results on world’s biggest economy

US midterm elections – live updates

After US midterms, what will lame-duck Trump mean for global economy?

US stocks have surged as investors digest the Democrats’ victories in the midterm elections, lifted by hopes that Donald Trump’s turbulent policymaking would be restrained and shaking off initial fears about the impact on growth in the world’s largest economy.

The Dow Jones rose close to 3%, its best day in over a year, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq and the benchmark S&P 500 gained about 1.5% each when markets closed on Wednesday afternoon, turning around overnight falls in US stock futures after the news that the Democratic party won control of the Senate and the House of Representatives.

The price of oil dropped sharply as traders assessed the impact of the Democrats’ win on the war in Iran. Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, fell below $100 a barrel for the first time since early October.

In a social media post on Wednesday afternoon, Trump took credit for the jump. “Stock Market just hit another Record High,” he wrote. “Your 401(k)s are through the roof. Record Setting All!”

However, the US dollar fell against the currencies of America’s major trading partners, hitting a one-month low on Wednesday while coming under pressure from falling bond yields. Investors moved into US treasuries, viewed as a haven from the political gridlock anticipated during the rest of Trump’s final term in office.

The dollar index, which measures it against a basket of six currencies, slid to its lowest level in a month, with the pound hitting its highest level since mid-September on the back of a fragile dollar, while the euro also made gains.

The dollar also slid against the yen and the Swiss franc, currencies that traders tend to turn to during times of uncertainty.

Meanwhile, the yield, or interest rate, on the benchmark 10-year US treasury bond has fallen 4.7 basis points to 4.918%. On two-year bonds it has dropped 3.7bps to 4.597%. Yields fall when bond prices rise.

Across the US, voters rejected Trump and the Republican agenda, with the Democrats securing Senate seats in traditional Republican strongholds such as Texas, Iowa, North Carolina and South Carolina.

Axel Rudolph, the chief technical analyst at the trading platform IG, said: “The scale of the losses will inevitably raise questions about Trump’s ability to push through his agenda over the next two years, and markets are already reacting. The dollar is under pressure as investors reassess the political outlook, while gold and silver are benefiting as safe haven plays.”

Futures trading initially indicated US stock markets would open sharply lower, with the Nasdaq expected to slide on fears over the prospects for AI companies. However, indicators later suggested Wall Street could open higher as Trump’s conciliatory tone and rises on European markets cheered investors.

European markets rose yesterday. London’s FTSE 100 was up 1.8%, Germany’s Dax rose by 2.2%, France’s Cac 40 was 2% higher and Italy’s FTSE MiB index rose by 2.2%.

Bank and clean energy stocks, which have borne the brunt of Trump’s policies, were among the top risers in Europe. Bank stocks rose by 2.8%, while Denmark’s Vestas Wind Systems jumped nearly 5% and Ørsted soared 7.4%.

“Some individual names are nursing significant losses today,” said Kathleen Brooks, the UK research director at XTB. “SpaceX is down 5% in the premarket, and Tesla is lower by more than 4%. Elon Musk is considered an anathema to most Democrats.”

Musk, the world’s richest person, pumped $446m (£331m) into the midterms, funding Republican-aligned political action committees and groups.

Brooks said investors were reacting to expectations that a Democrat-controlled Congress could mean greater scrutiny for AI companies, which could also cast doubt on a potential merger of Musk’s two companies.

The price of gold, a traditional haven asset, rose by 2.2%, soaring past $4,000 an ounce.

AI-related shares tumbled during Asian trading hours, on expectations that Democrats will want to bring in greater regulation of the sector.

Chris Turner, the global head of markets at ING, said: “Investors will be parsing what this all means. For example, Gina Hinojosa won the Texas governor’s race on a ticket of wanting an immediate moratorium on datacentre buildouts.”

He added: “Given AI’s role in powering the US economy, speculation over whether a new Democrat Congress would slow AI capital expenditure plans briefly hit markets.”

Jesper Koll, an expert director at the financial services company Monex Group, said: “The AI momentum has turned negative, with or without the Republicans having a majority. The starting point for financial markets into this election, particularly for the equity market, has been adverse on AI.”

Trump’s style of governing through executive orders has prompted some analysts to question whether the Democrats regaining control of Congress will have much change on US policymaking.

“There’s still a number of areas where Donald Trump can influence the markets – trade and tariffs, foreign policy and existing regulations,” said Tai Hui, a market strategist at JP Morgan Asset Management.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Jeremy Barr in Washington
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Fox News pundits hardly criticized the US president in midterms coverage but Trump was still quick to cast blame

US midterms 2026 live – latest updates

Track live results from all 50 states

Q&A: Ask your questions about Democrats’ win in the midterms

In the weeks leading up to Tuesday’s midterm elections, Donald Trump made clear that he would place some blame on his favorite cable channel, Fox News, if his party did poorly.

On election day, he didn’t disappoint.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Even before races really started to be called, Trump hit the network in multiple Truth Social posts, criticizing Fox for featuring Democratic pundit Jessica Tarlov; attacking Fox’s polls as “always the worst”; mocking some recent softness in the network’s year-over-year ratings trends and accusing Fox of being “AGAINST” him. Just before midnight, Trump directly placed blame on Fox News for the Republican party’s failure to hold on to the US House and Senate, writing that “FoxNews bears responsibility for these losses by constantly and consistently putting on the Dumocrat opposition, and worse.”

In a surreal moment, Trump then called into Fox’s election coverage around midnight and directly criticized the network’s polls as “terrible,” telling the network’s employees: “You ought to get yourself a good pollster, because your pollsters are the worst.” Fox News anchor Bret Baier pushed back gently, pointing out that “tonight, actually, the results are pretty close to what the Fox polls showed.” (Trump also made a dig about Baier – or Fox at large –not supporting him “when it wasn’t fashionable”.)

But while Trump was extremely critical of Fox News throughout the day and night, during more than six and a half hours of election night coverage viewed by the Guardian, commentators on the network seemed to take pains to not directly tie the party’s losses to Trump, and there were no suggestions that the party should back away from him.

Instead, several commentators on the channel turned the focus on voters for being “impatient” and wanting “instant gratification”, as host Jesse Watters put it just after 8pm. Many commentators said the president’s party historically performs poorly in the midterm elections. There were many attacks on Democrats, with conservative commentators in agreement that the party would overstay their welcome from voters and misinterpret their victory as a mandate, paving the way for Republican wins in 2028.

The only significant criticisms of the president focused on the White House’s messaging strategy and his decision to go to war in Iran.

“In some sense, Mr Trump was too successful in the first year and didn’t sell it enough in the second year,” said Larry Kudlow, a Fox Business Network host who served as Trump’s Director of the National Economic Council during his first administration.

Dana Perino, who served as press secretary to George W Bush, said: “From a messaging standpoint, a lot of times the administration has got too many balls in the air and it’s hard to figure out what is the headline we want to drive.”

And several commentators noted that voters seemed to be unhappy with the president’s decision to launch a war against Iran, particularly considering the rise in gas prices that resulted from it. Sean Hannity, the president’s biggest booster on the channel, agreed with Baier that the night’s outcome would have been different if he had not bombed the country.

“I think it’s prices. People are mad,” Watters offered later in the night.

Still, the overwhelming consensus from Fox’s election night panel – which included several former Trump administration employees, including his former press secretary Karoline Leavitt – was that the blame should not be squarely placed at the president’s feet. Instead, Leavitt singled out the media. “Unfortunately, I think the American people forgot about the good policy, [and] maybe listened to the lying media on the other side that is definitely in the back seat of the Democratic party,” she said.

Just before 10pm, Fox News host Will Cain said: “I look at the pros and the cons of the last two years under Donald Trump, and the pros significantly outweigh the cons.”

While primetime host Laura Ingraham acknowledged that the election was a “referendum on Trump”, she said that “overwhelmingly his policies have been phenomenal for the country. Overwhelmingly, the stuff he’s promised, he’s done, and it’s worked out fabulously.”

Despite his earlier comments, Hannity said that Trump’s policies “are rock solid”, that Iran “had to be done” and that his intervention will eventually be proven right.

One person who shared in the belief that the president was not responsible for the losses was the president himself. “I don’t view it as a hit on me,” Trump told the Fox News panel, adding that “historically, I think I’ll be judged for having done the right thing,” and largely placing the blame on the Republican candidates who were defeated. He repeated his contention that the outcome would have been different if he had been on the ballot.

This article was amended on 4 November 2026; a previous version incorrectly stated that Karoline Leavitt is Donald Trump’s most recent press secretary, when it is in fact Katie Zacharia.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Edward Helmore
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
CVS Pharmacy will be separate from CVS Health, housing major insurer Aetna and benefits manager Caremark

CVS Health, the largest US healthcare conglomerate valued at $117bn, has announced its plans split off its pharmacy chain from its health insurance and benefits businesses, ending an era in which healthcare companies grew into vast conglomerates.

In their announcement on Wednesday, CVS Health said they will split off its 9,000 pharmacies, in-store clinics and mail order prescription business into a business named CVS Pharmacy.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

A second company will keep the name CVS Health and house the major insurer Aetna and the giant pharmacy benefits manager Caremark, along with other businesses that provide home visits and primary care to older people.

The company has come under pressure from lawmakers and regulators over concerns that the healthcare giants, including CVS Health, UnitedHealth Group and Cigna, have become too dominant, leading to higher medical costs. The three companies control roughly 80% of the market. CVS Health in particular generated over $400bn in revenue last year.

A political pushback against healthcare gigantism has led Arkansas and Tennessee to pass laws aimed at preventing the companies from managing prescription benefits and running retail and mail-order pharmacies.

The Arkansas state representative Jeremiah Moore, a Republican who sponsored the state’s bill, told Politico last week: “The average American citizen is really tired of being pushed around and bullied, whether it be from the government or a monopolistic company.”

He added: “For far too long, they’ve taken advantage of these sick people, and it’s what I consider to be crony capitalism. They’re bending the rules to benefit their own bottom line.” Other states have proposed similar restrictions.

At the federal level, a bill introduced by the Missouri Republican senator Josh Hawley and Massachusetts senator Elizabeth Warren proposes an antitrust crackdown.

Hawley has described the legislation as “a major step toward restoring transparency and making healthcare more affordable for every American.”

David Joyner, CVS’s chief executive and chair, will run the healthcare solutions business.
 
 
 “Our history is defined by proactively evolving to stay ahead of what’s next in healthcare, and in today’s environment, that means delivering more affordability, greater access and a simpler experience,” said Joyner in a statement.

That marks a stark turnaround from CVS Health’s earlier opposition to legislative efforts to break up the healthcare giant, which a company spokesman said would “open the door to private equity stripping the entire U.S. healthcare system for parts”.

The announcement comes after a series of acquisitions that saw CVS Health expand into nearly every corner of the healthcare system. It began in 2018, when CVS and Aetna merged in a $70bn deal. Healthcare rivals, UnitedHealth and Cigna, also brought into the trend of harnessing an insurer, pharmacy benefits, and a mail-order business under one operation.

CVS Health, however, did not meet investors’ expectations for growth. In late 2024, its share price fell to $44, though it has since rebounded. The CVS Health breakup is planned for early 2028.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Jeremy Barr in Washington
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Journalists such as Jim Acosta and Scott MacFarlane are now competing against their former employers for eyeballs

On Tuesday, for the first time in more than 20 years, Jim Acosta, a former CNN stalwart, will not be working for a mainstream television network on election night.

Acosta, who left CNN last year after nearly 18 years at the network, is putting on his own live broadcast at the University of Virginia that will air on YouTube and his Substack platform.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

And in a sign of the times, Acosta will be joined for the broadcast, hosted by the university’s Center for Politics, by another star of linear television – Katie Couric, a former Today show co-host. (Don Lemon, another CNN alum and converted new media player, may also drop by, Acosta said.)

“If folks are looking for fresh faces and a different way of doing this kind of coverage, I think it’s going to deliver that,” Acosta said.

Acosta said he will be doing his best Steve Kornacki impression, giving analysis using an interactive, touch screen battleground map just like the NBC News data guru. “Yeah, I’m going to have to go to J Crew and get some new khakis.”

Rashida Jones, who serves as chief executive of Piers Morgan’s media company Uncensored, predicted that Tuesday’s midterms will come to be remembered as “the content creator election”, when independent journalists hosting streaming broadcasts give traditional networks a run for their money.

Jones was running one of those television networks, MSNBC (now called MS Now), during the 2024 presidential election, a role she held for four years. She is working to expand Morgan’s company by launching new shows and verticals beyond the “Piers Morgan Uncensored” streaming broadcast, which has about 4.5 million subscribers on YouTube.

The plan for election night is a several-hour-long live show hosted by Morgan from Washington DC, part of a three-day stint broadcasting from the US capital city.

“Our focus is going to be making sense of what’s happening in real time,” she said in an interview. “People aren’t coming to us because they’re looking for how this part of Michigan voted. It’s more the big picture themes and takeaways. Ultimately by the end of the night, people care about where did we land, less about the individual races.”

Jones said that traditional television networks will be facing more competition than past election cycles. “If I’m a network that’s got a guy at a board and a ticker at the bottom, and I just assume people are going to come, I don’t know that that’s baked in and that’s a given this cycle. And I think what we see [on Tuesday] will be on a smaller scale what we see for the general election … I think it’ll be the content creator election.”

Scott MacFarlane, a veteran reporter who resigned from CBS News in March seeking “some independence”, joined the progressive MeidasTouch network as its chief Washington correspondent and will be co-hosting its live election broadcast.

MacFarlane says the streaming show will lack the bells and whistles of a traditional television election broadcast, which is the point. “There will be no teleprompters and no scripts,” he said. “It’s straight to the point, direct, conversational and heavy on original reporting.” He added that “dramatic theme music and theatrical presentations would miss the moment”.

Still, many millions of Americans will be watching a traditional television network – or their streaming off-shoot – to keep tabs on the elections. On election night 2024, an estimated 42.3 million viewers watched television coverage – though viewership is obviously lower for non-presidential years.

“There are more places than ever for people to get their news and information, but there’s no place that has the depth, the scope, and the breadth that NBC News has,” said Hallie Jackson, an NBC News anchor, who is penciled in for nine hours of live coverage as part of the network’s election team, along with Savannah Guthrie, Tom Llamas and Kristen Welker behind the desk (along with Kornacki).

Jackson said the key to election night is hydration, and a regimen of healthy eating that she began last week. “You have to pace yourself. You have to stay hydrated. You have to have a secret pack of M&Ms for your blood sugar that you can come back to every hour.”

Sign up to How We Win

Bernie Sanders, Robert Reich, Stacey Abrams, Mehdi Hasan, Paul Krugman and other bold thinkers on how to defeat Trumpism and build a better future. From our opinion desk.

after newsletter promotion

Seni Tienabeso, vice-president of ABC News Live and Specialized Units, said the network has planned for a seven-hour-long broadcast, but could go much longer if a key call – perhaps for control of the US Senate or House – is on the horizon.

Asked how much effort is put toward the traditional television broadcast compared with digital and social media offerings, ABC News executives said the network is fully integrated. “For us, it’s about reaching the audience where they are,” Tienabeso said. “We don’t leave any of those arenas as secondary.” (The network’s coverage will also be aired on its ABC News Live digital channel, on Hulu, and on the Disney+ streaming service.)

Like most major networks and news organizations, ABC News relies on election results from the Associated Press – as well as a new voter survey conducted by the polling firm SSRS – to help make projections about key elections. Those decisions are made by a desk that is “holed off” from the rest of the newsroom, Tienabeso said, and is not primarily focused on beating rival networks. “We don’t pay attention to what competitors are doing,” he said. “Our decision desk makes the decision when they feel comfortable with their analysis of the race that they’re covering.”

On Tuesday, viewers watching CNN will be able to see the network’s decision desk in action, and will also have access to a new tool called CNN Sightline that will give insights into how a contest is leaning, based on both data and demographics. “I think it’s probably more transparency than we’ve ever had,” said David Chalian, CNN’s political director and Washington bureau chief.

CNN’s decision desk makes calls when they have at least 99.5% confidence that a certain candidate will win. “Speed is not part of that at all,” he said.

“In a time when voter confidence in elections is something that we constantly look at and is called into question, it only ups the seriousness of purpose with which we take this mission in projecting races,” Chalian added.

Chris Stirewalt, who serves as political editor for the cable network NewsNation and anchors the weekly show The Hill Sunday, said he doesn’t think that Republicans will be happy with the election results. He said that early returns from Ohio will be a good indication of whether “the rout is on” for Democrats.

Stirewalt is no stranger to election night, having been part of Fox News’ decision desk for several cycles before leaving the network in 2021. He said he values the finality of the process: “The conversation goes on and on and on, and then it’s over. And you count, look at the scoreboard, and then it’s done. I love that.”

While Acosta is best-known for his television work, he said he doesn’t miss CNN and is happy to be “starting something at the beginning” by working in creator-driven media. “And that’s kind of the exciting part of it, because who knows where this thing is going to take us?”
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: Jim Acosta will not be working for a mainstream television network on Tuesday night. He will be doing his best Steve Kornacki impression, giving analysis using an interactive, touch screen battleground map. Scott MacFarlane, a veteran reporter who resigned from CBS News in March, will be giving analysis.

https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.title: Dream ticket? Super-rich can sleep pretty with Singapore Airlines ‘largest double bed in the sky’
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.author: Lauren Almeida
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.text:
Cabin upgrade comes as airlines compete for wealthy customers in race to the top of luxury travel

Singapore Airlines has said it will offer the “largest double bed in the sky” as part of a S$2bn (£1.2bn) cabin upgrade as super-rich passengers demand ever greater levels of luxury travel.

The first-class premium cabins will feature what the airline claims is “the largest double bed in commercial aviation”.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

The bed for two people travelling together spans two adjoining seats and measures 203cm (80in) long and 152cm (60in) wide. A standard double bed mattress in the UK is 190cm long and 135cm wide.

The bed will include a mattress topper from the German luxury bedding company Paradies, a duvet and a choice of pillows.

Some business-class seats would be able to be made into a double bed, the airline said. The upgrade includes curved sliding doors to give passengers more privacy and ultra-high-definition 4K touchscreens.

A broader race to the top in luxury travel is under way, where a one-way ticket can cost upwards of £10,000. While Singapore Airlines was ranked as the world’s best overall airline by the researcher Skytrax this year, it has lost market share to rivals who have invested heavily in cabin upgrades.

In 2022, Emirates launched a fleet-wide $5bn retrofit programme, including refreshing its first-class suites with more space and updated tech. This year Air France introduced la Première, a redesigned first-class cabin, which the airline says is akin to a private jet experience. British Airways is also working on a new first-class cabin for its A380 planes.

The industry has been rocked by a rise in fuel prices this year triggered by the war in the Middle East, which has in turn pushed up air fares. However, Singapore Airlines has benefited from an increase in passengers routing their flights between Asia and Europe rather than taking connecting flights through the Gulf.

Singapore Airlines added that economy passengers would gain more leg space, as well as a new storage layout for personal items. All passengers would get upgrades to the in-flight entertainment service and an expanded meal selection, it said, and there would be onboard internet connectivity via Elon Musk’s satellite company Starlink.

The new cabins would be introduced from the second half of 2027, the airline said.

https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.title: Debt of poorest countries at record $9.4tn high, World Bank data shows
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.author: Heather Stewart Economic editor
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.text:
Cost of servicing external debt is preventing developing countries from investing for future

Debt owed by developing countries rose to a record $9.4tn (£7tn) last year, with the poorest paying the highest interest rates since the late 1980s, World Bank data shows.

The UK government is preparing to champion a “new drive on debt” as part of its presidency of the G20 next year – a move the prime minister, Andy Burnham, has linked to confronting the legacy of slavery.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

In its annual International Debt Report, the World Bank said the rising cost of servicing external debt was preventing some governments from investing for the future.

The increase in developing country debt last year, of 5.5%, was the fastest in four years, the report finds – driven by a rapid rise in private sector lending.

The World Bank’s chief statistician, Haishan Fu, said: “Access to international finance has improved, but the price of that finance has not. Low- and middle-income countries are borrowing more, paying more, and, in many cases, leaving less for long-term development.”

On average, the report found the poorest countries – those eligible for concessional lending from the World Bank – faced an average interest rate of 8.2% on new borrowing: the highest since the late 1980s. It also said preliminary data for 2026 suggested lending continued at a rapid pace – but at continued high interest rates as global financing costs rose.

The Bank highlighted recent borrowing by Laos, at an interest rate of 11.5%, the Republic of Congo, at 13.88%, and Kenya, at 9.2%.

Analysing the connection between a high debt burden and the ability to spend on domestic priorities, the World Bank found global shocks had more impact on the availability of food in heavily indebted countries.

“Food and nutrition security provides a concrete example of these interactions, illustrating how debt burdens may be closely associated with a decline in the affordability of a healthy diet during periods of global stress,” the report said.

Burnham has appointed the former Labour prime minister Gordon Brown to examine the feasibility of changes to the global debt regime in the run-up to the UK’s G20 presidency next year.

The UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, set out plans last month for a “new deal” for heavily indebted countries in a speech at the IMF annual meetings in Bangkok. The deal is likely to include proposals to mobilise the balance sheets of the World Bank and other multilateral development banks to buy back outstanding debt in an effort to extend repayment periods and bring down interest rates.

However, the situation is more complex than in the run-up to the Gleneagles summit in 2005 – when G8 countries signed up to write off billions of pounds worth of debt – because today’s creditors tend to be private-sector bondholders, not governments.

There have been growing demands in recent years for changes to the framework for international debt, including from African Union heads of state, and under the G20 chairs of Brazil and South Africa.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: UK found to be ‘dangerously’ reliant on China for critical minerals needed for defence and AI
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Lisa O’Carroll Senior staff correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
Delivering net zero also at risk, say MPs as they call for centralised policy and funding for mines and diversification

The UK is “dangerously” dependent on China for critical raw materials needed for the military, renewable energy infrastructure and AI, a parliamentary investigation has found.

MPs on the business select committee called for an urgent centralised policy and the creation of a “critical minerals finance facility” to help fund rare earth and other critical mineral mines, and deploy grants, equity and debt to accelerate a diversification programme.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

“Critical minerals are the alpha of the new economy,” said the committee’s chair, Liam Byrne. “We cannot rearm Britain, build AI or deliver net zero unless we secure the minerals these technologies depend on.

“Yet 16 years after China first weaponised its chokehold over rare earths, Britain remains dangerously exposed.”

It is the second time in a week that the government’s policy on China has been criticised by Byrne’s committee.

China has a stranglehold on the world’s supply of rare earths and other critical minerals, as well as their refined byproducts that are used in everything from military jets to car-locking systems and consumer products such as fridges and washing machines.

The committee heard that “the processing stage” was where the bottlenecks were, with China dominating the refining of seven categories of minerals, including refined lithium needed for electric vehicles and rare earths used in the fuselage and wings of military aircraft to help withstand temperature extremes.

MPs were told that demand for lithium alone would increase 45-fold between 2024 and 2030, leaving the UK in a high-risk dependency relationship with China.

The demand for rare earths needed for permanent magnets used in military jets and other applications would rise 16-fold in the same period as Britain was seeking to rebuild its military capabilities.

But with China capable of suddenly turning off rare earth supplies, as it did in 2025, a dependency on Beijing was a strategic vulnerability for the UK economy and national security, the committee found.

Separate restrictions on legacy chips after a row over a Dutch intervention in the China-owned Nexperia left the European car industry “days away” from stoppages last October.

The EU, the US and other countries faced the same risk of supplies of rare earths being cut off by China, and the committee said the UK was not putting enough effort into finding alternative supplies.

Donald Trump secured a one-year reprieve on global export restrictions on rare earths from Xi Jinping in October last year. This was extended to January 2027 after the Chinese president’s recent visit to Washington.

However, the reprieve means the UK is at the mercy of US-China relations, the report suggests.

Sign up to Business Today

after newsletter promotion

The most “realistic” solution was for the UK to work closely with G7 partners, the rest of Europe and Indo-Pacific countries, to “aggregate demand” and bring in new suppliers.

The committee said its investigation was frustrated by lack of transparency by the government.

“Parliament has no visibility of the capabilities the government is seeking to protect, the vulnerabilities it has identified, or the projects it is backing to reduce risk,” it said.

The committee has drawn up a 10-point plan that includes: working to identify domestic mining; refining and recycling opportunities and their costs; a strategy to encourage business to reduce procurement from China; a plan to unlock investment; and assess planning and permitting processes that may prove a barrier to mining.

As it stood, the committee said it could not be confident the government could satisfy any of its 10 tests.

“The UK requires new institutional and financial muscle,” it concluded.

A government spokesperson denied it did not have a critical minerals strategy saying it was delivering £400m “to ramp up domestic production and recycling” and forge new international partnerships.
 
 
 “Our strategy also sets clear goals for 2035, including meeting 10% of demand through domestic production and 20% through recycling, with no more than 60% of any critical minerals coming from any single country,” they added.

This article was amended on 6 November 2026. An earlier version said MPs were warned that there would be a 45-fold increase in demand for lithium between now and 2030; this should have said between 2024 and 2030.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: Activists across Europe prepare two days of protests against datacentres
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Dan Milmo Global technology editor
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
More than 100 campaign groups will join together in 15 countries this week to call for a halt to major AI projects

Protesters across Europe are planning two days of action against datacentres this week with demonstrations taking place in 15 countries.

More than 100 groups are joining together for the “Stop Dirty Data Centres” events on Friday and Saturday. They are calling for a moratorium on large projects, citing environmental and social costs that “we can no longer afford”.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Datacentres have become a lightning rod for concerns over artificial intelligence, given their role in developing and operating the cutting-edge technology. In the US midterm elections this week, opponents of datacentres were among the biggest winners for the Democrats.

Actions across the two days include: a protest outside the Polish parliament in Warsaw; a march in Dublin; a demonstration outside a Microsoft datacentre in Denmark; a “teach-in” near the site of a planned datacentre in Amsterdam; and an event in the Brick Lane area of east London, where a datacentre development has met local opposition.

Owen Espley, the campaign’s coordinator, said communities in the US and Europe are sending a message about data centres.

“Communities and civil society from across Europe are rising up to stop dirty data centres where they live and demand their politicians impose moratoria on large-scale data centre developments,” he said. “The US mid-term results reflect the concerns communities both sides of the Atlantic share about the harms of large-scale data centres.”

Organisers expect attendance at the European events to range from a handful at some to several hundred at larger gatherings such as in Brick Lane and in Dublin.

Groups backing the protests include Friends of the Earth, Greenpeace and Foxglove, a London-based campaign for “a fairer tech future”.

A weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our lives

after newsletter promotion

A key factor in national and local opposition to datacentres is their impact on the environment. By 2030, carbon dioxide emissions from AI datacentres will be six times the 2023 level, according to research by the Öko-Institut of Germany. In the UK, energy use by AI datacentres could cause the emission of up to 123m tonnes of CO2 – about as much as generated by 2.7 million people – over the next 10 years.

Various social impacts are listed by the pan-European campaign, from the impact of chatbots on mental health to the threat of AI eliminating jobs and the prioritisation of datacentres over housing. The tech industry argues that datacentres create jobs during construction and operation, and drive growth by supporting the development and deployment of AI.

About 250 global datacentre projects exceeding 100 megawatts in energy demand – equivalent to about 300,000 homes per project – were announced between 2021 and 2024, with North American schemes dominating the waiting list.

In the UK alone, there are 315 datacentres queueing to connect to the power grid, representing 73 gigawatts of demand compared with the entire country’s peak energy demand of 45GW.

https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.title: When her ‘soul cat’ died, she was bereft. Now she designs memorial jewelry to help others with pet loss
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.author: Ashley Stimpson
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.text:
A layoff and a leap of faith convinced Katie Teixeira she had what it takes to run her own business

I
n 2010, Katie Teixeira adopted a kitten found all alone in an abandoned house. The kitten – so tiny she fit in the palm of Teixeira’s hand – needed to be bottle-fed every few hours. For weeks, Teixeira set her alarm for middle-of-the-night feedings and drove home on her lunch break to care for the kitten she named Milo. As the cat grew, so did the connection between them.

“We just bonded,” Teixeira says. “Like mother and daughter.”

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Eventually, Teixeira and her husband adopted four more cats, but Milo, a tabby with white toes, maintained a special place in Teixeira’s heart. “People talk about soul animals,” she says. “Milo was my soul cat.”

When Milo died in 2021, Teixeira was bereft. She wanted a way to commemorate her. While Teixeira, who was working as a procurement analyst for CVS Health at the time, had seen pet memorial jewelry online, keepsakes that sometimes included the animal’s ashes or fur, “it just didn’t speak to me”, she says. “I’ve always been artistic and very crafty. So I was like, let me try doing something myself.”

It took a few years for inspiration to strike, but in 2023, Teixeira made a ring using a few of the whiskers Milo had shed while she was alive, crisscrossing them over a shimmering silver resin.

What happened next, she says, “happened very fast”.

When Teixeira wore the ring to her next volunteer shift at PawsWatch, the cat shelter near her home outside Providence, Rhode Island, she was inundated with requests from people who wanted their own. Soon, Teixeira was making dozens of pieces, which she began posting on her social media accounts. When one of her Instagram reels went viral, her inbox swelled with questions and requests. So Teixeira took two days off from work and built a website. Just three months after she made her first ring, Fallen Whiskers was born.

For a while, the business was Teixeira’s side hustle, a passion project that filled her nights and weekends and allowed her to support the shelter, where she donates a portion of her proceeds. But then, in 2024, she was laid off from her job of 20 years.

Friends and family encouraged her to make her side hustle a full-time gig.

“I remember saying to her, and I know it’s cliche, that when one door closes, another opens up,” says Donna Lilla, the operations manager at PawsWatch. “It just felt meant to be.”

But Teixeira wasn’t so sure.

“I was terrified,” she remembers. Her husband’s work as a heavy equipment operator could sustain the family only for so long. But her startup costs would be minimal; all she needed was a small stockpile of ring and necklace settings, the mica powder she used to create the resin backgrounds – and the whiskers, teeth and claws of pet owners who put their trust in her. She decided to test the business out, only for a few months.

Two years later, Teixeira fills about 15 orders a week for pieces that sell for $125 to $150. She has more than 100,000 Instagram followers. Her customers speak about her in adoring terms.

“She’s doing God’s work,” says Rebecca Snyder, a non-profit professional from Westchester county, New York, who remembers the day she lost her cat Emma as “literally the worst day of my life”. The pain was so overwhelming, the 40-year-old sought grief counseling.

Snyder says the matching teardrop ring and pendant necklace that Teixeira designed, with whiskers laid over a pearlescent green resin that matched the Maine Coon’s eyes, provided tremendous comfort: “I felt like I had done Emma justice by honoring her in such a beautiful way.”

Teixeira has incorporated whiskers, ashes, fur, teeth, claw sheaths, reptile skins, horse mane, hedgehog quills, bones and bits of favorite toys and blankets into cufflinks, bracelets, earrings and necklaces. (All materials must be shed naturally or collected after death, she said.) She has made a pendant of lion whiskers for a zookeeper mourning the big cat and another pendant of tiger whiskers for the sanctuary worker who cared for the rescued animal.

Fallen Whiskers is a part of a broader shift in how Americans view their pets. According to the Pew Research Center, 97% of owners consider their animals to be part of the family; more than half say their pet is as much a part of their family as a human member. Also on the rise: the amount of money pet owners are willing to spend on their animals, during their lives and afterwards, including on things like cremation, burial, memorial services and the kinds of bespoke consumer goods Teixeira produces.

Americans spent $157bn on their pets in 2025, up from $90bn in 2018, according to the American Pet Products Association.

“I’m still kind of wrapping my head around the fact that I am where I am right now,” Teixeira says of being able to earn a living from her passion project. “I guess I’ve made it.”

But “making it”, she’s learned, is very much a job that never ends.

When she started out, Teixeira tried to do her own accounting using QuickBooks but soon became overwhelmed. She decided to hire a part-time bookkeeper, the only individual on her payroll besides herself. “It’s just one thing I don’t have to worry about, and I can focus more on my customers and my orders,” she says.

Balancing her books has gotten much trickier in the last year. In April 2025, the Trump administration announced a 10% minimum tariff on almost all jewelry-related imports (with some countries and products facing much higher rates), a policy that affects Teixeira, who imports materials she can’t source in the US. A shaky market, meanwhile, has pushed investors into assets like precious metals, a trend that has essentially tripled what she pays for silver and gold.

“I have to extend that cost on to the customers,” she says. “It sucks – period.”

According to the Jewelers of America, an industry group that represents retailers and suppliers, these market shocks “pose a grave threat” to small jewelers like Teixeira, who rely on imported materials and operate on much thinner margins than big box stores. “The uncertainty of an escalating trade war can … potentially jeopardize the livelihoods of small retailers who form the backbone of the US jewelry market,” the group said in a position statement.

Teixeira says she is constantly monitoring her material costs, and, “as needed, adjusting on my side”, a time-consuming chore that takes her away from her workbench.

But according to Teixeira, managing costs isn’t the most difficult part of running Fallen Whiskers – it’s managing her emotions.

“The biggest challenge is the emotional weight of the work that I do,” she says. “Every day, I’m just diving into other people’s grief.”

That’s because Teixeira doesn’t just ask her clients for the fur and ashes they want included in their jewelry. She asks them to tell her the story of their bond with that animal. “And I’ve been there,” she says, “so it stirs up a lot of my own grief.”

While not a requirement, Teixeira says learning about the pet is a part of her creative process, as well as her way of helping other people through the pain of losing a companion.

“I was high-peak grieving, so writing was therapeutic for me,” says Natacha Hein, a clinical research contract specialist at Children’s hospital in Denver. “She helped me get over the hump.”

Hein stumbled upon Teixeira’s work online when she was looking for a way to memorialize Zazu, the “spicy” tabby that transformed the self-professed dog person into a cat person. “I wanted to feel like he was always around me,” Hein said.

The other shops she looked at “didn’t have that interaction piece. Their content felt scripted. There wasn’t a lot of warmth.” The conversations she had with Teixeira made her feel safe to send the jewelry maker precious, irreplaceable materials like fur and ashes. The day Hein received her ring, a smoky green the color of Zazu’s eyes, “was emotional as all hell”, she says. “I give Katie so much credit. It is a beautiful thing she is doing.”

So far, Teixeira has relied solely on word of mouth and daily posts on Facebook and Instagram to market Fallen Whiskers. Demand is growing, but Teixeira – who works on one piece at a time – isn’t in a rush to scale. “I don’t ever want it to feel transactional,” she says. That’s not to say the small-business owner doesn’t have aspirations.

“One day, I’d like to start my own cat sanctuary,” she says. “That’s my big, big dream.”
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.summary: Katie Teixeira adopted a kitten she named Milo in 2010. She and her husband adopted four more cats, but Milo, a tabby with white toes, maintained a special place in Teixi's heart. The Trump administration announced a 10% minimum tariff on almost all jewelry-related imports.

https://www.theguardian.com/money/us-mon.title: Financial bullying can ruin a marriage: first-person stories
https://www.theguardian.com/money/us-mon.author: Jana Kasperkevic
https://www.theguardian.com/money/us-mon.text:
When partners consider finances, when is it ‘my’ money, and when it is ‘our’ money? Guardian readers shared their experiences

A survey of about 1,000 Americans found that one in 10 would describe their partner as a financial bully. Our readers, however, insist that that might be a label easily assigned to a partner who is simply being financially responsible.

When we put out a call to out readers last week to see if any of them had similar experiences, we found that many of you wouldn’t define the actions described as financial bullying. Instead, quite a number of you insisted that keeping track of your partner’s expenses was simply budgeting and being financially responsible.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Adam: “Having disagreements about spending in a relationship is hardly bullying, it is natural and unavoidable and has happened since the dawn of money.”

Rebecca: “I thought it was called teaching financial responsibility.”

Sean: “Families should work together to maintain a budget, often one spouse is more reckless than the other, that’s not bullying, that’s being responsible.”

Sarah: “Financial bullying?! Sharing a life together and a bank account means both parties get to be involved in spending decisions.”

Nicole: “My husband knows how much money I spend. From a certain amount, I always ask him, if he’s OK with it. I won’t call it ‘financial bullying’, I call it ‘living together’. Someone has to keep an eye on the family’s money.”

Okay... but in all fairness, if you have a joint back account, and a budget, and one member of the party goes out and spends $250 unannounced on some superfluous item, then that's worthy of a conversation. And monitoring how much both people are spending is good practice.

There's nothing wrong with checking in, making sure that both parties in a relationship know how much they can spend on XY or Z.

I often look at charges and ask my husband what they are. Mostly, to make sure that anything unusual is not fraud. Secondly, if there is a huge charge for something we didn't discuss, to make sure he knows what our budget is and to stay within it. My husband often does not know what is in our bank account, flies off on work, spends a large amount of money on dinner and drinks, and then leaves me scrimping on grocery bills.

Does that make me a bully if I check our balance and warn him if his spending is going over the budget? You know, we also have rent and food to pay for, and only one bank account between us, of which I am the larger earner. My husband should feel ashamed if he blows our budget on expensive meals or jeans. Just as I should feel ashamed if I go out on a shopping spree that prevents us from buying food. Where does necessary budgeting and monitoring end, and bullying begin?

double quotation markMy ex-husband routinely spent our rent/bill/food money on restaurants, taxis and other things we really didn’t have the budget for. Finally I got sick of being behind on rent and always running out of money for food, and put my foot down. He refused to sit down and do a budget with me, saying “Why don’t you just do it?” So I did.

I made a budget of all his personal spending, and finally I had to make him choose between taxis to work and lunch at restaurants, which felt bizarre and incredibly uncomfortable for me. He chose taxis over lunch, and after that, whenever colleagues would ask him why he wasn’t joining them for lunch, he’d tell them that his wife wouldn’t allow it.

So my question is, who was the financial bully in this situation, me or him?

A reader from Arkansas says she was financially bullied by her then-husband for years:

double quotation markBut not the way you mean: when I suggested he cut back on his credit-card use on the card held in my name, he sharply increased his use, increasing our debt to $23,000 in a matter of months. That’s what I call financial bullying.

Even checking the accounts doesn’t stop financial ruin:

double quotation markA few years after we were married, my ex-husband developed a drug abuse problem. I was balancing the checkbook every month. He would take money out of our accounts to buy and sell drugs and not tell me. When the accounts wouldn’t match up, he would berate me for not being accurate. He spent all of our money and ran the credit cards up to the max.

When we got divorced we had two credit cards, one for the home and one for his “business” that never got off the ground. The agreement was that I would pay off the family card and he would pay off the business card. Of course, he never did and the creditors came after me – I wound up paying both of them off. My credit was wrecked for seven years.

double quotation markReading the comments here I guess none of the commentators has experienced this.

I have and it certainly was bullying. Talking about finances together is very different from keeping a tight eye on your partner’s spending and questioning every last penny. In my situation, this was coupled with a wholly one-sided approach to discussing joint spending which characterised what I suggested as ‘spending on me’ while what they wanted as ‘spending on us’.

Unless you’ve been in that sort of relationship, I recommend that you aren’t so quick to judge.

double quotation markBeen there too. Money I earned was “our money”, money she earned was “her money”. She was serious. She would get hysterical whenever I bought a magazine yet she felt she could blow hundreds in one shopping spree on whatever she felt like having.

A female reader living in New York wrote:

double quotation markI am in an arranged marriage, to a man who is self-made after a struggled childhood, with disregarded needs, as defined above. However, unless purchases are made to his own liking, he is extremely tight with money. For many years into my marriage – around five – I had no say in the type of food I ate or clothes I wore. My request for a choice of three types of breakfast cereals was seen as “an attempt to cremate his money”. My clothes came from Walmart or Value City.

When we went out, I was expected to eat at home, and could not have a $1 coffee or $1 hot dog in case I got a little peckish under the guise of ‘saving money’ and ‘aggressive savings targets’. If an eggplant spoiled in the refrigerator, the spoiled part was taken and smeared across my face and down my arms, to teach me the value of money. The rear of the television set was checked for warmth on arrival home from work to prove I had been watching TV all day and therefore ‘wasting electricity’. My grocery shopping was severely monitored, as I ‘made it my mission to waste money’.

I think it is important to note I had no earnings of my own during this period.

Fast-forward many years. Now I have my own earnings. My favorite shops are Nordstrom and Anthropologie [where I shop] on the regular and hide [purchases] in the closet. [I] accuse [my] better half of a bad memory when the clothes, bags and shoes make an appearance – with no apologies or regret whatsoever for my behaviours!

However, I think it’s fair to say that we have a sizeable bank balance and the mortgage is a year from being paid off in full.
https://www.theguardian.com/money/us-mon.summary: Survey of 1,000 Americans found one in 10 would describe their partner as a financial bully. But readers insist that they are simply being financially responsible.

https://www.theguardian.com/news/2026/ja.title: ‘I ain’t goin nowhere’: Gullah Geechee people fight off developers with a historic referendum
https://www.theguardian.com/news/2026/ja.author: Timothy Pratt in McIntosh county, Georgia
https://www.theguardian.com/news/2026/ja.text:
A citizen referendum, only the second of its kind in Georgia history, seeks to block a zoning amendment

I
re Gene Grovner stood behind his house on a recent morning, between chicken pens on one side and rows of winter collard greens on the other, holding a knife and skinning a raccoon splayed across a wood post.

“The meat is good roasted,” Grovner said. He pointed to the collards, a burst of green in the winter cold, and the chickens, with their eggs. “If you ain’t lazy, you can live good here,” he said, referring to Sapelo Island off the coast of southern Georgia.

Then he waved in a broad circle, pointing out the nearby modest homes of family members, all bearing the same last name as him, which Grovner, who is 70, says stretches nine generations back on Hogg Hummock.

The community is home to the Gullah Geechee people, descendants of enslaved west Africans who worked on cotton, indigo and rice plantations from North Carolina to Florida. In places like South Carolina’s Hilton Head Island, the Gullah Geechee population was nearly wiped out by development starting in the 1960s.

On Sapelo Island, post-enslavement, freed Black folks were granted land in Hogg Hummock in part because it was seen as marshy and less desirable than the rest of the island. It is the only remaining sea island community of Gullah Geechee people in Georgia.

“All that’s family,” Grovner summed up. “All those people who want to build houses here ain’t gonna close me in.”

Outsiders building large vacation houses was what was at stake in Tuesday’s election in McIntosh county, where Sapelo is located – only the second citizen referendum on a county plan or policy in Georgia history. (Nearby Camden county voters defeated a county plan to build a rocket-launching pad through a referendum in 2022.)

The referendum, brought about after more than 2,000 registered voters in the county signed petitions, allowed residents to vote on whether they were for or against a zoning amendment increasing the amount of residential square footage permitted in Hogg Hummock from 1,400 to 3,000.

Unofficial results released on Tuesday evening showed that nearly 85% of 1,869 county voters opposed the zoning increase.

Allowing larger houses to be built on the island would have opened the door to developers – “all those people” Grovner named – which then would raise taxes, making it harder for Gullah Geechee people to continue living on Sapelo, and potentially changing the island’s cultural and environmental landscape forever.

The number of Gullah Geechee people living on Sapelo has dwindled to between 30 and 40 residents, down from about 500 in the early 20th century. Dozens of the residents’ children and other family members have moved to the mainland over time. Nonetheless, many of these family members maintain ties to the island; some still own property and plan on retiring there.

“Every county in the state of Georgia is looking at” Tuesday’s results, said Kathleen Russell, editor of the Darien News – because any county’s residents can now mount a referendum and challenge zoning rules, she said.

The referendum made history in the region as well, as referendums “are incredibly rare in the majority of the south”, said Chris Melody Fields Figueredo, executive director of the Ballot Initiative Strategy Center. The reason: “States where formerly enslaved people lived, the state governments did not want those people to exercise their power,” Fields Figueredo said.

The ability to stage a referendum in Georgia comes from provisions in the state’s constitution. First, a certain percentage of a county’s registered voters signs a petition indicating they want to vote on a policy from the county’s elected representatives. The percentage varies based on the county’s population.

Once the threshold of confirmed signatures is reached and a referendum is authorized, it is “a form of holding power accountable, where systems of governance are challenged”, said Fields Figueredo.

The Gullah Geechee people who were leading the effort to hold the referendum first had to defeat the county’s legal challenges, based on assertions that zoning rules weren’t covered by language in the state’s constitution. It took a September state supreme court decision to give the green light to Tuesday’s election.

The Guardian spoke to a handful of the nearly 1,000 county residents who cast ballots during a two-week early voting period ending Friday. All had ties to Sapelo Island and Hogg Hummock, and felt strongly about the need to protect the community from unchecked development.

The unspoiled qualities that allow Gullah Geechee people to live close to nature also make the island a prime location for natural science; in the 1950s, Sapelo was the site of foundational research in the nascent field of ecology.

After casting his ballot on Thursday, Nick Macías described Sapelo as “an ecologically important island you don’t find anywhere in the world”. Macías, who works as assistant operations director at the island’s University of Georgia Marine Institute, pointed out that Sapelo was the only Georgia sea island with healthy communities of marsh grass – a keystone species, or one that other animals and plants in an ecosystem depend on for survival.

Allowing larger houses and increased development in Hogg Hummock “would put stress on the carbon footprint” of the island and displace Gullah Geechee people, he said: “When it comes to preserving the [Gullah Geechee] culture, it comes down to the next generation being able to live there.”

Also voting last week, Samuel – who didn’t want his last name used – had gotten off his job early as a trucker to cast a ballot. He has ties to Hogg Hummock through his wife, who has family there. “It’s a unique place,” he said. “You go there … and they treat you like family. They take you in.”

The trucker remembers first visiting as a teenager. “They showed me medicine for toothaches, using plants,” he said. As for the community’s ongoing struggles, he said, “I’ll fight for it till the end. They deserve it. It’s their place.”

One of Ire Gene Grovner’s relatives in Hogg Hummock is his brother, Bobby Gene Grovner. He’s renovating his home on the island, with plans of leaving it to his two daughters. “These ones who come with a pocketful of money, it ain’t gonna work,” he said, referring to developers with interest in the community’s land.

Still, Bobby Gene, who turns 67 later this month, said “it’s tiring” to have to fight in courtrooms and government halls for his community.

“I ain’t got but 40 years left!” he said, laughing.

His brother Ire Gene is involved in another unresolved legal battle, laying claim to several dozen acres of land that a 2024 lawsuit asserts was taken from his family by the state of Georgia in nearby Raccoon Bluff, a 698-acre plot of land on the island formerly inhabited by Gullah Geechee people. The lawsuit includes land deed records in Grovner’s family dating to 1875.

An ongoing case involving the subject of Tuesday’s referendum, filed by the Southern Poverty Law Center, asserts that the proposed zoning amendment was discriminatory. “The people in [Hogg Hummock] feel like they’ve been shut out,” said the SPLC attorney Miriam Gutman. “[They] want to pass their land onto their children and grandchildren. They want to be part of the conversation” about the community’s future, she said.

But even the immediate future after Tuesday’s result is unclear, as the McIntosh county attorney, Adam Poppell, recently stated that voters rejecting the county’s attempt to increase the maximum square footage allowed on the island doesn’t mean conditions will revert to what they were before: a limit of 1,400 sq ft. Instead, Poppell said, the election’s result leaves Hogg Hummock with “no zoning” – meaning anything could be built.

The county attorney did not answer a request for comment.

Dana Braun, attorney for the Hogg Hummock residents who mounted the referendum effort, said another lawsuit would be likely if the county insists on Poppell’s interpretation of where things stand. “The county apparently loves paying lawyers for losing battles,” he said.

After cleaning off his knife and preparing the raccoon on Friday, Ire Gene turned to face the chicken pens and the morning’s eggs. His position on the future of Hogg Hummock: “I ain’t planning on goin’ nowhere.”

This article was amended on 11 February 2026. A previous version misidentified a building in an image caption.
