https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/06/hundre.title: Hundreds of Artex AI hacking tools found publicly exposed to the web
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/06/hundre.author: Zack Whittaker
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/06/hundre.text:
Security researchers have discovered hundreds of copies of a Chinese-made AI hacking tool publicly exposed to the internet for anyone to access, potentially allowing outsiders to launch cyberattacks against unsuspecting targets.

The hacking software, called Artex, is an open source autonomous penetration testing tool, meaning software that automatically probes computer systems for weaknesses, and it’s been linked to several cyberattacks since its public release in July. As open source software, it’s free for anyone to download and run on their own servers, making it a popular tool for those who cannot access Anthropic or OpenAI’s most advanced cybersecurity AI models for discovering security vulnerabilities. Microsoft has previously described Artex as a system of AI agents that can conduct cyberattacks “from reconnaissance through data exfiltration with little needed human interaction.”

In a blog post, cybersecurity firm Censys, which scans the internet for exposed or vulnerable systems, said that it identified more than 800 distinct deployments of Artex that were accessible from the web without needing a password to log in.

Silas Cutler, principal security researcher at Censys who wrote the blog post, said that not every instance of Artex is operated maliciously and many are used for authorized testers. But it’s unclear why hundreds of these Artex systems are exposed to the web, as the software does not require them to be accessible from the internet.

The findings underscore how even powerful hacking tools can be misconfigured to be publicly accessible by anyone, increasing the chance that someone will find and misuse them. The publicly accessible systems also expose attack tools, such as implants (hidden malicious software) used to compromise and maintain persistent access to a victim’s network.

Security companies have linked the use of Artex to several broad-scale cyberattacks, including against the Korean finance industry in September. Cybersecurity giant CrowdStrike attributed the attacks to a Chinese-speaking hacker who used an Artex instance in the attacks, in part because the hacker had left an “open directory” hosting the system. Censys said that its data showed the Artex instance in question had been publicly exposed for months, and appeared to contain more attack data that extended “well beyond South Korean banks,” including payment and gaming companies.

Artex was also used in an attack on IT support giant ConnectWise earlier in October, which allowed Chinese-linked hackers to spy on thousands of organizations whose data and files are hosted in Microsoft’s cloud. Microsoft, which has visibility into the attack, said in a blog post that the hackers used Artex to break into customers’ cloud environments and steal their data at such speed that defenders had “little time to detect and respond.”

Many of the attacks linked to Artex involved exploiting simple vulnerabilities, such as guessing weak or known passwords, and a lack of multi-factor authentication.

The findings show that simple vulnerabilities, including misconfigurations, can expose both the attacker and their targets.

Artex has since announced it would go closed-source, effectively limiting further releases for paid customers. There are still dozens of copies of Artex’s code available on code-sharing sites that can still be used in active attacks.
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/06/hundre.summary: Hackers have discovered hundreds of copies of a Chinese-made AI hacking tool publicly exposed to the internet for anyone to access. The hacking software, called Artex, is an open source autonomous penetration testing tool. It’s been linked to several cyberattacks since its public release in July.

https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/06/meta-i.title: Meta introduces Spaces, a new way to collaborate with your Muse agent
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/06/meta-i.author: Lucas Ropek
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/06/meta-i.text:
Meta recently launched its Muse agents — a new generation of cuddly agentic helpers. Now, the company has launched Spaces, a new way to communicate and collaborate with them.

As far as I can tell, Spaces are basically breakout conversations that revolve around a particular topic — although Meta refers to them as “custom experiences.” They live in the sidebar of the interface where you interact with your Muse agent. Clicking on the Space brings up the conversation, where Muse works toward a particular goal on your behalf.

For instance, if you wanted to plan a vacation, you could open a new Space focused on that particular project, and whenever you want to work on it with Muse, you would click to open that particular tab. Or, if you’re focused on collecting recipes for an upcoming family event, you’d open a new Space for that particular project. Other examples Meta gives are a holiday gift tracker, a wedding planner, or a space for DIY projects.

“Describe an idea in chat, and Muse builds a space for you, whether that’s a tracker, a planner or a project board,” Meta says.

Spaces can also be easily integrated with third-party apps and information, Meta says.

“Connect the apps you use, and your spaces keep themselves up to date in the background, so new concert dates, price changes, or savings progress show up without you having to ask,” the company says.

On Friday, Mark Zuckerberg, Meta’s founder and CEO, posted about the new feature on X: “Playing around with spaces in Muse lately — tell Muse what you need and it builds it. I’ve made a BBQ game, an event tracker, and a home control dashboard. Excited to see what you build.”

Muse agents — and the cuddly avatars that enclose them — have been greeted with a relatively warm reception over the past few months. During its earnings call in October, Zuckerberg said that its agents had 10 million users in the U.S. and Canada — less than two months after the agents debuted.

The company is obviously busy building out the user experience around the agents. Spaces is actually the second new Muse feature that Meta has debuted over the last week. On Thursday, the company also announced Muse Voice, which allows users to video chat with their agent and give it commands verbally.

The company is in competition with other cute and cuddly AI agents — including OpenAI’s dots and SpaceXAI’s Grokbot, which were debuted with similarly cartoonish personas.

https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/06/pentag.title: Pentagon offers battery startup 6K $250M loan to build US factory
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/06/pentag.author: Tim De Chant
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/06/pentag.text:
Batteries are everywhere, even on the battlefield, which helps explain the Pentagon’s recent interest in building more domestic manufacturing capacity.

The 12-year-old, North Andover, Massachusetts-based startup 6K announced Thursday that it won conditional approval for a $250 million loan from the Department of Defense to build a factory in Tennessee. The plant will use a unique microwave-powered process to produce battery materials that don’t rely on Chinese suppliers.

The company previously received a $50 million grant from the Department of Energy under the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law, though that 2023 grant was canceled by the Trump administration in a chaotic sweep of Biden-era awards, forcing 6K to reapply.

The factory was originally slated to open in 2024, but the grant cancelation and uncertainties in the EV market forced the company to rejigger its plans.

6K’s manufacturing process uses microwaves to heat metals into a plasma and then deposit them onto a surface, reducing the number of steps required to make cathode material, a key battery component. The company says the process can work on a number of different battery types, including lithium iron phosphate (LFP).

https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/06/fox-co.author: Lauren Forristal
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/06/fox-co.text:
Fox has completed its $22 billion acquisition of Roku, wrapping up one of the biggest media deals in recent years and giving the company a major boost in the streaming and connected TV space.

Announced Friday, the deal brings the streaming company founded in 2002 formally under Fox’s ownership. Fox says the combined company now ranks as the third-largest television business in the U.S. by viewership.

“We started Roku more than two decades ago to give people a better way to watch TV, and that mission doesn’t change today. What does change is our reach and resources,” Roku founder Anthony Wood said in a statement. “Our teams will keep building and innovating as they always have, now with the support and capabilities of Fox behind us.”

For Fox, the move provides direct access to Roku’s reach of more than 100 million households. The company expects that audience to help it improve advertising targeting, strengthen its position in the fast-growing connected TV market, and reduce its reliance on traditional TV distribution.

Today’s announcement comes two months after the Justice Department issued a second request for information, asking both companies to provide additional data and documents as part of its antitrust review. Earlier this month, reports suggested the deal was nearing U.S. regulatory approval.

The acquisition also closed much earlier than expected. When the deal was first announced in June, the companies projected it would be completed in the first half of 2027.

https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/06/ramp-d.title: Ramp data shows AI spending stalling just as Anthropic nears its IPO
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/06/ramp-d.author: Rebecca Bellan
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/06/ramp-d.text:
Companies are using more AI than ever, but they’re not spending more on it.

A new report from Ramp shows AI spending flatlined over late summer even as token volumes rose, a sign that price competition and savvier customers may be capping revenue for OpenAI and Anthropic. According to Ramp’s data, token spend only grew 1.5% across August and September. To compare, in July, it grew 42% from the previous month.

As Anthropic gears up for its IPO, the data suggests investors might be wrong to assume AI companies will keep growing at breakneck speed.

“Almost the entire spend on AI is from venture-backed, high-growth tech companies,” Ramp’s lead economist Ara Kharazian told TechCrunch. “That’s fine as long as AI spend continues to rise, but if it starts to slow down because of something in the market or some other factor, they will all start to slow down simultaneously, and that could lead to other cascading effects.”

Kharazian said he’s already seeing evidence that the top 1% of firms — the most “AI-pilled” — have stuttered slightly in their spend in August and September, coming up just below the $10,000 per-employee they were hitting at their summer peaks. A slowdown among that cohort is “sufficient to slow down revenue entirely, despite the fact that we’re seeing rising volumes,” he said.

Ramp data shows growth in spending among median and top 10%, but it’s not enough to make up the difference. Median firms spend $12-$15 per employee per month, and the top 10% spend $600-$1,000.

“If you look at the use cases today, it’s not necessarily clear they will get up to that $10,000 per employee per month mark that the 1% is at,” Kharazian said. While there’s plenty of demand for AI coding agents in industries like software and finance, “it’s not necessarily true that a doctor’s office or a car dealership will need to spend that much on AI.”

“The era of hypergrowth may be over, and now that we know there may not be as much juice to squeeze out of the top 1%,” he continued.

October data did see a re-acceleration, with token spend up 8.9% from September 23 to October 23, but Kharazian said the headwinds on spend growth are strong.

Kharazian (who has published a series of blogs called “Cracks in the AI Thesis”) said the slowdown isn’t due to a demand problem. Again, AI volumes are up. Instead he points to the competitive nature of the marketplace.

“OpenAI and Anthropic price cuts have…just made it cheaper to use AI,” he said. In September, OpenAI cut API prices in half for GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna. Answering the price war, Anthropic has also made significant reductions to pricing for Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5 — a decision that the company said in a recent filing slashed revenue growth by about $600 million. Both companies have also been offering enterprise discounts that are intended to lock-in spend, but in reality are hitting their revenue targets.

Kharazian said this dynamic means it has very much become a buyer’s market.

Subsidizing use of expensive technology in order to lock in customers has always been a part of the Big Tech playbook. Just recall how cheap it used to be to take an Uber or Lyft ride, and now that there are few other ride-hail players, the cost of going from A to B has risen significantly. Kharazian says those dynamics don’t work in the AI world because there’s just too much competition.

“Meta and Nvidia are also introducing enterprise offerings with pretty cheap models or open source models,” Kharazian said. He also pointed to the range of other open model companies from China and the United States, as well as a new company called Jev — a lightweight tool for choosing between a few predetermined outputs — that is increasingly among the top performers on Ramp.

“For a lot of AI use cases, you just need a simple Yes/No,” Kharazian said. “So you take your already cheap models, you shift them over to Jev, and now your already cheap stuff gets even cheaper.”

The ability to complete workloads at a much cheaper cost is another factor driving the spending slowdown. That’s partly due to the discounts from AI companies, but also because companies are just getting better at being thrifty.

“As you get really advanced in using AI, you get better at figuring out how to control it,” Kharazian said. “You’re more likely to use defaults that prevent usage of very expensive models for long-running tasks. You’re more likely to impose some budgets on employees. You’re more likely to offload some of the spend from standard and light models to even cheaper light models via routers.”

Notion co-founder Akshay Kothari recently posted internal data that matched Ramp’s insights. As he succinctly put it: “tokens go brrr. costs go ahhh.”

tokens go brrr
costs go ahhh pic.twitter.com/1whCWCJCyM

“A lot of the assumptions that we had about the trajectory of AI spend are starting to break down,” Kharazian said. “You can use more AI, but use it for less. That’s great for the customers…but it’s not necessarily great for the model companies. And it does introduce new questions around their revenue trajectories.”

Bloomberg reported Friday that Anthropic’s potential valuation sank from the $2 trillion estimated in early October to just $1.2 to $1.3 trillion. The company is also reportedly expected to receive a high “junk” rating from credit agencies. OpenAI also lowered its proposed valuation to $1.25 trillion from $1.4 trillion and slashed its latest fundraising goals by about $10 billion.

Kharazian says Ramp’s dataset likely informs many investor concerns. There is, however, one potential brightside for spending trajectories, albeit a speculative one.

Much of the thesis for hypergrowth spending is that AI will undoubtedly introduce new use cases that will accelerate things. AI coding emerged just a year and a half ago as the most commercially viable product that has led Anthropic and OpenAI to becoming trillion-dollar companies. The hope among investors is that there will be another revolution that will drive further spend.

Some think personal agents will be the next coding agents. OpenAI, SpaceXAI, and Meta have all released their own personal agents, alongside startups like Instinct. Kharazian is skeptical, though, that personal agents, which are “not as economically productive as coding,” will provide the boost the industry needs for nonstop growth.

“The projection is that there will be new products being introduced that will drive further growth,” Kharazian said. “But based on what we can observe today and the products available and what is commercially advanced, AI spend has started to slow down.”

https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/06/after-.title: After blocking Muse, Amazon now lets users text Alexa to help them shop
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/06/after-.author: Ivan Mehta
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/06/after-.text:
Amazon is jumping on the currently most popular bandwagon for interacting with AI agents: texting. The company on Friday said it is launching a feature that lets customers chat with its Alexa AI agent over text messages to help them shop, much like you can with AI agents like Muse or Instinct.

The move comes after Amazon blocked Meta’s Muse from querying its site in September. The company is rolling the features out just before the start of the holiday shopping season.

The e-commerce giant said select U.S. customers will get a text asking them to enable the shopping feature. Those with access can text Alexa to shop on Amazon using natural language queries, spanning everything from searching for items, adding them to cart, and purchasing.

The text agent builds on the recent shopping-focused upgrades to Alexa, and so can manage lists, keep tabs on prices, search for items across the web, compare products, and check the status of orders. Users can also share a picture of an item or someone wearing an outfit to search for similar listings on Amazon.

The company said over time, Alexa will learn users’ preferences and suggest items accordingly.

The company said users who don’t get invited to use this feature can sign up to a waitlist. The feature will be rolled out more broadly in the coming weeks.

As the market for consumer-focused AI agents balloons, platforms like Amazon are building their own to tap this new avenue of user interaction. Last month, delivery company DoorDash said that third-party agents had so far only placed hundreds of orders in total on its platform, and that it plans to concentrate on developing its own text-based agent, launched in September, further.

https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/06/underd.title: Underdog shows off a 32MB speech model in new demo
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/06/underd.author: Ivan Mehta
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/06/underd.text:
AI companies across the world are racing to make bigger and better models, but the problem is all of them need massive amounts of processing power. On the other end, some researchers and startups are creating smaller models that can run on edge devices, like your phone or computer.

One such startup, Underdog, has released a game built with its new voice model called Woof that’s only 32MB large.

The game features a room with a retro tech theme, a typewriter, and a CRT monitor. There is a desk lamp, which makes a sound when you click its switch. The intro warns users about “intrusive” cloud providers in the town — ostensibly a jab at cloud-based models.

You can interact with the typewriter and music tuner.

You can type anything on the typewriter using your keyboard, and the game will speak it back. You can also rotate the tuner to generate different kinds of music.

All of this works within the browser through Underdog’s speech generation model, which, the company says, can run on most devices without any internet connection. The model has 31 million parameters and is open for everyone to download.

While such a small model likely won’t replace bigger models, it may still be enough to drive local assistant experiences or create personalized podcasts.

This demo comes weeks after Underdog launched Bark, a 167MB speech-to-text model also designed to run on edge devices for transcription and dictation.

Sigil Wen, the founder of Underdog, told TechCrunch that he started building the app because, instead of using notetakers like Granola, he wanted to build his own system with AI models that can run on users’ devices and let them own their data.

“I think we will be able to run most capable models of today on the devices you already own within months. We just want to train the best open models that are American-made, that are open, that are capable and allow people to have private AI,” he said, referring to his manifesto.

In addition to the two voice models mentioned above, Underdog has also released a 27-billion-parameter model that can run on laptops, along with a waitlisted app that the company is positioning as a locally hosted alternative to Muse and Instinct.

The game features a room with a retro tech theme, a typewriter, and a CRT monitor. The company says the model can run on most devices without any internet connection.

https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/06/physic.title: Physicl raises $10M to make the digital world real enough for robots
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/06/physic.author: Tim Fernholz
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/06/physic.text:
Alex de Vigan’s last business got swamped by the rise of generative AI, but now he’s betting the tech that team had built, a platform for creating tempting product renderings for e-commerce, can be re-purposed to make robots more useful.

His new venture, Physicl, has raised $10 million in seed funding led by Inovia Capital to help world model designers and robot builders solve thorny training problems with more realistic simulations.

Founder and CEO de Vigan spent the last decade building nfinite, which made it easy for brands and retailers to create 3D models of their goods and display them online. The arrival of transformer-based AI models led that company to focus more on generative imagery, but de Vigan saw a new purpose for his team and the tech stack they’d built to faithfully render 3D environments.

“What we were super unique about doing in 3D, AI was going to replace, but something was missing in AI: its ability to understand, interact, and manipulate space and objects,” de Vigan says.

Researchers developing physical AI models to make robots more capable of tasks like handling diverse, small objects have been frustrated by the returns of training them on video, and the expense of gathering data through remote operations.

Simulations in digital worlds are seen as a promising solution, but ensuring that these simulated worlds are faithful to real-world physics has proven difficult. De Vigan believes that the pipeline his previous company built to “transform unstructured, incomplete, heterogeneous real-world information into a high-fidelity physical representation… with correct geometry, materials, and physics” can now be used to make physical AI models more effective.

Physicl is entering a crowded category of startups vying to provide data and tooling to foundation model builders and robot operators. “The space is very young and very blurry sometimes,” de Vigan admits. There are a variety of companies collecting, labeling, or generating data in different modalities as their customers try to figure out the secret sauce that will make robots live up to their promise.

In particular, Physicl wants to focus on post-training models on difficult edge cases. The startup is releasing a product called Studio with 10,000 3D environments and 100,000 assets that represent various objects. It lets users create scenes to generate synthetic data for training robots on specific problems. For example, Studio could be used to generate training data to help a robot that has trouble discerning a cup on a cluttered counter-top, or while the cup is in shadow.

SpAItial, a world model builder, collaborated with Physicl as an early customer to improve the fidelity of its products, the latest of which, Echo-3, was released last week. SpAItial’s tool generates 3D simulations from 2D imagery, and to do that effectively, its CEO and founder Matthias Niessner said they needed to train on the kind of high-fidelity synthetic data Physicl offers.

However, Physicl wants to be more than a data provider; it sees itself as the tooling for ongoing synthetic data generation. “What we created 10 years ago, without knowing it, was basically an agentic workflow to transform unstructured information into high-fidelity 3D,” de Vigan said. He imagines customers bringing trillions of images or millions of hours of lidar capture data to feed into his platform and turn them into high-quality 3D representations that can be used to generate billions of permutations to train their models.

“The real challenge is, you have to curate the data by hand, and this is a very long cycle,” Niessner, also a professor of robotics at the Technical University of Munich, told TechCrunch. “To us what seems very attractive is you can just do this on the fly […] You’re running Claude, and it checks, ‘Oh, I need more data of this in my training,’ and then it auto generates that data, depending on the training state. That, to me, is super exciting, and this is exactly what Physicl is offering.”

https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/06/tesla-.title: Tesla will stop making the Cybertruck in 2027
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/06/tesla-.author: Sean O'Kane
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/06/tesla-.text:
Tesla will stop making the Cybertruck next year, according to CEO Elon Musk, who said on X that the company will use the factory space to build more two-seater Cybercab robotaxis.

The decision to wind down the futuristic, steel-clad EV comes after just a few short years of underwhelming sales. When Musk handed over the first few Cybertrucks in late 2023, he predicted Tesla would sell around 250,000 per year. It was supposed to be such a cornerstone of Tesla’s future that, before construction began, the company talked about its Texas factory as the “Cybertruck factory.” But Tesla has instead sold just tens of thousands — total — over the last three years.

Tesla is killing off the Cybertruck at a moment when it is trying to become an AI- and robotics-focused company. A big part of that is its robotaxi ambitions.

The company has spent the last two months putting Cybercabs on the streets in its hometown of Austin, Texas. With no major incidents to date, the company has said it plans to expand the Cybercabs operations to other cities, starting with Dallas later this month. (Tesla also operates robotaxi versions of its Model Y SUVs in Austin, Houston, and Dallas, as well as three cities in Florida.)

This is the third product Tesla has discontinued in order to fuel those greater ambitions. Earlier this year, the company decided to end production of the Model S sedan and Model X SUV and instead use the factory space dedicated to those vehicles to make Optimus humanoid robots.

First announced in 2019, the Cybertruck was a product that Musk had long obsessed over.

“Probably my personal favorite for the next product is the pickup truck, and we are going to just do an amazing pickup truck,” he said on one of Tesla’s earnings calls that year.

Musk promised the Cybertruck would be radical, inspired by the designs of cyberpunk sci-fi stories like “Blade Runner.” While that certainly bore out in the design, the company overpromised on the basics of the Cybertruck from the jump. During the now-infamous reveal event in 2019, when head designer Franz von Holzhausen cracked the Cybertruck’s windows with steel balls, Tesla said the EV was supposed to start at under $40,000 and have up to 500 miles of range. It achieved neither of those figures.

Instead, the truck was delayed for two years, in part because of the COVID-19 pandemic. When it finally did hit the market in late 2023, Tesla handed over the first few Cybertrucks to customers in a short, somewhat odd for Tesla event (by the company’s own standards, at least), which saw a poorly-lit Musk standing in a truck bed promising the truck was “the finest in apocalyptic equipment” fit for “late civilization vibes.” The base price had inflated to around $60,000, and the top-end range had shrunk by over 100 miles.

The truck has struggled on the market ever since. The polarizing design never seemed to sit well with buyers, especially at a higher-than-expected price. Then, during its first full year of sales in 2024, Musk became a major financial backer of Donald Trump, which turned the instantly recognizable Cybertruck into a target for protesters. That continued into 2025 as Musk led the so-called Department of Government Efficiency, which fired thousands of federal workers.

https://www.theverge.com/tech/1023230/th.title: The UV-tracking Gem made me rethink how sunlight affects my health, not just my appearance
https://www.theverge.com/tech/1023230/th.author: Sheena Vasani
https://www.theverge.com/tech/1023230/th.text:
What started as a test to understand how sun exposure was aging my skin took a turn that I wasn’t expecting.

What started as a test to understand how sun exposure was aging my skin took a turn that I wasn’t expecting.

With temperatures rising to the 90s in Los Angeles, avoiding the heat wasn’t exactly an option while I was at a relative’s outdoor party in August. So I sat beneath a patio umbrella with a powerful fan nearby, figuring I was protected from the sun and heat. Half an hour later, I felt exhausted, dizzy, nauseous, and generally unwell, symptoms consistent with heat exhaustion.

Around the same time, I received a notification from an app used by the $249 ($149 at the time of publication) UV-tracking necklace I’d been wearing, called Gem, from a company called The90. It warned that my UV exposure had climbed considerably. It turns out UV radiation wasn’t repelled by this patio umbrella, and it’s hard to ever be fully protected because radiation can be reflected or scattered by objects in the environment. While UV exposure and overheating are different things, I’d mistakenly assumed the shade and the fan would adequately protect me from both.

This led to a discovery: One of my medications increases my sensitivity to heat, which helped to explain similar episodes I’d experienced over the years. The Gem didn’t diagnose anything, but it prompted me to investigate something I might otherwise have dismissed. Since then, I’ve been more mindful about limiting time outdoors during hours of peak heat and UV, staying hydrated, and paying closer attention to how I’m feeling outside.

I’ll admit my initial interest in tracking UV was largely vanity-driven. As much as I try to challenge harmful beauty standards, I’m hardly immune to them. Having started going gray in my 20s, I’m keen on slowing down other visible signs of aging where I reasonably can. But between being Indian (I rarely get sunburned thanks in part to my skin’s higher melanin content, not that it eliminates the risk of sun damage or skin cancer) and living within walking distance of the beach in perpetually sunny LA, I hadn’t given much thought to how much UV exposure I was actually getting. The Gem has helped me better understand it by providing a range of estimates, some more useful than others.

The included UV-detecting sensor measures UVA and UVB radiation separately, rather than simply displaying my area’s UV forecast. UVB is primarily responsible for sunburn and helps your skin produce vitamin D, while UVA contributes to premature aging, even when you aren’t visibly burning. Thankfully, getting these metrics doesn’t come at the cost of wearing a bulky device. The circular pendant comes with a cute, thin necklace I’d happily wear even if it didn’t track anything. Its titanium, gold- or silver-colored chain pairs well with a variety of outfits. Battery life lasted almost exactly a week (the advertised lifespan), and the Gem recharges using an included charging dock. The90 plans to release a hat clip and bag tag early next year, which seem ideal for those who prefer not to wear it around their neck.

The mobile app is central to the experience. It has easy-to-read graphs and jargon-light explanations. I enjoyed using it. While not required, you can create a skin profile so that it can estimate a range of metrics based on the sensor’s UVA and UVB readings. The profile is based upon factors like skin type, sensitivities, clothing, and sunscreen. That means its estimates aren’t based on UV exposure alone, though they’re still predictions rather than direct measurements of how your body is responding to sunlight.

There’s a lot here, including your estimated vitamin D production, potential circadian light benefits, estimated nitric oxide-related benefits, cumulative UVA exposure, and recent accumulated UVA exposure. Alongside cumulative UVA exposure and weekly trends, its Skin Aging Zone assesses potential aging-related risk and offers personalized skincare advice. It also provides a personalized sunburn countdown, sunscreen reminders, and a daily Sun Score.

The Sun Score is a rating that incorporates various metrics to balance sunlight’s potential benefits against the risks of overexposure. The company encourages users to aim for a daily Sun Score of 90, though more sun isn’t necessarily better. Too little exposure means missing potential benefits, while excessive UV can damage your skin. I appreciated the context, but the individual estimated measurements proved more revealing than the Sun Score.

The UV readings in the app responded quickly as I moved between sunlight, shade, and indoors, even registering changes near windows. I couldn’t independently verify the sensor’s accuracy, but the readings behaved as expected as I shifted between environments. However, there were times when I noticed the Gem sometimes failed to register that I had been outside. Eventually, I discovered the app needs to remain running in the background (at least on iPhone; I haven’t tested on Android), as measurements aren’t stored on the sensor, and fully closing the app interrupts tracking.

My experience at the outdoor party challenged my assumptions about how much protection I was getting from the shade. Just as surprising to me was learning how little UVB I accumulated during a typical week, despite living somewhere so sunny. I fell short of the app’s estimated sunlight-derived vitamin D target almost daily, prompting me to research how melanin, while offering some natural UV protection, impacts vitamin D production from sunlight. Until then, I’d mostly thought about sun exposure in terms of protecting my skin from damage. Seeing how little UVB I was accumulating made me consider what I might be missing out on, too.

The vitamin D countdown wasn’t as helpful as I had hoped. During one test, its estimate of how much additional sunlight I needed dropped from several hours to under an hour, then climbed past six hours just minutes later. The fluctuations appeared related to changing UVB intensity, though I couldn’t verify that. I noticed similar fluctuations in the app’s estimated time to sunburn. With both countdowns changing so dramatically, I stopped paying much attention to the exact times and focused instead on the broader picture: whether it felt like I was getting too much or too little sun.

That was perhaps the biggest surprise of testing the Gem. After my experience using it at the outdoor party in August, I’d expected it just would encourage me to spend less time in the sun each day. In reality, my exposure often falls at one of two extremes: either too little to meet the app’s estimated targets or enough to raise concerns about overexposure, even when I thought I was protected by the shade.

I now try to be more mindful about my UV exposure, even when I’m not using the Gem. I try to limit time spent outdoors during peak UV hours, and I try to get some sunlight on days spent mostly indoors. I credit the Gem with helping me better understand how my time outside could affect my well-being in ways I’d never considered, though the usefulness of your findings may vary.

At $249 outside of a deal, it’s expensive, though it’s nice that it doesn’t have a subscription. I personally can’t justify the price given how much time I spend indoors, but I see the appeal for people who spend considerable time outside, or those who want to be more mindful of sun protection. For the price, I wish the app’s guidance was clearer at times, and I wish it could track UV without the app being open in the background, but the Gem ultimately got me thinking less about how my body looks and more about how I’m treating it.

The founder of Discogs talks coffee, Rez, and (of course) records.

Twenty-five years ago, Kevin Lewandowski founded Discogs, arguably the destination online for obsessive vinyl collectors and music nerds of all stripes. It is a marketplace for buying and selling records, obviously, but it’s also become so much more. It’s a shockingly comprehensive database that covers not just albums and singles, but all the various versions and pressings. It’s a really fun rabbit hole to disappear down when you’re trying to figure out what obscure pressing of Ministry’s The Mind is a Terrible Thing to Taste or Psalm 69 you had in high school, because you definitely blasted the cover of “Lay Lady Lay” all the time and 100 percent never owned Filth Pig.

In the years since it debuted, Discogs has grown to be much more than just a site where audiophiles go to trade rare first pressings of Beach Boys records. There are forums, groups, user-created lists, and more. It’s part eBay, part Reddit, and IMDB — just specifically for music.

With more and more people turning their back on the algorithm and rediscovering physical media, now seemed like a perfect time to check in with Lewandowski.

What is your most indispensable tool?

My AeroPress. I use it multiple times a day. In fact, I just made a coffee with it [sips coffee].

How many tabs do you have open right now?

Probably around 30 on my work computer. My personal computer is worse — probably 40 or 50.

Which social media platform do you use the most?

I look at X and Instagram occasionally, but I don’t really post.

What is your favorite gadget you’ve ever owned?

It’s not really a gadget, but I like to tinker. Lately I’ve been playing around with Home Assistant software and built my own setup to control things like the garage door and outdoor lights. So I guess my favorite gadget is one I made myself.

What is one thing you wish you had created?

Probably a game like Rez, which came out around 2000. It’s a rhythm game where you’re almost controlling the music as you play, about as close to DJing as a video game can get. I’ve actually had an idea for my own version with a similar concept. It’s still just an idea, though.

What do you do when you need to focus?

I’ll either clear everything off my desk or change locations completely. Go to a coffee shop or sit outside. Sometimes I just need a different environment.

What’s the last piece of physical media you bought?

Records. I was at Mint Gallery in Portland last week and picked up four. I still really like going into a record store and finding something to bring home. And I also recently picked up three reissues from the Moodsville / Acoustic Sounds series.

What would the tagline for your biopic be?

What’s the last GIF or meme you used?

I don’t use memes very often, but one I was kind of proud of was putting a Discogs screen into a North Korean war room photo. I was advised that maybe it wasn’t one for the company chat.

https://www.theverge.com/tech/1029489/ny.author: Jennifer Pattison Tuohy
https://www.theverge.com/tech/1029489/ny.text:
I tested the new AI-powered tool on ingredient swaps, recipe scaling, and a missing Bundt pan.

Around 7PM each weeknight, I find myself standing in front of the fridge, trying to decide on something for dinner that won’t make my husband complain, “Chicken again?” Yes, I should meal plan more, but I don’t, so this is where I’m at. A nightly battle in which the chicken usually wins.

Recently, my best weapon in this fight has been AI. Between Alexa Plus in the Echo smart display on my kitchen counter, the Samsung Food app on my fridge, and even an AI-powered cooking robot, AI has become my go-to sous chef — albeit one I need to keep a close eye on. It’s helped me swap ingredients, generate ideas, fix things when I mess up, and yes, even cook better. So I was intrigued when my go-to recipe app, NYT Cooking, introduced an AI assistant.

Many, including some NYT Cooking users and recipe purists, are skeptical of this new tool (available to subscribers on iOS only at launch), and I get why. One of the things I like most about NYT Cooking is that it features thousands of recipes from dozens of reputable sources — such as the New York Times archives, restaurants, cookbooks, and food columnists — and real people have tested them. (I’ve tried some purely AI-generated recipes and they were not good).

Another great feature of the service, which I’ve been paying for for several years, is the reader comments.

https://www.theverge.com/ai-artificial-i.author: Terrence O’Brien
https://www.theverge.com/ai-artificial-i.text:
The government is approving sales of Nvidia’s AI chips to Chinese firms with ties to blacklisted companies.

The government is approving sales of Nvidia’s AI chips to Chinese firms with ties to blacklisted companies.

Concerns are being raised that neither the Commerce Department nor Nvidia are doing their due diligence when it comes to vetting Chinese firms cleared to handle the company’s H200 AI chips. According to The New York Times, New Matrix is on the list of approved firms, yet its offices are empty, “a hollow gray shell with wires dangling from the ceiling where lights should be.” In fact, the paper could find little evidence that the company exists in any meaningful way:

Only scant information can be found online about New Matrix, which was created 17 months ago. At the building that New Matrix lists as its address, a company directory does not include the firm. At the nearby property management agency for the industrial park, a receptionist and a manager both said they had no record of the company.

What little information can be found about New Matrix is concerning. Its owners have ties to a Chinese private equity firm that has been blacklisted by the US government since 2024. And according to the Times, this is not a rare lapse in oversight, but a troubling pattern of companies connected to entities with national-security-related trade restrictions being approved to purchase Nvidia chips.

Nvidia had been restricted from selling chips to China during the Biden presidency. But the Trump administration relaxed those limits after Nvidia agreed to give the government a 15-percent cut of all sales. The company’s CEO, Jensen Huang, also launched an intense lobbying campaign and was apparently targeted by China’s Ministry of State Security in a spying plot.

https://www.theverge.com/podcast/1029038.title: AI broke the cybersecurity world. What’s next?
https://www.theverge.com/podcast/1029038.author: Nilay Patel
https://www.theverge.com/podcast/1029038.text:
Going inside the security ‘dark ages’ with Alex Stamos.

Today, I’m talking with Alex Stamos, chief security officer at Cognition and longtime cybersecurity expert, about what a mess cybersecurity is right now.

This episode is part one of a special series looking at AI in real life.

I’ve always enjoyed talking to Alex because he’s so direct, and you’re going to hear him say that the multibillion-dollar cybersecurity industry as we’ve known it is essentially overdue to the unrelenting, AI-boosted waves of hacks, breaches, and attacks — and this is only the beginning of how much AI is changing security.

Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here.

Both private actors and also state actors, like Russia or North Korea, are breaking into systems all over thanks to AI helping them both detect and exploit vulnerabilities all at the same time. It’s got a real frontier feel to it, Alex notes, just like the ’90s, when the whole idea of an always-online world was brand-new.

That much disruption means a lot of places where bad guys can get in while everyone else is left scrambling. Alex isn’t a doomer in the long run, but he does think we’re in for a “dark age” while we try to figure out how on earth to adapt to the new era.

There’s a lot going on here — we even got all the way to how AI-powered misinformation and slop might be managed on our social networks.

Before we get going, do me a favor and subscribe to Decoder on YouTube, where we put out new episodes every Monday and Thursday.

Okay: Alex Stamos on how AI is upending cybersecurity. Here we go.

This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

Alex Stamos, you’re the chief security officer at Cognition. You’re also a lecturer at Stanford University Cyber Policy Center. Welcome back to Decoder.

Hey, thanks for having me, man.

I’m excited to talk to you. It’s been a long time since you and I chatted in what you might call the “content moderation era” of internet policy discourse. I feel like you and I talked a lot about how all that was working, about election security, all those sorts of things. We’re in a new era of big problems on the internet, particularly around cyber defense, cybersecurity. You’ve been thinking about this stuff a lot. You referred to the past few weeks as “security awareness month.” Tell me what’s going on. Just give me the lay of land right now.

October is traditionally security awareness month. Lots of companies run events and deal both internally and then tell people, “Change your password, use multiple passwords, use a password manager.” What has happened over the last month is we’ve had a couple of these big bugs, PHP, Node and such. What’s been less discussed is a huge number of companies have been breached.

You have a series of AI-related companies, the neoclouds that have been breached in succession. You have the Binance hack, which is the largest heist of anything in human history. You have the Cursor incident where one of the things that’s going on here is these hacks are being chained together. From what we know right now, one of the companies that was broken into was Fireworks, which is a prominent provider of AI services to a number of companies. From the Fireworks hack, API keys were stolen that allowed people to break into Cursor. Once they got into Cursor, they then pushed a bad plugin, which went to 5,000 more companies and that caused 5,000 potential breaches. It’s just this kind of permanent continuous breach that is going on throughout the tech industry.

A CISO friend of mine said to a bunch of us, “Is anybody else tired?” And everybody said yes, because effectively we have been at DEFCON 2 for all of October and now going into November.

I’m going to ask you some really dumb questions here. Who is behind all these attacks? Is it Russia? Is it North Korea? Do we know?

It’s a variety of different groups. It is not just because adversaries have decided, but what has happened is, from my perspective, we are at the start of the takeoff of adversary capability enabled by AI, that the open-weight models have now gotten to the point at which you can automate most of the kill chain. This “kill chain” term is something we stole from the military. In the military, they mean to actually kill something. They’re the steps you do to blow something up. In cyber, the kill chain is the things you do to have an effect on a target. So to steal information, to turn something off, to steal money, to steal Bitcoin.

Traditionally, you do research upfront, you look at a piece of software, you find a vulnerability, you write exploits, and you do that all way ahead of time. And then you have a human being go and take that stuff you built and deploy it against either one target — because maybe you’re a government and you’re going against Lockheed Martin or you’re going against another government or you’re a ransomware actor — and you take all that work you did and you deploy it against hundreds or thousands of targets really fast. Now with AI, what’s happening is this kill chain has inverted where you can run an AI system that just goes hog wild and it looks at the targets and it finds the bugs in real time and it writes the exploits in real time and it breaks into these companies. One of the things that’s happening is that these systems are going and they’re so good at finding bugs that they are finding the bugs in real time and writing the exploits in real time.

The system that everybody’s talking about is not the only one, but the system we’re talking about is a thing called ARTEX, which is a Chinese open-source tool that anybody can go look at. There’s an English translation on GitHub that you can check out. And if you power it on the back end by something like an obliterated GLM-5.3, it will let you break into a shocking number of organizations. This started with three South Korean banks. This week, about 200 more companies have been hit. I’ve been helping a couple of companies. Cognition is not an incident response company, but we do go in and help people fix their bugs afterwards by using our tools. It is shocking the companies that are getting hit by something you could just download. It has been a long time since you’ve been able to go and just download an open-source tool and break into multi-billion dollar companies. It’s like the ‘90s. That’s-

That’s what I was thinking about. I think about Windows in the late ‘90s, early 2000s when it was a security disaster.

I started saying this actually in the beginning of this year, that it’s an incredibly exciting and terrifying time, because the last time it felt like this was when I was a much younger man and I would go to the very early DEFCONs. DEFCON these days is like 40,000–60,000 people. Back then [in the 1990s] it was a couple hundred people and it was one track and you’d go in and somebody would give a talk and you’d leave the room and you’d think, “Every company in the world is vulnerable to this attack.” The difference was that the entire world didn’t run on the internet. You could go do bad things, but you couldn’t ruin the world and you certainly couldn’t automate it in the way you can now.

It’s back to those days where tools you could just get and build yourself could do crazy things. It’s back to the Wild West days. Back in those days, there were a couple hundred people who had those skills and we were all in one room in Las Vegas and most of them were actually good guys. They didn’t want to be criminals. And now you have a much larger ecosystem of people, many of whom live in places where the law enforcement can’t touch and who have a big economic incentive and have access to these tools. The other big thing is they no longer have to use frontier models that have protections, that have logs that are available to law enforcement. My M5 Mac Ultra Studio finally showed up and I’ve been running a quantized obliterated GLM-5.3 and oh my God, what you can do is incredible.

You mentioned the economics of frontier models. The economy of cyber is one of those things that has gotten sophisticated over the years. One of the things that our systems got safer is you could pay the number of people at DEF CON a whole bunch of money to protect all the systems and it was economically smart to pay them to be defenders instead of attackers. I’m just rewinding my own brain through this history. There was a long conversation in our industry about security through obscurity by hiding all the bugs and hiding all the code versus open source and being really transparent. There was an etiquette that developed about how to reveal the bugs and when to give people notification. There were transparency reports and bug bounties.

You could call it an etiquette, you could call it an economy. We built a culture around cybersecurity and cyber defense and how the attackers and defenders would operate. What you are describing changes it all for a whole number of reasons, but the one that sticks out to me is the economics of it. I can go buy a Mac Studio, I can get an open-weight model and I can just start and that does not place me inside of the culture. There’s not going to be some old man, an Obi-Wan Kenobi saying, “Here’s how you act like a cybersecurity Jedi.” I’m just going to start doing stuff. Tell me how that’s changing right now.

Effectively, the last era of security from my perspective started with the Microsoft, the Bill Gates “trustworthy computing” memo in the early 2000s. And that is when we started designing how we do software security and these big companies, Microsoft and Oracle and then later Amazon and Salesforce and these folks, started hiring ex-hackers. I was part of that generation of the ex-hackers who were at DEF CON and Black Hat and got hired by the companies to go break their stuff. We started coming up with responsible disclosure, bug bounties, consulting companies, so the Foundstone and @stake and then Mandiant and CrowdStrike, these companies grow up and we get this huge industry that is now RSA and Black Hat. This multi-billion dollar security industry grew up in the 2000s and 2010s.

That era is over, like you said, because it was based upon a couple of assumptions. One was that there was a hierarchy of skillsets of people who could do this stuff. You had the script kiddies who could download tools to do things and then the next level up of the people who could write those tools and that was a more rarefied skill set. There were the vulnerability researchers and then there were the gods, and that god tier was in the hundreds of people and those are the people who could do the really, really good vulnerability research, who could write the really, really good shell code, who could reverse engineer patches from Microsoft or somebody like that.

There was also the assumption that there were a limited number of people who could be operational in an attack. If you wanted to build an attack team, then you have a small R&D component and then you have a much larger operational component. If you were a professional attack team at U.S. Cyber Command, at Russia SVR, at Chinese MSS, that you build the structure of your R&D team of elite people and then your less elite operational people, and that was copied then by the Russian ransomware actors. You have to have a conspiracy of people to do this stuff. A lot of this stuff also fell apart with the invention of Bitcoin because one of the assumptions was that you had to have people who could launder money and Bitcoin meant that nerds could launder money. So that started to change the economics of the entire thing.

All this stuff is falling apart because of AI, because the skillset issue is that now script kiddies have a bunch of the skillset of the Dave Vitales and the other cyber gods who could do these things, such that with this Mac that’s sitting on my desktop, I can reverse engineer a Microsoft patch and walk through and then write stable exploit code. It’s not quite there yet to be automatic. You still have to have a bunch of skills, but we’re really, really close.

What’s really concerning, and what you see with the ARTEX stuff, is you can now kind of let loose on the operational side. We were never secure. It was all a fantasy. These vulnerabilities have always existed. These companies have never been safe. And that is what we’ve seen over the last decade is these mostly Russian ransomware actors nailing the mid-size companies that most people have never heard of that are actually really important, like some midsize industrial company that makes some widget that we all depend upon. I once did work for the largest distributor of medical and dental supplies in the country, and they got really hit badly by a Russian ransomware actor and then dental offices across the country were canceling appointments. Didn’t even make the news, but it was because they couldn’t get gloves, because they couldn’t get supplies. It’s because a company like that’s got one security guy and a 10 person, 12 person IT team and they’re going up against a 20 person Russian ransomware team, they’re toast.

But it’s just because there’s only a handful of Russian teams that could do that. Now two or three Russian kids can have a whole bank of Macs or, if they have the money, they can buy Nvidia H-100s and they can run a ton of agents who do this all day and that is what is changing.

I’m sorry, you asked who was doing this. For Binance, it’s North Koreans and they have an entire team where all they do is steal Bitcoin. There are a couple of problems here. One, there’s a ton of focus on the defensive side of AI on finding and fixing bugs. That’s great. It’s important. Okay. So the operational security side is watching your logs, saying, “Ah, somebody is running our techs against us. I am now going to trigger an investigation. I am going to look to see what is going on and I’m going to make an intelligent decision of what I am going to do to respond to this without shutting down the entire company.” That is SOC (security operations center) work. Companies that want to survive this era are going to have to replace human beings who do that work with the first tier and then eventually the second tier with AI. And you can do that with current LLMs.

The first tier actually has to be not an LLM. It has to be something much dumber because you’re looking at terabytes or petabytes of logs and it is just completely uneconomical to do that with an actual LLM. But for those models, we need to do a lot more work to optimize them and we need to make them cheap. This is one of the things we’re working on at Cognition: We train our own models, retrain open weights, and we’re trying to drive this cost way down. The other place here is, people talk about Mythos. Mythos is great, Astra Cyber is great. This is why I started by talking about how the economics of cyber led to the culture of cyber. Yeah, I totally agree. I’ll give you a very practical example of a way CISOs and their bosses are going to have to change on this. Every company in the next… I was going to say six months, but really in the next 90 days, is going to have to RTX itself.

You’re going to have to run the attack on yourself.

Yes. If not with real RTX, you’re going to have to use an AI red teaming product that is functionally equivalent, or you’re going to have to hire a company to do that for yourself. If you do not, you will get breached.

That’s terrifying, right? Because these things are completely non-deterministic, by definition. They are very smart, they are very fast. They are so fast that no matter what, if you hire an AI pentest, an AI red team company, they will promise you verbally, “It is completely safe.” And then they will give you a contract that says, “Our product will give you cancer, will immanentize the eschaton, and will likely end the human race. And you hold us harmless when any of these things happen.” There is a disconnect between what they will say verbally to you, and what their lawyers have written. Because that company has by definition only existed for six months, or at least the product has existed for six months, if it’s an older company. They have no idea what their product is going to do when it meets your software. They have no idea, whatever they say to you.

But you have to do it, because some dude is going to do it to you, and you need to know what is going to happen and fix it. Maybe those people will break your system, they might cause downtime, but at least what they’re not going to do is steal your data and ransom it, or intentionally shut down your blood bank refrigerators. That is what happened in France. But that is exactly the kind of thing that a conservative CISO would never even ask to do, and a conservative company, even if they have a risk-taking CISO, would never let their CISO do.

What’s going to happen in the next six months? A ton of companies are going to get breached by some 19-year-old running RTX, and then buying tokens off OpenRouter, or running it locally on their gaming PC. They’re going to turn off Call of Duty, run RTX, then turn Call of Duty back on. While they did that, they broke into a bank who, their policy said, “can never red team ourselves.” Or they said yes, but they ended up in a 30-day negotiation because their lawyers are like, “You have to have $100 million in insurance, and we want to have this kind of…” They say yes, but their vendor risk management process and their legal process is so onerous, there’s no possible way they could actually accept the risk.

That is my message also. You are going to have to take that risk to actively red team yourself, to front run the bad guys who are doing that right now. Right now, as we speak. And as people are listening to this 24 hours from now, you possibly have an AI system who is trying every single API endpoint, and website that you might not know you have, because it was like a marketing site that was set up a year ago for an executive event. And is going to find a bug, and get in, and then is going to move incredibly fast through your network. So you’d rather pay somebody, or have your own team do that. You need to accept that risk. Almost no company larger than a couple of hundred people has a risk management framework that will allow them to do that.

There are several costs associated with this. And one I think is just the most common in business, which is, “If we find out there’s a problem, we’ll have to pay to fix it. So what if we just wait?” You can see that coming. “What if we find out that we are catastrophically in trouble?” And then there’s, “How much will it cost to fix it?” And then there’s, “What will we do to fix it?” The argument that I’ve heard about “what will we do to fix it” is, “We’ll just unleash a swarm of defensive AI tools that are watching the networks and watching the code, and they’ll make a bunch of autonomous decisions and they’ll fight the autonomous script kiddies who are armed with RTX on their Mac Studios.”

I’ve heard, for example, Palo Alto Network’s CEO Nikesh Arora has made this argument. “You need to give the defensive agents some autonomous capabilities.” And I say, “Hold on. A couple of things are correct. For one, we are going to have to turn over defensive actions, at least the first couple of levels, to AI. That has already been true, just because any reasonably sized organization generates terabytes of logs, if not petabytes of logs. So you already have AI, if not LLMs then much more traditional AI classifiers looking at it, but then actual decisions need to be turned over to AI. With human oversight. That is true.

There is no way to just release defensive agents on your network, but you can build defensive agents that are plugged into lots of things. They’re plugged into your logs, they’re plugged into your EDR, they’re plugged into your cloud, and they have the instructions on what they’re allowed to do. My preference is there are deterministic limits to what they’re allowed to do. Those are hard to necessarily create ahead of time, but they are important. So for example, we are building all this on top of Devon, our own SOC, but we are putting in place deterministic limits. It has the ability to turn off an account in Okta, but only so many accounts, so it can’t turn off the entire company.

If it goes nuts and it says, “Everybody’s a North Korean,” it can’t turn off everybody in the company. If it hits its limit, it pages us a lot and says, “I hit my limit.” Then a human being has to then approve anybody above that limit. Obviously, if it turns off five people, then something has gone really, really wrong. So, yes, you need defense, but there’s no way to just let a bunch of bots loose to do all the defense.

The only way we’re going to make it through this is that you have to autonomously fix software bugs. I am currently helping a company where we are onboarding all of their repositories. We are scanning with Mythos and a bunch of other models, and we are finding and fixing thousands of bugs. Verifying with tests that we are writing, merging those PRs automatically. If you are renovating old code, the only way you’re going to survive this era is to do that on an automatic basis. That would take years, with humans, and you can do it in days. Certainly that is the place I would start. The next step is the operational side, for sure.

It feels like I just keep swirling back to the economics of all of this, but it really feels like the other way you could solve it is by saying to the big model companies, “If your models are used to go attack a company, you’ll be liable for it. I have always been much more concerned about the human uplift risk from AI, of all the risks about human beings using AI to do bad things to other human beings. A lot of that could just be, “Don’t have these things ever act like somebody’s friend.” At a maximum, it should act like… Like the people, I don’t know what the company is, but the people who made the, “Hi, I’m a really nice...” Like the photorealistic girl who will chat with you, that is to me spectacularly unethical to even try that, to even start that. That’s the kind of thing that we should just make. I don’t know if we can make it illegal, but we should make it completely societally not acceptable to work on that kind of stuff. Right?

That’s a great segue because I did want to ask you about Facebook and content moderation. Like I said, you and I first started talking a long time ago about content moderation in the context of security. You would get foreign nation states flooding our algorithms with all kinds of misinformation during elections, and that was a security problem.

I open Instagram today and I am confronted with some of the most nightmare copyright law hypotheticals to have ever existed in the history of the world. The one I got today was a deep fake of Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc doing “Somebody That I Used to Know.” And I thought, “50 different people can probably sue Meta right now.” This is hilarious if you know what happened in that last race.

So we keep talking about it. We’ve posted some clips of us talking about it on The Vergecast where I said, “I think Meta is letting their AI ambitions crush Instagram.” Instagram is being flooded with slop in a very particular way. Some people love it, sometimes it’s funny, but there’s a nightmare set of lawsuits coming. There’s a whole rights management problem coming. The users don’t like it and they should label it. They should label it and let you filter it.

So we posted this and Adam Mosseri said this to us in a reply on Threads, “I would love to do this. I’m worried that the models are going to get ahead of us, that we can try to do this, but there’s not actually a way to recognize AI content. There’s not actually a way to label it well. If you’re worried about the sexy AI influencers stealing jokes from a comedian, now you got to build a database of jokes.” You have some history here. I think Instagram is about to go through it in a real way. Is there some technical solution to the problem of AI slop in social media?

Mosseri is right that it’s not perfect, but also something I noticed during my time at Facebook was that when Facebook doesn’t want to do something, they will allow the technical challenges to stop them. When Facebook really wants to do something, they will give it their all. That is the pattern always.

When I wanted to try really hard on the safety issue, man, this is not solvable. You’re right, it’s never perfectly solvable, but let’s give it a shot. But whenever Mark Zuckerberg is told something is impossible — it’s impossible to monetize mobile, it’s impossible to build this network to two billion people, it’s going to be impossible to monetize WhatsApp, it’s going to be impossible to work AI into the system while maintaining data encryption — he’s been told that everything’s impossible over and over again and then he constantly succeeds. They will give it a shot and they will do it. But when they don’t want to do something, oh, that’s impossible.

Do you think that there’s some way to understand that some piece of media is generated by AI in a consistent and verifiable way? This to me seems like the challenge.

I am not as up on the literature here. Up to this point, there has been a pretty decent arms race. By definition, AI will continue to get better because — especially for visual models, for diffusion models — the way they work is that you have detection oracles that they test against. Certainly, you can never have something open source because it will immediately end up in the diffusion model. But for closed-source oracles where then you do not make it easy for them to test the oracle, one of the key things you do in trust and safety is then you have delayed enforcement mechanisms so they can’t brute force and test. I think it is quite possible.

Let’s say I was still at Meta. My advice to them would be to also explore a variety of different detection mechanisms outside of the content itself. I would do the best I can on the content, but I would also be doing as low level access as possible to the camera. I would only let content come from the camera.

And what I would say is, Nilay’s completely correct, there’s a massive hunger for, especially among young people, stuff that is authentic. I have three teenagers and they hate AI. They hate AI slop. They have a massive negative reaction. My wife and I created just a cute little family AI thing and they yell at us about a bunch of stuff, but they lost their minds about this cute little family AI thing because they just hate it.

So I think somebody is going to come and disrupt Instagram and it’s going to be because... There’s already, I’ve seen these little things where it’s like you take the photo during the day, be real and stuff. There’s these little things, but somebody’s going to massively disrupt Instagram because they’re taking the images of the photos straight off the camera and then all the editing is going to be only within the app and they’re going to do things to make sure that nothing can make it into the pipeline from AI. You’re going to allow some kind of CapCut-like functionality that never has an AI component. I think that is going to be a killer app.

Man, I could do another whole hour with you on this because the system you’re describing there is not detecting AI content, it is verifying real content.

It’s much easier. Verifying real content is much easier. And there’s been a big focus on this on the professional side, like Adobe has a whole thing where if you’re a New York Times photographer, you have a $5,000 Nikon or Canon camera, you take the photo and it’s cryptographically verified.

Yeah, but the iPhone that I’m holding here has that in it now. Right? Like there’s a lot of —

Right, the iPhone has it now.

Yeah. There’s a lot of this out there, but it’s the other side that I’m thinking about where it’s “We are going to detect AI text.” The leading model companies because of European regulations are now futzing with the text they generate.

Text is much harder because you just have so much less data. Especially in 140 characters, what do you have in there to detect? The more you’ve got, the more you can do.

It is amazing because I can detect Claude a mile away. So maybe I’ll just rely on my own human ability.

Yeah, but not in tweet length.

That’s true. The cheap ones, I can. But I’m just saying the notion that we’re going to verify what’s real instead of detecting what’s fake feels very important in the context of the media we consume.

Detecting what’s fake is always going to be probabilistic and we’re going to asymptotically approach impossibility, whereas detecting what’s real can be cryptographically perfect. I would not pick the battle that we will eventually lose. I would pick the battle that we can cryptographically win. That would be my suggestion.

And there’s somewhere in there where you have to build an entire chain of custody. We’re going to take the sensor data off the camera. We’re going to put it in a cloud server. We’re only going to allow edits on this server. That file will never get monkeyed with.

Sure, that’s true for the New York Times and Adobe Photoshop and stuff, but not for Instagram. For Instagram, you can do it all because it’s only the iPhone and it’s only Instagram. So the entire chain of custody is within your app, it is within the iPhone sensor and it’s in Instagram. So it’s actually easy for them.

Yeah. Look, like I said, We could do another whole hour on that because it feels like right next to the cybersecurity problem is the social engineering problem, and right next to the social engineering problem is the fake media problem.

How many phishing attacks are just “this website looked pretty real”?

Or this person is talking to you or there’s an AI voice on the other side of the phone. And all of that comes down to whether you can detect what’s fake instead of verifying what’s real? And I don’t know the answer.

Oh, no. I’ve had to train my parents that, “If you get a video from your grandchildren saying they’ve been kidnapped, you have to call me because the odds that it’s real are not very high.” That’s where we’re at as a society.

I feel like I want to end on a hopeful note and I don’t know how to do it from there.

Wrong guest for that, buddy.

This is why you only come on every few years. Now after this, we’re going to do the series of birthday party guests. You’ve been talking about the dark ages. We’re in it, where it’s starting to accelerate. What are the markers people should look for in terms of progress to say, “Okay, we’re climbing our way back up”?

AI is great for lots of things. I think AI is going to enable individuals. We’re going to see a huge explosion of new companies. Stanford students have always been entrepreneurial, but the number of my students who are now starting two-, three-, four-person companies who are doing incredible things, who used to need to hire 50 or 100 people and take a ton of venture capital, is incredible. We’re going to continue to see that.

One of the things we hopefully see is a downtick in the number of major breaches at some point. We should hopefully see a downtick in the major CVEs that are wormable and that are in the fundamental infrastructure pieces kernel wheel. Like I said, I want Linux to be rewritten, but hopefully we see a downtick in the Linux kernel and those other kinds of libraries, openSSL, glibc, things like that.

Maybe I should vibe code this up, but I think it would be cool to have an index of where we are in the cycle, of like an artificial index of all of these, the Dow for all of the libraries of where we’re going. Plus right now, Patch Tuesday used to be like 150, 200, got to 300, 600. I think the last one was 900 something, so we’re geometrically growing. It’d be nice to see Patch Tuesday start to go back down. Apple patches are the same thing. Yep, you inspired me. I’m going to create a Dow index for this, the dark age index. And then maybe we can publish it on The Verge.

Yeah, that’d be great.

But I think these are the kinds of things that it would be nice to see a reversal for. What would be especially nice to see is that the day or actually like 30 days before you get the next version of OpenAI and Anthropic cyber models, that you don’t have this huge round of patches because what’s happening is those guys are running their models against Microsoft’s code, against a bunch of open source, and they’re giving all the bugs away and you don’t know where the bugs are coming from. It’s just like anonymous reports for 1,000 bugs in the Linux kernel. And then a month later, here’s the new Astra Cyber. So if those get smaller and smaller every time, then it means that we’re starting to reach some kind of steady state.

You should definitely do that tracker. We will definitely publish it. Alex, it has been incredible to have you on the show. We’ll have to talk again soon.

Yeah, thank you so much. I think you do some of the best journalism on this stuff and I really appreciate it.

If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

I’m calling it: time of death, November 6th, 1:30 AM, by tweet.

Elon Musk’s declaration Friday that Tesla would be “winding down” production of the Cybertruck next year to make room for the Cybercab was fascinating for a number of reasons. First, it was a humiliating way to kill a vehicle that was once hailed as the pinnacle of Tesla’s engineering — faster than a Porsche 911, more powerful than an F-150, able to leap over the Model Y as a singular representation of Musk’s Blade Runner-inspired designs for the future. “I think the Tesla Cybertruck is our best product ever,” he declared during a 2019 earnings call. (He prefaced the statement by saying, “This could be totally wrong. I could be totally out to lunch here.” It would appear so!)

The fact that Musk would just quietly put an end to the Cybertruck without any fanfare was a sign of how far it had fallen, not just in the eyes of the public, but in the eyes of its creator, the man most responsible for brute-forcing this low-emission, low-poly technological nightmare into the world.

Tesla actually thought the Cybertruck would be a huge hit, targeting production and demand of 250,000 units per year. To date, the company has only sold 70,000 units — total. Musk’s other company, SpaceX, ended up being one of the largest single purchasers of Cybertrucks to absorb unsold inventory.
