https://www.wired.com/story/apps-for-car.author: Jaclyn Greenberg
https://www.wired.com/story/apps-for-car.text:
All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

MY HUSBAND AND I are caregivers for our middle son, who has multiple disabilities and requires full-time support. We do our best to keep one another up to date on the activities that fill his daily life while also managing his numerous medical specialists, procedures, and therapies. We have to stay in constant communication while also working our jobs, caring for three teenagers, and managing a household. It’s tough.

We’re not alone in our struggles. According to AARP, in 2025, an estimated 63 million Americans cared for adults or children with a medical condition or disability. On average, these caregivers spend up to 27 hours per week providing care.

This caregiver crisis, where so many Americans provide ongoing, complex care and, as a result, endure poor health, financial strain, and isolation, is worsening as caregivers need more support and better systems.

Helpfully, to lighten the mental load, caregiver apps are aimed at families who are supporting seniors, children, or anyone with a diagnosis that needs regular management.

Every caregiver’s situation is different, and the apps and programs in this space reflect a diversity of needs.

Medisafe, which was created in 2013, tracks medications and sends reminders so users don’t miss a dose. The program can also notify a caregiver if a dose is missed. It gives its users the ability to track medical appointments, track their symptoms, and maintain a list of health care contacts and measurements. It also has a drug interaction checker where users can enter multiple medications to see if they are safe to take at the same time.

Caring Village, which was founded in 2015, has an appointment calendar, a to-do list, and a wellness journal where users can keep track of their loved one’s symptoms and moods, and even upload a photo. Caregivers can assign tasks through the app, create a care plan, and receive reminders to take medication. The app also comes with an AI assistant called Julia that can answer caregiving questions.

In 2022, Bret Koncak, based on his experiences with his two sons who have complex needs, cocreated Mejo, a web-based caregiver app. Users enter an individual’s medical history, which is then consolidated into a one-page summary that can be shared with caregivers, doctors, and therapists.

“A lot of people think that caregiving begins and ends with interactions with the health care system, but a lot of it is about what happens between care visits,” says Koncak. “That's what we're focused on.” For $6 a month or $60 a year, the premium version of Mejo gives users access to daily journaling, which they can share with other caregivers, so everyone stays on the same page without having to catch up verbally.

For now, information in Mejo is entered manually, but Koncak says his team is looking into ways to incorporate AI to help users come up with appropriate questions to ask during medical appointments.

Brett Rowell, whose son Briggs has cerebral palsy, is creating an app called Briggzy, so he and his wife, who work different hours, can more easily hand off their son’s care. Briggzy is currently in the testing phase, and Rowell hopes to launch it to a wider community in 2027.

“My wife took [our son] to most of the appointments because I worked 8 to 5 and she was off during that time,” said Rowell. “So the questionnaires alone, I don't know how to answer half of them unless I have Briggzy. My goal was to bring her mind into a shared space for me, so that way I can be helpful.”

Nasha Fitter, who has a daughter with a rare disease, launched Citizen Health in 2024 with cofounder Farid Vij to collect medical records for patients and store them in a secure portal. “With the users’ consent, we can extract information from those medical records, deidentify it, harmonize it, and start to pull an understanding of diseases through that,” says Fitter. “And then we feed that understanding back to patients so they would get a better sense of the trajectory of their child’s disease.” Citizen Health works with patient advocacy groups to support their research on drug development.

Six months ago, the company launched Ari, an AI “health teammate” that lets caregivers and patients track their loved one's care and symptoms by texting with it. Ari, currently in beta, can also access medical records, patient portals, and Google Calendar events, including specific appointment dates and surgeries. Ari notices caregiver patterns, such as whether they take medication at different times of the day and how that might impact symptoms. It prepares patients and caregivers for appointments by summarizing past medical information and providing appropriate questions to ask medical professionals. And it can help navigate insurance and government benefits.

Right now, Ari is only available for people with rare diseases, but the goal is to make it available and useful to all caregivers and patients.

I. Glenn Cohen, a bioethics and health law researcher and professor at Harvard Law School, is optimistic about AI in the health space overall. “For example, I think it will empower many patients to prep for questions they might want to ask their doctor before going in to see them.”

But he says that users should go into the process with their eyes open to understand the risks and what you're getting out of it, especially if a product is free or cheap.

Most of these devices are not medical devices, says Cohen. “As such, the FDA has not reviewed them, so their safety and efficacy remain a question mark, or it's the company's word for it that you have to take.”

The health information patients and caregivers plug into these AI tools is not protected by federal HIPAA statutes because the information is typically not coming from a covered entity. Instead, it comes from a person or from data collection at home. “If your privacy is important and you care about how the information is used, in some cases, all you can rely on is the contractual promises,” Cohen says. “They typically have language that absolves [the companies] from responsibility in many instances.”

He also warns that the information collected may not be only for the person receiving care, but may also include information about parents or other caregivers.

While I love the idea of keeping my son’s information all in one place so I can keep track of patterns, update his doctors without feeling emotionally drained, and easily hand off his caregiving needs to my husband, making sure we update the app regularly will be the key to actually seeing those benefits.

Denise M. Brown, CEO and founder of the Caregiving Years Training Academy, has seen many apps come and go because she says they can be tedious to maintain, especially when caregivers are already overloaded.

“We have to upload data to the app (care plans, schedules, tasks), and that’s a lot of work,” Brown says. “A physician, visiting nurse, therapist, or hospital discharge planner won’t log into the app to provide updates, which ends up falling back on the caregiver.”

At the end of the day, the need for caregiver apps is great, and many developers in this community, many of whom are caregivers themselves, are trying to do something to lessen the load.

“The technology and apps can open the door for broader seamless integration of care—and hopefully less stress on you as the caregiver,” says Nicole Howell, director of direct care workforce development at the National Council on Aging. But she says the final solution [to the overall caregiver crisis] will be something that not one family, not one caregiver can solve.

“It has to be all hands at the wheel. It has to be government. It has to be private. It has to be family members speaking up, saying the hard truth so we get the best of American ingenuity to move this to where we need to be.”

IF YOU HAVE holiday travel plans coming up, having a reliable power bank is a must. Sling a decent power bank in your pocket or bag and you can keep your phone and other gadgets topped up. But what if you want something a little more powerful? The best laptop power banks boast larger capacities and faster charging speeds, and the EcoFlow Rapid Pro is my top pick.

Both EcoFlow’s Rapid Pro models are on sale right now. The larger 27650 mAh-capacity Rapid Pro X is $170 ($80 off), and the 20,000 mAh Rapid Pro is $70 ($56 off). EcoFlow’s Rapid Pro X can deliver a total of 300 watts to power up a laptop, smartphone, and headphones simultaneously. It comes in just under the maximum capacity allowed on flights. This power bank has three USB-C ports, rated at 140 watts, 65 watts, and 65 watts, and a retractable 2-foot USB-C cable rated at 140 watts. This power bank supports almost every fast-charging protocol going (PD3.1, PPS, QC3.0, AFC, Apple2.4A, BC1.2, SCP, FCP, UFCS), but its greatest feature could be its super speedy recharge rate. If you don’t mind an extra purchase, Ecoflow’s dock can charge via the pogo pins on the bottom at 320 watts, enabling you to go from zero to 80 percent in just 20 minutes.

The smaller Rapid Pro matches its bigger sibling on most fronts, but has a lesser 20,000 mAh capacity, a maximum combined output of 230 watts with a 100-watt built-in 2-foot USB-C cable, a 100-watt USB-C port, and two 65-watt USB-C ports. It can also charge in under 20 minutes with the EcoFlow Rapid Pro Desktop Charger at $140 ($50 off). https://www.wired.com/story/he-ran-on-fi.title: He Ran on Fighting Data Centers. Now, He’s Going to Congress
https://www.wired.com/story/he-ran-on-fi.author: Molly Taft
https://www.wired.com/story/he-ran-on-fi.text:
WELCOME BACK TO Power Play! Senior writer Molly Taft has been tackling topics around this midterm season’s biggest issue: data centers. With the elections over, Power Play will be going on hiatus. But if you’ve got a question or thought for a story, feel free to shoot Molly an email at molly_taft@wired.com or reach them securely on Signal at mollytaft.76.

IF THERE’S ANY incoming congressional freshman who understands how voter anger about data centers supercharged this week’s election, it’s Will Lawrence.

A former member of the Democratic Socialists of America who helped found the Sunrise Movement, Lawrence centered his campaign on opposition to data centers from the beginning, months before many other candidates had caught on. It helped him win a challenging primary in Michigan’s 7th Congressional District against much-better-funded opponents, and this week, he defeated incumbent Republican Tom Barrett in one of the most expensive House races in the country. (Elon Musk’s America PAC chipped in $340,000 against Lawrence.)

For this last edition of Power Play, I caught up with Lawrence about what the future holds for data center developers and for voters concerned about them, and what his plans are when he gets to Washington, DC, next year.

MOLLY TAFT: I’ve seen some post-election takes that data centers weren’t as big of a factor for voters as media coverage may suggest. I’m curious as to what you heard from voters in the last weeks of the campaign about how data centers may be competing with other big issues in this election.

WILL LAWRENCE: What are the two headlines on the election? It's been about costs, and it’s about corruption. Data centers speak directly to costs and to the legalized corruption that's become ordinary business in our rigged economy. They’re taking tax breaks, they’re sucking up water, they’re proposing to use double or triple the total capacity of the grid in Michigan, they’re threatening people’s home values.

All of this is being done because the playing field is fundamentally slanted away from local communities and towards these mega corporations. People have attempted to exert community control and local oversight, and they've been challenged in court by these Silicon Valley companies.

You see an economy and a political order that is favoring the wealthy few over the many. It really makes a mockery of democracy itself. Why is it that we keep having to play whack-a-mole against these individual projects? It shows that people in Silicon Valley and Wall Street and DC have made these decisions for us, and it speaks of the lack of economic democracy.

There have been a lot of announcements from big tech companies in recent weeks, making promises to be more transparent, to use less water, to not use NDAs—OpenAI released a bunch of commitments the day after the election. Do you think these compromises are enough to sway people?

I haven’t seen any of the specific proposals. But if they’re feeling the heat, that’s good. What they've offered so far has been completely inadequate, and it's going to take a lot to win back trust.

There was just a new hyperscale data center proposed in the last week before the election in Delhi Township, south of Lansing, close to Mason. There was an announcement made by a local economic development agency and a would-be developer. They said, “This is going to be different. We're going to do a six-month community engagement process before we even decide if we are going to build a data center, but if we do, it's going to have all these protections. And we want to hear from you.”

The township board scrambled [to put together] an emergency meeting. Two hundred fifty people showed up, probably more than that—it was overflowing. And people said, OK, the answer is still no. It’s going to take a lot of work [from the companies] to convince anybody that anything has actually changed.

Have any tech companies reached out to you?

I haven’t spoken to any of these companies.

When you go to Washington in January, what are some of the first policies you’re going to try and work on around data centers?

I'm going to fight for a federal data center moratorium, and along with it, a pause on advanced AI development. The risks simply do not match up to the benefits at this time. We've got to have a conversation across all of the different stakeholders to determine what an appropriate regulatory agenda looks like.

Would that be a pause similar to what Senator Bernie Sanders has proposed, where it's contingent on AI safety regulations?

Yes. Safety here also means making sure that we're not sacrificing people and the planet to build data centers. We need to have appropriate regulations on both of those aspects.

What about using oversight or investigatory levers?

Certainly—it makes sense. We build cars here in Michigan. If GM put a car on the market that had a 1 percent chance of exploding on the highway and killing everybody inside, it would never go to market. If it did, they would be sued out of existence.

But these Silicon Valley companies, they tell us that they're actively developing a product that has a 10 percent chance of killing everybody on planet Earth. I mean, what are we talking about? This is obviously reckless endangerment, according to any existing standard of consumer protection law. There should be investigations into that, and there should be suits filed to provide a sanction against companies for engaging in unacceptable risks that are a public hazard.

It’s been a busy week for the WIRED newsroom! My colleague Tori Elliott and I tackled how data centers factored into the blue tsunami that swept the country on Tuesday. (Spoiler alert: Voters really, really want regulations on data centers.) Over on the Business desk, Caroline Haskins looked at how the election results are sending tech bros scrambling to find other locations to build data centers—including in space.

And earlier this week, WIRED’s global editorial director, Katie Drummond, sat down with New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani to talk about his first year in office. He told her that the movement against data centers gives him “a real sense of hope.” Read more from Katie and the mayor here.

WHILE THE FRIDAY after Thanksgiving has traditionally been the busiest shopping day of the year, Black Friday deals have gradually spread well beyond the day. First came Cyber Monday, then Cyber Week. Now, early Black Friday deals kick off before November has even started. The tricky part for early birds is knowing what’s a genuine deal and what’s likely to go even lower when Black Friday arrives.

The Reviews team at WIRED tracks prices on our favorite gadgets year-round, and we only highlight deals on devices we've tested and would recommend to our own friends and family. Some of these picks may be cheaper for Black Friday, but these are the discounts that have caught our eye so far.

Updated November 7: We've added new deals on Google Pixel 11 phones, Google Pixel earbuds, a Rocco minifridge, a Dreo space heater, and a Petkit automatic litter box. We've also checked for accuracy throughout. Louryn Strampe contributed to this story.

The best trackers for anyone with an iPhone; you can use them to keep tabs on your keys, luggage, bike, or whatever else you worry might go missing. Each AirTag location is marked clearly in the Find My app. The battery should last you a year, and we have a guide on how to replace your AirTag battery. Just please don’t use them to track people. This is the lowest price we have seen on the single tag, but it drops this low pretty frequently.

For Apple fans with an iPhone or MacBook, the Apple AirPods Max 2 are the best over-ear headphones. They offer great sound quality, effective noise cancellation, and good transparency modes. They are usually a little too pricey for our tastes compared to Sony and Bose options, but at $100 off, they look more tempting. Before you pull the trigger, they will likely drop by at least another $30 for Black Friday.

If you want to pair wireless earbuds with your iPhone and enjoy a seamless, feature-rich experience, you should snag the AirPods Pro 3. They are comfy, boast top-notch active noise cancellation, and can even translate some languages in real time. That said, they are at this price often enough that I hesitate to call it a great deal, and they will likely drop by another $20 for Black Friday.

At $10 below their all-time lowest price, this is a great deal if you're in the market for our top Android earbuds. The Pixel Buds Pro 2 are comfortable, have a long-lasting battery, and have clear sound with seamless noise cancellation. We think they're especially good for listeners with small ears. They might get cheaper for Black Friday or Cyber Monday, but likely not by much.

Google's full Pixel 11 lineup is on sale for less than we've seen all year long. Like some of these other tech deals, it's possible that we see prices drop a bit more later this month, but we don't anticipate it being by much. Each of these phones features incredible cameras and snappy performance, and they're available in a wide array of eye-catching colors. Whether you go with the base Google Pixel 11 or opt for the 11 Pro or 11 Pro XL, you'll be getting one of our favorite Android phones.

With a great camera, solid performance, and super-slick software features, the Pixel 10 Pro is an excellent Android phone. It also has proper Qi2 support for fast wireless charging, but more importantly, the magnets inside make it easy to attach to docks and chargers. Its bigger sibling, the Pro XL, has been my daily driver for most of the last year, and it has served me well. It has frequently dropped to this price before, but I still think it’s a good deal. Note that Amazon prices may vary based on the seller, so double check before adding to cart.

This is one of our favorite 3-in-1 chargers for keeping your iPhone, AirPods, and Apple Watch charged up from a single outlet. The unique feature is its height adjustability, enabling it to pull double duty as a tripod for shooting video or FaceTime calls with family or friends. It has been on sale (close to half price) for a while now but has never been lower than $60 at Best Buy. Snap it up while you still can.

Gadgets are too boring. I want more anthropomorphized devices in my life. Ugreen simply added a wee robot face to this wireless charger that changes its expression based on the charging status. I immediately like it more than all my old faceless chargers. The charging pad supports Qi2/MagSafe and tilts up to 70 degrees to reveal a second pad to charge AirPods or other wireless earbuds. It even has a USB-C port for a third gadget. At 40 percent off, this is the lowest price I’ve seen.

My pick for the best budget Wi-Fi router dips down to this price fairly often, but it’s a great deal for a Wi-Fi 7 router with four antennas, a 2.5-Gbps WAN, a 2.5-Gbps LAN, and three gigabit LAN ports. It’s only dual-band (2.4 GHz and 5 GHz), so there’s no 6-GHz option, and performance is limited, but for a small home with modest demands, this is a tough price to beat.

I always associate Black Friday with footage of excited shoppers struggling to carry huge TVs out of big box stores. The reality is that most Black Friday TV deals are on terrible models you should never buy. But this deal on LG’s 55-inch C6 OLED TV caught my eye. At $400 off the regular price, it is the cheapest it's ever been. The sale price on the 65-incher also makes it a better option than the entry-level LG B6 we just reviewed. Just make sure you pair it with a streaming device and disable the tracking.

This security camera records video at up to 2K at 30 frames per second, offers a 150-degree field of view, and connects directly to your Wi-Fi network. The Tapo app can detect motion (person, pet, vehicle) and enables you to set activity zones and privacy zones. The two-way audio is okay, and there’s a built-in alarm function. You can also slip a microSD card in for local recording. It lacks HDR, but it still earns a spot in our best outdoor security cameras guide. It has bounced between $90 and $65 for the last year, but it’s now down to $60.

It may not be one of the best video doorbells you can buy, but at this sale price, Blink’s latest wired doorbell is the cheapest option worth considering. It delivers reasonably good 2K footage and passable two-way audio, though it’s definitely less responsive than some other options on the market. If you want person detection and cloud storage, you’ll also need to spring for the subscription (from $3 a month). The battery version is also on sale at $39 ($41 off).

Permanent outdoor lights are a great way to avoid having to get up the ladder every holiday season. They offer simple white lighting, different colors, and also holiday-themed lighting effects. Eufy’s lights aren’t the brightest, but they hold up well against the competition and support Matter, so you can tie them into any smart home ecosystem. All lengths are on sale, but the 200-foot string has the best discount and is at its lowest price ever.

If you like to run an organized household, the best digital wall calendars are sure to appeal. You can use them to sync your digital calendars, create lists of chores, and plan your family meals. The Everblog HomeCal is our pick for folks who can’t stomach another subscription. It also works like a digital photo frame if you upload your snaps, and you can log into apps like Netflix and Spotify on it. This is the lowest we’ve seen it drop so far.

A good laptop docking station lets you convert your laptop into a desktop for a comfier experience when you’re working from home, and this compact beauty from Belkin is one of our top picks. GaN technology (gallium nitride semiconductors, a faster, more compact alternative to silicon) lets Belkin pack more ports than you can shake a USB-C cable at, including 96-watt power delivery, three 4K display ports, a gigabit Ethernet port, and more. This deal equals the lowest price we’ve seen.

Learning about the wildlife in your garden can be a lot of fun, and the best smart bird feeders are an ideal way to see which feathered friends are in the area. The thoughtfully designed Kiwibit Bird Feeder 2 has a removable 1.5-liter dual-hopper seed reservoir, is easy to clean, and boasts a solar roof to keep the camera charged up. It snaps 8-megapixel photos, captures 4K video, and includes a nifty AI bird-identification feature. We’ve seen it on sale before, but never this low.

This recently released designer minifridge from Rocco is being tested by WIRED editor Kat Merck, but so far, she likes it. It has a minimalist design, a dark glass door, and sliding drawers for smooth organization of all your must-have snacks and drinks. Some might use it for wine or beer, but I dream of this bedside for a crisp Diet Coke and some midnight charcuterie. Every color is discounted for Black Friday.

Our favorite space heater has only sold for less once before, and that price was a mere $5 cheaper than you'll get right now. Space heaters tend to get more expensive during the winter months. If you know you're in the market, this might be a great fit. It checks every box for safety, efficient heating, and aesthetics. It doesn't get too loud, and we like that the display can be dimmed and the control beeps can be muted.

Automatic litter boxes are sought after, but can be a hefty investment. This is a solid deal on our top pick. It should work well for most one- or two-cat households. It cleans efficiently and even has a deodorizing spray that it dispenses as needed. We wish the app were a little easier to use and more feature-rich, but if you won't miss bells and whistles like a camera inside or AI waste detection, this is a solid deal.

https://www.wired.com/story/the-american.title: The American Dream Wasn’t Built for Climate Change

THIS STORY ORIGINALLY appeared on Grist and is part of the Climate Desk collaboration.

TO SIERRA ISLEY, the American Dream brings to mind a home ringed by a white picket fence. “The house in the suburbs is just what you’re taught growing up,” the 26-year-old said. “You know, that’s what you see on TV.” What she wanted for her life was a bit different from that picket-fence ideal, but she still saw the prospect of buying her first house two years ago as a chance to live out what she called “that big dream that everybody has as a kid.”

Isley and her girlfriend, Jamie, were moving from Philadelphia to Asheville, North Carolina, and found a home they liked, a three-bedroom brick house with lots of natural light and a big tree out front. With some help from their parents, they put down a deposit and got their offer accepted. But when they went to sign the closing papers, a complication got in the way: The house had a huge lien on it. After consulting with lawyers, they decided to break the contract and hunt for an apartment to rent in Asheville.

It was a blessing in disguise. One month later, while Sierra and Jamie were still unpacking boxes and building furniture, the remnants of Hurricane Helene turned Asheville into a disaster zone. The basement of their apartment flooded, but they were luckier than some of their neighbors, whose homes had been destroyed.

Owning a home has long been seen as a cornerstone of the American Dream—a way to build wealth that you could use one day to pay for your children’s education and fund your retirement. That arrangement was always more precarious than it was made out to be. But as fires and floods damage homes and drive up insurance rates, pouring your life savings into a house has become riskier than ever. In a report called “Property Prices in Peril,” the firm First Street projected last year that climate risks could knock nearly $1.5 trillion off the value of American homes by 2055. For some people, the sociologist Rebecca Elliott wrote, “the American dream of homeownership may become a nightmare.”

Americans are beginning to grasp the threat that climate change poses to their aspirations. According to exclusive polling for Grist from the think tank Data for Progress, 58 percent of likely U.S. voters believe that climate change will hinder their ability to achieve the American Dream over the next 20 years, including 42 percent of Republicans. The survey suggests that people are worried that climate change will increase the cost of living, and such widespread concern very likely played a role in the major gains for Democrats last Tuesday.

The irony is that fossil fuels have long been promoted as necessary ingredients for the American “way of life.” Starting a century ago, oil and gas companies led extensive campaigns to tie their products to comfort and prosperity, a narrative that has been repeatedly deployed by politicians and oil industry executives to thwart climate action. President Donald Trump’s administration has often said that efforts to rein in fossil fuels threaten the American Dream. Earlier this year, when the administration scrapped Biden-era rules to cut emissions from cars, along with the Environmental Protection Agency’s authority to regulate climate change, it touted the effort as “restoring the American Dream.”

But the fossil-fueled American Dream is in the process of destroying itself. Greenhouse gas emissions from burning coal, oil, and gas have ushered in a new period of precarity, undermining the promise that each generation can expect a better life than the last. Scientific reports warn that climate change “imperil[s] the quality of life” for communities in the United States, disrupting livelihoods and cultural traditions.

Either Americans decide to reimagine what makes up the American Dream and abandon that oil-soaked version of prosperity, or climate change will dismantle it for them.

THE MEMORIES OF living through Hurricane Helene are still fresh in Isley’s mind. Hauling water from their flooded basement up to the toilet to flush it when the water ran out. Driving to Jamie’s parents’ house in Atlanta, holed up in a room with both of their cats until they couldn’t take it anymore. Coming back to Asheville and cooking meals in the Crock-Pot with disposable liners because even when the water was running again, it wasn’t safe to wash dishes with.

Two years later, Isley browses Zillow for fun, but she looks at homes through a post-disaster lens. “Now I have that fear in the back of my mind—anywhere near a river, or even a stream, if there’s a little bit of water on the map, I’m like, ‘Oh, no,’” she said. Jamie is trans, and after Trump was elected in 2024, the two of them briefly entertained the idea of moving somewhere with more protective policies, like California. But Isley’s mind immediately went to wildfires. Out of the question.

Isley had fled from hurricanes before, when she lived in Florida during college. She thought she’d be safe from them tucked away in the Blue Ridge Mountains. Asheville was supposed to be a “climate haven,” somewhere that would fare better than the rest of the country as the world warmed. Those promises were shattered when almost 14 inches of rain fell on Asheville over three days in September 2024. The French Broad River overflowed its banks, flooding homes and destroying parts of the town’s River Arts District. In western North Carolina, more than 74,000 homes were damaged and only about 4 percent had flood insurance, resulting in $9.5 billion in uninsured residential property losses.

Home values in western North Carolina have declined since the storm, especially in the hardest-hit counties. Asheville’s average home price shrunk 5 percent over the past year, while the national average increased 1.2 percent.

To some degree, housing markets are already pricing in the risk of increased environmental hazards. Homes within FEMA’s high-risk flood zones sell for 2.8 percent less, on average, than what they would otherwise sell for, according to a 2023 study published in the journal Nature Climate Change. The researchers found that homes exposed to flood risk were still overvalued by between $121 billion and $237 billion, though—and they identified Appalachia as a hot spot of overvaluation, one year before Helene hit. The devaluation of homes in high-risk zones is unfolding unevenly and causing “tremendous social harm,” said Elliott, a sociology professor at The London School of Economics and Political Science.

Homes are billed as a way for people to build wealth, but they can turn into a trap. After Superstorm Sandy devastated New York City and the New Jersey coast in 2012, many homeowners couldn’t sell their houses for enough money to buy a new place, leaving them stranded. Even homes that haven’t seen any kind of devastation are at risk of losing value as more people become wary of living in floodplains, coastal places exposed to storms, and wildfire-prone areas. “Those homes could become, in effect, economically worthless even before they are physically uninhabitable,” Elliott wrote in a study about property values and climate change.

Insurance is meant to offer a measure of safety when taking on a huge debt for a mortgage on a house. Douglas Heller, the director of insurance at the Consumer Federation of America, called it “the safety net for the American Dream.” But insurance rates are part of what’s making homeownership unaffordable for so many. Since 2020, property insurance costs have ballooned almost 80 percent, with the average single-family mortgage holder now paying $209 per month. Homeowners in the riskiest areas are paying substantially more, and many in California have been dropped by their insurers. Home insurance rates are rising faster in the Midwest than any other region, driven by the costs of severe storms.

“We are, for a lot of people, on the edge of a dysfunctional insurance marketplace,” Heller said. The more extreme weather we’re seeing is only part of the story: He argues that the insurance industry has become a “climate opportunist,” using climate change as an excuse to justify excessive rate increases.

People relying on Social Security benefits who own condos around Lake Tahoe are particularly vulnerable to rising rates, said Andrew Engler, the founder and CEO of Rock Rose Risk, who helps people in California protect their homes against wildfire and get their insurance premiums down. They’re facing ballooning homeowners association payments, to share the cost of insurance in a risky wildfire area, on a limited paycheck. If they try to move, their properties are worth significantly less because of the huge HOA bills, Engler said. Economists estimate that rising insurance costs linked to disaster risk have reduced the growth of home prices by more than $40,000 in the most hurricane- and wildfire-prone ZIP codes.

Renting might make you more nimble, but it doesn’t insulate you from these costs. One reason rents are going up is because landlords’ property insurance rates are increasing. “Whether you are a homeowner or a renter, we’re all paying for living under the increased risks of climate change,” said Caroline Nagy, the associate director of housing policy at Americans for Financial Reform. That makes it harder for people to save for a home—if that’s even a good idea anymore.

WHEN SIERRA ISLEY walks around her neighborhood these days, she sees the evidence of Helene all around her—in the form of banners with the slogan “Asheville Strong” and shirts that say “WNC Strong.”

One of the most surprising things about disasters might be the way that people who live through them rise to the occasion and come together. In the aftermath of the Helene, with the power and cell service knocked out, Sierra and Jamie walked all around town, talking to their neighbors to try to learn what had happened. People started congregating at the fire station where there was fresh water.

“It’s hard to put into words what that experience was like, but I’ve never felt more of a community, and really having to lean on my neighbors and feeling like my neighbors were leaning on me,” Isley said.

While the American Dream is usually all about independence and personal freedom, living through a disaster has a way of revealing how people depend on each other. The experience can prompt people to hold tightly to what they have, doubling down on protecting their communities, said Nick Tinoco, a sociology researcher in a doctoral program at the University of California, Los Angeles, who interviewed survivors of the 2018 Woolsey Fire in Los Angeles County. Some of the residents he talked to have taken things into their own hands and organized volunteer fire brigades and plan to stay behind to defend their neighborhoods during future fires.

As supposedly safe “climate havens” like Asheville experience more disasters, the idea that people can simply move out of harm’s way is losing its grip. “I think we have to just reckon with the fact that we’re going to have to make people secure in the places that they live,” Elliott said.

She thinks it’s time to rethink the bargain of the American Dream—the expectation that so much of a person’s economic future depends on the fate of a single structure. Many young people have begun to define success differently. A poll from Ipsos last year showed that 46 percent of baby boomers associate homeownership with the American Dream but only 13 percent of Gen Zers do, suggesting that there’s room for its defining features to change.

Sierra and Jamie couldn’t help but wonder what happened to the house they’d almost bought, and they drove over to check it out soon after Hurricane Helene hit. It was still standing, but they couldn’t see if there was any damage hidden inside. “Who knows if it flooded or anything like that, what kind of storm damage it took, and that would have immediately been our problem,” Isley said.

Living through Hurricane Helene didn’t just make Isley relieved she hadn’t bought a house in Asheville. It has shaped what she wants for her life, helping her discover a passion for public health and pushing her to want to work in emergency preparedness. Now she’s applying to schools to pursue a master’s degree in public health.

“I think I owe it to people like me, people in other rural communities who are going to face the same kind of climate change emergencies, to use my skills to help combat climate change and natural disasters,” Isley said. “I just feel such a calling.”

https://www.wired.com/story/cybertrucks-.title: The Cybertruck’s Death Is Actually Great News for EVs
https://www.wired.com/story/cybertrucks-.author: Brian Kahn
https://www.wired.com/story/cybertrucks-.text:
TESLA WILL END production of the Cybertruck at its Texas Gigafactory next year.

It’s a uniquely toxic electric vehicle, between its divisive design and Elon Musk’s embrace of you name it. That toxicity certainly contributed to subpar sales, along with a number of recalls.

But the end of the Cybertruck is also another sign that the era of big EVs—particularly big trucks—is waning. That’s great news for pedestrian and biker safety, but also for the battery supply chain at a time when more people need to get behind the electric wheel.

The Cybertruck uses a massive 123-kilowatt-hour battery that clocks in at around 1,600 pounds, or around a quarter of the vehicle's weight. That’s on par with the battery that powered Ford’s F-150 Lightning, another electric truck that was canceled late last year. (The company also killed a three-row EV in 2024.) Ford’s behemoth batteries ranged from 98 kilowatt-hours up to 131 kilowatt-hours.

Seeing both trucks canceled within a year of each other, while automakers have announced a bevy of smaller EVs and gas-powered autos with electric motors that can extend range, indicates there may be a shift afoot. Ford is planning to launch the Fathom next year. The sub-$30,000 electric pickup is expected to be about the size of the automaker’s compact gas-powered Maverick pickup. Though Ford hasn’t announced the battery sizes available in various trims, it’s a safe bet they won’t be anywhere near the size of the F-150 Lightning's or Cybertruck's. The company is also planning to relaunch the Lightning as an extended-range model.

Startup Slate is also launching a tiny electric pickup that can be converted to an SUV, with a bare-bones base model starting below $25,000. It also features a svelte battery and has seen a massive surge in preorders—though, to be fair, so did the Cybertruck, and we saw how that turned out.

Then there’s the Rivian R2, which launched this year. While the SUV isn’t as tiny or cheap as Ford and Slate’s vehicles—its battery has 88 kilowatt-hours of capacity and weighs in at around 1,200 pounds—it’s still smaller than the company’s flagship R1S. Rivian has also teased the R3, an even more-slimmed down SUV, in the coming years.

That’s not to say big EVs are dead. The Kia EV9, for example, is among the top 10 EVs by sales in the US, as is the R1S. There’s also a torrid resale market for the F-150 Lightning. But the rest of the top 10 new EV sales are all crossovers, sedans, or mid-sized SUVs with moderately sized batteries, and a number of newly announced EVs are trending on the smaller side or function as extended-range vehicles.

Building smaller vehicles is, of course, one way to make EVs cheaper. With less weight to propel, you can rely on a smaller battery. And given that the battery pack is the most costly component of an EV, that can in turn help automakers offer more affordable vehicles at a time when the price of so many other consumer goods is skyrocketing. That includes the current crop of EVs: The average transaction price for a new model is now $55,800, according to Cox Automotive.

Going small—or smaller, anyway—also means making the most of a limited battery supply chain. The vast majority of Cybertruck drivers are doing the same thing with their vehicles as Hyundai Ioniq 5 drivers: getting groceries, commuting, and driving kids to soccer games. But a standard-range Ioniq 5 driver is doing it with a battery about half the size.

After President Donald Trump’s administration killed EV incentives last year, sales plummeted. The Iran War and rising gas prices have led to an uptick in interest, though sales still lag behind the global average. (Used hybrid sales have also picked up, reflecting the pain people have been feeling at the pump.) Even with a Democratic-controlled Congress, EV incentives coming back under Trump are about as likely as defense secretary Pete Hegseth putting pronouns in his email signature. But should Democrats take the White House in 2028, marking the culmination of Woke 2.0, support for would-be EV buyers becomes much more likely.

Automakers pivoting to smaller cars could be much better positioned to meet pent-up demand if that happens, while also lowering the risks of delivery delays.

Even Elon’s announcement killing the Cybertruck points to where the market is heading: He claims Tesla is ending production to make room for cranking out more Cybercabs. The battery size in those vehicles? Just 48 kilowatt-hours.

Additional reporting by Aarian Marshall.

https://www.wired.com/story/rocco-black-.author: Kat Merck

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

IF YOU'VE BEEN coveting one of Rocco’s smart designer minifridges, you might be interested to know the brand's biggest sale of 2026 starts today, featuring the brand-new Rocco Essential for under $1,000 and the OG Classic in this year’s new Beige colorway, as well as white and two rare blue colors, for $1,495—as low as the Classic ever gets.

Today also marks the rerelease of the Classic's Icy Blue and Royal Blue, two rarely seen colors that Rocco says are not coming back after this year.

The Essential was just released in August and just began shipping in September; I'm currently testing it now. It's only been about a week and a half, but early impressions are positive. It has the same smart sight system as the Classic, but the biggest difference is obviously the look. Vintage-inspired fluted glass and rounded edges are out; sleek minimalism is in. The tinted dark glass door takes up the entire front, with a color-matched metal handle you can swap out for midcentury-inspired oak for an extra $95.

It's only got one temperature zone as opposed to the Classic's two, but my favorite part so far has been the interior—instead of the Classic's old-fashioned wire racks, the Essential sports smooth-glide drawers lined with a rubbery material and grip strips. This makes it much more accommodating to oddly shaped drinks and prevents cans (it can hold up to 77) from rolling around every time you open your Rocco. It also gets colder than the Classic model—down to 34 degrees Fahrenheit instead of 37. My main frustration so far is that the sight system has been a little spotty and slow to recognize when drinks have been removed, but I'm having that problem with the Classic as well, so it's not specific to this model. All colors (Cream, Sage, Graphite) of the Essential are currently discounted.

ROCCO (CERTAIN COLORS)

The handsome, vintage-inspired model is the one that started it all. Its thick steel body comes in a range of fun colors, the fluted glass refracts potentially drink-damaging light, and it comes with a color-matched metal tray so it can double as a bar cart. It's got two isolated temperature zones for red and white wine (or extra-crispy Cokes), plus five full-sized racks and one half-rack—enough for 88 cans or 27 bottles of wine. The wire racks don't pull out as smoothly as the Essential's rubber-lined drawers, but this is otherwise a top-of-the-line beverage cooler with an impressive 10-year warranty.

You can also control the interior lights from your phone. The sight system, however, is buggy—my Classic is currently displaying a rack of Dr. Pepper and Stella Artois bottles I had left over from a party in July (they were consumed not long after that), so I would not recommend buying one of these for the sight system alone. (Note this sale is on the Beige, White, Royal Blue, and Icy Blue Classic only.)

I’m partial to the Classic’s forest green, but even I've got to admit the blue hues look pretty good. They sold out almost immediately around this time last year, so if you've been wanting one and you see this, I wouldn't wait to add it to your cart.

With its built-in sleep tracking, it monitors your nightly sleep score, called your “Sleep IQ” number within the app. That data is compared with the firmness level you choose, known as your “Sleep Number” setting. The offer runs through December 7, and no promo code is needed—deals will be applied automatically.

This is probably the most luxurious smart bed the WIRED Reviews team has tested. (Read our review here.) You're probably not planning to drop ten grand on a bed today, but if you've been curious about smart beds, this may be a good one to check out. It has a unique design centered on temperature control, with built-in fans that make its surface noticeably cooler to the touch. The bed also monitors your bedroom's air quality and analyzes sleep metrics with an AI-powered sleep coach to give you feedback.

You can save $500 and get a $300 credit toward a future purchase when you buy a TEMPUR-ActiveBreeze System, TEMPUR-Breeze, or TEMPUR-LuxeAdapt mattress and a TEMPUR-Ergo Smart Base through December 1, with no promo code necessary.

When I die, bury me with this modular, supremely cooling mattress. It's part of Bedgear's new Night Ice collection, the most cooling beds I've ever slept on. It has a silky cover that's cool to the touch, top cooling layers that work together to dissipate heat effectively, and side mesh vents to increase airflow throughout the mattress. With this modular design, you can choose the same or different levels of firmness on both sides. The M5 above, plus Hybrid Performance and Sport Performance models below, are all discounted, and you can get a further discount if you buy one with an adjustable base. Sales run through December 7.

I slept on this cooling mattress for over a year and was super happy with it. It's one of the most consistently cooling beds I’ve tested, and it feels more luxurious than its price tag suggests.

IMHO, this is hands-down the best mattress you can buy for this price on the market today. It's cooling and comes in a few firmness levels.

This pillow has a cool-to-the-touch cover and adjustable filling, so you can tailor its density or fluffiness to your liking.

If you sleep sweaty, this is a great cooling pillow. Plus, it has two profile heights to choose from, depending on your preference.

https://www.wired.com/story/free-chinese.title: Free Chinese AI Models Are Getting Scary Good at Hacking
https://www.wired.com/story/free-chinese.author: Will Knight, Lily Hay Newman
https://www.wired.com/story/free-chinese.text:
OPEN-WEIGHT ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE models are now almost as capable of hacking into computer networks as the best closed ones, according to new research that heralds a much-anticipated turning point in the cybersecurity landscape.

Vals, a company that measures AI capabilities, set out to test how well different AI models could carry out complex, multi-step network instructions on mock corporate networks.

“The best frontier models, locked up inside the labs and available only through trusted access programs, are now starting to be matched by open models that anybody can download,” says Nikil Ravi, a researcher at Vals.

The company’s findings suggest that closed models no longer have a definitive edge in cyber skills, meaning recent efforts by frontier labs to limit access to their models, and thereby slow the proliferation of such capabilities, may potentially be moot.

The findings are also noteworthy given that the US frontier labs, particularly Anthropic, premised the limited release of new models—beginning with Claude Mythos Preview in April—on the idea that gated access would only buy time before advanced hacking capabilities were broadly available.

Anthropic's frontier red team lead, Logan Graham, told WIRED in April that the company’s Project Glasswing, which gives trusted access to the full capabilities of new models, was focused on getting those tools “in the hands of defenders to give a head start.”

“We need to prepare now for a world where these capabilities are broadly available in 6, 12, 24 months. Many things would be different about security,” he told WIRED at the time.

Seven months later, that transition seems to have arrived on schedule.

Vals tested AI models in two simulated scenarios, giving them various specific tasks to achieve. The first scenario involved a mock corporate network accessible through a public-facing website. The second involved two different company networks; a model needed to compromise the first in order to gain access to the second.

The researchers found OpenAI’s most advanced cyber model, Daybreak, which is available only to trusted partners, to be the most capable, completing 81 percent of the tasks it was given in an average of two tests. The Chinese open-weight model DeepSeek was not far behind, completing 73 percent of the objectives on average. The Vals researchers note that on some tasks, the two models scored equally.

The research also showed how much cheaper it is to use an open-weight model for this kind of task. Vals says it costs $17 to $46 in tokens for GPT-6-Sol to carry out an attack compared to $2 to $3 for DeepSeek. Open models are generally cheaper because they can be run on one’s own hardware. Rayan Krishnan, CEO of Vals, says this also provides a strong incentive for those playing defense to use open models rather than proprietary ones.

OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Much of the year in cybersecurity has played out as predicted, with AI automating core hacking tasks to help both attackers and defenders find a massive number of new vulnerabilities in code and rapidly probe networks for weaknesses. While the speed and scale of the findings, and the intensity of fixing uncovered software flaws, have all increased, experts are still debating whether AI has fundamentally altered the conceptual foundation and tenets of cybersecurity defense. In other words, it’s still not clear whether AI tools pose a new kind of threat or amplify the security challenges that have long existed.

The fact that open-weight models are now starting to match closed ones is crucial for understanding how criminal hackers can harness AI, and how companies and developers should respond. But in practice, real-world observation of cybercriminal and state-backed hacking activity has repeatedly shown in recent months that attackers are doing what they always do by conserving their resources and generally making do with older and less capable models—both proprietary and open—for most of their activity. And even with strict controls, defenders must assume that the best-funded and most highly motivated attackers have already had at least some access to closed models all this time.

“I am in general agreement that open-weight models are capable of producing advanced attacks and vulnerabilities today, especially when you consider the abliterated models that disable safety training by modifying weights,” says Alex Zenla, cofounder and chief technology officer of the cloud security firm Edera. “My caveat to this is that it is likely that the closed labs have trained additional, unreleased models exceeding these capabilities. So I would put this very much like a cat-and-mouse game. The labs see themselves as moving fast to outpace the open-weight models, to be able to secure vulnerabilities before the open-weight models find them. Unfortunately, I do think this may be the beginning of a dangerous security landscape.”

https://www.wired.com/story/rip-cybertru.title: RIP Cybertruck. You Were Unloved, Unwanted, and Utterly Absurd
https://www.wired.com/story/rip-cybertru.author: Jeremy White
https://www.wired.com/story/rip-cybertru.text:
ELON MUSK, IN a post on X, has officially called time on the Cybertruck, stating that “Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production.”

Produced for less than four years, the polarizing pickup is seemingly dying as it lived, with the news being greeted in a flurry of replies in praise of the EV as well as deriding it. James Star, claiming to be a Tesla employee, posted that it was “the saddest news! Cybertruck (was) the best car Tesla sold,” right next to a user called Captain Ford who simply replied to Musk with “Fuck that shitbox.”

Tesla has not responded to WIRED’s request for comment and clarification that the Cybertruck will no longer be made at all. The Cybertruck is exclusively made at Gigafactory Texas, as this is apparently the only Tesla facility equipped with the machinery required to manufacture the truck’s unique stainless steel body, which supposedly started to rust in some cases.

Despite whipping up a fevered number of reservations—allegedly more than a million according to Musk, who at the end of 2023 crowed that demand was “off the charts!”—the truck failed to sell, shifting less than 50,000 units in total by March last year.

EVWire cites Kelley Blue Book data suggesting that Tesla sold 11,586 Cybertrucks in the first three quarters of this year in the US, down 28 percent year-over-year, adding that Musk’s announcement post came about 80 minutes after Tesla raised US Cybertruck prices and paused new orders for the entry-level Dual-Motor AWD version.

The Cybertruck proved not only to be wildly unpopular, it was also beset by troubles before it even reached customers. In 2023, WIRED covered a leaked Tesla report dated January 25, 2022, that showed the Cybertruck had basic design flaws, and that the preproduction “alpha” version was struggling with problems with its suspension, body sealing, noise levels, handling, and braking.

In November 2019, when Musk stepped onto a stage in California to launch his new cyberpunk-styled electric pickup, he decided to demonstrate the strength of the “unbreakable” glass windows by hurling a steel ball at them. In what has now entered into public relations folklore, the demo truck’s windows smashed not once, but twice. Musk swore, then joked: “There’s room for improvement.”

There most certainly was. In April 2024, a recall was issued for the Cybertruck because its accelerator pedal pad could come loose and get trapped by interior trim, which had the frightening potential of pushing the car to full speed.

In March last year, Tesla had to recall nearly all the Cybertrucks it had then produced because a stainless steel trim panel could become detached from the vehicle while driving, blaming the problem on the wrong type of glue, which then had to be replaced with a new adhesive “not prone to environmental embrittlement.”

Back in May this year, Cybertrucks were struck down by the wrong type of grease, which meant that their wheels could potentially fall off. In what was then the EV’s 11th recall, it was declared that the Rear Wheel Drive (RWD) Cybertruck Long Range model might have faulty brake rotors. In a notice posted by the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, Tesla stated that “brake rotor stud holes may crack and allow the stud to separate from the wheel hub.” Such a situation might have seen some RWD Cybertruck owners merrily driving along only to then be disconcertingly overtaken by their own wheels.

Musk even tried to get President Donald Trump to buy one of his Cybertrucks, creating an impromptu Tesla showroom on the White House South Lawn, no less. But, sadly, even President Trump must have smelt something was off about the truck as instead he shunned the pickup and opted for a 200-mph Model S Plaid in ultra red, clearly impressed with the interior, remarking that “Everything’s computer!”

At the end of 2024, Karl Brauer, executive analyst at car ranking service iSeeCars, told WIRED that he’d calculated that the Cybertruck’s six recalls to date at the time made the EV “worse than 91 percent” of all other 2024 vehicles.

Yet, despite supposedly being so unreliable, the Cybertruck did find a small but loyal audience. WIRED profiled a number of owners last year, all fervently in love with their vehicles, but who were periodically forced to endure insults and taunts that they were Nazis, perhaps referring to an on-stage gesture Musk made at the start of 2025.

However, despite evidence seemingly to the contrary, Musk claims he is killing the Cybertruck, not because of its unreliability and staggering unpopularity, but because he wishes to focus instead on Cybercab, an autonomous EV that is central to Tesla’s robotaxi ambitions but itself has had a rocky start.

Currently operating in Austin only, with a fleet supposedly numbered only in the hundreds, Musk apparently wants to ramp up production dramatically since he confirmed on an earnings call the first cab came off the line in February.

Musk sees Cybercab as very much the vision of Tesla’s future. The CEO has even said that Tesla should no longer be regarded as an automaker but as a robotics and autonomous vehicle company. “Cybertruck was an incredible ⁠technology development platform and lives on through Cybercab,” Cybertruck lead engineer Wes Morrill said on X.
