Squarespace also announced layoffs this week, but explicit ties to AI remain inconsistent.

November 3, 2026, 1:12 pm ET

According to exclusive reporting by The Register, enterprise Linux provider SUSE will lay off one in 10 of its nearly 2,000-person workforce due to “automation and AI,” CEO Dirk-Peter van Leeuwen told staff via email.

Also: How many jobs is your state losing to AI?

Van Leeuwen noted that AI is rapidly changing how software companies function.

“AI capabilities are advancing exponentially, forcing us to radically reimagine our work,” he said, adding that “the organizational design and cost base that SUSE is built on today will not carry us forward successfully.”

He did not specify which roles would be terminated, but The Register reports that staff will be notified by Nov. 4.

AI is impacting many parts of the tech industry, including open source. Just last month, Linus Torvalds announced he had used Claude Code to write a Linux patch, which Linux enthusiasts read as an evolution of his stance on AI.

By some reports, businesses are finally seeing some ROI from AI after a few years of uncertainty. But that remains localized, ironically, to tech itself. As one economist recently noted, AI has primarily increased revenue per employee at major tech companies, while leaving most other companies unchanged.

The trade-off for that growth is, at least in some cases, layoffs. But layoffs credited to AI in some way don’t mean that human roles are always being replaced. Last month, Microsoft announced it would buy out 60,000 of its workers — some of which are in its Copilot division — to prioritize AI efforts, though it’s also likely the company is reacting to spending a significant amount of money on AI infrastructure.

Jobloss.ai’s layoff tracker shows primarily tech companies — including Uber, Salesforce, and GitLab — in its recent entries, but job loss attribution to AI is still mixed, and the number of roles cut isn’t always jarringly huge.

It’s also hard to tell whether a layoff strategically frames pre-AI plans as being due to AI capabilities or is actually a result of them. That question circulated around Block’s major layoffs earlier this year. Squarespace also announced layoffs of 19% of its staff yesterday, though company communications don’t explicitly name AI. Still, vibecoding has impacted website builders overall, though Squarespace itself has invested in AI offerings.

Also: Why replacing staff with AI backfires

Van Leeuwen’s email to staff acknowledged where SUSE has already begun to change, though it’s unclear whether he meant by adopting AI tools internally.

“Across SUSE, modern tooling is already changing our daily workflows, enabling teams to move faster with less operational overhead and flatter reporting lines. The requirement for some existing roles has greatly diminished. Other roles will evolve over the next few years,” he said.

While several tech companies have announced highly visible layoffs this year that they’ve also framed as related to AI, economists agree that the massive cross-industry layoff wave many fear has yet to arrive. Gartner even predicts that companies will actually rehire 30% of the employees they tried to replace with AI — and at a higher cost — by 2029 if they don’t “overhaul workforce planning.”

Still, AI investments, vibecoding, and shifting priorities are changing the software scene overall.

The HomeView Ultra is expected to feature a robotic arm and 9-inch display. Shades of Amazon's discontinued Echo Show 10?

November 3, 2026, 12:33 pm ET

The Apple HomeView is the company’s first dedicated smart home display, and new reports of how Apple plans to improve the product are already circulating. Apple is reportedly planning to announce a HomeView with a robotic arm as early as next year. The dynamic display is expected to cost up to $1,000.

Also: Apple’s HomeView may double as security camera

The HomeView isn’t even on the market yet — it will be available for purchase next week, starting at $299. This 7-inch smart panel features a speaker that doubles as a stand, and Apple will also sell a wall-mounted option.

As a smart home device, the HomeView is designed to serve as a platform for interacting with your Apple ecosystem, including Apple Home and Siri. It’s a smart dashboard that lets you view all your smart home devices and security cameras, as well as your calendar, messages, and other integrated apps.

The Information reported that Apple is rumored to be working on a higher-end smart display for 2027, with shipments starting in 2028. The new device, codenamed J595, may be branded HomeView Ultra and feature a robotic arm and a 9-inch display.

The new HomeView’s screen would be mounted on an articulated mechanical arm to swivel the display, tracking users during FaceTime calls to keep them on-screen. The device could feature proactive smart home automations, such as turning on devices or triggering a room scene when someone walks into the room.

Also: Google’s latest Home updates just fixed my biggest annoyances

The same report indicates that the hardware has been complete for a couple of years, but launch delays are attributed to software development issues. Integrating advanced AI features and proactive automation has, according to The Information, been a challenge for Apple.

A swiveling smart home display isn’t entirely new. Amazon used to sell an Echo Show 10 with a display that tracked users to keep them in the camera’s view during video calls, though this model has been discontinued.

However, one that works within the Apple ecosystem could change how users interact with their home interfaces, given the popularity of FaceTime calls and the prevalence of iPhone users.

Also: 4 big Amazon smart home announcements

A HomeView Ultra could even anticipate users’ needs by tracking people’s movements and automatically executing routines and scenes depending on where they are in the home.

While there’s reason to doubt whether most smart home users would welcome such technology in their homes or consider it too invasive, premium robotic smart displays indicate that companies are standardizing interactive central hubs for the home.

https://www.zdnet.com/home-and-office/so.author: Jada Jones

Home & Office

Speakers

New Sonos software and firmware updates are rolling out. Here's what you can expect.

November 3, 2026, 12:26 pm ET

Sonos’ promise to release its AI-upgraded voice assistant is nearing its “Fall 2026” deadline, and before fans can use the highly anticipated update, the company continues to make small improvements to its app and player features.

Also: Sonos Ace Ultra vs. Sonos Ace: Who should upgrade

This time, Sonos added System Health, a new in-app page to access a more comprehensive view of your system(s), though it’s only available on iOS for now. However, a new blog post states that iOS and Android users can expect volume presets, more interaction with the app miniplayer, and spoken voice prompts for the Ace Ultra headphones.

I poked around in the app and tried some of the latest features. Here’s what to expect.

If your system consists of multiple speakers, a mix of modern and legacy speakers, or multiple systems, you’re bound to experience a hiccup and be unsure which speaker is causing the issue.

It usually takes me some time to Google my issue and scroll through the Sonos Community forum, Reddit, or the official Sonos help documents to find suggestions and troubleshoot it. Sonos’ new System Health feature provides an overview of your systems, showing your network status and name, as well as the number of speakers and rooms in each system.

Also: I used Sonos’s new home theater feature – it’s a competition killer

According to Sonos’ blog post, System Health can detect a Double Network Address issue, which usually occurs when you introduce a new router to your home or plug a mesh system into your ISP-provided router. The result is two home networks, and your Sonos speakers will split their connection between them, flagging “System not found” errors, missing speakers, or connection dropouts.

System Health is in the Settings tab, under the Help Center menu.

Once you tap into your system, you can see all of its speakers, with unconnected speakers bearing a red “Not connected” badge, and wireless speakers showing a black “Powered off” badge when they’re off.

Then, you can see a speaker’s connection information, including status, Wi-Fi signal strength, signal/noise ratio, frequency, IP address, and more. You can also find its volume output, Trueplay setup status, line-in connection, voice control status, serial number, hardware model and version, and which Sonos platform it operates on.

System Health can also show you your account details, Sonos ID, Controller ID, and your current app build version. System Health comes after Sonos updated the System Updates tab, which now displays an overview of your app, system, and headphone update status. This page also links to the Sonos release notes.

Sonos’ blog post states that this feature is new and still open to change, especially if the Sonos community has a particularly overwhelming response to it. The blog post also disclaims that this feature is a first look, not a deep dive.

Review: Sonos Beam Ultra

However, after a brief first use, I see it as a great way to quickly access all the details you need about your systems and speakers, especially if you’re doing some rewiring, moving a speaker to a new room, or general troubleshooting.

System Health is rolling out to iOS users first. I updated my Sonos app in the App Store and was able to access it, but Sonos’ blog post states that this update is a phased rollout.

Updates to the Sonos app and its player are a long time coming. After receiving several new ways to control your speakers’ volume (I think we’re up to three), Sonos is realizing that granular volume control is a high priority for many Sonos users, including me.

The in-app volume dial is cool, and the interactive volume scrubber is a nice touch, but there’s nothing more jarring than wanting to play some tunes on my kitchen counter speaker, only for it to blast at 80% from when my husband was watching football the night before.

Sonos’ latest big update to volume this time around is Presets, a way to start playback in a specific room at a set volume. I haven’t found this feature in my app’s update yet, but I think it’s because my hardware needs an update. Presets will be available on iOS and Android.

Review: Sonos Ace Ultra

Fortunately, I did use another update to the Sonos miniplayer: swipe to skip. What a teeny, tiny but useful feature. It works just like the miniplayer in Apple Music and Spotify; when the app is open, you can swipe left to skip to the next song.

One major caveat: swiping right to replay a track doesn’t work — at least not yet. Swiping both ways seems like a given to me, so it feels odd that you can’t. Still, being able to swipe the miniplayer to the next track is better than always having the main player open to toggle tracks. This feature is also coming to iOS and Android.

Sonos’ miniplayer is getting so much better; you can swipe to the next track and easily control volume from it, even when you have the Ace or Ace Ultra connected (I tried). The in-app volume dial also works with Sonos headphones.

Also: Sonos Play vs. Sonos Move 2: Why I’d go with the $200 cheaper Bluetooth speaker

Speaking of the Ace Ultra, a firmware update is available. A new Vocal Guidance feature can announce the battery percentage when you power on the headphones, when the audio mode changes from ANC to Transparency, and which device your headphones are connected to via Bluetooth.

It feels like this update is the final stretch before Sonos 27voice arrives, as the release notes suggest. It appears Sonos is laying the groundwork for speakers to support the AI-powered voice assistant in Early Access. Once it’s here, I’ll test it as soon as I can.

https://www.zdnet.com/tech/windows-11-pc.author: Lance Whitney

Windows 11

The latest updates to Windows 11 offer improvements in speed, performance, and memory management.

November 3, 2026, 12:00 pm ET

The more memory your Windows PC has, the faster it should perform, especially when juggling multiple apps, files, and other data. My laptop has 32GB of RAM, while my desktop has a hefty 64GB, and both are absolutely zippy. Does that mean computers with only 8GB of memory, or even less, are also-rans? Nope, not according to Microsoft.

Also: How much RAM does your PC really need?

In a new blog post published Tuesday, Microsoft touted the gains in speed, performance, and memory management in Windows 11 achieved by the latest updates. These especially impact PCs with just 8GB of RAM, which can now run multiple apps and files faster and more efficiently than before.

To reach this goal, the company said it had three notions in mind.

The first was to make better use of the existing memory on each Windows 11 PC. The second was to protect the tasks that need to feel instant even as more memory gets used. And the third was to ensure that key apps and Windows require less memory. Yes, a computer with 16GB, 32GB, or 64GB of RAM can better handle more intensive activities. But Microsoft wanted to make sure that systems with 8GB could also keep pace.

Based on its own lab tests of PCs with 8GB of RAM, the company claims that Windows is now 20% more responsive and that multitasking is 40% faster than before the latest updates. Here’s how.

As more memory gets allocated, Windows must move inactive apps and files from RAM to the hard drive. When you need to access those apps and files again, you have to wait for Windows to move them from disk storage back to RAM. Normally, PCs with less memory have to do a lot of this disk swapping.

One way Windows eases the pain of this process is through compression. Here, the operating system shrinks less-active data into a smaller format so it can remain in memory. Though Windows has used compression for many years, Microsoft has fine-tuned the technology to determine how much to compress, when to move data from RAM to your drive, and when to fetch it back, especially on PCs with 8GB of memory.

Also: 5 apps I always install on new Windows PCs – most are free

As such, Windows can now keep up to 2GB more of your active data in memory rather than moving it to storage, Microsoft said. An inactive app, file, or browser that you leave open is less likely to have to reload from your hard drive when you return to it.

Opening the Start menu, launching File Explorer, right-clicking a folder or file, and searching for an item are all tasks that need to feel instant; otherwise, Windows itself feels sluggish. To achieve this on PCs with less RAM, Windows tries to prioritize certain actions you need to accomplish while backing off background tasks like search indexing, Microsoft said.

Here’s one example. After you update your computer and reboot, Windows has some housekeeping to do. But any setup work that occurs shouldn’t affect how long it takes to open an app or file.

Also: How to upgrade your ‘incompatible’ Windows 10 PC to Windows 11 – for free

The latest version of Windows 11 speeds up these types of tasks and interactions by up to 20% compared with the January 2026 version, according to Microsoft.

However, multitasking places the greatest strain on a PC with only 8GB of RAM. To analyze this, Microsoft said it conducted two tests on the same PC with 8GB of memory. One test measured the current version of Windows 11, while the other gauged the January 2026 flavor. Here, the testers opened 20 tabs in Microsoft Edge, kicked off a 4K video, and launched large files in Word, PowerPoint, and Excel, one after another. The current version of Windows is up to 40% faster than its predecessor, the company said.

To reduce the need for RAM among Windows and certain key apps, Microsoft said that it has improved how memory is managed and when it’s used.

As one example, memory is allocated to Word, PowerPoint, Excel, and Outlook more efficiently, resulting in a 360 MB savings in RAM. This maneuver also extends to third-party apps such as WhatsApp, which has reduced its memory requirements.

Also: 11 Windows apps I replace on every new PC (and the ones I keep)

On PCs with 8GB of memory, the Widgets app loads only when you open it and frees up about 200 MB of RAM when you close it. In Microsoft Edge, inactive tabs now go to sleep after 15 minutes, down from two hours previously, reducing overall memory allocation.

Across Windows, Microsoft 365, and Edge, those improvements reduced the growth in required memory by up to 900 MB, Microsoft said.

How does Microsoft test these scenarios to see whether the latest Windows updates and fixes are helping PCs with less memory?

“We test those fixes across a broader collection of over 20,000 PCs in our labs, including current 8 GB models, using automated workloads based on activities such as browsing, working in Microsoft 365 apps, joining video calls, and downloading files in the background and even using high-speed cameras to measure the time from an action, such as opening Start or launching an app, to the moment the result appears on screen,” the company explained.

Also: Why your RAM options cost 4X more now than last year

The ability to use Windows without much RAM on your PC is critical these days in light of the “RAMageddon” crisis. With AI companies scooping up massive amounts of memory and flash storage chips, remaining supply is limited, and the prices have surged. The more memory you add to a new or existing PC, the more you’re going to pay. That’s always been true, but now more than ever.

Of course, memory is only one part of the picture. Your PC’s processor and other hardware also play an important role. Here, Microsoft found that a 2026 Dell XPS 13 with 8GB of RAM showed 94% faster multi-core CPU performance than a 2021 8 GB model. But the same 2026 8GB PC performed on par with a 2021 16 GB system. This shows that memory does matter for multitasking, but that the processor also impacts performance.

Whether your Windows 11 PC has 8GB of RAM, less, or more, how can you take advantage of the latest enhancements? For that, you’ll want to make sure that you’ve updated to the newest version of Windows. That would be Windows 11 26H2, build 26300.9818 or later, according to Microsoft. But that includes the latest optional preview build released in late October. If you don’t want to install that one, you’ll be fine with build 26300.9711 for now.

Also: The best laptops: Expert tested and reviewed

To check, head to Settings, select System, and then click About. The section for Windows Info shows the current version and build. If you need to update, stay in Settings and go to Windows Update. Assuming your PC qualifies, you should find the latest Windows 11 26H2 build ready to install.

Beyond updating Windows, you also want to keep your apps current. If you use Microsoft 365, open any app in the suite, click the File menu, select Account, click Update Options, then select Update Now.

With most other apps, you have to update them manually or individually. To ease the process, consider a good software updater program. These will automatically scan most of your installed applications to identify which need updating, then download and install the updates for you.

One of Roku's most popular screensavers is about to make its last splash. Here’s how to switch before Dec. 1.

November 3, 2026, 11:40 am ET

A fan-favorite Roku screensaver is going away, and users aren’t happy.

Over the last several days, users with the Aquatic Life aquarium screensaver set as the default have noticed a message appearing when the screensaver opens. “Starting Dec. 1, 2026,” the message reads, “the Aquatic Life screensaver will no longer be available, and your screensaver will switch to Roku City.”

Also: The free Roku City screensaver game has me hooked

The screensaver, which displays a digital aquarium with tropical fish swimming back and forth, was available as a downloadable theme pack and was a popular pick for many years.

Users on Reddit quickly lamented the loss in many posts, with dozens noting that the aquarium was part of their daily routine. Roku responded to one post, saying, “That makes sense, and we hear you. Aquatic Life has a lot of loyal fans, and we’re passing your feedback along to the team.” The post noted that when “the fish swim off,” Roku devices with Aquatic Life will switch to Roku City.

You can browse to Settings > Theme > Screensaver to find another theme.

Several online reports indicate that the removal is a licensing issue and that the creator of the screensaver posted on Reddit that he removed the license after Roku’s sale to Fox. That thread has now been deleted, so the comment is unavailable. Roku hasn’t issued any statement of its own about why, but I have reached out to ask. I’ve also reached out directly to the screensaver’s creator.

If you’re looking for the exact screensaver, it’s still available as a 2-minute clip on Roku’s YouTube channel. It takes a few extra steps, but if you want to keep the screensaver running on your TV, you can create a YouTube playlist with just that video, set it to loop, and use the YouTube app on Roku whenever you want to see it.

Even though the announcement of the screensaver’s departure happened less than 24 hours ago, the comments section of that video is packed with users begging Roku to keep Aquatic Life.

Also: I started clearing my Roku cache, and it fixed my biggest TV complaint

Alternatively, you could open one of the many YouTube videos that have aquarium displays and let one of them run for as long as you want.

There are also several dozen aquarium apps for Roku. I checked out several of them, and while they don’t look exactly like the Roku one, they do fill the void. Note that if you opt for one of these, most of them do have ads that play before the aquarium starts.

Lastly, you can download the original app for your phone or computer from SereneScreen.

https://www.zdnet.com/tech/bank-phishing.title: This clever banking scam keeps phishing by faking its own demise – how it works
https://www.zdnet.com/tech/bank-phishing.author: Charlie Osborne
https://www.zdnet.com/tech/bank-phishing.text:
You won't see the 'suspended' sign because it's not meant for you.

November 3, 2026, 9:15 am ET

KELA researchers have exposed an active financial-scam infrastructure that hosts hundreds of fraudulent websites capable of faking their own suspensions to stay online. As of Oct. 25, 2026, 248 financial scam and phishing domains tied to 189 major US banks and financial services have been linked to the same infrastructure.

According to the cybersecurity firm’s report, published on Tuesday, the “Suspended” infrastructure operation runs websites that have cloned the official domains of victim organizations, with a particular focus on business banking. Many domains use the [keyword]-[bank].com format, slotting in keywords such as “secure,” “disable,” “protect,” and “cancel.”

Also: Beware of Bluetooth sniffers: How your favorite gadgets could be exposing your data

A handful of servers spread across two shared hosting providers run the backend of Suspended infrastructure, which has also been tied to phishing campaigns targeting cryptocurrency exchanges and government services in the UK, the Netherlands, Australia, and New Zealand. As a result, the researchers believe that either a single operator is behind the setup or that the server infrastructure is part of a wider phishing-as-a-service platform.

This phishing campaign stands out because of how the cybercriminals behind the scam are protecting it: by issuing takedown notices.

When you visit a website and see a message that it has been taken down or suspended, it’s usually because the domain has been associated with malicious or illegal activity, including phishing and scams. Law enforcement agencies, often with help from technology firms, find these websites, obtain the necessary court orders, and seize the infrastructure or accounts behind them to force a suspension through a registrar or hosting provider.

You see the notice, you move on — and this also goes for scanners and security teams.

However, in this case, the scam artists created a mechanism to show it themselves, to avoid being flagged and taken down. But it’s when they show it that matters.

The false suspension notice appears deceptively simple at first glance. A phishing kit embedded in the domain registers the IP address of each visitor, and on their second visit, they are shown a fake “account suspended” page. The kit is disguised as a challenge page similar to those legitimately used by Cloudflare.

Researchers also detected other decoys, including “Sorry, you’ve been blocked” notices, blank pages, and redirections to Google. Some pages also have reCAPTCHAs, and the researchers detected scripts that block browser developer tools, likely to slow analysis.

Also: Don’t use Muse? Meta’s AI agent can still access your private messages – here’s how

But why show fake suspension notices in the first place? To scanners and cybersecurity teams, it looks like someone else has already dealt with the malicious domain, and they can move on to the next suspicious website.

“That design targets exactly the people who could shut a site down,” KELA says. “A victim typically follows a link once. A scanner, a security team or a takedown provider checks a reported site and then checks it again to confirm, and the second check shows what looks like a completed takedown.”

As shown in the image below, while scanners would detect a suspension notice, victims would still see the cloned website, complete with lures to entice them into entering their information, leading to financial fraud and potentially identity theft. After all, one visit is enough.

As of this writing, there are 248 live domains, plus those taken offline after the researchers disclosed their findings to law enforcement; over 300 scam domains have been hosted on the same infrastructure since May this year. Unfortunately, this phishing campaign remains active, with new domains appearing every day.

One lead could reveal the operator: a remote desktop connection to the malicious infrastructure through a standard UK home broadband connection, but it has not been verified.

Use a phishing link checker to verify whether a URL is trustworthy, and remember that any email or message claiming to be from your bank may be fraudulent.

Typical signs of a bank phishing email include:

When it comes to organizations, KELA has released a free Bank Phishing Check tool that compares official domains and organizations against the websites uncovered during the firm’s research.

https://www.zdnet.com/innovation/claude-.title: Is Claude Code truly faster with message threads? I did the math on my logs
https://www.zdnet.com/innovation/claude-.author: David Gewirtz
https://www.zdnet.com/innovation/claude-.text:
Innovation
>
Artificial Intelligence

Claude Code’s update could save you time during demanding, hours-long coding sessions at no extra cost. But by how much? Here's my real-world result.

Senior Contributing Editor

Senior Contributing Editor

November 3, 2026, 8:11 am ET

Anthropic yesterday introduced message threads as part of Claude’s Messages API. Don’t confuse message threads with traditional human-to-human discussion threads. With message threads, entire conversations no longer have to be resent with each API call, saving roughly 35% of time-to-first-token when Claude requests contain 500,000 to 1 million tokens.

This feature is on by default for most Claude Code users. API users can turn it on using the “thread” parameter for API requests.

Token consumption remains unchanged, so this capability doesn’t provide a cost savings. The 35% savings is Anthropic’s measurement.

Also: Claude Code’s revised projects adds AI orchestration, but local developers must wait

Timing data from roughly 980 turns in my own Claude Code logs before this feature became available shows that Claude usually began a response about 3 seconds after each mid-task request when running contexts of 500,000 tokens and up. During five busy evenings last month, my conversations made roughly 100 to 225 model calls in a four hour stretch.

Using Anthropic’s reported 35% median time-to-first token reduction in a quick projection, Claude estimated a 2- to 4-minute savings per four hour work session.

Agents often send a bunch of requests to the model during each conversation. Before message threads, each message sent the entire conversation with each request.

Imagine if you’re in a very long texting chat with a friend. Now imagine if every time you sent a text to that friend, you also had to send every other text and every other reply along with that original text. That’s how model messaging has always worked. Except now, with message threads, there’s a better way.

Also: 75% of developers I surveyed prefer Claude Code – here’s why they choose it over Codex

With message threads turned on, agents only have to send what’s changed since the last turn. This reduces the amount of data transmission and increases responsiveness, what Anthropic calls time-to-first-token.

The benefit is seen most strongly in sessions that have a context of 500,000 to a 1 million tokens. About half of my sessions hit that context ceiling multiple times a night.

Anthropic reports that Claude’s message threads reduce median time-to-first-token by 35% for large requests. While my estimated savings of several minutes per session isn’t huge, the benefit increases with very long-running coding agents, and agents that transmit documents and image-heavy workloads.

For computer-using agents, all those screenshots “stay with the thread instead of being re-uploaded on every turn,” according to the Anthropic blog post on the feature.

Also: How I made a paid Mac app in 11 days with Claude – without writing a single line of code

While the time savings may not seem huge, in larger enterprise deployments or deployments where you want the AI to respond faster, any reduction in latency is a big deal and will be seen in any application of Claude technology that has a lot of back-and-forth turns with large data payloads.

Even though the addition of threads to the Messages API can reduce latency, token usage and therefore cost won’t go down. That’s because the model itself will still process the full conversation during every turn. Rate limits also don’t change.

Message threads and prompt caching can work together to reduce workload. Prompt caching has been around for about two years now, and it does save money. That’s because prompt caching allows the model to avoid re-processing prompts over and over (for example, in looping analysis calls).

On the other hand, the message threads capability does offer an extra smidge of performance, at no extra cost. So, there’s that.

Context is the size of the full session that Claude is currently working with. The rough human equivalent is current working or short-term memory. Most Claude Code sessions max out at a million token context, where a locally-hosted AI on my 128GB Mac Studio handles a context no bigger than 64K, or about 6% of the Claude Code context size.

Also: After the vibe-coding rush comes the debugging hangover

Compaction is a process where the AI attempts to reduce and eliminate extra information to fit the current session’s turns into the available context. An oversimplified analog is when you save a JPEG with quality turned way down in order to save space. You lose a lot of the visual fidelity, but you still get the main idea.

The larger the context you have, the longer you can go before the session has to initiate compaction. But there’s a gotcha. The larger the context you have, the more chance there is the model will lose track of what it’s working on or make reasoning errors.

Individual one-off requests also won’t see an improvement from message threads. Also, any conversation that delays longer than 5 minutes between turns will send the full message contents and not just the new stuff.

This feature doesn’t eliminate context management or compaction. But if your context is quite large, it will make responses a bit snappier.

Overall, message threads are a good thing, a solid if small innovation that increases responsiveness. While the feature doesn’t reduce costs, there’s also no additional cost for the additional performance, which is itself a win.

https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/claude.title: Claude Code's “Don't Ask Again” File Exposes Passwords and Keys in 1,122 Public Copies on GitHub
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/claude.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/claude.text:
Passwords and API keys that developers typed into commands they approved in Claude Code are sitting in public GitHub repositories, where anyone can read them.

When a user selects "Yes, and don't ask again," Anthropic's AI coding assistant can save the command, word-for-word, including the secret, in a project settings file.

Software security company Apiiro said yesterday that 1,122 public copies of that file hold at least one secret, though it did not test whether any still work. One company the researchers notified earlier this week confirmed its key had been live.

The file is .claude/settings.local.json. Removing it from a project does not undo the leak, because older versions stay in git history and in forks of the repository. The researchers' advice is to rotate first: change every password, token, and key the file has ever held, then clean up.

By default, Claude Code asks before it runs most shell commands. If the user picks "Yes, and don't ask again," it saves an allow rule in .claude/settings.local.json inside the project, according to its permissions documentation. Matching commands then run without asking in later sessions.

The rule covers only what the prompt offered. Sometimes that is a pattern, such as npm test *, and sometimes one exact command. When it is the exact command, any password or token typed into it is saved too, in plain text.

In public files, the researchers found saved commands with the secret still inside, and they reproduced the behavior with the latest models, Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1.

Claude Code tries to keep the file out of git. The first time it writes the file in a git repository, it adds the file to the user's global git excludes, its settings documentation says. Git on that computer then ignores the file in every repository.

That protection stays in one user's git settings on one computer. It does nothing for a file that was already committed, the researchers say. Claude Code never adds the file to the project's own .gitignore, so the protection does not travel with the project.

In 539 of the 1,105 repositories the researchers traced, a commit listing Claude as a co-author changed the file. They take this to mean Claude often commits the file itself.

Apiiro's search of public GitHub found 104,185 copies of the file in 103,617 repositories, its research write-up shows. About 1.1% of them, or 1,122 copies, hold at least one secret. Together they hold 1,379 different secrets.

A value counted as a secret when it matched a known key format, or when a password or token sat beside the address of a public server. An AI reviewer also had to agree. The researchers do not say whether anyone has used these secrets.

More than a third of the secrets open a database directly, including 379 database passwords. Others include 43 SSH logins for public servers, 42 tokens for GitHub, GitLab and npm, and 23 AWS keys.

Among the owners of these files are 63 organizations, mostly software companies of all sizes. The strongest cases include a database vendor's own admin-level cloud key and the owner password of a medical-records database, the researchers say.

As of Monday, every file with a secret was still on its repository's default branch, and in half of those repositories it had been there for at least 217 days.

Older versions of the file contain 734 more secrets across 509 repositories that are not present in any current copy, usually because the file was deleted. Forks spread the files further: 211 forks of 74 repositories carry the same secrets as the originals.

Secrets also sit in 298 of 76,011 copies of the shared .claude/settings.json file, which teams commit on purpose, mostly inside allow rules. Including those, the older versions, and saved agent chat logs, the total is 2,539 secrets across 1,994 repositories.

Of 16 coding agents whose documentation the researchers compared, Claude Code is the only one confirmed to save the full approved command in a project file by default.

For developers, the researchers recommend these steps:

Copies that never reach GitHub still matter, the researchers say. The file is plain JSON in the project folder, and it can also be left inside an npm package, a Docker image, a zip archive, or a synced folder.

Malware has previously looked for secrets on developer machines. In September 2025, the Shai-Hulud worm ran the TruffleHog secret scanner over infected computers, and the scanner flagged more than half of the files as secret.

Common secret scanners miss many of these files. The researchers ran gitleaks and TruffleHog over every copy, without the tools' verification step. Of the 1,122 files with a secret, gitleaks flagged 564 and TruffleHog 643, and neither flagged 215.

Most misses are passwords typed inside commands. Scanners look for known key formats, and a password after PGPASSWORD=, sshpass -p , or mysql -p looks like an ordinary word in an ordinary command line.

For security teams, the researchers recommend:

Claude Code users have reported this behavior before. An earlier bug report, filed on August 11, 2025, said approved commands with API keys and tokens were being stored word for word in settings.local.json.

An automated bot closed that report as "not planned" on January 3, after 60 days without activity.

As of today, the four related reports the researchers cite have all been closed by the same bot, the most recent yesterday. None got a reply from Anthropic, they say.
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/claude.summary: Claude Code tries to keep the file out of git, but it does not travel with the project. A reply from Anthropic is a reply from the group.

https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/instal.title: Installing the Fix for an Exploited WordPress Flaw Can Expose Some Sites One Last Time
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/instal.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/instal.text:
Some WordPress sites can still be attacked while they install the fix for an actively exploited flaw, according to Umut Bayram, the Picus Security researcher who found it.

The update that installs the fix still unpacks its files using the site's old, unpatched code, so an attacker who strikes at the right moment can run code on the server. The researcher advises blocking web access to the site's wp-content/upgrade folder before updating.

The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-119977, affects WordPress 4.7 through 7.1.3. During a core update that uses a complete package, WordPress unpacks a copy of the new version into a temporary folder inside wp-content/upgrade. That copy includes the WordPress installer, and the web server can usually reach it.

An attacker with no account who can determine the folder's name and access the installer before WordPress deletes the copy can end up running code on the server. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added the flaw to its catalog of known exploited vulnerabilities earlier this week.

WordPress released the fix last week in version 7.1.4 and in matching updates for older branches back to 4.7, all listed in its security advisory.

The fix gives the temporary folder a random name. But the update that installs the fix unpacks its files using the old code already on the site, as WordPress's updater code shows. On sites running 5.9 or later, that old code names the folder after the downloaded file, so the name can be predicted one last time.

Before the fix, an attacker could use the installer to write a new configuration file, wp-config.php, into the temporary copy. The update would then overwrite the site's real file with that file. The part of the fix that stops this already works during the update that installs it, because WordPress copies the files into place using the new code.

An attacker who catches the window during that update can still set up the temporary copy of WordPress with their own database, log in to it, and run PHP code with the web server's permissions before the copy is deleted, Bayram says in his technical write-up. From there, the attacker can read or write files in the live WordPress site.

Not every update exposes the installer, the researcher says. Complete packages always include the installer files. A smaller partial package, built for one specific starting version, exposes a site only if it happens to contain them.

On sites that allow automatic background updates, WordPress installs the fix automatically, via the same updater and the same steps.

The Hacker News checked WordPress.org's update service today for several versions. For updates within a branch, such as from 7.1.3 to 7.1.4, it offered a partial package, including for automatic updates. For a move from an older branch, such as from 7.0.7 to 7.1.4, it offered only complete packages.

On 4.4 through 5.8, the old code adds random characters to the folder's name. That hides the name unless the site leaks it some other way, such as in an error message, the researcher says.

Once 7.1.4 or a branch fix is installed, later updates use a random folder name, and a wp-config.php file in the temporary copy is never copied over the real one.

The researcher's first recommendation is to stop the web server from serving wp-content/upgrade at all. WordPress works with that folder directly on disk, so blocking web access does not break updates, he says.

The other safe route, he says, is a manual update done outside the web root, the folder the web server serves. Back up the site files and database, unpack the new release in a folder the web server does not serve, copy the core files into place without touching wp-config.php or wp-content, and then run the WordPress database update. This way, no temporary installer is ever created in a folder the web can reach.

WP-CLI's wp core update command is no substitute, because it runs the same updater and unpacks the package into the same folder.

WordPress 4.6 and earlier no longer receive security updates, so there is no fix for them. The researcher says the flaw goes back to WordPress 2.7, released in 2008, and that those sites should move to a supported version.

CISA's catalog addition earlier this week was based on evidence of active exploitation, but the agency did not describe the attacks.

Wordfence, the WordPress security company that assigned the CVE identifier, saw attack attempts begin nine minutes after it deployed a firewall rule for the flaw on the day of the release. Two of the busiest sources kept checking small groups of sites for about 14.5 hours, which the company says, in its attack analysis, aligns with attempts to catch the moment a site updates.

Its score for the flaw in the CVE record is 8.1 out of 10 on the CVSS scale. In its lab tests, the window lasted only seconds. WordPress's own advisory rates the flaw low.

Code that its authors describe as an exploit for the flaw has appeared in public GitHub repositories since earlier this week. One of them says its code also works on sites that still use a predictable folder during complete-package updates. Whether the code works has not been established.

For sites that stayed on an affected version after the release, Wordfence suggests looking for:

Bayram told The Hacker News on November 6 that whether a partial update is exposed depends on what that specific package contains. A partial package holds only the files that changed between two releases. If those do not include the installer files, the temporary copy cannot run as a WordPress installation, and the installer never becomes reachable.

A site also does not always get a partial package when one exists. WordPress falls back to a complete package if the site's core files do not match the official checksums or if the update is a reinstall.

The deciding factor, the researcher said, "isn’t partial versus complete. It’s whether the updater already installed on the site has been fixed."
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/instal.summary: fix is available for several versions of WordPress.org's update service. The fix was released in version 7.1.4 and in matching updates for older branches back to 4.7.7. The flaw affects WordPress 4. 7.7 through 7.3

https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/hacker.title: Hackers Target OpenSSH SSHole Flaw Within Hours of Disclosure, Gain Root on Honeypot
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/hacker.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/hacker.text:
Threat actors are attempting to exploit a recently disclosed security flaw impacting OpenSSH that can enable sign-ins to accounts that have no password set, according to Previdian.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-123158 (CVSS score: 8.1) and codenamed SSHole (or *sshole), impacts Linux systems that run OpenSSH on the musl C library with Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM) disabled, including Alpine Linux's default OpenSSH server configuration.

An unauthenticated attacker can supply an oversized password to access accounts that are deliberately configured without usable passwords, without having to steal credentials or SSH keys. The issue, discovered by security researcher Ozgun Kultekin, has been addressed in OpenSSH 10.6p2.

The underlying issue dates back to a patch introduced in 2016 to fix a username enumeration vulnerability tracked as CVE-2016-6210. Under specific conditions, the password-handling behavior in OpenSSH mistakenly interprets a failed password-hashing operation as successful authentication by producing the same value ("*") used to indicate that an account with password disabled at the system level.

An attacker can trigger the vulnerability to authenticate to certain password-disabled accounts using an arbitrary password between 257 and 1,024 bytes long, causing the hash attempt to fail and returning an asterisk. The sshd daemon then compares with the asterisk stored in the account's password field, leading to a successful login.

To be clear, successful exploitation requires at least one account with an asterisk (*) as its password hash. It does not allow attackers to bypass passwords on accounts with valid password hashes.

"A successful SSHole attack grants access with the compromised account's existing permissions," Safe Security said. "For enterprise, the consequences of SSHole depend on the privileges of the compromised account."

"While unauthorized SSH access is the immediate impact, attackers may also gain access to deployment credentials, application secrets, and connected infrastructure, potentially enabling lateral movement or service disruption."

It's worth noting that the vulnerability does not affect Dropbear, glibc-based Linux distributions, non-Linux systems, and systems that check passwords through PAM.

Threat intelligence firm Previdian said it observed the first exploitation attempt less than nine hours after the CVE publication, adding it has confirmed successful root access on a honeypot running Alpine Linux and OpenSSH. Telemetry data shows a total of eight exploitation attempts from an IP address geolocated to Japan.

"The observed source IP, 89.116.89[.]18, used oversized passwords to bypass authentication and ran reconnaissance commands including id, uname and hostname through non-interactive SSH sessions," Ryan Dewhurst, founder and CEO of Previdian, said in a statement shared with The Hacker News.

Affected users are advised to install OpenSSH 10.6p2 or their distribution's patched package, and then restart sshd. Alpine is also recommending that users investigate "Accepted password for" log entries involving accounts that should not accept password logins.

"Look in /var/log/messages for sshd lines reading Accepted password for an account that has no password (alpine, root, or any key-only user)," Alpine said. "Review doas use and recently created users, files and authorized keys on exposed machines. If you cannot rule out a login, treat the machine as compromised."
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/hacker.summary: The vulnerability was discovered by security researcher Ozgun Kultekin. It affects OpenSSH on the musl C library with Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM) disabled. An unauthenticated attacker can supply an oversized password to access accounts that are deliberately configured without usable passwords.

https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/openai.title: OpenAI Launches GPT-6 Cyber After AI Helps Find 81 Firefox Flaws, 948 Linux Exploits
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/openai.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/openai.text:
OpenAI on Thursday unveiled GPT‑6 Cyber, which it described as a major step forward in security research that brings together stronger cybersecurity capabilities with a step-change improvement in model alignment.

The new model is "more capable at finding and fixing vulnerabilities, and far more reliable staying within the boundaries researchers set," OpenAI said. It has classified the model as Critical in cybersecurity under its Preparedness Framework.

The artificial intelligence (AI) company said GPT‑6 Cyber is also better than its predecessors like GPT‑5.6 Cyber and GPT‑6 Astra when it comes to following task boundaries and avoiding exploiting out-of-scope services in 99.93% of cases, up from 94.49% for GPT-5.6 Cyber.

It also scores 48.5% on ExploitGym, a cybersecurity benchmark that evaluates the capabilities of AI agents to autonomously turn known software vulnerabilities into functioning, real-world exploits. In comparison, GPT-5.6 Cyber scored 32.1%.

OpenAI said the model enabled the discovery of 948 local privilege escalation exploits in Linux⁠ through an autonomous pipeline, along with 81 previously unknown high-severity vulnerabilities in Mozilla Firefox and a critical vulnerability in Brotli⁠ (CVE-2026-111497, CVSS score: 9.2).

GPT-6 Cyber is initially available through the API and Codex to select Daybreak Red customers as part of efforts to make the best cybersecurity-focused models available with an aim to help secure software before bad actors have a chance to detect and exploit vulnerabilities using AI-assisted approaches. The risk is compounded by the growing abuse of open-weight models with abliterated guardrails.

"When tested without deployment safety prompts, it avoided exploiting out-of-scope services in 99.93% of cases, up from 94.49% for GPT‑5.6 Cyber," OpenAI said. "With those prompts, GPT‑6 Cyber stayed within bounds 100% of the time."

OpenAI said it has implemented additional guardrails to flag misuse and ensure the model's actions fall within the scope of the user's intent and authorization. As of last month, the company announced plans to use content from Daybreak Blue sessions on personal accounts starting November 29, 2026, to "improve our models, including to help strengthen safeguards against cyber misuse" even when the "improve the model for everyone" setting is off.

"To prevent misuse of the Daybreak Red and Blue platforms, we have refined safeguards against assistance and capability development that could compromise industrial controls or safety-critical systems, interfere with equipment, or cause serious injury, catastrophic physical damage, or life-endangering service disruption," it noted.

GPT-6 Cyber's promise to stay within "rules of engagement" comes as OpenAI disclosed three misalignment incidents involving GPT-6 Astra and an internal research model. These incidents took place between July and October 2026 -

"In reviewed cases, Astra narrowed or stopped requested safety work without disclosing the restriction," OpenAI said. "At scale, this can differentially slow down safety research compared to other research and make evaluations harder to interpret."

"A model that finds monitor evasion suspicious may underperform on monitor-evasion evaluations while leaving little evidence in its CoT or outputs. The behavior becomes even harder to detect if models externalize less of this reasoning in CoT [chain-of-thought]."

The development also comes as California-based non-profit, Model Evaluation and Threat Research (METR), said Anthropic is developing its AI systems around twice as quickly as it was a year ago despite calls to slow down the technology's pace of improvement.

"As of October 2026, Anthropic is likely improving the capabilities of their models on well-specified tasks at around twice the rate they did between March 2024 and October 2025," METR said.

Google, for its part, has introduced new capabilities to CodeMender, its autonomous code-security agent, to facilitate secure isolation and flexible scanning, while adding human-in-the-loop checks for local write and command execution to mitigate the risks of malicious exploits.

https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/micros.title: Microsoft Paint RCE Fix Now Available, but Windows Update Won't Deliver It
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/micros.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/micros.text:
A fix for CVE-2026-83844, a remote code execution flaw in Windows Paint, is now in the Microsoft Store. Paint gets this fix only through a Store update, not through Windows updates.

The fixed build, 11.2609.401.0, was the newest Paint build in all ten countries The Hacker News checked today.

The flaw is an out-of-bounds read that could let an attacker run code over a network. Microsoft rates it as Important, with a CVSS score of 8.1, and says that a successful attack requires a deep understanding of the target system. The flaw was not known to be exploited or publicly disclosed when the company published it on October 13.

Brian Vitko of RFF, a device-management software maker, checked which Paint builds the Store offered in six countries earlier this week. He found that the newest in each was 11.2605.81.0, a build without the fix.

His test virtual machine has since moved to the fixed build on its own, through Store auto-update. That is one machine, and how quickly other PCs will get the build is not yet clear.

Microsoft's security advisory names 11.2609.401.0 as the fixed build. The CVE record for the flaw, which the company also publishes, still lists Paint as affected only below 11.2605.91.0. Its NVD entry shows the same range.

So a scanner that reads the CVE record would treat any build from 11.2605.91.0 up as fixed. A copy at 11.2609.401.0 or later passes under both numbers.

As recently as last week, the advisory gave 11.2605.91.0 as the fixed build, according to a forum question on Microsoft Q&A. The advisory's revision history still shows only its October 13 entry, with no note about the change.

Paint, like other Store apps, is installed separately for each user account on a PC. Windows can also keep a provisioned copy that it installs for each new user. A check of only the signed-in account can miss older copies.

Vitko's test write-up gives two commands to run in a PowerShell window opened as administrator. The first lists every user's copy of Paint, and the second lists the provisioned copy.

Get-AppxPackage -AllUsers -Name Microsoft.Paint | Select-Object Version, @{ n = 'Users'; e = { $_.PackageUserInformation.UserSecurityId.Username -join ', ' } }

Get-AppxProvisionedPackage -Online | Where-Object DisplayName -eq 'Microsoft.Paint' | Select-Object Version

For any copy below 11.2609.401.0:

The advisory lists no workaround or mitigation. Before the fix reached the Store, Vitko suggested removing Paint where nobody needs it, for every user and from the provisioned copy. He did not test that step.

An attacker could exploit the flaw by sending "a specially crafted packet to an affected service over the network," the advisory says, but it does not name the service. The attack would require no sign-in and no user assistance.

The flaw was not in the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog run by the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency when The Hacker News checked today. The catalog was last updated earlier this week.
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/micros.summary: Microsoft's security advisory names 11.2609.401.0 as the fixed build. The fix is an out-of-bounds read that could let an attacker run code over a network. The flaw was not known to be exploited or publicly disclosed when the company published it on October 13.

https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/malici.title: Malicious Browser Extensions Could Use Claude Dispatch to Run Code on Users' Computers
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/malici.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/malici.text:
A browser extension that can run scripts on claude.ai could make Claude Desktop run code on a person's computer, researchers at Forever Security, an endpoint security company, showed in a test.

The attack needs Dispatch, a Claude feature that lets people send tasks from their phone to Claude Desktop. The flaw that makes this possible can still be exploited, the researchers said earlier this week.

Claude Desktop is an AI agent that can run commands on the computer where it is installed. The researchers found that Dispatch also accepted an ordinary signed-in session on claude.ai, the Claude website, even though the site showed no link to it. That let an extension running on the site send Claude Desktop instructions as if the user had sent them.

The researchers say Anthropic, the company that makes Claude, told them on October 13 that Dispatch would be retired, with the end of October as the target. The Dispatch help page, last updated late last week, does not mention a retirement.

It says Dispatch is closed to new users and that people who already use it on some Pro, Max, and Ultra plans "can keep using it for now."

The attack needs two things, according to a technical write-up by Forever Security researcher Gal Weizman: an extension that can run scripts on claude.ai, and a person signed in to both claude.ai and Claude Desktop with Dispatch turned on.

The extension could be malicious, a legitimate one that received a compromised update, or a legitimate one with a security flaw. Dispatch itself only works while the computer is awake and the desktop app is open.

In the test, a script on the user's claude.ai page opened Dispatch and sent Claude four prompts as if it were the user. The prompts asked Claude to install an npm package.

Claude first hesitated over the unfamiliar package, but a follow-up message, delivered in the user's voice, got it to go ahead.

Claude asks before it acts, but those approval prompts appeared in the web page the extension controlled. The script clicked any "Allow" button every second, so no one had to be watching.

Claude then ran a global npm install, and the package's install script opened the Calculator app. No browser exploit was needed. The same step could have stolen files or installed a backdoor, given Claude's permissions on the computer, the researchers say.

The test was run with the browser and Claude Desktop on the same computer, and the researchers report no real attacks. Because Dispatch connects devices, the extension could also reach Claude Desktop on a different computer signed in to the same Claude account, they say. That case is described but not shown.

The same reach could link a home computer to a work laptop when someone uses a single personal Claude account on both devices, with Dispatch turned on. The researchers have seen personal Claude accounts with cross-device Dispatch turned on, on work computers at their customers.

The researchers reported the flaw to Anthropic on May 14. The company accepted it as valid on May 19 but closed the report as a duplicate of an issue it had already found internally, according to the researchers.

"Anthropic is retiring Dispatch, but not the design behind it," the researchers wrote, adding that two other Claude features, Claude Code Remote Control and Claude Cowork sessions, let extensions carry out the same attack. Their write-up does not include a test of those features, and they plan a follow-up post.

In Claude Desktop, Dispatch is part of Cowork and appears in the left-side panel. The Dispatch help page says users should know how to quickly disconnect or revoke access before turning the feature on, but it does not explain how.

https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/the-fl.title: The Flood is Coming And The Pipes Were Already Full
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/the-fl.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/the-fl.text:
An update on Athena, and some unsolicited predictions on what's coming next

On Saturday, Dario Amodei published We Must Pace the Frontier. I agree with him. Go read it if you haven't. I've spent the summer looking at what these models find, and the gap he describes between what they can do and what the rest of us are ready for is the one I've been staring at since May.

The hardest piece of his plan is the one that asks governments to coordinate. They're in a difficult spot: regulate too little and a US company accidentally builds the weapon, regulate too much and it gets built somewhere else, and open source isn't governable either way. Where governments can act is on consumption: not what the models can do, but what happens to what they find. Who gets a vulnerability first, how fast a fix reaches the people running the code, whether the operators who can't move on an attacker's timeline get a head start. That's what Gold Eagle is.

It matters because of where the risk actually lands. The danger in Dario's essay isn't a model in a lab. It's a model pointed at the power grid, the water system, the hospital network, all of it running on decades of software with the same exploitable design. The frontier is where the capability comes from. Consumption is where it does damage, and that's the end you can still defend.

So pacing has two ends. The frontier end is Dario's and the government's problem, and it's hard. The consumption end is ours: the disclosure processes, the patch pipelines, and the software itself, everything that has to absorb what the models produce. Pacing buys time on the frontier end. This post is a status report on how we're spending it, in three parts:

The short version: I'm more worried than I was in May, and more sure about what to do about it.

Athena has been taking in findings since June. The intake numbers are public: more than 40,000 findings, 42% of them critical or high, across more than 500 projects, with more than 2,000 patches produced. What hasn't been public is how much of that we've been sitting on. Generating fixes was never the bottleneck. Disclosing them responsibly, at a scale nobody has ever tried, is.

On September 28, we start. We're beginning with about fifty, and none of them are the scary ones. That's deliberate. The frightening findings, the live pre-auth RCEs, go through Akrites on embargo, which I'll come back to. The first 50 are low-stakes on purpose: a small batch to get the flywheel turning and find out what breaks before the thousands behind them hit it.

All 50 are silent fixes: vulnerabilities already fixed at head, sometimes years ago, where nobody ever filed a CVE. Your scanner has nothing to say about them, and the old versions are still running everywhere. This pattern showed up in Athena almost immediately. A big share of what the models find only affects old versions, because the models scan what's actually deployed, and what's deployed is old.

Two systems fail at once with silent fixes, and neither is anyone's fault. Upstreams typically won't merge fixes to old versions, and they're right not to: the code was rewritten years ago, there's no branch to merge into, and "upgrade" is the correct answer. And the advisory layer has nothing to work with, because CVEs don't get filed for things already fixed at head. It's the one class of finding where acting doesn't step on anyone else's process, because there isn't one.

For each one, where the project has no path for accepting fixes to old versions, we're doing three things.

We publish the patch. Plain .patch files, in a public Chainguard repo that says exactly what it is on the tin, under the project's original license. This is deliberately not a maintainer-of-last-resort move. We have plans for that, and I'll get to them below, but they're for projects nobody maintains anymore. These are active projects that already fixed the bug at head. We're not forking anything, not claiming stewardship, not creating a new namespace, and not inviting anyone to build from it. It's a place to put patches for the people who can't upgrade yet, and nothing more. The durable fix is still upgrading, but this step reflects today's reality, where most of what's deployed isn't upgraded.

We publish the advisory. A Chainguard OSV feed, with fully enumerated affected version ranges and the exact symbols affected. Not "some 2.x releases, probably." Athena partner scanners are integrating with it now, so these show up where your team already looks.

We ship the fix. Patched versions land in Chainguard Libraries for every Chainguard customer the moment the advisory goes live.

We're not planning to contact maintainers ahead of each of these. They already deal with more noise than anyone should, and we don't want to add to it, least of all for bugs they fixed years ago. If you maintain a project and you'd rather hear from us in advance going forward, or you have any other concerns about how this touches your project, let us know at cna@chainguard.dev and we'll happily work with you.

A silent fix used to be mostly harmless. Nobody had written the bug down, and finding it from a fix commit took real expertise and real time. That's over. A model can go from a public fix commit to a working exploit against every version that never got the fix in an afternoon. The finding exists whether we publish it or not. The only question is whether defenders get a copy, too.

Once people know about a bug, the world needs a signal to upgrade, and the signal the world already has is the CVE. Scanners, KEV, and every compliance regime key on it. Silent fixes had none. So, in support of the Gold Eagle initiative, and in partnership with CISA, Chainguard is in progress to become a CVE Numbering Authority, scoped to open source vulnerabilities processed through Athena where upstream already fixed the flaw without an identifier, or where no maintainer is left to assign one, and no more specific CNA covers the project.

The uncomfortable part: this will put new noise in your scanners. Old versions that scanned clean last week will light up. That's better than no noise and a breach. Silence in that channel was never safety, it was just nobody having looked yet.

We also go to great lengths to keep each advisory as narrow as it can be. Every entry is enriched with the exact introduced and fixed ranges across every release branch, not a single version floor, and carries module, class, and function level detail on what's actually affected. That's what reachability scanners need to filter out the false positives for your codebase, so the noise you do see should be the noise that matters.

The narrowness is the point. We assign only where there is no upstream to defer to. If a vulnerability exists at the latest version and the maintainer is reachable, the project's own CNA assigns it, and we are the reporter, never the assigner. Every assignment clears the same gates: a reproduced finding, never raw model output; a defensible commit range; affected versions in real use; the maintainer notified with a response window; and withdrawal if the maintainer shows us we're wrong. Projects that become their own CNA leave our scope. This is a transitional role, not a territorial one.

The map for everything else is simple. If a vulnerability exists at the latest version and the maintainer is reachable, that's Plan A, and it runs through Akrites, the shared disclosure body the Linux Foundation launched in June, and that we helped found. If it exists at latest and the project is unmaintained, that's maintainer-of-last-resort territory, and we're working with other Akrites members to stand that up inside Akrites, where it belongs. And Gold Eagle, the federal clearinghouse that came out of June's executive order, is the layer that gets prioritized findings in front of the critical infrastructure operators who can't move on an attacker's timeline.

We spent a good part of the summer waiting on both of those and helping build them. Akrites goes operational this month. I'll be straight about the tradeoff: one shared incident response team across dozens of organizations is slower at first than everyone acting alone. That's the cost of choosing "maintainers deal with one trusted counterpart" over "maintainers deal with thirty strangers," and we'd make it again. The disclosure and upstreaming numbers get published either way, pretty or not.

The second reason I'm worried is less about process and more about what I've seen. We joined Anthropic's Project Glasswing. Lots of organizations have, at this point, roughly 200 across 15-plus countries, so our joining isn't news on its own. What matters is what it means for Athena: we now have Mythos, and we're running it against the software we build and ship.

Here's the shape of one run, and I've picked it because it's the least reassuring result we have.

One widely used open source project. One run, about six hours. The harness came back with more than a dozen validated vulnerabilities, most of them pre-authentication remote code execution, reachable with no credentials and no operator action. Every one was reproduced three times in a clean VM before it counted, under the rule I'll describe in a minute: the model doesn't get to claim a finding, the host has to reproduce it. This is not an abandoned package. It's one of the most heavily scanned, tested, and fuzzed projects in the ecosystem, code that has survived years of expert review and relentless fuzzing. A model found all of it in an afternoon. These go through Akrites like everyone else's findings, and I'm not going to say more about the specific project here than that.

Here's what I'll say instead. Watching what these models find, and how long it takes a fix to reach anyone once they find it, is what worries me. It isn't the models themselves. It's the race between two clocks. On one, the industry is trying to absorb a short-term rush of findings through disclosure processes that were already behind. On the other, attacker capability is advancing toward the point where compromising critical infrastructure at scale becomes cheap. Right now, the second clock is running faster than the first, and I don't see anything that closes that gap on its own.

Which is the other reason the sandbox matters. Producing a finding like the one above means building and detonating a working exploit against real code, over and over, driven by an agent nobody is watching in real time. That is dangerous to run, and this summer has been a run of examples of people running it unsafely. The incident Dario built his essay around, OpenAI's agents breaking out of a cyber evaluation and ending up inside Hugging Face's production infrastructure, started with a zero-day in the package cache the agents had been given. Package infrastructure is what we build, so that one landed close to home. Pillar Security spent a week in July publishing sandbox escapes across Cursor, Codex, Gemini CLI, and Antigravity, and the finding that tied them together was that the agent almost never broke the sandbox head-on. It wrote a file it was allowed to write, and something trusted outside the box ran it later. None of these was a problem of insufficient sandboxes. They were a problem of insufficient sandboxing: the boundary existed, and everything interesting happened in the gaps around it. Denylists don't contain any better than containers do.

Everything Athena does, from developing an exploit to proving a patch closes the hole, runs inside a microVM, the same primitive our package builds, image builds, and CI have run on for years. Matt wrote up the architecture in July. The short version: every job gets a hardware-virtualized guest with its own kernel and a root filesystem built from scratch, egress is enforced at the hypervisor and allowlisted to package registries and nothing else, the first forbidden connection destroys the VM, and no credentials ever enter the guest. And because a shared primitive multiplies the blast radius of any weakness, we point AI agents at the sandbox itself with instructions to break it. Every finding lands as a failing test first, then the fix.

The harness that runs inside those sandboxes is the part I find most interesting, and it starts with a person. Ian Beer spent about six months writing a zero-click iOS exploit chain, and if you read the write-up as a search, you can see the shape of it: poke at a target, go deep, hit a dead end, back up, eventually connect enough dots to reach a working exploit. No human holds six months of that in working memory. He kept it in notes and pulled back the slice he needed each session. His notebook was the environment.

That's what we built, sharded across many agents in parallel: a tree search where every agent starts fresh with a scoped surface and a distilled trail of what's already known, and continuity lives in durable findings rather than anyone's context window. The rule I care most about is that the host casts the vote, never the model. A finding only counts if the host can replay it against a clean instance: the check fails before, the replay runs, the check passes after. Nothing enters the record until reality agrees, and that one rule is most of why the false positive rate is as low as it is.

A few things we learned building this, if you're working on something similar:

Put the pieces together, and the loop closes. Find, contain, fix, ship. All of it on one primitive.

None of this was possible on off-the-shelf infrastructure. Over the last year, we rebuilt our factory on three new primitives, and every one of them started as something we needed for ourselves before it was anything we could sell.

The sandbox is the microVM you just read about: the isolation boundary that lets us run untrusted code and hostile agents without the blast radius reaching anything that matters. The harness is the search that runs inside it, the thing that found those pre-auth RCEs. And the third is CI as a function: our own fleet stopped sending code out to a CI system a year ago. The checks run in the loop, and changes arrive already proven, at more than ten times the CVE volume we were handling before.

We built all three because we had to; we've been running our entire operation on them, and over the coming quarters, we're going to start opening them up directly. If you are running untrusted AI workloads, or trying to find real vulnerabilities in your own code, or drowning in CI that tells you less than you'd like, these are the tools we reached for. Soon you'll be able to reach for them too.

Here's the unsolicited prediction. Everyone is worried about Mythos zero-days right now, and almost nobody was keeping up with ordinary CVEs before any of this started. The median enterprise is months behind on patches that have had fixes, advisories, and scanner coverage for years. That's the system we're about to pour thousands of new findings into. Faster disclosure and faster patching only help the people who can move on them, and most of the world can't move at the speed a model sets. If you take one thing from this post, take this: the flood is coming, and the pipes were already full.

Which is why none of the above is the finish line. Everything in this post makes us faster, and all of it accepts a losing premise: that the goal is to keep pace with a discovery rate set by frontier models. The vulnerability classes those models exploit aren't defects in today's software. They're its design. Memory corruption, deserialization, injection, confused deputies: consequences of how the stacks under every enterprise application were built. You cannot patch your way out of an architecture.

So the endgame is new foundations: a stack built secure by construction, where the dominant vulnerability classes can't be written in the first place, filling the role Spring Boot fills today, across every enterprise language, underneath the frameworks and the registries they pull from. For forty years, migration costs protected every incumbent platform. Nobody rewrote the COBOL because nobody could afford to. Agents just collapsed that cost.

We're working on this, and I'll say more when there's more to say. Why us: we see the world's pre-disclosure findings before almost anyone, so we know which bug classes matter, and we have the one tool that can prove a foundation removed them. Point Mythos at it before you ship, and you know.

Dario is right that pacing buys time, and everything above is how we're spending it. But a paced frontier only matters if the software underneath survives the frontier we already have. If the dominant vulnerability classes can't be written, the critical infrastructure built on them can't be broken by them, and a frontier model in the wrong hands has far less to reach. Pacing limits the risk by slowing the capability. Foundations limit it by taking away the target, and that's the only version of this I can see that ends the treadmill instead of running faster on it.

The Programmer's Credo says we do these things not because they are easy, but because we thought they would be easy when we started. This is the first one where I didn't even think that. We're doing it anyway.

If you maintain a project any of this touches, or if you're finding vulnerabilities, join at chainguard.dev/athena. And if any of this sounds like something you want to build, we're hiring.
