"While environmental factors could have played a role, our findings most directly implicate the chytrid fungus, revealing that regional invasion of the pathogen coincided with these unexplained amphibian disappearances," Boyette said.

To investigate what happened, the researchers turned to an unexpected source of evidence: frogs preserved in museum collections decades earlier.

The Smithsonian's National Museum of Natural History houses specimens collected by William Ronald Heyer, a former curator of amphibians and reptiles. Heyer conducted five collecting expeditions at Boracéia, including two during the 1970s before the major population declines and three during the 1980s after the die-offs had occurred.

These preserved animals offered scientists a rare opportunity to examine the period before and after the mysterious disappearances. By testing specimens collected at different times, researchers could investigate when the pathogen arrived and how rapidly it spread.

The team analyzed samples from more than 370 preserved amphibians representing 17 species, searching for evidence of chytrid infection and tracking how frequently the fungus appeared over time.

Museum Specimens Reveal a Deadly Fungal Outbreak

The results revealed a striking change. None of the specimens collected before 1979 showed evidence of chytrid infection. Among those collected during the 1980s, however, more than half tested positive for the fungus.

This sharp increase suggests that the pathogen arrived and spread through the local amphibian community around the same time that frog populations were collapsing.

But the researchers also uncovered a surprising pattern.

Species that suffered the most severe declines showed no detectable signs of infection in the preserved specimens. Meanwhile, species whose populations remained relatively stable frequently carried the fungus.

At first glance, these findings might seem to contradict the idea that chytrid caused the disappearances. The researchers believe the explanation may lie in differences in how individual species respond to the disease.

Some frogs may have been naturally capable of tolerating the infection, allowing them to survive even when the fungus was present. More vulnerable species, on the other hand, may have died so quickly after becoming infected that few or no infected individuals were ever collected.

"It's important to keep in mind that not all species suffered catastrophic losses at Boracéia," Boyette said. "The species that didn't decline may have naturally tolerated the fungus, allowing them to become infected without suffering mass mortality. By contrast, the species that declined most dramatically may have been so susceptible that infected frogs died before Heyer could collect them."

Together, the results suggest that chytrid spread rapidly among frogs with little previous exposure to the disease, with potentially devastating consequences for species unable to withstand infection.

Decades-Old Collections Help Solve a Wildlife Cold Case

For Michael Campana, a genomicist at NZCBI who contributed to the research, the findings demonstrate the extraordinary scientific value of natural history museums.

Specimens preserved many decades ago can contain biological evidence that researchers at the time had no way of recognizing. Modern testing methods now make it possible to revisit these collections and investigate outbreaks that occurred long before the responsible pathogens were discovered.

"Museum collectors could not have anticipated how important their collections would be to our modern conservation challenges, but without them, we would never be able to detect pathogens that went unnoticed for decades and reconstruct disease outbreaks that would otherwise remain a mystery," Campana said.

Understanding these past outbreaks could also help scientists anticipate future threats.

One growing concern involves another fungal pathogen, B. salamandrivorans, which is threatening salamander populations in Europe and could pose a serious danger to salamanders in North America.

By reconstructing how earlier fungal diseases emerged, spread, and affected different species, researchers hope to improve their ability to recognize and respond to similar threats before they cause widespread damage.

Brazil's Frogs Show Surprising Signs of Recovery

Despite the devastating losses recorded decades ago, the latest findings also offer encouraging evidence of recovery.

Working with researchers from the University of São Paulo, the team made six visits to Boracéia between 2022 and 2024 to investigate the amphibians living there today.

Of the 17 species represented in Heyer's historical museum collection, researchers located 12 during their modern surveys. The remaining five were not found, leaving their current status uncertain and raising concerns that some may have disappeared from the site entirely.

Nevertheless, the surveys indicate that most amphibian species at Boracéia have recovered since the severe declines of the early 1980s.

The fungus has not disappeared. Chytrid infections are still present among local frogs, but the pattern of infection suggests that species once heavily affected by the disease may have developed greater tolerance over successive generations.

That increased tolerance could help explain why many populations have survived and rebounded despite continuing exposure to the pathogen.

The findings highlight an important distinction between infection and mortality. A species can carry a dangerous pathogen without necessarily suffering catastrophic losses, particularly if its members can tolerate the infection.

What the Discovery Means for Future Amphibian Survival

Although the evidence strongly implicates chytrid in the historic declines at Boracéia, the researchers caution that their findings apply to this particular location. The results cannot automatically explain amphibian disappearances elsewhere in the Atlantic Forest.

Still, the study provides a compelling explanation for a longstanding local mystery and demonstrates how scientists can use historical specimens to reconstruct outbreaks that would otherwise remain poorly understood.

The investigation is also continuing.

Researchers are now examining DNA recovered from museum specimens to identify the genetic mechanisms that influenced how amphibians responded to chytrid infections in the past. These analyses could help reveal why some species were devastated while others survived.

Separate projects are using ancient environmental DNA to help fill gaps in historical specimen records. This approach involves searching for genetic traces left behind by organisms in their surroundings, potentially providing evidence of species and pathogens that were never directly collected.

Together, these efforts could reveal a much clearer history of how chytrid emerged, spread, and affected amphibian biodiversity over the past century.

By uncovering the biological changes that helped some frogs survive and recover, scientists may also gain valuable insights into protecting vulnerable species from future fungal epidemics.

https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.title: 400,000-year-old teeth reveal a stunning twist in human evolution
https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.text:
For most of the 20th century, the model of human origins was a tree: with the trunk dividing into branches, and then twigs. Each species of human relative (hominin) was a neat, single branch.

As an undergraduate, I was taught that Homo sapiens was one of these branches that emerged in Africa, spread across the world, and displaced every archaic human it encountered.

Neanderthals, Homo erectus, and other ancient relatives were evolutionary dead ends – unfortunate cousins who left no descendants. In the 30 years since I left university, those early lessons are now radically revised.

That neat replacement story is now comprehensively wrong, largely thanks to studies like the one published in Nature by Qiaomei Fu from the Chinese Academy of Sciences and colleagues. The paper achieves something that would have seemed impossible a decade ago: it recovers meaningful biological information from H. erectus fossils far too old for DNA.

Instead of genetic sequences, the team extracted ancient proteins from the enamel of six teeth from three Chinese sites – Zhoukoudian (which, in the early 20th century, produced fossil remains known as “Peking Man”), Hexian and Sunjiadong – all dating to around 400,000 years ago.

Homo erectus is widely regarded as the first hominin to leave Africa; the evidence suggests this species had moved into Eurasia nearly two million years ago. It remains the most geographically widespread human ancestor that ever lived. The new study indicates that Homo erectus exchanged genes (probably through interbreeding) with Denisovans in East Asia roughly 400,000 years ago.

The study suggests that some of that genetic legacy, it now appears, was passed on to living people in the Philippines, Papua New Guinea, and across south-east Asia.

Tooth enamel is the hardest tissue in the body, and its proteins survive long after DNA has degraded beyond recovery. What the team found in those proteins is striking. All six specimens share a previously unknown amino acid variant – a tiny molecular signature, a single letter changed in the protein sequence, never seen in any other hominin alive or dead.

This variant clusters these east Asian H. erectus into a distinct group, confirming their identity and settling a long-running debate about whether the unusual Hexian fossils were H. erectus at all. A second variant they share, however, is not unique to H. erectus.

It also appears in Denisovans – a mysterious archaic (non-Homo sapiens) human group known mainly from a cave in Siberia. The corresponding genetic variant turns up in living people at frequencies of 21% in the Philippines and about 1% in India, distributed in a pattern that matches what we’d expect if it entered modern humans via Denisovan ancestry.

The most reasonable interpretation is that H. erectus populations in east Asia passed this variant to Denisovans through interbreeding, and Denisovans later passed it on to the ancestors of modern south-east Asians and Oceanians. This transfer of genetic material from one species to another is known as introgression.

The lineage we once thought was a dead end has, it turns out, left a small but detectable trace in living human genomes – a molecular thread connecting a Peking Man tooth to living people in Asia.

But the significance of today’s paper extends well beyond the specific variant or the specific populations involved. What it really shows is that interbreeding between archaic human lineages was not exceptional. It was routine.

Every major hominin lineage we have been able to examine genomically shows admixture. Modern humans outside Africa carry roughly 2% Neanderthal DNA. Papuans and Aboriginal Australians carry an additional 2–5% Denisovan ancestry.

West African populations carry genetic signatures from an unidentified archaic lineage. Even Denisovans themselves, as today’s study adds further weight to, received gene flow from something older and more diverged — likely H. erectus.

A 2019 review in the American Journal of Physical Anthropology documents at least three distinct introgression events from Denisovan-like populations into south-east Asian and Oceanic ancestors alone, some occurring as recently as 20,000 years ago. The picture is not one of clean lineages but of a tangled web of contact and exchange extending across millions of years.

The implications are far-reaching. Our genomes are not the product of a single unbroken lineage emerging from Africa. They are mosaics, assembled from contributions by multiple archaic groups, each adapted to its own regional environment.

Some of the Denisovan-derived variants in Papuan genomes, for instance, appear to influence immune function. The H. erectus-derived variant identified today has unknown functional consequences – that remains an open question – but the precedent from other gene variants that have introgressed (genes that have passed from one species into another) suggests that adaptation to new environments may have been part of the story.

Perhaps most intriguing is what the new paper implies about all the populations we cannot yet study. H. erectus survived in Indonesia until perhaps 100,000 years ago. Homo floresiensis, the diminutive “hobbit” species, was present on Flores when modern humans arrived. Another human lineage, Homo luzonensis, occupied the Philippines.

None of these populations have yielded DNA, and until today none had yielded any molecular data at all. Were they also absorbed, at least partially, into the human populations that replaced them? The genomic evidence from living people has not, so far, detected their signal clearly – but the tools available until recently were blunt instruments.

The proteomic approach demonstrated in today’s paper offers a way forward. If proteins can be recovered from H. erectus enamel at 400,000 years, the same approach applied to floresiensis or luzonensis material might finally reveal whether those lineages, too, contributed something to the humans who came after them.

The old metaphor of a tree – a single trunk branching into distinct species – has been quietly replaced in the scientific literature. It might be better to consider the process as a braided river, with many channels running partly together and partly apart, exchanging water continuously.

This new study is one more confirmation that when ancient human populations disappeared, they left traces of themselves behind.

https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.title: Dead stars could break one of physics' most famous limits
https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.text:
Some of the universe's dead stars may be capable of growing far more massive than a famous limit in physics was thought to allow. New computer simulations suggest that powerful magnetic fields hidden inside these stellar remnants could help them withstand crushing gravity and reach extraordinary masses.

The discovery challenges a long-standing understanding of white dwarfs, the dense cores left behind when certain stars exhaust their nuclear fuel and shed their outer layers. Although these stellar remnants are roughly the size of Earth, they can contain as much mass as the Sun or even more.

For white dwarfs without strong magnetic fields or rapid rotation, physicists have long recognized an upper mass boundary of approximately 1.4 times the Sun's mass. Known as the Chandrasekhar limit, this threshold plays an important role in understanding how some stars end their lives in spectacular explosions.

When a white dwarf made primarily of carbon and oxygen approaches this limit, the increasing pressure and density inside its core can ignite carbon, potentially setting off a powerful thermonuclear explosion known as a Type Ia supernova.

Scientists Discover How Magnetic Fields Could Break a Famous Cosmic Limit

New simulations by researchers from the Department of Physics at the Indian Institute of Science (IISc) and their collaborators suggest that the traditional mass limit may not apply to white dwarfs with sufficiently strong internal magnetic fields.

In one simulation, a magnetized white dwarf reached approximately 2.4 times the mass of the Sun, substantially exceeding the conventional limit of 1.4 solar masses.

"The idea started in 2011, when a summer student came to me and I gave him a problem quite casually: to check whether the Chandrasekhar limit can be violated by a magnetic field," explains Banibrata Mukhopadhyay, Professor at the Department of Physics and corresponding author of the study published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

The possibility of white dwarfs exceeding the Chandrasekhar limit is not entirely new. Theoretical physicists have explored these unusual objects, sometimes called "super-Chandrasekhar" white dwarfs, for decades.

Astronomers have also observed Type Ia supernovae that shine much more brightly than expected. These exceptionally luminous explosions have raised the possibility that some white dwarfs may reach masses as high as 2.8 times that of the Sun before exploding.

However, demonstrating that such massive white dwarfs could theoretically exist is only part of the challenge. Scientists also need to explain how an ordinary star could naturally develop into one.

Following a Star's Evolution From Birth to Death

"The important question was not simply whether a super-Chandrasekhar white dwarf is possible, but whether a star can actually evolve into one," says Zenia Zuraiq, first author of the study and PhD student at the Department of Physics. "Our simulations allowed us to follow that evolutionary pathway from the main-sequence star to the white dwarf, and show that under certain conditions, such a pathway is possible."

To investigate this process, the researchers modified a stellar evolution computer program called STARS, originally developed at the University of Cambridge.

The team expanded the software to account for magnetic fields and the cooling of white dwarfs. These additions allowed them to simulate how magnetized stars change over time, beginning with the main-sequence stage, when stars generate energy by fusing hydrogen into helium.

The simulations then followed the stars through their later evolutionary stages and into their final state as white dwarfs. Afterward, the researchers modeled a binary star system in which a white dwarf gradually pulls matter from a neighboring companion star.

This process, known as accretion, allows the white dwarf to gain mass over time. The researchers wanted to determine whether its growing magnetic field could change how much additional material it could support.

A Hidden Magnetic Force Helps Dead Stars Resist Gravity

The simulations revealed a surprising effect. Even a magnetic field that starts out relatively weak can become increasingly influential as a white dwarf accumulates matter.

As material builds up, the star becomes denser and contracts under its own gravity. This compression strengthens its internal magnetic field, which in turn provides additional pressure that helps counteract gravity.

The stronger magnetic support allows the white dwarf to hold more mass than would otherwise be possible. It also changes the familiar relationship between a white dwarf's mass and its size, potentially creating different maximum mass limit(s) depending on how magnetic fields behave inside the star.

One simulation illustrates just how dramatic the difference could be.

The researchers modeled a carbon-oxygen white dwarf with an initial mass of 1.02 times that of the Sun. It had formed from a main-sequence star that originally contained eight solar masses.

In the simulation, the white dwarf gradually accumulated material from its companion at a rate of 10⁻⁹ solar masses per year, equivalent to one billionth of the Sun's mass annually.

When magnetic effects were included, the white dwarf could reach approximately 2.4 solar masses. Without those effects, an otherwise comparable model reached the conventional limit of roughly 1.4 solar masses.

The results suggest that magnetic fields could fundamentally alter how massive a white dwarf can become.

The same mechanism may also help explain another astronomical puzzle. Some well-studied white dwarfs have unexpectedly large radii for their relatively low masses. Magnetic pressure could provide a possible explanation for why these stars appear larger than conventional models predict.

Could the Discovery Change How We Measure the Universe?

The implications could extend well beyond the evolution of dying stars.

Type Ia supernovae are among astronomy's most important tools for measuring distances across the cosmos. Because their peak brightness can be standardized, astronomers use them as cosmic reference points, often called standardizable candles.

By comparing how bright these explosions actually are with how bright they appear from Earth, researchers can estimate their distances. Such measurements have helped scientists investigate the universe's size, history, and ongoing expansion.

The Chandrasekhar limit has traditionally provided an important part of the physical framework for understanding these explosions. If white dwarfs reach similar masses before exploding, their energy output and brightness can be expected to follow broadly predictable patterns.

However, the new findings suggest that some exploding white dwarfs could have substantially different masses and internal magnetic fields.

Those differences could influence the properties and luminosity of the resulting supernovae, potentially helping explain why certain Type Ia explosions are unusually bright.

Understanding how magnetic fields affect these stellar explosions could therefore help astronomers refine their interpretations of supernova brightness and improve their understanding of cosmic expansion.

Although the findings come from computer simulations rather than direct observations of white dwarfs growing to these extreme masses, they offer a possible evolutionary pathway for stars that exceed the traditional Chandrasekhar limit.

The research suggests that one of astronomy's most famous mass limits may have important exceptions, with powerful magnetic fields allowing some dead stars to become far heavier than previously expected.

They say the Chandrasekhar limit may not apply to white dwarfs with sufficiently strong internal magnetic fields. The discovery challenges a long-standing understanding of white dwarf.

https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.title: The brain’s hidden fear mechanism may explain anxiety and PTSD
https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.text:
The brain has a remarkable ability to recognize danger, but new research suggests that this survival mechanism may also explain why people sometimes feel threatened in situations that are actually safe. The discovery offers a possible explanation for the intense fear responses associated with anxiety and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD).

For years, scientists believed that fear helps the brain distinguish more clearly between threatening and harmless experiences. However, a study led by researchers at the Douglas Research Centre at McGill University and the University of Toronto-Scarborough challenges that assumption. The findings, published in Nature Neuroscience, suggest that fear may have the opposite effect.

In experiments involving mice, researchers trained the animals to associate one environment with danger and another with safety. Instead of developing increasingly separate neural representations of the two locations, the animals' brain activity began to show overlapping patterns. In other words, the brain's representations of safe and dangerous experiences became less distinct.

"Our findings suggest fear may blur the boundary between danger and safety rather than sharpen it," said senior author Mark Brandon, Associate Professor in McGill's Department of Psychiatry and Researcher at the Douglas. "This could reshape how scientists think about anxiety and PTSD."

How Scientists Watched the Brain Process Fear

To investigate how these changes occur, the research team developed an unusual experimental setup that combined augmented reality with real-time brain imaging.

The researchers created a specialized arena in which mice could be virtually "teleported" between environments associated with danger and safety. By changing the sights and sounds surrounding the animals, scientists could make them experience different settings without physically moving them to another location.

At the same time, miniature microscopes monitored hundreds of neurons in the hippocampus, a brain region essential for learning and memory. This allowed the team to observe how the brain's activity changed as the mice transitioned between experiences associated with safety and threat.

"That gave us something conventional fear conditioning experiments cannot easily provide: a moment-by-moment view of the brain switching between competing maps of dangerous and safe memories," said Robert Rozeske, Assistant Professor in University of Toronto's Department of Psychology and lead author on the publication.

Why the Brain May Confuse Safety With Danger

Although mixing memories of safe and dangerous experiences might seem like a problem, the researchers believe it could serve an important evolutionary purpose.

The experiments suggested that overlapping memory representations allowed the brain to retrieve information about previous threats more rapidly. This could help an animal recognize possible danger and respond before it is too late.

Such a strategy comes with a trade-off. By prioritizing speed over accuracy, the brain may react to a potential threat even when the current situation is harmless. From a survival perspective, responding unnecessarily to a false alarm may sometimes be preferable to overlooking a genuine danger.

"The ventral hippocampus may be part of a system that prioritizes a rapid 'better safe than sorry' response," said Rozeske. "In other words, the brain may sacrifice precision for speed when danger matters."

The ventral hippocampus is a part of the hippocampus involved in processing emotionally significant experiences, including fear and anxiety. The new findings suggest that overlapping memory representations in this region may help the brain switch rapidly into a defensive state.

A Hidden Survival Mechanism May Help Explain PTSD

The discovery could also offer insight into why people with anxiety and trauma-related disorders sometimes experience powerful fear responses in situations that pose no immediate threat.

For someone with PTSD, an otherwise harmless sight, sound, or environment can trigger memories associated with a traumatic experience. The resulting fear can feel immediate and overwhelming, even when the person is objectively safe.

The researchers suggest that such reactions may arise, at least in part, when a normally useful survival mechanism becomes excessively sensitive. Instead of reflecting a system that has simply stopped distinguishing between different memories, these responses might involve a brain mechanism that shifts too quickly from recognizing safety to anticipating danger.

"Our study suggests that's not necessarily a broken pattern-separation system, but possibly an overactive version of a normal survival mechanism gone into overdrive," said Brandon. "That reframing could guide therapeutic approaches to address an overly fast transition to 'danger mode'."

Because the experiments were conducted in mice, additional research is needed to determine whether the same mechanisms contribute to anxiety and PTSD in humans. Nevertheless, the findings provide a new way to understand how fear influences memory and why a brain system designed to protect against danger might sometimes generate fear when no immediate threat exists.

Study Details and Funding

The study, "Overlapping representations in the ventral hippocampus support rapid fear memory retrieval," by Robert Rozeske and Mark Brandon, was published in Nature Neuroscience.

The research received support from the Canadian Institutes of Health Research and the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada.

https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.title: A tiny supercurrent could unlock quantum information without destroying it
https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.text:
One of the biggest obstacles in quantum computing is surprisingly simple to describe: how do you read information without changing or destroying it? Unlike the bits used in ordinary computers, quantum bits, or qubits, are extraordinarily sensitive to measurement. Trying to determine their state can cause that state to collapse, potentially erasing the very information scientists want to retrieve.

Researchers have now proposed a way to overcome much of this difficulty by using an unusual electrical signal produced by the qubit itself. Their approach focuses on a special type known as an "Andreev qubit," which can generate an oscillating electric supercurrent through its own quantum behavior. By monitoring this current, scientists may be able to determine the qubit's state without directly measuring it or significantly disturbing the information it contains.

The research, supported by FAPESP, was published in Physical Review B Letters. It was led by José Carlos Egues, a full professor at the São Carlos Institute of Physics at the University of São Paulo (IFSC-USP) in Brazil, and Yugui Yao of the School of Physics at the Beijing Institute of Technology in China. If experimentally confirmed, their method could simplify quantum computing by removing the need for extra qubits used in certain measurement techniques.

Why Measuring Quantum Information Is So Difficult

Conventional computers store information in bits that have one of two values, 0 or 1. These values can be checked repeatedly without changing the information. Quantum computers work differently because their qubits can exist in superpositions, meaning they can combine the states 0 and 1 in ways that are not possible with conventional bits.

This unusual ability is central to the potential power of quantum computing. However, it also creates a major vulnerability. Quantum states can be disrupted by interactions with their surroundings, including the instruments scientists use to examine them.

"In the conventional formulation of quantum mechanics, a projective measurement causes the system to assume one of the states associated with the measured quantity. Thus, if a qubit has been prepared in a certain superposition of 0 and 1, its direct measurement tends to destroy that superposition and, consequently, the information it contained," says Egues.

To minimize this problem, physicists developed techniques known as "quantum nondemolition measurements," or QND. Many of these approaches use an additional quantum system called an ancilla. Rather than measuring the original qubit directly, researchers transfer information to the ancilla and measure that auxiliary system instead.

The term "ancilla" comes from a Latin word meaning "slave" or "servant." In modern scientific usage, it describes something that performs a supporting function. Here, the ancilla acts as an intermediary, allowing researchers to obtain information while preserving the original qubit as much as possible.

Although effective, these procedures come with practical disadvantages. Scientists must prepare the auxiliary qubits, connect them to the qubits being studied, transfer information between them, and perform repeated measurements. These additional steps require time and equipment, and the complexity becomes increasingly significant as the number of qubits grows.

"Our strategy is different. Instead of transferring the information to an auxiliary qubit, we seek to obtain it from a signal produced by the qubit under study itself," says the researcher.

A Special Quantum Bit That Produces Its Own Signal

The proposed technique relies on the unusual properties of an Andreev qubit. Its name honors Soviet physicist Alexander Andreev (1939-2023), who identified a distinctive quantum process in 1964 that occurs where normal materials meet superconductors.

Superconductors are materials that can conduct electricity without electrical resistance under appropriate conditions. At the boundaries involving these materials, special quantum states known as "Andreev states" can form. In the system studied by the researchers, these states are confined to an extremely small region between two superconducting materials.

These quantum states can represent the basic values 0 and 1, along with superpositions of those values, making them suitable for storing quantum information.

"In the system under consideration, this region is a quantum dot - that is, a nanoscale structure in which electrons are spatially confined - formed in an indium arsenide [InAs] nanowire connected to superconducting materials on both sides. It's in this environment that the states characterizing the Andreev qubit are formed," Egues explains.

The key to the new approach is an electrical phenomenon called a "supercurrent." Unlike the current flowing through ordinary electrical conductors, a supercurrent moves without resistance.

The researchers found that when the Andreev qubit exists in a superposition, the supercurrent develops a component that oscillates over time. These fluctuations arise from quantum interference between the different states making up the superposition.

Crucially, the oscillations are not random. Their behavior contains information about the qubit's underlying quantum state, potentially allowing scientists to determine what that state is without directly measuring the qubit.

"It's precisely that property that we use to read the qubit. It's that supercurrent that lies at the heart of our proposal," the researcher points out.

How a Tiny Electrical Current Reveals Quantum Information

To understand how the technique works, it helps to consider how physicists describe a qubit's state mathematically.

One common representation is the "Bloch sphere," a geometric model in which every possible pure state of a single qubit corresponds to a point on the surface of a sphere. Two angles determine the location of that point.

The first angle describes how much each of the two basic states contributes to the superposition. The second describes their relative phase, which specifies how the quantum components are aligned with one another. Together, these two measurements provide the information needed to identify the qubit's state.

According to the new research, both pieces of information can be extracted from the supercurrent. Its steady component and the size of its oscillations reveal the relative contributions of the two basic states. Meanwhile, the timing of the oscillations provides information about their phase relationship.

"Our study showed that this information is encoded in the supercurrent itself. The supercurrent has a constant component and a fluctuating component. The value of the constant component and the amplitude of the oscillation reveal the proportion of each state (0 and 1) in the superposition, and the moment when that oscillation begins reveals the phase relationship between them. Thus, by measuring how the current varies over time, it's possible to reconstruct the initial state of the qubit," Egues explains.

This means the electrical current effectively carries a signature of the quantum information stored in the system. By observing how that signature changes over time, researchers could reconstruct the qubit's original state.

A Supercurrent That Oscillates Without Voltage

Another surprising feature of the proposed system is that the electrical current can oscillate without an externally applied voltage.

Ordinarily, producing an oscillating supercurrent in this type of superconducting system requires a voltage. This familiar phenomenon is called the "AC Josephson effect."

The researchers predict something different in their Andreev qubit. Here, the current's oscillations arise naturally from the qubit's own quantum evolution. No outside voltage is required to generate them.

"Our system generates a supercurrent that varies over time like an alternating current but without voltage. It's the very evolution of the qubit's state that produces that oscillation," says Egues.

This behavior is important because it transforms quantum activity occurring on an extraordinarily small scale into a detectable electrical signal. The current provides a connection between the microscopic world of quantum states and the larger physical systems scientists can measure.

That connection is what makes the proposed reading technique possible.

Detecting Quantum States With an Extremely Sensitive Sensor

The researchers envision placing the Andreev qubit inside a closed superconducting circuit, allowing its supercurrent to circulate continuously.

Next to the circuit would sit a SQUID (superconducting quantum interference device), a highly sensitive instrument capable of detecting extremely weak magnetic fields.

Whenever an electric current flows, it produces a magnetic field. Because the supercurrent in this system oscillates, the magnetic field it generates also changes over time.

The nearby SQUID could detect these tiny magnetic variations and use them to determine the behavior of the circulating current. Since the current contains information about the qubit's quantum state, the researchers could then reconstruct that state without measuring the qubit directly.

Egues compares the arrangement to two compasses that interact through a magnetic field.

"We can think of the qubit as one compass and the SQUID as another compass. The current in the circuit produces a magnetic field, and the SQUID 'senses' that field. Since the coupling between the two is very weak, the effect of the measuring instrument on the qubit tends to be very small."

The weak interaction between the sensor and the qubit is especially important. It offers a way to gather information while minimizing the disturbance that normally accompanies quantum measurements.

Reading Quantum Information With Almost No Disturbance

In quantum physics, observing a system is not necessarily a harmless process. A measuring instrument interacts with whatever it is attempting to measure, and that interaction can change the system's behavior.

This fundamental difficulty puzzled the earliest researchers studying quantum mechanics. It remains an unavoidable feature of quantum measurements today.

The proposed technique does not eliminate this effect entirely. The SQUID still interacts with the circuit, creating a small amount of feedback that can influence the qubit. However, the team's simulations suggest that this disturbance can be reduced to a level so small that it becomes effectively negligible.

"Our method doesn't eliminate the fundamental problem of quantum measurement. But it can approach the limit of a non-destructive readout and, at the same time, avoid the use of auxiliary qubits - the ancillas - employed in other non-destructive quantum measurement protocols," Egues notes.

The approach could also remove another complication found in some existing techniques. Because researchers would not need to restore the qubit to its original state after every measurement, they could make repeated observations as the state changes.

This would allow scientists to follow the qubit's quantum evolution over time, rather than obtaining information only through separate measurement and reset cycles.

Simulations Achieve Up to 99.85% Accuracy

To investigate whether the method could work outside ideal theoretical conditions, the researchers performed computer simulations designed to account for imperfections that would arise in real experiments.

These calculations included measurement noise, as well as the small amount of feedback introduced by the detection coil. The goal was to determine whether the qubit's state could still be reconstructed accurately despite these disturbances.

The results were encouraging. Depending on the number of measurements used, the simulations produced accuracies of 99.52%, 99.81%, and 99.85%.

According to the researchers, these values fall within the standard thresholds used in quantum error correction schemes, which are designed to manage errors in quantum information processing.

The findings suggest that the method could provide highly accurate quantum state reconstruction without the additional complexity of auxiliary qubits.

However, the technique has not yet been demonstrated experimentally. The results come entirely from theoretical analysis and computer simulations, so researchers still need to establish whether a physical device can achieve comparable performance.

Could This Make Quantum Computers Simpler?

Despite the lack of experimental confirmation, the researchers emphasize that their proposal does not depend on technologies that have yet to be invented.

The calculations use realistic properties drawn from existing quantum systems, and SQUID sensors are already established tools for detecting exceptionally weak magnetic fields and electric currents.

What remains to be built is the specific arrangement of components required to implement the proposed measurement technique.

"All the numbers we used are realistic. In principle, this can be achieved. In fact, we used parameters from existing systems in our calculations. What doesn't yet exist is that geometry, that setup that we proposed," he argues.

This makes the approach different from theoretical concepts that cannot be realized until scientists develop entirely new materials or manufacturing techniques. In principle, the necessary components already exist, although assembling them into the proposed configuration and demonstrating the predicted behavior remain important challenges.

The research offers two potentially significant advances.

From the standpoint of fundamental physics, it predicts that a qubit can produce an oscillating supercurrent resembling the AC Josephson effect, but without requiring an external voltage. Instead, the oscillations emerge from the qubit's own coherent quantum evolution.

From a technological perspective, the study shows how those oscillations could serve as a measurable signature of the qubit's internal state. By analyzing the electrical current, researchers could recover quantum information while causing very little disturbance to the system.

If future experiments confirm these predictions, the method could make reading Andreev qubits substantially simpler. Eliminating auxiliary qubits and repeated resets could reduce the equipment and procedures needed to retrieve quantum information.

More fundamentally, the work points toward an intriguing possibility: information hidden in the microscopic quantum world may be accessible through an electrical current produced by the quantum system itself, offering a promising new way to observe delicate quantum states without destroying them.

https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.title: Gene editing could replace a lifetime of medication, but there's a catch
https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.text:
Imagine receiving a single treatment that could keep your cholesterol under control for decades, potentially eliminating the need for daily medication. Advances in gene editing are bringing that possibility closer to reality. But scientists say the same technology that could revolutionize medicine also raises difficult questions about safety, permanent genetic changes, and unintended consequences.

Gene therapy is already being used to treat certain serious illnesses. These treatments can introduce working copies of genes, silence harmful genetic activity, or make changes directly to DNA. Unlike conventional medications that must be taken repeatedly, some genetic treatments are designed to work after just one administration.

More than 6,000 rare genetic disorders have been identified, although only a small proportion currently have targets that can be treated. Gene therapies have already achieved important successes against conditions such as spinal muscular atrophy and sickle cell disease.

Now, researchers are exploring whether similar approaches could help prevent or manage far more widespread health problems, including high cholesterol, heart disease, obesity, and diabetes.

That raises a fundamental question: Just because scientists can permanently change a person's genetic activity, does that mean they should?

In a perspective published in JAMA Internal Medicine, University of Michigan Health Frankel Cardiovascular Center cardiologists Eric D. Smith, M.D., and Venkatesh L. Murthy, M.D., Ph.D., outline how doctors and researchers should weigh the potential benefits of genomic therapies against their risks.

The two gene therapy researchers explain why these treatments are so promising, what makes them different from conventional medicines, and what must happen before they can be safely offered to millions of people.

Why One-Time Gene Therapy Is Different From Daily Medication

One of the most appealing features of gene therapy is the possibility of achieving lasting results without repeated treatments.

Traditional medicines generally work only as long as patients continue taking them. Genomic therapies operate differently because they act on genetic material itself. They may provide a healthy version of a gene, suppress a gene responsible for harmful effects, or modify a specific DNA sequence.

This makes it possible to develop treatments intended to work after a single dose. Such therapies are often called "one-and-done" treatments.

However, receiving a treatment only once does not necessarily mean its effects will last a lifetime.

Smith explains that many gene therapies use modified viruses to carry genetic instructions into cells. The immune system can recognize these delivery vehicles and develop a response against them. As a result, administering the same treatment again may be difficult or impossible, even if its benefits begin to fade.

Another important distinction concerns which cells are changed. Current gene therapies generally target somatic cells, which are the body's cells other than those involved in reproduction. Unlike germline editing, these treatments are not intended to create genetic changes that can be inherited by future generations.

Why Gene Editing Common Diseases Raises New Risks

For people living with rare, devastating genetic conditions, the benefits of gene therapy may clearly outweigh the potential dangers. Some patients have few effective treatment options, making even an experimental intervention worth considering.

The situation becomes considerably more complicated when the same technology is used against common diseases.

Conditions such as high cholesterol, heart disease, obesity, and diabetes already have established treatments. Many of these medications can be adjusted as a patient's condition changes or discontinued if troublesome side effects develop.

A permanent genetic intervention may not offer that flexibility.

Murthy also points to a major concern involving the number of people who might eventually receive these treatments. A serious side effect that occurs only rarely could still harm a substantial number of patients if a therapy is administered to millions.

For that reason, treatments intended for widespread use must meet especially demanding safety standards.

Five Questions Scientists Say Must Be Answered

To help determine when genomic therapy is appropriate, Smith and Murthy propose evaluating five essential factors:

The final question may be especially challenging.

Clinical trials typically involve relatively small groups of patients who are monitored for limited periods. Although these studies can identify many important safety concerns, they may miss extremely rare complications or problems that take years to develop.

Some adverse effects might only become apparent after a treatment has reached a much larger population.

The Problem of Tracking Risks That Could Emerge Years Later

Smith argues that long-term monitoring cannot be treated as an afterthought. It needs to be an essential part of how gene therapies are introduced into medical practice.

Patient registries, which collect information about people receiving particular treatments, have already shown how valuable extended follow-up can be.

However, therapies that could eventually reach millions of patients will require monitoring systems capable of operating on a much larger scale.

These systems must be independent and standardized so researchers can consistently evaluate whether treatments remain effective and whether unexpected health problems appear over time.

Without reliable long-term data, doctors may struggle to determine the full consequences of genetic interventions that cannot easily be reversed.

Could Some Genetic Changes Be Too Risky to Make Permanent?

Another concern is whether certain diseases or biological processes are suitable for permanent treatment at all.

Murthy emphasizes that developing the ability to alter a genetic target does not automatically make doing so the best medical decision.

Some conditions require careful adjustments to medication doses over time. In other cases, the difference between an effective treatment and a harmful one can be extremely small. Changing a biological process too much or too little could create serious complications.

Conventional medications offer an important advantage in these situations because doctors can modify or stop treatment as needed.

Permanent gene therapies generally lack that option.

Scientists may eventually overcome this limitation by developing genetic treatments with built-in biological "off-switches" or other methods for reversing their effects.

Until those approaches have been shown to work reliably, the ability to undo or adjust a treatment remains an important safety advantage of traditional medicine.

The Million-Dollar Challenge Facing Gene Therapy

Safety is not the only barrier to bringing gene editing into mainstream healthcare. Cost could also determine whether these treatments become widely available.

Some existing gene therapies have list prices above $1 million for a single patient, and several cost substantially more.

Such prices may be considered justifiable for certain rare, life-threatening conditions, particularly when treatment options are extremely limited.

But applying similar pricing to diseases affecting millions of people would place enormous financial pressure on healthcare systems.

Smith and Murthy argue that affordability and access must therefore be part of the discussion from the beginning.

Even a highly effective gene therapy could create new healthcare inequalities if only a small percentage of patients could obtain it. Researchers and policymakers must consider not just whether these treatments work, but also whether they can be delivered without making existing disparities worse.

Could One Gene-Editing Treatment Prevent Heart Disease for Decades?

Despite these challenges, the possibility of using gene editing to prevent common diseases is becoming increasingly realistic.

Researchers are already conducting early studies to investigate whether a single genetic treatment can produce long-lasting reductions in LDL, commonly known as "bad," cholesterol.

LDL cholesterol contributes to the buildup of fatty deposits inside arteries, which can increase the risk of heart attacks and other cardiovascular problems. Lowering LDL over extended periods is an important strategy for reducing cardiovascular risk.

If gene editing can safely produce sustained reductions, it could eventually offer a new approach to protecting cardiovascular health without requiring patients to take medication indefinitely.

However, promising early results will not be enough to justify widespread use.

Before these therapies become routine options for common conditions, researchers will need convincing evidence that their benefits last, their risks remain acceptably low over many years, and their costs are manageable. Reliable safeguards will also be essential.

For Smith and Murthy, the objective is not to hold back genetic medicine. It is to make sure that a technology with the potential to transform healthcare is introduced carefully and responsibly.

As gene therapy moves beyond rare disorders toward conditions affecting millions of people, the central challenge will be ensuring that the promise of lasting protection does not come at the expense of long-term patient safety.

https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.title: Scientists turn viruses into weapons against deadly superbugs
https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.text:
Viruses are usually associated with causing infections, but some can actually help fight them. Scientists are now working to turn these bacteria-killing viruses into treatments for dangerous infections that no longer respond to conventional antibiotics.

An international team of experts has taken an important step toward making this approach safer and more practical for medical use. Led by the German Society for Infectious Diseases (DGI), the group has developed the first internationally coordinated clinical guidelines for personalized phage therapy, a treatment that uses carefully selected viruses to attack harmful bacteria.

The effort involved 20 professional organizations, 18 international experts, including representatives from regulatory agencies, and two patient advocacy organizations. Together, they established more than 60 recommendations covering how phages should be selected, tested, manufactured, administered, and monitored. The guidelines also address laboratory infrastructure, quality control, treatment documentation, and priorities for future research.

The consensus statement was published in the journal Nature Medicine. Until now, doctors and researchers have lacked a unified international framework for many of the essential procedures and quality standards involved in using phages as medical treatments.

How Bacteria-Killing Viruses Could Fight Antibiotic Resistance

Antibiotic resistance is making bacterial infections increasingly difficult to treat around the world. As some bacteria develop defenses against commonly used medications, doctors may find themselves with few effective options.

One possible alternative involves bacteriophages, commonly called phages. These are viruses that naturally infect bacteria and can destroy them. Unlike many antibiotics, which can act against a broad range of bacteria, phages typically target particular bacterial species or even individual strains.

That precision makes phage therapy especially interesting, but it also creates a challenge. A virus capable of killing one strain of bacteria may have little or no effect on another. Before treatment begins, specialists must therefore determine whether a particular phage can successfully attack the bacteria responsible for a patient's infection.

Personalized phage therapy may be considered when established treatments have failed, are unavailable, or cannot be used safely. Research so far suggests that properly manufactured and administered phages generally have a favorable safety profile. However, controlled clinical trials have not yet provided sufficient evidence to establish how reliably the treatment works.

For that reason, the new guidelines do not recommend phage therapy as a routine treatment for bacterial infections. Instead, they emphasize carefully evaluating individual patients and using the approach only when the circumstances justify it.

Early Results Show Promise Against Difficult Infections

Although major questions remain, early clinical experiences suggest that phage therapy could benefit some patients with difficult infections.

In a Belgian case series involving 100 people who received phage treatment, 77 percent experienced an improvement in their clinical condition. In 61 percent of cases, tests could no longer detect the bacteria that the treatment had targeted.

These findings are encouraging, particularly for infections that are difficult to control with existing medications. However, observational studies cannot establish whether phages were responsible for the improvements or determine how well the treatment would perform in a controlled clinical trial.

Larger, carefully designed studies will be needed to clarify the effectiveness of phage therapy and identify which patients are most likely to benefit.

Finding the Right Virus for Each Bacterial Infection

A central challenge in personalized phage therapy is finding the correct virus for each patient.

Because phages are highly selective, laboratories must test whether a candidate virus can kill the specific bacterial strain involved in an infection. This process, known as a "phage match," should be completed as quickly as possible before treatment begins.

Timing matters because bacteria can change their susceptibility to phages during an infection. If multiple bacterial pathogens are present, specialists should test all of the relevant organisms rather than focusing on just one.

The guidelines recommend that treatment decisions involve a team of specialists, including the patient's physicians, clinical microbiologists, and recognized phage experts. This collaborative approach is intended to help clinicians select appropriate phages and determine whether treatment is justified.

The recommendations also establish expectations for cooperation among laboratories, phage manufacturing facilities, pharmacies, and clinical teams. Consistent testing methods and regular proficiency assessments should help ensure that results from different facilities are reliable and comparable.

Another priority is collecting detailed information about every treatment. The guidelines call for cases to be systematically documented and entered into registries, allowing researchers to compare clinical experiences, identify problems, and investigate unanswered questions.

"The standardization of quality criteria for the production of phages for personalized use, as well as the identification of infrastructural requirements, are essential components of the guideline and important prerequisites for reliable treatments," says Dr. Annika Claßen.

Claßen, a researcher with the German Center for Infection Research (DZIF), played a leading role in developing the recommendations. She also directs the "Translational Bacteriophage Research Group" at University Hospital Cologne.

Other major contributors include PD Dr. Silvia Würstle, Prof. Maria Vehreschild, and Dr. Simone Lieberknecht-Jouy of Goethe University Frankfurt. Vehreschild serves as deputy coordinator of the DZIF research area "Healthcare-Associated Infections," where Claßen, Würstle, and Lieberknecht-Jouy are also involved in research.

German Hospital Begins Using Personalized Phage Therapy

The potential of this approach is already being explored in clinical practice.

"The guideline provides physicians, pharmacists, and regulatory authorities with a common framework for safely and responsibly incorporating phage therapy into clinical practice," says PD Dr. Würstle, the corresponding author of the guideline.

At Frankfurt University Medical Center, Würstle is overseeing the development of the facilities and procedures needed to provide phage therapy in accordance with the new recommendations.

The medical center reports that ten patients have been successfully treated through its guideline-based phage therapy program since February 2026. The treatments use viruses individually selected to target the bacteria causing each patient's infection.

Among the pathogens treated are Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus, two bacterial species associated with infections that can be particularly challenging to manage, especially when antibiotic resistance is involved.

The method of delivering the phages depends on the infection and the patient's medical needs. Treatment may involve intravenous administration, inhalation, a nasal spray, or application through a sterile hydrogel.

These different delivery methods illustrate how personalized phage therapy can be adapted to specific clinical situations rather than relying on a single treatment approach.

New International Standards Could Shape the Future of Phage Therapy

Building a reliable system for phage treatment requires coordination across numerous medical and scientific specialties.

The guidelines highlight PhageNET DZIF, a network established and coordinated by Claßen, as an important platform for exchanging scientific knowledge and clinical experience.

By bringing together expertise in microbiology, clinical medicine, pharmacy, manufacturing, and regulation, the new framework aims to help specialists understand both the possibilities and the limitations of personalized phage therapy.

The recommendations were developed through a structured consensus process under the AWMF (Association of the Scientific Medical Societies in Germany). They are valid from January 5, 2026, through June 29, 2030, with the responsible committee reviewing them annually to determine whether updates are needed.

While phage therapy still requires stronger evidence from controlled clinical trials, these international standards establish a clearer path for its responsible development. For patients facing infections that conventional antibiotics cannot adequately treat, bacteria-killing viruses may eventually provide another valuable option.

https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.title: Scientists discover a surprising clue to autism's origins hidden in the placenta
https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.text:
Scientists are still working to understand why autism develops. Genetics are known to play a major role, but researchers have also found that conditions during pregnancy can influence the likelihood of autism spectrum disorder.

A new study from Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory (CSHL) has uncovered a surprising connection between inflammation during pregnancy, changes in the placenta, and the development of autism-like traits in male mice. The findings suggest that certain developmental disruptions may begin much earlier than previously recognized, potentially offering new clues about autism's origins.

"To truly understand autism spectrum disorder, we have to look beyond the brain," CSHL Associate Professor Lucas Cheadle says. "Our work suggests that maternal immune activation and changes within the placenta are a gateway to autism for some unique individuals."

Scientists Identify an Early Window of Vulnerability

To investigate how inflammation affects fetal development, Cheadle and his colleagues triggered an immune response in pregnant mice at different stages of pregnancy. They used a substance that mimics the immune system's reaction to a viral infection without actually introducing a virus.

The researchers discovered that mouse fetuses were especially vulnerable when inflammation occurred 12.5 days into pregnancy. According to Irene Sanchez Martin, a postdoctoral researcher in Cheadle's laboratory, approximately one-third of the fetuses showed developmental abnormalities within just 24 hours.

Scientists have investigated the effects of maternal immune activation for decades, but these findings reveal signs of developmental disruption earlier than researchers had previously observed.

Even more striking was the difference between male and female fetuses. Across every experiment, autism-like traits appeared only in males, while females continued developing normally.

This unexpected distinction could provide insight into why autism is diagnosed substantially more often in boys than girls. What makes the finding especially intriguing is how early the difference appeared, before many of the biological changes normally associated with sex-specific development.

"It's really fascinating, because we're looking at an age which precedes hormonal surges. It precedes sexual differentiation in the brain and many other regions. So, it's surprising there would be a sex-based difference this early."

A Surprising Connection Between the Placenta and Autism

To determine why some developing mice were affected while others appeared protected, Cheadle and Sanchez Martin examined the placenta, the organ that connects a developing fetus to its mother and supports its growth throughout pregnancy.

Their attention centered on specialized cells called spongiotrophoblasts, which occupy a region of the mouse placenta where maternal and fetal cells interact.

In fetuses that developed normally, this part of the placenta remained healthy. However, male fetuses showing developmental abnormalities also had visible damage to these specialized cells.

Spongiotrophoblasts play an important role in helping the mother's immune system tolerate the developing fetus. This protection is essential because the fetus carries genetic material from both parents and is not genetically identical to the mother.

The researchers found that maternal immune activation could interfere with this protective function. When these placental cells become damaged, the mother's immune response may begin affecting the developing fetus in harmful ways.

Why Female Fetuses May Have a Hidden Advantage

The findings raise another intriguing question: Why were male fetuses vulnerable while females appeared unaffected?

One possibility is that male embryos produce distinctive proteins that can trigger an unfavorable maternal immune response following a viral infection. Another explanation is that female embryos possess some form of protection that helps them withstand inflammation during this sensitive developmental period.

Cheadle says, "A protective mechanism may exist within the female that could be harnessed to help the male. We're trying to understand how autism emerges in both sexes," he explains. "The evidence says that there are potentially different mechanisms."

These possibilities suggest that biological pathways involved in autism-like development may differ between males and females. Understanding those differences could help researchers identify why some individuals are more vulnerable to certain environmental influences during pregnancy.

Cheadle's team plans to investigate both male and female mice more closely to uncover the mechanisms responsible for these contrasting responses. Their work could eventually identify new targets for treatments and lead to strategies for intervening earlier in developmental processes associated with autism.

Although the findings come from experiments in mice and do not establish that the same mechanisms cause autism in humans, they highlight an unexpected possibility: Important clues to autism's earliest development may lie not only in the brain, but also in the placenta and its interactions with the maternal immune system.

https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.title: All 5 genetic “letters” of DNA and RNA discovered in a 4.5-billion-year-old asteroid
https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.text:
A new study reveals all five fundamental nucleobases – the molecular “letters” of life – have been detected in samples from the asteroid Ryugu.

Asteroid particles offer a glimpse into the chemical ingredients that may have helped kindle life on Earth. The Ryugu samples were returned from space in 2020 by Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency’s (JAXA) Hayabusa2 mission.

In 2023, an international team reported they had found one of the nucleobases in these samples – uracil. Now, in a study published in Nature Astronomy, a team of Japanese scientists has confirmed all five nucleobases are present in this pristine asteroid material.

This means these ingredients for life may have been widespread throughout the Solar System in its early years.

Nucleobases are nitrogen-containing organic molecules that form the “letters” of genetic information in DNA and RNA. The five main nucleobases are adenine and guanine (known as purines), as well as cytosine, thymine and uracil (known as pyrimidines).

These molecules combine with sugars and phosphates to yield nucleotides – the building blocks of genetic material. Without nucleobases, the genetic code that allows organisms to grow, reproduce and evolve would not exist.

By studying purines and pyrimidines in Ryugu samples, scientists can reconstruct the chemical history of primitive asteroids. In turn, this gives us a better understanding of how the building blocks of life may have been formed and existed across the Solar System.

Hayabusa2 delivered a total of 5.4 grams of pristine asteroid material. Researchers have to use ultra-clean lab conditions to avoid contaminating it. They extracted organic molecules using water and hydrocholoric acid, and then purified them for further detection.

They found all five nucleobases in the two Ryugu samples they analysed, in roughly similar amounts.

The new results align with previous findings on space rocks. The Murchison meteorite that fell in Australia in 1969, and the Orgueil meteorite in France, 1864, have previously yielded a rich variety of organic molecules, including nucleobases.

Of course, meteorites that land on Earth can be contaminated by their journey and landing. But pristine samples from NASA’s mission to asteroid Bennu also yielded all five nucleobases in 2025.

Asteroids such as Ryugu, Bennu, and the parent body of the Orgueil meteorite are remnants of the early Solar System. They can preserve materials largely unchanged for about 4.5 billion years.

Interestingly, these asteroids show chemical differences. Murchison is enriched in purines, while Bennu and Orgueil contain more pyrimidines. It is thought this balance may be influenced by ammonia, a key molecule that can shape which nucleobases can form.

By peering into Ryugu’s relatively pristine samples and comparing them with meteorites like Murchison and Orgueil, researchers are tracing the cosmic journey of life’s probable molecular ingredients.

Their results suggest key components of genetic material may have formed in space and later delivered to the early Earth. In other words, the story of life on our planet may be deeply connected to the chemistry of such ancient asteroids.

Together, these discoveries show that carbon-rich asteroids throughout the Solar System contain diverse prebiotic chemistry. However, the precise mixture of molecules – such as the balance between purines and pyrimidines – varies depending on the asteroid’s chemical environment and history.

Because the Ryugu samples were collected directly in space and protected from Earth’s contamination, they provide one of the clearest views of ancient Solar System chemistry.

The discovery of all five nucleobases on Ryugu suggests the molecular ingredients of life may have been already forming in space billions of years ago. Asteroids may have helped deliver those ingredients to the early Earth – making the origin of life part of a much larger cosmic chemical story.

https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.title: Scientists discover new Alzheimer’s drug that repairs DNA damage and reduces brain inflammation
https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.text:
Scientists at King's College London have identified a promising new strategy for fighting Alzheimer's disease that could address several of the condition's damaging effects at the same time. Their research suggests that an experimental drug originally developed for spinal cord injuries may help repair damaged DNA, reduce inflammation, and target biological changes associated with the disease.

The drug, known as KCL-286, produced encouraging results in a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease. Unlike treatments that focus primarily on the buildup of toxic proteins in the brain, this approach targets additional processes that can begin long before the disease reaches its advanced stages.

One particularly promising advantage is that KCL-286 has already completed Phase 1 human safety and tolerability trials as part of its earlier development. This could significantly shorten the path toward further clinical testing, although its effectiveness against Alzheimer's in humans has not yet been established.

"KCL-286 is a first-in-class, orally bioavailable small molecule that has already successfully cleared Phase 1 human safety and tolerability trials. This will dramatically cut down the traditional multi-year timeline required for new drug development," commented Professor Jonathan Corcoran, Professor of Neuroscience at the Institute of Psychiatry, Psychology & Neuroscience at King's College London.

The drug is a small molecule that can be taken by mouth, making it potentially more convenient to administer than treatments that require injections or infusions.

Why Alzheimer's Disease Is So Difficult to Treat

Alzheimer's disease involves a complicated series of changes in the brain, making it particularly challenging to develop effective treatments. Two of its best-known features are the abnormal accumulation of proteins called amyloid-beta and tau.

Amyloid-beta can collect into sticky deposits between nerve cells, while abnormal tau proteins can form tangles inside them. These changes interfere with normal brain function and are associated with the progressive loss of neurons, the specialized cells responsible for transmitting information throughout the brain.

Much of the effort to develop Alzheimer's treatments has focused on these two proteins. Although medications that remove amyloid-beta have demonstrated modest but measurable clinical benefits, they do not fully address the many biological processes involved in the disease.

Researchers are increasingly investigating other changes that may contribute to Alzheimer's, including damage to DNA and inflammation in the brain. Both can appear early in the disease process, making them potentially valuable targets for treatments designed to slow its progression.

In the new study, KCL-286 helped repair breaks in DNA and reduce inflammation in mice with Alzheimer's-like disease. These findings suggest that targeting several harmful processes simultaneously could offer a broader approach than focusing on amyloid-beta or tau alone.

"Our findings demonstrate that KCL-286 not only targets DNA damage but also reduces inflammation, two processes that occur very early in Alzheimer's disease progression. This highlights its potential as a disease-modifying therapy rather than simply addressing symptoms," said Dr. Maria Goncalves, who project-managed the drug development.

How Vitamin A Pathways Could Help Fight Alzheimer's

The drug works by activating a particular protein involved in the retinoic acid pathway, a biological system associated with how the body processes and uses vitamin A.

Vitamin A is best known for supporting healthy vision, but it also plays important roles in cellular development, gene regulation, and nervous system function. Retinoic acid, a substance derived from vitamin A, helps control the activity of genes involved in several essential biological processes.

Earlier research found that disruptions in this pathway were associated with the formation of amyloid-beta deposits in the brains of rats. These deposits resemble a major pathological feature of Alzheimer's disease, suggesting that the pathway may be relevant to the condition.

KCL-286 activates a specific protein within this system, offering researchers a way to influence biological processes connected to brain health and cellular repair.

The drug had already demonstrated an ability to promote the repair of DNA double-strand breaks in earlier research involving neuropathic pain, a type of pain caused by damage or dysfunction in the nervous system.

That discovery led scientists to investigate whether the same mechanism might also help address DNA damage associated with Alzheimer's disease.

Repairing a Dangerous Type of DNA Damage

DNA contains the genetic instructions that cells need to function properly. Although cells have natural systems for repairing damaged DNA, some forms of damage are particularly serious.

One example is a DNA double-strand break, which occurs when both strands of the DNA molecule are severed. These breaks can disrupt normal cellular activity and threaten cell survival if they are not properly repaired.

"DNA double-strand breaks are like a rope snapping completely in two, rather than just fraying at the edges. We found that KCL-286 promotes repair of these breaks, allowing us to target a key feature of Alzheimer's disease," said Professor Corcoran.

The researchers had another reason to suspect that KCL-286 might be useful against Alzheimer's. Previous work by the same team at King's College London identified molecular pathways shared by acute spinal cord injury and Alzheimer's disease.

Because the two conditions involve some overlapping biological mechanisms, the scientists believed that a drug developed to address nervous system damage after spinal cord injury might also improve certain Alzheimer's-related changes in neurons.

Their new findings support that possibility, showing that KCL-286 can influence several cellular pathways involved in the disease.

A Promising New Direction for Alzheimer's Treatment

The results highlight a potentially important shift in Alzheimer's research. Rather than concentrating on one hallmark of the disease, scientists are exploring treatments that address several interconnected causes of brain damage.

KCL-286 is particularly interesting because it targets DNA damage and inflammation, two processes that can emerge early in Alzheimer's progression. Its previous human safety testing also provides a potential advantage over entirely new drug candidates that have not yet entered clinical development.

However, the Alzheimer's findings remain preclinical. Additional studies and human clinical trials will be necessary to determine whether the drug can safely slow disease progression or improve outcomes in patients.

Natasha Hill, one of the first authors on the paper, said: "To develop an effective treatment for Alzheimer's disease, we need to tackle multiple aspects of the disease. KCL-286 was able to target multiple disease-relevant cellular pathways, some of which are initiated very early in the disease course."
