As SNVs can be correlated due to linkage disequilibrium in the genomes, we conducted a grouping analysis to select the most significant SNVs within each linkage disequilibrium block as representative tags of the independent signals (between-SNV r2 < 0.01; Methods). We then identified 940 independent SNV-MWAS signals (Fig. 3d,e and Supplementary Table 10) and 13,198 SNVs with a high probability of contribution to phenotypic variation (posterior inclusion probability > 0.8) (Supplementary Note 5 and Supplementary Fig. 6). Power assessment found that 70.5% of signals have more than 0.80 power to be detected given the observed effect size, sample size, and MAF (Supplementary Note 6 and Supplementary Fig. 7) and showed a negative correlation between MAF and effect size (Fig. 3f, R = −0.29, P = 6.06 × 10−20). We also assessed replication across cohorts of different ancestries. Among the 940 signals, 215 had both SNVs and phenotypes available in the Dutch and Tanzanian cohorts, with 161 (74.9%) signals involving 8 different phenotypes supported by both cohorts. For example, 48 association signals of 23 species with age are supported by Dutch and Tanzanian cohorts (Extended Data Fig. 5).

Notably, among the 940 SNV–phenotype association signals, 65.74% showed no significant associations at the abundance level (linear regression, Bonferroni-corrected meta-analysis P > 0.05; Fig. 3d,e). To illustrate the added value of SNV associations, we systematically assessed the phenotypic associations with the gut microbiome at the species abundance, SNV and structural variant levels. Among the 62,464 species–phenotype pairs (Methods), 533 showed associations at SNV level, 460 (86.30%) showed associations only at SNV level, and just 5 (0.9%) showed associations at all 3 levels (Extended Data Fig. 6 and Supplementary Tables 11–13). These results suggest that SNV-based analyses provide complementary information to structural variant- and abundance-based analyses when investigating host–microbiome associations4,5,23.

Among 940 signals, 810 were linked with intrinsic factors and 130 with exposure factors (Supplementary Note 7). We found 152 pairwise signal combinations involving 26 intrinsic phenotypes (excluding age, sex and height), in which the same tag SNVs were associated with 1 or more exposure factors (Fig. 3g and Supplementary Table 14). To assess whether exposure factors confounded the association signals of the intrinsic factors, we included the exposure factors as covariates in a robust association test using LMM-based permutation tests (999 permutations) for the association signals shared between intrinsic phenotypes and exposure factors. Owing to data completeness requirements (phenotype, exposure and SNV all had to be observed in at least 100 samples), we could evaluate 66 signals. Of these, 54 (81.8%) remained significant in at least 2 cohorts after controlling for the exposure factors (permutation P < 0.05), suggesting that the exposure factors did not confound the majority of the SNV associations with intrinsic phenotypes.

Age showed the highest number of association signals (99 signals) involving 8,117 SNVs across 42 species (meta-analysis P < 5.42 × 10−11) (Fig. 3d and Supplementary Table 10). We next assessed how well microbial SNVs could predict host age (Methods). To this end, we trained a machine learning model in the DMP cohort and evaluated its predictive performance in the other cohorts. The model explained 12.8–42.0% of the variation in age (R2) in the test datasets (Supplementary Notes 8 and 9, Supplementary Figs. 8–10 and Supplementary Tables 15 and 16), suggesting the predictive potential of gut microbial genetics for host age.

The most robust signal was supported by four independent cohorts (meta P < 5.42 × 10−11; Fig. 4a, Extended Data Fig. 7 and Supplementary Table 10). This signal contains five SNVs in the genome of F. prausnitzii_I (species ID: 102274), and their associations were not confounded by other microbial features, including bacterial lineage, species abundance and structural variants (Extended Data Fig. 8 and Supplementary Note 10). Notably, all five age-associated SNVs are missense variants located in the sarA_2 gene (gene ID: 102274_01471). The most significant SNV was 102274_1617247 (effect allele: T, effect allele frequency = 17.38%, β = 4.93, meta-analysis P = 1.00 × 10−17), showing that individuals carrying the T allele were 4.9 ± 0.6 years older (mean ± s.d.) than those without the T allele (Supplementary Table 10). The linkage disequilibrium analysis showed that the lead SNV 102274_1617247 is linked with the other four missense SNVs (R2 > 0.2; Fig. 4a,b) in sarA_2, and significant signals were detected in all cohorts except 300OB (Fig. 4c,d). Notably, all 300OB participants are older than 50 years and show a higher frequency of age-associated alleles compared with the other four Dutch cohorts, which have younger average ages (Extended Data Fig. 9). In other words, the age-associated allele in the sarA_2 gene of F. prausnitzii_I was enriched in an older population. Moreover, replication of the association across the Dutch and Tanzanian cohorts (Fig. 4d) suggests convergent genetic changes during host ageing in different ethnic groups.

The sarA_2 gene is a homologue of the oppA gene, which encodes an oligopeptide-binding lipoprotein with a Tat pathway signal sequence in its N terminus. The protein product of sarA_2 also forms an outer-membrane unit of an ATP-binding cassette (ABC)-type transporter system responsible for the uptake of oligopeptides—the oligopeptide permease (OPP) complex (Fig. 4b). We thus hypothesized that the age-associated missense SNVs may influence the function of the SarA_2 protein (also known as OppA). To test this, we assembled the OPP complex based on the AlphaFold3 prediction, including the five subunits encoded by sarA, oppB_4, oppC_4, oppD_4 and oppF_4 (Fig. 4e). This structural comparative analysis revealed that the predicted OPP structure is similar to the substrate-binding protein-dependent ABC transporter systems of Mycobacterium tuberculosis H37Rv (Protein Data Bank (PDB): 8JA7)24 and E. coli (PDB: 6CVL)25, supporting the plausibility of the predicted ABC transporter architecture. The sectional view of the predicted OPP complex structure revealed a tunnel-like cavity, with the OppA subunit acting as a gate for the transportation tunnel (Fig. 4e). Notably, the age-associated SNVs we identify are located in the cavity of OppA that relates to the tunnel (Fig. 4f), which suggests that these SNVs may affect the transportation function of the protein complex.

To infer the potential ligand of the OPP complex and better understand the underlying age-related changes in transport function, we examined the functional annotations of each subunit of the complex in detail. The OppF_4 subunit, encoded by the gene 102274_01467, was annotated as a GsiA subunit of the transporter for glutathione, an antioxidant that can prevent the damage caused by oxidative stress for both eukaryotes and prokaryotes. We then compared the protein sequences of OppA, OppB_4, OppC_4, OppD_4 and OppF_4 with 3,239 existing protein sequences of the ABC-type glutathione transport system and found that all 5 subunits match existing protein sequences (E-value < 1 × 10−10; Methods), indicating that the OPP complex may function as a glutathione transport system. In silico molecular docking analysis further revealed that glutathione can bind to the pocket region of the OppA protein (Fig. 4g and Extended Data Fig. 10). This suggests that age-associated mutations may affect glutathione uptake efficiency and help F. prausnitzii_I better resist ageing-related oxidative stress in the intestinal environment.

Motivated by the structural characterization of age-associated SNVs in sarA_2, we further systematically depicted the effect of associated SNVs in relation to protein structures. To this end, we focused on 6,799 associated missense SNVs, which are related to 3,724 proteins. We retrieved high-confidence three-dimensional structures of 2,141 (57.49%) proteins with 3,705 associated missense SNVs from the ESM Metagenomic Atlas26 and AlphaFoldDB27. We then systematically characterized these SNVs in relation to structural properties, including relative solvent accessibility (RSA, how exposed a residue is to a solvent), distance to ligand (DTL, distance from the residue to the nearest predicted pocket centre) and distance to protein–protein interaction interface (DTPPI, distance to the closest residue within a predicted protein–protein interface region) (Methods). We designated SNVs in low-DTPPI regions (DTPPI < 10 Å) or low-DTL regions (DTL < 15 Å) as structurally important28,29,30,31,32. Out of 3,705 SNVs, 752 (20.3%) were structurally important by these criteria, including 246 and 528 SNVs affecting amino acid residues in low-DTL and low-DTPPI regions, respectively (Fig. 5a and Supplementary Table 17). These SNVs were associated with 40 different phenotypes (Fig. 5b,c).

Age was associated with 165 structurally important SNVs in 122 genes (Fig. 5d,e). Among these, 54 were identified to be low-DTL SNVs, including 3 of the 5 missense SNVs in the OPP subunit encoded by sarA_2. In addition, seven low-DTL SNVs were found to be located near a pocket region of the serpin domain-containing protein (gene ID: 104463_01487) in Vescimonas sp900548615 (Fig. 5d and Supplementary Table 18). Previous evidence suggested that microbial serpins can inhibit host serine proteases, thereby affecting many physiological processes, such as inflammatory responses33,34. Moreover, 114 age-associated SNVs were identified as low-DTPPI SNVs, including 7 SNVs in the Vescimonas sp003539495 gene (gene ID: 102612_00172) encoding an HTH marR-type domain-containing protein located in the protein–protein interaction region (Fig. 5e and Supplementary Table 18). The bacterial marR homologues are transcriptional regulators that can regulate the expression of many genes related to oxidative stress response35. The marR protein functions as a homodimer, and the age-associated mutations with zero DTPPI we identified were located in the dimerization interface where the two marR monomers directly interact (Fig. 5f,g). To assess how these SNVs may influence marR dimerization, we performed an in silico alanine scanning mutagenesis analysis, systematically replacing each amino acid residue with alanine and quantifying the changes in binding free energy. The age-associated SNVs were clustered in regions showing substantial shifts in binding affinity in the alanine scan (Fig. 5h,i), indicating that they may alter marR dimerization and consequently its regulatory activity. Collectively, this structure-informed analysis highlights how integrating protein-level information can pinpoint potential functional consequences of SNVs, thereby facilitating prioritization of variants for experimental validation.

Over the past decade, genome-wide association studies (GWASs) and metagenomics-based microbiome studies have enhanced our understanding of the roles of host genetics and the symbiotic microbiome in host health. However, the application of GWASs to metagenomic data remains limited. In this study, we took advantage of the growing number of large-scale, deeply phenotyped cohorts with gut microbial metagenomic sequencing data to conduct a PheWAS on 244 phenotype and exposure factors through a gut microbial SNV-MWAS. This identified 940 independent meta-analysis association signals between SNVs of 101 gut microbial species and 69 human phenotypes and exposures. All associations are detailed in an online catalogue (https://fulab.web.rug.nl/SNV-MWAS/).

To carry out this study, we had to resolve a few technical challenges. First, metagenomic sequencing can result in a high genotype missing rate for low-abundance species when sequencing coverage is insufficient. Second, construction of a population genetic structure based on metagenomic data, rather than on isolate assemblies, is problematic owing to the possibility of within-species strain mixture within the host individual20,36,37. We thus adapted several solutions to make our work feasible and plausible. We first filtered out species with insufficient genotype information. We then retained sample pairs with sufficient overlap in SNVs to permit construction of population genetic structure based on kinship. Further, to assess whether a sample was very likely to be dominated by a single main strain within the corresponding species, we adapted the idea of phaseability37,38 to estimate the phased haplotypes on the basis of the distribution of allele frequencies (quasi-phaseability). We then retained only quasi-phaseable samples that were dominated by a single main strain for the association analysis.

Out of 940 study-wide significant signals, 482 (51.3%) carry at least one missense change. It is notable, but perhaps not surprising, that a large proportion of associated bacterial SNVs are located in the coding region but do not alter the protein sequence. It is already known from human GWASs that most single-nucleotide polymorphisms associated with complex traits and diseases lie in non-coding regions or mark synonymous substitutions39,40,41. These single-nucleotide polymorphisms have been found to be more likely to have regulatory roles in gene expression or to serve as proxies for causal variants. Although functional exploration of synonymous substitutions in bacterial genomes remains challenging, previous evidence suggests that synonymous changes can themselves affect gene expression or protein folding. Synonymous substitutions have been shown to alter mRNA structures and protein levels42, to perturb co-translational protein folding in E. coli43, and to influence translational efficiency by altering the secondary structure of mRNA in Salmonella enterica44. Future studies may explore the effect of synonymous SNVs on expression or folding using metatranscriptome or ribosome profiling readouts, along with targeted perturbations in representative isolates.

This study provides a catalogue of microbial SNVs associated with various human phenotypes, offering a valuable resource for validation and hypothesis generation. However, our resource primarily includes samples from the Netherlands, with the DMP cohort supplying nearly three-quarters of samples. This imbalance amplifies the discovery power of the DMP and raises the spectre of winner’s curse inflation in the effect sizes inferred from that cohort alone45. Although we included the Tanzanian cohort to test for replication of associations in a genetically and geographically distant population, its smaller sample size limits the power of the replication analysis. In future, more large-scale cohorts with diverse genetic and lifestyle backgrounds should be integrated to enhance gut microbial SNV-MWAS in a multi-ancestry context, especially including non-European populations46. Moreover, the biological interpretation of these signals currently remains limited. Although we applied structural biology to assess the functional importance of SNVs, we need to take several further key steps to move from association signals to hypotheses. These include identification of causal variants; molecular readouts through metatranscriptomics, metaproteomics and metabolomics; and phenotypic readouts of microorganisms (such as growth rate, biofilm formation and energy utilization). Looking further ahead, experimental validation will be required to confirm the underlying mechanisms, including approaches such as culturing bacterial isolates with different genetic variants on human induced pluripotent stem cell-based organ-on-a-chip models to assess the effect of bacterial SNVs on human cells1,47.

The DMP consists of 8,719 individuals and is part of the Lifelines study, a multi-disciplinary prospective population-based cohort study that utilizes a unique 3-generation design to examine health and health-related behaviours in 167,729 people living in the northern Netherlands. Lifelines utilizes a broad range of investigative procedures to assess the biomedical, socio-demographic, behavioural, physical and psychological factors that contribute to health and disease, with a special focus on multi-morbidity and complex genetics48. Microbiome data generation for the DMP is described in Gacesa et al.12. In brief, fresh-frozen faecal samples were collected from participants of the Lifelines cohort. Microbial DNA was isolated using the QIAamp Fast DNA Stool Mini Kit (FSK, Qiagen) by the QIAcube automated sample preparation system (Qiagen). Metagenomic sequencing was performed at Novogene, China using the Illumina HiSeq 2000 sequencer.

LLD is a sub-cohort of Lifelines that was established to explore the risk factors of complex diseases. In LLD, 1,539 individuals were included, with multi-layers of omics data collected at baseline in 2013 (ref. 13). In the current study, high-quality metagenomic sequencing data were available for 1,135 individuals (474 male and 661 female participants). The average age of LLD participants was 45.04 years (18–81 years, s.d. = 13.60 years). The average BMI was 25.26 kg m−2 (16.67–48.56 kg m−2, s.d. = 4.18 kg m−2). Microbiome data generation for the LLD is described in Zhernakova et al.49. In brief, fresh-frozen faecal samples were collected, and DNA was isolated with the AllPrep DNA/RNA Mini Kit (APK, Qiagen, 80204). Sequencing was performed using the Illumina HiSeq platform at the Broad Institute, Boston. 1,135 metagenomic samples passed quality control.

Follow-up APK samples of LLD were collected for 338 individuals (150 male and 188 female participants) at a second time point. The duration between the two time points ranged from 3.33 to 3.92 years (mean = 3.53 years, s.d. = 0.12 years). At baseline, the mean age of participants was 48.2 years (18–80 years, s.d. = 11.7 years) and their mean BMI was 25.4 kg m−2 (17.6–43.3 kg m−2, s.d. = 4.08 kg m−2). At follow-up, the mean age was 51.7 years (22–84 years, s.d. = 11.7 years) and the mean BMI was 25.6 kg m−2 (16.1–37.6 kg m−2, s.d. = 4.0 kg m−2). Two aliquots of each stool sample were processed and used for DNA isolation and library preparation using two kits: FSK (Qiagen) and APK (Qiagen, 80204). WGS was performed on the Illumina HiSeq 2000 platform.

The 500FG is part of the Human Functional Genomics Project (HFGP) and consists of 534 individuals. The average age of 517 500FG-FSK participants was 28.47 years (18–75 years, s.d. = 13.69 years), and the average BMI was 22.75 kg m−2 (15.09–35.43 kg m−2, s.d. = 2.85 kg m−2). The metagenomic data generation was described previously14,15. In brief, DNA was isolated from 517 and 471 faecal samples with the FSK (Qiagen) and APK (Qiagen, 80204), and libraries were sequenced on the Illumina HiSeq 2000 platform.

The 300OB cohort was established by Radboud University Medical Center, Nijmegen, the Netherlands50. In total, 298 older individuals with metagenomic data (132 female and 166 male participants) with a high BMI > 27 kg m−2 were enrolled in 300OB. The average age of 300OB participants was 67.07 (54–81 years, s.d. = 5.39 years). The average BMI was 30.73 kg m−2 (26.28–45.47 kg m−2, s.d. = 3.48 kg m−2). All participants were included between 2014 and 2016. The metagenomic sequencing of faecal samples was done using a similar protocol and analysis pipeline to LLD.

The 1000 Inflammatory Bowel Disease cohort (1000IBD) consists of patients with IBD recruited at the specialized IBD outpatient clinic of the University Medical Center Groningen (UMCG) in the Netherlands16,51. IBD diagnosis was made based on accepted radiological, endoscopic and histopathological evaluation. The 1000IBD cohort is 60.70% female and 39.30% male. The mean age of participants was 42.61 (18–82 years, s.d. = 14.69 years) and their mean BMI was 25.44 kg m−2 (15–49.4 kg m−2, s.d. = 5.05 kg m−2).

For analysis among non-Europeans, we included 300TZFG, a population cohort of 323 individuals from both rural and urban areas in the Kilimanjaro region of northern Tanzania. This study is part of the HFGP. Metagenomic data generation was described previously18. In brief, bacterial DNA was isolated using the APK (Qiagen), and libraries were sequenced on the Illumina NovaSeq 6000 platform. The average age of 300TZFG participants with metagenomic data was 33.08 years (17.76–66.43 years, s.d. = 11.25 years). The average BMI was 24.98 kg m−2 (16.41–41.91 kg m−2, s.d. = 4.93 kg m−2).

The levels of 15 bile acids and C4 concentrations in fasting plasma were quantified by liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC–MS/MS) procedures, as previously described52,53. In brief, for sample preparation, 25 µl plasma was mixed with 250 µl internal standard solution to precipitate proteins. Samples were centrifuged at 15,800g, and the supernatant poured into a clean glass tube. The fluid was evaporated under nitrogen at 40 °C. Before measuring, samples were reconstituted in 200 µl 50% methanol in water. For the quantitative determination of bile acids, we used a Nexera X2 Ultra High-Performance Liquid Chromatography system (Shimadzu), coupled to a SCIEX QTRAP 4500 MD triple quadrupole mass spectrometer (SCIEX) (UHPLC–MS/MS). The LC–MS/MS system is controlled by Analyst MD 1.6.2 software. Bile acids were separated with an ACQUITY UPLC BEH C18 Column (1.7 µm, 2.1 mm × 100 mm) equipped with an ACQUITY UPLC BEH C18 VanGuard Pre-Column (1.7 µm, 2.1 mm × 5 mm) (Waters). Separation was achieved in 28 min using 10 mM ammonium acetate in 20% acetonitrile (mobile phase A) and 10 mM ammonium acetate in 80% acetonitrile (mobile phase B), flow 0.4 ml min−1.

The proportions of 15 bile acids (with suffix ‘_p’) were calculated by dividing by total bile acid concentration. Additionally, eight different total bile acid concentrations and ratios were calculated: (1) total bile acid (Total_BAs) = sum of all bile acid concentrations; (2) total primary bile acid (Total_primary_BAs) = sum of all primary bile acid concentrations; (3) total secondary bile acid (Total_secondary_BAs) = sum of all secondary bile acid concentrations; (4) ratio of secondary bile acids to primary bile acids (Secondary_primary_ratio) = Total_secondary_BAs/Total_primary_BAs; (5) ratio of CA to CDCA concentrations (CA_CDCA_ratio) = (CA + TCA + GCA)/(CDCA + TCDCA + GCDCA); (6) ratio of unconjugated bile acid to conjugated bile acid concentrations = (CA + CDCA + DCA + LCA)/(TCA + GCA + TCDCA + GCDCA + TDCA + GDCA + TLCA + GLCA); (7) ratio of dehydroxylated CA to deconjugated CA concentrations (CA_dehydro_deconju_ratio) = (DCA + TDCA + GDCA)/(CA + TCA + GCA); and (8) ratio of taurine-conjugated bile acid to glycine-conjugated bile acid concentrations (Taurine_glycine_ratio) = (TCA + TCDCA + TDCA + TLCA)/(GCA + GCDCA + GDCA + GLCA).

The stool level of short-chain fatty acids was measured using gas chromatography–mass spectrometry, as previously described54,55.

Trimethylamine N-oxide and its precursors betaine, carnitine, deoxycarnitine, and choline were measured using LC–MS/MS, as previously described56,57. In brief, an online cleanup of the sample was carried out using an analytic column containing a C18 stationary phase, prior to its introduction into the mass spectrometer. This stationary phase did not retain the analytes, but it did retain significant matrix interferences, such as (phospho-)lipids58.

Untargeted metabolic profiling of fasting plasma samples was conducted at General Metabolics using flow-injection–time-of-flight mass spectrometry on an Agilent 6550Q-TOF system, as previously described59,60,61.

Telomere length was assessed using an automated multicolour flow–fluorescence in situ hybridization (Flow-FISH) technique as previously described62,63. In brief, white blood cells were obtained by lysing erythrocytes in whole blood with NH4Cl. These white blood cells were then combined with bovine thymocytes, which have a known telomere length and serve as an internal reference. The cells underwent denaturation in formamide at 87 °C, followed by hybridization with a fluorescein-labelled (CCCTAA)3 peptide nucleic acid probe specific to telomere sequences. They were then counterstained with the DNA dye LDS751. Flow cytometry was used to measure the fluorescence intensity in granulocytes, total lymphocytes, and lymphocyte subsets (identified by antibodies specific for CD20, CD45RA and CD57). This fluorescence intensity, compared to internal control cells and unstained controls, was used to determine the median telomere length from duplicate measurements.

Signal joint excision circles produced during T cell development (sjTREC) expression was quantified using quantitative PCR (qPCR) as previously described63. In brief, DNA was extracted from whole blood using proteinase K digestion, phenol extraction, and isopropanol precipitation. We then used TaqMan qPCR on a ViiA 7 system (Life Technologies) to quantify sjTREC expression. The qPCR was performed on 75–100 ng of DNA in a 12 μl reaction mix with 18 µM of sjTREC primers (5′-TCGTGAGAACGGTGAATGAAG-3′ and 5′-CCATGCTGACACCTCTGGTT-3′) and albumin primers (5′-TGAACAGGCGACCATGCTT-3′ and 5′-CTCTCCTTCTCAGAAAGTGTGCATAT-3′) and 5 µM probes for sjTREC (5′-(FAM) CACGGTGATGCATAGGCACCTGC-3′ (TAMRA)) and albumin (5′-(FAM) TGCTGAAACATTCACCTTCCATGCAGA -3′ (TAMRA)). The PCR protocol was 50 °C for 2 min, 95 °C for 15 min, followed by 45 cycles of 95 °C for 15 s and 60 °C for 30 s. Reactions were done in duplicate. Fluorescence from probe cleavage was measured at the threshold cycle (CT). Valid results had a duplicate s.d. ≤ 1. Normalized sjTREC expression was calculated from the difference between average CT values of albumin and sjTREC.

We removed host genome-contaminated reads and low-quality reads from the raw metagenomic sequencing data using KneadData (v0.7.4), Bowtie2 (v2.3.4.3)64 and Trimmomatic (v0.39)65. In brief, the data-cleaning procedure includes two main steps: (1) filtering out human genome-contaminated reads by aligning raw reads to the human reference genome (GRCh37–hg19) and (2) removing adaptor sequences and low-quality reads using Trimmomatic with default settings (SLIDINGWINDOW:4:20 MINLEN:50).

We estimated the abundances of reference genomes in metagenomic samples using CoverM (v0.7.0)66 based on the identical reference genomes used in metagenomic SNV detection.

Structural variants were defined as within-species highly variable genomic fragments (>1 kb) across microbial genomes. Structural variants of the gut microbiome were detected from cleaned metagenomic reads using SGVFinder (v2.0)4 based on the identical reference genomes used by metagenomic SNV detection.

We characterized the SNVs for metagenomic samples using GT-Pro (v1.0.1) based on the pre-constructed sck-mer database11. In brief, a catalogue of 104 million biallelic SNVs in the core genomic region of 909 gut microbial species was initially constructed based on Unified Human Gastrointestinal Genome (UHGG) assemblies, the genotypes of the gut microbial SNVs were tagged by species-specific k-mers, and a k-mer-based gut microbiome metagenomic SNV panel was constructed. GT-Pro directly conducted genotyping for gut microbiota from metagenomic sequencing data by k-mer-searching and matching the genotype k-mers of the metagenomic SNV panel. GT-Pro output was further converted to SNV dosage format, with genotype indicating the frequency of the alternative allele.

We calculated allele frequencies based explicitly on the average reference or alternative allele proportions across samples:

For a given SNV across n samples, let:

Ri = relative abundance (proportion) of the reference allele in sample i (for example, 0.7)

Ai = relative abundance (proportion) of the alternative allele in sample i (for example, 0.3)

These values typically sum to 1 per sample if only two alleles are considered.

We then performed quality control in each cohort separately, filtering out SNVs with a high missing rate (>90%) or low MAF (<0.05) to get the cohort-specific common SNVs. We next counted the number of SNVs retained for each species in each cohort and removed species with a low common SNV number (<1,000). The manipulation and quality control of genotype datasets were conducted using PLINK2 (v2.0.0-a.6.9LM)67.

The genes of gut microbial reference genomes were predicted and annotated using Bakta68 (v1.10.1, database v5.1). The functional effects of the common SNVs were annotated using SnpEff (v5.1f)21.

For each species, we calculated the species-specific between-sample genetic dissimilarity Di,j measured by a Manhattan distance scaled by the number of shared SNVs within each sample pair using the parallelDist() function in R package parallelDist (v0.2.6). Sample pairs sharing <1,000 SNVs were skipped for the genetic dissimilarity calculation, and the corresponding Di,j were marked as missing values. To maximize the size of the retained sample with no missing value, we removed the sample with the highest number of missing values from the matrix in each round until there are no missing values in the matrix. We further calculated the between-sample genetic relatedness, Ri,j = 1 – Di,j, and the matrix MR containing Ri,j was used as the representative of population genetic structure. We performed principal coordinate analysis on the genetic dissimilarity matrices MD using the pcoa() function from R package ape (v5.7-1) with the parameter correction = “cailliez”.

To depict the linkage disequilibrium (LD) structure overview of each species, we randomly extracted 1,000 SNVs from the cleaned genotype dataset using plink2 (v2.0.0-a.6.9LM) with the parameters -thin-count 1000. We then calculated the LD as a squared correlation for all pairs of extracted SNVs using plink2 with the parameters -r2 inter-chr yes-really -ld-window-r2 0. We visualized the whole-genome LD structure using LDBlockShow (v1.40)69 with the parameters -SeleVar 2 -NoShowLDist 100000000 -OutPdf -OutPng.

The co-existence of multiple strains of a species within the host may bias the position of the sample in the population genetic structure and decrease the power of association analysis. For a given species, samples in which > 80% of the SNVs have the same allele in > 90% of the reads were considered quasi-phaseable, meaning the sample is very likely to be dominated by one strain of the corresponding species. The criterion and concept of quasi-phaseability were described before38,70.

We first manually integrated and curated the phenotypes from different cohorts and datasets to ensure the consistency of units. Each phenotype was analysed with a LMM that contained: (1) fixed effects for corresponding species abundance, age, sex and sequencing depth, and (2) a random-effect term capturing within-species population structure, with the variance–covariance of this random effect specified by the sample-by-sample kinship matrix (MR). When sex or age was the trait analysed, that variable was omitted from the covariate list. The LMM-based analysis was conducted using EMMAX (version beta-07Mar2010)71 with the parameters emmax -d 10 -t genotype.file -p phenotype.file -c covariate.file -k kinship.file -o output -Z. The association analyses were performed for each cohort and each species separately, with only the quasi-phaseable samples of the corresponding species included for the association analysis. For the SNV–phenotype pairs available in two or more independent cohorts (DMP, LLD1, 500FG, 300OB, IBD and 300TZFG), a follow-up meta-analysis was performed in the independent datasets (excluding the LLD2 and 500FG-APK datasets) using the Metal software (v2020-05-05)72 with default options (weighting cohort-based P values according to sample size). To ensure robustness and further reduce the chances of false discovery of identified associations, we conducted a permutational LMM with 999 times permutation following the Monte Carlo procedure within each cohort to assess the robustness of significant associations. Regional association plots showing LD structures on the gene regions covering the association signals were generated using LDBlockShow (v1.40)69.

The threshold of study-wide significance was determined by the total number of tested phenotype–SNV pairs (922,497,753) using the Bonferroni method: 0.05/no. of phenotype–SNV pairs = 5.42 × 10−11. Similarly, suggestive significance was determined using Bonferroni correction based on the total number of tested SNVs in each species and for each phenotype. Thus the suggestive significance did not control for the number of species and phenotypes involved in the study.

The SNVs could be correlated due to LD in the genomes. To count the number of independent association signals, we further conducted a grouping analysis that grouped interrelated SNVs by LD and picked the most significant SNVs within each LD block as representatives or tags of the independent signals (between-SNV r2 > 0.01, window size = 10,000 kbp) using PLINK2 (v2.0.0-a.6.9LM)67. The primary and secondary significance cut-offs used in PLINK2 were study-wide significance (5.42 × 10−11) and species-wide significance (species-specific) cut-offs. We visualized the local LD structure using LDBlockShow (v1.40)69 with the parameters -SeleVar 2 -NoShowLDist 100000000 -OutPdf -OutPng.

We performed a post-hoc approximate power analysis for the tag SNVs of significant associations using the genpwr package (v1.0.4) in R. The proportion of phenotypic variance explained (R2) was estimated from the observed effect size, standard error, observed sample size and MAF using the pheno_var_explained() function. Power was then calculated with power.calc.linear() under an additive genetic model and a study-wide significance threshold of α = 5.42 × 10−11. To evaluate the effect of sample size, power was also computed across fixed sample sizes (n = 100, 500, 1,000, 5,000 and 10,000) for the tag SNVs of significant associations.

As AlphaFold3 supports structure prediction for protein complexes, the three-dimensional (3D) structures of the OPP complex were modelled using AlphaFold3 (ref. 73) and visualized in ChimeraX (v1.10.1)74 and PyMOL (v2.5.7). However, according to the terms of use of the AlphaFold3 server, its output cannot be used in docking or screening tools (https://alphafoldserver.com/about). We therefore used local AlphaFold2 for monomer protein structure prediction and conducted in silico docking and other downstream analyses. To explore interactions between OppA/SarA_2 and glutathione, the protein structure of OppA/SarA_2 was first predicted using AlphaFold2 (v2.3.1)75 for both the wild-type and mutated protein sequences under monomer settings. The default reference databases and a template cut-off date of 14 May 2020 were used to guide the structure generation. For each experiment, five models were produced and further refined using graphics processing unit-based AMBER relaxation. The best model, based on pLDDT confidence scores (mean ≥ 90), was selected for downstream analysis, excluding the low-confidence N-terminal residues. The glutathione structure was downloaded from PubChem (https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/) and converted into PDB format. Ligand-binding pockets in the OppA/SarA_2 structure were predicted using P2Rank (v2.5)76, focusing on residues with high ligand-binding probabilities (>0.6) from top-scoring pockets (probability > 0.85). These residues were then used as active sites in HADDOCK (v2.4)77,78, a docking platform that generated 200 structural complexes for each variant. The top four docked poses from the best-scoring cluster were selected and energy-minimized in water. Binding free energies (ΔG) were estimated using PRODIGY-LIG (v1.1.4)79,80, and PLIP (v2025)81 was used to identify non-covalent interactions. As a docking benchmark, a literature-derived82,83 tripeptide panel representing basic (KAK, KWK, KKK), neutral (AAA, GFG, GAG) and acidic (EEE, DED) chemistries was docked to the same OppA binding site using the same set of active residues defined for the glutathione docking in HPEPDOCK (v2.0)84. All the resulting complexes were refined through water minimization in HADDOCK (v2.4)77, and binding free energies were estimated with PRODIGY-LIG (v1.1.4)79.

The protein structural property analysis was conducted using an internal pipeline (https://github.com/GArcho44/snvs-annotation-pipeline). In brief, to interpret effect of SNVs at the protein structure level, only missense variants in coding regions were retained. Functional gene annotations from Bakta (v1.10.1)68 and UniProt (https://www.uniprot.org/)85,86 enabled linkage of genes to protein sequences within UniRef100 and consequently to structure entries in the AlphaFold Database (AlphaFoldDB, v2022)27. Recognizing that many genes lacked direct matches in UniRef100, we applied a homology-based approach to expand structural coverage. Gene coding sequences were extracted using GffRead (v0.12.7)87 and translated to proteins with EMBOSS transeq (v6.6.0)88. The resulting sequences were queried against AlphaFoldDB and ESM Metagenomic Atlas (version 1 November 2022, https://esmatlas.com/)26 using DIAMOND BLASTP (v2.0.15)89, retaining only full-length matches with ≥98% identity. When multiple matches occurred, the best match was selected by identity score, preferring AlphaFoldDB entries when there was a tie. Protein accessions (UniProtKB or MGnify) were then used to retrieve high-confidence structural models (mean pLDDT ≥80) via custom application programming interfaces. Multiple per-residue properties were measured on these curated protein models to functionally annotate the structural properties of SNVs. Relative solvent accessibility (RSA) was calculated using DSSP (v3.0.0)90,91, normalizing surface exposure per residue against empirical maxima. Ligand-binding pockets were detected using fpocket (v4.2.1)92 and rescored with fpocketPRANK to boost detection sensitivity. Binding residues were defined from pockets with druggability score > 0.5. Each residue’s distance to ligand (DTL) was computed based on the minimal Euclidean distance to the closest pocket centre. Protein–protein interaction interfaces were predicted using PeSTo (model version i_v4_1)93. Residues with interface confidence scores > 0.5 were grouped into clusters based on spatial proximity (Cα–Cα < 10 Å), and only high-confidence clusters (average score > 0.8, pLDDT > 0.7 and ≥6 residues) were retained. Each residue’s distance to protein-protein interface (DTPPI) was calculated based on Euclidean distance to closest residue of predicted interface.

The 3D structure of the marR homologue dimer was modelled using AlphaFold3 (ref. 73) and visualized with ChimeraX (v1.10.1)74. Protein-protein interface analysis, specifically in silico alanine scanning, was performed using the mCSM-PPI2 web server94.

The original gene annotation was conducted using Prokka (v1.13.3)95, and the age-association signal was identified in the gene annotated as sarA (UniProtKB: P31306), which is located next to oppB, oppC, oppD and oppF. The sarA gene encodes a periplasmic oligopeptide-binding protein, SarA, and contains an oppA gene family domain. According to the literature96,97, OppABCDF is a typical oligopeptide permease (OPP) or ABC transport system complex. Therefore, sarA, oppB, oppC, oppD, and oppF could form a gene cluster whose products can assemble into an oligopeptide ABC-transport system complex.

To confirm whether the gene organization of these five genes is conserved as a gene cluster across different bacterial genomes within the F. prausnitzii taxonomic clade, we conducted a gene cluster search using cblaster (v1.3.20)98 in 17,496 assemblies of F. prausnitzii from publicly available databases such as UHGG (v2.0.2)99, SPIRE100, and our in-house F. prausnitzii MAG and isolate genomes6. We found that all 5 genes co-occur in 2,185 F. prausnitzii genomes, situated close to each other (maximum distance between any 2 hits in a cluster <20 kb). The F. prausnitzii species with the complete OPP operon are Faecalibacterium butyricigenerans (223), Faecalibacterium duncaniae (3), Faecalibacterium longum (1,568), F. prausnitzii _I (372), Faecalibacterium sp900539945 (1), Faecalibacterium sp934514285 (15) and 3 unclassified genomes. Therefore, the SarA gene and the other four genes (oppB, oppC, oppD and oppF) do form a gene cluster or operon that is conserved in its gene organization within the F. prausnitzii genome. We also conducted 3D structure prediction using AlphaFold3 for the protein complex, compared it to the experimentally derived structures, and found that the predicted structure is similar to experimentally validated ABC transporter structures in M. tuberculosis (PDB: 8JA7)24 and E. coli MetNI (PDB: 6CVL)25. Therefore, the SarA with the OppA domain can function as OppA and can assemble with the other four subunits to form an OPP complex.

To further identify the potential ligand of this OPP complex, we conducted gene function annotation with Bakta (v1.11.0)68. We found that one of the five genes in the OPP gene cluster was annotated as an ABC-type glutathione transport system ATPase component (gsiA). We then compared the protein sequences of SarA (OppA), OppB, OppC, OppD and OppF to 3,239 existing protein sequences of the ABC-type glutathione transport system using blastp (v2.16.0 + ). We found that all five proteins match existing protein sequences of the ABC-type glutathione transport system (E-value < 1.00 × 10−10). The OPP complex may therefore function as a glutathione transport system.

To identify the genes from reference genomes potentially related to nicotine degradation, we obtained sequences of 92 proteins involved in two nicotine-degradation pathways from the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) (KEGG entries: M00810 and M00811) and searched for them in the genes of 909 reference genomes using tblastn (v2.14.1-gompi-2023a)101. In total, we identified 2,434 genes similar to known nicotine-degradation genes (E-value < 1.00 × 10−10).

We constructed a host age prediction model based on light gradient-boosting machine implemented in the R package lightgbm (v3.3.5). To ensure generalizability of the model, we used tidymodels (v1.1.0) to conduct nested cross-validation with a five-times-fivefold split for the outer loop and a fivefold split for the inner loop to assess the predictive power of gut microbial SNVs on host age. To avoid information leakage for the samples collected from individuals with close microbiome kinship, samples from the same lineage group were assigned to the same split dataset (either internal train dataset or internal test dataset) using the group_vfold_cv() function during the nested cross-validation procedure. We defined lineage groups using all SNVs used for age model training, pooled across species. Pairwise sample distances (scaled Manhattan distance) D were computed, and kinship was then defined as K = 1 – D. From D = 1 – K, we built a neighbour-joining tree and rooted it to orient the cut. Lineage groups were assigned by a single tree-height cut at h = (1 – c)/2 with kinship cut-off c = 0.9 (thus h = 0.05, equivalent to distance cut-off 0.1). Each descendant clade crossing this cut was then treated as one lineage group. In all cross-validation runs, we used a set of predetermined hyperparameters: trees = 2000, tree_depth = 15, min_n = 30, sample_size = 0.6, mtry = round(0.2 * total_feature_number), and learning_rate = 0.01. We estimated the importance of features using Shapley additive explanation, which assigns each feature an importance value for a particular prediction. After 5 × 5 rounds of fivefold cross-validation, we calculated the median importance value of each SNV feature, sorted the SNV features from high to low median importance values, cumulatively summed the median importance values until we reached 95% of the total sum of importance values, and took the counted SNV features as the predictive features for the final model. Because lineage groups were defined using SNVs pooled across species, this approach captures overall microbiome kinship but may not fully prevent information leakage for individual species whose species-specific kinship structure differs from the overall pattern.

The partial correlation test was conducted using the pcor() function of R package ppcor (v1.1). For the partial correlations between gut microbial SNV age and other biological age indices and between gut microbial SNV age and host intrinsic phenotypes, we used partial Spearman’s correlation, adjusting for chronological age. For the partial correlations between gut microbial SNV age and untargeted blood metabolome, we used a partial Pearson correlation, adjusting for chronological age, sex and blood creatinine level.

Per-cohort linear mixed model association results were combined by meta-analysis, with study-wide significance defined as P < 5.42×10−11. Robust associations required nominal significance (Ppermutation <0.05) in two or more cohorts with consistent effect direction and confirmation by permutation testing (Ppermutation <0.05 in ≥ 2 cohorts). Linked SNVs (r² > 0.01 within 10 Mb) were grouped to yield independent signals. Numbers in blue indicate counts after each filtering step.

The bar plot shows the ratio of SNV impact category in the associated SNVs of each phenotype (number of associated SNVs >10), all phenotypes, and all common SNVs (background). Phenotypes are sorted by the ratio of start/stop codon variants and missense variants. The horizontal dashed red line is the reference line indicating the ratio of start/stop codon variants and missense variants in the background (0.176). The red “+” and blue “-” indicate significant enrichment and depletion, respectively, of start/stop codon variants and missense variants compared to the background SNVs (Two-sided Chi-squared test, P < 0.05). Significant enrichment was observed for Lifelines protein diet score (P = 2.01 × 10−4), on-a-diet behaviour during the past month (P = 1.09 × 10−10), thrombocyte count (P = 2.92 × 10−4), waist circumference (P = 0.0366), beta blocker intake (P = 0.0193), and sex (P = 0.0211). Significant depletion was observed for BMI (P = 0.0104), DBP (P = 0.0376), HbA1c (P = 0.0467), lymphocyte count (P = 0.00281), SBP (P = 0.00360), and body weight (P = 0.0357). P values were not adjusted for multiple comparisons.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.title: A spatiotemporal cancer cell trajectory underlies glioblastoma heterogeneity
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.author: Omer Ali Bayraktar
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.text:
Nature (2026) Cite this article

Cancer cells show highly heterogeneous and plastic states in glioblastoma, an incurable brain tumour1,2,3,4,5. However, how these malignant states arise and whether they follow defined cellular trajectories across tumours is poorly understood. Here we generated a deep single-cell and spatial multi-omic atlas of human glioblastoma that pairs transcriptomic, epigenomic and genomic profiling of 12 tumours across many regions. We identify that glioblastoma heterogeneity is driven by spatially patterned transitions of cancer cells from developmental-like states towards those defined by a glial injury response and hypoxia. This cellular trajectory regionalizes tumours into distinct tissue microenvironments and manifests in a molecularly conserved manner across tumours as well as genetically distinct tumour subclones. Consistently, using a new deep-learning framework to map cancer cell states jointly with clones in situ, we show that tumour subclones are finely spatially intermixed through glioblastoma tissue microenvironments. We validate this cellular trajectory by using somatic mutation-based hierarchies in vivo and an experimental patient-derived organoid model ex vivo. Finally, we show that this cancer cell trajectory is intimately linked to myeloid heterogeneity and unfolds across regionalized myeloid signalling environments. Our findings define a stereotyped trajectory of cancer cells in glioblastoma and unify glioblastoma tumour heterogeneity into a tractable cellular and tissue framework.

The extensive tumour heterogeneity of glioblastoma (GB), an incurable adult brain cancer, presents a major obstacle to treatment. Nearly two decades of molecular profiling has found that malignant cells exist across a spectrum of cellular states within each tumour, resembling developmental neural progenitors as well as mesenchymal-like and injury response states1,2,3,4,5. These states are suggested to vary in abundance across tumours and stratify GBs into subtypes1,2. Furthermore, patient-derived xenografts have shown that malignant cells can transition across cellular states, indicating their plasticity2,6. Despite these extensive efforts, we still do not understand how cancer cells diversify into distinct states and give rise to GB heterogeneity. In particular, whether malignant cells follow stereotyped or variable cellular trajectories across GB tumours is unknown. A cancer cell trajectory that is conserved and tractable across GBs would present a highly attractive therapeutic target.

Single-cell, bulk and spatial genomics have revealed stereotypical aspects of GBs. Several malignant cell states can be detected within each tumour2,5,7 and their single-cell transcriptional profiles can be mapped onto an axis between developmental-like (dev-like) and injury response-associated gene expression programs4,8. Genetic heterogeneity1,2 and tumour microenvironment (TME) signals9 also influence malignant cell state identity. Furthermore, these states show a recurrent spatial organization across tumours5,10. Yet, these observations have not been linked together to resolve malignant cellular trajectories in GB, in part due to the lack of multimodal profiling efforts that can integrate insights from various cell and tissue atlassing technologies. Here we address this challenge by means of deep single-cell and spatial multi-omic profiling of human GBs and identify that a stereotyped spatiotemporal trajectory of cancer cells gives rise to GB heterogeneity.

To comprehensively profile GB heterogeneity, we generated a single-cell and spatial multi-omic atlas of 12 isocitrate dehydrogenase wild-type (IDH-wt) primary GB tumours (Fig. 1a and Supplementary Table 1), combining three main approaches. First, we profiled each tumour across many sites, ranging from 4 sites (roughly 1.25 cm3 each) for most cases to 15 sites effectively covering one whole tumour (Extended Data Fig. 1a and Supplementary Fig. 1), spanning 57 tumour sites in total. Second, we generated paired single-nuclei and spatial omic data from each sampling site, profiling consecutive tissue sections with single-nuclei joint transcriptome sequencing and chromatin accessibility sequencing (‘multiome’ snRNA + ATAC-seq) and Visium spatial transcriptomics (ST) (Fig. 1a). Select sites were assayed with orthogonal Xenium ST and immunohistochemistry, as well as whole-genome sequencing (WGS) of tumour microbiopsies (Supplementary Fig. 1). Third, we profiled large numbers of nuclei (more than 1 million) and spatial tissue sections (more than 0.3 million spatial transcriptomes across 97 Visium sections) (Supplementary Table 2). The resulting ‘GBM-space’ dataset, accessible on a user-friendly interactive webportal11 (www.gbmspace.org/), enables comprehensive multimodal characterization of GB and presents a unique holistic tumour atlas for cancer research.

To examine GB heterogeneity, we first annotated malignant and TME cell states in our multiome data. After standard data processing workflows, we filtered nuclei on the basis of quality of both RNA and ATAC profiles, resulting in 1,025,329 nuclei with more than 85,000 nuclei per tumour on average (Methods, Fig. 1a and Extended Data Fig. 1b,c). We then annotated transcriptomic cell states in snRNA-seq data and examined ATAC data in a companion study to map GB gene regulatory networks12.

We integrated snRNA-seq data using scVI13 to account for batch variations, then distinguished malignant clusters on the basis of inferred copy number (CN) gain of chromosome (chr.) 7 and loss of chr. 10, as well as enrichment of known GB expression programs2 (Fig. 1b and Supplementary Figs. 2 and 3). Subclustering yielded 28 malignant clusters, including 10 highly common clusters present across 50% of the tumours, as well as 71 TME clusters (Fig. 1c and Supplementary Fig. 4).

We annotated malignant clusters by relating them to GB cell state gene programs described in ref. 2 and developing human brain single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) data14 as well as gene-set enrichment analysis (Methods and Supplementary Fig. 5a,b). As a result, we hierarchically grouped malignant clusters into four main classes and nine subclasses of GB cell states that were each observed across several tumours (Fig. 1c,d, Supplementary Fig. 4a and Supplementary Table 4).

Two main classes of GB cell states resembled distinct developmental progenitors: neural progenitor-like and oligodendrocyte progenitor-like (NPC-OPC-like) and neuronal progenitor-like and neuronal-like (NPC-neuronal-like) cells. These two dev-like states matched those previously described in ref. 2 and expressed respective developmental markers of oligodendrocyte (PDGFRA, OLIG1) and neuronal lineages (MYT1L, STMN2) (Fig. 1c and Supplementary Note 1).

The third main GB cell state showed a transcriptomic spectrum from astrocyte progenitor (AC-prog)-like to gliosis-like (that is, glial injury response) and hypoxic states, broadly expressing core astrocyte markers (SLC1A3, GFAP) (Fig. 1c). Whereas AC-prog-like cells showed Neftel ‘AC-like’ signatures and resembled developmental glioblasts, AC-gliosis and gliosis-like cells expressed genes related to wound healing and injury response (VIM, SERPINE1) and angiogenesis (VEGFA) and the remaining cells were defined by hypoxia (HILPDA) (Fig. 1c). The gliosis-hypoxic cells were initially described as mesenchymal-like states1,2 defined by Neftel ‘MES1-2’ programs. Recently, they were reinterpreted as more similar to reactive astrocytes responding to injury4 and glial wound healing states4,8. Here we adopted the latter nomenclature that better reflected malignant cellular trajectories in our atlas (sections below). The final main malignant state represented proliferative cells. Although dominated by G2M and S phase gene expression, we resolved that these cells represent actively cycling analogues of main GB cell states (Fig. 1c, Supplementary Fig. 6a and Supplementary Note 1).

GB cell states showed substantial inter-tumour and intra-tumour heterogeneity. Most tumours showed a dominant GB cell state among the main classes (for example, NPC-OPC-like for AT5 and 9) (Fig. 1d, left). However, despite their stratification, each tumour contained substantial fractions of both dev-like and AC-gliosis-hypoxia cells. Two tumours (AT4 and 10) showed near equal proportions of both classes, whereas in others, the minority states represented 5–21% of all malignant cells (Fig. 1d and Supplementary Table 4). Individual sampling sites also contained a mixture of GB states broadly reflecting the parent tumour (Supplementary Fig. 8b,c). Yet, we could often identify at least one site per tumour with a unique cell state composition. In a striking example, tumour AT10 showed distinct dominant GB cell states at each site (Fig. 1d, right). Consistent with other studies5,7,15, these observations show that single biopsies can be confounded to stratify GB tumour phenotypes.

We also captured all main cell lineages in the GB TME (Supplementary Figs. 4b and 7). Although OPCs, mature oligodendrocytes and myeloid cells were the most abundant, we also annotated fine-grained neurons, astrocytes, lymphocytes and vasculature (Supplementary Note 1). Taken together, our single-nuclei transcriptomic atlas presents a deep, fine-grained cellular census of malignant and TME states in GB.

Next, we examined the spatial organization of GB cell states. To resolve fine GB states in Visium ST data, we mapped malignant and TME clusters from each patient’s snRNA-seq profile to their matched Visium data using cell2location16 (Fig. 2a). Whereas integrating paired snRNA-seq and ST accounted for inter-tumour heterogeneity, it also enabled us to link GB spatial organization to malignant cell trajectories, subclonal organization and TME signalling that we subsequently inferred from snRNA-seq.

GB cell states showed striking segregation across all tumours. In particular, gliosis and hypoxia cell states segregated from dev-like states (Extended Data Fig. 2), consistent with previous surveys10,15. GB states also showed regional heterogeneity across tumour sampling sites (Extended Data Fig. 2 and Supplementary Fig. 8c). We also observed concordant spatial mapping results between cell2location and alternative computational methods, especially for highly abundant GB cell states (Methods and Supplementary Fig. 10a–c).

We then asked whether GBs have a conserved spatial architecture. To determine whether malignant and TME cells assemble into stereotyped tissue microenvironments (TMs), we first identified spatially colocalized cell states (that is, microenvironments) per tumour by means of non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) of cell2location results16 (Fig. 2a and Methods). This resulted in 192 factors across our cohort (Supplementary Table 7 and Supplementary Fig. 11a), which we then clustered by their cell state similarity to identify 16 TMs that recurrently appear across tumours (Fig. 2b).

We annotated the recurrent GB TMs on the basis of their cellular composition and anatomical location (Fig. 2b,c and Supplementary Note 2). ‘Tumour’ TMs represented malignant, immune and vasculature states in the tumour core, whereas ‘infiltrated’ TMs spanned non-malignant neurons and glia in the surrounding infiltrated regions (Fig. 2b,c). Most tumour TMs were defined by their distinct GB cell state composition and appeared across many tumours (Extended Data Fig. 3). Core malignant TMs such as Dev-like (OPC), Dev-like (AC), Proliferative, Gliosis transition, Gliosis and Hypoxic 1 were detected in more than 50% of tumours, whereas others such as Dev-like (Neuron) and Hypoxic 2 were rare. Crucially, 8 out of 12 tumours (for example, AT3, AT10) showed nearly the full complement of core TMs (Extended Data Fig. 3a), suggesting these features are fundamental to GB organization. Finally, we recapitulated these TMs with cell2location alternatives on our GB atlas and on public GB Visium ST datasets10,15 (Methods and Supplementary Fig. 12).

Previous ST studies have mapped hypoxic ‘mesenchymal’-like states at the necrotic core and dev-like states at the infiltrating edge of tumours10,15. Correlating GB TMs with tumour anatomy showed Dev-like TMs occurred in the cellular tumour compartment bordering the infiltrating tumour and leading edge. By contrast, Gliosis and Hypoxia TMs were localized further from the infiltrating regions, forming layered zones around perinecrotic and necrotic areas (Fig. 2c, Extended Data Fig. 3a and Supplementary Note 2).

To quantify their precise spatial arrangement, we calculated the pairwise spatial proximities of GB TMs across all tumours (n = 97 Visium sections) into a network graph (Methods). This showed that GB TMs are ordered along a main anatomical axis between the infiltrating tumour edge and the necrotic tumour core (Fig. 2d). Dev-like (OPC) was found closest to infiltrated white matter. Dev-like (AC) spatially overlapped with the Dev-like (OPC), yet extended deeper into the tumour towards successive layers of Gliosis transition, Gliosis and Hypoxia (Fig. 2d). Dev-like (Neuron) was similarly positioned near the infiltrated regions when present (Fig. 2c). In tumour AT15 that we profiled in whole, these gradual transitions from dev-like TMs to gliosis and hypoxia were observed across each sampling site (Supplementary Fig. 13a,b).

We validated these observations with orthogonal 315-plex Xenium ST data (n = 17 sections from 8 tumours) annotated at the single-cell level by means of snRNA-seq integration (Methods). This validated malignant cell state zonation, in which dev-like states bordered infiltrated regions marked by neurons, contrasting with the gliosis and hypoxia states situated further around necrosis (Fig. 2e and Supplementary Fig. 13c). Profiling centimetre-scale tumour sections revealed this pattern at each sampling site (Fig. 2e), indicating stereotyped spatial organization throughout each tumour. Xenium also enabled us to validate the accuracy of cell2location predictions on GB data (Methods and Supplementary Fig. 14).

GB TMs also reflected TME organization. ‘Vasculature’ captured pericytes, VLMCs and endothelial cells, anatomically correlated with microvascular proliferation and hyperplastic blood vessels, and was found in close proximity to Dev-like (AC) and (OPC), Gliosis transition and Proliferative malignant TMs (Fig. 2b,d and Extended Data Fig. 3a). Two ‘Immune’ TMs captured distinct myeloid cell compartments (last section). Among infiltrated regions, ‘White matter’ was found in close proximity to tumour leading edge (Fig. 2c,d), consistent with being a main GB invasion route17,18,19.

Taken together, we reveal stereotyped stepwise spatial transitions of malignant cells from dev-like to gliosis and hypoxia states in GB.

We proposed that the stereotyped spatial transitions of GB states relates to their cellular trajectories. Specifically, we proposed that as GB tumours expand at their leading edge into normal brain tissue, the dev-like malignant cells progressively transition towards gliosis and hypoxia states. To test this, we first examined putative malignant trajectories related to gliosis and hypoxia.

In the snRNA-seq data, we observed an expression gradient of astrocyte, injury response and hypoxia-related genes through AC-gliosis-hypoxia states (Fig. 3a). The AC-prog-like states showed the highest levels of developmental and homeostatic astrocyte gene expression (EGFR, SLC1A3, AQP4, ALDH1L1). These were downregulated in AC-gliosis-like cells and replaced by a transcriptomic program resembling astrogliosis, including genes from the integrin–N-cadherin pathway (ITGAV, ITGB1, CDH2) associated with glial scar formation20. This program expanded in gliosis-like cells to genes associated with JAK–STAT signalling (JAK2, STAT3, SMARC4), wound healing (ANXA2, ANXA5, YAP1, F1, AKAP12), cytokine production (IFI16, IL6R, IL1R1) and coagulation (SERPINE1), as well as angiogenesis and hypoxia (VEGFA)21,22,23. This trajectory terminated in hypoxia (HILPDA, BNIP3L, VEGFA) and stress-response gene expression (JUN, FOS, HSPA1B) (Fig. 3a and Extended Data Fig. 4a). Transcriptome-wide pseudotime analysis produced consistent results (Methods and Supplementary Fig. 15).

Whereas they were previously thought to resemble mesenchymal cells2, we observed negligible and non-specific expression of key epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition regulators (for example, SNAI1/2, TWIST1/2, ZEB1/2) in gliosis-hypoxia states24,25 (Extended Data Fig. 4a). Hence, our nomenclature places these states in the more specific biological context of glial injury response and hypoxia, putatively stemming from developmental astrocyte-like malignant cells.

The molecular trajectory was correspondingly patterned in space, manifesting as concentric segregation of AC-gliosis-hypoxia states in ST data (Fig. 3b,c and Extended Data Fig. 4c). AC-prog-like cells resided in the non-necrotic cellular tumour in the Dev-like (AC) microenvironment. AC-gliosis-like and gliosis-like cells formed Gliosis transition and Gliosis microenvironments, respectively, that spatially intermixed to varying degrees. In tumours such as AT10, AC-gliosis-like was located at the margin of the cellular tumour and gradually transitioned into gliosis-like within the perinecrotic zone. Hypoxic cells were located either within or adjacent to the tumour necrotic core. The marker genes of these states showed consistent zonated expression with ST and immunohistochemistry (Fig. 3b and Extended Data Fig. 4b).

Taken together, we identify putative GB cellular transitions from developmental astrocyte-like to gliosis then hypoxia states, unfolding across an anatomical axis from tumour expansion towards hypoxia and necrosis (Fig. 3d).

To explore GB cellular transitions, we then asked whether dev-like and gliosis-hypoxic states could emerge within the same tumour subclones (that is, genetically related malignant sublineages). Initially, we performed copy number aberration (CNA) inference to our multiome data, jointly calling clones from tumour snRNA-seq and snATAC-seq profiles (Fig. 4a and Supplementary Note 3). Distinguished by chr. 7 and chr. 10 CNs, most tumour subclones contained both dev-like and gliosis-hypoxic cells (Fig. 4b and Supplementary Fig. 16b,c), with the minority states making up an average of 15% (ranging from 3% to 49%) of each clone. Whereas subclones tended to show similar GB state compositions, three tumours contained individual subclones with divergent states. For example, tumour AT10 clone 0 was marked by chr. 17p loss and chr. 17q gain and was preferentially enriched for NPC-neuronal-like states, whereas AT10 clone 1 was enriched for AC-gliosis-hypoxia (Fig. 4b).

To identify CNAs and subclones at the DNA level, we performed WGS on 100–200 × 100–200-μm sized tissue regions of interest (ROIs) by means of laser capture microdissection (LCM)26 (Fig. 4c). We profiled several ROIs across two sampling sites of two tumours (AT3, AT10), generating 61 high-quality WGS profiles (Supplementary Fig. 17). Notably, one ROI from AT10 showed a CN loss in chr. 17p and gain chr. 17q, validating our multiome CN calls. We then defined tumour subclones in multiome data on the basis of the CN events validated by means of LCM-WGS27 (Extended Data Fig. 5a). In AT10, this validated chr. 7 gain and chr. 10 loss in malignant cells and distinguished two subclones based on chr. 17 alterations (Fig. 4d). Both subclones contained a mixture of dev-like and gliosis-hypoxia cells, with clone L0 enriched for NPC-neuronal-like cells and marked by chr. 17 CNs (Extended Data Fig. 5b,c), mirroring our multiome findings. Hence, paired multi-omic evidence demonstrates shared clonal origins of dev-like and gliosis-hypoxia cell states.

Next, we examined spatial organization of GB subclones and whether each subclone spans dev-like to gliosis-hypoxia TMs. In the multiome data, we detected many subclones within each centimetre-scale tumour sampling site (Fig. 4b and Supplementary Fig. 18a). Different sampling sites showed largely consistent clonal composition, with exceptions including AT10, in which the chr. 17-altered clone 0 is predominantly located in one site (Fig. 4b). These data indicate coarse spatial intermixing of GB clones, as shown in refs. 5,7.

To investigate finer-scale clonal organization, we examined our LCM-WGS data (roughly 100 × 100 µm resolution). Considering GB clonal intermixing and that our LCM cuts span many cells, we used PyClone-VI28 to infer clonal population structure of LCM ROIs on the basis of single nucleotide variant (SNV) allele frequencies (Fig. 4c). Focusing on AT3, our most comprehensively profiled tumour, we identified 14 SNV clusters (that is, putative subclones) across 35 ROIs (Supplementary Fig. 18c). Individual SNV clusters were present across several LCM ROIs and individual ROIs contained several SNV clusters, indicating clonal intermixing at fine spatial resolution (Fig. 4e).

Clustering ROIs on the basis of their subclonal composition revealed broad spatial clonal domains spanning several millimetres (Fig. 4e and Extended Data Fig. 5g). Broad spatial gradients of intermixed subclones demarcated these domains (Supplementary Note 4). Different tumour sampling sites showed more extensive clonal differences than suggested by multiome CNA inference (Extended Data Fig. 5g), probably owing to the better sensitivity of SNV-based clone calling. Inferring the AT3 phylogeny (Methods), we observed a high degree of spatial intermixture between ancestral (that is, 12), mid-timed (that is, 9) and late (that is, 4) SNV clusters (Fig. 4d,e and Supplementary Figs. 18c and 19).

Individual clones and clonal domains spanned diverse GB cell states and TMs resolved on the adjacent Visium sections (Supplementary Fig. 18c). As our LCM-WGS dataset was limited to two tumours, we then surveyed clonal organization across our Visium dataset. To resolve GB subclones intermixed within Visium spots, we developed the SpaceTree computational framework that leverages scRNA-seq to jointly deconvolve tumour subclones and cell states in ST data (Fig. 4f). SpaceTree integrates reference scRNA-seq and query ST datasets by means of a multi-task graph neural network architecture coupled with label propagation, enabling joint spatial mapping of clones and cell states annotated in scRNA-seq (Supplementary Fig. 20a and Supplementary Computational Note).

We benchmarked SpaceTree on ST data simulated from our GB snRNA-seq profiles, finding that it offers spatial clone deconvolution accuracy near alternative tools at notably reduced computational cost (Supplementary Computational Note). We then applied SpaceTree to integrate our GB snRNA-seq and Visium ST data per tumour site, leveraging our cell annotation and multiome clone calls. As expected, SpaceTree distinguished tumour versus normal and/or infiltrated regions on the basis of the spatial mapping of malignant versus diploid and/or TME clones, respectively (Extended Data Fig. 5h,j and Supplementary Note 4).

SpaceTree revealed widespread spatial intermixing of subclones across all tumours (Fig. 4g and Supplementary Fig. 20b), quantified as high clonal entropy in Visium spots dominated by malignant cells and TMs (Fig. 4h and Supplementary Note 4). SpaceTree also resolved broad spatial subclonal domains that overlapped with diverse malignant cell states (Extended Data Fig. 5i and Supplementary Fig. 20c,e). For example, AT15 subclones 0, 3 and 4 each overlapped with both dev-like and gliosis-hypoxia cell states (Fig. 4g). Yet, we also observed regional clonal enrichment, such as clone 3 contributing more heavily to gliosis-hypoxia (Fig. 4g) and the AT10 clone 0 marked by chr. 17 CNs enriched in tissue areas with NPC-neuronal-like cells (Extended Data Fig. 5i). Finally, we observed concordant spatial clonal mapping between SpaceTree and LCM-WGS (Extended Data Fig. 5g and Supplementary Note 4).

In summary, we present a new framework for GB subclonal spatial architecture (Fig. 4i), in which individual subclones finely spatially intermix and organize into broad clonal domains cutting across GB TMs.

Given their shared clonal origins in single-cell and spatial data, we proposed that dev-like cells continuously transition into gliosis and hypoxia states during the rapid expansion of GBs, which double in size every 50 days (ref. 29), and that our ‘snapshot’ snRNA-seq profiling can capture the different stages of such transitions. To infer cellular trajectories from snRNA-seq, we used cell2fate, a probabilistic RNA velocity model30 (Extended Data Fig. 6a).

We applied cell2fate to the snRNA-seq profiles of individual tumour subclones, avoiding confounding genetic differences across clones and tumours, and reconstructed robust trajectories from 23 out of 58 subclones (Extended Data Fig. 6b,c and Supplementary Note 5). Most of these subclones (18 out of 23, more than 78%) showed temporal transitions from dev-like to AC-gliosis-hypoxia and the rest were dominated by an individual state and often showed low transition scores (less than 0.2; 6 out of 7, 86%) (Fig. 5a and Extended Data Figs. 6b–e and 7a).
