https://www.space.com/space-exploration/.title: Voting in space: NASA astronauts cast ballots from International Space Station
https://www.space.com/space-exploration/.author: Mike Wall
https://www.space.com/space-exploration/.text:
"Yes, you can even vote from space!"

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The three Americans currently living off Earth just made sure their electoral voices were heard.

Anil Menon told us today (Nov. 3) that he and fellow NASA astronauts Luke Delaney and Jessica Watkins voted in the U.S. midterm elections from the International Space Station (ISS).

"Yes, you can even vote from space! All three U.S. crew members had the privilege of voting from space station. We filled out an electronic ballot and sent it securely to the election officials," Menon wrote in an X post this morning.

Yes, you can even vote from space! All three US crew members had the privilege of voting from space station. We filled out an electronic ballot and sent it securely to the election officials. https://t.co/hJCExQ2nKrNovember 3, 2026

That post included a 29-second video, in which Menon — wearing, like many of us today, an "I voted" sticker — shows us his "voting booth."

It's actually his room on the ISS, Menon explained. "Inside of it is my computer, where I was able to fill out an electronic form and send it to Harris County so I could vote today," he said.

Most NASA astronauts register to vote in Texas' Harris County; it's home to Johnson Space Center in Houston, the agency's human spaceflight hub.

Americans have been able to vote from space since 1997, when Texas passed a law allowing this to happen. The first person to take advantage of the legislation was NASA astronaut David Wolf, who cast his ballot from Russia's Mir space station that same year. (The ISS didn't welcome its first crew until November 2000.)

"Just like any other American away from home, astronauts may fill out a Federal Post Card Application to request an absentee ballot," NASA officials wrote in an astronaut-voting explainer.

The process is somewhat involved, however.

"After an astronaut fills out an electronic ballot aboard the orbiting laboratory, the document flows through NASA's Tracking and Data Relay Satellite System to a ground antenna at the agency's White Sands Test Facility in Las Cruces, New Mexico," they added. "From New Mexico, NASA transfers the ballot to the Mission Control Center at NASA Johnson and then on to the county clerk responsible for casting the ballot. To preserve the vote's integrity, the ballot is encrypted and accessible only by the astronaut and the clerk."

Delaney and Watkins launched to the ISS on Oct. 1 on SpaceX's Crew-13 mission. Menon has been there since mid-July, arriving aboard a Russian Soyuz spacecraft.

The trio currently share the orbiting lab with four other people — Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk and cosmonauts Anna Kikina, Pyotr Dubrov and Sergey Teteryatnikov. Kutryk and Teteryatnikov are members of Crew-13, whereas Dubrov and Kikina shared the Soyuz with Menon.

Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. https://www.space.com/entertainment/spac.title: 'OGame' developers explain how the browser-based sci-fi game has lasted 24 years ahead of the huge Orion update
https://www.space.com/entertainment/spac.author: Fran Ruiz
https://www.space.com/entertainment/spac.text:
The OG sci-fi browser game is still going strong.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If you were on the Internet in the early 2000s looking for free browser games to play, OGame was a blooming sci-fi strategy sensation that couldn't be ignored. With online servers providing the structure for a living and evolving universe where players fought, traded, and created empires from scratch, its limited visual presentation was no issue.

Times have changed, but GameForge hasn't gone anywhere. OGame has been ported to mobile devices, and content updates have kept it alive and fresh for much longer than a plethora of installable MMO games.

With the Orion update, which will hit the newly launched universes (servers) on November 6, OGame is introducing conflicts against non-player-character (NPC) enemies, wave-based battles, co-op missions, and completely new systems that can also be disrupted by other players.

The game's endurance and such a major reinvention are stunning achievements, so we asked GameForge's Martin Liedtke (Director, Products of Browser Games) and Enrico Mareth (Senior Project Manager for OGame PC and Mobile) about the many challenges of working on OGame alongside the community for so long, what Orion is bringing to the table, and what's next for this worldwide phenomenon.

Some quotes have been editorialized and lightly trimmed for better flow.

"OGame has an enduring core: You build an interstellar empire, and your decisions matter... Keeping it fresh means adding meaningful choices to that foundation," said Liedtke. "Orion adds missions against automated opponents (PvE) alongside missions open to other players (PvP)... It supports different appetites for risk."

The GameForge veteran noted, however, that it's the community that "supplies another kind of freshness" after the studio releases the new content. "We develop the systems; players create much of the history."

Part of this approach is keeping tabs on how very different kinds of players approach what's available. "Some commanders concentrate on their economy; others enjoy expeditions or carefully coordinated fleet operations... Orion follows that approach; more experienced players can dig into fleet composition, progression, and cooperation. The aim is to offer worthwhile choices."

Liedtke also noted that "OGame's PvP has become a sophisticated contest of information and coordination" over time. Some players like to scout targets and organize combined attacks when enemy fleets are vulnerable. Those battles resolve automatically, but it's the planning that "can be remarkably intricate," especially after so many years of updates.

The PvE in Orion doesn't sacrifice any of those intricacies or density. In fact, it's adding a "more structured layer" that gives players clear objectives. In most cases, they'll have to cooperate to obtain better rewards. "There is a strong case for introducing that kind of cooperative PvE earlier. It gives players another reason to build and use fleets together."

Over two decades later, how people choose to engage with OGame has changed, pushing GameForge to consider supporting new platforms. Today, mobile devices have become essential to free-to-play games' success over time.

Mareth told us their importance "has made touch controls, navigation, and clarity on smaller screens central development considerations," even if thousands of players still remain attached to PC as their main platform. "We're currently working on a design overhaul of the app, combining what we've learned with players' feedback."

Liedtke also said there is more overlap between PC and mobile players than you might imagine.

"The same player might check their empire on a phone and spend a longer session planning in the browser." Liedtke also noted that "Different playstyles also have different needs," adding that activities like mining and trading fit "comfortably" into short mobile sessions, but complex fleet operations benefit from sitting in front of one's PC.

While it's a game of interstellar conflict and sci-fi spaceships, OGame does take a lot of inspiration from real-life science, even if it stretches that science well past its limits. "When ships are destroyed in battle, the debris field can form a moon around a player's planet," explains Liedtke. "The chance (of that happening) is linked to the real lunar cycle: it is higher around a full moon than a new moon."

He noted it's a "playful connection" to astronomy, "rather than a simulation of how real moons form," but the developers thought it was cool to influence the game via things that happen in our own sky.

This possible in-game "event" also led to one of the best examples of player ingenuity in OGame: Moonshots. Liedtke explained that "players organize deliberate battles and exchange sacrificial fleets to help one another obtain those valuable moons. They have turned destruction into a cooperative project. For a designer, the lesson is to examine what players can achieve together, as well as what an individual action rewards."

As the team figured out how to develop "the more imaginative side of science fiction" in OGame's universe, they also decided to explicitly use deuterium for fusion research and as fuel. Star Trek fans will recognize this as the starship fuel of that universe, but it is a real substance: one of two stable isotopes of hydrogen. "Those scientific references give the universe familiar foundations," remarks Liedtke.

In OGame's shared galaxy, Orion is introducing "anomalies" as a central new feature, which Liedtke described as "mission sites you uncover with a new scanner" before it's required to send in ships. "Combat missions ask you to hold position against waves of automated fleets; peaceful missions put your cargo ships to work collecting rewards." The twist is these missions are open to co-op... but also to rival commanders that can attack the objectives marked as PvP. While you can theoretically ignore them, better rewards await for daring commanders.

With PvE bringing all sorts of new design opportunities to the table, Liedtke pointed out the Orion update "gives us a foundation to learn which kinds of missions players find rewarding" as GameForge looks to the strategy MMO's future. "Personally, I would like to explore encounters that make commanders reconsider what to send and how to work together. Discovery becomes more interesting when it changes your plan."

Sounds exciting, though Liedtke quickly added that this isn't an official announcement of future features.

OGame's 25th anniversary is in 2027, and while the team is tight-lipped on what the team has planned, Liedtke noted that "Reaching a quarter of a century in 2027 will be an extraordinary moment for OGame. We owe that longevity to the team's continued work and, above all, to the players who keep building empires, forming alliances, and giving this universe its stories."

OGame is available on PC (via browser and GameForge's own platform) and on mobile devices via the App Store and Google Play. The Orion update arrives on November 6, 2026.

Fran Ruiz is our resident Star Wars guy. His hunger for movies and TV series is only matched by his love for video games. On top of writing features and other longform articles for Space.com since 2021, he is a frequent collaborator of VG247 and other gaming sites. He also serves as associate editor over at Star Wars News Net and its sister site, Movie News Net.

https://www.space.com/space-exploration/.title: Dimorphos in sight: Europe's Hera probe gets its 1st look at battered space rock (photo)
https://www.space.com/space-exploration/.author: Andrew Jones
https://www.space.com/space-exploration/.text:
"With this image, the smaller Dimorphos asteroid becomes visible for the first time."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Europe's Hera planetary defense spacecraft is closing in on the binary asteroid system targeted by NASA's DART deflection test, and can now tell the two rocky bodies apart.

Hera is nearing the end of its voyage to the Didymos asteroid system, having launched on a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket in October 2024. The spacecraft snapped the image of Didymos and the smaller Dimorphos on Oct. 18 from a distance of 795 miles (1280 kilometers) from the pair, which are currently about 122 million miles (197 million km) from Earth.

"With this image, the smaller Dimorphos asteroid becomes visible for the first time," Michael Kueppers, Hera project scientist at the European Space Agency (ESA), said in a statement. "Before this acquisition, the spacecraft was still resolving the Didymos system as a single dot. But now, even though Dimorphos is made up of only around one pixel in this initial image, it is clearly well separated from its parent body."

The Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) smashed into Dimorphos in September 2022, changing the asteroid's orbit in a pioneering planetary defense demonstration. Hera's job is to survey the damage and refine our understanding of the impact, as well as the asteroids themselves.

Hera performed braking maneuvers earlier in October to slow its approach and put it on course to rendezvous with the binary system. The spacecraft is designed to make follow-up observations of the asteroids using 12 payloads, providing new insights that will prove valuable for planetary defense efforts. The mission also carries a pair of cubesats for a closer look and eventual landing on the 495-foot-wide (151 meters) Dimorphos.

For now, Hera is continuing its approach and preparing for arrival, with a big reveal expected to occur later this month.

"Our views will grow much sharper as Hera comes closer," said ESA's mission manager Ian Carnelli. "We will unveil the first detailed images of Dimorphos — the first object in the solar system to have had its orbit measurably shifted by human action — on 25 November."

Andrew is a freelance space journalist with a focus on reporting on China's rapidly growing space sector. He began writing for Space.com in 2019 and writes for SpaceNews, IEEE Spectrum, National Geographic, Sky & Telescope, New Scientist and others. Andrew first caught the space bug when, as a youngster, he saw Voyager images of other worlds in our solar system for the first time. Away from space, Andrew enjoys trail running in the forests of Finland. You can follow him on Twitter @AJ_FI.

https://www.space.com/astronomy/hubble-s.title: Hubble Telescope sees cosmic 'cat's tail' that could wrap around Earth and the sun 500 times
https://www.space.com/astronomy/hubble-s.author: Robert Lea
https://www.space.com/astronomy/hubble-s.text:
"It's a testament to how much these massive planets really influence their surrounding dust and icy bodies out to hundreds of astronomical units."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Using the Hubble Space Telescope, astronomers have investigated a cosmic cat's tail, finding it likely formed after two Pluto-sized bodies smashed together.

The feature, nicknamed the Cat's Tail, extends out from the debris disk known as Beta Pictoris which is located in a planetary system located 63 light-years away. This tail would put that of the average tabby to shame: It's so long that it could curl around the sun-Earth system about 500 times. That's about as long as 200 trillion house cats.

The major difference between our solar system and the planetary system that hosts the Cat's Tail is the latter's relative youth. While our solar system is around 4.6 billion years old, Beta Pictoris is a cosmic kitten no more than a few million years old. That means it is still host to collisions between planetary bodies similar to the ones that rocked the solar system during its infancy.

The team behind this research gained new insights into the Cat's Tail using 14 years of observations. This allowed them to solve the long-standing mystery of the violent conditions under which it formed.

"The Cat's Tail is thought to be the aftermath of a collision between large bodies — think something like Pluto," team leader Arin Avsar of the University of Arizona said in a statement. "Oddly, this feature had previously only been seen with the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), which detects infrared light, but remained invisible at shorter wavelengths, which has puzzled the community for a while."

Comparing Beta Pictoris and our solar system, one thing rapidly becomes apparent: our cosmic neighborhood is relatively well-ordered. The planets orbit the sun with most space rocks neatly delegated into bands: the main asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter, and the Kuiper belt out beyond the orbit of Neptune.

However, this is a stark contrast to the solar system's violent and chaotic youth. Back then, the solar system was host to an infant star surrounded by a swirling disk of gas and dust in which collisions between bodies called planetesimals — the building blocks of planets — were commonplace.

Astronomers can't look back to the solar system's infancy, so to learn more about how our cosmic backyard took shape, they study nearby young planetary systems. Systems like Beta Pictoris. That doesn't mean it has been quick to divulge its secrets, though.

"We think the Cat's Tail has eluded our observations in visible light until now because of what it's made of," Avsar explained. "It consists almost entirely of what we call organic refractory material, which is heavily carbon-based. These long chains of carbon atoms absorb visible light, so they're quite black."

This new study revealed that the feline feature is cat-like in more ways than just its shape. It's also pleasingly fluffy, Hubble observations suggest. That's because the grains that compose it are extremely porous.

"How you can get dust grains that small that are as porous as we see here no one really understands, and that's part of why we study this feature," Avsar said.

"It's possible that the velocities involved in the collisions were so high that the carbon grains vaporized, turned into gas, and then recondensed as they cooled, and that's how they became so porous," team member Kevin Wagner of the U of A said.

The scientists also discovered a hitherto undiscovered feature in the Cat's Tail — a warp that seems to be the result of an interaction between the trail of material and one of the planets in the system, Beta Pictoris b, a gas giant planet 10 times more massive than Jupiter.

"This gives us another line of evidence into how giant planets influence comets through their immense gravitational force," Avsar said. "It's a testament to how much these massive planets really influence their surrounding dust and icy bodies out to hundreds of astronomical units [one astronomical unit being the distance between Earth and the sun]."

The team's research was published last month in The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

https://www.space.com/stargazing/solar-e.title: The 2027 'eclipse of the century' will plunge real Star Wars filming locations into darkness
https://www.space.com/stargazing/solar-e.author: Jamie Carter
https://www.space.com/stargazing/solar-e.text:
On Aug. 2, 2027, the moon's shadow will sweep across Tunisia, giving Star Wars fans a rare chance to experience a total solar eclipse at the real-life filming locations of Tatooine.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Aug. 2, 2027, the moon's shadow will sweep across some of the most iconic filming locations from Star Wars, plunging them into darkness during what's being called the "eclipse of the century".

The path of the 2027 total solar eclipse will cross southern Tunisia, where several locations were used to bring the fictional desert planet Tatooine to life. From the dunes of Mos Espa to the rocky Jundland Wastes, Star Wars fans will have the rare opportunity to experience totality at the very places where their favorite scenes were filmed

But not every famous filming location will experience totality, so choosing where to watch will be crucial. Here are four locations that fall directly in the moon's shadow. All times, totality durations and historical cloud cover data come from Time and Date.

Location: south of Chott el-Gharsa, Tozeur Governorate, southwest Tunisia

Start of totality and duration: 10:06 a.m. CET; 2 minutes, 9 seconds

With a massive budget and three prequels to make, Lucasfilm built a new film set that would double as the Mos Espa spaceport on Tatooine for The Phantom Menace and Attack of the Clones. This is where Qui-Gon Jinn, Obi-Wan Kenobi, Jar Jar Binks and Padme get stranded, where they meet Anakin Skywalker and where the podrace takes place. Now abandoned, it's in the middle of nowhere, between two huge salt lakes and subject to the intense heat and moving Eriguet dunes — but it is firmly within the path of totality. Nearby are two other shooting locations — the Ong Jemel outcrop, where Darth Maul arrives on the scene, and Yardang, where Qui-Gon and Darth Maul battle — the first-ever lightsaber duel filmed on location.

Location: Jebel Sidi Bouhlel canyon, Dghoumès National Park, Tozeur, southwest Tunisia

Start of totality and duration: 10:06 a.m. CET; 3 minutes, 37 seconds

Often called "Star Wars Canyon" by fans and crew, Maguer Gorge in Jebel Sidi Bouhlel doubled as the Jundland Wastes of Tatooine in Star Wars: Episode IV — A New Hope. It's where Luke Skywalker is attacked by Tusken Raiders, where Obi-Wan Kenobi first appears and where Luke and Obi-Wan discover the slaughtered Jawas. The canyon also provided the distant view of Mos Eisley — the famous "wretched hive of scum and villainy." On Aug. 2, 2027, you'll likely be pointing your macrobinoculars at the eclipsed sun rather than Tusken Raiders.

Steven Spielberg later filmed here for Raiders of the Lost Ark, including the scene in which Indiana Jones threatens to destroy the Ark with a bazooka. Just south of Dghoumès National Park is a desert oasis called Bouhlel Sdada, used for the archaeological dig scenes in Raiders.

Location: Ajim city center, Médenine Governorate, Djerba island, Tunisia

Start of totality and duration: 10:10 a.m. CET; 3 minutes, 55 seconds

Chance of clouds: 19%

Djerba Island's palm trees, beaches and Mediterranean horizons will make it a popular destination for eclipse chasers after a long totality away from the heat and crowds of Luxor in Egypt. It's also home to three notable Star Wars filming locations. The original movie's Mos Eisley footage was shot here, with Ajim doubling as a Stormtrooper checkpoint ("These are not the droids you're looking for"), the Cantina exterior, and an alley near Docking Bay 94 where stormtroopers watch the Millennium Falcon blast off. In reality, it's an abandoned bakery.

Location: Ajim outskirts, Médenine Governorate, Djerba island, Tunisia

Start of totality and duration: 10:09 a.m. CET; 4 minutes

Chance of clouds: 19%

Just north of Ajim, this mosque — originally a fisherman's house — was used as a stand-in for "Old Ben's" house, where Obi-Wan Kenobi gives Luke Skywalker a lightsaber. It was used purely for photography, and no actors set foot here. It was also cut from the movie's Special Edition in 1997, so you'll only find it in the original version. Completists might also want to check out Sidi Jemour Mosque to the north, which was used for scenes with Biggs Darklighter that didn't even make the final cut. IYKYK …

Tunisia's Star Wars locations are spread across the south, so the easiest way to see several is on an organized tour or with a private driver and guide. Tozeur is the main base for visiting Mos Espa, Ong Jemel and Jebel Sidi Bouhlel, with local operators offering half-day and full-day 4x4 excursions into the desert. Djerba Island is the other major hub for three sights. Longer multi-day tours typically connect Tozeur with Matmata, home to Hotel Sidi Idriss — the Lars Homestead — as well as Djerba.

One tour company, Star Wars Tours, is running a (sold-out) special departure called "Eclipse tour from the Outer Rim" that witnesses totality at the Mos Espa set. Other Star Wars-focused tour operators include Galaxy Tours, though one-day trips to the Mos Espa set from Tozeur are also available.

Tunisia is surely one of the most attractive destinations for the Aug. 2, 2027 total solar eclipse. Historical cloud cover is exceptionally low, while totality reaches around five and a half minutes near the centerline. It also offers established tourism infrastructure and generally lower August temperatures than Egypt, making it an obvious alternative for eclipse chasers hoping to avoid the biggest crowds around Luxor.

You can, of course, visit the Star Wars sets in the days before or after the eclipse. For Tunisia's maximum duration of totality, consider Sfax, where darkness lasts 5 minutes, 41 seconds, or nearby Chaffar Beach, with its long, open Mediterranean coastline. Offshore, the low-lying Kerkennah Islands get around 5 minutes, 39 seconds. Inland, Sidi Bouzid offers about 5 minutes, 33 seconds beneath typically dry skies, while the spectacular Roman amphitheater at El Jem gets 4 minutes, 23 seconds. On Djerba Island, meanwhile, beaches and extensive resort infrastructure make combining an eclipse chase with a conventional Mediterranean vacation particularly easy — with a view of Mos Eisley thrown in for good measure.

Jamie is an experienced science and travel journalist, stargazer and eclipse chaser who writes about exploring the night sky, solar and lunar eclipses, the Northern Lights, moon-gazing, astro-travel, astronomy and space exploration. He is the editor of WhenIsTheNextEclipse.com, author of A Stargazing Program For Beginners, co-author of The Eclipse Effect, and a senior contributor at Forbes.

https://www.statnews.com/2026/11/07/new-.title: Lowering blood pressure after stroke or with diabetes poses challenges, in research and practice
https://www.statnews.com/2026/11/07/new-.author: Elizabeth Cooney
https://www.statnews.com/2026/11/07/new-.text:
CHICAGO — High blood pressure has earned its reputation as the silent killer. If someone has diabetes or has had a stroke, the risk of serious cardiovascular events posed by hypertension climbs even higher.

Three studies presented Saturday at the American Heart Association’s scientific sessions reported on recent attempts to lower blood pressure in people with these challenging medical histories, and how medical care should reach across specialties to treat them. One small but diverse trial tested a common diuretic after a stroke, another looked at intensifying treatment to reach lower-than-standard post-stroke blood pressure goals, and the third looked at going lower in people living with type 2 diabetes.

Each of the scientists leading the studies and the experts commenting on them at a media briefing emphasized the role of blood pressure. Adding a widely available drug earlier held promise for controlling blood pressure, but it was a split decision between the effects of lower numbers post-stroke and with diabetes.

By Elizabeth Cooney and Matthew Herper

By Casey Ross and Brittany Trang

WASHINGTON — The Biotechnology Innovation Organization is joining the legal fight against the Trump administration’s pilot program aimed at aligning drug prices in Medicare with prices charged in peer countries.

BIO and two California-based biotech trade groups filed a complaint Friday in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California asserting that the Global Benchmark for Efficient Drug Pricing demonstration, known as GLOBE, oversteps Medicare’s statutory authority. The complaint seeks to halt the model.

The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

https://www.statnews.com/2026/11/07/aha-.title: STAT+: Failure of Novartis Lp(a) drug raises questions about cardiovascular strategy
https://www.statnews.com/2026/11/07/aha-.author: Elizabeth Cooney and Matthew Herper
https://www.statnews.com/2026/11/07/aha-.text:
CHICAGO — Lipoprotein(a), a genetic risk factor for cardiovascular disease carried by 1 in 5 people, is the target of novel therapies trying to cut down heart attacks, strokes, and deaths in those at risk. The growing field of research aimed at the particle took a hit earlier this year when top-line results showed an experimental drug reduced Lp(a) but failed to lower serious outcomes.

More details of the study, funded by Novartis, were revealed Saturday at the American Heart Association’s scientific sessions and published simultaneously in the New England Journal of Medicine.

In the Phase 3 trial, the drug pelacarsen dramatically lowered Lp(a), a mashup of lipids and proteins that at high levels can heighten the risk of severe heart problems. But despite lower Lp(a), the HORIZON trial showed no difference in heart attacks, strokes, urgent coronary revascularization, or deaths in participants followed for almost five years who were randomly selected to take the drug or a placebo.

https://www.statnews.com/2026/11/07/aha-.title: STAT+: Despite Novo drug’s failure, cardiologists say they will still pursue anti-inflammatories
https://www.statnews.com/2026/11/07/aha-.author: Elizabeth Cooney
https://www.statnews.com/2026/11/07/aha-.text:
CHICAGO — Out-of-control inflammation is often called the root of all evil in cardiovascular and metabolic disease. Recent clinical trial results, described in brief in July, showed that while an experimental drug could lower two biomarkers of inflammation, it didn’t limit serious heart events in patients with severe illness.

The Novo Nordisk study, called ZEUS, showed that the monoclonal antibody ziltivekimab reduced levels of the inflammatory cytokine interleukin-6, or IL-6, but that drop did not translate into fewer heart attacks, strokes, or deaths in the treatment group compared to those taking a placebo. Once top-line results were disclosed, Novo halted two other trials of the drug called HERMES and ATHENA after a data monitoring committee found in September they were unlikely to succeed.

The ZEUS results were detailed further on Saturday at the American Heart Association’s scientific sessions and published simultaneously in the New England Journal of Medicine.

The Trump administration is facing another lawsuit over its sweeping changes to Medicaid less than a week after a federal judge ruled that implementation of work requirements would cause “irreparable harm.”

The complaint from four states, filed Thursday, alleges that the overhaul will lead to “irreparable sovereign, fiscal, and public-health harms” and that the administration does not have the authority to force states to implement these changes. Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield filed the suit in the U.S. District Court in Oregon, joined by Minnesota, New Mexico, and Washington.

The lawsuit arrives less than 60 days before the Jan. 1 deadline outlined in Republicans’ One Big Beautiful Bill, which passed in 2025. It would require a Medicaid recipient  to work, volunteer, or attend school for 80 hours a month to keep health insurance, with a few exceptions for disability.

WASHINGTON — The Trump administration’s MAHA agenda has been derailed by corporate interests and the influence of money, a recently departed administration official told the podcaster Joe Rogan in a recording released Friday.

Calley Means, a key Make America Healthy Again leader who worked in the White House and highest levels of the federal health agencies until last month, said top White House officials were altering policies in response to industry influence and funding.

Means pointed to the fight over glyphosate, an herbicide many MAHA advocates argued causes grave health consequences. He recounted an “almost violent reaction” from industry groups that pressured agencies against researching or restricting the substance. He said a White House official later presented Means with a policy to boost its production — noting it was “not up for discussion.”

Amid a sweep of Democratic victories in Tuesday’s midterms, some online commentators jokingly declared “Woke is back.”

There was little congressional pushback over the past two years as the Trump administration terminated hundreds of grants meant to chronicle and remedy medical inequities, shuttered programs intended to diversify the science workforce, and opened investigations into universities and medical schools it accused of discriminating against white and Asian applicants. Will that change now that the Democratic Party has won control of the 120th Congress?

Two newly elected candidates with science credentials told STAT they hope to change that: Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, an epidemiologist and former health disparities researcher, and incoming Rep. Jasmine Clark of Georgia, a microbiologist who will be the first Black woman with a STEM Ph.D. in Congress.

By Theresa Gaffney and Jonathan Wosen

The political environment is about to get friendlier for hospitals.

With Democrats gaining control of the House and Senate, hospitals will not have to worry about Republican-led efforts to cut Medicaid payments further. In fact, Democrats have explicit goals to prioritize measures that are financially beneficial to the hospital industry.

Within the first 100 hours of the next Congress, which starts in January, Democrats want to advance policies that would reverse Medicaid cuts outlined in President Trump’s tax law and “permanently restore” the enhanced subsidies for Affordable Care Act plans that expired earlier this year, according to a memo from party leaders. Democrats even plan to block a niche drug discount model, despised by hospitals, that the Trump administration proposed.

Novartis has acknowledged seven previously unknown instances in which tumors were found in children who were treated with its spinal muscular atrophy therapy, a surprising development that has raised concerns among families, physicians, and patient advocacy groups, STAT writes. The cases, which for the moment are being seen as only a potential safety signal, were publicized on Thursday by an advocacy group and on a Facebook page after Novartis earlier this week disclosed the information to neurologists. One advocacy group, SMA Europe, issued a statement saying that regulatory authorities are now examining the cases.

Four of the eight people appointed by U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. https://www.statnews.com/2026/11/06/wome.text:
In September, the Gallup-Pivotal Women’s Health Survey reported that 34% of U.S. women strongly or somewhat agreed that a health care provider minimized or dismissed their symptoms in the past five years. Thirty-three percent reported being misdiagnosed or unable to get a diagnosis, compared with 21% of men reporting these experiences.

Medical records tell a different story. An epidemiologist and a sociologist, we recently released a study where we paired electronic medical records with detailed interviews with 87 women. We talked to these women about their pain and illnesses, work, family, poverty, violence, and encounters with the health care system.

Fifty-three of the women described a trust-breaking encounter with a health system, but only seven of them had medical records that documented mistrust. Thirty-two women reported experiencing a misdiagnosis, but misdiagnosis was only documented for eight of these women. Thirty women reported that they felt that clinicians treated them with disrespect, but this was not documented in the records anywhere.

https://www.statnews.com/2026/11/06/what.title: Most people haven’t heard of kratom. What is it, and who’s using it?
https://www.statnews.com/2026/11/06/what.author: Theresa Gaffney
https://www.statnews.com/2026/11/06/what.text:
Over the last few years, the kratom plant and supplements made from it have garnered increasing attention from public health leaders. This broad category of products, which largely skirts any regulation, has seen major surges in potency, while becoming omnipresent on smoke shop and gas station shelves. Health officials have warned that concentrated compounds like 7-hydroxymitragynine (7-OH) are an emerging public health threat, and federal policies to limit their availability are pending. In the meantime, multiple states and smaller localities have issued emergency bans on 7-OH, and in some cases, on all kratom products.

Despite the messaging and rising use, few Americans are familiar with kratom or the newer derivative products. They’re made with compounds that have scientific names like 7-OH, mitragynine pseudoindoxyl (MGPI) and dihydro-7-hydroxy mitragynine (MGM-15) but are often sold on shelves with names like Dozo Perks, Roxy, and UltraOhmz Pseudo Supreme. New survey data from the Annenberg Public Policy Center show about two-thirds (66%) of Americans have never heard of kratom. Among those who had at least some familiarity, few understood the difference between its natural leaf form and more synthetic products.

That confusion carries over to the associated risks. In the survey of nearly 2,000 people, 66% were unsure if kratom products posed a serious public safety hazard. And most people didn’t understand health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s stance on regulation — a question that’s become complicated by repeated reports of kratom industry lobbying influence on the DEA’s proposed action.

By Elaine Chen and Damian Garde

By Casey Ross and Brittany Trang

https://www.statnews.com/pharmalot/2026/.title: STAT+: Pharma’s trade group spent heavily on search ads to sway public opinion
https://www.statnews.com/pharmalot/2026/.author: Ed Silverman
https://www.statnews.com/pharmalot/2026/.text:
The lobbying group for the U.S. pharmaceutical industry spent an estimated $59 million on search advertising over a recent seven-year period to influence how Americans view the highly charged issue of prescription drug costs, according to a new analysis that used data to model the spending.

Of that, the Pharmaceutical Research & Manufacturers of America spent roughly $32 million on ads linked to insurance and health plan searches, while $28 million was spent directing people to its web pages and domains criticizing pharmacy benefit managers, which drugmakers argue are the true culprits behind the rising prices for many medicines.

Spending also surged around well-publicized legislative and regulatory actions, such as when Medicare began drug price negotiations in 2023. In all, PhRMA used more than 283,500 distinct keywords to generate 17.1 million paid visits from 2019 through 2025, according to an analysis published in Clinical Pharmacology & Therapeutics.

https://www.medscape.com/viewarticle/pan.title: Pancreatic Surveillance Findings Common, Mostly Stable
https://www.medscape.com/viewarticle/pan.text:
More than half of carriers of pathogenic germline variants (PGVs) in BRCA1, BRCA2, ATM, or PALB2 undergoing pancreatic cancer surveillance had at least one imaging finding. However, most were benign or low-risk and remained stable over short-term follow-up.

“These data provide a foundation for counseling [high-risk individuals] on the expected frequency and evolution of pancreatic imaging findings,” the study authors wrote. While surveillance findings are common, they added, “importantly, these findings are mostly benign and stable during the short-term follow-up period.”

The study, led by Samantha Kasselman, MS, CGC, of the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia, was published online in JCO Precision Oncology.

The cohort was predominantly female (72%) and white (89%), and may not represent the broader population of high-risk individuals. Imaging outcomes may be affected by inter-reader variability and detection bias, and few participants had both EUS and MRI simultaneously, limiting modality comparison. Follow-up was short, and the solid mass sample was small.

The study was supported by the Basser Center for BRCA and several family research funds. Several co-authors reported consulting, speaker, or research ties to industry. Full disclosures are available in the original article.

https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.title: Topol lists missed opportunities in CV care
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.author: Erik Swain
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

CHICAGO — There are many opportunities for improving cardiovascular health that cardiologists have missed, Eric Topol, MD, said at the American Heart Association Scientific Sessions.

Topol, the founder and director of Scripps Translational Research Institute and professor of molecular medicine and executive vice president of Scripps Research, who received the James B. Herrick Award of Outstanding Achievement in Clinical Cardiology from the American Heart Association, outlined a number of practices that he said cardiologists should be doing, but are not.

An American College of Cardiology scientific statement on exercise prescriptions released in October had been needed for a long time, Topol said.

“We should be ... taking detailed histories of each patient’s physical activity and getting a very individualized plan for that person because it is driving healthy aging and cardiovascular aging in a very favorable way,” Topol said. “In fact ... exercise is the No. 1 thing to promote youthful aging, especially in the cardiovascular system. So this whole thing about the end of aging, I don’t think so, but we do know one way to change the course toward a youthful, healthy aging process.”

Polygenic risk scores do an excellent job of risk prediction for various forms of heart disease, but they are not used much in clinical practice, Topol said.

“Polygenic risk scores [are available] for all of the cardiovascular outcomes, but especially noteworthy is coronary artery disease,” Topol said. “I still don’t understand why every patient has not [received], as long as they’re willing, their polygenic risk scores across all common cancers, atrial fibrillation and coronary disease. It costs $20 to do a [single nucleotide polymorphism] array. Unfortunately, there are companies out there charging $300 for what should be $20. This should be widely available, and health systems should be providing this to all their patients who would like to get it.”

As one example, Topol said, genetic markers do a far better job determining who is at risk for aortic dissection than the standard practice of considering an aorta wider than 5 cm as high risk and one narrower than that as low risk.

There are several examples of portable diagnostic technologies that are better than standard tools but are not being used regularly by cardiologists, Topol said.

“Why aren’t we doing a six-lead [ECG], which takes a few seconds in every patient, with or without taking their pulse?” he said. “I have done this routinely for many years, and it gives a lot of insight about conduction disturbances, which you’re not going to get from a pulse or even auscultation. Why isn’t this routine?

“Then there’s [handheld ultrasound]. I haven’t used a stethoscope to examine the heart for over a decade. And when I ask about this, some cardiologists say, ‘Well, I don’t get reimbursed for that.’ Well, do you get reimbursed for using a stethoscope? This is the modern stethoscope. You can see everything in seconds and share it with the patient.”

Routine medical images can reveal a lot about CV conditions even if they were not performed for CV reasons, but most cardiologists do not take advantage of this, Topol said.

“There’s a long list of every type of medical image [that] can deliver, provide much more data and evidence of abnormalities than what is the reason for getting the scan in the first place,” he said. “Every single type of medical image has a rich embedment of data that is left on the table and is not being provided. The great example for us is the chest X-ray. A single chest X-ray is better than the atherosclerotic cardiogram. It’s substantially better than a risk score. Why aren’t we using it? There is an AI tool that spots heart disease in less than 2 seconds, picking up all sorts of diagnoses that are commonly missed. And then what about the mammogram for breast artery calcification? The state of Maryland has made it the law that it has to be in the readout for every mammogram that a woman undertakes. That should be done for every mammogram.”

Retinal images are perhaps the most useful diagnostic tool in medicine, and have been shown to indicate calcium in arteries and predict subclinical coronary atherosclerosis, myocardial infarction and stroke, Topol said.

“We’re not using that information,” Topol said. “And that is extraordinary. [Two papers have] shown us the prediction capacity of a retinal image is astounding. And in fact ... all the cardiovascular diseases can be predicted from the retinal image, which is so easy to obtain. “In the future, cardiologists and primary care doctors and eventually patients and consumers will take their own retinal image. But right now this can be done in less than 20 seconds without pupil dilatation, and that image can be interpreted by AI, and we’re not yet doing it. It’s a great opportunity.”

Awareness of the impact of arterial inflammation on heart disease has grown in recent years, but it has not translated to a lot of diagnostic action, Topol said.

“This is such an important pivot in cardiovascular medicine,” Topol said. “We know atherosclerosis is growing; it’s progressing over multiple decades. But the one thing that takes this over the top and leads to events is inflammation, and now we even have a way, FDA-approved, to quantify the inflammation in each of the coronary arteries: the [fat attenuation index] score (CaRi-Heart, Caristo Diagnostics).”

Topol E. Opening session. Presented at: American Heart Association Scientific Sessions; Nov. 6-9, 2026; Chicago.

Disclosures: Topol reports serving on scientific advisory boards for Abridge, Aevius, Danaher, Microsoft and Mercor.

https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.title: Lower blood pressure target after stroke reduces heart risk
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.author: Scott Buzby
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

CHICAGO — Targeting systolic blood pressure of less than 120 mm Hg more effectively reduced major cardiovascular events in patients with prior stroke or transient ischemic attack vs. a target of less than 140 mm Hg.

OPTIMAL-STROKE was the first trial to be adequately powered to determine the effects of intensive BP control on prevention of major CV events in patients with prior stroke of TIA, and the results were presented at the American Heart Association Scientific Sessions and simultaneously published in The New England Journal of Medicine.

“Elevated blood pressure is the most important risk factor for recurrent stroke. Almost all patients after stroke leave on antihypertensive therapy, but what we don’t know is how low should we go,” Gisele Sampaio Silva, MD, PhD, MSc, professor of neurology at the Federal University of São Paulo and head clinical trialist in neurology at Albert Einstein Israelite Hospital in São Paulo, said during a press conference. “The SPRINT trial actually set the stage for the use of lower blood pressure thresholds with a goal of less than 120 mm Hg in patients with high cardiovascular risk factors, but this trial actually excluded patients with previous strokes, and other prophylaxis trials were either underpowered or were performed in a specific and limited stroke population. So our question was a very straightforward one: What is the benefit of targeting a systolic blood pressure of lower than 120 mm Hg vs. lower than 140 mm Hg to prevent major cardiovascular events in patients with prior ischemic stroke or TIA.”

OPTIMAL-STROKE was a multicenter, open-label, randomized trial conducted at 30 sites in Brazil, for which researchers enrolled 4,368 participants with high BP and a history of stroke or TIA and were clinically stable for 48 hours (mean age, 64 years; 48% women).

Participants were randomly assigned to intensive antihypertensive therapy with a systolic BP target of less than 120 mm Hg or standard treatment with a systolic BP target of less than 140 mm Hg, according to the study methods.

The primary outcome was a composite of CV death, nonfatal MI, nonfatal stroke or hospitalization for unstable angina or heart failure.

The mean systolic BP reached during follow-up was 122 mm Hg in the intensive-treatment arm and 135.2 mm Hg in the standard-treatment arm (between-group mean difference, 13.1 mm Hg; 95% CI, 12.5-13.8).

During a median of 3.9 years’ follow-up, a component of the primary outcome occurred in 10.9% of the intensive-treatment group (3.25 events per 100 person-years) and 13.5% of the standard-treatment group (4.11 events per 100 person-years), Silva said during the press conference.

The hazard ratio for the primary composite outcome was 0.79 with intensive vs. standard BP lowering among people with hypertension and prior stroke or TIA (95% CI, 0.67-0.94; P = .007), according to the presentation.

Researchers reported that renal outcomes were more common in the intensive-therapy group vs. standard-treatment group (3.9% vs. 2.2%).

“This was primarily driven by a sustained drop in renal function; potentially a hemodynamic effect. We can discuss this further because there were no increase in the risk of end-stage renal disease. There was no increase in dialysis and no increase in renal mortality,” Otavio Berwanger, MD, PhD, cardiologist and clinical trialist at George Institute for Global Health UK, Imperial College London, said during the press conference.

Overall incidence of serious adverse events was comparable between the two study arms, according to the presentation.

“In patients with a previous ischemic stroke or TIA, a systolic blood pressure target below 120 mm Hg reduced major cardiovascular events compared with a target below 140 mm Hg,” Berwanger said during the presentation. “Overall, serious adverse events were similar, but renal events were more frequent with intensive treatment.”

After the presentation, Cheryl D. Bushnell, MD, MHS, FAHA, professor and vice chair of research in the department of neurology at Wake Forest University School of Medicine, discussed the implications of OPTIMAL-STROKE for this patient population.

“SPRINT was a similar design with a goal of less than 120 mm Hg systolic with intensive blood pressure lowering, and so that is what our colleagues were able to accomplish in the stroke population, which can be very challenging,” Bushnell said. “There are a lot of times when patients are discharged from the hospital, and they have carotid stenosis, they have a middle cerebral artery stenosis and everybody’s nervous about lowering their blood pressure too much. This abolishes some of the concerns that a lot of neurologists and primary care physicians have had on cerebral perfusion.”

Sampaio Silva G. LBS.02: Treating the clot or controlling the blood pressure: Improving outcomes after stroke. Presented at: American Heart Association Scientific Sessions; Nov. 6-9, 2026; Chicago.

Disclosures: Berwanger reports receiving research funding from Bayer. Bushnell reports consulting for Bayer. Sampaio Silva reports advising for Bayer and Boehringer Ingelheim.

https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.title: Ziltivekimab cuts inflammation but not CV events in ZEUS
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.author: Katie Kalvaitis
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

CHICAGO — Ziltivekimab, a novel interleukin-6 inhibitor, lowered inflammatory markers but not major adverse CV events compared with placebo among adults with atherosclerotic CVD and chronic kidney disease in the ZEUS trial.

“Cardiovascular inflammation is highly prevalent. It remains a mechanistically compelling therapeutic target. The CANTOS, LoDoCo2 and COLCOT trials have already proven that lowering inflammation lowers risk,” Paul M. Ridker, MD, MPH, director of the Center for Cardiovascular Disease Prevention at Brigham and Women’s Hospital, said during a press conference at the American Heart Association Scientific Sessions. “Our challenge is what drug for what patient group.”

Play Video
Paul M. Ridker, MD, MPH, discusses the results of the ZEUS trial presented at the American Heart Association Scientific Sessions.

The ZEUS trial was designed to evaluate a novel anti-inflammatory therapy in a higher-risk patient population than the previous inflammation trials — patients with established ASCVD, chronic kidney disease and systemic inflammation, which was defined as a high-sensitivity C-reactive protein level of 2 mg/L or more. This is a group with high risk and considerable unmet need, according to Ridker.

The researchers tested ziltivekimab (Novo Nordisk), a monoclonal antibody that targets IL-6, a downstream inflammatory molecule.

“What the ZEUS trial was trying to figure out is can we go downstream from IL-1 to target IL-6,” Ridker told Healio.

Researchers enrolled 6,376 adults (mean age, 69 years; 27.5% women; 4.2% Black; 24.3% Asian; mean BMI, 30.3 kg/m2) who were randomly assigned to once-monthly subcutaneous ziltivekimab 15 mg or placebo. Most patients (92%) also had hypertension, 66% diabetes and 42% heart failure. The baseline median IL-6 level was 4.9 pg/mL and median hsCRP level was 4.5 mg/L.

The results of ZEUS were previously announced in July by Novo. The full data were presented in a late-breaking science session and simultaneously published in The New England Journal of Medicine.

At 24 months, the ziltivekimab group had a 64% reduction compared with placebo in hsCRP and a 76% reduction in free IL-6, in addition to other inflammatory markers including serum amyloid A, fibrinogen and lipoprotein(a). Increasing tertiles of hsCRP and IL-6 are associated with increasingly high risk for MACE and death, according to the presentation.

During a median follow-up of 33 months, the primary efficacy endpoint — a three-point MACE endpoint that included death from CV causes, nonfatal MI or nonfatal stroke — occurred in 17.6% of patients assigned ziltivekimab compared with 17.7% assigned placebo (HR = 0.99; 95% CI, 0.88-1.11; P = .84), according to the results.

Looking at individual components of the three-point MACE endpoint, death from CV causes occurred in 11.1% of the ziltivekimab group and 11.2% of the placebo group (HR = 0.99; 95% CI, 0.86-1.15), nonfatal MI in 4.5% of the ziltivekimab group and 4.6% of the placebo group (HR = 0.97; 95% CI, 0.77-1.22) and nonfatal stroke in 3.6% of the ziltivekimab group and 3.9% of the placebo group (HR = 0.92; 95% CI, 0.71-1.18), according to the results.

The researchers also evaluated a four-point MACE endpoint, which included hospitalization for unstable angina requiring urgent coronary revascularization, which occurred in 18.4% of patients assigned ziltivekimab and 18.5% assigned placebo (HR = 0.99; 95% CI, 0.88-1.1).

There was no difference in a composite kidney event endpoint, which included sustained reduction in estimated glomerular filtration rate of 40% or more, death from kidney failure or CV causes or kidney failure, which occurred in 20.2% of the ziltivekimab group and 19.3% of the placebo group (HR = 1.05; 95% CI, 0.94-1.17).

Death from any cause was reported in 16.9% of the ziltivekimab group and 17% of the placebo group (HR = 0.99; 95% CI, 0.88-1.12).

Serious adverse events occurred in 54% of patients in both treatment groups. Serious infections were reported in 20.4% of the ziltivekimab group and 17.9% of the placebo group.

“At one level, while this is a neutral study, it’s a study we are learning a great deal about. As someone in the vascular biology community excited about inflammation, this is actually a big study because it’s telling us where we should go, what’s going to be next and how ultimately do we improve patient care,” Ridker told Healio.

Ridker discussed possible reasons for the neutral findings in ZEUS. Compared with CANTOS, which was a positive trial of IL-1 beta inhibition, ZEUS, which was a neutral trial of IL-6 inhibition, evaluated a much higher risk population, he said.

“Perhaps [the ZEUS participants] simply have nonmodifiable disease,” Ridker told Healio. “Was it too late in the process? Was the horse already out of the barn?”

Ridker noted that participants in ZEUS were about 10 years older than those in CANTOS, had longstanding diabetes, more HF and 72% had a high kidney disease class.

“We know lowering inflammation works. Now, we have to figure out what’s the right drug for the right person. Maybe we take that IL-6 inhibitor and give it to lower-risk patients; those ongoing trials will happen. Maybe instead of moving downstream to IL-6 we consider moving upstream to something called the NLRP3 inflammasome itself, which controls the regulation of IL-1. Many new drugs are being developed that target the NLRP3,” Ridker told Healio.

The ongoing HERMES and ARTEMIS trials will provide additional evidence on the effects of ziltivekimab in different populations, including those with HF with preserved and mildly reduced ejection fraction and also acute coronary ischemia.

I think that maybe exploring ziltivekimab in a less high-risk population would be critical, maybe not in the setting of chronic kidney disease. Other IL-6 receptor agents that don’t just target the ligand could be of interest. This does put the focus on upstream agents. Looking at the NLRP3 inflammasome, there are agents being tested now that they already have data showing they significantly lower inflammatory markers. I think if you start upstream you may have a more significant impact on all those downstream pathways. It’s like whack-a-mole; if you block one pathway, does something else pop up? We just don’t see that. The ZEUS trial does not shut the door on inflammation, but I think it does raise the possibility of a different strategy to target it.

Ridker PM, et al. LBS.01. The Eugene Braunwald late-breaking science session: Translating science into prevention: Lessons from landmark trials. Presented at: American Heart Association Scientific Sessions; Nov. 6-9, 2026; Chicago.

Disclosures: Ridker reports consulting for Agepha, AngioWave, Arrowhead, AstraZeneca, BioAge Labs, Boehringer Ingelheim, Cardiol Therapeutics, CSL Behring, Eli Lilly, GSK, HeartFlow, IQVIA, Merck, Mirador, NewAmsterdam, Nodthera, Novartis, Novo, SOCAR, Tourmaline Bio and Uppton and receiving research grants/contracts to his institution from Bristol Myers Squibb, Esperion, Kowa, National Cancer Institute, NHLBI, Novartis, Novo and Pfizer. The ZEUS trial was supported by Novo.

https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.title: Pelacarsen does not reduce CV events in patients with high Lp(a)
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.author: Erik Swain
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

CHICAGO — In patients with cardiovascular disease and high lipoprotein(a), pelacarsen did not reduce risk for major adverse CV events compared with placebo, according to results of the Lp(a)HORIZON trial.

As Healio previously reported in September, Ionis and Novartis, the developers of pelacarsen, an antisense oligonucleotide shown to reduce serum Lp(a) and the first drug specifically targeting Lp(a) to report CV outcome trial results, announced the drug failed to achieve the primary endpoint in Lp(a)HORIZON. The full results were presented at the American Heart Association Scientific Sessions and simultaneously published in The New England Journal of Medicine.

At least four other novel drugs targeting Lp(a) are expected to report results of CV outcome trials in the next few years.

“Although these results are disappointing, they provide scientific insights that help inform future research efforts,” Healio | Cardiology Today Editorial Board Member Steven E. Nissen, MD, MACC, chief academic officer of the Sydell and Arnold Miller Family Heart, Vascular & Thoracic Institute and the Lewis and Patricia Dickey Chair in Cardiovascular Medicine at Cleveland Clinic, said during a press conference. “The Lp(a)HORIZON trial is not the end of the story. Ongoing trials are studying different populations, such as primary prevention and aortic stenosis, and different therapies, such as [small interfering] RNA. A single trial does not provide definitive evidence of a lack of benefit of lowering lipoprotein(a) as a strategy to reduce cardiovascular risk. We will hopefully be able to move on and keep these studies going. I am worried that people ... will bail out on the Lp(a) hypothesis. That would be a tragic outcome.”

For Lp(a)HORIZON, Nissen and colleagues randomly assigned 8,350 patients with established CVD and Lp(a) of at least 70 mg/dL (148 mmol/L), of whom 8,322 were included in the efficacy analysis, to receive subcutaneous pelacarsen 80 mg once monthly or placebo. The mean age was 60 years, 27% were women and 78% were white.

The average Lp(a) level was 236 nmol/L at baseline, which at 12 months dropped to 64.4 nmol/L in the pelacarsen group, a 77.7% reduction, but stayed steady at 233.4 nmol/L in the placebo group, Nissen said during the press conference.

At a median follow-up of 4.7 years, the primary endpoint of major adverse CV events, defined as CV death, nonfatal MI, nonfatal stroke or urgent coronary revascularization, occurred in 12.3% of the pelacarsen group and 12.1% of the placebo group (HR = 1.02; 95% CI, 0.9-1.15; P = .76), Nissen said.

Among patients with baseline Lp(a) of at least 90 mg/dL (192 nmol/L), the primary endpoint occurred in 12.3% of both groups (HR = 1; 95% CI, 0.87-1.15; P = .99), according to the researchers.

Nissen said there were no differences between the groups in the individual components of the primary outcome:

The rate of serious adverse events was 37.3% in the pelacarsen group and 41.1% in the placebo group, Nissen and colleagues found. The rate of adverse events leading to drug discontinuation was 20.6% in the pelacarsen group and 7.5% in the placebo group, while the overall rates of drug discontinuation were 35.1% in the pelacarsen group and 18.3% in the placebo group, Nissen said.

“These results apply to this [antisense oligonucleotide] and secondary prevention patients,” Nissen said during the press conference. “Background therapy was optimized with baseline LDL cholesterol and blood pressure among the lowest achieved of any CV outcome trial, which may have precluded showing further benefits.”

In a series of extended analyses that were also presented and were simultaneously published in NEJM Evidence, the researchers found no differences between the groups in the primary outcome under the following circumstances:

The researchers also found the primary endpoint results did not vary by baseline Lp(a), LDL, high-sensitivity C-reactive protein or time between qualifying CVD event and enrollment.

“There are plenty of examples of when the first drug in a class failed for a variety of reasons, maybe which we didn’t fully understand, and we went on and continued to test the hypothesis and we got better results, so I really think you cannot close the door with a single negative trial,” Nissen said during the press conference. “But yes, it does lower our expectations for the likelihood of success. It’s going to be my mission to convince the people who pay the bills, which is industry, not to pull the plug on the hypothesis, because we really need to understand more about who benefits and who doesn’t.”

This was about as neutral a trial as a trial can get. Nothing moved the needle: the main analysis, the subgroup analyses, the on-treatment analyses all showed no difference.

The big take-home is this was truly a negative trial. A trial where the agent moved the biomarker 80%, but the curves just were right on top of each other, is a little disappointing. It’s certainly a big outcome, but just not the one we were hoping for.

This was one shot on goal. There are other shots on goal, but I think that the floor has been raised. We are dealing with different trial designs, different drugs and different potency. But I think what this tells us is that the bar is now high for a secondary prevention trial. A primary prevention trial or a high-risk primary prevention trial could be very different.

Step one is we have to wait until we see the other secondary prevention trial. I think that the olpasiran (Arrowhead/Amgen) trial will be next. This is a different trial, a different drug with different tolerability and more potent Lp(a) lowering. I think if that doesn’t work, then we need more serious conversations about what we’re doing with Lp(a), but I don’t think the story’s over.

Lp(a)HORIZON told us, though, that the floor for preventive pharmacotherapy, especially after events, is a high floor. We’re doing a good job. But it might mean that in that population, there’s just a little less room for treating some of the residual risk, at least with this drug.

What changes when we go back to clinic? Right now, nothing changes. For all my patients, we’re still checking Lp(a) because we know it is a powerful, genetically predicted risk factor for coronary heart disease.

For our post-MI patients, it tells us we need to be aggressive about following the guidelines, have them on antiplatelet therapy and drive their LDL cholesterol down low. Nissen said this was one of the best-treated populations we’ve seen in a CV clinical trial, and we have to replicate that. We have to get them on good lipid therapy and good antihypertensive therapy and treat their diabetes with drugs we know reduce risk. And I think if we do that, we can tell our patients, we have mitigated a lot of what we see from that residual risk, and we have some trial data to back that up that a well-treated population does really well. The only thing that changes is I can no longer say I think we’re going to have a drug right around the corner.

A lot of us were expecting a different outcome, and obviously it’s disappointing, but this is why we do outcome trials, because the biology is good and the genetics is good. We have a lot more questions than we have answers, and I look forward to the next time we have an Lp(a) outcome trial, which will hopefully be positive.

Nissen SE, et al. LBS.01. The Dr. Eugene Braunwald late-breaking science session: Translating science into prevention: Lessons from landmark trials. Presented at: American Heart Association Scientific Sessions; Nov. 6-9, 2026; Chicago.

Disclosures: Nissen reports receiving institutional research grants from Arrowhead, AstraZeneca, CRISPR Therapeutics, Eli Lilly, Hygieia, Kalexo Bio, NewAmsterdam Pharmaceuticals, Novartis and Silence Pharmaceuticals, receiving travel reimbursement from Lilly and consulting for Amgen. He does not accept personal compensation from drug and device companies. Please see the study for all other authors’ relevant financial disclosures. The Lp(a)HORIZON study was funded by Novartis.

https://www.healio.com/news/womens-healt.title: How men and women are ‘treated differently’ across medicine
https://www.healio.com/news/womens-healt.author: Emma Bascom
https://www.healio.com/news/womens-healt.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

Women are less likely to receive active management for the same medical conditions as men, according to research published in PLOS One.

Miriam Veenhuizen, MD, an honorary lecturer in University of St. Andrews School of Medicine, and colleagues reviewed 41 papers, 38 of which were retrospective case series that evaluated patient records. Thirty-three reported finding “a significant difference” in the treatment of men and women patients.

This was consistent across many different specialties. Major disparities included:

Veenhuizen told Healio the research is “important for healthcare providers both for their day to day working and for planning research projects,” but “we do not know for sure if there were any clinical implications of our findings.”

“We do know that men and women were treated differently despite this not being advised in guidelines. We don’t know if this leads to poorer outcomes for either sex. We have to consider that patient choice may have played a role in the differences found,” Veenhuizen said.

The researchers also were “not aware of any clinical reason for women to be less likely to be given analgesia for pain,” but that was “a consistent finding across the literature,” according to Veenhuizen.

“In our review, analgesia use was only studied in prehospital medicine,” she said. “In other research papers, the authors have recommended a guideline for pain management in prehospital medicine to try and make the decision more protocol driven.”

The researchers concluded that there are “persistent sex-based differences in the treatment of patients” in medicine. The most consistent finding across multiple specialties was that women were statistically less likely than men who had comparable clinical characteristics “to receive invasive or intensive treatments.” And, when they were treated conservatively, women “were less likely to receive guideline-compliant therapy.”

Veenhuizen said that, to reduce these disparities, “more research should be done, and more emphasis should be given on equality, diversity and inclusivity in the education of healthcare providers.” According to a press release, the researchers now plan to test whether these same patterns will appear in generative AI outputs, “which are trained on this literature and on clinical records, and which could entrench these differences at scale if left unchecked.”

“Overall, this is a societal issue and likely found across all workplaces. In order to improve disparity, we need to recognize it and more research needs to be done to address it,” Veenhuizen said.

Miriam Veenhuizen, MD, can be reached at mav3@st-andrews.ac.uk.

Disclosures: Veenhuizen reports no relevant financial disclosures.

https://www.healio.com/news/orthopedics/.title: Legal risks associated with peptides for practicing physicians
https://www.healio.com/news/orthopedics/.author: Gary W. Herschman, JD; Mark Yacura, JD
https://www.healio.com/news/orthopedics/.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

Physicians prescribing peptides that have not been FDA approved continue to face a myriad of potential legal and regulatory risks.

While prescribing FDA-approved semaglutide (Ozempic and Wegovy, Novo Nordisk) and tirzepatide (Zepbound and Mounjaro, Eli Lilly) for their approved uses presents few regulatory issues for physicians, many other unapproved peptides prescribed and promoted for various uses are currently being produced by compounding pharmacies.

Physicians who prescribe, source, promote or administer peptides that are not FDA approved or have not been included in FDA’s bulk substances lists face significant potential regulatory, civil and even criminal risks.

Prescribing or compounding peptides that violate FDA rules, such as utilizing bulk drug substances that FDA has not deemed safe and placed into FDA’s bulk substances list, can lead to disciplinary action, fines or revocation of a physician’s state medical license by the state medical board where he or she practices.

In July 2026, the FDA’s Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee (PCAC) voted to recommend adding six peptides to the FDA’s Section 503A bulk substances list, which would enable compounding pharmacies to compound these peptides under strict parameters without concern for current FDA enforcement action. The FDA is, however, not legally bound to follow these recommendations as the PCAC recommendations are only advisory, and the FDA can accept, reject or take substantial time to act on them.

On Oct. 14, 2026, FDA issued an interim policy statement to the White House stating it intends to use “enforcement discretion” and would pause enforcing against pharmacies sourcing these six bulk peptide substances for compounding. On Oct. 27, 2026, the White House Office of Management and Budget affirmed the FDA policy proposal. On Oct. 30, the formalized policy was published by the Federal Register. FDA’s enforcement discretion regarding these six peptides will remain in force until final rulemaking regarding their inclusion in FDA’s bulk drug substance list is completed or if and until safety issues regarding any of these peptides becomes apparent to the FDA.

Nevertheless, many state boards of pharmacy and state attorneys general have authority under their state’s laws to take independent enforcement actions against unapproved compounded peptides regardless of federal committee recommendations or any FDA policy.

Beyond state administrative action risks to physicians, federal prosecutors have presented evidence to grand juries who have indicted licensed physicians for prosecution for ordering peptides that have not been approved by the FDA from overseas or unverified third-party intermediaries and dispensing them to patients.

Sourcing or selling unapproved, misbranded or research-use-only peptides can result in federal criminal actions against physicians who prescribe or dispense such peptides or promote them for clinically unproven uses. Thus, purchasing peptides from unverified online vendors or research-only suppliers — rather than licensed, compliant compounding pharmacies — places legal liability on the prescriber for any product contamination, mislabeling or purity failures.

If a physician markets unapproved peptides as capable of preventing or treating disease or a medical condition without competent and reliable scientific evidence, the physician is potentially subject to civil fraud, deceptive trade practice or consumer protection lawsuits at both the federal and state level.

Administering or recommending experimental or off-label peptides that lack rigorous, placebo-controlled human clinical trials exposes physicians to malpractice lawsuits if patients experience serious adverse reactions, unexpected side effects or death.

Further, physicians have a legal duty to inform patients if a therapy is experimental and the prescribed or dispensed peptide is not approved by the FDA, lacks long-term human safety data or the physician fails to disclose all potential side effects.

Failing to adequately document and secure proper informed consent exposes a physician to legal claims if untoward side effects or serious or life-threatening adverse events materialize.

Gary W. Herschman, JD, and Mark Yacura, JD, are members of Baker Donelson and can be reached at www.bakerdonelson.com.

Disclosures: Herschman reports being a healthcare transaction attorney for more than 30 years and being co-chair of the healthcare transactions group at Baker Donelson. Yacura reports no relevant financial disclosures.
