https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.title: GLP-1s confer better glycemic, CV outcomes than metformin
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.author: Erik Swain
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

CHICAGO — Among adults with prediabetes and obesity, those taking a GLP-1 receptor agonist were more likely to achieve normoglycemia compared with those taking metformin, researchers reported.

Those taking a GLP-1 were also had reduced risk for death, CV outcomes and progression to type 2 diabetes compared with those taking metformin, according to the results.

“Nearly 40% of U.S. adults have [prediabetes], and up to 10% progress to diabetes each year,” Vinicius de Sousa Barzon Serra, MD, research fellow in the department of cardiovascular medicine at Mayo Clinic in Scottsdale, Arizona, told Healio. “Metformin is still the standard first-line medication, alongside lifestyle modification. GLP-1 medications are now widely used for weight loss, and about one in 10 U.S. adults may be taking one. We wanted to know how they compare with metformin in patients who have both prediabetes and obesity. We looked at blood sugar reversal, progression to diabetes and cardiovascular outcomes. To do that, we used TriNetX data covering more than 250,000 patients across 104 institutions.”

For the study, presented at the American Heart Association Scientific Sessions, Serra and colleagues matched 128,846 adults with prediabetes and obesity taking a GLP-1 receptor agonist with 128,846 adults with prediabetes and obesity taking metformin. Matching was based on demographics, comorbidities, medications and laboratory values. The mean age was 52 years and 76% were women. The primary outcomes were reversion to normoglycemia and progression to type 2 diabetes. Participants were followed for approximately 3 years.

The rate of reversion to normoglycemia during the study period was 37.3% in the GLP-1 group and 29.3% in the metformin group (HR = 1.53; 95% CI, 1.51-1.55; P < .001), while the rate of progression to type 2 diabetes was 25.1% in the GLP-1 group and 37% in the metformin group (HR = 0.69; 95% CI, 0.68-0.7; P < .001), Serra and colleagues found.

Compared with the metformin group, the GLP-1 group also had reduced risk for all-cause mortality (HR = 0.59; 95% CI, 0.55-0.63), acute heart failure (HR = 0.74; P < .05), ischemic stroke (HR = 0.8; P < .05), acute myocardial infarction (HR = 0.84; P < .05), cardiac arrest (HR = 0.58; P < .05) and atrial fibrillation (HR = 0.92; P < .05), Serra and colleagues found.

“The direction of the results was in line with what we expected,” Serra told Healio. “GLP-1 medications produce substantial weight loss, and weight loss is known to help prevent type 2 diabetes. We saw a 1.5-fold higher chance of reversing blood sugar to normal and a 31% lower risk of progression to diabetes. The size of the association with all-cause mortality (41% lower) and with cardiovascular events was larger than I would have predicted. I would interpret it cautiously. This is an observational analysis based on diagnosis codes and prescription records. These findings are preliminary and need confirmation in prospective studies.”

There was no difference between the groups in risk for ventricular tachycardia.

“The main effect these findings could have is on shared decision-making between doctors and patients,” Serra told Healio. “Metformin remains a safe, inexpensive first-line option with a long track record. This work is less about replacing one medication with another and more about discussing additional options with specific patients. It may add to the case for considering GLP-1 medications earlier, rather than waiting until type 2 diabetes develops. Lifestyle changes, including diet and exercise, remain an essential part of prediabetes treatment. Cost and access are also practical considerations.”

“This is an important finding because the GLP-1 receptor agonists are commonly used today, and this is a population that in the transition from prediabetes to diabetes are at increasing risk for cardiovascular disease,” Robert Eckel, MD, FAHA, emeritus professor of medicine at the University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus and past president of the American Heart Association, said in a statement made available to the media. “So, the finding is not surprising to me, and I think the explanation is yet to be clarified, but likely in part relates to the amount of weight reduction that ensued. The Diabetes Prevention Program was an incredibly important program done several decades ago that showed that lifestyle intervention was really important in delaying the transition from prediabetes to type 2 diabetes, and the bottom line from all those lifestyle interventions was the amount of weight that was lost. Yes, that included nutritional approaches and approaches to modifying physical activity, but the weight reduction was really which was most telling, and we know with GLP-1 receptor agonists, you get a fair amount of weight reduction. And of course, that varies depending on which GLP-1 receptor agonist was utilized. Some caused much more weight loss than others, and I think the data need to be shared and published for us to review it more carefully.”

https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.title: Contemporary hormone therapy does not worsen cardiovascular risk
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.author: Erik Swain
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

CHICAGO — In a long-term study, menopausal hormone therapy did not raise risk for heart attack, stroke, blood clots or death in women aged 45 to 59 years, researchers reported at the American Heart Association Scientific Sessions.

“In November 2025, the FDA removed the black box warning from hormone replacement therapy products, and we have since seen a steep rise in the number of women starting hormone therapy (HT). Much of that momentum is driven by media coverage and social media rather than by clinical consultation. Because the original warning bundled cardiovascular disease together with breast cancer, dementia and endometrial cancer, its removal has been widely read as meaning that HT now carries no risk at all,” Ronen Arbel, PhD, FESC, FAHA, head of innovation and research at Community Medical Services Division, Clalit Health Services, Tel Aviv, and associate professor, Maximizing Health Outcomes Research Lab, Sapir College, Sderot, Israel, told Healio. “Women are arriving at their physicians not to ask whether they should take HT, but to request it, and some say explicitly that they want it to lower their cardiovascular risk. Clinicians need real data to answer that question, in either direction. The existing evidence did not provide it: The randomized trials that shaped a generation of practice used higher-dose formulations that are largely obsolete, in women who began treatment many years after menopause. Clalit’s electronic health records let us ask a more contemporary question: current formulations, women who start at the age they actually start, and long enough follow-up to matter. We held to a strict target-trial design, which is why we are confident in what we found.”

The researchers analyzed a retrospective, observational matched cohort of 52,330 women aged 45 to 59 years, half of whom initiated HT and half of whom did not, who were free from atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, venous thromboembolism and cancer at baseline.

After a mean follow-up of 12 years, Arbel and colleagues observed no differences between the groups for the following outcomes:

“The findings are consistent with [the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists’] recommendation to start HT within 10 years of menopause onset and before age 60, and with the FDA’s 2025 decision,” Arbel told Healio. “They also help settle the long shadow cast by the Women’s Health Initiative, which led a generation of physicians and patients to abandon HT altogether.”

The results did not vary by type of HT or route of administration, according to the researchers.

“The genuine surprise was venous thromboembolism: 174 events with HT vs. 175 without: no excess risk at all, and no meaningful difference between oral, transdermal and gel preparations,” Arbel told Healio. “Other studies have reported an advantage for transdermal routes, and there is a plausible pathophysiologic explanation: avoidance of hepatic first pass. Our data suggest that oral tablets are equally safe in this population.”

Arbel said the lessons from the study include that “HT should be prescribed to treat menopausal symptoms — not as cardiovascular prevention. That is the honest message to give a woman who asks for it on cardioprotective grounds”; that “women and their clinicians are not confined to the small number of transdermal products available. Oral formulations widen the options, and with them the likelihood of finding a regimen a woman will actually stay on”; and that “these results should not be extrapolated beyond the population we studied: women with established cardiovascular disease, prior thromboembolism or cancer were excluded, as were women initiating treatment well after menopause.”

Arbel noted several limitations. “This is an observational study, so it cannot prove causation,” he said. “Although the groups were matched on age, BMI, blood pressure, lipids, diabetes, smoking status and socioeconomic status, factors not captured in the health records — physical activity, diet and severity of menopausal symptoms — may still differ between them. Women were also classified by the first formulation they received, without accounting for later changes in type or route of administration."

Abstracts presented at American Heart Association scientific meetings are not peer-reviewed, and the findings are considered preliminary until published as a full manuscript in a peer-reviewed scientific journal.

Arbel R, et al. Abstract MDP0654. Presented at: American Heart Association Scientific Sessions; Nov. 6-9, 2026; Chicago.

Disclosures: Arbel reports no relevant financial disclosures.

https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.title: Data support monotherapy approach after uncomplicated LAAC
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.author: Scott Buzby
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

Monotherapy was noninferior vs. dual antiplatelet therapy at 6 months for death, stroke or major bleeding after uncomplicated left atrial appendage closure, according to data presented at TCT 2026 and simultaneously published in JAMA.

Six-month results from the open-label, multicenter, randomized SIMPLAAFY trial showed that reduced-dose non-vitamin K antagonist oral anticoagulation (NOAC) or aspirin alone was noninferior to DAPT in patients who underwent left atrial appendage closure (LAAC) with the Watchman FLX Pro device (Boston Scientific).

“After left atrial appendage closure, a short-term full-dose non-vitamin K antagonist anticoagulation ... or 6 months of dual antiplatelet therapy is administered during device endothelialization,” Saibal Kar, MD, interventional cardiologist at Los Robles Hospital and Medical Center in Thousand Oaks, California, said during a press conference. “Balancing the bleeding risk and thromboembolic risk is always a challenge. The randomized evidence of simplified antithrombotic strategies are quite limited. The objective of this trial was to evaluate the safety and efficacy of two postimplant monotherapies, either reduced-dose NOAC or baby aspirin alone, compared to conventional dual antiplatelet strategies.”

Researchers randomly assigned 1,857 patients who underwent uncomplicated LAAC in a 1:1:1 fashion to 6-month DAPT followed by aspirin, 3-month reduced-dose NOAC followed by aspirin or 12-month aspirin only (mean age, 76 years; 43% women; mean CHA2DS2-VASc score, 4.2), according to the presentation.

The primary outcome was a composite of all-cause death, stroke, systemic embolism or major bleeding at6 months.

Compared with 6-month DAPT, both reduced-dose NOAC (RR = 0.75; 95% CI, 0.48-1.18; risk difference, –1.7 percentage points) and aspirin monotherapy (RR = 0.49; 95% CI, 0.29-0.82; risk difference, –3.5 percentage points) met criteria for noninferiority (P for noninferiority for both < .001), Kar said at the press conference.

Rates of ischemic stroke were the same in each group (0.7%), the researchers reported.

Risk for all International Society on Thrombosis and Haemostasis bleeding was lower in the aspirin monotherapy (RR = 0.43; 95% CI, 0.29-0.64; P < .05) and reduced-dose NOAC groups (RR = 0.57; 95% CI, 0.4-0.81; P < .05) vs. 6-month DAPT, according to the presentation.

“There was significant reduction in bleeding in both the monotherapy arms compared to DAPT,” Kar said during the presentation. “Actually, this was even more pronounced with the patients who were just assigned to baby aspirin.”

The researchers reported the lowest rates of device-related thrombus occurred in the reduced-dose NOAC group (0.9%), followed by the aspirin monotherapy group (2.7%) and the DAPT group (3.4%).

“Monotherapy strategies were noninferior to dual antiplatelet therapy for the composite of death, stroke, systemic embolization or major bleeding at 6 months,” Kar said during the presentation. “Both monotherapy strategies reduce clinically relevant bleeding compared to dual antiplatelet therapy. The 45-day [device-related thrombus] appeared lowest with the reduced-dose NOAC. Ischemic stroke rates were the same in all the three groups, and longer-term efficacy outcomes will be analyzed at a prespecified endpoint at 12 months. These findings support that simplification of antithrombotic management of uncomplicated left atrial appendage closure may be individualized according to competing bleeding and device thrombotic risks and patient preferences.”

Kar S. Late-breaking clinical trials: Session II, in collaboration with The New England Journal of Medicine. Presented at: TCT Scientific Symposium; Oct. 31-Nov. 3, 2026; San Diego.

Disclosures: Kar reports consulting for Abbott and receiving research support from Boston Scientific. The study was funded by Boston Scientific.

https://www.healio.com/news/endocrinolog.title: Hepatitis B vaccination important for people living with diabetes
https://www.healio.com/news/endocrinolog.author: Susan Weiner, MS, RDN, CDN, CDCES, FADCES; Arpan Mohanty, MD, MSc
https://www.healio.com/news/endocrinolog.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

In this Diabetes in Real Life column, Susan Weiner, MS, RDN, CDN, CDCES, FADCES, talks with Arpan Mohanty, MD, MSc, about why hepatitis B warrants greater attention in diabetes care and what to know about vaccination, screening and more.

Weiner: What is the clinical guidance for hepatitis vaccination for people living with diabetes?

Mohanty: The American Diabetes Association recommends hepatitis B virus vaccination for all adults with diabetes younger than 60 years. For those aged 60 years or older, vaccination should be considered based on individual risk factors, such as exposure risk, living situation and other health conditions, consistent with Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices guidance.

Weiner: What populations are at increased risk?

Mohanty: Adults with type 1 or type 2 diabetes have a higher risk for HBV. Among adults aged 19 to 59 years, the risk for acute infection is about twice that of people without diabetes. Diabetes may impair immune responses, reducing the likelihood of HBV clearance and increasing the risk for chronic infection. Risk may be especially high in long-term care settings or when blood glucose monitoring equipment is shared or not properly disinfected. In addition, vaccination is particularly important for people with diabetes, as they are more likely to develop metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), which can lead to metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), cirrhosis or liver cancer. Preventing HBV with vaccination helps protect a liver that may already be vulnerable.

Weiner: Describe the overlap of chronic kidney disease, diabetes, hypertension, inflammation and coordinated cardiometabolic management for people living with diabetes and hepatitis.

Mohanty: In patients with diabetes, hepatitis or liver inflammation most commonly results from viral infection, alcohol-associated liver disease or MASH, the inflammatory form of MASLD. MASLD and MASH frequently coexist with obesity, hypertension, dyslipidemia and CKD and should be viewed within the broader cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) framework.

These conditions share common drivers, including insulin resistance, excess adiposity, endothelial dysfunction and chronic systemic inflammation. The relationship between MASLD and type 2 diabetes is bidirectional: Type 2 diabetes increases the risk for MASLD progression while MASLD may worsen insulin resistance and glycemic control. Consequently, MASLD, particularly when fibrosis is present, is associated not only with liver-related outcomes, including cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma, but also with a higher risk for major adverse cardiovascular events.

Management should therefore be coordinated, rather than organ-specific. Therapies selected to improve glycemic control and protect the heart and kidneys may also reduce liver fat or injury while newer liver-directed treatments can slow or potentially reverse fibrosis in patients with MASH. Viral hepatitis also warrants prompt treatment. Hepatitis C virus cure may improve glycemic control and is associated with reduced kidney and CV complications. A coordinated CKM-liver strategy can therefore address shared risk factors while improving outcomes across the liver, heart and kidneys.

Weiner: Dialysis populations have historically experienced higher rates of HBV exposure. What enhanced infection control measures and monitoring situations should be implemented?

Mohanty: Patients receiving hemodialysis remain at increased risk for HBV and HCV because of frequent blood exposure, shared treatment environments and impaired immune function, which increases susceptibility to infection and reduces vaccine responsiveness. Prevention should begin before admission to an outpatient dialysis unit.

The CDC recommends baseline testing with hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg), antibody to hepatitis B surface antigen (anti-HBs) and antibody to hepatitis B core antigen (anti-HBc) for all patients starting hemodialysis. Susceptible patients should be vaccinated as early as possible, ideally before dialysis begins. For patients vaccinated after dialysis initiation, higher-dose regimens are recommended, followed by anti-HBs testing 1 to 2 months after series completion. Patients who do not achieve protective immunity should receive a second vaccine series. Ongoing HBV surveillance should be guided by immune status. Patients who remain susceptible should undergo monthly HBsAg testing, whereas vaccine responders should have anti-HBs levels checked annually and be revaccinated if titers fall below 10 IU/L. Patients with immunity from prior infection generally do not require additional routine HBV testing. In addition, patients should also be screened for HCV at dialysis initiation and every 6 months thereafter. Screening for viral hepatitis is also important when transferring to another dialysis center or changing treatment type, after a blood exposure, and whenever a new HBV case is identified in the unit.

Infection control within the dialysis unit is equally important. Standard precautions, meticulous hand hygiene, appropriate use of personal protective equipment, safe medication and injection practices, disinfection of dialysis stations and shared equipment, and maintenance of water quality should be consistently enforced. Patients who test positive for HbsAg should be promptly isolated and dialyzed using dedicated equipment, with unit-specific exposure protocols implemented to reduce transmission.

Weiner: How can hepatitis be prevented, detected and treated in the diabetes population? Which members of the healthcare team should support these efforts?

Mohanty: Hepatitis prevention, detection and referral for treatment should be integrated into routine diabetes care. The key steps are to assess vaccination status, complete recommended screening and ensure timely follow-up of positive results. Prevention begins with HBV vaccination. The ADA Standards of Care recommend vaccination for adults with diabetes aged younger than 60 years and individualized vaccination for those aged 60 years or older. Vaccine response may be reduced by older age, obesity, CKD, immunosuppression and diabetes itself. The two-dose CpG-adjuvanted vaccine (Heplisav-B, Dynavax) provides higher seroprotection and a shorter completion interval than conventional three-dose regimens. Postvaccination serologic testing is important when confirmation of immunity is clinically necessary, including for patients receiving hemodialysis, immunocompromised individuals and healthcare personnel.

Detection has been simplified by universal adult screening. All adults should undergo HBV screening at least once with HbsAg, anti-HBs and total anti-HBc, as well as one-time HCV antibody testing with reflex RNA testing. Repeat testing is indicated for those with ongoing risk. In diabetes care, the operational priority is to confirm that screening has been completed, document the results and establish a reliable follow-up pathway.

Patients with positive results should be referred promptly. Chronic HBV can be effectively suppressed, and HCV is curable in most patients, including those with advanced CKD. HCV cure may also improve glycemic control and reduce kidney and CV complications. Antiviral selection and monitoring may intersect with renal function, lipid management and glucose-lowering therapy.

The optimal model for hepatitis prevention and treatment often requires coordinated, interprofessional care, which depends on the clinical context and institutional resources. Primary care clinicians and endocrinologists can assess vaccination and screening status and initiate referrals while nurses, medical assistant and pharmacists can use standing orders, administer vaccines and track series completion. Diabetes care and education specialists can reinforce the relevance of hepatitis to diabetes outcomes; nephrology and dialysis teams can oversee dialysis-specific surveillance and infection control; and hepatology or infectious disease specialists can screen for hepatitis, manage confirmed infection and advanced liver disease. Each institution should establish a clear coordination point, assign responsibility for each step and embed hepatitis care within the diabetes pathway to prevent incomplete vaccination, missed results and unclosed referrals.

Weiner: How can we improve prevention, detection and treatment in underserved and at-risk communities?

Mohanty: Improving hepatitis prevention and care in underserved communities requires embedding services in the settings where people with diabetes already receive care, including primary care, endocrinology, pharmacies, dialysis units and diabetes education programs. Each setting should first identify its implementation gaps, such as low vaccination rates, incomplete screening or loss to follow-up, assess their magnitude and local causes, and tailor interventions accordingly.

Strategies to improve vaccination and screening include standing vaccination orders, opt-out testing and electronic health record prompts, which can reduce missed opportunities and help address disparities. Testing should also be available beyond traditional clinics through community health centers, mobile programs, shelters, correctional facilities, syringe-service programs and other settings that reach people with limited access to care.

Treatment access can be expanded through telehealth and task-shifting. Primary care clinicians, nurse practitioners and other trained nonspecialists can treat uncomplicated HCV with specialist support, allowing hepatology resources to focus on patients with cirrhosis, complex coinfection or treatment failure. Telehealth and Project ECHO (Extension for Community Healthcare Outcomes)-type models can extend expertise to rural and safety-net settings, although telephone-based options may be needed for patients with limited internet access.

Finally, improving outcomes requires addressing barriers that commonly interrupt care, including transportation, insurance coverage, medication costs, housing instability, limited health literacy and stigma. Community health workers, peer navigators, social workers and culturally and linguistically tailored education can help patients move from screening to treatment without being lost to follow-up. The most effective approach is a coordinated, context-specific system that combines easier access, automated workflows, community partnerships and clear ownership of follow-up.

Weiner: Is there current research available on other hepatitis treatments?

Mohanty: Research in MASH treatment is advancing rapidly, an especially important development for people with type 2 diabetes who are at high risk for MASLD/MASH and resultant progressive liver fibrosis. Resmetirom (Rezdiffra, Madrigal Pharmaceuticals), a thyroid hormone receptor-beta agonist, and semaglutide (Wegovy, Novo Nordisk), a GLP-1 receptor agonist, are now FDA-approved for adults with noncirrhotic MASH and moderate to advanced fibrosis, in conjunction with lifestyle modification. Incretin-based therapies remain particularly relevant to diabetes care. Phase 2 trials of tirzepatide (Mounjaro/Zepbound, Eli Lilly) and survodutide (Boehringer Ingelheim) have shown improvements in MASH, weight and cardiometabolic risk. Fibroblast growth factor 21, or FGF21, analogs, including efruxifermin (Novo Nordisk) and pegozafermin (Roche), have also shown promising effects on liver fibrosis and metabolic parameters and are now being evaluated in phase 3 trials. These advances also reinforce the importance of identifying fibrosis early so eligible patients can benefit from approved therapies or clinical trials.

Arpan Mohanty, MD, MSc, is a hepatologist at Boston Medical Center and assistant professor of medicine at Boston University Chobanian & Avedisian School of Medicine. Mohanty can be reached at endocrinology@healio.com.

Susan Weiner, MS, RDN, CDN, CDCES, FADCES, is a registered dietitian, author, nutrition expert and media spokesperson who translates nutrition science into practical strategies for daily life. She is coauthor of The Complete Diabetes Organizer and Diabetes: 365 Tips for Living Well and serves as the Healio | Endocrine Today Diabetes in Real Life column editor. She can be reached at susan@susanweinernutrition.com; Instagram @susanweinernutrition; X @susangweiner.

Winn Career Development Award; consultant fees in the past 2 years from Boehringer Ingelheim, Madrigal, Medpace and Takeda; and serving as site principal investigator for industry-sponsored clinical trials funded by Atea Pharmaceuticals, Bausch Health, Inventiva, Kowa, Madrigal, Meridian Biosciences, Novo Nordisk and Takeda. https://www.healio.com/news/primary-care.title: Gloria Steinem believed in this lifestyle medicine pillar
https://www.healio.com/news/primary-care.author: Resa E. Lewiss, MD, DipABLM
https://www.healio.com/news/primary-care.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

See all articles from Lewiss on Lifestyle Medicine

In February of 2020, I sat with Gloria Steinem for a podcast episode. We talked about her writing, her professional life and her visible voice.

We met at her New York City brownstone for an in-person conversation. When we sat down to record, she offered me a piece of her raisin bran muffin — the oversized ones you can typically buy at an NYC bodega.

As an emergency and lifestyle physician interested in health and chronic disease prevention, I asked her what she did to stay healthy. Lifestyle medicine is a medical specialty that uses lifestyle interventions to prevent, treat and reverse chronic noncommunicable diseases such as diabetes, obesity, high blood pressure and cancer.

Clinicians focus on behaviors in six main health areas: food and nutrition, movement and exercise, restorative sleep, decreasing stress, avoiding harmful substances, and being in community. She seemed healthy and my physician's brain was curious.

I imagined she had a movement and exercise regimen that included walking the streets of the Upper East Side. And I was sure her food choices were intentionally nutrient-rich and minimally processed.

“I don’t come from a place, a family or a generation that did sports or cared about nutrition,” she said. “I mean, I sort of grew up on candy bars and ice cream. So, I still don’t have very good habits in that regard. I don’t walk regularly. I’ve never played a sport in my life.”

She said her main exercise was running through airports, noting she was often late for flights. I smiled.

My curiosity continued. “What do you do to stay healthy?”

She replied with a tone and response connoting something self-evident: “I have friends. There’s, I mean, people who — however different we are — we share the same kind of general hopes and humor and whatever it is. And I could not possibly do without that. Those are our chosen families.”

A 2023 study showed that people possessing a positive sense of community had lower rates of anxiety, depression and loneliness. It seems being in community is not just good for mood and mental health, though, because a 2016 systematic review and meta-analysis showed a noncommunicable disease association. What the authors called “poor social relationships,” including loneliness and social isolation, were associated with increased risk for coronary heart disease (29% increased risk) and stroke (32% increased risk).

Most of us intuitively know that social connectedness and social networks feel good. They positively affect our emotional well-being, and it turns out our physical health and longevity, too. The Harvard Study of Adult Development identified social connections as the single most important predictor of longevity and happiness with a positive mortality benefit. There is a 50% greater likelihood of survival among people with stronger social relationships compared with people with weaker social relationships.

Steinem emphasized the importance of storytelling. She said that storytelling is life-giving and one of our most necessary things next to air food and water. When I asked why she believed physicians were particularly poised to use their voices for good, she said, “Well, I think we all have a story. No matter whether we’re literate or physicians or whoever we are, it doesn’t matter, we have a story. And it is a story unlike anyone else’s. We need to be able to tell that story and to discover the similarities and the differences from other people’s stories. It’s absolutely crucial.”

Steinem, who died at age 92, visibly demonstrated the preventive health benefits of strong positive social connections and community. We saw this in the way she brought people together in her Manhattan brownstone. That living room and gathering place was ground zero for storytelling, activism, advocacy, conversations, and even a podcasting conversation with me.

Resa E. Lewiss, MD, DipABLM, is a lifestyle medicine and emergency medicine physician. She is an adjunct professor of emergency medicine at the Warren Alpert Medical School of Brown University. She produces and hosts The Visible Voices Podcast and is the co-author of the leadership book MicroSkills: Small Actions, Big Impact. She can be reached via her website resaelewiss.com.

https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.title: High-potassium DASH diet appears safe for patients on BP therapy
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.author: Maddy Grieco
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

The Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension diet did not raise risk for hyperkalemia among Black adults on blood pressure-lowering therapy, according to data presented at the American Heart Association’s Hypertension Scientific Sessions.

In 2025, Healio reported that the Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension (DASH) diet ranked highest among U.S. News & World Report’s heart-healthy diets.

“The DASH diet is a well-known, proven nutrition pattern that is known to improve blood pressure,” Marian Budu, MBBS, MPH, the clinical research coordinator of the GoFresh trials at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, said in a press release.

However, the diet includes foods that are high in potassium, which may cause hyperkalemia among people with different degrees of kidney function who are also using BP medications, Budu said.

To assess the impact of the DASH diet on serum potassium levels, Budu and colleagues conducted a secondary analysis of the GoFresh and GoFreshRx randomized trials, which included 356 Black adults from the Boston region with high BP (mean age, 53 years; 70% women; systolic BP, 120 mm Hg to < 150 mm Hg; diastolic BP, < 100 mm Hg) and varying degrees of kidney function.

The researchers assigned the participants to a group that received weekly DASH-patterned groceries — which aimed to include 4,700 mg daily potassium and a 2:1 potassium-to-sodium ratio — or to a self-guided diet using a monthly stipend for purchasing groceries for 3 months.

The medications the researchers analyzed included NSAIDs and three BP classes: ACE inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers, potassium-sparing diuretics and beta-blockers.

Budu and colleagues found that mean serum potassium levels did not significantly differ between the two groups after the intervention, suggesting a high-potassium diet was not linked to increased risk for hyperkalemia among Black adults using BP medications.

For instance, for those on ACE inhibitors/ARBs, the changes in serum potassium over 3 months included –0.03 mmol/L for the grocery group and 0.08 mmol/L for the self-directed group, for a difference in change between the two groups of –0.05 mmol/L. The difference in change for the other therapy classes ranged from –0.1 mmol/L for both NSAIDs and beta-blockers to 0.07 mmol/L for potassium-sparing diuretics.

The finding persisted regardless of baseline estimated glomerular filtration rate, although the study did not include patients with stage 4 or stage 5 kidney disease, according to the researchers.

“High-potassium groceries can be safely recommended to adults taking potassium-raising medications across a broad range of kidney function,” Budu told Healio. “Future trials should focus on looking at changes in adults with higher baseline potassium levels and stage 4 or 5 kidney disease.”

Marian Budu, MBBS, MPH, can be reached at cardiology@healio.com.

Budu M, et al. Moderated poster #TH157. Presented at: American Heart Association’s Hypertension Scientific Sessions; Oct. 7-11, 2026; Arlington, Va.

Disclosures: Budu reports no relevant financial disclosures.

https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.title: Coronary sinus reducer not beneficial in patients with ANOCA
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.author: Erik Swain
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

In patients with refractory angina and coronary microvascular dysfunction but no obstructed coronary arteries, a coronary sinus reducer did not improve coronary microvascular function, symptoms and quality of life, researchers reported.

The single-center investigator-initiated REMEDY-PILOT trial, presented at TCT 2026, compared the performance of a coronary sinus reducer (Shockwave Reducer, Shockwave Medical) with a sham procedure at improving endocardial myocardial perfusion reserve, symptoms and quality of life.

“In patients undergoing investigation for angina with nonobstructed coronary arteries, coronary microvascular dysfunction is observed in about 40% of patients. This condition is common,” Kevin Cheng, MA, BMBCh, MRCP, BHF clinical research fellow at Imperial College London and the Royal Brompton Hospital, said during a presentation. “Patients with coronary microvascular dysfunction experience a significant burden of symptoms [that] impairs quality of life and incurs excess healthcare costs. Trials [that] have employed a treatment strategy stratified by the results of microvascular function testing have demonstrated the potential benefits of pharmacologic approaches to improving symptoms and quality of life in these patients. However, despite this, a significant proportion of patients continue to experience life-limiting angina.”

Two previous sham-controlled trials showed that the coronary sinus reducer improved patient- and physician-reported angina in patients with refractory angina secondary to advanced coronary artery disease, but there had not previously been a sham-controlled trial of the device in patients with angina but no obstructive CAD (ANOCA) and coronary microvascular dysfunction, Cheng said.

REMEDY-PILOT included 54 patients (median age, 64 years; 44% women; 91% with Canadian Cardiovascular Society Angina class III or IV) randomly assigned to receive treatment with the coronary sinus reducer or a sham procedure.

The primary endpoint of change in segmental endocardial myocardial perfusion reserve at 6 months was similar in both groups (adjusted treatment effect, –0.03; 95% CI, –0.22 to 0.15; P = .72), Cheng said during the presentation.

The secondary endpoint of segmental endocardial/epicardial ratio at stress also did not differ between the groups (adjusted relative treatment effect, 1.004; 95% CI, 0.954-1.057; P = .88), he said.

The change in number of daily angina episodes also did not differ (OR = 0.92; 95% credible interval, 0.42-2.04; probability of benefit = 0.41), he said.

There were also no differences between the groups in change in six domains of the Seattle Angina Questionnaire: physical limitation, angina stability, angina frequency, treatment satisfaction, quality of life and summary score, according to the researchers.

There was only one device-related adverse event, a case of tamponade in the coronary sinus reducer group, Cheng said.

“REMEDY-PILOT is the first randomized, double blind, sham-controlled stratified treatment trial of a coronary sinus reducer in patients with refractory angina, ANOCA and [coronary microvascular dysfunction],” Cheng said during the presentation. “Coronary sinus reducer implantation was acceptable and safe. The coronary sinus reducer did not improve [cardiac magnetic resonance] perfusion metrics, symptoms or quality of life over a sham procedure. Ongoing analyses and additional studies are needed to define a role for reducer therapies in ANOCA and [coronary microvascular dysfunction].”

This was a well-done double-blind, randomized, sham-controlled trial. That’s huge, especially in this space. A couple of caveats to it is we don’t know the invasive physiology, such as coronary reserve, resistances or reaction to acetylcholine, we just have MRI-based perfusion, which is not widely used in the United States. So we don’t have a good sense of the population enrolled into randomization.

Any time you have extremely neutral trial results like that, it kind of makes you wonder, was that the right population to study? It appears to be some mixed disease, coronary disease, obstructive and nonobstructive disease, and there was no testing for vasospasm. A lot of patients could have had vasospasm, and coronary sinus reduction is not going to help them. So, my main takeaway would be that I’m not certain this was the most appropriate population with which to test this therapy.

Because this trial was smaller, with 54 patients, and there are other trials, and many other patients have been using this for over a decade now, I don’t think it’s going to derail things too much. However, it will make us be very careful with our selection for patients who would be candidates for the coronary sinus reducer in order to optimize their care and the success of the therapy to improve symptoms in patients with refractory angina.

We need to look at not only the obstructive refractory angina, but the nonobstructive patients. There is a lot of work to do mechanistic-wise: We need to look carefully at measures of coronary flow and/or resistance. I think that will help us identify the populations that are going to be most benefited. Plus, newer iterations of the device will come out that will make it safer, easier and potentially more efficacious, if we make prudent decisions on patient selection.

Cheng K, et al. Late-breaking clinical trials: Session I, in collaboration with The Lancet. Presented at: TCT Scientific Symposium; Oct. 31-Nov. 3, 2026; San Diego.

Disclosures: Cheng reports receiving honoraria from Johnson & Johnson Medtech.

https://www.healio.com/news/hematology-o.author: Josh Friedman
https://www.healio.com/news/hematology-o.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

This is a modal window.

AMA wants the FDA to hold botanical products derived from substances such as cannabis and kratom to the same scientific standards they maintain for approving other conventional drugs.

In a letter to the FDA, John J. Whyte, MD, MPH, AMA CEO and executive vice president, noted AMA is “deeply concerned” about the widespread use of these “natural” products without research-based evidence, and “strongly recommends” the FDA regulate them and determine their efficacy through research and clinical trials.

“As botanical manufacturers develop increasingly potent products in everything from gummies and powders to oils and injections, consumers are becoming the real-world guinea pigs — and suffering tragic consequences, including dependence, substance use disorders, overdose, and death,” AMA President Willie Underwood III, MD, MSc, MPH, said in a press release. “Calling something ‘natural’ doesn’t make it safe. We need science, not social media hype, to determine what belongs in our medicine cabinets.”

AMA “supports innovation in drug design and development,” but also “urge extreme caution” when products are marketed outside of the scientific process, including botanical health products, Whyte wrote.

Anita Gupta, DO, PharmD, MPP, FASA, adjunct assistant professor of anesthesiology and pain medicine at Johns Hopkins School of Medicine, applauded AMA’s insistence on holding botanical drugs “accountable.”

“We need better standards across the board to ensure that we’re proving safety and efficacy for all ingested products,” she told Healio. “Day in, day out, patients come in to see their doctor, and they don’t routinely mention these products, herbal, botanical, natural, however you want to describe them, because they don’t think of them as drugs. That needs to change. These products can impact bleeding, blood pressure and metabolism of certain drugs. It’s critical that we and patients treat botanicals for what they are, drugs that belong on a medication list.”

For instance, products made from kratom, a tropical tree from Southeast Asia, have been frequently used to self-treat various conditions, including anxiety, coughing, depression, diarrhea and pain, according to FDA.

Healio previously reported the number of poison control calls related to kratom exposure increased 1,200% between 2015 and 2025.

Whyte described AMA as “pleased” with the Drug Enforcement Agency emergency action against kratom compounds mitragynine pseudoindoxyl, commonly known as MGPI, MGM-15 and MGM-16.

“The AMA supports legislative and other efforts banning synthesized, purified, or derivative products from kratom for marketing, distribution, promotion, and sale, including but not limited to unregulated mitragynine along with the 7-hydroxymitragynine [7-OH] and MGM-15 market,” Whyte said. “Accordingly, the AMA has worked with multiple medical societies to support new laws protecting consumers from kratom and 7-OH products within their states.”

Gupta emphasized the dangers of kratom should be taken “seriously.”

“People often self-treat with kratom when other medications for pain are not working appropriately, or their treatments have failed in some way,” she explained. “Kratom has morphine effects, and 7-OH, which is a known compound derivative of kratom, has morphine effects. This is a red flag. Uncontrolled products are not the answer to pain treatment failure. There are rigorous trials for approved medications that we have very clear understanding how to dose, and we really need to have patients understand the risk.”

Gupta noted the same type of research that has been put into cannabis is needed for kratom.

Healio has reported on multiple investigations into cannabis, healthcare and outcomes, including:

AMA continues to support “adequate and well-controlled” studies investigating cannabis and related cannabinoids, and “encourage expanded research,” Whyte wrote.

He added AMA wants “sufficient funding” and supply of products and placebos for studies, and “safeguards for cannabis clinical research protocols and the development of a model informed consent form for institutional review board evaluation.”

Whyte implored the FDA to “not” allow political interests to “overrule scientific evidence.”

Gupta described the current time as historic for the number of nonregulated products individuals take for their health, and emphasized “natural is simply a marketing word, not a safety standard.”

“If a product is potent enough to really help someone for a medical condition, it is also potent enough to cause harm,” she said. “It should have to prove itself the same way every other drug does on the market.”

Anita Gupta, DO, PharmD, MPP, FASA, can be reached at www.anitagupta.com.

Disclosures: Gupta reports serving as a former US FDA special government employee, senior advisor to Milken Institute, advisor to Gates Foundation and member expert to World Economic Forum.

https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.title: CT guidance noninferior vs. IVUS for some undergoing PCI
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.author: Scott Buzby
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

Coronary CT-planned and -guided percutaneous coronary intervention was noninferior to intravascular ultrasound-guided PCI for 12-month target vessel failure, a speaker reported.

The finding was among patients with chronic coronary syndrome or stabilized non-ST elevation acute coronary syndrome.

The results of the investigator-initiated, international, open-label, randomized, noninferiority P4 trial of coronary CT-guided vs. IVUS-guided PCI for patients with an indication for revascularization were presented at TCT 2026 and simultaneously published in The New England Journal of Medicine.

“Coronary CT has evolved tremendously over the years. ... You see, for the first time, the disease in three dimensions, which is something that makes the interpretation of it very intuitive,” Carlos Collet, MD, PhD, director of cardiovascular imaging, physiology and translational therapeutics at the Cardiovascular Research Foundation, said during a press conference. “We went in-depth in the analysis of the calcium. Calcium is one of the Achilles' heel of PCI, so we provide a very comprehensive analysis of the calcium, including thickness, length, arc, location, density, etc.

“On top of that, we added the physiology in terms of [CT-guided fractional flow reserve] that basically show whether that lesion was significant or not,” Collet said. “In other words, appropriateness of the PCI, but also the physiology tells us where would a stent make a difference. For a stent to actually increase the flow, it needs to have a translation of pressure gradient. The trial hypothesis was the following: Can a CT-guided PCI strategy achieve similar outcomes compared to IVUS-guided PCI, with the context that IVUS-guided PCI is the best in terms of standard of care.”

Researchers enrolled 1,105 adult patients with chronic coronary syndrome or stabilized non-ST elevation ACS and a clinical indication for revascularization and randomly assigned them to coronary CT- or IVUS-guided PCI (median age, 65 years; 22% women). Key inclusion criteria included having at least one epicardial lesion with a stenosis diameter of more than 70% and CT-guided fractional flow reserve of 0.8 or less, Collet said during the press conference.

The primary endpoint was a composite of target vessel failure at 12 months, including CV death, target vessel MI or ischemia-driven target vessel revascularization, and the noninferiority margin was 4.5 percentage points.

“CT-guided PCI was a strategy that mandated the review of what we call the ‘structured PCI package,’ and the IVUS-guided PCI mandated IVUS before and after the intervention,” Collet said during the press conference. “[The package] was a comprehensive analysis of the CT to provide a number of details and was reviewed by all the physicians before the procedure. In addition to that, we designed software to integrate this 3D reconstruction inside the cath lab, and we synchronize that with the C-arm in order to provide real-time guidance during the PCI.”

At 12 months, the rate of target vessel failure was 4.1% in the CT-guided PCI arm and 4.6% in the IVUS-guided PCI arm, for a risk difference of –0.42 percentage points (95% CI, –2.82 to 1.99; P for noninferiority < .001; P for superiority = .73).

Six patients in the coronary CT group and nine in the IVUS group had clinical procedural complications, according to the study.

Procedural time was approximately 17 minutes shorter with coronary CT- vs. IVUS-guided PCI and the CT approach required less contrast volume (–20 mL; 95% CI, –25 to 0; P < .001), Collet said at the press conference.

Contrast volume was lower in the CT group compared with the IVUS group (150 mL vs. 170 mL; difference, –20 mL; 95% CI, –25 to 0; P < .001), he said.

Radiation exposure was numerically lower in the CT group (35.6 Gycm2 vs. 38.5 Gycm2; difference, –2.91 Gycm2; 95% CI, –9.03 to 3.8; P = .07), according to the researchers.

“CT-guided PCI was not inferior to IVUS-guided PCI with respect of target vessel failure at 12 months. CT guidance shortened the procedures and resulted in less contrast use and numerically lower radiation. These results support a path for PCI planning and procedural guidance in selected patients undergoing PCI,” Collet said during the press conference.

The P4 trial is encouraging. CT-guided PCI isn’t ready for prime time right now, but it’s just around the corner, potentially in the next 2 to 5 years. There are a lot of things dependent on it. We’re going to need more proliferation of the software, interpretations and education regarding coronary CT and the advanced coronary CT scanners, which are not that common, even in the U.S. We’ll see a migration to CT-guided PCI, but it’s going to take some time, additional resources and education.

It’s all very doable, and less invasive if we can avoid using an IVUS catheter. Any time there’s another catheter or a procedure vs. just imaging, there’s a possibility for a complication.

There are some limitations. This was a group of patients with fairly low complexity, and their event rate was low, which was great, but maybe not as much as what you would see in the real world. It’s not going to be for everybody, because there are going to be a lot more complex patients where it would be difficult for CT to manage. You’re going to probably need additional imaging help either with coronary physiology or IVUS beyond CT. But I can see coronary CT being the primary place to start, and these others being adjunctive as needed.

The lower procedural time and contrast volume with CT-guided PCI will likely translate into real-world practice, and that’s a definite advantage they’ve shown with the study. On the other hand, we need to understand there was time spent with the CT angiogram prior to the procedure. That’s time that’s not included with the invasive procedure, and also the radiation and contrast that was used with that initial CT angiogram. That should be added on to what was used in the actual procedure vs. IVUS. It was great that there was less time and less contrast, but that’s not taking into account the preprocedural planning.

P4 was the first late-breaking trial presented, and there’s a reason for that. It looks like something that’s very positive with potential for the near future. I look forward to seeing its development on both sides: the proliferation of this next level of technology, and the education of cardiologists to make this a reality.

Collet C, et al. Late-breaking clinical trials: Session I, in collaboration with The Lancet. Presented at: TCT Scientific Symposium; Oct. 31-Nov. 3, 2026; San Diego.

Disclosures: Collet reports consulting for Abbott Vascular, AngioInsight, Boston Scientific, CryoTherapeutics, Heartflow, Medtronic, Siemens Healthcare and SpectraWAVE; receiving grant support from GE Healthcare and Shockwave Medical; holding stock options in Cathflo and Medyria; and holding a patent licensed by Abbott Vascular. The study was supported by unrestricted research grants from GE HealthCare and Heartflow to CoreAalst.

https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.title: TAVR benefits high-risk patients with moderate aortic stenosis
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.author: Erik Swain; Scott Buzby
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

In patients with moderate aortic stenosis with at least one at-risk feature, transcatheter aortic valve replacement was linked to reduced risk for death or a heart failure event at 2 years compared with clinical surveillance, data show.

“This is going to be a turning point in the way that we see patients with moderate aortic stenosis,” Philippe Généreux, MD, director of the structural heart program at Morristown Medical Center in New Jersey, said during a press conference at TCT 2026.

For the PROGRESS trial, simultaneously published in The New England Journal of Medicine, Généreux and colleagues randomly assigned 744 patients (mean age, 78 years; 39.1% women; 45.6% at low surgical risk) with moderate aortic stenosis and at least one at-risk feature, defined as a symptom or structural or functional abnormality known to be tied to faster disease progression or adverse cardiovascular outcomes, to receive TAVR with a balloon-expandable valve (Sapien 3, Edwards Lifesciences) or clinical surveillance.

The primary safety outcome of death, stroke, life-threatening bleeding, stage 4 acute kidney injury, hospitalization for a device- or procedure-related complication and valve dysfunction requiring reintervention at 30 days occurred in 5.9% of patients, and the upper bound of the 97.5% confidence interval of 8.8% beat the performance goal of 13.7% (P < .001), Généreux said at the press conference.

The primary effectiveness outcome of all-cause death or an HF event with or without hospitalization at 2 years occurred in 16.7% of the TAVR group and 23.9% of the surveillance group (risk difference, 7.2 percentage points; 95% CI, 13.1 to 1.3; HR = 0.67; 95% CI, 0.48-0.93; P = .02), Généreux said during the press conference, noting the number needed to treat to prevent one event at 2 years was 14.

“Moderate aortic stenosis is not benign, and these patients would benefit from earlier referral to a valve clinic for comprehensive evaluation to establish the optimal management strategy,” he said.

There was no difference between the groups in all-cause mortality (TAVR, 8.4%; surveillance, 7.3%; HR = 1.14; 95% CI, 0.67-1.93; P = .61), but HF events occurred less often in the TAVR group (10.8% vs. 19%; HR = 0.55; 95% CI, 0.37-0.81; P = .002), he said, noting there was a significant difference in HF hospitalization (7.4% vs. 14.9%; HR = 0.48; 95% CI, 0.3-0.77; P = .001).

In the surveillance group, 10.6% of patients had TAVR by 6 months, 27% had it by 1 year and 57.4% had it by 2 years, Généreux said. Among those who underwent TAVR, 81.4% had progressed to severe aortic stenosis, he said.

In the TAVR group, Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire overall summary score rose 15.5 points within 30 days of the procedure, whereas in the surveillance group, it declined 9.3 points, but rose 22.3 points within 30 days of the procedure among those who underwent it, he said.

“Rather than waiting for progression to severe aortic stenosis, PROGRESS supports TAVR for patients with moderate [aortic stenosis] and at-risk features,” Généreux said at the press conference.

The PROGRESS trial represents an important advance in our understanding and management of moderate aortic stenosis. The findings demonstrate that early intervention with TAVR can significantly reduce adverse clinical outcomes compared with clinical surveillance, with the benefit driven predominantly by a reduction in HF events and hospitalizations rather than mortality.

What is particularly important about this trial is that it challenges the longstanding perception that moderate aortic stenosis is a relatively benign condition that can simply be monitored until it progresses to severe disease. We are increasingly recognizing that moderate aortic stenosis is not necessarily benign, particularly in patients who are already symptomatic or have evidence of cardiac dysfunction. These patients may experience meaningful clinical deterioration while under surveillance, and waiting for the traditional thresholds for intervention may not always be the optimal strategy.

PROGRESS provides compelling evidence that earlier intervention may change that clinical trajectory in appropriately selected patients.

I was particularly impressed by the rigor of this study. Unlike some of the earlier investigations in moderate aortic stenosis, PROGRESS enrolled a substantial number of patients, incorporated careful clinical and echocardiographic assessments and evaluated clinically meaningful outcomes. The separation of the event curves is particularly noteworthy and reinforces the potential benefit of intervening earlier in the disease process. Importantly, the findings also suggest improvements in patients’ quality of life, which should never be underestimated when evaluating the value of a therapeutic intervention.

However, these results also raise several important questions.

No. 1, how do we identify the patients with moderate aortic stenosis who are most likely to benefit from earlier intervention? Not every patient with moderate aortic stenosis will necessarily require TAVR, and understanding the clinical, anatomical and physiological characteristics that predict progression and adverse outcomes will be essential.

No. 2, what are the implications for younger patients? The trial focused on an older population, and extending these findings to younger individuals requires careful consideration of valve durability, future coronary access, the potential need for repeat interventions and the overall lifetime management of aortic valve disease.

No. 3, how should these findings influence clinical practice, future guidelines and regulatory decisions? PROGRESS provides important randomized evidence supporting consideration of TAVR earlier in the course of aortic stenosis. At the same time, we need to carefully evaluate the balance of benefit and procedural risk, the durability of these outcomes and their applicability to broader patient populations.

This is also where real-world evidence becomes critically important. Through initiatives such as the Society of Thoracic Surgeons/American College of Cardiology Transcatheter Valve Therapeutics Registry, we have an extraordinary opportunity to understand how these findings translate into everyday clinical practice, evaluate outcomes across different patient populations and continue to refine our approach to patient selection and lifetime management.

For me, the most important message from PROGRESS is that we need to rethink how we approach aortic stenosis across the entire spectrum of disease severity.

We have made tremendous advances in transcatheter valve technology, and we now have the ability to treat patients more safely and effectively than ever before. The next frontier is determining not only whom to treat, but when to intervene to achieve the greatest long-term benefit.

Ultimately, our goal should not simply be to wait for patients to develop severe aortic stenosis. It should be to understand the disease trajectory, recognize those at risk of clinical deterioration, and intervene at the right time to prevent heart failure, preserve quality of life, and improve long-term outcomes.

PROGRESS is an important step toward that goal.

Généreux P, et al. Late-breaking clinical trials: Session II, in collaboration with the New England Journal of Medicine. Presented at: TCT Scientific Symposium; Oct. 31-Nov. 3, 2026; San Diego.

https://www.healio.com/news/endocrinolog.title: TSH suppression after thyroidectomy tied to adverse bone outcomes
https://www.healio.com/news/endocrinolog.author: Michael Monostra
https://www.healio.com/news/endocrinolog.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

Long-term levothyroxine therapy after differentiated thyroid cancer may lead to adverse bone outcomes, but more research is needed on other potential adverse effects, according to a review article published in Thyroid.

Fadi Esttaifo, BHSc, MSc, medical student at the University of Ottawa and research assistant at Sunnybrook Research Institute in Toronto, and Mohammad Jay, MD, an endocrinologist, head, neck and adrenal endocrinology clinical fellow and PhD candidate in clinical epidemiology and healthcare research at University of Toronto, said levothyroxine therapy is used long term in some patients after a thyroidectomy to suppress thyroid-stimulating hormone levels and reduce risk for cancer recurrence. However, Esttaifo and Jay said, this treatment could lead to other adverse health outcomes.

“As patients live longer, it becomes increasingly important to consider not only cancer outcomes, but also the potential consequences of treatment,” Esttaifo and Jay told Healio. “We conducted this review to better understand which patient- and treatment-related factors are associated with these adverse effects, with the goal of supporting more individualized treatment strategies that balance cancer control with long-term health.”

Researchers searched three databases for studies examining postsurgical levothyroxine therapy for differentiated thyroid cancer and adverse outcomes related to treatment published from 2011 to February 2026.

There were 35 studies enrolling 11,819 patients included in the review. Of the studies, 51.4% examined skeletal outcomes and 40% assessed cardiometabolic outcomes. Neuro-psychological outcomes were assessed in 11.4% of studies and reproductive and muscular outcomes were ascertained in one study each.

The most common patient-level factors assessed in the studies were BMI in 25.7%, age in 22.9% and sex in 14.3%. The most common treatment-level factors assessed were circulating free thyroxine and free triiodothyronine levels in 37.1% of studies, treatment duration in 17.1% of studies and daily levothyroxine dose in 8.6% of studies.

In studies examining skeletal outcomes, older age was linked to lower bone mineral density, impaired bone microarchitecture and osteoporosis in multiple studies. Associations between BMI and skeletal outcomes varied among the studies and differed based on levothyroxine exposure. Sex-specific associations with skeletal outcomes also varied.

Greater TSH suppression was the treatment factor most commonly linked to adverse skeletal outcomes such as lower BMD, osteoporosis, increased fracture risk and higher bone turnover markers. Additionally, longer levothyroxine treatment duration was linked to osteoporosis or bone loss.

“The relatively consistent associations with adverse skeletal outcomes highlight the importance of assessing a patient’s overall risk of osteoporosis and fractures, taking into account factors such as menopausal status, previous fractures, underlying bone health and other established skeletal risk factors, alongside the intensity and duration of TSH suppression,” Esttaifo and Jay said.

Data were limited regarding associations between demographics and cardiometabolic outcomes. Some studies found lower TSH or higher free T4 were associated with cardiac rhythm abnormalities, cardiac dysfunction and cardiac mortality. However, three studies found no link between TSH suppression and atrial fibrillation. Some studies found TSH suppression was tied to higher cholesterol levels, and one study found higher levothyroxine dose was linked to diabetes and hypertension.

There were few associations found with neuropsychological outcomes in the review. Multiple studies reported that increased anxiety and insomnia were linked to lower TSH or higher free T4. Data on reproductive and muscular outcomes with levothyroxine were limited.

Esttaifo and Jay said the study identified several research gaps, but it also called attention to the importance of following up with patients after levothyroxine is initiated. They also emphasized the importance of patient counseling and shared decision-making throughout the process.

“In clinical practice, TSH targets should be reassessed periodically as a patient’s cancer status and overall health evolve,” Esttaifo and Jay said. “While decisions about the appropriate degree of TSH suppression must also consider cancer recurrence risk and response to treatment, our review did not evaluate the oncologic benefits of different TSH targets. Rather, our findings provide evidence about potential treatment-related harms that can be considered alongside oncologic factors when making these decisions.”

Esttaifo and Jay said there is plenty of evidence assessing skeletal outcomes, but more research is needed to examine other adverse effects with TSH suppression as well as looking at the cumulative effect of therapy.

“Ultimately, an important next step is developing and validating clinical prediction models that integrate baseline patient characteristics, existing health conditions and longitudinal treatment exposure,” Esttaifo and Jay said. “Such models could help clinicians estimate an individual’s risk of adverse effects and incorporate this information alongside their anticipated oncologic benefit when making personalized treatment decisions.”

Fadi Esttaifo, BHSc, MSc, can be reached at endocrinology@healio.com.

Mohammad Jay, MD, can be reached at endocrinology@healio.com.

Jay M, et al. Thyroid. 2026;doi:10.1177/10507256261499041.

Disclosures: The authors report no relevant financial disclosures.

https://www.healio.com/news/primary-care.title: ‘Pay attention and look deeper’: How clinicians can identify, help sex trafficking victims
https://www.healio.com/news/primary-care.author: Andrew (Drew) Rhoades
https://www.healio.com/news/primary-care.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

LAS VEGAS — Healthcare visits may be one of the few opportunities to identify a sex trafficking victim, so it is important for clinicians to be aware of the warning signs, a speaker at OMED said.

In 2025, 21,457 individuals in the United States were victims of sex trafficking, according to the National Human Trafficking Hotline.

Susan Norris, MSEd, founder and executive director of Rescuing Hope, said data indicate over 80% of sex trafficking victims are seen in women’s centers, urgent care or EDs, yet “no one asks the critical questions.”

“Pay attention and look deeper,” she said.

According to Norris, sex trafficking is defined as a commercial sex act induced by force, coercion or fraud among adults aged 18 years or older, and any commercial sex act among youth aged under 18 years.

She noted that coercion or fraud are the likeliest ways of inducing sex trafficking — although force “used to be 4% of all trafficking cases, now the data is telling us it’s 0.02%.”

One of the most frequent ways victims are affected “that people don’t see as sexual exploitation or sex trafficking is pornography,” Norris said. “We are seeing more peer-to-peer sexual assault than ever before because of pornography — 25% of all people who are addicted to pornography are females. Our culture is a pornified culture.”

She explained that traffickers — who can also be parents or caregivers — will trauma-bond with victims by exploiting their vulnerabilities, such as prior sexual abuse and unmet emotional or financial needs.

Clinical presentations that may be indicative of sex trafficking include:

Norris also highlighted behavioral signs. For example, the patient “may or may not act like they’re totally with you, and then any given thing, like a man walking in the room, could cause them to suddenly act differently,” she said. “They may not be able to look you in the eye: a trafficker will not allow their victims to look someone in the eye except for when that person is paid for that time with you.”

If a clinician suspects a victim of sex trafficking, Norris said “you need to find a way to get that individual separated.”

“You have words that half the population do not understand, and you have HIPAA on your side,” she said.

For example, clinicians could tell a potential sex trafficker, “‘We need to take an X-ray of her arm, and we’ve got to go back to the other part of the hospital. Because of HIPAA regulations and other patients there, I can’t take you,’” Norris said.

She added that it is crucial to interact with victims in “ways that you can speak with them where they feel safe and empowered.”

“You need to make sure that they have freedom to make a choice anywhere that you can,” she said. “You may not have a lot to offer them, but ask, ‘Can I get you some water? Would you like a blanket?’ Anything that you can offer them where they feel like have an ounce of control is hugely important.”

Norris advised following typical procedures used in the events of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) incidences.

“Make sure you’re dealing with what they’re there for, and follow the processes for confidentiality, but use your resources,” she said. “If you’re a mandatory reporter, use your social workers. There are a lot of different organizations and people that can help you along the way.”

Norris S. Human trafficking: Risk factors, recognition, and medical management. Presented at OMED; Oct. 22-25, 2026; Las Vegas.

Disclosures: Norris reports no relevant financial disclosures.

https://www.healio.com/news/womens-healt.title: Testosterone therapy may lead to CVD risk in postmenopausal women
https://www.healio.com/news/womens-healt.author: Emma Bascom
https://www.healio.com/news/womens-healt.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

Testosterone therapy may be associated with a higher risk for CVD for postmenopausal women, according to research presented at The Menopause Society’s annual meeting.

Xuezhi (Daniel) Jiang, MD, PhD, a professor at Drexel University College of Medicine’s department of obstetrics and gynecology, and colleagues wrote that they conducted a cohort study to analyze the connection between testosterone therapy and CVD in postmenopausal women.

“Cardiovascular disease remains the number one killer of women, and studies like this are important as long-term safety data on testosterone use in women are lacking,” Stephanie Faubion, MD, MBA, FACP, MSCP, medical director for The Menopause Society, said in the release.

Jiang and colleagues conducted a retrospective cohort study with the TriNetX U.S. Collaborative Network, including 3,164 women each in the control and testosterone therapy cohorts after matching was complete. They estimated hazard ratios with Kaplan–Meier and Cox proportional hazards analyses.

The researchers found that, for women who are postmenopausal, testosterone therapy was linked to a significantly higher hazard of incident composite CVD compared with those who had no exposure (3.8% vs. 0.5%; HR = 8.08; 95% CI, 4.72-13.82). The event rates were low, but “the observed association was consistent across multiple cohort definitions,” Jiang and colleagues wrote.

The results remained consistent in sensitivity analyses that compared women who received testosterone and baseline menopausal hormone therapy with women who only received the baseline therapy (3.2% vs. 0.5%; HR = 6.73; 95% CI, 5-9.05) and in evaluations excluding women with any baseline menopausal hormone therapy after menopause from both of the cohorts (3.1% vs. 0%, P < .001).

“Our findings identify a potentially important cardiovascular safety signal associated with testosterone therapy in postmenopausal women. Although absolute event rates were low, the consistency of the association across multiple analyses warrants further prospective investigation,” Jiang said in a press release.

The researchers also noted that, considering “the potential for residual confounding inherent to observational studies” and the observed hazard ratio magnitude, their results “should be considered hypothesis-generating and warrant prospective validation.”

“The findings are a reminder for healthcare professionals to carefully balance individualized risks and benefits when prescribing testosterone,” Faubion said.

The study was interesting because it uses TriNetX, which is a very large database. The problem with large databases is [with such a large] control group, how do you really compare with normal healthy women? And why were they given it? What dose were they given? What did they obtain? And what level was attained? Using large databases like this is a wonderful tool, but it’s more hypothesis-yielding than is an actual finding because the numbers are so large that sometimes it’s easier to find something that’s statistically significant.

They’re finding that it increases cardiovascular disease. That may be right. I mean, look at women with PMOS. These are women who have excess testosterone production from the ovaries. This is a group that seems to be prone to more cardiovascular disease. So, one might say this makes sense. But the problem is that, in these large data sets, it’s so easily misled. It might have an effect, but the doses that are being used in women really are quite low because everyone’s afraid of the masculinization that might take place. So, I’m really quite hesitant about thinking that it’s going to cause cardiovascular disease.

That doesn’t mean I would recommend treatment. I think if you’re very careful, if there’s a population that really is low in testosterone, that the ovaries are removed, there could be a role for testosterone in small groups of people. But I do not think there’s a role for testosterone for women in large populations.

Jiang X, et al. Testosterone therapy and cardiovascular risk in postmenopausal women: A retrospective propensity-matched cohort study. Presented at: The Annual Meeting of The Menopause Society; Oct. 20-24, 2026; San Diego.

Disclosures: Jiang reports no relevant financial disclosures.

https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.title: Acute MI in cancer potentially underdiagnosed, undertreated
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.author: Scott Buzby
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

Patients with cancer may have lower rates of acute MI but higher rates of CV death vs. the general public; however, revascularization for MI reduces risk for CV death vs. medical treatment alone, a speaker reported.

Researchers posited that patients with cancer who experience an acute MI may be underdiagnosed and undertreated due to a healthcare disparity, according to data presented at the TCT Scientific Symposium and simultaneously published in JACC: Asia.

“Patients with cancer are inherently at increased risk of coronary atherosclerosis and arterial thrombosis associated with traditional risk factors, hypercoagulability and persistent systemic inflammation. In addition, cytotoxic chemotherapy and thoracic radiotherapy can induce significant vascular injury, leading to acute MI,” Seung Hun Lee, MD, PhD, associate professor at Chonnam National University Hospital in Gwangju, South Korea, and colleagues wrote in the simultaneous publication. “Although current guidelines emphasize the importance of revascularization in acute MI patients, patients with cancer have been undertreated with invasive revascularization for acute MI compared with patients with noncancer. Moreover, the latest guidelines for patients with cancer recommend more conservatively that revascularization is recommended for cancer patients with a meaningful life expectancy, if prognosis and bleeding risk are appropriately weighed. However, limited evidence is available regarding the prognostic impact of revascularization in patients with cancer.”

The researchers conducted a retrospective, nationwide, population-based cohort study using data from the South Korean National Health Insurance Service database to compare the incidence of acute MI among patients with cancer vs. a cohort without cancer matched via propensity score. The researchers also compared the prognostic impact of revascularization vs. medical treatment alone in patients with cancer, according to the study.

The study included data from 682,030 patients with cancer (mean age, 62 years; 51% men), of whom 13.5% were current smokers, 39.9% had hypertension, 20.8% had diabetes and 25.7% had hyperlipidemia; and the same number of individuals without cancer. The most common cancer was gastric cancer, followed by colon, thyroid, breast, lung, hepatic, prostate and pancreatic cancer.

Researchers reported that the risk for CV death among patients with cancer was significantly higher vs. the general population without cancer (adjusted HR = 2.5; 95% CI, 2.47-2.54; P < .001) with estimated incidence rates of 1,692.4 per 100,000 person-years in patients with cancer and 796.3 per 100,000 person-years in those without cancer.

Risk for MI was lower among patients with cancer vs. the general population without cancer (aHR = 0.93; 95% CI, 0.9-0.96; P < .001) with estimated incidence rates of 156.5 per 100,000 person-years in patients with cancer and 191.7 per 100,000 person-years in those without cancer, according to the study.

The researchers observed the highest risk for CV death among patients with pancreatic, hepatic, lung and hematologic cancer.

The highest risk for acute MI was observed among patients with lung cancer and hematologic malignancy, according to the study.

Risk for CV death was lower for patients with cancer who underwent revascularization for MI compared with those who had medical treatment alone (aHR = 0.82; 95% CI, 0.73-0.92; P < .001), researchers reported.

“The high competing risk of death, particularly early after cancer diagnosis, may reduce the time at risk for nonfatal ischemic events, thereby lowering the observed acute MI incidence even when early hazards are elevated; this is consistent with the pronounced early event clustering and later attenuation of acute MI risk,” the researchers wrote. “Competing-risk estimates indicate that both revascularized and medically managed acute MI events were less common among patients with cancer. These findings suggest that lower risk of acute MI cannot be fully attributed to a trend toward less invasive management for patients with cancer; it also reflects broader dynamics of events in the context of significant competing mortality.”

Lee SH. PCI in patients with cancer or cirrhosis. Presented at: TCT Scientific Symposium; Oct. 31-Nov. 3, 2026; San Diego.

Disclosures: Lee reports no relevant financial disclosures.
