https://fortune.com/2026/11/07/olive-oil.title: So much ‘liquid gold’ could hit the market that the world’s top producer is withholding output—but supplies can’t stay ‘extra virgin’ for long
https://fortune.com/2026/11/07/olive-oil.author: Jason Ma
https://fortune.com/2026/11/07/olive-oil.text:
A bumper harvest of olives threatens to jolt the olive oil market, prompting the world’s top producer to suppress supplies for the first time ever.

On Friday, Spain’s agriculture ministry ordered farmers to hold back 12% of their production until the end of September 2027, requiring them to store supplies on their farms or at third-party facilities.

“The measure aims to ensure farmers’ profitability and also to protect the interests of olive oil buyers,” it said, according to the Financial Times, adding that “greater stability to the market” will benefit producers and consumers.

While the move is unprecedented, the European Union allows olive oil supplies to be held back, unless it leads to excessive market distortion.

The current harvest season for so-called “liquid gold” began in September, and favorable weather this past spring promises to reverse years of drought and heat that kept olive production low.

This season, Spanish olive oil production is projected to jump 23% to 1.6 millions tons, marking the fourth-largest harvest ever. The agriculture ministry seeks to keep 188,000 tons off the market.

But expectations for more supply have already sent olive oil prices down. At mills in Andalusia, they averaged 2.93 euros per kilogram last weekend, down about 15% in about two months.

The olive oil industry has pushed back against the government’s attempt to prop up prices, pointing out the market is global while the order only applies to Spanish producers.

Kyle Holland, senior analyst at commodity data firm Expana, also noted that olive oil degrades over time, telling that FT that after several months in storage ”very quickly that olive oil is not going to be extra virgin anymore.”

He added that top olive oil buyers already have hefty supplies, so ordering farmers to store away some production would have little immediate impact on prices.

Spain isn’t the only country dealing with wild swings in key commodities.

The Quebec Maple Syrup Producers, which oversees Canada’s strategic syrup reserve, recently warned the stockpile will be completely empty by February.

While new supplies will continue to be produced, the reserve won’t be able to help ease any wobbles in output, which depends heavily on the weather and can be volatile.

Demand has increased in recent years as producers have diversified to more market beyond the U.S., but last year saw an especially big spike after President Donald Trump launched his global trade war.

To get ahead of anticipated tariffs, Americans rushed to buy up Canadian syrup supplies. As a result, total syrup exports jumped nearly 16% last year, up from 9% growth in 2024.

Meanwhile, the Iran war has forced oil-consuming countries around the world to drain crude stockpiles. In the U.S., the Strategic Petroleum Reserve has fallen to the lowest level since 1982.

Elsewhere, Japan has a rice reserve that had to be drawn down last year as prices soared amid bad weather and looming threats from natural disasters that sparked panic buying. But this year, Japan has already swung to a record surplus.

And China tapped its strategic pork reserve in 2019 after an outbreak of swine fever sent prices higher. But this year, prices have slumped as the anemic consumer economy has weighed on demand while the government’s prior encouragement to boost production has now resulted in oversupply.

Pork prices have plunged 39% over the last four years. To help prop up the market, China has repeatedly purchased pork for the strategic reserve.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/07/alabama-p.title: Alabama Power spent more than $6 million on ads last year — and customers can be billed for half of them until 2029
https://fortune.com/2026/11/07/alabama-p.author: Dennis Pillion, Inside Climate News
https://fortune.com/2026/11/07/alabama-p.text:
This article originally appeared on Inside Climate News, a nonprofit, non-partisan news organization that covers climate, energy and the environment. Sign up for their newsletter here.

On a busy election day, the Alabama Public Service Commission requested that Alabama Power voluntarily stop billing customers, effective immediately, for television commercials and other ads it buys to promote various aspects of its business.

Alabama Power is the largest electricity provider in Alabama, with territory covering about two-thirds of the state. Though it is a monopoly, the company spends millions each year on advertising, touting its reliability, customer service and other aspects of its business.

In recent months, the company has launched a series of television commercials touting a rate freeze it announced late last year amid heavy criticism over rising electricity prices.

A state law passed earlier this year will prohibit Alabama Power from including the costs of those commercials in customers’ electric bills, meaning the powerful utility will have to find all of the dollars in corporate profits. But the new law won’t take effect until 2029.

Currently, Alabama Power is allowed to bill customers for half of its non-public safety advertising costs.

During Tuesday’s meeting, PSC President Cynthia Lee Almond moved to “request” that Alabama Power voluntarily begin excluding those costs immediately.

“I don’t see any reason why we shouldn’t go ahead and take steps now to begin that process, rather than waiting until Jan. 1, 2029,” Almond said during the meeting.

Almond then made her motion, which was not on the meeting agenda, but came after the regular report from the commission’s electricity division.

“I move that the commission request that Alabama Power consent to exclude all advertising expenses from retail rate setting until after Dec. 31, 2028, when the new law takes effect,” Almond said. “Assuming Alabama Power consents, this interim measure would be reflected in its [Rate Stabilization and Equalization] filings for 2027 and 2028.”

Commissioners Jeremy Oden and Chris Beeker IV voted yes after a brief discussion.

According to the company filings with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, Alabama Power spent more than $6 million in general advertising last year, roughly $4 per customer. It’s unclear from the federal filing how much of that total was passed on to customers or how much might be impacted by the new prohibition.

Alabama Power did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Daniel Tait, executive director of Energy Alabama, said the move was a boon to Alabama Power customers, who faced some of the highest electric bills in the country in recent years.

“We are grateful for the leadership of President Almond and the full commission for acting to end customers paying for Alabama Power’s advertising,” Tait said. “Once in place, Alabama will have one of the strongest customer protections in the nation on this front.”

This will be among the last actions of the commission under its current construction before a major overhaul takes effect.

In January, the commission will expand from three members to seven. Outgoing Gov. Kay Ivey has appointed four new commissioners, who will take office in January, including the PSC’s two first-ever Black members.

Oden and Beeker will also leave the commission in January after being defeated in Republican primaries. Cullman County Sheriff Matt Gentry will take Oden’s Place 1 seat, and former state auditor and PSC Commissioner Jim Zeigler will replace Beeker in Place 2.

Zeigler, a perennial candidate in Alabama across several decades, will return to the commission 48 years after leaving the PSC. He served one term from 1975-1979, during an era of skyrocketing energy costs and protracted political battles over electric rates between Alabama Power and then-Gov. George Wallace.

Almond will be the sole remaining member of the current commission.

The new seven-member commission will be overseen by the state’s first secretary of energy, who will be selected by Gov.-elect Tommy Tuberville. The new secretary will set the commission agenda, and overruling the secretary will require a vote of five of seven commissioners.

Tuberville has not yet announced his pick for secretary of energy. The only statutory requirement is that the secretary “must have experience in utility regulation or energy policy or a related field.”

https://fortune.com/2026/11/07/in-n-out-.title: In-N-Out’s billionaire owner vows iconic chain ‘will always be’ in California and says leaving the state would be the ‘dumbest business decision ever’
https://fortune.com/2026/11/07/in-n-out-.author: Jason Ma
https://fortune.com/2026/11/07/in-n-out-.text:
Lynsi Snyder, president and owner of In-N-Out, moved her family to Tennessee recently but reaffirmed that the iconic burger chain will never abandon California.

In an interview with actor Terry Crews that In-N-Out posted online, she was asked how the company will retain its California DNA as it expands to more states around the country.

“This is where we started. It’s where we are now, and it’s where we will always be,” Snyder replied.

Her grandparents opened the first In-N-Out in Southern California in 1948, and the company has gradually expanded to other parts of the state—and to other parts of the country.

While far from being the biggest chain, it retains a cult following that has helped its expansion as people who moved out of California make pilgrimages when restaurants open in new states.

But Snyder, who grew up in Northern California, revealed last year that she and her family were moving to Tennessee, saying that raising kids was difficult in the state and that “doing business is not easy” there either.

That sparked fears In-N-Out might leave California, prompting the burger heiress—who is worth an estimated $7.3 billion—to clarify that her departure from the state doesn’t mean the company will too.

In a video posted to her Instagram page last year, Snyder told followers: “We’re not leaving California, or leaving our roots behind. Each one of our locations is here to stay.”

Still, there has been a corporate exodus from California to states like Texas, where Elon Musk has relocated the headquarters for Tesla and SpaceX.

In-N-Out has also clashed with state authorities, such as when it refused to comply with officials and request that customers must show proof of vaccination to make purchases during the pandemic.

And the company reluctantly raised prices after California imposed higher minimum wages for fast-food workers in 2024.

But during her latest interview, Snyder addressed the fears about In-N-Out, which maintains headquarters in California and Tennessee.

“There were rumors about ‘they’re gonna close all their California stores.’ I’m like what where did this even come from? That’s unimaginable. I can’t even imagine that — dumbest business decision ever,” she said.

Snyder added that In-N-Out continues to grow in California, with “lots of stores” slotted for the other cities in the state.

At the same time, the company has expanded to Nevada, Arizona, Utah, Texas, Oregon, Colorado, Idaho, Washington and Tennessee. Snyder suggested that Mississippi, Arkansas, and Oklahoma are under consideration, with New Mexico also in the works.

But she insisted the company is taking a slow and steady approach to growth that won’t compromise on the quality of its food her grandparents’ values, adding that In-N-Out won’t be able to accommodate every request to open a new location.

As for her own family’s relocation to Tennessee, Snyder described it as “kind of a God thing” and said she originally wanted to move to Colorado because she loves the mountains.

But her husband floated the idea of going to Tennessee instead. While they already had made plans, she recalled that “something just kind of clicked.”

“I felt it and then started looking at it, just praying, and I’m like ‘I think you’re right. I think that’s where we’re supposed to go,'” Snyder said.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/07/florida-p.title: Florida’s new property tax cuts could defund the police, fire fighters and EMS in small towns, threatening ‘rural dark ages,’ former GOP lawmaker says
https://fortune.com/2026/11/07/florida-p.author: Jason Ma
https://fortune.com/2026/11/07/florida-p.text:
The blue tsunami that swept across the country on election day petered out in Florida, where voters continued to elected Republicans to statewide offices and approved a massive cut to their property tax bills.

Amendment 3 expands the so-called homestead exemption, shielding more of a home’s assessed value from taxation. It will nearly triple from $51,400 currently to $150,000 in 2027 and increase again to $250,000 in 2028.

It also lowers the cap on annual assessments on rental and commercial properties from a 10% hike to 5%. The amendment doesn’t apply to school-related property taxes but creates a path for abolishing non-school property taxes completely.

State economists have projected that local governments will lose nearly $5 billion in the first year and nearly $12 billion a year once the exemption is fully phased in.

But while Amendment 3 requires remaining tax revenue go toward public safety and other local services, it doesn’t mandate that police, fire and emergency medical services be funded first or that they receive a minimum level of funding.

Proponents argued that lowering property tax bills would provide relief as higher inflation worsens the cost of living. But sheriffs, police chiefs, fire chiefs and local government officials came out against the plan as they face a steep hit to their budgets.

To be sure, local governments can raise revenue in other ways, such sales taxes and fees. But they can crash in bad economic times and are unlikely to completely offset losses from Amendment 3.

“In the end, though, essential services would still almost certainly be affected,” University of Tampa economists Abigail Hall and Aaron Wood wrote in the Conversation. “Funding for police, fire and emergency medical services is primarily the responsibility of local governments, and, for most counties, they make up the largest line item in their annual expenditures. Reducing property taxes would amount to a direct hit, especially in smaller, less-populated counties.”

Leading up to election day, Pinellas County Sheriff Bob Gualtieri estimated the county’s general fund could lose about $180 million in the first year after the measure passes, adding that the sheriff’s office accounts for half of the county’s spending, which mostly covers personnel costs.

That means the county could have fewer deputies available to respond to calls, with community policing programs, marine patrols and K-9 units also facing cuts, he warned. In addition, the county’s emergency medical services fund could suffer a $20 million reduction.

“I think there’s no doubt — zero — that there has to be position cuts,” Gualtieri told WLRN last month.

Outgoing Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, who backed Amendment 3, has dismissed such warnings as “fearmongering” and suggested state grants could offset any budget shortfalls to local agencies. Florida Realtors, another backer, insisted the measure could be implemented without compromising the essential services.

Still, some details are lacking, and a special session of the legislature could be called to spell out exactly how the amendment will work.

Jeff Brandes, a former Republican state senator and president of the Florida Policy Project, wrote in an op-ed for Florida Politics on Friday that grants can’t fill recurring revenue shortfalls.

And unlike big cities like Miami, which can hike hotel taxes and lean on other tourism-related sources, small inland towns have fewer options to generate tax revenue.

He pointed to research from the Florida League of Cities, which found that at least 90% of homestead values will no longer be taxable in 108 of Florida’s 411 cities. And in 33 counties, at least seven in 10 homesteads fall below the $250,000 exemption limit.

“The amendment itself sends no reimbursement to fiscally constrained counties, the poorest and most rural places with the least room to absorb a loss, and nothing in the amendment guarantees that police and fire will be protected,” Brandes said.

“That is how rural Florida slides into rural dark ages: slower emergency response, crumbling roads, shorter library hours, shuttered recreation programs. Fewer services discourage investment. Less investment thins the tax base. A thinner tax base means fewer services. The dark ages won’t arrive all at once. They’ll arrive one closed fire station at a time.”

Because fire departments could see drastic cuts, Florida homeowners may end up paying higher insurance bills, offsetting savings from property taxes.

Insurance Services Office, a private insurance-data company, evaluates local fire protection and assigns ratings that insurers can use in underwriting.

“A reduction in fire protection services in a community can lead to a lower ISO rating,” a spokesman for the Insurance Information Institute told Bloomberg. “The ISO rating is among numerous risk factors property insurers use to underwrite homes in Florida and could potentially cause premiums to increase if the rating is downgraded.”

Amendment 3’s effects could extend to the state’s broader economy as well. In a pre-election analysis from the Tax Foundation, the think tank described the measure as not just a tax cut, but a fundamental restructuring of local government finance.

Since Florida doesn’t a state income tax, property taxes are a reliable source of revenue, even in economic downturns, and they reduce need for higher taxes on labor, entrepreneurship, capital formation, and consumer spending, it said.

“The elimination of a substantial portion of the property tax base does not eliminate the cost of local government services,” the Tax Foundation pointed out. “Amendment 3 would create highly distortive tax shifts, change who pays, and change how those costs are distributed. The result would be economically harmful both to Florida communities and the state overall.”

https://fortune.com/2026/11/07/berkshire.title: Berkshire Hathaway stock is a haven again as investors flee AI bloodbath while its own portfolio takes a hit amid reshuffling
https://fortune.com/2026/11/07/berkshire.author: Jason Ma
https://fortune.com/2026/11/07/berkshire.text:
Investors are seeking shelter from the AI storm in Berkshire Hathaway after shares of the conglomerate had lagged the broader market since Warren Buffett announced his departure as CEO last year.

Berkshire’s class B stock is up 13.6% so far this year, beating the S&P 500’s 7.8% gain. The outperformance has come as Wall Street rotates out of once high-flying tech stocks that rode the AI boom. Since Oct. 1 alone, Berkshire stock has soared 14% while the S&P has fallen about 4%.

That mirrors other years that saw major market upheaval. Most recently, Berkshire gained 4% in 2022 when the Federal Reserve launched an aggressive rate-hiking campaign that sent the broad market index down 18%.

Still, Berkshire’s own closely followed portfolio hasn’t been immune to recent market swings. According to its third-quarter earnings report filed on Saturday, investment gains plunged 46% from a year earlier to $9.4 billion.

Berkshire’s top stock holdings remained Alphabet, American Express, Apple, Bank of America and Coca-Cola during the quarter.

While a more detailed filing later this month will reveal its precise moves, the quarterly earnings report showed that Berkshire bought $2.4 billion of stocks during the period and sold some $2.8 billion.

The company grew its stake in “commercial, industrial, and other” equities by $2.3 billion on a cost basis, and cut its stake in “banks, insurance and finance” by $400 million.

Meanwhile, CEO Greg Abel, who took over from Buffett at the start of this year, continued to draw down Berkshire’s massive cash pile and accelerated stock repurchases.

It repurchased $9.6 billion of its stock in the third quarter, more than double the pace in the second quarter. And in the first four weeks of the fourth quarter, Berkshire bought back about $2 billion more in stock.

With a broad array of firms under the Berkshire umbrella, the conglomerate remains focused on traditional businesses like railroad BNSF, Brooks running shoes, See’s candies, and Forest River RVs.

Abel added to that strategy in July, when he agreed to buy home builder Taylor Morrison for $6.8 billion. That broke a long drought without any major acquisitions as Buffett bemoaned the lack of good bargains.

Berkshire’s holdings in the traditional economy have paid off. In the third quarter, its railroad, energy and manufacturing businesses delivered strong profits, though insurance underwriting tumbled.

That’s as the AI boom has not only supercharged the tech sector but also industries that benefit from the hundreds of billions of dollars being spent on data center construction as well as electrical grid upgrades.

As a result, U.S. GDP has been running hot, expanding 3.4% in the third quarter, accelerating from 2.2% in the second quarter.

But the Democratic sweep of gubernatorial races in data center hot spots like Texas, Ohio and Georgia is expected to slow down the AI buildout and the overall economy.

https://fortune.com/article/why-did-airb.title: Billionaire Brian Chesky’s social-worker parents told him to pick a high-paying career. He went to art school—and started Airbnb with 3 air beds
https://fortune.com/article/why-did-airb.author: Sasha Rogelberg
https://fortune.com/article/why-did-airb.text:
Before Airbnb had over 9 million listings worldwide, there was one sole lodging: three inflatable air beds at CEO Brian Chesky’s San Francisco home. He had quit his job and packed up all his belongings in a Honda Civic to make a cross-country move, and couldn’t pay his rent. That’s when he noticed all the local hotels were booked because of the Industrial Designers Society of America’s International Design Conference in San Francisco, and a business was born.

“We called it the air-bed-and-breakfast,” he told Fortune in 2017 at a World’s Greatest Leaders event.

Chesky and Airbnb cofounder Joe Gebbia were hooked on the idea of making money and meeting new friends through their makeshift accommodations, so they opened their home to three guests: “What if you could book someone’s home the way you could book a hotel anywhere in the world?” Chesky said about their inspiration. They launched Airbnb with Gebbia’s former roommate Nathan Blecharczyk in 2008.

Chesky’s social-worker parents in upstate New York (he was born in Albany) told him to pursue a high-paying career, but much to their chagrin he went to art school instead, at the famous Rhode Island School of Design.

“I’m going to become an artist,” Chesky recalls telling his mom, to which she responded: “You somehow managed to pick the only job in the world that pays less than a social worker. You’ll get paid nothing.”

Today, Chesky doesn’t have to worry as much.

Airbnb has a market capitalization of $112 billion, above its level from before the pandemic, which threatened its very survival as a business. The company lost 80% of its business in the first months of the pandemic, and Chesky reorganized it in a scramble for survival.

A post shared by FORTUNE (@fortunemag)

Though Chesky’s creativity is what birthed (and saved) Airbnb, it also meant business veterans did not initially take him seriously.

Chesky’s design background was at first a hindrance to a budding Airbnb. While looking for $150,000 to fund an estimated 10% of the company, Chesky met with over 20 potential investors, all of whom turned him down.

“Joe and I were designers, and as far as they were concerned, designers didn’t start companies,” Chesky said. “We didn’t look like a tech founder, which is ridiculous because I don’t think you should ever hire somebody because they look like something else. You want a new thing.”

Investors didn’t take an interest in Airbnb until it began designing presidential-candidate-themed cereal boxes, which eventually got the attention of Paul Graham, founder of startup accelerator Y Combinator.

“Creative companies are companies that tap into a sense of imagination,” Chesky told Time. “That they might come up with new breakthrough ideas, that people that were only beholden to near-term measurable outcomes won’t ever have.”

Success at Airbnb has been a double-edged sword. Explosive growth has forced the company to refocus at times.

During the pandemic, Chesky told Fortune in 2023, he even opened his own home as an Airbnb to better understand the host experience and lived in various Airbnbs across the country for six months, where he discovered inconsistent and unnecessary practices across hosts, including complicated rent agreements.

Airbnb still faces challenges as waves of short-term rental regulations in New York and across Europe, where cities are implementing phase-outs, prohibiting rentals for less than 30 days, or no longer renewing tourist apartment licenses, for example. In the U.S., housing advocates have fought against Airbnb, according to the AP, claiming short-term rentals have essentially become hotels.

Airbnb has pushed back against regulations, saying that short-term rental bans would limit affordable accommodations for travelers.

Last month, Airbnb implemented a new “reasonable house rules and requests” policy, where the company has stopped asking guests to “complete tasks that require significant effort or time, or would typically be performed by a cleaner,” such as stripping the bed, washing and putting away dishes, or taking trash offsite. The new policy, which will go into effect on rentals booked on or after Nov. 20, has drawn pushback as hosts threaten to boycott or hike cleaning fees, and been a pleasant surprise to customers.

https://fortune.com/article/starter-home.title: Starter homes cost $1 million in a record 242 U.S. cities—proof the affordability crisis has hit the homes meant for first-time buyers
https://fortune.com/article/starter-home.author: Sydney Lake
https://fortune.com/article/starter-home.text:
They waited out the pandemic boom. They saved longer, rented longer, delayed longer, and watched the typical first-time homebuyer age climb to a record 40. Now, the buyers who did everything right are running into a new problem: The Northeast just became the fastest-growing region for million-dollar starter homes in the country.

It’s especially imperfectly timed for millennials entering their peak household spending years and beginning to form their own families (or at least try to).

A Zillow report published in June counts a record 242 U.S. cities where starter homes cost $1 million or more—triple the 80 cities that cleared that mark before the pandemic, and up from 226 a year ago.

The share of first-time buyers has fallen to half the historical norm. For millennial parents in the Northeast—now in their late thirties and early forties, often with kids, hunting for more space—the numbers have a specific shape.

New Jersey had just one million-dollar starter city before the pandemic. Now it has 26. New York used to have 12; now it has 41. The two states added 15 cities to the list in the past year alone—faster growth than anywhere else in the country. The New York City metro area now leads all with 63 cities where a starter home runs $1 million or more.

That growth didn’t happen in a vacuum. Six of the 10 most competitive housing markets in the country are in the Northeast, per Zillow’s 2026 analysis, a region where new construction has chronically lagged and inventory deficits run deepest. California still leads the raw count with 105 cities, but the Northeast is where the crisis is actively spreading.

“A housing shortage a decade in the making ran headlong into intense demand with mortgage rates at historic lows, driving up home values at a record pace,” Zillow senior economist Kara Ng wrote. For Northeast buyers, those forces have compounded.

First-time homebuyers are historically younger, although the typical age of first-time buyers climbed to an all-time high of 40, according to a National Association of Realtors report released in November 2025. In fact, the housing market has gotten so unaffordable that the number of first-time homebuyers fell to half the historical norm last July.

A rising price floor on starter homes only pushes that first home purchase further out of reach. And it’s a problem that’s worsened, especially during the past couple of years.

“For homebuyers, the prevalence of million-dollar cities significantly—greatly—strains what is already the worst housing affordability since at least the 1980s,” Christopher M. Naghibi, executive vice president and chief operating officer at First Foundation Bank, told Fortune in 2024 when Zillow released a report about the number of U.S. cities with $1 million median-priced homes. “Prospective buyers in these markets face higher barriers to entry, needing ridiculously large down payments and higher incomes to afford homes.” That still holds true today.

Zillow defines a starter home as one in the lowest third of home values in a given region. As of June, the typical starter home nationwide was worth $198,649, up 1.7% from a year earlier. But in well over 200 U.S. cities, starter home prices are a whopping five times as high as that. It’s a phenomenon that keeps spreading, and into places it never used to touch.

Zillow chalks it up to the effects of the pandemic housing boom.

Before 2020, the list of cities with $1 million starter homes was almost all coastal. Colorado was the only non-coastal state with a million-dollar starter-home city. Now 26 states have at least one, up from nine before the pandemic. Texas, Wyoming, and Illinois each have multiple examples.

California still leads with 105 cities, but the fastest growth is in the Northeast. New York and New Jersey added 15 cities combined over the past year. New York is now up to 41, from just 12 before the pandemic. New Jersey is at 26, up from one.

The New York City metro area tops all metros with 63 cities where a starter home runs $1 million or more. San Francisco follows with 37, then Los Angeles with 33, San Jose with 13, and Miami and Seattle with eight each. The trend aligns with Zillow’s 2026 hottest markets analysis, which found six of the 10 most competitive housing markets are in the Northeast, where new construction has lagged and inventory deficits run deep.

The pandemic reset the cost of buying a home. A housing shortage a decade in the making collided with surging demand and historically low mortgage rates, pushing values up at a record pace. Those effects have stuck.

The squeeze on millennials and Gen Z has been building for years. Baby boomers, sitting on paid-off homes or cheap pandemic-era mortgages, have edged younger buyers out of the market in record numbers. The cost has pushed some Americans to delay milestones like marriage and kids, and others to co-buy homes with friends or partners just to split the bill.

Others have done the opposite—had kids first, rented longer, and are now hunting for space in a market that moved against them.

“We’re seeing a reshaping of the housing ladder,” Alexandra Gupta, a real-estate broker with the Corcoran Group, previously told Fortune. “Some first-time buyers are turning to long-term renting or even co-living models because the idea of owning a home has become so out of reach.”

There are modest signs of relief. Conditions are slowly turning friendlier for buyers. Zillow found the typical buyer now breaks even versus renting after about six years, down from more than eight in late 2023. More inventory and slower price growth mean buyers who are financially prepared are in better shape than they had been.

But “financially prepared” is carrying a lot of weight in 242 cities where there are $1 million starter homes. For a young buyer there, the costs pile up fast: a bigger down payment, a higher monthly mortgage, and a steeper climb before they achieve the American Dream.

No wonder that dream is largely happening in Texas.

A version of this story was published on Fortune.com on June 17, 2026.

https://fortune.com/article/acely-ceo-ro.title: This CEO lived on canned soup and took just two days off for his daughter’s birth. Now, he admits he lost sight of proper work-life balance
https://fortune.com/article/acely-ceo-ro.author: Preston Fore
https://fortune.com/article/acely-ceo-ro.text:
The grind to success can be long, punishing, and it can quietly take more than it gives.

Ron Schneidermann knows that better than most.

After scaling his first company, Liftopia, into a business with more than $60 million in annual revenue, he went on to become CEO of AllTrails, the popular hiking map app. Today, he leads test-prep startup Acely. But looking back across his career, he says he had to learn the hard way what real work-life balance actually costs—and what it’s worth.

While building Liftopia, a digital marketplace for ski resorts, that mindset came at a personal price. Schneidermann worked out of a cramped San Francisco apartment, turned spending less than $15 a day into a kind of endurance test, and went two years without taking a salary, surviving largely on canned soup.

The tradeoffs even extended into his family life. When his first daughter was born four years into Liftopia, he took just two days off work. Three years later, he allowed himself just a week for his son’s birth—and thought that was progress.

“I look back, I was just able to justify it as ‘that’s just part of the grind’… but you never get that time back,” Schneidermann told Fortune. “That was a mistake.”

It’s not an easy admission in startup culture, where sacrifice is often worn as a badge of honor and overwork is normalized as the price of ambition. But Schneidermann, now in his late 40s, has since reframed the experience entirely.

“For everything that was frustrating, that went wrong, that I regretted about Liftopia, I was able to take the inverse and turn it into a strength,” he said.

By the time he joined AllTrails in 2015, that mindset shift was already underway. He eventually became CEO in 2019 and instituted a company-wide ritual: the first Friday of every month, AllTrails shut down and employees were encouraged to go outside.

In August 2025, he took on the new challenge of becoming CEO of Acely. This time, he’s bringing those hard-won lessons with him from the start. Instead of monthly trail days, the company now runs a monthly “hackathon,” where its less than a dozen employees pause routine work for the whole day and experiment with AI tools and new ideas—no meetings, no KPIs, no deliverables.

Even before Schneidermann had his eyes on entrepreneurship, he was learning career lessons the hard way.

In the late 1990s, he was a student at UCLA studying mass communication and business while also working at Abercrombie & Fitch to help pay for his studies. However, he ended up getting fired three separate times because he “never liked it” enough to muster the proper decorum.

Similarly, after graduating in 2000, he landed a job at Accenture working as a business process consultant. Once again, though, he found it not aligning with the life he wanted to have. And despite the lucrative salary of working at a Fortune 500 consulting firm, he quit.

“It was a great experience. I’m grateful for it, but I hated it,” he said. “I hated it, and I told myself, I am never going to take a job for money again. Life is too short.”

That realization eventually pushed him toward startups.

Through a friend of a friend, he landed a role at Hotwire, then a travel startup that was later acquired by Expedia, and it became his entry point into the tech world. Looking back, Schneidermann said that early career path offers a lesson he wishes more young workers would take seriously: relationships matter as much as résumés, especially in a job market where traditional entry-level pipelines are narrowing.

“Really invest in your network,” he said. “There’s a small pond at the end of the day. If you stay in it long enough, you are going to know everyone, and everyone you know are going to be leaders somewhere.”

Schneidermann’s point may resonate with Gen Z at a time when employers say early-career workers are struggling with basic professional norms. A 2024 survey found that six in 10 bosses admitted they had already fired Gen Z employees hired straight out of college, citing poor communication, lack of professionalism, and disorganization.

For Schneidermann, the issue isn’t just skills—it’s mindset. Too many young workers treat networking as transactional, when in reality it’s built on consistency, reputation, and how you show up over time. That starts with small, often overlooked behaviors.

“There’s a human on the other end. Don’t ghost people and just show up,” he said.

The same principle applies more broadly to career growth. Rather than chasing the perfect role or obsessing over credentials, Schneidermann emphasized curiosity as the real differentiator.

“Just approach everything with a curious mindset,” he added. “Just constantly try to be learning and exploring.”

That philosophy has carried through multiple career pivots, including his most recent move to Acely, a startup with no obvious connection to his background. After being approached by an executive search firm, he took the job in part because his high school–aged daughter had recently used the product for SAT prep. She was among its over 50,000 active users.

For Schneidermann, the challenge was one he was eager to take on. From his perspective, he didn’t need to be an expert in the industry—he just needed to be willing to learn it.

A version of this story was published on Fortune.com on April 25, 2026.
https://fortune.com/article/acely-ceo-ro.summary: Ron Schneidermann is now CEO of hiking app AllTrails, the popular hiking map app. He says he learned the hard way what real work-life balance actually costs and what it's worth. Schneidermann says he was able to turn his experience into a strength.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/07/data-cent.title: The battle for megawatts: why restricting data centers is a strategic mistake
https://fortune.com/2026/11/07/data-cent.author: Serhiy Tokarev
https://fortune.com/2026/11/07/data-cent.text:
In Ireland, data centers consume nearly a quarter of the country’s electricity. New grid connections around Dublin were effectively frozen for three years. Under revised rules, new projects must provide generation or storage capacity onsite or nearby. Amsterdam previously imposed a moratorium on new facilities, while Frankfurt regulates their location through zoning.

In July 2026, New York State introduced a moratorium of up to one year on certain environmental permits for new large data centers. State officials said the pause would allow them to assess the facilities’ impact on the power grid and the environment. As of May 2026, data center projects representing nearly 12 GW of potential demand were in the state’s grid interconnection queue.

Should governments restrict data centers when power grids cannot keep pace? I believe they should expand power supply and grid capacity instead.

As co-founder and general partner of Roosh Investment Group, I have been investing in technology companies for over five years. Our portfolio includes AI infrastructure, and energy is now a key focus. This experience has shown me how access to energy infrastructure influences investment decisions. Reliable power is increasingly becoming a decisive factor in a company’s ability to scale and attract capital.

As businesses rely more on AI, control over its models and infrastructure matters more. A foreign provider’s decision to change terms, raise prices, or restrict access could affect entire industries. Domestic computing capacity gives countries more control over the infrastructure their businesses depend on.

This helps explain the intensity of U.S.–China competition in AI. American companies hold leading positions across the AI stack, from advanced models and chips to major cloud platforms. Washington views the power supply for data center infrastructure as a national security issue.

Beijing is pursuing a state-led strategy. Its “Eastern Data, Western Computing” program directs the development of computing capacity toward western China, where energy and land resources are more readily available. At the same time, the country is expanding power generation at scale. According to the International Energy Agency, China added nearly 500 GW of renewable capacity in 2025—more than 60% of the global increase.

Europe, meanwhile, risks falling further behind. Brussels plans up to seven AI gigafactories and at least a tripling of EU data center capacity within five to seven years. Yet some countries are slowing construction, while European businesses still rely primarily on American cloud providers. Restrictions do not remove demand for AI; they risk pushing investment abroad and reinforcing that dependence.

Data centers’ hunger for power should be understood in the context of wider electricity demand. According to the International Energy Agency, they accounted for only around 70 TWh of the 800 TWh increase in global electricity consumption in 2025. Industry, air conditioning, heat pumps, and electric vehicles contributed far more.

The challenge is rapidly growing demand concentrated in a handful of locations. Power must reach new computing capacity in time.

In the U.S., lead times for large transformers now exceed two years, compared with roughly 50 weeks before the pandemic. Morgan Stanley estimates that U.S. data centers could face a power shortfall of around 49 GW by 2028. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has acknowledged that power has become the company’s binding constraint. Some of its GPUs are sitting in inventory with nowhere to plug them in.

Dedicated gas-fired plants offer no quick fix. GE Vernova, Siemens Energy, and Mitsubishi Power produce around two-thirds of the world’s gas turbines, and their factories are booked years ahead. GE Vernova reported 116 GW in gas power equipment orders and slot reservations, while targeting annual turbine output of 20 GW in the third quarter of 2026.

The hardware itself adds another challenge. A server rack once required 7–12 kW. Systems built around NVIDIA’s GB200 consume 120–132 kW per rack. Conventional air cooling is no longer sufficient at that power density, so new facilities must be designed for liquid cooling from the outset.

Tech giants are securing power themselves. Microsoft agreed to buy electricity from the 835 MW Three Mile Island reactor, which is being restarted to serve its needs. Google’s agreement with Kairos Power calls for small modular reactors, with the first expected online by 2030.

Governments cannot rely on corporate initiative alone. They must plan energy and digital infrastructure together: expand grids, accelerate transformer production, streamline connections, and encourage long-term power purchase agreements, generation near data centers, and storage.

Ukraine’s experience shows how a crisis can accelerate the deployment of local generation. War and repeated attacks forced the country to rapidly deploy local power sources where the centralized grid could no longer guarantee a reliable supply.

My experience investing in technology companies has shown me that reliable infrastructure is essential for business growth. In Ukraine, companies have long had to manage energy risks. They need reliable electricity, backup power, and plans for potential outages. This also matters to investors. A company’s ability to operate during power outages affects how they assess its potential for growth.

Ukraine already has around 1.8 GW of distributed gas-fired generation, with more than 500 MW under construction. It is also streamlining grid connection and permitting procedures.

Ukraine’s experience cannot be directly applied to large AI data centers. But it illustrates how making energy resilience a priority can accelerate investment in additional generation and changes to connection procedures, even under extreme conditions.

Powering new data centers will require coordinated action by governments, grid operators, and businesses. Governments can plan sites for new facilities. Grid operators can reserve capacity for them in advance. Businesses can invest in their own power plants, storage, and cooling, and reduce electricity use during peak hours in exchange for faster grid connections. A combination of grid supply, gas-fired plants, nuclear power, and renewables can help meet demand where no single source is sufficient.

The ability to build and power data centers quickly is likely to become an increasingly important factor in investment decisions. An advantage in the AI race will depend not only on access to models and chips, but also on a country’s ability to expand computing capacity, generation, and grids together. Restricting data center development may temporarily ease grid pressure, but it can also deepen dependence on foreign infrastructure and technology.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/07/alignable.title: Big Tech’s AI race will save small business owners time. It won’t find them customers
https://fortune.com/2026/11/07/alignable.author: Eric Groves
https://fortune.com/2026/11/07/alignable.text:
Meta, Google, OpenAI and Anthropic are racing to become the small business owner’s AI assistant. Meta brought its Muse agent to small businesses in September. Anthropic and OpenAI now package tools aimed squarely at owners, and Google is building the same features into tools millions of them already use.

That competition is good for Main Street. But it’s a race to save owners time, and time isn’t what keeps them up at night. What keeps them up is where the next customer will come from.

A word on where I sit. I run Alignable, a network of 10 million small business owners, so I have a stake in this argument. Alignable also co-hosts small business AI training with Anthropic, one of the companies named here. Read what follows with that in mind. But I also have something the assistants don’t: 13 years of data on how small businesses actually find work.

Start with where customers come from. In our surveys, members say about 85% of their customers come through referrals. Not ads, not search, not cold email. People who already trust them.

Across 35,000 local communities, our members have formed 226 million business connections. Most of them never become a relationship that sends work either way. The owners who grow through their networks aren’t the ones with the most connections. I’ve told owners for years that 50 warm relationships beat 500 cold contacts. That’s a rule of thumb from experience, not a number we’ve measured. But the owners who win do keep a small set of relationships active and leave the rest alone.

And most owners are sitting on more opportunity than they know. When members tell us what their ideal customer looks like, we can count how many of those businesses sit one introduction away: connected to someone the owner already knows. Among members whose ideal customers show up in their extended network, the typical one has about 190 of them a single introduction away. For one in four, it’s more than 600.

The next customer is rarely a stranger. They’re one relationship away, through someone the owner hasn’t talked to in months.

Those relationships aren’t random, either. In my experience, three kinds do most of the work: customers who talk you up, businesses that serve the same customer without competing with you, and a handful of people who open doors. The best referral partner usually isn’t a peer in your own industry. It’s the business your customer calls right before or right after they call you: the realtor and the home inspector, the accountant and the financial planner.

Ask any of the big assistants how to get more referrals and you’ll get a solid list of best practices. Ask an assistant that sits on a map of business relationships and it can tell you something specific: three nearby businesses serve your ideal customer, one of them already knows two of your clients, and you haven’t spoken to your best referral partner in four months.

That’s the difference between advice and action. A general assistant can’t answer that question, because the answer lives in data it doesn’t have.

The early numbers bear this out. In Bluehost’s 2026 study of 350 U.S. owners, 78% said AI saves them time every week. But 43% have seen no change in revenue. Time saved only matters if it goes somewhere that pays.

Too often it goes into volume. Forbes recently told the story of Paul Birrell, a New Jersey owner whose automation loop sent roughly 400,000 emails in three days. His reaction: “I don’t have 400,000 customers.” Everything we see says growth comes from the opposite: judgment about the few people who matter.

AI will reach small business owners in three forms. The first is the personal assistant the giants are fighting over. It delivers time, and the assistants are converging fast.

The second is AI built into the systems that already hold the business’s own data. Intuit knows the books. Shopify knows the store. That AI delivers control: it can flag a cash crunch six weeks out or spot the product quietly losing money.

The third is AI built on the relationships between businesses: who knows whom, who serves the same customers, who sends work to whom. That’s the one that delivers growth, and it’s the one almost nobody is talking about. At Alignable, ours is called Allie.

The giants have real advantages, and they’ll connect to the other two kinds. Meta’s Muse already plugs into QuickBooks, Shopify and Stripe, and the others are adding similar connections. The open question is who the intelligence works for. Meta makes nearly all of its money selling ads, and an assistant built by an ad company will tend to find that the answer involves more advertising. The data that actually works for the owner describes how their business runs and who in their community can help it grow.

Use a personal assistant every day. The time savings are real.

Then decide, in advance, where the reclaimed hours go. Put them on the calendar against the work that generates revenue, and the most neglected item on that list is relationships. Write down the 50 people most likely to send you business. Most owners can name 10 without trying. Those 10 are where AI should be pointing you.

There are about 36 million small businesses in the U.S., and more than 80% of them have no employees. For those owners, AI isn’t a department upgrade. It’s a capability they never had. Owners should take the better tools the giants’ race produces. But the biggest gains won’t come from saving an hour. They’ll come from knowing which 50 relationships to spend it on.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/07/alignable.summary: Meta, Google, OpenAI and Anthropic are racing to become small business owners' AI assistants. For those owners, AI isn't a department upgrade, says Fortune.com's John Sutter.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/08/cathie-w.title: Cathie Wood 'always feels better when the market is worried' — here's why
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/08/cathie-w.author: Chloe Taylor
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/08/cathie-w.text:
Ark Invest CEO Cathie Wood told CNBC on Friday that a “wall of worry” is gripping markets.

But she said worry among investors cements her view that the bull market has further to run.

Stocks sold off sharply on Thursday before staging a tentative recovery on Friday.

Ark Invest CEO Cathie Wood is shrugging off this week’s market jitters, telling CNBC on Friday that concerns among investors actually reinforce her optimism that further gains lie ahead.

U.S. equities sold off sharply on Thursday, reversing the initial rally seen in the wake of the midterm elections. AI-related stocks led the rout, sending the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite into correction territory. On Friday, tech stocks staged a tentative recovery.

Much of the sell-off on Thursday was driven by concerns that a Democrat-led Congress would lead to a slowdown in data center construction. But concerns about artificial intelligence – particularly when it comes to capital expenditure, cash flow, debt and circular financing – have sparked multiple bouts of volatility over the course of this year.

Wood, whose firm manages various funds focused on tech and innovation, told CNBC there was a “wall of worry” pervading financial markets right now. But her decades of experience as an investor give her a somewhat unconventional view of the state of play.

“I experienced the tech and telecom bubble, and you know there really wasn’t much worry about it,” she said. “It was the 80s and the 90s, and it was a bull market, and people were just assuming this would go to the moon, that is not how this [the AI trade] has evolved.”

She explained that “from the beginning,” many investors have been concerned about how much firms are spending on AI development, how rapidly the spending is taking place, and how the hyperscalers have moved from extreme levels of positive free cash flow to negative free cash flow.

“So it’s been unsettling the markets for quite some time,” she said. “I always feel better when the market is worried, because that tends to suggest a more durable bull market, and I don’t think we’ve derailed this bull market.”

In 2025, her flagship Ark Innovation ETF
 gained more than 35%, far outperforming the S&P 500′s 16.4% rise and the Nasdaq Composite’s 20.5% rally.

Asked on Friday whether markets were anywhere near the end of the current bull run, Wood replied: “I don’t think so.”

“I think we’re in the middle of a technology revolution,” she said, pointing to the development of technologies like robotaxis and AI agents.

One thing that did risk becoming a “showstopper,” Wood noted, was the rising cost of capital.

Interest rates and bond yields have risen sharply this year as the U.S.-Iran war pushes inflation higher across the globe. Yields on corporate bonds have been rising too, with creditors demanding greater compensation for lending to companies.

“This correction is partly caused by what’s going on in the bond markets,” Wood said on Friday.

“I had been saying for quite some time that the wall of worry has been built by senior leaders in the financial world who were young during the bubble,” she said.

“It’s the elder statesmen and women of the industry who are keeping this wall of worry in place, and that’s not bad. Now you can add the bond investor to that. Bond investors in the old days weren’t necessary for technology. It was software. It was low fixed cost. It was viral apps, very high margins. [AI] is high fixed cost, so bond investors are experiencing or taking a journey into the technology world, really that they haven’t very much before.”

But she noted that AI hyperscalers were somewhat insulated by opportunities for growth.

“If a company thinks that taking on debt is going to accelerate its momentum, meaning its growth rate, it hardly matters what happens to interest rates for those companies,” Wood explained.

Wood said her advice to investors in the current volatile environment was to identify their high-conviction positions and double down on them as the market shifts.

“When you see a rally in a volatile environment, take some profits. When you see a sell-off, you’ll have the psychological wherewithal if you have taken profits to move back in,” she said.

“That’s what we do. So what we do during periods like this is concentrate towards our highest conviction names. So that’s what we’ve been doing in the last week or so. Our SpaceX position has gone up. If anything, the controversy around data centers on Earth is giving data centers in space a bigger opportunity.”

In 2027, Wood said she expects the equity rally to continue.

“This is two steps forward, one step back,” she said of the post-election turbulence. “The revolution will become clearer and clearer next year, and I think the market will do well.”

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/07/trump-uf.title: Trump offers UFC chief Dana White press secretary job
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/07/trump-uf.author: Megan Sauer
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/07/trump-uf.text:
President Donald Trump offered UFC president and CEO Dana White the job of “Press Secretary of the United States.”

White posted a picture of himself on Instagram stories standing behind the press secretary’s lectern in the White House, with the caption, “On to the next chapter.”

It was unclear whether White had accepted the position or was simply acknowledging the president’s request as a joke.

President Donald Trump offered UFC president and CEO Dana White the job of press secretary on Saturday.

In a post on Truth Social, Trump said: “I am pleased to announce that the Great Dana White, a violent Fighter and Warrior, has been offered the job of Press Secretary of the United States.”

“We need these people to defend us against the Lunatic Left,” Trump wrote. “Dana will be a Press Secretary like none other. Dana, please take the job!”

CNN, citing a source, reported White had declined the president’s offer.

Earlier Saturday, White posted a picture of himself on Instagram stories standing behind the press secretary’s lectern in the White House, with the caption, “On to the next chapter.”

It was unclear whether White had accepted the position or was simply acknowledging the president’s request as a joke.

Trump said that he was offering White the job of “Press Secretary of the United States,” but the president’s spokesperson is called the “White House press secretary.” Trump also recently speculated about considering Trump loyalist and rapper Nicki Minaj as press secretary, in an interview with podcaster Benny Johnson.

Trump said the job offer to White extended to his assistants, “even though some are not from our Country.” The so-called assistants Trump named included current and former UFC mixed martial arts fighters from countries such as Brazil and Russia.

In October, White House press secretary Katie Zacharia left the position just five days after her stint as Karoline Leavitt’s replacement began.

The president told reporters he suggested Zacharia quit after her first and only press briefing, where, in her six minutes answering questions behind the lectern, she only took questions from three conservative outlets.

“I just spoke to her about it. I said, ‘Katie, is this for you?’” Trump said outside the White House on Oct. 16.

The president’s appeal to White follows Friday’s announcement that Trump’s deputy chief of staff, Stephen Miller, would be promoted to chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles.

Trump’s stunning shake-up came just three days after Democrats won a landslide victory in the midterm elections, gaining majority control in the House and Senate.

The president and White have a longstanding friendship. During Trump’s first campaign in 2016, White praised the then-Republican nominee and called him a “fighter.”

“Nobody took us seriously. Nobody. Except Donald Trump. Donald was the first guy to recognize the potential we saw in the UFC and encouraged us to build our business,” White said.

And for his 80th birthday in June, President Trump hosted a UFC match — dubbed UFC Freedom 250 — on the White House’s South Lawn.

The White House and the UFC didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

— CNBC’s Kevin Breuninger contributed to this report.

CORRECTION: This article has been updated to correct the spelling of Karoline Leavitt’s name.

It was unclear whether White had accepted the position or was simply acknowledging the president’S request as a joke.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/07/anthropi.title: Anthropic IPO meets AI backlash after midterms show stinging rebuke of data centers
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/07/anthropi.author: Ashley Capoot
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/07/anthropi.text:
Anthropic’s IPO could thrust the company into the spotlight at a moment when AI is very unpopular in the U.S.

In the midterm elections, voters opposed data center-related ballot measures in 40 out of 41 cases.

More than half of voters said AI data centers were a “crucial” or “major factor” in who they supported for Congress, according to an exit poll from NBC News.

Americans were unequivocal at the ballot box this week as they expressed disdain for tech billionaires and mistrust of artificial intelligence. With that backdrop, Anthropic is about to try to go public.

The AI company is gearing up for a potentially historic IPO, likely targeting mid-November for its Nasdaq debut. CNBC reported on Friday that Anthropic investors see the company aiming for a valuation of $1 trillion to $1.5 trillion, down from a target of $2 trillion that had been floated in recent months.

From Wall Street to Main Street, it’s becoming a tougher environment for Anthropic. The Nasdaq on Thursday suffered its steepest drop in 19 months, and it’s down to start November after October marked its worst month since March 2025. Chipmakers and neoclouds, the companies most closely tied to the AI buildout, are getting hit the hardest.

Voters rebuked AI in Tuesday’s midterm elections, while sending Democrats to sweeping congressional victories across the country. Candidates who advocated for more stringent AI regulation won handily in states like Michigan, Ohio, Texas and Georgia, which will all now have Democratic governors, and local communities opposed data center-related ballot measures in 40 out of 41 cases.

More than half of voters said AI data centers were a “crucial” or “major factor” in who they supported for Congress, according to an exit poll from NBC News.

“People don’t want a data center going near them if it’s just going to house AI that’s going to help a big tech company profit,” Maura Austin, a behavioral scientist at the University of Virginia, told CNBC. “What Anthropic is doing when they’re going public with such a high valuation is they’re really leaning into that big tech, billionaire kind of caricature. I expect that’s not going to go well with the public.”

Anthropic has long tried to position itself as a safety-conscious company that takes AI’s potential risks and benefits seriously. CEO Dario Amodei co-founded the company alongside a handful of researchers who defected from OpenAI
, now its chief rival. Anthropic is best known for developing a family of AI models called Claude, and it primarily sells its products and services to other businesses.

The company’s enterprise focus has helped it avoid becoming the public face of AI, leaving that distinction to OpenAI and CEO Sam Altman. But with Anthropic poised to become the first pure-play AI company to hit the public market, minting a number of new billionaires and many more millionaires in the process, a heightened level of scrutiny is coming.

“Being a public company, just that by itself pushes you in the limelight,” Reena Aggarwal, a professor of finance at Georgetown University, said in an interview. “And then AI is such a hot-button issue that Anthropic will be in the limelight even more.”

Matt Kennedy, a senior IPO market strategist at Renaissance Capital, said that’s not necessarily a bad thing for Anthropic.

Public markets force greater transparency, he said, and the company could attract new users through its debut. And since AI has become such a mainstream conversation topic, several private companies are already household names.

“I would say that a public company does not deserve more criticisms than a comparable private company,” Kennedy said. “So Anthropic should not be put in a harsher public spotlight than OpenAI just because it’s public.”

Anthropic declined to comment.

AI backlash accelerated over the summer after a series of high-profile safety and security incidents rattled the public. As concerns mounted, the debate over data centers intensified, while tech’s hyperscalers simultaneously boosted their forecasts for capital expenditures, each reaching into the hundreds of billions of dollars.

Anthropic and OpenAI depend on state-of-the-art data centers to train models and serve customers, and they’re trying to build out capacity as quickly as possible to meet demand. Anthropic said in an amended IPO prospectus this week that it has entered into purchase commitments and lease agreements with an aggregate committed spend of about $895.4 billion, “substantially all of which is related to compute and infrastructure.”

Americans grappling with inflation and stubbornly high gas prices have grown worried that the facilities could exacerbate environmental harms, raise utility bills and contribute to job loss. For many, a proposed data center in their backyard became the physical manifestation of the widespread antipathy toward AI.

In the risk factors section of its prospectus, Anthropic said opposition to data center development has become more organized across jurisdictions, and that the company’s public profile could draw particular scrutiny to projects associated with it.

Nicole Greene, an analyst at Gartner, said she expects that Anthropic’s executives have long been prepared to contend with AI backlash, especially given the disruptive nature of the technology.

“There’s going to be big emotions,” Greene told CNBC. “With big emotions and feelings — fear and excitement — comes heightened scrutiny.”

Amodei acknowledged the souring sentiment around AI in a post on X in August. He said it’s the result of a “crisis of trust,” and that people believe companies, the government and the tech industry are always “cooking up some new way to screw them over.”

Rebuilding public confidence is going to be an uphill battle as the company begins providing quarterly financial updates.

The University of Southern California published a survey on Monday that found that 71% of respondents don’t trust big tech companies to act in society’s best interest “at all” around data center development.

“Once you’ve lost trust, it’s hard to gain it back,” Wändi Bruine de Bruin, a professor at the University of Southern California’s Schaeffer Institute, said in an interview. “The numbers are not good.”

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/07/berkshir.title: Berkshire Hathaway more than doubles buybacks in third quarter as earnings decline
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/07/berkshir.author: Fred Imbert
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/07/berkshir.text:
Berkshire Hathaway repurchased about $9.6 billion of its stock in the third quarter, more than double the second-quarter amount.

Third-quarter operating earnings fell 5.8% to $12.705 billion as insurance underwriting and investment income declined.

Berkshire Hathaway
 said Saturday it accelerated its share repurchases during the third quarter, as operating and overall profits took a hit.

The Greg Abel-led conglomerate bought back $9.6 billion worth of Berkshire stock. That’s more than double the $4.5 billion repurchased in the second quarter and brings the company’s total buybacks for 2026 to about $14.4 billion.

The sharp increase came as Berkshire’s operating earnings — those from wholly-owned businesses — fell year over year, as profits from its insurance business pulled back.

Berkshire operating profits totaled $12.705 billion, down 5.8% from $13.485 billion in the year-earlier period. Insurance underwriting tumbled 43% year on year to $1.352 billion, while insurance investment income declined 14% to $2.734 billion. Berkshire’s railroad, energy and manufacturing businesses all saw earnings grow year over year.

The company’s overall earnings, which include Berkshire’s sprawling stock market portfolio, also dropped 28% in the third quarter to $22.112 billion from $30.796 billion a year prior. Investment gains for the company fell nearly 50% to $9.407 billion.

Despite the earnings pullback, Berkshire stock has outperformed recently amid a massive rotation out of technology stocks. Class A shares are up more than 12% over the past month, while the S&P 500 has dropped 5.5% in that time. Year to date, Berkshire has gained 13%, while the broad market index is up just 7.8%.

Berkshire’s five largest equity holdings remained the same in the third quarter: Alphabet
, American Express
, Apple
, Bank of America
 and Coca-Cola
.

Berkshire’s cash hoard also grew 3% in the third quarter $377.435 billion from $365.514 billion in the second quarter. However, excluding rail and utility cash along with T-bill payables, the conglomerate’s cash holdings totaled $352.3 billion, down 1.9% quarter over quarter.

— CNBC’s Alex Crippen contributed reporting.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/07/dave-weh.title: Meta chief strategy officer Dave Wehner leaves to join AI infrastructure startup Fireworks as CFO
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/07/dave-weh.author: Megan Sauer
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/07/dave-weh.text:
Meta chief strategy officer Dave Wehner is leaving the company to become CFO of Fireworks.

Fireworks is an AI inference and model-training platform that helps companies customize and run open models.

Fireworks was valued at $17.5 billion in a July Series D and is in early talks to raise again at a possible $30 billion to $40 billion valuation, Business Insider reported.

Dave Wehner, Meta’s
 chief strategy officer, is leaving the company for four-year-old AI startup Fireworks.

At Fireworks — an AI inference and model-training platform focused on open models that was valued at $17.5 billion during a Series D fundraising round in July — Wehner will assume the CFO role, he announced on X on Friday.

Wehner will be tasked with scaling the company’s finances and operations, Fireworks CEO Lin Qiao said in a statement to CNBC.

“Fireworks has the right mission for the moment,” Wehner wrote on X, adding: “I’ve become increasingly bullish on what they are building. There’s a remarkable depth of technical talent here, coupled with a very practical focus on what customers need.”

The AI startup, founded in 2022 by former Meta and Google
 employees, is a platform that lets developers customize and run open models for their businesses. Its latest investment round was led by Atreides Management, Index Ventures and TCV, but Fireworks is also backed by Nvidia
 and Sequoia Capital. Business Insider reported that it is in early talks to raise funds again at a possible $30 billion to $40 billion valuation.

Wehner joined Meta, then called Facebook, in 2012 and was the company’s chief financial officer from 2014 to 2022.

“Dave helped guide Meta through tremendous growth and complexity over 14 years, and brought disciplined thinking to some of our hardest company-level decisions,” Meta COO Javier Olivan said in a statement to CNBC.

Fireworks is notably smaller than Meta — the tech giant has about a $1.56 trillion market capitalization as of Friday’s close — and its competitors, which include OpenAI and Anthropic.

“Dave told me he wanted to get back to a smaller company where he could build toward a big impact again,” Fireworks’ Lin wrote in a LinkedIn post on Friday. “He sees AI as the defining technology shift of his lifetime and wants to help shape what comes next.”

The company’s size has not made it immune to the risks and complications often associated with AI technology. In October, the company found “a security incident involving unauthorized use of internal Fireworks credentials,” in which “an unauthorized third party accessed environment variables used in evaluation jobs in a limited number of customer accounts,” it said in a press release.

“Based on our investigation at this time, we have not detected evidence of unauthorized access to customer models, datasets, training data, personal information, or inference traffic within the Fireworks security perimeter or control,” the release said.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/07/iran-war.title: Risk of Iran war escalation remains high despite Democratic sweep in U.S. midterm elections
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/07/iran-war.author: Spencer Kimball
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/07/iran-war.text:
Crude oil prices sold off this week as investors hoped the Democratic victory in the U.S. midterm elections would force an end to the Iran war.

But tensions remain high in the Middle East, with the Gulf states still bracing for escalation, analysts say.

The Democrats’ options are limited until they take control of Congress in January.

And President Donald Trump has reiterated that he will not allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon.

The U.S. and Iran are careening toward renewed war despite growing hopes this week that the Democrats’ decisive midterm election victory will bring the conflict to an end, analysts say.

Crude oil prices fell more than 16% over the last five trading days after U.S. Vice President JD Vance publicly blamed the Republicans’ stinging loss on the war. Vance’s remarks raised questions about whether the administration still has support to continue the conflict with Iran.

The Democrats plan to use their comfortable majorities in both chambers of Congress to pass a war powers resolution that demands President Donald Trump end the war. But tensions in the Middle East have not eased since the election, and the Democrats aren’t sworn in until January, the analysts say.

“Throughout the week, we were struck by the divergence between deepening escalation concerns in the Gulf and the headline-driven off-ramp optimism of market participants thousands of miles away,” Helima Croft, head of global commodity strategy at RBC Capital Markets, told investors in a note Friday.

Late Saturday, U.S. Central Command said it disabled a St. Kitts-flagged ship after the tanker ignored multiple warnings and attempted to leave the region after visiting an Iranian port, according to media reports. Iran state media also reported on explosions on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, as well as several blasts occurring in the port of Jask. CNBC couldn’t independently confirm the reports.

Several oil tankers have also come under attack near Oman since the election, killing one seafarer, according to maritime security agencies. Iran’s Houthi allies in Yemen continue to fire missiles at neighboring Saudi Arabia.

Meanwhile, the U.S. military buildup continues, with a third carrier strike group en route to the region. The consulting group Rapidan Energy sees an 80% chance that fighting will resume as diplomacy stalls.

Trump told reporters Thursday that he will make a decision soon on whether to attack Iran again.

“I would rather not destroy the rest of the country if possible but maybe I’ll have to,” Trump said in the Oval Office. “You’ll know soon enough.”

“We’re locked and loaded,” the president said. “If we have to do the rest of the Iran thing, we’re very much locked in.”

Crude oil prices will vault above $100 a barrel again in response to renewed fighting, said Bob McNally, president of Rapidan and a former energy advisor to President George W. Bush. Brent crude, the international benchmark, traded above $97 on Friday, while U.S. crude was around $90.

“President Donald Trump is determined as a legacy item, almost at all costs, to prevent Iran from getting a nuclear weapon, having them give up their nuclear capabilities,” McNally told CNBC’s “Squawk Box Asia” on Friday.

“The Iranian regime, on the other hand, is not willing to do it,” the analyst said. The escalation dynamic remains in place so long as that core difference between the U.S. and Iran persists, he said.

The risk of war is still alive, especially since Trump no longer faces future elections, said Amos Hochstein, a former energy advisor to President Joe Biden. Gasoline, diesel and jet fuel prices would all surge as a consequence, Hochstein told CNBC’s “Power Lunch” Friday.

Tehran has been taunting the Trump administration since the election. The social media account of Iran’s Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei said the “process of the U.S.’s collapse has accelerated” after the midterm results.

And Congress is unlikely to pass a war powers resolution until Democrats take control in January. Trump can veto such a resolution anyway.

The main leverage Congress will have is the power of the purse, Croft said. Government funding expires on Dec. 11, and negotiations for another continuing resolution could drag into 2027, she said. This would give Democrats more leverage when they take power in January, the analyst said.

“Importantly, deferring funding decisions would not immediately constrain Trump’s ability to conduct military operations, but could significantly reshape the administration’s longer-term funding outlook,” Croft told investors.

Trump discussed diplomatic efforts to de-escalate tensions in the region with the emir of Qatar during a Friday phone call, according to Qatar’s state news agency.

An unnamed senior Iranian official told Reuters on Thursday that Tehran sent a nuclear proposal to the U.S. through Qatar. Tehran will only discuss the proposal after the U.S. meets its demands, the Iranian official told Reuters.

Trump seemed to dismiss the diplomatic efforts Thursday.

“Iran will never have a nuclear weapon,” the president said. “They’re not doing anything without our approval. It doesn’t make any difference what they’re looking at,” he said of the diplomatic efforts.
