Sales of its new GLP-1 obesity pill Foundayo were under Wall Street's expectations for the third quarter. Lilly now expects  Eli Lilly posted earnings of $7.48 per share for theThird quarter.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/08/ai-recru.title: AI is speeding up recruitment — and putting agency fees under pressure
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/08/ai-recru.author: Lindsay Dodgson
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/08/ai-recru.text:
AI is cutting time spent on candidate search and screening, according to recruitment-industry surveys and company data.

Recruiters interviewed by CNBC are split over whether AI-driven efficiency will push agency fees down or make human judgment more valuable.

Some recruiters expect consolidation and job cuts as automation expands, while others say relationship-building and specialist assessment will support fees.

Artificial intelligence is speeding up parts of hiring — and that could force recruitment agencies to rethink how they charge.

David Berwick, owner of Adria Solutions, a recruitment agency based in Stockport, England, said that as AI takes on more of the work involved in making a placement, clients may question what their fees actually pay for. Agencies often charge employers a percentage of a successful candidate’s first-year salary.

“If a recruitment agency is simply finding CVs and forwarding them to employers, AI is making that service increasingly difficult to justify,” Berwick told CNBC. “Businesses can already automate much of that work themselves.”

A 2026 survey of nearly 300 recruitment professionals in the U.K. and Ireland by U.S. recruitment software provider Bullhorn found that 37% said AI had made candidate screening between 26% and 50% faster. LinkedIn’s 2025 UK Future of Recruiting report also found that talent acquisition professionals experimenting with or integrating generative AI saved an average of 18% of their working week.

Major recruitment firms are already putting that automation into practice. Swiss staffing company Adecco said in February that it had six AI recruitment agents operating in the U.K. and France, with the U.K. tools saving around 15% of the time spent on recruitment processes.

The U.K. was the first market in the Adecco Group to test these AI recruitment agents, according to Niki Turner-Harding, the company’s senior vice president for the U.K. and Ireland. Across the group, AI has supported more than 2.5 million candidate interactions, around half outside normal working hours, the company said.

But although the agents support the recruitment process, they don’t make hiring decisions, Turner-Harding said. That responsibility remains with a human recruiter, and candidates can always ask to speak to a person.

“People don’t go into recruitment because they love admin. They go into it because they like working with people, solving problems and building relationships,” she told CNBC. “So, what we’ll see is recruiters spending less time on process and more time actually recruiting.”

Matt Collingwood, managing director of recruitment firm VIQU Group in Birmingham, England, told CNBC he sees automation as an opportunity to give recruiters more time to build relationships, rather than simply making the same service cheaper. VIQU’s turnover has grown by 47% over the past 18 months, partly as a result of that approach, he said.

“The businesses best placed to succeed will be those that combine technology with strong relationships and genuine expertise,” he said. “I see every reason for our fees to hold firm, or even increase, if the value we deliver continues to grow.”

Still, Collingwood predicted that only a third of today’s recruitment agencies may survive the next five years. Others expect deep job cuts. James Wright, founder of London-based executive hiring firm Velocity Leadership, said AI now allows him to do work that previously required a team of five.

He pointed to the large global executive search firms, sometimes known as the SHREK firms — Spencer Stuart, Heidrick & Struggles, Russell Reynolds, Egon Zehnder and Korn Ferry — which dominate C-suite and board-level recruitment. These businesses could face significant pressure to shrink their workforces, he said.

“They have this huge hierarchy of analysts, researchers, consultants, and managing partners,” he told CNBC. “At least 60, 70% of them are going to be out of a job, I think.”

While some recruiters expect to hold their fees, others think that AI will eventually push the cost of hiring down.

Paddy Lambros, founder and CEO of London-based AI recruitment platform Dex, said the industry is long overdue for an overhaul.

“Recruitment as a way of doing things isn’t very effective no matter how you look at it,” he told CNBC. “It’s very expensive, it’s very slow. One of the reasons that the fees are so high is that it’s such an inefficient process.”

Lambros argued that AI is contributing to a hiring market flooded at both ends, with candidates sending out thousands of automated resumes and employers struggling to sift through applications.

“The solution is not giving every candidate an AI, giving every client an AI and then making the AIs fight — that’s just a massive waste of time,” he said. “Technology has to be used in a way that supports both sides.”

Others argue AI will make human judgment more valuable, not less. Chris Stirling, managing director of U.K. specialist recruitment firm Stirling Q&R, told CNBC that the value of recruitment firms will increasingly lie in their ability to assess candidates.

Software can find a hundred people with terms like “QA” or “regulatory” in their profile in seconds, he said, “but it cannot tell a biotech founder whether a candidate has actually built a quality system from scratch or only maintained one.”

“AI is making the easy part of recruiting faster,” he said, “which is exactly why the fee now has to be earned on the hard part.”
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/08/ai-recru.summary: Recruiters interviewed by CNBC are split over whether AI-driven efficiency will push agency fees down or make human judgment more valuable. Some recruiters expect consolidation and job cuts as automation expands. Others say relationship-building and specialist assessment will support fees.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/06/cramer-c.title: Cramer’s week ahead: AI data center stocks face another hurdle and so does the Fed
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/06/cramer-c.author: Alexa LoMonaco
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/06/cramer-c.text:
CNBC’s Jim Cramer warned that next week’s earnings from leading neoclouds pose another test for AI data center stocks.

Cramer highlighted earnings from CoreWeave and Nebius, alongside key inflation reports that could shape the Federal Reserve’s next interest rate decision.

CNBC’s Jim Cramer on Friday said that next week’s earnings from leading neoclouds could test investor confidence in the battered data center trade.

Stocks rebounded to end a turbulent election week, which saw investors dumping companies tied to the artificial intelligence infrastructure build-out after Democrats flipped the House and Senate and some key gubernatorial seats. Following the worst day on Wall Street in 19 months, Friday’s gains were welcome but not to be trusted. Cramer remained skeptical of any recovery, as he also had been about what proved to be Wednesday’s short-lived midterm rally.

Cramer argued that concerns about data center spending and financing have yet to be resolved. “It felt like a dead cat bounce,” the “Mad Money” host said, referring to Friday’s largely positive market. “I know we are never going to get an all clear. But it still feels like there are plenty of sellers lurking, just waiting for stocks to make a bigger recovery so they can get out.”

With that backdrop, Cramer turned to the week ahead.

Constellation Energy
 reports before the bell, offering an early look at how political uncertainty could affect the power infrastructure supporting AI data centers.

On Holding
 reports earnings, but Cramer remains cautious on the athletic footwear. He said the industry feels increasingly crowded. “I am going to pass on this one,” he said.

The consumer price index also arrives Tuesday morning, with Cramer looking for a meaningful slowdown in inflation. He warned that persistently high prices could prompt Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh to raise interest rates again. The Fed hiked rates in September for the first time in three years.

After the close, neocloud CoreWeave
 reports in what could be one of the week’s most consequential earnings releases. Cramer said the heavily indebted neocloud needs to explain how it plans to finance its expansion and manage its borrowing costs.

Corteva
 reports in an otherwise quiet session. Cramer said the agricultural chemicals company has fallen sharply out of favor with investors and wants to better understand what’s weighing on its stock.

Nebius
, another high-profile neocloud, reports before the bell, providing another major test for the AI infrastructure trade following results from CoreWeave. Cramer said investors will be looking for strong new orders, completed data centers and a robust pipeline of future projects. “What I don’t want to hear is that the sites they are building are coming in late and overbudget,” he said.

Cisco Systems 
also reports Thursday evening. He said the networking provider may be oversold, but would wait to see how the market responds to CoreWeave and Nebius before buying.

Applied Materials
 reports as well. Although the semiconductor equipment maker’s shares have fallen sharply from their highs, Cramer cautioned that a steep decline alone does not make a stock attractive. “Remember, we don’t care where a stock comes from. We just care about where it is going,” he said.

Kraft Heinz
 holds an investor meeting Thursday. Cramer remains optimistic about CEO Steve Cahillane’s ability to unlock shareholder value, citing his track record at Kellogg.

The producer price index comes in Friday, offering another important reading on inflation.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/06/tesdonal.title: SpaceX says Google exec Don Harrison has resigned from its board
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/06/tesdonal.author: Lora Kolodny
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/06/tesdonal.text:
SpaceX board member Don Harrison, a Google executive, resigned from his role at Elon Musk’s company.

The resignation was disclosed in a filing from SpaceX, which thanked Harrison for his service with the company.

Google parent Alphabet is the largest institutional investor in SpaceX, with a $74 billion stake.

SpaceX
 said on Friday that longtime Google
 executive Donald Harrison has resigned from the rocket maker’s board of directors.

Harrison has worked at Google since 2005, and is the search giant’s president of global partnerships and corporate development. In a regulatory filing, SpaceX said “Mr. Harrison’s decision to resign was not due to any disagreement with the Company on any matter relating to its operations, policies, or practices.”

SpaceX thanked Harrison for his “many contributions and his years of dedicated and outstanding service” to the company.

The announcement comes roughly five months after SpaceX went public in the largest IPO on record. Google parent Alphabet maintains close ties with SpaceX, having invested in Elon Musk’s company in 2015, when it was valued at about $12 billion.

Alphabet is now the largest institutional investor n SpaceX, with a stake worth $74 billion as of Friday’s close. SpaceX’s current market cap is about $1.8 trillion.

Google is a key customer of SpaceX, and has agreed to pay the company’s AI division up to $920 million a month for compute capacity from its data centers in the area around Memphis, Tennessee. The companies also recently worked together to launch Google AI chips into orbit via Project Suncatcher.

“While Don is stepping down from the board, we remain deeply supportive of SpaceX’s mission and are excited to continue our long-standing partnership,” Google said in an emailed statement.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/06/investor.title: Investors brace for lower Anthropic valuation, calling $1.5 trillion a 'stretch'
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/06/investor.author: Kate Rooney,Caleigh Keating
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/06/investor.text:
With the tech selloff this week, some Anthropic investors now expect Anthropic to list below a $1.5 trillion valuation, with some saying that number could dip to $1 trillion.

That’s below prior expectations for a valuation of $2 trillion, the target when the company filed confidentially with the SEC.

The Democratic sweep in the midterms this week further increased fears that the buildout will slow.

Following tech’s selloff on Wall Street this week, some investors are lowering their expectations for Anthropic.

The artificial intelligence company had been looking toward a $2 trillion valuation in its IPO up until recently, but stakeholders told CNBC that even $1.5 trillion is now in doubt, with one investor calling that number a “stretch.”

Anthropic declined to comment.

The change in sentiment comes alongside growing concerns about the outsized spending by AI companies and a sharp post-midterm slump in the market. The Nasdaq plummeted more than 5% on Thursday, its steepest drop in 19 months, reflecting fears that Democrats’ newfound power in Washington, D.C., and a nationwide rebuke of AI will lead to a slowdown in the buildout of data centers.

Bearishness on the AI trade was on the rise before the election. The Nasdaq suffered its worst month in October since March 2025, led by declines in chipmakers and neoclouds.

Anthropic is set to list on the Nasdaq
, under the ticker ANT, and is gearing up for an expected debut in a matter of weeks. Last month, Anthropic was reportedly seeking a valuation as high as $2 trillion. As of May, the company was privately valued at $965 billion.

With the latest market turmoil, one investor said $1 trillion to $1.25 trillion is a more likely valuation target, although that could change with market conditions. The investors asked not to be named because they’re not authorized to speak about the matter.

Gil Luria, an analyst at D.A. Davidson, told CNBC that, “Investors will expect the IPO to be priced at least at the low end of previous expectations.”

“The market really needs this IPO to go well and the bankers on the deal surely understand that,” Luria said. “The best way to set Anthropic up for success is to price the deal well.”

The company is expected to kick off its roadshow next week.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/06/openai-b.title: OpenAI bugging suspect Alfozan pleads not guilty
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/06/openai-b.author: Jordan Novet,Dan Mangan
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/06/openai-b.text:
The Saudi national charged with planting a listening device in the headquarters of OpenAI while he worked there pleaded not guilty during an appearance in San Francisco federal court.

Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, was sent back to jail after the brief hearing. Alfozan has been held without bail since his arrest on Oct. 9.

A grand jury indicted Alfozan on Oct. 27 on a single count of interception of oral communications, court records show.

The Saudi national charged with planting a listening device in the headquarters of OpenAI while he worked there pleaded not guilty on Friday during an appearance in San Francisco federal court.

Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, was sent back to jail after the brief hearing. Alfozan has been held without bail since his arrest on a criminal complaint in early October.

He faces a maximum possible sentence of five years in prison if convicted in the case.

A grand jury indicted Alfozan on Oct. 27 on a single count of interception of oral communications, court records show.

Prosecutors say that he put a recording device in a television in an executive conference room at OpenAI’s offices in San Francisco on Sept. 28.

Alfozan’s lawyer declined to comment after the hearing before Magistrate Judge Peter Kang.

The judge ordered Alfozan to next appear in court on Nov. 17.

Alfozan is a venture partner in a Saudi Arabian venture capital firm, Raed Ventures.

“He currently serves as Engineering Lead at OpenAI, with a focus on AI Agents and the data platform,” Alfozan’s bio page on Raed’s site says.

Prince Khalid Bin Bader Al Saud, a member of Saudi Arabia’s royal family, is a venture partner in the same firm.

Alfozan’s case comes as U.S. companies such as OpenAI are making rapid advancements in developing artificial intelligence agents, and as concerns grow about the potential theft of AI tech from those companies.

In June, President Donald Trump, in an executive order on AI innovation, said it was U.S. policy “to protect American ingenuity and intellectual property from exploitation and theft by adversaries; and to cultivate America’s advanced AI-enabled capabilities.“

Trump has had a close relationship with Saudi Arabia. But he has also taken steps during his second term in the White House to limit the number of visas for highly skilled foreign workers.

OpenAI earlier this year held discussions with Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, the country’s sovereign wealth fund, about investing in the company.

— Jordan Novet reported from San Francisco

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/06/tech-exe.title: OpenAI, Arm and Qualcomm executives react to post-midterm AI sell-off
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/06/tech-exe.author: Caleigh Keating
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/06/tech-exe.text:
A Democratic sweep of Congress and many governorships in the midterm elections Tuesday prompted market fears of a data center slowdown.

Stocks sold off sharply Thursday, with major indexes posting their worst day since April 2025, before recovering some of those losses Friday.

Executives at some major tech companies reiterated to CNBC the importance of continuing the data center buildout, but expressed skepticism that the worst of the slowdown fears would materialize. Others pointed to strengths in their businesses that would be unaffected by data center concerns.

As a post-midterm rally Wednesday turned into a steep sell-off Thursday, tech executives sought to look through the notion that potential data center constraints could be catastrophic for their businesses.

In response to a Democratic sweep of Congress as well as a sizeable number of state governorships and legislatures in the midterm election Tuesday night, stocks initially rallied Wednesday, posting their best day in more than 18 months as President Trump accepted the blowout results with little fanfare.

The tide quickly turned Thursday, however, with stocks selling off sharply as investors feared a potential slowdown in the data center build-out after wins by candidates in favor of data center regulation in states like Texas and the possibility that the artificial intelligence trade may be past its peak. Tech led the sell-off, with the “Magnificent Seven” losing over $1 trillion in aggregate market cap.

Stocks recovered some of their losses Friday.

Here’s how tech executives reacted to the midterms and sell-off threat:

Haas characterized the postelection fear as “very, very short term thinking” and not likely to be a major threat to Arm’s
 business in the long term, but said the U.S. must keep investing in the data center build-out before the rest of the world catches up.

“If the U.S. hesitates in any way, shape, or form in terms of data center build-out, the rest of the world is ready and willing. There is just huge demand for this capacity,” Haas told CNBC’s “Squawk on the Street” Thursday.

Friar told CNBC’s Sara Eisen Friday that OpenAI will continue investing in data center infrastructure after voters resoundly rejected data centers in their backyards during the midterm election. The company will also focus on community concerns, including electricity. “We will never raise your electricity bill,” Friar said.

“When I think about the midterms, I need to keep thinking about how do we keep investing to meet that customer demand. It starts early with having built relationships with all of the hyperscalers, and it will continue to mean that we raise capital,” Friar said.

“If the midterm means more focus on data centers and communities, we’re going to keep doing the work to get into those communities and to build trust with them.”

Amon said the anxiety about the future of the data center build-out doesn’t pose a significant threat to the chipmaker’s business, as data center infrastructure is just one segment. Qualcomm
 slid 9.49% in Thursday’s sell-off before recovering some losses Friday.

“The whole market is down, but I think the Qualcomm story is a little bit different,” Amon told CNBC’s Jon Fortt Thursday. Unlike traditional PC and data center chipmakers, Qualcomm has historically focused on low-power consumption computing. “The story of Qualcomm is what we have done outside that on the data center specific question.”

Levie told “Squawk on the Street” Thursday that productivity gains meant AI “is clearly going in one direction,” but said a tendency for industry messaging to coalesce around “doomerism” can exacerbate the public perception problems AI companies face.

“I think it’s a little bit easier to rotate it toward maybe the more risk-oriented messages, and that’s something that our industry needs to work on clearly. But ultimately, obviously, the consumer needs to see the direct benefit, and that’s something that will just take time,” said Box’s
 Levie.

Risher said the dour market sentiment wasn’t concerning for Lyft’s
 business, as consumer sentiment and bookings remained strong.

“I wouldn’t get too distracted about the short term stuff of what’s going on in the market. If I look at the consumer, for example, we just had the biggest Halloween we’ve ever had,” Risher told CNBC’s “Squawk Box” Friday.
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/06/tech-exe.summary: Stocks sold off sharply Thursday, with major indexes posting their worst day since April 2025. Tech executives expressed skepticism that the worst of the slowdown fears would materialize.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/06/open-ai-.title: OpenAI will keep investing in AI data centers despite election results, CFO tells CNBC
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/06/open-ai-.author: Ashley Capoot
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/06/open-ai-.text:
OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar said the company will continue to invest in artificial intelligence infrastructure despite the results of the midterm elections.

Voters across the country on Tuesday voiced their support for candidates who have pledged to place restrictions on data center development.

OpenAI needs infrastructure built as quickly as possible as it rapidly develops new services and models and pushes toward an IPO.

OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar on Friday said the company will continue to invest in artificial intelligence infrastructure, even after voters strongly opposed data centers during Tuesday’s midterm elections.

“When I think about the midterms, I need to keep thinking about how do we keep investing to meet that customer demand,” Friar told CNBC’s Sara Eisen in an interview at the Citi TMT Leadership Summit in Pebble Beach, California. “It starts early with having built relationships with all of the hyperscalers, and it will continue to mean that we raise capital.”

Out of 41 local ballot measures across 10 states, voters backed restrictions or rejected pro-development measures in all but one, according to an analysis by Ballotpedia and additional results gathered by CNBC on Wednesday. Opposition to the facilities mounted swiftly over the summer as Americans grew worried about their potential to harm the environment, raise utility bills and contribute to job loss.

Investors have turned skeptical on the AI trade of late due to a combination of higher borrowing costs, concerns about soaring debt and public backlash toward the industry. The Nasdaq on Thursday suffered its steepest drop in 19 months, led by a plunge in shares of the chipmakers and neocloud companies most closely tied to the AI buildout. The stocks rebounded some on Friday.

OpenAI depends on data centers to train its AI models and serve customers, and Friar said she doesn’t think the election results dramatically changed anything for the company. On Thursday, OpenAI published a policy blueprint and a series of commitments that it pledged to apply to company-owned and -operated data centers in the future.

“If the midterm means more focus on data centers and communities, we’re going to keep doing the work to get into those communities and to build trust with them,” Friar said.

OpenAI confidentially filed its prospectus with the Securities and Exchange Commission in June, and Friar said Friday that the company would continue to look into a 2027 debut. Anthropic, OpenAI’s chief rival, is trying to go public first, with an aim to hit the Nasdaq in mid-November.

Anthropic’s revenue in the first nine months of the year jumped roughly 1,200% to $33.2 billion, according to its prospectus. The company said it has entered into purchase commitments and lease agreements with an aggregate committed spend of about $895.4 billion, “substantially all of which is related to compute and infrastructure.”

OpenAI is in talks to raise funding at a $1.25 billion pre-money valuation, Friar said Friday. She said “a good CFO always raises money when she can” and that the round is ongoing.

The company has closed an initial $11 billion portion of that funding round, CNBC confirmed on Friday, and it could raise up to an additional $9 billion in the coming weeks. Bloomberg was first to report the $11 billion portion.

“The demand for AI is real,” Friar said. “I don’t think anyone’s arguing with that, or if they are, I think it’s a losing argument.”

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/06/ai-data-.title: AI stocks hammered by midterm shock as data center buildout becomes a 'war of attrition'
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/06/ai-data-.author: Kai Nicol-Schwarz
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/06/ai-data-.text:
AI and semiconductor stocks sold off sharply Thursday as investors reassessed the data center build-out after Democrats won control of Congress.

The election rout landed on an AI trade already under pressure from high interest rates, heavy capital spending and questions about returns.

By Friday morning, U.S. tech stocks were showing signs of recovery, but the market blip is a warning of potentially rougher roads ahead for the AI boom in America.

This report is from this week’s The Tech Download newsletter. Like what you see? You can subscribe here.

The Democrats’ stunning rout of the Republicans during the midterms this week wasn’t just a stinging rebuke of President Donald Trump, but also a potential roadblock to huge plans to build artificial intelligence data centers across the country.

Since the landmark results came in, tech and AI stocks have been jolted by market volatility.

The most valuable tech companies in the U.S. and Europe were hit with a massive sell-off on Thursday as investors got nervous.

Nvidia
 lost 9.3%, with AMD
 shedding 17.3%, Microsoft
 3.6%, Micron
 17.5%, Broadcom
 10.4%, Tesla
 10.8% and SpaceX
 9.1%.

Neoclouds, which rely on their ability to serve AI computing power and are involved in massive data center projects, were also hit particularly hard. Nebius
 dropped 15%, Iren
 fell 17% and CoreWeave
 10% on Thursday.

By Friday morning, U.S. tech stocks were showing signs of recovery, but the market blip is a warning of potentially rougher roads ahead for the AI boom in America.

“The tumble in tech stocks that took hold in the immediate aftermath of the US midterm elections resumed as investors contemplated what a Democrat-controlled Congress may mean for tech regulation and the overall AI boom,” wrote Kyle Rodda, senior financial market analyst at Capital.com in a note on Thursday after the bell.

There were dozens of local ballot measures in 10 states up for a vote on Tuesday that would place restrictions on the construction of data centers in different ways, CNBC reported on Wednesday.

“The regulatory and political risks arise at a time when the proverbial AI trade was already on shakier foundations,” said Rodda.

Earnings season had been an “overall disappointment” for the markets, he added, with Magnificent Seven results so far “undershooting growth expectations and flashing warning signs that the pace of AI spending is slowing down.”

Now, Rodda wrote, the risk that the investment boom could be slowed further “by measures as potentially disruptive as moratoriums on new data center construction, investors are rushing to the exits on so-called AI trades.”

Opposition to data centers in the U.S. is a long-standing issue.

Between January 2024 and May 2026, at least 46 AI data center projects across 20 U.S. states, representing more than $170 billion in announced investment, were blocked, withdrawn or stalled following community opposition, according to research carried out by think tank International Data Center Authority, or IDCA.

The midterms will weigh on investors’ minds, Dan Ives, partner at Yorkville Ives & Co., said in a note on Wednesday morning.

“For tech investors the big focus is will these mid-term elections slow the pace of the planned 800 to 1,000 datacenters across the US fueling the AI Revolution…the answer in our view is a clear YES,” he wrote.

Democrats taking control, particularly over the Senate, will create some major hurdles for AI over the next two years, Ives added.

The figures floating around on the scale of projected AI infrastructure spending are eye-watering.

Goldman Sachs estimates that AI-related capital spending could total about $7.6 trillion from 2026 through 2031, across computing, data centers and power.

But, heading into the election, AI stocks were already looking shaky on Wall Street.

Chipmakers, neoclouds and other data center-related companies sold off in October on concerns about rising interest rates and overspending. Many hyperscalers have turned cash flow negative as they spend hundreds of billions of dollars on AI infrastructure.

“AI pushback is bipartisan but local, making the buildout pricier rather than stalling it,” said Dominique Toublan, head of U.S. credit strategy at Barclays Investment Bank, in a note from Wednesday.

“The AI race shifts from a prisoner’s dilemma to a war of attrition: scarce power favors the biggest balance sheets.”

By Thursday morning, after speaking to investors over the past 24 hours, Ives said it was a confusing time for Wall Street tech backers trying to “discern the poker game in the Beltway and how this will truly impact the AI Revolution buildout.”

The impact could be significant.

“Putting all the pieces together we believe Big Tech capex growth rate now peaks in 2027 vs our previous view that would not happen until 2028/2029,” he said.

Chinese AI lab Moonshot turned to Europe for Nvidia Blackwell access amid U.S. China curbs, sources tell CNBC.

CrowdStrike
 launches AI kill switch that it says can stop internal agents that go rogue.

Meta
 seeks to raise up to $25 billion in debt sale as AI spending jumps.

Brookfield plans for a $27 billion AI data center at UK power station.

Elon Musk’s Tesla
 and SpaceX
 lose over $420 billion in combined market cap after midterms.

Blue Origin pushes launch to January 2027 as it races to rebuild damaged launchpad.

Elsewhere in midterm-land, it’s not just data centers in the crosshairs.

Democrats’ sweep of Congress likely resets the political calculus for crypto, my colleague Tanaya Macheel writes.

The result? It could usher in a more adversarial approach in Washington and push industry-friendly legislation like the Clarity Act to the back burner, she says.

The election rout landed on an AI trade already under pressure from high interest rates, heavy capital spending and questions about returns.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/06/tech-sto.title: Nasdaq sell-off batters Asian chip stocks as SK Hynix, Samsung, Softbank, TSMC tumble
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/06/tech-sto.author: Lee Ying Shan,Jenny Lee
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/06/tech-sto.text:
Asian technology stocks tumbled Friday, tracking a sharp sell-off on Wall Street overnight that sent the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite into correction territory.

Asian technology stocks tumbled Friday, tracking a sharp sell-off on Wall Street overnight that sent the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite into correction territory as renewed concerns over artificial intelligence spending rattled investor sentiment.

South Korean chipmaker SK Hynix plunged 10.44%, while Samsung Electronics shed 6.35%. LG Innotek and LG Display fell 7.02% and 4.45%, respectively, as selling pressure spread across the country’s technology sector.

The rout came as investors worried that Democrats’ sweeping victory in the U.S. midterm elections could lead to tighter restrictions on data-center development, potentially slowing demand for AI chips and related infrastructure.

In Japan, semiconductor-related stocks also fell, with chip-testing equipment maker Advantest
 plunging 4.99%, while Tokyo Electron
 slid over 5%. Technology investment giant SoftBank Group
 tumbled 10.83%.

Shares of memory chipmaker Kioxia Holdings
 fell 8.72%, while Renesas Electronics
 declined 5.74%.

In Taiwan, semiconductor stocks also came under heavy selling pressure, with contract chipmaker TSMC
 sliding 4.69%.

China was also caught in the regional sell-off, with the tech-heavy STAR Market and the ChiNext Artificial Intelligence Index both tumbling more than 4%.

The declines followed a brutal session on Wall Street, where the Nasdaq Composite sank 5.5%, amid mounting concerns over the sustainability of the AI investment boom and returns on massive data-center spending. It closed more than 10% below its recent peak. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index plunged 12.2%.

European stocks were broadly lower on Friday, but technology was among the least-impacted sectors, with losses of around 0.25% in morning deals. Chip stocks ASML and ASMI rose 4% and 3%, respectively.

The sell-off in Asian equities has been exacerbated by investors unwinding positions, stop-loss selling and heightened volatility, Timothy Moe, chief Asia Pacific equity strategist at Goldman Sachs, told CNBC’s “Squawk Box Asia” on Friday.

He added that potential political opposition to U.S. data center construction may affect demand and profits for Asian AI hardware suppliers.

“If there’s concern about the speed and magnitude of buildout in the U.S., then obviously that’s going to put all that into question,” he said. “The market’s tendency is always to shoot first and ask questions later. I think that’s exactly what’s happening now.”

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/05/jim-cram.title: Jim Cramer explains why no AI stock seems safe from the market carnage
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/05/jim-cram.author: Alexa LoMonaco
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/05/jim-cram.text:
CNBC’s Jim Cramer said AI stocks are becoming increasingly difficult to value as uncertainty over the future of the data center build-out raises questions about their long-term growth prospects.

Cramer highlighted Nvidia, Micron and AMD as examples of companies delivering strong results but facing risks that could undermine their valuations if AI infrastructure spending slows.

CNBC’s Jim Cramer said Thursday that uncertainty over the future of a data center build-out has made artificial intelligence stocks increasingly difficult to value, leading to the steep selling over the past two sessions.

The sell-off swept across the AI trade, hitting everything from chipmakers to companies supplying power and electrical equipment for data centers. The iShares Semiconductor ETF
 (SOXX) fell 3% Wednesday and another 10% Thursday, while GE Vernova
 and Sandisk
 dropped 7% and 22%, respectively, on Thursday. Investors are concerned that regulatory hurdles and opposition to new data centers could slow the build-out, undermining the growth forecasts supporting chipmakers’ valuations.

“We don’t know what to pay for any of the stocks connected to the data center and that’s why this moment is so fraught,” the “Mad Money” host said.

Cramer pointed to Nvidia
 as a prime example. The AI chipmaker trades at roughly 12 times next year’s earnings with an expected growth rate of 70%, making it appear remarkably cheap. But those earnings projections assume demand will remain strong for years to come.

“That’s an incredible bargain,” he said. “But it is not a bargain if, the following year, it can’t grow any further, because the U.S. won’t permit new data centers as fast as they do now.”

Memory maker Micron
 also faces risk. The company’s long-term take-or-pay contracts provide some revenue visibility even if customers don’t take delivery of their chips. However, Cramer said he’s unsure how sturdy those contracts would be if any signees fell on especially hard times and didn’t have the money to pay.

Advanced Micro Devices
 presents another valuation dilemma. Cramer praised its latest earnings as “one of the best quarters I have ever seen” and highlighted CEO Lisa Su’s projection that the broader data center market could eventually reach $1 trillion.

“If that’s the case then you can buy her [CEO Lisa Su’s] stock right now,” Cramer said. “Do you want to? The stock was at $188 in March. By that token, $404 seems awfully high to me. Maybe that’s the real problem.”

Ultimately, Cramer said the question is whether regulatory hurdles will significantly slow data center construction or merely delay it. Until the outlook becomes clearer, even exceptional earnings outlook may not be enough to justify AI stocks’ valuations.

Cramer’s Charitable Trust, the portfolio run by CNBC’s Investing Club, owns shares of NVDA and MU.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/05/jim-cram.title: Jim Cramer says the AI sell-off isn't over, but it isn't another dot-com crash
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/05/jim-cram.author: Alexa LoMonaco
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/05/jim-cram.text:
CNBC’s Jim Cramer warned that the sell-off in AI stocks likely has further to run, but said the downturn is different from the dot-com crash because many of today’s hardest-hit companies have profitable businesses.

Cramer urged investors to maintain sufficient cash and not to panic.

The steep sell-off in artificial intelligence stocks likely has further to go, CNBC’s Jim Cramer predicted Thursday — but he urged investors not to panic.

Growing opposition to new data centers following the midterm elections has raised doubts about future AI infrastructure spending, sending shares of companies tied to the buildout sharply lower. Micron
 tumbled 17%, GE Vernova
 dropped 7% and Sandisk
 plunged 22% on Thursday. All three stocks were also crushed in Wednesday’s session.

“I wish I could say that today’s flush was the bottom,” the “Mad Money” host said, before cautioning that there may be more downside ahead, though he didn’t believe this was an internet bubble redux. Cramer argued that today’s AI companies are fundamentally different from the speculative businesses that collapsed during the dot-com bust.

“But I look at the charts, and there still seems like there’s no support for so many Tech stocks, especially the semis, because they ran so much on the way up. However it might feel, it’s actually an orderly decline because unlike 2000, these are mostly lucrative companies with stocks that went too high.”

Investors had pushed AI stocks too high by assuming the rapid pace of data center construction would continue indefinitely, Cramer said. Smaller developers such as CoreWeave
, Iren
 and Nebius
 face particular risks because they borrowed money to finance projects that could now face regulatory delays.

“That’s what I am chiefly worried about,” he said. “That’s the real problem. That’s what could really hurt the stock market. ... Right now, no one of significance is defaulting on their debt. The only issue with the debt is that it’s connected to those neocloud companies that I mentioned. That’s not enough to sink us.”

Cramer suggested that a swift sell-off could help the market work off the excesses of the AI boom more effectively than a prolonged downturn.

“I for one am glad they are ripping the Band-Aid off this market rather than slowing trying to take it off a little bit each day,” he said.

For investors, Cramer recommended maintaining sufficient cash. While semiconductor stocks could face further declines, he pointed to falling interest rates, signs of easing inflation and the possibility of an end to the Iran war as reasons for optimism.

“If you have cash you won’t panic,” Cramer concluded. “You won’t be complacent, either. You will be clear-headed and that’s how you will lose less money until things get better. They always do.”

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/05/iren-ear.title: Neocloud IREN says $4 billion in annualized revenue being delayed due to customer request
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/05/iren-ear.author: Kif Leswing
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/05/iren-ear.text:
After a dramatic plunge in its stock price, IREN said some revenue is being delayed from 2026 until early next year.

IREN said in its earnings report that AI cloud revenue more than doubled from the prior quarter.

The neocloud segment is getting crushed on Wall Street because of concerns about whether capital will be available for the companies to continue expanding.

Following a 26% post-election plunge in its stock price, neocloud IREN
 said in its earnings report on Thursday that over $4 billion in annual recurring revenue projected to land in 2026 has been pushed out to at least January.

IREN said the move, which could extend payment to February, is due to “a customer-requested change and supplier timing.”

On the company’s earnings call, IREN co-CEO Daniel Roberts said Microsoft
 is the customer.

“They made a request to reconfigure and upgrade some of the network infrastructure and the purpose of that was really to enable the 200 megawatts of capacity to service these latest-generation frontier models,” Roberts said.

Shares of IREN rose in extended trading, but that comes after a 55% drop over the past month.

The company said revenue climbed 66% from the prior quarter to $228 million, beating the $221 million average analyst estimate, according to LSEG. AI Cloud revenue more than doubled to $200 million. IREN gets the rest of its revenue from bitcoin mining, which was its primary business before the company pivoted to AI.

IREN’s net loss narrowed to $263 million from $684 million the prior period. Year-ago figures weren’t included in the earnings release.

The company is being closely watched by investors as the AI trade shows signs of unwinding, particularly following the Democratic sweep in Tuesday’s midterm elections. Concerns are mounting that cash-burning companies reliant on debt are going to have a hard time meeting their obligations as interest rates rise and lenders back out of the market. The Nasdaq had its worst day on Thursday since April 2025.

“Capital markets have become more selective in the last few weeks, and the questions have undoubtedly moved from how big the contract is to whether it can be delivered, financed, and run at a profit,” Roberts said on the call.

CoreWeave
, which is set to report earnings on Tuesday, has plunged 60% in the past month. Nebius
, which reports next Thursday, is down 48% over that stretch.

IREN said revenue backlog increased 22% from the prior period to $20.3 billion, with “approximately two-thirds with investment-grade counterparties.” The $4 billion ARR target is fully contracted and funded, the company said.

“There is a disconnect between what we’re seeing in public market and what we’re seeing at the customer level,” Roberts told CNBC’s Seema Mody.

Still, Iren said it planed to shell out $15 billion in capital expenditures the rest of this fiscal year, including $9 billion in cash and committed financing, and $6 billion in “target” financing, which is “subject to market conditions.”

The neocloud said that prices for its compute continue to rise and that it expanded an existing contract with a leading frontier AI lab. It said it has contracts with Nvidia
, Microsoft and 13 other customers.

Roberts said that some data center construction in the coming year would be backed by Nvidia and Microsoft, but about a third would be to companies that are willing to offer large prepayments for the capacity.

“We just had a customer agree to fund 90% of the GPU capex,” Roberts said, referring to graphics processing units.

IREN said that community opposition can be addressed by tapping local suppliers, using water efficiently and creating jobs.

“I think whether it’s Texas, whether it’s Australia, whether it’s Spain, everywhere, all we’re seeing is people wanting to ensure that data centers pay their own way and do the right thing, and it it feels completely reasonable,” Roberts said.

IREN said it deliberately hadn’t yet bought all of the GPUs it needs for next year to reduce risk.

—CNBC’s Isabel O’Brien contributed to this report.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/05/tesla-sp.title: Elon Musk's Tesla and SpaceX lose over $420 billion in combined market cap after midterms
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/05/tesla-sp.author: Lora Kolodny
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/05/tesla-sp.text:
Elon Musk’s Tesla and SpaceX lose over $420 billion in combined market cap in the two days after midterms.

As Democrats control the House and Senate, and Texas flips blue, investors expect Musk and his companies to face probes and steeper regulatory hurdles to their AI and merger ambitions.

Musk was the biggest backer of GOP candidates and causes in the midterms and most of those he backed were defeated by Dem opponents.

SpaceX
 and Tesla
 shares declined by about 9% and 11%, respectively, on Thursday afternoon with investors concerned that Elon Musk could face new congressional probes — and his companies stricter regulation — following the U.S. midterm elections.

The declines, which correlated with a broader tech sell-off, brought aggregate market cap losses for SpaceX and Tesla to over $420 billion since Tuesday’s close.

Musk’s wealth, which had topped $1 trillion after SpaceX’s initial public offering in June, is now down below $800 billion, having dropped about $90 billion in the past week, according to Forbes. He is still the richest man in the world.

Musk was the biggest donor to GOP candidates and causes in the midterms, with his financial contributions exceeding $470 million, the Financial Times first reported.

Despite his bolstering the GOP war chest, most of the candidates Musk backed lost their races.

Democrats won control of both the House and Senate. And in Texas, where both Tesla and SpaceX are headquartered, Democrats Sen.-elect James Talarico and Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa beat longtime Musk allies, state Attorney General Ken Paxton and Gov. Greg Abbott.

Deutsche Bank analysts wrote in a note out on Wednesday, “While policy is naturally hard to predict, we could envision SpaceX facing some incremental headwinds in this type of backdrop.”

Gov.-elect Hinojosa “made data centers a major campaign issue,” the analysts noted, calling for “a moratorium on new approvals until the legislature passes stronger protections on water use, electricity costs, local control, and incentives,” and criticizing tax breaks for large facilities.

Tesla and SpaceX are both building out AI infrastructure in Texas, and are planning to build Terafab, a massive facility, which will include a data center and sprawling semiconductor factory, in Grimes County, Texas.

SpaceX also plans to build out a “supercomputer” at its Starbase, Texas, launch facility and company town, according to company job listings.

Deutsche Bank analysts also wrote that SpaceX’s Texas compute capacity could now be at risk of delays. Capital expenditures by the company may need to increase to meet the requirements of tighter, anticipated regulations around data center buildout, the analysts wrote.

Musk and SpaceX have been instructed to preserve records concerning restrictions imposed on a military version of the Starlink satellite internet service in Ukraine, CNN first reported, citing an aide to a Democratic senator. The restrictions hampered the country’s ability to defend against attacks by Russia.

Additionally, regulatory scrutiny could block chances for Musk to merge SpaceX and Tesla, an idea he has promoted, while acknowledging shareholders’ approval would be required first.

SpaceX and Tesla had lost about $456 billion in market cap by the close of business on Thursday.

--CNBC’s Nick Wells contributed reporting.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/05/blue-ori.title: Blue Origin pushes launch to January 2027 as it races to rebuild damaged launchpad
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/05/blue-ori.author: Annie Palmer
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/05/blue-ori.text:
Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin has delayed its New Glenn return to flight to January 2027, after previously targeting a launch by the end of this year.

Blue Origin CEO Dave Limp said the company has moved swiftly to repair a launchpad that was damaged by the New Glenn explosion in May, but he noted that the work hasn’t been easy.

“This small adjustment doesn’t diminish what we’ve accomplished or the importance of the work still ahead,” Limp said.

Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin has delayed a return to flight for its flagship New Glenn rocket to January 2027, later than its earlier target of the end of this year, as it rushes to recover from a major explosion in May.

Blue Origin CEO Dave Limp told employees in a memo Wednesday that the company’s launch timing slipped as a result of delays with reconstructing its Cape Canaveral launchpad, including due to bad weather over the summer.

“This small adjustment doesn’t diminish what we’ve accomplished or the importance of the work still ahead,” Limp wrote in the memo, which was viewed by CNBC. “Returning New Glenn to flight remains our top priority — it’s worth it.”

The Financial Times earlier reported the memo. The January 2027 time frame is about 10 days later than Blue Origin’s earlier launch target, a person familiar with the matter told CNBC. The person asked not to be named because the matter is internal.

The New Glenn explosion in May, which occurred during a hot-fire test, badly damaged Blue Origin’s Florida launchpad. The company was slated to deploy 48 satellites for Amazon
’s Leo internet-from-space service just a few days later.

Limp told CNBC’s Morgan Brennan that the first analysis he had after the explosion was that the company couldn’t fly again until mid 2028.

“And we just didn’t accept that,” he said. “We just said we’re going to get back to flight this year.”

Since then, the company has moved swiftly to repair the launch facility and reworked its pad configuration. Bezos told Fox News last month that the company was still expecting New Glenn to fly again in December.

Limp said Blue Origin has made great progress on the recovery, but he noted that “rebuilding at this pace hasn’t been easy.”

“Your collective work on our return to flight has been nothing short of remarkable,” Limp wrote. “In just six months, Team Blue has accomplished what many thought would take years.”

The mishap was inconveniently timed, as Blue Origin has been working to ramp up its launch cadence in an effort to compete with its chief rival, Elon Musk’s SpaceX
, for commercial and government customers.

The New Glenn delays have hampered Amazon’s Leo constellation buildout, for which it relies on Blue Origin for a portion of its launches. Amazon has turned to other providers, including United Launch Alliance and Arianespace, in the interim, especially as SpaceX has phased out Falcon 9 launches to prioritize testing its enormous Starship rocket.

NASA has also tapped Blue Origin for several contracts in the agency’s Artemis return-to-the-moon program, including a lunar lander.

The company announced new investments in its Florida launch facilities last month with the goal of supporting multiple flights per week by the end of the decade.

Limp told CNBC on Thursday that Blue Origin has its first customer for a lunar mission, which will be flying in 2028.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/05/qualcomm.title: AI meltdown: Nvidia and Qualcomm drop more than 9%, pushing Nasdaq to worst day since April 2025
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/05/qualcomm.author: Kif Leswing,Caleigh Keating
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/05/qualcomm.text:
Companies tied to the AI buildout are all selling off as concerns mount about a slowdown following the midterm elections.

The Nasdaq plunged 5.5% on Thursday, its worst day since April 2025.

Chipmakers like AMD, Micron and Applied Materials all suffered double-digit percentage drops.

Chipmakers plummeted on Thursday, with Nvidia
 pushing the Nasdaq to its worst day in 19 months, after this week’s midterm election results raised concerns on Wall Street that the artificial intelligence buildout is poised to slow down. Neoclouds like CoreWeave
 tumbled for a second straight day.

Qualcomm
 contributed to the selloff after issuing a disappointing earnings forecast for the current quarter. Qualcomm and Nvidia both dropped more than 9%, with the latter losing almost $450 billion in market cap. The Nasdaq slied 5.5%, its steepest slide since April 2025.

The environment has gone from bad to worse for companies intimately tied to AI infrastructure, as the combination of rising interest rates, ballooning capital needs and the Democratic sweep in Congress has led to increased fears that wide swaths of the market are going to be weighed down by too much debt and too little revenue.

“The technology is still going to continue on in terms of its development, but if there is a slowdown in the actual development and the buildings and the infrastructure and so forth, that’s what stocks are going to trade off,” said Peter Boockvar, chief investment officer at OnePoint BFG Wealth Partners, in an interview with CNBC’s “Squawk on the Street.”

Advanced Micro Devices
, Micron
 and Applied Materials
 all suffered double-digit percentage losses on Thursday. Elon Musk, who contributed hundreds of millions of dollars to try and get Republicans elected in Texas and elsewhere, saw shares of his public companies, SpaceX
 and Tesla
, each drop more than 9%.

In Tuesday’s election, the states with the most ambitious AI data center plans all turned blue. Democrats won key contests for governor and the Senate in Texas and Ohio, while also coming up victorious in the gubernatorial race in Georgia, where Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff also cruised to reelection.

There were 41 local ballot measures in 10 states up for a vote on Tuesday that would place restrictions on the construction of data centers in different ways, according to Ballotpedia. Voters sided against data centers in each measure except one in Harwood, North Dakota, according to an analysis by Ballotpedia and additional results gathered by CNBC on Wednesday.

On Wednesday night, at the Wall Street Journal Tech conference, Meta
 President Dina Powell McCormick told the audience that building data centers is “going to be harder” following the elections. She added that one of the victorious governors had said that, “As soon as we get past the inauguration, let’s meet because we don’t want to lose this investment in our town. We don’t want these jobs to go elsewhere,” according to the Journal.

Meta, like its hyperscaler peers — Alphabet
, Amazon
 and Microsoft
 — has laid out an ambitious path for infrastructure development, with spending plans that extend well past $100 billion a year. Meta went free cash flow negative in the latest quarter, joining Alphabet and Amazon, which turned negative in the prior period. The hyperscalers each dropped between 2% and 4% on Thursday.

Qualcomm on Wednesday became the latest chipmaker to report booming growth in its data center business, though it’s still a relatively small unit for the company. Qualcomm had $650 million in data center revenue during the quarter, mostly from customizing and connectivity work, CEO Cristiano Amon said.

“We don’t have a demand issue; it’s a supply issue,” Amon told CNBC in an interview. “If I had more supply, I would probably be doing better.”

The problem for Qualcomm and fellow chipmakers Intel
 and AMD is that the global memory shortage is jacking up prices, making it harder to get key supplies and leading to surging prices for consumer devices.

Intel last week reported a 78% jump in data center revenue, but the stock got crushed due to a weaker-than-expected forecast from the memory shortage. And AMD said this week that sales in its data center business more than doubled in the latest period.

Investors are looking past the numbers and questioning the sustainability of that growth, and whether buyers of the technology will be able to put it all to use.

“There’s going to be a knee-jerk reaction, and that could lead to some delays, and that’s going to be some concerns,″ Richard Clode, a portfolio manager at Janus Henderson, told “Squawk on the Street.” “We’re not going to solve for that in terms of knowing the answers to that anytime soon, unfortunately.”

— CNBC’s MacKenzie Sigalos contributed to this report.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/05/crypto-m.title: Democratic sweep puts crypto on defensive in Washington
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/05/crypto-m.author: Tanaya Macheel
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/05/crypto-m.text:
The new Congress is likely to focus more on scrutinizing President Trump’s personal crypto dealings over industry-friendly legislation like the Clarity Act.

Democrats have historically been less supportive of crypto than Republicans, though that divide has been narrowing as more Democrats embrace the industry and its potential.

The stakes extend to stablecoins, banking access, tokenization and other priorities that the crypto industry sees as important to ensuring U.S. dominance in the global market.

Democrats’ sweep of Congress likely resets the political calculus for crypto, ushering in a more adversarial approach in Washington and pushing industry-friendly legislation like the Clarity Act to the back burner.

With crypto critics like Sherrod Brown, D-Ohio, returning to the Senate and Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., retaining significant influence over financial policy, analysts say the new Congress is likely to focus on scrutinizing President Donald Trump’s personal crypto dealings over supportive industry legislation.

For years, crypto fought an uphill battle in Washington, asking for clear operating rules, but often landing on the receiving end of regulation by enforcement. That shifted after Trump’s 2024 election victory, giving the industry a reprieve and seat at the policy table.

“We see Sherrod Brown winning in Ohio as damaging the crypto industry’s political clout as the industry worked to defeat him,” Jaret Seiberg, TD Cowen’s Washington analyst, said in a note Wednesday. “We did not think Clarity could advance over the next two years. This makes us more confident in our prediction.”

The crypto industry spent more than $200 million to sway the midterms, hoping to get leaders elected that could push a comprehensive crypto market structure bill over the finish line after the Clarity Act stalled in the Senate.

Seiberg emphasized that Democrats “will investigate Trump’s crypto entanglements including World Liberty Financial” and said “the resulting political environment may make it impossible to advance a version of Clarity that the crypto sector could back.”

Mike Townsend, Charles Schwab’s managing director of legislative and regulatory affairs, said he expects “Democrats to push next year for a version of the bill that is much tougher on cryptocurrency companies.”

The stakes extend beyond market structure legislation via Clarity. Stablecoin innovation; decentralized finance, or DeFi, development; banking access; tokenization; and sensible tax policy are priorities the industry sees as important to ensuring the U.S. remains competitive in the global crypto economy.

The industry will need continued bipartisan engagement to ensure these priorities aren’t sidelined by changing political dynamics. And Democrats have historically been less supportive of crypto than Republicans, though that divide has narrowed as more Democrats embrace the industry.

The implications of Democrats’ big win aren’t all bad. Crypto has reached a level of financial integration that could be difficult to reverse, with its future increasingly centered on establishing crypto as financial infrastructure. Even with the Clarity Act potentially stalled until 2028, key financial regulators can help advance the industry through rule-making.

Coinbase’s vice president of U.S. policy, Kara Calvert, points out that the election results point to a historic shift in the makeup of the incoming Congress, with a record number of pro-crypto voices expected to join its ranks.

“With last night’s results, the 120th Congress is on track to have more new pro-crypto members than we’ve ever seen in any freshman class,” she said. “Crypto is 100% bipartisan, and that’s why the future of finance does not rest on either political party or a single election night. Democrats and Republicans alike know that clear rules protect consumers and keep innovation in the U.S.”

As of Thursday morning, 19 candidates characterized as pro crypto by the advocacy nonprofit Stand With Crypto have been elected to the Senate versus eight Senate candidates it characterizes as anti crypto. In the House, 228 pro-crypto candidates have been elected versus 106 the group deems anti crypto.

Several races have not been called, but Fairshake — the super PAC launched in 2023 to support pro-crypto candidates regardless of party — has so far won 29 of the 34 races it spent on, per Reuters, including three of the six House candidates it prioritized by spending a baseline of $1 million on their campaigns.

Dante Disparte, chief strategy officer and head of global policy and operations at Circle, emphasized Circle’s bipartisan approach and readiness for new Senate and House leadership, but said it “may take longer to get Clarity tabled again.”

That bipartisan support may offer a blueprint for what comes next, but even if crypto legislation stalls, progress can continue, said Joseph Chalom, CEO of ether treasury company Sharplink.

“We expect the Clarity Act to remain on hold through 2028. Even so, there is a clear path forward for stablecoins … and for the tokenization of public equities under the SEC’s five-year innovation exemption,” he said. “Technological progress is rarely rolled back. Once the benefits of faster settlement, lower costs and markets that never close become clear to investors and institutions, this shift will be very difficult to reverse, regardless of who wins the White House in 2028.”

Near-term, investors should expect more volatility as the market tries to figure out how crypto regulation may shift under a Democratic Congress.

The impact of the blue wave “should vary considerably across assets,” said James Butterfill, head of research at CoinShares. “We would expect U.S. crypto equities to be more sensitive than bitcoin, particularly businesses reliant on new regulatory permissions. Established, compliant operators could even benefit from greater scrutiny of competitors. So miners who already have data centers set up are likely to remain in high demand by AI hyperscalers.”

— CNBC’s Talia Kaplan contributed reporting.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/05/markets-.title: Markets cool after the monster midterm rally with Musk's stocks under pressure
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/05/markets-.author: Leonie Kidd
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/05/markets-.text:
This is CNBC’s Morning Squawk newsletter. Subscribe here to receive future editions in your inbox.

Hello, this is Leonie Kidd with today’s edition of Morning Squawk.

Cooler heads are prevailing after the monster rally that drove the best day for the Dow in over a year and a half.

Investors are now assessing the impact of a new Democratic controlled Congress and how that changes the market landscape.

Futures are mixed across Wall Street after the Dow closed its best day since April 2025, soaring over 1,500 points on the Democrats’ decisive midterm victory.

A huge boost for stocks came from the plunging oil price. Brent and WTI have settled lower after falling over 8% in Wednesday’s session. That came as the Trump administration admitted the role the Iran war had played in the poor Republican results.

It has been a mixed handover from Asia, where Japan’s Nikkei
 and South Korea’s Kospi
 fell sharply amid a deepening tech rout, despite strength across the wider market. European stock markets are broadly higher.

President Donald Trump told CNBC’s Eamon Javers in a brief call late Wednesday that he can work with Democratic majorities in the next Congress on “many more things than people understand.”

The pressure is still on Elon Musk’s companies.

Tesla
 and SpaceX
 are down once again in premarket trading, after falling over 3% during yesterday’s session.

One of the biggest early decliners is Qualcomm
. Shares are down over 9% in premarket trading after fourth-quarter smartphone chip sales missed estimates.

CNBC’s Morning Squawk recaps the biggest stories investors should know before the stock market opens, every weekday morning.

Subscribe here to get access today.

Cryptocurrencies are cautiously higher overnight as investors assess how much the new Democratic composition for Congress will impact Washington’s view.

Bitcoin
 is hovering around the $80,000 mark, lifting the broader crypto space.

Analysis: The Democrats have one chance to extract concessions from Trump

The electoral sweep by Democrats on Tuesday night injects a new, unstable dynamic into the single biggest political risk to financial markets in the coming year: the debt limit. Unless a defeated Republican Party makes a swift and unlikely show of unity to take the issue off the table in its last few weeks in power, the protracted fight that will unfold is set to be nastier than ever, adding volatility to an already shaky bond market.

— CNBC’s Sean Conlon, Spencer Kimball, Pippa Stevens, Luke Fountain, Matt Peterson and Mike Winters contributed to this report.

Jack Sommers edited this edition.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/05/moonshot.title: Chinese AI lab Moonshot turned to Europe for Nvidia Blackwell access amid U.S. China curbs, sources tell CNBC
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/05/moonshot.author: Kai Nicol-Schwarz
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/05/moonshot.text:
Chinese AI lab Moonshot has looked to gain access to advanced Nvidia chips hosted at facilities in Europe, sources told CNBC.

Chinese AI companies’ use of Nvidia chips has become a key geopolitical flashpoint between the U.S. and China.

U.S. export controls restrict the shipment of Nvidia’s most advanced chips to China, but remote access via overseas data centers offers a loophole.

Moonshot AI, a Chinese artificial intelligence lab that the White House accused of accessing Nvidia
 advanced chips remotely in East Asia, has sought access to the chips through data centers in Europe, sources have told CNBC.

Deals have been discussed this year for Moonshot to rent capacity from neoclouds hosting Nvidia graphics processing units, or GPUs, at facilities in Europe, four people familiar with the matter said. They asked not to be named because they were discussing private information.

Nvidia’s effective monopoly over the most powerful chips has made U.S. export controls a key tool in Washington’s effort to preserve its advantage over China in the AI race. American AI labs such as OpenAI and Anthropic are locked in a training and pricing battle with Chinese developers, including Moonshot AI, which makes the Kimi family of models.

Moonshot was looking to lease capacity powered by Nvidia’s Blackwell systems, advanced chips currently subject to those export controls which effectively ban their import into China, three of the sources told CNBC.

In July, the White House said the Chinese AI lab had accessed Nvidia’s Blackwell chips via a facility in Thailand.

U.S. export controls restrict the shipment of Nvidia’s most advanced chips to China, but remote access via overseas data centers offers a loophole. Current law does not give regulators broad authority to control companies’ access to those chips through cloud services hosted overseas.

Moonshot, Nvidia, the White House, the U.S. Department of Commerce, China’s embassy in the U.K. and its Ministry of Foreign Affairs did not respond to a request for comment.

Chinese developers have made notable capability gains in the past six months and greater access to Nvidia chips could put even more pressure on their American rivals.

To lease Nvidia computing power in Europe, a Chinese AI company would typically rent capacity from a non-Chinese neocloud or data center operator that can purchase advanced chips.

Moonshot was interested in leasing capacity on clusters for inference, which refers to serving models to end users, in Europe, two of the sources said. One of the sources said they were also aware of interest in clusters for training.

Talks for arrangements that would see Moonshot rent access to clusters of 8,000 or more Blackwell GPUs hosted in the region have taken place, one source said. They described the Chinese AI lab as “very aggressive” in its pursuit of more computing power.

One of the sources told CNBC that talks on securing Moonshot compute in Europe had taken place since the White House said it had done so via Thailand. Moonshot did not comment at the time.

Founded in 2023, Beijing-based Moonshot AI is one of China’s leading model builders. It released a new model in July that Moonshot said closed the gap with leading systems built by Anthropic and OpenAI.

The model saw significant uptake as a cheaper alternative to U.S. offerings. Chinese AI models have surged in global adoption in 2026, amid capability gains and lower costs than U.S. rivals.

Around the time Kimi K3 was released, Moonshot said demand had stretched its capacity, and it temporarily paused new subscriptions to prioritize compute for current members. “We’re adding capacity as fast as we can and will reopen new subscription spots in batches,” the company said in a LinkedIn post.

Leasing AI compute is a booming industry, with customers, or offtakers, typically taking capacity for a fee and paying an upfront cost to secure the deal, which is a percentage of the lifetime contract value.

One source said it had been proposed that Moonshot pay 30% to 50% more upfront than a non-Chinese offtaker would.

Arrangements with Chinese customers can be more lucrative upfront, as neoclouds and financing firms look to hedge against a potential future ban of remote access agreements.

In Washington, lawmakers have proposed the Remote Access Security Act (RASA) to expand U.S. export controls to include the cloud-based access of critical hardware and software. It passed the House of Representatives in January but has not passed the Senate.

The Financial Times reported on Tuesday that the chip giant told cloud providers selling access to their chips that they must sell at least 51% of services to non-Chinese customers.

Asked about the reports earlier this week, an Nvidia spokesperson said: “America cannot win the AI race unless America’s AI infrastructure wins worldwide — if the world’s clouds rely on foreign-made chips, the model and application layers will be foreign-built as well.”

Nvidia said in August that Washington had licensed some sales of its H200 AI chips, an older generation, but that “such sales were restricted” by the Chinese government, which has sought to boost domestic chipmakers by limiting access to Nvidia chips.
