https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/05/meta-spa.title: Voters rejected AI data centers over resource concerns. Here's why measuring water usage is hard
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/05/meta-spa.author: Katie Tarasov
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/05/meta-spa.text:
Huge 1GW data centers from OpenAI, Meta, SpaceX, Amazon, Google and others were a key issue in the midterms, largely due to concerns over power and water use.

Liquid cooling keeps water use low inside many modern AI data centers, but external cooling still requires large power or water draw in hot climates.

CNBC visited data centers and spoke to researchers to find out the truth about how data centers use water.

Voters made it clear this week that they want to see limits put on data centers for artificial intelligence, passing 40 of 41 proposed ballot measures that would place restrictions on some of the more than 2,000 new facilities planned for communities around the nation.

Water and power top the list of ratepayers’ concerns. But calculating how much each data center draws from local resources is an elusive task, with operators typically reporting usage figures companywide instead of site by site.

Giant 1-gigawatt AI data centers from the likes of Meta
, Google
, Amazon
 and SpaceX
 can consume up to 10 million gallons of water per day, according to Shaolei Ren, a data center researcher and professor at University of California, Riverside.

The exact number varies greatly depending on what type of hardware is inside a data center, where it’s built, and what method is used to cool the servers and the building as a whole.

The complex ways data centers use water have left room for misinformation from both the builders and those fighting against them. CNBC talked to experts to get a clearer picture.

Data centers need serious internal cooling methods to keep chips and servers from overheating.

Legacy data centers, filled with lower-power servers used for things like networking or storage, are often air-cooled. Large fans move hot air away from the servers and outside the building.

But modern AI data centers are filled with high-power, denser graphics processing units, or GPUs, which Ren said can run so hot that the servers can “boil your eggs.”

Water is about 3,000 times more efficient for cooling down these GPUs, according to Equinix sustainability head Christopher Wellise.

GPUs “run at such a high wattage, a high temperature, you would need nearly hurricane-force winds to actually cool them down if you were just using air,” Wellise told CNBC in an interview.

That’s why the latest rack-scale AI systems, Nvidia
’s Vera Rubin and Advanced Micro Devices
’ Helios, rely on liquid cooling. Most large AI data centers use a closed-loop liquid cooling system that uses very little water on a daily basis.

At an Equinix
 data center in San Jose, California, CNBC got an up-close look at the closed-loop liquid cooling system used to keep temperatures down in a row of eight Nvidia Grace Blackwell racks owned by AI marketing startup Alembic.

Equinix builds colocation data centers, where companies like Alembic rent space to run their own server racks, while Equinix supplies the power, network connections, interconnectivity and cooling.

Like many data center operators, Equinix doesn’t disclose water consumption at individual sites. In 2025, Equinix operations as a whole consumed 1.2 billion gallons of water, up 10% from a year prior.

Despite closed-loop internal cooling like what Equinix uses in San Jose, total water consumption is far more dependent on an additional cooling process that happens outside the data center.

“How do we reject the heat from the closed loop to the ambient environment?” Ren said. “That’s where the water usage comes in.”

In Lebanon, Indiana, for example, Meta is building a 1GW data center that it says uses a “closed-loop, liquid-cooled system that recirculates the same water and will use zero water for a majority of the year.”

Water allocation for the site, however, could ramp up to 8 million gallons per day by 2031, according to the company’s law firm. Meta says that figure represents peak usage on the hottest days. “We anticipate rarely reaching this maximum usage level, currently projected as only a few days per year,” Meta told CNBC in a statement.

That’s because the hottest days of the year will require more water for that external cooling process, removing the heat from that separate internal closed-loop system.

There are two primary methods for this external cooling process at a data center: dry cooling and evaporative cooling. While dry cooling uses far less water, it can require far more power, especially in hotter climates where many of these AI data centers are being built.

“There’s no sort of silver bullet,” Wellise said. “At some point you need to eject that heat out to the atmosphere. And that’s where those trade-offs occur.”

Dry cooling relies on fans to blow air across heat exchangers, using the ambient air to cool it down. Those fans are less effective when the outside temperature is high, so data centers turn on refrigeration units to cool down the air first.

“That’s a very power-intensive process, and that’s exactly why we have power shortages in the summer,” Ren said. “Because everybody else turns on their AC.”

Evaporative cooling, meanwhile, uses very little power. The hot water circulates through cooling towers or over wet pads that are exposed to air, and the portion that evaporates carries heat away with it. Large amounts of water can be lost through that evaporation on the hottest days.

In between these two extremes, hybrid methods are common as companies try to find a balance.

Some data centers, like Equinix’s in San Jose, use dry cooling in the colder months and evaporative cooling when it’s hot outside. In Indiana, Meta relies on dry cooling and keeps power consumption down in hotter months by spraying a mist to cool the air instead of relying solely on refrigeration units.

Near some data center projects, Meta, Amazon, Microsoft and others are building water treatment plants to help treat and recycle the necessary water. Meta, for example, spent $100 million on a new water and wastewater system near its data center in Kuna, Idaho.

Outside Memphis, Tennessee, Elon Musk pledged $80 million to build a water recycling plant that’s meant to turn treated municipal wastewater into cooling water for SpaceX’s Colossus data centers. The first data center there, Colossus 1, came online rapidly in 2024, but construction on the water treatment plant was put on hold in April of this year.

Colossus 1 has a water allocation of up to 1.28 million gallons per day, although it hasn’t yet reached that threshold, according to the local utility, Memphis Light, Gas and Water.

Tech firms are also building their own power plants on some data center campuses in an effort to secure enough supply, but those also consume a large amount of water. Colossus gets energy from gas-powered turbines it installed on-site, which have been the subject of multiple lawsuits over alleged Clean Air Act violations and noise pollution.

Meanwhile, some chip companies are directly working on ways to bring the heat of a chip down so less cooling will be needed to begin with.

South Korean startup DeepX makes an AI processor it says runs up to 100°F cooler than competitors. Hyundai Motor
 will use the DeepX chip in robotics offerings.

SK Hynix
, the world’s leading maker of high-bandwidth memory, told CNBC in July that it’s working on a low-heat memory technology called iHBM that can reduce thermal resistance by 30%.

At Equinix, Wellise said each new site undergoes a water risk analysis to determine which external cooling method to deploy in areas with scarce water.

“Communities are beginning to ask the right questions. They’re concerned about water consumption,” Wellise said. “We take resource consumption, resource use very seriously.”

https://insideclimatenews.org/news/07112.title: Climate Change Is Bringing Dengue Fever to the High Himalayas
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/07112.author: Story by Avery Schuyler Nunn, photos by Yuri Segalerba
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/07112.text:
The warming of Nepal’s mountains is dramatically transforming some of the grandest landscapes on Earth, leading melting glaciers to collapse, thawing permafrost that can slide from steep peaks and crumbling ice dams to release vast lakes. But other impacts are barely the length of a fingernail.

As the alpine cold recedes, disease-bearing mosquitoes are taking its place. Over the past decade, researchers have documented Aedes aegypti—the primary mosquito species responsible for transmitting the dengue virus—at elevations up to 2,500 meters (8,200 feet). Its expansion into Nepal’s mid-hill and high-altitude regions is driving a major shift in the geographic footprint of insect-borne diseases in the Himalayas.

“In Nepal, Dengue used to be the problem of lower altitude regions, mainly the disease of Terai (the lowlands of Nepal and India),” says Sunita Baral, a research associate at Nepal Health Research Council. “When we were younger we used to hear and even experience the mosquito bite in Terai and we used to ignore going there during the monsoon and post-monsoon. But after a few years, a dengue outbreak occurred in hilly regions like Kathmandu and mosquitoes began to appear here.”

According to a literature review published in January in the journal Clinical Infection in Practice, dengue transmission in Nepal has escalated over the past two decades from localized outbreaks to major nationwide epidemics.

First reported in the country in 2004, the virus caused major public health crises in 2019, 2022 and 2023. Transmission is no longer restricted to the lowland Terai region along the border with India; sustained outbreaks now occur routinely in densely-populated areas at higher elevations. Recent health data reported by local Nepalese media shows the virus has reached 76 out of the country’s 77 districts, with roughly 9,000 recorded infections and at least six deaths in 2025 alone.

“Climate change has a huge impact on geographical distribution and establishment of these vectors in a new area,” explained Ishan Gautam, an associate professor at Tribhuvan University in Kathmandu. “Years ago they were only found in the tropical regions, but they have migrated thousands of meters up to Kathmandu Valley.”

The expansion is driven by a combination of changing climatic patterns, population mobility and unplanned urbanization. Higher average minimum temperatures allow Aedes mosquitoes to survive and reproduce at altitudes that previously acted as natural thermal barriers.

At the same time, rapid urban growth in cities like Kathmandu has created severe water infrastructure challenges. Chronic shortages lead residents to store water in open drums, buckets and construction cisterns, providing optimal breeding conditions for both Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus mosquitoes. Flash floods from unusually strong monsoons have overwhelmed municipal drainage systems and washed out water pipelines in cities like Kathmandu, leaving more standing water for breeding mosquitoes.

“They lay eggs in different types of building habitats, so as they disperse and continue to lay eggs in varying places, the population continues to increase,” Gautam continued. “Dengue vectors are rapidly increasing.”

Beyond climate conditions and urban density, specific biological characteristics of a given vector can accelerate the speed of disease transmission. According to Gautam, infected mosquitoes frequently bite seven to eight individuals before reaching repletion–the state of being fully engorged with a blood meal.

This high feeding frequency means a single infected vector can transmit the virus to multiple hosts within a short time frame, creating a transmission chain driven by a mix of biological compulsion and favorable climate conditions.

Despite these growing risks, public health response efforts are constrained by a widespread lack of community preparedness.

“Many of the communities who are at risk are not aware of dengue vectors and their likelihood of contracting dengue disease,” Gautam noted. “They don’t know about all of the potential breeding sites, so they aren’t able to eliminate them.”

The presence of multiple distinct strains of the virus circulating in Nepal further heightens the risk to public health. A secondary infection with a different strain significantly increases the likelihood of severe dengue, which can cause plasma leakage, severe bleeding and organ impairment.

Additionally, both Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus serve as vectors for other insect-borne diseases. Chikungunya is already documented in Nepal, and health officials warn that established vector populations create a serious risk for local Zika virus transmission.

“Due to the news of dengue outbreaks, communities are becoming more aware of dengue, but still they do not recognize mosquito breeding sites around their houses,” said Baral. “In newly affected mountain communities, dengue is still relatively unfamiliar, which can delay recognition and response.”

Because dengue-carrying mosquitoes bite during early morning and late afternoon hours, when most residents in the affected communities are awake and active, relying on bed nets while sleeping provides a false sense of security.

The implications extend beyond the emergence of individual diseases. Together, the presence of two competent vector species and multiple dengue serotypes suggests that Nepal’s mountain regions are becoming increasingly suitable for forms of transmission once associated primarily with warmer lowlands.

The warming trends unfolding in the Himalayas mirror shifts happening across tropical highlands globally, from the Colombian Andes to communities in Costa Rica’s central valley. Historically, these high-altitude regions were shielded from vector-borne illness because lower temperatures slowed mosquito development and virus transmission.

Erin Mordecai, an infectious disease ecologist at Stanford University, highlights that rising temperatures have already increased global dengue burdens by roughly 18 percent over historical baselines, hitting cooler highland regions hardest.

“This is projected to get much worse if we continue emitting huge amounts of carbon, but averting carbon emissions can limit the expansion of this devastating disease,” she said. “Nepal is a particularly troubling case because it is a carbon-negative country—it sequesters more carbon than it emits—and yet it is experiencing some of the most dramatic early effects of climate change, including expanded mosquito-borne disease burden.”

Response efforts in Nepal continue to face logistical and institutional hurdles. Disease surveillance systems in Nepal suffer from underfunding and underreporting, meaning local outbreaks are often detected late. Because a large proportion of people infected with dengue show only mild symptoms or remain asymptomatic, passive hospital-based surveillance captures only a fraction of total community transmission.

Without a widely available dengue vaccine in Nepal, control strategies rely heavily on Integrated Vector Management (IVM). Experts emphasize that mitigating future epidemics will require systematic community campaigns to eliminate standing water, structural improvements to municipal water infrastructure to reduce storage dependency and aggressive public education initiatives.

“My biggest fear is that climate change, rapid urbanization and increasing human movement will continue to create favorable conditions for Aedes mosquitoes to establish in areas that were previously unsuitable,” said Baral. “This means more communities that have little previous experience with dengue could become vulnerable. I am also concerned that outbreaks may become more frequent and less predictable.”

In some remote Himalayan communities, the first source of care may not be a hospital but from an amchi—a traditional healer using Sowa Rigpa, a centuries-old Tibetan medical practice. Amchi diagnose illness with methods such as pulse reading, examination of the tongue and urine and detailed conversation with the patient, but may not recognize the symptoms of dengue and other mosquito-borne infections that are new to the region.

Amchi Khedup Loden Gurung packs Sowa Rigpa medicines and checks a patient’s pulse in a clinic in Jomsom, Mustang. Amchi are traditional healers trained in Sowa Rigpa. Diagnosis is based on pulse reading (nad-par), visual examination of urine and tongue, and dialogue with the patient.

Although Amchi remain deeply trusted providers, their position outside formal disease-surveillance systems can make it harder for health authorities to recognize an emerging outbreak unless traditional practitioners and local health posts are closely connected.

Even if they are, as Aedes mosquitoes expand into previously unsuitable terrain, Baral worries the burden on the country’s healthcare capacity will escalate rapidly.

“We need to prepare now,” she warned, “rather than responding only after major outbreaks occur.”

Still, she remains hopeful that with targeted investments in research and community engagement, Nepal’s public health network can curb the threat before it spreads further.

“With sustained investment in surveillance, research, and community engagement, we have an opportunity to reduce the impact of dengue before it becomes even more widespread.”

https://insideclimatenews.org/news/07112.title: Democrats Vow to Reset “Values and Agenda” for House Natural Resources Committee
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/07112.author: Interview by Steve Curwood and Jenni Doering, Living on Earth
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/07112.text:
From our collaborating partner “Living on Earth,” public radio’s environmental news magazine, an interview by host Steve Curwood and Jenni Doering with U.S. Rep. Jared Huffman.

Congressional committees originate legislation and oversight investigations, and under the seniority system—as Democrats take control and their senior members presumably become chairs—many House committees have broad subpoena powers.

U.S. Rep. Jared Huffman has represented northern California’s second district since 2013 and is an environmental lawyer in line to chair the House Committee on Natural Resources. This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

STEVE CURWOOD: Representative Huffman, what can we expect to be a top priority from you and your committee when it comes to energy?

JARED HUFFMAN: On all of the subjects before our committee within our jurisdiction, it’s going to be a two-part agenda. We’re going to have to do oversight and investigations to make up for the fact that we haven’t really had a Congress for the last two years. There haven’t been checks and balances. So we will be digging into and investigating so many different things on energy and other subjects that we oversee.

But then we’ve got to move an affirmative policy agenda as well. And we can’t, in my opinion, constrain ourselves to just what Donald Trump might sign into law. I think we’ve got to advance an agenda that reflects our values and our priorities, even if we draw some vetoes from this president. There’s enormous value in drawing that contrast.

JENNI DOERING: Just how important do you think energy and access to affordable energy was in these midterm elections?

HUFFMAN: It was part of the affordability backlash that I think helped shape this blue wave, for sure. The fact that electricity bills, utility bills have been skyrocketing as Donald Trump pays offshore wind developers to walk away from projects that could bring cheap, reliable, clean energy onto the grid, as he does everything he can to strangle clean energy—the cheapest, fastest form of energy that can help lower utility bills.

I think people connected those dots, and they also put together the connection with the corruption, with just the fact that the fossil fuel industry was so programmed with Donald Trump on all of this and was making money hand over fist, war profiteering. Donald Trump boasted, in his words, “We are making a killing on the war in Iran” while people were struggling to afford fuel. All of that helped shape the election in a big way.

CURWOOD: I think it’s fair to say that in many campaigns we didn’t hear the words “climate change” or “climate emergency,” and yet, to what extent do you think the concern about the climate is part of this blue wave?

HUFFMAN: Climate is part of it, even if it wasn’t articulated with that specific phrase. When you look at the inability to get [home] insurance or the inability to afford insurance. When you look at skyrocketing food costs. When you look at the fact that American consumers found themselves stuck on the fossil fuel roller coaster once again because Donald Trump had burned the bridge to clean electric vehicles—or at least tried to do so—while the rest of the world is moving forward in a way that will liberate them from that fossil fuel roller coaster. These were significant elements, and climate was on the agenda, whether folks realized it or talked about it as such or not.

DOERING: How is the climate crisis affecting your district and your constituents? What are you hearing from them?

HUFFMAN: I’m hearing them kind of stunned that in the middle of sunny days, at high tide, we have coastal areas underwater because of what’s called a Kelvin wave—this pulse of warm water that’s moving up the West Coast due to El Niño, which is more intense because of human-caused climate change. The reality really comes home when you’re in the middle of a sunny day, there’s been no storm and you have roads and bike paths and trails and coastal buildings underwater.

CURWOOD: You’ll become chair, in a few weeks, of the House Energy and Natural Resources Committee. Looking at your newfound power, what’s at the very top of your list to get done while you have this opportunity to influence things?

HUFFMAN: We need to do a permitting reform bill on our terms. That’s going to be high on my priority list, if I’m allowed to do it. When we get back to Washington, everybody’s going to be consumed with this fight over the Senate permitting reform deal, a deal that was cut behind closed doors by four people—two of whom are coal-state Republicans—a deal that was written largely by the oil and gas industry. I think waking up after that profoundly huge blue-wave statement by the American people, people—I hope—are going to question why we would constrain our permitting reform ambition to this, which was negotiated with zero leverage for Democrats.

Why wouldn’t we give Democrats a chance to use this newfound power to cut a better deal that doesn’t throw the Endangered Species Act and Native American tribes and the Clean Water Act and all of these other core values under the bus, and a deal that ends the war on clean energy, so that we can give the next president a chance to lead on climate action instead of tying his hands, which is one of the things that this bill would do.

CURWOOD: To what extent is that going to move ahead, though, in a lame duck session?

HUFFMAN: They’re going to try to jam it [through]. That’s very clear. This deal is premised on a very rapid, no-hearings push through the Senate and the House. A lot of the votes have already been lined up, and it is just a good old-fashioned jam job that is going to hit us as soon as we get back to town next week.

DOERING: Part of this permitting bill fight that you’re referring to is public lands. When it comes to the lands that all Americans hold as a public trust, what are your priorities with the Natural Resources Committee?

HUFFMAN: Our public lands are an intergenerational trust. We’ve always understood them to be something that weren’t just there for us to extract and monetize and exploit to the maximum degree for the here and now. It was something that needed to be stewarded and passed on to people we’ll never know in better shape than we found them.

That entire trust has been broken by this administration. We have a Secretary of Interior who talks about our public lands like they’re assets on a corporate balance sheet, like they can just be leveraged and given away and liquidated and monetized like you would a corporation in some sort of a private equity deal. That all has to change, and I think our opportunity in the next Congress will be to reset that trust.

DOERING: One of the things that the Trump administration has proposed is this land swap with a private developer for parts of Yosemite National Park. What are some of the concerns that you have on this front as a congressman from California?

HUFFMAN: This is the kind of thing you just don’t do. Yosemite is one of our most sacred places, not the only one, but certainly a beloved part of our public land portfolio. And to simply give part of it away in order

to facilitate the interest of a private developer—not to enhance the park, not to improve public access or anything else, but to just cut a deal—that’s sort of the poster child of what’s wrong with this administration. Nothing is sacred with these folks. Nothing about tribal lands, national monuments, our pristine oceans, any of these public trust resources that we are supposed to steward for future generations. They just see it all as a grift, as a chance to make some money and to dole out favors to their friends. This is so outrageous, and the backlash has been so loud, including from some Republicans, that I think we should be able to stop it. But it tells us a lot just the fact that they were even considering it.

CURWOOD: You’ll have subpoena power come sometime in January. What rocks do you want to turn over for the public to understand when it comes to natural resources for the United States?

HUFFMAN: Lots of rocks. We want to dig into these mineral deals where the administration has taken equity stakes in companies where members of Trump’s inner circle just happen to have financial interests. We want to look at ethical lapses by senior members of this administration. We want to look into the very shady operations of the Freedom 250 entity and the way they hijacked America’s 250th celebration, and the way they have reprogrammed funds that were supposed to go to national parks and other public lands into these other activities, and in some cases into Donald Trump’s vanity projects, which are also on our agenda for oversight and investigation.

CURWOOD: You’re not referring to the arch, are you?

HUFFMAN: One of several vanity projects, amazingly. That joy ride is going to stop.

CURWOOD: What power do you have in this lame duck situation? They have the White House. They have both parts of Congress, and if they put things on a fast track, they can jam things through. Yes or no?

HUFFMAN: Well, you’re right. A lame duck is very fluid, and it is kind of hard to predict what happens and why. I think the fact that there was such an overwhelming mandate from voters for the Democrats makes it harder for them to really roll the Democrats in the lame duck. Democrats, I hope at least, are a little fortified and less willing to let themselves just be rolled, but we’ll see. There will be two months of chaos, and it’s going to be a wild ride until we seat the next Congress. So stay tuned. A lot of weird stuff can happen in a lame duck.

DOERING: Earlier this year, you introduced, along with Chairman [Arkansas U.S. Rep. Bruce] Westerman, this bipartisan Great American Outdoors Act 250. Tell us about why the bipartisan aspect is important, and how that might help this move forward. And what’s the current status?

HUFFMAN: That’s a good example of something good that could happen in the lame duck, because there’s overwhelming bipartisan support for the Great American Outdoors Act.

This is a fund to tackle the deferred maintenance backlog on our public lands, and especially at our national parks. And it’s something that some members of the Republican conference look at as an expenditure, something that we have to go find an offset for. They think that whatever it’s going to cost, you will have to make a parallel cut in some social program or something. That’s why the bill hasn’t advanced at this point.

But in a lame duck, we might be able to get past that objection. I don’t think you have to offset or find cuts to pay for this because this is money we already owe. I regard this as a debt that we have incurred. That’s what deferred maintenance is. It’s stuff you were supposed to have done all along, but you failed to do, and we are now catching up. So the idea that we would need to do cuts for what we were supposed to have been doing all along, I think, is just fundamentally flawed, and that’s the argument that we’ll make, if we can find enough Republicans to get on board. Mr. Westerman and I are shoulder to shoulder in supporting this bill. The president has said he would sign it, so I think there’s a chance.

CURWOOD: You were an environmental lawyer before you became a member of Congress. After decades in this space, how are you feeling today about the future of environmental protection and stewardship and the climate in the United States?

HUFFMAN: We’ve taken some hits, and I can’t sugarcoat the amount of damage that’s been incurred for the past two years. We have gone from leaning into climate action and environmental protection and environmental justice to taking several steps backward, and actually a scorched-earth agenda that has attempted to not only roll back that progress but to kind of burn the bridge and make it harder to rebuild that progress. That’s what we have to start tackling.

I don’t want to overpromise, but what I can say for sure is that the values and the agenda are going to get reset, and we’re going to work like heck to begin repairing all of this damage and get us back in a forward posture on public lands protection, on clean water, clean air, on environmental justice, and on climate action.

https://insideclimatenews.org/news/07112.author: By Bob Berwyn
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/07112.text:
As global climate negotiators and government officials convene for the annual United Nations climate summit, the scientific organization they rely on to guide their decisions is mired in gridlock and short on funds.

Since 1990, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change has produced influential global reports in cycles. Its 2013 and 2014 reports provided the scientific foundation for the 2015 Paris climate agreement, which continues to shape international climate policy. But the IPCC suspended its mid-October meeting without approving a budget for next year or agreeing on a timetable for publishing upcoming reports.

The political disputes that derailed the meeting rattled many of the scientists who devote hundreds of hours, often without pay, to assess the latest climate research across dozens of disciplines, from ice sheets and glaciers to forests and agriculture. Their work not only tracks the science of a changing climate, it also identifies ways to cut greenhouse gas emissions and helps communities adapt to increasingly severe climate impacts.

More than 100 IPCC scientists expressed their concern about the future of the panel in an Oct. 19 open letter, asking political leaders to provide it with adequate resources. The scientists reaffirmed their commitment to the work, but warned that, as climate impacts intensify, governments must ensure the panel can produce timely assessments of climate risks and potential solutions when they are needed. They also called for a process that gives all countries an equitable voice, rather than allowing wealthy, industrialized nations to dominate.

The IPCC will resume its session online in December, after the annual COP, the Conference of Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change. This year’s event, COP31, begins next week in Antalya, Turkey. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change continually informs the negotiations with science updates, but political tensions have affected its budget and timelines for upcoming reports.

Governments decide voluntarily each year how much to contribute to the panel’s annual budget of $9.7 million, about the cost of producing a major movie. That pays to keep the meetings running, covering travel, scientific support and workshops, especially for developing countries.

Next year’s budget remains uncertain, but a concerted push by nations to increase funding at the upcoming climate summit in Turkey could be effective, history shows. In 1999, at COP5, an urgent funding appeal in the meeting’s final decision document helped the IPCC maintain momentum for its third and fourth cycles of updated climate reports.

Repeated reminders from the annual climate COPs helped sustain funding through the early 2010s, leading up to the landmark Fifth Assessment Report that is the scientific basis of the 2015 Paris Agreement, which aims to limit human-caused warming as close to 2.7 degrees Fahrenheit (1.5C) as possible.

The United States has, at times, contributed as much as one-third of the IPCC’s annual budget. The Trump administration’s withdrawal of funding over the last two years, along with the U.S. government’s withdrawal from the panel, likely contributed to stalling the IPCC process, said Bob Kopp, a climate scientist and professor at Rutgers University, who signed the Oct. 19 letter and has worked on several of the panel’s reports.

Despite the loss of federal support, the United States still has a significant scientific presence in the current assessment cycle, Kopp said. The U.S. Academic Alliance for the IPCC was formed in 2025 by the American Geophysical Union, bringing together colleges and universities to help ensure continued U.S. scientist participation without federal support. He said the U.S. has the largest percentage of contributing authors of any country, about 7.5 percent, and that the alliance nominated more authors for the current cycle than the U.S. government did for the previous one.

“I’m very pleased that civil society in the U.S. has managed to fill some of this gap,” he said. “But we can also see from what’s happening among the governments and the IPCC budget that there’s only so much civil society can do on its own.”

Key IPCC reports are scheduled to track whether countries are living up to what they promised in the Paris Agreement, said Carl Schleussner, a climate scientist with Climate Analytics and the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis. Without a timeline for those reports, scientists can’t plan their IPCC-related work schedule, he said.

The delay in the IPCC’s process reflects a range of complex factors, against a backdrop of deteriorating international cooperation. Among them are concerns raised by a group known as the Like-Minded Developing Countries, including India and China. They are questioning whether the panel’s scenarios fairly represent the range of possible climate pathways for all countries, according to reports by observers with the International Institute for Sustainable Development’s Earth Negotiations Bulletin.

Davide Faranda, another IPCC author who signed the letter, said he’s concerned that a breakdown of international collaboration could lead to climate information being weaponized.

If the IPCC fails to provide that timely, widely available knowledge, major powers like the United States or Russia could try to keep climate assessments private to gain strategic advantages through knowledge of climate impacts on agriculture, natural resources, national security and other sectors, he said.

“I think that everyone is aware that climate change now is hitting the entire world like a hammer … and the consequences are here,” said Faranda, who studies climate extremes at the French National Center for Scientific Research in Paris. “Having a report that is transparent and accepted worldwide is important.”

The delays in IPCC decision-making may also reflect the broader redistribution of power in a volatile world. He said the process “should respect that there are new equilibria” emerging.

“We cannot have the deliberations driven only again by European and British and American scientists,” he said. “We have to make it more inclusive. We have to respect the fact that there are countries that are developing fast, and they need to have a stronger voice also in the IPCC.”

The panel’s overall role may be shifting, added Mike Hulme, a professor of human geography at the University of Cambridge who has studied the IPCC.

In the late 1980s and early 1990s, the IPCC mission was clear, he said: detect if the climate is changing and whether humans are causing the warming. The panel answered those straightforward scientific questions by the mid-1990s. After that, things became more complicated.

The climate crisis, he said, raises deep and fundamental questions about the trajectory of human development on the planet. Today, the IPCC grapples with questions that have significant political implications, including how to address global warming through mitigation, adaptation, geoengineering and carbon removal.

The resulting political tension can slow the IPCC’s work, Hulme said. That tension, he added, is also reflected in questions about the coal-producing status of the current two COP31 host countries, Turkey and Australia, and of previous hosts with economies heavily dependent on fossil fuels.

“These political things are very much in the foreground right now,” Hulme said. “The idea that the IPCC can somehow run through that fire with some sort of fireproof clothing on is a non-starter.”

https://insideclimatenews.org/news/06112.author: By Nicholas Kusnetz, Lauren Dalban
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/06112.text:
Alan Armstrong of Oklahoma entered the U.S. Senate to fill a vacancy in March with a clear priority: pass permitting reform that he argued was necessary based on his experience leading a major natural gas pipeline company.

Now, as he prepares to leave office, that goal is within reach—with big potential benefits for the company and him personally.

The bipartisan permitting bill slated for a vote next week would overhaul regulations for building all kinds of projects. But it also includes provisions Armstrong promoted that could push through a disputed pipeline that the Williams Companies, his former employer, has tried to build through New York for more than a decade.

When state regulators denied a water quality permit for the Constitution pipeline in 2016, it was a rare rebuke for an industry unaccustomed to having government officials block its projects. Provisions in the new bill would limit New York’s authority to deny it again.

Williams is now asking federal regulators to revive their approval of the pipeline from more than a decade ago.

Armstrong continued to hold at least tens of millions of dollars in Williams stock as of Oct. 22, according to his most recent financial disclosures. He also hired three former Williams colleagues to his staff, one of whom maintained his role as senior vice president and general counsel at the company while temporarily serving as Armstrong’s chief of staff in the Senate.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act would greatly restrict states’ and tribes’ ability to deny or place conditions on water quality certifications. The bill would also make other changes to accelerate approval of Constitution and other pipelines, including restricting judicial review and scaling back certain environmental reviews.

Environmental lawyers say changes to what’s known as a Section 401 certification of the federal Clean Water Act appear tailored to help a small number of gas pipeline projects. One of the companies that would benefit most is Williams, where Armstrong served as chief executive and chairman for 15 years until his appointment in March by Oklahoma’s governor to fill a vacated U.S. Senate seat.

Williams has already received extraordinary support from the Trump administration.

President Donald Trump claimed he made a deal with New York Gov. Kathy Hochul to get the Constitution pipeline built, which she denies. Environmental Protection Agency Administrator Lee Zeldin has pledged support for the pipeline, and his agency is finalizing a rule change that would restrict states’ and tribes’ ability to condition permits in order to safeguard water quality, similar to the permitting bill.

In October, the U.S. Department of Energy said it would devote up to $42 million under the Defense Production Act to pay permitting costs for the project.

Armstrong’s office did not respond to questions for this article, though he has frequently criticized what he calls a broken regulatory system that drives up costs.

“When every pipeline, transmission line, power plant and industrial project is treated as something to stop rather than something to build responsibly, the costs do not disappear,” Armstrong said in a Senate speech in July. “They accumulate slowly, until families are paying more, reliability is deteriorating, and investment is moving elsewhere.”

Williams spokesperson Blake Jackson said the company supports the permitting bill “and all its provisions to provide a tech-neutral and level-playing field for all energy infrastructure.”

Some residents of upstate New York see things differently.

Anne Marie Garti, a lawyer who owns a home near the Constitution pipeline route, fought the project the first time around. From the start, “there was a huge amount of opposition,” Garti said, “and skepticism.”

The Constitution project would run 125 miles from the Pennsylvania shale gas fields across upstate New York, eventually connecting to other interstate pipelines. The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, also known as FERC, oversees interstate gas pipelines. But states retain authority under the Clean Water Act, which requires energy companies like Williams to apply for water quality certifications.

Garti called these permits the “weak link” in the regulatory process. Taking inspiration from an earlier permit denial in Connecticut, she and other residents focused their fight on the pipeline’s potential effects on 251 streams along its route. State regulators said 87 of those streams provided trout habitat.

Building the pipeline would require digging trenches across streams, diverting their flow and clearing trees and brush along their banks. The work would send sediment into clear waters, raise temperatures and temporarily damage habitat for trout and other species, according to the New York Department of Environmental Conservation’s 2016 denial.

State regulators rarely reject water quality permits, which are needed not only for pipelines but many federally regulated projects. In a recent survey of 24 states by the Association of Clean Water Administrators, no state reported a denial rate higher than 3.5 percent—most said they’d never denied a permit.

New York denied the certification for Constitution in 2016, saying the company had failed to address the project’s water quality impacts and had not provided sufficient proof that Williams would comply with state standards. The denial kicked off years of legal wrangling. In 2020, Williams said it would not pursue the pipeline and a federal appeals court ruling later vacated the federal permit.

Another permit denial followed in 2019 for a second Williams project: the Northeast Supply Enhancement (NESE) pipeline that would have run from New Jersey across the New York harbor. A few other pipeline proposals in the Northeast and mid-Atlantic faced similar fates, while in some cases regulators imposed conditions to protect waterways.

The bipartisan permitting bill would severely limit states’ ability to impose these restrictions in the future. Currently, states or tribes can consider the full scope of how pipeline construction and operation would affect waterways—for example, how clearing trees could increase erosion on banks, or how contaminated runoff could enter the water.

The permitting bill would limit states to considering only direct discharges when reviewing projects. It would also shift the burden of proof. Instead of requiring pipeline companies and other developers to show their projects would protect water quality, state regulators would have to prove they would cause harm.

Regulators would also face a higher standard of evidence to make their case, and they would have to prove any conditions they impose would be the least burdensome for the company to address water quality concerns.

“This bill moves in the wrong direction,” said Nancy Stoner, a senior attorney at the Environmental Law & Policy Center, a Chicago-based advocacy group. “The provisions in it on the clean water side are all negative.”

Williams revived its applications for the Constitution and NESE pipelines last year. In a reversal, New York and New Jersey approved NESE, but a federal court recently overturned New Jersey’s water quality permit after environmental groups sued. The ruling dealt another setback to Williams’ plans, at least for now.

In an earnings call this week, T. Lane Wilson, senior vice president and general counsel at Williams, said the company would still have its permit if the bill had been in effect when courts reviewed New Jersey’s approval.

Garti, the lawyer who fought the Constitution pipeline, said the water quality provisions in the permitting bill appear aimed at pushing through pipeline approvals for projects in the Northeast.

“They have learned all the arguments that we have made over these past, let’s say, 15 years, and they’re undermining each and every one of them,” Garti said.

Meanwhile, Williams is asking FERC to reinstate its original construction approval for the Constitution pipeline from more than a decade ago and to waive the requirement for a state permit. New York and environmental groups filed lawsuits over those moves, questioning whether FERC can revive an application that a federal court vacated in 2021.

Ken Lovett, a spokesperson for Hochul, said the state is suing to defend its permitting authority, arguing that Williams wants “to circumvent New York’s permitting process.”

Armstrong and Williams have pushed for years to make it harder for New York and other states to block pipeline projects.

Last year, when Armstrong was still at Williams and chair of the National Petroleum Council, which advises the Department of Energy, the group published a “permitting blueprint to build.” The recommendations included restricting the conditions under which states could review water quality permits.

In December, Williams was one of two pipeline companies that joined the American Petroleum Institute in a teleconference with officials at the White House and the EPA, which had proposed the rule to limit states’ Clean Water Act authority. Two months later, the company filed comments with the EPA expressing “strong support” for the proposal.

Williams gained a new connection to Congress in March, when Armstrong was appointed to finish the Senate term of Markwayne Mullin, who was tapped to lead the U.S. Department of Homeland Security.

From the start, Armstrong made permitting reform a top priority. With only months to advance his agenda—Oklahoma law barred Armstrong from seeking a full term—he quickly got to work. He delivered his first Senate floor speech on permitting reform, calling New York’s rejection of the Constitution pipeline a “political veto.”

Armstrong appointed former Williams colleagues to his staff, including two who had worked on government and regulatory affairs. For chief of staff, he tapped Wilson, the senior vice president and general counsel, who had recently celebrated Armstrong’s appointment to the Senate, saying the odds of passing permitting reform “just went way up.”

Despite his new role, Wilson did not leave his position at Williams, according to Jackson, the company spokesperson. Instead, he “altered his responsibilities, management structure and communications to address potential conflicts of interest, including an organizational separation from the Williams Government Affairs & Outreach team and preemptive and ongoing recusal from any meetings between the Williams Government Affairs & Outreach team and Sen. Armstrong or his legislative staff,” Jackson said.

Wilson worked as Armstrong’s top aide from April 13 to July 10. During that time, he declined to draw a salary from Williams, Jackson said, adding that the arrangement was approved by the Senate Select Committee on Ethics. Oklahoma’s other senator, Republican James Lankford, chairs that committee.

In June, Armstrong introduced legislation to reform the federal permitting process. Though the bill never came to a vote, it attracted 20 co-sponsors and some of its provisions made their way into the bipartisan permitting bill.

As a senator, Armstrong has maintained a significant financial stake in Williams. As of March 5, he held more than 2.7 million shares of the company’s stock, worth nearly $200 million at the time, according to a securities filing. Since then, he has sold between $5.5 million and $26 million worth of Williams stock and stock options, according to Senate financial disclosures.

At the time of his appointment, Armstrong reported nearly $69 million in income from Williams, including unvested stock compensation.

When he stepped down as executive chairman to serve in the Senate, Williams’ board elected to grant him the stock awards he would have received had he remained in the position until his expected retirement in July, so that he “would not be financially penalized for his public service.” That concession was worth about $2.8 million at the time.

Senate ethics rules are notoriously forgiving, said Donald Sherman, chief executive of Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, a government watchdog. Because Armstrong’s legislation and the permitting bill could benefit entire industries and not Williams uniquely, the senator does not appear to have violated the rules, Sherman said.

But, he added, Armstrong’s role raises particular issues because he was never elected, so voters didn’t have the chance to scrutinize his financial ties.

“The entire premise of the lax ethics regime in the Senate and Congress generally is these people are elected and they file financial disclosures before they are elected. He did neither,” Sherman said. “Just because something isn’t illegal doesn’t mean it’s not corrupt.”

While Armstrong’s office did not reply to Inside Climate News, a spokesperson told the news site Sludge, which reported on his financial ties last month, “Senator Armstrong consulted and complied with all Senate ethics rules during his unexpected transition from private citizen to U.S. Senator.”

Jackson, the Williams spokesperson, said the changes to the water quality permitting process would allow all pipelines and transmission lines “to receive a fair and transparent review process.”

Tyson Slocum, director of the energy program at Public Citizen, a consumer advocacy group, said Armstrong’s role “taints a lot of the negotiations.” While proponents have said the bill would promote renewable energy, Slocum said, “at the end of the day this is a pro-fossil-fuel compromise that gives massive benefits to the oil and gas industry.”

It is unclear whether Armstrong will cast a vote on the permitting bill. Republican Kevin Hern, elected Tuesday to Oklahoma’s U.S. Senate seat, has sought to be sworn in as soon as the election results are certified. The state’s attorney general said the law is behind him.

But the bill is expected to face its first vote next week and Armstrong has said he is intent on holding the seat until then.

“I’ve been kind of the voice with industry, and there’s a lot of conflict with industry,” Armstrong told Tulsa World after the election, adding that the bill was likely to face amendments on the Senate floor. “There’s trade-offs to be made. Getting these amendments done in a way that can hold the coalition together, I can play a very critical role in that.”

https://insideclimatenews.org/news/06112.title: Global Campaign Seeks to Curb Emissions of World’s Most Potent Greenhouse Gas
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/06112.author: By Phil McKenna
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/06112.text:
The German government has launched an international initiative to curb emissions of sulfur hexafluoride, an exceptionally potent greenhouse gas that it says has long been overlooked in efforts to address climate change.

Announced this week at a United Nations Environment Program meeting in Kigali, Rwanda, the “Global SF6 Pledge” urges countries to commit to monitoring, reporting and reducing emissions of the synthetic gas from the electric power sector, where it is used as an insulator in high-voltage equipment.

Pound for pound, SF6 is 24,300 times more effective at warming Earth’s atmosphere than carbon dioxide and remains in the atmosphere for 1,000 years. Although the United Nations identified it as one of six key greenhouse gases in the 1990s, it has received relatively little attention from policymakers.

“It’s a gap,” said Philippe Lempp of Germany’s international development agency, which is implementing the pledge. “We need to take care of this one because it’s something that we cannot rely on countries to do themselves.”

More than half of all sulfur hexafluoride emitted globally comes from China, a country that is rapidly expanding its electric grid. The country’s state-owned electric power companies recycle only about 30 percent of the gas they discard each year, with the remainder likely released into the atmosphere, a recent Inside Climate News analysis concluded.

“The pledge finally turns the spotlight on SF6, but until the world’s largest grid builder matches that ambition, we’re only treating half the leak,” said Richard Ferris, senior counsel at the Institute for Governance and Sustainable Development, a Washington, D.C.-based environmental research and advocacy organization.

China’s central government released its National Climate Change Response Plan in July, which called for an SF6 management plan to reduce emissions of the pollutant. The pledge and the attention it brings could hasten China’s efforts, Ferris said.

“China will continue to work with all countries to strengthen international cooperation on climate change, contributing to a green transition and the sustainable development of humanity,” Liu Chang, spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in Washington, D.C., said in a written statement. Liu did not directly respond to a question about whether China intends to sign the pledge.

Countries that sign the SF6 Pledge commit to strengthening monitoring and reporting of SF6 emissions while supporting efforts to reduce releases of the pollutant. SF6 emissions can be cut by recycling rather than venting used gas, reducing leaks from high-voltage equipment and using alternative gases or technologies as electrical insulators.

The European Union and the United Kingdom are the first to endorse the pledge, which officially launches this month at the United Nations’ global climate conference in Antalya, Turkey. The U.S. State Department declined to comment.

The United States released 328 metric tons of sulfur hexafluoride in 2023, primarily from the electric power sector, the most recent year for which data are available, according to U.S. Environmental Protection Agency data. This equals the annual climate pollution of 1.9 million automobiles, based on the agency’s greenhouse gas equivalency calculator.

The EPA has repeatedly extended the deadline for large greenhouse gas emitters—including those that release SF6—to report their climate pollution, as the agency considers scrapping reporting requirements entirely under an executive order by President Trump.

The pledge joins a growing list of voluntary initiatives, such as the Global Cooling Pledge and the Global Methane Pledge, that aim to reduce climate pollution. More than 150 countries have signed the methane pledge.

The SF6 pledge would provide a valuable platform for international cooperation, but “voluntary commitments must be backed by national regulations and accountability,” said Avipsa Mahapatra, climate campaign director for the Environmental Investigation Agency US, a Washington, D.C.-based nonprofit organization, in a written statement. “Success should not be measured by how many countries sign the pledge, but by how quickly countries stop installing new SF6-dependent equipment where alternatives are available, reduce emissions from existing equipment, and establish credible pathways toward eliminating SF6 emissions.”

Efforts should also target other industries that use and emit SF6, including semiconductor manufacturing, Mahapatra said.

The U.S. and Europe have significantly reduced emissions from their electric power sectors in recent decades through gas recycling, leak prevention and the adoption of alternative gases and technologies. The European Union took another step in that direction in January, when it began phasing out SF6 in new electrical equipment.

“It’s something that can be done,” Lempp said of global SF6 emissions reductions. “And with the right push, it will be done.”

https://insideclimatenews.org/news/06112.title: Billions of Gallons of Raw Sewage Are Pouring Into the Chicago River After Storms
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/06112.author: By Brett Chase, Chicago Sun-Times
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/06112.text:
This article originally appeared in the Chicago Sun-Times. It has been republished with permission.

Joe Gamble knows what to expect when he arrives at work at the Bridgeport Art Center after days of heavy rain.

“There was raw sewage floating in the creek,” Gamble says after storms in early October. “The wind carried the smell for at least a block or two.”

The Bridgeport Art Center sits along the south branch of the Chicago River at a spot known as Bubbly Creek, a small body of water that marks the south fork of the river and divides Bridgeport and McKinley Park.

It’s a really disgusting spot after big storms.

Layers of feces, condoms, tampons and other items flushed down toilets float past and get stuck in the low-lying trees along the shoreline. There are so many condoms that they’ve picked up a nickname: “Chicago whitefish.”

More and more people have been drawn to the river in recent years for recreation, many of them taking to the water in canoes and kayaks.

Bubbly Creek appeals particularly to beginner rowers and paddlers because it’s calm and easy to navigate. After storms, though, it often stinks so badly that the smell clings to Gamble’s clothes even after he’s left the area.

“I am sometimes tolerant of smells,” says Gamble, who works at the Chicago Maritime Museum, “but it’s a different level.”

The culprit behind the stench? A sewage pumping station on Racine Avenue south of the Bridgeport Art Center building. The Racine Avenue pumping station has big pumps that help move sewer water—both wastewater and stormwater—to a treatment facility where it’s sanitized, then sent on to the Chicago Sanitary and Ship Canal, then the Des Plaines and Illinois rivers and ultimately to the Mississippi River down to the Gulf of Mexico.

But sometimes the Metropolitan Water Reclamation District of Greater Chicago, the government body that operates the station, says heavy rains mean it needs to dump untreated sewage directly into the river to prevent flooding of homes.

And it’s a lot of sewage. This year, the Racine station, which is nearly 90 years old, has dumped more than 10 billion gallons of sewage into the river. That’s more than it has since 2019. In Chicago, stormwater and wastewater go into one big sewer.

Like what happens at the Racine station on the South Side, the water reclamation district’s North Branch pumping station—at Lawrence Avenue and the river on the North Side, on the border of Albany Park and Lincoln Square—has spewed nearly 2 billion gallons of untreated sewage this year into the north branch of the Chicago River.

And all of this is happening despite the billions of dollars in taxpayer money that has been spent over 50 years on the Deep Tunnel project, the sprawling system of more than 100 miles of underground tunnels and massive reservoirs designed to capture floodwater in the Chicago area and help protect the river and Lake Michigan from pollution.

The Deep Tunnel is one of the many ways that government officials in Chicago and engineers have tried to adapt a big city that originally was built on a swamp and remains highly prone to flooding to its environment.

But climate change has complicated those efforts. It’s contributing to intensifying weather patterns that bring storms that drop rain faster and harder than ever before. That overwhelms our sewers, streets and homes.

These intense storms can bring us more than 8½ inches of rain in just 24 hours.

But Chicago’s sewer system, designed decades ago, can handle just 2 inches of rain before flooding is likely.

All of that sewage flowing into Bubbly Creek and the north branch of the river isn’t just gross. It also poses a health risk for people with weak immune systems because of the bacteria and other pathogens the water carries. The contaminated water also can wreak havoc with nature, wiping out fish populations for weeks. That’s bad for the larger ecosystem, something that environmental advocates and government officials have been working over the last three decades to restore.

Tara Hoffmann, executive director of Recovery on Water, a group that has a rowing team for breast cancer survivors, says she worries about keeping its members safe in the sometimes nasty water. Some of the women have compromised immune systems following their cancer treatment. And they are out on the water, rowing, much of the time during warm weather months.

Hoffmann recalls a particularly bad day on the creek in June, when the women were paddling through excrement.

“One of the first things you notice,” she says, “is fish up at the surface, gasping for air. They’re just desperate to breathe.”

District officials say the more intense storms we’re seeing mean that Chicago needs more flood prevention measures in addition to the Deep Tunnel, like creating green spaces and tapping other strategies in an effort to capture water before it reaches the sewers. The district has designed nearly 300 flood mitigation projects, many of them still in the planning stages.

Raw sewage is a clear threat to the river’s water quality, says Phil Nicodemus, who’s the research director for the organization Urban Rivers, which works to turn urban waterways in Chicago into wildlife sanctuaries.

“It dumps a bunch of nutrients into the water at the same time,” Nicodemus says of the sewage. “That causes a massive oxygen drop, which causes a huge die-off. If that happens enough times throughout the year, you might be talking about a whole summer without much oxygen at all. That creates an enormous problem for wildlife.”

On a late summer day, Nicodemus traveled in a pontoon boat with a team surveying the floating ecosystems near River Park on the North Side, not far from the North Branch pumping station. He steered the boat. Urban River team members jumped into the water and collected bug samples. These will be studied to help provide insights on water quality.

Other experts also are examining the problem of these raw sewage dumps in the river.

Bubbly Creek, formerly a dumping area for discarded animal carcasses from the old Union Stockyards, was studied after a large sewage spill in 2023. What research biologist Austin Happel from the Shedd Aquarium found was disturbing.

The Chicago River provides a home to hundreds of animal species, and the sewage is having a dramatic impact on them, according to Happel. He has found that oxygen levels dropped while nitrogen levels rose significantly. Fish swam off and didn’t return until weeks later.

“There’s a stark shift in the food chain,” Happel says.

Oxygen in the water gets depleted. That makes it impossible for fish and other water life to exist. For weeks on end, the fish will disappear from the water, which flows into the south branch of the Chicago River.

The Deep Tunnel system includes more than 100 miles of massive tunnels hundreds of feet underground. The tunnels—basically giant pipes—range in diameter from under 10 feet to 35 feet. They help stormwater flow to two former rock quarries in the south and southwest suburbs that can hold billions of gallons of water.

Cleaner water was one of the main reasons it was decided in the 1970s to build the Deep Tunnel, formally known as the Tunnel and Reservoir Plan. The Deep Tunnel also is supposed to ease flooding in and around Chicago. The costly flood control measure has worked to a degree, but not entirely. This is why the Chicago area still sees chronic flooding and the Chicago River continues to be tainted by sewage.

The intensity of the rains we now see is too much for the tunnel and reservoir system to handle as envisioned. It’s being overwhelmed.

This summer, the biggest of the two quarries—the Thornton reservoir in South Holland—became filled with stormwater for the first time since it was opened in 2015. That mean it contained nearly 8 billion gallons of sewage. And it still hasn’t completely drained.

To the west of Chicago, the McCook reservoir in Bedford Park has filled up 10 times this year. Since it was opened in December 2017 through last year, that 3.5 billion gallon reservoir had filled to capacity only five times.

McCook is now undergoing an expansion. Eventually, it’s expected to hold 10 billion gallons of sewage water when it’s completed in 2032. The water reclamation district previously told the EPA the expansion would be finished three years sooner, in 2029.

In the race against time and nature, “The efforts aren’t keeping up,” Nicodemus says.

Margaret Frisbie, executive director of the environmental advocacy group Friends of the River, agrees. As more people turn to the river for recreation, Frisbie says, the problems are being more widely noticed.

The answer, she says, will rely on a mix of many new and innovative smaller projects, including moves to create more green space across Chicago and to create structures that capture rainwater before it gets into the sewers, where it ultimately can overwhelm the current system.

This year has been a whopper for rain, with more than 37 inches already recorded at O’Hare Airport and more rain forecast this weekend.

That’s a big hurdle, according to Frisbie.

“I don’t think you can engineer your way out of that,” she says.

https://insideclimatenews.org/news/06112.title: Election Shakeup Threatens Bipartisan Deal to Speed Energy Projects
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/06112.author: By Dan Gearino, Marianne Lavelle
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/06112.text:
Democrats’ electoral sweep has shaken the ground beneath a permitting reform bill in Congress, raising doubts about whether the measure has enough support to advance in an initial Senate vote scheduled for Monday.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) said on Thursday in a statement to POLITICO that he opposed the bipartisan bill in its current form, joining some fellow Democrats and environmental groups in raising concerns that the legislation would revise federal laws such as the National Environmental Policy Act.

Even before Jeffries’ statement, mounting evidence showed support for the bill was wavering.

The legislation, called the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, has support from business groups tied to renewable energy and fossil fuels. They tout its potential to reduce consumer energy costs by bringing new supplies online. The measure would ease regulatory barriers to build energy projects of just about every type—clean and dirty—and it would weaken the Clean Water Act, the Endangered Species Act, the National Environmental Policy Act and the National Historic Preservation Act.

And a new report by Kevin Kircher, a mechanical engineering professor at Purdue University, attempts to quantify the proposal’s broader emissions consequences, identifying potential harms that previous analyses may have missed by examining only parts of the bill.

The Senate is scheduled to vote Monday on whether to begin debate on the bill. Its co-sponsors are Sens. Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.V.), Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), Mike Lee (R-Utah) and Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.)

Chris Moyer, founder of Echo Communications Advisors, said Democrats’ overwhelming wins in the midterm elections have changed the landscape for the bill. He previously hoped Congress would pass it in the lame-duck session, which begins next week, but has since changed his mind.

“The numbers we’re looking at in the House and Senate are just massive and Democrats will have a ton of leverage,” Moyer said in an interview. He previously worked on Capitol Hill as an aide to the late Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid.

Republicans will control the House and Senate in the lame-duck session, but Democrats will have comfortable majorities when the 120th Congress begins in January. Democrats will soon have more clout to address crucial clean energy roadblocks, like long queues for interconnection to the electric grid, without the trade-offs currently in the legislation that could speed the building of fossil fuel infrastructure in sensitive areas, Moyer said.

“If there’s a way to address some of the concerns that are being raised from the environmental and public lands standpoint and from the Tribal standpoint, and also preserve a lot of the good things that have been negotiated already, that’s something it seems there should be interest in this Congress in working on,” Moyer said. “It can be part of the affordability agenda that the incoming majorities are going to focus on.”

Scott Segal, a longtime environmental policy expert with the Washington, D.C., law and lobbying firm Bracewell, which represents both fossil fuel and renewable energy interests, sees little chance that the legislation will pass by the end of the year.

“In a situation where one side has won a tremendous landslide, they are usually not set to do a lot of lame-duck production,” he said in a post-election webinar. “With something like permitting reform, the Democrats might rightly say that they’d like to negotiate their own version of it.”

Although it might be difficult to imagine Democrats finding common ground with Trump on the issues, Segal noted that some of the most significant U.S. environmental and energy laws have been enacted during periods of divided government in Washington: for example, the National Environmental Policy Act and the original Clean Air Act in 1970, the big Clean Air Act amendments in 1990, and the Energy Independence and Security Act of 2007.

“When there’s a distribution of leverage, you can create the conditions for advancing legislation, provided that people on both sides of the aisle don’t let the perfect be the enemy of the good,” Segal said. “Almost every major environmental statute occurred under exactly these circumstances, with Dems controlling both houses of Congress and a strong Republican in the White House.”

Rep. Sean Casten (D-Ill.) said Wednesday that he is waiting to see an amendment drafted by the bill’s Senate co-sponsors before deciding whether he supports the legislation. The amendment, whose text has not been disclosed, responds to some of the objections, including that the bill may tie the hands of a future president’s ability to oppose projects.

“There were some pretty significant structural problems with the first version that came out,” Casten said in a conference call that primarily focused on election results.

Kircher, the Purdue mechanical engineering professor, published his report on the bill this week, aiming to provide a more comprehensive assessment than previous analyses, which focused largely on the power sector provisions and overlooked other parts of the legislation with potential emissions implications.

Kircher built a model that calculates the bill’s potential effects, comparing a baseline of 2025 data with a hypothetical 2025 in which the measure was law. He found the bill would increase revenue and jobs in both fossil fuel and clean energy industries, with larger increases for fossil fuels. The bill also would likely increase energy-related greenhouse gas emissions and deaths attributable to air pollution from fossil fuels.

He weighed the trade-offs between negative effects, such as air pollution deaths, and positive ones, such as accelerating renewable energy construction. For example, he found that clean electricity revenue would increase by $2.1 million per life lost due to additional pollution from fossil fuels. This is much less than the roughly $12 million per-life cost standard that the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency has used to evaluate environmental policies, he said.

“I am for making reasonable compromises to get the good things we want out of our energy system, such as accelerating renewable energy development,” Kircher said in an interview. “That said, I don’t think the compromises in this version of BAAJA are reasonable, and I have a hard time seeing that changing without a major overhaul of the bill.”

Other analyses have found a net emissions benefit, with lower emissions under the bill than a baseline scenario. Much of the benefit comes from provisions that make it easier to build transmission lines and connect more renewable energy projects to the grid. But by focusing solely on power-sector benefits, the analyses miss some of the bill’s most concerning parts, Kircher said.

Opposition to the permitting bill has grown as environmental advocates have scrutinized it. One concern is the bill’s “permit certainty” provision, designed to protect renewable projects from the kind of moves the Trump administration has made to stall already approved projects. But environmentalists warn the provisions also could make it tougher to challenge fossil fuel projects, even when new evidence emerges of harm to water or land resources.

Environmental groups praised Jeffries’ criticism of the bill.

“We’re grateful that Leader Jeffries made a very wise move that sends a good faith signal that he’s accounting for the full range of interests in the Democratic caucus and is rightly cautious about sparking a bloody factional fight days after a historic political victory,” said Erik Schlenker-Goodrich, executive director of the Western Environmental Law Center.

Meanwhile, clean energy business groups have not wavered in their support for the bill, even as criticism has intensified. They are highlighting the potential to reduce consumer prices after an election in which affordability was a top issue.

“BAAJA is the best opportunity Congress has to lower prices right now, and they should not delay action on that,” said Dylan Reed, managing director of federal and political affairs for Advanced Energy United, a trade group, in a Thursday conference call. “We support passage of that bill and getting it done before the end of this Congress.”

https://insideclimatenews.org/news/06112.title: As Data Centers Move In, Iowa Residents Fight Plans for a New Gas Plant
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/06112.author: By Anika Jane Beamer
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/06112.text:
FAIRFAX, Iowa—Nearly 50 people gathered at the American Legion Post on a July evening to learn about a proposed natural gas plant less than three miles from town. Seated in folding chairs, they pulled out their phones and typed responses to a simple question: How are you feeling?

The words “angry,” “disgusted” and “scared” flashed across a TV screen at the front of the room.

For many, the meeting drudged up a familiar feeling of frustration.

Nine months earlier, Interstate Power and Light, an Iowa-based subsidiary of Alliant Energy, had abandoned plans to build a natural gas-fired power plant in Fairfax after fierce opposition from residents and leaders at the nearby Eastern Iowa Airport.
