https://grist.org/elections/midterms-202.title: What a historic ‘blue wave’ midterm means for climate action
https://grist.org/elections/midterms-202.author: Grist staff
https://grist.org/elections/midterms-202.text:
The Democratic Party won a commanding victory in Tuesday’s midterm elections. As of Wednesday morning, the party had secured control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives, as well as several state governments. The party’s strong performance, driven in part by voters’ anger over inflation and the war in Iran, reached into traditional Republican strongholds like Ohio and South Carolina. The sweep will have profound consequences for climate action in the United States, even with President Donald Trump still in the White House.

Flipping control of Congress will allow the Democrats to hinder Trump’s numerous attempts to roll back federal climate policy. In the first two years of Trump’s term, party leaders could do little more than write strongly worded statements to administration officials. They were powerless to stop the suspension of clean energy funding, the elimination of climate rules for power plants and motor vehicles, and the hollowing out of agencies like the U.S. Forest Service and the Federal Emergency Management Agency.

Now, the party will have a lot more leverage. Democratic senators and members of Congress can issue subpoenas to force administration officials to testify before Congress, and could even impeach Trump administration figures over funding clawbacks and staff reductions that Democrats have called unlawful. Democrats will also have control over must-pass funding bills, and Trump will have to negotiate with them in order to avoid a government shutdown. This could lead to the restoration of some funding for energy and climate resilience programs that Republicans have been trying to whittle down. With majorities in the Senate and the House, the party could even seek to reimpose some of the clean energy tax credits that Republicans rescinded last year.

Turnover at the state level, where officials are still counting votes, may be even more significant. Democrats gained full control of the state government in Wisconsin, Arizona, and Pennsylvania, according to election analysts, ending in some cases decades of Republican or divided government. This could allow the passage of meaningful climate policy in much of the country for the first time. In Pennsylvania, for instance, state House Democrats have said they intend to pass bills making it easier to build community solar, warehouse solar, and battery energy storage, as well as preventing local governments from banning renewables. In Georgia, Democrats flipped both the governor’s mansion and control of the Public Service Commission, which regulates electric utilities.

While Trump’s approval ratings are underwater on almost every major issue, energy prices were among the most salient issues in many races. The gasoline price hike caused by Trump’s invasion of Iran was perhaps the most consequential, but voters in many places were also concerned about their heating bills (Maine) and homeowner’s insurance premiums (Florida). In state races in Texas and Ohio, and in bellwether House districts like one in central Pennsylvania, skepticism over the AI boom may also have driven voters to oust incumbents who supported data centers.

Here are some of the most consequential outcomes for climate change and the environment. We’ll continue to update this post as more results and analysis come in.

Upon taking office, the Trump administration attempted to withhold billions of dollars in climate money, much of it from the landmark Inflation Reduction Act signed into law by Joe Biden in 2022. These freezes threw a number of major climate projects into limbo — the Department of Energy halted experimental projects for hydrogen production in Pennsylvania and decarbonized cement in California, while the Environmental Protection Agency froze a $7 billion community solar program.

Those days may soon be over. Chellie Pingree, the lead Democrat who oversees funding for the Environmental Protection Agency and Interior Department on the powerful House Appropriations Committee, says that she has prepared a long list of investigations and subpoenas for Trump administration officials, including EPA chief Lee Zeldin. She also intends to use the power of the purse to force the administration to spend climate money. Funding bills could include provisions that would deny agencies core operational funds or restrict travel money for leading officials unless they doled out solar and energy funding as Congress previously instructed them to.

“We can put a lot more teeth into the next appropriations bill,” she said. “We can say, ‘OK, fine, if you’re not going to spend the money, we have the power to withhold other funding.’”

Texas joined other Southern states in flipping blue for the first time in decades. Senator-elect James Talarico, a Democrat, supports an all-of-the-above energy strategy, which includes protecting oil and gas jobs while also growing renewable energy. This moderate approach proved important in a state that provides over 40 percent of the nation’s oil and gas.

As a state representative, Talarico authored and introduced the Texas Climate Action Act in 2021. While the bill did not advance, it aimed to establish targets for reducing greenhouse gas emissions and set energy efficiency standards, with an emphasis on local resiliency.

Talarico beat out Republican Ken Paxton, the state’s attorney general, who is widely considered friendly to the oil and gas industry. He’s been embroiled in scandal for years and was impeached in 2023 by the Texas House. Paxton’s track record likely helped Democrats obtain this victory.

Montana is on track to send a Democrat to the House of Representatives for the first time in over 30 years. Sam Forstag, a former wildland firefighter and union leader, claimed victory in the state’s competitive western district seat over Republican Aaron Flint, who conceded the race early Wednesday morning. The Associated Press estimates that 13 percent of ballots remain uncounted as of midday Wednesday.

Forstag ran his campaign on the affordability issues facing many Montanans and emphasized rising power bills, the need for data center regulation, and protecting public lands from attacks. The 31-year-old decided to run for office after experiencing Trump’s massive cuts to federal land management agencies, including wildland firefighting. Forstag received early endorsements from Representative Alexandra Ocasio-Cortez of New York and Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont.

In an interview with Montana Free Press in October, Forstag said he wanted to “invest in transmission” and ensure “next-generation energy projects, wind and solar, have the actual resources that they need to get off the ground.”

Their districts were redrawn to eliminate them, but voters in Florida’s 14th and Ohio’s 9th districts respectively reelected Kathy Castor and Marcy Kaptur anyway.

Castor — referred to as a “climate hawk” by Politico — has spent much of her long career in Congress raising the alarm about climate change. Between 2019 and 2022 she chaired the House Select Committee on the Climate Crisis, and has otherwise made reducing carbon pollution and preparing communities for climate impacts central to her legislative agenda. In March, she backed the Energy Bills Relief Act, which proposed restoring energy upgrade tax credits and connecting more clean energy to the grid. She has also strongly opposed data centers in the Tampa area that she serves, warning that the facilities could drive up her constituents’ utility costs while straining local water supplies.

Kaptur is the longest-serving woman in the House. She has been a leading opponent of the Department of Energy’s efforts to redirect Inflation Reduction Act money away from clean energy and toward fossil fuels. She has alleged that these redirections violate federal law, and would likely lead investigations into the Energy Department’s actions in a Democratic-controlled Congress. The Ohio state Legislature redrew her district to encompass more conservative areas along Lake Erie, but she held on to her seat comfortably.

— Jake Bittle and Sachi Kitajima Mulkey

Stunning results are still coming in from the Lone Star State. For the first time in over 30 years, a Democrat has won a seat on the Texas Railroad Commission, the regulatory agency that oversees the state’s oil and gas industry. Jon Rosenthal defeated Republican candidate Bo French, who made a racist social media post about South Asian students celebrating at a University of Texas football game that drew national bipartisan backlash.

“To the dude that posted the online poll last summer, asking who’s a bigger threat to America and the only two choices were Muslims and Jews — tonight this Jewish engineer sent that motherf*cker home,” said Rosenthal in his victory speech, referring to another racist post by French.

Rosenthal asserts that good jobs and clean air can — and must — coexist. He supports an all-of-the-above energy strategy and capturing natural gas. He also wants to “turbocharge” the plugging of inactive oil and gas wells, which leak methane. The Railroad Commission is currently considering rules on that, spurred by state legislation passed last year.

Rosenthal will join two Republican commissioners, meaning it’s likely he will be outvoted on many issues.

Democrats secured both Public Service Commission seats on the Georgia ballot, giving the party majority control of the powerful utility regulation board for the first time in 30 years.

Democrat Peter Hubbard successfully defended his District 3 seat against a challenge from former commissioner Fitz Johnson, while Democrat Shelia Edwards defeated Republican Josh Tolbert to take the District 5 seat.

The commission regulates utilities, including the behemoth Georgia Power, meaning commissioners have final say over how the state’s largest utility makes energy and how much customers pay for it. The board has drawn increased scrutiny in recent years because of a series of rate hikes and the scramble to produce enough energy for the massive spike in demand that Georgia Power predicts will result from the data center boom. The utility’s plans to meet that demand rely heavily on fossil fuels.

Georgia is one of 10 states where utility regulators are elected rather than appointed.

After years of financial woes and operating deficits, some residents of the California Bay Area were concerned that this year’s midterms might signal the downfall of public rail options in the region, leaving them stuck in its infamous traffic. But the Regional Transit Measure, which sought to enact a sales tax to fund local transit agencies for another 14 years, easily won a majority vote. It is expected to raise $1 billion each year to keep trains up and running.

Colorado rail supporters have also claimed victory for Measure 7A, which will establish a permanent sales tax to extend Colorado Connector passenger trains between Pueblo and Fort Collins. The coalition that campaigned for the measure argued that the expanded railway would reduce emissions equivalent to 29,000 cars in the area.

Other states had transit wins, too: More than 70 percent of voters said yes to Seattle’s Proposition 1, which would double the dedicated transit tax and support more frequent bus service. And Lawrence, Kansas, increased its transit sale tax to fund service for another 10 years.

— Sachi Kitajima Mulkey

Colorado voters roundly rejected an effort to enshrine a right to natural gas in the state Constitution, which would have been a first in the country. Amendment 82 proposed giving homes and businesses a right to use gas stoves for cooking and heating, as well as giving distributors and utilities a right to sell the fossil fuel. Since the Constitution trumps all else, the ballot measure’s approval could have jeopardized local and state efforts to shift away from fossil fuels and electrify buildings, prompting court challenges to climate policies. The measure also raised concerns that it could protect access to natural gas for power-hungry data centers.

Only 46 percent of voters supported Amendment 82 as of late Wednesday morning, far beneath the 55 percent a constitutional amendment needs to pass. That protects the Colorado Public Utilities Commission’s Clean Heat Plan, which requires utilities to cut natural gas emissions by 41 percent by 2035.

In western North Carolina, where Hurricane Helene caused billions of dollars of damage two years ago, Democrat Jamie Ager defeated Republican Jennifer Balkcom for an open seat in the House of Representatives. Ager, a longtime farmer, made the area’s slow hurricane recovery a centerpiece of his campaign. He criticized Representative Chuck Edwards, who dropped out of the race after a sexual harassment scandal, for doing too little to deliver aid for Asheville and its surrounding counties. Grist reported last month that at least some voters blamed Republicans for the slow recovery. In a rally held on the eve of the election, President Trump promised to deliver more hurricane aid money, but only if North Carolina elected Republicans. The district around Asheville did not take the bait — not only did Ager win the state’s 11th House District, but Democrat Roy Cooper, the state’s former governor, easily won a Senate race, flipping a seat that had been held by Republicans.

William Lawrence, a co-founder of the climate activism group Sunrise Movement, has prevailed in a razor’s-edge House of Representatives race in central Michigan. Lawrence, a 36-year-old progressive, ousted freshman Republican Tom Barrett in Michigan’s 7th Congressional District, a bellwether area encompassing Lansing and its suburbs. He made opposition to data centers a focal point of his campaign, calling for a national moratorium on data center development. He also aligned himself with activists and residents who have opposed large-scale renewable energy projects in the Lansing area. In an interview with Grist last month, Lawrence said that many utility-scale solar projects don’t benefit the communities around them.

In one of the night’s biggest upsets, Texas state Representative Gina Hinojosa ousted incumbent Governor Greg Abbott after campaigning on a data center moratorium and accusing Abbott of selling out to the tech industry.

And at least three legislative seats flipped blue after Democrats aggressively criticized Republican incumbents for being too friendly to data centers. Democrat Sherrod Brown defeated Republican Jon Husted in Ohio’s special Senate election after state Democrats put up billboards stating: “See that data center? Jon Husted did that.” Likewise, Democrat Paige Cognetti beat Republican Rob Bresnahan in Pennsylvania’s 8th Congressional District after she ran television ads associating Bresnahan with data centers and comparing tech companies to polluting mining corporations. (Bresnahan has owned stock in data center companies.) And in South Carolina’s Senate race, voters pushed Annie Andrews to a surprise win over incumbent Darline Graham after Andrews highlighted that a new pro-data center super PAC spent $1.5 million dollars on ads for her opponent, whom she nicknamed “Data Center Darline.”

Both Husted and Bresnahan had previously welcomed data centers to their regions, but later attempted unsuccessfully to pass regulations constraining them once the facilities became a hot-button issue. Data centers are massively unpopular with voters across the political spectrum, polls have shown. The facilities have become a growing source of demand for electricity from fossil fuels.

— Austin Corona, Sachi Kitajima Mulkey, and Jake Bittle

Further down the ballot, it’s hard to find a place where data centers didn’t lose. In addition to the marquee congressional and governor’s races where voter sentiment about the AI boom may have helped oust Republican incumbents, dozens of towns and cities passed pauses or bans on data center development, according to The Washington Post. In many cases, these restrictions passed by enormous margins — in Sunbury, Ohio, where Amazon proposed a $2 billion project, voters rejected the facilities by an almost 60-point margin.

The AI issue also upended local elections, and perhaps the best example is in Pine Island, Minnesota. Google has proposed building a large new data center there, one that would be powered exclusively by clean energy and would include big subsidies for electric ratepayers. But voter outrage over the project caused a previous mayor to resign and led a first-time politician to mount a campaign against the interim replacement. That challenger, Mark Lang, won with well over 60 percent of the vote.

Representative Jared Moskowitz, a Democrat, easily hung onto his seat in Congress, surviving a challenge from Scott Singer, a Trump-backed Republican, in Florida’s redrawn 25th Congressional District. His third-term victory defies the right-wing effort to make his district significantly redder with new boundaries and keeps one of America’s most vocal FEMA reformers in Congress.

Moskowitz, once appointed Florida’s emergency management director by Governor Ron DeSantis, championed bipartisan legislation to pull FEMA out of the Department of Homeland Security and make it an independent, Cabinet-level agency — just as the Trump administration seeks to cut its funding and shift more responsibility onto states. He has also introduced bills that would let states voluntarily administer federal disaster housing and public assistance, and proposed a reinsurance backstop that would help cover catastrophic losses after disasters like hurricanes.

— Sachi Kitajima Mulkey

Voters in Michigan passed a measure to limit corporate spending in elections, and in a nationwide first, successfully went after the state’s electric and gas utilities. Supporters of Proposal 2 leveraged ratepayers’ growing dissatisfaction with utilities around power bills, unreliable service, and data centers. The measure is one of the most ambitious attempts in the country to limit corporate influence in politics, which it aims to do by preventing utility-funded political action groups and utility executives from contributing to state political campaigns. Groups that oppose the measure have contended that Prop 2 will stifle corporations’ speech protections under the Supreme Court’s Citizens United decision in 2010. Shortly before midnight on Tuesday, a conservative policy group sued the state in federal court, saying that everyone from journalists to nonprofit organizations could lose speech and privacy rights under the new measure. And while experts said the measure likely won’t get all utility money out of politics, Prop 2 advocates maintain it’s a step toward accountability.

Republican Byron Donalds has defeated Democrat David Jolly for occupancy of Florida’s governor’s mansion. Donalds, who currently represents Florida’s 19th Congressional District, will be the state’s first Black governor. He doesn’t believe humans play any role in global warming, but he’s more willing to discuss the issue than the current governor, Ron DeSantis, who signed the state’s infamous “don’t say climate change” law.

That matters in a state especially battered by sea level rise, coastal erosion, and storms. The skyrocketing costs of home insurance were a central issue in this race, and Donalds promised to bring them down by increasing competition in the state’s private market. In 2025, Donalds notably co-introduced bipartisan legislation with Democrat Jared Moskowitz to reform federal disaster aid by making FEMA an independent Cabinet-level agency. In the weeks before voters went to the polls, he also pledged investment in restoring coastal habitats. Donalds seems likely to carry on DeSantis’ other environmental policies, such as supporting data center development and attacking wind and solar projects.

— Sachi Kitajima Mulkey

Republican Senator Ashley Moody defeated the progressive Democrat Angie Nixon to retain her seat, which Florida Governor Ron DeSantis appointed her to last year. Moody’s brief stint in Washington hints at what’s to come: She introduced a resolution to overturn Biden-era efficiency standards and supported the so-called One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which ended federal tax credits for clean energy installations like rooftop solar and batteries. Previously, as Florida’s attorney general, she joined a lawsuit challenging emissions reduction targets on highways.

But in Florida, a state grappling with coastal erosion and rising sea levels, some environmental protections are popular across party lines: Last year, even as Trump pushed to open offshore drilling in other states, Moody introduced the American Shores Protection Act to ban the practice off Florida’s coast through 2032.

— Sachi Kitajima Mulkey

This story has been updated with analysis of additional races and trends.

https://grist.org/solutions/electric-avi.title: Electric aviation is taking off in unexpected ways
https://grist.org/solutions/electric-avi.author: Benton Graham
https://grist.org/solutions/electric-avi.text:
The call came from a home in Hyde County, a rural expanse of coastal farmland and marsh in North Carolina. Paramedic Quinn Reece jumped into an electric aircraft with one seat, two wings, and eight propellers. It is called a BlackFly, and at about 14 feet long it looks like an oversized drone. Moments later it rose like a helicopter, then flew like an airplane.

As she raced toward the emergency at about 60 mph, a dispatcher described the location. Reece quickly realized that the app the county uses for emergency response had given the wrong location. Because she had flown over the area before, Reece had an idea of the correct location. She zipped over in the aircraft, confirmed where the call had come from, and relayed the information to paramedics headed that way. She was on the scene and administering care 20 minutes before they arrived.

That is exactly what Brook Cox, the county’s emergency medical services chief, hoped to see. She launched the six-month trial with a company called Pivotal in March to see if its BlackFly could help medics more quickly reach patients in a county that covers 1,459 square miles of land and water. The county conducted more than 300 training flights prior to using the aircraft for two 911 calls.

Air taxis and flying cars have long defined the promise of electric vertical takeoff and landing aircraft, or eVTOLs. This is the vision the Federal Aviation Administration has highlighted through the eVTOL Integration Pilot Program, which works with manufacturers to test the emerging aircraft in real-world settings. Last week, Archer Aviation announced plans for aerial taxi services in three Texas cities and Joby Aviation began demonstrations in Florida.

Grist thanks its sponsors. Become one.

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

Hyde County is among those exploring more immediate uses for these machines. The FAA program considers emergency medical response an important application, particularly in rural areas. Similar aircraft powered by the sun that can stay aloft for weeks are being developed to monitor climate threats like wildfires, methane emissions and ice melt.

The great promise of electric aviation is to help decarbonize flight. These developments point to a fast-approaching future for electric aviation. It just might not arrive in the form we expected.

Kristina Menton, Pivotal’s vice president of flight, points to a December 2024 flight as proof the technology could be a boon to EMS. A BlackFly took off from a Los Angeles County fire station and landed in a backyard in Malibu, demonstrating it could fly directly to a private address.

Menton acknowledged that single-seater aircraft are a new approach for a field that has typically employed separate crews for flight and EMS operations. BlackFly’s simplified controls allow one person to serve as both pilot and medic. “The aircraft is a breeze,” Cox said. “It really takes the guesswork out of it because you have a screen and you have all these prompts that you have to go through.”

Grist thanks its sponsors. Become one.

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

Carl Dietrich, who founded Jump Aero in 2019 to build electric aircraft for EMS, sees Pivotal’s work as proof of concept rather than competition, something that can only help the sector grow. “It shows that other organizations believe that this is a real opportunity,” he said.

Jump Aero is building a different kind of aircraft, the JA1 Pulse, which has been in development for seven years. Dietrich expects it to reach 288 mph, compared with 63 mph for the BlackFly. He said eVTOLs aren’t necessarily replacing helicopters or ambulances, but adding something new to emergency response: an aircraft that is easy to fly and can launch almost immediately without warming up.

“It’s ideal for rapid response missions because you don’t pay any maintenance penalty for going to full power instantly,” he said. This is particularly important in a field that aims to arrive within eight minutes of a call, while rural response times average nearly 15 minutes.

There are, of course, limitations, including battery range and weight capacity. The BlackFly can travel 20 miles on a charge and carry 200 pounds, while the JA1 Pulse is good for 70 miles and 350 pounds. The aircraft clearly aren’t meant to transport patients; their utility lies in being able to quickly reach an emergency and stabilize a patient until an ambulance arrives. Reece carried a cardiac monitor, airway supplies, and a “primary response bag” of essential gear that would allow her to assess a patient and begin treatment immediately.

Rural areas may present an easier path to introducing the technology, said April Zhang, director of advanced air mobility at the University of South Florida’s Center for Urban Transportation Research. “In the urban area, it’s probably more challenging to find the right landing and takeoff sites,” she said. Menton said other counties are already looking at Hyde County’s experience and considering similar programs.

Zhang points to the eVTOL Integration Pilot Program as a way for manufacturers and public agencies to collaborate on applications. Beyond EMS, she sees traffic surveillance and cargo deliveries as other potential uses.

FAA policy may also give public agencies an easier path to using eVTOLs than commercial operators. Andrew Mearns, a commercialization consultant at Multicopter Aerospace Consulting, said EMS organizations can often operate under the FAA’s public aircraft rules, which could allow them to fly without the credentials required of a commercial pilot.

Cost is another appeal. Pivotal’s model sells for $190,000, while Mearns said helicopters can cost from $500,000 to $10 million. Operating costs will vary with the specific model, but generally speaking an electric aircraft might be about 80 percent cheaper than a similarly sized machine that burns fossil fuels, Mearns said.

Emergency response is one avenue where electric aviation is beginning to find a practical use. Another is taking shape much higher in the atmosphere.

Unmanned stratospheric aircraft can reach altitudes of 65,000 feet, about twice as high as commercial aircraft. Solar-powered versions can remain aloft for weeks or months, making them well suited to long-term environmental monitoring.

“If you imagine these solar-powered aircraft just circling the L.A. County area, collecting soil moisture, vegetation moisture data, with complex math models and deep learning mapped to that, you can have improved risk profiles better than the models that are currently there,” said Craig Mascarenhas, an aerospace researcher at Harvard University. The aircraft could also spot fires more quickly and help map them for first responders.

Mascarenhas leads engineering research for Harvard’s branch of the Stratospheric Airborne Climate Observing System, where he is helping develop and deploy solar-powered electric aircraft with Electra.Aero, MIT and others. He said their applications go beyond wildfires.

“It’s hurricane monitoring and tracking, methane emiss monitoring, understanding ice dynamics across the world,” he said. “The instruments will be swapped, but the topology of the aircraft will remain the same.”

The aircraft themselves could offer environmental benefits too. Mascarenhas said eVTOLs could reduce greenhouse gas emissions when they replace fuel-burning helicopters, but the climate case is less clear when they replace efficient ground transportation.

“Vertical flight is inherently energy-intensive, and an electric aircraft is not necessarily more energy-efficient or lower-carbon per passenger-mile than an electric car, bus, or train,” he said.

For Pivotal, EMS in Hyde County is just the beginning. Menton said the company’s broader vision is to “revolutionize transportation” by making short electric flights accessible to more people.

But for now, some of the technology’s most immediate uses may be the specialized applications already being tested in places like Hyde County and high above it.

Correction: This story originally underestimated how much cheaper an eVTOL aircraft might be to operate.

https://grist.org/solutions/louisiana-mi.title: Louisiana’s accidental blueprint for restoring its coast
https://grist.org/solutions/louisiana-mi.author: Tristan Baurick
https://grist.org/solutions/louisiana-mi.text:
Arthur Matherne is used to speeding his airboat across a southeastern stretch of the Louisiana coast where lakes and bayous have widened as the Gulf of Mexico’s salty water has moved in, dissolving marshes and swamps.

But in one tucked-away patch of the Barataria Basin’s 1.6 million acres, the semi-retired tour guide eases off the throttle as he tries to remember his way through channels that have grown tighter by the year. Grasses are overtaking the shallows, and oak branches are spreading overhead, dangling Spanish moss over waterways he once barreled through.

“All this, it’s filling in,” Matherne said after shutting off his airboat’s roaring propeller. “Right here, it used to be three feet of water. Now it’s three inches.”

What Matherne is seeing is a striking reversal of a pattern that has defined southern Louisiana for the past century. While much of the coastal zone has receded at about 11 square miles per year from erosion and other forces compounded by climate change, the wetlands here are gaining ground.

Grist thanks its sponsors. Become one.

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

The reason is just a few miles away. Near Luling in St. Charles Parish, the Davis Pond Freshwater Diversion has funneled Mississippi River water into the basin since the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers built it in 2002 to combat saltwater intrusion. But something unexpected happened. The diversion also carried the muddy river’s sediment into the wetlands, raising the bottom and helping create new land.

“It’s had this unintended consequence of building land,” said Jacob Berkowitz, an Army Corps of Engineers wetland scientist. “This became one of the strategies that’s considered a key to addressing coastal land loss in Louisiana.”

Yet even as Davis Pond demonstrates the land-building potential of river diversions, Louisiana has abandoned its most ambitious attempt to put that approach to work. Last year, the state canceled the massive Mid-Barataria Sediment Diversion, a $3 billion project inspired by Davis Pond and once heralded by the state as “the largest and boldest environmental restoration project in U.S. history.” Though it broke ground in 2023, work stopped shortly after Governor Jeff Landry, a Republican and one of the diversion’s most prominent critics, took office in 2024. He officially terminated the project, which would have been located 20 miles south of New Orleans, in July 2025.

Landry called the diversion a costly and ineffective “experiment” that would harm the commercial fishing industry by flooding parts of Barataria Bay with too much fresh water and sediment, pushing out shrimp and burying oysters.

Grist thanks its sponsors. Become one.

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

“This project is going to break our culture,” Landry told state lawmakers in 2024. “It will destroy the shrimping industry — which is already struggling — and destroy the oyster beds.”

Landry’s administration also canceled a companion project — the $1.8 billion Mid-Breton Sediment Diversion, aimed at reviving dying wetlands southeast of New Orleans.

Despite Landry’s opposition to these projects, his administration is quietly planning more diversions along the Mississippi, albeit on a smaller scale.

Officials with the Louisiana Coastal Protection and Restoration Authority, or CPRA, declined to discuss the state’s diversion plans, but a Verite News review of the authority’s budget documents indicates the state plans to spend at least $340 million on five projects over the next several years that would divert Mississippi River water to restore coastal wetlands. That represents a big increase over past spending on diversions. Since 2007, CPRA has completed just three diversion projects totaling $47 million, according to the agency’s 2027 annual plan.

While some state leaders may disparage diversions, CPRA scientists still believe using river water to rebuild land and restore wetlands is a sound approach. At its core, a diversion mimics how the Mississippi functioned before levees walled off its floodplain, preventing the river from overflowing its banks or breaking through them at points called crevasses, according to Brian Gossman, a CPRA coastal scientist, who spoke at a public lecture in March.

“The natural process that we’re attempting to harness is the Delta cycle,” Gossman said. “It’s the same process that built all of coastal Louisiana over millennia. We’re just using it in a targeted way.”

Nearly all of the CPRA’s diversion spending would go to one project — the restoration of Maurepas Swamp, a Chicago-sized wetland along the west edge of Lake Pontchartrain, about 25 miles from New Orleans.

The $334 million project, which broke ground in 2024, will install gates in the Mississippi River levee near Garyville in St. John the Baptist Parish and channel up to 2,000 cubic feet per second of water into Maurepas, which remains one of the country’s largest swamps despite losing thousands of acres of cypress and tupelo forest. Levees built in the early 1900s cut the swamp off from fresh water and sediment, leaving its trees vulnerable to saltwater intrusion.

According to CPRA, the diversion will rebuild lost land and flush out stagnant, salty water, rejuvenating about 45,000 acres. It’s set for completion late next year.

The authority hasn’t totally given up on diverting sediment into the Barataria Basin. After canceling the Mid-Barataria Sediment Diversion, the agency dusted off an earlier, much smaller version of the project: the Medium Diversion at Myrtle Grove. Proposed more than 25 years ago, the project would divert up to 15,000 cubic feet of river water per second into the basin — about one-third of Mid-Barataria’s typical operating rate. To speed up the creation of marsh, the authority would also dredge sediment from the Mississippi and pump it directly into the basin.

The Myrtle Grove project’s timeline and budget are unclear. CPRA’s budget documents indicate about $1.7 million could be spent on it between 2027 and 2029, but the full cost will likely be much more. In 2012, the project was estimated at $278 million, or about $480 million in today’s dollars.

CPRA’s spending plans would also boost the Davis Pond diversion. The agency has proposed spending $3 million, shared with the Army Corps, to study how the diversion could be operated to build more land.

Research led by Tulane University in 2019 suggested that boosting the diversion’s average flow from 1,000 cubic feet per second to between 4,000 and 7,000 cubic feet per second could deliver more sediment to nearby wetlands. But if the flow is too high, researchers warned, the sediment will be flushed away.

In St. Charles Parish, home to Davis Pond, finding ways to increase the diversion’s flows has strong support. In its 2025 habitat restoration plan, the parish endorsed the proposed CPRA study, citing criticism that the diversion’s operations were “not being aggressive enough” to maximize its benefits.

Watching Davis Pond’s silty flows creep past his airboat, Matherne agreed the diversion should release more water and sediment. “Right now, it’s like pissing in an Olympic-size swimming pool,” he said. “We need more flow.”

The Army Corps built the diversion to improve oyster beds that had become too salty as coastal marshes receded. Oyster abundance in the area has fluctuated since the diversion was built, but recent monitoring data suggest populations on public beds were above their 10-year averages in 2024, according to Danielle Richardi, a CPRA coastal scientist. Shrimp catches south of the diversion hit a nearly four-decade high that same year, she said.

Matherne said he’s seen a marked increase in wildlife. Alligators are more plentiful, he said, pointing out more than a dozen of the reptiles as his boat traveled the maze of waterways near the diversion. “All the alligators you see — that’s a fraction of what’s out there,” he said. “Come back at night, and you’ll see their eyes shining all over.”

Several studies have documented how accumulated sediment has built land near the diversion, although researchers in recent years have reached conflicting conclusions about the overall impact on wetland acreage.

In 2019, Louisiana State University coastal sciences professor Eugene Turner challenged conventional thinking about river diversions with a study linking Davis Pond to increased wetland loss. Turner found that the annual rate of wetland loss near Davis Pond nearly tripled after the diversion began operating, increasing from 0.36 percent to more than 1 percent. The increase was greater than in nearby wetlands unaffected by the diversion.

One explanation might have to do with what’s in the water. While the diversion was intended to restore the Mississippi’s pre-levee connections to surrounding wetlands, the river’s water has changed dramatically over the past century. It now carries high concentrations of nitrogen and phosphorus, much of it from fertilizer and manure runoff from farms and wastewater discharged by cities upstream. Turner argues that the excess nutrients produce wetland plants that are, essentially, flabby and weak.

“If your garden is fertilized too much, it puts all its growth aboveground,” he said. “It falls over because its roots never had to work hard.”

Turner believes that lower nutrient levels encourage plants to develop stronger root systems, making marshes more resistant to erosion. He likens some of the apparent land gains from diversions to a “green toupee.” The wetlands may look as though they’re filling in, but strong winds or currents can easily strip away the vegetation.

Two of Turner’s colleagues disputed his findings in a 2023 study. John White and John Day, also LSU coastal sciences professors, found that the first 20 years of Davis Pond’s operations had actually led to a net gain of 1.3 square miles of land. Their study said Turner came to an “erroneous conclusion” by incorrectly using data “that was clearly labeled as inappropriate for the task.”

The researchers asserted that Turner’s satellite data were too imprecise to distinguish small patches of wetlands from open water, potentially making land appear to have disappeared when it hadn’t.

Turner stands by his findings, arguing they more accurately portray how diversions affect coastal wetlands and warn of the damage they can cause if poorly managed.

Opponents of the Mid-Barataria diversion regularly cited Turner’s research and added several more concerns, including CPRA’s projections that the huge diversion could bury oyster beds under sediment and that added fresh water would likely push shrimp farther offshore, making them harder to catch. Combined with the project’s $3 billion price tag, those concerns cratered political support.

“Considering the uncertainties and questionable environmental outcomes recognized by various agencies … it was necessary to abandon the current project,” CPRA Chairman Gordon Dove wrote in a column in The Times Picayune.

Although CPRA has yet to fully explain its new approach to diversions, smaller and cheaper projects appear to be a priority. Turner welcomes that shift, but argues diversions should also operate at lower flows to avoid washing away vegetation that he believes excessive nutrients have weakened. He also recommends building diversions in areas with sandy soils rather than the soft, unstable soil in many marshes.

“It’s not that they won’t work,” Turner said. “These diversions give you lessons. We should learn from them.”

https://grist.org/business/energy-transi.title: On Wall Street, the ‘energy transition’ includes natural gas and data centers
https://grist.org/business/energy-transi.author: Austin Corona
https://grist.org/business/energy-transi.text:
Blackstone, one of the largest private equity firms in the world, officially changed the name of its dedicated energy investment fund to include the phrase “energy transition” in 2022, having already ceased investing in oil and gas production five years earlier. The pivot toward a new energy future has not diminished interest in the fund. In mid-October, Blackstone announced that the fund pulled in $8.7 billion in investor money this year, reportedly turning away an additional $3 billion to stay under its maximum investment cap.

Blackstone’s is one of several energy transition funds at private equity firms that have consistently grown over the past decade. That growth has continued even as general climate-oriented investment has fallen over the last few years. Colloquially, “energy transition” refers to the shift from fossil fuels to renewable energy that is necessary to limit the worst impacts of climate change. But on Wall Street, the term can mean something a bit different. Some transition funds — including Blackstone’s — see opportunities for profit in natural gas, data centers, and rising electricity costs.

“I know a lot of the investors out there do consider gas a transition fuel,” said Ryan Loughead, a senior associate and former climate solutions analyst for BloombergNEF, an energy research firm.

Private equity funds take new investor money every few years and then use it to buy existing companies, maximize their profits, and then sell them, returning the money from the sale to investors. Unlike publicly traded companies, whose stocks are available for anyone to buy, private equity firms typically take investments only from large organizations, like pension funds, or very wealthy individuals, and they have faced criticism for prioritizing returns at the expense of workers and the environment.

Grist thanks its sponsors. Become one.

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

The transition to renewable energy has been a booming business for private equity firms. “Transition funds” in private equity have raked in $178 billion between 2021 and the beginning of 2026, triple the amount raised by comparable funds dedicated to fossil fuels and general energy, according to Loughead’s research. They’ve maintained their popularity even as other forms of climate-related investments have flagged in the United States, with climate-related venture capital on track to suffer its worst year this decade. (While private equity funds buy out established companies, venture capital funds make smaller investments in startups.)

These shifts have coincided with changes in federal policy, as well as the overall economy. The Biden administration’s signature climate law once spurred innovation in new technologies, but Republicans in Congress repealed most of that legislation last year. Meanwhile, the tech industry’s data center buildout is creating surging demand for electricity and drawing trillions of dollars from investors.

In the financial industry, the energy transition has grown into a sophisticated economic trend with established players and markets, said Dan Cohn, an energy finance analyst with the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis, a think tank focused on the energy transition. Private equity funds don’t typically demonstrate investor interest in a budding industry so much as a view that the industry is becoming economically important.

“Investors are sensing oncoming scarcity [of electricity] and are positioning themselves accordingly,” Cohn said. “That speaks to both the moment of rising electricity demand, but also the maturity of clean energy technologies.”

Grist thanks its sponsors. Become one.

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

But while these funds seek to capitalize on high demand for electricity, they don’t all show a clear commitment to reducing emissions. Blackstone’s fund is explicit in its view that methane gas, a fossil fuel and the primary component of natural gas, is essential to the energy transition. The fund no longer invests in oil and gas fields, but it does invest in natural gas plants. When Blackstone rebranded it in 2022, the fund’s director, David Foley, explained why natural gas plants were still on the table. “A lot of the capital invested in the energy transition is going into simple renewable power generation assets like solar and wind,” he told an industry publication. “While this is important, just adding renewables to the grid doesn’t necessarily mean you can shut down and remove existing sources of power, such as coal and gas.”

This year, the fund announced investments in six companies, including a natural gas plant operator and a data center cooling technology company, alongside a company focused on renewable energy development and some transmission and grid technology companies. Blackstone did not reply to a request for comment.

Meanwhile, the private equity firm Brookfield governs its transition funds partly through an explicit commitment to decarbonization and emissions reductions. The company has said it can invest in natural gas in cases where it replaces dirtier fossil fuels, but Brookfield has also drawn criticism for describing gas expansion as part of the energy transition.

Similar funds in Europe, like Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners’ Energy Transition Fund, are far more focused on clean energy sources like green hydrogen, with little emphasis on natural gas.

“‘Energy transition’ is a flexible term,” Cohn said. “And I’m unsurprised to see either the gas or electrical equipment and data center-related companies in some of these funds. That is perfectly consistent with how I know some investors think about the energy transition.”

BlackRock, another private markets giant unrelated to Blackstone, explicitly defines “transition” investing as something different from “sustainable” investing: “not all sustainable strategies are transition, and not all transition strategies are sustainable,” its website reads.

That partial overlap could complicate investors’ claims about how sustainable their portfolios are.

At least three major government-managed investors in Blackstone’s energy transition fund have explicit climate investing goals. The Oregon Treasury, Minnesota State Board of Investment, and San Francisco Employees’ Retirement System all have some form of climate-related goal or plan for their investments. These entities have committed a combined $525 million to the fund, according to Private Equity International, an analytics firm.

These investors did not reply to requests for comment before publication of this article, but the wide range of standards for climate- and energy-related investments has already created confusion. In Oregon, a state representative formally asked the state’s treasury this year to more clearly define what it reports as “climate-positive” investments, which it uses as a category in its public reports.

Investors may have a financial incentive to include gas in their view of the energy transition. Transition funds that include gas tend to have slightly higher returns than those that don’t, Loughead said. And Loughead and Cohn both said the massive rush to invest in the data center boom has permeated funds nominally concerned with the clean energy transition.

Off Wall Street, the question of whether natural gas and data centers have a role to play in the energy transition is hotly debated. Natural gas has cut emissions from the power sector when it has replaced coal, while data centers have spurred investment in grid improvements and clean energy sources. But using natural gas still produces significant emissions — both when it’s burned and when it leaks out of infrastructure — and data centers are spurring more fossil fuel use, potentially slowing progress on global power sector emissions. Plus, some grids are already finding ways to provide reliability with cleaner alternatives to gas, like batteries, which can store renewable energy to use when the sun isn’t shining and the wind isn’t blowing. Most climate and environmental groups argue emphatically that gas should not be seen as a transition fuel.

“Natural gas no longer functions as a credible bridge in the energy transition,” wrote Shruti Shukla, a senior advocate on international energy at the Natural Resources Defense Council in a 2025 article, adding that the fuel “risks slowing decarbonization, raising system costs, and locking economies into avoidable volatility.”

And in the long run, it may not even come to be seen on Wall Street as a questionable investment, according to Cohn. As fuel price spikes continue driving the world toward renewables, fossil fuels may become less and less attractive as investment opportunities.

“There are other very prominent solutions like solar, wind, and batteries, which will mature and continue to see price declines, and so the view that you need gas is increasingly contested,” Cohn said.

This post has been updated to more accurately characterize the nature of BlackRock’s business.

https://grist.org/economics/american-dre.title: The American Dream wasn’t built for climate change
https://grist.org/economics/american-dre.author: Kate Yoder
https://grist.org/economics/american-dre.text:
To Sierra Isley, the American Dream brings to mind a home ringed by a white picket fence. “The house in the suburbs is just what you’re taught growing up,” the 26-year-old said. “You know, that’s what you see on TV.” What she wanted for her life was a bit different from that picket-fence ideal, but she still saw the prospect of buying her first house two years ago as a chance to live out what she called “that big dream that everybody has as a kid.”

Isley and her girlfriend, Jamie, were moving from Philadelphia to Asheville, North Carolina, and found a home they liked, a three-bedroom brick house with lots of natural light and a big tree out front. With some help from their parents, they put down a deposit and got their offer accepted. But when they went to sign the closing papers, a complication got in the way: The house had a huge lien on it. After consulting with lawyers, they decided to break the contract and hunt for an apartment to rent in Asheville.

It was a blessing in disguise. One month later, while Sierra and Jamie were still unpacking boxes and building furniture, the remnants of Hurricane Helene turned Asheville into a disaster zone. The basement of their apartment flooded, but they were luckier than some of their neighbors, whose homes had been destroyed.

Owning a home has long been seen as a cornerstone of the American Dream — a way to build wealth that you could use one day to pay for your children’s education and fund your retirement. That arrangement was always more precarious than it was made out to be. But as fires and floods damage homes and drive up insurance rates, pouring your life savings into a house has become riskier than ever. In a report called “Property Prices in Peril,” the firm First Street projected last year that climate risks could knock nearly $1.5 trillion off the value of American homes by 2055. For some people, the sociologist Rebecca Elliott wrote, “the American dream of homeownership may become a nightmare.”

Grist thanks its sponsors. Become one.

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

Americans are beginning to grasp the threat that climate change poses to their aspirations. According to exclusive polling for Grist from the think tank Data for Progress, 58 percent of likely U.S. voters believe that climate change will hinder their ability to achieve the American Dream over the next 20 years, including 42 percent of Republicans. The survey suggests that people are worried that climate change will increase the cost of living, a concern so widespread that it’s expected to sway the midterm elections on Tuesday.

The irony is that fossil fuels have long been promoted as necessary ingredients for the American “way of life.” Starting a century ago, oil and gas companies led extensive campaigns to tie their products to comfort and prosperity, a narrative that has been repeatedly deployed by politicians and oil industry executives to thwart climate action. President Donald Trump’s administration has often said that efforts to rein in fossil fuels threaten the American Dream. Earlier this year, when the administration scrapped Biden-era rules to cut emissions from cars, along with the Environmental Protection Agency’s authority to regulate climate change, it touted the effort as “restoring the American Dream.”

But the fossil-fueled American Dream is in the process of destroying itself. Greenhouse gas emissions from burning coal, oil, and gas have ushered in a new period of precarity, undermining the promise that each generation can expect a better life than the last. Scientific reports warn that climate change “imperil[s] the quality of life” for communities in the United States, disrupting livelihoods and cultural traditions.

Either Americans decide to reimagine what makes up the American Dream and abandon that oil-soaked version of prosperity, or climate change will dismantle it for them.

The memories of living through Hurricane Helene are still fresh in Isley’s mind. Hauling water from their flooded basement up to the toilet to flush it when the water ran out. Driving to Jamie’s parents’ house in Atlanta, holed up in a room with both of their cats until they couldn’t take it anymore. Coming back to Asheville and cooking meals in the Crock-Pot with disposable liners because even when the water was running again, it wasn’t safe to wash dishes with.

Two years later, Isley browses Zillow for fun, but she looks at homes through a post-disaster lens. “Now I have that fear in the back of my mind — anywhere near a river, or even a stream, if there’s a little bit of water on the map, I’m like, ‘Oh, no,’” she said. Jamie is trans, and after Trump was elected in 2024, the two of them briefly entertained the idea of moving somewhere with more protective policies, like California. But Isley’s mind immediately went to wildfires. Out of the question.

Isley had fled from hurricanes before, when she lived in Florida during college. She thought she’d be safe from them tucked away in the Blue Ridge Mountains. Asheville was supposed to be a “climate haven,” somewhere that would fare better than the rest of the country as the world warmed. Those promises were shattered when almost 14 inches of rain fell on Asheville over three days in September 2024. The French Broad River overflowed its banks, flooding homes and destroying parts of the town’s River Arts District. In western North Carolina, more than 74,000 homes were damaged, and only about 4 percent had flood insurance, resulting in $9.5 billion in uninsured residential property losses.

Home values in western North Carolina have declined since the storm, especially in the hardest-hit counties. Asheville’s average home price shrunk 5 percent over the past year, while the national average increased 1.2 percent.

To some degree, housing markets are already pricing in the risk of increased environmental hazards. Homes within FEMA’s high-risk flood zones sell for 2.8 percent less, on average, than what they would otherwise sell for, according to a 2023 study published in the journal Nature Climate Change. The researchers found that homes exposed to flood risk were still overvalued by between $121 billion and $237 billion, though — and they identified Appalachia as a hot spot of overvaluation, one year before Helene hit. The devaluation of homes in high-risk zones is unfolding unevenly and causing “tremendous social harm,” said Elliott, a sociology professor at The London School of Economics and Political Science.

Homes are billed as a way for people to build wealth, but they can turn into a trap. After Superstorm Sandy devastated New York City and the New Jersey coast in 2012, many homeowners couldn’t sell their houses for enough money to buy a new place, leaving them stranded. Even homes that haven’t seen any kind of devastation are at risk of losing value as more people become wary of living in floodplains, coastal places exposed to storms, and wildfire-prone areas. “Those homes could become, in effect, economically worthless even before they are physically uninhabitable,” Elliott wrote in a study about property values and climate change.

Insurance is meant to offer a measure of safety when taking on a huge debt for a mortgage on a house. Douglas Heller, the director of insurance at the Consumer Federation of America, called it “the safety net for the American Dream.” But insurance rates are part of what’s making homeownership unaffordable for so many. Since 2020, property insurance costs have ballooned almost 80 percent, with the average single-family mortgage holder now paying $209 per month. Homeowners in the riskiest areas are paying substantially more, and many in California have been dropped by their insurers. Home insurance rates are rising faster in the Midwest than any other region, driven by the costs of severe storms.

“We are, for a lot of people, on the edge of a dysfunctional insurance marketplace,” Heller said. The more extreme weather we’re seeing is only part of the story: He argues that the insurance industry has become a “climate opportunist,” using climate change as an excuse to justify excessive rate increases.

People relying on Social Security benefits who own condos around Lake Tahoe are particularly vulnerable to rising rates, said Andrew Engler, the founder and CEO of Rock Rose Risk, who helps people in California protect their homes against wildfire and get their insurance premiums down. They’re facing ballooning homeowners association payments, to share the cost of insurance in a risky wildfire area, on a limited paycheck. If they try to move, their properties are worth significantly less because of the huge HOA bills, Engler said. Economists estimate that rising insurance costs linked to disaster risk have reduced the growth of home prices by more than $40,000 in the most hurricane- and wildfire-prone ZIP codes.

Renting might make you more nimble, but it doesn’t insulate you from these costs. One reason rents are going up is because landlords’ property insurance rates are increasing. “Whether you are a homeowner or a renter, we’re all paying for living under the increased risks of climate change,” said Caroline Nagy, the associate director of housing policy at Americans for Financial Reform. That makes it harder for people to save for a home — if that’s even a good idea anymore.

When Sierra Isley walks around her neighborhood these days, she sees the evidence of Helene all around her — in the form of banners with the slogan “Asheville Strong” and shirts that say “WNC Strong.”

One of the most surprising things about disasters might be the way that people who live through them rise to the occasion and come together. In the aftermath of the Helene, with the power and cell service knocked out, Sierra and Jamie walked all around town, talking to their neighbors to try to learn what had happened. People started congregating at the fire station where there was fresh water.

“It’s hard to put into words what that experience was like, but I’ve never felt more of a community, and really having to lean on my neighbors and feeling like my neighbors were leaning on me,” Isley said.

While the American Dream is usually all about independence and personal freedom, living through a disaster has a way of revealing how people depend on each other. The experience can prompt people to hold tightly to what they have, doubling down on protecting their communities, said Nick Tinoco, a sociology researcher in a doctoral program at the University of California, Los Angeles, who interviewed survivors of the 2018 Woolsey Fire in Los Angeles County. Some of the residents he talked to have taken things into their own hands and organized volunteer fire brigades, and plan to stay behind to defend their neighborhoods during future fires.

As supposedly safe “climate havens” like Asheville experience more disasters, the idea that people can simply move out of harm’s way is losing its grip. “I think we have to just reckon with the fact that we’re going to have to make people secure in the places that they live,” Elliott said.

She thinks it’s time to rethink the bargain of the American Dream — the expectation that so much of a person’s economic future depends on the fate of a single structure. Many young people have begun to define success differently. A poll from Ipsos last year showed that 46 percent of baby boomers associate homeownership with the American Dream, but only 13 percent of Gen Zers do, suggesting that there’s room for its defining features to change.

Sierra and Jamie couldn’t help but wonder what happened to the house they’d almost bought, and they drove over to check it out soon after Hurricane Helene hit. It was still standing, but they couldn’t see if there was any damage hidden inside. “Who knows if it flooded or anything like that, what kind of storm damage it took, and that would have immediately been our problem,” Isley said.

Living through Hurricane Helene didn’t just make Isley relieved she hadn’t bought a house in Asheville. It has shaped what she wants for her life, helping her discover a passion for public health and pushing her to want to work in emergency preparedness. Now she’s applying to schools to pursue a master’s degree in public health.

“I think I owe it to people like me, people in other rural communities who are going to face the same kind of climate change emergencies, to use my skills to help combat climate change and natural disasters,” Isley said. “I just feel such a calling.”

https://grist.org/culture/american-dream.title: Exclusive: Most voters believe climate change threatens the American Dream
https://grist.org/culture/american-dream.author: Kate Yoder
https://grist.org/culture/american-dream.text:
In his inaugural address in January 2025, President Donald Trump promised that “the American Dream will soon be back and thriving like never before.” Apparently, that required undoing policies to tackle climate change: The Trump administration has invoked “the American Dream” as a justification to propose ending mandatory reporting of greenhouse gas emissions, reverse rules to cut emissions from cars, and deregulate coal.

Voters, on the other hand, view climate change itself as a problem for their aspirations. Exclusive polling for Grist from the think tank Data for Progress shows that 58 percent of likely U.S. voters believe that the warming climate will hinder their ability to achieve or maintain the American Dream over the next 20 years — including 42 percent of Republicans.

“We identify a strong concern about climate change as a threat to achieving the American Dream,” said Grace Adcox, a senior climate strategist at the progressive think tank.

Percentage of respondents who say climate change will affect their ability to achieve or maintain the American Dream over the next 20 years, by how much

The survey, conducted this spring with 1,167 likely voters, shows that more than half see the cost of living as the biggest threat to reaching the American Dream today. That tracks with other political polls this year as well as reports on rising inflation. A recent analysis from Investopedia found that the typical elements of the American Dream — owning a home and a new car, raising kids, and other milestones — now add up to a price tag of $5.3 million per household. Only 2 percent of voters surveyed named climate change and extreme weather events as the central threat.

Share of likely voters who named each as the greatest threat today to their ability to achieve or maintain the American Dream

5 percent said they didn’t know.

Why do so many people think climate change will hurt the American Dream, if it’s so close to the bottom of the list of their concerns today? One likely reason is that people are making the connection between climate change and the rising cost of living. More than half of voters are very worried about climate change making life more expensive over the next 20 years, according to the Data for Progress poll. That’s higher than the share of voters who are worried about warmer temperatures, extreme weather, crop failures, and degraded natural areas.

Climate change is already showing up in household bills. A study from MIT earlier this year found that families in the United States were paying between $400 and $900 more each year because of the effects of global warming, from higher utility bills to climbing insurance premiums, with costs above $1,000 in the hardest-hit counties.

Share of likely voters who are very worried about each effect of climate change in the next 20 years, by party

Ahead of the midterm elections this week, climate advocacy groups have been talking about high energy costs, a top issue for voters in battleground districts. They have championed wind and solar as cheaper sources of energy and have argued that Trump’s efforts to block offshore wind farms and slow down other renewable energy projects will drive up costs.

While Trump has been talking about the “Green New Scam” and emphasizing the costs of taking climate action, that message doesn’t appear to be gaining much traction with voters. When participants in the Data for Progress poll were asked to choose between phrases that captured their views on climate policies, very few of them — only 6 percent — opted for “an expensive burden on working people.” Even Republicans didn’t pick that characterization, identifying climate action instead as a distraction from more important issues or a misguided approach based on faulty information. The most common phrase respondents chose to describe their views on climate policies was “a critical step to protect our environment.”

“That really is interesting, and suggests that potentially voters are not going to be as susceptible to the sacrifice or expense framing, despite this top-down use of the rhetoric,” Adcox said.

https://grist.org/indigenous/doge-cuts-c.title: DOGE cuts cost tribes $470M, gutting funding for climate projects
https://grist.org/indigenous/doge-cuts-c.author: Joseph Lee
https://grist.org/indigenous/doge-cuts-c.text:
Every year, Kotzebue, a small city in northwest Alaska, has a three-month window to receive all the diesel fuel it will use throughout the following year. It sits on a gravel spit that juts into Kotzebue Sound just north of the Arctic Circle, and is accessible only by air and sea. Ice keeps freight barges from reaching it for most of the year.

The community relies on diesel for 75 percent of its power, and residents put about 20 percent of their income toward buying it. That’s more than three times the average energy burden for low-income households nationwide.

“We’re pretty much at the mercy of world markets,” Chad Nordlum, who is the energy project manager for the Native Village of Kotzebue, told Grist. “Right now, with the Iran war going on, the diesel prices are very high and we’re locked in to much higher prices than we’ve had in the past. There’s really nothing the community can do about diesel prices, but what we can do is produce our own energy.”

That’s why Nordlum was so excited about a $20 million grant from the Environmental Protection Agency to support a wind energy project. The funding, announced in 2024, was part of a larger $150 million allocation for tribal infrastructure in Alaska. Nordlum says it would have lowered the community’s reliance on diesel to about 40 percent to 50 percent and given the tribe more control over energy and economic decisions.

Grist thanks its sponsors. Become one.

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

But the Trump administration canceled the grant in May 2025. More than a year later, the project remains paused.

That cut was among hundreds of millions of dollars the Department of Government Efficiency pulled from Indian Country, and part of a broader pattern of funding rollbacks and underinvestment in Indigenous communities. Two new reports from the Brookings Institution show that the so-called One Big Beautiful Bill Act killed many of the funding streams established by the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act, while DOGE eliminated another $468 million, about half of which was allocated for environmental and natural resources. Another 11 percent targeted agriculture. Those projects include climate resiliency plans, renewable energy projects, and jobs programs.

According to Brookings, despite historic investments flowing into Indian Country after the pandemic, a massive underinvestment in Indigenous communities continues. Not only is that a violation of the federal government’s trust and treaty obligations to tribes, it is hindering Indigenous efforts to protect the environment and address climate change. The report authors are calling for policy changes that would ensure tribes receive funding, regardless of political winds.

Rob Maxim, who is Mashpee Wampanoag and a fellow at Brookings Metro, said climate and environmental funding is especially crucial for Indigenous communities because they are often the most severely impacted by climate change, especially after years of underinvestment.

Grist thanks its sponsors. Become one.

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

“The actions that the Trump administration is taking are particularly significant, but it’s not totally out of trend with previous administrations,” he said. “And what we wanted to show was that actually this underinvestment is kind of the default for the U.S. rather than a blip.”

The true aberration was the unprecedented levels of funding after the pandemic. That funding, which came under the Biden administration, included over $700 million in climate, energy, and infrastructure funding for tribes. It covered projects like development of climate action plans, food systems analysis, and more. For example, the Hopi Tribe was to receive a $25 million grant to install solar panels for 600 homes. That grant, and the entire $7 billion Solar for All program, were cut.

Maxim says that funding for Indigenous communities is a federal obligation based on treaties and other agreements with tribes and should be standard and irrevocable. “The funding that was flowing to Indian Country was not being done on the basis of race or DEI, and it was absolutely not illegal,” he said. “It was aimed at the promotion of tribal sovereignty and the well-being of tribal citizens and tribal communities, and so that is, you know, an obligation that the U.S. government maintains.”

The White House and the EPA did respond to requests for comment.

Glencora Haskins, a senior research associate and applied research manager at Brookings Metro, said that the administration had targeted funding to tribes, with “tribal” being the most frequently flagged term. “I think that there was a very surface-level view of what a lot of these programs were doing, rather than any deep interrogation of the types of systemic infrastructure deficits that programs were trying to fix,” Haskins said.

In Native communities throughout Alaska, and around the country, energy and infrastructure needs are especially acute because of increasingly frequent and destructive storms, wildfires, and other climate-driven disasters.

Haskins and Maxim recommend that Congress pass legislation that bars the cancellation of grants and contracts for tribes, and stipulates that all funding for Indigenous nations and communities is in service of trust and treaty obligations even if it is from a program with a different stated purpose. They also call for a statutory requirement that money should flow directly to tribes rather than having them seek reimbursement from the U.S. Treasury.

In Kotzebue, Chad Nordlum hopes the political tide will turn enough to get the funding for the wind project moving. In the meantime, he is working on a smaller solar project that he hopes will help alleviate the community’s energy challenges.

“Our main goals are energy security and economic development for the tribe, which is ultimately being able to invest in our own community, help make the lives of people here a little more sustainable,” Nordlum said. “We want our community to continue on into the future. We have to get a handle on our energy prices and availability.”
