https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/8.title: ‘Don’t bring your camera’: Filmmakers face extortion in Lagos
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/8.author: Pelumi Salako
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/8.text:
Lagos, Nigeria – Half an hour after Nurudeen Sanni and his crew began shooting a documentary in Ajah, several men surrounded them and demanded 100,000 naira (about $75) before they could continue filming.

As the crew negotiated, one of the men slapped a crew member who tried to protect the cameras. A scuffle broke out, and the men produced knives and cutlasses. The crew fled, but one member was stabbed in the neck and seriously injured, Sanni said.

“The painful part was that we saw a member of our crew being beaten and we could not do anything,” said Sanni, a 40-year-old sound recordist.

His experience illustrates the risks that filmmakers, content creators, photographers and journalists say they face while working on the streets of Lagos, Nigeria’s largest city and commercial hub.

Men locally known as agberos, a term commonly used for street touts, including some who collect levies from commercial transport operators, have been accused of demanding money from people filming in public and threatening those who refuse to pay.

In August, music video director ThankGod Omori, known professionally as TG Omori, described a night shoot in Ikoyi that was disrupted at about 3am by a crowd demanding money. He said he left the set in the hands of his assistant directors and security personnel, with one scene still unfinished. The following morning, he learned that the men had broken through a gate and injured a security guard who had refused them entry, according to Nigerian newspaper PUNCH.

Actress and content creator KieKie has also described being confronted by men after filming a short video in Obalende. She said they initially demanded one million naira (about $750), but she paid approximately 700,000 naira (about $525) after negotiations. For a separate shoot around Kara, near Berger, she said she spent close to 500,000 naira (about $375) on security.

Stanley Ikechukwu, an analyst at Lagos-based risk advisory firm SBM Intelligence, said creators regularly reported harassment and extortion. He described the situation as a “war on camera”.

Nabila Okino, an analyst at global risk advisory firm Africa Practice, said filmmakers were particularly vulnerable because abandoning a location could mean losing time and money.

“Because filmmakers often need to shoot in specific locations, those demanding money know that there is a cost to abandoning a location and starting again, which gives them leverage to extract cash,” she told Al Jazeera.

For journalists, the consequences extend beyond the cost of filming. Threats and harassment can prevent reporters from covering events and leave some communities and incidents underreported.

When Karina Adobaba-Harry covered the demolition of Makoko in January for News Central, the Nigerian television channel where she works as a camera operator, men in the area approached her crew and demanded money before they could film.

“That was funny to me because we are here to tell your story, you want the government to hear your voice … and you want us to still pay you. That sounded ridiculous to me,” she told Al Jazeera.

Adobaba-Harry said she regularly encountered men demanding payments while reporting. Some left when she explained that she had no money; others threatened to seize or damage her camera. She said reporters had sometimes paid out of their own pockets or used miscellaneous funds provided by their employer.

Ikechukwu said such incidents could affect what the public learns about events in the city.

“A reporter who is harassed or whose camera is seized while covering a flood, a fire, or a protest is not just being robbed, the public is being denied information. It creates self-censorship. Reporters will start avoiding certain areas, and the news will only come from ‘safe’ places,” he told Al Jazeera.

For small production teams, unexpected payments add to the cost of camera rental, location fees, crew wages and transport. Some also budget for security or money they may be pressured to hand over after arriving at a location.

Adobaba-Harry said she had learned to change her demeanour when confronted by men demanding money.

“Sometimes, you have to take up the persona of the agbero so that when they see that you are not as calm, they will leave you,” she said.

She said many victims did not report incidents because they doubted that complaints would lead to action.

“Even if you report, chances that you will find the guys there [are] low. It is seen as a normal thing in Lagos, except if your life is in danger. But if it is just a case of wanting to take money from you, nobody will care,” she said.

Ikechukwu said the risk of being targeted had become another consideration for filmmakers planning a shoot.

“A filmmaker has to budget for ‘settlement’ on top of camera rental, location, crew, and food. It increases cost. It kills spontaneity; you cannot just see a beautiful Lagos moment and capture it. You have to think, ‘Will I be harassed?’” he said.

Okino said authorities should work with community leaders, market and park associations and other local groups to establish clear rules for filming in public spaces and ensure harassment and extortion are not tolerated.

Foreign content creators documenting Lagos have also reported harassment. In September, Chinese travel content creator Xiao Jony shared a video of men confronting him while he was filming at a market in the city.

He said they demanded money and that, over a stretch of about 10 kilometres (6.2 miles), he encountered more than 20 checkpoints where people asked him for payment. It remains unclear who operated the checkpoints or whether they were linked to any government agency.

Okino said such experiences could discourage tourists and production companies from filming in Nigeria.

“They may decide that the cost and risk of producing content in Nigeria outweigh the benefits. At the margin, that could mean choosing neighbouring countries with more predictable and straightforward filming environments instead,” she said.

Ikechukwu said videos showing tourists being harassed could undermine efforts to promote Nigeria abroad.

“We tell the world, ‘Come to Lagos,’ but our own behaviour says, ‘Don’t bring your camera,’” he said.

Gbenga Omotosho, Lagos state’s commissioner for information and strategy, said nobody had the authority to demand money from people taking photographs or filming in public.

“If there are ruffians who are saying that before you can take a picture, before you can walk the street, you have to pay them money, that is not acceptable; that kind of case will be handled by the police, the government will not stand for that nonsense,” he told Al Jazeera.

For photojournalist Jean-Fidele E Ananou, the threats have changed how he documents Lagos. He used to go out daily to photograph what he describes as the beauty of the city. He has since stopped because of concerns for his safety and equipment.

“When you think about the whole thing, it just doesn’t make sense. When you see other people from other countries taking pictures of their country, it just makes you wonder why can’t it be the same here. It’s just a really crazy menace,” Ananou, 31, told Al Jazeera.

“For photojournalists and street photographers, it is getting increasingly difficult to tell stories,” he said.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/8.summary: One crew member was stabbed in the neck and seriously injured, according to a Lagos state official. The threat of harassment could discourage tourists and production companies from filming in Nigeria.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/8.title: The anti-Netanyahu: Can Gadi Eisenkot give the world a different Israel?
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/8.author: Simon Speakman Cordall
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/8.text:
Israeli President Isaac Herzog has tasked the leader of the Yashar (“Straight”) party, Gadi Eisenkot, with assembling a government after elections left no political alliance with a majority in the Knesset.

Eisenkot, a former military chief of staff, will now have 28 days, with the possibility of a 14-day extension, to put together a government before Herzog allows an alternative leader, most likely Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, to try to do the same. If this fails, then new elections would be called.

But as things stand, Eisenkot is unlikely to be able to form a majority government of the kind Netanyahu has relied upon to force through his right-wing policy agenda.

He may have to rely upon the support of at least one of the two parties representing the ultra-Orthodox community, which have often been allies of Netanyahu. It will also be critical for him to persuade some of the more right-wing elements of his opposition bloc to get the support of Arab parties outside the government.

How far he will be able to go in this is uncertain for a man whom observers described as less comfortable with the subterfuge and political guile often attributed to Netanyahu.

Eisenkot emerged as the leader of his volatile opposition bloc just days before the October 27 elections, and even then, messaging from within the coalition appeared confused, contradictory and seemingly absent of any central coordinating figure.

So far, any support from the ultra-Orthodox United Torah Judaism Party, which has broken with its traditional ally Shas in declining to endorse Netanyahu, is likely to come in return for the continuation of the de facto shield afforded to young ultra-Orthodox men who refuse military service.

Support from parties representing Palestinians with Israeli citizenship, even if offered from outside the government, is likely to come in return for at least some meaningful effort to tackle the violent crime wave that has been allowed to engulf Palestinian communities inside Israel.

They will also want the epidemic of violent settler pogroms, which have swept through the occupied West Bank with the seemingly active encouragement of Netanyahu’s government partners – particularly far-right Ministers Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich – to stop.

But Aida Touma-Sliman, a Knesset member from the left-wing Hadash party and a member of the Palestinian-led Joint List, said developments in recent days showed that Eisenkot doesn’t want to rely on Palestinian voters.

“He appears much more willing to compromise with the ultra-Orthodox religious parties, particularly over the law governing military conscription, than risk being seen to depend on Arab support.”

One of the primary issues that whoever leads the country next will have to deal with is Israel’s standing in the United States. Israel’s reputation has fallen to an all-time low among the American public due to the genocidal war on Gaza and the US-Israel war on Iran, which Netanyahu is accused of convincing US President Donald Trump to start.

On the eve of what turned out to be disastrous midterm elections for Trump, he announced an end to the $3.8bn military aid package extended to Israel annually.

Irrespective of the last-minute announcement, Trump’s Republican Party suffered historic losses, and senior officials, including Vice President JD Vance, blamed the war on Iran.

Carnegie Endowment senior fellow Aaron David Miller acknowledged Israel’s reputation in the US was at a low ebb, one that Eisenkot – with his discomfort over the public stage and reluctance to speak in English – would need to address.

“Perceptions of Israel are fairly entrenched. Essentially, the public’s been watching the region in split screen since 2023. On one screen, there’s the carnage inflicted by Hamas on October 7 [2023], and on the other, there’s the death and destruction unleashed by Israel in response.”

“In the eyes of many, Israel is no longer David but Goliath,” he told Al Jazeera. “Ahead of Eisenkot may be the toughest US landscape any Israeli prime minister has to navigate.”

For now, at least, Eisenkot has the backing of the majority of Israelis as much for what he isn’t as for what he is.

Unlike Netanyahu, the well-polished son of a privileged Ashkenazi Jewish family who has nevertheless sought to leverage the grievances of Mizrahi Jews, Eisenkot represents a more genuine package.

Born in Tiberias to parents from Marrakesh and Casablanca, he grew up in the equally remote southern port city of Eilat before joining the army at 18, later rising to the rank of chief of staff. He then followed the well-worn path of senior Israeli military officers into politics, eventually serving in the national unity government assembled by Netanyahu after the Hamas- led attacks on southern Israel on October 7, 2023.

Described by both allies and opponents as both “menschy” (decent) and “schlumpy” (unkempt), Eisenkot’s careworn appearance reflects, at least in the eyes of some voters, his personal connections with the October 7 attacks and subsequent genocidal war on Gaza.

His son Gal was killed in Jabalia in northern Gaza in December 2023 while taking part in the war, followed a day later by his nephew Maor.

In November 2024, another nephew, Yogev Pazy, was killed in Gaza. This has created a persona around Eisenkot at odds with Netanyahu’s family, whose relatively glamorous lifestyle appears far removed from the Israeli public’s current situation.

“He seems very military in his bearing, very steady and a man you don’t always know what he’s thinking,” Yossi Mekelberg, a senior fellow at Chatham House, said. “I think he’s offering what Israel needs above all else right now: a sense of normalcy and the understanding that there are rules that apply equally and to everyone, including the government.”

But this will make little difference for Palestinians. Eisenkot is the architect of the Dahiyeh Doctrine, which advocates the use of disproportionate force and widespread destruction against civilian communities resisting Israeli force. It is far from clear if Eisenkot’s appointment as premier will make any difference to the yawning gulf in rights between Jewish and Palestinian citizens of Israel.

Eisenkot was reported to have expressed resentment at having to sit alongside such far-right figures as Ben-Gvir and Smotrich during his eight-month tenure in the national unity government. But he has nevertheless overseen punishing policies upon both Palestinians and Arabs in neighbouring states.

As chief of staff, Eisenkot oversaw brutal operations against Palestinians in Gaza and the West Bank as well as overseeing extensive air strikes against Iranian targets and arming rebels in Syria.

From 2015 to 2018, years overlapping with his tenure, United Nations figures record about 650 Palestinians killed by Israeli forces or in conflict-related incidents. The toll included 295 deaths in 2018 alone. Among them were 189 Palestinians killed and thousands wounded during the Great March of Return protests in Gaza, including 35 children.

A UN commission later found reasonable grounds to believe that Israeli forces under his command had committed serious violations of international law, some potentially amounting to war crimes or crimes against humanity.

During the 2006 war in Lebanon when Eisenkot is credited with having devised the Dahiyeh Doctrine, Israel killed 1,109 people, about 860 of whom were civilians. There are no numbers for the tens of thousands of people killed under Eisenkot’s tactic in the years since.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/8.summary: Gadi Eisenkot has been tasked with assembling a government after elections left no political alliance with a majority in the Knesset. He will now have 28 days to put together a government before Herzog allows an alternative leader to try to do the same. If this fails, he will be the architect of the Dahiyeh Doctrine,

https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.title: Hossam Hassan sacked as Egypt head coach over ex-wife scandal
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.text:
The Egyptian Football Association (EFA) has dismissed national team coach Hossam Hassan, citing concerns over the image and stability of the national side after a series of controversies surrounding his marital life.

The EFA said on Saturday that it had reviewed recent events and their “negative impact on the positive image and stability” of the national team before deciding to part company with Hassan and his coaching staff, adding that “maintaining stability of the team is top priority”.

Ali Maher, currently in charge of club side Ceramica Cleopatra, was appointed his successor.

The move came three days after Egypt’s Supreme Council for Media Regulation banned Hassan from appearing on media platforms over a case linked to his private life and former wife.

Local media reported lawyers representing Hassan had filed a complaint against his ex-wife, Dina Mostafa, known publicly as “Dan Adam”, alleging forgery of official documents and bigamy.

Those allegations were denied by her representatives.

On the pitch, a 0-0 home draw with Angola in a Nations Cup qualifier in September came under scrutiny after Hassan substituted talisman Mohamed Salah in the 60th minute.

The Trabzonspor forward left the national team camp, and the EFA said he avoids playing on artificial pitches and, therefore, would miss the qualifier against South Sudan that same month, which Egypt won 5-0.

Hassan’s future had already been under scrutiny following a string of disputes after Egypt’s run to the last 16 of the 2026 World Cup, the country’s best-ever performance at the tournament.

The former striker, who took charge in March 2024, also led Egypt to the semifinals of the Africa Cup of Nations before a fourth-place finish.

Hassan, who received a three-match ban from FIFA after criticising the referee following Egypt’s knockout World Cup defeat by Argentina, left the national team after 38 matches in charge, winning 21, drawing 10 and losing seven.

Former Egypt attacker Mido said in September the situation had “gone out of control” and called for officials to intervene.

Maher, 52, will take charge before Egypt’s Africa Cup of Nations qualifying matches against Malawi on November 13 and 17.
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.summary: Hossam Hassan has been sacked as Egypt's national team coach. The EFA said it had reviewed recent events and their “negative impact on the positive image and stability’ of the national team. Hassan's future had already been under scrutiny following a string of disputes.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/8.title: Mapping how France’s protest wave spread across Europe
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/8.author: Hanna Duggal
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/8.text:
France’s protest movement is showing little sign of easing, nearly two months after high school students first walked out over crumbling classrooms.

On Saturday, 146,000 people rallied across the country, including 46,000 in Paris, according to the Ministry of the Interior, while unions put the figures at 250,000 and 75,000.

Turnout was down from previous weeks, but police used tear gas and batons on protesters in Paris and fired tear gas canisters at hundreds of people blocking a road in central Lyon, France’s third-largest city. About 70,000 security personnel were deployed, days after an estimated 575,000 people joined a union-organised rally.

The protests have expanded to cover a range of issues, from high fuel prices to wages and social housing, and in some cases, the demonstrations have been marred by looting and violence. Police have been accused of using excessive force, with officers using barricades, tear gas and batons against protesters.

Al Jazeera maps where demonstrations, including riots, have taken place across Europe.

An analysis of data from Armed Conflict Location & Event Data (ACLED) found that between September 15 and October 30, more than 1,200 protests and riots of 100 or more people took place across France over education, public services and the cost of living.

The movement began in mid-September in high schools, where students complained of overcrowded classrooms, a lack of teachers and crumbling buildings. It soon broadened into protests against the rising cost of living, drawing in trade unions and the “yellow vests” movement, with rioting and looting on the sidelines.

On October 17 alone, more than 500,000 people protested nationwide, according to government estimates.

ACLED CEO Clionadh Raleigh said on October 19 that ACLED had recorded an average of 20.5 demonstrations a day in France over the past five years. “During the current protest cycle, that has jumped to almost 66 a day, more than three times the usual rate,” she said.

Protest cycles typically last about 20 days, or 36 for major movements, Raleigh said. By ACLED’s count, this one had reached 45 days and was still going.

“But the most striking difference is the level of confrontation,” she said. “Almost a quarter of events, 24.2 percent, have been classified as riots, compared to a median of just 1.9 percent in previous cycles. Only the unrest following the death of Nahel Merzouk in 2023 recorded a higher proportion.”

The police response has also drawn criticism. On October 28, four United Nations experts mandated by the Human Rights Council expressed alarm at the “excessive use of force” by French authorities in dispersing the student protests.

“The scale of the arrests and detention, affecting several thousand people, mainly minors, appears disproportionate and deters demonstrators from exercising their freedoms of expression and peaceful assembly,” they said in a statement.

In the northern city of Lille, a teenager lost a hand when a grenade exploded as school protesters clashed with police.

France is not protesting alone. Since mid-September, demonstrations over rising living costs, low wages and a lack of public services have broken out in 30 other European countries, from Portugal to Poland.

Between September 15 and October 30, more than 1,700 protests and riots of 100 or more people took place across Europe, according to an analysis of ACLED data.

Although protests in other countries did not reach the same scale as the rallies in France, they may be a sign of discontent spilling over, Alberto Alemanno, professor of European Union law and policy at HEC Paris Business School, told Al Jazeera last month.

“France is the epicentre of this movement … and there are signs now that this is spreading beyond France,” Alemanno said.

France has led the demonstrations, but protests have also broken out across Europe at the same time, driven by a common thread of underfunded education, rising living costs and unaffordable housing.

According to an analysis of ACLED data, France saw more than 1,200 protests and riots between September 15 and October 30, followed by Spain (173), Italy (160), Germany (70) and Portugal (33).

In Spain, tens of thousands of people rallied in early October after parliament rejected two emergency housing decrees on October 2, dealing a blow to Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez’s minority government.

In Italy, demonstrations over the cost-of-living crisis and unaffordable housing have led to clashes with police.

In Portugal, tens of thousands of protesters marched against the cost-of-living crisis, low wages and an inability to access housing in major cities.

https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/.title: As AI data centres guzzle energy, can we harness their wasted heat?
https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/.author: Nick Clark
https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/.text:
As the rapid growth of AI data centres compounds the world’s energy crisis, engineers in Denmark have found a way to make use of the vast amounts of “waste heat” generated by these centres, which is usually lost to the outside air.

There are more than 12,500 data centres around the world and more are coming online every day, straining global energy infrastructure and resources.

Beyond consuming hundreds of billions of litres of water, these systems not only place a massive demand on the global electrical grid, but are likely to be contributing to global warming on a massive scale as well.

The International Energy Agency (IEA) has reported that, in 2024, data centres used 485 terawatt hours of electricity, the equivalent of 1.5 percent of the world’s total energy supply – or the total electricity generation of Germany.

And this figure will double to 3 percent by 2030, with an exponentially growing proportion driven by AI development. This comes as nations are seeking energy independence and need to drastically cut their CO2 emissions.

Indeed, the United Nations Economic Commission for Europe has warned that the rapid expansion of AI hyperscalers – the large-scale cloud service providers like Google, Amazon and Microsoft – and the vast data centres required to support them – pose a “growing threat to electricity systems worldwide”.

The proliferation of data centres is causing widespread anger. In the Netherlands, police arrested protesters against the construction of a new Microsoft data centre close to Amsterdam on Friday. Meanwhile, Elon Musk has earned the ire of residents of Texas, where he moved his AI and SpaceX operations to take advantage of tax breaks. Texans voted in their first Democratic senator – James Talarico – in nearly 40 years in this week’s midterm elections despite Musk sinking hundreds of millions of dollars into campaigns for the Republican Party.

The Bitten supercomputer, which was launched in May this year at the University of Southern Denmark in Sonderborg, is the go-to AI resource for academic research across the country. It provides the AI computing power required for deep data analysis and complex scientific simulations.

But like supercomputers and AI data centres everywhere, Bitten’s capability matches its power consumption. Twenty-four hours a day, its specialised processors generate extreme amounts of thermal energy as they handle the workload.

Now, instead of just allowing that energy to dissipate like AI centres elsewhere, 100 percent of the waste heat is recovered by advanced liquid cooling technology designed by the Danish engineering company Danfoss. This replaces traditional air conditioning and fans that vent to the outside air.

The new system pumps coolant directly over the high-temperature processing chips, completely absorbing the waste heat. That heat can then be channelled directly into Sonderborg’s municipal district heating network to help the town’s 75,000 residents stay warm.

Kristian Strand, president of Danfoss Climate Solutions, told Al Jazeera that whenever we take a picture or upload a document, we activate processing in a data centre.

“That creates heat which we have to remove,” he said. “With the waste heat recovery system, at the end of the process you basically have a tap of hot water coming out of the data centre. That hot water can then be used not only to heat homes but in industrial processes, too.”

Across the world, a colossal amount of energy from industrial processes just vanishes into the atmosphere. Strand told Al Jazeera that Danfoss calculated heat wasted across Europe in one year could power the entire city of Paris for 48 years, while roughly two-thirds of the world’s energy is expelled as excess heat.

The United States hosts more data centres than any other country by far, currently about 4,000. They draw down 5 percent of the nation’s electricity. Yet the US recovers very little heat because it has nowhere to go.

“We should be building data centres where their heat can be used, not just where land is cheapest,” said Jan Rosenow, professor of energy and climate policy at the University of Oxford.

Scandinavia has been leading the way on capturing waste heat, Rosenow said. “Meta’s data centre in Odense in Denmark recovers around 100 GWh a year, enough for 6,900 homes. And Stockholm in Sweden has been feeding data centre heat into its network since 2014.”

At Danfoss, other potential sources of waste heat are being showcased, from supermarket fridge systems, to factories and wastewater treatment plants.

Its engineers recently replaced two carbon-intensive gas boilers at Sonderborg Hospital with a heat pump system that captures waste heat from medical equipment like MRI scanners, and from temperature regulation systems in operating theatres, wards and corridors.

This heat used to be vented outside via cooling towers. Now, the hospital is energy independent for nine months of the year and can feed heat back into the district heating network, saving significant sums on heating bills.

“There was a very good business case for making this happen,” said Lasse Bo Madsen, head of technical services at Sonderborg Hospital. “The project will pay for itself inside two years, and it means we will be able to spend more money on patient care and new equipment, like scanners.”

According to Kristin Strand, this technology is a huge opportunity to save energy and reduce carbon emissions. “We have a vast untapped source of energy in waste heat,” Strand said. “Putting that energy to use reduces reliance on fossil fuels while also making business sense.”

As the AI boom accelerates and new data centres come online, each demanding enough electricity to power a small city, Danfoss believes the scalability of this new waste-heat technology could help ease the soaring demand that is currently stretching global supply.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/8.title: Saudi Aramco building in Riyadh damaged in ‘attempted’ attack
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/8.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/8.text:
A building belonging to Saudi Aramco in Riyadh has been damaged after an attempted attack, Saudi Arabia’s energy ministry said.

The administrative building was damaged by “falling shrapnel” and there were no injuries or fatalities, Saudi state media reported on Sunday, citing a senior source at the ministry.

Several news agencies reported that a tower belonging to the Saudi oil giant in the King Abdullah Financial District (KAFD) of Riyadh was damaged.

The reports came after the Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen’s Houthis said its air defences had destroyed several ballistic missiles launched by the Iran-aligned armed group towards the kingdom.

Two of the missiles were launched towards Riyadh, while another targeted the kingdom’s Eastern province, Major-General Turki al-Maliki, the coalition’s spokesperson, said in separate posts on X on Sunday.

The coalition also intercepted and destroyed two missiles in the southern region, as well as a drone launched by the Houthis, al-Maliki said.

The Houthis, also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), have escalated attacks on targets in Saudi Arabia since a truce in Yemen’s war collapsed in July.

The Iran-aligned group has carried out attacks on the King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, the Ras Tanura and Rabigh oil refineries, and other airports and Aramco facilities across the kingdom.

At least 13 people were killed and more than 300 wounded in a Houthi strike on the Riyadh airport on October 10.

The attacks come as fighting intensifies across Yemen between the Houthis and government forces, who launched the Dawn of Yemen operation aimed at retaking Houthi-held territory, including the capital, Sanaa, last month.

The Houthi-run Health Ministry spokesperson, Anees al-Asbahi, said on Saturday that 33 people, including eight women and 13 children, were killed after Saudi-led coalition air attacks on the village of al-Shariyah, near Sanaa.

In a post on X, al-Asbahi said at least 39 others were wounded in the attacks on Saturday, which targeted homes, roads, paramedics and civil defence teams in the village, located in the Bani Hushaish district east of Sanaa.

There was no immediate comment from the Saudi-led coalition on the reported strikes. Al Jazeera could not independently verify the reports.

Media outlets affiliated with the Houthis reported on Sunday that various areas of the Shada border district in Saada province have also been subjected to artillery shelling.

Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree earlier claimed that the coalition had carried out 105 air strikes and missile attacks over 24 hours targeting Sanaa and seven other governorates, taking the total number of strikes since the escalation began to 4,369.

On Friday, an attack on a market in Taiz province killed 30 people. The Houthis blamed it on Saudi air strikes, while Yemeni government forces accused the Iran-aligned group of firing a ballistic missile at the site.

According to the United Nations, more than 1,600 people have been killed and almost 300,000 displaced since a 2022 ceasefire collapsed in July after the Houthis announced a blockade of Saudi ports.

In September, the Houthis seized much of Yemen’s Red Sea coast in a lightning offensive, while government forces launched a campaign to reclaim Houthi-held territory in October.

Heavy rain has flooded tens of thousands of displaced people’s tents in war-devastated Gaza, Palestinian authorities said, leaving many without shelter.

Since early Saturday, displaced families have been seen fleeing camps in parts of Gaza City and other northern areas of the territory, as well as parts of central Gaza, after they were inundated by rainwater.

Gaza authorities said about “70,000 tents sheltering tens of thousands of displaced people were flooded on the first day” of rains.

The statement also noted the “collapse of dozens of cracked walls and roofs, which caused injuries”, some of them critical, in various areas of the war-devastated territory.

Palestinian Civil Defence spokesman Mahmoud Basal told the news agency AFP on Saturday his teams had received more than 1,500 calls during the night from residents requesting urgent assistance after their tents were flooded, explaining that the agency “is operating without any equipment or capabilities”.

“We have issued an urgent distress call to the international community and humanitarian organisations to intervene immediately to save hundreds of thousands of displaced people from the flooding of their tents.”

“We cannot face the consequences of this storm on our own,” Bassal added.

https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.title: Is unconditional support for Israel becoming a liability for Republicans?
https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.author: Said Arikat
https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.text:
The sweeping Republican defeat in the November 3 midterm elections may have opened a debate that, until recently, would have been almost unthinkable within the party: whether the United States should fundamentally reconsider its relationship with Israel.

For decades, unwavering support for Israel was a defining feature of Republican identity, sustained by evangelical Christians, the conservative foreign policy establishment, influential lobbying organisations, and a deeply entrenched congressional consensus. Now, following the electorate’s repudiation of Donald Trump and his administration, that consensus is showing unmistakable signs of strain.

The clearest indication came from Vice President JD Vance, who acknowledged in an unusually candid post-election assessment that dissatisfaction with America’s relationship with Israel was among the reasons Republican voters abandoned their party. Identifying four concerns driving former Trump supporters towards Democrats, Vance cited the Iran war, the cost of living and inflation, the principle of putting America first, and, significantly, changing the American relationship with Israel.

His admission was remarkable not simply because of what he said, but because of who said it. As the administration’s second-highest official and a potential Republican presidential contender in 2028, Vance effectively acknowledged that unconditional support for the Israeli government is no longer politically cost-free, even within the Republican coalition.

More importantly, he brought into the open a question Republican politicians have traditionally been reluctant to entertain: whether America’s commitment to Israel continues to serve America’s own interests.

Does this represent a genuine reassessment, however, or merely an attempt to explain an electoral disaster and reposition the party for 2028?

There are compelling reasons to believe that something more consequential is under way. The Republican alliance with Israel has rested on several overlapping foundations: evangelical Christian support, strategic and intelligence cooperation, military interests, and conservative political organisations that have made backing Israel an almost unquestionable test of political loyalty.

But those foundations are increasingly being challenged by a younger generation of conservatives, particularly within the emerging America First movement, who question why American resources and military commitments should be directed towards foreign conflicts while economic pressures mount at home.

Their scepticism does not necessarily reflect sympathy for Palestinians or opposition to Israel’s existence. Rather, it challenges the assumption that American and Israeli interests are automatically identical. Increasingly, these voters want to know why Washington should continue providing extensive military assistance, diplomatic protection, and political support regardless of the policies pursued by the Israeli government.

The wars in Gaza and Iran have brought that question into sharper focus. Israel’s devastating military campaign in Gaza, the resulting humanitarian catastrophe, and Washington’s continued military and diplomatic backing have imposed mounting moral, diplomatic, and strategic costs on the United States. The subsequent confrontation with Iran further exposed the dangers of allowing Israeli security priorities and regional calculations to influence American decisions about war and peace.

Vance’s intervention, therefore, did not emerge from a political vacuum. It reflects tensions that have been developing within the Republican electorate for years. Earlier polling had already identified declining enthusiasm for Israel among younger Republicans, even as traditional constituencies remained considerably more supportive. The Chicago Council’s 2026 survey also found declining Republican favourability towards Israel compared with 2022, although Republicans continued to favour maintaining or increasing military assistance. The picture is consequently not of a party abandoning Israel, but of one increasingly divided over the terms and consequences of the relationship.

That division could become central to the Republican Party’s struggle over its post-Trump future. By identifying dissatisfaction with Israel policy as a factor in the electoral losses, Vance has effectively legitimised a debate that conservative politicians have long avoided. He has also signalled that the issue could become an important point of differentiation among potential presidential contenders preparing for 2028.

For Trump, the contradiction is particularly damaging. He built his political movement around putting America first and ending costly foreign entanglements, yet his presidency has become closely associated with extraordinary support for Benjamin Netanyahu’s government, including military cooperation, diplomatic backing, and confrontation with regional adversaries.

The Iran war has made that contradiction harder to defend. Voters who supported Trump expecting him to prioritise domestic concerns may reasonably question why the United States became entangled in another Middle Eastern conflict, particularly when the consequences include economic uncertainty, higher energy costs, and resources diverted from domestic priorities.

While Trump has acknowledged that the Iran conflict contributed to Republican losses, he has continued defending the decision to launch it. Vance, meanwhile, has been more explicit in recognising the political price of the administration’s foreign policy choices. That difference could become an important fault line within the Republican leadership.

Yet recognising the political costs of the relationship is not the same as changing it. The institutional forces sustaining the US-Israel alliance remain formidable. Congressional Republicans have traditionally supported substantial military assistance, while evangelical organisations, influential donors, lobbying networks, and defence sector interests continue to exercise considerable influence. Beyond domestic politics, the relationship encompasses intelligence sharing, military technology, regional security arrangements, and decades of diplomatic commitments.

Consequently, even an administration persuaded that unconditional support carries electoral risks could find it difficult to translate that recognition into meaningful policy. Changing the rhetoric is considerably easier than changing military appropriations, arms transfers, diplomatic positions, and the strategic architecture underpinning the alliance.

Nevertheless, the midterm results have altered Washington’s political calculations. With Democrats controlling both chambers of Congress, continued military assistance and diplomatic protection will face greater scrutiny. Republicans contemplating their political future must also consider whether defending every decision of the Israeli government remains electorally advantageous, particularly among younger voters and independents whose support increasingly determines national outcomes.

The real test, therefore, will not be what Republican politicians say in the aftermath of their defeat, but what they are prepared to do. Will they support conditions on military assistance? Reconsider automatic diplomatic protection when Israeli policies violate international law? Challenge settlement expansion and annexationist ambitions? And will they recognise that a sustainable regional settlement must address Palestinian freedom, security, and political rights rather than treating them as secondary considerations?

These are the questions that distinguish a genuine reassessment from electoral opportunism.

For Palestinians, the stakes are considerable. A meaningful Republican shift could create political space for greater accountability, a less permissive American approach to Israeli military operations, and renewed pressure for a political settlement grounded in Palestinian rights. But expectations should remain measured. A change in Republican rhetoric does not necessarily translate into a change in America’s strategic priorities, much less an immediate departure from decades of established policy.

Ultimately, the significance of the midterm defeat may lie less in an immediate transformation of American policy than in the erosion of an assumption that has governed Washington for generations: that support for Israel is politically untouchable. The Republican Party now faces a choice: ignore the warning or recognise that its political future may depend, in part, on responding to it.

The alliance is not about to disappear. But the political immunity that has long shielded it from serious scrutiny may finally be eroding. Whether that erosion produces a substantive change in American policy towards Israel remains the defining question of the post-election period.

He cited Iran war, cost of living and inflation, the principle of putting America first, and significantly, changing the American relationship with Israel.

https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.title: There is reason to hope that the Democrats might deliver this time
https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.author: Jonathan Smucker
https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.text:
In the days since the midterm elections in the United States, many commentators have argued that the “blue tsunami” signalled a popular rejection of US President Donald Trump, but not a new love for Democrats. They are right to warn that if the Democratic Party fails to deliver, it will likely face the same kind of anti-incumbent anger in the next election cycle.

I have personally spilled loads of ink arguing that the Democratic old guard’s embrace of neoliberalism is a huge part of what created the crisis conditions that enabled Trump’s rise to power in the first place, and has severely hampered their ability to stop him over the past decade.

But this election cycle was different in remarkable ways. To put it in plain terms, the Democrats started “sucking less” — not all of them, but a lot of them. And this recent demonstration of “sucking less” is what is presently providing me with at least an ounce of hope that the party might actually manage not to blow this historic opportunity.

How did the Democrats “suck less”? First off, there was a proliferation of progressive economic populist candidates who explicitly took on powerful corporations and positioned themselves clearly as fighters for working-class people. The economic populist insurgency within the Democratic Party gained significant ground in this cycle.

Some might wonder, what took so long? For one, it’s easy to forget that the electoral insurgency within the GOP had an eight-year head start on the insurgency within the Democratic Party — and that head start has been enormously consequential.

In the wake of the 2008 financial meltdown, it was, ironically, conservative anti-establishment energy that first captured populist momentum through the Tea Party. With the help of organisations such as FreedomWorks, that energy was quickly channelled into Republican Party primary contests. By 2014, Tea Party activists had unseated GOP House Speaker Eric Cantor and set the stage for Trump.

Nearly three years after the Tea Party kicked off, Occupy Wall Street was the left’s opening salvo in the populist era. By framing a popular class conflict (the 99% vs the 1%) and naming popular villains (Wall Street and big banks), Occupy dramatically changed the national “common sense” about the evils of runaway inequality.

But the grassroots movement was allergic to the electoral realm. Senator Bernie Sanders’ 2016 presidential run brought Occupy’s core message onto electoral terrain, but it wasn’t until the 2018 midterms — with the election of Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (AOC) and “the Squad” — that the left’s capacity for electoral insurgency caught up with where the right already was in 2009.

Since then, independent progressive organisations such as Justice Democrats, the Working Families Party, Democratic Socialists of America, the Sunrise Movement, and countless local and statewide organisations (for example, PA Stands Up and PA United in my home state of Pennsylvania) have been developing their capacity for recruiting and supporting working-class champions to run for office.

This has been a profound development. Over the course of a decade now, in fits and starts, this groundswell of independent grassroots organising has broken the Democratic Party establishment’s virtual monopoly on candidate recruitment. The 2026 midterms demonstrated a significant increase in capacity to run working-class champions for Congress.

And without diminishing the importance of this long-term organisational investment, it is clear that 2026 also saw an organic proliferation of candidates who ran as champions of the working class. This organic proliferation didn’t happen by chance: It was the result of a profound shift in common-sense notions of what constitutes a winning message.

Over the past decade, a growing chorus of voices in Congress and on the campaign trail has taken up the message Bernie originally popularised, arguing for the same reforms and overhauls, from passing Medicare for All and making housing and childcare affordable, to reining in artificial intelligence (AI) and taxing the rich.

But it took a confluence of events to finally start to break into the mainstream of the Democratic Party in the 2026 cycle.

One key event, unfortunately, was Trump winning a second term. An important casualty of Trump’s second victory was the median Democratic voter’s faith in party leadership. The arc of results and consequences from 2016 to 2024 suddenly cleared the fog, exposing a damning narrative about the party leadership’s negligent qualifications when it came to winning elections.

All that stuff they told us about Bernie being “too far left”, all their wisdom about “electability” was nonsense. The acceleration of the party’s already severe bleed of working-class voters in 2024 and its alarming spread to Black and Latino voters exposed the utter bankruptcy of Democratic leader Chuck Schumer’s lauded affluent suburban swing voter strategy.

The next key event was more uplifting, thankfully. In 2025, in a moment when progressive hopes were at their lowest ebb, suddenly Democratic Socialist Zohran Mamdani showed up out of nowhere with one of the most captivating and inspiring mayoral campaigns in US history, winning the Democratic nomination for mayor of New York City, and then the election.

Mamdani’s incredible message discipline centred around one word: affordability. With a discredited party leadership, mostly missing in action, Mamdani effectively filled a leadership and vision vacuum. Meanwhile, Bernie and AOC were crisscrossing the country, filling stadiums and energising the base with their “Fighting Oligarchy” tour.

On the eve of the 2026 midterm season, economic populism had become the only thing on offer, the only thing that seemed to credibly have a chance. Suddenly, a whole lot of Democratic candidates and officeholders were talking about affordability and the working class.

One of the few things party leadership did right in 2026 was not derailing this growing populist message and momentum. So while Schumer and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries remain unpopular, a movement among the rank-and-file and a new crop of economic populist candidates managed to land a coherent and compelling narrative.

An orthodox Marxist might argue that the explanation for the Democratic Party’s failure over the past decade to connect to working-class voters is straightforward: It doesn’t want to bite the hand that feeds it, in other words, billionaires and powerful corporations that provide millions in campaign contributions.

While big money undoubtedly provides significant incentives, I take a perspective more like sociologist Max Weber’s, where the political class has an important degree of “relative autonomy”. Most political operatives genuinely want to win elections, but their ideas about how to do so are constrained and distorted by the elite cultural milieu in which they are embedded.

It’s taken a full 10 years since Trump’s first victory for economic populism to finally break into the elite bubble of the liberal consultant class, or at least to bypass it and finally approach a critical mass of candidates and officeholders in the Democratic Party who grasp how the world has changed, what hardship and precarity most Americans are experiencing, and how to win working-class voters back.

In his 2016 run for president, Bernie was not “ahead of his time”. He was reading the times perfectly. What he was ahead of was an out-of-touch Democratic Party establishment, whose misreading of the times enabled a dangerous authoritarian pseudo-populist to ascend to power and set America’s downward spiralling course for a decade now.

Tuesday’s historic “blue tsunami” was not only the result of Trump’s failures. The 2026 midterm election cycle also saw the start of the remaking of the Democratic Party to be a party that — as Bernie steadfastly exhorts us — fights for the working class.

Yes, sure, Bernie probably would have won the general election back in 2016 and 2020. But more to the point today: Bernie is winning. That is to say, by finally moving towards an economic populist agenda and a commitment to America’s working class, the Democratic Party might just be starting to find its popular voice.

Tuesday’s results do not mean US voters have sworn loyalty to the Democratic Party. But they have given it another chance. A chance to deliver and improve people’s lives. It would be wise and electorally prudent to deliver… bigly.

https://www.wired.com/gallery/best-touch.author: Simon Hill
https://www.wired.com/gallery/best-touch.text:
All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

THE OBVIOUS WAY to keep Jack Frost from nipping at your fingers is to slip on a pair of toasty touchscreen gloves. People have been wearing gloves for centuries, with the shift from mittens to individually wrapped fingers the biggest upgrade in all that time. But traditional gloves don’t play nicely with our smartphones. Sure, you could stab uselessly at the touchscreen before slipping your glove off to use your phone. But wouldn’t you rather snag a good pair of touchscreen gloves?

All these gloves have some material or fingertip technology that works with touchscreens, but some are better than others. I tested each pair in this guide with my phone—I answered calls, browsed the web, and sent text messages—and also considered comfort, grip, and warmth, using them in 30- to 40-degree Fahrenheit weather. These are my favorites.

Updated January 2026: We've added heated gloves from Venustas, streamlined our picks, and updated our suggested settings.

Before diving in, I strongly recommend you increase the sensitivity of your phone’s touchscreen. Here’s how:

On an Android phone: Go to Settings, Display and touch, Touch sensitivity, and toggle on Increased sensitivity. These settings may vary slightly on different Android phones.

On an iPhone: Go to Settings, Accessibility, Touch, and tap Haptic Touch or 3D & Haptic Touch and select Fast. You should also consider tweaking some of the settings in Settings, Accessibility, Touch, and Touch Accommodations.

The Glider Gloves offered the most control and accuracy among the touchscreen gloves I tested. The Canadian manufacturer uses conductive copper in the yarn, so every touch registers. You can tap and swipe with any part of your hand, pinch to zoom, and use all your fingers, not just the tips.

I found these gloves very comfortable, with a soft brushed interior that feels seamless and textured silicone grip sections on the palm and fingers, ensuring your phone won’t slip. The trade-off is that they are not thick, so they won’t be warm enough for extreme cold, and they’re not waterproof, so forget about snowballs. Sizes feel on the small side at first, though they loosen up when you wear them in, and a tight fit allows for maximum typing accuracy.

These are popular gloves, so they do sell out sometimes.

If you prefer knitted gloves, Moshi’s Digits are great. These are very warm and comfortable, with effective touchscreen capabilities so you can use all your fingers and thumbs—I can type quite accurately with these gloves on.

Moshi includes rubber strips in a wavy pattern to enhance grip, which is crucial because the knitted fabric is slippery. Unfortunately, the inner microfleece lining sometimes separates from the knitted outer layer. The weave is also quite loose, and my pair began to fray after I caught a finger on something during a snowball fight. (They’re not great for snowballs either.) If you want them to last, keep them dry and look after them.

If you crave a classic style, these leather gloves from Kent Wang are nice. They come in black, dark brown, and tan, and they look polished enough for the office but can blend in with any outfit. The deerskin leather is wrinkle-resistant, durable, and treated with a touchscreen-friendly layer that the manufacturer promises won’t wear off.

These gloves work well with touchscreens, but it took me some practice to type because of the seams at the fingertips. You will want a snug fit for best results. These gloves are also comfortable and cozy, with a lovely cashmere lining (that explains the price). They can cope with rain or the odd snowball.

Even the most responsive touchscreen gloves can leave you feeling like a clumsy illiterate when you try to speed-type a text, and many phones require a fingerprint scan to unlock. Luckily, you have fingerless options, and these clever fold-over mittens from the Heat Company are my favorite.

They are wind- and water-resistant, with goatskin leather palms and long cuffs to keep you cozy. But what I love about these gloves is the two-fold-back sections, a mitten top to cover your fingers (with a pocket for a hand warmer), and a separate thumb cover, with sewn-in magnets to keep them out of the way when open. I often use my thumb to unlock my phone and both thumbs to type, so the option to only expose my thumbs is ideal. These gloves are decently warm, but if it’s especially chilly, they can be combined with the Merino Heat Tube Liners ($39), which have long cuffs and another pocket for hand warmers.

For colder climates or folks who need toasty hands, heated gloves could be the way to go. I’ve tried a few pairs and have always been disappointed, until I slipped on these gauntlets from Venustas. They have three heat settings, activated by the color light-up button on each glove. The cozy fleece lining is very comfortable, they are adjustable for a tight fit, and they have a nonslip palm. The fingertips work well for tapping and swiping on a touchscreen, but they’re chunky, so typing is tricky. There’s also a plastic clip for joining them together when they're off, so you never lose one.

The big catch is that each cuff has a zipped compartment to store a battery, and you’ll have to remember to charge them. The lowest heat setting can last up to 10 hours, but it wasn’t warm enough for me in the biting wind of my daily coastal walk, and you only get three hours from the high setting.

Some of the touchscreen gloves we tried fell short of a recommendation for one reason or another.

Verloop Twist Knit Touchscreen Gloves for $35: Gloves don’t have to be gray, as these vibrant, eye-catching, fun color combinations prove. I tested the Twist Knit Touchscreen Gloves in magenta and cobalt, and they proved an instant hit with my daughter. The tips of the thumb, index finger, and middle finger are touchscreen-friendly. She found it easy to swipe around and even type with some practice, but you need a snug fit to type at speed and use your thumbs. These gloves are cozy, with ribbed cuffs, and they are machine washable but not waterproof.

Black Diamond Lightweight Screentap Gloves for $35: Thin gloves can maintain your dexterity but still provide some warmth. There’s a suede patch on the palm that acts as great padding for when you hold an umbrella or steering wheel. It’s easy to use the touchscreen with my thumb, so these are great for one-handed use, and I can type at close to normal speed. These gloves also have an elasticated wrist for a snug fit and a plastic clip for joining them together when they're off, so you never lose one. They’re not especially warm, and they feel a little slippery.

Canada Goose Mixed Media Gloves for $175: Slipping on these gloves feels heavenly because the brushed inner lining is incredibly comfortable. They are warm too, with a soft shell and leather exterior. Sadly, the touchscreen performance is disappointing. You can type with any finger or your thumb, but it takes more determination than with other gloves on our list. I became fairly capable with my thumb after some practice, but using my index finger was hit-and-miss, with touches frequently not registering.

Marks and Spencer Knitted Gloves for $20 or £10: A gift from my in-laws, these knitted gloves from reliable UK retailer Marks and Spencer are pretty good. They keep your hands cozy but also have special touchscreen pads on the index finger and thumb tips. I can swipe, tap, and type reasonably well with these gloves on.

Graphene-X All Rounder Bio-X Gloves for $119: With a classy look, high-tech graphene material on the back, and plant-based bio leather on the palm and fingers, these gloves are certainly unique. They're comfy too, but they completely failed to keep my hands warm. The touchscreen material works, and I had no trouble tapping and swiping, but the joins and squared-off shape on the fingertips made it almost impossible to type accurately.

Trendoux Winter Gloves for $12: These affordable gloves have tips on the index fingers and thumbs that work with touchscreens, but the seams on the inside make them tricky to type with and a little uncomfortable. They are slim, so not especially warm, but the finish is smooth and water-resistant, with rubbery anti-slip dots on the palm and other fingers. I like the clip for snapping them together when you take them off.

Maybe you already have non-touchscreen gloves you love, or you simply don't fancy any of our picks. There are a couple of alternatives worth considering:

A stylus: It may seem old school, but a stylus allows you to use your phone accurately without taking your gloves off and will work with any smartphone or gloves. The Bargains Depot 2-in-1 Stylus ($9) worked well in our testing.

A handwarmer: If you brave the cold gloveless or use one of our thinner picks above, you might want to have a rechargeable handwarmer waiting in your pocket. My favorite is the VQ Rechargeable 10,000-mAh Power Bank Hand Warmer (£30), but it's only available in the UK. Folks in the US can find a ton of similar options on Amazon.

https://www.wired.com/story/macbook-pro-.title: The Apple MacBook Pro M5 is on Sale, and a Top MacBook to Buy Right Now
https://www.wired.com/story/macbook-pro-.author: Luke Larsen
https://www.wired.com/story/macbook-pro-.text:
All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

LAST MONTH, APPLE refreshed the 14-inch MacBook Pro with the latest M6 chip. It's powerful, has great battery life, and the mini-LED screen is bright. There are all kinds of great attributes about this laptop, but you probably shouldn't buy it. At least, not right now.

While the updated M6 is a perfectly capable laptop in its own right, it fits a bit awkwardly into the current lineup of MacBooks. It's identical to the previous-gen M5 model, which came out in late 2025. But here's the problem: Despite having the exact same laptop specs (save for the chip difference), you can currently get the M5 for $200 less on Amazon and Walmart.

If you're thinking that upgrading from the M5 to the M6 must be worth $200, I'm not so sure. The M6 comes with two additional CPU and GPU cores, which is the origin of most of its gains. While that's not nothing, it's one of the smaller gen-over-gen Apple Silicon performance bumps in the past six years. The main difference is in AI performance, thanks to the second 16-core Neural Engine and faster memory bandwidth on the M6. In day-to-day work—or even in content creation workflows—I just don't think the difference will be very noticeable between the two models. That's especially true since the base 14-inch MacBook Pro isn't a true pro laptop in terms of performance. It uses the same M5 chip that's in the MacBook Air and iPad Pro, after all. The only other real difference is in wireless connectivity, where you get the bump to Wi-Fi 7 with the M6 model.

If you're going to buy the 14-inch MacBook Pro M5, though, you should also be considering the 15-inch MacBook Air. The main difference between these two laptops is the quality of the display. The mini-LED panel on the MacBook Pro is much brighter and more colorful, allowing for some very impressive HDR performance. It also has more ports, such as HDMI and an SD card slot. My favorite small feature is its USB-C ports on both sides of the laptop, allowing for charging from either direction.

The 15-inch MacBook Air is actually on sale today, too. The model with 16 GB of memory and a terabyte of storage is at its lowest price since June: $1,549. That's $150 off Apple's retail price.

So, whether you opt for the thinner 15-inch MacBook Air M5 or the 14-inch MacBook Pro M5 with its better screen, you have great deals to enjoy. The same just can't be said as of now for the M6 MacBook Pro.

https://www.wired.com/story/world-models.title: World Models Will Soon Be Inescapable. Here’s What You Need to Know
https://www.wired.com/story/world-models.author: Reece Rogers
https://www.wired.com/story/world-models.text:
IT’S 2016, AND you’re wandering around the neighborhood at dusk. On the prowl, you’re swiping on a smartphone to catch that elusive Snorlax and grow your collection in Pokémon Go. You, alongside hundreds of millions of other players, are enjoying a mixed-reality game built around lovable characters. What you don’t realize is that these scans of your environment will one day help robots navigate obstacles and interact with objects.

Niantic, the creator of Pokémon Go, sold the game last year and pivoted hard into one of Silicon Valley’s buzziest AI topics right now: world models. “We’re very much about reconstructing the real world,” says Brian McClendon, Niantic Spatial’s chief technology officer. He hopes to leverage its trove of world data to build replicas. Unlike the text-based nature of large language models, world models use visual inputs and can generate digital environments that simulate physics.

This software is poised to seep into everyday life, without you necessarily ever interacting directly with world models. 2027 could be a major year for the expansion of home robotics and driverless cars, both of which are bolstered by advances in world models. It’s time to better understand how these bots think.

“So with a language model, you have a sentence, and it will predict the next word in the sentence,” says Oliver Cameron, the CEO of Odyssey, an AI lab focused on world models. “With a world model, you give it a visual state of the world, an image, and it will then predict the next visual state of the world.” These 3D generations can be used as digital training grounds. “They’re simulations, but they look and feel real,” he says.

McClendon sees these world models as helping robots practice without physical movement or being in intended environments. He says someone could take photos of where the robot is intended to function, generate a 3D model, and then let the software run “millions of simulations” to train the robot on the space’s parameters.

It’s not just humanoid robots that could use simulated practice; driverless cars also improve using world models. Without a human behind the wheel, split-second software reactions are paramount.

“Importantly, a world model must be able to react to the actions that we take in the world, and so it must understand physics, cause and effect, and how other objects and people change their actions in response to our own,” says Jamie Shotton, chief scientist at Wayve, which builds world models designed for cars.

Wayve’s generative world model is powered, in part, by dashcam footage. The startup uses it to recreate hazardous roads and other unsafe conditions that would not be practical to test in real life.

Beyond physical applications, developers are also analyzing how world models could impact video games. Since physics and 3D rendering are core to video games, major players like Tencent are investing in their own world models.

You can expect large AI companies, like Google, to keep boasting about their latest world-model improvements. Investors are also throwing money at insurgent big names in computer science that are turning their attention to the technology. Yann LeCun, Meta’s former chief AI scientist, raised over a billion dollars recently to fund his Advanced Machines Intelligence startup. Additionally, famed Stanford computer scientist Fei-Fei Li launched a startup in 2024 called World Labs, which AMD acquired this year for over $8 billion.

Even if you plan on avoiding autonomous cars and domestic bots altogether, world models are already warping the labor market behind the scenes. To simulate our physical world, AI labs need real people to record it. Earlier this year, I strapped an iPhone to my forehead and recorded hours of videos in my apartment. I recorded my hands folding laundry, washing dishes, and pouring Diet Coke, selling the video data through an app for a fairly measly payout. As more companies attempt to build better world models, even more gig work may demand this kind of data collection.

Between chasing virtual monsters in 2016 and selling videos of my chores in 2026, these systems are ingesting more and more of my physical life. Now I can’t stop picturing the digital ghost of some humanoid robot trapped inside a simulation of my bedroom, endlessly folding my boxers with its metallic claws—getting slightly better with every pass. I’m sorry I didn’t tidy up first.

https://www.newscientist.com/article/259.title: Antipersonnel mines have returned in Ukraine and now threaten the world
https://www.newscientist.com/article/259.author: David Hambling
https://www.newscientist.com/article/259.text:
Antipersonnel (AP) mines seemed to be on the way out in 1997, when 122 countries signed the Ottawa Treaty to ban them. But in 2026, such mines are making a comeback.

“These things are both cheap to produce and offer a level of sophistication that actors couldn’t hope to reproduce for a hundred times the price only a few years ago,” says Seán Moorhouse, an explosive ordnance disposal consultant.

How Ukraine became a drone factory and invented the future of war

AP mines come in two forms. Blast mines, weighing 100 grams or less, are typically scattered by aircraft. Activated by pressure, blast mines are designed to maim. Larger fragmentation mines, laid by combat engineers, have tripwires and spray lethal fragments in all directions.

https://www.statnews.com/2026/11/08/hear.title: STAT+: Why the latest heart drug failures should make us all more skeptical of AI hype
https://www.statnews.com/2026/11/08/hear.author: Matthew Herper
https://www.statnews.com/2026/11/08/hear.text:
The next time someone tells you that artificial intelligence, or any other new technology, is going to cure every disease, point them to the effort to fight heart attacks and strokes, which together are the largest killer in the developed world.

Because again and again, pharmaceutical researchers have learned the same hard lesson: technologies that were supposed to speed new medicines to patients have fallen short. Two studies presented Saturday at the annual meeting of the American Heart Association are a perfect example. A new understanding of genetics was supposed to increase the odds of success – and did anything but.

One study showed that a Novartis drug, pelacarsen, had no effect on the rate of heart attacks and strokes despite lowering a substance in the blood called lp(a), which genetics said should  reduce cardiovascular risk. Another large study, from Novo Nordisk, of an anti-inflammatory targeting a protein called IL-6 also showed no benefit.
