https://fortune.com/2026/11/08/ceo-four-.title: A CEO gave his employees Fridays off. Three years later, revenue is up about 160%
https://fortune.com/2026/11/08/ceo-four-.author: Bilin Lin
https://fortune.com/2026/11/08/ceo-four-.text:
In late 2022, Jake Kurtz, founder and CEO of Tampa-based social media agency Brick Media, wanted a better work-life balance. He had a wild idea: What if everyone worked just four days a week?

After seeing European companies experiment with shorter workweeks on social media, he launched a 90-day pilot in January 2023, giving employees Fridays off without cutting their salaries. By April, he had made the schedule permanent.

Nearly four years later, Brick’s revenue has grown dramatically. According to figures the company provided, revenue jumped 73% in 2023, another 39% in 2024, and 8% in 2025. Compounded, that’s roughly 160% growth in three years.

Kurtz believes some of that success traces back to the four-day workweek, though he doesn’t claim the schedule alone explains it. He bets that giving employees a reason to stay makes the company more efficient and more competitive, even as workplace researchers say the four-day week has faded from the hybrid-work conversation and some leaders who tried it have dialed it back.

At Brick, employees work four nine-hour days, Monday through Thursday. That’s a 36-hour week, four hours short of the traditional 40, with paid lunch breaks included. Employees are still considered full-time and eligible for benefits.

That puts Brick between a compressed 40-hour week and the 32-hour model some researchers advocate. At Fortune‘s Workplace Innovation Summit in May, University of Georgia psychology professor Malissa Clark argued that the point of a four-day week is to cut eight hours, not cram 40 hours into four days.

Brick’s schedule also contrasts with the long hours common in the related public relations field. Muck Rack’s State of PR 2026 report found that 55% of PR professionals surveyed had worked more than 40 hours the previous week.

Social media doesn’t exactly take weekends off, but Kurtz said clients have been surprisingly understanding of the arrangement, and most content shoots, meetings and other work can be planned ahead of time.

Employees still occasionally handle small tasks on Fridays or weekends, which he described as taking “five minutes here and there.” He estimated that more serious emergencies requiring several hours of work happen roughly once or twice a quarter. In those cases, nonexempt employees are eligible for overtime if they work more than 40 hours in a week, and the company brings in freelance contractors when needed.

The rule he goes by: Don’t bury employees in work.

Brick served 56 clients in all of 2022, compared with 85 in just the first half of 2026, according to Kurtz. A social media manager typically handles six or seven clients, with seven the upper limit.

Once employees approach that threshold, Brick hires more people instead of piling more work on existing staff. That’s one reason revenue has grown so quickly. It’s also why profit margins have stayed roughly unchanged since 2022, Kurtz said, as payroll has risen alongside revenue.

Employees also work from home most of the time. Only one of the four working days requires a trip to the office.

For Kurtz, keeping employees happy is as much a business strategy as a cultural one.

“If I can keep people here longer, and they like their job, and they’re communicating with similar people all the time, it just makes the business a lot more efficient,” he told Fortune.

Experienced employees don’t need everything spelled out. Kurtz said colleagues who have worked together for years can sometimes resolve something in a two-minute hallway conversation that might otherwise take 30 minutes.

He believes that efficiency translates into better client relationships and, ultimately, more business. Of the 20 new leads Brick received in October, 16 came from referrals, according to Kurtz.

The company’s resignation numbers suggest employees are increasingly willing to stay. Brick recorded six voluntary departures in 2022, before the schedule change, compared with two in 2023, two in 2024, three in 2025, and none so far in 2026, according to figures provided to Fortune. Its workforce has grown from 15 employees at the end of 2022 to 25 today.

Asked whether Brick could have achieved the same success with employees onsite five days a week and working frequent overtime, Kurtz said, “No, I really don’t… I think people would leave Brick Media for like a $5,000 raise.” He said he knows some employees have had better offers and chosen to stay.

“People have a hard time leaving the four-day schedule once they experience it, because they start to realize that life is way more than just the salary,” he said.

It’s the same case ThredUp CEO James Reinhart made on Clark’s panel at the Fortune summit, where he warned that companies sticking with five-day weeks will lose the competition for top talent.

For Andrea Echeverry, Brick’s director of client experience, who has been with the company since before the schedule change, switching to four days hasn’t meant doing less work.

“I think we have just found more ways to be more efficient with our time,” she told Fortune.

She doesn’t mind squeezing the same workload into four longer days. In fact, she prefers it. Echeverry said “hustle culture has played a role,” explaining that people her age are still willing to work long hours but take a different approach to the traditional “work hard, play hard” mentality.

She is a working mother whose husband also works full-time, and Fridays are now for spending time with her child and running personal errands.

To Echeverry, it’s part of a generational shift in attitudes toward work. Rather than accept traditional workplace arrangements simply because previous generations did, she believes younger workers are more willing to question the norm.

She isn’t alone in ranking balance over pay. In Randstad’s global Workmonitor 2026 survey, 46% of workers named work-life balance as their main reason for staying in their job, compared with 23% who cited competitive pay and benefits.

“We’re sort of like redefining work-life balance,” she said.

Kurtz doesn’t think every company needs to give employees Fridays off. Instead, he advises other CEOs to “think about what would make your employees want to work at your company.”

“I just think that there’s a happy middle ground where you can still have a really good life and a really good business,” he said. “And if you can also extend that to your employees, then it’s not only a feel-good thing for the culture; it’s actually a business advantage that your competitors won’t have.”
https://fortune.com/2026/11/08/ceo-four-.summary: Jake Kurtz, founder and CEO of Tampa-based social media agency Brick Media, launched a 90-day pilot in January 2023. Nearly four years later, Brick’s revenue has grown dramatically.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/08/france-fo.title: Unrest in France looks like a ‘pretty big foreshadowing’ to economists nervously eyeing national debt at 126% of GDP
https://fortune.com/2026/11/08/france-fo.author: Eleanor Pringle
https://fortune.com/2026/11/08/france-fo.text:
When U.S. markets watched as Paris metaphorically imploded just weeks ago, the consensus reaction was: “Let’s not do that.”

Unrest ripped through the French capital after protesters initially highlighted failings in the public school system. The action snowballed into widespread expressions of dissatisfaction with the cost of living and job prospects.

The macroeconomic health of the European nation is not in great shape: unemployment was 8.3% in Q2, real GDP growth was 0.4%, and wage growth was 1.7% at the national level. And underpinning it all is public debt, currently at 116% of GDP, with 30-year bonds topping 5.4% at the time of writing.

And the U.S. bond market, flirting with a wrap on the wrist for its own policymakers presiding over mounting debt, stalled. In fact, 10- and 30-year Treasury yields even declined.

“There’s a reason that the U.S. has pulled back a little bit in the last few weeks [and] why France has not,” Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union, told a Bipartisan Policy Center (BPC) event last week. “It’s a couple of key indicators that differentiate us from France and suggest … that we still have a little bit of room to have these debates now, in the context of a K-shaped economy.

“We’re at about 100% debt-to-GDP; they’re at 120% debt-to-GDP. They are further along that crisis curve, and they are growing at about 0.5%. We’re growing at just over 2%. That’s a pretty big difference. ”

While economists largely agree that policymakers are perhaps naive in their hopes to simply grow the U.S. out of a debt crisis, starting from a point of strength rather than stagnation gives the economy a better chance of rebalancing its debt-to-GDP ratio.

But Long added that France also differs from the U.S. in that the former has exhausted much of its revenue-generating capacity through taxes. Per the OECD, the “tax wedge” (the difference between labor costs to the employer and the corresponding net take-home pay of the employee) for French workers is 47.2%, according to its most recent data. The U.S., on the other hand, is down at 30%.

“It’s certainly not easy to raise taxation in the U.S., but from a financial world perspective and the bond market perspective, there’s a lot more room to experiment and to grow in the United States than there is in France,” Long added. “To me, the biggest warning sign from France is really not just the K-shaped economy effect, but the generational effect that’s going on and to see young people really driving this latest protest … from the disparities that they’re seeing generationally, and that seems like a pretty big foreshadowing [of] what we could see here as we creep towards 120% debt to GDP.”

As with any debt, the question of repayment isn’t if but when—and that’s the question budget experts are asking the public and politicians to think about.

Phil Swagel, the director of the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office, said policymakers have a series of choices to make: How they might prepare for growth to slow if spending is cut, which forms of tax to explore, and so on.

“The other set of choices that you can think about with the deficit is about which generation is paying, so the longer we wait to make changes, that means some generations are … missing out on their share of the burden of the adjustment,” Swagel told the BPC event, “and then who within each generation will pay a tax.”

He explained: “The longer we wait means some generations, in some sense, don’t share in the burden of the adjustment. Then, who within each generation is affected? I think there’s a societal consensus it will be progressive, not in the political sense, but in the sense that households with relatively high lifetime incomes will have more of a share of the adjustment. But that’s a societal preference, and there’s lots of room for disagreement in there.”

https://fortune.com/2026/11/08/social-se.title: ‘No vote, no warning, just plain math’: Social Security is six years from an automatic 22% cut—and most Americans have no idea
https://fortune.com/2026/11/08/social-se.author: Lena Borrelli
https://fortune.com/2026/11/08/social-se.text:
More than one in five Americans don’t know that their Social Security checks could be cut by roughly 20% in about six years, according to a recent TIAA survey on Social Security.

The program’s retirement trust fund, which pays benefits to retirees and survivors, is projected to run out of reserves in the fourth quarter of 2032, according to the 2026 Social Security Trustees Report. After that, incoming payroll taxes would cover only 78% of scheduled benefits. The resulting 22% cut would apply across the board, including to people already collecting.

“Insolvency is a slightly misleading word for what the Trustees are projecting,” says Martin Mulyadi, YHB Endowed Chair in Accounting and Professor of Accounting at Shenandoah University. Payroll taxes keep flowing after 2032, he notes: “Social Security is not running out of money in 2032. It is running out of savings.”

The stakes are large. Social Security pays monthly benefits to more than 71 million people, and it provides the majority of income for 43% of seniors, according to AARP. The Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget (CRFB) estimates that a 22% cut would cost a typical dual-income couple retiring in 2033 about $16,900 a year.

CRFB has warned that the program is “on a collision course toward insolvency,” and Fortune has reported that its finances haven’t looked this bad since 1983. The alarm grew louder after the trustees confirmed the 22% cut in June.

“America has a 25 trillion dollar problem,” says Michael Liner, a disability attorney and founder of Liner Legal, a law firm that specializes in Social Security disability benefits. “The gap between what Social Security has promised and what it can actually afford to pay.”

The trustees now put that 75-year gap even higher, at $29.3 trillion in present value, up from $25.1 trillion in last year’s report. If nothing changes, Liner says, the cut arrives automatically: “No vote, no warning, just plain math.” For many retirees, he adds, it will be “the difference between getting by or not.”

Social Security is funded mainly by payroll taxes. For decades, those taxes exceeded what the program paid out, and the surplus built up reserves in two trust funds: the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance (OASI) fund for retirees and survivors, and the Disability Insurance (DI) fund.

That changed in 2021, when the retirement fund’s costs began exceeding its total income, according to the Congressional Research Service. Reserves have been covering the difference ever since.

“In 2025, Social Security took in about $1.45 trillion and paid out about $1.61 trillion, and reserves covered the gap,” Mulyadi says.

The disability fund is in better shape; the trustees don’t project it running dry at any point in the next 75 years. If Congress legally merged the two funds, combined reserves would last until 2034 and then cover 83% of benefits, according to CRFB. That would require a change in law, and it wouldn’t close the underlying shortfall.

The public has noticed. In a June 2025 survey, just 36% of Americans told AARP they were confident in Social Security’s future, the lowest level since 2010.

Much of the pressure is demographic. Social Security now serves roughly twice as many beneficiaries as it did in 1980, when about 35.5 million people collected. Lower birth rates mean fewer workers paying in, retirees are collecting for longer, and declining immigration has shrunk the pool of workers paying payroll taxes.

Inequality plays a role, too. Payroll taxes apply only to earnings up to a cap, $184,500 this year, and high earners’ pay has grown faster than everyone else’s. The share of total wages subject to the tax fell from almost 87% in 1984 to roughly 83% today, according to Roosevelt Institute research reported by CBS News.

“The Social Security trust fund is under strain because Congress has failed to update the program for the economy we actually have,” said Elizabeth Wilkins, CEO of the Roosevelt Institute, a progressive think tank. “Too much income now flows to the top, where it escapes Social Security taxation.”

The last time Social Security came this close, Congress acted. The 1983 amendments gradually raised the full retirement age from 65 to 67 and, for the first time, subjected some benefits to federal income tax.

“We’ve had two instances in our history where it was suggested Social Security was going to go insolvent,” says Ernie Wingard, an advisor at Capital Choice Financial Group, “and in both of those instances, at the last minute, Congress was able to come to an agreement that saved it.”

That 1983 fix was designed to keep the program solvent for 75 years. If the retirement fund runs dry in 2032 as projected, it will have lasted about 50.

Lawmakers have plenty of levers. Options modeled in the American Academy of Actuaries’ Social Security Challenge tool and in Social Security Administration analyses include:

“Any fix has to close that gap through some mix of more revenue, such as a higher payroll tax rate or a higher cap on taxable earnings, and slower benefit growth, such as a later full retirement age or changes to the benefit formula,” Mulyadi says. “Each option has trade-offs, and the longer Congress waits, the larger each adjustment has to be.”

The fight is over the mix. In a debate covered by Fortune, two economists who disagreed on whether to phase out Social Security still agreed that wealthy Americans would have to pay more. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, meanwhile, argued in June that economic growth can shore up the program without benefit cuts.

“This is absolutely something that can be fixed,” says Nancy LeaMond, AARP’s executive vice president and chief advocacy and engagement officer. “Congress has hundreds of tools in its toolbox to strengthen Social Security and fill that gap of 20 percent or so without cutting the payments that Americans have earned for a lifetime of hard work.”

“This should be a wake-up call: Congress needs to act,” AARP CEO Myechia Minter-Jordan said in a June statement. “Americans have worked hard and paid into Social Security their entire lives, and they deserve to count on it when they retire.”

Whatever lawmakers choose, they have about six years to choose it.

For households, Mulyadi recommends planning with a range rather than a single number. “Log in to your my Social Security account at ssa.gov, look at your projected benefit, and test your retirement budget at about 75 to 80% of it,” he says.

“If the plan still works, a cut is an inconvenience,” he says. “If it doesn’t, you still have time to save more, work a little longer, or rethink when to claim.”

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/08/france-p.title: In pictures: France protests draw 146,000 as clashes erupt for fourth straight weekend
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/08/france-p.author: Jack Sommers
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/08/france-p.text:
France’s Interior Ministry counted 146,000 demonstrators nationwide Saturday, including 46,000 in Paris, as protests entered a fourth consecutive weekend.

Police used tear gas during clashes at the end of the Paris march, while authorities reported at least 360 arrests nationwide.

Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu is due to meet labor and employer representatives Monday to discuss wages and purchasing power.

Protesters clashed with police in France on Saturday as demonstrations over living costs and public services entered a fourth consecutive weekend and drew students, trade unions and members of the revived “Yellow Vest” movement onto the streets.

The country’s Interior Ministry counted 146,000 demonstrators nationwide, including 46,000 in Paris. A youth union alliance put attendance at 250,000 nationally and 75,000 in the capital. At least 360 people were arrested across the country, AFP reported, citing a ministry tally.

Police used tear gas against people throwing projectiles as the main Paris march ended at Place de la Nation, per AFP. Garbage cans were set alight as protesters and police clashed in several cities, according to Le Monde.

Police blocked a separate, banned Yellow Vest gathering at Place de la Concorde and arrested two movement leaders, Le Monde reported.

The Yellow Vests emerged in 2018 in opposition to fuel-tax increases, before broadening into a movement protesting high living costs and the policies of President Emmanuel Macron.

The turnout was lower than on the previous three weekends. It was also below union-led demonstrations on Nov. 5, when the Interior Ministry counted 575,000 people nationwide.

The protests began in late September with high-school students demanding better conditions, before university students and unions joined.

This weekend’s protests come after French lawmakers rejected the revenue section of the 2027 budget, as the government wrestles with addressing public anger while trying to rein in its finances.

The government’s original proposal now goes to the Senate, which is scheduled to begin debating it Nov. 20.

Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu is due to meet labor and employer representatives Monday to discuss wages and purchasing power.

https://insideclimatenews.org/news/08112.author: Story and photos by Keerti Gopal
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/08112.text:
Second of two stories about the effort to support Lahaina fire survivors’ health in the long, hard aftermath. Read the first story, about the Maui Wildfire Exposure Study, here.

LAHAINA, Hawaiʻi—As Mikey Burke walked into her acupuncture appointment on a Wednesday morning in May, she felt the energy shift, just as she always does.

Noelani Ahia, 51, an acupuncturist and Hawaiian healer, greeted Burke, 42, with a smile and a hug, and led her away from the sunlit, open-air courtyard of the Lahaina Comprehensive Health Center and into a dark room, walled in with dividers and empty except for a single bed, a chair and a few small tables. As they settled in, they spoke about Lahaina.

Burke, a mother of four, has been going to the local health center since her home burned down three years ago in the deadliest U.S. wildfires in more than a century. Sometimes, it feels like these appointments are the only time she can truly breathe.

“I don’t think people realize how hard a time people are still having,” said Ahia, who directs Maui Medic Healers Hui, a community organization that operates out of the state-run center. “Pretty much no one is fine.”

“And we’re almost worse off now than we were right after the fires,” Burke replied.

“Can you say a little bit more about that,” Ahia asked, softly.

Burke’s appointment was one day before a construction crew would pour the cement foundation of her family’s future home, and the same week that the Maui Wildfire Exposure Study might be shutting down for good.

As she started to speak, Burke fought back tears.

“The fire was a point in time,” she began, her voice breaking as she laid out a chronology that disaster survivors know all too well.

In the immediate aftermath, the first, most acute trauma was that everything was gone, she explained. But now there’s a slower, unrelenting ordeal of all that has fallen apart since.

It’s not just about the destruction of her family’s house, which she’d fought for years to find and secure. It’s her family’s mental health, the loss of friends and neighbors who were priced out and moved away, the fights to address water access, regain local control of land rights, advocate for her children’s Hawaiian immersion school and protect her people’s ability to be Hawaiian in this place that has been taken over by colonizers and corporate interests again and again. She and her neighbors have to be strong for every battle. Everything feels too important; nothing can fall through the cracks.

It was in this building that Burke found out about the Maui Wildfire Exposure Study, a University of Hawai‘i research project both quantifying the health impacts of the wildfires and helping survivors navigate them. Burke participated in MauiWES with her husband and four boys, and it was through the study that she learned that her twins, then just 10, were showing signs of post-traumatic stress disorder. It was also how she’d enrolled them in therapy.

Noelani Ahia inserts acupuncture needles in Mikey Burke’s leg, part of her practice with Maui Medic Healers Hui.

But keeping the study funded had been an ongoing struggle, and a few days before Burke’s acupuncture appointment, organizers held a weekend-long event to collect survivors’ health information for what they feared could be the last time.

It made Burke angry. She’d seen what the study had done for her boys. She felt how deeply her community was still struggling. If no one tracked her community’s health, then how would they know, years from now, how the fires changed them? How would they know how to heal?

“There’s always something that we have to fight,” she continued, her tears now falling fast. “We can’t even just be in our own grief.”

The Maui wildfires on Aug. 8, 2023, destroyed more than 2,200 buildings and killed more than 100 people. The Burkes were among the nearly 13,000 displaced.

For months after the fires, Mikey, her husband, Rob, their four sons and four dogs were shuttled between family and friends’ homes, hotel rooms and finally to the two-bedroom, one-bathroom rental where they’re now living, another waystation in the long wait for a new home.

Three years out, she was still meeting people who hadn’t heard about the Lahaina Comprehensive Health Center or MauiWES, who had been so swept up in surviving, day-to-day, they hadn’t had time to seek support. It was clear to her there was a pressing need for these health resources.

In the dimly lit room at the health center, the magnitude of it all rose and took over. She fell into Ahia’s arms, shaking, and the older woman stroked her back with strong, fluid movements.

“I’ve got you,” Ahia said. “You’re carrying so much.”

Burke took a deep breath through her tears.

“Just for today, just for this little bit of time, we’re gonna set it down,” Ahia continued, her voice low and calm. “We’re going to take the pōhaku out, even though the pōhaku is your kuleana.”

Her worldly responsibilities, her kuleana, are like pōhaku, stones, weighing her down every day, Ahia explained. But for now, she could set them aside.

Burke’s shoulders softened, the tension of the morning dissipating.

This is a central part of Ahia’s work. Her clients come in with a lifetime of wounds, small and large, their nervous systems shot by unending, compounding traumas. She refers to it as colonial inflammation, how years of layered injustices pile on and manifest in a physiological response to stress. A Native Hawaiian diaspora kid who grew up on the continent and returned to Hawai‘i as a young adult, Ahia blends teachings from Hawaiian healing and traditional Chinese medicine into her practice.

She co-founded what grew into Maui Medic Healers Hui in 2019 to care for protesters opposing an observatory on Mauna Kea, a volcano on Hawai‘i island considered sacred by many Native Hawaiians. After the 2023 fires, the organization mobilized to support survivors. Now, many of Ahia’s patients are still feeling the disaster’s aftershocks.

“Can I share a thought?” Ahia asked cautiously, and Burke nodded, her breathing slowing down.

“Before the fires, we all knew about the colonial bullshit that we all go through and how difficult it is, but we had our regular daily lives to keep us busy so we didn’t always have to see it and acknowledge it,” Ahia said.

Burke nodded again as Ahia continued.

“But one patient said to me that now that everything is literally, physically gone, there’s nowhere to hide. So all the pieces of the historical trauma and the current colonial structure that we’re still being oppressed by are screaming at us,” she said.

Lahaina was once the royal seat of the Hawaiian Kingdom and had a lush, green landscape with abundant waterways. But centuries of colonial extraction—first through sugar and pineapple plantations run by American and European companies and then through tourism—diverted water away from Lahaina and helped create today’s arid conditions.

The 2023 fires added fuel to West Maui’s longstanding water conflict. They also highlighted challenges to land ownership for Native Hawaiians and other long-time local families dealing with insurance shortfalls, foreclosure threats, complicated rebuilding requirements and long waitlists for housing.

“The wound is wide open and it’s constantly having dirt put in it,” Ahia continued. “We have to help each other take the dirt out of the wounds.”

Burke and many of her neighbors saw in the aftermath of the fires an opportunity to change course and rebuild with local priorities at the forefront. She helped found the Lahaina Community Land Trust, a nonprofit that works to help families rebuild and keep land in local hands.

For Burke, standing up for Lahaina doesn’t feel like a choice. It’s her kuleana, her responsibility. She can’t imagine another way of being than to be in the fight.

But even as she advocates for resources to help her neighbors, Burke hesitates to accept help for her own family, which faces the same challenges. The aid could go to someone else who needs it more, she tells herself.

“We shouldn’t have to be this strong and resilient,” Ahia said, and Burke laughed in agreement. “So for right now you don’t have to be strong or resilient, you can just be unmasked.”

Burke climbed onto the table, lay on her back and closed her eyes. Ahia swabbed each of her ears and began placing acupuncture needles in her hands and feet.

Her hands over Burke’s chest, Ahia began a pule ho‘ōla, a healing prayer. Her voice reverberated as she chanted, asking for the heavens to open, the rain to fall, the earth and its people to be nourished.

Burke was distracted when she arrived that morning, thinking about the lei she had to make for her twin boys’ fifth-grade graduation later that day. Flowering trees used to be abundant, found in every neighbor’s backyard. In recent years they’d dwindled as gentrification pushed local families away. Then the fires came, burning most homes and trees down. Now, she knows of just a handful of flowering trees remaining in Lahaina, their blossoms in high demand. Just one more thing the flames took.

Burke comes to the center for talk therapy as well as her sessions with Ahia. Her twin boys attend therapy and a weekly video gaming group. Her husband, a transplant from California, doesn’t like talking about his feelings and isn’t drawn to talk therapy. But his body is showing the toll of the stress from the fires and a lifetime of manual labor.

Rob had an appointment scheduled for September, just before his 45th birthday, to remove a lesion on his nose, his latest bout with skin cancer. And when MauiWES ran tests on him, he learned that he—like many wildfire survivors here, including his wife—had elevated levels of heavy metals in his body and breathing problems. He listened to Mikey talk about her experience at the center and agreed to sign up for acupuncture and lomilomi massage there, too.

A few hours after Mikey Burke’s appointment, in the room next door, 11-year-old Makoa Burke was laser-focused on smashing Mario to a pulp.

He’d taken a couple of hits so far, but it was still early in the game. He was facing straight ahead, camo baseball hat turned to one side, eyes narrowed with concentration, feet fidgeting in and out of his Crocs.

Then, Makoa’s avatar ballooned on screen and his hammer came down hard on his opponent. A few feet away, Kaleohano Burke spun his chair around, eyes wide, watching his twin brother’s victory with glee. His lei were lying on the table, but he still wore the gray kīhei, knotted at his left shoulder, from their fifth-grade graduation ceremony that day. Raising a hand covered in bright orange powder, he scarfed down a Cheeto.

Makoa’s eyes remained trained on the screen.

“I’m surviving,” he said to the room, or maybe to himself. “No more dying.”

Christopher Knightsbridge, a therapist who works on the MauiWES study, sat quietly to the side of the room and watched the boys, leaning back in his chair with his hands behind his head.

As the hour went by, the table piled up with empty bags of Doritos, SunChips and the clear crowd favorite, Cheetos. About half an hour in, the Capri-Suns had run out, so Kaleohano cracked open a pack of organic apple juice boxes.

Since the fires, Mikey and Rob Burke had seen changes in their sons. Kaleohano began having nightmares and Makoa, who had always been a fiercely independent child, hovered around his parents, distraught at a hint of separation. They’d get triggered by smoke from a neighbor’s barbecue, unsettled until their parents took them to the source and proved, beyond a shred of doubt, that it was something distinct from the fire they’d fled as it burned their home, their street and nearly their entire town clear to the ground.

For months, the Burkes knew their kids were struggling. They were too. But the family was in survival mode, and addressing their mental health was one item on a long and impossible to-do list that included insurance paperwork, emergency housing, school, the logistics of rebuilding and continuing to support their community, where they counted their family lucky—sheltered and at least visibly uninjured. On top of everything, both parents had busy jobs: Rob as a construction worker and Mikey as the new West Maui community liaison for the state’s largest utility, Hawaiian Electric, which dealt with legal fallout after the fires.

Mikey remembers being in a state of shock when MauiWES staff said both boys were showing signs of PTSD. But Knightsbridge walked her over to the front desk of the center and helped her sign them up to see one of the mental health counselors there for free. In their second year of testing with MauiWES, after regular therapy and Knightsbridge’s gaming group sessions, their mental health scores had returned to a normal range.

The gaming group is separate from formal therapy, but Knightsbridge sees it as a part of the center’s holistic approach to healing. Many of the children he sees are navigating instability at home and trauma from the fires. The gaming group gives them a reason to leave their homes and socialize. Sometimes, it’s a safe, low-stakes space to open up.

But everything feels precarious. That week, it looked like MauiWES would be shutting down. And after leaving the Department of Health in the spring, Knightsbridge was working at the center on a federal emergency response grant that was nearing an end. He lives on O‘ahu but was spending half of most weeks on Maui, and he couldn’t imagine leaving his patients.

The next morning, Rob Burke stood surveying a construction crew at the site of the family’s former and future home. The sun beat down hard from a cloudless sky, and the empty lot offered no shade for the workers.

This was therapy for Rob. Watching as their build began at last was the first time since the fires that he felt he could really breathe.

Rob was dressed to shield his skin from the sun: dark sunglasses and a black, long-sleeve zip-up with the hood pulled over his head. From under each sleeve and on one leg beneath knee-length shorts, thick, bold tattoos emerged. The only other skin left uncovered was his nose, already bright pink and sunburnt.

Rob does finishing work for Crescent Homes, a local company, and plans to take that on at his family’s home too. For now, the house was just a grid on the ground under the blazing sun. Pipes stuck out where the bathrooms and laundry room will take shape.

Rob jokes that his body, his pale skin and Irish blood, wasn’t made for Hawaiʻi. But his soul was. Even with his home burned to ash and skyrocketing prices for seemingly everything, he couldn’t imagine leaving Lahaina. The place is special. It’s the land, its spirit, its mana. As soon as he moved here, he could feel it. It’s the only place Mikey had ever wanted to bring up their kids. Now, he feels the same way.

Mikey had just parked her car and was walking up the road to their house. In contrast to Rob’s head-to-toe sun protection, she was dressed for summer in denim shorts, a short-sleeved button down and a baseball hat that read, “You Are On Native Land.”

As he spotted his wife, Rob brightened, then quickly sobered. As excited as he was, he knew this would be a difficult day for her.

She approached Rob and they hugged, the weight of the morning left unsaid. Before long, a cement truck backed in from the street, and by a quarter to 10, the crew started pouring the foundation. Cement churned in the truck and was pushed through a crane before it gushed out of a vertical pipe and filled the grid on the ground.

Behind her sunglasses, Mikey began to cry. Rob pulled her into another hug as she shook with the sobs.

It was May, nearly three years since the fires, and they were only just starting to rebuild. She and Rob are taking on the job as owner-builders, without a general contractor. She doesn’t know when they’ll be able to get the materials to start building its frame. The length of the road ahead, full of unending unknowns, scares her. Her oldest son will be 18 by the time they’re ready to move back in, if they’re lucky. He might not even want to live here anymore.

The sun stayed high as the hours ticked by and the crew—most of whom Rob knew from work—labored steadily, pouring and smoothing the concrete. Rob passed around cool drinks and pizza.

As the day progressed, Mikey’s mood gradually lifted. The slab pouring felt like a metaphor. The foundation of the house, the start of their homecoming, the beginning of a new chapter in their family’s life. As the ground hardened, she and Rob could see it all beginning to take shape.

Around 1 p.m., Mikey left to pick up her kids a little early from school—she wanted them to be there to see this.

On the brief drive, she passed a neighbor’s home on the corner that was in the midst of construction. She remembered the beautiful house that had burned down, built in Lahaina’s plantation-era style and renovated by the current owner’s father, who has since passed away. That house was his legacy.

Throughout the burn zone, Lahaina was reemerging. The streets were bustling daily with construction crews in pickup trucks. A single block could house every stage of the construction process: a fully built home next to a wooden frame, beside two stories of scaffolding plastered with Tyvec paper flapping in the wind. Scattered throughout were empty lots, where homeowners moved away, sold their land or just haven’t been able to start building yet. Of the more than 2,200 structures destroyed by the fires, just over 300 have been rebuilt three years later.

Mikey picked up her son Maleko, then 16, at Lahainaluna High School and drove to Princess Nāhiʻenaʻena Elementary School just below it.

“We’re pouring slab today,” she said with a smile to the women working the front desk as she signed out the younger boys, Makoa, Kaleohano and Kaimana, 9. The sun was high and the foundation already dry enough for the workers to walk on when she and the boys arrived.

As the afternoon dragged on, cars drove by, honking at the family and rolling down their windows to yell greetings and congratulations. The Burkes waved, shouted alohas and threw shakas at a cousin whose home was rebuilt by Habitat for Humanity down the block, a friend who lives in an apartment building that was burnt down and rebuilt a few streets over, a Hawaiian language teacher from the boys’ school, his grandchildren returning their waves from the back of his pickup.

While Maleko stood close to his dad, the three younger boys walked the perimeter of the site, climbing the stone wall behind the house and playing with tennis balls and their kendamas, Japanese wooden toys made of a handle, ball and string. They did tricks for the crew and weaved on and off the sidewalk, running up and down the block.

Before the fires, they were just beginning to fall into a neighborhood crew of kids their age. They’d run to each other’s houses for movie nights in someone’s yard, to ride bikes along the street or to get shave ice from a seller on the corner.

The neighborhood they’re renting in now has few kids and no sidewalks. It’s not built for play.

It’s another item on Mikey’s list of many worries since the fires. They might have lost the chance to build those bonds, moving back only after aging out of that magical era when their lives could revolve around exploring their neighborhood with a little goonie squad.

As she fretted, a blonde-haired boy from the neighborhood rolled in on a scooter, recognizing the boys and stopping to play. They laughed on the sidewalk, passing their kendamas back and forth.

The road ahead was long and full of challenges. Mikey knew she would have to continue to fight—to avoid foreclosure and secure insurance funds, to find building materials and  trustworthy contractors, to make time for the family’s health in the midst of everything else. The boys would soon have to stop seeing their therapist as the emergency funding ran out. She didn’t know what would happen to MauiWES.

But that day, something was taking shape.

It was nearly 3 p.m., the sun still high. The boys sat in the back of their father’s truck, eating pizza and making each other laugh. Rob and Mikey took shade under a lone tree on the sidewalk, each leaning on a branch as they faced their land. And across the new foundation of the Burkes’ future home, the crew kneeled as they smoothed out the corners of the now-hardening concrete.

As the summer began, Ruben Juarez and Alika Maunakea—the two University of Hawai‘i researchers leading the study that got the Burke boys into therapy—looked for a Hail Mary.

They met with local funders. In June, they flew to Washington, D.C., to talk with their state’s congressional delegation and a handful of program officers at the National Institutes of Health and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, explaining their vision for an expansion of MauiWES that would combine screening and data collection with care navigation, referrals and community outreach in mobile clinics across the island.

They’re calling the initiative HO‘ĀLA-Maui, using a Hawaiian word that means to re-awaken or restore as an acronym: Health Outreach ‘Āina-based Lifecourse Alliance.

Long term, they are dreaming even bigger.

Juarez and Maunakea want to use what they’ve learned to build a new national blueprint for responding to disasters: a combination of data collection and care rooted in Mauli Ola, a Hawaiian concept that describes how physical, mental, social and environmental health and well-being are inextricable.

At the end of June, they got a breakthrough.

An email from NIH announced that one of their applications had been approved: $2.2 million over three years from the National Institute on Minority Health and Health Disparities.

It was enough to bring staff back to MauiWES.

And after that, the funds began to flow in earnest.

On July 1, Maui County officials allocated another $2 million to the HO‘ĀLA initiative, to focus on the remote corners of the island that are most impacted by healthcare shortages.

In mid-August, an NIH grant Juarez and Maunakea applied for a year and a half earlier was approved: $3.6 million for a five-year study on a new 1,000-person cohort to better understand the impacts of wildfire exposure and legacy pollutants from the state’s plantation history on lung and heart health—a follow up to their recent findings. And in September, NIH granted them another $3.7 million over five years for further research on health impacts to children.

Juarez and Maunakea believe that these funds, along with some renewed charitable support, are enough to keep the effort going.

On a hot evening in mid-July, the two professors walked northbound along the lakefront trail in downtown Chicago.

They were there for just a few days, attending a symposium on science and safety. The next afternoon, Maunakea would speak about MauiWES on a panel about ecosystem resilience.

Juarez looked out at Lake Michigan, the water glistening, tinged purple with the promise of a soon-setting sun, and remarked how much it looked like the ocean.

They walked for a bit before stopping at a little outdoor restaurant with a view of the sailboats docked in the harbor. The sun began to set as they ate and sipped their drinks—Maunakea, a piña colada and Juarez, a glass of rosé.

Maunakea was thinking about climate change. Hawaiʻi is experiencing rising temperatures and sea levels, coastal erosion, ocean warming and acidification, coral bleaching, changes in rainfall, greater wildfires and more intense storms and hurricanes triggering flooding and landslides. This year, the state has faced relentless, back-to-back disasters that leave little time to recover in between and lay bare systemic gaps in the state’s healthcare system. It makes this work, combining research with intervention, all the more urgent.

Sitting on Chicago’s lakefront, the two men felt cautiously optimistic.

Juarez and Maunakea have shared their findings with researchers studying the impacts of 9/11 debris exposure on first responders in New York City and water contamination in Flint, Michigan. They have consulted with a team in Los Angeles implementing a similar project to track health impacts from the 2025 fires there. As wildfires roared through Utah and Colorado in June and killed four wildland firefighters, the MauiWES team connected with a local researcher almost immediately to talk about potential next steps. And after tensions with their state’s health department, they were feeling hopeful about working more closely with the agency.

As he and Maunakea finished their dinner, Juarez was enthralled by dozens of spiders of all different sizes that surrounded them on the lakefront, running up and down nearly invisible threads of silk between shrubs, their chairs and the umbrella that shaded their table. He’d never seen so many in his life.

They reminded him of Lahaina, the web of interwoven social and environmental dimensions of the community. Everything connected, but easily broken by a single disruption.

“You just need one thing to destroy this web,” Juarez said. “You have a disaster, and it’s gonna shock all of them at the same time.”

“Or they’ll recover and build a new one,” Maunakea said.

“It depends on how resilient they are,” Juarez said.

Maunakea, seemingly unimpressed with the metaphor, stared pointedly at him, and Juarez laughed.

By then the sun had set. The two men walked back to their hotel, stopping for gelato on the way.

As they flew back to Oʻahu two days later, wildfire smoke from Canada swept in over the lake and shrouded Chicago in a thick yellow haze.

https://insideclimatenews.org/news/08112.text:
First of two stories about the effort to support Lahaina fire survivors’ health in the disaster’s long, hard aftermath.

LAHAINA, Hawaiʻi—Early on a Saturday morning in May, Ruben Juarez took the 45-minute flight from Oʻahu to Maui, just like he’d done dozens of times over the past three years.

This one felt different.

Juarez landed in Kahului Airport with his partner, Alika Maunakea, and drove on a long winding highway beside the piercing blue ocean until they reached the Lahaina Comprehensive Health Center.

A cool breeze wafted in from the Pacific less than half a mile below as they set up stations for blood collection, lung function tests and mental health check-ins, directing a team of Ph.D. students and local healthcare providers. Then they waited for the fire survivors to arrive.

On Aug. 8, 2023, Maui was hit with the deadliest wildfires the U.S. has seen in over a century. They killed at least 102 people, displaced nearly 13,000 residents and destroyed more than 2,200 buildings. Three years later, just 15 percent have been rebuilt.

Juarez, an economist, and Maunakea, a biomedical scientist, never expected to focus on disaster recovery. But after the fires, they were thrust into the space by the overwhelming scale of need. The two University of Hawaiʻi professors dreamed up the Maui Wildfire Exposure Study, or MauiWES, as a form of rapid response: an effort to track the impacts of the fires on survivors’ health.

Three years and 2,500 participants later, the study has blossomed into a combination of research and intervention, a web of community organizations working together to give participants not just free testing but also therapy, food assistance, cash support and help connecting with doctors and insurance. Some even say the study saved their lives.

The researchers hope MauiWES could become a national blueprint for public health response after disasters. Experts across the country are paying attention. One longtime disaster researcher, David Eisenman at the University of California, Los Angeles, said the study’s holistic approach is “singular.”

But critical federal support to keep the effort going for at least a decade was running out, and its renewal was uncertain—grant applications had been met with silence for months. And just two weeks before Juarez and Maunakea landed on Maui, state funding they were counting on fell through.

Now, here they were at what might be their last big event to understand how survivors were doing and what help they needed.

Juarez was distraught: It felt like the end. But Maunakea, usually the pessimist of the pair, refused to believe it. He felt the study had to continue. The need was too great. They would find a way.

At the health center that Saturday morning, Maunakea greeted Lisa and Nilsson Panis, a pair of siblings born and raised in Lahaina. As he checked them into the study, he explained what they’d do that day. Urine samples to track environmental exposures. Saliva collection for biomarkers of stress and aging. Blood tests for metabolic function. Two assessments of lung health. Recordings of blood pressure, height and weight. A mental health screener.

At the end of it all, they’d meet with a volunteer physician who would help them understand their test results, and they’d each walk away with $100, compensation for their time.

“We’re trying to do this every year,” Maunakea told the Panises.

He was determined to make that happen.

The lobby of the health center had a dark stain on its ceiling where water had leaked in just a month before.

The building—run by the state’s Department of Health and loaned to MauiWES for the weekend—sits near the base of the sprawling West Maui mountains. That weekend, the foothills above the center were covered in dry, yellowing grass that was nonetheless much greener than usual, courtesy of recent Kona low storms.

The storms swept water damage into construction sites and homes that had just been rebuilt. They busted up highways and caused torrential flooding, triggering millions of dollars in damage across the county. They also kicked off an unusually verdant spring, with flowers blooming on the trees outside the center and along the highway below. Wetness that early can heighten the fire risk later in the year, fueling grass and brush growth that dries out and becomes plentiful tinder, susceptible to heat and strong winds.

Lisa Panis had an appointment with MauiWES that day, but she was hoping they’d have room for her older brother, too. In a fluorescently lit room just beside the center’s main lobby, she introduced Nilsson to Maunakea and explained that he had been a first responder after the wildfires, cleaning up debris in the burn zone. Maunakea immediately instructed the Ph.D. students working the check-in desk to sign him up, along with Nilsson’s girlfriend, another survivor.

MauiWES had limited resources, especially with funding so up in the air. But on an island already suffering from a severe healthcare provider shortage, Maunakea and Juarez didn’t like turning anyone away.

Lisa Panis, a participant in the Maui Wildfire Exposure Study, has struggled with her mental and physical health since the fires, and her family is still in temporary housing.

Maunakea listened to Nilsson explain what his life looked like in the months after the fires: 12-hour days, seven days a week, clearing the burn zone for a construction company. He wore full-body gear to keep as much of the dust out as possible, but he still ended each day coated in grime. Though he’d never been tested, Nilsson felt confident the constant inhalation of ash and the debris that covered his body as he worked had impacted his health.

“We tried to push all the dust down with water,” Nilsson said to Maunakea, describing the cleanup. “But you cannot get everything.”

“Are you still doing that, or pau?” Maunakea asked.

“Pau,” Nilsson replied. Finished. Now he was working as a mason, bringing his sister on whenever he could. It wasn’t steady. He hoped jobs would pick up in the summer.

The Panis siblings’ father is descended from Filipino immigrants who came to the island to work on the sugar plantations more than a century ago, during a period when American and European companies brought indentured laborers from the Philippines to work under brutal conditions for extremely low pay. The plantations, established before Hawaiʻi’s illegal annexation by the United States and continuing another century after, sucked water out of Lahaina’s once green and fertile hills.

That set the stage for modern-day wildfire risks, now worsened by climate change, and cemented a pattern of local disenfranchisement that continued as the tourism industry took hold.

For years, the Panises had experienced the harder realities of life in Lahaina, like gentrification and unstable housing and employment. On the day of the fires, Nilsson was meant to fly back from Las Vegas to spread the ashes of two siblings who had passed away just weeks apart that spring. Lisa was living with an aunt whose home would not survive. She remembers standing on the field next to the post office where she and her brothers played football as kids, watching as flames engulfed the town above and below her.

After they finished checking into the study, the Panis siblings moved through the stations, a sort of medical assembly line: urine samples, then blood tests, then blood pressure, then spitting into a tube. A few feet away, Juarez coached another participant on how to blow into a spirometer to test lung function.

“Sigue, sigue, sigue,” he said, reminding the man to keep breathing out. Throughout the day Juarez greeted Spanish-speaking participants, acting as one of a handful of interpreters who walked people through the study’s tests in English, Spanish and Tagalog.

Juarez was pulled into Maui’s recovery because of his connections to Lahaina’s abundant immigrant community. One-third of Lahaina residents were born outside the U.S., many in Asia or Latin America. Juarez moved from Mexico to Houston for a doctorate at Rice University, then to Oʻahu for a job at the University of Hawaiʻi. There, he met Maunakea, and as neighbors in the university’s faculty housing, they fell in love.

When they met, Juarez’s research was focused on social networks and Maunakea’s on health disparities in disease. After the fires, Maunakea was drawn to Maui by his connections with people working to address the disproportionate public health burdens faced by Native Hawaiians across the islands. Although he lives on Oʻahu, his great-grandmother, a Native Hawaiian healer, was born in Kula, an upcountry Maui community that was also badly impacted by the 2023 fires.

He and Juarez met with community leaders and healthcare workers on Maui soon after the fires. They became part of the MauiWES advisory board, consulting on design and implementation. For many study participants, that grounding made a big difference.

Mikey Burke, a Native Hawaiian mother of four who grew up in West Maui, remembers an influx of mental health practitioners from the continent who swarmed to Maui after the fires. They roamed the lobbies of hotels where she and other displaced families were sheltered. But though they were well-intentioned, they felt largely unapproachable. She gravitated toward local organizations like Maui Medic Healers Hui, which was working with MauiWES. It was something in their mannerisms, the way they spoke to her, the normalcy and familiarity they offered.

In the months after they lost their home, Burke, her husband Rob and their four young sons were shuttled between temporary shelters, family homes and rental properties. She could see that her twin boys, just 8 years old when the fires hit, were struggling. But it wasn’t until they got screened by MauiWES that addressing their mental health shot to the top of her lengthy to-do list. The study team told her that both boys were showing serious signs of post-traumatic stress disorder, and got them connected with a free therapist right away.

The Burkes aren’t an anomaly. The study found widespread emotional distress and trauma in adults and children, and connected many with therapists.

On an island with a severe shortage of physicians, MauiWES was also most early participants’ first time seeing a doctor after the fires. Over the past three years, the team made some big saves.

In August 2024, one year after the fires, a former trauma nurse named Amy Jackson had such a low hemoglobin count that it wasn’t registering on MauiWES’ testing system. The team urged her to go to the emergency room immediately. Jackson had signed up for the study because the cash would be a good birthday present for her daughter. If it wasn’t for that, she wouldn’t have gotten checked out at all.

At the hospital, she remembers a doctor telling her he was amazed she was still alive. She was admitted and treated, and she credits MauiWES with saving her life.

In February 2024, another participant presented with symptoms suggesting a serious lung infection. Volunteer physicians were concerned and said she needed medical attention right away. But she was an undocumented immigrant and one of the 10 percent of study participants who had both lost their jobs in the fire and weren’t eligible for state insurance.

Juarez coordinated with Roots Reborn—a local organization supporting Maui’s immigrant community—and reached out the next day to ask an insurer with a charitable health coverage program to consider an emergency enrollment.

She got the insurance and then the treatment she needed. She’s one of more than 200 participants Juarez estimates have been connected with private insurance via Kaiser Permanente because of interventions from MauiWES and Roots Reborn. He was happy to see her now, in good spirits and good health, coming in for her follow-up at the May collection event. He thought the immigrant population had the most to lose from the study ending.

The team still had so much to do.

After her lung test, Lisa Panis stood underneath the stain on the lobby’s ceiling and waited for her brother. The Panis siblings stay strong for one another. But she’s experienced depression since the fires, like many other survivors, and her tests revealed elevated levels of several toxic metals in her body.

In their first, smallest cohort, about six months after the fires, Juarez, Maunakea and their colleagues found that about half of study participants were experiencing breathing problems that suggested ongoing, residual impacts from wildfire smoke. They’ve also found that poor lung function was linked to elevated levels of heavy metals in participants’ urine, including some of the same metals the health department found in the burn zone.

After looking at so many test results, Maunakea can guess with considerable accuracy what neighborhood a participant lives in just by seeing the distribution of metals in their body. Some of that contamination may predate the fires. But the health implications are the same.

Before Nilsson Panis left for the day, Juarez gave him a T-shirt with the MauiWES logo—a sun rising behind the island—and a hundred-dollar bill. Then he ushered him over to the front desk, where a case manager who works for the Department of Health was waiting.

She asked Nilsson if there was anything he might need help with.

He paused for a moment before answering. Maybe some assistance with food, he said. He also asked about opportunities to volunteer and help other survivors.

The case manager took down his email.

The next day Maunakea supervised a group of staff and volunteers administering lung function tests. A participant wearing a neon-yellow baseball hat and flower-patterned shorts walked in and took a seat.

“It’s unfortunate that you guys didn’t get more additional funding from the legislative session this time,” Ekolu Lindsey said to Maunakea as he took a break from breathing hard into a plastic mouthpiece.

It had been MauiWES’ most recent funding attempt: A bill sponsored by the state senator for West Maui, Angus McKelvey, would have allotted $3 million to keep the study going and expand the number of children it could serve. But at the last minute, the bill failed to make it through.

“I get it, they went for the bigger-ticket items, but the health part is also a big-ticket item that didn’t take precedence,” continued Lindsey, who is the president of a grassroots land trust organization on Maui. “I don’t think they understood, because probably none of them went through it.”

Maunakea agreed. He had thought that public health would be more of a priority in the wildfire recovery, especially in a state with a doctor as a governor. But funding MauiWES has been an ongoing challenge.

The study’s first cohort, in early 2024, began with charitable funding from the Hawaiʻi Community Foundation and Kaiser Permanente, while the researchers pursued government support. That summer, they got $2.3 million from the state. And almost one year after the fires, they received a $1.4 million grant from the National Institutes of Health’s minority health disparities program.

That support quickly turned precarious after Donald Trump retook office and slashed funding for programs focused on diversity or health disparities, along with a wide swath of academic research.

The MauiWES researchers hoped to renew their federal funding and keep the study going for at least a decade. But heading into the May event, applications they submitted to the agency had been languishing without a decision for more than a year. By that time, the NIH had lost 23 percent of its staff under the Trump administration, almost double the reduction across the entire federal government, according to an analysis by Inside Climate News.

The MauiWES researchers started getting national recognition in the disaster recovery space, speaking on panels and presenting at conferences on the mainland, hoping that might drum up more cash. But private funding wasn’t enough to keep the study going, and the speaking engagements had yet to pay off. More state funding seemed like Juarez and Maunakea’s best hope.

Initially, the team had strong backing from the state’s Department of Health, which wrote enthusiastic letters of support for federal grants. But as the study progressed and the researchers began publicizing their results, the agency pushed back.

The Department of Health had earlier screened 557 West Maui residents for lead in their blood, saying in May 2024 that so few had elevated levels that it was not necessary to screen the general population for toxic substances identified in the burn zone.

“On the basis of these results with lead as an indicator of exposure, we do not expect to find health impacts caused by toxins in the wildfire ash,” agency director Kenneth Fink said in a statement at the time.

But lead is just one of the toxic substances the department found at elevated levels in burn zone ash, and it’s undetectable in people’s blood relatively quickly after exposure, unlike some other substances found in the burn zone. Environmental health experts questioned why the department used a limited sampling of lead to draw broad conclusions about the burn zone as a whole.

Then MauiWES found elevated levels of heavy metals associated with heart and lung issues and cancer risks in a cohort of more than 1,200 fire survivors.

The findings seemed to contradict the Department of Health’s assertion that the burn zone was safe. Emails and letters Inside Climate News obtained through public records requests suggest that agency staff quickly moved into damage-control mode.

The day after Honolulu Civil Beat published a story about the preliminary findings last year, a naturopathic doctor on Maui emailed state toxicologist John Jacob for information about the effects of heavy metals like arsenic, nickel, cadmium, mercury and lead on psychological function. Her clients had been tested by MauiWES and registered high levels of those metals, she wrote.

Jacob forwarded the email to colleagues at the Department of Health.

“I don’t want to affirm what UH is stating,” he wrote, referring to the University of Hawaiʻi. “The panic has begun!”

A few days later, agency staff discussed whether to stop assisting MauiWES with data collection. Fink, the director, said staff could continue for now, but he felt the department’s recommendations on study design had been either inadequate or disregarded. “If the latter, I would need to reevaluate our involvement,” Fink wrote to colleagues.

In October, the Department of Health sent a letter to the University of Hawaiʻi, criticizing MauiWES’ reliance on sampling survivors who showed up—as opposed to a randomized cohort—and its findings of elevated heavy metals in their urine.

The university defended the research in its response and explained that MauiWES was not claiming a definitively causal relationship between the fires and the heavy metals.

Although the team remained committed to working with the state, Juarez said he saw the Department of Health’s letter as an attempt to censor their research. Academics not involved with MauiWES told Inside Climate News the exchange seemed unusual for a university and a state agency, and they did not think the health department’s dismissal of burn-zone dangers was warranted based on the limited information it had collected.

The agency’s director said in a statement to Inside Climate News that discussions about the best way to approach research “are a normal and healthy — and often essential — aspect of scientific collaboration.”

“While our perspectives may differ, both DOH and UH remain committed to respectful dialogue and evidence‑based inquiry,” Fink wrote in his statement. “Most importantly, the public needs clear, accurate, and consistent information about how the wildfires may have affected their health. Residents deserve timely communication they can trust — free of speculation and grounded in the best available data.”

In an emailed statement to Inside Climate News, Jacob acknowledged that the researchers’ approach was acceptable but said that not disclosing limitations could “result in confusion among the general public.”

In defense of the agency’s own approach to quantifying post-wildfire health risks, a department spokesperson said in an email that a structured soil sampling technique allowed staff to use the lead screening as a “reasonable indicator for population exposure.”

In internal emails in January, agency staff discussed a bill with funds earmarked to keep MauiWES alive. They agreed to keep a close watch on the effort. “Especially since we are not satisfied with their science,” wrote Jacob, the toxicologist.

In the end, a department subagency was among those submitting testimony in support of the funding. But that wasn’t enough to push it through. When the bill fell short with still no word on federal money, it looked like the end of MauiWES.

At nearly 5 p.m. on Sunday, the team packed up while finishing tests for the last few stragglers. Most of the staff and volunteers had to catch a flight back to Oʻahu in a couple of hours, but Christopher Knightsbridge, a therapist working on the study’s research team, would stay on Maui a few more days to see patients in person.

Knightsbridge was overcome with pure frustration. All weekend, he’d done mental health check-ins with participants still focused on getting by, day by day. He felt certain the study was having an impact. He saw it every week. And he was still concerned about what he’d been hearing in his sessions. He wanted his patients to wake up and feel like they were living, not simply fighting to survive. For that, they needed more support, not less.

Knightsbridge poured everything he had into supporting survivors’ mental health in recovery. He spent half of most weeks away from his wife and young children on Oʻahu to see patients still dealing with ongoing crises: survivors in temporary housing and unstable employment, people with cancer diagnoses, young children whose lives were turned upside down by the fires. He’s seen serious PTSD symptoms, depression and even suicidal ideation from kids as young as 6.

That same week, he sat in his video gaming group for kids at the health center with two of Mikey and Rob Burke’s sons, the twins dealing with PTSD. Knightsbridge was seeing both boys for therapy and organized the gaming group as another form of support, a low-stakes place for kids to open up. But the federal emergency grant supporting his position—separate from MauiWES’s funding—was also about to run out.

On the other side of the lobby, Juarez stood in a doorway, gutted. The study had made painfully apparent the gaps in healthcare access on the island, and it felt like their work was just beginning. The thought brought him to the brink of tears. Throughout the weekend, he heard from worried participants who asked if the study was going away. He didn’t want to let them down.

Near the entrance to the courtyard, Maunakea carried a table from the hallway back into one of the offices, tired but heartened by how many people had come through. Sitting with returning participants, learning about their recovery journeys and watching how they were putting the pieces back together was energizing for him. Healing is a communal task in Lahaina. The study leaned into that.

Maunakea knew the next disaster was just around the corner. He believed Maui could adapt and offer a model to the rest of the world for building resilience to the steep challenges climate change brings.

Maybe, he thought, that would be the ultimate lesson from the study: that documenting and addressing health inequities in the wake of a disaster helps communities withstand what they cannot escape.

Toward the end of the day, more survivors arrived without appointments after hearing about the study from family and friends. By closing, he estimated the team had turned away more than a dozen new people, taking down their names in case funding came through. Maunakea met people that weekend who said they’d known about the study for several years but hadn’t felt ready to participate until now. It hammered home to him how crucial it was for their work to go on.

The team would find a way to continue the study, Maunakea felt certain. He didn’t know how, but he saw no other choice. If his great-grandmother was alive, she would have said: ‘O ka pono ke hana ‘ia a iho mai nā lani. Continue to do good until the heavens come down to you.

He believed that this study is pono, and that the community wanted and needed this service. So somehow, iho mai nā lani. The heavens would come down.

Inside Climate News’ Peter Aldhous contributed to this story.

Israel is not finished with Iran, its defence minister said Sunday, as he renewed charges that Tehran is pursuing nuclear weapons, which the Islamic republic has long denied.

"With regard to Iran, the mission is still not complete. Iran is trying to renew its efforts to obtain nuclear weapons – alongside other grave efforts that place the State of Israel in real danger," Defence Minister Israel Katz said at a ceremony.

The US military has announced it will create a 20-member task force to find ways to disrupt land routes into Iran that it says are used for shipments of weapons and illicit materials.

The restrictions would expand on a US naval blockade of Iranian ports during the two countries' eight-month war, in which Tehran has also restricted passage through the critical Strait of Hormuz trade route, choking global energy supplies.

The task force's work "will further constrain Iran's ability to finance terrorism, rebuild weapons factories, and replenish their military," US Central Command chief Brad Cooper said in a statement posted on X on Saturday.

The team of both civilian and military personnel based in Florida would coordinate with US government agencies on "preventing the movement of advanced weapons systems, dual-use technologies, sanctioned materials, and illegal revenue streams across Iran's land borders and the Caspian Sea," the statement added.

At least 33 people were killed and dozens more were injured in Saudi airstrikes on a village near Sanaa on Saturday, Yemen’s Houthi-run health ministry said.

The ministry said the strikes hit homes in the ‌town of Bani Hushaysh, a Houthi stronghold, and that most of those killed were ​women and children.

Abdul-Aziz al-Dailami, director of Sehatuna Hospital in Sanaa, said many victims remained trapped under the rubble, including first responders.

A ​Saudi ​Energy Ministry official said on ​Sunday ‌that ⁠an ‌administrative building belonging to ⁠state oil giant Saudi ​Aramco ‌in Riyadh had been ‌targeted in ​an attempted attack on the capital's financial district, with falling ​debris causing limited ​damage ​to the ​building with no injuries or fatalities.

The incident, which the ⁠ministry said caused limited damage, came after the Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted two missiles fired by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis towards ‌Riyadh.

Good morning and welcome to our liveblog on the situation in the Middle East.

We will keep our eyes on several things today, from the attack on Riyadh’s financial district to the government coalition talks in Israel.

https://www.france24.com/en/sport/202611.title: France beat Fiji to reclaim top spot in Nations Championship
https://www.france24.com/en/sport/202611.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/sport/202611.text:
France stormed back to the top of the northern hemisphere Nations Championship table with a dominant but flawed 54-17 victory over Fiji on Saturday.

Victory came at a cost, with fly-half Romain Ntamack, aligned alongside captain Antoine Dupont at half-back for the first time since March 2025, seemingly dislocating his shoulder in the build up to France's third try.

READ MORE
France cruise to second Nations Championship victory beating Japan 42-15

With Matthieu Jalibert already out injured, France will face world champions South Africa next week without either of their best fly-halves.

And they will need to put in a vastly improved showing to stand any chance of avoiding a 10th defeat in their last 11 clashes with the Springboks.

Props Jean-Baptiste Gros and Sipili Falatea, winger Aaron Grandidier-Nkanang, centre Kalvin Gourgues, full-back Theo Attissogbe, replacement forward Charles Ollivon and Dupont crossed the whitewash, with a penalty try making it eight scores for the hosts.

They are two points ahead of Ireland in the standings ahead of England's clash with Australia on Sunday.

Fiji, who started the match in Lyon with 10 France-based players, including their entire backline, were typically physical but slumped to a fourth straight defeat in the inaugural Nations Championship.

Their much-vaunted backs struggled to fire, although centre Vinaya Habosi beat four defenders to score and Selestino Ravutaumada added a second consolation try.

The Top 14's most prolific finisher, Jiuta Wainiqolo, who was playing in his adopted home, was unable to make an impact, though.

Neither did France's own wing wizard, Louis Bielle-Biarrey, although he did set up one try.

Fiji showed early ambition, turning down a straight-forward three points to kick to touch, but France stole the line-out.

After a breathless and error-strewn start to the game, Gros burrowed over for the opening try on 15 minutes, only his second for France.

That changed the complexion of the game, with France gradually starting to purr.

A penalty try soon followed, with Mesake Vocevoce sent to the sin-bin for collapsing a maul, and then Falatea burst through tacklers to score.

In the phase before Falatea's score, Ntamack injured his shoulder as he stretched for the line.

The Toulouse playmaker left the field visibly in pain.

Grandidier-Nkanang secured the attacking bonus point before half-time after Vilimoni Botitu, a late change to the Fiji starting XV as Isikeli Rabitu was reportedly sick, spilled the ball in his 22.

The hosts led 26-3 at the break, with Simione Kuruvoli's penalty Fiji's only reward.

France, though, were error-prone in the second half and struggled to turn their dominance into points.

It took them 19 minutes to add to their tally, with Gourgues going over in the corner on his first start for Les Bleus.

That seemed to open the floodgates as Bielle-Biarrey sent Attissogbe away for France's sixth try.

But Habosi struck next out of the blue before Ollivon barged over from close range.

Ravutaumada added a breakaway score but Dupont had the final word.

France are two points ahead of Ireland in the standings ahead of England's clash with Australia on Sunday. France will face South Africa next week without either of their best fly-halves.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-08/j.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

The shattered windows of a car dealership in Toyohashi, Aichi Prefecture. (AP:  Kyodo News)

Central Japan was shaken by a strong earthquake on Sunday that shattered store windows and caused people to flee buildings, leaving at least 22 people injured, according to local media.

A wide area near Aichi Prefecture was affected, including the tourist city of Kyoto, and the nearby prefecture of Yamanashi, where Mount Fuji is located.

Japan's Meteorological Agency warned people to brace for possible strong quakes in the coming week, especially the next two to three days.

A strong earthquake has shaken central Japan, shattering store windows, causing people to flee buildings and leaving at least 22 people injured, according to local media.

Japan's Meteorological Agency said Sunday's quake was a magnitude-5.7, while the US Geological Survey reported it at magnitude-5.5.

Smaller aftershocks were reported.

A wide area near Aichi Prefecture was affected, including the city of Hamamatsu, the ancient capitals of Kyoto and Nara and nearby prefectures of Yamanashi, where Mount Fuji is located, as well as Gifu.

Japanese TV footage showed shattered store windows and scattered shards of glass on the streets.

A bookstore was left with mounds of books that had flown off the shelves.

The injuries included people who fell from stairs while they were trying to flee.

The quake, which struck at 1:04am (local time), was located about 40 kilometres below the Earth's surface in Shizuoka Prefecture.

Aichi and Shizuoka are neighbouring regions. They are far enough from Tokyo that the quake was not felt there.

Experts warned residents of the possibility of more earthquakes in central Japan this week. (AP: Kenzaburo Fukuhara)

The meteorological agency warned people to brace for possible strong quakes in the coming week, especially the next two to three days.

"Please be on the lookout for mudslides, falling rocks and the possible effects from rainfall," Ayataka Ebita, an agency official, said.

He said no apparent change was detected to the Nankai Trough plate, where scientists say a megaquake can possibly hit.

The Shinkansen bullet trains were running at slower speeds in the affected areas as a precautionary measure. Sometimes quakes can damage the railways the trains run on.

A book store employee had to clean up after the earthquake in Toyota in Aichi Prefecture. (AP:  Kyodo News)

Japan is located in an area that is prone to earthquakes.

Authorities frequently instruct people to stock up on bottled water, food and batteries, have plans ready to hide under tables and keep comfortable walking shoes at hand.
