https://www.npr.org/2026/11/08/nx-s1-601.title: In Maine, a new approach to practicing medicine in the sky
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/08/nx-s1-601.author: Elaine Appleton-Grant
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/08/nx-s1-601.text:
Elaine Appleton-Grant

Flight nurse Denise Saucier begins loading a stretcher and equipment into a helicopter on the tarmac at LifeFlight of Maine's Bangor headquarters. It takes only a few minutes for the crew to prepare for takeoff.

Clipboard in hand, pilot Will Bradbury stands near a helicopter at LifeFlight of Maine's Bangor headquarters. He's running down emergency landing tips with his crew.

"If we need to get out quickly because of smoke or fire, just watch the terrain so that you're not walking uphill into the rotors," he reminds flight nurse Denise Saucier and paramedic Brian Merklin.

The team is getting ready to take off on a medical transport flight. Saucier folds herself into the compact helicopter. She's worked for the air ambulance service for seven years and still calls it a dream job.

Dream job or not, the life of a flight clinician is hard and, given the headwinds slamming rural healthcare, getting harder.

Pilot Will Bradbury runs down emergency landing tips with his crew ahead of a flight from LifeFlight of Maine's Bangor headquarters.

Since 2015, demand for medical flights in Maine has doubled. In 2025, LifeFlight crews flew 3,031 flights, more than one every three hours. This year, demand is up another 10%.

Nationwide, air medical services are filling the gaps left behind as rural hospitals close, convert to outpatient-only rural emergency hospitals, or stop offering unprofitable services like labor and delivery.

And, as Medicaid cuts estimated by the Congressional Budget Office at $911 billion over ten years take effect, it's going to get worse. Hundreds more rural hospitals or maternity departments are at immediate risk of closing. With every closure, medical care gets further away.

And, increasingly, ground ambulance stations, many of which are also struggling to keep their doors open, can't meet the need. That leaves flight clinicians like Saucier and Merklin seeing more patients every day.

"We're seeing this across the board. The need for air medical services is increasing year over year," says Nicholas George. He runs the ETHOS Database, a national tracking system for air medical programs.

When the rural health care system breaks, EMS — on the ground and, increasingly, in the air — is the backstop.

For stories on the science of healthy living, subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.

Every week or two, Saucier finds herself on a flight to one of Maine's thousands of islands. Occasionally, crews even land in the state's vast forests and mountains, then take snowmobiles to reach patients.

But "scene calls" to roadside — or trailside — accidents are less than 10% of LifeFlight's transports. (They're a higher percentage in urban areas.)

Most are interfacility transports, like today's. They'll stabilize a patient at a small, local hospital and fly them to a larger, better resourced one.

Saucier glances out the window for hazards. The view still reminds her of the role the organization plays in Maine, one of the country's most rural states.

"You go so long of a distance without seeing any houses, any roads," Saucier says. "It really hits home how rural Maine is and how necessary EMS is in the state."

And the pressure is on air ambulances as ground services in Maine are increasingly strained. The system is so fragmented that patients can fall through the cracks. Last year, a woman in a small northern Maine town died while the county dispatch center called 10 ambulance services. None responded.

Pilot Will Bradbury guides the helicopter during a flight over rural Maine (right). The view out the window includes some of the many lakes near Bangor (left).

Air ambulance services, though, come with unique challenges, particularly since the COVID-19 pandemic. It's been difficult to retain staff with the medical expertise to treat everything from heart attacks to injuries to fragile newborns, and who can stick with the demanding job without burning out.

Almost a quarter of ground-based EMS workers leaves the field every year. While there's no comprehensive staffing data for air medical services, flight clinicians face a slew of unique stresses, including dangerous conditions; long shifts and unpredictable hours; ever-increasing training and certification requirements; and significant mental health burdens. And then there's the pay, which is low throughout emergency medical services.

For years, LifeFlight retained only 60% to 70% of its workers, says CEO Joe Kellner.

"This is a really hard job," Kellner says. "By their job description, they are seeing people on their worst day, over and over again."

A specialty ambulance designed to transport newborns who need critical care. Northern Light is one of Maine's large hospital systems; it works in partnership with LifeFlight of Maine. By the end of the year, Maine will have lost 12 of its labor and delivery departments, causing a statewide shortage of birthing centers.

This year, for the first time in nine years, LifeFlight is nearly fully staffed. One of the nation's handful of independent nonprofit air medical companies, LifeFlight has taken an innovative approach to the problems that plague the industry, including a combination of better training, higher pay and in-house mental health support.

Mike Abernethy, an EMS expert and retired emergency medicine professor at the University of Wisconsin, considers the company one of a handful of model programs for the industry. LifeFlight of Maine is a nonprofit, unlike much of the industry, which is dominated by for-profit businesses with reputations for charging exorbitant prices.

"There's just absolutely no comparison in the aviation and medical quality of these programs" versus an average for-profit air medical business, Abernethy argues.

When Kellner, a paramedic himself, became CEO in 2023, he began addressing the recruitment and retention problems. What LifeFlight calls the "Critical Care Academy," a six- to eight-month orientation program, is intended to address both issues.

Emergency critical care advances quickly. So most clinicians need regular education, both to remain successful on the job and to get hired in the first place.

Seen through the window of a control room, Chuck Hogan, LifeFlight of Maine's chief clinical officer, (left) stands next to a "breathing, bleeding" dummy in a fake hospital room. He's preparing for a simulation of an emergency, designed to test clinicians' skills.

On another day at headquarters, four instructors sit in a claustrophobic control room. Through a window looking into what appears to be a hospital room, paramedics Daniel Horne and Brad Alleger are undergoing an annual skills assessment, a simulation of a real-life medical crisis.

Dr. Dave Saquet turns on a mic and coughs. "It's hard to breathe," he whispers urgently. "It hurts everywhere."

His voice seems to be coming from the patient — a breathing, bleeding mannequin lying on a hospital bed.

"What happened to you?" Horne asks.

"My house was on fire," Saquet chokes out.

A wall monitor displays the patient's vital signs — which Saquet is manipulating on his laptop.

Medics and nurses here do simulations often, both to pass the Critical Care Academy, and also to stay up to date on occasional but critical events, like emergency births, newborn resuscitation, and burns. Before the assessment ends, the paramedics will have tried and failed to intubate the patient. After that "failure," they performed an emergency procedure to enable breathing, switching from the mannequin to a pig trachea.

Because it's hard to find recruits qualified enough for the rigorous training, the company also started a mentorship program for people considering applying. Some even attend the academy, gaining skills even if they'll never work for LifeFlight.

Success comes slowly: Recently, LifeFlight hired one of last year's mentees.

Kellner instituted an unusual change that he says even nurses endorse: LifeFlight raised paramedics' pay to match flight nurses' compensation. Industrywide, paramedics make less. That keeps costs down, which is why pay equity is rare. Kellner believes the change has helped with recruitment.

Another experiment: LifeFlight hired a full-time mental-health counselor.

EMS workers' rates of post-traumatic stress injury, anxiety and depression are more thanfive times higher than the average American's.

"That has led people to leave this profession," Kellner says.

That was true for paramedic Brian Merklin, who was working for a different service in Nevada during the pandemic.

"We got hit really hard," he says. "The crews were just flying nonstop. We did four-day shifts, so for 96 hours we were just going, going, going."

About a third of the staff quit, he says. "They were getting air medical service plus COVID, right in the teeth."

Eventually, Merklin too needed a break. He left the profession for a few years. Then, when he felt the urge to fly again, he found LifeFlight.

A LifeFlight of Maine helicopter and crew at the company's base at Bangor International Airport in Maine.

The helicopter, which took off from Bangor, lands on a community hospital's rooftop helipad. Merklin and Saucier hurry to the patient's side. Most LifeFlight patients are unconscious or too ill to consent to share their stories, so the details are private. The injuries are shocking. If this patient doesn't get to a trauma center quickly, they might die.

Merklin and Saucier are unfazed.

But it's this kind of incessant trauma exposure that makes mental health support for first responders so invaluable.

Merklin serves on a peer support team.

"There's a lot of lip service paid … to the cost to your mental health in this profession. But this is the only place I have ever worked that actually provided support," he says. "I would love to see it take hold in other areas."

If counseling keeps two or three people from leaving, it's a wise investment, Kellner argues: "The cost of training somebody new into our organization is about $100,000."

As both air and ground EMS become even more essential, the task is to recruit and keep more people like Merklin and Saucier.

Because, if hundreds more hospitals do close, highly trained EMS workers may be the only people standing between patients dying and getting the care they need.

Elaine Appleton Grant's reporting was supported by the National Institute for Health Care Management.

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/08/nx-s1-539.title: Climate change is altering the colors we see in the world: an illustrated journey
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/08/nx-s1-539.author: Connie Hanzhang Jin
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/08/nx-s1-539.text:
Imagine the bright tones of coral under the sea. What do you see? What colors come to mind?

One of the ways that climate change will alter — or has already altered — our world is by shifting the familiar colors of nature. When warming ocean waters bleach the vibrant colors of coral to white, that’s one example.

“Many young scientists who are working on coral reefs don’t realize that what they’re seeing is vastly degraded,” says Anya Salih, a scientist who has studied coral reefs and their fluorescent colors for decades. “It’s often hard to perceive how it was to what it is now.”

This change of color isn’t just aesthetic. For coral, bleaching leaves them vulnerable to disease and other stressors that can lead to death. In other situations, these color changes have more complex impacts, ones that scientists are still trying to understand.

An illustrated journey

A shifting landscape in the Arctic

Every summer, massive climate-driven wildfires spread soot across huge swaths of the Arctic, covering the ice in a blanket of black particles. Soot pollution from oil and gas operations, as well as commercial shipping and increased tourism, contributes to the problem at both poles.

The dark particles coat white snow and soak up heat from the sun, exacerbating melting that was already happening more quickly because of climate change. Increased melting in the Arctic leads to sea level rise, which threatens communities across the world. And the soot itself pollutes the air and water it seeps into.

“We know that the high northern latitudes are warming faster than the rest of the planet,” says Douglas Morton, an Earth scientist at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center. These changes are shifting the colors of the Arctic landscape.

Source: National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration

Beyond the Arctic ice at the pole, farther south, lie vast regions of permafrost: soil that has remained frozen for years.

But the warming climate is causing permafrost to thaw.

And in some places, crack and collapse.

As permafrost thaws deeper into the soil, nutrients become more available and plants can grow deeper roots. These conditions can stimulate plant growth and enable larger vegetation like trees to gain a foothold, turning the landscape greener.

These established plants also trap snow in the winter, insulating the plants from the cold and promoting further plant growth.

These conditions can stimulate plant growth and enable larger vegetation like trees to gain a foothold, turning the landscape greener.

These established plants also trap snow in the winter, insulating the plants from the cold and promoting further plant growth.

A 2020 study in Nature Communications used satellite data to estimate Arctic vegetation over time, sampling thousands of sites across Alaska, Canada and western Eurasia. The researchers found that between 1985 and 2016, about 38% of the sites showed greening.

“Not everywhere in the Arctic is green,” says Logan Berner, a terrestrial ecologist with the University of Alaska Southeast, who led the study. “But there’s enough greening that if you look at the average greenness of the Arctic over time, it’s going up.”

According to Berner, who grew up in southern Alaska, this consistent increase in average greenness tracks strongly with an increase in summer temperatures.

Annual rate of greening, 2000-2025

Annual rate of greening, 2000-2025

Annual rate of greening, 2000-2025

Source: NOAA’s Arctic Report Card 2025

Though the Arctic might seem far away from us, Berner notes that it’s a “bellwether for the kinds of impacts that climate change can have.” And increased greening can negatively impact the people who live in the Arctic and rely on its natural resources. For example, as shrubs expand across northern lands, they can shade out berry patches that people rely on for food; changing weather patterns can also affect the timing of fruit and its quality.

“People have coined the term that lakes are sentinels in the landscape,” says David Butman, a professor at the University of Washington who focuses on biogeochemistry and satellite remote sensing. Lakes react quickly to changes in the environment, so measuring lake color through satellite monitoring can help quantify those changes.

Butman worked on a 2021 study in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America (PNAS) that measured green wavelengths in more than 400,000 lakes in the boreal Arctic zone in North America. Researchers found that green values declined by 15% between 1984 and 2019, meaning that, to the naked eye, these lakes got significantly darker.

Thawing permafrost is a possible reason. As it thaws, soil can mix with lake water, making it darker. The researchers found that the greatest declines happened in warmer and wetter regions.

The darker a lake gets, the more heat it can store, according to Butman. “You can imagine, you know, a black car and a hot day,” he says. The darker a lake is, the longer it stays warm after the summer, disrupting the natural timings of processes like fish life cycles and algae production. When soil or other outside material sinks to the bottom of a lake, microbes consume oxygen to break it down, leading to the production of methane, a potent planet-heating gas.

On a global scale, many lakes fall within the green-blue color spectrum. Bright blue lakes, often depicted in illustrations, are rarer than green lakes.

In 2022, scientists Xiao Yang and Catherine O’Reilly led a study in Geophysical Research Letters that analyzed the color of more than 85,000 lakes. They found that blue lakes are generally found in northern places with cooler summers and are covered in ice in the winter, such as Moraine Lake in Canada or Lake Baikal in Russia.

Globally, approximately 31% of the Earth’s lakes are blue.

Yang and O’Reilly predict that fewer blue lakes will exist as summers get warmer and winter ice cover decreases due to climate change.

The birds and the bees

Many animals have appearances that blend in with their surroundings for survival. When those surroundings start to shift, animals such as the snowshoe hare begin to stand out. The snowshoe hare’s white winter fur sticks out with less snow on the ground, leaving it more vulnerable to predators.

Researchers haven’t found evidence that hares are adapting the timing of their molts to align with their changing winter. But some insects have already changed coloring. North American male dragonflies, for instance, have adapted to warmer climates by losing color on their wings, according to a study in PNAS.

Losing some of the heat-absorbing color can help the dragonflies stay cooler, but the males also lose color that helps attract females. And researchers predict this will continue to be the case in the future as the climate continues to warm. An even tinier example is a specific kind of bee.

Sevan Suni is an associate professor at the University of San Francisco who studies interactions between plants and pollinators. She has been going to Costa Rica for the last 15 years to study a group of bees commonly known as orchid bees.

These bees are the sole pollinators for about 200 species of orchids in Central and South America. Their bodies look almost jewel-like, with shiny iridescent shells.

Year after year, Suni noticed that one species of bee, the champion’s orchid bee, seemed to shift color from blue-green to orange-red. She and others discovered that, in hotter areas, the number of orange-red bees has increased over time while the number of blue-green bees has decreased.

The areas that increased in temperature faster over time also had more of the red-orange bees. It’s unclear what’s driving this change. The darker blue-green color could be hotter, absorbing more heat. Or the blue-green bees may be more vulnerable since the color of their environment is changing. Due to deforestation in Costa Rica, they may be less camouflaged in a less green environment. Either way, Suni has concerns about potential impacts.

“As a biologist, I’m always interested in biological variation,” she says. “It worries me a little bit if the blue-green morph has an important ecological function and they’re getting less prevalent over time.”

A last gasp of hidden color

Warming ocean waters bleach colorful corals, turning them white. The corals expel symbiotic algae, losing a food source and becoming more vulnerable to disease. Corals can recover after bleaching, but the longer and more frequent the bleaching, the more difficult recovery is. In some cases, corals turn stunningly fluorescent and colorful at the start of bleaching and after — a last bright gasp of life.

These neon colors, usually visible only under ultraviolet light, are always present to some degree, says Anya Salih. Salih, a fellow at the University of Technology Sydney, has studied coral reefs and their fluorescent colors for decades. She dives at night to scan reefs with blue lights.

“Sometimes when I dive with people who are not used to seeing this, I would have to hold their tank so that they don’t turn upside down,” she says, “because in that very colorful, psychedelic world, you lose the perspective of up and down in the water.”

Algae in healthy coral absorb sunlight for energy. When the algae leave due to stress, turning the coral white, more light travels through the remaining skeleton.

The coral becomes white and bleaches, making it more vulnerable to disease and death. Sometimes the coral turns colorfully fluorescent before bleaching.

A healthy coral and algae depend on each other. The coral provides the algae a place to live, and the algae provide the coral with its main sources of nutrients and color.

If stressed, often because of higher ocean temperatures, algae leave the coral.

A 2020 study in Current Biology found that this excess light encourages coral to produce the shockingly colorful pigments. This tends to occur when heat stress is mild and coral cells can still function. These colorful pigments act as a kind of sunscreen barrier protecting the coral from light damage, which encourages algae to return. Researchers believe corals that bleach colorfully have a higher chance of recovery.

Salih has seen reefs glow, bleach and recover, even multiple times. Still, climate change is causing ocean temperatures to rise, creating more bleaching. “So the scope for recovery is low,” she says.

Source: National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration

Coral bleaching has ripple effects on the larger ecosystem of the reef. A 2022 study in Global Change Biology found, for instance, that fewer fish with colorful bodies were found in the Great Barrier Reef following a specific bleaching event. In the future, reef ecosystems might be less diverse, bright and colorful.

“The neon glows of the reefs are a stress response. It’s a cry for help,” says Salih. “They’re fighting for their survival. They’re using their colors to protect themselves. But in many ways they’re failing in many parts of the world. And the reefs are collapsing.”

Now imagine a glacial lake. A pristine ice sheet at the North Pole. Or the vibrant shades of coral.

Color can be a fleeting, subjective thing, simply how one perceives light reflecting off a surface. But it’s also how we see and know our world, and our world is slowly changing around us, even if we don’t notice.

Salih remembers when she accompanied a group of scientists to an Australian reef. “I was also recently on that reef, which was dying, pretty much,” she says. “And they’d never been on the reef and they thought it was beautiful.”

Annual surface air temperature data, Arctic greening data and coral reef bleaching-level heat stress data from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration

The Arctic greening data shows the change in maximum yearly NDVI value from 2000 to 2025. NDVI, or Normalized Difference Vegetation Index, is a commonly used vegetation index that uses satellites to measure near-infrared and red light as a proxy for chlorophyll levels over an area of land. Higher NDVI values indicate healthier vegetation, and lower values indicate stressed vegetation or barren areas.

Coral reef bleaching process diagram based off National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration graphic

Global lake color data from Xiao Yang, Catherine O’Reilly et al. They used satellite imagery from 2013 to 2020 to measure the most common water colors in a representative sample of more than 85,000 lakes worldwide. Dominant wavelength values are measured on the Forel-Ule scale, a standard reference scale used to estimate the color of bodies of water. Around 11,000 lakes, out of the 17,785 blue lakes believed to show sensitivity to temperature changes, are predicted to shift from blue to non-blue.

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/07/nx-s1-602.title: Oklahoma tribes say proposed legal changes put ancestral lands in Ohio at risk
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/07/nx-s1-602.author: Adriana Martinez-Smiley
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/07/nx-s1-602.text:
Adriana Martinez-Smiley

The Trump administration has proposed changes to the National Historic Preservation Act that could endanger historic sites significant to tribal nations across the country. Oklahoma tribes say that puts ancestral lands in Ohio at risk.

Tribal leaders in Oklahoma whose ancestral lands are across the country in Ohio say sacred sites are under threat. Changes favored by the Trump administration to the National Historic Preservation Act could weaken much needed protections, they say. Reporters at member stations WYSO and KOSU take us to both places.

ADRIANA MARTINEZ-SMILEY, BYLINE: I'm Adriana Martinez-Smiley in Ohio, which is home to hundreds of earthworks sacred to Native Americans, like the Miamisburg Mound, one of the largest conical mounds in the eastern United States, rising 65 feet.

MICHELLE COLLINS: Once you get up there, you can just sit and kind of take in a view, a really fantastic view, of the Miami Valley.

MARTINEZ-SMILEY: Miamisburg Mayor Michelle Collins calls the structure awesome.

COLLINS: You're talking something that's a couple thousand years old.

MARTINEZ-SMILEY: The mound was built by the Indigenous Adena Culture. The National Historic Preservation Act, which has been around for 60 years, protects sites like this. Section 106 of the Act allows states, tribes or local governments to consult with federal agencies on development proposals and redesign projects to mitigate harm to sites.

However, the Advisory Council on Historic Preservation, a federal agency, and Congress are separately proposing changes. Their revisions would narrow what's considered damaging to a site and make consultation optional. Democratic Senator Martin Heinrich of New Mexico says the current rules also cause too much of a delay when it comes to approving energy projects.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

MARTIN HEINRICH: America needs to be able to build things in years, not in decades.

MARTINEZ-SMILEY: Advocates say the proposed changes should streamline the permitting process. However, tribal officials say the changes could undermine the responsibility the federal government has to cooperate with tribal nations.

SARAH LIESE, BYLINE: I'm Sarah Liese in Oklahoma. There are 38 federally recognized tribal nations in the state. For some, Ohio was once their home, but they were forcibly displaced to Oklahoma due to broken treaties and federal policies in the 18th and 19th centuries. Chief Ben Barnes of the Shawnee Tribe says the National Historic Preservation Act should remain as is.

BEN BARNES: The Section 106 consultation process allows the Shawnee Tribe and other tribes to make sure that sacred sites, such as the earthworks in Ohio or ancestral burial grounds or places of sacred memory, are preserved.

LIESE: Barnes says they also want to protect the spaces where they currently live, and it's key that Native Americans still have a say in the process with no optional provision about their involvement.

BARNES: We have a very large gas line that runs across Oklahoma to Springfield, Missouri. And one day, that gas line is going to need to be disturbed or going to need to be enlarged or need to be repaired. And without having Section 106 processes, they can do that without ever consulting the people that gather in that place to worship.

LIESE: Blake Norton, an official with the Citizen Potawatomi Nation, says these sites are much more to them than places needing development. He likens it to stripping away the humanity of his ancestors and disregarding the relationship Native Americans have to these spaces.

BLAKE NORTON: And for what? So a project can be completed? So that capitalism can continue?

LIESE: In a statement, Senator Heinrich says he's speaking with tribal leaders about possible compromises on the bill. For NPR News, I'm Sarah Liese in Oklahoma.

MARTINEZ-SMILEY: And I'm Adriana Martinez-Smiley in Ohio.

https://www.theguardian.com/news/2026/no.title: How African philosophies inspired a new approach to staging film festivals in Manchester
https://www.theguardian.com/news/2026/no.author: Chris Osuh Community affairs correspondent

See My World, an event highlighting the pan-African thought via film, poetry and dance, builds on momentum sparked by local activists and creatives

African philosophies including exploring how lessons from the past can shape the present and near future have inspired a film festival coming to Manchester.

See My World, a day dedicated to independent creators from across the African diaspora in the north of England, will take place at the Contact theatre on 21 November.

The festival is part of See My World’s year-round programme showcasing pan-African arts, culture and events.

It reflects the determination among creatives and activists in Manchester to build on the legacy of the 1945 Pan-African Congress in Manchester – which connected luminaries of postwar independence movements with a shared vision of liberation – after last year’s 80th anniversary commemorations.

See My World’s CEO and artistic director, Tunde Adekoya, said this month’s film festival was taking inspiration from across the spectrum of pan-African thought, including the works of Kenyan writers John Mbiti, an Anglican theologian who died in 2019, and Ngũgĩ wa Thiong’o, the author of the groundbreaking 1986 book Decolonising the Mind who died last year.

Both writers rejected the colonial conceit that African thought was inferior, stressed the importance of community and saw reclaiming African ways of knowing as essential to a people’s self-understanding.

While Mbiti sought common ground between African religions and Christianity, Ngũgĩ was a Marxist. He argued colonialism was motivated by cultural and economic conquest, and that European powers used language as their sharpest instrument. Ngũgĩ famously abandoned English to write in Gikuyu, a Bantu language mainly spoken in Kenya and criticised the role missionary Christianity played in colonial rule.

Adekoya said: “It’s a day dedicated to pan-African and global majority films from the north of England with exclusive premieres of documentaries we’ve been working on, which weave together expressions of liberation through art forms like poetry and dance.

“The whole idea is that it’s like a playground in search of strategies of liberation, using the festival as a way to explore different philosophies.

“John Mbiti explores the philosophy and spiritual understandings of time through the concept of Sasa na Zamani – in which the past informs everything that happens moving forward. That reflects how we constantly go back to pan-African histories to inform how we progress.”

Film-makers have been invited to submit films lasting up to 30 minutes from across genres, with no screening fees charged.

As well as submissions, the festival will feature documentaries produced by See My World. They include Homage, a “cinematic love letter to dance” that traces a culture through present-day portraits illustrating dance artists and archival material from Manchester, telling a story of joy, loss, migration, rhythm and resistance. Meanwhile, Poetic Justice explores how pan-African thought and Manchester’s poetry scene speak across decades.

Adekoya added: “The idea is that we would go against the norm of how film festivals are, because when we think about decolonisation, we think about how structures have been created to alienate and exclude communities.

“So we thought our film festival would look more at how we make film accessible and how stories that deserve to be seen get seen. Throughout the day we will have different activities, from exhibitions to explorations of our performances, discussions, Q&As, insights into directors’ processes, and workshops.

“We’ve been looking for literature and concepts that inform us and give us an understanding of who we truly are. And as works from thinkers like John Mbiti have come into our sphere, they have really emboldened us to think differently about our place in the world and what we do.”

See My World film festival runs from 2pm to 11pm on Saturday 21 November at Contact theatre, Oxford Road, Manchester.

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: Who’s who at Cop31: key players at the climate talks
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Fiona Harvey Environment editor
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
What are the relationships and dominant interests in play, as the summit kicks off after a bitter row over its hosting?

Hosting Cop was a key pledge from Australia’s prime minister, Anthony Albanese in 2021, while in opposition, before his successful election campaign. But arcane rules meant the country had to wait its turn to bid and was then embroiled in an angry row with Turkey over the hosting. The final compromise put Australia in charge of the negotiations which will take place in the Turkish city of Antalya. The bitter taste left by the row lingers and Australia has seemed to some a rather half-hearted host. The country’s media has been much quieter on Cop than previous host countries, and although Albanese will speak at the opening of the leaders’ segment, he is unlikely to stay long.

Chris Bowen, Australia’s climate and energy minister, will be in daily charge of the negotiations. As aspects of Australia’s energy supply also fall under his portfolio, he has been in the sometimes uncomfortable position of having to boost fossil fuels while insisting on the need for a clean energy transition.

Yet Australia has a positive story to tell on decarbonisation: while remaining one of the world’s major fossil fuel exporters, the country has also invested heavily in renewables, and solar power has now expanded so much that consumers are sometimes offered free electricity.

Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, Turkey’s autocratic president, showed little interest in climate and environmental concerns before bidding to host this year’s Cop summit.

In the last five years, Cop has also been held in Egypt, the United Arab Emirates, Azerbaijan, all in the same broad region. This has given an outsize role to the Arab group of countries, who are neighbours in the region and have a strong interest in ensuring that fossil fuel interests – including their lobbyists – are well represented.

Australia runs the overall direction of the negotiations, and Turkey’s government, with the environment minister, Murat Kurum, has control of the action agenda, a programme of voluntary initiatives. Erdoğan has used this to push forward a key interest of his wife, Emine Erdoğan, in cutting waste and promoting the circular economy. She has called for an end to “throwaway culture” and for recycling instead of landfill – though Turkey still has sites that leak vast quantities of methane.

Fatih Birol, the head of the International Energy Agency and one of the world’s leading energy economists, is understood to be one of the advisers behind this year’s emphasis on electrification, displacing fossil fuels with electricity for heating, transport and industrial uses. This could halve the amount of energy we need, and is the next biggest step, after boosting renewable energy generation, needed for a low-carbon world.

The recently re-elected President Lula da Silva will come to Cop31 for his first trip abroad after winning his historic fourth term, and will bring two roadmaps, one a global plan for the transition away from fossil fuels, the other for halting and reversing deforestation. These are non-binding, and contain no deadlines or firm requirements from governments, but show a series of steps that governments can take to achieve these goals.

Xi Jinping, the president of China, will not come to this year’s Cop, but his country’s rapid energy and industrial transformation will determine the course of the planet’s future. China is the world’s second biggest economy and the biggest emitter of greenhouse gases, making up nearly a third of global annual carbon output, owing mainly to the use of fossil fuels to power its explosive economic growth for the last 25 years. But it has also invested in renewable energy, which is reshaping the global energy business.

Xi may not be present in Antalya, but the top officials he sends will know that petrostates – including Russia, Saudi Arabia and the UAE – are his important allies. However, countries pushing for a low-carbon future may be more important still – as China’s customers.

For several months this year, India’s prime minister, Narendra Modi, mulled an intriguing proposition: to host the Cop33 UN climate summit in 2028. In the end, India withdrew its bid in April without specifying why, leaving the field open. India is torn between its burgeoning clean energy sector – it now has the world’s third biggest installed capacity of renewable energy, after China and the US – and its coal sector, which still supplies about 70% of electricity, and has close links to Modi.

Bhupender Yadav, India’s environment minister, who leads its Cop delegations, enjoys a mutually supportive relationship with the UK’s Ed Miliband, and a reputation as a forward thinker.

The attention of Donald Trump has been fixed on the crucial midterm elections, a verdict on his second term as president that has shown Republicans the electoral dangers of an unpredictable White House. No US delegation is expected at Cop31, and soon Trump’s withdrawal of the country from the UN framework convention on climate change will mean none can take part.

Trump’s shadow was felt at Cop30 in Belem last year, as he started to dismantle the US’s renewable energy sector and boost fossil fuels, setting the US on course to start increasing greenhouse gas emissions again, after decades in which they fell. But his administration’s unpopularity with the US electorate, and a drought and fire-filled summer, has bolstered the pro-climate stance of scores of Democratic congresspeople and state governors, despite a campaign of “climate hushing” before the midterms. Some of them, and a scattering of business leaders, may attend Cop31.

Andy Burnham will attend Cop for the first time this year, after a mixed record on the climate since taking office. During the record-breaking heatwaves and droughts of this summer, the British prime minister was criticised for failing to speak out on the climate crisis. He subsequently made strong interventions affirming his support for the UK’s target of reaching net zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050, but then backed the Jackdaw gasfield. No decision has been announced on the Rosebank oilfield yet.

The planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essential

after newsletter promotion

From December, Burnham will have a much bigger opportunity to craft climate policy on the international stage: the UK will take over the revolving presidency of the influential G20 group, which comprises the world’s biggest developed and developing economies. The Guardian understands that the UK will emphasise building resilience against the impacts of the climate crisis as a key focus of the G20 for its year-long presidency.

Miliband, now foreign secretary, and a veteran of many Cops in government and opposition, is expected to accompany the prime minister to the leaders’ summit segment of Cop31. Miliband was hailed, in public and private, by many participants last year for his patient bridge-building that helped Brazil to rescue a deal from the fractious final hours of Cop30.

At this year’s UN general assembly, he also briefed other governments on the findings of the UK’s joint intelligence committee, which warned that the impact of collapsing ecosystems around the world posed a national security risk, threatening food shortages, mass migration and potential nuclear war.

The energy and net zero secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, will head the UK’s Cop31 delegation for the final negotiations in the last days of this fortnight of talks, after the leaders have departed.

The EU has faced a quandary over its climate convictions in recent years. Far-right populists are on the rise, pushing climate denialism, and the bloc has backed down from some key regulations, watering down its green deal package, loosening the strings on corporate climate liabilities, delaying rules on trade in goods from deforested areas, and extending the phase-in of new car rules. The failure of Europe’s car industry to move decisively to electric vehicles – preferring lobbying against emissions standards, which has turned out to be a poor strategy as consumers turn in droves to cheap-to-run EVs – has led to threats to slap tariffs on China.

The EU commission president, Ursula von der Leyen called this summer’s record-breaking heatwaves and drought a “summer of truth” that must be answered: she is now confirmed for the summit. Wopke Hoekstra, the Dutch climate commissioner, will oversee the final stages of the talks for the EU, and is expected to make competition with China a key focus.

Cop31 will mark the final outing at a UN climate summit for António Guterres, the UN secretary general, who has regularly intervened powerfully on this subject. A successor to Guterres has still not yet been chosen – the US has tried to get Viktor Orbán, the far-right former president of Hungary, into the role, or a former minister from the United Arab Emirates, Lana Nusseibeh.

Simon Stiell, the determined executive secretary of the UNFCCC, will oversee the talks, with an added twist to his job this year, having to liaise between the two co-hosts as well as the fractious parties.

Saudi failed to confirm with the Guardian before Cop who would lead its delegation, but the country’s recent behaviour at international climate meetings tells its own story. The country has a long history of obstructing the UN climate negotiations, though its behaviour was sometimes muted when the US intervened. With Trump in the White House, Saudi has felt emboldened to interfere further, with allies including Russia, Venezuela, members of the Arab group, and the Like-Minded Developing Countries grouping.

At Cop30, the Saudi delegation refused to allow even an oblique mention of the pledge to “transition away from fossil fuels”, made at Cop28 in Dubai in 2023, in the final text until the final moments.

At recent meetings of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, Saudi led a small group of countries – including China, India, Russia and Kenya – that fought to delay publication of the next comprehensive assessment of climate science. Publication of the landmark report, which is expected to warn of catastrophic impacts from further temperature rises, was expected in 2028, in time for Cop33 at which countries will assess their progress on meeting emissions-cutting goals under the Paris agreement, a process known as the “global stocktake”. Delaying it by a year or more, as Saudi wants, would mean a loss of urgency for the global stocktake, and could help countries to get away with inadequate measures on decarbonisation.
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.summary: Australia's prime minister has been in charge of negotiations for the Cop summit. Andy Burnham will attend Cop31 for the first time this year. The UK will take over the revolving presidency of the influential G20 group.

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: Cop31: what is at stake at the UN climate summit and what can it achieve?
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Fiona Harvey Environment editor
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
Delegates from more than 190 countries are gathering in Turkey for climate talks, but the US will be absent

As the planet faces unprecedented human-caused global heating, heads of government are meeting for the next fortnight for the latest round of climate talks. We ask why it matters and what is likely to be achieved.

From 9-20 November, world leaders, ministers and high-ranking officials from more than 190 countries are expected to convene in Antalya in Turkey, for the annual UN climate talks. This year, the summit will be hosted by Turkey, but in an unusual twist the negotiations will be presided over by Australia in a compromise deal struck after the two countries vied for the presidency.

While nearly all of the 196 original signatories of the 2015 Paris climate agreement are expected to be present, one glaring absence will be the US, whose president, Donald Trump, has withdrawn from Paris.

Australia will take charge of the formal negotiations where countries thrash out the details of work programmes such as the “just transition”, climate finance and putting the world on track to stick as closely as possible to the Paris agreement goal of limiting temperature rises to 1.5C above pre-industrial levels.

Turkey will take charge of the “action agenda”, the voluntary agreements that work towards the Paris goals but are not legally binding: programmes on cutting waste and achieving a circular economy, cutting methane, improving food security, and – perhaps most important – the electrification of the global economy.

The Paris goal of 1.5C has been breached, but the UN argues that rapid action to cut greenhouse gas emissions would limit the “overshoot” and allow for a return to lower temperatures by the end of this century. For that to happen, countries need to break dependence on fossil fuels and adopt low-carbon technologies faster. The two roadmaps from Brazil – on the “transition away from fossil fuels” and on halting deforestation – will present ways of doing so.

Developing countries are also in dire need of help to cope with the hastening impacts of the climate crisis. After the disaster in Nepal, the country has been granted access to the global fund for “loss and damage” – the rescue and rehabilitation of communities stricken by climate-related disasters. But it is not enough, and poor countries also lack the means to adapt their infrastructure to worsening extreme weather.

Rich countries have been cutting their overseas aid, while rising interest rates have loaded further debt on to the poor.

It was not until 2023 at Cop28 that the final agreement directly addressed fossil fuels for the first time, due to long-term strident opposition from producing countries. The agreement included a resolution to “transition away from fossil fuels” but no deadline or plan for doing so. It is still tricky to get fossil fuels directly on to the Cop agenda, which requires consensus from nearly all parties, but this year the issue will be addressed through a non-binding “roadmap” for the global transition away from fossil fuels.

Given the tense and fragile geopolitical situation – some commentators believe we are already in the midst of an unacknowledged third world war, while inflation and a rising far right are upsetting economies – countries might be tempted to settle for a quiet meeting.

But there are hopes for a better outcome, which could include: acceptance of the plans Brazil has produced and a promise to carry them forward; progress on climate finance for developing countries; a resolution to the row over climate science that has plagued recent meetings of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change; and the fleshing out of the “just transition mechanism” designed to help workers reliant on fossil fuels to adjust to a low-carbon economy.

Progress is also possible through Cop-related means outside the formal negotiations. Earlier this year, more than 60 countries, including the UK, the EU and dozens of developing nations, gathered in Colombia to vow to “transition away from fossil fuels”. This “coalition of the willing” could be boosted at Cop31 by new members, as well as fresh impetus from the recent success of political movements in several countries – Brazil, Canada, Serbia, Hungary and the US in states that decisively rejected Donald Trump at the midterms.

Several prominent members of the US Congress may attend, along with businesspeople and US civil society groups, so there will be representation beyond the White House’s absence. Trump appears intent on boosting fossil fuel interests as much as possible in the US, but with oil prices still high after his war in Iran, the economics of low-carbon energy look ever more favourable.

The geopolitics and the technology. Although the winds of conflict have upended international relations, they have also shown countries can benefit from the energy security that results from decentralised renewable generation. China’s oil imports, for instance, are likely to be down about 12% this year owing to a massive uptake of electric vehicles, and its renewable generation capacity has now outstripped coal. This is saving billions of dollars for consumers and businesses as the oil price soars.

Solar is booming in Africa at last, while in Pakistan a consumer-led rooftop revolution now produces about a quarter of the electricity used. Close to half of new cars in countries from Vietnam to some EU members are now electric.

Electrification will be a key focus of Cop31, and the high efficiency of electric technology means it could reduce the amount of primary energy use by half across the world, according to University of Oxford professor Jan Rosenow.

Politically, the re-election of Lula as president in Brazil has also cheered climate supporters. Lula will attend Cop, his first international visit since re-election, and is likely to be a fiery presence, showing progressive parties around the world how to win while championing the climate.

Officials say suspect holds far-right views and three people found dead at his home were his parents and sister

Polish prosecutors have opened a terrorism investigation after a 24-year-old man opened fire in a busy market square in Kraków, killing six people including a Briton and injuring 17, in an attack that authorities said was probably inspired by far-right ideologies.

Police confirmed on Sunday that three people found dead at the gunman’s home after the attack on Saturday afternoon were his father, 53, mother, 52, and sister, 21.

As two days of national mourning began, the national prosecutor’s office said on social media it had launched an investigation into “the killing of six people … using a firearm, and the attempted murder of many others, including police officers, this act constituting a terrorist offence”.

The rare mass shooting has shocked a country that was considered safer than many of its western European neighbours, and has deepened concern after several school stabbings in October that left one woman dead and which officials said were linked to extremist content online.

The Kraków suspect, a Polish national, drove into the city’s main square in the heart of the old town, which is usually packed with tourists, at top speed at about 3pm on Saturday. Wearing military-style fatigues and a bulletproof vest, he started shooting at random as he took what the Kraków police spokesperson Katarzyna Cisło described as a “wild ride” around the square.

The interior minister, Marcin Kierwiński, said the suspect, who was apprehended and taken to hospital after being wounded in an exchange of fire with police, was fascinated with far-right ideologies and held “very radical” and “ultra-nationalistic” views.

Four women and two men were killed, including a British citizen, Polish police said. Three of the victims were Polish women and the remaining two have not yet been identified. Five of the wounded are foreign nationals from Britain, Austria, Germany, Portugal and Russia.

Two police ⁠officers were also among the injured, one of whom is in a serious condition. The suspect underwent surgery in hospital, where he is under heavy police guard.

The bodies of the suspect’s parents and sister were found at the family home in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, a town about 100 miles north-east of Kraków. Police said they had probably died of gunshot wounds.

Mourners have left candles in tribute to victims in the square, which was still partially cordoned off on Sunday. Flags across the country have been lowered to half mast, as have European flags outside the European Commission in Brussels “in solidarity with the Polish people”, the commission said.

The Polish defense minister, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, called the shooting an “act of terror” on the people of Kraków, Poland’s second largest city, which receives 15 million visitors a year, most of them passing through the main square.

Kraków authorities said the square and adjoining streets “as well as sections along the perpetrator’s escape route will be closed for several hours”. Police in Warsaw, the Polish capital, said security had been bolstered there.

Maria, a 20-year-old employee at a cafe in Warsaw, told Reuters she “almost burst into tears” when she heard about the attack in Kraków. “Recent events – not just this one, but things happening lately – are really affecting our sense of security,” ⁠she said.

The daily newspaper Rzeczpospolita said in an editorial that the mass shooting had brought a “brutal end ​to an era in which Poland was ​considered an island of safety”.

The UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, said: “I’m shocked and saddened by the appalling shooting in Kraków today,. My thoughts are with the families of those who have lost their lives, everyone injured and all those affected by this senseless violence.”

The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said his country stood in solidarity with its neighbour, calling the shooting a shocking crime.

France’s Emmanuel Macron described “shock and disbelief following the tragic shooting in Kraków”, while the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, said: “The events in Kraków have deeply affected me,” adding that Germany stood with Poland “as a friend and partner in these difficult times”.

Italy’s prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, expressed condolences to Poland “following the vile and unacceptable act of violence”.

https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/n.author: Kim Willsher
https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/n.text:
Luc Corlouër made ‘deal’ with Prix Goncourt winner Philippe Jaenada over his research into model Louise Cansot, murdered in Paris in 1949

For almost eight decades the artists’ model Louise Cansot, the subject of the novel winning France’s most prestigious literary prize this year, was one of Paris’s forgotten murder victims.

After her body was found near the Seine in September 1949, city police wrote off the young woman, immortalised as “the girl of 100 portraits”, as loose, libertine and – worse – an unmarried mother. They closed their investigation after just four months having made little effort to find her killer.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

But long before the author Philippe Jaenada began researching his, Prix Goncourt-winning novel, L’Inconnue du Quai de Javel (The Unknown Woman of the Quai de Javel), another writer from the Breton village where Cansot was born had already spent decades researching her story.

Luc Corlouër might have felt aggrieved but in a rare show of literary solidarity, the two writers decided they would both publish books. As part of what he calls “the deal”, Corlouër handed Jaenada his notes.

“We agreed we would write our respective books, which are very different. And after all, the star was him, not me,” Corlouër told the Guardian. “By giving him the subject I knew he would make a really superb book. He is a great novelist.”

Cansot, nicknamed Lise, was born in Tréguier, on the Côtes-d’Armor in north-west France, the daughter of a shoe repairer. In 1937, aged 16, she left her family and moved to Paris where her beauty attracted the attention of the celebrated Montparnasse artists, who jostled to have her pose for them.

When war broke out and most of the artists fled south, Cansot remained in Paris working as a film extra, waiter and dancer at the Folies Bergère. She had a five-year-old daughter, Nathalie, whom she left with a nanny in the suburbs until she could raise the money for an apartment, but with the painters gone and no steady income, her situation became increasingly desperate.

On 7 September 1949, her body was found on the Quai du Javel, now known as the Quai André-Citroën, in the 15th arrondissement, south-west of the Eiffel Tower. Detectives initially identified four possible murderers but rapidly filed the case as unsolved.

Jaenada, the author of 17 novels, discovered the story while looking through old newspapers in the French National Library.

By then, Corlouër had already amassed maps, images, photos, paintings, documents, letters and newspaper cuttings on Cansot. His book, La Tragédie du plus beau modèle de Paris (The Tragedy of the Most Beautiful Paris Model) was finally published on 19 August – the same date as Jaenada’s novel – and is based on the documentary information about the case and the victim.

Corlouër says his interest in Cansot was piqued in 1981, when he met an elderly woman at the war memorial in Tréguier. “She told me one name was of a local girl, Annick Cansot, run over by a German truck during the war. When I said: ‘How terrible,’, she said even worse was that her older sister had been murdered in Paris.

“I decided I had to know about Louise Cansot and what happened to her, so I began researching, but my book was a failure. It was a novel about a murder investigation that did not identify the murderer. It was rejected by one publisher after another.

“I thought there was only one person capable of writing such a book: Philippe Jaenada, whom I had already met at a literary salon. Then one day he contacted me. He told me he was interested in the case but said he wouldn’t do anything without me.

“So, I entrusted him with my research. I gave it to him and he did the best investigation imaginable. He dissected all the information and found things I didn’t even think of.”

The original 300-page police report on Cansot’s murder concluded that she was a woman of “ill repute” and newspaper reports speculated that she was a sex worker, alcoholic or drug addict.

In his 530-page book, Jaenada gives a more sympathetic portrayal of the victim, and suggests the name of the man he believes strangled Cansot after inviting her to visit a flat she hoped to rent. His research included reading 74 out of the 75 novels by Georges Simenon featuring Inspector Maigret in 1940s Paris.

Corlouër said it was unsurprising the police had not made the same effort to find the killer back then.

“Lise was a very modern girl at least 50 years ahead of her time,” he said. “She dressed well, was intelligent and free in her choice of lovers. But when she was killed, what journalists and the police saw was a young woman who was a bit libertine, had a baby out of wedlock, had jobs they didn’t think were proper jobs and posed for painters. To them, she had brought what happened on herself.”

Corlouër said he and Jaenada had wanted to rehabilitate Cansot’s reputation after 77 years of slander. “In the police report it’s more or less written that she deserved it. And the defamation continued after her murder,” he said.

Corlouër also revealed how the authors traced Cansot’s daughter Nathalie, now 80, who was raised by another sister, Valentine.

“I don’t want to say too much because it would spoil the end of Philippe’s novel, but when we found her, the first thing she said was she didn’t want to hear a word about her mother and that Lise was a prostitute,” Corlouër said.

“She was raised by her aunt, who was very jealous of Lise and who for years told the girl her mother was disreputable. Nathalie was very surprised when Philippe and I told her this was not true, that her mother was an amazing woman.

“When she heard this, she did not cry. She’s tough like her mother, but she was amazed. So there is a kind of happy ending to this tragic story.”

Margaret Parkes and her husband, in their 80s, want Allan Grimson to reveal location of their son Simon’s remains

The mother of a teenage Royal Navy sailor who vanished 40 years ago has called for a “serial killer” suspected of murdering him to finally reveal where her son’s body is hidden.

Speaking as Simon Parkes’ suspected murderer, the former navy petty officer Allan Grimson, was sentenced for sexual offences against four boys and men, Margaret Parkes, 80, said time was running out for her and her 84-year-old husband, David, to find out what happened to their son.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

She said they had not been able to hold a funeral and the not knowing had hung over the family for four decades. “It never goes away, it never will. It’s affected our lives tremendously. I think we’re totally different people to how we were before it happened,” she said.

They still hope their son’s remains may be found. “That’s what keeps you going, that you will know,” she said. “Whether Grimson will admit it, I’m very doubtful. I would like it to happen but I doubt it. I think it’s something to do with power, maybe. I try not to think of him as a person, I just think of the victims.”

Parkes, a retired primary school teacher, said she felt Grimson, 67, should never be released. “He should be kept in for ever. He shouldn’t be in the community. He shouldn’t be let out on parole. He’s not going to change.”

Grimson has been in jail for more than 25 years after admitting killing two young men, both of whom had been in the navy in the late 1990s in Portsmouth. The sentencing judge in 2001 described him as a “serial killer in nature if not by number”.

In July this year, Grimson was convicted by a jury of sexual offences against four boys and men, the youngest only 14, also in the 1990s, and on Friday the judge Paul Dugdale jailed him for another 22 years for these crimes.

The judge told Grimson: “You remain dangerous. You still pose a significant risk to members of the public.”

He said Grimson had targeted vulnerable boys and young men whose trust he had abused. They had suffered “lifelong” harm, the judge said as he praised their “staggering courage” in coming forward now.

Dugdale said Grimson would not be eligible to be considered for parole until just before his 80th birthday, but added that his life sentence for the two murders meant he may never be freed.

Margaret Parkes followed the trial in the summer from her home near Bristol. Her son’s disappearance was mentioned during legal argument when Dugdale acknowledged that Grimson was a suspect.

She was impressed by the four men who gave evidence against Grimson. “They’ve come forward after all these years and they’ve been traumatised all their lives and to go through a court case it must have been dreadful, but so important to them. You can’t bring back what he’s taken away,” she said.

Her son vanished in Gibraltar on 12 December 1986 when the ship he was serving on docked in the British overseas territory. He has never been found. Grimson, who was serving on the same vessel, has long been suspected of killing Simon, though he denies it.

Parkes said her son had been looking forward to getting back to England and was going to be posted at a navy air station in Somerset. “He was just a youngster – 18, well, almost 19. He was liked by everyone. He was just fun. He enjoyed life,” she said.

“When he disappeared it was dreadful, such a shock. You just went into automatic mode really. All we had was a phone call. The navy said that he’d gone awol. We had about 10 or 12 years of not having any support or any contact with anyone. We’re just ordinary people. We didn’t know how to deal with authority. The press were the only ones that every now and again would bring it up.”

In 1999, Grimson led British police to the bodies of Nicholas Wright, 18, and Sion Jenkins, 20, whom he had murdered in Hampshire on the same date – 12 December – in successive years, 1997 and 1998.

Parkes said: “The police came and said they were looking back because it was 12 December he killed them and Simon disappeared on the 12th, so that was the link to begin with.”

Over the years, there have been searches in Gibraltar but Simon’s remains could not be not found. It means the family have not been able to obtain a death certificate.

In 2020, the Parole Board recommended Grimson be moved to an open prison to prepare him for freedom. “He was very, very close to being released,” Parkes said. “We couldn’t believe it but were helpless to do anything.”

His chance of liberty was scuppered when the four men came forward to describe the offences Grimson had committed against them between 1994 and 1999.

Parkes once asked Grimson directly what happened to her son. “I did write him a letter when he was in prison, years and years and years ago. But nothing came of that,” she said.

She was still struck by Grimson telling police when he was arrested for the murders of Wright and Jenkins that killing was “better than sex”. She said: “You can’t change that mentality in a person. I think he’s tried to be a very good boy in prison, a model prisoner probably, but I think he should stay in for as long as possible.”

There is another chance for the family. An inquest for Simon is finally due to be held in Gibraltar next year after a campaign by a local journalist, Ros Astengo, who is writing a book about his case.

Parkes and her husband have health issues. She said: “We’ll go over if we can manage it.”

Does she think she will find the answer to what happened there? “Who knows?” she said. “It’s taken such a long time to get to this point. We might not be here next year.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Chris Stein in Washington
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Midterms success gives party potent leverage over Trump – expect tough campaigns of investigating and lawmaking

“C
osts, chaos, corruption”: after almost two years spent relentlessly criticizing Donald Trump for failing to address those three, broad political concerns, Democrats won a monumental return to power in Tuesday’s midterm elections that will give them potent new leverage over the president.

Now the question becomes: what will they do with it?

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

While party leaders say their exact strategy remains under discussion, all signs point to Democrats embarking on aggressive campaigns of both investigating and lawmaking, with the aim of giving their eventual nominee the ammunition they will need to win the 2028 presidential election.

“We are going to make sure that those candidates running for president of the United States aren’t getting asked about plastic-straw bans. Instead, we should be talking about all of the legislation that we pass out of the House, pass out of the Senate, and force to Donald Trump’s desk,” Greg Casar, the chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, told reporters on Wednesday.

He envisioned “passing bold legislation that people called for, every single week, off of the floor of the House and the Senate”, pointing to bans on price gouging, Super Pacs and stock trading by lawmakers as priorities. “If [Trump] vetoes it, then that is the platform upon which candidates can run in 2028, and then we can get signed into law in 2029,” Casar said.

That election is still two, long and unpredictable years off. And despite flipping seats across the country, the Democratic party brand remains deeply unpopular.

But Democrats have reason to feel confident: Republicans suffered such a cataclysm Tuesday that they lost Senate seats they’d held for decades, and House seats drawn specifically to elect only Republicans.

It was the biggest midterm defeat for an incumbent party in more than 50 years, but the power Democrats have gained in Congress is not unlimited. Trump is still set to inhabit the White House until January 2029, and can veto bills that do not pass with overwhelming support.

And the Senate filibuster – which Democrats used to block many bills that Republicans attempted to pass along party lines over the first half of Trump’s second term – remains in place. Now the shoe is on the other foot: Republicans can use it to stop any incoming Democratic legislation that does not have 60 votes in a chamber. Ballot counting is still ongoing, but if the two outstanding Senate races are won by their candidates, Democrats and their allies will have 56 seats.

Congress’s incoming leaders have made clear those obstacles will not stop them from at least trying to enact legislative solutions to the problems they campaigned on fixing.

“We made a promise to the country that we would fight for an affordable America, and we intend to keep it,” said Hakeem Jeffries, who is set to become speaker of the House of Representatives when the new Congress convenes after the new year.

He named as priorities reimplementing premium tax credits for Affordable Care Act (ACA) health plans as well as undoing the cuts to the Medicaid insurance program that Republicans approved last year. Jeffries also promised legislative action to make Trump undo his tariffs, and end the conflict with Iran.

“Everything we do maps onto three promises, the very same three we ran on, turning from a critique into a to-do list: lower costs, make your government work for you, clean up the corruption,” Chuck Schumer, who is expected to be the next Senate majority leader, said during an appearance at the Center for American Progress, a liberal thinktank.

One thing that does not seem to be on the table: impeaching Trump, for a third time. During his first term, Senate Republicans rescued the president after two impeachments, first on charges of leveraging aid to undermine his political rivals, and then again after his supporters attacked the Capitol on January 6.

While Democrats have accused Trump of violating the law and the constitution regularly during his second term, they appear clear-eyed about Republicans’ willingness to force the president from office.

“I haven’t had a single member of the House Democratic Caucus talk to me about impeachment,” Jeffries said. “We’ve been relentlessly focused on affordability and on accountability.”

When it comes to the latter, Democrats have no shortage of ideas. After publicly issuing a warning to potential targets to “lawyer up,” Robert Garcia, who will lead the investigative House oversight panel, told reporters this week to expect inquiries related to allegations of corruption in Department of Homeland Security (DHS) contracting, stock trading by lawmakers, corporate profiteering and the government’s release of files related to disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein.

Noting he’d sent more than 200 demands for information to the Trump administration and others, Jamie Raskin, who is expected to lead the House judiciary committee, said “go back and read my letters” when discussing who he would investigate next year. His letters carried no legal force, because he was in the congressional minority, but that will soon change – once the Democrats take committee gavels next year, they can issue subpoenas.

The party also doesn’t lack for ideas when it comes to addressing concerns about affordability, a major issue for voters in the elections.

It was Democrats’ demands to extend the ACA subsidies that led to the record-long government shutdown last year, and their candidates made warnings about the impending Medicaid cuts prominent in their campaigns.

The outgoing Republican congressional majorities have so far rejected attempts to address either issue, but Democrats did have some luck coaxing the majority to vote for war powers resolutions intended to end the conflict with Iran – one measure did pass, but the president has thus far ignored it.

“Trump has the ability to block our efforts to lower costs for American families, root out corruption in Washington, end the chaos in our streets and overseas,” Schumer acknowledged.

“But if he does that, I have no doubt the American people will rebuke him and his party just like they did in the election.”

So far, Trump, who cannot run again in 2028, has oscillated between saying he’d be willing to work with Democrats, and defiantly posting on social media an image of a red cap with the word “Veto” written on it.

The Democratic victories in the midterms came only after at-times anguished primaries that underscored the divides between the left and centers in the party, and over contentious issues like aid to Israel.

In the wake of their wins, leaders of the party’s ideological factions have taken tones of unity and cooperation – which could be aided by the fact that the Democratic majorities in both the Senate and House are expected to be so large that intraparty fights could be less impactful.

Kristen McDonald Rivet, who leads freshman lawmakers on the centrist New Democrat Coalition, acknowledged that when it comes to healthcare – a marquee issue for everyone in the party – “people want big change”.

“Some people’s approach to that is Medicare for all. Others are talking about Medicare for all who want it,” McDonald Rivet told reporters.

“There’s all kinds of ways to solve the solution, but I actually do not see that as a place of combat with other members of the caucus. It’s actually an incredibly hopeful thing that we are going to debate what big thing we can do around healthcare.”
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: Democrats won a monumental return to power in Tuesday's midterm elections. The party's new strategy is to investigate and lawmaking. The aim is to give their eventual nominee the ammunition they will need to win the 2028 presidential election.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Hannah Harris Green
