Australia swarmed Samoa to make its way into the World Cup final. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer )

They say you can't fight city hall, but sometimes against Australia, it feels like you're flat out breaking a few windows.

The Kangaroos cruised into the World Cup final by turning Samoa's dream into a recurring nightmare via their 44-12 win in Sydney on Sunday night.

As New Zealand did the night before, Australia won this on the finer margins.

Spirit filled the night through the anthems, where tears again flowed freely, and the Siva Tau, which ended with Brian To'o and Tino Fa'asuamaleaui sharing a moment more powerful than words can say.

Moments like that are the big things, the reason these matches matter in the first place. And it's what makes them feel like more than a game but through the blinding emotion there is still a game to be won.

To do it when it really matters, you need to do all the little things and Australia proved it's the little things that make up life right from the start as, not for the first time, its science defeated Samoa's magic on the big stage.

Against any other team, it might not matter that Francis Manuleleua and Jazz Tevaga, two middle forwards, found themselves defend together off a scrum. It's not the done thing, but you can get away with it.

But the Kangaroo punished Samoa for that lapse when Tom Dearden took them and threw a dummy everyone knows is coming but nobody seems to know how to stop for the first try of the night.

Like the hardest teachers, Australia stressed the same lesson over and over again and Samoa's inability to change the course meant frustration took hold, which only made things worse.

Three times in the first half alone, Samoa conceded a penalty, a set restart and a try in quick sequence. For the final 19 minutes of the half, they got to their kick just twice.

Give Australia that much ball and field position and you're asking for punishment.

The Kangaroos ran up the tries and carried a 26-2 lead into the break that killed off the game as a contest and robbed the blue wave in the stands of their power.

Samoa's army of fans were silenced by Australia.  (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer )

The harder the Samoans tried and the more venom they played with, the more it turned to a choking bile in their throats.

Spencer Leniu dropped the ball with his first touch, got sin-binned for dissent, then dropped the ball with his first touch on return.

They did what they could to the end, and twice had tries chalked off by the barest of margins. But in the end Australia were too clinical, too clever, too willing and able to exploit every little edge on offer until it all added up to a comfortable win.

Samoa's poor discipline — Adam Gee pinged them for a combined 12 restarts and penalties in the end — and errors would have been much to overcome against most sides and most sides aren't packing Australia's heat.

The Kangaroos will face New Zealand in the final of the Rugby League World Cup after overwhelming Samoa 44-12 at Sydney Football Stadium. Follow live.

Reece Walsh, raced in a brilliant hat-trick to continue his dazzling tournament and put himself right in the frame to be awarded the Golden Boot on Thursday as the best international player of the year.

The Broncos firecracker was the explosion and the fuse was lit by Cameron Munster and Harry Grant, who were in total control of every aspect of the match throughout.

Pat Carrigan and Tino Fa'asuamaleaui were both strong in the middle in a performance that should help restore a little of the Australian forwards battered reputation.

The win would have been a personal triumph for Fa'asuamaleaui given the Samoa international copped plenty from the crowd.

The Pacific nations have given this World Cup so much and they feel like the future of Test football. But this game was a reminder of the power of old money and that the most dangerous creatures in these waters are still Kangaroos.

There is a reason, for all the improvement Samoa and Tonga have made in recent years, they only have one win over Australia from a combined 10 attempts.

It's the same reason Australia has only lost one game from 18 starts in the set restart era, which is the same reason they haven't lost a game on home soil in 11 years.

Samoa's frustration was palpable as the game slipped away. (Getty Images: Spencer)

To climb the green and gold mountain, you need to be as close as perfect as reality can allow because need a way to douse their firepower and blunt their smarts while getting just about everything right yourself.

New Zealand have the team to do it, to the point they should be favourites for the final. But it's no guarantee they will because team as fierce and skilled as Samoa, for all their might and power, couldn't really get themselves in the fight.

After all their growth, it is the last step they need to take but perhaps the longest of all.

The Kangaroos are as ruthless as they are well-drilled, as fast as they are merciless.

That is why, even as the Davids have gotten bigger, Goliath still reigns.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: 800 Rally in Tokyo to demand North Korea abductees’ immediate return
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
A national rally calling for the immediate and collective return of all Japanese citizens abducted by North Korea decades ago was held in Tokyo on Sunday, attended by about 800 people, including Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi.

“The parents of abductees are living each day on the edge,” Takuya Yokota, the younger brother of Megumi Yokota, who was abducted to North Korea in 1977 at the age of 13, said at the rally. “I want everyone to continue fighting with us with a strong determination never to give up until all abductees return home.”

Takuya, 58, is head of the Association of Families of Victims Kidnapped by North Korea and one of the organizers of the rally.

Sakie Yokota, Megumi’s 90-year-old mother, who is the only remaining parent among the families of government-recognized abductees still awaiting the return of their loved ones, said, “I feel indescribable heartache and sorrow because a family member I raised with great care was taken away.”

“For almost 50 years, we have been unable to save her. We must continue to show, with one united heart, that we will never allow the abduction issue to be left unaddressed,” Sakie said.

Koichiro Iizuka, 49, the eldest son of abductee Yaeko Taguchi, who was kidnapped in 1978 at the age of 22, said: “Once the new year begins, it will be 49 years since my mother was abducted. I absolutely cannot accept allowing that to stretch to 50 years.”

Addressing the gathering, Takaichi said: “I feel very sorry that the abductees have not yet been able to return home. I am determined to make a breakthrough during my tenure, and my mission will not end until the day their families can embrace their loved ones again.”

The rally adopted a resolution calling on North Korea to return all abductees while members of the parents’ generation are still alive.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.summary: A national rally calling for the immediate and collective return of all Japanese citizens abducted by North Korea was held in Tokyo on Sunday. The rally adopted a resolution calling on North Korea to return all abductees while members of the parents’ generation are still alive.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: What the end of U.N. peacekeeping in Western Sahara means
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
TUNIS – For the first time in more than three decades, the U.N. Security Council has failed to renew the mandate for its peacekeeping mission in North Africa’s disputed Western Sahara.

The vast mineral-rich desert territory, home to significant phosphate reserves and fishing resources, was a Spanish colony until 1975.

It is largely controlled by Morocco but has been claimed for decades by the Algeria-backed Polisario Front, and remains on the U.N. list of nonself-governing territories.

Why are the peacekeepers leaving?

Morocco considers Western Sahara part of its territory and has proposed autonomy under Moroccan sovereignty, while the Polisario seeks full independence.

The U.N. mission, MINURSO, was created in 1991 to organize a self-determination referendum that has never taken place.

Its mandate expired on Oct. 31 after Russia and the United States vetoed rival Security Council resolutions.

Washington proposed extending the mission while effectively dropping the referendum option and making Morocco’s autonomy plan the basis for future talks.

Eleven of 15 council members supported that approach, but Russia rejected it as one-sided.

Instead, Moscow sought to renew MINURSO unchanged, only for Washington to block the move.

“Washington has been enthusiastic about imposing a solution, but it’s explicitly biased in this conflict,” said Jacob Mundy, a Western Sahara expert and professor at U.S.-based Colgate University.

The U.S. recognized Western Sahara as Moroccan in 2020 when Rabat normalized ties with Israel under a deal backed by U.S. President Donald Trump.

Morocco backed the U.S. proposal but also saw a smaller victory in Russia’s veto, which effectively ended MINURSO’s mandate.

Rabat welcomed the mission’s end as “an important step toward the definitive closure” of the issue at the U.N., adding its initial functions were now “outdated.”

“For Morocco, the veto was the second-best option,” said Riccardo Fabiani, senior analyst at the International Crisis Group.

Moroccan Foreign Minister Nasser Bourita met Russian counterpart Sergei Lavrov in Moscow two days before the vote, and later admitted Rabat had not tried to stop Russia from using its veto.

Rabat sees MINURSO’s exit as “the end of U.N. scrutiny ... and another step towards normalizing Moroccan control over the territory,” Fabiani explained.

Morocco “was going to win either way,” added Hamish Kinnear of U.K.-based consultancy Verisk Maplecroft.

“If the U.S.-drafted resolution passed, Morocco’s plan would have been established as the only framework for a political solution — effectively ruling out the possibility of a U.N.-facilitated referendum,” he explained.

U.N. peacekeepers were first deployed with the consent of both Morocco and Polisario, but “what Morocco is saying now is it no longer consents to MINURSO,” Mundy said.

What do other sides say?

The Polisario said it would hold Morocco “fully responsible for any serious repercussions” for regional security following the council’s vote.

Algeria, Morocco’s regional rival and host to thousands of Sahrawi refugees, said Russia’s veto was “inevitable,” arguing the U.S. proposal’s “excessive partiality” sought to “legitimize a situation of occupation.”

For Morocco, U.N. efforts have long stalled, with Bourita recently saying the kingdom was “free to choose the path and framework it wants.”

Rabat’s autonomy plan has already gained growing support from countries including France, Britain and Spain.

Last year, the Security Council gave the plan unprecedented backing, calling it the “most feasible” solution.

But for many analysts, the issue is still far from over.

The U.N. has already begun winding down MINURSO, and said this month the liquidation process should be completed “as soon as possible.”

The organization stressed, however, that the mission’s departure does not affect the Sahrawi people’s “inalienable right to self-determination.”

Morocco promptly said it was “coordinating and supporting” the mission’s exit.

“Morocco is now betting to continue to normalize its control over Western Sahara while trying to remove it from the U.N. list of non-self-governing territories,” analyst Fabiani said.

But the end of MINURSO could also remove a long-standing buffer between Morocco and the Polisario.

Without peacekeepers on the ground, Kinnear said Morocco would have “greater latitude to conduct operations against the Polisario.“

The kingdom has reiterated its commitment to a ceasefire despite repeated Polisario violations since 2020. But tensions with Algeria have remained high since Algiers severed diplomatic ties in 2021.

Last month, Algeria said it was deploying troops to Niger to protect energy assets, which many saw as an unusual break from its traditional non-intervention policy.

“That was no coincidence,” Mundy said. “I think it’s a signal.”

“Algeria feels surrounded — with Libyan instability driven by the Emirates on one side and Morocco being closely allied with Israel on the other,” he added.

Kinnear said direct clashes between Morocco and Algeria were unlikely, but “Rabat will have to weigh Algiers’ increasingly assertive foreign policy in the context of Western Sahara.”
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.summary: The U.N. Security Council has failed to renew the mandate for its peacekeeping mission in North Africa's disputed Western Sahara. Morocco considers Western Sahara part of its territory and has proposed autonomy under Moroccan sovereignty. The U., U.S. and Russia vetoed rival Security Council resolutions.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.title: AI safety advocates make gains after $110 million midterm fight
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.author: Emily Birnbaum
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.text:
Candidates who favor stricter oversight of artificial intelligence racked up wins in key congressional races, aided by a pro-regulation political funding group backed in part by Anthropic at a time when Americans are increasingly uneasy over the rapidly developing technology.

Public First, funded by Anthropic co-founder Dario Amodei and other AI safety advocates, poured more than $63 million into the midterms to promote candidates aligned with its goal of stricter regulation, according to the group’s numbers.

The architects of two of the country’s most sweeping state-level AI laws — Colorado’s Manny Rutinel and California’s Scott Wiener — will be among the incoming U.S. House members elected with help from Public First, bringing energy and expertise to Congress. Ten of the 17 congressional candidates the group backed were elected.

https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/soci.title: Defects at Hong Kong MTR station ‘unimaginable’, engineers and lawmakers say
https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/soci.author: Wynna Wong,Leopold Chen
https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/soci.text:
MTR Corp is urged to strengthen oversight and let frontline workers flag construction problems after about 30 defective columns were found at Tung Chung West station

The mistakes that left about 30 columns defective at a Hong Kong railway station under construction were “unimaginable”, lawmakers and engineers have said, adding that the repairs were expected to be straightforward and unlikely to delay the project.

The MTR Corporation was also urged on Sunday to set up a reporting mechanism that would allow frontline workers to flag problems during construction.

The comments came a day after the Buildings Department revealed that about 30 columns at the MTR’s Tung Chung West station, now under construction, were defective as the concrete had failed to reach the upper ceiling, leaving steel reinforcement bars exposed.

The MTR Corp said earlier it had ordered the main contractor to stop work after a routine inspection in October found it filling the heads of the columns with patching material without prior approval.

Aaron Bok Kwok-ming, the engineering sector lawmaker who is also deputy chairman of the Legislative Council subcommittee on matters relating to railways, said filling concrete into columns was a simple task and such a mistake should not happen.

“Filling in concrete is something large companies like Bouygues-Dragages Joint Venture are familiar with. Such mistakes are unimaginable and very rare,” said Bok, referring to the contractor.

He added that fixing the problem would be simple, but the contractor was obliged to agree on a remedial plan with the MTR Corp rather than pressing ahead on its own.

“For the next step, the MTR Corp should oversee the contractor in coming up with a remedial plan and implementing it and document the work with photographs,” he said, estimating that the construction period would not be extended because the work could run alongside other tasks.

“The contractor should also investigate within its own team why this happened because it should not have happened,” he added.

It remains unclear how many columns the site has in total, or how long the remedial work will take.

Mark Chong Ho-fung, a lawmaker from the political party Roundtable, said the MTR Corp should disclose whether basic steps such as concrete filling fell within the scope of its inspections, so the public could judge whether it had properly discharged its supervisory duties.

“To make sure each step is carried out in strict compliance with the agreed approach, the MTR Corp should also set up a reporting mechanism that allows frontline workers to flag practices that deviate from the plan,” he said.

“The MTR Corp may not be able to check every detail in its inspections and reporting would be an effective way of doing so.”

He added that the MTR Corp should also release information on the structure’s current safety, noting that conflicting assessments from professionals based on photographs circulating online had emerged after the incident.

Edward Chan Sai-cheong, former chairman of the Structural Division of the Hong Kong Institution of Engineers, suspects a step required to complete the columns – filling the gaps at their tops with grout – was planned but somehow left unfinished.

He explained that such gaps could be deliberately left during top-down construction, with the sequence of work set out in approved plans.

Under that method, steel columns inside the concrete columns can support the floors above while construction continues elsewhere and filling the gaps with grout allows the completed columns to carry their full permanent loads.

That meant grouting did not necessarily have to hold up other work, provided it was completed before the additional loads associated with the next construction stage were applied.

“In theory, it should not affect the overall construction schedule,” Chan said.

He said grouting generally took relatively little time. The gaps would first need to be inspected and prepared, then checked to ensure the grout had filled the spaces; further grouting or patching could be required if the results were unsatisfactory.

Chan said the construction stages should already be specified in approved plans, although substantial remedial work could require revised plans to be submitted to the relevant authorities.

The Buildings Department has said temporary supports beneath the floor slabs meant the defects posed no structural danger.

It required an investigation report and remedial proposals by mid-November, while the Highways Department has separately demanded a detailed report from the MTR Corp within two weeks.

Authorities have maintained the Tung Chung line extension’s 2029 completion target, and the MTR Corp has said the main contractor would bear all costs associated with the remedial work.

The South China Morning Post has contacted the MTR Corp and the contractor, Bouygues-Dragages Joint Venture, for comment.
https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/soci.summary: MTR Corp urged to strengthen oversight and let frontline workers flag construction problems. 30 defective columns were found at Tung Chung West station under construction. The repairs were expected to be straightforward and unlikely to delay the project.

https://www.dw.com/en/gaza-rains-add-mis.title: Gaza: Rains add misery to humanitarian catastrophe
https://www.dw.com/en/gaza-rains-add-mis.text:
With most homes damaged or destroyed by the war, Gazans are facing worsening humanitarian conditions due to heavy rain.

Heavy rains sweeping across parts of the Middle East this week have flooded tens of thousands of tents in Gaza's displaced persons' camps.

According to authorities in the enclave, at least 70,000 tents have been flooded over the past day, where tens of thousands of people took shelter.

No fatalities had been reported, although some people were injured.

Some of the tents have been washed away due to the weather, with mattresses and blankets soaked with water.

More than 1.6 million residents of Gaza's 2.1-million population now live in tents or other makeshift shelters due to Israel's war in the enclave.

UN data says some 80% of the enclave's structures have been damaged during the war, with two-thirds destroyed, leaving Gaza's residents — many of whom were displaced multiple times during the war between Israel and Hamas — to either live in tents or risk their lives and seek shelter in buildings that could be on the verge of collapse.

The Higher Presidential Committee for Church Affairs in Palestine released a statement appealing for humanitarian aid for the Gaza Strip due to the situation.

According to the committee, some 950,000 people are living in areas "vulnerable to flooding," with more than 400,000 living in areas of "high levels of risk."

"Heavy rainfall is compounding an already catastrophic humanitarian situation, leaving displaced families and those who have lost their homes exposed to the elements and deprived of the most basic necessities of life," the statement said.

Some 74,000 people have been killed in the Gaza Strip since October 7, 2023. The war was triggered when Islamist Palestinian organization Hamas and its affiliates launched a terrorist attack in Israel's south, killing some 1,200 Israelis, most of whom were civilians. The militants also kidnapped 251 hostages.

The UN, EU, US and Israel, among others, consider Hamas to be a terrorist organization.

A UN commission of inquiry, as well as many leading human rights organizations, have accused Israel of committing genocide in Gaza. Israel has rejected the accusation, saying its army is acting in accordance with international law.

More than 1.6 million residents of Gaza's 2.1-million population now live in tents or other makeshift shelters.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c50m.title: Dormice 'thrive' at National Trust site
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c50m.text:
Habitat work and a monitoring scheme have helped hazel dormice thrive at a National Trust site, despite declines elsewhere, experts have said.

Killerton National Trust has 100 nest boxes across its estate in Devon. Rangers weigh and record details of each mouse between April and October.

The trust said the animals "continue to thrive" in the area - a sign it was "doing something right" by creating a "healthy, diverse and well-connected habitat for wildlife".

The People's Trust for Endangered Species said populations had declined by over two thirds in the UK since 2000. Experts said the decline was largely down to "habitat fragmentation".

The trust hopes the mammals, which typically weigh between 20g and 40g, will have gained enough weight to begin hibernating in the coming weeks and survive the winter ahead.

Fi Hailstone, senior ranger for the National Trust at the Killerton estate, said: "When we have warmer weather, it wakes them up and when we have wet springs, that affects their ability to forage when they do wake up.

"So having a resilient ecosystem with lots of shelter for them, lots of scrub, lots of things for them to eat [is important]."

"They love bramble, and I know that bramble has a bit of a bad reputation with a lot of gardeners," Hailstone said.

"But bramble is the life source, really. It has flowers in the spring, it has berries on it.  It's also protective in terms of cover from other predators, so it's a really great place for them to nest."

When they are not hibernating, they are shy and nocturnal.

Hailstone said Devon was "a bit of a stronghold for dormice" because "there is such a strong hedge network".

"We've been monitoring our dormouse population at Killerton since 2018, and during that time, we've noticed that they are fairly stable, which does buck national trends."

Hailstone said: "We are finding them in new areas which indicates them spreading across the estate.

"We think this is because we're planting a lot more hedges, a lot more trees."

"We might be planting lots of woodland now, which is great, but we won't see the effects of that for dormice for another 100 or so years," Hailstone added.

"It's really important to manage the woodlands that we already have in a positive way."

Anyone who finds a dormouse in the winter is urged not to pick it up but to alert the RSPCA or local animal shelter.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c50m.summary: Killerton National Trust has 100 nest boxes across its estate in Devon. Wildlife experts say the animals are thriving despite declines elsewhere. The trust hopes the mammals will have gained enough weight to begin hibernating in the coming weeks.

https://www.nytimes.com/live/2026/11/08/.title: Here’s the latest.
https://www.nytimes.com/live/2026/11/08/.author: Bayliss Wagner
https://www.nytimes.com/live/2026/11/08/.text:
Sunday morning news shows will be dominated by the winners of Tuesday’s election, while ballots continue to be counted in Alaska and Mississippi.

A number of candidates who won marquee midterm races were set to appear on the Sunday morning news shows, where they were expected to discuss election outcomes and their future plans after the Democratic landslide.

Even in an age of changing media consumption, the Sunday shows still hold the potential to set the agenda. Prominent Republicans are largely staying away as their party trades blame over its blowout defeat, while a parade of Democrats will appear amid a debate over the future of their suddenly crowded ranks.

Among the guests to watch: Hakeem Jeffries, the House Democratic leader who is set to become the first Black speaker of the House; Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, a Michigan Democrat who won a bruising race and will be the first Muslim senator; and Governor-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms of Georgia, who will be the nation’s first Black female governor. All are appearing on ABC’s “This Week.”

Senator-elect Adam Hamilton, whose stunning victory in Kansas was among Democrats’ biggest upsets, and Governor-elect Byron Donalds, a Republican who made history as the first Black person elected governor of Florida, will both appear on NBC’s “Meet The Press.”

Three leading progressives, Mayor Zohran Mamdani of New York (“Fox News Sunday”), Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont (CNN’s “State of the Union,” NBC) and Senator Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts (CBS’s “Face the Nation”) will appear as well. The Sunday shows will also include some winning House candidates and some potential presidential contenders.

Fewer prominent Republicans will appear on the shows after the avalanche of losses they suffered. Guests to watch include Attorney General Todd Blanche (Fox) and Representative French Hill of Arkansas (CBS).

Here’s what else we’re covering:

Mississippi and Alaska still tallying: Democratic Senate candidates held slim leads in Mississippi and Alaska, but a winner has not been declared in either race. Some competitive House races are also still up in the air. Democrats have clinched 254 House seats so far, three shy of tying the high-water mark for either party this century.

Democrats’ feuding factions: At a moment of opportunity for the party, its long-feuding factions are seizing on the midterm results to make their case for tacking to the center or to the left. Read more >

Demographic shifts: White, working-class voters, Black voters, Latino voters and young voters all lurched leftward in Tuesday’s elections, driving Democrats’ biggest triumph in a generation. Read more >

Shane Goldmacher and Tim Balk

Campaigns spent billions of dollars on ads this year. Some worked. Some didn’t. Some were stirring. Some were cringe.

Most will be quickly forgotten. A few will be remembered.

Here are some of the most memorable, influential and sometimes incoherent spots of a 2026 midterm election that resulted in one of the biggest Democratic landslides in modern history:

Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, Republican of Mississippi, wasn’t supposed to even be in a competitive race. But in the closing stretch, national Republicans redirected money and President Trump made a trip for a rally to try to save her.

But it was one of her missteps in a TV interview that her Democratic challenger, Scott Colom, packaged into a viral clip about her dismissal of the price of beef.

“You know you have so many proteins to choose from,” Ms. Hyde-Smith had said.

The spot features a parade of Mississippians mocking the idea.

“Pick another protein? She done lost her damn mind. I’d rather pick another senator,” one woman says.

The spot did not run on television. But Mr. Colom’s post on X featuring the video was widely viewed. And in perhaps the nation’s closest Senate race — as of now still uncalled but with Mr. Colom narrowly leading — it drew attention to the Democrat on one of the year’s defining issues: costs.

By the end of the election, there was more than $120 million of advertising referring to the convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

But one of the earliest Democrats to seize on linking Mr. Epstein to his Republican opponent was the former Senator Sherrod Brown, Democrat of Ohio. He ran an ad in the spring accusing Senator Jon Husted of having “taken the most money from associates of Jeffrey Epstein” of all 535 members of Congress. (The ad highlighted more than $100,000 in campaign contributions Mr. Husted had received in the past from Leslie Wexner, who was the source of much of Mr. Epstein’s wealth; Mr. Husted’s campaign noted that Mr. Brown himself had received campaign donations in the past from Mr. Wexner’s wife.)

In a year when Democrats tried to push a message that Republicans were serving themselves and the elites over everyday Americans, the closing line foreshadowed the hits to come: “Who’s he really working for?”

Mr. Brown won the race.

Some admakers still produce spots on instinct and intuition. But many are rigorously tested both before and after for how much they move voters.

Of all the ads that the House Majority PAC, the top House Democratic super PAC, ran this year, one stood alone as the most effective: This spot highlighting allegations Representative Max Miller, Republican of Ohio, faced from his ex-wife. The ad ticks through some of her accusations, including that he scalded her with hot water from a skillet and fractured his daughter’s collarbone. (Mr. Miller has denied the domestic abuse allegations and claimed that his ex-wife has mental health challenges.)

The ad moved Mr. Miller’s favorable rating by 15 points, and shifted the race itself nearly 10 points, according to testing data shared by the House Majority PAC.

The race was one of the ugliest in the country after many Republicans — including Senator Bernie Moreno of Ohio, whose daughter is Mr. Miller’s ex-wife — tried to get Mr. Miller to quit the race. Mr. Miller lost.

Mr. Trump launched Islamophobic attacks on Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate nominee in Michigan, calling him a “jihadist” while Republicans suggested he had ties to terrorists.

The El-Sayed campaign countered in many ways — including with a memorable ad.

“Where did Abdul El-Sayed come from?” a wide-eyed older white woman intones ominously, shot in noirish black and white.

Then the ad shifts to color.

“Here!” she shouts gleefully, sitting on a sofa with another older white man. “We’re his grandparents!” The words “Livingston County, MI” appear on the screen.

The cheeky spot had $1.8 million spent on it, according to AdImpact, starting right after the Democratic primary, in a bid to neutralize the coming attacks.

Mr. El-Sayed won the race.

As of Friday, former Gov. Paul LePage of Maine was one of the few Republicans ahead in the vote counting to flip a Democratic seat that had not been redrawn.

In a district that borders Canada and has pockets of French-speaking populations, Mr. LePage ran a memorable ad in which he took a hard line on illegal immigration.

The spot showcased the depth of his ties to the community — he says in French that French was his first language in Lewiston — and worked in his record as governor, while pitching himself as a supporter of legal immigration, but opposed to illegal immigration.

Former Gov. Paul LePage is the first candidate I can recall running a bilingual French-English ad — and using it to take a hard line on illegal immigration pic.twitter.com/gO4TSchafD

One perennial challenge for candidates is to push back on accusations from rivals without repeating the allegations. James Talarico, the Democratic nominee in Texas, took a creative approach to that: He ticked through how his experience was different from Ken Paxton’s, his Republican rival, and then he unloaded on Mr. Paxton.

“Ken Paxton says I don’t have his experience and he’s right. I’ve never been indicted for fraud,” he says, walking through a warehouse as 3-D words flash across the screen, “I’ve never been reported to the F.B.I. for bribery. I’ve never been impeached by my own party. ”

Mr. Talarico on Tuesday became the first Democrat to win a Senate race in Texas since 1988.

NEW AD: “Ken Paxton says I don't have his experience — and he's right.I’ve never been indicted for fraud. I’ve never been reported to the FBI for bribery. I’ve never been impeached by my own party.And I’ve never given a sweetheart deal to a pedophile.” pic.twitter.com/2umvnSzZzg

Even Senator Roger Marshall’s own team knew this one was a bad idea.

But when they said no, Mr. Marshall, a Kansas Republican, went ahead anyway. Without his senior campaign team’s knowledge, he arranged for a film crew to produce a spot defending his past lawsuits as an obstetrician against his patients, some of whom eventually faced arrest.

Mr. Marshall was determined to clear his name in the closing days — and thus drew more attention to the story. (The New York Times reported in September that Mr. Marshall had filed lawsuits against more than 700 patients, seeking payments of their debts, and at least 81 were arrested for missing court dates. Others faced wage garnishments and Mr. Marshall routinely charged an 18 percent interest rate on the outstanding debts.)

“I never had anyone arrested,” Mr. Marshall says in his would-be ad.

He had sent it to some campaign aides and top leaders moved to block its release. Mr. Marshall began personally texting it to people and it was posted by a local talk-radio host. Mr. Marshall was defeated on Tuesday, as a Democrat won a Senate seat in Kansas for the first time in nearly a century.

With 3 days left to #ElectionDay, here’s part of the closing argument from @RogerMarshallMD. #kansassenate pic.twitter.com/PB5tCX8cn1

An ad from Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican nominee for governor of Ohio, quickly rocked his race, divided Republicans across the country and became a symbol of the ugly tenor of the midterms.

The explosive spot shows the estranged mother of Mr. Ramaswamy’s Democratic opponent, Amy Acton, describing her as a liar and urging voters not to support her.

Ms. Acton said she had not spoken to her mother since she was 12, after her stepfather was charged with raping her. The sitting governor of Ohio, Mike DeWine, a Republican, said he found the ad “deeply, deeply troubling” and “just plain wrong.”

Other Republicans, including Mr. Trump, closed ranks around Mr. Ramaswamy.

Vice President JD Vance, a former Ohio senator, said he was “disgusted” to see Republicans “whining” about the ad.

Former President Barack Obama, visiting Ohio to campaign, said he did not “know what’s happened where the standards of behavior have gotten so low that somebody can run an ad like that.”

Mr. Ramaswamy lost to Ms. Acton on Tuesday.

In North Carolina, an ad for the Republican Senate nominee, Michael Whatley, appeared to boomerang and boost Democrats.

The ad, from the flagship super PAC for Republican Senate candidates, the Senate Leadership Fund, featured Ronald Hayes, whose son had been murdered. It blamed the Democratic Senate nominee, former Gov. Roy Cooper, for crime in North Carolina.

The ad had a flaw, Mr. Hayes, a Democrat, told news outlets. He had no problem with Mr. Cooper, he said, and had been misled by Republican operatives about the subject of the commercial.

Mr. Cooper’s campaign rushed out an ad to highlight Mr. Hayes’s account.

“Michael Whatley: Lies, deceit,” a voice in the Cooper campaign’s ad says. “He should never be in the Senate.”

The Cooper campaign spent more money on the pushback ad than anything else all cycle, according to AdImpact’s data, nearly $3 million.

Carter Wrenn, a Republican strategist in North Carolina, said Mr. Cooper’s ad was effective in tarnishing Mr. Whatley’s credibility.

“Because it was true what Cooper was saying,” Mr. Wrenn said, adding that Mr. Whatley’s allies looked “sloppy.”

Mr. Cooper won by a wide margin.

In the waning days before the election, Senator Susan Collins of Maine ran an ad that stunned some Republicans and that Democrats quickly promoted.

The ad showed a retired Maine telecaster, Bill Green, dismissing the Democratic nominee Troy Jackson’s work as a logger. “We’re not talking about buying a cord of wood here,” Mr. Green says. “We’re sending someone to the U.S. Senate.”

Democrats said it was elitist. Mr. Jackson used it to focus attention on a crisis facing Maine residents: heating oil costs that were soaring because of the war in Iran. Half the homes in Maine are heated with fuel oil, and the rising prices became a central issue in the race.

Mr. Jackson said the race was “about a cord of wood” and about Mainers’ struggles to heat their homes. On Halloween, Mr. Jackson walked the streets of Portland, Maine, dressed as a cord of wood, mocking the commercial.

Lance Dutson, a Republican strategist in Maine and a former aide to Ms. Collins, said the ad carried a “tone of condescension” and left an impression that Ms. Collins was out of touch on a crucial issue.

“How that got on the air, I have no idea,” Mr. Dutson said.

Mr. Jackson defeated Ms. Collins.

Hi, I watched hundreds and hundreds of political ads this year as I covered the 2026 elections. Commercials matter because they are one crucial way that campaigns reach voters who don't want to consume political news. Here are just some of the ones that stood out — for better or worse. What stood out to you?

Lisa Lerer and Reid J. Epstein

Lisa Lerer and Reid J. Epstein are national political correspondents who have covered presidential campaigns since 2008.

A pastor in Kansas. A Paralympian in Iowa. A former Presbyterian seminarian in Texas.

Democrats expanded their map this week with big wins in traditionally red states that the party had all but written off for years by making appeals to moderate, independent and Republican voters.

At the same time, progressives won key races in two purple states, Michigan and Maine.

The combined victories amounted to a sweeping triumph that will send an ideologically diverse crop of new Democratic lawmakers to Congress in January, but internal debates are already emerging about what lessons the party should draw ahead of the 2028 presidential campaign.

For centrists, the results demonstrate that the best way to flip conservative strongholds where their party has long struggled is through embracing moderate candidates and positions that appeal to a broader array of voters. Progressives argue that the victories in Maine and Michigan show that left-wing populists can energize the party’s liberal base and win back some of the working-class voters who had flocked to President Trump.

The debate arrives at a moment of unusual opportunity for the Democratic Party, which will hold large majorities in Congress next year and will seek to carry its midterm momentum into the 2028 cycle.

The discussion over the party’s direction is already playing out as donors, officials and politicians converge at party meetings and liberal gatherings across the country to take a victory lap and plan for the future. And as potential presidential contenders accelerate their quiet planning, they are using the results to make a case for the next nominee — and, possibly, themselves.

“There’s a ton of non-MAGA Republicans and independents that are giving Democrats a second look and a second chance,” Rahm Emanuel, the former Chicago mayor, who is considering a presidential run, said in an interview. “I don’t happen to think socialism is the way to win their hearts and minds.”

He added: “We don’t want to be identified with that anymore.”

Representative Ro Khanna, a California progressive who has also been teasing a bid, had a different assessment.

“The results show that there is no electoral penalty for being a progressive,” he said in an interview. “The stale talking points of the establishment, which lost twice to Trump, about who they deem electable or not electable is totally out the window.”

The early skirmishes are the latest round of a decade-long dispute over the Democratic Party’s direction and strategy.

In the first few months of this year, it appeared as if progressives had the upper hand. Liberal insurgents knocked off moderate rivals in blue districts in New York, New Jersey and Colorado, and they prevailed in Senate primaries in Maine, Michigan and Minnesota.

But in the general election, the moderates roared back, using explicitly bipartisan appeals to win by notable margins in states that had not elected Democrats to the Senate in years or, in the case of Kansas, nearly a century.

In Iowa, Josh Turek, the party’s nominee for Senate, ran a closing-stretch TV ad about how he opposed transgender athletes participating in youth sports. In Kansas, Adam Hamilton, a pastor who until this year had been a registered Republican, offered direct appeals to Trump voters and described himself as “a liberal conservative and a conservative liberal” who was above party politics. And in Texas, James Talarico embraced a “politics of love” that leaned away from partisanship and focused on “top versus bottom,” or the rich and powerful against ordinary Americans.

While all three men embraced economic populist platforms that promised to lower costs and raise taxes on billionaires, they also denounced what Mr. Hamilton called the “hyperpolarization in Washington.”

“Those candidates ran on that kind of pragmatic platform, saying we’re going to focus on the issues that impact our community, and we’re going to be independent voices, not putting parties and politics first,” said Representative Adam Gray of California, a Democrat who is the chairman of the moderate Blue Dog PAC. “They did better than their progressive counterparts. I think you’re going to see that in the data.”

Progressives rode a different path to victory.

The party’s Senate candidates in Maine, Michigan and Minnesota placed left-wing rallying cries at the center of their campaigns, promising to establish “Medicare for all”; calling to dismantle the Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency; and accusing Israel of committing genocide in Gaza.

In Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed combined some of those promises into a call-and-response slogan: “Money out of politics, money in your pocket and Medicare for all.”

In an interview, he credited his victory to his willingness to try to upend the political system. He suggested that not everyone in his party was on board with that idea.

“I think one of my big critiques of Democrats has often been that we just treat the symptom and not the disease,” he said. “Some people want to treat the disease without treating symptoms, right? You’ve got to treat both.”

He wasn’t the only progressive feeling bullish. Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont, the dean of congressional progressives, claimed near-total victory in an interview. Of the candidates he endorsed, the only one who did not win was Angie Nixon, a democratic socialist who fell just short in the Florida Senate race.

Mr. Sanders said Democrats should not hesitate to press a progressive agenda next year in Congress. He argued that Americans had voted for major changes, including wealth taxes, a higher minimum wage, universal health care and ending foreign wars.

“They want a government that stands up for the working class, that takes on the oligarchs, that delivers for working families,” he said. “We can no longer engage in same old, same old, status quo policies.”

In the House, Representative Greg Casar of Texas, the chairman of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, boasted that his group would expand its ranks by 25 members next year. He cast the midterms as a generational victory for the progressive movement.

Progressive winners of House races included Will Lawrence, a co-founder of an environmental group, the Sunrise Movement, who flipped a Republican-held district in Michigan; Brian Poindexter, who defeated a scandal-tarred Republican in northeast Ohio; and Randy Villegas, who prevailed in a redistricted House seat in California.

“This election cycle, the progressives made a big new bet that by endorsing populist candidates in seats Trump won big, we could show that a populist progressive message can win anywhere,” Mr. Casar said in an interview. “And that paid off.”

He added, “Progressive ideas won.”

With so many Democratic wins, not all the ideological lanes were quite so clear.

Both moderates and progressives claimed some credit for the party’s flips of Republican-held seats by Sam Forstag, a union leader and smoke jumper in western Montana; Bob Brooks, a Pennsylvania union leader; and Rebecca Cooke, a Wisconsin political fund-raiser.

Democratic leaders have tried to downplay the party’s divide. Senator Chuck Schumer of New York, who is widely expected to become the next majority leader, and Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York, who is poised to become speaker, stressed unity. They said all of the party’s candidates had run by focusing on the cost of living, corruption and the Iran war.

“Whether they were progressives or moderates, they were saying the same things,” Mr. Schumer told reporters.

Still, some officials in both wings of the party interpreted the results through the prism of what kind of Democrat would be best to nominate for president in 2028.

With the jockeying for the presidential race escalating this week — Gov. JB Pritzker of Illinois released a memo on Wednesday promoting his proposed agenda for the next two years — the fight over the party’s direction will unfold both in Congress and in the early primary states.

A chief target of the centrist scrutiny was Mr. El-Sayed, who won in Michigan after his party sent its full armada to help him.

Former President Barack Obama and former Vice President Kamala Harris stumped for him. Mr. Schumer’s super PAC invested $67 million into the race even though Mr. El-Sayed said he would not back Mr. Schumer to be party leader.

In the final weeks, some party officials quietly grumbled that a more centrist candidate would have cost less and freed up money for Democrats to expand their playing field of competitive races into places like Florida and Mississippi, where a moderate candidate leads a Senate race by just over 2,000 votes as counting continues.

Progressives, for their part, noted that Mr. El-Sayed had been undercut by his moderate primary rival’s surprising late endorsement of the Republican nominee.

Broadly, centrist Democrats have argued that progressive candidates, despite winning, underperformed in blue or purple states. Democrats are on track to win the national popular congressional vote by about 13 percentage points, according to estimates by The New York Times. Mr. El-Sayed won his Senate race by seven points, Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota by 10 and Troy Jackson of Maine by six.

“The people who won handily in states Democrats haven’t won in decades were the people who practiced the politics of addition, not the politics of subtraction,” said Neera Tanden, the president of the center-left Center for American Progress.

Some other Democrats were already looking ahead to the next race.

Even before the polls closed on Tuesday, aides to Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York released a five-page memo detailing her contributions to midterm Democrats and again articulating her thinking about whether to seek the 2028 presidential nomination.

“In the coming days and weeks, much will be discussed about the future of the Democratic Party and 2028. You may be asked whether you support her running for president or for Senate in New York or staying in the House of Representatives,” the memo concluded. “We’d recommend you rely on the details of this memo and answer that Rep. Ocasio-Cortez will continue to do what she’s always done: look for ways to do the most good for the most people.”

Democrats of all stripes won sweeping victories on Tuesday. Progressives in Maine and Michigan. Centrists in Kansas and South Carolina. A 39-year-old incumbent in Georgia, a 69-year-old former governor in North Carolina. Even before all of the votes in all of the races are done being counted, an intraparty fight over credit has begun. Moderates say they did better — and the math seems to back them up. Progressives said their victories in political battlegrounds proves they can win anywhere. For both wings of the party, the ultimate test is coming up as the 2028 presidential primary season kicks off.

Michael Kruse contributed reporting from Detroit.

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.title: Second world war veterans outnumber former PMs for possible last time on Remembrance Sunday
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.author: Matthew Weaver
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text:
Andy Burnham takes part for first time alongside eight ex-premiers as 12 veterans participate in ceremony

Second world war veterans outnumbered former prime ministers for what could be the last time at the national service of remembrance at the Cenotaph in central London.

The number of veterans from that conflict has dwindled to about a dozen, the oldest of whom was Jeffrey Brereton who served in the RAF. He volunteered for the RAF in 1940, at the age of 19, and served as a mechanic on Hurricane aircraft during the Battle of Britain.

The number of former prime minister has swelled to nine, all of whom attended as Andy Burnham took part in the ceremony for the first time. They included John Major, 83, the oldest living former prime minister; Keir Starmer the most recent ex-premier; and Liz Truss the shortest-serving.

Some of the spouses of former prime ministers joined Burnham’s wife Marie-France van Heel on a balcony overlooking Whitehall. She was flanked by Victoria Starmer and Hugh O’Leary, Truss’s husband; Theresa’s May’s husband Philip; Gordon Brown’s wife Sarah, and Rishi Sunak’s wife Akshata Murty.

Reform UK’s leader, Nigel Farage, laid a wreath for the first time. Only leaders whose parties hold six seats or more are entitled to take part, and over the last year defections from the Conservatives have taken Reform beyond that threshold to eight MPs.

Other politicians who laid wreaths included Kemi Badenoch, Sir Ed Davey, Shabana Mahmood and Sir Lindsay Hoyle.

The first wreath was laid by King Charles, who was dressed in a field marshal’s uniform. He was joined by his son, William, wearing the black uniform of a lieutenant colonel of the household cavalry.

Minutes before the ceremony, one of the soldiers in the parade on Whitehall was taken away on a stretcher after fainting. Charles led the two-minute silence which was broken only by a crying baby in Whitehall.

A gun was fired to mark the end of the silence before the last post was sounded by the buglers of the Royal Marines. After the service about 10,000 veterans took part in a march-past with more than 300 different armed forces and civilian organisations represented.

Some veterans waved and saluted as they began the march after the wreath-laying ceremony. Some of the older members were in wheelchairs and one group, many of whom were adorned with medals, rode mobility scooters.

after newsletter promotion

They were applauded by the crowd as they marched swiftly through Whitehall. The youngest taking part was eight-year-old Ronan Doncaster, who walked in honour of his father: a guardsman with the first battalion Coldstream Guards who died in April 2024.

In Enniskillen in Northern Ireland, the Irish taoiseach, Micheál Martin, and the Northern Ireland secretary, Chris Bryant, attended a memorial service. In 1987, the event was targeted by an IRA bomb that killed 11 people on the day and a 12th victim, who never woke up from a coma, years later.

In Scotland, the first minister, John Swinney, led tributes at a service outside Edinburgh City Chambers. A military parade marched down the Royal Mile from Edinburgh Castle, led by the RAF Central Scotland Pipes and Drums.

A service attended by veterans, faith leaders and representatives of the Armed Service was also held in George Square, Glasgow, with a silence at 11am followed by a wreath laying ceremony.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: ‘We feel the love’: Epstein survivors overwhelmed by messages of support at pop-up art exhibition
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Victoria Bekiempis
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Visitors to a touring show drawing attention to Epstein’s crimes have left thousands of ‘powerful’ notes – and survivors say it means a great deal

When Danielle Bensky first went to The Donald J Trump and Jeffrey Epstein Memorial Reading Room, she didn’t know what to expect.

“What happens if I walk in and survivors’ names are just plastered everywhere?” Bensky wondered about the reading room, a traveling exhibition of Epstein investigative files, first held in a New York City gallery this May. “I was a little worried in the beginning that this would be a form of exploitation for survivors.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

“Instead, it was just so beautifully done.”

The reading room is meant to bring attention to Epstein’s crimes and law enforcement’s decades-long failure to act. The former financier, who counted numerous high-profile men among his associates, was arrested in 2019 for sexual abuse of teen girls but killed himself in jail.

While Ghislaine Maxwell was arrested and found guilty of luring teen girls into Epstein’s orbit, documents reveal that law enforcement officials were well aware of their crimes decades prior. Survivors have called for greater transparency and legal actions against any other participants in their sexual abuse.

Bensky also didn’t know what would happen when David Garrett, founder of event organizer the Institute for Primary Facts, floated an idea to make the exhibit more interactive. There was a cork board in the final room and Garrett told Bensky he was going to keep it there when this exhibition opened to the public, so visitors could leave notes.

“I was like, ‘Oh, that’s such a great idea,” said Bensky, who is among the Epstein survivors pushing for accountability and justice. “That’ll be so cool to see.”

About a week after the reading room officially opened, Bensky returned and saw “at least six or seven corkboards that were full and overflowing with notes”. There were notes with drawings and notes with abject sadness and “sometimes, it was pure rage”.

“Sometimes, it would be a note directly to a survivor. Sometimes it was a note directly to themselves, and it got everybody involved,” she said. “Even members of survivors’ families were leaving notes. It was just a really beautiful display of our democracy.”

Bensky said the notes have given her hope amid years of institutional failures.

“Being seen in this process has been pretty remarkable.” Visitors have written, “We’re here with you, we stand with you, and we believe you” – demonstrating the “really beautiful empathy that comes with every single note”, Bensky said.

“There have been days where I felt like I couldn’t really do much. I felt really debilitated,” Bensky said. “The reading room can be a lot when you’re walking through your trauma all day, and you’re meeting all kinds of people.

“But so many of us will just go and sit in the room with all the notes and read the notes, and it’s like, ‘Wow, what an extraordinary thing to actually be seen and be believed by so many people at this point.’”

Liz Stein, an Epstein survivor, expressed similar sentiments about the power of these notes.

“It started out with one bulletin board, and I will never forget seeing that one initial bulletin board and just really feeling like, ‘Oh my goodness, people are really reacting to that,’” Stein said. When the first reading room installation ended, these notes “took up the better part of the downstairs of the exhibit”.

“The love that people show us is overwhelming, and every time we do these events with the reading room, every single time, people hug us, they tell us what we mean to them, and a lot of times they’ll say, ‘But it doesn’t matter. I’m just someone you don’t know from somewhere you don’t live,’” Stein said.

“And it’s like, no, we might not know your individual names, but we feel the love.”

“This wall with the note cards is a really tangible visual representation of how much support we have, and that fuels us in a way that I don’t think people quite understand.”

Garrett said that the idea for a notes space came at the last minute. He thought that people might experience deep emotions from the exhibit and might feel the need for support.

So, organizers put up a cork board with information about the national suicide prevention hotline as well as resources for those experiencing gender-based violence. Without thinking about it too much, Garrett decided to leave some extra notecards and pens.

“We just put them out and said, “if you want to write a note to the survivors, you can do that,” he told the Guardian. “We didn’t think that we would need more than that two foot by three foot corkboard.”

“By the end of the first day, not only was the corkboard full, but [notes] were taped up all around the cork board.” After just one day, visitors had left about 300 cards.

For the next 10 days, the producer would buy more cork boards everyday. There were 30 by the time the reading room ended its initial exhibition. “Every surface on that basement downstairs was full of cork boards and full of cards.”

The reading room would come to have seven stops – New York City; Washington DC; Des Moines, Iowa; Columbus, Ohio; Detroit, Michigan; Dallas, Texas; and Fort Lauderdale, Florida – and a traveling bookmobile that made about two dozen stops. In total, visitors left approximately 12,500 or 13,000 notes, Garrett said.

The reading room kicked off several months before highly contentious midterm elections dealt Republicans numerous blows which, some commentators said, was due to voters rejecting Trump. The president and Maga Republicans have been saddled by his administration’s handling of the files since he took office.

The White House rejected criticism of Trump’s handling of the files.

“Just as President Trump has said, he’s been totally exonerated on anything relating to Epstein,” White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said.

“And by releasing thousands of pages of documents, cooperating with the House oversight committee’s subpoena request, signing the Epstein Files Transparency Act, and calling for more investigations into Epstein’s Democrat friends, President Trump has done more for Epstein’s victims than anyone before him.”

Trump’s DoJ rebuffed criticism of their handling of these files and condemned the reading room.

“This sham tour is traveling to politically competitive areas and shamefully using victims as political pawns,” a DoJ spokesperson said in a statement.

“The non-profit’s fundraising ploy, which often hosts candidates for office, is a disgrace. It’s thanks to this Department of Justice that they even have those files, released in compliance with the Epstein Files Transparency Act under the most transparent administration to date.”

The words from supporters, both in person and notes, have provided encouragement to keep pushing for justice in spite of institutional roadblocks, Stein said.

“Your courage is louder than the people who tried to silence you,” was among Stein’s favorite notes. Another, Stein recalled, said: “One of these girls could have been me or my friends.”

“Money and power should not dictate justice,” Stein said of another memorable note.

Bensky also recalled one particularly powerful message.

“There was one that was just so simple,” Bensky recalled. “I think it literally just said: ‘It wasn’t your fault.’”
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: The Donald J Trump and Jeffrey Epstein Memorial Reading Room is a traveling exhibition of Epstein investigative files. The White House rejected criticism of Trump's handling of the files.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Tom Perkins
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Trump administration has gutted regulations that protect lives and natural resources as pipeline build-out continues

Datacenters are spurring a boom in fossil fuel pipeline projects at a time when the Trump administration is gutting rules that protect from disasters along the lines, a new review of federal records shows.

The report, compiled by the Environmental Integrity Project, also found pipelines are being built to meet demand for natural gas exports fueled by wars in Ukraine and Iran. Federal records identified almost 200 pipeline projects that are proposed or in the works, and would collectively span 17,000 miles (27,000km).

Not signed in before? Create a free account

Not only has the Trump administration targeted laws that protect the environment and human health from pipelines’ risks, it has also pledged not to enforce regulations around them, the report adds.

The findings bring into focus a little-considered environmental threat in artificial intelligence and datacenter proliferation – the US already records about 1.7 pipeline accidents, spills, fires or explosions per day, and these projects would almost certainly lead to more.

The pipelines could help supply the at least 98 gas-fired power plants proposed to serve datacenters, and, if all the lines are completed, they would transport about 40% more natural gas daily than what the system carries today.

“This is the largest boom in a couple decades … and it coincides with all this deregulation,” Alexandra Shaykevich, research manager with the Environmental Integrity Project, said. “That’s concerning because the pipelines do usually operate safely, but they can leak and explode, and so there are big risks for communities across the United States.”

Most of the pipelines would carry natural gas across 42 states, though many of them are concentrated in several fossil fuel-producing regions. About 42 are in or cross Texas, 27 are in Louisiana, and nine each are in Pennsylvania and Illinois.

Advocates say they’re especially worried because of the wide-ranging attacks on foundational environmental protections, from the Clean Water Act to the Endangered Species Act, that until recently have been wielded to stop the riskiest projects, protect from accidents or hold polluters accountable.

The report states that over 25% of the projects have requested an expedited environmental review, and the administration is largely using legally dubious mechanisms to push them through, like invoking the “energy emergency”. That has accelerated permit approvals, reduced the scope of environmental studies, and limited public and community input, the report alleges.

Meanwhile, the administration has used the Defense Production Act to push through projects over the objections of states. In March, it jump-started the Santa Ynez oil pipeline in Santa Barbara, California, despite the state shutting it down in 2015 following a major spill that harmed about 150 miles (240km) of coastline. The act is also being used to attempt to ram through controversial plans for the 125-mile (200km) Constitution pipeline that would run from Pennsylvania to upstate New York, which the latter has opposed.

The Trump administration in January issued a memo stating that it would “refrain from taking any enforcement action” against companies that violated Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration regulations. By 2025, it had already cut the average number of enforcement actions initiated in half, recording only 117.

The administration is also raising the risk of accidents and explosions by allowing companies to increase the pressure of pipelines in densely populated areas and letting them conduct fewer pressure tests, the report alleges.

It has made changes like this despite the regularity of accidents, including some that are deadly. The report points to a March 2023 disaster in which a crack in a gas pipeline in West Reading, Pennsylvania, caused an explosion in a chocolate factory that killed seven workers and injured 10 others. Last month, two workers were killed when a New Mexico pipeline exploded.

The pipelines could also destroy thousands of acres of federally protected wetlands. At least 81 of the projects are expected to damage more than 19,000 acres (7,700 hectares) of federally protected wetlands, the report found. This also comes as the Trump administration attempts to strip 94% of federal wetland protections.

The dangers of this are felt in south-west Louisiana, which holds a large concentration of pipelines because of the high number of export terminals along the Mississippi River. These already cut through and harmed sensitive wetlands and fishing grounds, said James Hiatt, executive director of For a Better Bayou.

“The people who live here carry the risks and bear the burden while the profits go elsewhere,” Hiatt said.
