https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5x2.title: Surgeon having lunch near Krakow shooting undoubtedly saved officer's life, colleague says
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5x2.text:
One of two surgeons who treated victims on the streets in the aftermath of a mass shooting in Krakow, Poland said his colleague"undoubtedly" saved the life of a gravely injured police officer.

The pair were eating near the city's Main Market Square on Saturday when a gunman began firing at random, killing six and injuring 15.

The doctors raced to treat both the attacker and two officers shot while subduing the perpetrator.

On Sunday, the officers - both hailed as "true heroes" by the prime minister for preventing further deaths - emerged from comas.

Prosecutors launched a terror investigation after ministers previously said the 24-year-old Polish attacker - who remains in a critical condition - was apparently inspired by "far-right ideologies".

A British national and Austrian woman were among those killed alongside four Poles.

Professor Michal Pędziwiatr and Dr Mateusz Wierdak were having lunch in central Krakow with their families when they heard gunshots, local media reported.

"Suddenly my son ran up and said: 'Dad, they're shooting at people there, people are falling to the ground'," Pędziwiatr told news outlet Fakt.

Pędziwiatr said when they got to the scene, they treated both the apparent attacker and the police officers.

"When it comes to saving lives, it doesn't matter who is who," he added.

Once the shooting stopped, Pędziwiatr said he took care of the other victims and the perpetrator, while Wierdak began working on the police officer who was shot in the chest during the gunfight.

"He, to put it colloquially, stuffed all the bandages into [the police officer's] chest and stuck his hands in," he told Fakt.

"If not for that, I don't know how things would have turned out, as there was a long wait for the ambulance."

Meanwhile, Pędziwiatr said he called John Paul II Hospital where the Department of Thoracic and Cardiac Surgery is located.

"I insisted they take him there because, in my opinion, he had the best chance of survival there, where there were specialists for precisely this type of injury," he told Fakt.

According to local media, Wierdak is a renowned surgeon in Krakow. The University Hospital in Krakow states Pędziwiatr is head of General, Oncological, Metabolic and Emergency Surgery.

The police officers have been identified as senior constables Jakub Kulik and Artur Morański.

The attacker has not yet been named by authorities.

When his house was searched after the attack in central Krakow, the bodies of his parents and sister were found.

The National Public Prosecutor's Office in Poland launched an investigation into the attack with a unit specialising in "terrorist offences" taking the lead.

Separately, reports emerged that six Dublin Civil Defence volunteers also assisted in the aftermath of the shooting.

James McConnell, an officer, told RTE News the group were on a city break and were close to the main square when the shooting happened.

The volunteers who are trained to provide medical care immediately sought to help injured people, providing "CPR and haemorrhage control".

Witnesses who were close to the attack described panic and confusion around the square as it unfolded.

Ruby Catherine Warren, from London, heard gunfire and "yelled at my friends to run and we all sprinted for our lives".

Not knowing where the gunman was - or if there was more than one - they "just kept sprinting", eventually finding a hotel to hide inside.

Tom Brook, from West Yorkshire, was inside a McDonald's near the square when he heard "multiple gunshots and saw people running for cover".

"I then walked into the square and saw paramedics working on someone outside [a shop] and there was a dead body covered in foil blankets 20 meters away," he said.

The suspect wore full military tactical gear during the attack and was described as having a military-grade weapon - but the government said he was not a member of the Polish armed forces.

Poland's Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said "everything suggests" the suspect was "fascinated by far-right ideologies" and held ultra-nationalist views.

The rampage began shortly before 15:00 local time (14:00 GMT) on Saturday in the historic centre of Krakow.

Footage showed the attacker's vehicle speeding through the centre of the city, and people fleeing as the sound of gunfire rang out.

The glass fronts of shops were shattered by bullets and a tram was shot at during the attack, which police say lasted for around three minutes.

The mayor of Krakow said he had submitted an urgent request for the two officers injured while stopping the attacker to be awarded titles of honorary citizens of the city.

Main Market Square reopened on Sunday evening after a security cordon was lifted.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5x2.summary: Polish police officers hailed as "true heroes" by Polish prime minister for preventing further deaths. Two surgeons treated both the attacker and two officers who were shot while subduing the perpetrator. The officers were eating near the city's Main Market Square when a gunman began firing at random. Six people were killed and 15 injured in the attack

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwvg.title: Seven dead and more than 100 injured after trains collide in Egypt
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwvg.text:
At least seven people have died in a train crash near the Egyptian city of Giza, with more than 100 injured.

The country's railway authority said two trains travelling south from Giza and Cairo collided, causing several carriages to derail and fall down an embankment.

Images from the scene showed people looking inside overturned carriages for injured passengers as a massive emergency response was launched.

Egyptian President Abdul Fattah al-Sisi said he had ordered state authorities to "investigate the circumstances of the accident, and hold accountable anyone found to have been negligent".

The public prosecutor's office warned the death toll could rise.

The government said hospitals in the area had been put "on heightened alert" as they dealt with a massive influx of patients.

Egypt's health minister Dr Khaled Abdel Ghaffar said people were being treated for broken bones and head injuries.

The Egyptian Red Crescent said it was providing aid and psychological support to victims and their families at the scene.

The driver of one of the trains was among those who died in the crash, the ministry confirmed.

The first train involved in the crash was travelling from Giza to Fayoum, south of Cairo, when it crashed into the rear of another service heading south from Cairo to Aswan, which was stationary on the tracks.

Images from the scene showed some carriages had overturned, with the body of at least one appearing to have split in two.

Trains between Giza and the Upper Egypt region were suspended as cranes were dispatched to remove the wrecked trains. The railway authority has not said how long it expects this to take.

The collision occurred in the area between Kafr Ammar and Al-Raqqa stations in Al-Ayyat, close to where Egypt's deadliest train tragedy occurred in February 2002, when a fire engulfed a passenger train travelling from Cairo to Luxor.

In that incident, more than 370 people were officially reported killed, although some estimates put the toll considerably higher.

Two further crashes in the area in 2009 killed dozens more.

There were calls in Egypt on Sunday for the transport minister to resign over the latest deadly rail disaster.

Foreign leaders and dignitaries have shared condolences and support for the victims.

Saudi Arabia's ministry of foreign affairs expressed "solidarity" with Egypt and wished those hurt a speedy recovery.

Turkey's ambassador to Egypt wrote on X that he extended "heartfelt condolences and sincere sympathy" to the victims, their families, and the Egyptian people.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwvg.summary: Egypt's president orders state authorities to investigate the crash. The public prosecutor's office warns the death toll could rise. The collision occurred in the area near the city of Giza. The first train involved was travelling from Giza to Fayoum, south of Cairo, when it crashed into the rear of another service.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm70.title: Homes and temples glow across India to mark Diwali
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm70.text:
Millions across India are celebrating Diwali, the Hindu festival of lights, illuminating homes, temples, offices and streets with oil lamps and colourful lights to symbolise the triumph of light over darkness.

The festival falls on the darkest night of the Hindu lunar month of Kartik, when the moon is not visible in the sky.

Although Diwali traditions vary across India's regions and communities, the festival is widely marked by prayers, family gatherings, the exchange of sweets and the lighting of firecrackers.

But the celebrations come amid growing concerns over air pollution, particularly in northern India.

Seasonal weather conditions and the burning of crop residue contribute to deteriorating air quality, while firecrackers set off during Diwali can make the situation worse.

Air pollution in the Indian capital Delhi has reached such hazardous levels that it is the most polluted Diwali festival in a decade. New measures to improve air quality do not seem to have been successful.

India's financial capital, Mumbai, has also experienced high pollution levels in recent weeks.

In an effort to limit pollution, India's Supreme Court on Monday permitted the manufacture, sale and use of certified "green" firecrackers in Delhi and surrounding areas for a limited period.

These firecrackers are designed to produce 20-30% fewer emissions than conventional fireworks. But critics have questioned how effective they are at reducing pollution and raised concerns that conventional firecrackers could still make their way into the capital from neighbouring states.

Despite the debate over fireworks, Diwali is about much more than firecrackers.

The festival celebrates the return of Lord Ram to Ayodhya after his victory over Ravan, the main antagonist in the Hindu epic Ramayana, and symbolises the triumph of good over evil, light over darkness, and knowledge over ignorance.

In the days leading up to the festival, families clean and decorate their homes with flowers, colourful lights and traditional oil lamps known as diyas.

The celebrations also bring families and friends together for prayers, elaborate feasts and the exchange of gifts, and lots of traditional Indian sweets.

Colourful patterns known as rangoli are created at entrances to homes, while markets bustle with shoppers buying festive essentials beneath brightly lit decorations.

The celebrations began on 6 November with Dhanteras, when buying gold, silver or new utensils is considered auspicious and believed to bring good fortune.

The second day, known as Chhoti Diwali, or small Diwali, is marked by the lighting of oil lamps and, in some households, setting off firecrackers.

The third day is the main celebration, when families offer evening prayers to Lakshmi, the Hindu goddess of wealth and prosperity, before gathering for festive meals and fireworks.

The fourth day is celebrated differently across India, with family gatherings and New Year festivities in some communities. The fifth and final day, known as Bhai Dooj, celebrates the bond between brothers and sisters.

The festival is also celebrated by Sikhs and Jains along with other important religious observances.

Sikhs mark Bandi Chhor Divas, or Prisoner Release Day, commemorating the release of their sixth guru, Guru Hargobind, from imprisonment at Gwalior Fort in the early 17th Century.

For Jains, Diwali marks the attainment of moksha, or liberation from the cycle of rebirth, by Lord Mahavira, the 24th and last Tirthankara, or spiritual teacher, of the current era.

With Indian communities spread across the world, Diwali is also celebrated internationally, with families and friends coming together for festive gatherings and exchanging gifts.

The festival is considered an auspicious time to make new purchases, which many believe bring prosperity and good fortune. India's stock exchanges even hold a special one-hour trading session for investors who consider buying and selling shares on Diwali favourable. Known as Muhurat trading, it will take place on 8 November this year.

Although rooted in Hindu traditions, Diwali is celebrated by people across different faiths and communities.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm70.summary: Diwali is the Hindu festival of lights, lights, and fireworks. It is celebrated across India's regions and communities, but it is also celebrated internationally. The festival is celebrated by people across different faiths and communities.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckly.title: Iran executes three men for 'armed unrest' after January protests
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckly.text:
Iran has executed three men accused of carrying out armed unrest during January's anti-government protests, according to state media.

Hassan Dioband, Hamid Kazemi and Reza Zanganeh were accused of throwing Molotov cocktails and grenades, using bladed weapons and firearms, and setting fire to public facilities in the city of Karaj, west of Tehran, Iran's state news agency Tasnim reported.

The executions are the latest in a series linked to the protests, including those of people accused of having ties to Israel and the United States.

The number of executions in Iran has increased since US-Israeli strikes on the Islamic Republic began in late February.

The protest movement initially sparked in December last year by the high cost of living rapidly evolved into widespread anti-government demonstrations that peaked on 8 and 9 of January.

Iranian authorities reported more than 3,000 deaths, and blamed the violence on "terrorist acts" orchestrated by the US and Israel.

However foreign-based NGOs gave higher figures and the BBC received multiple accounts from Iranians of security forces opening fire on unarmed protesters.

Tasnim reported that the three men were executed after the Supreme Court upheld their convictions and found them guilty of "participating in operational activities on behalf of the Israeli Zionist regime, the United States and hostile groups".

The damage allegedly included an electricity substation in Karaj which caused power outages in some areas.

Dioband was arrested on 11 January after investigations identified him as a suspect in attacks on public property and incitement to violence.

Ten others accused of taking part in the unrest under his supervision were later arrested.

Reuters news agency reports that they received prison terms of 5 to 10 years.

The latest executions in Iran come after the UN human rights chief Volker Türk said he was alarmed by the rise in death penalties.

In August, Türk said at least 56 people had been executed on national security-related charges since 19 March, including 27 in cases linked to January's nationwide anti-government protests.

Iran is thought to be the world's second-most prolific executioner after China. Last year, it put to death at least 2,159 people, according to Amnesty International.

The human rights group said that was the highest figure on record since 1981 and included 45 executions of suspected dissidents on national security-related charges.

A train collision has killed at least seven people and injured dozens in northern Egypt.

Footage showed multiple overturned carriages and dozens of people surrounding them.

One train was travelling from Giza to the Fayoum oasis, south west of Cairo, while the other was heading from Cairo to Aswan in the south.

It is yet unclear what caused the accident but Egyptian President Abdul Fattah al-Sisi said an investigation was underway and would "hold accountable anyone who proves their negligence".

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cxnv.title: Paramedic sustains multiple injuries in hospital assault
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cxnv.text:
A female paramedic has been seriously assaulted at Altnagelvin Hospital in Londonderry while responding to someone in need of medical assistance.

Police said the attack happened at about 17:45 GMT on Saturday and a suspect has been identified.

The Northern Ireland Ambulance Service (NIAS) said the paramedic sustained injuries to the back of her head, neck, face and hands during the attack. They said she is also believed "to have suffered concussion".

They added that the incident happened after the NIAS received a call to provide medical assistance to a male patient who was being transported by ambulance to the hospital, following initial treatment.

The NIAS said the "attack lasted a number of minutes".

"On arrival at the hospital, and while being transferred from the stretcher to the chair, the patient delivered a punch to the face of one of the paramedics who was helping him".

"The force of the blow knocked her down and knocked her glasses off her face," they said.

"The other paramedic tried as best she could to intervene but couldn't get into a proper position to help, after the assailant also attempted to punch her.

"He then turned his attention back to the first paramedic and started a sustained attack on her as she lay helpless."

Jenny Keane, chief executive of the NIAS, said she was "horrified and outraged" to hear of the assault.

"This incident is particularly disturbing given that it was perpetrated by an adult male on a female paramedic, while her other female colleagues did what they could to help.

"This was a sustained assault on a paramedic who has a career of over 37 years, caring for her local community.

"Although her physical injuries, of which there are many, may heal over the coming days and weeks, I would be concerned at the psychological and emotional impact this may have on her and others involved."

Keane said NIAS staff "must be free to go anywhere without the fear of being assaulted, quite simply for delivering care and compassion to someone they have been called to assist".

Social Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP) Foyle assembly member Sinéad McLaughlin, who knows the paramedic personally, said she was "absolutely appalled by this vicious attack on a woman".

She said she found the incident and the extent of the paramedic's injuries "deeply upsetting".

"We cannot allow attacks on healthcare workers to become something that is simply accepted as part of the job.

"We need to send a clear message that this will not be tolerated, and the safety of our frontline workers must be a priority."

Sinn Féin assembly member Philip McGuigan said there must be "zero tolerance" of attacks or abuse against health and social care workers.

"Reports of this attack are deeply disturbing.

"Health service workers go above and beyond to save lives and keep people safe, often working in very challenging circumstances," he added.

"They, and all workers, should never have to face abuse, attack, intimidation or threats in the workplace."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c680.title: Secondary schools told to stop teaching GCSEs before Year 10
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c680.text:
Secondary schools will be told not to teach GCSEs early as part of a major shake-up of how children in Years 7 to 9 are taught.

The government plans to make Key Stage 3 a more distinct education phase, urging schools to focus less on exams and more on a "richer, more engaging" experience.

The changes come in response to two reviews that found pupils were increasingly becoming disengaged in their early teenage years, affecting attendance and achievement, the Department for Education (DfE) said.

The move will mark a reversal of the approach taken by the previous Conservative government to focus the first three years of secondary school on core subjects and on doing well in assessments.

Former Education Secretary Michael Gove prioritised English, maths and science, while raising grade boundaries, making exams harder and limiting resits.

He also made GCSEs linear, meaning they are sat all in one go at the end of Year 11 instead of over the course of Key Stage 4.

These reforms meant teachers started preparing pupils for exams at an earlier stage at the expense of teaching unexamined parts of their subject.

Education Secretary Lucy Powell said: "The early years of secondary school should be a time when children are excited to go to school and engage in the specialist and much broader teaching on offer, and where they find their passion and develop a love of learning."

She added that ringfencing Key Stage 3 studies would allow for "more time to develop deeper understanding, as well as a richer experience that will engage more young people in their passions".

The DfE has pledged a "more engaging offer" in subjects like drama, PE, music and languages, which have seen a decline in students taking them, when it publishes its new curriculum later this year.

It says persistent absence nearly doubles among pupils between Year 6 and Year 9, from 13% to 15%.

The department pointed to a recent survey commissioned by the International Baccalaureate that found GCSE prep dominated Key Stage 3 learning in England, with 57% of teachers saying it was the leading influence on the curriculum.

"The pressures of GCSEs and an overcrowded curriculum are resulting in too many children receiving a narrower offer during Key Stage 3 and being rushed towards exams without grasping the fundamentals or developing deeper understanding," Powell said. "I'm putting a stop to that."

A 2015 Ofsted report suggested that Key Stage 3 may be "wasted years", echoing the view at the time that pupils aged 11-14 lacked a clear motivation to work hard.

However, the government faced criticism at the time that its reforms made each exam far more significant, meaning teachers refocused lessons only on what could come up in them.

Reacting to the DfE's announcement on Sunday, Lib Dem education spokeswoman Munira Wilson MP said school was "more than drilling kids for exams" but cautioned against "micromanaging" teachers.

She added that a new curriculum "alone won't get children back into the classroom", noting that "too many pupils are missing school because of anxiety and unmet mental health needs" while "schools can't offer more drama, music and languages without the teachers to teach them".
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c680.summary: Government plans to make Key Stage 3 a more distinct education phase. Move comes in response to two reviews that found pupils were becoming disengaged in their early teenage years. Move will mark a reversal of the approach taken by the previous Conservative government.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw1m.title: Ofsted faces fresh calls to halt graded school inspections in England
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw1m.text:
A second head teachers' union has called for a halt to graded Ofsted inspections in England, saying it is "increasingly concerned about the welfare and morale" of its members.

The Association of School and College Leaders (ASCL) also raised the prospect of potential strike action, saying a new grading system had become an "overbearing mess".

On Friday, Ofsted's chief inspector Sir Martyn Oliver said an independent survey of education providers showed it was "on the right track" with inspections.

The Department for Education (DfE) said ministers were "working with Ofsted and school leaders to ensure accountability is fair, proportionate and focused on helping every school get better".

ASCL's announcement comes after another union, the National Association of Head Teachers (NAHT), said changes Ofsted made to inspections just under a year ago had been severely harmful to school leaders' welfare.

ASCL said it had passed a motion of no confidence in "the ability of Ofsted's leadership to address the damage being done by the new inspection system", adding that it was "increasingly concerned about the welfare and morale of members".

Pepe Di'Iasio, general secretary, said the union did not take the step "lightly", but added Ofsted's "warm words about recognising wellbeing pressures... have not been matched by the action necessary" and that "negotiation [had] hit a brick wall".

"The current system is not fit for purpose. It is an overbearing mess and urgently needs to be reviewed," he said.

ASCL called on the government to pause inspections and review the system, and said it would survey members on whether to hold an informal ballot on industrial action if there was no change.

In response, Ofsted said it had "worked hard to reduce the pressure of inspection in recent years, but we know workload and wellbeing remain a challenge".

"We are working with the Department for Education on this and we will keep listening to feedback from professionals as we continue to improve what we do," a spokesperson added.

England's schools inspectorate introduced the report card system to replace its previous one or two-word judgements last November, following the death of head teacher Ruth Perry, who took her own life after Ofsted downgraded her school from "outstanding" to "inadequate".

An inquest ruled that an Ofsted inspection had contributed to her death in January 2023.

That led to a change in how Ofsted assessed schools, bringing in report cards designed to grade schools on several areas, rather than focusing on one overall grade.

Last month, the NAHT said testimonies from its members, seen by the BBC, suggested some school leaders had faced "intolerable" pressure because of the new inspections, leaving them "overwhelmed" and "anxious".

It warned the system could pose a "risk to life" if changes were not forthcoming.

An independent report, commissioned by Ofsted to evaluate its new framework, concluded this week that leaders were "generally positive" about their inspection experience, and that it was "more collaborative and accounts for context better than previous inspections".

But it also said nearly half (48%) of school leaders who responded to its survey said their staff's mental wellbeing had been negatively affected "a fair amount" or "a lot" by a recent inspection.

The interim report was based on focus groups and nearly 700 responses from school, college and early years leaders who were invited to complete a survey following inspections this year. A full report is due to be published next year.

Sir Martyn said: "The data published today shows that we are on the right track.

"I know that workload and wellbeing in education continue to be challenging, and I don't take that lightly.

"We will keep listening to feedback from professionals and parents alike as we continue to improve what we do."

The DfE said "inspection and accountability are vital, but they must reflect the reality of what is happening in schools, recognise the context they are working in, and support improvement rather than add to the pressures they already face".

The Association of School and College Leaders also raised the prospect of potential strike action. Ofsted chief inspector Sir Martyn Oliver says an independent survey shows it is on the right track.

https://www.nytimes.com/live/2026/11/08/.text:
Republicans faced questions about the future of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth while Hakeem Jeffries, the House Democratic leader, said he was a “hard yes” on a vote expected this week. Attorney General Todd Blanche promised to staunchly defend cabinet officials.

Bayliss Wagner and Robert Jimison

Senior officials from both parties clashed on the Sunday morning news shows, with Democrats emboldened by sweeping midterm wins signaling that they would intensify their fight against the Trump administration.

Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the Democratic leader who is poised to become speaker in the next Congress, and Senator Bernie Sanders, the Vermont independent, both addressed the possibility of impeaching Trump cabinet members — an effort that could move forward even before the new class of freshman lawmakers is sworn in.

Mr. Jeffries said he was a “hard yes” on a vote to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth that is expected to come to the House floor this week, pushed by Representative Thomas Massie, a Kentucky Republican and Trump foil who lost a primary to a challenger backed by the president. During an interview on ABC’s “This Week,” Mr. Jeffries said that Mr. Hegseth had “abused his power, undermined our national security and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran.”

Mr. Sanders, who caucuses with Democrats and is set to take control of the Health Committee in the next Congress, expressed openness to an impeachment effort against Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. during an interview on CNN’s “State of the Union.”

On CNN’s “State of the Union,” Attorney General Todd Blanche said that the Justice Department would strongly defend any Trump administration officials whom the House Oversight Committee moved to investigate or potentially impeach. That could include Mr. Hegseth and Stephen Miller, the White House aide who was promoted this week to chief of staff, Mr. Blanche said.

The interviews were part of a flurry of Sunday news show appearances from party leaders and candidates who won marquee midterm races.

Some Republicans voiced concern about Mr. Trump’s war in Iran. Representative French Hill, Republican of Arkansas, expressed dissatisfaction with the handling of the war, but stopped short of endorsing an effort to impeach Mr. Hegseth, saying he wanted to hear the case against him. “I want to hear the debate on it to see if it merits impeachment,” Hill said during an interview on CBS’s “Face the Nation.”

While Democrats ramped up criticism of the Trump administration, they were also navigating some internal discord of their own. Senator-elect Adam Hamilton, the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in Kansas since 1932, reiterated on CNN’s “State of the Union” that he would not support Senator Chuck Schumer of New York remaining the Democratic leader in the chamber. Mr. Schumer’s aides have said he has already locked down enough support to be elected majority leader.

Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, appearing on ABC’s “This Week,” downplayed his past criticism of Mr. Schumer. “Senator Schumer and I figured out how to work together,” Mr. El-Sayed said.

Here’s what else we’re covering:

Mississippi and Alaska still tallying: Democratic Senate candidates held slim leads in Mississippi and Alaska, but a winner has not been declared in either race. Some competitive House races are also still up in the air. Democrats have clinched 254 House seats so far, three shy of tying the high-water mark for either party this century.

Demographic shifts: White, working-class voters, Black voters, Latino voters and young voters all lurched leftward in Tuesday’s elections, driving Democrats’ biggest triumph in a generation. Read more ›

A precinct’s memory card containing missing votes has shaken up a race for a seat in Georgia’s House of Representatives, where party control has not yet been decided.

According to Brad Raffensperger, Georgia’s secretary of state, unofficial results showed a Republican incumbent trailing his Democratic challenger. Then, Seminole County’s board of elections determined that a memory card with election results hadn’t been properly uploaded.

After those votes had been counted, State Representative Gerald Greene, the Republican incumbent, appeared to be leading, Mr. Raffensperger said in a statement on Friday.

On Sunday morning, The Associated Press hadn’t made calls in four of the Georgia State House races, including in the district where Mr. Greene is running, State House District 154, which is in the state’s southwest corner. So far, 90 seats have been called for Democrats and 86 for Republicans; a majority would require 91 seats.

The memory card revelations came after the secretary of state’s office identified a discrepancy between the number of voters who checked into polling places on Election Day and the votes reported by the Seminole County board of elections.

“Therefore, the Election Summary Report marked ‘Unofficial and Incomplete’ was just that (unofficial and incomplete),” said Ronald Foskey, elections supervisor in Seminole County.

Mr. Raffensperger called the oversight “unacceptable,” announcing on Friday that he had opened an investigation into the delayed vote upload.

“Every vote matters, and in a close election, even a relatively small number of unreported ballots can change the outcome,” Mr. Raffensperger said in a statement.

On Tuesday, Keisha Lance Bottoms, a former mayor of Atlanta, was elected governor of Georgia, becoming the first Black woman to hold the state’s top office and the first Democrat in more than 25 years. Republicans will hold the majority in Georgia’s State Senate.

Harry James, Mr. Greene’s Democratic opponent, said he was confused by the memory card mishap.

“Just trying to keep an open mind till we get some understanding of what happened or how it happened,” he said.

Mr. Greene did not immediately respond to requests for comment. The deadline for counties to certify their general election results is Monday.

Reporting from Washington

Representative Hakeem Jeffries, the Democratic leader poised to become the next speaker of the House, said on Sunday that he would support impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, joining the growing calls to remove one of President Trump’s top cabinet secretaries after overwhelming Republican defeats in last week’s elections.

Mr. Jeffries said that he was a “hard yes” on a resolution to impeach Mr. Hegseth that was expected to come to the House floor this week — the first time the top Democrat has publicly expressed support for the idea.

“The so-called secretary of defense has abused his power, undermined our national security and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran,” Mr. Jeffries said during an interview on the ABC morning program “This Week,” adding, “Pete Hegseth has got to go.”

Democrats, emboldened by their decisive victories in the House and the Senate last week, have begun laying the groundwork for an aggressive oversight agenda aimed at Mr. Trump and his administration. But increased bipartisan pressure, especially on Mr. Hegseth, since the election suggests that a political reckoning could come before the new Congress begins.

Representative Thomas Massie of Kentucky, a Republican who is retiring at the end of his term after losing a primary to a challenger backed by Mr. Trump, is expected to force a vote in the House this week on impeaching Mr. Hegseth.

Mr. Massie first moved to bring the impeachment resolution to the floor before the midterms. That prompted Speaker Mike Johnson to call an early recess to avoid voting on the measure. Impeachment resolutions are privileged motions in the House and when introduced must be taken up within two days.

Because that effort expired, Mr. Massie must renew his notice to force action on the measure, which he is expected to do when the House returns this week, again setting off a two-day clock to take up the resolution.

Even if the House were to vote to impeach Mr. Hegseth, however, it would be unlikely to lead to his removal from office, which requires a two-thirds majority in the Senate. Only two cabinet officials have been impeached in U.S. history, and neither was removed from office by the Senate.

Mr. Jeffries predicted “incredibly strong support” among Democrats for the resolution on Sunday and said they would discuss the issue when they return to Washington this week.

Attorney General Todd Blanche said on the CNN talk show “State of the Union” on Sunday that the Justice Department would defend members of the administration like Mr. Hegseth from investigations or impeachment efforts. “Department of Justice represents members of the executive,” he said, adding that he “would be very worried” if he were a Democrat threatening to investigate administration officials.

On Saturday, Mr. Trump wrote on social media that the calls for impeachment amounted to “extortion at the highest level” and ordered the Justice Department to investigate those making the push.

Some Republican lawmakers are also signaling openness to the case against Mr. Hegseth, even as they have stopped short of endorsing impeachment.

“I want to hear the debate on it to see if it merits impeachment,” Representative French Hill, Republican of Arkansas, said during an interview on the CBS program “Face the Nation.”

Mr. Hill, who won re-election on Tuesday by fewer than 4,500 votes, expressed dissatisfaction with the administration’s handling of the war with Iran but cautioned that poor performance did not necessarily rise to the level of impeachment.

“If you don’t think he’s done a good job conducting his job, that doesn’t mean per se that he has committed an impeachable offense,” he said. He added that if Mr. Hegseth was not carrying out his mission properly, “the president ought to make a change there.”

Representative James R. Comer, Republican of Kentucky, has also raised questions about Mr. Hegseth’s leadership and future, warning that it was “very possible” that enough lawmakers would vote to impeach him.

In a NewsNation interview on Friday, Mr. Comer did not explicitly express support for removing Mr. Hegseth, instead saying, “That’s going to be a decision that President Trump’s going to have to make.”

Beyond the Pentagon, lawmakers have expressed varying levels of support for personnel changes across the administration.

Representative Marlin Stutzman, Republican of Indiana, criticized the appointment of Stephen Miller as the next White House chief of staff, calling it a “bad mistake.”

And Senator Bernie Sanders, the Vermont independent who is likely to lead the Senate’s health committee in January, said on Sunday that he was open to impeachment efforts against Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

Evan Gorelick contributed reporting.

Representative Marlin Stutzman, Republican of Indiana, said it was “a bad mistake” for President Trump to promote Stephen Miller, the architect of the administration’s mass deportation campaign who was elevated to chief of staff this week, and that he should have been fired instead.

“If your team takes a beating as badly as we took this last week, you have to fire people,” Stutzman said in an interview on CNN’s “Inside Politics Sunday.” “You don’t promote those who were in charge of what was supposed to be delivered.”

Stutzman added, however, that he would not vote to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth as the House moved toward a vote this week because Hegseth answers to Trump as commander in chief. He said that he thinks Trump’s cabinet “is phenomenal.”

Representative-elect Nancy Lacore, a South Carolina Democrat and former Navy admiral who was abruptly fired last year by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, said Hegseth has committed “probably plenty” of impeachable offenses. But she added that she believed those proceedings “will be handled” before she begins her term in January — a reference to an impeachment push driven by Representative Thomas Massie, a Kentucky Republican.

“It’s all part of the problem with the corruption and the lack of strategy, which is doing nothing but really driving up costs for people,” Lacore said in an interview on CBS News’s “Face the Nation,” adding that Hegseth is “the most unqualified secretary that this nation has seen.”

California voters have rejected a ballot measure that would have streamlined development for large projects like housing, roads, hospitals and power infrastructure, according to The Associated Press. It would have shortened the length of environmental reviews and made it more difficult to bring challenges, moves that opponents warned could ease the path for the construction of data centers.

Representative French Hill, Republican of Arkansas, expressed dissatisfaction with the handling of the war in Iran but stopped short of endorsing an effort to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, saying he wanted to hear the case against him. “I want to hear the debate on it to see if it merits impeachment,” Hill said during an interview on CBS’s “Face the Nation.”

“If you don’t think he’s done a good job conducting his job, that doesn’t mean per se he has committed an impeachable offense,” he said, adding that if Hegseth was not carrying out his mission properly, “the president ought to make a change there.”

Governor-elect Byron Donalds, Republican of Florida, said in an interview on Fox News that “we really are the last state that’s going to be committed to conservative policies” after the party’s losses in the midterm elections. Republicans in Florida won all their statewide races this week, though they lost their supermajority in the state House.

“I think that when people in Texas and these other states realize what the Democrats are going to do, they’re going to look to Florida and say, ‘No, that’s how we want our states to operate,’” Donalds said, adding that his focus as governor would be on gas and grocery prices. Because the Iran war had raised energy costs, he said, President Trump ought to end it quickly and “finish the job.”

Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, appearing on ABC’s “This Week,” downplayed his past criticism of Senator Chuck Schumer of New York, the Democratic leader. “Senator Schumer and I figured out how to work together on the three pragmatic goals we had,” El-Sayed said. “We wanted to take back the Senate. We wanted to win this Michigan seat. And he wanted to see me elected.”

But El-Sayed did not say whether he would support Schumer becoming majority leader. “I want to see who else is in the running,” he said.

Attorney General Todd Blanche said in an interview on CNN’s “State of the Union” that the Justice Department would strongly defend any Trump administration officials whom the House Oversight Committee decided to investigate or potentially impeach. That could include Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Stephen Miller, the White House aide who was promoted this week to chief of staff, Blanche said.

“Department of Justice lawyers represent members of the executive,” Blanche said. “And I would be very worried if I was a member on that committee,” he added, referring to the oversight panel.

In an interview on CNN after the attorney general, Representative Robert Garcia, Democrat of California and the chairmain-in-waiting of the House Oversight Committee, criticized Blanche’s position. “It is ridiculous that we have the attorney general saying to the American public that somehow he’s going to defend administration officials when his job is to defend the Constitution,” Garcia said, adding: “He is threatening our committee. He’s trying to stop us from doing real oversight.”

Senator Bernie Sanders, the Vermont independent who is set to take control of the Health Committee in the new Congress, expressed openness to an impeachment effort against Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. during an interview on CNN’s “State of the Union.” Sanders added that he would call for Kennedy to testify on Capitol Hill and press him on a number of policy decisions. “I’m open to all ideas,” Sanders said.

Senator-elect Adam Hamilton, the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in Kansas since 1932, reiterated on CNN’s “State of the Union” that he would not support Senator Chuck Schumer of New York remaining the Democratic leader in the chamber. “Whether it’s fair or not, Chuck Schumer is seen as a more divisive figure by many people,” Hamilton said. “And I think we need somebody who’s going to bring us together.” Schumer’s aides say he has locked down enough support from Senate Democrats to be elected majority leader.

Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the Democratic leader who is poised to become the majority leader when his party assumes power in January, said he was a “hard yes” on the vote to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth that is expected to come to the House floor this week when representatives return to Washington. In an interview on ABC’s “This Week,” Jeffries said that Hegseth had “abused his power, undermined our national security and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran.”

While Jeffries had previously said he would like to “push out” the defense secretary, this appears to be the first time he has explicitly supported an impeachment effort against Hegseth, an influential member of the Trump cabinet.

Senator-elect James Talarico, Democrat of Texas, played himself in a cameo last night on “Saturday Night Live.” During the cold open, as President Trump (played by James Austin Johnson) rationalized his party’s wipeout in the midterm elections, he began listing and mocking Democrats who won their races. After Johnson’s Trump complained about Talarico, whom he called “Talafreako,” the real Talarico walked into the frame.

“Hi America, I’m James Talarico, the guy who’s been texting you every day asking for $5,” he said, continuing: “But I think, Mr. President, if we can work together, we can make life better for everyday Americans. It’s clear people want something new. They want something different. I’m talking, of course, about S.N.L.’s cold opens. How many of these Trump freezers are they going to do?”

As ballot tabulation continues in the Mississippi Senate race, most of the 233 provisional ballots cast by students on campus at Jackson State University had to be rejected, said Felicia McClinton, an election commissioner in Hinds County, one of the most populous counties in the state. The majority of those rejected ballots had been cast by students who were not properly registered to vote, McClinton said in an interview on Saturday. In other cases, they had voted in the wrong precinct, she added.

Scott Colom, the Democrat, has taken a roughly 2,600-vote lead over the Republican incumbent, Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith.                                                                        With such a tight margin, there is a lot of attention in the state on mail ballots and provisional ballots, also known as affidavit ballots, which are used when a voter’s eligibility cannot be immediately confirmed at the polls. Mississippi counties must certify their election results by Friday, Nov. 13.

Gov. Josh Shapiro, Democrat of Pennsylvania, said in a recorded interview with NBC’s “Meet The Press,” that he believed Senator John Fetterman would face “a robust primary challenge” if he seeks re-election in 2028. Fetterman, a Pennsylvania Democrat, has won favor with Republicans and rankled many in his party. “I think that there’s no question that people are lining up to run, and he has to decide if he’s going to run,” Shapiro said, according to a transcript of the interview provided by NBC.

Shapiro, who was re-elected on Tuesday by a wide margin and is seen as a potential 2028 presidential candidate, declined to answer specific questions about his political future. Asked whether he would commit to serving out his full four-year term, he said he was focused on being governor.

Shane Goldmacher and Tim Balk

Campaigns spent billions of dollars on ads this year. Some worked. Some didn’t. Some were stirring. Some were cringe.

Most will be quickly forgotten. A few will be remembered.

Here are some of the most memorable, influential and sometimes incoherent spots of a 2026 midterm election that resulted in one of the biggest Democratic landslides in modern history:

Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, Republican of Mississippi, wasn’t supposed to even be in a competitive race. But in the closing stretch, national Republicans redirected money and President Trump made a trip for a rally to try to save her.

But it was one of her missteps in a TV interview that her Democratic challenger, Scott Colom, packaged into a viral clip about her dismissal of the price of beef.

“You know you have so many proteins to choose from,” Ms. Hyde-Smith had said.

The spot features a parade of Mississippians mocking the idea.

“Pick another protein? She done lost her damn mind. I’d rather pick another senator,” one woman says.

The spot did not run on television. But Mr. Colom’s post on X featuring the video was widely viewed. And in perhaps the nation’s closest Senate race — as of now still uncalled but with Mr. Colom narrowly leading — it drew attention to the Democrat on one of the year’s defining issues: costs.

By the end of the election, there was more than $120 million of advertising referring to the convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

But one of the earliest Democrats to seize on linking Mr. Epstein to his Republican opponent was the former Senator Sherrod Brown, Democrat of Ohio. He ran an ad in the spring accusing Senator Jon Husted of having “taken the most money from associates of Jeffrey Epstein” of all 535 members of Congress. (The ad highlighted more than $100,000 in campaign contributions Mr. Husted had received in the past from Leslie Wexner, who was the source of much of Mr. Epstein’s wealth; Mr. Husted’s campaign noted that Mr. Brown himself had received campaign donations in the past from Mr. Wexner’s wife.)

In a year when Democrats tried to push a message that Republicans were serving themselves and the elites over everyday Americans, the closing line foreshadowed the hits to come: “Who’s he really working for?”

Mr. Brown won the race.

Some admakers still produce spots on instinct and intuition. But many are rigorously tested both before and after for how much they move voters.

Of all the ads that the House Majority PAC, the top House Democratic super PAC, ran this year, one stood alone as the most effective: This spot highlighting allegations Representative Max Miller, Republican of Ohio, faced from his ex-wife. The ad ticks through some of her accusations, including that he scalded her with hot water from a skillet and fractured his daughter’s collarbone. (Mr. Miller has denied the domestic abuse allegations and claimed that his ex-wife has mental health challenges.)

The ad moved Mr. Miller’s favorable rating by 15 points, and shifted the race itself nearly 10 points, according to testing data shared by the House Majority PAC.

The race was one of the ugliest in the country after many Republicans — including Senator Bernie Moreno of Ohio, whose daughter is Mr. Miller’s ex-wife — tried to get Mr. Miller to quit the race. Mr. Miller lost.

Mr. Trump launched Islamophobic attacks on Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate nominee in Michigan, calling him a “jihadist” while Republicans suggested he had ties to terrorists.

The El-Sayed campaign countered in many ways — including with a memorable ad.

“Where did Abdul El-Sayed come from?” a wide-eyed older white woman intones ominously, shot in noirish black and white.

Then the ad shifts to color.

“Here!” she shouts gleefully, sitting on a sofa with another older white man. “We’re his grandparents!” The words “Livingston County, MI” appear on the screen.

The cheeky spot had $1.8 million spent on it, according to AdImpact, starting right after the Democratic primary, in a bid to neutralize the coming attacks.

Mr. El-Sayed won the race.

As of Friday, former Gov. Paul LePage of Maine was one of the few Republicans ahead in the vote counting to flip a Democratic seat that had not been redrawn.

In a district that borders Canada and has pockets of French-speaking populations, Mr. LePage ran a memorable ad in which he took a hard line on illegal immigration.

The spot showcased the depth of his ties to the community — he says in French that French was his first language in Lewiston — and worked in his record as governor, while pitching himself as a supporter of legal immigration, but opposed to illegal immigration.

Former Gov. Paul LePage is the first candidate I can recall running a bilingual French-English ad — and using it to take a hard line on illegal immigration pic.twitter.com/gO4TSchafD

One perennial challenge for candidates is to push back on accusations from rivals without repeating the allegations. James Talarico, the Democratic nominee in Texas, took a creative approach to that: He ticked through how his experience was different from Ken Paxton’s, his Republican rival, and then he unloaded on Mr. Paxton.

“Ken Paxton says I don’t have his experience and he’s right. I’ve never been indicted for fraud,” he says, walking through a warehouse as 3-D words flash across the screen, “I’ve never been reported to the F.B.I. for bribery. I’ve never been impeached by my own party. ”

Mr. Talarico on Tuesday became the first Democrat to win a Senate race in Texas since 1988.

NEW AD: “Ken Paxton says I don't have his experience — and he's right.I’ve never been indicted for fraud. I’ve never been reported to the FBI for bribery. I’ve never been impeached by my own party.And I’ve never given a sweetheart deal to a pedophile.” pic.twitter.com/2umvnSzZzg

Even Senator Roger Marshall’s own team knew this one was a bad idea.

But when they said no, Mr. Marshall, a Kansas Republican, went ahead anyway. Without his senior campaign team’s knowledge, he arranged for a film crew to produce a spot defending his past lawsuits as an obstetrician against his patients, some of whom eventually faced arrest.

Mr. Marshall was determined to clear his name in the closing days — and thus drew more attention to the story. (The New York Times reported in September that Mr. Marshall had filed lawsuits against more than 700 patients, seeking payments of their debts, and at least 81 were arrested for missing court dates. Others faced wage garnishments and Mr. Marshall routinely charged an 18 percent interest rate on the outstanding debts.)

“I never had anyone arrested,” Mr. Marshall says in his would-be ad.

He had sent it to some campaign aides and top leaders moved to block its release. Mr. Marshall began personally texting it to people and it was posted by a local talk-radio host. Mr. Marshall was defeated on Tuesday, as a Democrat won a Senate seat in Kansas for the first time in nearly a century.

With 3 days left to #ElectionDay, here’s part of the closing argument from @RogerMarshallMD. #kansassenate pic.twitter.com/PB5tCX8cn1

An ad from Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican nominee for governor of Ohio, quickly rocked his race, divided Republicans across the country and became a symbol of the ugly tenor of the midterms.

The explosive spot shows the estranged mother of Mr. Ramaswamy’s Democratic opponent, Amy Acton, describing her as a liar and urging voters not to support her.

Ms. Acton said she had not spoken to her mother since she was 12, after her stepfather was charged with raping her. The sitting governor of Ohio, Mike DeWine, a Republican, said he found the ad “deeply, deeply troubling” and “just plain wrong.”

Other Republicans, including Mr. Trump, closed ranks around Mr. Ramaswamy.

Vice President JD Vance, a former Ohio senator, said he was “disgusted” to see Republicans “whining” about the ad.

Former President Barack Obama, visiting Ohio to campaign, said he did not “know what’s happened where the standards of behavior have gotten so low that somebody can run an ad like that.”

Mr. Ramaswamy lost to Ms. Acton on Tuesday.

In North Carolina, an ad for the Republican Senate nominee, Michael Whatley, appeared to boomerang and boost Democrats.

The ad, from the flagship super PAC for Republican Senate candidates, the Senate Leadership Fund, featured Ronald Hayes, whose son had been murdered. It blamed the Democratic Senate nominee, former Gov. Roy Cooper, for crime in North Carolina.

The ad had a flaw, Mr. Hayes, a Democrat, told news outlets. He had no problem with Mr. Cooper, he said, and had been misled by Republican operatives about the subject of the commercial.

Mr. Cooper’s campaign rushed out an ad to highlight Mr. Hayes’s account.

“Michael Whatley: Lies, deceit,” a voice in the Cooper campaign’s ad says. “He should never be in the Senate.”

The Cooper campaign spent more money on the pushback ad than anything else all cycle, according to AdImpact’s data, nearly $3 million.

Carter Wrenn, a Republican strategist in North Carolina, said Mr. Cooper’s ad was effective in tarnishing Mr. Whatley’s credibility.

“Because it was true what Cooper was saying,” Mr. Wrenn said, adding that Mr. Whatley’s allies looked “sloppy.”

Mr. Cooper won by a wide margin.

In the waning days before the election, Senator Susan Collins of Maine ran an ad that stunned some Republicans and that Democrats quickly promoted.

The ad showed a retired Maine telecaster, Bill Green, dismissing the Democratic nominee Troy Jackson’s work as a logger. “We’re not talking about buying a cord of wood here,” Mr. Green says. “We’re sending someone to the U.S. Senate.”

Democrats said it was elitist. Mr. Jackson used it to focus attention on a crisis facing Maine residents: heating oil costs that were soaring because of the war in Iran. Half the homes in Maine are heated with fuel oil, and the rising prices became a central issue in the race.

Mr. Jackson said the race was “about a cord of wood” and about Mainers’ struggles to heat their homes. On Halloween, Mr. Jackson walked the streets of Portland, Maine, dressed as a cord of wood, mocking the commercial.

Lance Dutson, a Republican strategist in Maine and a former aide to Ms. Collins, said the ad carried a “tone of condescension” and left an impression that Ms. Collins was out of touch on a crucial issue.

“How that got on the air, I have no idea,” Mr. Dutson said.

Mr. Jackson defeated Ms. Collins.

Hi, I watched hundreds and hundreds of political ads this year as I covered the 2026 elections. Commercials matter because they are one crucial way that campaigns reach voters who don't want to consume political news. Here are just some of the ones that stood out — for better or worse. What stood out to you?

Lisa Lerer and Reid J. Epstein

Lisa Lerer and Reid J. Epstein are national political correspondents who have covered presidential campaigns since 2008.

A pastor in Kansas. A Paralympian in Iowa. A former Presbyterian seminarian in Texas.

Democrats expanded their map this week with big wins in traditionally red states that the party had all but written off for years by making appeals to moderate, independent and Republican voters.

At the same time, progressives won key races in two purple states, Michigan and Maine.

The combined victories amounted to a sweeping triumph that will send an ideologically diverse crop of new Democratic lawmakers to Congress in January, but internal debates are already emerging about what lessons the party should draw ahead of the 2028 presidential campaign.

For centrists, the results demonstrate that the best way to flip conservative strongholds where their party has long struggled is through embracing moderate candidates and positions that appeal to a broader array of voters. Progressives argue that the victories in Maine and Michigan show that left-wing populists can energize the party’s liberal base and win back some of the working-class voters who had flocked to President Trump.

The debate arrives at a moment of unusual opportunity for the Democratic Party, which will hold large majorities in Congress next year and will seek to carry its midterm momentum into the 2028 cycle.

The discussion over the party’s direction is already playing out as donors, officials and politicians converge at party meetings and liberal gatherings across the country to take a victory lap and plan for the future. And as potential presidential contenders accelerate their quiet planning, they are using the results to make a case for the next nominee — and, possibly, themselves.

“There’s a ton of non-MAGA Republicans and independents that are giving Democrats a second look and a second chance,” Rahm Emanuel, the former Chicago mayor, who is considering a presidential run, said in an interview. “I don’t happen to think socialism is the way to win their hearts and minds.”

He added: “We don’t want to be identified with that anymore.”

Representative Ro Khanna, a California progressive who has also been teasing a bid, had a different assessment.

“The results show that there is no electoral penalty for being a progressive,” he said in an interview. “The stale talking points of the establishment, which lost twice to Trump, about who they deem electable or not electable is totally out the window.”

The early skirmishes are the latest round of a decade-long dispute over the Democratic Party’s direction and strategy.

In the first few months of this year, it appeared as if progressives had the upper hand. Liberal insurgents knocked off moderate rivals in blue districts in New York, New Jersey and Colorado, and they prevailed in Senate primaries in Maine, Michigan and Minnesota.

But in the general election, the moderates roared back, using explicitly bipartisan appeals to win by notable margins in states that had not elected Democrats to the Senate in years or, in the case of Kansas, nearly a century.

In Iowa, Josh Turek, the party’s nominee for Senate, ran a closing-stretch TV ad about how he opposed transgender athletes participating in youth sports. In Kansas, Adam Hamilton, a pastor who until this year had been a registered Republican, offered direct appeals to Trump voters and described himself as “a liberal conservative and a conservative liberal” who was above party politics. And in Texas, James Talarico embraced a “politics of love” that leaned away from partisanship and focused on “top versus bottom,” or the rich and powerful against ordinary Americans.

While all three men embraced economic populist platforms that promised to lower costs and raise taxes on billionaires, they also denounced what Mr. Hamilton called the “hyperpolarization in Washington.”

“Those candidates ran on that kind of pragmatic platform, saying we’re going to focus on the issues that impact our community, and we’re going to be independent voices, not putting parties and politics first,” said Representative Adam Gray of California, a Democrat who is the chairman of the moderate Blue Dog PAC. “They did better than their progressive counterparts. I think you’re going to see that in the data.”

Progressives rode a different path to victory.

The party’s Senate candidates in Maine, Michigan and Minnesota placed left-wing rallying cries at the center of their campaigns, promising to establish “Medicare for all”; calling to dismantle the Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency; and accusing Israel of committing genocide in Gaza.

In Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed combined some of those promises into a call-and-response slogan: “Money out of politics, money in your pocket and Medicare for all.”

In an interview, he credited his victory to his willingness to try to upend the political system. He suggested that not everyone in his party was on board with that idea.

“I think one of my big critiques of Democrats has often been that we just treat the symptom and not the disease,” he said. “Some people want to treat the disease without treating symptoms, right? You’ve got to treat both.”

He wasn’t the only progressive feeling bullish. Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont, the dean of congressional progressives, claimed near-total victory in an interview. Of the candidates he endorsed, the only one who did not win was Angie Nixon, a democratic socialist who fell just short in the Florida Senate race.

Mr. Sanders said Democrats should not hesitate to press a progressive agenda next year in Congress. He argued that Americans had voted for major changes, including wealth taxes, a higher minimum wage, universal health care and ending foreign wars.

“They want a government that stands up for the working class, that takes on the oligarchs, that delivers for working families,” he said. “We can no longer engage in same old, same old, status quo policies.”

In the House, Representative Greg Casar of Texas, the chairman of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, boasted that his group would expand its ranks by 25 members next year. He cast the midterms as a generational victory for the progressive movement.

Progressive winners of House races included Will Lawrence, a co-founder of an environmental group, the Sunrise Movement, who flipped a Republican-held district in Michigan; Brian Poindexter, who defeated a scandal-tarred Republican in northeast Ohio; and Randy Villegas, who prevailed in a redistricted House seat in California.

“This election cycle, the progressives made a big new bet that by endorsing populist candidates in seats Trump won big, we could show that a populist progressive message can win anywhere,” Mr. Casar said in an interview. “And that paid off.”

He added, “Progressive ideas won.”

With so many Democratic wins, not all the ideological lanes were quite so clear.

Both moderates and progressives claimed some credit for the party’s flips of Republican-held seats by Sam Forstag, a union leader and smoke jumper in western Montana; Bob Brooks, a Pennsylvania union leader; and Rebecca Cooke, a Wisconsin political fund-raiser.

Democratic leaders have tried to downplay the party’s divide. Senator Chuck Schumer of New York, who is widely expected to become the next majority leader, and Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York, who is poised to become speaker, stressed unity. They said all of the party’s candidates had run by focusing on the cost of living, corruption and the Iran war.

“Whether they were progressives or moderates, they were saying the same things,” Mr. Schumer told reporters.

Still, some officials in both wings of the party interpreted the results through the prism of what kind of Democrat would be best to nominate for president in 2028.

With the jockeying for the presidential race escalating this week — Gov. JB Pritzker of Illinois released a memo on Wednesday promoting his proposed agenda for the next two years — the fight over the party’s direction will unfold both in Congress and in the early primary states.

A chief target of the centrist scrutiny was Mr. El-Sayed, who won in Michigan after his party sent its full armada to help him.

Former President Barack Obama and former Vice President Kamala Harris stumped for him. Mr. Schumer’s super PAC invested $67 million into the race even though Mr. El-Sayed said he would not back Mr. Schumer to be party leader.

In the final weeks, some party officials quietly grumbled that a more centrist candidate would have cost less and freed up money for Democrats to expand their playing field of competitive races into places like Florida and Mississippi, where a moderate candidate leads a Senate race by just over 2,000 votes as counting continues.

Progressives, for their part, noted that Mr. El-Sayed had been undercut by his moderate primary rival’s surprising late endorsement of the Republican nominee.

Broadly, centrist Democrats have argued that progressive candidates, despite winning, underperformed in blue or purple states. Democrats are on track to win the national popular congressional vote by about 13 percentage points, according to estimates by The New York Times. Mr. El-Sayed won his Senate race by seven points, Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota by 10 and Troy Jackson of Maine by six.

“The people who won handily in states Democrats haven’t won in decades were the people who practiced the politics of addition, not the politics of subtraction,” said Neera Tanden, the president of the center-left Center for American Progress.

Some other Democrats were already looking ahead to the next race.

Even before the polls closed on Tuesday, aides to Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York released a five-page memo detailing her contributions to midterm Democrats and again articulating her thinking about whether to seek the 2028 presidential nomination.

“In the coming days and weeks, much will be discussed about the future of the Democratic Party and 2028. You may be asked whether you support her running for president or for Senate in New York or staying in the House of Representatives,” the memo concluded. “We’d recommend you rely on the details of this memo and answer that Rep. Ocasio-Cortez will continue to do what she’s always done: look for ways to do the most good for the most people.”

Democrats of all stripes won sweeping victories on Tuesday. Progressives in Maine and Michigan. Centrists in Kansas and South Carolina. A 39-year-old incumbent in Georgia, a 69-year-old former governor in North Carolina. Even before all of the votes in all of the races are done being counted, an intraparty fight over credit has begun. Moderates say they did better — and the math seems to back them up. Progressives said their victories in political battlegrounds proves they can win anywhere. For both wings of the party, the ultimate test is coming up as the 2028 presidential primary season kicks off.

Michael Kruse contributed reporting from Detroit.

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/08/nx-s1-603.author: Willem Marx
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/08/nx-s1-603.text:
A view through the destroyed walls of a kindergarten shows a large bomb crater and a damaged residential apartment building following a missile attack in Kyiv, Saturday, Nov. 7, 2026.

European officials will turn up for the U.S.-mediated peace talks between Russia and Ukraine in the United Arab Emirates this week, France's foreign minister said Sunday, days after the Kremlin had insisted there could be no role for European powers at the meeting.

"France will be there and will ensure that Europe's voice is heard," Jean-Noël Barrot told French radio. He did not say who would represent Paris, or whether French or other European officials would take part directly in negotiations, or simply observe.

The meetings, which are set to take place in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday and Wednesday, had previously been presented as a three-way session between Washington, Moscow and Kyiv.

The Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov had earlier ruled out a European role, saying the trilateral format had already been agreed.

Talking to a Russian news channel on Friday, he accused European governments of failing to decide who speaks for them, while acknowledging that security talks would at some point require Europe's involvement.

On Thursday, President Trump met Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev and said a coming agreement was "going to involve more than Ukraine," adding he could even say it "might involve all of Europe."

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told CNN on Friday that he had not been given details of the agreement Trump had referenced, and warned: "For me, it's not simple, and it can be dangerous." He invoked the 1945 Yalta conference, where Allied leaders settled Europe's division without the involvement of several affected countries.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, right, and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy attend a press conference in Berlin, Germany, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026.

This will be the fourth round of talks between the two warring nations brokered by the Trump administration, and the first since those in Geneva this February. Earlier U.S.-brokered meetings have made little progress, and the chances of a breakthrough have been reduced as the Trump administration focused on its war with Iran.

Moscow confirmed it would return to the negotiating table only following a visit by U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg in October. Those talks saw Putin announce the release of an American prisoner from a Russian jail — an apparent Kremlin gesture to President Trump's earlier lifting of sanctions on Russian diesel exports. Ukraine was vehemently opposed to the fuel sales — arguing they helped replenish Moscow's war chest.

Witkoff has said the agenda for these latest talks will include postwar security arrangements and de-escalation of the conflict and humanitarian issues, shortly after Melania Trump helped broker a limited ceasefire that allowed humanitarian aid to enter a town inside Russian-occupied Ukraine.

Russia's delegation will again be led by Vladimir Medinsky, a hardline Putin aide who has participated in most talks with Ukraine since the unsuccessful first set of discussions all the way back in March 2022.

For the first time, these talks will also include Deputy Foreign Ministers Sergei Ryabkov and Mikhail Galuzin, as well as Yury Zhigarlovsky, a deputy head of the General Staff's operations directorate, alongside military intelligence chief Igor Kostyukov.

This more senior lineup could indicate that Moscow is readier than before to address thorny political and military questions. But the U.S. think tankInstitute for the Study of War suggested some of those same Russian officials have in fact previously sought to slow down previous talks or push harder on Moscow's demands.

The gaps between the two countries remain substantial. Russia has demanded that Ukraine give up large parts of its territory and renounce NATO membership. Zelenskyy has repeatedly insisted any security commitments should be clearly spelled out, including who would act, and how, if Russia attacked again.

Russian President Vladimir Putin, right, interacts with people at the monument to merchant Kuzma Minin and Prince Dmitry Pozharsky, leaders of the struggle against foreign invaders in 1612, in Red Square in Moscow, Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026, during National Unity Day celebrations.

Some analysts expect little. In an op-ed for the Atlantic Council think tank, the former U.S. ambassador to Ukraine John Herbst argued that Putin had rejected every U.S. proposal Kyiv accepted and preferred participating in peace talks than pursuing actual peace. "Perhaps the only outcome of the talks," he wrote, "will be to agree to another round."

The meetings in the United Arab Emirates also follow Democrats' midterm victories, which Zelenskyy said could improve Ukraine's chances of more U.S. aid.

Russia, too, may be looking to push for the Trump administration's outlines of a Ukraine deal — before a Democratic-controlled Congress arrives come January.

Also hovering over the talks — the prospect of Trump, Xi, and Putin gathering for a trilateral meeting at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China later this month. While details remain murky, all sides have confirmed discussions are underway.

And as officials travel to Abu Dhabi to talk peace, the war has raged on regardless.

Zelenskyy said Russia fired 36 ballistic missiles at the Kyiv area overnight Saturday, with only four intercepted, accusing Moscow of treating diplomacy "as a form of aggression."

In southern Ukraine, the death toll from a guided-bomb strike Monday on an aid distribution site in Komyshuvakha rose to at least 55.
