“America took a giant step back in History with the results of the last Election,” Trump claimed in a post on his Truth Social platform on Sunday morning, citing the sharp sell-off in global markets, fueled a rout of US tech stocks. “But have no fear, we will be back, BIGGER AND STRONGER THAN EVER BEFORE!”

Despite Republicans losing control of both chambers of US Congress in Tuesday’s decisive US midterm elections, and voters across the country expressing frustration with key pillars of Trump’s controversial agenda, from the Iran war to sweeping tariffs, the administration appears set to press ahead.

Miller’s promotion has stoked expectations that Trump is poised to double down on an aggressive immigration crackdown, stoke cultural war battles, and refuse concessions to the new Democratic majority in Congress. The move “signals the administration is going to ⁠have a fighting-from-a-bunker approach the last two years”, Dan Eberhart, a Trump donor and energy executive, told Reuters.

Trump abruptly announced on Saturday that he had offered White, whom he described as “a violent Fighter and Warrior”, the role of White House press secretary, which has been largely vacant since Karoline Leavitt departed the administration this summer. Leavitt initial replacement, Katie Zacharia, lasted five days in the job.

“Dana will be a Press Secretary like none other,” said Trump. “Dana, please take the job!”

After Trump also threatened Democrats planning to conduct oversight of his administration and family, announcing he had ordered the US Department of Justice to “look into” them, attorney general Todd Blanche told CNN’s State of the Union on Sunday that “there could be” investigations. Republicans have faced “dangerous” threats, Blanche claimed, without specifying what crimes he believed had been committed. “You have to draw the line.”

Democrats have made clear that Miller and Elon Musk, the world’s richest man and a close Trump ally, are likely to be targets of congressional investigations once the party retakes control of Congress in January.

Congressman Robert Garcia, a Democrat from California, who is set to chair the powerful oversight committee in the House of Representatives next year, said on Sunday that investigations are set to explore Musk’s involvement in the Department of Government Efficiency’s mass firing of federal workers last year, and Miller’s role in Trump’s immigration crackdown. “I think there’s a lot ⁠of interest – not just from our committee, but from committees across the Congress – to speak to Mr Musk,” Garcia told CNN.

Representative Jamie Raskin, poised to become the chair of the House judiciary committee, has also requested information on the business dealings of Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner and son Donald Trump Jr.

With 33 of 35 Senate races called, the Democrats had won 54 seats to the Republicans’ 44. Votes are still being counted in Alaska, which had long been seen as a key battleground, and Mississippi, a previous Republican stronghold which remains too close to call.

Congressman James Comer, a Republican from Kentucky who currently heads the House oversight committee before his party cedes control to Democrats, told Fox News that the committee is going to dedicate the last two months of this congress investigating Alaska over the controversy surrounding its Senate race.

Trump has already threatened Democratic candidate Mary Peltola with criminal prosecution over reports that her campaign was linked to the recruitment of a second “Dan Sullivan” in Alaska’s Senate race, with the same name as the Republican candidate.

Democrats meanwhile embarked on a victory lap this weekend, celebrating their historic wins on Tuesday. Democratic candidates won after running on policies that would “change working peoples’ lives”, New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani told Fox News on Sunday.

“We are seeing a moment in time where working class Americans have made very clear that they are tired of waiting,” said Mamdani. “They are tired of being told, again and again, that there is less for them to make ends meet, while we see the world’s first trillionaire emerge in Elon Musk.”

But there has been friction within the party regarding the incoming congressional leadership, with Chuck Schumer set to become the next majority leader in the US Senate Hakeem Jeffries widely expected to become House speaker.

Senator-elect Adam Hamilton of Kansas – the first Democrat the state has sent to the US Senate in almost a century – told NBC’s Meet the Press on Sunday the Schumer is a “kind of polarizing figure” adding: “It feels like it is a time for fresh and new ideas, and somebody who can unite us instead of dividing us.”

The celebrations continued, though.

During a Saturday Night Live skit this weekend, a member of the cast impersonated Trump attacking James Talarico, the Democrat who ran for US Senate in Texas, and called him “Talafreako” – only for Talarico himself to walk out on stage.

“That’s senator Talafreako,” he said, to loud cheers, after becoming the first Democrat to win statewide office in Texas since 1994.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Abdul El-Sayed’s Oxford years: PhD, political influences and sporting distinction
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Sammy Gecsoyler
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Michigan senator-elect’s former peers recall his time at university in Britain – and his love of coronation chicken sandwiches

In the cold, twilight days of 2008, inside the University of Michigan’s fortress-like Fleming administration building, one student was given a particularly adulatory sendoff.

Mary Sue Coleman, president of the university at the time, convened a ceremony for the latest Rhodes scholar heading to the University of Oxford: Abdul El-Sayed. “There is no doubt among anyone who crosses his path that he will achieve all he sets out to accomplish and more,” she declared to a room full of the university’s leaders, calling the medical PhD student the “epitome of the engaged intellect”.

She even recalled Bill Clinton’s response to a speech made by El-Sayed in 2007, with the former US president remarking: “I wish every person in the world could have heard you speak today.”

For those who ran into El-Sayed months later in autumn 2009 when he finally crossed the pond, these words of praise rang true. “He always seemed very driven,” says Elias Rothblatt, who played lacrosse alongside Michigan’s senator-elect more than 15 years ago. El-Sayed was captain of Oxford’s lacrosse team and student journalists at the time described him as a “defensive master” in the sport.

Rothblatt, 36, who works in fintech, says El-Sayed was a “very fierce competitor” on the field and a “wonderful” captain. “He had a great sense of humour. He struck a really good mix of being friends with other people on the team but also setting the tone and helping lead the team and keep things, keeping serious.”

Off the field, Rothblatt says, El-Sayed was equally “fun and friendly”. He says: “It was always a pleasure to run into him. He was with his wife sometimes and she was wonderful too.” El-Sayed also had a fixation on a resolutely British sandwich: coronation chicken. Speaking to the Times, Ricardo Chasebi, owner of a now-closed cafe in Oxford’s covered market, recalled El-Sayed’s order as a grilled ciabatta filled with coronation chicken, cheddar, peppers and red onion that was topped with lettuce and tomato.

He eventually placed El-Sayed’s version on the menu, naming it “the Abdul”. The senator-to-be was so keen on Chasebi’s sandwiches that he would call ahead from the airport and say: “I’ll be in Oxford in two hours, don’t shut until I get there.” El-Sayed even handed Chasebi a copy of his doctoral thesis, where he thanked the cafe owner in the acknowledgments for “nourishing my stomach and my soul”.

Rothblatt has tried the Abdul sandwich. “It’s good,” he says. El-Sayed also had a penchant for Nando’s, organising meetings there with his fellow Rhodes scholar cohort.

While he eventually settled into Oxford life, things didn’t start smoothly for El-Sayed. He did not enjoy his course at first and flew back to Michigan two weeks before his first term ended. And based on a recent outburst, where he told a Sky News reporter: “You know how many votes I want to get in the UK? Zero,” you might assume he was, at best, apathetic about his time in Britain. But that is not the case. In his memoir, Healing Politics: A Doctor’s Journey into the Heart of Our Political Epidemic, El-Sayed wrote: “My classmates in Oxford taught me more than I could learn in any classroom.” And in several articles El-Sayed wrote for the Guardian, he expressed an appreciation for Britain and, in particular, its political system.

after newsletter promotion

In one piece, where he declared that UK democracy had the “upper hand” on the US, El-Sayed expressed his awe at a parliamentary hustings in Tower Hamlets, east London before the 2010 general election where all of the candidates were of Bengali heritage, reflecting the demographics of the local area. He opined: “As an Arab-American, the likelihood of ever having the opportunity to vote for an Arab-American candidate for national office during my lifetime is minimal.”

But this week, he did have the opportunity to do so, being able to cast the ballot for himself. He was joined by more than 2.5 million others who followed suit and elected El-Sayed as the country’s first Muslim senator.

Rothblatt is “very excited” to see what El-Sayed will do in the Senate. “I think he’s going to do a fantastic job. Back then, he was a talented, ambitious person who had some really good ideas about what he wanted to do in the world. Now he’s continuing to bring those to life,” he says.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: The political playbook that unraveled US transgender rights in the past decade
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Maggie Mertens
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
From the military to healthcare, Trump systematically dismantled Obama-era protections for transgender rights

S
helby Chestnut remembers turning on the news in 2016 and hearing something he didn’t expect. Then- attorney general, Loretta Lynch, had just announced a federal lawsuit to block HB2 in North Carolina, otherwise known as the “bathroom bill”. Lynch said the law, which made it illegal for transgender people to use a public restroom that did not align with the sex listed on their birth certificate, was reminiscent of those passed during the Jim Crow era that restricted public facility use by race. Then, she addressed transgender Americans directly: “But no matter how isolated or scared you may feel today, the Department of Justice and the entire Obama administration wants you to know that we see you; we stand with you; and we will do everything we can to protect you going forward.”

HB 2 was repealed within the year. Chestnut said he thought at the time: “Oh this is the next phase of protections for trans people.”

Not signed in before? Create a free account

But instead of the beginning of legal protections for transgender Americans – the past decade has become the exact inverse. This was made abundantly clear during the midterm elections, where even during a “blue wave” of tsunami proportions, ballot initiatives targeting transgender people were passed even in Democratic strongholds like Washington and Colorado.

Just how much have things shifted? North Carolina experienced mass boycotts of the state in 2016 over that bathroom bill – including almost 200 corporate leaders asking for the repeal of the law, and the NCAA March Madness basketball tournament pulling seven games from the state in protest – a huge economic and cultural blow. But this year Kansas and Idaho have both passed bathroom bill laws without any kind of similar public outcry, though facing challenges in court. In Idaho, a person who uses the bathroom of the gender that does not match the sex they were assigned at birth could be charged with a misdemeanor punishable by up to one year in prison for the first offense. The second offense would be considered a felony, punishable by up to five years in prison – for using the bathroom.

The intervening decade changed the rhetorical, political and legal landscape to be nearly opposite of that in 2016 regarding the civil rights of transgender Americans. Meanwhile, culturally the transgender population has gone from a curious minority (approximately 1-3% of Americans are transgender) that needed protecting to an outright punching bag. Former college swimmer Riley Gaines has made a career out of speaking out against trans women participating in sports. Fox News spent three weeks of the summer airing at least 130 segments whipping up concern about the possibility of trans athletes playing in the WNBA – a league where no trans women have ever played. Books that mention trans characters are routinely banned from schools and libraries, and Disney erased a trans character’s storyline from an animated Pixar series in 2024 before the show could even be released.

While Trump often took rhetorical shots at social issues during his first term, he only used executive power to specifically target the rights of transgender Americans a couple of times, often simply to undo ways the Obama administration had specifically sought to protect them. His second term has taken a vastly different tack. But why did laws targeting this particularly tiny part of the American population grow so rapidly?

“It’s been a long, long 10 years, to say the least,” said Chestnut, the executive director of the Transgender Law Center.

***
 
 Back in 2016, before the November election, it had been just one year since the supreme court decision on Obergefell v Hodges made marriage equality the law of the land. The LGBTQ+ movement was at a “high point” in terms of political capital, says Marie-Amélie George, a professor and legal historian at Wake Forest Law School whose research focuses on the history of LGBTQ+ legal rights.

“There was a renewed movement for all types of anti-discrimination protections to expand upon the victory of the marriage equality campaign, and the [response to] HB2 was really very much a sense of commitment to LGBTQ rights,” George said.

This often took the form of legally applying anti-discrimination laws to trans people, according to Elana Redfield, a federal policy expert at the Williams Institute at UCLA. “At the time, there was this open question about whether laws that were designed to protect against sex discrimination applied to transgender people,” Redfield said. While the Obama administration had made some overtures towards protecting trans people under those laws, Trump mostly followed a more restrained legal tactic, by rescinding Barack Obama’s moves.

So while the Obama administration ended a ban on transgender troops in the US military, and passed official memorandums and executive orders that medical providers could not deny access to trans patients under nondiscrimination rules, that trans prisoners should be housed based on their gender identity, and that Title IX protected transgender students – the Trump administration issued rules withdrawing guidance on all these fronts in his first term.

At the same time, these moves were a clear signal to groups like the Transgender Law Center that it was time to get ready for a backlash, according to Chestnut. Until then, the Transgender Law Center had been one of the only litigation groups arguing that laws and ordinances banning trans people from bathrooms or other public spaces were an infringement on civil rights – cases they had largely won. But the situation seemed ripe for a turning of the tides.

“At that point, we convened a coalition which birthed some of our guiding principles over the last 10 years,” Chestnut said.

Their coalition of litigation and advocacy specialists was prescient. By the last year of Trump’s first term, Idaho passed a law targeting trans athletes playing school sports, saying that transgender athletes were not allowed to play on women’s or girl’s sports teams. It was the first such state law to pass and was highly controversial.

When Joe Biden took office in 2021, he again rolled back the executive orders and mandates Trump had made regarding the ways federal anti-discrimination law could affect trans Americans, including lifting the ban on trans troops, and including trans students in Title IX protections – swinging a pendulum back the other way along ideological lines.

But those moves were now extremely politicized. And during the four years of the Biden presidency, the backlash arrived as a hurricane. By 2024, 26 states had passed laws similar to Idaho’s banning trans students from playing school sports. So-called “red states” didn’t stop at sports participation, either. During the same time period of the Biden presidency, 27 states passed laws restricting access to gender-affirming care for trans youth, despite all the major US medical associations supporting access to this type of care for youth as best medical practice.

One of the reasons trans rights were targeted by the political right was probably the lack of a “red wave” during the 2022 midterm elections, according to George. After the disappointing election, the American Principles Project, a conservative thinktank, conducted a study on how Republicans might have fared better at the ballot box. Ultimately, the group made recommendations that have “framed the evolution of the anti-trans playbook”, says George.

She points out that one of the major findings was on voter opinion in battleground states. “Voters of all demographics tended to support Republican positions on transgender issues … that indicated that trans rights could be a really successful political issue.”

Ultimately, along with an influx of funding and organization from groups like the Alliance Defending Freedom, a conservative Christian legal advocacy group that helped overturn Roe v Wade and is classified as an anti-LGBTQ+ hate group by the Southern Poverty Law Center, these political messages led to the rash of state laws restricting trans civil rights from sports, medical care, identity cards and – again – public bathrooms.

“I don’t want to discount the fact that some of the conservative leaders are evangelicals who firmly believe that there are two sexes and that it is immutable,” says George, “but I think there is also a strong political element.

“Some of it may be backlash to liberalism, particularly the Democratic party under Biden, and some of it is political opportunism because once you see that it works in one state, that makes it easier to adopt in another.”

And once the formula was seen to work well in the states, the 2024 presidential election followed suit. In fact, Trump dedicated much of his campaign time to making promises about transgender-related issues, from sports to healthcare. One of the most aired political ads in the final days of the campaign that year was “Kamala is for They/Them. Trump is for You.”

The mountain of anti-trans laws on the books, plus the political success of Trump campaigning on the issue in battleground states set up a much different second Trump term than the first. “The groundwork was there,” said George. “What is different is the speed at which the Trump administration has seized upon them. But I think that is part and parcel of a different strategy on the part of his administration coming in the second time … where if you do all of these things at once, it’s harder for the other side to respond.”

On his first day in office, Trump issued an executive order that essentially redefined the legal meaning of “sex” as the genetic makeup of a person at the time of conception. Even though most medical experts say this is an unscientific explanation (a fetus’s sexual characteristics take weeks to evolve and are not always cut and dried) it was effective, says Redfield. “In other words, the president is saying that it is now the policy of the federal government not to recognize the existence of transgender people, non-binary people, or intersex people.”

That changed the way the federal government could target trans people from day one. “I think it’s pivotal, because it addressed a known ambiguity, and it then gives a categorical approach to the entire federal government … and that was carried out in such a dramatic, expansive and exhaustive way that it’s likely to have ramifications for decades,” Redfield says.

This particular executive order affected three large sectors of the federal government immediately: data collection, federal funding and identity documents. These were hugely impactful for the trans population, according to Redfield, because any statistical information being gathered by the federal government on the American population of transgender, intersex or non-binary people ended abruptly – information that is often used to figure out where federal programs and funds are needed. Funding via grants provided by federal agencies were also cut off entirely to any projects that were determined to even acknowledge the existence of transgender people. And finally, the state department was instructed to stop issuing passports that did not match the sex at birth of the individual, or those with an X gender marker for intersex or non-binary individuals, taking away a basic civil right to identity documents.

But it didn’t stop there. Healthcare, sports and education all became targets of the Trump administration’s legal attention against trans Americans nationwide, after the wave of state laws that had passed under Biden.

Within a month, Trump had issued orders that directed the Department of Health and Human Services to end gender-affirming care for minors nationwide via cutting off federal funding for institutions providing the care, and directing Medicare and Medicaid to not cover the costs of that care.

And he kept the rhetoric about sports at a fever pitch. On National Girls & Women in Sports Day, he issued an executive order entitled “Keeping Men Out of Women’s Sports”, a wide-reaching order that said states or organizations with laws that allowed trans student athletes to compete in women’s or girl’s sports categories were at risk of being in violation of Title IX and/or losing federal funding. The order also directed the Department of Education to prioritize Title IX investigations on this matter. Later, the gutting of that department’s office of civil rights, by the so-called “department of government efficiency” (Doge), has meant that Title IX investigations have been decimated. The few that remain have targeted institutions with policies that are inclusive of trans people, whether in sports, or admissions (such as at Smith College), in lieu of true inequities in women’s sports or gender discrimination, harassment or assault complaints.

Though nearly every action at the federal level has been targeted by lawsuits, the broad legal attack on a certain group of people has had an impact, even in “blue” states. For instance, the largest sports governing bodies have changed rules to disallow trans athletes from competing in women’s division, including the NCAA, and now, even the International Olympic Committee, which will host the next Summer Olympics in Los Angeles in 2028. Meanwhile, even moderate Democrats, such as the California governor, Gavin Newsom, Iowa senator-elect Josh Turek, South Carolina senator-elect Annie Andrews, and Texas senator-elect James Talarico, have made statements that they are against allowing trans kids to participate in girls’ sports.

Last week, four states, Nebraska included, passed ballot initiatives that would ban trans girls from participating in school sports. Three are far from deep red: Washington, Colorado and Arizona. Arizona’s includes private sports clubs, and Washington’s even goes so far as to require medical sex verification for all girl athletes in the state.

This is at a time when more than 40 hospitals with gender clinics have shut down or paused their services for minors – even in blue states, even when lawsuits have been successful – often out of fear of losing federal funding.

Nearly every principal in the Trump administration, from JD Vance to the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, has taken up an anti-trans stance as a priority, both in word and action. And now the supreme court of the United States has ruled in favor of state laws that ban trans athletes and gender-affirming care – rulings that may take years to be overturned, if they ever are.

When it comes to issues of civil rights for a targeted community, there are always steps forward and backward, says George. “It’s important to keep in mind that the states are a patchwork, and that there are lots of states moving against trans rights, and counter-moves with states protecting trans rights, and those states are disproportionately populated. So it’s inaccurate to say that everyone is moving in lockstep against trans rights.”

Notably, some big midterm winners won for Democrats in battleground states while maintaining support for trans rights, such as Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and Senator-elect Troy Jackson in Maine.

But the constant drumbeat of headlines over the past 10 years about laws targeting trans people and political rhetoric stoking fear about them, has resulted in a change in public opinion. Between 2022 and 2025, for instance, American sentiment for laws or policies that protect trans people from discrimination has gone down eight points overall, according to Pew Research. While the differences in Republican- and Democrat-identified voters are still stark (just 5% of Republicans favor requiring health insurance companies to cover gender-affirming care, for instance, while 40% of Democrats do) the loss of support is seen across the political spectrum.

This played out in the midterm results, according to Redfield. “You see a tremendous opportunity for inclusive policy with this blue wave, but there is a sobering reminder from the passage of all these ballot initiatives that the discourse in the country has really negatively affected the lives of trans people and will continue to for some time.”

And those studying this political process closely hope voters and politicians alike will see that the federal government has proven that any group could be targeted using this same playbook.

Chestnut believes that the more people understand this connection between attacks on the transgender community and other groups having rights taken away, the more effective political organizing could be. “I think trans people might be the testing case for a broader attack,” he says. “What we’re looking at is a complete restriction of bodily autonomy of all people that are not cis, white, Christian and conservative. Whether that’s immigration, trans people or people seeking abortions, or voters’ rights.” All of these laws and political rhetoric together, could be what opens the door to “much bigger discrimination”.

Chestnut thinks the movement’s future lies in building coalitions to protect all targeted groups. “We learned that if you want to come for immigrant communities and take them away from their homes and families, then you will lose elections. The way that America has finally started to unite on the tragedy that is immigration enforcement in this country is remarkable. We can do that for the trans community, too.”

Higgins scores twice as Cincinnati win fourth straight

Game was NFL’s second at Real Madrid’s Bernabéu

Joe Burrow threw for three touchdowns and rushed for another and the Cincinnati Bengals’ offense kept rolling to defeat the Atlanta Falcons 34-17 in Madrid on Sunday for their fourth straight win.

Ja’Marr Chase had eight receptions for 142 yards in the first half, and Tee Higgins added two touchdown catches at Real Madrid’s Santiago Bernabéu stadium. Chase finished with 10 catches for 155 yards and a touchdown.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

After his 47-yard touchdown catch in the first quarter, Chase celebrated with Higgins in bullfighting style, with Higgins mimicking a bull by putting his hands on his head and Chase playing the matador with an imaginary cape.

The Bengals (6-2) have scored 30 points or more in four straight games for the first time since 1997. It was the second consecutive defeat for the Falcons (3-6).

Burrow, who completed 24 of 29 passes for 271 yards Sunday, had thrown five touchdown passes and rushed for another in overtime in the team’s 43-36 win over the Tennessee Titans last week.

Playing under the closed roof of the Bernabéu, Falcons quarterback Michael Penix Jr played better than in the rain in a 16-0 loss to the Buccaneers in Tampa Bay last week, but threw a late interception to go along with his opening-drive touchdown to tight end Charlie Woerner. Penix was 20 of 31 for 162 yards with a touchdown and interception and added 50 yards rushing.

Running back Bijan Robinson had 42 yards on three carries on the Falcons’ first drive. He ended with 100 yards rushing and a touchdown on 19 carries and 47 yards receiving on six receptions.

It was the second NFL regular-season game in Madrid after the Miami Dolphins beat the Washington Commanders 16-13 in overtime in last year’s inaugural game in the country. It was the seventh game in a record nine-game schedule outside the US for the NFL this season. The remaining games will be played in Munich, Germany and Mexico City.

A crowd of 78,660 people was on hand on Sunday in the Spanish capital. Bengals fans appeared to outnumber Falcons supporters. The lights at the Bernabéu suddenly went out just as the Bengals were taking a snap inside the final two minutes, prompting the down to be replayed.

Emma Peschel scores on US debut in Group A win

Americans outscore opponents 12-0 through two games

Sweden bounce back with 4-1 victory over Finland

Emma Peschel celebrated her international debut with a goal as the United States shut out Germany 5-0 at the women’s ice hockey world championship on Sunday.

The 22-year-old defender scored with a wrist shot from the point to make it 2-0 in the opening period of the Group A game.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

Casey O’Brien opened the scoring and added an assist in her second game for the US, having marked her debut with a goal and an assist in Friday’s 7-0 victory over Switzerland.

Alex Carpenter extended the lead to 3-0 in the second period before Abbey Murphy and Joy Dunne completed the rout with third-period goals.

Captain Hilary Knight registered an assist to extend her world championship records to 54 assists and 122 points. Defender Caroline Harvey added two assists, giving her five through the opening two games.

Goaltender Gwyneth Philips stopped all 13 shots she faced as the Americans recorded their second straight shutout, having outscored their opponents 12-0 to open the tournament.

“Today was another solid win under our belt, Germany is a talented team,” US coach John Wroblewski said. “We’re going to take the positives from this game and focus on turning our attention to our next test against Austria tomorrow.”

The Americans have won 10 of the past 14 world championships and arrived in Denmark as reigning world and Olympic champions, having claimed the 2025 title in the Czech Republic and gold at the Milan-Cortina Games in February, beating Canada in overtime in both finals. They will face Austria in another group-stage contest in Esbjerg on Monday.

All but one member of the American roster plays in the Professional Women’s Hockey League.

In Group B in Herning, Sweden bounced back from an opening 5-1 defeat to Canada with a 4-1 victory over Nordic rivals Finland. Hilda Svensson scored on the power play and added an assist.

Canada were scheduled to face Japan later on Sunday in Herning, while the Czech Republic were due to meet Switzerland in Esbjerg.

https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.title: US employers keep passing rising healthcare costs to workers. There are better options
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.author: Gene Marks
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.text:
Choosing a healthcare plan can be extremely complicated, but it’s necessary to attract and retain good workers

A
gain, healthcare costs are going up. According to a recent study from Mercer, total health benefit cost per employee in 2027 is expected to rise 8.2% – after employers’ planned cost-reduction measures (without action, employers told Mercer their existing plans would rise about 11%). This would be the highest increase since 2003.

And, again, we see the same reaction from employers. The Wall Street Journal recently reported that even as healthcare costs have gone up, the share of these costs coming out employees’ paychecks has “shot up” even faster.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

Healthcare costs always rise. Naturally, employers are concerned about their bottom line. But is the right approach to pass these cost increases to employees? Or perhaps this is just a little shortsighted, if not lazy. Particularly when many employers – specifically smaller companies, of which 44% don’t provide any health benefits at all – have options instead of just making their people pay more.

For example, offering an individual coverage health reimbursement arrangement (ICHRA) plan is a potential answer. Under this type of plan an employer doesn’t need to purchase group health insurance. Instead, a reimbursement is made to employees for when they get their own healthcare coverage.

An HRA isn’t for everyone. But it’s a good answer, particularly for small business owners. And it’s why ICHRA adoption grew between 73% and 128% among employers with fewer than 100 employees.

Another way to cut costs is by leaning into health savings accounts, or HSAs. If a company already has a high-deductible group insurance plan, it’s usually very easy to attach an HSA plan to it. Setting up an HSA plan incurs a nominal cost but with it employees can contribute their own pre-tax dollars to these accounts and then use the savings to pay for healthcare expenses including deductibles, copays, prescription drugs, many OTC medicines, and dental and vision expenses that may not be covered under the insurance policy.

An HSA enables employees to reduce their taxable income which in turn helps them save money on their healthcare. Workers like these plans because there’s no required distribution and the money grows tax free. Plus, if they change jobs they can take their savings with them. It’s an easy, inexpensive benefit to provide that cuts costs.

Once only a consideration for the biggest of companies, a growing number of smaller employers are now also choosing to self-insure. Some of my clients have signed up for level funded plans, with which they reimburse their employees for healthcare expenses up to a certain amount and then purchase stop-loss coverage to cover larger claims.

When a company self-insures, they start paying more attention to the out-of-pocket expenses their employees are paying. Because of this, a growing number of companies are negotiating rates with local urgent care centers, healthcare providers and pharmacies, and requiring their employees to use them to best control their costs. Amazon and other online pharmaceutical providers are now offering aggressive discounts on products under corporate plans.

For many of us, choosing a healthcare plan is more complicated than designing a bridge. It’s like you need a PhD in healthcare to understand all the ins, outs, deductions, credits, co-pays, networks and nuances, and you need an MBA to properly estimate your costs to decide on what plan is right for your family. Paying a consultant to work directly with employees to help them choose the right plan (or maybe go to the health exchanges or Medicare for older employees) not only helps them make smarter, more cost-effective decisions but also helps you cut back on a company’s healthcare contributions.

Any or all of these strategies can play a big part in controlling healthcare costs, both at the corporate and employee level. So why don’t more companies do this? Because it takes time, effort, resources. It’s a lot of work. Rather than doing this, most employers just pass the cost to their employees and move on.

But moving on isn’t a great idea. This type of laziness has its risks. At some point, the costs get too high and, considering that healthcare is always one of the most requested benefits, can have an impact on both attracting and retaining workers. The labor market is tight. Most of my clients continue to hunt for talented workers. The ones putting in the effort to offer these types of plans are more attractive to workers and position themselves not only to better control their costs but to grow.

https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.text:
Applications due on 3 December for new generation of explorers who can ‘shape humanity’s future in space’

Nasa has launched a callout for a new generation of astronauts as it searches for explorers who could live and work on the moon.

Opening applications for the latest expansion of its Artemis program, the US agency said successful candidates would help “shape humanity’s future in space” as it builds a base on the moon and plans the first crewed missions to Mars.

The news was announced on Saturday during a Kennedy Space Center air show promoting lunar exploration, as well as advances in aviation and technology.

“This is an extraordinary time to join Nasa’s astronaut corps,” said Nasa administrator Jared Isaacman. “The people we select could walk on the Moon, live and work at the Moon Base, and help pioneer the systems and operations that will ultimately carry crews to Mars.”

Nasa expects to make its final selection in late 2027 to begin training the next class of astronaut candidates. The agency last opened applications for new astronauts in 2024, ultimately accepting 10 new astronauts out of more than 8,000 applicants in September 2025.

“For those who apply, becoming a Nasa astronaut is more than a career opportunity,” said Scott Tingle, chief astronaut and chair of the Astronaut Selection Board at Nasa’s Johnson Space Center in Houston. “It is a chance to join a legacy of explorers who have pushed the boundaries of discovery and play a role in the missions that will shape humanity’s future in space.”

Since the 1960s, Nasa has selected 370 people to train as astronaut candidates for increasingly challenging missions. The agency currently has 32 astronauts active in the astronaut corps.

Isaacman and other agency leaders recently laid out Nasa’s ambitions to return Americans to the moon in 2028. Both SpaceX and Blue Origin intend to support a crewed lunar landing.

All applicants must be US citizens, Nasa said, and have either a master’s degree in science, technology, engineering or mathematics; medical qualifications; training as a pilot; or two years’ work on a relevant doctoral program.

Three years of “related professional experience” are also required.

Applying pilots must have either 750 hours of pilot-in-command time of a high-performance jet, 1,500 total flight hours in another fixed-wing aircraft, or 1,000 total flight hours in a rotary-wing aircraft.

Applicants have until 11.59pm ET on Thursday, 3 December, to submit their applications.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: The Guardian view on Ordnance Survey maps: still a superior way to navigate the landscape | Editorial
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Editorial
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
The 225th anniversary of the organisation’s first publication is an opportunity to celebrate its unique contribution to our sense of place

I
n his one-paragraph short story, On Exactitude in Science, Jorge Luis Borges imagines an empire in which the level of cartographical ambition is so high that a map is made on a one-to-one scale with the imperial territory. The quest for perfect accuracy doesn’t end well. But the earliest map-makers for Ordnance Survey, which this week marked the 225th anniversary of its first publication, might have empathised with the obsessive dedication.

The 1801 OS map of Kent was 10 years in the making, its military-led production inspired by fears of Napoleonic invasion. But as Rachel Hewitt points out in Map of a Nation, her stirring account of the Ordnance Survey’s early years, its genesis also lay in an Enlightenment-based enthusiasm for comprehending and accurately representing reality. During the course of the 19th century, the entirety of the British isles was meticulously mapped through fog, rain, wind and sun, in what was described as “a wild and arduous exercise”. The surveyors, armed with theodolites, measuring chains and notebooks, saw themselves as footsoldiers serving in the ranks of Reason as they brought intellectual order to the landscape.

These days, the topographical legacy they left behind is updated through satellites, GPS and digital technologies. But just as significant has been the cultural impact of OS maps on the wider population, amid expanded access to leisure time. Science and art combined in the 20th century, as the commercial potential of small-scale productions for tourists and ramblers was recognised. Sales shot up as covers began to depict motorcars venturing down country lanes, pipe-smoking backpackers plotting a route through the Forest of Bowland, and couples wandering through the Chilterns.

One should not over-romanticise. There is a darker, controlling side to the history of maps, not least when it comes to who got to define borders and names. In his play Translations, the writer Brian Friel portrays the cultural impact of colonial power by following two British surveyors across Ireland, as they impose toponymic order on a recalcitrant Celtic landscape.

But viewed from the age of satnav instructions and Google Maps, there is a charm to cartography that the passive reception of a monotone order to “turn right after 50 metres” will never match. As well as being models of precision and order, the best maps are also a form of mysterious and evocative art, inviting us to proactively explore the world and firing up the imagination. Hewitt quotes from a 19th-century poem in which a woman yearning for her soldier husband “taught her finger” to “stray o’er the map”, tracing the represented distance between them. Countless map-readers have similarly immersed themselves in contour lines, symbols and coded colours, in order to visualise landscapes that they are about to encounter for the first time.

The rise of digital technologies means that the sight of a map poking out of a rucksack or spread awkwardly across the passenger seat of a car is less common than it used to be. But the tactile delights of vinyl records are being rediscovered and celebrated by younger consumers, amid a surge of nostalgia for the analogue age. Hopefully, the peculiar pleasures of attempting to tame an OS Landranger, as it flaps uncontrollably on a windy hillside, will also continue to be enjoyed by generations to come.

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: Beef industry quietly squashes part of its own science curriculum after ranchers protest
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Zach Boren
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
Lesson for teenagers included how cattle’s methane emissions contribute to climate crisis, but it was then scrapped

A beef industry-funded effort to teach teenagers about cattle’s climate impact was quietly scrapped following backlash from some ranchers, who disputed the premise that cows contribute to global heating.

The episode is the latest example of the livestock industry’s decades-long battle to determine what US children learn about cows and the climate.

The American Farm Bureau Foundation for Agriculture (AFBFA) and its Food and Agriculture Center for Science Education produce a free science curriculum used by around 1.2m students across more than 100 school districts nationwide.

Late last year, the foundation announced a new lesson exploring “how cattle produce methane and its role within the broader environmental and biological systems”.

Within months it had been removed, following online criticism from ranchers, with Brett Kenzy, prominent South Dakota farmer, telling a trade paper “it’s not fair claiming that cows are harming the environment because they’re not”. Kenzy, who chairs a committee of the Ranchers-Cattlemen Action Legal Fund United Stockgrowers of America (R-CALF USA), called the lesson a “slap in the face”.

“We did take it down,” Rick Henningfeld, the AFBFA education director, told an audience at CattleCon, the beef industry’s annual convention, in February. “We heard the feedback, and we are editing it, and our hope is to get it back up quickly,” according to a recording of the event shared with the Guardian.

It hasn’t yet returned. A new lesson on cattle digestion, published in July, makes no mention of methane or climate.

Since the 1990s, the beef industry has worked to shape what children learn about its products. Today, officials behind the curriculum say it “eliminate[s] negative perceptions” of the industry for “future consumers”.

The curriculum is funded by a mandatory levy on cattle sales called the “beef checkoff”. A foundation spokesperson said the topic “cannot be a 45-minute lesson”. The foundation said it is working on a longer version, reviewing research “related to the biogenic cycle” with help from unnamed researchers and university experts. It said the July lesson was “not a replacement”.

Animal agriculture advocates often claim the biogenic cycle – in which atmospheric methane breaks down within about 12 years into carbon dioxide that is then reabsorbed by grass – means cattle methane contributes little additional global heating.

But mainstream climate researchers point out that biogenic methane – which comes from living sources such as organic waste, rice paddies and livestock – is a leading cause of climate crisis, even when emissions aren’t rising.

“About 0.3C [roughly 20%] of global warming to date is maintained by our ongoing biogenic methane emissions,” said Carl-Friedrich Schleussner, a climate scientist at the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis. “Cutting these emissions is essential to slow global warming and keep peak warming as low as possible.”

The lesson, “Methane & Cattle: A Climate Connection”, was designed to help high schoolers understand “how the natural digestive processes of cattle contribute to methane emissions and influence atmospheric dynamics”.

Using figures from the UN’s Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, it showed that methane is a far more powerful greenhouse gas than carbon dioxide, though it has a short atmospheric life. The lesson also contained an error, stating livestock accounts for about 2% of human-caused methane emissions, when the true figure is a little over 30%, said Drew Shindell, a climate scientist at Duke University.

Shindell, who chaired the UN’s 2021 Global Methane Assessment, said it was “a shame the ranchers would block students from learning about the world they will inherit”.

“The role of methane in climate change is not controversial, having been measured in the lab long ago and confirmed in satellite observations of the energy emitted by the Earth,” he said.

The backlash began with Jim Mundorf, a rancher, podcaster and longtime critic of the beef checkoff. After seeing a Facebook post promoting the curriculum, Mundorf wrote an analysis on his blog, Lonesome Lands, describing the methane lesson as “one of the most infuriating things I have laid eyes on” and attacking it as condescending to farmers.

“Blaming cattle for climate change is no different than blaming volcanos, or the oceans, or lightning strikes that cause wildfires,” he wrote.

The post was republished by the ranchers coalition of CPAC, the influential conservative group, and amplified across the farming community.

“I put [the blog] out to the world. Hopefully it catches on,” Mundorf said in an interview. “And it did. I get phone calls and emails from people involved with farm bureau who were also upset about [the lesson].” According to Mundorf, farm bureau contacts later told him “they don’t think it’ll be used anymore”.

At CattleCon, responding to an audience question about the “social media heat”, Henningfeld confirmed the lesson had been removed after “feedback from some farm bureau members and some producers”.

Henningfeld said the foundation would develop a new producer review of everything published by the program, to make sure “the science is represented, the needs of the teachers [are] represented, the needs of our awesome producers shows up”.

The foundation said its review process “invites a group of producers to suggest topics and review draft materials”.

But some aren’t convinced. “What happens when those goals conflict?” said Glenn Branch, deputy director of the National Center for Science Education. “The censorship in the recent episode suggests that the needs of the producers prevail.”

Vivayic, a Nebraska-based consultancy that develops the program for the foundation, said the curriculum’s goal is for students to make sense of real scientific data.

A study published in October by Jennifer Jacquet and Loredana Loy, both from the University of Miami, examined how the NCA, a precursor of today’s National Cattlemen’s Beef Association (NCBA), responded to early climate science.

Drawing on archival documents, they found that in the 1980s and 1990s the group treated global warming as a public relations problem, working to downplay US cattle’s methane emissions rather than trying to cut them.

In 1991, the study found, NCA pressure led Random House to end reprints of a Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles children’s book that linked cattle to global warming.

“Influencing K-12 education has been part of the National Cattlemen’s strategy for decades,” Jacquet said.

NCBA declined to comment.

In September, the US Department of Agriculture (USDA), which oversees all agricultural checkoff programs, ordered them to end support for environmental, social and governance (ESG) initiatives as well as net-zero and climate-neutrality targets. The USDA said it had no role in the decision to remove the methane lesson.

“This is compatible with what I see happening,” Jacquet said. “The livestock industry is winning with the Trump administration and does not even need to fake that it cares, let alone that it is doing anything.”
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.summary: The lesson was removed after backlash from some ranchers. NCA worked to downplay US cattle’s methane emissions rather than trying to cut them.

https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.title: Half of NHS trusts in England lack funds earmarked to cover maternity leave
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.author: Tobi Thomas Health and inequalities correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.text:
Physiotherapy services hit particularly hard compared with other areas of healthcare such as nursing, union finds

Almost half of the NHS trusts in England have no earmarked funding to cover staff on maternity leave, according to analysis that raises fresh concerns about pressure on physiotherapy services.

Freedom of information requests sent to the trusts by the Chartered Society of Physiotherapy (CSP) found that 49% had neither a dedicated budget nor a policy to permit overspending to pay for maternity cover.

Where funding does exist, the analysis revealed that physiotherapy appears to be treated less favourably than other areas of healthcare. More than one in five trusts (22%) said their maternity cover arrangements did not extend to physiotherapy staff, compared with only 9% for nursing posts.

The CSP said failing to plan for maternity leave risked leaving overstretched teams to shoulder the same workload with fewer people, meaning patients waiting longer for treatment and rehabilitation. The findings are also especially stark given that women make up about 79% of the NHS physiotherapy workforce.

The CSP’s director of practice and development, Ash James, said it was deeply concerning that physiotherapy teams were significantly less likely than their nursing colleagues to have access to funding for maternity cover.

“When a physiotherapist goes on maternity leave, the patients needing treatment don’t disappear. Without cover, already overstretched colleagues are left trying to absorb the workload, potentially leaving patients waiting longer for the rehabilitation they need,” he said.

“This is happening against a backdrop of recruitment freezes, disappearing posts and growing demand for care. It is yet another example of physiotherapy services being stretched beyond their capacity. Trusts must ensure maternity cover arrangements are available fairly across clinical professions, while the government must urgently lift recruitment freezes and invest in the physiotherapy workforce.”

Earlier research suggested that stroke patients and others who need intensive physiotherapy were receiving poorer care because hospitals lacked adequate space and equipment.

That research found four out of 10 NHS physiotherapy staff had lost or expected to lose dedicated rehabilitation space. In a survey of more than 2,000 members by the CSP, six out of 10 said their rooms had been taken over by other clinical teams, with some blaming a lack of funding or managers who did not prioritise their work.

The body is calling for equal access to maternity cover funding across NHS professions as well as urgent action on recruitment freezes and staff shortages in physiotherapy.

The chair of the Patients’ Association, Alastair Henderson, said the gaps in cover had direct consequences for patients. “When services are already stretched, losing staff without adequate replacement can mean longer waits for treatment and rehabilitation, less access to specialist expertise and greater pressure on remaining teams,” he said.

“Patients should not have to wait longer or miss out on the care they need because the NHS has failed to plan for or cannot afford to cover predictable staff absences.”

https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.title: Older women are as varied and individual as we have ever been | Letters
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.author: Guardian Staff
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.text:
Thank you, Jo Brand, for not offering us a formula for growing older, writes Dr Denise Taylor. Plus a letter from Louise Mothersole

I found Jo Brand’s reflections on approaching 70 wonderfully refreshing (‘It’s far too late for me to go to the gym every 10 minutes’: Jo Brand on ageing, raging, fitness and grief, 2 November). Here is a woman who doesn’t feel obliged to turn ageing into another self-improvement project. She can be angry, grumpy, less adventurous than she once was, and still enjoy her life.

We hear so much about ageing well, ageing positively and ageing successfully. We are encouraged to exercise more, eat better, remain productive, find our purpose and keep reinventing ourselves. Much of this advice is well intentioned, but collectively it can make growing older seem like another job we are expected to perform.

As a 69-year-old psychologist who researches and writes about later life, I question this narrative. Of course, looking after our health matters. But ageing isn’t a competition, and we shouldn’t have to demonstrate that we’re making the most of every remaining year.

I was particularly struck by Brand’s comments about older women being treated as though they are all alike. We are as varied, contradictory and individual as we have ever been. Some of us want adventure; others want a quieter life. Some are still working, others are delighted to have left employment behind. And our feelings about ageing can change from one day to the next.

Perhaps what makes Brand’s interview so appealing is that she doesn’t offer us a formula for growing older. She simply describes her experience, with humour, honesty and a willingness to acknowledge what is difficult.

We need more of that. Less instruction on how to age successfully, and more freedom to grow older in our own way.
Dr Denise Taylor
Chartered psychologist and author of ThriveSpan

I would like to reassure Jo Brand that approaching 70 is certainly not too old to get fitter and healthier. My partner (aged 73) and I (64) were dedicated couch potatoes. Our evenings were spent with wine, cheese and chocolate. Neither of us had ever done any sport or fitness activity until April of this year when we began the Couch to 5K challenge.

We now run 5km three times a week, every week. We’re not quick (40 minutes) but we do it and feel so much better for it – so virtuous that my halo lights our evening runs.
Louise Mothersole
Bournemouth, Dorset

https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.title: It is time the government treated hunger and obesity as two interlinked problems | Letter
https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.author: Guardian Staff
https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.text:
The cabinet committee the MPs want should become the delivery arm of a statutory right to adequate food, writes Prof Kent Buse of the World Obesity Federation

Your report (UK government’s obesity plan ‘doomed to fail’, MPs warn, 30 October) arrives a fortnight after the Right to Food UK Commission asked the same prime minister for the same thing: a legal duty on government, a minister responsible for it, and an independent body reporting to parliament.

Each report sees half the problem. The Health and Social Care Committee wants prevention and treatment run as separate workstreams, and stops at urging ministers to stand up to the food industry. The commission sees hunger as a question of income and rights, but says little about the quality of the diet that low incomes buy. The same food system, and the same households, produce both hunger and obesity. Whitehall treats them as two problems, with two sets of ministers and no shared accountability, and so neither is solved.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

The remedy is to combine the two asks. The cabinet committee the MPs want should become the delivery arm of a statutory right to adequate food, in the sense the UN covenant on economic, social and cultural rights already gives it: enough food, and food that nourishes. That duty needs measurable targets, an independent commission reporting annually to parliament, and conflict-of-interest rules that keep manufacturers and retailers out of the policy process, as tobacco control has required for 20 years.

Mr Burnham praised the Right To Food campaign at prime minister’s questions on 14 October. Ministers are due back before MPs within three months with a plan. Combining the two reports would give that plan something it currently lacks: a structure that holds government to account for what people eat.
 
 Prof Kent Buse
 
 Co-chair, Policy and Prevention Committee, World Obesity Federation

https://www.theguardian.com/wellness/202.title: Tired all the time? What to know about B12 and if it actually boosts energy levels
https://www.theguardian.com/wellness/202.author: Keren Landman
https://www.theguardian.com/wellness/202.text:
Med spas are raving about vitamin B12 shots as a pick-me-up. But do they actually make you feel more energized?

I
f you spend time on social media, you may have seen med spa owners and employees describing vitamin B12 shots as a pick-me-up. When they’re run down or facing a busy week, they say, a quick injection gets them through. Some med spas say many people feel an energy lift within a day or two and recommend a shot every few weeks.

B12 is essential to your health, and people who don’t get enough of it can feel exhausted or worse. But most people already have plenty of B12, and for them, extra doses aren’t likely to help.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Here’s what you need to know about what B12 does, who runs low on it and when to get tested.

Vitamin B12 is found naturally in animal foods like meat, fish, eggs and dairy, and it’s added to some breakfast cereals and nutritional yeasts. It helps your body make red blood cells and DNA, and it keeps your nerves working properly. It also plays a role in turning food into energy, which is where its reputation as an energy booster comes from.

When people don’t have enough B12, they can develop anemia, memory problems, depression and fatigue, says Andrea Dean, a hematologist at Loyola University medical center in Chicago. If their levels are seriously low, they can also develop numbness and tingling in their hands and feet.

Eating foods rich in vitamin B12 isn’t enough to ensure you have adequate levels. To absorb this vitamin, your stomach needs to produce adequate acid, along with a protein called intrinsic factor.

When people have B12 deficiencies despite a balanced diet, it’s often because they have a condition that reduces stomach acid production (like gastritis) or pernicious anemia, an autoimmune condition in which the stomach stops making intrinsic factor.

About 4% of US adults have low B12 levels, and deficiency is more common in adults 60 and up. Other factors that raise the risk include having weight loss or stomach surgery, digestive conditions like celiac or Crohn’s disease and overusing alcohol.

Taking the diabetes drug metformin or acid-reducing medications for a long time can also lower B12 levels. Vegans and some vegetarians can become deficient too, unless they eat fortified foods or take a supplement.

For people who feel fatigue or mental slowing due to low B12 levels, treating the deficiency can restore their energy. But if your B12 levels are already adequate, getting more won’t make you feel less worn out or improve your athletic performance. Dean compares it to filling up a car: if the gas tank is already full, adding more gas won’t make the car go faster.

Some people who feel more energetic after a B12 shot may be experiencing a placebo effect. “We know that some of this is just all mental,” says Dean. For med spa owners who endorse the injections, it’s also financial: The shots cost a typical US spa less than $1 a piece and are sold to consumers for $25 to $75 each. The profits add up when patients get weekly shots.

There’s not much risk to spas who sell these shots. B12 is generally safe, even at high doses, because your body gets rid of what it doesn’t need, and Dean says she has never seen anyone overdose on it. But if your B12 levels are normal, injections are unlikely to be worth their cost.

Fatigue has many possible causes, including poor sleep, low thyroid hormone and low iron. “It’s not just B12,” says Dean. So if you’re tired most of the time, it’s worth seeing a clinician who can look for the cause.

A B12 level is a simple blood test that your primary care doctor can order. In many US states and the UK, you can also order one yourself online through commercial labs. However, the results can be tricky to interpret on your own because you can be deficient even when your result looks normal. Most labs consider levels to be low if they’re less than 200 or 250 pg/mL, but Dean treats anyone with a level below 400 pg/mL. For people with borderline levels and symptoms, doctors can order two more blood tests, called methylmalonic acid and homocysteine, to help confirm a deficiency.

If your level is low, your doctor should also figure out why, because the cause affects how it’s treated. Sometimes your medical history explains it, but otherwise, your doctor may test you for pernicious anemia.

B12 can be taken as a pill or given as a shot. Shots deliver the vitamin into a muscle or under the skin, which skips the gut entirely.

That makes shots the best choice for people with severe deficiency, nerve symptoms or conditions like pernicious anemia that keep them from absorbing B12. When someone has nerve symptoms, “we don’t play around,” says Dean.

For many others, pills work just as well. High doses of oral B12 raise blood levels about as effectively as injections, and they cost less.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/8.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/8.text:
Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, has warned that Tehran will “rain down hell” if the United States resumes attacks, serving Washington with an ultimatum in an attempt to end the two countries’ eight-month war.

“Our 2-day proposal stands: meet the requirements, including end to war on all fronts, and you will see results,” Araghchi wrote in a post on X on Sunday.

“Or choose war, and see our alert and battle-hardened warriors rain down hell,” he said.

US President Donald Trump said on Sunday that renewed strikes on Iran are “highly unlikely” if negotiations progress over Tehran’s nuclear programme and the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz.

“It depends on whether or not they sign a very strong agreement,” Trump said when asked about continued US strikes on Iran during a phone interview reported by CNN. “I would [continue], if necessary, but we hit them really hard,” he added.

Trump warned that US forces have three aircraft carriers stationed in the region “fully locked and loaded”, ready to continue strikes if need be. He also said that the US has 38 bridges in Iran’s crosshairs that US forces “can knock down in literally one hour”.

Iran’s Foreign Ministry also quoted Araghchi in an earlier statement on Sunday that said Iran would “not go easy on American targets” in the region.

Araghchi’s statements came after reports by state media that an oil tanker caught fire earlier that morning after hitting a naval mine east of the Strait of Hormuz, citing Iran’s navy.

The navy claimed the ship’s identification systems were turned off and it was travelling in the no-go zone of the strait.

An adviser to Iran’s commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps’ Aerospace Force made threats that echoed those of the Iranian foreign minister and said that weapons have been “secured for years to come”.

“The armed forces are at the ready, and if the enemy makes a mistake, Iran’s response will be devastating and severe,” warned IRGC Brigadier-General Ali Belali in a statement on Telegram.

“As senior commanders of the armed forces have pointed out, we have upgraded our capabilities in the post-Ramadan War period,” Belali said.

The back-and-fourth between Iranian and US leaders comes following US midterm elections in which the Democratic Party won control of both chambers of Congress, soundly defeating Trump’s Republican Party.

Araghchi alleged that negotiations have been delayed as a result of the elections, but he awaits the path forward, Iranian state media reported.

“It will take some time for things to settle down and for the atmosphere to become conducive to the mediators resuming their visits,” the foreign minister said. “We have to wait.”
