You can get a temporary break from the $200 price hike that hit both Air sizes this summer.

You can get a temporary break from the $200 price hike that hit both Air sizes this summer.

If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

The latest 13-inch MacBook Air is currently available for $1,099.99, marking the second time we’ve seen this $200 discount following the company’s hefty price increases over the summer. Although the base model — which features Apple’s M5 processor, 16GB of RAM, and 512GB of storage — often sold for around $950 to $1,000 shortly after it launched in May, savings have been rare since July, making the current deal worth flagging. Amazon, Best Buy, and B&H Photo are all honoring the price across all color options.

If you’d prefer something with a larger screen, a six-speaker array instead of four, and slightly more power (with two additional GPU cores in the M5), Apple’s 15-inch MacBook Air is also on sale for $200 off. Amazon, Best Buy, and B&H Photo are each selling the 16GB RAM / 512GB SSD configuration in most colors for $1,299.99.

Although it’s pricier than the newer MacBook Neo, the Air offers better value in numerous ways. It’s an ideal choice if you want faster performance, as it offers double the RAM and a speedier CPU with more cores. You also get twice as much storage, better speakers, a backlit keyboard, and a larger, higher-resolution screen. Given said differences, it’s easy to see how the Air’s improvements might make it worth the extra cost for some people.

If you’re still on the fence, though, I’d recommend reading my colleague Antonio G. Di Benedetto’s reviews, both of which were published before the summer price increases.

https://www.space.com/entertainment/lege.title: Legendary sci-fi magazine 'Starlog' returns as a yearly release, just in time for its 50th anniversary
https://www.space.com/entertainment/lege.author: Jeff Spry
https://www.space.com/entertainment/lege.text:
Before the rise of online entertainment sites, this is where genre fans got their news

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

"Starlog" was one of the greatest sci-fi and fantasy magazines ever, and after a 17-year absence, it's being resurrected.

The legendary sci-fi mag went dark back in 2009 as part of the wave of popular publications folding due to years of declining readership and subscriptions. But as of Nov. 13, this geek favorite periodical returns as an annual print edition, and it's available for pre-order now.

It’s another indication of digital fatigue in the world, and fans of a certain age will recall the pleasure of poring over each colorful issue packed with in-depth interviews, behind-the-scenes photos, TV guides, classic movie retrospectives, book reviews, con news, and VFX features.

"Starlog" launched in 1976, in the pre-"Star Wars" days, under the leadership of editor-in-chief Terry O’Quinn. It first arrived with artist Jack Thurston's beautiful painted "Star Trek" cover, featuring William Shatner as Captain James T. Kirk and Leonard Nimoy’s Spock, set against the U.S.S. Enterprise near a shimmering black hole.

The magazine continued to inform the science fiction community about upcoming sci-fi TV shows and blockbuster Hollywood films for over three decades; I fondly recall reading each informative and entertaining monthly issue cover-to-cover.

Just in time to honor its 50th anniversary this year, "Starlog" blasts back into the sci-fi universe with Issue #375 showcasing cover artwork created by Armenian artist Gabriel Yeganyan. Its geek culture legacy, covering iconic franchises like "Star Wars," "Star Trek," and "Alien," will now live on thanks to Fangoria Holdings and io9 co-founder Annalee Newitz, editor-in-chief.

"During its original 33-year run, 'Starlog' documented science fiction as it evolved across film, television, books, technology, and culture," said 'Fangoria's Tara Ansley.

"Fifty years after the magazine first launched, the line between science fiction and the real world has become increasingly difficult to separate. That makes this an especially interesting time to bring 'Starlog' back. Technology may change, but the most compelling questions have always been about people: how we live, what we create, and what kind of future we want to build."

"Starlog" reloads for its first annual edition after a long hiatus on Nov. 13. You can pre-order the first issue (Issue 375 in continuity) on the Starlog website.

Jeff Spry is an award-winning screenwriter and veteran freelance journalist covering TV, movies, video games, books, and comics. His work has appeared at SYFY Wire, Inverse, Collider, Bleeding Cool and elsewhere. Jeff lives in beautiful Bend, Oregon amid the ponderosa pines, classic muscle cars, a crypt of collector horror comics, and two loyal English Setters.

https://www.space.com/space-exploration/.title: On this day in space! Nov. 8, 2005: Europe launches Venus Express, its first mission to Venus
https://www.space.com/space-exploration/.author: Hanneke Weitering
https://www.space.com/space-exploration/.text:
Venus Express had to survive harsh radiation at Venus, but it persevered for nine years.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Nov. 8, 2005, Europe launched its first mission to Venus. The spacecraft was called Venus Express.

Venus is a hothouse planet, one where the atmospheric pressure can easily crush an unprotected spacecraft. Even from orbit, Venus Express had to survive harsh radiation. But the spacecraft lasted for more than nine years.

During that time, Venus Express saw a weird vortex swirling around Venus's south pole. It also saw possible signs of active volcanoes. Venus Express also discovered that the planet generates its own auroras. These auroras happen when particles from the sun hit charged particles in the atmosphere.

Late in the Venus Express mission, controllers told the spacecraft to dip down into Venus's clouds — even though the spacecraft wasn't designed to do this. It performed well, but eventually it stopped listening to commands. The spacecraft burned up in the atmosphere in January 2015.

Venus Express established ESA as the third world organization to successfully send a probe to study Venus, following the United States and Soviet Union. (Japan's JAXA became the fourth five years later.)

"By studying Venus, scientists learn how Earth-like planets change over time," reads a summary of the planet's exploration prepared by The Planetary Society. "Orbital studies [like Venus Express] hint that Venus may have hosted habitable oceans before becoming inhospitable."

"By studying Venus, we can learn how Earth-like planets evolve and what shapes planets throughout the galaxy into temperate, lush worlds instead of sweltering hothouses. Venus also helps scientists model Earth’s climate, and may serve as a cautionary tale on how dramatically a planet’s climate can change," wrote the Society.

ESA returned to Venus in 2018 when BepiColombo, its joint mission with JAXA, used the planet's gravity to redirect its path toward the planet Mercury.

Want more space history? Check out our full On This Day In Space Story archive and watch our On This Day In Space videos on YouTube.

Hanneke Weitering is a multimedia journalist in the Pacific Northwest reporting on the future of aviation at FutureFlight.aero and Aviation International News and was previously the Editor for Spaceflight and Astronomy news here at Space.com. As an editor with over 10 years of experience in science journalism she has previously written for Scholastic Classroom Magazines, MedPage Today and The Joint Institute for Computational Sciences at Oak Ridge National Laboratory. After studying physics at the University of Tennessee in her hometown of Knoxville, she earned her graduate degree in Science, Health and Environmental Reporting (SHERP) from New York University. Hanneke joined the Space.com team in 2016 as a staff writer and producer, covering topics including spaceflight and astronomy. She currently lives in Seattle, home of the Space Needle, with her cat and two snakes. In her spare time, Hanneke enjoys exploring the Rocky Mountains, basking in nature and looking for dark skies to gaze at the cosmos.

https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.title: Single iron infusion improves exercise capacity in HFpEF
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.author: Erik Swain
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

CHICAGO — In patients with iron depletion and heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, an infusion of ferric derisomaltose improved various measures of exercise capacity compared with placebo, researchers reported.

For the IRONMET-HFpEF trial, presented at the American Heart Association Scientific Sessions and simultaneously published in Circulation, Gregory D. Lewis, MD, director of heart failure at the Mass General Brigham Heart and Vascular Institute and professor of medicine at Harvard Medical School, and colleagues randomly assigned 65 patients with HFpEF and iron deficiency 2:1 to a single IV infusion of ferric derisomaltose (FDI; Monoferric, Pharmacosmos Therapeutics) or placebo.

“Patients with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction have marked reductions in exercise capacity,” Lewis, who presented the findings, told Healio. “There’s a huge unmet need to improve upon functional capacity in these patients. It turns out more than half of them have iron deficiency, so that’s what the target was.”

All patients had iron deficiency, defined as ferritin level of less than 100 ng/mL or ferritin level of less than 300 ng/mL with transferrin saturation level of less than 20%. The median age of patients was 68 years, 72% were women, the mean baseline transferrin saturation was 16%, the mean baseline level of ferritin was 57.8 ng/mL and the median baseline peak oxygen uptake (peak VO2) was 12.7 mLkg1min1 in the FDI group and 12.1 mLkg1min1 in the placebo group.

Most studies of iron-based therapies for patients with HF have been conducted in patients with reduced, not preserved, ejection fraction, Lewis said during the presentation.

“We made measurements of hepcidin, a marker in the bloodstream that is a measure of how well patients can absorb iron,” Lewis told Healio. “It was abnormally elevated in patients with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. As a result, we could predict that an oral iron supplement would not be helpful. So we purposely used an intravenous formulation. Ferric derisomaltose is a safe way to give high doses of intravenous iron in a single infusion.”

At 12 weeks, the primary outcome of peak VO2 improved by 1.2 mLkg1min1 (95% CI, 0.6-1.7) in the FDI group but did not change in the placebo group (0.1 mLkg1min1; 95% CI, 0.7 to 0.9; least-squares mean difference, 1.1 mLkg1min1; 95% CI, 0.2-1.9; P = .02), Lewis and colleagues found.

“We know that iron plays an important role in exercise capacity in patients with heart failure, since iron is involved not only in oxygen transport to the muscles, but also in mitochondrial function, which the skeletal muscles require to generate energy,” Rajeev Malhotra, MD, associate director of the Cardiopulmonary Exercise Laboratory at the Mass General Brigham Heart and Vascular Institute, associate professor of medicine at Harvard Medical School and the senior author of the study, told Healio. “The clinical endpoint is a gold-standard measurement of oxygen uptake in heart failure patients.”

At the end of the study, transferrin saturation in the FDI group was 9.4 percentage points greater than in the placebo group (95% CI, 4.9-13.9) and ferritin was 182.6 ng/mL greater (95% CI, 127.7-237.5) compared with the placebo group (P < .001 for both), according to the researchers.

Oxygen at the anaerobic threshold, 6-minute walk test distance and NYHA class all improved in the FDI group compared with the placebo group (P < .05 for all), but there was no difference between the groups in change in Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire overall summary score, Lewis and colleagues found.

There were no serious adverse events in the FDI group, Lewis said during the presentation.

“We saw improvements in multiple different measures of exercise capacity,” Lewis told Healio. “Patients could walk farther in 6 minutes, they could achieve higher peak oxygen uptake, their ability to do aerobic exercise improved. We feel these are all meaningful endpoints for patients living with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, particularly with a safe therapy like this. We would like to see larger and longer studies to confirm the durability of these functional benefits that we observed. Fortunately, we know these medicines are effective at keeping iron stores elevated for extended periods of time. Additional studies will be quite important for this field, but we are very encouraged by the results of IRONMET.”

Gregory D. Lewis, MD, can be reached at cardiology@healio.com.

Rajeev Malhotra, MD, can be reached at cardiology@healio.com.

Lewis GD, et al. Featured science: Heart failure care for normal phenotypes. Presented at: American Heart Association Scientific Sessions; Nov. 6-9, 2026; Chicago.

Disclosures: Lewis and Malhotra report serving as advisors for Pharmacosmos. Lewis also reports past service on a scientific advisory board for American Regent. The other authors report no relevant financial disclosures.

https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.title: ‘Smart alerts’ boost volunteer arrivals for suspected cardiac arrest
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.author: Scott Buzby
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

CHICAGO — A “smart alerting” algorithm selecting cardiac arrest volunteer responder by estimated travel time boosted volunteer arrival before emergency medical services.

The algorithm ruled out volunteer responders too far from the scene of suspected cardiac arrest or who were unable to arrive before an ambulance, potentially reducing futile dispatches and keeping volunteers engaged with the smartphone alerting system, according to new data presented at the Resuscitation Science Symposium of the American Heart Association Scientific Sessions.

“Many regions in Europe and also in the U.S. have smartphone alerting systems. These systems register volunteers who are ready to save your life. If somebody nearby ... experiences out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, then these volunteers are alerted through the smartphone app,” Michael Mueller, DEAA, MME, FERC, chief physician of the department of anesthesiology, intensive care and emergency medicine at Artemed St. Josefskrankenhaus Freiburg in Germany, said during a press conference. “The system knows the position of the first responders, they are alerted, and they can run to the location and deliver chest compressions, give ventilations and defibrillate the patient. They can bridge the time until the ambulance arrives.

“However, when we alert volunteers, it would be nice to alert those who can reach the scene prior to the ambulance. Our goal when developing smartphone alerting systems is to have the shortest time until the first compression,” Mueller said. “The other goal or objective of smartphone alerting systems is the shortest time to the first defibrillation shock. To reach this, we have developed a modern alerting algorithm [that] takes into account the mean of transportation.”

The researchers therefore evaluated whether alerting volunteer responders based on their predicted arrival time — smart alerting — rather than by their physical distance to the cardiac event, may allow responders to arrive ahead of emergency medical services (EMS) and bridge CPR.

Mueller and colleagues conducted a prospective, randomized trial comparing smart alerting with fixed-radius 600 m and 2,500 m alerting strategies to notify volunteers of suspected out-of-hospital cardiac arrest.

The study was conducted in Freiburg from January to July 2024, and sent 1,482 volunteers to 823 suspected cardiac arrests across all three trial arms, according to the study methods.

The primary endpoint was rate of volunteer arrival before EMS.

Volunteers dispatched using the 2,500 m (57%) and smart alert systems (58%) more frequently arrived at the scene before the ambulance compared with those alerted via the 600 m system (31%).

Smart alerts significantly increased pre-EMS arrival compared with the 600 m alert system (risk difference, 27 percentage points; 95% CI, 19-34; P < .001) but was not significantly different vs. the 2,500 m strategy, according to the presentation.

The researchers reported that more volunteers on average reached the patient when dispatched using the 2,500 m and smart alerting strategies compared with the 600 m strategy (1.9 vs. 0.8).

Among volunteers who reached the scene, more than twice as many dispatched with the 2,500 m and smart alerting strategies brought an automated external defibrillator before the ambulance arrived (28% with the 2,500 m strategy vs. 27% with smart alerting vs. 11% with the 600 m strategy), according to the study.

Moreover, volunteers who accepted the alert but were deliberately not sent by the smart alerting system would have most likely not arrived before the ambulance, based on the system’s algorithm. By reducing futile dispatches, this method may keep more volunteers engaged with the alerting system, Mueller said.

“With smart alerting, the system sends a pre-alert, asks them how are you traveling, calculates the route, and 31% of the responders are rejected by the system because the system knows they will arrive later than the ambulance,” Mueller said during the press conference.

The researchers acknowledged limitations of the present study, including that only system performance was measured, not patient survival, and that the alert strategies were randomized by day of the week rather than by emergency type.

“If you know CPR and a smartphone alerting system is active in your region, please register because you can make a difference if the ambulance needs longer than 3 to 5 minutes,” Mueller said during the press conference. “If you are responsible [for] an ambulance system or emergency system, you should consider establishing a smartphone alerting system because it’s great to have a volunteer there before the ambulance arrives.”

Mueller M, et al. LBRS.01. Late-breaking resuscitation science abstract session. Presented at: American Heart Association Scientific Sessions; Nov. 6-9, 2026; Chicago.

Disclosures: Mueller reports no relevant financial disclosures.

https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.title: No clinical benefit for PCI in stable coronary artery disease
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.author: Erik Swain
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

CHICAGO — In follow-up lasting up to 25 years, percutaneous coronary intervention did not reduce death or MI in veterans with stable coronary artery disease, according to new data from the COURAGE trial.

The results are the same as the primary outcome reported in 2007 after a median of 4.6 years and a follow-up analysis reported in 2015 after a median of 11.9 years.

“These findings do not support a routine strategy of elective upfront PCI to reduce long-term death or MI in patients with stable CAD,” Neel M. Butala, MD, assistant professor of medicine (cardiology) at the University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus and medical director of structural heart disease and intervention for the VA Eastern Colorado Healthcare System, said during a presentation.

The new analysis, presented at the American Heart Association Scientific Sessions and simultaneously published in JAMA, included 959 veterans (mean age, 63 years; 98% men; 78% white) from the COURAGE trial for whom outcomes could be ascertained via VA Corporate Data Warehouse administrative and laboratory data. Median follow-up was 15 years and maximum follow-up was 25 years.

Butala said the extended analysis was undertaken after the ISCHEMIA trial, which also showed no difference between PCI and medical therapy for death and MI in patients with stable CAD, had a lower rate of spontaneous MI but a higher rate of procedural MI in the PCI arm.

“One can imagine, if these trends continue, there may be a significant difference,” he said. “So the key question remained, would this diverge in outcomes with longer observation?”

According to the researchers, the estimated 25-year cumulative incidence of the primary outcome of death or MI was 91% in veterans assigned optimal medical therapy and 93.3% in veterans assigned PCI plus optimal medical therapy (HR = 1.01; 95% CI, 0.88-1.15; log-rank P = .89).

The estimated 25-year incidence of death was 82.2% in the medical-therapy group and 83.9% in the PCI group (HR = 0.98; 95% CI, 0.85-1.13), the estimated 25-year incidence of MI was 54% in the medical-therapy group and 54.6% in the PCI group (cause-specific HR = 1.01; 95% CI, 0.85-1.2), the estimated 25-year incidence of first revascularization in the medical-therapy group was 53.5% and the estimated 25-year incidence of repeat revascularization in the PCI group was 50.4% (cause-specific HR = 0.87; 95% CI, 0.73-1.03), according to the researchers.

There were no differences between the groups in event-free survival at any 5-year time point, or in time lost to MI or revascularization at any 5-year time point, or in any prespecified subgroups, Butala said during the presentation.

Limitations include that the study population was overwhelmingly male and had high baseline CV risk, that the sensitivity of MI is imperfect due to the data collection method, and that patients were treated with outdated technologies such as bare-metal stents, he said.

In the extended analysis, “the treatment effects were generally consistent with the adjudicated results during the trial period,” Butala said.

In a discussant presentation, Rasha Al-Lamee, MBBS, PhD, clinical academic interventional cardiology consultant at Imperial College Healthcare NHS Trust in London and British Heart Foundation Intermediate Research Fellow and professor of cardiology at Imperial College London, said that COURAGE “was the first trial that really started to shape what we believed in terms of what we could do in the cath lab. And over the years and the decades since COURAGE was published, we’ve obviously all become a little bit more sound, and perhaps a bit more conservative about who we think we should revascularize in terms of improving outcomes in stable coronary artery disease. But interventional cardiologists have still had lots of questions. They constantly say, “Well, it wasn’t long enough and I don’t really know what happens to a 50-year-old man if I don’t revascularize him over decades.’ They say, “I don’t think this applies to my population of patients that I treat every day and we shouldn’t be using that data.’ But actually, what [Butala and colleagues have] proven to us is that event rates in these patients remain very low and that over the long term, a significant proportion of patients in the optimal medical-therapy group, nearly half, did not require revascularization.”

She said the extended analysis “is a very important piece in understanding stable coronary artery disease and categorizing that many of our patients actually do well with [optimal medical therapy]. You can see yourself talking to a patient who you’re going to manage conservatively and using some of this data. But I hope that we will, as you dig into the data more, be able to understand more about what changed in these patients over time and whether their [optimal medical therapy] changed over time.”

Butala NM, et al. Featured Science: Stable ischemic heart disease: What happens in the long run. Presented at: American Heart Association Scientific Sessions; Nov. 6-9, 2026; Chicago.

Disclosures: Al-Lamee reports advising for AstraZeneca and Johnson & Johnson, consulting for Medtronic, Philips and Shockwave Medical and holding equity in Orbita Systems. Butala reports receiving consultant fees from Boston Scientific, Catch Bio, Emboline, HiLabs and Shockwave Medical and holding equity in HiLabs. Please see the study for all other authors’ relevant financial disclosures.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/08/tocquevil.title: How a Frenchman’s book on ‘Democracy in America’ nearly 200 years ago explains the midterms, from data centers to Texas
https://fortune.com/2026/11/08/tocquevil.author: Nick Lichtenberg
https://fortune.com/2026/11/08/tocquevil.text:
I turned to Alexis de Tocqueville, having read about him for years and never actually read him myself, after the Nov. 3 midterms handed Democrats a “blue tsunami” the likes of which I haven’t seen in my 43 years. Texas went blue down the line. And in 40 of 41 local votes across 10 states, Americans chose to limit data centers.

Within days, $3.2 trillion of AI-related stock market wealth was wiped out as investors bet the election winners would slow the AI buildout. Texas holds one-fifth of the planned data-center pipeline, and its governor-elect has promised to ban new approvals until the state legislature acts.

I had been privately skeptical, because data centers are the bedrock of the massive industrial boom powering most of America’s GDP growth. From an economic perspective, being anti-data center is like being pro-recession, I assumed, but Tocqueville’s Democracy in America explains a lot of what has really gone on in America for centuries.

Tocqueville was a young French aristocrat who toured the United States in 1831 and published Democracy in America in two volumes, dated 1835 and 1840. The Library of America calls it arguably “the most perceptive and influential book ever written about American politics and society.” One big idea he offered was what he called the “general equality of condition” among Americans, meaning how widely property and status were spread around. And this, he proposed, is the fact that the rest of American life comes out of. He argued that Americans hold tight to their property, care more about equality than liberty, and organize locally to get what they want. The data-center industry made its plans without accounting for any of that, and it’s an open question whether the Democrats who just won a landslide really understand it, themselves.

Most Gen Xers can barely remember a wave like this one. The closest historical comp is the 1974 blue wave that swept aside the corruption of the Nixon Watergate era. The 2026 midterms suggest a scrambling of the calculus of red states and blue states much like Donald Trump’s shocking election did a decade ago, when the “blue wall” of Pennsylvania, Wisconsin and Michigan crumbled.

Nationally, Democrats have so far flipped seven Senate seats and are on track for at least 258 House seats. They took a majority of governors’ mansions for the first time since 2010, and Trump acknowledged that Democrats had secured both chambers. Down the ballot, voters in 10 states decided 41 local measures on data centers, and in 40 of the 41 they favored limits on development. In NBC’s exit poll, 76% said they would oppose a new data center in their community. There were many stunners, like Kansas electing its first Democratic senator since 1932, but Texas stands out as the signature shock.

The Lone Star state went blue across its statewide offices. Beyond the Senate and governor’s races, Democrats won agriculture commissioner, attorney general, land commissioner, comptroller, lieutenant governor and railroad commissioner. They have taken the state House for the first time since 2002. Gina Hinojosa unseated Gov. Greg Abbott and will be the first Democrat elected governor of Texas since Ann Richards in 1990, and the first ever Hispanic person to hold the office. The Texas House looks likely to have its first female and first Black speaker in the form of 87-year-old Senfronia Thompson, who took office in 1973.

Reading Tocqueville in this climate is downright spooky. He wrote in 1835 that American political bickering at first looks to a stranger “so incomprehensible and so puerile” that he can’t decide whether to pity the people or envy the happiness that lets them argue. I personally thought as much for months about the issue of data centers — a massively overstated environmental risk but a massively understated political and emotional issue — until voters proved they were not messing around.

Look closer, Tocqueville wrote, and nearly every faction of American political life comes down to one side trying “to limit,” and the other “to extend, the popular authority.” Five years later, in his second volume, he explained what made Americans different from the Europeans watching them. “The great advantage of the Americans is that they have arrived at a state of democracy without having to endure a democratic revolution; and that they are born equal, instead of becoming so.” Two centuries on, that birthright came out on Nov. 3 as a mass of voters told the Republican Party, and the data-center builders, something like “No, I don’t think so.”

Property, unlike aristocratic Europe where it is passed down from along family lines for centuries, is what keeps the whole thing from flying apart for most Americans, who are “possessed of sufficient property to desire the maintenance of order, yet not enough to excite envy.” Tocqueville observed that “the passions engendered by property are keenest and most tenacious amongst the middle classes.” And because equality leaves each person weak on his own, Americans band together to form what he called “associations,” without which they “become powerless if they do not learn voluntarily to help one another.”

Tocqueville also prophesied that Texas would hold the key to the American future. “The inhabitants of the United States are perpetually migrating to Texas, where they purchase land; and although they conform to the laws of the country, they are gradually founding the empire of their own language and their own manners,” he wrote, a decade before Texas joined the Union.

Texas has spent the 2020s proving him right. It added 391,243 residents in the year to July 2025, more than any other state for the third year in a row, reaching 31.7 million. It produced $2.9 trillion in GDP in 2025, and holds one-fifth of the planned 253-gigawatt data center pipeline nationwide. The five fastest-growing American cities, the Census Bureau revealed in May, were all in Texas, some for the second year running.

This year, Texas put every one of Tocqueville’s arguments on the ballot at once. Landowners fought transmission lines after a 2023 law cut the time regulators have to consider them from 365 days to 180. Groups like Save Rural Texas organized against data centers, and while Abbott ordered an audit of every data center in the grid queue, Hinojosa called for a statewide moratorium, vowing days before the vote to “stop the data center takeover.” Then the voters made clear in resounding fashion how they felt about property, equality and popular authority.

For a lot of voters this year, equality came down to the cost of living. In Gallup’s final preelection survey, 44% of voters called income and wealth distribution extremely important, the highest reading in the three midterms Gallup has measured it, up from 32% in 2018 and 31% in 2014. On PJM, the grid running from Illinois to New Jersey, the independent market monitor puts data centers at $6.3 billion of the latest auction’s $16.4 billion in capacity charges, and at $29.4 billion, or 46%, across the last four auctions. In the October ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos poll, 57% of Americans called home energy and utility costs unaffordable, up from 45% in February.

On property, Tocqueville wrote that “the heart of man is not so much caught by the undisturbed possession of anything valuable as by the desire, as yet imperfectly satisfied, of possessing it, and by the incessant dread of losing it.” The data-center fears, environmental concerns aside, cut straight to the American dread of losing one’s property. In August, a University of Texas/Texas Politics Project poll found 57% of Texas voters opposed a data center in their community, including 43% of Republicans and 60% of rural voters. The other side claims property, too. Texas Policy Research, a free-market think tank, argues Texas should protect private property rights and free enterprise while making large electricity users pay the costs they impose on the grid.

The “associations” that Tocqueville observed were so obvious in this election season they hardly need mentioning. Data Center Watch, a tracker maintained by AI research firm 10a Labs, counted 833 opposition groups across 49 states by March 2026, up from 396 at the end of 2025. In June, Seattle’s city council voted unanimously for a one-year ban, making it the largest U.S. city to pass one. None of these ran through Washington.

Tocqueville spelled out the lesson in 1840: Americans describe their civic life in terms of self-interest. “The Americans… are fond of explaining almost all the actions of their lives by the principle of interest rightly understood,” he wrote. “They show with complacency how an enlightened regard for themselves constantly prompts them to assist each other.”

When they do something public-spirited, in other words, they insist it is in their own interest. They “seldom allow that they yield to emotions of this kind; they are more anxious to do honor to their philosophy than to themselves.” He didn’t mean that as an insult, calling the principle “the best suited of all philosophical theories to the wants of the men of our time,” and “their chief remaining security against themselves.”

That’s what most readings of the data-center fight, including mine, missed. From outside it looks like people guarding their power bills and their land. Others suspected the opposition was manufactured, even from China. The experts Fortune spoke to in June found it organic, with little evidence to support claims of China’s interference. The people in the fight talk about bills and property, as Tocqueville said they would, and they organized and voted in 41 places.

Americans misread themselves on the bigger question, too. Before the vote, fewer than half expected free and fair midterms, according to a University of California, San Diego, survey. Experts weren’t much sunnier. In Bright Line Watch’s October survey, their median forecast of a free and fair election was 75%, and one article in Political Science Quarterly argued the country had descended into soft competitive authoritarianism. But Tocqueville reasoned in the chapter “Why Great Revolutions Will Become More Rare” that a country of small owners has too much to lose to blow itself up.

“Nations are less disposed to make revolutions in proportion as personal property is augmented and distributed amongst them,” he wrote. Americans’ revolutions come through the ballot box when equality feels threatened. The contrast with Germany and France, where disaffected Gen Zers’ protests have turned violent in the streets, looks straight out of the late 18th century.

Democrats would be making a Tocqueville-sized mistake to read Nov. 3 as a conversion. The border counties that swung toward them had swung the other way two years earlier. In 2024, Trump won all four counties in the Rio Grande Valley, a region Democrats had swept in almost every presidential election since at least the 1920s. In Texas, where Democrats won their largest House majority since the 1993 session, several Democratic flips were decided by mere hundreds of votes. In Kansas, Hamilton won as an “independent-minded Democrat.” He avoided association with national Democrats and said he wouldn’t support Sen. Chuck Schumer for another leadership position, even though his campaign took $5 million from a PAC associated with Schumer.

The voters who elected them were following the bills, the land and the town meeting and will surely follow them again.
https://fortune.com/2026/11/08/tocquevil.summary: The 2026 midterms suggest a scrambling of the calculus of red states and blue states. Texas added 391,243 residents in the year to July 2025, more than any other state for the third year in a row.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/08/us-debt-a.title: The market bloodbath just exposed Wall Street’s true fears about U.S. debt, top economist warns
https://fortune.com/2026/11/08/us-debt-a.author: Jason Ma
https://fortune.com/2026/11/08/us-debt-a.text:
There have been competing theories to explain why Treasury yields have risen so much this year, but last week’s brutal stock selloff debunked one of them, according to a top economist.

The 10-year yield has eased in recent weeks as investors seek shelter in Treasuries. But before the latest dip, it shot up more 100 basis points, soaring above 5% and at one point hitting the highest level in 24 years.

The run-up began after the Iran war started in late February, sending oil prices up and raising expectations that the Federal Reserve will hike rates to fight suddenly resurgent inflation.

At the same time, hyperscalers have been flooding the bond market with fresh debt to finance massive capital spending and the AI infrastructure boom, which has kept the U.S. economy running hot and inflation sticky.

That’s competed for investors’ dollars as the Treasury Department taps the bond market to finance the federal government’s $2 trillion budget deficit—and pay interest of the $40 trillion in U.S. debt.

Some on Wall Street have downplayed the spike in yields, saying the deluge of AI debt has crowded out U.S. bonds and forced the Treasury to offer investors higher returns at auctions.

But Robin Brooks, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, doesn’t buy that explanation. In a Substack post on Saturday, he said the past week’s market selloff represented a “natural experiment” that puts the competing arguments to the test.

“On one end of the spectrum are people like me who think this is a rising fiscal risk premium as our public debt grows out of control,” he wrote. “On the other end are folks who say it’s hyperscaler debt issuance that’s pushing up yields, so there’s no sign fiscal policy’s in trouble.”

Brooks said corporate borrowing is nowhere near where it was in the IT bubble of the early 2000s, while public borrowing is historically high and more likely driving up yields.

He pointed to the bond market’s reaction to the latest monthly jobs report, which showed payrolls grew by more than double the consensus estimate.

Compared to previous upside job surprises, the two-year yield rose more than what hot economic growth could explain, undercutting the idea that U.S. growth depends on AI as well as the argument that AI is responsible for higher yields.

Brooks also cited the market-implied yield for a 10-year security 10 years from now, which gauges the premium investors demand for the risk of holding Treasuries long term. Such risks include the trajectory of U.S. debt and deficits.

If the AI bubble was pushing up long-term yields, then this “10y10y forward yield” would’ve fallen alongside the 10-year and two-year yields.

“It didn’t and that in my mind further cements the case for the fiscal risk premium,” he said.

“The midterm elections and the AI sell-off that’s ensued have given us the perfect natural experiment to disentangle what’s going on with long-term yields. They’re up because of mounting fiscal stress, not because of AI.”

U.S. debt warnings have been piling up recently. Last month, the Treasury Department’s final tally on fiscal year 2026 showed that the federal budget deficit widened to $1.99 trillion, 12% worse than the $1.78 trillion gap in fiscal 2025.

That came as revenue increased 3% to $5.4 trillion, lagging behind the 6% bump in spending to $7.4 trillion. Social Security and Medicare were the biggest line items, but in third place was interest payments on the national debt, topping defense spending and Medicaid.

Gross interest costs for fiscal 2026 came in at $1.36 trillion, Treasury data show, with an average interest rate of 3.53%. That’s more than double the rate in 2021, just before the Federal Reserve embarked on an aggressive tightening cycle to rein in inflation.

Net interest payments rose 8% to $1.05 trillion, outpacing increases in total spending, revenue and GDP. In fact, it exceeds real GDP growth of about 2% as well as nominal GDP growth of about 6%.

Fiscal 2026’s net interest costs translate to about $2.9 billion a day, and the Peter G. Peterson Foundation estimated they represent 3.2% of GDP, breaking the previous record set in 1991.

“Higher interest begets more debt, and greater debt begets higher rates and higher interest. Eventually, the whole thing could come crashing down,” Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget President Maya MacGuineas said in September.

“That’s why Washington needs a fiscal intervention now, before it’s too late. The President, the Treasury Secretary, and Congressional leadership need to understand the severity of this issue. There are no easy fixes, and we can’t just wish this problem away.”

https://fortune.com/2026/11/08/gen-z-per.title: Gen Z pushes back on ‘performative availability’ as only 8% of workers say it won them a promotion
https://fortune.com/2026/11/08/gen-z-per.author: Cordell Jones
https://fortune.com/2026/11/08/gen-z-per.text:
Every generation entering the workforce has its work ethic put on trial. For Gen Z, the charge is a reluctance to stay reachable once the workday ends.

New survey data suggests the bargain they are questioning is lopsided. In a June 2026 survey of 1,006 U.S. employees by Software Finder, 69% said being available after hours has not meaningfully improved their careers. Just 8% credit it with a promotion, and 12% with a raise or bonus.

The costs are easier to find. Forty percent of respondents said after-hours availability has worsened their work-life balance, 38% said it has raised their stress, and 32% said it has worsened burnout.

That gap between sacrifice and reward comes as employers grow stingier with advancement. Workday data reported by Fortune showed promotion rates fell in 10 of the 11 industries it tracks in the first half of 2025.

The survey splits respondents into always-on workers and those who set firmer boundaries around their time off. The always-on group does report more upside: 57% say their availability helped their career, compared with 8% of boundary-setters.

Promotions are another story. Only 17% of always-on workers credit their availability with a promotion, though that still beats the 2% of boundary-setters who do.

The trade-off is steep. Always-on workers were 2.8 times as likely as boundary-setters to report worsened burnout, 2.6 times as likely to report worsened work-life balance, and 2.4 times as likely to report worse sleep.

Even time off offers little relief. Some 73% of workers check work messages on vacation, and 51% have answered a work email while away.

Stepping back carries its own risk, and workers know it: 49% worry that setting boundaries could hurt their careers. That fear has some basis. In a 2025 study covered by Fortune, managers rated employees who unplugged after hours as more productive but less committed and less deserving of promotion, even when their performance reviews were identical.

This is where the generational divide shows up. Gen Z respondents were the least likely to feel pressure to respond after hours, at 65%, compared with 72% of both millennials and Gen X.

Feeling less pressure has not spared them the toll. Burnout worsened for 34% of Gen Z workers, the same share as millennials, compared with 26% of Gen X.

Jeff LeBlanc, a lecturer at Bentley University, describes the old bargain as “performative availability” in a recent Fast Company column: treating visibility, rather than results, as proof of commitment. He argues Gen Z’s resistance challenges workplace norms, not a lack of drive. “Gen Z hasn’t shown that they don’t value hard work,” he writes.

Millennials and Gen X, many now in management, may be part of the problem. LeBlanc writes that those generations “might be compounding these expectations” for the workers who report to them.

The strain extends well beyond one survey. In Deloitte’s 2026 Gen Z and Millennial Survey of more than 22,500 respondents in 44 countries, 48% of Gen Zs and 45% of millennials said they feel burned out.

Those same respondents are rethinking the climb itself. As Fortune reported in June, only 6% of Gen Zs and millennials in the Deloitte survey named reaching a leadership position as their top career goal.

Emma Codd, Deloitte Global’s global inclusion leader, put the stakes plainly in the report: “When showing up becomes more important than being well, inequities deepen, and the cost shows up in burnout, attrition, and lost potential.”

https://fortune.com/2026/11/08/black-fri.title: Holiday fares hit a 10-year high. A Black Friday deal may only get you back to last year’s price
https://fortune.com/2026/11/08/black-fri.author: Martie Bowser
https://fortune.com/2026/11/08/black-fri.text:
A 15% Black Friday discount on a Christmas hotel room this year comes to about $167 a night. That is roughly what the average Christmas room cost a year ago.

Black Friday falls on Nov. 27 this year, followed by Cyber Monday on Nov. 30 and Travel Tuesday on Dec. 1, and airlines, hotels and cruise lines are expected to compete for bookings across all three. For budget-conscious travelers, the question is whether a markdown matters when starting prices have already jumped.

According to Hopper’s 2026 Holiday Travel Index, domestic round-trip Thanksgiving flights are averaging $402, up 31% from 2025. Christmas fares are up 23%, with round trips averaging $452. Hopper projects this will be the most expensive holiday travel season in a decade.

Elevated jet fuel prices are behind the climb, making deep holiday discounts less likely. For most carriers, fuel is the second-largest cost after labor. Delta said after its third-quarter results that its jet fuel costs rose 60%, an increase of $1.6 billion from a year earlier.

Travelers have absorbed most of that. CEO Ed Bastian said in July that he expected Delta to pass close to 100% of its higher fuel costs on to customers in the third quarter, and the airline’s revenue per seat mile rose 15%.

On the earnings call, Bastian said the market “has accepted these price points.” He also said, “Hopefully, we will see fuel recede into the next year at some point, and that’s when I think you’ll see the real earnings power of this franchise be amplified.” As Fortune reported, that suggests higher fares could stick even if fuel prices ease, as long as demand holds up.

Other carriers, including American, United and Southwest, have cut less profitable routes, tightening supply as demand peaks. U.S. airfares were up 22.4% in September from a year earlier, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, as airlines chose higher fares over fuller planes.

Domestic hotel prices are splitting. Hopper reports that Thanksgiving rates are running about $170 a night, comparable to 2025, while Christmas rates average $197 a night, up 18% from a year ago.

Hopper expects rates to rise and availability to fall as the holidays near, which changes the math on any sale. A promotional price may only bring a surge-priced room back to last year’s rate.

With capacity tight and costs elevated, there is little room left for deep discounts. DaShawna Carpenter, owner of Skyy Travel Mavens, says the shopping holiday has lost some of its punch in travel.

“Black Friday is definitely becoming weaker,” she says. “While I think you can genuinely find legitimate savings, I have found that prices are sometimes inflated to appear cheaper during the sale periods. So it’s more of a marketing campaign than anything, especially for travel.”

She says Travel Tuesday tends to offer the best deals of the three days but cautions that most of them are bundled. “Most of the deals are attached to packages rather than flights alone, so it’s hard to say whether there are huge fare deals or not.”

That distinction matters for anyone hoping to save on airfare alone. A package price blends airfare, lodging and extras, which makes it difficult to see what the flight itself costs.

Even when a discount does apply to airfare, Carpenter says, the savings may be narrower than they look. “Some airlines apply discounts to airfare but leave fuel pricing, taxes, and other fees the same.”

Her advice is to arrive with a reference point rather than be swayed by a lower sticker price. “A traveler has to be knowledgeable in what the fare normally costs to really understand the discounts and what they are comparing it to.”

November and December have historically been slow booking months, and Carpenter notes that the discount-day “marketing campaigns have helped fill that gap.” The sales are less about generosity than about smoothing demand in a quiet window for trips later in the year.

That is also why missing them is not a big deal. “If you don’t buy on any of these marketed ‘discount days,’ there will definitely be other chances to catch a discount,” she says.

Carpenter’s read on traveler spending is consistent with carriers’ decision to hold prices high. “We found out during COVID that travel is somewhat recession- and virus-proof,” she says. “Travelers are going to remain committed to their vacations and I’ve found they cut back on other things in order to keep their travel plans up.”

She also credits buy now, pay later services such as Klarna, Afterpay and Affirm with making travel more attainable and consistent, even for price-sensitive travelers.

For travelers eyeing next year, Carpenter’s advice centers on comparison shopping rather than chasing a single flash fare.

For this holiday season, timing matters more than coupons. Hopper had advised booking holiday flights and hotels before Halloween and expects prices to keep rising as the dates approach, so waiting for a sale works against the trend.

Fares on the Sunday after Thanksgiving can top $600, Hopper notes, while flying on Thanksgiving Day, Black Friday or Cyber Monday is cheaper. This year, the best Black Friday travel deal may be a seat on a plane that day.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/08/stock-mar.title: Stocks will tumble much further as AI investment will slow next year then fall in 2028 and drag GDP down too, economist predicts
https://fortune.com/2026/11/08/stock-mar.author: Jason Ma
https://fortune.com/2026/11/08/stock-mar.text:
Investors have already taken a severe beating recently, but there’s much more stock market carnage in store as the AI investment boom wanes, according to Capital Economics.

In a note on Friday, Chief Economic Adviser Vicky Redwood said AI still has potential to boost productivity but is bearish about the amount of revenue that can be generated to sustain the rate of investment.

A handful of hyperscalers are expected to spend $800 billion this year, double from a year ago, and invest an estimated $1 trillion or more in 2027. Many forecasts assume annual capital expenditures will remain above $1 trillion for several years.

But Redwood calculated that annual AI-related revenues earned from external customers would have to explode by 10-fold by 2030 to justify all that spending. While that’s possible, it implies a much more severe and rapid disruption to the economy than currently seen, such major displacement of existing businesses and labor.

As a result, she thinks investment will continue to rise next year but at a slower pace—then fall outright in 2028 by around 10%.

Given that higher AI investment added 0.3 percentage point to U.S. GDP growth last year, a capex slowdown should trim that much from its recent growth rate, Redwood estimated, and a 10% capex drop might take 0.1% off GDP.

That’s actually just a slight haircut, especially compared to more AI-dependent economies in Asia. Taiwan’s real GDP growth next year should be around 3 percentage points lower, and South Korea’s should be 1 point lower, with a further drag in 2028.

Meanwhile, the stock market will price in the looming AI capex drop even sooner. Redwood expects the S&P 500 will be 12% below its current level by the end of 2027, putting it 17% off its early-October peak.

“We expect considerably larger falls in tech-heavy indices,” she added. “A tightening of financial conditions driven by factors such as higher energy prices or term premia could also make financing investment hard.”

Lower stock prices will also feed into the economy via the wealth effect, which fuels consumer spending. The market’s rally over the past year lifted GDP by around 0.4%, according to Redwood, so a stock selloff should produce an economic drag of similar scale.

Despite the warnings about capex, GDP and stocks, AI will continue to work its way into the economy and improve productivity, helped by the infrastructure that’s already been built and the new investment that’s on the way, albeit at a slower rate.

In fact, capex could remain relatively high even after declining, Redwood pointed out, as hyperscalers keep spending to replace depreciating equipment, exploit economies of scale, and stay ahead in the “winner-takes-most” AI race. They could also spread out any investment declines over several years instead of all at once.

“The bottom line for the U.S. economy is that we expect slower GDP growth in 2028, but not a major downturn,” Redwood wrote. “Admittedly, recessions have sometimes followed previous capex booms and busts, including in the early 2000s after the dotcom bust. However, a fall in capital spending alone has generally not been sufficient to cause a recession.”

At the same time, AI adoption should continue to expand, boosting productivity and supporting output growth. Redwood estimated that AI will increase U.S. productivity by about 1% per year for several years.

She does not expect an abrupt collapse in AI investment or a severe economic downturn when the boom ends.

“Rather, we expect investment to adjust to a more sustainable pace, with sufficient capacity still being added to support further growth in AI usage,” she concluded.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/08/pentagon-.title: ‘On par with what the DoD pursued during the Cold War’: Pentagon’s war stockpile plan hits a minerals wall
https://fortune.com/2026/11/08/pentagon-.author: Bilin Lin
https://fortune.com/2026/11/08/pentagon-.text:
The Pentagon wants to stockpile enough critical minerals, fuel, and munitions on American soil to keep fighting a major war even if cyberattacks and sabotage knock out factories and power grids at home. One defense expert says the scale of the planned effort is “on par with what the DoD pursued during the Cold War.”

The minerals may be the hardest part. The U.S. produces less than 1% of the most common type of rare-earth magnet it uses, and China, which dominates the processing of many critical minerals, has kept American companies short even in peacetime.

The initiative, known as FORTRESS America, short for Federal Operations for Resilience, Troop Resources, Energy, Supply, and Survivability, was formally established on Sept. 30. It is designed to keep U.S. forces operating if a conflict disrupts domestic power grids and manufacturing supply chains, and it is the same program behind the Pentagon’s push for major bases to plan for 90 days without the grid.

Stockpiling materials isn’t unusual for the U.S. military, Bryan Clark, a senior fellow at the Hudson Institute, told Fortune. What distinguishes FORTRESS is its planned scale and its shift toward domestic reserves rather than overseas stockpiles.

During the Cold War, the Pentagon stored as much or more war matériel overseas, near anticipated battlefields in Eastern Europe or Northeast Asia, Clark said. FORTRESS instead focuses on protecting supplies inside the United States, reflecting growing concern that American factories could themselves become targets.

China could disrupt U.S. industrial production through cyber operations, drones, electromagnetic warfare, or attacks carried out by people inside the country, Clark warned. U.S. agencies have already warned that Chinese state-sponsored hackers had positioned themselves inside American critical infrastructure.

That concern has a recent precedent in Europe. On Dec. 29, 2025, cyberattacks hit about 30 renewable energy sites, a manufacturing company, and a heat and power plant serving nearly 500,000 customers in Poland. Polish officials linked the attacks to Russia’s Federal Security Service and said the attackers tried to destroy industrial systems, but the country avoided a major outage.

Building stockpiles on the scale Clark described runs into a stark industrial reality: America’s defense industry remains deeply reliant on foreign supply chains for its raw materials.

In 2025, the U.S. imported about $60 billion worth of critical minerals other than rare earths, including nickel, lithium, cobalt, graphite, and tungsten, according to the Peterson Institute for International Economics.

The gap is most acute in rare-earth magnets. U.S. demand for the most common type reached roughly 48,000 metric tons in 2025, while domestic sources supplied just 300 metric tons, according to Arthur D. Little data reported by Reuters. U.S. companies are on track to have capacity for about 5,000 metric tons by the end of this year, roughly a tenth of last year’s demand.

The shortage has already reached factory floors. Ford, No. 22 on the 2026 Fortune 500, idled its Chicago Explorer plant for a week in May 2025 when rare-earth supplies ran short.

China has repeatedly tightened rare-earth export controls, and American companies are still struggling to secure enough supply, Reuters reported on Nov. 6, citing U.S. officials. That day, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer pressed Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng to fully carry out Beijing’s commitments on rare earths and other critical minerals.

A major war could further disrupt overseas production and shipping routes, making it harder for the Pentagon to replenish its stockpiles.

To reduce foreign dependence, Clark said, the Pentagon is pursuing a dual approach: building raw-material reserves while funding domestic mining and processing capacity.

Tungsten, a stockpiling priority Clark identified, illustrates why building reserves takes more than government spending.

The U.S. hasn’t commercially mined tungsten since 2015, when cheaper imports undercut domestic production, according to Scientific American. Its net import reliance for the metal exceeded 50% in 2025, according to the U.S. Geological Survey.

In September, tungsten manufacturer The Elmet Group won a Defense Logistics Agency contract worth up to $2 billion to supply tungsten ores, concentrates, and sodium tungstate to the National Defense Stockpile. Only $150 million of that is guaranteed. The Pentagon also committed $450 million to Elmet, including about $150 million earmarked to restart the Springer tungsten complex in Nevada.

Yet Elmet said it won’t begin deliveries to the stockpile until additional supply becomes available. To avoid diverting existing tungsten from American manufacturers, the company plans to wait until new production comes online from investments in Nevada, Australia, and Spain.

The deal illustrates a problem FORTRESS could face across the board: signing supply contracts doesn’t immediately put minerals into government vaults.

The cost of FORTRESS also remains uncertain. A senior defense official told reporters on Oct. 20 that officials are still assessing costs, Air & Space Forces Magazine reported. The magazine estimated the broader initiative could cost “scores of billions of dollars, if not hundreds of billions.”

To help cover the bill, the Pentagon is exploring public-private partnerships, Dale Marks, assistant secretary of defense for energy, installations, and environment, told Breaking Defense.

Even with capital flowing, analysts warn that supply chain independence can’t be rushed.

“The Pentagon is unlikely to meet the goals in the near term,” Clark said, pointing to the structural difficulty of rapidly stockpiling both finished weapons and raw minerals.

Chris Berry, a minerals industry analyst, told Reuters it will “take many more years” to build the infrastructure needed to compete with China’s dominant supply chain.

The first test comes soon. Starting Jan. 1, 2027, federal rules require defense contractors to stop buying rare earths, magnets, and tungsten from China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea. Washington has repeatedly granted waivers because domestic supply falls short, Reuters reported in July.

For the Pentagon, building the physical reserves may prove far harder than announcing them.

The U.-S. defense industry remains deeply reliant on foreign supply chains for its raw materials. Washington has repeatedly granted waivers because domestic supply falls short.

https://fortune.com/article/how-long-wou.title: The average worker would need to save for 52 years to claw their way out of the middle class and be classified as wealthy, research reveals
https://fortune.com/article/how-long-wou.author: Orianna Rosa Royle
https://fortune.com/article/how-long-wou.text:
The exact number of years of saving it would take for the average worker to claw out of the middle-class bracket has been revealed—and it’s nearly half a century.

Sobering research released in October 2025 from the think tank Resolution Foundation shows that for aspirational Brits looking to move up the wealth ladder, the average worker would need to save their earnings for 52 years to raise £1.3 million ($1.7 million). That’s the amount needed to move from the middle and become as wealthy as the richest 10%.

And it gets worse: That’s with zero bills being paid.

“Wealth gaps in Britain are now so large that a typical full-time employee saving all their earnings across their entire working life would still not be able to reach the top of the wealth ladder,” wrote Molly Broome, formerly a senior economist at the Resolution Foundation and the lead author of the report.

And for those who happen to be born in the working class, the odds are increasingly stacked against them.

“Wealth mobility in Britain is low. People that start life wealthy tend to stay wealthy, and vice versa,” Broome added.

As the saying goes, money makes money. The report revealed the key driver of widening inequality is the “passive” gains. Essentially, those who bought property and invested their money have seen their wealth balloon since 2010.

As inflation squeezes workers in a cost-of-living vise, paired with a job crisis, and AI threatening to make it even worse, the salary it takes to be considered rich keeps climbing further out of reach. And the issue is transatlantic.

Even in the U.S., workers say they’d need at least $2.3 million to feel rich. Meanwhile, separate research highlights they’d need a staggering $4.4 million to achieve the American Dream—the house in the suburbs, two children, an annual vacation, and a new car in the driveway. Achieving those milestones would cost over $1 million more than most Americans will make in their lifetime, according to an Investopedia calculation.

With median weekly earnings of full-time workers averaging $1,232, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, it would take over 35 years of full-time work to feel rich with $2.3 million in the bank. That’s before a single bill is paid, and still $2.1 million short of affording the American Dream.

It would take the average American worker nearly 70 years without a single expense being paid to reach that $4.4 million benchmark—far longer than most people will work in a lifetime. And that’s without even considering inflation, any unexpected financial shocks, or automation’s impact on the future of work.

A version of this story originally published on Fortune.com on December 23, 2025.

The average British worker would have to save for 52-years to reach that benchmark.

https://fortune.com/article/warren-buffe.title: Warren Buffett says ‘accumulating great amounts of money’ doesn’t achieve greatness—He still lives in a $31,500 Nebraska home and clipped coupons
https://fortune.com/article/warren-buffe.author: Emma Burleigh
https://fortune.com/article/warren-buffe.text:
Many entrepreneurs strive to one day add “millionaire,” or even “billionaire,” to their list of achievements: It’s a sign that they’ve finally made it in business. But billionaire investing mogul Warren Buffett hit back at the notion that eye-watering net worths equate to excellence.

“Greatness does not come about through accumulating great amounts of money, great amounts of publicity or great power in government,” Buffett wrote in his final Berkshire Hathaway shareholder letter last November.

The 96-year-old “Oracle of Ohama,” known as one of the most successful investors of all time, is the 10th richest person in the world, boasting a fortune of $163 billion. But that doesn’t mean he’s splurging on mansions and driving luxury cars off the lot. He’s been thrifty throughout his seven-decade professional career, despite adding billions to his name.

Known for eating at McDonald’s, driving a beat-up old car, and living in his modest Nebraska home, it’s clear his bank account hasn’t changed his ways. Instead of feeling powerful by lavishing in the spoils of his riches, Buffett finds true value and greatness in non-material pursuits.

“When you help someone in any of thousands of ways, you help the world,” Buffett continued. “Kindness is costless but also priceless. Whether you are religious or not, it’s hard to beat The Golden Rule as a guide to behavior…Keep in mind that the cleaning lady is as much a human being as the Chairman.”

Buffett’s golden rule is that everyone should be treated with kindness and respect, no matter if they’ve built a unicorn company, or are a junior-level worker. And he has treated the world’s most powerful business leaders the same way, unwilling to shell out on fancy meals to impress them.

The Berkshire Hathaway icon is known for stopping by McDonald’s for a cheap eat, choosing to order two sausage patties, an egg and cheese, or a bacon egg and cheese—all less than $4. He loves the fast-food chain so much he even took Bill Gates there for lunch years ago, instead of wining and dining him at a swanky restaurant. One time, the entrepreneurial pair were at a McDonald’s in Hong Kong, and Gates recalled laughing when Buffett offered to foot the measly bill, pulling coupons out of his pocket. But for the hedge-fund mogul, every penny counts.

The same money philosophy applies to Buffett’s major life purchases. The former CEO still lives in the same five bedroom, two-and-a-half bathroom Omaha home he bought for $31,500 back in 1958. The house would be worth around $1.4 million today—far more affordable than the luxurious pads Buffett can afford—yet he said he “wouldn’t trade it for anything.” Buffett’s true fondness for the home lies in the memories of raising his three kids on the property, not its market value.

Uber-rich people boasting net worths like Buffett may also be tempted to ball out on indulgences like expensive cars. But the investing magnate isn’t interested in getting behind the wheel of a Lamborghini or Aston Martin; he once drove a 20-year-old car because he felt it was safer than driving a speedy luxury alternative. And at one point, his license plate even read as “THRIFTY.”

Whether it be mansions or sports cars, Buffett steers clear of making major purchases that reflect his bank account. In fact, he feels giving in could be counterproductive to his happiness.

“I do not think that standard of living equates with cost of living beyond a certain point,” Buffett said at a Berkshire Hathaway shareholders meeting in 2014. “My life would not be happier…it’d be worse if I had six or eight houses or a whole bunch of different things I could have. It just doesn’t correlate.”

A version of this story was published on Fortune.com on November 12, 2025.

https://fortune.com/article/jamie-dimon-.title: Jamie Dimon says the bigger your job gets, ‘the less you know—literally.’ The CEOs too insecure to admit it are the ones who get into trouble
https://fortune.com/article/jamie-dimon-.author: Marco Quiroz-Gutierrez
https://fortune.com/article/jamie-dimon-.text:
Jamie Dimon, one of the banking industry’s longest-serving CEOs, has thoughts on why some CEOs rise to the occasion while others flounder—and it has little to do with how much they know about business.

Dimon, who has served as CEO of JPMorgan Chase, the largest U.S. bank by market cap, for more than 20 years, said on the Master Investor Podcast earlier this year, that more than anything, insecurity is one of the biggest threats to a CEO’s career and their company’s success.

As Dimon puts it, when executives climb the corporate ladder, they often go from being an expert overseeing one area of the business they know well to a generalist responsible for other areas of the company they know less well.

“The bigger job you get, the less you know—literally—about the job,” he told the podcast’s host, Wilfred Frost.

Some CEOs handle that transition well, he said. They seek out people with expertise in areas they lack and don’t get embarrassed when they don’t know something.

But for others, this change is a recipe for insecurity.

“It becomes PowerPoints, you know, make them look good, don’t tell them the bad news. And that is what causes the problem,” he said.

Dimon said this type of insecurity, more than arrogance, speaks to a deeper weakness in leadership that causes other issues. A CEO needs to be able to absorb criticism and turn it into a plan for improvement, especially when it comes to customer complaints, he said.

“You’re not going to hurt my feelings by telling me we have a crappy product,” he said. “If you’re right, I’m gonna thank you for letting me know.”

In fact, Dimon said in an October interview with the Wall Street Journal executives should take a note from the leadership style of Ted Lasso, the relentlessly positive protagonist of the Apple TV series of the same name. Lasso, he said strikes a great balance between two leadership traits he said are needed in upper management, both a drive to win as well as empathy and humility.

“I love Ted Lasso,” Dimon said. “He comes in and he doesn’t know anything about football, and he’s just gracious. He’s working with people—their insecurities, their bad behavior, their work ethic—and he’s getting them to function as a team.”

Dimon’s record gives his leadership advice added weight. During his tenure, he has turned JPMorgan into a $894 billion banking giant. His “fortress balance sheet” strategy, which emphasizes high liquidity and conservative risk management, was key to helping the bank survive the 2008 recession. Dimon has also helped grow the bank over the past two decades by acquiring competitors in turmoil, such as Bear Stearns in 2008 and, more recently, First Republic Bank in 2023.

His latest comments on insecurity are also consistent with his previous warnings that “bureaucracy, complacency, and arrogance,” can take down otherwise successful companies.

In April, Dimon said the best way to tackle these problems is to “get rid of the jerks,” or bureaucratic managers who care more about the process than the outcome. Holding back information, as might happen with an insecure CEO, breeds “rope-a-dope politics,” a reference to Muhammad Ali’s evasive defense strategy, which he has also said creates unnecessary debate and hinders results.

Dimon’s philosophy aligns with that of other successful current and former CEOs. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella previously told Fortune he encouraged his employees to maintain a growth mindset rather than be content and complacent.

Nadella also tried to shift the company from a “know-it-all” culture to a “learn-it-all” culture where employees are encouraged to approach problems with curiosity. Ray Dalio, the founder and former CEO of Bridgwater Associates, also pushed for “radical transparency” during his tenure, encouraging employees to challenge one another openly and confront mistakes without defensiveness.

The JPMorgan CEO, who also serves as chairman of the board, practices what he preaches. For the past 20 years, he has stepped out of every board meeting to give board members time to discuss without the pressure of his “forceful” personality, he said. He has previously said leaders like himself must earn the trust of their employees every day. Part of doing that, he argued, is being willing to admit mistakes without taking criticism personally.

“I’m not trying to do the thing that I want to do, I want to do the right thing for the company,” he said Monday.

A version of this story was published on Fortune.com on July 21, 2026.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/08/nvidia-j.title: Nvidia investigates CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with alleged Chinese spy
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/08/nvidia-j.author: Kif Leswing,Kamaron McNair
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/08/nvidia-j.text:
CEO Jensen Huang told Nvidia staff in an email that he had an affair and that the company’s board has opened an independent investigation into allegations that the woman is a Chinese spy.

U.S. intelligence agencies have expressed concerns that the woman, Alice Huang, has been passing information to Beijing, according to reports.

Ms. Huang is affiliated with a cloud company and an Nvidia customer called Megaspeed, which has been accused of helping restricted Chinese companies acquire Nvidia AI chips.

Nvidia has opened an investigation into co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang’s relationship with a businesswoman who intelligence agencies say is a Chinese spy.

U.S. intelligence agencies have expressed concerns that the woman, Alice Huang, who is affiliated with a cloud company and an Nvidia customer called Megaspeed, has been passing information to Beijing, according to reports in The New York Times and the Financial Times.

Huang told Nvidia staff in an email on Sunday that he had an affair with the woman and that Nvidia’s board of directors had opened an independent investigation into the spying allegations.

“I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did,” Huang wrote in the message. “I am deeply sorry.”

An Nvidia spokesperson said that Huang was committed to continuing as CEO of Nvidia without interruption.

In a statement, the Nvidia board said it would investigate the allegations that Huang had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.

“While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board’s inquiry will examine all available information,” Nvidia’s board said in a statement.

The allegations come as Nvidia has become the center of a trade dispute between China and the U.S. as AI is seen as increasingly critical to national security.

The U.S. restricts exports of Nvidia’s most advanced AI chips to China, though it has approved exports of certain older, slower models.

Megaspeed, which Ms. Huang is affiliated with, has been accused of helping restricted Chinese companies acquire Nvidia AI chips. Nvidia representatives previously said that Megaspeed had already been investigated for evading export controls.

Nvidia’s Huang has pushed for broader AI chip exports to China, saying it is better for the U.S. if the world uses and builds on American technology. He has also aligned with President Donald Trump on American artificial intelligence policy and its infrastructure buildout.

In his note to staff, Huang said he was “proud and grateful” to be an American.

Three House Republican committee chairs sent a letter to Huang on Wednesday asking him to sit for a closed-door briefing with lawmakers on Nov. 18.

Nvidia reports third-quarter earnings on Nov. 17 and will hold a major conference in Washington, D.C., at the end of the month.
