https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/f.title: Live: PM says he will engage with Trump 'respectfully' on Iran war
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/f.author: Joshua Boscaini
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/f.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Government and Politics

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese says he will raise the Iran war with US President Donald Trump when the Quad meets on the sidelines of ASEAN in Manila.

Follow all the updates in our live blog.

Choose what information you see below by using filters

Communications Minister Anika Wells says she's open to further negotiations to pass the government's Digital Duty of Care laws in the Senate.

Wells told ABC New Breakfast she'd like to see bipartisan support for the online safety legislation, but she's not disclosing what ground she's willing to give.

"I welcome any amendments being put by any parliamentarian that strengthen or improve these laws," she said.

A Senate inquiry into the legislation will be held today and tomorrow, hearing from parents and experts about the proposed changes, which passed the lower house last month.

Wells says the industry has been unregulated and operating like the "wild west" for 20 years.

"We think big tech needs to be held to account, and if you build it, you should be responsible for its harms," she said.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has urged the opposition to support savings measures currently before parliament.

The government is trying to pass savings measures, including winding back the over-65s private health insurance rebate, to pocket $3 billion.

But the Coalition and Greens have opposed them and Labor doesn't have a majority in the Senate, so they are held up.

"We function as a government, a united government with a sense of purpose governing in what are difficult global times," Albanese says.

"It stands in stark contrast to the alternative, which is a rabble, essentially, of dysfunction of One Nation, the Liberals, the Nationals and others on the right and the Greens being a protest party on the left."

The prime minister has been asked about Resolve Political Monitor polling showing just 20 per cent of people trust the Albanese Government.

The poll published in the Sydney Morning Herald and The Age newspapers shows just over 40 per cent of Australians blame Labor for rising living costs.

The ABC reported that PM held an honorary membership for a golf club in his electorate that received a $6 million grant.

Asked if Labor's election commitments have affected that trust, Albanese says the opposition made over 2,000 commitments.

"One of the things that happens in elections is that people put commitments in order to advance their position. That has happened in every election that I've been involved," Albanese says.

Anthony Albanese says he will engage with the US president "respectfully and diplomatically" in relation to the war in the Middle East.

The prime minister says the war in Iran will be a topic of discussion with Donald Trump on the sidelines of the ASEAN conference in Manila.

"I'll engage constructively as I've developed a constructive relationship with President Trump," Albanese says.

"Australia has for some time now repeatedly said that there is a real impact of the conflict in the Middle East. Everyone knows that's the case."

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has defended his government's economic record and management of inflation.

Inflation rose to 4.3 per cent in the 12 months to September, according to Australia Bureau of Statistics data.

Albanese says inflation is lower now than what the government inherited when it came to power in 2022.

"It's also a fact that, unlike the budgets that we inherited, we have produced savings in every single budget and every single economic statement that we've made," Albanese says.

Pressed on that, the PM has shifted attention to the war in the Middle East and the impact it has had on global inflation.

"We have seen inflation rise around the world. We saw last week interest rates increase, not just in Australia, but the Bank of England for the first time in a long while increased interest rates," he says.

"I accept and my government accepts completely that there are pressures on Australian families. We accept that as well, that we need to find savings in the budget."

Anthony Albanese has been asked about emissions from coal and gas exports from Australia which have nearly doubled since 2005.

He's been asked if it puts Australia in a awkward position going into COP 31 negotiations in Antalya in Türkiye this week.

The prime minister says emissions are measured at the point of emission, otherwise there would be "double counting".

"Australia is playing an important role in reducing our emissions. In the December quarter of last year was the first time that renewables reached above 50 per cent of emissions," Albanese says.

The prime minister is taking questions now and is asked about staffing allocations for crossbench MPs and senators, who have consistently raised the issue with the government.

Anthony Albanese has brushed off the question and says it was a system that was put in place by the former government.

"One of the things that we did was to increase, through the minister, an additional staffer for every member of the House of Representatives and every senator," Albanese says.

But pressed on the matter, Albanese repeats it was a system that he inherited and it's a matter for the minister.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has stepped up for a press conference at the National Emergency Management Agency in Canberra.

Albanese says Australia is well into the high-risk weather season and is urging Australians to prepare for the worst from a super El Niño.

He's announcing a support package to strengthen bushfire risk management and to support the mental health and wellbeing of emergency responders.

The prime minister says additional funding will be directed to the Australian Fire Danger Rating System and national bushfire intelligence capability.

"We've already had fires in the Northern Territory and floods in Queensland already. We're already seeing warm and dry conditions expected for much of the summer, supercharged by the El Niño impact," Albanese says.

"Whilst we can't predict exactly when extreme events will occur, what we can do is to make sure that we're prepared and that the government stands ready to respond."

Emergency Management Minister Kristy McBain says the additional $12 million will be split, with $5.8 million directed to the fire danger rating system, $2.6 million to intelligence and $3 million to first responder wellbeing.

Shadow Veterans Affairs Minister Michael McCormack says the decision to scrap the sale of four historic defence sites was necessary.

McCormack says the decision to move defence personnel out of the Victoria Barracks site before Christmas and without a permanent home will hit morale in the Australian Defence Force.

Speaking to ABC Radio National Breakfast, McCormack says the government shouldn't be selling off Defence heritage.

"They've made the right decision on these four sites, yes, and they'll work with the Australian War Memorial. But what about the other 63 sites? Now, they're just selling these off to prop up their ailing budget bottom line. That's the real crux of the issue," McCormack says.

"We should be teaching our young people the value of our heritage, of our military heritage [and] the fact that there are 103,000 names on the Roll of Honour at the Australia War Memorial in Canberra, of people who fought and died so that we could live in relative peace and security and safety."

Listen to the full interview via the link below.

Defence Minister Richard Marles says the decision not to sell off four historic defence sites won't have a big impact on the budget because their commercial value is limited.

Labor planned to sell 67 defence sites after an independent estate audit in February, to generate $1.8 billion for the government.

But yesterday, Labor backtracked on its decision to offload four high-profile sites earmarked for sale.

They include the Victoria Barracks in Sydney, Victoria Barracks Melbourne, Fort Queenscliff and Point Cook (RAAF Williams).

Speaking to ABC Radio National Breakfast, Marles says the Department of Finance will seek to manage them in a way that maximises community and commercial use.

"There will be some financial return, but it was never imagined that there would be a lot from these sites. The accounting of the disposal of the whole of the 67 sites, in that sense, remains unchanged," Marles says.

Labor MP Ed Husic says he thinks Australia is being "lured" into a "frenzy" building artificial intelligence data centres by big tech companies.

The former industry minister has been outspoken on the need to have stronger guardrails for the development of artificial intelligence in Australia.

Earlier this year, the prime minister unveiled a set of standards for artificial intelligence to provide clear rules for data centres, forcing them to minimise water use and underwrite or supply their own power.

Speaking to ABC News Breakfast, Husic says building data centres is "as popular as getting a heat rash".

"People don't want them, and understandably so, because they are putting such big pressure on our economy. Even the RBA [Reserve Bank of Australia] is concerned by how much pressure this build is doing," he says.

"They [Australians] are concerned about the risks that come with AI. They are concerned that AI will not just do them, Australians, out of a job but their kids out of a job as well.

"Just saying we need to build more data centres so we can get access to frontier models … won't really cut it in the minds of Australians. I am worried that we are attracted to the lure of a late night TV commercial: 'Act now or you will miss out.'"

Anika Wells says she accepts Australians are feeling under pressure, with new polling showing just 20 per cent of Australians trust the prime minister.

A Resolve Political Monitor poll published in the Sydney Morning Herald and The Age shows just over 40 per cent of Australians blame Labor for rising living costs.

Speaking to Channel Nine, the communications minister says people have a right to feel under pressure and want to send a message to the government.

"People are under a lot of pressure and these are difficult and tricky times, and Australians want their lawmakers, their governments to know that that's understandable and that's and that's their right and we hear that feedback," Wells says.

"That's why we're here in Canberra to work on MYEFO [mid-year economic and fiscal outlook], to deliberate on what savings we can make ahead of MYEFO, just as we have in all previous budget packages."

Social Services Minister Tanya Plibersek and Shadow Treasurer Tim Wilson have clashed on the private health insurance rebate for over-65s.

Labor has been under pressure to find savings as inflation and government spending rise as a share of GDP.

In May's budget, the government proposed winding back the private health insurance rebate for over-65s, in what will save the budget $3 billion.

But Labor has so far been unsuccessful passing the changes through parliament, because the Coalition and Greens won't support the measure.

"This is about people on the same income getting the same rebate, not based on age," Plibersek tells Channel Seven.

"How is it fair that two households on the same income get different rebates? That's what we're proposing and that's what Tim's opposing."

But Wilson says the measure is an "assault on pensioners" and will cause more elderly Australians to end up in the public hospital system.

"You get those people off the private health system, they go on the public health system and the cost for the taxpayer soars," Wilson says.

A Senate inquiry is set to get underway today into the government's proposed Digital Duty of Care legislation.

Communications Minister Anika Wells says algorithms and AI tools need to be regulated to protect people from online harms, and tech companies will be slapped with fines of $109 million if they fail to mitigate the risks.

The legislation also aims to ban nudify apps and to give social media users the choice to opt in or out of the algorithm on their feeds.

The legislation was introduced to the House of Representatives and passed in October, without Coalition support.

Experts and parents will give evidence during the two-day inquiry, and Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young has said she will "kick the tyres and hold Big Tech's feet to the fire to ensure these laws have teeth".

Hello and welcome to our federal politics live blog! It's great to have you here early on a Monday morning.

I'm Josh Boscaini joining you live from Parliament House in Canberra, here and ready to bring you all of today's federal politics news.

We're likely to hear a bit about Labor's proposed Digital Duty of Care legislation, which will face scrutiny at a Senate inquiry kicking off today.

Let's get right into the day and see what happens!

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/a.title: Live: ANZ posts $7.3 billion profit as Wall Street lifts on AI rebound
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/a.author: Stephen Letts
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/a.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Wall Street made up some ground on Friday thanks to renewed buying of AI stocks, but still shed close to 3 per cent over the week.

ANZ has posted a $7.3 billion full-year profit, marginally beating expectations, while the ASX is poised to edge higher today.

Follow the day's financial news and insights from our specialist business reporters on our live blog.

Disclaimer: this blog is not intended as investment advice.

Choose what information you see below by using filters

NAB has announced it has appointed financial industry veteran Ian Saines as chair-elect to replace Philip Chronican who will stand down from the board after 11 years with NAB, including eight as chair.

Saines will join the board in March 2027 and become chair in July 2027.

He is a former senior executive of Commonwealth Bank, Challenger Limited, Zurich Capital Markets Asia and Bankers Trust Australia.

He was also a director of Macquarie Bank from 2022 until his resignation to join the NAB board.

ANZ CEO Nuno Matos says the bank is on track to deliver on its cost-cutting and productivity strategy outlined soon after he joined the bank in May 2025.

ANZ posted a $7.3 billion net profit, and its $7.6 billion cash profit was slightly ahead of analyst forecasts.

The cash profit strips out one-off items including $585 million restructuring costs related to 3,500 redundancies.

Net operating expenses fell by 7% to $11.1 billion.

Net interest margin — the difference between the bank's cost of borrowing and the rate it charges customers — contracted 2 basis points to 1.53%, with ANZ noting increased competition in lending.

"The results we are announcing today demonstrate the significant progress we have made through disciplined execution in the first year of our ANZ 2030 strategy," Mr Matos said in a statement to the ASX.

"We are on track to deliver all five immediate priorities on time.

"Competition for capital to fund data centres, government spending and the energy transition has intensified, with this expenditure super-cycle, combined with inflationary supply side shocks, driving interest rates higher globally.

"Against this backdrop, the economies across our geographic footprint remain relatively resilient."

Mr Matos added that the bank was on track to deliver the integration of Suncorp Bank by June 2027.

By Stephanie Chalmers

Aussie shoppers have flocked to David Jones in the days since the department store's collapse into administration, according to the receivers.

FTI Consulting, which was appointed by David Jones' lender Hilco last week, said "foot traffic and sales throughout David Jones stores and online have been at record levels, reinforcing the public's love for David Jones and support for an iconic Australian brand".

The highly publicised financial collapse will have no doubt encouraged some shoppers to hunt for a bargain or perhaps attempt to redeem any outstanding vouchers or gift cards.

The receivers say it's business as usual, confirming the retailer "remains full operational" and placing orders to replenish stock from "suppliers that have confirmed trading agreements".

They do note, however, "limited instances of brand partners withdrawing from some stores".

National consumer affairs reporter Michael Atkin had this piece on what shoppers need to know:

By Stephanie Chalmers

Nvidia says it is initiating an independent investigation after a media report alleged CEO Jensen Huang had a close relationship with a Chinese businesswoman who passed information to Beijing.

In a message to Nvidia employees, Huang admitted to being unfaithful to his wife and took "full responsibility" for his actions.

The New York Times reported last month that US authorities were investigating Alice Huang, a former executive of Singapore-based company Megaspeed, which buys AI chips from Nvidia.

US authorities have scrutinised Megaspeed over suspicions it helped Beijing gain access to advanced AI chips that are barred from shipment to China.

"The NVIDIA Board is initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort," the company said in a statement.

"A committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel, will oversee the investigation."

The company said on Sunday (US time) that, while its board has no reason to believe that either US national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, its inquiry will examine all available information.

Huang fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it, it added.

Huang said in a message to employees: "I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry."

Addressing his colleagues, board, partners and shareholders, Huang said: "My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility. I am fully committed to NVIDIA and will work to earn back your confidence."

A Nvidia spokesperson said Huang was "committed to continuing to lead NVIDIA as CEO without interruption".

Top Republicans in the US House of Representatives have called on Huang to brief Congress this month about the report.

The ANZ has lifted its provisions of for credit impairment to $582 million, an increase of $141 million on last year.

The individual provision charge was raised by $33 million, but the bank says portfolio losses remain low, reflecting strong overall credit quality.

The collective provision charge was raised by $108 million, which reflects portfolio growth along with emerging risk from higher interest rates and cost-of-living conditions becoming more challenging for the bank's customers.

Iraq has reached understandings with the United States to allow Iraqi oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz via a shipping lane near Oman, Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein said in an interview with Al Jazeera.

He said Iraq's losses from the Iran war and disruptions to oil exports had reached $US60 billion.

Iraq's oil exports recovered in October after a sharp drop the previous month.

Exports rose to about 3.5 million barrels per day from 2.65 million bpd in September, according to Iraqi energy officials.

The ANZ has posted a 23% jump in statutory profit to $7.27 billion.

Its preferred measure of cash earnings, which strips out one-off items, came in at $7.59 billion, up 31% on last year and slightly ahead of the consensus analyst forecast.

The final dividend of 83 cents per share takes the full year payout to $1.66/share, the same as last year and slightly lower than expectations.

US tech stocks pulled out of their recent nosedive on Friday but still left Wall Street looking a touch shabbier and a trillion or so dollars lighter over the week.

The broad market benchmark, the S&P 500, gained as well, but the blue-chip Dow closed lower.

Over the week US stocks shed 2.7% while the Japanese market was down more than 9%.

However, not every market suffered — Chinese shares rose 1.7% across the week, Europe gained 0.6% and the ASX came out 1.3% higher after a volatile week.

This week looks to be starting on a mildly positive note as well.

ASX 200 futures, when they closed on Saturday morning (AEDT), pointed to a marginal gain of around 0.2%.

In the US most of the buying action was in AI-related stocks.

The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index gained 4.2% after slumping in its biggest one-day drop since April 2025.

Nvidia rose nearly 3%, after its worst day since January 2025, when the emergence of low-cost Chinese AI model DeepSeek hammered markets.

Other heavyweight chipmakers, including AMD, Intel and Micron Technology closed up between 5% and 11%, while Elon Musk's Tesla and SpaceX were also up 4% and nearly 9% respectively after losses earlier this week.

"Most of the disruption of the AI buildout will not probably occur but it's just the uncertainty of the change in government from Republican-led to Democratic-led, not only at the federal level but the state, local levels," Sparrow Capital Management portfolio manager Gerry Sparrow told Reuters.

"That's causing some disruption in the expectations of investors … The volatility around elections or any political event, whether it be war or terrorist attack, is always going to disrupt the market."

The sentiment was helped by good economic news with stronger than expected jobs data.

Non-farm payrolls grew 165,000 in October, beating the consensus forecast of 70,000, and the unemployment rate came in at 4.1%, compared to prior of 4.2%.

Wages growth also ticked higher.

Those numbers kept a rate hike from the Fed in December very much in play and drove the US dollar higher.

The Aussie dollar shed more ground against the greenback.

It finished the week down 2.3% to reach its lowest level since March, unable to withstand the combination of strong US data, risk aversion on global markets and a softer domestic growth outlook.

Gold slipped a tad (-0.1%) thanks to the higher rates and US dollar but gained more than 5% for the week to close above $US4,000/ounce again.

The slide in oil prices halted on Friday, with Brent crude futures edging higher (just 3 US cents/barrel).

Over the week, Brent fell 17%, its steepest weekly percentage fall since the start of the COVID pandemic and its biggest in absolute terms.

Copper fell to its lowest level since July as traders mulled over the implications of a slower rollout of data centres in the US and across the globe.

Good morning and welcome to another day on the ABC markets and finance blog.

Stephen Letts from ABC business team limbering up for a blow-by-blow coverage of the day's events, where every post is hopefully a winner, but none should be construed as financial advice.

Wall Street closed higher, supported by a rally in AI-related stocks.

The ASX looks like shrugging off Friday's decline with futures trading pointing to a marginal gain on opening.

It's a busy day ahead.

ANZ is due to release it FY26 results before the market opens.

The key figure to keep your eye on is the consensus forecast for a cash profit of $7.5 billion, which would be 9% when excluding significant items.

Dividends are expected to be marginally higher — $1.70/share compared with $1.66/share last year.

We will also hear from RBA assistant governor and chief economist Sarah Hunter this morning.

On the data front, we'll get the latest consumer and producer inflation data from China in the afternoon.

The game's afoot, so let's get blogging.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/f.title: Eisenkot is trying to form government in Israel. Here are five ways it could go
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/f.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
World Politics

Gadi Eisenkot appears at his party headquarters following the announcement of exit poll results. (Reuters: Shir Torem)

Former Israeli military chief Gadi Eisenkot has now been asked to try to form a new coalition government, meeting Israel's President Isaac Herzog in Jerusalem on Sunday to receive his invite to start negotiations.

But his pathway to power is not entirely easy, and the next few weeks could involve some creative political arithmetic and manoeuvring to get over the line.

So, what are the options from here?

The reason Gadi Eisenkot has been tapped for the first shot at forming a coalition is because of what happened late last week.

Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar party, has been Benjamin Netanyahu's main opponent in the election. (Reuters: Shir Torem)

The president sat down with representatives of each of the political parties that won seats at the election, and asked them to endorse either Mr Eisenkot or the incumbent Benjamin Netanyahu — given the two men are the leaders of the two largest parties in the next Knesset.

All of the anti-Netanyahu parties from across the political spectrum, including the two Arab-Israeli or Palestinian-Israeli parties, backed Mr Eisenkot:

That's a total of 67 seats in the 120-seat Knesset backing the main rival to Benjamin Netanyahu.

The prime minister only secured votes from most of his current coalition:

That's a total of 46 seats in the Knesset.

The other ultra-Orthodox Jewish party, United Torah Judaism (UTJ), did not back either candidate with their seven seats — despite spending most of the last four years backing in Mr Netanyahu.

Getting the endorsements to start negotiations is important, as it puts Mr Eisenkot in the box seat to form a new government and end Mr Netanyahu's time at the top.

At the moment, they are united by a common goal of giving the current prime minister the boot.

But convincing them to put aside longstanding grievances and policy differences could be difficult, and loyalty to principle also isn't guaranteed.

Mr Eisenkot is in a prime position to form a new government and end Mr Netanyahu's leadership.  (Reuters: Clodagh Kilcoyne)

Israeli media is speculating Gadi Eisenkot could try to press ahead with forming a minority government, which would include all of the Jewish anti-Netanyahu parties:

That's a total of 48 seats out of the 120 on offer in the Knesset.

The only way that could work is if the two Arab-Israeli parties, the United Arab List and the Joint List, agreed to effectively green-light the government's agenda on the floor of the Knesset — promising not to block things like budget legislation.

There's an immediate problem with this approach — the leader of Yisrael Beiteinu, Avigdor Liberman wants a majority government.

His opposition to working with the Arab-Israeli parties goes as far as relying on them working outside of a formal coalition.

As a result, he is reportedly looking at trying to entice the ultra-orthodox parties of UTJ and Shas to join forces with the rest of the "change" camp.

Mr Liberman could change his tune. But at this point, he seems to be digging his heels in.

This would be a coalition of all of the Jewish parties that are critics of Benjamin Netanyahu, and the two ultra-Orthodox parties who've helped to prop up his right-wing government over the past four years:

That's a total of 61 seats — the barest of majorities.

While this would effectively kill off the fierce and at times racist arguments being put forward about the Arab-Israeli vote, it brings its own problems.

Mr Eisenkot and other members of the so-called "change" camp have all campaigned on wanting to force men from the growing ultra-orthodox community, known as the Haredi, to complete compulsory military service.

This has been one of the most controversial issues of the past three years, since Hamas's deadly attacks against Israel on October 7, 2023 — the pressure on the Israel Defense Forces as it fights on multiple fronts.

In 2024, the Israeli Supreme Court tore up the sweeping exemptions from service afforded to Haredi men — effectively ending the principle that they should be given permission to avoid being drafted because they are students of the Jewish faith, and work to safeguard the future of the religion.

Early exit polling and results show incumbent Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc is likely to secure more seats than the opposition, but still falling short of the majority required to form government.

UTJ and Shas had been demanding the Netanyahu government reimpose the exemptions.

Even Avigdor Liberman, the man now reportedly talking to them, campaigned on ending "draft dodging".

If this scenario were to become reality, it would demonstrate a commitment to the principle of ousting Mr Netanyahu over loyalty to pre-election policy platforms.

It could also be a calculation that anti-Arab sentiment in the Israeli community is more toxic than anti-Haredi views.

This would be a coalition of the anti-Netanyahu Jewish parties, and the two Arab-Israeli parties:

That would be a total of 67 seats — the strongest majority possible on the current numbers without Mr Netanyahu's Likud. More on that below.

But the only way this would happen is if the strident opposition to the Arab-Israeli parties is parked in favour of toppling Mr Netanyahu.

It is also a government that would come under attack from the prime minister and right-wing forces in Israel given the ongoing allegations of foreign interference in the election prompting a surge in support for those parties.

This is something Benjamin Netanyahu has started pushing more and more in the last week or so — encouraging Gadi Eisenkot to work across the aisle with him to form a broad, Jewish-Israeli coalition.

It would look something like this:

That gets total of 75 seats in the Knesset — a considerable majority.

The inconclusive result of the Israeli election with neither Netanyahu nor the opposition gaining majority, means weeks of messy and complicated negotiations.

The problem here is that Mr Eisenkot and the other "change" camp parties have spent the past few years insisting Mr Netanyahu is the embodiment of everything wrong with the government and needs to go.

Mr Eisenkot has also ruled it out, even as Mr Netanyahu continues to insist it is the way forward.

This scenario also does not include the far-right Otzma Yehudit, led by national security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, and Religious Zionism, led by finance minister Bezalel Smotrich.

They are seen as even more problematic than Mr Netanyahu by members of the "change" camp.

Gadi Eisenkot has at least 28 days to form a new coalition.

Mr Herzog can give Mr Eisenkot more time to form a government. (Reuters: Bernadett Szabo)

President Isaac Herzog can extend that by another 14 days of he thinks there's a chance at a deal, and it just needs a bit more time.

At the end of that process, he can ask another candidate to have a go.

But if that also fails, Israel would be on track for another election sometime early in the new year.

Same too if one of the other scenarios play out, and the government collapses — a fresh vote could be ordered.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/w.title: Wallabies' woes mount after terrible Twickenham outing
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/w.author: Simon Smale
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/w.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Harry Wilson and the Wallabies have a tough task to turn things around. (Getty Images: RFU/Dan Mullan)

When Max Jorgensen sprinted away to score the Wallabies' first try on the stroke of half time, supporters may have felt a faint stirring of half-remembered joy.

Just two years earlier, Jorgensen raced down that same touchline, albeit running in the other direction, to snatch a thrilling victory at the death.

That the try came at the end of a magnificent move of swift ball movement and rapid running imbibed a justified sense of hope in where the national team was heading.

The possibilities that victory seemed to promise were endless.

Two years ago, it felt like the Wallabies were building.

Back in the present and Jorgensen's solo score, via an intercept pass against the run of play, meant that the Wallabies only trailed England by 9 points at half time, sugar-coating a desperate first half in which that was the Wallabies' only line break.

Max Jorgensen scored a superb try at the end of the first half to keep the Wallabies in touch. (Getty Images: David Rogers)

And it would only get worse.

The Wallabies came away from Twickenham having lost a third-straight match by a big score, conceding a record total against an England team that has now won 12 of their past 14 matches against them.

Incredibly, coming into the game, England were the team under pressure.

Steve Borthwick's team won just a single game in the Six Nations, and that was only against the basket case Welsh, to finish fifth on the ladder.

In fact, England, the richest and best-equipped nation in world rugby, had only won three of their eight matches in 2026.

A report in The Times on match week suggested a deepening rift between the head coach and his players that put further pressure on Borthwick, although senior players angrily denied those claims in the lead-up to the game.

The Wallabies had hoped they could use that distraction to put England to the sword, build on the sensational victory against South Africa in Perth and prove that the All Black thrashings were merely aberrations built on the kryptonite qualities Eden Park holds over the side.

Rob Valetini should start against Scotland next week. (Getty Images: PA Images/Ben Whitley)

Instead, it is the Wallabies who leave south west London in even deeper trouble than before, with time running out to effect reasonable change.

The Wallabies's spring tour started in the worst possible way, as England ran rampant at Twickenham to pile the pressure on coach Les Kiss.

Despite the closeness of the half time score, in truth the Wallabies barely featured in the opening 40 minutes.

England, rampaging forward with impunity, had dominated.

In fact, it was only the hosts' errors that had kept the Wallabies in touch at all — Jorgensen's intercept score included.

England's speed at the breakdown had the Wallabies on the back foot.

Their bravery with the ball in hand contrasted dramatically with the Wallabies' insipid defence, forced too narrow by the pace of England's outside backs.

Les Kiss appeared to grow increasingly angry in the coaching box throughout the first half and well into the second.

Les Kiss appeared to be seething at times in the contest. (Getty Images: CameraSport/Bob Bradford)

But heading into the break within touching distance, despite the way they had played, could have given the Wallabies a boost.

Sadly, the Wallabies came out for the second half just as insipidly as they started the first.

Within 15 minutes of the restart, England were 38-10 up and the game was well and truly over, with all but one of the Wallabies' tries essentially a gift from England errors.

"I am disappointed, there is frustration," Kiss told the BBC after the match.

"A credit to England, they kept us in our third in the first half and made their way into our tryline area. They were very good and clinical.

"This wasn't a true reflection of us but that is what happened."

If Wallabies fans want to look for positives, they will have to spend a long time searching.

Ben Donaldson and Filipo Daugunu did OK off the bench: In the short time they were together on the field they had a combined total of four clean breaks, while the rest of the team had just three in total.

But those are thin straws to clutch at.

Henry Slade crashed into Max Jorgensen to deny him a second try in the second half. (Getty Images: PA Images/Ben Whitley)

The worry for the Wallabies now is how to arrest this slide.

Maro Itoje said pre-game that this match would be crucial ahead of any potential meeting at the World Cup, which could occur at the quarterfinal stage if projections bare out.

"Each game is new but there's no doubt that against teams you're going to play down the line, you want them to know that you've got their number," Itoje said.

"We want to win this weekend for this weekend's sake, but we also want to win because we don't want to give the opposition an inch.

"We want to show ourselves and show England fans that we've turned a corner.

"For that reason, this game is huge."

Henry Pollock scored two tries as a flanker playing on the wing. (Getty Images: Patrick Khachfe)

One match does not change an entire mindset, but if Itoje believes England may use it to turn a corner, what direction are the Wallabies now heading in?

"We need to be better," Kiss said simply.

"Losses like that make you sit back and make you take an internal look into a few things.

"It is important to not look too far and too wide, we need to narrow down a few things that we can work on together.

"It is a disappointment tonight but we have seven days to turn that around."

The problem is that seven days may not be anywhere near enough.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/q.title: New housing model giving older women a home 'for the rest of my life'
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/q.author: Lexy Hamilton-Smith and Meghan Dansie
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/q.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

By Lexy Hamilton-Smith

Topic:
Housing Policy

A new co-housing model has opened its doors to five women in Brisbane. (ABC News: Pete Mullins)

Five women who have turned to couch surfing and loved ones to keep a roof over their heads have landed their forever homes as part of an Australian-first co-housing development.

They have paid $120,000 each and signed a 50-year lease, ensuring they will never be kicked out.

Ann Singh, 79, was left struggling financially after a divorce, so like many others, moved from rental to rental and took on house sitting.

Tonight she will finally sleep in her own unit at Darra, south-west of Brisbane.

Ann Singh is relieved to have a lease will last the rest of her life. (ABC News: Meghan Dansie)

"It's emotional, to wake up in my own space with my own things around me," she said.

"It is such a perfect solution for women like me who had a little bit of money but not enough to buy a property.

Ann Singh was left struggling financially after a divorce. (ABC News: Meghan Dansie)

It is a dream come true, thanks to a charity called Sharing with Friends and is the result of seven years of dogged determination.

Each woman will live in their own private, self-contained studio unit, with a kitchen and courtyard.

If they are in the mood for company, there is also a shared kitchen and living room as well as a central courtyard.

The co-housing model caters specifically to older women who are the fastest-growing group of homeless people in the country.

A rendered image shows the central courtyard of the complex. (Supplied: Sharing with Friends)

Robyn Duffy-Jones is one of Ms Singh's new neighbours and, at 60 years old, is the youngest of the group.

The single mother has rented all her life, and was rejected by banks when she tried to borrow money to buy a house in her mid-50s.

Then, Queensland property prices started to soar.

Ann Singh and Robyn Duffy-Jones have welcomed the security the project offers. (ABC News: Meghan Dansie)

Ms Duffy-Jones said there were times she thought she might end up in a tent, which "terrified" her.

"Where are you going to live is a fundamental right, [it is] such a scary thought to not have a roof over your head," she said.

When she heard about the Sharing With Friends project, she jumped at the opportunity, describing it as "a saviour".

Women and girls make up 60 per cent of the estimated 289,000 people who seek help across Australia, according to the latest statistics from the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare.

"I've always wanted to own my own home, it's always been a dream of mine," she said.

The $120,000 investment was determined by the fact that at the time it was the average amount a woman at retirement age had in their super fund.

Sharing With Friends president Susan Davies said they were motivated to try something new after hearing countless stories of single, older women struggling to find a decent place to live.

"It's a real systemic failure in this country. No one was doing anything about helping this group of women and we decided to do something," Ms Davies said.

"We call them the missing middle. They had too much to qualify for social housing, but absolutely not enough to afford to buy anywhere.

"So if they are renting, they are facing drawing down on their savings and basically living in fear of eviction, and being thrown onto the street."

The number of homeless women over 55 has surged, with census data from five years showing a 40 per cent increase over the past decade.

Robyn Duffy-Jones has been renting with her two sons for years. (ABC News: Meghan Dansie)

The first group of women to live at the Brisbane co-living development chose each other through a series of workshops run by the charity.

Ms Davies said generous philanthropic donations got the project off the ground, amid rising construction costs and planning delays.

"We've had virtually no help from government," she said.

The charity owns the land, but the women have to pay for electricity and rates, just like any home owner.

When they want out, or after death, their initial investment is returned with CPI added in.

"One of our women just said to me, 'I finally have a home, before this I was worried I would be one of those people whose whole life would be being pushed around in a shopping trolley,'" Ms Davies said.

Each woman will have her own self-contained studio unit. (Supplied: Sharing with Friends)

Sharing with Friends want to roll out this model across Australia but say local councils and governments need to cut back on red tape and include the model into their planning acts.

"The system has to change so that we can replicate this quickly," Ms Davies said.

"We knew we needed to come up with something affordable and sustainable."

A rendered image of one of the studio units. (Supplied: Sharing with Friends)

She said with the average woman now having about $150,000 in their super fund and increasing costs, the next project would need a "buy-in" of about $200,000.

Architect Eloise Atkinson designed the model pro bono, with the aim of creating a sense of community with friendship at the core.

"These women are choosing to live there, they're choosing to live together," she said.

"There's the shared space, there's the communal garden, but then there's your own space."

Robyn Atkinson said it aims to provide the women with a sense of privacy and access to community.  (ABC News: Edward Gill)

Ms Atkinson said some of the bigger councils should lead the way, so planners around the country understand how the models work.

"That it is not a boarding house, which is the category we have had to have it approved," she said.

"The first couple of years will be the real test."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/m.title: Couple wants the BOM to replace them with a weather station
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/m.author: Annie Brown
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/m.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Weather Statistics

Merrillyn and Ernie Cole record weather data for the Mitta Mitta Valley and want the reporting to continue.  (ABC Rural: Annie Brown)

Ernie and Merrillyn Cole, from Mitta Mitta in north-east Victoria, have collected weather data for the Bureau of Meteorology since 1963.

The couple, now in their 80s, want an automatic weather station to be installed, so they can travel.

The BOM has not said if it will install a weather station at Mitta Mitta, but it is keen for another volunteer to come forward.

After 63 years of recording the weather from the same house in north-east Victoria's Mitta Mitta Valley, Ernie and Merrillyn Cole are asking the Bureau of Meteorology (BOM) to install an automatic weather station so they can take a break.

The Coles are now in their 80s and want to travel more, but they are worried about the maintenance of accurate local weather records.

The couple arrived in Mitta Mitta in 1963, when Mr Cole was a forestry officer with the state government.

Part of his job was to report the weather to the BOM from a weather station outside their house.

Ernie and Merrillyn Cole have lived in the same house since 1963.  (ABC Rural: Annie Brown)

In order to help Mr Cole get to work early, Ms Cole took over.

"Quite often I'd have a baby on one hip and a toddler and down to the weather box we'd go," she said.

Sixty-three years later, the couple live in the same house and continue to send rainfall totals to the BOM.

They have always enjoyed doing the job, but they want to move on and hope technology can assist.

Ernie Cole, 86, checks the rain in the Mitta Mitta Valley.  (ABC Rural: Annie Brown)

"We've been pressing for an automatic weather station here," Mr Cole said.

"We'd just like to make sure that the weather is looked after, after we've gone."

The weather has been recorded in Mitta Mitta since 1915.

Mr Cole inherited earlier records from the local postmistress when he took over in the 1960s.

Merrillyn Cole still keeps notes on the weather and rain totals.  (ABC Rural: Annie Brown)

He said for any future data to remain accurate, it had to be measured in the exact same place.

When Mr and Ms Cole are away, friend and neighbour Russell "Ned" Kelly records the rain for them.

Russell Kelly is a local pilot who helps the Coles.  (ABC Rural: Annie Brown)

Mr Kelly is a retired pilot and operates the local airfield.

"Being a pilot, you're always interested in the weather," Mr Kelly said.

"I'm pretty au fait with the micro-climate we have in the Mitta Valley."

Mr Kelly said rainfall can vary greatly across the valley.

"If you go another 10 kilometres, there's another 300 millimetre rainfall, for example," Mr Kelly said.

Mitta Mitta and the surrounding area has a population of 171, according to the 2021 census. (ABC Rural: Annie Brown)

Mr Kelly has also pressed the BOM to install a weather station at the Coles' house.

"Rainfall over the past 100 years is actually on a steady decrease.

"Without a station here, the local farmers would not be aware of that."

The BOM operates a network of more than 650 automatic stations across Australia to collect real-time weather.

Since the 1980s, the technology has slowly replaced manual weather stations, monitored by people.

About 3,000 manual observation sites remain in operation.

The in-ground rain gauge is fenced off.  (ABC Rural: Annie Brown)

A statement from the BOM did not confirm or deny plans to install an automated weather station in Mitta Mitta.

But it did point out there were two automated weather stations 39km away and another automated rain gauge 6km away.

"The bureau has no plans to discontinue volunteer rainfall observations at Mitta Mitta," a spokesperson said.

Ms Cole has noticed a change in the way weather data is used by the BOM in recent years.

It was once a daily phone call with information about temperature, wind, frost and fog.

Ernie Cole hopes the recording of Mitta Mitta rainfall continues.  (ABC Rural: Annie Brown)

"Twelve months ago, the BOM told me not to worry about ringing the rain through anymore unless we had a big deluge," she said.

At 86 and 82 years old, the Coles will continue to collect weather data until they no longer can.

But Mr Cole said they hope to travel more, and Mr Kelly has also put off holidays in the past to cover for them.

The Coles look forward to doing more travelling.  (ABC Rural: Annie Brown)

"If we had an automatic weather station, we wouldn't have to go and ask people to do the rain for us," Mr Cole said.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/m.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

A man has been charged after the Melbourne incident.  (ABC News)

Detectives have charged a 51-year-old man with murder and intentionally causing injury after a stabbing in Melbourne on Friday.

Delivery rider Feng Jianming was fatally stabbed when the man allegedly attacked him and another delivery rider.

The man is expected to appear before the Melbourne Magistrates' Court today.

A 51-year-old man has been charged after a fatal stabbing in Melbourne's CBD on Friday that left another man injured.

The man is accused of tampering with two delivery drivers' bikes on Frederick Way, near the Queen Victoria Market, just after 8pm.

Victoria Police said the pair confronted the man before a physical altercation occurred.

Father of two Feng Jianming was one of the delivery drivers and was allegedly stabbed during the confrontation.

The 47-year-old Chinese national died at the scene.

Feng Jianming died after the incident. (Supplied)

The second deliver driver, a 34-year-old man, suffered serious injuries.

He was taken to hospital where he remains.

The 51-year-old Footscray man has been charged with one count of murder and intentionally causing serious injury.

He is expected to appear before the Melbourne Magistrates' Court today.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/t.title: Seven dead and 100 injured after trains collide in Egypt
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/t.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Transport Accidents and Incidents

A train travelling south crashed into the rear of another train, according to the Transportation Ministry. (AP Photo)

A train collided with the rear of another train and derailed near Cairo in Egypt on Sunday.

At least seven people have died and more than 100 people were injured, the Ministry of Health said.

Emergency teams and cranes have been dispatched to clear the wreckage.

At least seven people have been killed and more than 110 injured in a passenger train collision in Egypt's Giza province.

A train that was travelling between Giza and Fayoum collided with the rear of another train travelling from Cairo to Aswan, Egyptian authorities said on Sunday.

The collision occurred in Al-Ayyat district in Giza province, on the edge of Cairo, and caused the train to derail from its tracks.

The Ministry of Health confirmed seven people had died, and more than 110 were injured in the train collision.

Egypt's health ministry said the crash had injured at least 110 people. (AP Photo)

Emergency teams and cranes were dispatched to the scene to clear the wreckage and restore train services to their normal schedule as soon as possible, the Egyptian Railway Authority said.

President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi ordered a swift investigation and said anyone found negligent should be held accountable, according to a separate statement.

The crash occurred in al-Ayyat district in Giza province, about 52 kilometres south of Cairo. (AP Photo)

Egypt's public prosecutor's office said investigations were underway to determine the technical reasons behind the crash.

Egypt has one of the oldest and largest railway networks in the region and accidents involving casualties are common, though the government has been investing billions of Egyptian pounds to modernise the network.

Egypt's president said in a social media post that he had ordered an investigation into the crash. (AP Photo)

Casualties were taken to nearby hospitals for treatment, the Egyptian Ministry of Health said.

Last September, a train driver and his assistant were injured after two freight trains collided in the same district.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/a.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Aunty Lorna Corbett says she's enjoyed sharing her cultural knowledge with the university students. (ABC News: Stephen Opie)

Traditional owners from across the country have come together to learn what it takes to become an archaeologist in a new program based at Ityamaiitpinna Yarta Glenthorne National Park.

It's hoped the pilot program will encourage more First Nations people to pursue a career in the field, and share their cultural knowledge with archaeology students.

Traditional owners hope the federally-funded program will become a mainstay, with funding secured for the next five years.

Deep within Ityamaiitpinna Yarta Glenthorne National Park, in Adelaide's southern suburbs, tools tinker against the earth beneath silver-striped gumtrees.

Eleven traditional owners from across Australia work alongside a group of Flinders University archaeology students to unearth history.

There is no shortage of colonial history at the park, which was formerly Glenthorne Farm — a warhorse training ground, a colonial house, and research station.

In the few days the traditional owners and students have been on site, they have found colonial era bottles, a medicine bottle, part of a glass pane and a window frame.

The traditional owners and students are at the site as part of a new five-day course designed by the Australian Resources Sector, Flinders University and traditional owner groups.

The federal government-funded program teaches students and traditional owners the theoretical and practical skills involved in excavation, archaeological surveying and ground-imaging.

Ashley Wedding-Corbett says he hopes to use his experience to do field work on Country. (ABC News: Stephen Opie)

Western Australian traditional owner Aunty Lorna Corbett, a member of the Palyku-Jartayi Aboriginal Corporation, said she valued being able to participate in something she believed "should have happened many years ago".

"I think it's very important to have Aboriginal people right across Australia to be called upon in the initial stages of anything to do with Country," she said.

"Creating this workshop, allows us to go out there … and be involved in what decisions they make on Country."

Palyku and Noongar man Ashley Wedding-Corbett, who is also a Palyku-Jartayi member, said he hoped to use his experience to do field work on Country.

"It'd be awesome to do that where I live … to try and get into that kind of environment and be out there actually doing it," he said.

While the program does not give participating traditional owners formal qualifications in archaeology, they do receive a certificate equivalent to one graduate level topic in archaeology.

Ian Moffat says traditional owners have been "doing as much teaching" as they have done learning. (ABC News: Stephen Opie)

Professor of Archaeological Science at Flinders University Ian Moffat said the training added to the traditional owners' cultural knowledge.

"Sadly, archaeology in Australia has done a terrible job at bringing First Nations people to universities and providing practical training," he said.

"Our traditional owner partners are the people that are on Country, managing heritage."

Mr Moffatt said the traditional owners "have been doing as much teaching … as they have doing learning", by sharing their cultural knowledge with the students.

"We really appreciate them coming, sharing their cultural knowledge, sharing their perspectives and the best way to manage heritage in Australia," he said.

Aunty Lorna said she had enjoyed sharing her cultural knowledge with the Flinders students.

"It's just like a two-way learning … whether it's here in the classroom or in the field," she said.

The university has secured funding to run the program over the next five years.

Traditional owners hope the program will become a mainstay, saying it is a crucial step to help preserve and pass down cultural knowledge to the next generation.

"It's very important for our culture to keep those histories," Ms Corbett said.

"That's why oral history is very important.

"We are here today because of our ancestors."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/a.title: The questionable sales tactics prompting people to switch their super
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/a.author: Nassim Khadem
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/a.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Superannuation

Australians switching superannuation are urged to be cautious of telemarketers.  (ABC News: Alistair Kroie)

Over 17 months, unqualified and unlicensed telemarketers urged Australians to switch about $678 million of their investments — mostly their superannuation savings — into riskier schemes.

That is among the findings the corporate regulator, the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC), unveiled today in a review focusing on 15 Australian financial services licensees operating between January 2025 and June 2026.

The report looked at the practice of telemarketers, also known as lead generators, using social media advertising and telephone calls to identify consumers and introduce them to licensed financial advisers.

These advisors would then switch their superannuation out of APRA-regulated funds in a practice known as lead-generation.

Earlier this year, ASIC announced it would be looking into the firms that allow these lead generators to operate.

Unlicensed telemarketers who cold call and make unsolicited approaches to consumers to convince them to switch their super will be banned under long-awaited reforms.

The regulator found that the licensees obtained about 7,639 new clients through lead generation services over the period, which represented about 35 per cent of total new clients for these licensees.

This resulted in more than $678 million being switched or invested, with about 90 per cent coming from superannuation savings.

Licensees deducted $9.8 million in up-front advice fees from clients and clients agreed to a further $4.5 million in annual ongoing fees.

ASIC says the high-profile collapses of Shield and First Guardian — which left almost 12,000 investors losing over $1 billion of their retirement savings — illustrate the potential impact when financial services providers do not act in the best interests of Australian investors.

Earlier this year, Assistant Treasurer Daniel Mulino announced that unlicensed telemarketers who cold call and make unsolicited approaches to convince people to switch their super will be banned.

Under the law, only a licensed financial adviser can give a consumer advice about their investments.

The collapses of the First Guardian and Shield schemes have exposed deep flaws in the regulation of Australia's $4.3 trillion superannuation sector.

But ASIC's review found the 15 licensees used unlicensed lead generators to lure Australians into investment schemes.

The regulator said these lead generators took activities beyond simple referral, including lead qualification, appointment setting, fact-finding, product research and discussing investment performance or Statements of Advice (SOA) recommendations.

In one case, a lead generator had assisted with advice implementation.

ASIC also said some lead generators had used potentially misleading statements, fear-based claims, and non-like-for-like performance comparisons to persuade investors to switch their super.

"Many Australians invested in the funds because their financial adviser failed to act in their best interests and many of these people were advised to make these investments after being approached by a lead generator," ASIC said in its review.

It found involving lead generation in financial advice was likely to be "inconsistent with the obligations that apply to financial advisers" and their authorising licensees.

This included the obligation to act in the best interests of the clients and to only provide personal advice if appropriately authorised.

ASIC said some licensees were failing to supervise or understand what was happening within their networks.

Five of them did not have controls or standards in place that prohibited, or were likely to identify, high-risk superannuation switching by their authorised representatives.

A further four licensees were operating businesses that had some features of "high-risk superannuation switching", the review said.

Alan Kirkland says consumers should be wary of lead generators.

ASIC commissioner Alan Kirkland said lead generators use "slick sales tactics to convince people to switch their super" and that this "can expose Australians to serious financial harm".

"Our message to advice licensees is clear: we will continue to take enforcement action under current laws where we find evidence of serious consumer harm."

Super Consumers Australia chief executive Xavier O'Halloran said ASIC's findings exposed "the greed driving high-risk super switching schemes".

"Good advisers don't need to cold call people to get clients," he said.

Xavier O'Halloran says good financial advisers do not cold call prospective clients.  (ABC News: Daniel Irvine)

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/r.title: Aged care bed crisis hits boiling point for families waiting years
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/r.author: Amelia Walters
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/r.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Betty Cameron says her husband, Darryl, "hoped his heart would give out before he got to this point". (ABC Riverland: Amelia Walters)

Betty Cameron has been waiting two years for an aged care bed for her husband in South Australia.

She is now looking interstate to find him a bed due to the delays.

The state government says 10,600 additional federal residential aged care places are needed nationally each year in the next two decades to meet demand.

Horrendous, horrible and sleepless nights.

This was how 74-year-old Betty Cameron described the past two years trying to find her husband a residential aged care bed in South Australia.

Darryl Cameron has late-stage dementia, and is living in NDIS-funded supported independent living care.

With his health declining, Ms Cameron was told her husband's funding is likely to cease in three weeks, with Mr Cameron now facing hospitalisation if an aged care bed is not secured.

"He always said he hoped his heart would give out before he got to this point."

Betty Cameron says the aged care bed crisis is taking a physical and mental toll.  (ABC Riverland: Amelia Walters)

Mr Cameron's NDIS provider, Hola Support, said his funding was being reviewed through an NDIS tribunal process.

The couple live three hours away from Adelaide in the state's Riverland, a drive Ms Cameron said is unfeasible to do each day if her husband were relocated.

Some days Darryl Cameron smiles, and other days he cannot get out of bed. (Supplied: Betty Cameron)

She was left to look interstate in Mildura, about 150 kilometres away, for a suitable facility she could visit daily due to unavailability in the Riverland.

"I want to be there every day with him. I want to have fun and just interact with him until he does pass away," she said.

Darryl Cameron (centre) was a die-hard Adelaide Crows supporter.  (ABC Riverland: Amelia Walters)

Ms Cameron said the process has taken a significant mental toll on her and she has felt unseen by a system meant to help.

"Some days I feel like punching everyone out, and other days I'm alright," she said.

"I get more days of wanting to punch people out than I do good days.

"When this is all sorted, I'll be right. But until then, nah, I'm a mess some days."

The aged care crisis is a national issue, with all states and territories seeking ways to find solutions.

South Australia is the oldest mainland state and has the longest wait times in the country for residential aged care beds.

There are also about 500 people in hospital waiting for a residential aged care bed in the state. Four years ago, it was only 60.

Lisa Turton believes incentives should be handed out to attract more aged care staff to the sector.  (ABC Riverland: Amelia Walters)

NDIS support coordinator Lisa Turton said aged care bed shortages have been an issue for more than a decade.

She said some families are having to make life-altering choices because of the delays.

The number of those in hospital who are waiting for an aged car bed has increased by 830 per cent in the past four years. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

Ms Turton believed infrastructure across the state needed to be fast-tracked, with regional areas prioritised.

"[There should be] a focus on getting more staff to the area that are passionate about this field, or offering incentives and supporting people to find their passion in supporting others."

Conducting a roundtable with stakeholders last week, South Australia's Minister for Health and Wellbeing, Blair Boyer, said the state government would leave "no stone unturned" to address the aged care crisis.

"[The statistics] will continue to grow and potentially be much higher next year if we don't get some action and support from the federal government, who are responsible for aged care in this nation," he said.

Blair Boyer says the federal government needs to step up.  (ABC News: Daniel Taylor)

The minister hoped to generate 650 new beds from a recent no-interest loan scheme for developers, as well as create 600 beds inside part of the old Women's and Children's Hospital.

"Last year, just 800 beds were added to the system."

A spokesperson for the federal Minister for Aged Care and Seniors said delayed discharge is a nationwide challenge and it invested $600 million in 27 state and territory initiatives to reduce delayed discharge.

"We're supporting the construction of around 5,000 additional residential aged care beds [nationally] each year," the spokesperson said.

The spokesperson said 268 beds were slated across five Adelaide sites as part of the 5,000-bed plan.

Ensuring her husband has dignity is front of mind for Ms Cameron.

She said securing an aged care bed is the only way he would receive the consideration and care he deserves.

"Just think about these people who have put in years looking after this country. Giving something back to them, that's what they need to do," she said.

Betty Cameron says her husband, Darryl, has a wicked sense of humour.  (Supplied: Betty Cameron )

Ms Cameron will continue to try to savour the special moments with her husband where she can until a bed is secured.

"He is just beautiful. I love it when he remembers my nickname, Betty Spaghetti," she said.

"If he comes out with that or if he just looks at me and says, 'I love you darling,' it makes my day."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/i.title: Trump championed oil, but instead he fuelled an electro revolution
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/i.author: Nathan Morris
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/i.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Electric Vehicles

Donald Trump and Elon Musk made a pitch for Tesla vehicles at the White House, but the Iran war has arguably had a greater impact. (Reuters: Kevin Lamarque)

During the 1979 Iranian oil crisis, US president Jimmy Carter gave a speech that would likely resonate today.

"Solar energy will not pollute our air or water. We will not run short of it. No one can ever embargo the Sun or interrupt its delivery to us," he said.

Rising fuel prices were crippling the world, and energy sovereignty was front of the president's mind. Behind him as he spoke was a new solar hot water system he had installed at the White House.

President Jimmy Carter inspects solar panels on the roof of the White House's West Wing in 1979. (Supplied: Harvey Georges)

But while Carter's solar prophecy took decades to realise, experts say Donald Trump's decision this year to start a war with Iran has accelerated global electrification efforts and may be considered a tipping point in the shift from fossil fuels.

Renewables continued to grow in the US under Trump even before the war — despite his opposition. Solar generation is up 20 per cent, coal is down, and a record 86 gigawatt hours (GWh) of renewable projects are planned.

And now that voters have stripped Republican control of Congress, the economic momentum behind renewables may be even harder to derail.

Soaring oil prices during the 1970s drove a shift toward fuel-efficient cars and accelerated research in new energy sources, such as solar.  (Supplied: US National Archives)

Unlike the oil shocks of the past, this time, consumers have real electric alternatives, and the cost of installed solar and batteries has fallen 90 per cent since 2010. But the biggest story of the war has been the unprecedented rise of electric vehicles (EVs).

Since the US and Israel began bombing Iran in February, both the fuel price and the sale of EVs have risen sharply around the world.

"I think Donald Trump is the best salesperson for electric vehicles the world has ever seen," said Gabrielle Kuiper, an energy expert affiliated with the CSIRO and the ANU.

"Everywhere is recognising that why would you be reliant on liquid imported fossil fuels when you can generate your own electricity with sunshine or with wind and then you can drive an electric vehicle."

In Australia, EVs now make up close to a quarter of all new car sales, lining up with the global average, and in September and October 2026, battery electric cars outsold petrol cars.

Global EV sales were already rising before the Iran conflict, but growth has surged in emerging markets and places dependent on liquid fuel imports.

Euan Graham, an analyst with global think tank Ember Energy, said a massive EV boom is taking place in South-East Asia.

"Vietnam, Singapore, Thailand, now as well as Indonesia [are] all really picking up in their rate of EV sales and it's more than just the actual sales of cars themselves," he said.

"The best-selling car in Vietnam is a VinFast car, which is a domestic manufacturer that already completely dominates the Vietnamese market and is now expanding overseas."

Based in Vietnam, VinFast is now a leading manufacturer of EVs in South-East Asia. (Reuters: Nguyen Ha Minh)

While the Australian government's efforts to secure fuel supplies have minimised shortages domestically, other countries have been hit hard.

Three-quarters of the world imports fossil fuels, and about 75 per cent of the world's oil supply is traded by sea.

Countries are taking direct action to reduce dependence on imported fuel.

In May, Laos suspended the import of internal combustion engine (ICE) vehicles, following Ethiopia's 2024 decision to ban the imports.

In Europe, despite concerns about the impact of imported Chinese cars, EV sales have reached record levels, including in auto-manufacturing powerhouse Germany, where sales hit 37 per cent in October.

The US is the only country where EV sales have fallen as US automakers pivoted back to ICE cars in the aftermath of the 2024 Trump victory.

It is a bitter irony for a country that has just delivered a verdict on high gas prices.

EVs might be the headline-grabbing story of 2026, but electrification more broadly continues to grow.

"Around the world last year, about three quarters of the growth in electricity demand came from solar alone. And in some countries, solar was providing all of the growth already," Graham said.

Australia's booming battery fleet, and the threat of a gas tax, have seen electricity prices drop since the start of the war, but overseas they have shot up as the conflict disrupted the supply of gas exports from Qatar.

In response, heavy fossil fuel users like South Korea are investing hundreds of billions in renewables.

In Vietnam, plans to build the country's biggest gas-fired power station have been scrapped to shore up energy sovereignty.

Wind turbines along the Sinchang Windmill Coastal Road on Jeju Island, South Korea. (Supplied: Слава Ли/Pexels)

Anna Freeman from the Energy Efficiency Council said the soaring cost of fossil fuels has made the economics of renewables more compelling.

"Prior to this crisis, we were on track to spend $US4 trillion a year on oil and gas globally," said Anna Freeman, from the Energy Efficiency Council.

Freeman also leads the Electrify Now coalition, which published research this week forecasting this year's total oil and gas bill could be over $US5 trillion.

"We will be spending an additional $1.2 trillion, not for any additional products, just that is the price premium associated with this fossil fuel crisis," Freeman said.

"By contrast, we can deliver the net zero energy transition for $3.5 trillion per year," Freeman said.

"And that gets us so much more because it builds us a more efficient and a more affordable and a more secure energy system."

A recent report from Ember found that the global electric car fleet has helped save about $20 billion in crude oil costs in the six months since the US-Israel war with Iran.

But there are some hard numbers that grind against the electrification narrative. EVs may now make up about a quarter of new car sales, but make up only five per cent of cars on the road.

Coal, oil and gas still supply about 60 per cent of the world's final energy. And record growth in renewables in 2025 of 887 terawatt hours (TWh) did outpace electricity demand of 849TWh, but not by much.

Satellite imagery reveals the staggering rise of solar farms around the world in recent years.

Electrification will be a key focus of the UN's annual climate summit, the Conference of Parties — or COP31 — this week.

In June, the UN set a goal of 35 per cent electrification by 2035.

"The world is entering the age of electricity. At COP31, we will flick the switch," wrote COP31 president-designate Murat Kurum, in a special report on electrification by the IEA last month.

It is welcome news for Kylie Turner, the sustainable economies lead at Monash University's Climateworks Centre, who describes electrification as "the unloved child of the energy transition."

"At COP28 in Dubai, the world signed up to a global pledge to triple renewables and double energy efficiency, and the piece of the puzzle that's missing is actually electrification."

Almost 50 years after Jimmy Carter declared solar "feasible and cost-effective," Ember Energy analyst Euan Graham says the economics of electrification have moved beyond politics.

"I'm most optimistic about transforming the power sector because it's gone far beyond climate targets," he said.

"In terms of economics and the speed at which they can be built, clean technologies — especially wind, solar and batteries — are just winning."
