Following reports of Nvidia's chief Jensen Huang becoming involved with a Chinese spy, Huang offered an apology for cheating on his wife. Meanwhile, the US tech company pledged to investigate the alleged espionage.

US tech giant Nvidia said on Sunday it would investigate claims that its CEO Jensen Huang was targeted by "foreign intelligence efforts."

Multiple media outlets, including The Financial Times, recently reported on American intelligence sharing information on Huang's extramarital affair with a Chinese woman. The woman, according to US intelligence sources, had been recruited by China's Ministry of State Security.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The reports identified her as Alice Huang, an executive for Singapore-based company Megaspeed. The US is investigating the company over suspicions that it was helping Beijing bypass export restrictions and obtain cutting-edge AI chips. According to The New York Times, the company has bought Nvidia chips worth billions of dollars in the last two years.

US lawmakers have invited the Nvidia chief to brief them on the reports.

On Sunday, Nvidia's top executive admitted to being "unfaithful" to his wife of 40 years.

"My actions hurt her and our children," Jensen Huang wrote in an email sent to Nvidia staff. "There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

He also said he was he committed to protecting the company and "supporting America's national security."

Huang was born in Taipei and spent part of his childhood in Taiwan before moving to the US. In 1993, he and two other people launched Nvidia, a company that grew to become a leading manufacturer of computer graphic cards and then an essential supplier of computer chips in the AI boom.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The 63-year-old Nvidia CEO is one of the richest people in the world, according to the Forbes magazine, with his $162.2 billion (€145.5 billion) net worth as of Sunday putting him roughly on par with globally renowned investor Warren Buffet.

In their statement, Nvidia's board of directors said Huang will remain the head of the US-based company while the probe is taking place.

Huang "fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it," according to their statement.

The board said a group of "independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel, will oversee the investigation."

At the same time, the heads of the $4.5 trillion company said they had "no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised."

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/08/nx-s1-603.title: NASA is looking for astronauts to live and work on the Moon
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/08/nx-s1-603.author: Chandelis Duster
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/08/nx-s1-603.text:
The NASA logo is seen at NASA's Johnson Space Center, Friday, Aug. 28, 2026, in Houston.

If you have dreams of going to the moon, you now have a chance. NASA is accepting applications for those interested in becoming an astronaut.

The candidates selected to be astronauts would not only test spacecraft but would also live and work on the moon in a future moon base, said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman in a statement released on Saturday.

"Those missions will demand technical excellence, sound judgment, teamwork, and courage," the statement said. "NASA's astronaut corps has always called on remarkable Americans willing to take on extraordinary challenges in service to the nation."

There are currently 32 active astronauts in NASA's astronaut corps. Since NASA missions began in the 1960s, the agency has selected 370 people to train as astronauts, according to the agency.

The applicant process is extremely competitive. Out of more than 8,000 applicants for NASA's last astronaut class, only 10 candidates were selected.

While any U.S. citizen can apply and there is no official age restriction, applicants will need to have a master's degree in a STEM-related field such as engineering or math.

In a recent change, a nursing degree qualifies.

"Nursing degrees are now included in the STEM definition," Anna Schneider, NASA spokesperson, told NPR on Sunday. "Master's-level nursing degrees now meet the minimum educational requirement, whereas nursing degrees were previously excluded."

In addition, NASA is requiring a minimum of three years of related professional experience after completing a degree.

In lieu of a master's degree and working experience, NASA will consider those in a PhD program (in STEM), doctors or pilots with extensive flight experience.

FILE - This detail of a July 20, 1969 photo made available by NASA shows astronaut Neil Armstrong reflected in the helmet visor of Buzz Aldrin on the surface of the moon.

If chosen, the selected astronauts will undergo training that will last for two years. NASA said astronauts will prepare for critical and difficult missions such as landing near the moon's South Pole.

To achieve its goal of returning humans to the moon in 2028 – the first time since 1972 – NASA is relying on private companies such as Blue Origin and SpaceX to develop systems and spacecraft.

During a Nov. 7 press conference on the Artemis III moon mission's progress, Isaacman said he is "very confident" the mission will launch in 2027.

The starting salary is $164,395 and applications will be received through Dec. 3.

A 15-year-old boy has been stabbed outside a south-west Sydney high school, police say. (ABC News: Floss Adams)

A 15-year-old boy has been taken to hospital after being stabbed multiple times outside a school in Sydney's south-west.

NSW Police said emergency services were called to Myall Road in Casula just before 8:30am, after receiving reports of an assault outside Casula High School.

Officers were told the boy was stabbed several times in the abdomen.

The teenager was treated by paramedics at the scene and was taken to Liverpool Hospital in a serious but stable condition.

A crime scene has been established and police are investigating.

Royal Commissions

Public hearings for Victoria's royal commission examining allegations of corruption on government building sites have begun in Melbourne.

It comes as the state's election campaign enters the final three-week stretch ahead of polling day on November 28.

Follow our live coverage below.

Choose what information you see below by using filters

Mr Young says future blocks will explore the integration of organised crime into the construction industry.

He says members of organised crime were often given "large payments" for services that amounted to "little more than intimidation and menace".

Mr Young says other future hearings will deal with how government money was allocated, and how certain public projects were decided.

Mr Young lists what he calls "themes" of the royal commission's investigation into corruption on government work sites.

He notes these are all allegations at this stage, and some have been denied.

Among the themes, Mr Young says:

Counsel assisting Chris Young KC covers what the royal commission has already uncovered in its preliminary work.

Mr Young says more than 110,000 documents have already been requested by the commission, and hundreds of notices have been sent out.

Secret hearings have also been held already, with witnesses interviewed in private.

The hearing today will examine the events of June 2022 at the Gap Road project in Sunbury.

The project involved the removal of a level crossing and the construction of a new rail bridge and underpass as part of the Sunbury Line Upgrade.

On June 6 and 7 in 2022, there was a work stoppage.

After a meeting at the CFMEU offices on June 7, work resumed with control of the site transferred to the union.

The royal commission will investigate what occurred, what arrangements were made, what they cost and what the government knew.

Establishing the royal commission was Ben Carroll's first act as premier, a move that distanced him from predecessor Jacinta Allan.

But any hope the public would reward Carroll and Labor for calling the inquiry quickly evaporated.

The government didn't receive a poll bounce from changing leaders — it thus seems unlikely voters will reward Labor over the next fortnight if hearings expose fresh corruption claims.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Japan works to shield Takaichi from any Xi snub at China summit
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
Japan is trying to ensure Xi Jinping doesn’t snub Sanae Takaichi when they meet at a major leaders’ summit in China this month — their first encounter since a furor over Taiwan derailed ties.

When Takaichi attends the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation conclave in Shenzhen, Japanese officials expect the host leader to greet her with at least a customary handshake. Ties between Japan and China, however, have over the past year hit one of their lowest ebbs since the countries normalized relations in 1972 — throwing such a reception into doubt. Xi shook then-Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe’s hand the last time China hosted APEC back in 2014 during an earlier period of strained ties, but unlike today the groundwork for that detente had been laid months in advance.

Japanese officials have sought reassurances from China that Xi will give Takaichi the same treatment as other world leaders, according to people familiar with the matter. Tokyo will protest anything unusual planned for the conference on Nov. 18-19, added the people, who weren’t authorized to discuss private matters.

“Over the past year, Beijing has personalized its rhetorical attacks against Japan, many of which focus on demonizing Takaichi to an unusual degree,” said Jeremy Chan, a senior analyst at the Eurasia Group and former U.S. diplomat. “That increases the chances China could find an opportunity at APEC to personally embarrass her by downgrading her status or criticizing Japan.”

Underscoring the risks, Xi publicly rebuked Canada’s then-Prime Minister Justin Trudeau during a Group of Twenty summit in Indonesia in 2022 after a yearslong spat — a tense exchange caught on camera. Seating plans and family photos both pose other opportunities for Takaichi to be sidelined.

Asia’s top two economies have been at loggerheads since Takaichi last November said a Chinese attack on Taiwan could pose an existential threat to Japan. While that’s long been the view among Japanese leaders, others had avoided stating it publicly. Her remarks came only a week after she met Xi on the sidelines of the APEC summit in South Korea — timing that appeared to intensify the Chinese anger.

In retaliation, China has choked exports to Japan of the rare earths over which it holds a near monopoly and are critical to its neighbor’s semiconductor and auto industries. U.S. manufacturers that rely on Japan for certain magnets are also hurting, prompting Donald Trump to ask Xi in September to ease the measures.

Takaichi’s visit to China is particularly fraught because Xi appears to have personally demanded she retract her remarks on Taiwan, according to some Japanese officials. So far, Japan’s first female premier has refused — and pushed ahead with a security agenda that has further angered China.

Plans for maritime boundary talks with the Philippines announced in May to resolve their overlapping maritime border east of Taiwan upset China, along with suggestions from leading government officials in Tokyo that they may discuss revising a ban on the entry of nuclear weapons into Japan.

Chances for a Takaichi-Xi meeting at the APEC summit are low, people familiar with the planning said. Encounters are likely to be limited to customary interactions as part of APEC’s formal program, such as the leaders’ dinner, where Xi is expected to meet and greet each leader.

Trump and Russia’s Vladimir Putin are also set to hold a trilateral with China’s top leader at the APEC arena — marking the first time in post-World War II history the heads of those three nuclear-armed powers have huddled. For Takaichi, that raises the risk of looking isolated from Washington, which is Japan’s sole formal ally.

Takaichi has a chance to catch Trump in Manila at the ASEAN summit days before the Chinese conference, giving her a channel to convey a message to Beijing. That’s a tactic she used in September on the sidelines of the United Nations in New York, seeking to ensure Tokyo’s interests weren’t traded away at Trump’s White House summit with Xi.

Chinese Premier Li Qiang will also attend ASEAN, where he could meet Takaichi — technically his counterpart, given she isn’t a head of state.

While China’s ties with Japan had been rocky for decades over disputes spanning Tokyo’s invasion of its neighbor in the 1930s to competing territorial claims, relations had stabilized in the months before Takaichi swept to power. China’s reaction to the views of Takaichi, who visited Taiwan’s President Lai Ching-te in April 2025 months before becoming leader, has changed the relationship.

China has urged its citizens — who made up about a quarter of all visitors to Japan before the spat — to avoid its Asian neighbor, citing safety risks. It’s also curbed seafood imports and put Japanese companies on lists that control or monitor their access to Chinese products with military uses.

Classifying a Chinese invasion of Taiwan as an existential threat to Japan could provide the legal basis for Tokyo to deploy its military as part of a collective response with the U.S.. That prospect has fueled a narrative in China that Japan is returning to its militaristic past under Takaichi, which Tokyo has denied.

While APEC in 2014 helped deliver a detente, that was preceded by a meeting between senior officials days before the summit where Tokyo offered an olive branch. Chinese state media touted that huddle as a “diplomatic win” after Japan “for the first time” acknowledged the two countries’ claims over disputed islands.

There have been no such exchanges this time. Chinese officials have only met with figures outside Takaichi’s cabinet. When former Japanese prime minister, Yasuo Fukuda, died last month, Xi bypassed Takaichi and sent a condolence letter directly to his wife.

Komeito, a party known for its ties to China and the former coalition partner of Takaichi’s ruling Liberal Democratic Party, helped lay the groundwork for the Xi-Abe sit-down. When Takaichi became prime minister, Komeito exited the coalition.

Going into APEC, Japan’s leader just needs to handle things calmly and steadily, said Masaki Taniguchi, a professor of political science at the University of Tokyo.

“There’s no need to provoke China unnecessarily,” he added. “Conversely, Japan has absolutely no reason to kowtow to China either.”
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.summary: Ties between Japan and China have hit one of their lowest ebbs since 1972. Takaichi's visit to China is particularly fraught because Xi appears to have personally demanded she retract her remarks on Taiwan.

https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.title: ‘This happened very quick’: Beau Lamarre-Condon reenacts shooting Jesse Baird during double murder trial
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.author: Kat Wong and Ima Caldwell
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text:
Former police officer has pleaded not guilty to murdering Jesse Baird and Luke Davies in Paddington in early 2024

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Beau Lamarre-Condon has demonstrated in court how he claims he shot Jesse Baird, acting out his movements in the witness box in Sydney.

The former police officer is accused of fatally shooting Baird and his partner, Luke Davies, with his police service weapon in Baird’s Paddington home in Sydney on 19 February 2024.

He has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder and one charge of aggravated break and enter.

Giving evidence under cross-examination on Monday, Lamarre-Condon re-iterated his claim that Baird was holding a knife while struggling with the officer in the house.

Lamarre-Condon told the New South Wales supreme court that the knife was next to his throat, which led him to push Baird back with his right arm.

The crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield asked Lamarre-Condon to stand up and demonstrate, telling the accused: “Put your rosary beads down while you do that.”

The officer reenacted the struggle for the jury, with Hatfield describing his movements.

“[The accused] with his left arm out at shoulder height, demonstrated pushing Jesse Baird’s right hand with the knife away from him, so that the left arm was fully extended,” the prosecutor told the jury.

“[Lamarre-Condon] gestured pulling the pistol around the area around his belt … then held it up at around chest or shoulder height and demonstrated with a bent elbow firing a shot towards the right shoulder of Jesse Baird.”

Lamarre-Condon told the court he “discharged a shot” and said he was aiming towards Baird’s right shoulder.

“My arm did extend … I don’t know to what extent … there was constant movement in this struggle,” the accused told the court. “That’s as clear as I can be. This happened very, very quick.”

Hatfield said the officer last week said he was pinned by Baird during the struggle and asked if Lamarre-Condon was now suggesting “something different” by claiming he was constantly moving.

Lamarre-Condon said he was pinned directly before he pushed back and fired the shot, telling the court there was “constant movement” before that.

Asked what Baird and Davies were wearing, Lamarre-Condon said both men were only in their underwear and were not wearing shoes.

During his evidence-in-chief last week, Lamarre-Condon stood by his decision to fire the first shot but claimed a second bullet was “accidentally” fired.

On Monday, he re-iterated he did not intend to fire the second shot at Baird.

The trial before Justice Natalie Adams continues.

https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.title: Only 6.4% of stroke survivors receive enough therapy, finds ‘damning’ report
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.author: Denis Campbell Health policy editor
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.text:
Stroke Association says widespread lack of rehabilitation hinders patients’ chances of regaining physical and mental function

Fewer than one in 15 stroke survivors are getting the amount of therapy the NHS should provide to maximise their chances of recovery, a report has revealed.

The figure was a “damning” indictment of the widespread lack of rehabilitation for patients, which was hindering their chances of regaining physical and mental function, the Stroke Association said.

Only 6.4% of those in England, Wales and Northern Ireland who have a stroke receive the three hours a day of rehabilitation therapy at least five days a week to which they are entitled.

The finding is disclosed in the latest annual report of the Sentinel Stroke National Audit Programme (SSNAP), which is based on stroke care data from hospitals in the three countries.

Almost 100,000 people a year in the UK have a stroke. It is the single largest cause of complex disability and can leave survivors struggling to walk, talk or swallow. The ageing population, and an increased number of people with high blood pressure or diabetes, could cause the annual figure to rise to 115,483 by 2030.

All stroke patients should get three hours of physiotherapy, speech and language therapy, and occupational therapy to help them recover from the brain injury they have suffered, whether they are still in hospital or have returned home to continue their rehabilitation.

That is set out in National Institute for Health and Care Excellence guidelines intended to guide NHS practice in England and Wales. They are also followed in Northern Ireland.

However, during January to March this year – the latest figures available – only 6.4% of patients received that amount, down from the 7.5% who did so in October to December 2024.

The average amount of therapy stroke survivors in the three countries received in the first quarter of this year was 40 minutes, six minutes less than in late 2024. Some patients received only 15.2 minutes, while the maximum received was still only 57.3 minutes, the SSNAP audit showed.

In addition, only 68% of patients received continuing help with their rehabilitation once they had been discharged from hospital, the report found.

“These damning figures expose the deeply troubling reality that too many vulnerable stroke survivors are being left without the care and support they need, both in the critical days after their stroke and in the months and years that follow,” said Juliet Bouverie, the Stroke Association’s chief executive.

“The brain injury caused by stroke can change every aspect of a person’s life in an instant and last for a lifetime. Stroke is both a medical emergency and a long-term condition which touches on almost every aspect of NHS and social care.

“Yet too often, our health and care system focuses on treating the emergency rather than considering the importance of what comes after that – and these shocking statistics reveal the true extent of that.”

Bouverie said services for stroke survivors “are already overstretched to breaking point” as the charity published a new report showing that stroke costs the UK an estimated £25.7bn a year.

after newsletter promotion

More than half that sum (£13.7bn) goes on the social care costs of helping survivors. The wider societal costs, such as people no longer being able to work and relatives having to give up work to care for survivors, amount to another £6.7bn. Welfare benefits to patients and income tax not collected because they had had to stop work came to £2.4bn alone, the charity estimated.

The Department of Health and Social Care did not comment on the overwhelming majority of stroke patients not receiving enough rehabilitation. Instead it stressed the NHS’s efforts to improve care.

“Hundreds of people every day suffer a stroke, and the NHS is working hard to get them the rapid support and long-term rehabilitation they will often require,” a spokesperson said.

“In our 10-year health plan last year, we pledged to reduce premature mortality from heart disease and stroke by a quarter within a decade, and our cardiovascular disease modern service framework, published in July, aims to accelerate that progress.

“The NHS is also working to increase the delivery of thrombolysis and thrombectomy rates as a key intervention to support improved outcomes in patients who have had a stroke,” they added.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/8.title: Chancellor Merz to nominate Aigner as Germany’s first woman president
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/8.text:
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz will nominate Bavarian politician Ilse Aigner for Germany’s next president, which would make her the country’s first female head of state.

Merz made the announcement at a dinner for leaders of his centre-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) party on Sunday.

Aigner, speaker of the Bavarian state parliament, belongs to the Christian Social Union (CSU), the Bavarian sister party of the CDU.

If her nomination is confirmed at a CDU and CSU meeting on Monday, she would almost certainly be formally elected.

According to German political practice, coalition parties must agree on a common candidate. The governing coalition is made up of the CDU, the CSU and the Social Democratic Party (SPD).

The SPD has frequently voiced its support for Aigner as president.

The German president is elected by the Federal Convention, convened solely to choose the president. It will decide on incumbent Frank-Walter Steinmeier’s successor on January 30.

Steinmeier, a Social Democrat, took office in 2017, and will reach the limit of two five-year terms in March 2027.

Germany’s president holds a largely ceremonial position, signing legislation into law and formally appointing ministers.

But the president can play the role of a neutral arbiter, above party politics, and acts as a symbol of national unity.

The CSU put forward Aigner’s name earlier this year, but the CDU held back from endorsing her while Merz considered alternatives, straining relations between the parties.

Aigner, 61, began her political career in local politics before being elected to federal parliament in 1998.

She served as agriculture minister under former Chancellor Angela Merkel before returning to her home state of Bavaria, where she became speaker of the state parliament in 2018.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/08/pentagon-.title: The Pentagon is reportedly ramping up economic warfare and espionage. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with a suspected Chinese spy shows why
https://fortune.com/2026/11/08/pentagon-.author: Jason Ma
https://fortune.com/2026/11/08/pentagon-.text:
AI chip leader Nvidia launched an investigation into reports CEO Jensen Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence campaign—just as the U.S. has intensified its own efforts at economic warfare.

Nvidia’s board released a statement Sunday that a committee of independent directors and an outside counsel will oversee the probe, adding that Huang supports the review and plans to cooperate.

“The Board prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders,” it said. “While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board’s inquiry will examine all available information.”

The announcement followed reports that Huang had a romantic relationship with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, whom U.S. intelligence suspects was working as a spy for China.

According to the New York Times and Financial Times, the Nvidia boss admitted to the affair and apologized in an internal message to company employees.

“I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry,” he said in the message.

Representatives for Nvidia and Megaspeed didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.

U.S. officials believe Alice Huang was recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security, sources told the FT, and surveillance revealed that she was feeding information to China, according to the New York Times.

Jensen Huang, who isn’t related to Alice, is a central figure in the U.S. AI industry, leading a company that develops world-class chips powering large language models.

Its technology is so sensitive that the Trump administration has restricted exports of Nvidia’s most cutting-edge products to China while President Donald Trump has often cited the U.S.-China AI rivalry as a reason for not slowing down development.

Meanwhile, Megaspeed is a Singapore-based data center company that quickly became one of Nvidia’s top customers in Asia, purchasing more than $4.8 billion in chips over the past two years.

But the U.S. also investigated Megaspeed last year for allegedly helping smuggle restricted AI chips into China, which the company has denied.

News of the Nvidia’s probe into Huang comes weeks after reports indicated the U.S. defense and intelligence communities are getting more aggressive about industrial espionage.

Sources told the Washington Post that the Pentagon is planning a spying program that deploys “nonofficial cover officers” who pose as executives—a covert effort in a larger economic warfare campaign.

Politico also reported that the Defense Department is quietly building an elite agency to covertly sabotage foreign technology programs that could threaten U.S. military superiority.

The Technology Support Office was established in April by reorganizing two classified intelligence programs that have been secretly carrying out technology sabotage at a smaller scale since 2023.

The Pentagon has denied the reports.

“This query appears to be built on information that is simply not true. Whoever is feeding you these claims are either badly misinformed or deliberately leading you astray to peddle their fantasies,” it told both outlets.

But other signs point to the U.S. taking economic warfare more seriously. In September, CIA Deputy Director Michael Ellis said the U.S. is expanding espionage against China by targeting companies in sensitive areas like AI, biotechnology and chips.

Also this year, the Pentagon formed the Economic Defense Unit for “deterring, denying, disrupting, and helping to defeat adversaries through economic means,” sources told DefenseScoop.

AI in particular has emerged as such an important technology that the Defense Department has been more heavy-handed with U.S. companies as well.

Anthropic’s AI models were used in the military, but a dispute between the San Francisco-based startup and top brass led to a schism just as the Iran war started.

CEO Dario Amodei has said the company is patriotic and seeks to defend the U.S., but wouldn’t allow its AI to be used in mass domestic surveillance or autonomous weapons.

The Pentagon insisted it would use the AI in lawful scenarios and refused to abide by any limits from the company that would go beyond those constraints.

After failing to reach a compromise earlier this year, Trump ordered the Pentagon to phase out Anthropic’s technology. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth also designated the company a supply-chain risk, meaning contractors can’t use it for military work.

Last month, an appeals court ruled the supply-chain risk designation is illegal, but the Pentagon confirmed it’s no longer using any Anthropic tools.
https://fortune.com/2026/11/08/pentagon-.summary: Nvidia's board says it will investigate whether its secrets were compromised. The company's CEO Jensen Huang has admitted to an affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang. The U.S. intelligence suspects Huang was working as a spy for China.

US President Donald Trump has backtracked on his White House press secretary job offer to UFC boss Dana White. (Reuters: Eric Lee)

United States President Donald Trump has backtracked on his announcement to offer Ultimate Fighting Championship CEO Dana White the vacant White House press secretary role, saying he was "only kidding".

While speaking to reporters before boarding Air Force One in Florida on Sunday evening, local time, Mr Trump said he still expected to speak with Mr White on Monday.

Mr Trump also said he believed Mr White "loves the idea" of the job offer.

In his initial Truth Social post on Saturday, local time, Mr Trump described Mr White as "a violent Fighter and Warrior" and said he could appoint several well-known UFC stars as his assistants.

Donald Trump's original Truth Social post in which he announced the offering of a White House posting to Dana White. (Supplied: Truth Social/@realDonaldTrump)

On the tarmac in Florida a day later, the president said the nature of the post was a sign it was a joke.

He then told reporters that he was kidding five consecutive times in the same address.

"If you saw the assistants, I posted the greatest wrestlers and UFC fighters in the world, right? Like Khabib, like Justin Gaethje who's phenomenal … You would've thought that people would've said, 'He's having a good time,'" Mr Trump said.

"I was only kidding, but Dana loves the idea and there's only one Dana … It was just a little fun.

"This was an example of something where I was kidding."

Following Mr Trump's Truth Social post, Mr White then posted his own image that appeared to show him standing at a White House lectern in the press briefing room, with a caption that read: "On to the next chapter".

The reaction image posted on social media by Dana White. (Supplied: Dana White)

The White House press secretary posting has remained vacant for close to a month after Katie Zacharia left the position less than a week into the role.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/b.title: Live: Beau Lamarre-Condon cross-examined in double murder trial
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/b.author: Millie  Roberts
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/b.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Beau Lamarre-Condon is back in the witness box at the NSW Supreme Court in Sydney. (ABC News: Sharon Gordon)

Beau Lamarre-Condon is being cross-examined by the prosecution in his double murder trial.

Last week, he gave evidence in the witness box. He has pleaded not guilty to murdering Jesse Baird and Luke Davies in early 2024.

Follow our live coverage here.

Choose what information you see below by using filters

"I said, 'please don't shoot me I'm not here to hurt you I'm not a threat. Get out'," Lamarre-Condon says.

Davies raised the gun from the accused's chest up to his head, he claims.

"That's when immediately I saw his left index finger go on the gun ... trigger. I got up, I grabbed with my left hand his left wrist," he says.

He says his right hand, with a phone, is pressed up to Davies's forearm.

The phone drops and its screen smashes.

Lamarre-Condon says he turns Davies's left wrist, now holding the gun, with his left hand to pivot him away.

"It's then discharged obviously it's hit Luke and exited."

"I see him with the firearm, he's got both hands on the gun," he says.

He claims Davies says: "I'm going to f**king shoot you."

He puts his hands to the surrender position and lowers himself to the floor.

The phone is still in his hand and he tells him to "get out" with a "shoo" motion, waving away from his body, and towards the front door.

"I'm not a threat, you can have the gun ... and get out."

Lamarre-Condon says he was near storage boxes when he first saw Davies.

"Luke was standing in front of Jesse Baird's front door and blocking the front door," he says.

"I was facing towards the front door."

He says Davies was facing towards him and the kitchen, and his back was towards the front door.

He says he picks up the phone from the kitchen and dials Triple Zero (000) heading towards the front door.

He says he wanted to flag an ambulance or paramedics down from the street.

St Vincent's Hospital is nearby.

"I was moving very quick, it was urgent ... I know I was 100 per cent calling Triple Zero while I was moving," he says.

"I never disconnected the Triple Zero call."

He says he said "get out" to Davies and he replies "f**k off" after listening back to the call.

His visor was down while on the call.

"I didn't need to take my helmet off I was not doing CPR or resuscitation," he says about why it was still on while attending to Baird.

"Was it a deliberate decision to leave both phones in your car?" Hatfield asks.

"It was a deliberate decision," Lamarre-Condon replies.

He says he didn't need his phones to get his possessions back.

Lamarre-Condon says he was looking in the house for a phone, and saw one on the kitchen counter.

"Was it obvious to you he was dead?"

"No. I knew he was unresponsive," Lamarre-Condon says.

He's being asked if he could see a "massive gunshot wound" to Baird's mouth.

"Wasn't it obvious he'd been shot through his head? ... Wasn't there a lot of blood?" Hatfield asks.

He says he's being "truthful" when he replies lots of blood could have come from "anywhere".

Lamarre-Condon is being asked about kneeling near Baird and entering "police mode", trying to see if he was alert and putting him in the recovery position.

"I was kneeling next to his body at this point," the accused says.

He did not have gloves on at this stage, but can't remember if he took them off upstairs or shortly after this point.

Lamarre-Condon says he thought he could feel a pulse on Baird's wrist.

"I was just trying to see if I could get Jesse up, see if I could get a reaction," he says.

Baird was laying on his back at this stage.

Lamarre-Condon agrees the second shot happened within a "couple seconds" of the first.

"It was unintentionally discharged towards Jesse," he says.

He says it was not aimed.

"I've never had an intention or thought" to hurt Baird, he says.

He says he did not "intentionally discharge the second shot".

"It's the case you executed him with that second shot," Hatfield says.

"I never executed Jesse Baird."

"I also had a hold of Jesse's right arm with my left hand so that is further grip ... and during the fall, after the shot was discharged I was already pulling back," Lamarre-Condon says about how the gun would have flung backwards.

It's a flicking motion in a backwards direction towards his right shoulder.

"You're holding the handle the whole time and the trigger finger must have been loose? Hatfield asks.

"At one point," he says.

"Trigger wouldn't have been loose if I was pulling backwards ... you squeeze tight.

"After it was discharged and there was no more motion of Jesse ... it would have been loose?"

He says the gun would have been "arms length" away from Baird when it discharged.

Lamarre-Condon is being asked about his evidence last week, in relation to his struggle with Baird.

The floor plan of the kitchen and lounge room is on the screen.

He says the gun went "backwards" in the "vicinity of the living room".

"Jesse must have gone back over the box, fallen back to his right and you must have gone with him," Hatfield says, saying the door to the living room would be to the left.

"No, it would have been to the right," he replies.

Lamarre-Condon says if the gun was yanked left or right, it would have flung towards the living room.

The prosecutor suggests it would have gone behind him or to the ceiling instead.

Hatfield has asked the accused what Baird and Davies were wearing when he came across them in the home.

He says both men were in their underwear and neither were wearing shoes.

Hatfield has given Lamarre-Condon a copy of a computer-assisted floor plan of the Brown Street terrace and asked him to mark various items on the document.

He’s marked where he says there were cardboard storage boxes in the hallway and kitchen, where he later saw a mattress in the courtyard, and the location of a mobile phone which he says he picked up after Baird was shot to call emergency services.

Lamarre-Condon has been shown a photograph of the kitchen and been asked to point out where he was pinned against a wall.

He describes it as an area in the right corner, where the wall and the kitchen counter meet.

Lamarre-Condon has been asked by Crown Prosecutor Brett Hatfield SC to demonstrate the movements involved in a struggle he says he had with Baird in the kitchen of the Brown Street terrace.

He has previously testified that he was wearing a helmet at this point, and that Baird was holding a knife, “lunged” at him, and then at one point the knife was close to Lamarre-Condon’s throat before he pushed Baird back and fired a shot at Baird's shoulder.

“This was really, really quick and we were moving,” the accused says of the struggle.

“There was movement, constant movement in this struggle.”

Hatfield has asked whether this evidence was different to something he said last week — that he was “pinned” during the struggle.

Lamarre-Condon insists it’s not different, and at one point he was pinned near a wall.

This is the third day Lamarre-Condon has been in the witness box.

Last week, he was questioned by his defence barrister John Stratton SC.

Afterwards, the Crown began their cross-examination for a short period before court adjourned on Friday.

Crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield SC is expected to pick up his questioning of the accused in the NSW Supreme Court today.

We are back into cross examination, with Beau Lamarre-Condon being asked to revisit the moment he shot Jesse Baird the first time in the Paddington share house.

“This was very, very quick … I was aiming towards his right shoulder,” he said.

He gestured pulling his pistol from around his belt area, lifting it up to chest or shoulder height.

There were some technical difficulties after this point.

We're picking things up from here on out, and will loop back with what you missed shortly.

Lamarre-Condon has pleaded not guilty to murdering Jesse Baird and Luke Davies in February 2024.

Court reporter Jamie McKinnell explained what he testified here:

Thanks for joining us. Today we're back in court for Beau Lamarre-Condon's double murder trial.

He'll continue being cross-examined by the prosecution after giving evidence last week.

https://www.scmp.com/week-asia/politics/.title: Why Indonesia’s death penalty lives on, even as executions dwindle
https://www.scmp.com/week-asia/politics/.author: Aisyah Llewellyn
https://www.scmp.com/week-asia/politics/.text:
A report on the high number of convicts on death row in Indonesia has prompted legal experts to urge judges to focus on rehabilitation

A new report on the persistent use of capital punishment in Indonesia’s courts has raised questions about the rulings despite an unofficial moratorium on executions.

There were 639 people on death row in Indonesia as of April, an increase from 596 as of August 2025, according to a report by the Indonesian Commission for the Disappeared and Victims of Violence (KontraS) published in October.

Titled “Capital Punishment Policy Has Changed, Yet the State Has Not Reformed”, the report shows that the number of criminals facing death sentences more than doubled as of April compared with 2019.

Indonesia has not executed anyone since July 2016, when three Nigerian nationals and one Indonesian were killed by firing squad for drug-related offences.

Under Indonesia’s new Criminal Code, which was passed into law in 2023 and came into force in January this year, the death penalty is classified as a “special punishment” to be used as a “last resort”.

The legislation provides for a 10-year probation period for those sentenced to death, after which their sentences can be commuted to life imprisonment if they have shown good conduct and commitment to change while incarcerated.

Legal experts have regarded the provisions as a compromise in place of complete abolition.

Usman Hamid, the director of Amnesty International Indonesia, said many judges, particularly in courts of first instance, were still inclined to interpret the law conservatively, rather than embracing the concept of rehabilitation.

Despite the new Criminal Code, there was “only a partial shift” in the thinking of judges, Hamid said.

“Judges maintain a conservative perspective regarding the specific types of crimes that warrant a capital sentence. While there has been a shift in practice, it has not yet succeeded in halting the imposition of death sentences.”

Under Indonesian law, the death penalty can be imposed for serious crimes including premeditated murder, terrorism, drug trafficking, gross human rights violations such as genocide and treason.

Judicial motivations for continuing to impose the death penalty vary, and one of them is that the death penalty is the most favourable outcome for such offences, according to legal experts.

“In certain situations, securing a death sentence is even viewed as an achievement. It can bring media attention to the prosecutors or judges involved, who are then perceived as having succeeded by imposing the ultimate penalty,” said Albert Wirya, director of the Legal Aid Institute for the People.

What was concerning was that the number of death sentences remained high in 2024 and 2025, Wirya said. He pointed out that the possibility for a death sentence to be commuted might have swayed judges into favouring capital punishment.

Under Indonesian law, the final decision of whether to grant or deny the commutation of a death sentence to life imprisonment after 10 years lies with the sitting president.

As such, judges may feel that the eventual outcome of a case is not for them to decide, according to Wirya.

“This suggests that judicial motivation to impose the death penalty will persist,” he said. “Therefore, the complete abolition of the death penalty remains essential in Indonesia.”

Indonesia, however, has yet to introduce procedures to allow inmates on death row to apply for their sentences to be commuted.

Without such procedures, these inmates’ suffering would be prolonged due to the uncertainty, Wirya said.

“Unfortunately, the fate of those on death row remains unaltered. More than 100 individuals sentenced to death have already served over 10 years in prison. Yet they are unable to apply for a commutation of their sentences because the necessary implementing regulations have not yet been established.”

Beyond Indonesia, the legal approach to capital punishment varies considerably across other parts of Southeast Asia.

In the Philippines, Cambodia and East Timor, capital punishment is prohibited.

Brunei and Laos retain the death penalty for certain offences but have not executed a convict for decades, while Thailand has not done so since 2018.

Malaysia has removed the mandatory death penalty for certain offences and gives its courts sentencing discretion in such cases.

Myanmar resumed executions in 2022 after more than three decades.

Singapore continues to carry out executions, with Amnesty International recording 19 in the first nine months of 2026, all for drug-related offences, compared with 17 in 2025.

Abdul Fickar Hadjar, an expert in Indonesian criminal law, said the evolution of the Criminal Code was a reflection of changing societal norms.

“This is not a matter of public or political pressure but, rather, it reflects the aspirations prevalent within Indonesian society at the time the Criminal Code was being drafted in 2023,” he said.

An inmate whose death sentence has been commuted to life imprisonment could also potentially have the sentence further modified to a jail term of up to 20 years.

“These provisions illustrate that the application of the law is intended to evolve in tandem with the prisoner’s personal improvement, reflecting the core purpose of the penal system, [which is] the rehabilitation and restoration of the individual’s humanity,” Hadjar said.

Human rights lawyer Ranto Sibarani said Indonesian judges had “failed to grasp the spirit behind the abolition of the death penalty as part of a global trend that underpins the new Indonesian Criminal Code”, focusing instead on imposing punitive sentences.

“Sadly, nothing will change as long as courts remain focused solely on maximising punishment, rather than focusing on education and rehabilitation.”
https://www.scmp.com/week-asia/politics/.summary: There were 639 people on death row in Indonesia as of April, an increase from 596 as of August 2025. Indonesia has not executed anyone since July 2016, when three Nigerian nationals and one Indonesian were killed by firing squad for drug-related offences.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6ly.title: Aramco Tower hit in heart of Saudi capital as Houthis launch fresh strikes
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6ly.text:
The Aramco Tower, a skyscraper in the Saudi Arabian capital's central financial district, had been hit by an air attack.

A statement issued via the Houthi-controlled Saba news agency confirmed the group had targeted Riyadh's business zone on Saturday, without mentioning the Aramco Tower by name.

The Saudi energy ministry said the tower had suffered only "minor damage" and no one had been killed or injured.

Footage authenticated by BBC Verify shows more extensive damage to the building, with at least one floor appearing to have been badly hit by a missile or drone strike.

Windows on more than one level appear to have been shattered by the strike.

The Houthis also said Riyadh's airport and Aramco oil storage facilities were targeted in separate strikes. Saudi Arabia said its air defences had intercepted and destroyed several missiles.

The strikes were the latest claimed by the Yemen-based armed group against targets deep inside Saudi Arabia, which the Gulf power has struggled to contain in recent months.

It came a day after the Houthis accused a Saudi-led coalition of killing at least 33 people, including women and children, in an air strike on Yemen.

Footage broadcast by Houthi-run television channel Al Masirah showed rescuers pulling bodies from the rubble of several buildings in al-Shariyah, a town to the east of the capital, Sanaa.

Saba said 39 people had been injured in the strike. Saudi Arabia has not commented.

A Saudi-led coalition has been fighting the Houthis for more than a decade in support of Yemen's internationally recognised government, which has lost control of a large swathe of the country to the rebel group.

Although the conflict had largely been dormant in recent years, fighting has intensified following the outbreak of the Iran war.

An informal ceasefire unravelled in July after the Tehran-backed Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.

The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they have called a Saudi blockade of their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport Saudi Arabia said had been to prevent an Iranian aircraft from landing there.

Major fighting has since resumed between Houthi forces and troops aligned with Yemen's Saudi-backed government.

The United Nations says more than 1,600 people have been killed and more than 300,000 displaced since fighting resumed.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6ly.summary: Saudi energy ministry says the tower suffered only "minor damage" The Saudi energy ministry said no one had been killed or injured in the strike. The strikes were the latest claimed by the Yemen-based Houthis against targets deep inside Saudi Arabia.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmd7.title: New contract will make it 'easier' to get GP appointments
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmd7.text:
A new contract with general practitioners (GPs) will make it "easier" for patients to get appointments, the health minister has said.

The Department of Health (DoH) said it will give an additional £40m across two years for "improvements in patient access and primary care activity".

Last year, GP partners in Northern Ireland voted in favour of taking collective action as part of their fight for increased funding for general practice.

Robbie Butler said he welcomes the NI General Practitioners Committee's (NIGPC) "commitment to rebuild a constructive working relationship with the department and to end the current collective action".

A GP contract is a formal agreement between GP partners or practices and the DoH to provide general medical services.

The total in-year value for the 2026/27 General Medical Services Contract agreed between the department and the NIGPC is worth a further £17.384m, including £13.3m of recurrent funding into core GP services, according to the DoH.

In a statement, Butler said: "Difficulties getting an appointment with their GP is one of the issues people raise with me the most, which is why during negotiations I have been very clear that the financial package must deliver more appointments and services for people who need them."

Adding that he is "pleased" that the NIGPC is to take part in the Neighbourhood Model of Health and Wellbeing.

The neighbourhood plan commits to establishing a neighbourhood-centred health and social care system.

In May 2025, the former health minister Mike Nesbitt imposed a disputed financial package on Northern Ireland GPs after they rejected the deal.

The move had triggered a work to rule, which included doctors ignoring non-essential paperwork, limiting appointments to the British Medical Association (BMA) recommended safe limit of 25 per day and the withdrawal of noncontractual services.

BBC News NI health correspondent Marie-Louise Connolly

Northern Ireland needs more GPs to deliver much needed appointments for the public.

Acquiring more GPs needs considerable long-term investment and what the department has announced appears to fall short of what general practice has said is required.

Recently GPs told Stormont's Health Committee that general practice in Northern Ireland received less than 6% of the entire health budget.

Dr Frances O'Hagan said that wasn't nearly enough to fund the number of doctors required in each practice to meet growing demand.

While she said 10% of the health budget was the minimum they could accept - 15% was a longer term ambition.

Those figures translate closer to £80m per year as opposed to the £20m allocated by the health minister,

Clearly what is good about the funding announcement is that it ends a 12 month dispute between the department and GPs.

At least, if required, new negotiations can begin again.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmd7.summary: Department of Health will give an additional £40m across two years for "improvements in patient access and primary care activity" Last year, GP partners in Northern Ireland voted in favour of taking collective action.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3dx.title: Nvidia launches investigation into CEO's affair with suspected Chinese spy
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3dx.text:
US tech giant Nvidia has opened an independent investigation following reports its CEO Jensen Huang had a relationship with a suspected Chinese spy.

The company, one of the most valuable in the world, said its board had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised, adding that the CEO was committed to continuing to lead the company.

Separately, Jensen Huang admitted to having been "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children.

US intelligence officials believed that Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, who had a close relationship with Jensen Huang, was a spy for Beijing, according to a New York Times report.

Jensen Huang said he took "full responsibility" for what he did, adding that he had fallen short of his responsibilities to Nvidia's employees, board and shareholders.

Nvidia is one of the world's largest companies and seen as central to making the hardware for emerging AI technologies, and Jensen Huang has been in charge of it for more than 30 years.

He said: "I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry."

His statement continued: "Regarding the national security concerns raised in news reports, Nvidia's Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation. I support the investigation and will cooperate fully.

"I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American."

A separate statement issued by Nvidia's board of directors said it would begin an investigation in "light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort".

It continued: "The Board prioritises US national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of Nvidia and its shareholders.

"While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information."

US President Donald Trump said he had not spoken to the Nvidia boss since news of the investigation emerged.

"I just know he's a fine person, but you never know what's going on," Trump told reporters, adding that he had "done an amazing job for our country".

Jensen Huang rescued Nvidia from almost going broke on more than one occasion, and he took a punt on AI a long time before the rest of the world did.

His decision to make Nvidia chips, originally designed for gaming, become the best in the business for AI development, has now paid off in spades and the company is worth trillions.

This is a big blow for a man who is renowned for being a workaholic, a perfectionist and someone who expects incredibly high standards from his staff.

Alice Huang, who is of no relation to Jensen Huang, is linked to Singapore-based data centre firm Megaspeed.

The company told the New York Times last month its current leadership took the allegations seriously and had appointed external legal advisers to conduct an internal investigation.

Nvidia is a central player in AI infrastructure, providing chips to leading AI model developers including OpenAI and Meta.

The microchip manufacturer is worth some $4.5 trillion, making it one of the most valuable companies ever.

China has previously rejected allegations of an espionage operation targeting Nvidia's chief, describing the claims as "groundless speculation".

US intelligence agencies had been monitoring Alice Huang and concluded that she was acting on behalf of the Chinese government, according to unnamed sources cited by The New York Times.

Surveillance reportedly revealed communications between Alice Huang and an American citizen, who was subsequently identified as Jensen Huang through a process known as "unmasking".

It remains unclear what information Alice Huang – who is also known as Huang Le – allegedly passed to Beijing, how valuable it was, or when she is believed to have begun gathering intelligence.

Alice Huang did not respond to the paper's request for comment.

Last week, members of Congress wrote to Jensen Huang, asking him to appear before them in the light of the reported relationship.

Three House Republican committee leaders asked the CEO to appear later in the month, to talk about Nvidia's "security protocols against foreign adversary espionage" given his reported relationship with Alice Huang.

"Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC's [China's] access to sensitive US technology and information.

"The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge US technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress," the letter said.

Nvidia's AI chips have been a major focus of the rivalry between the US and China, and Washington has previously imposed controls on where its advanced products can be sold.

The H200, Nvidia's second most advanced semiconductor, had previously been restricted by Washington over concerns that it would give China's technology industry an edge over the US.

In January, the Trump administration said it would allow the company to sell its H200 chips to Chinese customers under certain conditions.

The company said it will begin an investigation into the allegations. The CEO said he took "full responsibility" for what he did, adding that he had fallen short of his responsibilities. He admitted to having been "unfaithful" to his wife

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck7v.title: Doing these things now will help you save money at Christmas
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck7v.text:
How soon is too soon when it comes to thinking about Christmas and your finances?

The answer, of course, is that it is never too soon. Save early and the cost becomes more manageable.

The squeeze is harder for some than others, with charity Barnardo's warning that some parents will skip meals so their kids get a Christmas dinner with the trimmings.

But, debt advice charity StepChange is offering tips to everyone, to avoid Christmas spending leading to a financially painful new year.

The best way to avoid a difficult January, it says, is to make a realistic plan before the spending begins.

Small decisions now can make a big difference later. Its tips include:

"Christmas is a time when we want to enjoy ourselves and make things special for the people we care most about," said Vikki Brownridge, chief executive of StepChange.

"But it can also put a lot of pressure on household budgets, and it is key to take steps to get ahead of any January financial blues."

If you are concerned about Christmas leaving you in debt, then it is best to seek advice well before things become unmanageable.

The independent MoneyHelper website has a guide to finding free debt advice near you.

There are also tools to work out if you are receiving all the benefits and grants you are entitled to, and tips on how to draw up a budget.

And it is really important to watch out for scams at this time of year. Fraudsters will take any opportunity to catch you out, especially when you are under pressure financially.

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/08/nx-s1-603.title: Nvidia launches investigation into CEO's alleged relationship with Chinese spy
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/08/nx-s1-603.author: Rebecca Hersher
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/08/nx-s1-603.text:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang delivers his keynote on the company's GTC event in Berlin, Germany, Wednesday, Oct. 21, 2026.

The massive artificial intelligence chip maker Nvidia says it is launching an internal investigation, after reports that the company's CEO was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy.

In the statement announcing the investigation, Nvidia cited recent reporting by The New York Times, which alleges Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was the target of a Chinese intelligence operation that sought to send advanced Nvidia AI chips to China.

"While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information," the statement from the company's board of directors reads in part.

The Times released a series of reports over the last two weeks detailing Huang's alleged relationship with a woman named Alice Huang, who is accused of being a spy for China. The two are not related. NPR has reached out to the Chinese Embassy in Washington, D.C. but has not received a response.

"Alice Huang is a Chinese national. She's a Chinese businesswoman who had something of a mysterious and meteoric rise," Times reporter Ana Swanson explained on NPR's technology podcast Machine Gods.

Alice Huang ran a Singapore-based company that purchased nearly $5 billion in Nvidia chip technology, Swanson says. "At the same time, she was also seen personally with Jensen Huang on a couple of occasions after some industry events in Taiwan. They were photographed together both at a bar with other suppliers and then also out to dinner with some other executives."

The reporting by the Times suggests Alice Huang may have helped China get around U.S. limits on exports of powerful AI chips.

According to Nvidia, Huang sent an email to his employees on Sunday, acknowledging the relationship, and apologizing for being unfaithful to his wife.

"I support the investigation and will cooperate fully," Huang wrote. "I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America's national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American."

Last week, three Republican members of Congress sent a letter to the Nvidia CEO requesting that he brief lawmakers about the relationship, and about the company's "security protocols against foreign adversary espionage."

Nvidia dominates the global market for AI chips, and has seen explosive growth in recent years, as NPR has reported. The company started as a manufacturer of chips for computer graphics, which later turned out to be crucial for training artificial intelligence.

Nvidia's CEO and President Trump have repeatedly appeared in public together in recent years. According to Huang, Nvidia is helping to fund the construction of a new ballroom at the White House.

NPR does not offer or accept money for coverage or interviews.
Anyone who makes such an offer or request is not an NPR employee and does not represent NPR.
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/08/nx-s1-603.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is accused of being in a close relationship with a Chinese spy. The New York Times reports that Huang was the target of a Chinese intelligence operation. The two are not related.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.title: Kyle Larson joins Nascar’s all-time greats with third Cup title in six years
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.author: Agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.text:
Larson becomes first repeat champion since 2010

Hendrick driver clinches title in opening stage

Ryan Blaney wins season finale at Homestead

Kyle Larson is now a three-time Nascar champion.

Larson clinched his third Cup Series title in six years early in Sunday’s 400-mile season finale at Homestead-Miami Speedway, becoming the first back-to-back champion since Jimmie Johnson in 2010. Johnson won five consecutive titles beginning in 2006.

The 34-year-old Larson also became the 11th driver in Nascar history to win three Cup titles, joining an exclusive club that includes seven-time champions Richard Petty, Dale Earnhardt and Johnson. Jeff Gordon won four titles, while Lee Petty, David Pearson, Cale Yarborough, Darrell Waltrip, Tony Stewart and Joey Logano each won three.

Ryan Blaney won the race for Team Penske, passing Tyler Reddick of 23XI Racing with just over a lap remaining as NBA legend Michael Jordan watched from pit road. Reddick finished second, followed by William Byron, Christopher Bell, Bubba Wallace and Denny Hamlin.

But the biggest celebration belonged to Larson, who finished 12th. He stopped near the start-finish line for a smoky burnout before exchanging high-fives and hugs with his team and children. He then climbed atop his No 5 Chevrolet with the championship flag and all three of his children to celebrate.

Larson had been the overwhelming favorite to lift the Bill France Cup long before the green flag dropped.

He entered the weekend with a 67-point lead over Bell and needed only nine points to secure the championship. He earned one point for starting the race and seven more by finishing fourth in the opening stage. When Bell failed to win that stage, he was mathematically eliminated from contention.

Larson responded to crew chief Cliff Daniels breaking the news over the radio with a deadpan assessment: “That was anticlimactic.”

Hendrick Motorsports owner Rick Hendrick, celebrating his team’s 16th Cup championship, radioed Larson to congratulate him during the ensuing caution period.

“Now you can go ride the wall,” Hendrick joked.

Larson obliged, only to cut a right-rear tire and be forced to pit out of sequence, effectively ending his hopes of winning the race.

“I got the word that we clinched it, and I started driving like an idiot,” Larson said. “I’m more mad at myself.”

The mishap mattered little after a remarkable postseason in Nascar’s Chase for the Championship. Larson ended a 51-race winless streak by winning three of the previous nine playoff races and finished in the top 10 in eight of them.

He produced a similarly dominant finish in 2021, his first season with Hendrick, winning four of the final five races, including the championship finale at Phoenix Raceway.

His second title came in dramatic fashion last year at Phoenix. Taking advantage of a late caution, Larson’s crew opted for two new tires rather than four, allowing him to leapfrog sentimental favorite Denny Hamlin on pit road with two laps remaining. Hamlin could not catch him.

This year’s championship was considerably less suspenseful. Larson’s advantage was so commanding that he was the only Cup driver invited to Nascar’s championship media day on Thursday, an experience he described as awkward.

Any concerns about how Larson and his No 5 Hendrick Motorsports team would handle the pressure appeared unfounded by Saturday’s qualifying session.

“They were debating on if a hot dog is a sandwich and if cereal is a soup,” Larson said. “So I would say they were pretty relaxed. I was surprised by all that.”

With three Cup championships secured, Larson’s place among motorsport’s most versatile drivers is becoming increasingly difficult to dispute.

Parnelli Jones, Mario Andretti, AJ Foyt and Stewart are widely regarded among the greatest American drivers for their success across multiple disciplines.

Jones won in sprint cars and stock cars around the time he captured the 1963 Indianapolis 500. Andretti won four IndyCar titles, the 1967 Daytona 500 and the 1969 Indianapolis 500. Foyt won four Indianapolis 500s and the 1972 Daytona 500, while Stewart claimed the 1997 IndyCar championship and three Cup Series titles before moving into top-level NHRA drag racing.

Larson has twice competed in the Indianapolis 500 and has won the Rolex 24 at Daytona, three Chili Bowl Nationals and four Knoxville Nationals. His third Cup title further strengthens his case for a place alongside those legends.

“He wins in everything he does, and they’re all completely different cars and tracks,” said retired driver and NBC Sports analyst Jeff Burton. “And he’s racing against the best in every discipline.”
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.summary: Kyle Larson becomes first back-to-back champion since 2010. Larson becomes 11th driver in Nascar history to win three Cup titles. He is the first back to back champion since Jimmie Johnson in 2010.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.title: Jeffries backs Hegseth impeachment as Democrats vow probes of Trump allies
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.text:
United States House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries has thrown his support behind impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, as the Democratic Party prepares to use its incoming congressional majorities to probe President Donald Trump’s administration.

In a Sunday appearance on the Television show This Week with George Stephanopoulos, Jeffries weighed in on the upcoming impeachment resolution, anticipated for the coming days.

“I’m a hard yes on the Hegseth resolution,” Jeffries said. “The so-called secretary of defence has abused his power, undermined our national security, and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran.”

The impeachment resolution has been spearheaded by outgoing Republican Representative Thomas Massie of Kentucky, a vocal critic of the US-Israel war on Iran.

“Pete Hegseth has got to go,” Jeffries added. “I believe there will be incredibly strong support for that resolution.”

Jeffries is poised to become the next speaker in the House of Representatives after Democrats notched a historic victory in the November 3 midterm elections.

Both the House and the Senate flipped into Democratic control, with the left-wing party making some of its biggest gains in the lower chamber in more than half a century.

Democrats are expected to use their new congressional majorities to launch investigations into the Trump administration.

There have also been concerns, voiced by Trump himself, that he and other top officials could face impeachment.

In Sunday’s interview, Jeffries said the Democratic majority would move “aggressively” in its first 100 days in office, both to address affordability and “unprecedented corruption” under Trump.

“We are committed to cleaning up the mess wherever it’s found,” Jeffries said. “That’s in Congress, in the Supreme Court, and with respect to this administration.”

Currently, Republicans hold a government “trifecta”, with control of both chambers of Congress and the presidency. The Supreme Court also boasts a conservative supermajority, shaped by three Trump appointees.

But a new Congress will be sworn in on January 3. In the coming weeks, Democrats will choose their party leaders for both chambers.

Representative Robert Garcia formally announced his bid to lead the House Oversight Committee in a letter to colleagues on Thursday.

The committee is the chamber’s principal investigative panel, with the power to subpoena witnesses and documents.

On Sunday, Garcia told CNN that Stephen Miller‘s influential role in the Trump administration warranted investigation.

Miller, who was named last week as White House chief of staff, has been closely associated with Trump’s hardline immigration policies since his first term as president.

“What we think is that Stephen Miller is the architect of this horrific, unjust policy happening across the country,” Garcia said, pointing to policies of separating immigrant families and accusations of due process abuses.

“Stephen Miller is at the centre of major policy decisions that are happening in the administration, and it does deserve oversight and investigation.”

Garcia also signalled interest in questioning businessman Elon Musk over his leadership in the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), a federal initiative that led to widespread federal workforce cuts at the start of Trump’s second term.

DOGE also sought access to sensitive government data, including Americans’ personal information.

“What happened with DOGE, in particular, and the federal employees losing jobs the way they did and people’s data likely being compromised, I think, is very serious,” Garcia said.

Congressional committees have the power to hold hearings, subpoena witnesses, and demand documents, giving lawmakers a constitutional check on the executive branch.

The House can also impeach administration officials if a simple majority votes in favour.

Conviction and removal, however, require a two-thirds vote in the Senate, a high bar even with Democrats controlling the chamber.

The White House was quick to draw its own battle lines.

Speaking on CNN’s State of the Union on Sunday, Attorney General Todd Blanche said there could be investigations into Democratic lawmakers over their “threatening” rhetoric.

He added he was ready to counter Democratic efforts to probe and impeach Trump officials.

“If that’s what this new incoming leadership wants to do, we are ready,” said Blanche, a former personal lawyer for Trump. “If you work in this administration, you have a lawyer. It’s me.”

Trump, meanwhile, made similar remarks in a Truth Social post on Saturday.

He called on the Justice Department to investigate Democrats over their plans to haul his allies before congressional committees, branding them as “SLEAZEBAGS” who “should go to jail”.

“The threats being made by the Democrat Party against innocent Republican Donors and Party Members are absolutely unprecedented, and totally illegal,” the president wrote.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/liveblog/.author: Kristina Harazim,Adam Hancock
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/liveblog/.text:
Oil prices have fallen in early trading in Asia after the US president said he was highly unlikely to order new attacks on Iran as long as there is progress in talks to end the war.

Brent crude prices fell over half a percent to $97.67 a barrel, while US oil futures also dropped to $90.51 a barrel, according to the Reuters news agency.

Trump made his remarks even as both countries reported hitting ships in or near the Strait of Hormuz.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio says there has been no progress on talks to end the war on Iran, due to what he called Tehran’s “unacceptable” and in some cases “outrageous” demands.

Speaking to reporters at the Homestead Air Reserve Base in Florida, Rubio said mediation efforts were continuing.

“I don’t have any progress to report to you,” he said. “You have a number of countries that continue to engage them with different ideas, but I wouldn’t say we’re on the verge of a breakthrough. The president would always prefer to solve this and every problem diplomatically. Sometimes that’s not possible, unfortunately.”

But if there’s a chance for a deal, “we’ll explore it,” he said. “Right now, it hasn’t been very productive because the Iranian demands are simply not just unacceptable, but in some cases outrageous and ridiculous and really not realistic,” he added.

Rubio made the comments before his flight to Paris where he is due to attend the G7 Foreign Ministers meeting.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi says there has been no progress in talks with the US and that Tehran is waiting to see if Washington’s position will change after the ‘shock’ of the midterms.

Hello, and welcome to our continuing coverage of the United States and Israel’s war on Iran.

Stay with us for the latest developments, reactions and analysis of the war and its fallout across the globe, including in Yemen and Saudi Arabia.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/8.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/8.text:
The mayor of the Mexican border town of Rio Bravo has been found alive after being abducted in the violence-ridden Zacatecas state in northern Mexico.

Federal officials said Miguel Angel Almaraz was released by his captors on Sunday, hours after being taken to the city of Zacatecas.

He was abducted while travelling with family and friends in a region that straddles the states of Zacatecas and San Luis Potosi on Saturday, when his car was intercepted by armed men, who let the others go.

Almaraz’s relatives were able to reach a town in San Luis Potosi, where they alerted authorities about the incident, according to the state’s Security Department.

Almaraz is the mayor of Rio Bravo, a municipality of about 110,000 people in Tamaulipas state, 11km (7 miles) from Mexico’s border with Texas, United States.

He was acquitted of money laundering charges in 2015, after being imprisoned for six years.

He is a member of the conservative National Action Party, but was previously associated with the left-wing Party of the Democratic Revolution.

It is unclear why Almaraz was taken. Authorities say they are investigating the case, including who might be involved in the abduction.

Zacatecas state is known for activity involving the Jalisco New Generation Cartel and the Sinaloa Cartel, both accused of attacking civilians and politicians.

A car bomb exploded outside a municipal police headquarters in Ojo Caliente, Zacatecas state, in August, injuring 11 people and damaging about 30 homes. Officials said the attack may have been retaliation by an organised crime group after a recent arrest.

In June 2021, police discovered the bullet-ridden bodies of 18 men after an apparent gun battle between suspected drug cartels in Zacatecas state.
