https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Evan Gershkovich on prison, Russia and liberty
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: Alexander Marrow
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
When masked agents of Russia’s FSB security service wrestled Wall Street Journal reporter Evan Gershkovich to the floor of a restaurant in the Urals city of Yekaterinburg on March 29, 2023, he became the first U.S. journalist to be arrested on espionage charges in Russia since the Cold War. He was later sentenced to 16 years in prison before being freed in an East-West prisoner swap in August 2024. Gershkovich, the Journal and the U.S. government all strongly deny the allegation that he was a spy.

In his recently released book “This Cursed Beautiful Land,” Gershkovich, an American citizen whose parents emigrated from the Soviet Union before he was born, details his experience in prison and the cast of characters that he met along the way, from cellmates to investigators. All the while, he continued reporting, uncovering details of what he says was an elaborate FSB sting operation and the mechanics of the swap that would ultimately set him free.

Speaking to Reuters from Canada, the latest stop on a global book tour, Gershkovich reflects on his arrest, his time in prison and Vladimir Putin’s Russia.

This conversation has been edited and condensed for clarity.

In the book, we read of your two personas: the American, Evan, and the Russian, Vanya. How do they differ and does Vanya live on now that you’re out of prison?

My American friends always would say that I’m super pessimistic, and then my Russian friends would say that I’m much too optimistic. I always thought that it was in between, but in prison I clearly became more Vanya in the sense that my reaction was I can’t change anything about this. It was this fatalistic resignation to the reality. I had American friends saying, “We’re gonna get you out tomorrow.” And I knew that wasn’t the case. This was gonna be a really hard swap. So it’s resigning yourself to it and also treating it with dark humor.

You can’t deal with the situation, so you might as well laugh at it. And then I get back after the swap and that side starts receding (and) Evan starts coming back. I’m living in the Western world again, I’m speaking English all the time. But I think I found a perfect balance. My girlfriend’s Russian, my family hasn’t changed, so I speak Russian in my daily life, but I’m not so fatalistic and deeply resigned to the situation around me anymore. I think my optimism is back.

Let’s go back to your arrest in March 2023. Did you feel vulnerable then?

I actually felt more vulnerable in late 2022 than I did in early 2023, when I was no longer followed (overtly by security agents). In late 2022, the environment was shifting. The community of foreign correspondents (were thinking): Has this unwritten rule of us being treated as quasi-diplomats changed?

And then there was the address when (President) Vladimir Putin told the FSB to do a better job of catching spies. I was talking about this with a colleague who has Russian citizenship and a foreign citizenship and we still thought that if you’re a foreigner, you still have this special (status). So I gained this false sense of security in early 2023 that I think (the FSB) helped me feel. There was a naivete, of course, but I think I was just misreading signals. They’d done a good job of making me feel more comfortable.

You write in the book at one point that you felt some pride at being on the inside, a thought that you immediately pushed out of your mind. Looking back now, how do you reflect on the experience?

I think it’s easier for the person in prison, in a way. Once you get your bearings and you understand what’s happening to you, you can figure out, okay, I can handle this in a certain way. But your loved ones, it’s a black box to them the whole time. And there’s a helplessness to it and that never really goes away. But having ended up there, I think one coping mechanism I had was I can’t really change the fact that I’m here now and I have to accept it.

And it is, frankly, an interesting place to be. So I might as well report on it and try to understand it and come away with something valuable for the rest of us. We have all these brilliant books about the Gulag and that history in the Soviet period because Stalin and his government arrested scores of writers and journalists, and we came away with some of the Soviet Union’s best literature.

The difference with mine is I have a foot in both worlds. I wasn’t a Soviet citizen or a Russian citizen getting arrested. I was an American with a Russian-Soviet background. So I can try to place myself in that canon of literature, but also be doing the work of the foreign correspondent and explaining this place that has been an enigma to foreigners for so long, and be your tour guide into this place.

You moved from Moscow’s Lefortovo prison to a larger prison in Yekaterinburg and really seemed to take it in your stride. Did you feel yourself hardening while in Lefortovo?

Absolutely. I had this one cellmate (in the second prison); I describe him as a street kid, a street brawler, a kind of “patzan.” He had a very stoic way of approaching prison. I’m naturally a bit stoic and he had a really tough exterior. And I think that started happening with me. I had decided I won’t let myself cry, but I also won’t let myself get angry at the system. So what happens is you start crafting this toughened exterior over time. And I think that’s a coping mechanism and a survival tactic. When I got to the second prison, I was starved of and dying for human interaction. It’s almost like no matter what, I was probably more steeled to it and more ready for it, but I was also so eager to have any kinds of conversations that I could have after 15 months of serious isolation.

How has your experience shaped your view of Russia?

I think to be disillusioned with a place, you had to have had illusions in the first place. I’ve described my arrest as a shock, but not a surprise, because it’s not a surprise that they might do a thing like that.

To me, it was a shock that they crossed this red line of not treating a foreign correspondent anymore like a quasi-diplomat who you kick out. We know from independent polling that more than two-thirds of Russians want the war to end. But they also don’t seem to want to state their opinion about the war because that can land them in prison for up to 10 years. So, are they pro-Putin but anti-war? Are they pro-war but anti-Putin? Are they anti-both? We don’t really know. And prison felt like a lot of the same kinds of characters, people who had checked out politically.

I met a prison guard who told me he was trying not to focus on what was going on around him. And I asked him what he thinks about the war, and he tells me he can’t talk about that. So that was, I think, a confirmation that even people in the system don’t agree with everything that’s going on.

You intersperse the book with snippets of wisdom from the books you read during your time in prison. How many did you read?

I think it was 75. Prisoners are some of the best readers because you’re so isolated from the outside sensory world that when you read it’s an incredibly intoxicating experience. It’s very psychedelic. I mean, reading already is, right? You just have words on a page and then you imagine images from these words on a page, but in prison it’s especially so because you’re really living it. It felt like talking to real people when I was reading.

https://www.dw.com/en/pope-leo-urges-arg.title: Pope Leo urges Argentina's Milei to put people before the economy
https://www.dw.com/en/pope-leo-urges-arg.text:
Pope Leo XIV has urged Argentina to protect democracy and ensure economic growth benefits the poor, delivering a message to President Javier Milei over austerity, social welfare and political divisions.

Pope Leo XIV arrived in Argentina on Sunday, urging to protect democracy and ensure economic growth benefits the poor.

The pope's remarks were widely watched for criticism of President Javier Milei's harsh austerity programs and cuts affecting social services.

While Leo did not address the government's policies directly, he said "the economy must be at the service of the people, rather than people being at the service of the economy."

Talking to Milei and other government officials, he pointed to the plight of those who, "despite hard work, nonetheless struggle to meet their household's needs."

With regards to democracy, he said it was "part of Argentina's heritage that needs to be safeguarded."

The visit to Buenos Aires marks the second leg of the pope's South America tour and is the first papal visit to Argentina in nearly 40 years.

The 71-year old pontiff, who underwent surgery for lung cancer less than a month ago, arrived from Uruguay and is scheduled to visit several cities in the Catholic-majority country before continuing to Peru on Wednesday.

Milei's policies have in the past drawn strong criticism from Argentina's Catholic Church, particularly cuts affecting social services, pensions, disability assistance and public universities.

The Argentine leader, a close ally of US President Donald Trump, has defended his aggressive spending cuts as necessary to stabilize the country's ailing economy and curb inflation.

Annual inflation has fallen from more than 200% to approximately 33% under his administration, but households continue to face financial pressure, and there's been anger over public-sector layoffs and business closures.

In the past, he agressively dismissed criticsm from the Catholic Church, going as far as calling Leo's predecessor, Pope Francis, an "imbecile." He had later though softened his tone and met with Francis in Rome.

On Sunday, Milei struck a significantly more conciliatory note, praising Francis as an "exceptional figure" and the "most important Argentine in history."

Pope Leo also stressed the need to safeguard democracy in the country.

"Those who exercise authority have a duty to act with prudence, to acknowledge the limits of the power entrusted to them, and to direct their decisions toward the good of the entire community."

The Pope's words carry particular significance ahead of Argentina's presidential election in 2027, in which Milei has said he will seek another term.

The president's aggressive rhetoric and frequent attacks on journalists and political opponents are widely seen as part of an increasing political polarization in the country.

Leo told Milei that strengthening democracy required a "willingness to listen" and the "careful use of words."

His visit marks the first time a pope has traveled to Argentina since John Paul II's trip in 1987. It also brings renewed attention to the legacy of Francis, the country's first pope, who died in April 2025 without returning to his homeland during his 12-year papacy.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmwy.title: Society needs to act to help white working-class pupils, inquiry says
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmwy.text:
Action from "across society" is needed to help improve the educational outcomes of white working-class children, the co-chair of an independent inquiry looking into the issue has said.

The inquiry's first report, published this summer, concluded that once-in-a-generation reforms were needed to fix a system "not serving the interests of white working-class children".

The next phase will focus on early years children and teenagers aged 14 to 19, aiming for a stronger start at primary school and improving older students' routes through education into successful careers.

Education Secretary Lucy Powell said she was "backing" the inquiry to "get to the heart of the barriers holding children back".

Inquiry co-chair and former education secretary Baroness Morris said the next phase of the inquiry's work will consider "what needs to be done".

"This isn't just the responsibility of schools but calls for action from across society," she said.

The Independent Inquiry into White Working Class Educational Outcomes was commissioned by the multi-academy trust Star Academies, and is supported by the Department for Education.

It spoke to thousands of young people and their parents, as well as hundreds of teachers.

Education data about white working class pupils was also analysed as part of the year-long review, looking at the 1.25 million young people in England who are white British and in receipt of free school meals.

The inquiry found a growing belief among white working-class families that the current education system does not guarantee future success.

In the summer, the inquiry also acknowledged that the true scale of white working-class disadvantage is "likely to be substantially larger", as the education data they looked at did not include families who were on low incomes but did not receive free school meals.

Since then, all families receiving Universal Credit have become eligible for free school meals.

Under the new phase of the inquiry, practical recommendations for government, schools, colleges and other organisations working with white working-class communities will be developed.

This action will include a research programme looking at the routes taken by teenagers aged 14 to 19, investigating how schools can work with communities to provide clearer pathways into further study and successful employment.

The new phase of the inquiry will also look at how schools can ensure the transition from primary to secondary school builds strong foundations.

"Right now, too many white working-class children are falling behind at every stage of their education," Powell said.

"That is why I am backing this independent inquiry to get to the heart of the barriers holding children back - from their first steps into school, through to the opportunities and choices they have as teenagers into further study, training or work."

It comes after Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced plans to open up new technical routes from age 14 in England over the summer.

The prime minister said he was "on a mission" to reduce the number of young people not in education, employment or training - known as "Neet".

Currently, nearly a million young people are classed as Neet.

Former minister Alan Milburn's interim report found that children who are not school-ready at aged four or five are nearly three times as likely to be Neet by ages 16 to 17.

A final report by Milburn is expected to set out his recommendations for tackling the issue in the coming weeks.

https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.title: Wagga Wagga family members of alleged DV murderer charged with being accessories after the fact
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.author: Caitlin Cassidy
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text:
Danielle Madgwick died in regional NSW in September after suffering multiple stab wounds to her upper body

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Family members of a man accused of the domestic violence murder of a 23-year-old woman in south-western New South Wales have been charged with being accessories to the alleged crime.

Emergency services were called to a Wagga Wagga home on the morning of 19 September where they found Danielle Madgwick suffering multiple stab wounds to her upper body. She died at the scene.

That same evening, Adam Mark Perrim, 31, who was alleged to be Madgwick’s partner, was arrested and charged with alleged domestic violence murder. He briefly appeared in court but did not apply for bail and was remanded to reappear on 18 November.

On Monday, NSW police said they had raided on the weekend the same house where Madgwick was found. Officers arrested two men, aged 18 and 56, and a 53-year-old woman in connection with the alleged murder in mid-September.

The trio was taken to Wagga Wagga police station, with each individual charged with being an accessory after the fact to murder. They appeared in court on Saturday for a committal hearing and were refused bail to next appear on 23 December.

Court documents state those arrested on the weekend were Perrim’s brother, Bailey Perrim, his father, George Maxwell Richard Perrim, and his mother, Julie Ann Collins.

Police will allege in court all three knew Madgwick.

Her death was one of three separate cases across the state investigated as domestic violence-related homicides that weekend.

The New South Wales premier, Chris Minns, said at the time the alleged crimes were “shocking” and his thoughts were with the families and communities of the three women.

Sign up to Breaking News Australia

Get the most important news as it breaks

after newsletter promotion

Madgwick’s father, Heath Madgwick, paid tribute to his daughter on social media last month on what would have been her 24th birthday.

“Words cannot describe the amount of emotions, thoughts and feelings that have been experienced over the last 4 weeks,” he wrote.

“There’s been enough tears to fill the world’s oceans over and over, I miss you like you wouldn’t believe, your beautiful smile, your silly laugh, our goofy video calls, the groan and eye roll I’d get with every ‘dad joke’, those are memories I’ll treasure for a lifetime.”

According to the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, a woman was killed every 11 days in 2024-25 by her intimate partner.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.title: Drone attack suspends production at Iraq’s Khor Mor gasfield
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.text:
A drone attack on the Khor Mor gasfield in the semi-autonomous Kurdish region of northern Iraq has caused a fire at the facility and cut power to the region, according to Iraqi and Kurdish officials.

The Sunday night attack left more than 70 percent of the Kurdish region without power.

It was not clear who was responsible for the attack or whether it was related to the United States and Israel’s war on Iran.

Al Jazeera’s fact-checking agency Sanad has verified footage of smoke and flames rising from the vicinity of the gasfield in the Sulaimaniyah governorate.

Omid Ahmed, spokesperson for the Kurdistan Regional Government’s Ministry of Electricity, said the attack suspended gas supply to power plants in the cities of Erbil, Sulaimaniyah, Bazian, Chamchamal and Duhok, the official Iraqi News Agency (INA) reported.

The strike knocked between 2,500 and 2,800 megawatts of electricity generation off the grid, he said.

He added that the ministry would provide electricity to critical facilities, such as hospitals and water treatment plants, by operating hydroelectric power stations and other plants that run on alternative fuel.

Al Jazeera’s Peter Smith, reporting from Baghdad, cited security sources as saying the explosive-laden drone struck the Khor Mor gas storage facility, reducing the energy grid’s capacity by 70 to 80 percent.

Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi said there were no casualties as a result of the attack, based on an initial assessment, the INA reported.

Al-Zaidi also directed that a joint investigative committee be formed with the relevant authorities in the Kurdish region to investigate the circumstances surrounding the attack, INA reported.

The attack comes amid heightened regional tensions. A drone strike hit the same facility last year, with no group having claimed responsibility.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/china-wh.title: China wholesale inflation hits over four-year high as consumer measure slows
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/china-wh.author: Lim Hui Jie
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/china-wh.text:
Producer prices in China grew at the fastest rate since June 2022, accelerating for the third month in a row.

The PPI for October came in at 5.7%, compared to the 5.3% expected by economists polled by Reuters.

Consumer inflation in China slowed to 0.7% in October, its first deceleration after two straight months of increases.

The figure missed expectations of a 0.8% rise from economists polled by Reuters, and was lower than the 0.9% seen in September.

The Chinese economy has shown some signs of expansion recently. It grew faster than expected in the third quarter, and September saw a sharp beat in retail sales.

https://www.france24.com/en/france/20261.title: Europe to press US on Ukraine peace and Iran at Paris G7 ministers talks
https://www.france24.com/en/france/20261.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/france/20261.text:
Foreign ministers of the G7 group meet in Paris from Monday for two days of talks expected to see European powers press the United States to seek a fair settlement for Ukraine in the war against Russia and deter Washington from further military action against Iran.

Ministers from the leading industrialised nations of Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States will be gathering with preoccupations strikingly similar to those of the last such meeting in March.

Russia's war against Ukraine following the February 2022 full-scale invasion of its neighbour is grinding towards its fifth anniversary. And Washington is still not ruling out new attacks against Iran even after the defeat of President Donald Trump's Republicans in the midterms.

All eyes will be on US Secretary of State Marco Rubio who is due to attend both days, unlike the March meeting where he only came for one.

READ MORE
Kremlin says meeting between Putin and Zelensky at Miami G20 'impossible'

This G7 ministerial meeting, one of the final acts of the French G7 presidency that saw President Emmanuel Macron host Donald Trump for the leaders' summit this summer in the lakeside resort of Evian, had long been scheduled to be held in the southern port city of Marseille.

But at the last minute the event was moved to Paris, with only scheduling reasons given for the change.

The visit by Rubio -- seen by US media as a potential candidate to succeed Trump -- will be his first abroad since the midterms. Washington will also in 2027 take over the G7 presidency from France.

The meeting coincides with US-mediated talks with Moscow and Kyiv in Abu Dhabi scheduled for Tuesday and Wednesday on ending the Ukraine war, with Europe concerned Kyiv must not be forced to accept disadvantageous conditions.

French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot told RTL radio that on this occasion "Europeans will be represented and France will be in Abu Dhabi to participate in these talks".

Trump stoked fears of a US pivot toward the Kremlin by predicting a "very big" deal with Russia involving not only the Ukraine war but "all of Europe".

Jared Kushner, the US president's envoy and son-in-law, said the United States was working on "a broader European security architecture that can help establish the conditions for lasting peace", a concept met with scepticism in the past by Europe.

On Iran, Trump has not ruled out new strikes, including at so-called Pickaxe Mountain, a suspected nuclear site which Tehran denies is such a facility. Europeans, however, are eager to see a resolution and shipping traffic return to normal in the Strait of Hormuz energy transit hub.

"We're dealing with them now," Trump said of the Iranians Friday. "They want to make a deal very badly."

READ MORE
G7 & co: Who rules the new world?

The sidelines of the meeting will also see the French finance ministry hosting on Monday a donor conference to raise funds to repair the dome protecting the nuclear reactor that exploded in Ukraine's Chernobyl in 1986 after it was damaged in a Russian strike last year.

Around 500 million euros is required but only just over half has been raised so far with a target date of spring 2027 to muster the rest of the funds, the French finance ministry told AFP.

Even though the meeting was moved to Paris, Marseille will still host the launch of a network of 14 global ports uniting to combat drug trafficking, which has become a major scourge in the southern city, Barrot said.

As he addressed reporters while preparing to leave for France, Rubio declined to comment directly on Trump's and the Republicans' crushing loss in the US midterm elections.

"It is not uncommon to have a division of power in this country," Rubio told reporters, alluding to the fact that Trump will now see both houses of Congress controlled by the Democrats.

Asked about widespread protests in France, Rubio added that he was not worried and trusted US counterparts on the ground who advised him it is safe to attend the G7 meeting.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/t.title: Alcaraz downs Shelton in final to claim maiden Paris Masters title
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/t.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Carlos Alcaraz's Paris Masters triumph made it five title wins in the calendar year. (Getty Images: Ibrahim Ezzat/NurPhoto)

Carlos Alcaraz has beaten Ben Shelton in the final of the Paris Masters, winning the tournament for the first time in his career.

Alcaraz downed the American 7-6 (5), 7-5, exacting revenge after being beaten by Shelton in the US Open semifinal earlier this year.

The Paris win took Alcaraz's total to five titles for the calendar year and 29 titles overall.

Carlos Alcaraz says he feels proud of taking "one step forward mentally" after following up his Vienna title last week with a 7-6 (5), 7-5 victory over Ben Shelton in the Paris Masters final.

The Spanish showman, who missed more than four months of the season because of an injured right wrist, continued his late-season surge in style.

He has won all three finals he has reached since the US Open two months ago.

Alcaraz took his total to five titles for the year and 29 overall, including the Japan Open last month.

The second-seeded Alcaraz threw his arms out wide in celebration after clinching victory on his second match point with a two-handed backhand winner down the line at the indoor Plenitude Arena.

The seven-time grand slam champion cracked a broad smile and briefly appeared to cry after earning a ninth Masters title and first in Paris.

"It is something I have been chasing for a long time. Some of the toughest defeats I ever had in my career I have had here," Alcaraz said.

"Finally, I got my level here. I found the right path and the right way to do things."

With the season-ending ATP Finals in Turin starting next Sunday he feels in a good position to win that trophy for the first time, too.

"I would say this week I made one step forward mentally," Alcaraz said.

"Trying to be positive, trying to stay strong mentally. I'm happy I controlled my emotions every single match."

Alcaraz won for the fourth time in five meetings with Shelton, who had beaten Alcaraz in a quarterfinal marathon at the US Open ending at 3:33am.

Shelton went on to reach the final, where he lost to Alexander Zverev.

There was to be no late marathon finish between Carlos Alcaraz and Ben Shelton this time around. (Getty Images: Ibrahim Ezzat/NurPhoto)

Alcaraz saved six break points in the first set of Monday morning's final and overcame a break of serve in the second set by breaking the third-seeded Shelton straight back, no mean feat considering Shelton had 12 aces compared to six for Alcaraz.

"He is always in a position to attack after that serve," Alcaraz said.

"It is really difficult to dominate that ball. It is not only coming fast, it is coming with a lot of power."

Alcaraz, 23, did not drop a set in Vienna. But it was harder work in Paris and he almost went out on Friday, saving two match points against Taylor Fritz in their quarterfinal.

Shelton, 24, was seeking his eighth title overall and third Masters, having twice won the Montreal title.

The American recently added Juan Carlos Ferrero to his coaching staff, following on from Alcaraz's split with long-time coach Ferrero last year.

There is clearly no animosity between the players over that. Both congratulated each other's shots, and Alcaraz made a point of walking around the net to hug Shelton and pat him on the chest after winning.

Both blessed with speed and agility, Alcaraz and Shelton drew each other to the net throughout, trading low, angled volleys.

Ben Shelton says he learns a lot from playing in big matches against the best. (Getty Images: Sport News/Quality Sport Images)

Pushing the other to the extremities of the court, there were some improbable retrieves, including one by Shelton in the ninth game when the American almost did the splits.

Shelton had an early advantage when he had Alcaraz 0-40 down in the fourth game. The Spaniard went on to save four break points before finally holding.

In the second set, Alcaraz was 4-2 down but broke Shelton back when he hit a forehand long from the back of the court.

After that he definitively changed the momentum.

Shelton was "frustrated" at the missed opportunities, especially against someone like Alcaraz.

"The window is small. If you miss your chance, it's likely that another isn't going to come," he said. "It also speaks to his level, his ability to be clutch."

That is the next step for Shelton, who believes this defeat and the US Open final loss to Zverev will serve him well.

"When you get to play against the best consistently in big matches, I think that you learn so much," he said.

"Now going to Turin against the eight best players in the world, that's the positions that I want to be in."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/c.title: Coach Aloisi oversees stunning capitulation in Chinese Super League title race
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/c.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Chengdu Rongcheng head coach John Aloisi said he would not be drawn on whether he would resign after the team's spectacular capitulation.  (Getty Images: Masashi Hara)

Chengdu Rongcheng needed just one point from its final four games to claim the Chinese Super League title.

John Aloisi's team went on to lose all four games, surrendering a 14-point lead and the title to Dalian Yingbo, which had a better head-to-head record.

Socceroos legend Aloisi brushed away questions about whether he would resign after the capitulation.

John Aloisi's hopes of beginning his new coaching adventure with a title have spectacularly failed after the former Western United mentor's side capitulated on the final matchday.

The Socceroos legend was looking to become the next Australian to guide a team in China's top league to a championship after Kevin Muscat led Shanghai Port to glory in 2024 and 2025.

Aloisi's Chengdu Rongcheng were in the box seat to do so, leading the competition by 14 points with five rounds remaining and needing to pick up just one point to secure a maiden title.

The Sichuan club had also been top of the standings since the opening day, but things began to unravel when they lost three consecutive games while their main chasers, Dalian Yingbo, recorded three successive victories.

Going into the final matchday on Sunday, Dalian began three points behind Chengdu and defeated Tianjin Jinmen Tigers 3-1 in front of 60,000 fans.

Aloisi's club still only needed a point, but by 63 minutes in, they were 3-1 down to their final opponents Shandong Taishan.

Brazilian forward Wellington Silva did pull one back for Chengdu but they couldn't find the all-important equaliser, and Dalian claimed the title.

While Chengdu had a superior goal difference, the Chinese Super League prioritises head-to-head records between teams level on points and Dalian had won both meetings between them.

Footage showed furious fans yelling at Aloisi and his players at the team hotel following the match, with police stepping in to push the angry supporters back.

"We are indeed very disappointed not to have won the championship. We are in a very despairing state. There is nothing else to say," Aloisi told local media via a Chinese translator.

"I want to say sorry to everyone. We certainly know that our fans have travelled a long way to fight alongside us and support us.

"Right now, my only feeling is one of great dejection and disappointment, because we could see the trophy right in front of us, but could not get it."

Aloisi came to the Chinese Super League in January hoping to replicate the success he found with Western United in the A-League.

He led his team to the competition's championship in the 2021/2022 season, but his coaching career was thrown into limbo when the Melbourne-based club was placed into "hibernation" following legal issues and financial collapse last year.

He brushed away questions about whether he would resign because of the failure to secure the title in China.

"Now is not the time to talk about this," Aloisi said.

"As a team, together with the club and everyone, we need to review where we fell short in our past five matches. We need to face our problems, and then work on those aspects."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/a.author: Jano Gibson
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/a.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Transport Accidents and Incidents

TT-Line says the new Spirit of Tasmania vessels are no longer using autopilot in Port Phillip Bay as a precaution. (ABC News: Harrison Tippet)

The two new Spirit of Tasmania ferries have suffered separate steering faults near Geelong in recent weeks.

Operator TT-Line has revealed the ships are no longer using autopilot during their transit of Port Phillip Bay.

The Australian Transport Safety Bureau is investigating the steering incidents, with a report due by the middle of next year.

The operator of the new Spirit of Tasmania ferries has suspended autopilot use during transits of Port Phillip Bay as it probes the ships' steering faults.

Spirit IV was on its fifth-ever passenger voyage last Thursday when its primary steering system failed as it neared the bay en route to Geelong.

The issue occurred when the steering control was switched from autopilot to manual mode.

A back-up steering system ended up being used, and a tugboat was called to escort the ferry to Geelong, delaying its scheduled arrival by about four hours.

A track map shows Spirit IV made several turns outside Point Lonsdale before entering Port Phillip Bay. (ABC News: Hamed Akrami)

The incident came after a separate steering fault caused its sister ship, Spirit V, to briefly move outside the bay's charted shipping lane during a trial voyage in October.

TT-Line explains 'frustratingly minor' steering issue that caused four hour delay

Both matters are now under investigation by the Australian Transport Safety Bureau.

On Monday, TT-Line chairman Ken Kanofski said last week's incident on Spirit IV involved a "frustratingly minor issue".

"There's an ongoing investigation, and I don't want to prejudice that by kind of declaring exactly that everything's been dealt with," Mr Kanofski told 936 ABC Hobart.

"When Spirit IV docked in Geelong, an inspection found a frustratingly minor issue with mechanical electrical processes in the steering console itself.

Ken Kanofski, pictured in May, says the steering issue on Spirit IV was caused by a "frustratingly minor issue". (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

Mr Kanofski said the autopilot, which allows a ship to automatically follow a pre-determined route, is no longer being used when approaching and departing Geelong.

"So at the moment, we're not using autopilot in the bay, in Geelong, in Port Phillip Bay," Mr Kanofski said.

However, the autopilot will still be used once the ship reaches the open waters of Bass Strait, he said.

Mr Kanofski said the autopilot was never used for the ferries' arrival and departure at Devonport, in Tasmania's north-west.

"Obviously in Geelong you come in through the heads, and you've got quite a long way to navigate to get to port.

"In Devonport it's a very short distance, and so that's always been a completely manual process.

"But we've taken a range of interim measures to ensure that the ships and the passengers are safe, and that's our number one priority here."

The new Spirit of Tasmania ferries began carrying passengers across Bass Strait in late October. (Supplied: David Wallace)

The ABC has asked TT-Line when it plans to resume its use of autopilot during transits of Port Phillip Bay.

On Sunday, Spirit IV conducted an exercise off Devonport that was described by TT-Line as a "planned, routine check of its equipment".

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Cities turn to private parking garages for vehicle storage amid flood risks
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
As torrential rain and flooding become increasingly frequent, more local governments are partnering with private businesses to make multistory parking garages and other facilities available as storage sites for vehicles.

During the heavy rains brought about by Typhoon Dujuan in September, many facilities were opened free of charge under such agreements.

Challenges remain in the initiative, however, including in matters such as securing facilities in safe locations designated on a city’s flood hazard map, informing residents of their availability and ensuring that drivers can evacuate safely after parking their vehicles.

The city of Kashiwa in Chiba Prefecture opened temporary parking areas at municipal facilities and the Aeon Mall Kashiwa shopping center on Sept. 21 and 22 as the typhoon approached.

At the mall, about 400 parking spaces, including part of its multistory parking garage, were made available free of charge.

The city publicized the arrangements through disaster-prevention emails and social media. The drivers of 42 vehicles used the facility.

According to the city’s disaster prevention and safety division, it had previously signed an agreement with the mall covering the supply of food and other necessities during disasters.

The city requested the mall to also open its parking facilities after heavy rain in August left unprecedented damage, including flooded vehicles found in various parts of the prefecture.

The typhoon in September marked the third time the arrangement with the mall had been put into effect.

“We have strengthened cooperation with the mall based on previous experience, and this allowed us to reduce the time needed to open the parking area,” said Taisuke Katakami, an official of the division.

The city of Shizuoka has had agreements with supermarkets, pachinko parlors and other businesses since 2024. It now has 13 participating locations offering a total of about 2,500 parking spaces.

Residents in areas without access to such facilities have called for the program to be expanded.

However, increasing the number of sites is challenging because facilities must be located in areas designated as safe on the city’s flood hazard maps, according to its crisis management division.

The program accepts vehicles only, meaning after leaving their vehicles, drivers must either return home or evacuate to another location.

“The municipal government will make every effort to provide information promptly so that drivers can evacuate safely after leaving their cars,” an official of the division said.

Meanwhile, the city of Hiroshima, which was hit by torrential rain and floods in July 2018, has secured about 4,800 parking spaces at nine locations, including supermarkets.

The facilities serve as evacuation sites for people who have difficulty evacuating on foot, such as older residents, as well as those who wish to evacuate with their pets or those wanting to shelter in their cars.

At two of the locations, including an outlet mall, city officials are dispatched to help manage the sites when they are opened.

The city first signed an agreement with a private facility in 2021, allowing people to take shelter in their vehicles as a way to avoid being infected with COVID-19.

“With floods occurring frequently across the country in recent years, public interest in evacuating vehicles has grown further,” an official at the city’s disaster prevention division said, adding that the city continues to approach private businesses to secure more evacuation sites.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.title: Japan says three-day yen intervention lifted currency in summer
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.text:
Japan has said it intervened in the currency market three times over the summer to prop up the yen, confirming previously reported actions that included Tokyo’s first coordinated operation with the U.S. to support the currency in nearly three decades.

The data showing three days of intervention came as a surprise, as traders had previously thought action came over two days. Tokyo bought a daily record of ¥7.98 trillion ($50.4 billion) on July 30 and another ¥5.55 trillion and ¥1.87 trillion in the following days, according to the daily intervention data for last quarter released by the Finance Ministry on Monday.

The total amount of ¥15.4 trillion over those three days marked Japan’s largest monthly spending on yen-buying intervention. Japan and the U.S. previously confirmed they had jointly entered the currency market on July 31, their first coordinated operation to support the yen since 1998.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.title: ‘Feeling guilty’: price hikes a tough sell in Japan despite inflation
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.text:
When Japan’s “symbol of affordability” Uniqlo decided to increase the price of its basic socks last month, it sparked a backlash before the clothing titan made an immediate U-turn.

That came after Italian-style family restaurant chain Saizeriya issued an almost groveling apology as it decided to add ¥20 ($0.13) to the price of its trademark Milanese Doria, lamenting its “lack of effort.”

The very public angst — including in one of the world’s most recognizable clothing brands — highlights the struggles Japanese firms face as they battle rising costs in a country where decades of deflation have nurtured a consumer class averse to higher prices.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.title: Tokyo’s office rent boom spurs deals as Blackstone plans sale
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.author: Natalie Wong
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.text:
Interest rates at a 31-year high have yet to dent the office market in Tokyo, where surging rents are boosting investment activity.

Commercial-property investment across Japan hit ¥2 trillion ($13 billion) in the third quarter, the highest volume for the equivalent period since 2007, according to data from brokerage firm Jones Lang LaSalle (JLL). Office deals occupied 36% of the total deal volume — the largest portion — and nearly 70% of total investments were in the Tokyo region.

“Rent is increasing so investors are still able to see huge amounts of rental upside, especially if the current building’s office rent is lower than the market rate today,” Koji Naito, research director of capital markets at JLL Japan, said in an interview.

https://www.scmp.com/news/people-culture.text:
To ensure accuracy, a lawyer suggests the programme mandate a user agreement and hire experts to verify reports

A digital map of bed bug sightings has gained popularity in China but has also sparked controversy by allowing users to flag hotels where they claim to have found the insects with a single click.

Since its launch on September 21, the app has attracted 200,000 users, who have marked more than 600 hotels across China. Any user can flag a hotel on the map after claiming to have spotted bed bugs there, and the marks are visible to all users.

Some hotels have defended themselves, saying they were wrongly flagged, China Business News reported.

https://www.dw.com/en/germany-chancellor.title: Germany: Chancellor Merz to nominate Aigner for president
https://www.dw.com/en/germany-chancellor.text:
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz announced that he will nominate Ilse Aigner for federal president, paving the way for her to be the first woman to hold the office. DW has more.

This is a roundup of the top stories from and about Germany on the weekend of Saturday, November 7, and Sunday, November 8, 2026:

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz announced to the Christian Democrat Union (CDU) party heads his intention to nominate Ilse Aigner as the country's next federal president, according to the dpa, AFP and Reuters news agencies.

She will replace Frank-Walter Steinmeier when he steps down at the end of his term early next year.

Aigner, who hails from Bavaria's conservative Christian Social Union (CSU) and is the president of the Bavarian state parliament, would be the first woman to hold the German president's position should she be elected on January 30.

Steinmeier is a member of the junior coalition partner SPD.

Merz will officially pitch Aigner's name for the job on Monday, when party leaders will gather to choose a joint candidate.

SPD and Green Party representatives have already voiced support for her candidacy.

The city of Moscow has officially unveiled a new commemorative plaque honoring one of communist East Germany's top Cold War spies, Markus Wolf.

The plaque was initially installed by Russia's Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR) at Nizhny Kislovsky Lane 8 in September to mark the site where Wolf and his family, who were religious Jews and communists, lived between 1934 and 1945 after fleeing Nazi Germany.

Wolf would go on to spend nearly 30 years at the top of the foreign department of East Germany's Ministry for State Security, or Stasi, and was considered one of the Cold War's ultimate spymasters.

The spymaster was long known as "the man without a face" by Western intelligence services because they had no idea what he looked like.

Wolf's ability to place agent Günter Guillaume within West German Chancellor Willy Brandt's inner circle, ultimately leading to Brandt's 1974 resignation, is considered to be one of his greatest successes.

Wolf's widow Andrea reportedly expressed her gratitude for the honor in a letter addressed to "all Russian friends." Wolf died in Berlin on November 9, 2006, at the age of 83.

The Berlin Police and the Berlin Public Prosecutor's Office on Sunday evening issued a joint statement announcing that they believe that a body found in an abandoned house in Brandenburg is in fact that of Lisa T., a 13-year-old Berlin girl who went missing on her way to school Tuesday morning.

Police in Brandenburg found the body, as well as an injured male whom they believe to be responsible for the child's death, when they acted on a tip from locals alerting them of a break-in.

Authorities say the man is in critical condition at a nearby hospital where he is under police guard. Further, authorities say the man's injuries were self-induced.

Police are now working to ascertain the man's identity.

On Friday, the police said that the girl had likely not disappeared voluntarily. On Saturday, they said that it must be assumed that she had been the victim of a crime.

Veteran keeper Manuel Neuer has been added to the list of walking wounded at Bundesliga top team FC Bayern Munich, suffering a torn foot tendon in his team's 2-1 victory in Mainz.

Neuer, who posted on social media that "an injury never comes at the right time, but it's part of the game," left the match just before the half.

Bayern released a statement saying that the champion goalie would be "out for the time being."

Though no further information was given, media reports suggested Neuer could be out for at least two months.

"I've been through this before, and I'll get through this one, too," said Neuer. "From now on: full focus on recovery. Until then, I will support the boys on the pitch wherever I can."

A two-time Champions League winner, Neuer made club history at the start of the match — his 550th in Germany's Bundesliga — as the oldest ever player to take the pitch for Bayern at age 40 years and 225 days.

The veteran's absence will only compound Bayern's injury woes as they battle on without head coach Vincent Kompany — who is recovering from an illness — as well as Jamal Musiala, Luis Diaz, Ismael Saibari and Serge Gnabry — all of whom are on long-term injured reserve.

As authorities in Poland try to make sense of yesterday's deadly shooting in Krakow, lists of victims' nationalities have been made public.

Of the six victims shot and killed at the city's market square on Saturday, four were women and two were men. Three of the women and one of the men were Polish, while the remaining woman was from Austria and the man from the UK.

Austrian, British, German, Portuguese and Russian passport holders were among the 15 individuals wounded by the Polish gunman.

German Federal President Frank-Walter Steinmeier's office on Sunday posted a statement of support on X, writing: "In this difficult hour, Germany stands in mourning and solidarity with Poland and its citizens."

Further, Steinmeier expressed his condolences to Polish President Karol Nawocki, saying, "my thoughts are with the victims and their families."

Researchers have confirmed the loss of the Schwarzmilzferner, the last glacier in the Allgäu Alps on the border between Germany and Austria.

Estimates by researchers say that the eastern Alps could be completely ice-free by 2070 due to climate change and rising global temperatures.

The glacier was located on the Austrian side of the mountain range at an altitude of 2,450 meters (8038 feet).

It can no longer be considered a glacier as it has lost over 4 meters in thickness and around half its volume earlier this year, glaciologist Cristoph Mayer told the dpa news agency.

Mayer said that the glacier will likely disappear "completely" by next summer.

The rapid melting came as Europe was hit by a massive heatwave over the summer of 2026.

"Even if there is heavy snowfall in winter, the ice masses are shrinking rapidly. Summers have now become too hot for them," Mayer said.

"As things stand, I expect the entire Eastern Alps to be ice-free between 2060 and 2070."

A 22-year-old man took down the German flag at the Reichstag building in Berlin and replaced it with a Palestinian flag, police said on Sunday.

The Reichstag building is the seat of the lower house of German parliament, the Bundestag. The large German flag that flies in front of the building is known as the Unity Flag, or Flagge der Einheit in German, as it commemorates the German reunification of 1990.

The man climbed up the flagpole using a climbing harness at around 11:30 a.m. local time (1030 UTC) and threw the German flag to the ground, police said.

He lowered himself back down on his own, according to police, after which he was taken into custody.

He was supported by two other men aged 20 and 32, according to the report.

Police have launched an investigation into a suspected case of denigration of the state and its symbols, damaging public property and trespassing.

The Palestinian flag was removed with the assistance of the fire department.

As the mast hoisting cable had been damaged in the incident, the German flag could not be immediately raised again.

A camel survived a collision with a bus in southern Germany.

The accident occurred on a rural road in Riedering, a town southeast of Munich in the state of Bavaria.

According to police, three camels escaped a fenced pasture, with one of them ending up on the road on which the accident occurred when the bus drove past it at 8am local time.

While the camel did not sustain any injuries, the bus suffered an estimated €500 ($552) worth of damage.

Bavarian Premier Markus Söder has spoken out in favor of military conscription in remarks seemingly in response to Defense Minister Boris Pistorius, who this week said he believed the draft was not necessary in the near future (see earlier entry in this blog).

"If our democracy is important to us, we have to stand up for it. That's why it is clear: We need true military conscription again," he wrote on X.

"Germany is threatened in a way it has not been in a long time," Söder wrote. "That is why we have to keep strengthening the Bundeswehr."

Söder, who also leads the conservative Christian Social Union (CSU), which forms part of Germany's coalition government, said the current large investments in equipment and infrastructure were not enough on their own.

"A new concept of defense for the country and its allies also needs more soldiers," he wrote.

In remarks published on Saturday, Pistorius told newspapers from the Funke media group that the Bundeswehr currently had some 190,000 members, the highest level in 13 years, meaning that voluntary recruitment measures were working.

"If this trajectory continues, we will have no problems with growth," he said, and there would not have to be "a discussion about conscription of whatever kind."

During Gen Z protests last weekend, young demonstrators called among other things for an end to any considerations of reintroducing military conscription.

Germany's largest union, IG Metall, has called on workers at a Mercedes-Benz plant outside Berlin to walk out for two hours on Monday amid stalled wage negotiations.

Employees at local car supplier Gestamp in Ludwigsfelde, a town south of Berlin, have also been called upon to take part in the industrial action.

IG Metall is demanding 5% more pay for the around 96,000 employees in the metal and electrical industry in the states of Berlin and Brandenburg as part of a 12-month collective wage agreement, as well as job and location security.

The strike is being called after the union failed to reach agreement in a third round of a wage dispute.

During a second round of talks, the employers presented a coordinated nationwide offer of a one-off payment next year and a 1.3% pay rise in July 2028, which was rejected by the union as inadequate.

Young people are increasingly denying the facts of the Holocaust or downplaying its horrors, according to the head of the Anne Frank Zentrum in Berlin.

In remarks made to the Catholic news agency KNA ahead of the 88th anniversary of the November pogroms in Germany, Veronika Nahm said that people attending traveling exhibitions organized by the center sometimes asked, "Is that even true?"

She said that people downplaying or denying the Holocaust was particularly apparent in social media posts connected with the center.

She said there were comments such as, "Why do you commemorate Anne Frank, why not a child in Gaza?"

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Nahm attributes the rise in such opinions to ignorance rather than bad intentions on the part of young people, saying they were not as well-informed on the topic in schools as they were 15 years ago.

"There has been a generational change of teachers. For many older teachers, it was close to their hearts, and it was mentioned in many places and subjects during lessons. That is different today," she said.

Nahm said it was important that visits by young people to sites commemorating the Holocaust be used to strengthen their feeling of empathy, something that worked particularly well with the story of Anne Frank.

The Anne Frank Zentrum in Berlin is a partner organization to the Anne Frank House in Amsterdam.

Anne Frank was a Jewish girl who hid in that house during the 1940-1945 German occupation of the Netherlands and wrote a famous diary, later published, about her experiences and feelings.

She was discovered and deported by the Nazis and died in the Bergen-Belsen concentration camp in early 1945.

The November pogroms, during which Jews and Jewish property and institutions were attacked, took place on November 9-10, 1938, across the German Reich at the instigation of Germany's Nazi regime.

Most people in Germany favor the government imposing a cap on prices for gasoline and diesel, a survey has shown.

The government is currently debating such a cap, which would replace a current fuel tax rebate that runs out at the end of the year.

According to the survey by the NIM Institute, 71% of the people asked said they would like the government to control fuel prices.

Altogether 66% of respondents were in favor of levying a windfall tax on oil corporations, which have been turning in massive profits amid shortages caused largely by the war in Iran.

Other measures to relieve the pressure on motorists amid surging fuel prices were less popular, according to the survey.

Just 56% of respondents wanted to see a rise in the allowed tax deduction for commuters, and just 52% favored direct payments from the state to drivers on low incomes.

German Environment Minister Carsten Schneider has said he hopes agreement will be reached on measures to limit global warming at the UN Climate Change Conference over the next two weeks.

"The faster global emissions fall, the faster we can bring the temperature curve back down to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit). At the same time, we must do more to protect people from the effects of heat waves, droughts and floods," Schneider said.

Schneider was referring to the target of limiting global warming to 1.5 C compared with pre-industrial levels agreed on under the Paris climate accords.

The UN said last month, however, that this target will be missed within the century, with most nations failing to reduce their greenhouse gas emissions by a significant amount.

Schneider also said moving toward electricity as the main source of energy was the best way to combat climate change, which is being driven largely by the human burning of fossil fuels such as oil and gas.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Schneider will be the only German Cabinet member to attend the  COP31 summit, which kicks off in Turkey on Monday.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz has decided to skip the event, citing "other commitments."

His decision has drawn considerable criticism, with leading German climate activist Luisa Neubauer saying it sent "the worst possible signal to the international community."

"It is unworthy of Germany and an insult, particularly to those nations around the world that are already facing an existential threat from rising sea levels," she said.

Media reports say Merz is planning a visit to an Italian restaurant with his wife and daughter for his 71st birthday on Wednesday while the summit is underway, leading Neubauer to describe his non-appearance as a "Bella Italia absence."

Nearly 200 states will convene for the summit in Antalya.

Police in Berlin are still looking for a 13-year-old girl who disappeared on the way to school on Tuesday.

In a statement, Berlin police said they could not rule out that the girl, who has been identified as Lisa T., "has been the victim of a crime."

"Based on the current state of the investigation, it is assumed that the child did not leave her home environment voluntarily," police said.

Around 220 police officers were deployed in the Marzahn district of the German capital on Saturday, with a police spokesman saying that the search was time-consuming because of the large number of houses and parks in the area.

The search began on Friday, supported by sniffer dogs and a police helicopter.

Women on the executive boards of Germany's leading listed companies were earning almost as much on average as their male colleagues in 2025, a study by consultancy EY says.

According to the study, female board members at companies listed on the DAX, MDAX and SDAX indices, not including chief executives, earned an average of €2.20 million ($2.45 million) last year.

That is a rise of 2.4% from 2024.

Their male counterparts, on the other hand, saw a nearly 2% reduction in their pay down to €2.23 million, which reduced the pay gap from €121,000 to €26,000.

The study also found that there were more women serving on executive boards in 2025 than a year previously, with 101 female board members compared with 88 in 2024 and just 33 in 2013.

"Women on executive boards are no longer the exception. That is also reflected in salaries," said EY partner Jens Massmann.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: Pope Leo delivers stinging rebuke of Milei’s austerity measures during Argentina visit
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Agence France-Presse
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
Pontiff tells Argentina’s president the economy must benefit all on second stop of 12-day Latin America tour

Pope Leo XIV has delivered a stinging critique of Argentine president Javier Milei’s harsh austerity measures, insisting growth must benefit all in a speech met with rapturous applause in Buenos Aires.

“The economy must be at the service of the people, rather than people being at the service of the economy,” he said on Sunday, shortly after landing in Argentina on the second leg of a Latin America tour.

Leo stressed the plight of those who, “despite hard work, nonetheless struggle to meet their household’s needs”.

He spoke out in defence of the poor and pensioners, insisting that “particular concern be shown for those affected by illness, dependency and disability” – a veiled reference to the government’s controversial cuts to disability assistance.

He also told Milei, known for his foul-mouthed diatribes, that strengthening democracy required a “willingness to listen” and the “careful use of words”.

Leo, 71, is on an ambitious 12-day tour of the continent, just three weeks after undergoing surgery for lung cancer.

The visit is the first by a pontiff to Argentina in nearly four decades, and Leo was met with calls to help mend deep divisions in the country after three years of austerity under Milei.

Argentina is the home country of the late pope, Francis, who Milei famously insulted for his pro-poor teachings.

Leo said he was “retracing” Francis’s steps.

Argentines are hoping the leader of the world’s 1.4 billion Catholics will help unite the country, which is bitterly divided between supporters and opponents of Milei.

“Just like the World Cup unites us, hopefully the pope will too,” said Liliana Deblauwe, a 68-year-old retired teacher who waited with hundreds of people to see the pope visit a monument to liberation hero Jose de San Martin.

Hundreds more chanting “Papa Leon” (Spanish for Leo) gathered outside the presidential palace, where he was hosted by Milei.

Brian Inacio Rodriguez, a 26-year-old job seeker, spent five days travelling overland from Ushuaia, at the very tip of South America, to see the pontiff.

He said he hoped he brought “much peace to Argentina”.

Leo arrived in Buenos Aires from Uruguay, where he began his first trip as pope to Latin America, the world’s most Catholic continent which is becoming increasingly secular.

In Uruguay, he condemned drug violence and urged an end to child poverty.

In Buenos Aires, he insisted on the importance of “personal integrity” in public office, stressing that “corruption undermines the confidence of citizens in their institutions.”

The Argentine stage of his visit aims to boost the flagging faith of a country left disappointed by Francis’s failure to visit during his papacy.

It will also act as a litmus test of support for the church. In a recent University of Buenos Aires poll, 57.7% of people identified as Catholic, down from about 90% in the 1960s.

Leo will visit a home for disabled people and a prison and celebrate three open-air masses.

The church has said it expects 7 million to attend the various events.

Milei came to office on a promise to revive Argentina’s ailing economy and tame runaway inflation by shrinking the welfare state, targeting public hospitals, universities and pensioners in particular.

The poverty rate has swung wildly since he came to power – increasing to 32.3% in September.

A close ally of US president Donald Trump, with a similar combative style, Milei had a tense relationship with Francis.

On the campaign trail the cost-cutting economist called his countryman an “imbecile” for championing social justice.

Once in office, however, he softened his tone, but he continues to heap insults on the press and opposition.

His relationship with Leo has so far been cordial, but the local Catholic church has heavily criticised him for treating key social services solely as a budgetary constraint.

Milei has also been criticised for restricting several democratic freedoms, including the right to protest. But he maintains a loyal supporter base for drastically reducing inflation.
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.summary: Pope Leo XIV is on a 12-day Latin America tour of the continent. He is on the second leg of his 12- day tour of Latin America. He has been criticised by Argentina's president Javier Milei for austerity measures.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/a.title: 'Dedicated' apprentice jockey critical after race meet fall
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/a.author: Lily Plass
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/a.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Ms Neale is known as a dedicated rider in racing circles.  (Supplied: Instagram )

Apprentice jockey Izzy Neale remains in hospital in critical condition after falling off her horse during the Cotton Cup in Warren.

Her horse, Marnoo, was euthanased after sustaining a near foreleg injury.

A scheduled race meeting for today in Scone has been postponed in response.

An apprentice jockey is fighting for her life after falling from a horse during a race in western NSW on the weekend.

Izzy Neale was riding in the Cotton Cup at Warren on Sunday when she suffered head injuries following a fall at the 400-metre mark during a 1,600m event.

The 22-year-old was treated onsite before being airlifted to Dubbo Hospital for further medical care, where she remains in a critical condition.

The horse she was riding, six-year-old Marnoo, suffered a near foreleg injury and was euthanased.

"The thoughts and heartfelt support of Racing NSW and the entire racing community are with Izzy, her family, friends and colleagues during this extremely difficult time," Racing NSW posted in a statement on X.

Fellow jockey Diego Montes de Oca was also dislodged from his horse, Shadow Dane.

He was transported to Dubbo hospital via road for injuries to his foot.

A Racing NSW spokesperson said Montes de Oca had since been discharged from hospital.

"Diego sustained soft tissue injuries to his left foot, with no fractures identified," the spokesperson said.

In a statement on social media, the Warren Jockey Club said its thoughts were with Izzy and her loved ones.

"The racing community is a close-knit one, and moments like these remind us just how much we stand together," the club said.

"We are all hoping for the very best for Izzy and are sending her strength, courage and our sincerest well wishes."

Race caller Colin Hodges said the mood turned "very glum" after Neale was dislodged in front of the roughly 600 people in the crowd

The veteran caller of 57 years said he still remembered her first race at the Condobolin Picnic Races in 2024, where she pulled off an upset.

"She'd driven hundreds and hundreds of kilometres to western NSW," he said.

"[The horse] was probably the outsider of the whole race meeting."

Ms Neale won her debut race at Condobolin.  (Supplied: Instagram )

Mr Hodges said Neale had assured her trainer at the Condobolin meet that she would ride well despite the odds.

"She certainly did because the horse was back running midfield and she just got into the perfect spot and won," he said.

Neale has had 88 wins out of 699 starts.

"She's become very, very successful," Mr Hodges said.

In a statement on X, Racing NSW said it had postponed a meet in Scone today following consultation with jockeys and trainers that were set to take part.

"The decision follows the serious race fall involving apprentice jockey Izzy Neale at Warren yesterday," the statement said.

Racing NSW will be conducting an inquiry into the incident.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/n.title: Teenage boy avoids jail over Sydney terror attack planning
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/n.author: Sarah Gerathy
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/n.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

The boy had just turned 14 when he was charged with committing acts in preparation for a terror attack in 2024. (AAP: Jessica Hromas)

A 16-year-old boy has been spared jail for preparing a terror plot after being exposed to extremist content on social media.

The boy was 14 when he was arrested in August 2024 after researching how to make a pressure-cooker bomb and potential target locations.

The judge found the planning "was not sophisticated".

A teenage boy who admitted he considered carrying out a mass terror attack at the Sydney Opera House after being exposed to extremist content on TikTok has been spared a prison sentence after a Supreme Court judge found there was "very little chance" of him reoffending.

The 16-year-old was handed a three-year community corrections order for the offence, which carries a maximum sentence of life in prison.

The boy, who cannot be identified, had just turned 14 when he was arrested at his Western Sydney home by federal police in August 2024 and charged with committing acts in preparation for a terror attack.

He pleaded guilty in August this year.

The court heard the teen had sought out online instructions about how to make a pressure-cooker bomb and researched potential target locations, including the finishing line of the Sydney Marathon at the Sydney Opera House.

But in sentencing, Supreme Court Justice Stephen Campbell found the level of planning was at the least serious end of the scale.

"The research was not sophisticated and he took no steps to cover his tracks" the judge said, noting the teen had not made any attempts to obtain the materials to make a bomb or settled on a date for an attack.

The teen told the court he had first been exposed to extremist material on TikTok which he found "interesting", and it led to him viewing increasingly violent material including some from Al Qaeda and recruitment propaganda from the Islamic State group.

The court heard that over a five-week period in 2024 the teen had shared extremist material with others online, praised Al Qaeda on encrypted messaging apps and attempted to contact the surviving Boston Marathon bomber in a US jail via email.

But the judge suggested the communications showed a "high level of naivety" and noted that the boy repeatedly "ducked" or "fobbed off" the question when the people he was chatting to asked him if he was going to carry out an attack.

He said when the boy was asked if he would try to make a bomb he had replied: "For now I cannot try to make it because my parents will see … but later on I will, inshallah."

When the same correspondent asked him if he wanted to learn how to plan an attack the teen replied: "For now I am just learning how to make [a bomb] but not planning."

"I accept his evidence that he was hesitant at best … about actually carrying out an attack."

Justice Campbell said since his arrest the teenager had renounced Islamic extremism and would benefit from continuing to live in a "loving home", with his parents who were from the persecuted Hazara minority in Afghanistan.

He said the couple had friends from a variety of cultural and religious backgrounds and had counselled their son that extremism was against their interpretation of Islam.

"The compelling evidence of remorse and acceptance of legal responsibility persuade me that his prospects of rehabilitation are excellent, "Justice Campbell said.

The teenager was handed a three-year community corrections order and told he must hand over the password to his phone to a youth justice officer, continue to undertake any deradicalisation or education programs as instructed and not have access to any encrypted messaging apps.

After he was sentenced he returned to sit between his parents in the courtroom, where his mother briefly rested her head on his shoulder and his father smiled.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Man arrested following string of attacks on women on Tokyo street
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
A 39-year-old man has been arrested over a physical attack on a woman on a street in Tokyo in October, with police suspecting he is behind a string of other similar attacks that took place on the same evening, according to investigative sources.

Hikaru Hamaguchi was arrested after he allegedly slapped a university student in her 20s across her left cheek while she was walking on a sidewalk in the Jimbocho district of Tokyo’s Chiyoda Ward at around 9 p.m. on Oct. 17. Hamaguchi fled by train after the alleged attack but was later apprehended at another station in Tokyo.

The sources said Hamaguchi is suspected of having attacked a total of seven female high school and university students over a period of about 15 minutes, punching some in the abdomen and delivering jumping kicks to others as he walked past them on the street.

The attacks appeared to have been random, and all seven victims are believed to have suffered minor injuries.

The Metropolitan Police Department is investigating the possibility that there were additional victims and is looking into the suspect’s motive.

The incidents came to light after police received a series of reports from several victims as well as witnesses of the alleged attacks.

The attacks appeared to have been random, and all seven victims are believed to have suffered minor injuries.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Man arrested after Ishikawa woman’s body found in forest
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
KANAZAWA, ISHIKAWA PREF. – The body of a woman was found in a forest in Ishikawa Prefecture following a statement by a man who was arrested for allegedly confining her.

The Ishikawa Prefectural Police arrested the man, Takashi Utsunomiya, 49, from the city of Hiroshima by Sunday. He is suspected of confining the woman, a 26-year-old resident of the Ishikawa city of Nonoichi, in a car and taking her from Nonoichi to Komatsu against her will from around 5:15 a.m. to 2:30 p.m. on Oct. 30.

Utsunomiya told the police that he killed the woman, Saya Nakada, and left her body in a mountainous area. Investigators found the body in a forest in the city of Awara in Fukui Prefecture, which borders Ishikawa, on Saturday.

Based on his statement, the Ishikawa police department will continue investigating the case and will consider murder charges.

The victim was employed at a restaurant and was believed to be dating Utsunomiya.

An autopsy determined that Nakada died of acute suffocation, indicating she was strangled or smothered, and that about a week had passed when her body was discovered.

Nakada consulted the Ishikawa police department in July, saying that she wanted to break off her relationship with Utsunomiya.

On Thursday, her parents reported to the police that they were unable to contact their daughter.

Utsunomiya emerged as a suspect partly from analysis of security camera footage. He was detained in the city of Hiroshima on Friday.

Utsunomiya told police that he put Nakada in the car but that he did not force her to get in the vehicle, according to investigative sources.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Iran suggests blasts are not U.S. attacks as both sides report ships hit
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
CAIRO – Iranian media suggested explosions in southern Iran on Saturday evening were related to Iranian military activities rather than U.S. strikes while both sides reported that shipping had been hit in or near the Strait of Hormuz.

Iran’s state television said officials had not confirmed any missile strikes on Iranian territory following blasts heard in several areas, including on Qeshm Island in the strait.

U.S. President Donald Trump had hinted at renewing major attacks on Iran after last week’s U.S. midterm elections but there has been no sign of a large-scale U.S. military operation, which Iran has said it would respond to by striking U.S. and Israeli targets.

Both sides have continued strikes on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, however, restricting exports of energy and other commodities vital to the world economy.

Iran’s state television said the evening explosions might be related to Iranian military activity in the waterway, where Iran said two vessels had hit mines and a third had caught fire.

The U.S. said its air force had disabled a vessel in the Gulf of Oman beyond the strait.

Tasnim news agency said two missiles had struck Qeshm Island, with no official information on possible damage. Neither Iran nor the U.S. has commented on that report. Washington said on Nov. 2 that it had struck the island in a limited defensive measure against Iranians using surface-to-air missiles against U.S. assets.

Since the U.S. and Israel began attacks on Iran in February, Tehran has sought the upper hand by hitting vessels in the Strait of Hormuz to block Gulf energy exports, while U.S. forces began blockading movements to and from Iranian ports in April.

The U.S. military said on Saturday evening that its air force had fired at the stern of a commercial vessel in the Gulf of Oman, disabling it as it tried to get through the blockade.

Iran’s Revolutionary Guards Navy said two oil tankers had caught fire after hitting mines while attempting to pass through an “unauthorized route” in the Strait of Hormuz. A third tanker had also suffered an explosion and caught fire, the semi-official Fars news agency reported later.

The reported strikes could not be confirmed.

Monitors from the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said a bulk carrier and military forces were involved in an incident in the Gulf of Oman, approximately 18 nautical miles east of the United Arab Emirates’ city of Khor Fakkan, with damage unknown. It was unclear if it was related to the reported U.S. attack.

A conflict between Iran-aligned Houthis in Yemen and Saudi Arabia has escalated this month, enlarging the wider Middle East war.

On Sunday, Saudi Arabia’s energy ministry said an administrative building belonging to state oil company Saudi Aramco in Riyadh had been damaged by falling debris after an attempted attack, with no injuries or fatalities reported.

Qatar, which has been mediating in talks to try to end the conflict that has shaken the world economy, on Saturday denied reports that the U.S. and Iran had failed to reach a deal.

The Qatari prime minister had affirmed that both sides were continuing to work toward an agreement, it said.

Iran has submitted a nuclear proposal to Washington through Qatar, a senior Iranian official said on Thursday, saying the U.S. was reviewing it but discussions would depend on Washington first meeting Tehran’s seven demands.

These include sanctions relief, access to frozen assets and war reparations, while Washington insists nuclear issues must feature in initial talks.

On Saturday, the U.S. military said it was launching a task force to crack down on the movement of advanced weapons and other sanctioned material to Iran via its land borders and the Caspian Sea — part of economic measures to try to pressure Tehran.

Iran’s Revolutionary Guards dismissed the plan as “wordplay,” saying it would not work because Tehran had made preparations and communicated closely with its neighbors.
