https://www.scmp.com/news/asia/southeast.title: Singapore minister says Cop31 has ‘enough to work on’ without new targets
https://www.scmp.com/news/asia/southeast.author: Reuters
https://www.scmp.com/news/asia/southeast.text:
Despite geopolitical ‘headwinds’, there is room for progress on issues such as climate adaptation, environment minister Grace Fu says

“I think that we are not expecting a major upgrade in mitigation targets” at ‌the annual UN talks in Turkey, Grace Fu told reporters. “But we have enough, even within the Paris Agreement, with what we have already agreed on. There is enough to work on.”

Delegations from nearly 200 countries are meeting in Antalya for the 12-day Cop31 conference, seeking to thrash out more steps on reducing emissions. They are set to negotiate on areas including electrification, limiting the rise in global temperatures and climate finance.

The climate negotiation process has come under criticism. Fu’s Panamanian counterpart, Juan Carlos Navarro, told a recent UN biodiversity conference that the need to ‌secure unanimity allowed single delegations to “torpedo” progress.

There are also calls to broaden the funding base, with now-prosperous economies like ⁠China and Middle East ⁠petrostates still classified as developing countries – which are not obliged to contribute to climate financing.

“Like many multilateral fora, there’s a frustration about lack of progress and how maybe ‌the systems have not kept up with the latest geopolitical realities,” Fu said. “It’s about how we have that change and where the leadership is coming from. I don’t ‌see that ‌leadership for such drastic change appearing at this COP.”

Fu said the ultimate aim was ‌to “shape the behaviour” of businesses.

“I’m hoping ‌that we will not have to prosecute, but the fact that it’s there will just make businesses realise that there are consequences and that they will do the right thing to avoid being prosecuted,” she said.

“It’s really just do whatever that is legally required of you, so that you don’t cause harm to others. And that harm is not just to Singaporeans, it’s to Indonesia and Indonesians.”

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.title: Moldova launches new power line to Romania to cut reliance on Russia
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.text:
Moldova has officially launched a new power line connecting the country to neighbouring Romania and the European grid to reduce its reliance on Russian energy.

“For decades, Moscow used energy to blackmail us,” Moldovan President Maia Sandu said on X on Sunday.

“No more: Moldova buys zero Russian gas,” she added.

Moldova, a country of 2.6 million people wedged between Romania and Ukraine, received most of its gas from Russia via its pro-Moscow separatist region of Transnistria and pipelines running through Ukraine.

“Thanks to this project, we are strengthening our electricity transmission capacity, diversifying our means of supply and reinforcing the connection of the Republic of Moldova to the European energy system,” Sandu said during the power line’s inauguration ceremony on Sunday in the capital, Chisinau.

She also said that “two more power lines to Romania are on the way”.

European Commissioner for Energy Marta Kos, who was at the ceremony, said Moldova could now “buy energy where it is cheapest”.

The 400-kilowatt extra-high-voltage line, which runs from the city of Vulcanesti to Chisinau, allows Moldova to cut reliance on the Cuciurgan thermal power plant in Transnistria.

“Every time Moldova dares to choose something other than what Moscow wants, they threaten to cut our electricity,” said Sandu.

Dubbed the “energy independence line”, the power grid was launched two years after the date Moldovan authorities initially promised.

Last month, Moldova’s parliament approved a government-requested state of emergency until November 20 as it tries to ease gas shortages amid soaring world energy prices.

Some in Europe have blamed Moscow for the skyrocketing gas prices, accusing it of withholding additional supplies to put pressure on the continent.

European-aligned states in the Black Sea region say they are experiencing renewed attacks allegedly carried out by Russia.

Last month, Romania blamed Russia for a drone strike that sank a cargo ship off Romania’s Black Sea coast, killing one crew member and leaving three others missing.

Ukraine, Romania and Bulgaria have called on NATO to “fast-track the additional surveillance capabilities” to protect commercial shipping in the Black Sea, as fighting in Russia’s war on Ukraine escalates.

NATO said it would send more maritime patrol aircraft, radar systems and drones to the ⁠⁠⁠⁠Black Sea.

Lance Morris is set for another stint on the sidelines after injuring his left hand during a party. (Getty Images: Cricket Australia/Jason McCawley)

Australian Test hopeful Lance Morris has suffered an injury to his non-bowling left hand during a party.

It continues a horror run for the 28-year-old, who has managed just 26 Shield appearances since making his first-class debut in 2020.

Morris is set to consult a hand specialist to determine the extent of the injury. There is no timeline on his return to playing.

Test hopeful Lance Morris is again under an injury cloud after hurting his hand at a social event following Western Australia's one-day clash against England on Saturday.

It is understood Morris was at a party when he cut his non-bowling left hand.

Morris is set to consult a hand specialist today to determine the extent of the injury, and a timeline on his return to playing.

It comes just over a year after Morris had spinal fracture surgery he hoped would save his cricket career, after struggling to string games together in recent years.

Morris (centre) picked up three wickets in Western Australia's tour match against England at the weekend. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

There were encouraging signs in Saturday's outing as Morris finished with figures of 3–29 off 10 overs, claiming the wickets of England superstar Joe Root, as well as Tom Banton and Gus Atkinson.

Morris was called into Australia's Test squad in late 2022 after an impressive start to the Sheffield Shield season, with some considering it a matter of time until he made his Test debut.

However, since then he has managed just three one-day internationals, six Shield matches and 22 Big Bash games, due to a wretched injury run.

Ahead of last season Morris underwent stabilisation surgery, a process that involves bolts and wire being put into his lower back.

Australia's chairman of selectors confirms the omission of Marnus Labuschagne after an extended lean run of form at the Test level.

Just last week he told ABC Sport's Tom Wildie he hoped to bowl faster than ever after the procedure, hopeful it would not affect his pace and strength.

"That [a loss of pace] was a huge question for me leading into the surgery because I knew that was the asset that made me potentially selectable for red-ball cricket," he said last week.

"I had to look around at other guys that have had the surgery, the likes of Jofra [Archer], Jasprit Bumrah, the guys that have returned to Test cricket at the same speed if not better.

"I've got one eye on the speed gun at all times to see where things are at, but I'm pretty happy with where it's at."

With regular fast bowlers Josh Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc and Captain Pat Cummins all well into their 30s, Australia is expected to soon be looking for other pace bowling options in the Test arena, with Morris long considered a likely contender for a spot in the eleven.

NSW Police says the 10-year-old boy died at the scene on Mulligans Flat Road in Sutton. (ABC News: Abbey Haberecht)

Police are appealing for information after a 10-year-old boy was killed in a car crash on Mulligans Flat Road in Sutton last month.

Investigators say the boy died at the scene after the vehicle, a Holden sedan, left the road, hit a tree, and then caught alight on Friday, October 23.

Emergency services were called to the scene near the ACT border at around 6:45pm.

NSW Police is urging anyone who may have information about the fatal crash to contact them. (ABC News: Floss Adams)

The 39-year-old male driver, and two female passengers aged 33 and 35, were able to get out of the vehicle.

They suffered burns and other injuries, and were taken to Canberra Hospital for treatment.

Inquiries into the incident are ongoing, conducted by the NSW Police Crash Investigation Unit.

Authorities are urging anyone with information about the incident, or anyone with dash-cam footage that may be relevant, to contact Crime Stoppers.

Police say they believe a body found in Walhalla this morning is that of missing Warrnambool man Geoffrey. (Supplied)

Police believe a body found in Victoria's Alpine region is that of a 76-year-old Warrnambool man who disappeared on Wednesday.

Geoffrey, whose surname has not been released by police, went missing about 6pm in Walhalla, a former gold-mining town north of Morwell in Gippsland.

He was last seen on Church Road on Wednesday evening, and was believed to be visiting historical sites in the region.

Geoffrey disappeared about an hour's drive west of Cowwarr, where an unrelated search continues for a missing 17-year-old boy.

A police spokesperson said a report would be prepared for the coroner after the discovery of a deceased male in Walhalla this morning.

Police said the body was yet to be formally identified but was believed to be that of missing 76-year-old man Geoffrey.

The death is not being treated as suspicious.

Police said family members were initially concerned about Geoffrey's disappearance due to a medical condition and it being out of character.

Netflix’s “Did Someone Happen to Mention Me?” isn’t just about one thing: It’s a love letter to filmmaking, a take on “King Lear,” a poignant exploration of father-child relationships and a showcase for its star, Koji Yakusho, all set in motion by a seemingly anti-vaccine premise.

A second pandemic results in a lockdown in Japan, so when Yakusho’s Gen Takasegawa can finally return to Tokyo after a successful run as King Lear at London’s Globe Theatre, he finds that his two ex-wives, his children, his fans and the world have forgotten him — because the vaccine against the virus causes amnesia.

Within the first few episodes, he’s shouting at a line of people waiting for the vaccine not to get jabbed — an off-color plot point at a time when pseudoscience is rampant. Strangely, the show never pits the people who chose to get vaccinated against those who didn’t, even though that is the fundamental tension for Gen. It tries to stay entirely apolitical and never references any ongoing discourse around vaccination.

Instead, the show mostly leaves the mechanics of its premise in the dust, preferring to platform the myriad talents of its star.

“Did Someone Happen to Mention Me?” cycles through several riches-to-rags arcs for Gen as he rebuilds his life and career, adopting the everyman name Taku Tanaka and working at a sentō (public bath). Buoyed by his co-worker Tetsu Okamoto (Kento Kaku), who also moonlights as a playwright, Taku starts working as an extra on TV and film sets.

Meanwhile, Taku bonds anew with his daughter Ema (Yuumi Kawai), who works in a maid cafe, and tries to repair his relationships with other loved ones who don’t remember him.

A Shakespeare fan will spot and likely enjoy the thematic similarities to “King Lear,” which is experiencing renewed popularity in Japan. The play, which centers on the vulnerability of growing old, being forgotten, and the paranoia that comes with it, is understandably resonant in one of the world’s most rapidly aging societies, and those same fears, wants and regrets are explored in “Did Someone Happen to Mention Me?”

There is a scene where Taku pretends to be a yakuza boss to threaten the high-powered man stalking Ema, only for his threats to turn into a tearful plea and lament over his failings as a father.

Yakusho doesn’t overshadow the supporting cast, though. In the same scene, Ema stands up for herself in an impassioned speech, which Kawai delivers with a deftness that skirts melodrama. Even Kaku’s comic relief has a thread of earnestness that makes him more of a sidekick than a punching bag.

The rest of the cast, including Hayato Isomura, Kenichi Matsuyama and Noriko Eguchi, hold their own and their scenes never feel like plot fodder. They offer enough depth to their characters to transcend the two-dimensional archetypes of wife, friend or anyone else defined solely by their relationship to Yakusho’s lead.

The 10th and final episode is a tongue-in-cheek black-box stage-play version of the nine that preceded it. It would be easy for this to feel tedious and self-serving. Instead, it’s not only emotionally satisfying but also genuinely funny.

The 10th and final episode is a tongue-in-cheek black-box stage-play version of the nine

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Eisenkot gets chance to form Israeli government after vote
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: Dan Williams
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
Israeli election challenger Gadi Eisenkot got the first attempt at forming a new government, putting him a step closer to ending Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s record tenure.

Eisenkot was formally handed the mandate on Sunday by Israeli President Isaac Herzog, who noted the “immense” challenges facing the country. Eisenkot will have up to six weeks to try to form a coalition that accounts for the majority of 120 parliamentary seats. Failure would mean the task likely reverts to Netanyahu, who for now continues to govern in a caretaker capacity.

While neither candidate’s political camp won a clear parliamentary majority in the Oct. 27 vote, Eisenkot’s nomination was supported by a majority of parties. The centrist ex-general said he was already negotiating to cobble together what he called a “national emergency government” to oust Netanyahu, under whose hard-right coalition Israel has been mired in war and deepening international isolation.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.summary: Gadi Eisenkot was formally handed the mandate on Sunday by Israeli President Isaac Herzog. He will have up to six weeks to try to form a coalition that accounts for the majority of 120 parliamentary seats. Failure would mean the task likely reverts to Netanyahu, who for now continues to govern in a caretaker capacity.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Japan to launch online reporting system for nursing care accidents
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
The Health, Labor and Welfare Ministry will launch an online system next April to directly receive reports from nursing care providers when accidents, such as falls or medication errors involving care recipients, occur at their facilities.

The system is intended to help central and local health authorities quickly identify accidents, enabling them to analyze the causes and develop measures that could help prevent similar incidents.

Nursing care providers are currently required to report accidents to municipal governments. However, municipalities are not required to share the information with the central government.

As a result, the national government has been unable to obtain a comprehensive picture of such incidents, making it difficult to analyze nationwide trends and consider improvements.

Reports from care providers are also sometimes submitted on paper, creating an administrative burden for both providers and municipalities.

Under the new system, information entered by care providers will be automatically sent to the central and local governments.

This will allow municipalities to identify accidents more quickly while enabling the national government to collect comprehensive data on incidents across the country.

The ministry will also standardize accident-reporting forms, which currently vary among municipalities.

The online system will provide common information fields, such as the location and time of an accident, the care recipient’s level of required nursing care and any injuries sustained, as well as the provider’s response and analysis of the cause. The standardized format is expected to improve reporting accuracy.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.summary: The Health, Labor and Welfare Ministry will launch an online system next April. The system is intended to help central and local health authorities quickly identify accidents. Nursing care providers are currently required to report accidents to municipal governments.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
WEST PALM BEACH, FLORIDA/WASHINGTON – U.S. President Donald Trump’s decision to elevate loyalist Stephen Miller to run his White House indicates that he plans to ramp up confrontation in his final two years in office and block outside political and economic pressures, Trump administration officials and other Republicans say.

Voters delivered a historic rebuke to Republicans in Tuesday’s midterm election, but with Miller as White House chief of staff, the Trump administration is expected to continue its aggressive immigration crackdown, amplify cultural conflicts and give no ground to a Democratic-controlled Congress, say officials and experts. They say wavering Republicans will face increased pressure to stay in line, while businesses may have a harder time making their case to the White House.

“This signals the administration is going to have a fighting-from-a-bunker approach the last two years,” said Dan Eberhart, a Trump donor and energy executive.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.summary: Trump administration expected to continue aggressive immigration crackdown, experts say. Experts say wavering Republicans will face increased pressure to stay in line. Businesses may have a harder time making their case to the White House.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.author: Yasutaka Tamura
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.text:
Mizuho Financial Group is carving out a lucrative niche in Japan’s equity capital market by bridging the ravenous U.S. demand for artificial intelligence fundraising and its home country’s deep pool of retail savings.

Anthropic’s listing is the third in a string of blockbuster deals where Mizuho snagged a key role, looking to raise as much as $3.5 billion from Japanese investors. It shows that the bank is able to leverage its success in building a U.S. business to compete on a market traditionally dominated by Nomura Holdings where domestic deals have hit a drought.

The Claude chatbot maker is following SpaceX in bringing a mega deal to the Japanese market, attracted to its cash-rich retail investors and a streamlined offering process. The country’s households have about ¥2.4 quadrillion ($15 trillion) in financial assets, with roughly half parked in currency and deposits, according to the Bank of Japan.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck1w.title: Cruise ship pianist rescued from sea after nine hours in Pacific Ocean
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck1w.text:
A cruise ship pianist was found treading water around 20 miles (32km) off the Californian coast after falling overboard, according to US media reports.

Two fishermen discovered the Royal Caribbean employee near Catalina Island on Friday and officials believe he may have been in the Pacific Ocean for nine hours, according to CBS News, the BBC's US news partner.

"I'm like, 'Yeah, it's a human being. Stop the boat; let's get all of our lines in," Grant Garrett was quoted as saying, recalling the moment he and Sean Norton spotted him.

The man, who has not yet been identified, was taken to hospital in a stable condition, the US Coast Guard told the BBC, adding it was investigating the incident.

The fishermen say the man identified himself as a pianist on a 14-deck cruise ship called the Ovation of the Seas.

"The only thing he said to me was, 'Thank you. I thought I was gonna die,'" Norton said.

The Coast Guard said in a statement it had received a report from "a Good Samaritan who recovered a conscious individual from the water".

The person was handed over to Newport Beach Lifeguards, who confirmed he was an employee of the Ovation of the Seas cruise ship, it said.

Lifeguard officials believe he may have fallen overboard at around 02:30, about nine hours before he was discovered.

"It was approximately 15 to 20 miles offshore, pretty much in the middle of the ocean," Newport Beach Lifeguard Battalion Chief Adam Yacenda told CBS.

Norton credited the man's survival to unusually warm ocean temperatures.

"You have this crazy super El Niño year. This guy was in the water for probably 10 hours, but the water's 76 degrees," Norton said, which equates to about 24C.

"A different year, no way he makes it," Norton said.

The developing El Niño climate phenomenon is now the strongest on record, according to scientists monitoring the Pacific, with ocean temperatures about 3.05C above average.

In a statement to the BBC, a Royal Caribbean Group spokesperson said: "We are providing support and assistance to our crew member during this difficult time.

"To respect the privacy of our employee, we have no additional details to share."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck1w.summary: Cruise ship pianist found treading water around 20 miles off California coast. Two fishermen found him near Catalina Island on Friday. The man was taken to hospital in a stable condition, the US Coast Guard says. The pianist was found by lifeguards and was taken over by a Good Samaritan.

https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.title: ‘Outrageous and racist’: premier responds to NSW One Nation candidate’s claim Australians are being ‘demographically replaced’
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.author: Anne Davies
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text:
Chris Minns and human rights commissioner lambast comments made by Stuart Bonds, who leads party’s NSW upper house ticket

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The New South Wales premier and the Australian Human Rights Commission have criticised comments by the man who heads One Nation’s upper house ticket in NSW after he said Australians faced demographic replacement unless “mass migration” was curtailed.

Chris Minns described Stuart Bonds’ comments as “frankly outrageous and racist”.

Minns said the replacement theory being espoused by Bonds was “just a conspiracy theory that’s been imported from the US here to Australia”.

Bonds will be the first candidate on the rightwing party’s NSW upper house ticket and on current polling is likely to be elected in March’s state election.

He made the incendiary remarks at an anti-immigration rally in Sydney’s CBD on Sunday. Several hundred people attended amid a sea of Australian flags.

At least one neo-Nazi, Joel Davis, was spotted among them, as well as rightwing figures including the national director of the Family First party, Lyle Shelton, who was previously head of the Australian Christian Lobby.

“Make no mistake, we are being demographically replaced inside our own nation,” Bonds told attendees after referring to abortion rates in Europe, the US and Australia.

“If we don’t support Australian mothers having Australian children, we are going to pay for other cultures’ children to be brought up in our lands.”

He warned that unless it was stopped it would be “impossible to reverse”.

Bonds told the crowd that a country was “a shared culture, a shared border, a shared flag, a shared language and a dominant religion”.

“After 240 years, we are told we’re still on stolen land, and we’re meant to apologise for being here,” he said.

“Yet, in the same vein, we’re expected to believe that an immigrant arriving yesterday is as Australian as you and me. I don’t accept that people like the Bondi shooters are as Australian as you and me. I don’t accept that.”

The race discrimination commissioner, Giridharan Sivaraman, said comments that some Australians were superior to others sowed “division and hate”.

“The idea that migrants can never truly be Australian ignores both our history and our shared future,” he said on Monday.

“Australia has always been shaped by successive generations of people who came here from around the world and helped build the nation we know today. It has the longest continuous culture in the world.

“Throughout history, periods of uncertainty have often seen minority communities cast as scapegoats. Today, migrants are too frequently portrayed as the cause of Australia’s challenges.

“Reducing complex problems to a simple narrative that migrants are to blame is not only inaccurate, it risks fuelling division, exclusion and racism. Migrants are not separate from the Australian story. They are central to it.”

Bonds told the rally that the “socialist plan” was to “destroy and bring down and tear down the fabric of your civilisation” pointing to European countries “on fire”.

He said Australia was going down a path “of becoming a special economic zone within Asia,” and that it needed to “re-establish ourselves as a proud Australian nation”.

Minns said voters should ask themselves which portfolio Bonds would have were One Nation to win the election.

“Trade, education, Treasury? I mean, what job will this bloke have in a Coalition-One Nation government?” Minns said.

“And are we going to see some distancing from those kind of views and those horrific perspectives or points of view from the Coalition?”

Comment was sought from the Coalition’s spokesperson on multiculturalism, Mark Coure, and from One Nation’s NSW headquarters.

Bonds’ comments were also reverberating in Canberra.

The federal minister for multicultural affairs, Anne Aly, said Australians with migrant backgrounds were not replacing Australians – they simply were Australians.

“Questioning someone’s right to belong because of their race or ancestry is not a debate about immigration,” she said.

“It’s divisive, dangerous and goes against everything we stand for as Australians.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Trump tells 60 Minutes that deportation policy was ‘too tough’
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: David Smith in Washington
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
President makes unusual acknowledgement that one of the defining policies of his second administration had become a political liability

Donald Trump has admitted that his deportation policy was “too tough” and has offered to strike an immigration deal with Democrats in a concession following the Republicans’ disastrous defeat in the midterm elections.

In an interview on the CBS network’s 60 Minutes broadcast on Sunday, the president acknowledged that the aggressive crackdown had hurt him politically and said he was open to an arrangement to allow some undocumented immigrants to remain in the US.

Trump was asked by 60 Minutes correspondent Ross Douthat whether his deportation policy had gone too far. “I think it was too tough,” he said. “I think it might be too tough, yeah. And a lot of people would say that it’s great. But a lot of people think it’s too tough.”

The president’s comments offered an unusually frank acknowledgment that one of the defining policies of his second administration had become a political liability. But they were seemingly at odds with his decision on Friday to elevate Stephen Miller, the architect of his immigration crackdown, to White House chief of staff.

Since Trump returned to office, sweeping Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) raids at workplaces, homes and public spaces have ensnared people with no criminal records, separated families and spread fear in immigrant communities. Federal agents fatally shot two US citizens, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, during operations in Minneapolis earlier this year.

The president claimed that his policy “both helped and hurt”, since people gave him an “A+ for closing up the border” and “very high marks for getting the bad ones out”. But he admitted: “I get hurt because we also took people that had good jobs, that created one violation, or breaking of the law, and that was that they came into the country illegally.”

Trump added that there were competing views within the country about whether undocumented immigrants should be deported or allowed to remain if they were working and paying taxes. He said some people believed that “they should be allowed to stay if they’re good people working in a landscaping company” and “in some cases, paying taxes”.

Trump said he believed an agreement with Democrats was achievable, allowing some long-term undocumented residents to stay while continuing to remove people convicted of serious crimes. He proposed targeting killers, rapists and drug dealers while making an accommodation for people who had been in the country for 10 or 15 years.

“Let the people that are here, and in some cases here for 10 and 15 years, work a deal for them,” he said. He described the proposal as something that could be negotiated, saying: “I think that’s something that’s actually doable.”

Trump suggested Democrats were receptive to a compromise, saying some had already contacted him. Asked whether he could refrain from name-calling for six months to secure an agreement, he replied: “Very easily.”

Trump also blamed the war with Iran and higher petrol prices for much of the Republicans’ midterms defeat, agreeing with an assessment by his vice-president, JD Vance, that the conflict had been a major factor. He also cited what he described as growing dislike of Israel.

He maintained, however, that the military campaign had been justified and said he would make the same decision again. “My answer is an emphatic yes because you can’t let Iran have a nuclear weapon,” he said.

Trump insisted the war had been won and predicted that Tehran would eventually negotiate a deal. He acknowledged that the military campaign might not have been popular in the short term, saying: “I think historically, this will be a very good decision. Is it a good decision for today and tomorrow? Maybe not.”

He said he was not looking to escalate the conflict after the midterms.

On the economy, the president conceded that his administration had failed to communicate its achievements effectively, despite repeatedly claiming that employment, investment and stock market figures were at record levels. “I think it was bad messaging, maybe by me,” he said.

Trump signalled an openness to safeguards for artificial intelligence, despite having previously favoured allowing technology companies to police themselves rather than imposing sweeping government restrictions. “I don’t mind guardrails,” he told 60 Minutes. “But I don’t wanna put us in a deep second position.”

The interview also raised questions about the substantial increase in Trump’s personal wealth since his return to the White House.

Douthat cited a Forbes estimate that Trump’s net worth had increased by $3bn from the autumn of 2024 to the autumn of 2025. Trump initially suggested that the increase reflected the general performance of the stock market and said his finances were managed by his son.

Asked about his family’s cryptocurrency business, World Liberty Financial, in which he is a co-owner and which has attracted investment from people connected to the United Arab Emirates, Trump defended the arrangement by saying: “I know nothing about it.”

But Dan Alexander, a Forbes senior editor who calculates the net worth of wealthy individuals for the magazine, challenged Trump’s explanation in a lengthy thread on X, arguing that the president’s increased fortune could not be explained simply by stock market gains.

Alexander identified several sources including cryptocurrency ventures that generated more than $1bn in proceeds and the appreciation of tokens retained by Trump, overseas licensing agreements that expanded the value of his branding business, and the removal of an almost $500m financial penalty in his New York civil fraud case.

Trump also offered a glimpse of the Republican succession battle ahead of the 2028 presidential election, saying he might endorse a candidate but had not decided whether to intervene. Asked whether he expected to endorse a successor, Trump replied: “Probably. Not necessarily.”

He described the Republican party as having a strong field of potential candidates and praised secretary of state Marco Rubio while declining to rule out other contenders.

The president said his endorsement would carry considerable weight but suggested he might be better off staying out of the contest. He also expressed confidence that the “Make America great again” movement could survive without him as its leader, describing its defining principles as strong borders and a strong military.

At the end of the interview, Trump was asked whether he could forgive political opponents including former FBI director James Comey and former House speaker Nancy Pelosi, even before the judgment of God. Trump said: “The answer is no. I want to be honest, no.”

Douthat followed up: “Mr President. You have had the most charmed and remarkable life of any American in my entire lifetime and you are telling me that before the judgment throne of God you couldn’t find it in your heart to forgive some of your enemies? After all that’s been given to you? Come on. Help me out here.”

But Trump remained adamant, insisting: “I probably cannot do that, no, because I do hate some of my enemies and I always will.”

Douthat then noted that many presidents are remembered with a single line such as “He freed the slaves” or “He won the cold war” and asked what line will Trump’s presidency be remembered with.

The president said simply: “That I made America great again.”
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: Trump admits deportation policy was 'too tough' and offered to strike a deal with Democrats. He said he was open to an arrangement to allow some undocumented immigrants to remain in the US. Trump also blamed the war with Iran and higher petrol prices for much of the Republicans’ midterms defeat.

https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/1.title: Asian stock markets climb after earlier tech rout
https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/1.author: John Power
https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/1.text:
Asian stock markets have rebounded after last week’s tech rout triggered by the Democratic Party’s sweeping victory in the United States midterm elections.

Key indexes in Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and Hong Kong made substantial gains on Monday, following a rebound on Wall Street on Friday.

In Tokyo, the benchmark Nikkei 225 was up 3.45 percent as of 04:00 GMT.

In Taipei, the Taiex was 5.72 percent higher, while the Kospi in Seoul was up 1.68 percent.

Hong Kong’s Hang Seng Index was up 0.19 percent.

Futures for Wall Street’s benchmark S&P 500 index and the tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 were up 0.60 percent and 0.59 percent, respectively.

They had dipped earlier following US-based chip giant Nvidia’s announcement that it would investigate its CEO over his romantic relationship with a woman accused of being a Chinese spy.

Nvidia’s board of directors said that while it had confidence in CEO Jensen Huang and had no reason to believe that national security or company secrets were compromised, the independent inquiry would examine “all available information”.

The board said Huang supported the inquiry and pledged his full cooperation.

“The Board prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders,” the company said.

The stock market rebound comes after the US midterm results prompted a $2.5 trillion sell-off on Wall Street on Thursday amid concerns that Democratic-controlled legislatures could slow the rollout of data centres used to power AI.

The tech rout spilled into Asia on Friday, with the Nikkei 225, Kospi and Hang Seng Index plunging about 6 percent, 9 percent, 1.3 percent, respectively.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.title: Rubio says war on Iran unpopular but ‘necessary’ to stop nuclear threat
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.text:
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said President Donald Trump launched the war against Iran to safeguard the world from Tehran’s nuclear ambitions.

Rubio told reporters in Florida on Sunday that Trump “identified a very real threat” in Iran and had worked to stop it from pursuing a nuclear weapon.

Trump addressed “difficult challenges for the security of our country – doing it isn’t necessarily popular, but necessary”, Rubio added.

On diplomatic efforts to end the war, Rubio said, “I wouldn’t say we’re at the verge of a breakthrough”. He added that although Trump prefers a diplomatic solution, Iranian demands are “not just unacceptable, but in some cases, outrageous and ridiculous and really not realistic”.

Rubio comments came after Trump had said that “a lot of people didn’t like” Vice President JD Vance recent comments blaming the US-led war on Iran for the Republican Party’s crushing defeat in last week’s US midterm elections.

Trump said that although he mostly agreed with Vance, he did not regret the decision to go to war against Iran. It “will go down as one of the best things we ever did”, he said, adding that if Tehran were to have a nuclear weapon, “they would blow up the world”.

Trump also told CNN in a phone interview on Sunday that as long as Washington sees progress in negotiations with Tehran and they sign a “strong agreement”, it is “highly unlikely it’s going to be necessary” for the US to resume strikes.

For Iran’s part, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Sunday that it was “time for the White House to make its own” decision on the war.

“American voters have made their choice,” Araghchi wrote on X, referring to the midterm election results.

He added that Tehran’s “2-day proposal stands: meet the requirements, including end to war on all fronts, and you will see results”.

“Or choose war, and see our alert and battle-hardened Warriors rain down hell.”

Iran has offered to reopen the strategic Strait of Hormuz to commercial shipping within two days if the United States meets its conditions.

Trump is set to meet Qatari Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani at the White House on Monday, according to his official schedule.

Tehran is reviewing proposals presented by Qatar aimed at addressing differences with Washington, according to the Associated Press news agency.

In recent days, Rubio has also denied “unfounded” speculation that he was quitting as the top US diplomat to run for higher office in 2028.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.summary: Rubio said Trump had worked to stop Iran from pursuing a nuclear weapon. He said that if Tehran were to have a nuclear weapons, ‘they would blow up the world’

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.title: Mexico arrests alleged major leader of Jalisco cartel
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.text:
Authorities in Mexico have announced the arrest of an alleged leader in the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG), one of the country’s two main criminal groups.

Rafael Alvarez, alias “R2”, who is suspected of heading CJNG’s “Los Rs” cell, was arrested in an operation in the city of Zapopan, in the Guadalajara metropolitan area, on Sunday, as a result of intelligence shared by the US Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA)⁠, according to Mexico’s Navy.

“This cell is mainly ⁠linked to extortion, drug trafficking, homicide, illegal deprivation of liberty, kidnapping and attacks against authorities,” Mexico’s Security Minister Omar Garcia Harfuch said.

He added that victims of the group’s extortion included “business owners and avocado producers”.

Harfuch said on X that Alvarez was wounded in a shootout that broke out during the arrest and is receiving medical care.

Alvarez has an outstanding arrest warrant in Mexico for aggravated homicide and another warrant for ⁠extradition to the US, Harfuch also said.

Authorities, including those from Mexico’s National Intelligence Center, also took part in the operation, which captured 19 other people.

Alvarez is linked to the killing of at least 19 people, including last year’s murder of Carlos Manzo, the popular crime-fighting mayor of Uruapan in Mexico’s avocado-producing Michoacan state.

The CJNG, which operates in the states of Jalisco and Michoacan, was designated a “foreign terrorist organisation” by the US government in 2025 and is known for violent tactics and attacks on authorities.

It competes with the Sinaloa Cartel for drug trafficking into the US.

Since the death of the CJNG founder, Nemesio “El Mencho” Oseguera, in a military operation in February, several of its top leaders have been apprehended.

But there are still reports of kidnapping for ransom in the areas where the cartels are active.

An estimated 134,000 people are believed to be missing across Mexico, with Jalisco recording the country’s highest numbers of disappearances.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: ‘Last generation’: ‘Kristallnacht’ survivor, 94, bears witness
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
BERLIN – For George Shefi, a 94-year-old survivor of Nazi Germany’s “Kristallnacht,“ bearing witness to the pogroms targeting Jews is his final “mission” — all the more urgent in the face of a renewed wave of anti-Semitism.

“Our generation is the last generation that can tell the true story,” Shefi said ahead of Monday’s 88th anniversary of the events, also remembered as the “Night of Broken Glass.”

The wave of violence unleashed by the Nazi regime on Nov. 9 to 10, 1938, saw at least 90 Jewish people killed and 1,400 synagogues set alight across Germany.

Shefi, born Spiegelglas in 1931, was just 6 years old when the anti-Semitic riots shook his home city of Berlin.

His mother did not let him out of the house in the capital’s Schoeneberg district for three days, but when he finally emerged, he was confronted with a radically changed city.

“My school was burned down,” he said, speaking last Thursday at a ceremony at the New Synagogue in Berlin organized by the International March for the Living, a Holocaust remembrance group.

“I remember very clearly a hat shop which was broken into, glass all over the place, women’s hats all over the place. That made a big impression on me.”

Another of his memories is of a stationery shop owner being “jeered” by dozens of onlookers while clearing up anti-Semitic graffiti.

“They wrote in big letters: ’This store belongs to a Jewish pig who is married to a Christian sow.’”

Months later, just before the outbreak of World War II, George was placed on a train that would take him to safety in the United Kingdom, in a rescue effort known as the Kindertransport that saved almost 10,000 children.

His mother dropped him off at a train station before getting in a taxi to a different stop, where more children were due to be picked up.

“Unfortunately, I saw her running on the platform, but she never saw me. And that’s the last time I saw her.”

George was taken to stay with distant relatives in London before being evacuated to the rural English county of Lincolnshire.

He received one letter from his mother during the war, via the Red Cross, and never heard from her again.

He later found out that she was deported to Auschwitz, arriving at the death camp on Jan. 30, 1943.

“As far as I could calculate, she was murdered the same day.”

Some 6 million Jews were killed in the Holocaust.

After a brief stay in the United States, Shefi settled in Israel following the war.

In the past 25 years, he has traveled back to Germany to tell his story, sharing his experience with more than 12,000 schoolchildren.

His message for German students: “I want to convince you that you’re not allowed to forget the Holocaust.”

Shefi has told them that “you’re not responsible for what was, but you’re responsible for the next 20, 30 years when you grow up and you’re going to lead this country.”

But the world has changed in the decades since Shefi first began retelling his story.

Anti-Semitic offenses in Germany have surged from around 1,400 in 2015 to 6,500 last year, according to police figures.

The situation has worsened since the Oct. 7, 2023, attacks led by Hamas against Israel and the subsequent war in the Gaza Strip.

Meanwhile, Germany’s culture of Holocaust remembrance is under threat, with the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) often railing against what it calls a “cult of guilt.”

In September, an AfD-backed motion passed in the eastern town of Heidenau banning the creation of new “Stolpersteine,” small public inscriptions commemorating the victims of Nazi persecution.

George was well aware of the development.

“I think it has to be fought tooth and nail,” he said at the Berlin ceremony.

“People have to wake up to it, and if you want to keep this country democratic, you have to start immediately to fight against such situations.”

Soon to turn 95, George is still engaged in what he calls his “mission” to combat anti-Semitism.

“We are the ones that have to tell, as long as we can, the truth.”

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: War drove refugees into Turkey. Climate change is making it harder to leave.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
Even after the start of Syria’s civil war in 2011, beekeeper Muhammad Salih regularly traveled along the country’s northern border with Turkey in search of the best spots to produce the honey that sustained his family. It wasn’t until four years later, when Islamic State militants took control of his hometown and killed his brother-in-law, along with his seven children, that Salih decided it was time to move for good.

“We buried them and crossed into Turkey,” said the 46-year-old, who now lives in Karkamis, a small Turkish town near the Syrian border. “I had to sell all 250 of my beehives for a third of what they would have been worth if I hadn’t been in such a rush.”

But while Salih has left sectarian violence behind, he hasn’t been able to escape extreme weather. Drought has cut his honey production in half over the past five years. This year, the rains returned but brought intense flooding and hail that destroyed the flowers his business depends on.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.title: Berkshire plans first Japan bond offering since April
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.text:
Berkshire Hathaway has hired banks for its first yen bond sale since April as it prepares to raise more funds in Japan.

Berkshire mandated Mizuho Securities and BofA Securities for a potential benchmark yen bond offering that’s expected in the near future, subject to market conditions, according to people familiar with the matter.

The company has been issuing yen-denominated bonds at a pace of twice a year. The latest offering would come as Japanese firms have slowed domestic bond sales. New issuance has recently thinned after a surge of supply in October widened the additional yield, or spread, that domestic corporate bonds offer over government debt.

This will be Berkshire’s second yen bond offering since Warren Buffett stepped down as chief executive officer. Investors will focus on how much of a premium the company offers and how much demand it attracts. In April, it sold six tranches with maturities ranging from three to 30 years, totaling ¥272.3 billion ($1.7 billion). That was among its largest yen bond offerings, behind its debut issuance in 2019 and its October 2024 sale.

“Berkshire has name recognition in Japan because of its investments in Japanese stocks,” said Takashi Fujiwara, lead fund manager in the fixed-income investment department at Resona Asset Management. “There should be demand for the bonds depending on the spread.”

https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/tran.title: Man dies after being hit by bus in Hong Kong’s North Point
https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/tran.author: Roetta Wang
https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/tran.text:
Fatal accident occurred at junction of King’s Road and Tin Chong Street in North Point on Monday morning

A man in his 60s has died after being struck by a bus in Hong Kong’s North Point.

The fatal accident happened at the junction of King’s Road and Tin Chong Street at around 8.17am, with police and ambulance personnel arriving at the scene after a report by the Citybus driver.

Police said the victim suffered severe head injuries and was unconscious before being rushed to Pamela Youde Nethersole Eastern Hospital in Chai Wan, where he was certified dead at 8.54am.

An investigation into the cause of the crash is under way.

The Citybus involved in the accident was operating on Route 38, between Chi Fu Fa Yuen and North Point Ferry Pier. Photos from the scene showed severe cracks to the left side of its windscreen.

Following the collision, all Chai Wan-bound lanes on King’s Road near Tin Chong Street were temporarily cordoned off, but normal traffic flow has since resumed.

The South China Morning Post has contacted Citybus for comment.

Spencer Leniu will have a delayed start to his next NRL season after being sanctioned over a gesture made towards the referees. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

Samoa's Spencer Leniu has been suspended for two matches after making a money gesture at the referees in his side's loss to Australia in the Rugby League World Cup semifinal.

If Leniu contests the grade three contrary conduct charge and loses his appeal, he will incur an additional one-match suspension.

Leniu will miss Parramatta's first two games of the 2027 NRL season, including the team's game in Las Vegas.

Parramatta's marquee off-season recruit Spencer Leniu is poised to miss the first two games of the 2027 campaign — including the Eels' trip to Las Vegas — after being sin-binned in Samoa's World Cup semifinal loss to Australia.

Leniu was sin-binned by referee Adam Gee for dissent late in the first half of Sunday's 44-12 loss to the Kangaroos in Sydney.

The prop made a money gesture with his hand as he walked towards the tunnel, a sign that many interpreted as the Samoan forward questioning the integrity and impartiality of match officials.

Rugby league's Davids have gotten much bigger in recent times but Australia's win over Samoa in the World Cup semi-final was a reminder of Goliath's power.

Leniu was handed a grade three contrary conduct charge on Monday.

The 26-year-old, who will join Parramatta after winning the 2026 premiership with Sydney Roosters, will miss the club's opening two games of the season, which includes their trip to the US to face Gold Coast.

In the unlikely event he contests the charge, Leniu would incur an additional one-game ban if he were to lose his appeal.

The prop's outburst came during a frustrating night for Samoa, from which Samoan halves Ronald Volkman and Jarome Luai have avoided suspension for dangerous contact.

Samoa were on the wrong end of a 9-4 penalty count and coach Ben Gardiner suggested Gee had handed the Kangaroos several "home-ground calls".

"It was a real home-ground advantage for Australia," Gardiner said.

"They had the music pumping in the background and we had a lot of Samoan fans here to support us, which was brilliant.

"But they got the home-ground calls, got a really good start and then it was just too hard for us to chase back from there."

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: How a digital bank’s collapse toppled Paraguay’s president
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
ASUNCION, PARAGUAY – For years, Paraguay’s digital bank, Ueno, stood out as a homegrown success story, luring roughly half the country’s people to open accounts and offering many the opportunity to hold a bank account for the very first time.

But over just five days last week, the bank collapsed, freezing the savings of nearly 3 million customers — in a country of 6.5 million people — and triggering the country’s deepest political crisis in more than a decade.

On Friday evening, Paraguayan President Santiago Pena was impeached after attempting to resign, and his vice president, Pedro Alliana, was sworn in as his replacement.

Authorities quickly arrested Pena, an economist and close ally of U.S. President Donald Trump, and prosecutors charged him on Saturday with breach of trust and administration for personal gain. A judge ordered him held in pretrial detention at a military facility.

Pena has denied wrongdoing and his attorney, Ricardo Preda, told journalists that he is pleading not guilty to the charges.

The scandal has triggered public protests and sharp rebukes from the opposition.

“We are facing the biggest corruption scandal in our democratic history,” said opposition Sen. Rafael Filizzola on Friday. “This impeachment is a first step toward ensuring justice is served.”

Manuel Ferreira, a Paraguayan economist and former finance minister, echoed much of the public anger over the case. “This was a modern-day Bonnie and Clyde,” he said. “They didn’t rob us with a pistol, they robbed us with an app. The head of the gang was the president of the republic.”

Until March 2025, Pena had been a business partner of the group that owns Ueno Bank. After his election in 2023, he tapped Ueno’s former president, Carlos Carvallo, to lead the central bank.

Carvallo resigned as central bank chief earlier last week. Prosecutors charged him on Saturday with breach of trust, producing false public documents and administration for personal gain. They sought his pretrial detention, which was approved by a judge.

Carvallo did not respond to a request for comment. It was not immediately clear if he had entered a plea in the case.

Pena’s lawyer, Preda, objected to the impeachment, saying that ousting a president during a bank resolution could itself be destabilizing.

“What sets a serious country apart is not that its banks don’t fail, but how it responds,” Preda said on Friday. “If there is one thing that undermines confidence in the financial system, it is attempting to oust the president without evidence.”

Ueno was launched in 2021 as a sleek, millennial-friendly banking app that quickly won over Paraguayans who had been underserved by brick-and-mortar institutions.

It soon became deeply embedded in Paraguay’s payments system. It paired its digital offering with physical branches, later sponsoring sports teams, businesses and events. As of June, public institutions — including Paraguay’s state pension fund — held roughly $850 million in accounts with the bank.

But in recent months, internal regulatory reports warning of excessive lending to certain companies were leaked to local media outlets ABC and Ultima Hora, triggering political scrutiny of the bank’s lending practices.

Following growing public pressure, Paraguay’s central bank on Tuesday put Ueno into resolution — its strongest measure short of immediate liquidation — after determining that Ueno had breached minimum solvency requirements, locking millions of customers temporarily out of their accounts.

The central bank said on Saturday that the equivalent of $160 million had since been paid out to nearly 1.2 million savers under the state deposit guarantee scheme.

Authorities have promised that depositors will be reimbursed and say the crisis is confined to Ueno. But analysts say the damage to Paraguay’s reputation as a stable investment destination in South America may linger far longer than the bank resolution itself.

“This is the moment when Paraguay must demonstrate that its institutions are functioning,” Ferreira said.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.summary: Paraguay's digital bank, Ueno, collapsed last week, freezing the savings of nearly 3 million customers. President Santiago Pena was impeached after attempting to resign. He was charged with breach of trust and administration for personal gain.

https://www.scmp.com/news/china/politics.title: Fire in northern China high-rise building kills 14, injures dozens more
https://www.scmp.com/news/china/politics.author: Phoebe Zhang
https://www.scmp.com/news/china/politics.text:
The building in downtown Taiyuan, the capital of Shanxi province, contained flats, a hotel and children’s education centres

Fourteen people have been killed and dozens more hospitalised after a fire broke out in a high-rise building in northern China.

That night, 38 people were sent to hospital, including five people who had died. By Monday morning, the death toll had increased to 14, state news agency Xinhua reported.

“All-out efforts are being made to treat the injured, follow-up work is under way and the cause of the fire remains under investigation,” the district government said.

According to real-estate platform Lianjia, the building was a mixed-use residential and commercial block.

A member of staff at a hotel in the building told Jimu News on Sunday that he thought the fire started on the fifth floor and that some people were injured on the eighth floor. He helped firefighters search for survivors while some parts of the building were still on fire, he added.

Pictures from the Jimu News report show that besides hotels, the building also has restaurants and academic training centres for children.

The building is located in downtown Taiyuan, close to hospitals, schools, commercial centres and tourist sites.

https://www.dw.com/en/g7-ministers-meet-.title: G7 ministers meet as Europe seeks greater say in Ukraine peace talks
https://www.dw.com/en/g7-ministers-meet-.text:
With Washington preparing negotiations with Moscow and Kyiv, European leaders fear Ukraine could face pressure to accept a bad deal. Iran tensions and the threat of renewed US strikes are also on the agenda.

Foreign ministers from the Group of Seven (G7) leading industrialized nations are set to meet in Paris on Monday and Tuesday for talks on how Europe can be part of US efforts to end Russia’s war on Ukraine and how to urge Washington to not resume military action against Iran.

The meeting will bring together leading diplomats from Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States.

It coincides with US-mediated talks between Moscow and Kyiv in Abu Dhabi scheduled to begin on Tuesday.

European governments are concerned the the US might be pushing Ukraine to a settlement favoring Russia. US President Donald Trump, in the run-up to the Abu Dhabi talks, said a "very big" deal was in the making, suggesting Ukraine could emerge from a settlement with altered ‌borders.

"I think we're gonna have it done, and I think it's ‌gonna happen ​and they're gonna end up with a little bit different shape Ukraine," Trump told broadcaster CBS. The US president also said the deal would involve all of Europe.

About the talks in Abu Dhabi, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot told RTL radio that "Europeans will be represented and France will participate in these talks."

European leaders have long insisted that any deal to end the war should include the continent's participation in the talks and that any settlement should not come at the expense of Ukraine's sovereignty.

When asked about the US plans for a possible agreement to end the war in Ukraine, Barrot said he did not know the details but stressed that no deal affecting the European security architecture could be done without the Europeans.

Particular attention at the upcoming meeting will be on US Secretary of State Marco Rubio who will attend both days unlike the last G7 meeting where he came only for one.

Rubio suggested that recent discussions had made progress on security guarantees for Ukraine and the wider European region. Trump's envoy and son-in-law Jared Kushner has also described US efforts to develop a broader European security framework.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has in the past expressed doubts over proposals for a new European security framework, suggesting that any such debates should follow, rather than precede, efforts to end the war.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The G7 ministers are also expected to discuss US tensions with Iran, as Trump has not ruled out additional military strikes against the country.

Washington has previously considered targeting suspected nuclear facilities, including the site known as Pickaxe Mountain, following the US midterm elections last week. Tehran denies that the location is a nuclear facility.

European governments are seeking a diplomatic resolution rather than a resumption of military action. Gobal attention is particularly on the restoration of normal shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical route for international energy supplies.

Trump recently said that Iranian officials were keen to reach an agreement, suggesting negotiations remained possible.

The Paris gathering is among the final major diplomatic events of France's G7 presidency. The United States is scheduled to assume the group's rotating presidency in 2027.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqkg.title: Government's EV targets expected to be reduced this week
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqkg.text:
The UK government's electric vehicle (EV) targets are expected to be reduced this week in a move likely to be welcomed by carmakers but opposed by environmental groups.

Under the current rules, 80% of new cars sold in the UK must be electric by 2030 but industry groups have long called for "urgent relief".

New petrol or diesel cars are due to be phased out by 2030 and by 2035 all new cars must be zero emission.

But the speed of the transition to electric has been hotly debated, including within the cabinet.

The government has been consulting on reducing its 80% rule and a significant reduction is now expected.

Downing Street has insisted no decision has been made.

A government source told the BBC it would approach the issue in a "pragmatic and balanced" way.

If ministers do decide on a steeper watering-down of the rules, it will arguably be interpreted by some - alongside the approval of the Jackdaw gas field - as Prime MInister Andy Burnham prioritising economic considerations over environmental ones.

Sustainability groups say any weakening of the 2030 target will threaten the UK's long-term electrification and climate goals.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/europe-f.title: From supermarket fridges to passenger flights, a wave of threats is testing Europe's defenses
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/europe-f.author: Chloe Taylor,Elsa Ohlen
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/europe-f.text:
Europe has faced a number of security threats this month, including cyberattacks on refrigeration systems at supermarkets and hoax bomb threats which disrupted dozens of passenger flights.

Experts told CNBC that such attacks can create economic damage, public anxiety and pressure on governments even without open military conflict.

Cyberattacks, bomb threats against passenger flights, civil unrest and suspected acts of sabotage across Europe have raised questions about the continent’s resilience — and how prepared it is to defend itself against modern security threats.

Hackers remotely manipulated refrigeration systems at supermarkets across Europe last week, forcing retailers to discard spoiled food and exposing vulnerabilities in everyday infrastructure.

French blood-bank refrigeration systems were subsequently targeted in what appeared to be a similar incident, while a wave of suspected hoax bomb threats disrupted dozens of flights across the continent, forcing diversions and, in some cases, fighter jet escorts.

The week culminated with bomb threats targeting European news outlets, including the U.K.’s Sky News and Irish public broadcaster RTÉ.

The incidents come against a backdrop of heightened geopolitical tensions and domestic unrest across parts of Europe, with civilian infrastructure potentially becoming an increasingly attractive target for hostile actors.

While authorities have not established who was behind the attacks or whether they were connected, defense and security experts warn that disruption to everyday services can have consequences far beyond the immediate economic damage.

If Russia were responsible, such attacks could be intended to demonstrate the costs of Europe’s continued support for Ukraine, said Sidharth Kaushal, a research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute, or RUSI.

“I think it’s more about cost imposition,” Kaushal told CNBC. “Convincing the European political leadership that the costs of a war can come home to them.”

Russia didn’t immediately respond to a CNBC request for comment.

On Monday, supermarkets in Belgium, Luxembourg, Sweden and the Netherlands found that refrigeration systems had been set to as much as 50 degrees Celsius, or 122 degrees Fahrenheit, affecting retailers including Ahold Delhaize, IKEA, Colruyt Group and Carrefour.

It followed an October cyberattack that targeted hundreds of French supermarkets, causing fires, fridges to overheat and food to spoil. The incidents highlighted vulnerabilities in food-supply infrastructure.

They also highlight the role of private companies in national resilience, as internet-connected equipment can be exploited to cause physical disruption.

Fredrik Blix, cybersecurity expert at Visente and associate professor at Stockholm University, told CNBC that the supermarket attacks required very little technical sophistication since vulnerable refrigeration control systems were connected directly to the public internet, allowing potential attackers to find and exploit them.

“These attacks, they don’t really require any specific advanced knowledge to carry out,” he said, adding that some systems were protected only by default passwords or easily guessed credentials.

“This is why this is so cheap to do,” Blix said, warning that the publicity surrounding the incidents could encourage copycat attacks. “Anyone can do it, and it does not require any resources from a country or anything like that.”

Cyberattacks have become more common over the past decade as societies have become more digital and vulnerable systems have become easier to access, Blix said. However, he noted that mounting geopolitical tensions have also made European countries more alert to potential hybrid warfare threats, leading to scrutiny by both governments and media.

While Blix acknowledged the possibility of a state or state-backed actor being behind the attacks, he said the more likely scenario is someone testing the boundaries and “having some fun.”

Kaushal said the incidents should be viewed within the larger context of suspected sabotage and hybrid threats across Europe, including damage to undersea cables in the Baltic Sea.

“If this was an event in isolation, one might say ‘okay, we should view it on its own merits,’ but when you view it in the backdrop of all of that, it becomes less clear,” he said, also citing death threats against European defense executives and a bomb placed on a DHL aircraft in 2024.

European governments are contending with greater uncertainty over U.S. security guarantees after decades of underinvestment in defense, while facing a rise in unconventional but potentially devastating threats.

Hybrid warfare combines tactics such as cyberattacks, sabotage and disinformation to destabilize adversaries without triggering open military conflict.

Countries’ abilities to withstand hybrid threats vary substantially across the continent, according to Kaushal. While Finland and Sweden have well-developed civilian defense programs reflecting their Cold War experience, much of Europe’s infrastructure was built around economic efficiency rather than defense needs.

“As one goes further west in Europe, the level of preparation, both against hybrid attacks, but also just simple missile attacks of the kind that we’ve seen in Ukraine, is far less great,” he said.

“Every attack generates a bit of resilience,” he said, citing NATO’s increased focus on threats to underwater cables and gas pipelines after the 2022 Nord Stream sabotage.

Oana Popescu-Zamfir, a senior research fellow specializing in European security at RUSI, said the recent incidents showed Europe had lagged in “preparing for something that we have known would be coming.”

“We’ve been slow in adjusting to a new reality,” she said. “We still tend to conceptually divide between peace and wartime, and that is no longer the case because we’re not at war, but we’re also not in peace time.”

She said Europe was likely to face sustained hybrid attacks designed to achieve military objectives without conventional military force.

Popescu-Zamfir said Russia could draw on networks of proxies in Europe, some directly controlled and others more loosely coordinated, making responsibility difficult to trace directly to the Kremlin.

She told CNBC that “the damage that can be done is huge” in targeted attacks on internet-connected systems, citing the potential disruption of blood reserves.

The attacks are not a “piece of cake for Russia to carry out, but they’re also not rocket science,” she said, adding that they “can do tremendous damage in concrete terms and in terms of the psychological impact on our societies and the feeling that we are unprotected.”

Blix said companies can take relatively straightforward steps to reduce their exposure.

“These are basic cyber hygiene things... You should not be allowed to connect industrial control systems and this kind of operational technology directly online without any proper security around it,” he said.

Responsibility is split among product manufacturers, maintenance providers and grocery chains, making accountability unclear as each points to the others.

Blix said maintenance companies sometimes prioritize convenience by enabling remote access despite manufacturers’ security guidance, while retailers may fail to enforce adequate cybersecurity standards among suppliers.

“What worries me is that we don’t really do anything,” Blix said, adding that “we are shuffling a lot of papers” and “doing a lot of risk assessments” but failing to take meaningful action.

Europe has also seen widespread unrest in recent months, adding political pressure as households grapple with high living costs.

Domestic political and economic tensions can also give foreign adversaries opportunities to deepen divisions, said Alexander Anderson, president and director of policy at the Centre for International Security and Economic Strategy.

He told CNBC that Russian and potentially Chinese influence operations may work to amplify those divisions.

“But we should be careful not to dismiss legitimate domestic grievances as the product of foreign interference,” he said. “Doing so risks misunderstanding both the causes of political instability and the methods through which hostile actors seek to exploit it.”

Weeks of nationwide protests, riots and strikes have increased pressure on the French government, complicating efforts to rein in public finances and deepening existing political divisions.

In Spain, demonstrations and a parliamentary impasse over the housing crisis led Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez to call a snap election. The vote is scheduled for Nov. 29. The far-right Vox party is expected to make gains, putting Sanchez’s left-leaning government at risk of losing power.

Germany, Italy, Portugal and Albania have also seen unrest over rising living costs in recent weeks.

On Friday, protesters in Amsterdam tried to enter a Microsoft
 data center, Reuters reported.

Meanwhile, elevated energy prices, persistent inflation, sluggish growth and large budget deficits are pushing up borrowing costs and leaving governments with less room to support struggling households.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/s.title: Looking for new fillings for sandwiches and wraps? We have you covered
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/s.author: Anna Chisholm
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/s.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Hetty Lui McKinnon says this vegetarian muffuletta is a diversion from the original, but no less satisfying. (ABC News: Hetty Lui McKinnon)

As we farewell soup and stew weather, we welcome perfect conditions for sandwiches and wraps.

These creative and versatile options could be served up at almost any time of day, and there's no need to spend hours babysitting a simmering pot.

In fact, most of these recipes involve minimal (if any) cooking time and many can be prepared (or partially prepared) ahead well before hunger strikes.

Have a batch ready to toast in a sandwich press as you need them, Lina Jebeile says. (ABC News: Lina Jebeile)

Lina Jebeile loves prepping these omelette breakfast sandwiches for suhoor (the pre-dawn meal during Ramadan) but says they are also a winner year-round.

Because they reheat beautifully in a sandwich press, they are a compelling contender for any busy mornings or office lunch.

Simple to make, easy to customise and perfect for prepping ahead.

Why confine this sanga strictly to mornings?

To make this layered roast vegetable sandwich vegan, simply omit the cheese. (ABC News: Hetty Lui McKinnon )

Hetty Lui McKinnon says this vegetable sandwich is perfect for picnics, but there's nothing stopping you from eating it inside too.

Inspired by one of America's iconic deli sandwiches, this vegetarian iteration of muffuletta uses roasted vegetables rather than cold cuts and the olive salad infuses every bite with a zesty punch.

This sandwich can also be made ahead. Just reach for some bread (focaccia or ciabatta recommended).

This recipe makes a chickpea filling for sandwiches or wraps, or for you to scoop up with crackers, Heidi Sze says. (ABC News: Heidi Sze)

Use this nourishing smash from Heidi Sze as you see fit, but between two slices of your preferred bread is an obvious (and delicious) choice.

This smash filling takes just 10 minutes and relies on a tin of inexpensive chickpeas as a base.

You can also play around with different flavour combinations, depending on your preferences and what you have handy. Trade parsley for chives, gherkins for capers or mayonnaise for plain yoghurt.

Loi Nguyen's version of traditional banh mi, a dish influenced by both French and Vietnamese cuisines. (ABC TV: Steve Brown)

Influenced by both French and Vietnamese cuisines, this is Recipe of the Year contestant Loi Nguyen's take on a traditional crispy banh mi.

It uses thinly sliced marinated rump steak along with the classic combination of pickled carrots, mayonnaise and chilli sauce.

Marinating the chicken ahead of time takes the pressure off cooking at night. (ABC News: Heidi Sze)

Store-bought flatbreads, herby chicken, crunchy vegetables and a garlicky sauce are combined into an easy and satisfying meal in this recipe from Heidi Sze.

If weather and energy levels allow you could cook the chicken element of this meal on the barbecue, or even make the flatbread yourself.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/l.title: Shark bite survivor Leah Stewart shows 'incredible' wound recovery
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/l.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Shark attack victim Leah Stewart has shown the extent of her leg wound. (Supplied: Instagram)

Leah Stewart says her leg wound has now healed and she is no longer at risk of infection.

The 35-year-old was attacked by a great white shark on June 13 at Coogee Beach in Sydney's east.

Ms Stewart underwent more than a dozen surgeries including the amputation of her left arm.

Almost five months after miraculously surviving a great white shark attack in Sydney's east, Leah Stewart says her leg wound has healed and she is no longer at risk of infection.

Ms Stewart was finishing up her swim at Coogee Beach on June 13 when she was mauled by a 4-metre-long great white shark.

The attack left her with multiple injuries and required more than a dozen operations, including the amputation of her left arm.

In an online update, Ms Stewart said the shark took a "chunk" of her leg and that doctors were unable to save her quad muscle and outer hamstring.

Leah Stewart shows the device that helped her wound heal. (Supplied: Instagram)

She said doctors used a surgical implement, DermaClose, to help gradually close the wound and despite not passing a skin graft her bite was finally able to scar.

"I am really proud of my own body and the amazing team at St Vincent's and I survived the great white, so I've got a cool scar to show for it," she said in the update.

Ms Stewart, who last week celebrated her 35th birthday, said recovering from her leg wound had "been a journey".

"But the fact of the matter is, I can use my legs and I don't have to wrap it up every time I have a shower or be worried about infection because now it is closed.

"So thank you for following along. I am just so happy this is the best update for me."

Ms Stewart also shared a video of her rescue on the day of the attack, showing lifesavers drag her to shore.

The teacher and mother from Coogee has spent months recovering from her injuries, being bitten across her arms and legs and suffering extreme blood loss.

Leah Stewart has now shown the full extent of her injuries. (Supplied: Stewart family)

She was placed in a medically induced coma for more than a week at St Vincent's Hospital.

In August she described in an interview the great white being only "30 centimetres" from her face.

"In my head, I was like, 'You ugly f***er, you are not taking me away from my daughter,'" she said.

"And I twisted myself around and I just started punching it over and over and over again. Just punch, punch, punch.

"It was like fighting a dinosaur. It was so big. It was like punching a brick wall."

Last week Ms Stewart said she was undergoing EMDR therapy to help her "process the event" which left her unable to sleep and suffer daily nightmares.

Eye Movement Desensitisation and Reprocessing is a treatment where the patient is asked to recall a traumatic or emotionally distressing memory while using guided eye movements.

"It's been life-changing for me. I feel like I'm finally getting my life back," she said.
