https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/h.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Mia Petterson said more people were shopping online and looking for second-hand or vintage goods. (ABC News)

Amid the uncertain future of a major department store and the predicted slowing of retail spending, the value of retail goods and services has grown in the ACT.

A marketing expert says the "personalisation" of the industry has been a major change impacting this new era of spending.

One Canberra business owner says developing a relationship with her customers was "the only way to survive".

When Mia Petterson was younger, her mum ran a retail store on Lonsdale Street in Braddon, in Canberra's inner north.

Fast forward to 2026, and Mia is following in her footsteps.

The 28-year-old curates vintage and second-hand items for her Blonde Concept store — which happens to be on the very same street her mum's was on.

Giving a personal touch to business is a priority for vintage and second-hand shop owner Mia Petterson. (ABC News)

"So the name, obviously not a huge amount of creativity involved in that, just got to be honest.

Since her mum's days working in the industry, Ms Petterson said retail had "100 per cent" changed, with buyers shifting towards secondhand and online purchasing.

Social media has become a huge part of the way people shop, too.

Dr Andrew Hughes, a marketing lecturer at the Australian National University, said businesses who use social and digital platforms to boost and maintain engagement were more likely to succeed.

"Nowadays [shopping] combines the social factor as well," Dr Hughes said.

Nationally, retail turnover is predicted to slow to 1.5 per cent next financial year, from 2.8 per cent, according to the latest quarterly forecast by Deloitte Access Economics.

But in the ACT, government data shows a near one per cent rise in the value of goods and services produced by the retail industry, indicating its increased value to the broader ACT economy.

Dr Hughes said retail results are often a "mixed bag", but successful businesses in the ACT that have managed to connect in multiple ways with their customers "are really a case study in how to do marketing well".

"They have good connection with their consumer base, they do good service provision and they're active on socials," he said.

Dr Andrew Hughes said the 'personalisation' of retail was impacting whether businesses sink or swim. (ABC News: David Sciasci)

Ms Petterson said developing a relationship with her customers was "the only way to survive".

"I think one of my main priorities has always been creating a really comfortable, inviting environment for shoppers where they feel like they can try anything on, chat to me, like chat to the girls who work here, and I want people to leave feeling inspired," she said.

Mia Petterson followed after her own mum in running a retail store on Lonsdale Street, Braddon. (ABC News)

This personalised approach is something Dr Hughes believes will become a trademark of success in a new era of retail — and something that Australia's premier department store brand David Jones failed to adapt to.

"We're in a different environment," Dr Hughes said.

"People still spend, but the spending is linked in with experiences which are more personal to who they are.

David Jones's suppliers tell the ABC they could see "the writing on the wall" as payment times got longer and telephone calls went unanswered.

Dr Hughes said keeping up with younger markets was also key for retail businesses.

"For a lot of the younger markets, the most common thing I hear nowadays is, if I can't afford a [house], I'll spend some more money on retail," he said.

"Good for them, I get where they're at, you need some fun in life.

Retail success is a "mixed bag" in the nation's capital, according to one expert. (ABC News)

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.title: Pressure still on Man United boss Carrick despite dramatic Villa draw
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.author: Philip O'connor
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.text:
MANCHESTER, ENGLAND – Manchester United manager Michael Carrick is facing another international window filled with uncertainty after his side slipped into the Premier League relegation zone despite a sensational comeback to claim a 4-4 home draw with Aston Villa.

United is 18th on eight points after 10 games, one behind Coventry City, and for long periods of Sunday’s game looked like a disjointed, rudderless side, with collapses in concentration at the start of each half proving costly for Carrick’s men.

Alysson opened the scoring for Villa after two minutes and Nicolas Jackson added a second two minutes later, but United looked to be motoring when Bruno Fernandes pulled one back with a penalty and Youri Tielemans levelled just before the break.

United again conceded twice in quick succession at the start of the second half to goals from John McGinn and Leon Goretzka but Joshua Zirkzee threw them a lifeline in stoppage time and Patrick Dorgu headed the equalizer in the 96th minute.

“I don’t feel happy,” Dorgu said, despite his late heroics. “We are in a bad situation. We need to fight together to get out of it. Draw better than a loss, but we had the better opportunities.

“Everyone needs to look at themselves and ask if they are doing enough. We need to fight for the manager, for the club and get out of this together ... we need everyone to come back sharp from the international break and start getting wins.”

After the final whistle, Carrick said he thought his side had done enough to win but individual errors had cost them.

“I thought we were the better team for a large part of the game. We’re making it difficult for ourselves with the goals that we’re giving away, and not just giving away one — it’s kind of two in succession that put us in such a difficult position,” he told Sky Sports.

“Then (we) came back into the game and had a lot of the game, and then could have won it in the end, so disappointed that we haven’t won again.”

United fans unfurled banners calling for a change of ownership and booed and whistled some players as they were replaced, but the supporters celebrated with abandon when their side snatched a point at the death.

“They are desperate to get behind us and for us to give them something to go on, they’ve showed that there’s frustration and disappointment at times, I think we all feel that, but they’re right behind the boys,” Carrick said.

“They were (there) right till the end today, and they were after the final whistle as well.”

Asked about his own future after another underwhelming display, Carrick remained tight-lipped.

“We haven’t won enough games, but I expect to move forward and keep working on things that we’ve been working on and showing a lot of the good (we showed) in the game today, tighten up on a few mistakes and win football matches,” he said.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.summary: Manchester United manager Michael Carrick is facing another international window filled with uncertainty. United are 18th in the Premier League after a 4-4 home draw with Aston Villa. The Red Devils are one behind Coventry City and one behind Manchester City.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Private high schools remain out of reach for many despite tuition-free policy, survey finds
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
Tuition-free private high school education began in April, but families still face a heavy financial burden from expenses other than tuition, including admission fees and other school charges.

Nearly 30% of students from financially struggling households said they could not consider private high schools as an option when choosing where to study, according to a survey by international nonprofit organization Save the Children Japan.

The survey was conducted online in May and June among households participating in a child benefit program run by the Tokyo-based organization. It received 550 valid responses, including 125 first-year junior high school and high school students from across Japan and 425 parents.

Asked how the high school tuition-free policy had affected their choice of school, 27% of first-year senior high school students responded they had been unable to consider private schools as an option because they thought they would face expenses other than tuition.

Meanwhile, half of the parents whose children attend private high schools cited as a major concern when enrolling them the possibility that their children might have to leave school for financial reasons.

The survey showed that the average school fees, including facility maintenance and air-conditioning charges incurred when entering a private high school was ¥147,526 ($932), more than double the figure recorded a year earlier.

Admission fees averaged ¥173,135, about 1.2 times the previous year’s level. Expenses for uniforms, sportswear and commuter passes also increased.

More than 60% of parents and junior high school and high school students said they wanted computers and tablet devices, which are expensive for families to purchase, to be provided as school-owned equipment.

Subsidies or grants for purchasing such devices were available to 54.7% of students at public schools, compared with just 7% at private schools. Families whose children attend private high schools spent the average of about ¥100,000 for the purchase.

“Rising prices and the resulting financial strain are affecting children’s right to education, particularly those from economically disadvantaged households,” said Mitsue Tashiro of the organization.

Yuji Shirakawa, a professor specializing in sociology of education at Chiba University who helped with the survey, said, “Schools need to reconsider their practices regarding admission fees and other charges, and take measures such as providing learning materials as school-owned supplies and promoting the transfer of used items from graduating students to incoming students.”
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.summary: Nearly 30% of students from financially struggling households said they could not consider private high schools as an option. The survey was conducted online in May and June among households participating in a child benefit program. The average school fees, including facility maintenance and air-conditioning charges, were more than double the figure recorded a year earlier.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/environment.title: COP31 to open in Turkey, with climate goals under pressure from war and AI
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/environment.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/environment.text:
ANTALYA, TURKEY – Representatives from nearly 200 countries will gather on Turkey’s Mediterranean coast on Monday for two weeks of climate talks, as war-driven energy security fears, surging artificial intelligence power demand and U.S. disengagement put new pressure on the fight against global warming.

The U.S. war with Iran has nations scrambling for oil cargoes and firing up coal plants; the rapid rollout of AI is pumping up power demand; and the world’s top historic greenhouse gas emitter is shunning climate cooperation for the second year running.

All that has created a challenging backdrop destined to complicate efforts by COP31 host Turkey to land a strong deal, according to observers.

“It’s hard to be optimistic,” said John Holdren, a professor of environmental policy at Harvard University.

Turkey’s COP31 presidency has centered this year’s U.N.-sponsored summit on a goal to electrify more than a third of the global economy by 2035, up from around a fifth today. It is asking nations to sign onto a pledge supporting that target.

Theoretically, such a goal could help reduce planet-warming emissions by speeding the global shift away from fossil fuel-powered vehicles, furnaces, boilers, cookstoves, and other greenhouse gas-emitting equipment.

But climate advocates have criticized the pledge because it does not require that the additional electricity come from low-carbon sources. This has set up an early fight over whether electrification alone should count as climate progress.

A coalition of countries, including South Pacific island nations most vulnerable to sea level rise, are pushing more generally for a clearer global roadmap away from fossil fuels — a perennially controversial topic at climate summits.

Many oil- and gas-producing nations, including Saudi Arabia, argue that fossil fuels can still form a substantial part of the global energy mix in a climate-friendly world, provided they are paired with technologies that reduce or capture emissions.

Pressure is mounting for faster action on climate change.

A report by the United Nations Environment Program published in October said the world is already set to overshoot 1.5 degrees Celsius of warming above preindustrial times, the threshold set at the 2015 Paris climate summit.

2026 also stood out with a series of extreme heat waves across Western Europe and a glacier collapse in Nepal that caused a catastrophic flood that killed more than 1,450 people, with thousands still missing.

“This year has proven to be one of the years with the highest casualties by the climate-induced disasters,” said Manjeet Dal, an adviser to the Least Developed Country bloc and south Asia director of Climate Analytics.

The Iran war has underscored the world’s attachment to fossil fuels, as has Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the ensuing sanctions on Moscow’s energy exports. Some say disruptions from the wars have also clarified the benefits of turning to renewables.

The Iran war, now in its ninth month, severely disrupted Middle East oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, lifting fuel prices around the globe and leading governments to scramble for new supplies.

U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration has encouraged policies maximizing oil, gas, and coal production to address the Mideast disruptions. South Korea, India, Thailand and other Asian nations, meanwhile, have increased their reliance on coal or taken steps to boost coal-fired power generation.

“A lot of people who previously might have been embarrassed to argue for continuing very high use of fossil fuel are now feeling empowered to make that case,” said Holdren of Harvard.

At the same time, the deployment of renewable energy has also risen, driven by surging exports of cheap clean tech from China, cheering advocates for ambitious climate action.

“The war has strengthened the case for accelerating the energy transition. The United States is something of an outlier in this regard,” said Andre Correa do Lago, a Brazilian diplomat who presided over last year’s COP.

AI has also added a wrinkle. The technology’s rapid rollout is driving a surge in global power demand, contributing to rising greenhouse gas emissions. But its benefits are proving irresistible, even to climate and environment activist groups.

COP31 host Turkey will call on governments, businesses and other institutions at the conference to sign a pledge outlining principles to ensure AI is developed and deployed sustainably.

Business advocates said they want just one thing from COP31: clarity.

“Delivery cannot remain a slogan or be left to voluntary initiatives,” said John Denton, the secretary general of the International Chamber of Commerce. “COP31 must send clear policy signals that give businesses the confidence to invest in electrification and the wider energy transition — and turn adaptation needs into bankable projects.”
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/environment.summary: U.S. war with Iran has nations scrambling for oil cargoes and firing up coal plants. The rapid rollout of AI is pumping up power demand, and the world’s top greenhouse gas emitter is shunning climate cooperation for the second year running.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Poland mourns victims of Krakow shooting amid security fears
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
KRAKOW – Poland began two days of national mourning on Sunday after a gunman killed six people in Krakow’s historic main square, an attack the government said may have been inspired by far-right ideology.

Saturday’s shooting shocked a country that had prided itself on being safer than many of its Western European neighbors, and deepened public concern about extreme views following school stabbings in October that officials have linked to inflammatory content online.

Nationalist opposition politicians, however, questioned the grounds on which the government said far-right ideology could have led to the shooting that left 16 people wounded in addition to those killed.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.summary: Poland's government says attack may have been inspired by far-right ideology. Six people killed in Krakow's main square, including 16 people wounded.

PARIS – Carlos Alcaraz gained a measure of revenge on Ben Shelton on Sunday as the seven-time Grand Slam champion beat the American 7-6 (7-5), 7-5 to win the Paris Masters for the first time.

In defeating the man who ended his U.S. Open title defense earlier this season, the 23-year-old claimed the ninth 1000-level title of his career.

Unlike their five-set quarterfinal epic in New York two months ago, the clash in Paris lasted just under two hours.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.author: Gabriel Araujo
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.text:
SAO PAULO – Mercedes secured its ninth Formula One constructors’ world championship and completed a title double on Sunday in a wet Sao Paulo Grand Prix won by McLaren’s Lando Norris from pole position for the second year in a row.

The title was Mercedes’ first team crown since 2021 and came a week after 20-year-old Italian Kimi Antonelli made headlines as the youngest drivers’ champion with four races to spare in Mexico City.

Red Bull’s Max Verstappen finished second, putting on a masterclass from 21st on the grid due to engine penalties, in a race that started and ended in the rain.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.author: Amy Tennery
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.text:
Coco Gauff shredded her shoes but stayed one step ahead of Jessica Pegula to defeat her compatriot 6-4, 6-7 (7-5), 6-2 on the first day of the WTA Finals at Indian Wells on Sunday, while Czech Linda Noskova got the better of Marta Kostyuk 6-2, 6-4.

Gauff had beaten Pegula three months ago in Cincinnati and had the right formula once again, as the 2024 winner showed superb versatility in a round-robin clash between the top two Americans in the season-ending championship.

The frequent rivals were 5-5 in their head-to-head record before Sunday and appeared perfectly matched through a tight opening set, where Gauff got the break from the baseline on the fourth set point.

https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.title: Victorian election 2026: Concern and scepticism among Labor MPs as new poll shows party trailing One Nation
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.author: Benita Kolovos Victorian state correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text:
Ben Carroll refuses to be drawn on latest opinion poll that puts Labor at all-time low of just 18%, behind One Nation on 21% and the Coalition on 33%

Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast

Victorian Labor MPs are both sceptical and seriously concerned about a new poll ahead of the state election showing the party trailing third behind One Nation, with its primary vote at an all-time low of just 18%.

The DemosAU/PremierNational, first published by the Herald Sun on Monday, showed Labor’s primary vote share has crashed seven points to 18%, putting it in third place behind the Coalition’s 33% and One Nation’s 21%. At the same time, the Greens improved their primary vote to 17%, an increase of three points since September.

It means the Coalition now leads Labor on a two-party preferred basis 56-44, compared with 52-48 in September.

George Hasanakos, DemosAU’s head of research, said if the poll were replicated on election night then many contests across the state would be between the Liberals or Nationals and One Nation, which would then result in a “clear Coalition majority”.

“If that happens, One Nation has to poll really, really well to have a chance of winning, because Labor and Greens preferences will flow to the Liberals,” he said.

On election night, the Victorian Electoral Commission plans to conduct a two-candidate-preferred count, or 2CP, between the two candidates it expects to finish with the most support after preferences are distributed. The commission is selecting the indicative 2CP for each seat based on polling, analysis of preference flows and results from previous elections. It will not publish the indicative 2CPs before election day to avoid influencing voter behaviour.

Hasanakos added that he “double, triple, quadruple checked” the result of the “extraordinary” poll, which had 1,562 respondents, an effective sample of 818 and a margin of error of 3.4%.

“We went to the trouble of a bigger sample here, and I stand by it,” he said.

Ben Carroll repeatedly refused to say whether he was worried about the poll at a press conference in South Melbourne on Monday morning.

“What I’m focused on every day is fighting for working people and making sure that every Victorian that goes into the ballot on November 28 knows that under my government you have a government on your side that will fight for you,” he told reporters.

“The alternative is a Liberal-One Nation government that will fight against you – they’re going to shrink the economy, cause a recession and make life difficult for every single Victorian.”

But the result has sparked serious concerns among the Labor caucus, even though some MPs are sceptical about the 18% figure. Inside Labor’s campaign headquarters, they are treating the result as an “outlier” and point to other public polls that have their primary vote in the 20s.

Several Labor MPs, unauthorised to speak publicly, have told Guardian Australia there are many in the caucus questioning their party’s strategy.

This includes a focus in recent days on crime – an issue that is typically a Coalition strength. On Sunday, Carroll announced a $204m plan to enable judges to sentence low- and mid-level youth offenders to a new rehabilitation detention program while on Monday he announced $70m to recruit 200 more police reservists to re-open stations and build and upgrade more stations.

“Caucus is really angry and deflated, because this is all happening because of him,” one MP

“Even if it’s higher than 18, and we get back into something with a 2 in front of it, the experiment has been an epic fail, the campaign is in freefall, and it’s about to get a whole lot worse.”

Another MP said the focus on crime was “diabolically stupid strategy” as the government had years to tackle community concern around rising rates.

The opposition leader, Jess Wilson, on Monday said her party had a focus on “getting tough on crime”, including by introducing Aidan’s Law, to toughen sentencing for attacks on people who step in to protect others.

Carroll immediately matched the commitment to introduce the proposed law, named after 22-year-old Aidan Becker, who was fatally stabbed at Mernda station after stepping in to protect a 14-year-old during an alleged violent robbery.

It comes as Pauline Hanson rejected reports by The Age and 60 Minutes on Sunday that her former national campaign director, Sean Black, continues to secretly work for One Nation in Victoria.

Black was in 2018 was jailed for rape and subsequently lost his appeal against the conviction but was then rehired by One Nation in 2020 as a campaign director after serving his time. Hanson sacked him after political pressure earlier this year.

She told the Australian Financial Review on Monday “the day that I sacked him [Sean Black] that was the day he finished up”.

https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.author: Josh Halliday North of England editor
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.text:
Minister says Labour hoping to offer bed to every rough sleeper in England but cites chronic housing shortage

Andy Burnham’s pledge to tackle rough sleeping by getting “everyone in for Christmas” is in jeopardy amid rising numbers of people on the streets and a severe housing shortage.

Official figures show an increase of nearly 1,000 people sleeping rough in England between January and June, the latest month for which figures are available.

There were 8,748 rough sleepers in England in June, the highest number since November 2025, according to government statistics.

Only 15% of those were found accommodation by the end of June, the lowest level since August 2025 as councils struggle with the growing demand for temporary and affordable housing.

The homelessness minister, Florence Eshalomi, said the government hoped to offer a bed to every rough sleeper by Christmas but that there was a chronic shortage of suitable housing.

Asked whether every person on the streets in England would be offered accommodation in the next six weeks, she said: “We’re hoping to offer that, but what we are definitely offering is a route off the street for everyone who wants to take up that offer.”

A “route off the street” may not necessarily involve housing, Eshalomi said.

“For some people it will be a route into accommodation, for some people it could be a … dedicated plan around their mental health or substance misuse, so that’s what we are committed to.

“The offer of a bed will be there for people who want that. We cannot force people off the streets – we’ve got to respect that as well – but that offer will be there.”

Burnham has pledged to offer every rough sleeper in England a safe route off the streets or wider support as a central part of his premiership.

Councils across England have said the number of homeless families is growing as a result of the chronic shortage of affordable housing, record demand for temporary accommodation and the long-term freeze of local housing allowance, meaning rents far outstrip the welfare available to those on low incomes.

Frontline professionals are also concerned about the impact of the prisons early release scheme, with some offenders being released without stable accommodation, as well as a flood of no-fault evictions before the practice was banned on 1 May.

A record 135,600 households in England were living in temporary accommodation such as B&Bs and hostels at the end of March 2026, according to official figures. This is about 90% higher than a decade ago and 4% higher than the previous year.

In a speech in Downing Street when he became prime minister on 20 July, Burnham said: “I will soon go through that door behind me and issue my first instruction: to end rough sleeping in our country.”

The next month, he announced increased funding of £442m as part of what he called the “national drive to get everyone in for Christmas”.

In October he set out a further £432m in funding from March 2027 so that people would be “offered a safe route off the streets this winter” and support to the end of this parliament.

Eshalomi, who was appointed by Burnham in July, previously described the freeze of local housing allowance as one of the “systemic barriers” and a “big sticking point” in reducing homelessness.

Speaking on a visit to a temporary accommodation facility in Manchester last week, she said the area was not “best policy” and that she raised it “constantly with colleagues … with the Treasury”.

Asked whether she raised it with fellow ministers before John Healey’s budget last month, she said: “I’ve been an MP since 2019. I’ve been raising it since then.”

Eshalomi said she was working with councils and housing associations in England to bring thousands of empty or derelict properties into use to help tackle rough sleeping.

She said ultimately the solution was “building those homes”.

“It’s around making sure we’re building more social and affordable homes so that people don’t have to find themselves choosing between not having enough money and support to live in a private rented sector.”

https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.author: Julia Kollewe
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.text:
Coffee shop chain targets growth north of London with extra 500 outlets in big boost for youth employment

Starbucks has set out plans to hire 7,500 new baristas over the next five years, in a boost to youth employment as the chain pins hopes for future growth on the north of the country.

The US coffee shop chain, which employs more than 18,000 people in the UK, said the hiring spree would focus on the Midlands, north of England, Wales and Scotland, as it targets growth north of the M25.

The roles are expected to staff 500 new coffee shops which Starbucks hopes to open across the country by 2031. The company set out the growth plan earlier this year after shutting dozens of underperforming outlets in Britain last year as part of a $1bn (£750m) global restructuring.

Darren King, who runs Starbucks UK, said: “We’re deeply focused on how we can help more young people into these positions, starting by making entry-level roles as accessible as possible.”

Starbucks is a large youth employer and set out its plan before an official report into the number of young people not in education, employment or training, known as Neets, which hit a record high above 1 million at the start of the year.

The rise in worklessness was dealt a blow in the run-up to the budget last month, as UK employers cut back on hiring amid worries about rising costs and the outlook for the British economy, according to a monthly survey.

The number of people taking up permanent jobs across the UK fell for the first time in four months, according to the latest jobs report from KPMG and the Recruitment & Employment Confederation, compiled by S&P Global. Recruitment for temporary roles also fell, for the first time since March.

Jon Holt, the chief executive and UK senior partner of KPMG, said: “October saw employers pull back on hiring in the month leading up to the budget, ending a run of more positive news over recent months. Renewed geopolitical and economic uncertainty weighed on confidence, with further energy price shocks and a global bond sell-off pushing borrowing costs higher.”

Holt added: “Businesses will now be assessing whether the measures announced in the budget give them enough stability to absorb the external pressures and higher costs they face. But with the Bank of England increasing interest rates and inflation set to continue rising over the coming months, there is a risk the green shoots we had been seeing in the jobs market could stall.”

https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/n.title: The efficiency trap: why optimising everything can backfire, badly
https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/n.author: Steven Strogatz and Alex Townsend
https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/n.text:
From roundabouts to the stock market, relentless streamlining could be making the world more dangerous

W
e have all been there: packed shoulder to shoulder on the train while the person beside us coughs and sneezes. A protective flu jab offers some reassurance, but so does the thought that there will be a hospital bed for you, should you need it. Yet, in England, about 95% of adult hospital beds were occupied at the height of flu season last year.

If hospitals were hotels, that level of occupancy would be good business, and we would commend them for their efficiency. But do we really want a hospital to have so few beds in reserve that it’s just one bad flu week away from having to treat patients in corridors?

This is the subtle thing about efficiency. We usually assume that more of it must be better. But we can become so focused on improving one thing that we lose sight of the others. You can try to arrange your calendar so that every minute is accounted for, but you’ll soon start running over and end up behind. A gap between meetings might seem like inefficiency, but it’s what allows your schedule to recover when something unexpected happens.

Mathematicians have a name for the pursuit of efficiency. We call it optimisation. Give us something to minimise or maximise – cost, time, fuel, profit – and we will try to find the best possible answer. For most of human history, people optimised by common sense. But computers have enormously expanded what can be effectively tackled, from airline schedules to supply chains. The gains for society have been extraordinary. But there are at least three traps to beware of in the relentless pursuit of optimality.

The hospital bed story illustrated the first one: weakening a system’s robustness by squeezing out too much slack. An empty bed can be redundant on a quiet Tuesday night, but it’s somewhere precious to put the next patient when flu cases surge. If you judge a system by its performance under ordinary conditions, you can lose the ability to cope with extraordinarily challenging ones.

A second trap is having a too-narrow definition of “best”. Take the city of Milton Keynes. Designed by urban planners in the late 1960s, it has an American-style grid system. As the city began to be built out, roundabouts rather than traffic lights became a defining feature of its road junctions; today there are about 130 of them. The roundabouts were great for traffic flow, but they came with a now-notorious cost. Have you ever taken the coach from Oxford to Cambridge? An hour in, you get great views of Milton Keynes, but a busload of queasy passengers, as the coach negotiates one roundabout after another. Slow down, swing left, curve right, accelerate. It’s hard to appreciate the seamless merging of vehicles when your stomach is churning.

Traffic flow is important, to be sure. Engineers find it convenient to optimise because it’s relatively easy to measure. Passenger comfort, on the other hand, is harder to quantify. In a case like this, optimisation gives you the best answer to the question you asked, but can deliver unwelcome answers to questions you failed to consider.

A third trap appears when attempts to optimise collide. Even if every part of a system is acting optimally, the system as a whole may not. On 6 May 2010, US financial markets gave a dramatic demonstration of the effect. In the middle of an already falling market, the S&P 500 suddenly plunged another 5% in just five minutes. The whipsaw on the upside was even wilder; within 10 minutes, the market had recovered. Hundreds of individual securities briefly traded at absurdly low prices.

One trigger for these violent fluctuations was an automated program selling 75,000 futures contracts, worth more than $4bn. Other automated traders reacted nearly instantly. Then their responses fed back on one another, and liquidity evaporated. The algorithms’ actions may have been individually sensible in isolation, but they combined to produce collective turmoil.

Which brings us to artificial intelligence. AI is one of the most spectacular triumphs of optimisation in history. During training, enormous numbers of parameters are repeatedly adjusted so that a model gets better at predicting language, writing computer programs, answering scientific questions and giving legal advice. Unfortunately, AI now has the potential to make all three optimisation traps more treacherous than ever. The first trap – the urge to remove the slack – could tempt organisations to dispense with the human oversight that looks redundant in the age of quicker-witted algorithms. Why retain experienced staff when a machine can handle the routine chores? But in cutting that human capacity, you may lose the ability to spot and handle exceptional circumstances.

The second trap – a blinkered view of what “best” means – arises if we regard intelligence as whatever scores highest on a leaderboard. We are remarkably good at building AI systems that do well on measures such as user satisfaction, but we are finding it much harder to optimise them for judgment or empathy. Indeed, researchers have found that training algorithms on human preferences can encourage AI to sycophantically agree with us rather than tell us uncomfortable truths.

Then there is the third trap. AI systems are increasingly interacting with one another, often at blinding speeds and in vast numbers – especially in the era of agentic AI – and we worry that their interactions could generate unpredictable, dangerous behaviour. Recently, an OpenAI agent broke into a non-public Medicare statistics portal in Australia, while public logs suggested that hundreds of other agents were coordinating attempts to gain access to Australian government health data. Although those attempts have not been shown to be part of the Medicare breach, they certainly revealed something disturbing: hundreds of agents apparently working together in unauthorised ways. The concern here goes beyond what any given AI may or may not do; it’s about what happens when swarms of them join forces.

As optimisation becomes more powerful, avoiding these traps becomes more important. The challenge is not simply finding the best answer. It is deciding what “best” really means – and knowing what not to optimise away.

Steven Strogatz and Alex Townsend are mathematics professors at Cornell University and the authors of Big Math (John Murray).

The Efficiency Paradox: What Big Data Can’t Do by Edward Tenner (Vintage, £16.99)

The Unaccountability Machine: Why Big Systems Make Terrible Decisions (Profile, £11.99)

Optimal Illusions: The False Promise of Optimization by Coco Krumme (Bantam, £25.99)

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.title: Turkiye pushes electrification top of climate agenda as COP31 set to open
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.text:
The United Nations climate conference COP31 is set to open on Monday in Antalya, Turkiye, against the backdrop of the US-led war on Iran, which has underscored the world’s attachment to fossil fuels.

Turkiye has said it would centre electrification on the COP31 agenda, launching the non-binding 35-by-35 Global Electrification Pledge, which aims to make electricity account for at least 35 percent of global energy demand by 2035.

Electricity currently accounts for about one-fifth of global total final energy consumption, according to the International Energy Agency.

Turkiye says the “35 by 35” will speed up the shift to renewable sources of energy while strengthening energy security.

“This year’s energy crisis has shocked us… everyone now understands that energy that you import is energy that you do not control,” the COP31 president and Turkiye’s environment minister, Murat Kurum, said on Thursday.

“Electrification is the answer. It protects communities from volatile global markets and cuts emissions.”

COP31’s aim is “to usher in the age of electricity”, he said.

The climate conference’s priority areas also include zero waste, methane reduction, climate-resilient cities, green industrialisation, education and implementation of national climate plans.

However, climate advocates have criticised the pledge, arguing it does not require that additional electricity come from low-carbon sources.

This has set up a debate on whether electrification alone should count as climate progress.

A coalition of countries, including South Pacific island nations most vulnerable to sea level rise, is pushing more generally for a clearer global roadmap away from fossil fuels.

Many oil and gas producing countries, including Saudi Arabia, argue that fossil fuels can form a substantial part of the global energy mix, provided they are paired with technologies that reduce or capture emissions.

The US-Israel war on Iran has severely disrupted oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, raising fuel prices around the globe and leading governments to scramble for alternative sources.

US President Donald Trump has encouraged policies maximising oil, gas, and coal production to address the Middle East disruptions.

South Korea, India, Thailand and other Asian nations have increased their reliance on coal or taken steps to boost coal-fired power generation.

At the same time, the deployment of renewable energy has also risen, driven by surging exports of cheap clean technology from China.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.summary: COP31 is set to open on Monday in Antalya, Turkiye, against the backdrop of the US-led war on Iran. The UN climate conference is set for the first time in the past year. The conference is expected to focus on the global energy supply shift to renewable energy.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.title: A joke or test? Why Trump floated UFC’s Dana White as his press secretary
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.author: Ahmed Diab
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.text:
For a brief period over the weekend, it looked like United States President Donald Trump had zeroed in on a new White House press secretary: Dana White.

A stocky former fighter with a shaved head and a penchant for wearing black, White currently serves as the chief executive of Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC), a mixed martial arts company that counts Trump among its fans.

But on Sunday night, after hours of speculation, Trump put an end to the rumours he himself started.

“I was only kidding. But Dana loves the idea,” Trump said from an airport tarmac in West Palm Beach, Florida. “And there’s only one Dana. He’s great.”

Just a day earlier, Trump had posted a message to his Truth Social platform, purporting to offer White the press secretary job.

“I am pleased to announce that the Great Dana White, a violent Fighter and Warrior, has been offered the job of Press Secretary of the United States,” Trump wrote on Saturday.

He proceeded to explain – in seemingly tongue-in-cheek style – that he had asked White to bring along fighters like Islam Makhachev and Khabib Nurmagomedov as “assistants”.

The post was accompanied by images of the muscle-bound fighters, several of them baring their teeth.

“We need these people to defend us against the Lunatic Left. Dana will be a Press Secretary like none other,” Trump continued in his post. “Dana, please take the job!”

Trump has a history of unconventional picks for public office. The press secretary role remains vacant after Trump briefly appointed political commentator Katie Zacharia to the job in October.

Zacharia lasted five days, the shortest tenure of any White House press secretary in history.

Critics questioned her legal credentials and her job performance. At her inaugural briefing, she struggled to deliver her opening remarks, and the meeting ended within 15 minutes.

White would likewise have been an out-of-the-box choice to serve as press secretary. But political insiders say Trump has an affinity for pushing the envelope of what is acceptable in Washington, DC.

“Knowing President Trump as I do, I believe he was partly serious,” Rob Arlett, a Republican strategist and former Delaware campaign manager for Trump, told Al Jazeera.

“He and Dana White share a longstanding friendship and business relationship dating back more than 25 years, when Trump supported the UFC by hosting events at his Atlantic City casino. Their mutual loyalty and trust remain strong.”

Arlett believes Trump often floats ideas publicly to gauge reactions before deciding his next move.

It’s also part of the president’s strategy, he said, to generate headlines, test public opinion and assess the response.

Born on July 28, 1969, in Manchester, Connecticut, White is a two-time college dropout and former boxer who turned a passion for fighting into a billion-dollar enterprise.

He is also one of Trump’s longtime political supporters. In December 2015, White endorsed the Republican leader’s bid for the presidency, even though Trump was considered a long shot at the time.

“You will never hear me say a negative thing about Donald Trump,” White told TMZ Sports. “Donald will get my vote.”

Trump went on to win the 2016 presidential election in his first successful bid for public office.

The two men’s careers have been intertwined for decades, though. White began his career running gyms in cities like Boston and Las Vegas, and eventually, he started to manage champion fighters like Tito Ortiz and Chuck Liddell.

It was the 1990s, and both men were competitors in a new competition circuit known as the Ultimate Fighting Championship.

The tournament was designed to bring different martial arts, like jujitsu and wrestling, together in one arena.

White would ultimately be credited with transforming the sport into an international commercial success.

He became president of the UFC in 2001, after the businessmen Frank and Lorenzo Fertitta bought the company for $2m.

But the sport was struggling at first, according to White’s own account. Critics slammed its tournaments as too violent and unregulated.

“It was basically considered a blood sport,” White told the Republican National Convention in 2016, as he rallied on behalf of Trump’s campaign. “State athletic commissions didn’t support us. Arenas around the world refused to host our events. Nobody took us seriously. Nobody – except Donald Trump.”

During the first year of White’s leadership at the UFC, Trump arranged to host the tournament at his Taj Mahal casino in Atlantic City, New Jersey. He did so again the following year.

White credits the move with helping the UFC gain mainstream acceptance.

“Donald was the first guy that recognised the potential that we saw in the UFC and encouraged us to build our business,” White said.

He has since campaigned for Trump in the 2016, 2020 and 2024 elections, donating tens of thousands to his campaign. In 2020, for instance, White donated $1m to America First Action, a pro-Trump political action committee.

Trump and White have continued to enjoy a close relationship since the Republican leader’s return to office.

In June, Trump hosted a UFC tournament on the White House lawn as part of the festivities for the 250th anniversary of US independence.

And over the weekend, White acknowledged he had plans to meet Trump in Washington, DC, on Monday.

“I’m flying to Washington, DC, right now,” White told reporters at a news conference. However, he appeared dismissive of the prospect of joining Trump’s administration.

“I’ve got a lot of jobs already,” he quipped. Since 2023, White has served as the CEO of the UFC, as well as its president.

White has no previous government experience. But some experts say that might not be disqualifying under Trump’s leadership.

“Trump likes to think outside the box and be the first to do something to stand out from the others,” Ihsan Alkhatib, a lawyer and political science professor at Murray State University in Kentucky, told Al Jazeera.

“But the position requires a set of skills that Dana White doesn’t have,” Alkhatib added.

The lack of experience prompted some critics to question Trump’s decision-making abilities when he first floated the idea of naming White as press secretary.

Still, Alkhatib explained that other presidents have likewise faced pushback over decisions to appoint unconventional candidates to public office.

The scenario is “not as unusual as it might sound”, Alkhatib said, offering an example. “George W Bush wanted to elevate his personal lawyer and White House counsel, Harriet Miers, to the US Supreme Court, and she was definitely not qualified for the position.”

White’s appointment, however, would likely have generated further controversy had Trump pursued it.

White has been married to Anne Stella since 1996, but in 2022, a video posted on social media showed White slapping her during an argument at a New Year’s Eve party in Mexico.

White later apologised for his behaviour. In a statement to the media at the time, he said, “There’s no defense for this, and people should not be defending me, no matter what. All the criticism I’ve received this week is 100% warranted.”

Trump had four White House press secretaries during his first term, from 2017 to 2021. So far, during his second, he has had two: Karoline Leavitt and Zacharia.

The post has been vacant since October 16. Trump is still without a chief spokesperson.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.summary: Dana White is the chief executive of Ultimate Fighting Championship. White has been married to Anne Stella since 1996. White is a two-time college dropout and former boxer.

https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/08/is-jen.title: Is Jensen Huang’s job on the line? Yale’s Jeffrey Sonnenfeld estimates it’s “about a 50-50”
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/08/is-jen.author: Connie Loizos
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/08/is-jen.text:
Nvidia’s board announced Sunday that it’s launching an independent investigation after CEO Jensen Huang told staff he was unfaithful to his wife. But this isn’t a case of just another CEO having an extramarital affair. The romantic interest is Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, whom U.S. officials believe is a Chinese spy who was feeding information back to Beijing. In short, the stakes reach well beyond Nvidia, given how many tech and financial partners depend on its place at the center of the booming AI economy. “I’m responsible for an entire industry,” Huang recently told Bloomberg in a sit-down.

A spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in Washington dismissed the allegations in late October as “groundless smears and slanders,” and no one has been charged. But U.S. intelligence officials reportedly briefed President Donald Trump about their concerns a year ago, and unnamed senior officials inside the Trump administration told the Times that they doubt Huang could have remained unaware all that time of Alice Huang’s intelligence-gathering role for China. When Trump was first briefed, the Times reported, officials didn’t believe Huang knew, and isn’t clear whether their assessment has changed. The board, meanwhile, says it sees no sign that national security or company secrets were compromised, and that Huang is staying on.

The question now is whether Huang can survive this. To think through what could come next, this editor spoke Sunday with famed professor Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, senior associate dean for leadership studies at the Yale School of Management and founder of the Chief Executive Leadership Institute, which has hosted Huang at its CEO summits. Sonnenfeld likes Huang, he said, and he called Huang’s career salvageable but put the odds at “about a 50-50.” He also had a lot more food for thought.

First, the reputational damage. Until now, Huang has been “revered and trusted by everybody in technology,” Sonnenfeld noted. But he called this episode “remarkably poor judgment.” Even if Huang was merely naive, he said, “any employee in Nvidia other than him would be fired over this,” and the recklessness alone would mean “an irretrievable loss of confidence.”

Sonnenfeld suggested that Huang’s saving grace could be what social psychologists call idiosyncrasy credits, if he can prove he was being duped. The term comes from Edwin Hollander, a social psychologist who proposed in a 1958 paper that people earn latitude in a group by showing competence and following its rules. Huang has been earning latitude since he co-founded Nvidia in 1993. But all that goodwill can run out when a screw-up looks self-serving or touches the group’s core norms. Here that group includes Nvidia’s board, its roughly 42,000 employees who are bound by security rules, and, in a looser sense, the U.S. government, given it restricts its exports.

We also talked about precedents, except, as it turns out, there really are none. Executives who survive personal scandals usually pick up where they left off at another company, Sonnenfeld observed. Former HP CEO Mark Hurd is one example example. Between 2005 and 2010, he turned HP to the top of the industry by revenue, then was pressured to resign after he filed inaccurate expense reports that hid a personal relationship with a contractor. Oracle hired him about a month later. Huang has no equivalent move to make because Nvidia is his company

As for the bench at Nvidia, that doesn’t really exist either. While there is typically a hierarchy inside companies of Nvidia’s scale and importance, Huang has kept things as flat as possible, with about 60 direct reports by his own account. That structure makes it hard to figure out who would succeed him from inside (though his children, both of whom work at Nvidia, are the sometimes the subject of succession speculation). That won’t stop the worldwide guessing game that’s sure to follow in the coming weeks. And boards in crisis often reach for a “messianic solution” from outside, Sonnenfeld said, floating former Google CEO Eric Schmidt as one idea.

Nvidia’s role at the center of a massive and complex circular financing web is what makes this particular predicament especially tricky. Nvidia isn’t just the biggest provider of chips driving the AI boom but also largely the bank behind the buildout. In addition to stakes in hundreds of smaller startups, Nvidia has invested in OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI, CoreWeave and Nebius. In August, it also signed preliminary agreements with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR aimed at mobilizing more than $500 billion over time, and Huang has said Nvidia could backstop up to a quarter of it. The move was widely interpreted as a way to spread risk. Still, a leadership crisis at the center is how a stumble becomes a spiral.

So what’s Nvidia’s board likely doing right now? Sonnenfeld noted that Huang’s advocacy for selling advanced chips to China had already made people anxious. Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, whose company Nvidia has backed, had a lot to say about selling chips to China at Davos back in January, likening it to “selling nuclear weapons to North Korea.”

Now the board’s independent members — meaning everyone but Huang — will have to establish what technology reached China if any, and by what routes, including by better understanding Nvidia’s relationship with Megaspeed. The Singapore cloud company, which grew out of a Chinese gaming business and became Nvidia’s largest buyer in Southeast Asia, bought roughly $2 billion of its chips, the New York Times reported in October 2025, raising broader questions about whether it was helping China circumvent U.S. export restrictions, either by re-exporting the chips to China or renting them to Chinese customers remotely. (An Nvidia spokesperson told The Hill after the Times report that the allegations were “thoroughly investigated and debunked last year.”)

In the meantime, Huang will keep running the company, Nvidia said Sunday. That’ll be a tall order, even for a CEO who already spends much of his time traveling the world to promote Nvidia. For starters, three House chairmen want a closed-door briefing from Huang on November 18. Nvidia is also reporting its newest earnings on November 17. Sonnenfeld expects that even if Huang keeps the title, he’ll have to hand off some of the day-to-day decision-making.

Only one thing is certain right now. Huang doesn’t own the kind of super-voting stock that would cement his power at Nvidia. Sonnenfeld often argues for dual-class structures that empower founders, and he says Huang’s success without one has been the best counterargument to that case. But if Huang had one, Sonnenfeld continued, removing him would be harder.

This episode may be remembered as a pivotal moment for how the tech industry guards its secrets. Sonnenfeld argues tech has been “way too lax” compared with defense contractors that face clearance regimes. The arrest last month of an OpenAI engineer points to the same problem. He was accused of hiding a recording device behind a TV in an executive conference room, and while OpenAI has said it has no indication that model weights, source code, or customer data were accessed, the case highlights how exposed tech companies are to people who get close.

Huang may well survive the investigation (Sonnenfeld hopes the board clears him of knowingly aiding anyone). The bigger test comes when Nvidia’s employees, customers and partners, and, indirectly, the millions of Americans with Nvidia in their 401(k) plans, have to decide whether an AI economy built largely on the judgment of Huang still makes sense.
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/08/is-jen.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told staff he was unfaithful to his wife. The stakes reach well beyond Nvidia, given how many tech and financial partners depend on its place at the center of the booming AI economy.

https://foreignpolicy.com/2026/11/09/heg.title: Is Hegseth the New Rumsfeld?
https://foreignpolicy.com/2026/11/09/heg.author: Julian E. Zelizer
https://foreignpolicy.com/2026/11/09/heg.text:
My FP: Follow topics and authors to get straight to what you like. Exclusively for FP subscribers. Subscribe Now | Log In

With the midterm elections over, the future of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth hangs in the balance. Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, who is set to be speaker of the house, announced this weekend that he would vote in favor of a resolution to impeach Hegseth. The Defense Secretary is one of the most controversial figures in President Donald Trump’s cabinet, and has purged the Pentagon of many top officials widely perceived as highly effective. He has repeatedly made provocative culture-war comments that have little to do with national security. And most damaging to his reputation, Hegseth has become the face of the war in Iran.

No matter how unpopular the U.S. military operations have been, Hegseth has stood behind the president. He has defended the pledge to eliminate Iran’s nuclear program and to establish a stronger foothold in the region, even as voters, including those in red states, flocked to the polls to express their disapproval of the administration’s foreign policy.

With the midterm elections over, the future of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth hangs in the balance. Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, who is set to be speaker of the house, announced this weekend that he would vote in favor of a resolution to impeach Hegseth. The Defense Secretary is one of the most controversial figures in President Donald Trump’s cabinet, and has purged the Pentagon of many top officials widely perceived as highly effective. He has repeatedly made provocative culture-war comments that have little to do with national security. And most damaging to his reputation, Hegseth has become the face of the war in Iran.

No matter how unpopular the U.S. military operations have been, Hegseth has stood behind the president. He has defended the pledge to eliminate Iran’s nuclear program and to establish a stronger foothold in the region, even as voters, including those in red states, flocked to the polls to express their disapproval of the administration’s foreign policy.

What happens next remains to be seen. Some Republicans privately hope Hegseth will resign, either voluntarily or under pressure, so that Trump can replace him with someone who has a more favorable public presence and clearer strategy for bringing U.S. involvement in the war to an end. Most Democrats are wary about initiating impeachment proceedings against Trump, given that he has only two years left in office and has historically benefited politically when under attack. Hegseth, however, remains a possible target for impeachment. Pursuing him, potentially with some Republican support, would allow Democrats to demonstrate that they are serious about holding the administration accountable.

Twenty years ago, Defense Secretary Donald Rumsfeld lost his job after becoming the face of an unpopular war. The question now is whether Hegseth will meet the same fate.

When President George W. Bush announced his nomination of Rumsfeld to be secretary of defense on Dec. 28, 2000, following a highly divisive election recount, most experts considered Rumsfeld one of the most qualified people for the job. A Navy veteran of the 1950s, he had served in the U.S. House of Representatives from 1963 to 1969. He then left legislative politics to become President Richard Nixon’s director of the Office of Economic Opportunity, and later counselor to the president and director of the Cost of Living Council. In 1973, Nixon named him U.S. ambassador to NATO. After Nixon resigned in disgrace over the Watergate scandal in August 1974, President Gerald Ford appointed Rumsfeld as White House chief of staff, and in 1975, Ford nominated him as secretary of defense, a post he held until President Jimmy Carter took office in 1977. Rumsfeld then spent many years working in the private sector while remaining involved in politics as a champion of neoconservatism.

His nomination as was greeted as a sign that the new President Bush would surround himself with a team of seasoned experts. After 9/11, Rumsfeld, who had a close and long-standing relationship with Vice President Dick Cheney, emerged as an important voice within the administration, helping to develop and implement a counterterrorism strategy intended to prevent comparable attacks on U.S. soil. In October and November 2001, the success of the military operations against the Taliban regime in Afghanistan was praised as evidence of his strategic prowess. The same was true in 2003, when the United States went to war with Iraq and Baghdad fell within weeks. On May 1, Bush declared an end to major combat operations beneath a “Mission Accomplished” banner, and in December, U.S. forces captured Iraqi leader Saddam Hussein.

Beneath those successes, however, things were already going wrong for Rumsfeld and for the war. The first major trouble came when looting broke out across Baghdad in April 2003, including at the Iraq Museum and the National Library and Archives. It soon became clear that the Pentagon had done little planning for the aftermath of Hussein’s downfall. “Stuff happens,” Rumsfeld told reporters, brushing off their questions about the looting. Meanwhile, the U.S. military failed to find stockpiles of weapons of mass destruction, which had been the main justification for the war.

By the 2006 midterms, the Iraq War was deeply unpopular. Large numbers of U.S. ground troops were still struggling to establish political stability and contain sectarian violence, and they were suffering heavy casualties. The 2003 decision to disband the Iraqi army proved enormously costly, and in April 2004, a weeknight 60 Minutes broadcast had revealed widespread abuse of detainees of Abu Ghraib prison. Although the story was initially framed as the work of a few rogue soldiers, it soon became clear that the abuses were connected to Pentagon policies authorizing harsh interrogation methods. Rumsfeld privately offered to resign several times, but Bush refused to accept.

There had also been scattered calls from Congress to force the issue. In May 2004, New York Rep. Charles Rangel introduced eight articles of impeachment against Rumsfeld in response to the revelations of Abu Ghraib.

After their tours of duty, many soldiers returned with post-traumatic stress disorder and could not get the support they needed to transition back to civilian life. Democrats made the war a central theme of the 2006 campaign, presenting it as evidence of Republican misrule: Bush’s deeply flawed and unnecessary decision to go to war with Iraq in the first place, made with strong congressional Republican support, compounded by the failure to plan for what would happen once the government collapsed. In September 2006, Republicans were able to block a vote on a nonbinding statement from Senate Democrats expressing a “sense of the Senate” that Bush replace Rumsfeld. “To fight a war on terror,” New York Sen. Charles Schumer said during the floor debate, “you need to be both strong and smart. And with Secretary Rumsfeld in this administration, you do see a great deal of strength but you don’t see enough on the smarts.” Behind the scenes, White House chief of staff Andrew Card lobbied the president, unsuccessfully, to replace Rumsfeld, too.

Rumsfeld himself was an issue. His approval ratings, which had stood at 71 percent in 2003, had fallen to 44 percent in Gallup polling by January 2006. That spring, in what Time called “The Revolt of the Generals,” six retired generals called for Rumsfeld to resign. “When I introduce the Secretary of Defense to my troops, I’m going to be a loyal subordinate,” Army Major General John Batiste told the magazine. “But it was boiling inside me. Every time I looked at him, I was thinking about … that s___ war plan, I was thinking about Abu Ghraib, and I was thinking about the challenges I had every day trying to rebuild the Iraqi military that he disbanded.”

The defense secretary puts stunts over substance. The U.S. should send him on permanent leave.

One lawmaker lays out the case for indicting the defense secretary.

The secretary of defense is now the most influential senior official in the Trump administration.

Still, Bush stood by his man. Responding to critical editorials and calls for Rumsfeld’s resignation, Bush told the press on April 18: “Don Rumsfeld is doing a fine job. He’s not only transforming the military, he’s fighting a war on terror. … I hear the voices, and I read the front page, and I know the speculation. But I’m the decider, and I decide what’s best. And what’s best is for Don Rumsfeld to remain as the secretary of defense.” Whenever the issue came up in conversations with the White House, Robert Draper wrote in his 2007 book, Dead Certain, Bush doubled down. “The moment someone would say ‘Fire Donald Rumsfeld,’ Donald Rumsfeld would get a new lease on life,” said a White House aide.

The criticism did not abate. On Sept. 25, 2006, six weeks before the election, Batiste and two other retired generals told the Senate Democratic Policy Committee that Rumsfeld was unable to handle the job. On Saturday, Nov. 6, the newspapers associated with the Military Times Media Group published an editorial titled “Time for Rumsfeld to Go.”

Although Bush had publicly defended Rumsfeld into the final days of the campaign, the outcome made continued support all but impossible. A number of issues drove the election, including corruption, the cost of living, and healthcare, but opposition to the Iraq War was chief among them. Democrats won control of the House and Senate.

The president realized that he needed to change course. According to Rumsfeld, Cheney had given him advanced warning that Bush planned to finally accept his resignation. On Nov. 8, Bush announced that he was nominating Robert Gates as the new secretary of defense. “America is safer and the world is more secure because of the service and the leadership of Donald Rumsfeld,” Bush said. The decision was a blow to Cheney, who counted on Rumsfeld as an ally, and a victory for the foreign policy realists who served under President George H.W. Bush.

The leadership shake-up paved the way for a basic shift in strategy, announced in January 2007: from a U.S. mission focused on fighting insurgents and handing security over to newly constituted Iraqi forces, to a so-called surge of additional troops whose mission was to protect the Iraqi population and win their support against the insurgency.

Many Republicans privately expressed regret that Bush had not made the decision earlier, which might have given the GOP a fighting chance to hold its majorities. As New York Times reporter Adam Nagourney put it, then-Rep. Rahm Emanuel, an Illinois Democrat, “gave private thanks that the president had not robbed the Democrats of a potent issue by firing Rumsfeld before the campaign was engaged.”

The war in Iran is not nearly as large as the Iraq War, and there is no ground war, but Trump’s policies have proven to be extraordinarily unpopular from the start, and as prices rise, the war has only become more controversial. There is little love for Hegseth, even among Republicans. Not only does he embody much of what critics think is wrong with Trump 2.0, but because he is not the president, Republicans feel freer to attack him.

Rumsfeld’s resignation offers a template for today’s Republicans who are angry about what has happened in Trump’s second term, and it could be that Hegseth will now go. But even if he leaves—or if Congress forces him out—it is unlikely to bring a fundamental change in policy. The Trump White House has centralized power in the president himself, so he will remain the source of policy decisions and the focus of attacks. Despite Democratic victories in last week’s midterms, Trump is unlikely to change course. It would take budgetary and investigative pressure from Congress to make that change.

Julian E. Zelizer is a columnist at Foreign Policy and a professor of history and public affairs at Princeton University. He is the author of The Long View, a newsletter putting the news in perspective. In 2027, Norton will publish his new book, Rumble on the Promenade: The Clash of Justice and Power at the 1964 Convention. X: @julianzelizer

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/c.author: Phoebe Pin
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/c.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Beau Lamarre-Condon is accused of murdering Jesse Baird and Luke Davies. (ABC News: Sharon Gordon)

Beau Lamarre-Condon has denied planning to "assassinate" Jesse Baird and intentionally shooting Luke Davies.

Mr Lamarre-Condon has been in the witness box at his double-murder trial since Thursday and maintained he acted in self-defence.

He said he cared for Mr Baird and was "emotional" after the shootings after being accused of acting "relaxed".

Beau Lamarre-Condon has rejected the suggestion he "executed" his former partner and deliberately shot the television presenter's new boyfriend, during at times tense exchanges with the Crown prosecutor in his double murder trial.

Mr Lamarre-Condon has been in the witness box since Thursday, and is about seven weeks into his trial in the NSW Supreme Court in Sydney.

He is accused of stalking Jesse Baird before allegedly using his police-issued pistol to shoot him and Luke Davies in a Paddington share house on February 19, 2024.

He has pleaded not guilty to all charges and has argued he acted in self-defence.

The former police officer has told the court he intentionally shot Mr Baird once after he was startled by Mr Lamarre Condon, who said he had been trying to retrieve his belongings after their casual romance ended.

He had been wearing a motorcycle helmet at the time, with Mr Lamarre-Condon saying he had wanted to get his things without being recognised.

Last week he said Mr Baird had "lunged" at him with a knife, defending his decision to fire the first shot at his ex partner in an attempt to disarm him.

Mr Baird was shot twice during the incident, the trial has heard. (Instagram)

During cross-examination, prosecutor Brett Hatfield SC on Monday put to Mr Lamarre-Condon that he had intended to kill Mr Baird.

"You executed him with that second shot," Mr Hatfield said.

"I never executed Jesse Baird," Mr Lamarre-Condon replied.

The court was played a recording of the Triple Zero (000) call the 31-year-old said he made with the intention of getting Mr Baird medical help.

But he said he was discovered by Mr Davies, who Mr Lamarre-Condon said was holding his police pistol, which had been flung into a hallway in scuffle, and yelling at him to "f*** off".

A struggle over the gun ensued, according to Mr Lamarre-Condon's evidence, with the accused maintaining his finger was not on the trigger when the pistol discharged and Mr Davies was shot.

Mr Lamarre-Condon told the court Mr Davies got hold of his police pistol after the struggle with Mr Baird. (Instagram)

Mr Hatfield later pressed Mr Lamarre-Condon about the helmet, jacket and gloves he said he took from a food delivery worker's motorbike before entering the Paddington house.

Mr Lamarre-Condon denies purchasing the helmet and high-vis clothing before the shootings. (Supplied: NSW Supreme Court)

The former police officer said he decided to use the clothes to disguise his identity to avoid a confrontation with Mr Baird and a report of harassment being made against him.

"I wasn't intending on stealing it I was intending to put it straight back," he said.

Mr Hatfield put to Mr Lamarre-Condon that he purchased the helmet and other items before deciding to put his "plan to assassinate Jesse Baird into action".

He did not raise his voice under cross-examination but appeared to grow frustrated at times, and at one point accused Mr Hatfield of "putting words in [his] mouth".

At another point, Mr Lamarre-Condon appeared to chuckle when the court was shown CCTV footage of him twice relieving himself near his car in the hours before he entered the Paddington home.

While waiting to make sure no-one was home, he said he "pissed in a water bottle".

"I really needed to go toilet," he said.

He was quizzed about footage that appeared to show him laughing at a sushi train restaurant the day after the shootings.

"You were remarkably relaxed," Mr Hatfield said.

New CCTV footage of Beau Lamarre-Condon a day after Jesse Baird and Luke Davies's deaths has been released.

Mr Lamarre-Condon maintained he was "detached" from the incident.

In his evidence in chief, Mr Lamarre-Condon said he experienced poor mental health related to bullying by some NSW Police officers.

He told the court he had planned and attempted suicide in October 2023, saying his mother forced him to visit a doctor and psychiatrist as a result.

Mr Hatfield put to Mr Lamarre-Condon that the suicide attempt did not occur.

"You weren't suicidal, you were homicidal," he put to Mr Lamarre-Condon.

"You're trying to get sympathy for these claims."

Mr Lamarre-Condon became emotional as he rejected the suggestions.

"This is the real life I was living at the time unfortunately," he said.

He was questioned at length about a conversation he had with a friend in December 2025 in which he discussed what happened inside the Paddington property.

Mr Hatfield put to Mr Lamarre-Condon said he did so with the intention of influencing what the other man would later tell the trial in evidence.

This led to a number of tense exchanges in court.

"Not once have I said to lie … I just want the truth to be told," Mr Lamarre-Condon said.

"Stop making speeches, would you?" Mr Hatfield said.

Mr Lamarre-Condon was expected to continue to give evidence on Tuesday.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/v.author: Judd Boaz and Emma D'Agostino
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/v.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Royal Commissions

The commission heard that contractors were wary of the CFMEU's influence. (AAP: Joel Carrett)

A two-week block of public hearings for Victoria's Big Build royal commission have started.

The first day of hearings explored the events leading up to a stop-work at a Sunbury level crossing removal site in June 2022.

The public hearings continue until November 20, days out from the state election.

Victoria's Big Build royal commission has heard a major contractor was wary of the "unprecedented access" the CFMEU had to government ministers, as well as alleged threats against subcontractors.

A level crossing removal project at Sunbury, in Melbourne's outer north, was the focus of the first day of a two-week block of public hearings.

The royal commission is exploring a number of themes, including allegations related to the conduct of the CFMEU (Construction, Forestry, Mining and Energy Union) on sites.

Victoria election 2026 live updates: For all the latest news from the campaign trail, read our blog.

Counsel assisting the commission Chris Young KC noted that all of the themes being canvassed were allegations at this stage, some of which had been denied.

Events related to a work stoppage at the Gap Road project in June 2022 were the focus of Monday's hearing.

Work ceased on June 6 and resumed on June 7 after control of the site was transferred to the CFMEU.

The commission heard that project costs blew out by an estimated $6 million.

Passages from several internal memos from site contractor John Holland were read out during today's hearing, including allegations about the CFMEU's relationship with the Victorian government.

Monday's hearing focused on the Gap Road level crossing removal at Sunbury in Melbourne's north. (Supplied: Victorian government)

"It is worth noting the significance of the CFMEU's relationship with the Andrews government in Victoria and the impact this is having and will have in the future in respect to client relationships," a memo dated to 2017 said.

"The union movement played a critical role in the election of the government, both organisationally and financially. The premier is factionally aligned with the Socialist Left and the CFMEU is the key industrial organisation in that faction.

"We also understand the CFMEU have unprecedented access to ministers and other key Victorian government stakeholders.

The commission heard that John Holland was increasingly cautious in its interactions with the CFMEU, with documents describing an escalating campaign by the union on the Gap Road site leading up to the June 2022 stop-work.

The construction sites of the Victorian government's Big Build have become hotbeds for allegations of criminal wrongdoing, corruption and serious misconduct.

Allegations of threats of violence against subcontractors were also aired during today's hearing.

One instance was captured in notes from an internal contractor meeting about conduct on site ahead of the June 2022 stop-work.

"CFMEU are putting pressure on Wagstaff [Piling] not to work tonight, said 'you guys better not turn up tonight otherwise we'll smash you during the day'," Mr Young said, reading from a transcript.

The commission heard that police and WorkSafe Victoria were notified, but that Victoria Police took no action as it was regarded as an occupational health and safety issue.

Wagstaff Piling subsequently told firms they would not be working, citing pressure from the union.

The commission heard about events leading up to the June 2022 stop-work at Gap Road. (Supplied: Victorian government)

The royal commission has already received a raft of information, including private hearings and requests for more than 110,000 documents.

The hearings come as Victorians prepare to head to the polls for the November 28 state election.

Premier Ben Carroll today denied any knowledge of the CFMEU's access to senior government officials and ministers.

"What today's hearings show is that I am a premier that will make the tough decisions," Mr Carroll said.
