BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Jensen Huang is one of the world's most influential figures in the AI industry. (AP: Julia Demaree Nikhinson)

The chief executive of Nvidia, the world's most valuable company and a close ally of US President Donald Trump, has admitted to having an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.

Jensen Huang, who heads the tech giant that dominates the world's AI chip industry, sent a memo to staff acknowledging the affair after reports emerged the woman worked for China's Ministry of State Security.

Nvidia's board has launched an independent investigation into whether Mr Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort.

The story centres on the Nvidia chief executive's relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen and executive at Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed, a customer of Nvidia.

In October, The New York Times reported Megaspeed was under scrutiny for possibly steering advanced Nvidia AI chips to Beijing, which are barred from shipment to China.

US officials reportedly concluded Ms Huang was a Chinese intelligence asset and developed a close relationship with Mr Huang.

An image shared by software company Net Thunder on LinkedIn in 2024, which it says shows Alice Huang sitting alongside Jensen Huang at an event in Taiwan. (Supplied: NetThunder/LinkedIn)

The NYT reported Mr Trump was briefed on the intelligence findings about a year ago and did nothing.

Further reporting over the weekend said US officials had intelligence Ms Huang was working for China's Ministry of State Security.

The Financial Times also reported the development, saying a memo circulated among top policymakers shortly before Mr Trump flew to Beijing for a summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping earlier this year.

The Chinese government dismissed the NYT report as "groundless speculation".

Mr Huang is an influential ally of Mr Trump and a leading figure in the US's efforts to dominate the AI race against China.

Mr Huang co-founded California-based Nvidia in 1993 and has served as president and chief executive ever since.

Leading AI companies such as Anthropic and OpenAI rely on Nvidia's hardware to operate, so the company wields a lot of power in the US and across the industry.

The founder of the world's most valuable AI company has the ear of Donald Trump when it comes to the risks and potential of the cutting-edge technology.

Nvidia surpassed Microsoft in June 2025 to become the world's most valuable company. A recent Forbes report said the company hit a market capitalisation of more than $US5 trillion ($7 trillion).

Mr Huang previously lobbied Mr Trump to lift a ban on the sale of advanced AI chips to China, arguing the restrictions accelerate Beijing's own development of the technology.

Mr Huang was born in Taiwan and raised in Thailand before he emigrated alone to the US to attend boarding school at 10 years old.

He met his wife, Lori, at university and the pair have been married for over 40 years.

Jensen Huang, with his wife Lori Huang, speaking to Tim Cook during a state dinner for Xi Jinping in September. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images/AFP)

Nvidia announced on Sunday, local time, it had launched an independent probe "in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort".

It said while the company's board had "no reason to believe" either US national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the probe would "examine all available information".

Nvidia said a committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel, would oversee the investigation.

Mr Huang will remain chief executive during the inquiry.

"Today's news will not slow Nvidia," company spokesperson John Rizzo said in a statement.

It is unclear if the CIA is also investigating.

The White House and CIA declined to comment to both the NYT and FT. Ms Huang could not be reached for comment by either outlet.

Shortly before Nvidia announced the probe, Mr Huang admitted to his affair with Ms Huang in a lengthy memo to staff.

He said he was "unfaithful" to his wife and there was "no excuse" for his actions, adding he was "deeply sorry".

Addressing the "national security concerns raised in news reports", he said he would fully cooperate with the investigation".

He said he was "committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America's national security".

I owe my family and all of you an apology.

I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.

Throughout my life, my family has given me love and support. They deserve my honesty and loyalty. Instead, I let them down and damaged the life we built together. I take full responsibility for what I did and the hurt I caused, and I accept the criticism that comes with it.

To my wife and family: I love you. I know an apology cannot undo what I have done. I hope our family will heal and that, over time, I can earn back your trust.

To my colleagues at NVIDIA, including those I have worked alongside for decades, and to our board, partners, and shareholders around the world: you deserve better from me.

Leading NVIDIA is the privilege of my life. My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility. I am fully committed to NVIDIA and will work to earn back your confidence.

Regarding the national security concerns raised in news reports, NVIDIA's Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation. I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company, and I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America's national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American.

My family bears no responsibility for my choices. I do. Please give them privacy.

After Nvidia announced its investigation, Mr Trump said he had not spoken to Mr Huang about the allegations but said he had "done an amazing job for our country".

"I have not spoken to him about it. I just know he's a fine person, but you never know what is going on," Mr Trump told reporters.

Donald Trump reportedly was briefed a year ago about Jensen Huang's relationship to Alice Huang and her ties to Chinese intelligence. (Reuters: Evan Vucci)

When asked if he would take Mr Huang on his trip to Asia next week, Mr Trump said: "I don't know, but I'd certainly take him."

Secretary of State Marco Rubio said he could not comment on the matter.

"I just can't comment because of the nature of it," he told reporters on his way to a G7 meeting in Paris.

"And I also can't comment on an internal corporate matter that's going on with Nvidia."

Top Republicans in the US House of Representatives have called on Mr Huang to brief Congress this month about the reports.

Chris Coons, a Delaware Democrat who will chair the Senate's foreign relations committee from January, shared the NYT report on social media with a pledge to open an investigation.

"The more I learn about the insane relationship between the Trump Administration, Chinese spies, and AI billionaires, the more I'm convinced there is nothing this administration does that isn't corrupt," he said.

Bloomberg's North Asia correspondent Minmin Low said there was uncertainty about what could come next.

"Will there be stricter restrictions when it comes to US investment overseas? Does this delay Nvidia's billions of dollars that are being poured into areas like advanced packaging and to its suppliers in Asia?" she told ABC's News Channel.

"If you look at the market reaction today, it seems like markets are quite resilient … investors are not seeing this as a change to the fundamentals of the AI trade.

"Of course, there is some short–term sentiment that is shaken at the moment, but a lot really rests on the ongoing investigation."

Scams and Fraud

The government is reviewing potential fraud in the Victim Assist Queensland scheme. (ABC News: Nick Haggarty)

The Queensland government is investigating potential fraud within the Victim Assist Queensland scheme.

The scheme offers payouts for expenses related to recovery from crime and paid out almost $244 million in the 2024-25 financial year.

Youth justice minister Laura Gerber has not ruled out tightening the scheme's criteria to clamp down on possible fraud.

The Queensland government is reviewing potential fraud in a vital scheme providing financial support to victims of crime, the ABC understands.

Victim Assist Queensland (VAQ) offers payouts for expenses relating to recovery from crime, including counselling and legal fees, moving costs, or one-off lump sums to primary victims of violent crime.

The scheme has seen a dramatic increase in applications and payouts in recent years, totalling almost half a billion dollars.

In the 2024-25 financial year, it paid out almost $244 million, up from $100 million the previous financial year, and just under $40 million in 2022-23.

Youth justice minister Laura Gerber refused to rule out tightening the scheme.  (ABC News)

Amid reports of rorts in the scheme, youth justice minister Laura Gerber put fraudsters on notice.

"Our priority is supporting victims, including domestic and family violence victims, and any financial assistance fraud is not only a crime but takes support away from victims in their time of need," she said.

"We strongly urge anyone with allegations of fraud to come forward with information."

Ms Gerber would not rule out tightening the scheme's criteria to clamp down on dodgy claims, or answer questions about any internal investigations to assess its effectiveness.

In some cases, victims can access compensation through VAQ without having reported to police, including through a doctor or psychologist.

Gillian O'Brien, Sexual Violence Prevention Association director, urged the government to consider any sweeping changes to VAQ's operations carefully.

"If there were any changes to assessment processes, the last thing I would want to see is going backwards to requiring police reporting for all matters," she said.

Gillian O'Brien is the director of the Sexual Violence Prevention Association. (Supplied: Gillian O'Brien)

"Sexual assault and domestic violence are traumatic enough, and highly under-reported, often committed by someone the victim knows and trusts, and this would be a significant barrier for many victims to apply to the scheme."

Ms O'Brien said VAQ made a significant difference to many people's lives and had many safeguards in place to prevent fraud.

"There are always going to be risks and unethical people with any financial assistance scheme.

"While checks and balances need to be in place, we need to ensure we don't place undue burden on victim survivors to prove they are worthy."

As of December 31, VAQ had already paid out more than $125 million this financial year.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Peer-support program for healthier aging gains ground in Sendai
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
A volunteer program aimed at preventing frailty among older people has been gaining momentum in Sendai, marking its fifth year of operations in the city.

The program encourages people to help others of their own generation stay healthy, and more than 200 volunteers are now taking part.

Frailty is a condition in which people become physically and mentally weaker as they age, increasing their risk of needing long-term care.

At a training session for new volunteers held on Sept. 24 at Sendai Choseien, a care home for older people in Sendai’s Aoba Ward, 31 people participated, exceeding the planned capacity of 25. The session teaching practical skills followed a classroom lecture held on Sept. 10.

Wearing light-green T-shirts identifying them as volunteers, participants learned how to carry out practices that are performed during frailty checks. These included measuring calf circumference, testing speech clarity with a machine and practicing standing up from a chair using only one leg.

Hiroko Tanaka, a 76-year-old local resident who attended the training, said, “I wanted to contribute to society while I’m still healthy.”

Experienced volunteers helped with the training.

Miki Kato, a 73-year-old resident of the Iwakiri district in the city’s Miyagino Ward who has been involved in the program for five years, said, “The good thing (about being a volunteer in this program) is that you can get to learn knowledge from physical therapists who conduct frailty checks with us.”

She has become so enthusiastic that she has even made her own picture-story show to explain frailty prevention, and brings it to checkup events.

The frailty checks were developed by Katsuya Iijima, a 61-year-old physician who heads the Institute of Gerontology at the University of Tokyo, and other experts. A volunteer program that organizes and conducts the checks in local communities was launched in 2015 in the city of Kashiwa in Chiba Prefecture, and similar programs are now active in more than 100 municipalities across Japan.

Sendai introduced its program in fiscal 2022, beginning in the Iwakiri district. The city now has 203 registered volunteers, including members of eight neighborhood-based groups organized through community support centers as well as volunteers who receive individual training and are sent to events across the city.

Two more neighborhood-based groups are scheduled to launch in fiscal 2026, in the city’s Aoba Ward and Taihaku Ward.

In general, people age 65 or older can become frailty prevention volunteers. They help conduct frailty checks at community support centers and local health events.

Speaking at a lecture in Sendai on Sept. 1, Iijima stressed the importance of residents supporting one another.

“It is important for people of the same generation to take part in the checks together in a relaxed, friendly atmosphere, rather than relying solely on health screenings organized by local governments,” Iijima said.

There is also a practical incentive for volunteers. Those who help with the checks receive 300 points for each session through a local volunteer reward program for active older residents. Each point is worth one yen and can be used at participating stores.

Kazuhiro Naito, head of the Sendai Municipal Government’s community-based integrated care promotion division, said, “Working as a volunteer offers benefits to people such as becoming healthy themselves and building stronger ties with others in their communities.”

“I hope that the network of residents supporting one another will continue to grow, even if only gradually.”

The program encourages people to help others of their own generation stay healthy. More than 200 volunteers are now taking part in the program.

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.title: Stop undermining Jim Chalmers, environment minister urges Labor colleagues
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.author: Tom McIlroy Political editor
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text:
‘It’s pretty obvious that there are all sorts of people making all sorts of comments,’ Murray Watt says after budget savings meeting

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The environment minister, Murray Watt, has urged ministers to stop undermining the treasurer, Jim Chalmers, as Labor struggles to sell its budget and looks to cut popular clean energy subsidies to help with the fight against inflation.

Cabinet ministers met again on Monday to discuss potential budget savings to be included in next month’s mid-year update, part of efforts to reducing spending to ease pressure on the economy.

Watt was asked about speculation of tension between the treasurer and the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, and whether he’d like to see an end to “undermining and leaking” against Chalmers.

“Yes, I would,” Watt said. “As a member of the government, I take seriously the responsibility to work together to support government policies and also to get our work to support each other in what are very difficult times.

“I think that Jim Chalmers is doing an excellent job as a treasurer in what are very difficult economic times; many of the features that are impacting on our economy are sort of well outside any treasurer’s control, and I very much support Jim Chalmers in his efforts.”

Watt conceded Chalmers was being undermined from within Labor.

“It’s pretty obvious that there are all sorts of people making all sorts of comments.”

A new round of opinion polls added to Labor’s political pain on Monday, with the Resolve Political Monitor in the Age and Sydney Morning Herald showing Labor’s primary vote falling to 28 percentage points, down from 34.6% at last year’s election.

The Coalition also dropped one point to 22%, while One Nation was steady at 25%.

A Redbridge poll in the Financial Review showed Labor’s primary vote slipped two percentage points to 26%, while the Coalition’s jumped four points to 25%. One Nation was down one point to 28%.

Monday’s meeting of the expenditure review committee of cabinet comes after last week’s interest rate hike from the Reserve Bank. The governor, Michele Bullock, said while it is up to governments to manage their budgets independently of the RBA, public and private spending had caused “excess demand” in the economy.

Watt accused the Coalition and minor parties of leaving existing spending proposals to linger in parliament, including savings from changes to the private health insurance rebate for over 65s.

Get the most important news as it breaks

after newsletter promotion

“Let’s not forget that for all of their demands that we find more savings, the Coalition currently are blocking the government from saving $10 billion in measures that are before the parliament,” Watt said.

Albanese has confirmed spending in the public service will be scrutinised as the government looks for savings in the budget update, expected in the middle of December. Last year, departments and agencies were asked to identify potential savings of as much as 5% from their annual budgets, part of the government’s efforts to cut lower-priority spending.

Spending on Labor’s $7bn home battery subsidy program and incentives for electric vehicle purchases could be reined in.

Announced in April 2025, the batteries program was originally designed to cost about $2bn. More than 600,000 systems have been installed, but the program could have means testing rules added.

Separately, subsidies designed to promote uptake of electric vehicles has cost the budget far more than originally anticipated.

Angus Taylor announced an opposition “red tape razor gang” on Monday, designed to reduce the burden on business from costly regulation.

https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.title: Fixing UK’s youth jobs crisis demands much more investment, TUC boss warns
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.author: Richard Partington
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.text:
Paul Nowak also calls on government to avoid arbitrary benefit cuts before much-anticipated Milburn report is published this week

Fixing Britain’s youth jobs crisis will require ministers to drastically increase investment in employment support while avoiding arbitrary cuts to benefits, the head of the trade union movement has said.

Before an important official report expected next week, the general secretary of the Trades Union Congress, Paul Nowak, said the government had a “once in a generation chance” to secure young people’s futures.

In an interview with the Guardian before the highly anticipated Milburn review into young people and work, he said the costs of increasing job support, education and training would be outweighed by economic gains that would help to ease the pressure on the welfare state.

“There is no solution that is cost-free,” he said. “The government is going to have to be prepared to invest in securing the future of those young people, but also to invest to secure what is the future of our economy.

“This is where the government is going to have to be clear. Of course as a country it’s right to invest in our physical infrastructure, but also we have to invest in social infrastructure too.”

Ministers are braced for the report by Alan Milburn, the former Labour health secretary, to recommend welfare cuts to fund job support for almost a million young people who are not in education, employment or training (Neet).

The report was delayed until after the budget amid fears that the call for welfare cuts would sit uneasily alongside the tax and spending plans of the chancellor, John Healey.

Andy Burnham has said the surge in young people who are Neet is an “economic catastrophe and a moral failure” and that tougher benefits rules and more help for young people will form part of his government’s response to the Milburn report.

Sign up to Breaking News UK

Sign up for the Breaking News UK email to get newsletter alerts direct to your inbox

after newsletter promotion

The prime minister has been at pains to take a cautious approach to avoid a repeat of the welfare rebellion, which forced Keir Starmer and Rachel Reeves into an embarrassing and costly U-turn on planned disability benefit cuts within a year of coming to power.

Calling on Burnham to focus on delivering a step change in employment support, Nowak said increased investment would help to bring down the benefits bill by getting more young people into work.

“We can’t afford to not do this stuff, as the benefits bill will go up if young people are not supported,” he said.

“I don’t think this government is going to repeat the mistake of the previous attempt at benefit reform, where you make arbitrary cuts, [and] where you have an impact on some of the most vulnerable people without thinking about how you support people into work.”

There is rising concern over youth worklessness. Most Britons now see the youth jobs crisis as one of the biggest problems facing the country – ranking it second only to the cost of living and above NHS waiting lists, housing, crime and immigration, according to polling by the research company Focaldata for the Jobs Foundation.

The employment charity, co-founded by the Conservative peer Matthew Elliott, is behind a national campaign to tackle worklessness that launches on Monday. It includes a pledge, backed by a group of leading employers – including Amazon, Pret a Manger, NatWest, Marks & Spencer and Shell – that have committed to support young people who have been overlooked for work.

A government spokesperson said: “We are determined to turn the tide on youth unemployment which has been years in the making.

“We have already pledged £2.5bn in youth employment support, which will deliver almost 500,000 opportunities to earn and learn, while engaging with business including some of Britain’s biggest retail and hospitality brands to create up to 200,000 jobs for young people.

“Further reform will follow the Milburn review, which will be published in the autumn.”

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: British people don’t trust Palantir – it’s not too late to reverse the NHS’s dependence on it | Ben Coleman
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Ben Coleman
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
We can’t allow our health data to be locked into the control of a US tech firm. It won’t be easy, but next spring the job of clawing it back must begin

Ben Coleman is Labour MP for Chelsea and Fulham and a member of the health and social care committee

N
ext March, Palantir’s £330m contract to run NHS England’s federated data platform (FDP) ends. Ministers must decide by Christmas whether to extend it. They should move on from Palantir, and transition to new suppliers that put the NHS in full control of its technology and patient data.

I sit on the health and social care committee. In June, we recommended no extension – people don’t trust Palantir, its benefits are contested and other tools could deliver the same or similar advantages. The debate so far has been whether to drop Palantir. The harder question is what replaces it. The tempting solution is to hire a single British firm. But that would not give the NHS the control it lacks: the freedom to switch supplier without losing what it has built.

Currently, NHS teams build applications on Palantir’s software platform. The NHS owns the applications and rents the platform. The aim is to join up hospital data to manage waiting lists, plan operations and get patients home. We need clarity about what will happen if the Palantir contract ends. How easy would it be to move the applications to another supplier? Will there be disruption that affects patient care?

Ministers assure me the NHS is not locked into Palantir’s service. Local NHS data teams, British tech firms and thinktanks tell me they are not convinced. A ministerial response to the committee in August left questions open. It said the NHS owned, or had a right to use, the applications built on the platform, but that some arrangements would end with the contract. It did not say which. Owning your applications is useless if they won’t work elsewhere.

It also said the government would explore how to move the applications on to a different platform only if the contract ended, and it declined to audit which Palantir tools hospital trusts depend on. Surely ministers need to know this now?

The NHS’s dependence on Palantir worries the national data guardian, too. She told ministers this month that “concerns about interoperability, vendor lock-in and data sovereignty must be addressed”, including by considering open standards. Open standards are shared, published rules for how health information is recorded and labelled, so that software from different suppliers can work together, much as any UK plug fits any UK socket.

In an FDP based on national open standards, regions could choose their own suppliers to build the software they need, from in-house NHS developers to small British firms. Data would stay with each region and be shared only under strict permissions. Suppliers could be swapped without starting again.

Britain has the skills to do this. Nigel Shadbolt, co-founder of the Open Data Institute, told our committee there is “nothing to suggest that the UK lacks the talent or capability to produce an equivalent to what Palantir offers”. For example, Greater Manchester’s integrated care board already runs its own analytics platform, while NHS OneLondon joins up patient records across the capital.

It is not too late to reverse the dependence on Palantir. The Guardian reported recently that 16 trusts and health boards say they do not use the platform. Some tried it and reverted to old systems. The British Medical Journal says a third of signed-up trusts have never logged in and many barely use it. The case for change is about more than avoiding lock-in. A data platform works only if patients trust it, yet mistrust of Palantir means opt-outs are growing.

The FDP’s benefits are also uncertain. Palantir claims a 14% fall in discharge delays, but the Health Foundation has found no noticeable change. Just one trust, Chelsea and Westminster in my constituency, accounts for 84% of the claimed national cut in outpatient waiting lists. Even NHS England now says cause and effect are unproven. I’ve asked its chief executive, Jim Mackey, why it lets Palantir claim otherwise.

A full evaluation is not due until 2029. Mackey told our committee that an independent review now would be “helpful and necessary” but could not be done before the decision.

after newsletter promotion

Then there is sovereignty. Britain needs to be able to build and control its own health tech, including AI, and not leave the NHS dependent on a US company.

Could an open system be ready by March? Probably not. So ministers should agree only a short transition, on new terms, while it is built. That transition should do four things. Freeze new applications on Palantir’s platform. Run it for at most two years, with leaving made easier over time. Publish what the FDP does and costs, which tools trusts depend on and how an exit would work so others can bid. And make Palantir prove there is no lock-in by moving one application off the platform within a year.

Beyond the FDP, the planned single patient record, which will bring each person’s health records together, must be open, too, or it will tie the NHS to a single supplier on a far larger scale.

Data sovereignty means more than keeping health data on British soil. If Britain wants sovereign AI in health, it needs a system it controls. A British Palantir would not give it that. Open standards would.

Ben Coleman is Labour MP for Chelsea and Fulham and a member of the health and social care committee

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.title: Smog blankets New Delhi as Diwali firecrackers worsen air quality
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.text:
Heavy smog has blanketed New Delhi after firecrackers lit up the Indian capital during Diwali celebrations, worsening the seasonal pollution crisis.

Diwali, the Hindu festival of lights, was celebrated across India on Sunday. Despite restrictions on fireworks, New Delhi residents celebrated the festival of lights with firecrackers throughout Sunday evening, releasing smoke and fine particulate matter into the atmosphere.

On Monday morning, the Air Quality Index exceeded 350 in several parts of the capital, categorised as “severe” and posing significant health risks, according to the World Health Organization’s (WHO) recommended exposure thresholds.

Last month, India’s Supreme Court put in place restrictions to limit Diwali pollution, allowing only approved “green firecrackers” under specified conditions for three-hour windows on Saturday and Sunday. The approved crackers produce fewer emissions but are not pollution-free.

On Wednesday, days before Diwali, toxic air pollution in New Delhi surged to more than 30 times the WHO’s recommended daily limit, data from air monitors showed.

New Delhi, home to 30 million people, persistently ranks among the world’s most polluted capital cities.

The issue is exacerbated during the winter, when cooler temperatures, low wind speeds and stagnant atmospheric conditions prevent pollutants from dispersing.

Vehicles account for 23 percent of New Delhi’s winter pollution, while biomass burning, including farm stubble fires, contributes 20 percent, according to India’s Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change.

The result is a thick haze that can linger over the capital and surrounding areas for days.

The air quality index exceeded 350 in several parts of the capital on Monday morning. The issue is exacerbated during the winter when cooler temperatures, low wind speeds and stagnant atmospheric conditions prevent pollutants from dispersing.

https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/.title: ‘Tents don’t protect us’: Rains flood displaced Palestinians in Gaza
https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/.author: Maram Humaid
https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/.text:
Az-Zawayda, Gaza Strip – On Saturday night, water began rushing into Jaber al-Kaseeh’s tent in central Gaza’s az-Zawayda area, waking him and his family as heavy rain swept across Gaza. Soon the tent’s floor was flooded, soaking mattresses, carpets, blankets and spoiling what little food the family had managed to keep.

“Everyone woke up and stayed awake, asking their neighbours about the extent of damage and inquiring about children,” Jaber, who is in his 70s, told Al Jazeera.

He described the area outside the displacement camp, where thousands of Palestinians have taken refuge, as a swimming pool.

More than 70,000 tents have been flooded since heavy rains began late on Friday, according to Gaza’s Government Media Office. Hundreds of thousands of displaced Palestinians are sheltering in locations considered “highly vulnerable” to more flooding.

More than a year after the so-called “ceasefire” deal was signed between Israel and Hamas, Israel has continued to flout the terms of the agreement, blocking the entry of goods into Gaza, including 60,000 mobile homes and 200,000 tents.

Only 20,000 tents have been allowed in, and mobile homes have remained parked on the Egyptian side of the border, many of them for more than two years.

This is the fourth winter for Jaber and his family living in a tent house in the az-Zawayda area. Originally from Beit Lahiya in northern Gaza, Jaber has been displaced several times, like most Palestinians since Israel launched its genocidal war on October 7, 2023.

More than 90 percent of Palestinians have been displaced, many of them multiple times, by the war that has attracted global condemnation.

Jaber says his camp was flooded three or four times last winter, forcing many families to leave. Around 40 tents still remain there, but the latest flooding has left them in even worse condition.

“All the tents are now damaged, torn and covered in mud,” Jaber told Al Jazeera.

“We urgently need tents, tarpaulins, plastic sheets, mattresses, blankets and carpets to protect us from the difficult days ahead.

“We keep hearing about tents and tarpaulins being distributed, but we have received nothing.

“We had hoped the mobile homes and temporary housing units promised under the ceasefire deal would allow us to rest and return to a life of safety and peace. But it was all just words in the air. We have seen nothing.”

Jaber’s experience reflects the wider shelter crisis facing displaced Palestinians across Gaza. Despite the “ceasefire” agreement, which included provisions for temporary housing units, tents and heavy machinery to clear rubble, large numbers of families remain in makeshift shelters exposed to winter weather.

Under the first phase of the agreement, along with temporary housing units and tents, heavy equipment was also supposed to be allowed in to remove rubble and help restore damaged infrastructure.

But the arrival of mobile homes and heavy machinery has been delayed as Israel has found excuses to restrict their entry into the enclave of 2.3 million people.

Trucks carrying mobile homes and equipment have reportedly been waiting on the Egyptian side of the border while Palestinians live in misery in dilapidated tent camps.

According to the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), Gaza requires approximately 121,000 tents and 561,000 tarpaulins, while available stocks remain far below what is needed.

For Om Hani Hamouda, a displaced woman from Beit Lahiya now sheltering in al-Zawayda, replacing her worn-out tent with a caravan has become a dream.

“We did not expect that the first rainfall would leave us in this condition,” she told Al Jazeera. “These tents do not protect us from the cold, storms or rain. Whenever winter comes, everyone holds their breath.”

Hamouda had hoped the ceasefire agreement would allow her family to return to northern Gaza or at least receive a caravan or building materials to secure better shelter. But she said there had been no sign of progress.

“We are asking for a dignified life. We want these tents to be replaced with caravans. Even a simple caravan would be better,” she told Al Jazeera.

Hamouda’s family has been displaced around 15 times during the war. She spent more than 15 years living and working in the United Arab Emirates before returning to Gaza nearly two years before the war began.

“My children cry because they miss the life we had there,” she said. “Life here is so difficult. There is no life in any sense.”

Ramy Abdu, chairman of the Euro-Mediterranean Human Rights Monitor, told Al Jazeera that large quantities of tents, caravans, prefabricated housing units and shelter equipment remain stranded at Gaza’s borders because of Israeli restrictions.

He said that while more than 1.5 million displaced Palestinians were facing another winter in worn-out tents, even people living in houses and apartments remained exposed to the elements because of the extensive damage to homes and infrastructure.

“Today, we cannot even say that those living in houses and apartments are safe from extreme weather because, with around 85 percent of homes destroyed or damaged, every family is exposed to some degree of harsh weather conditions,” Abdu said, adding that Israel continues to reject shipments containing timber and emergency shelter kits, depriving families of the ability to repair homes that could otherwise accommodate them.

Abdu said Israel, as the occupying power, was legally obligated under the Fourth Geneva Convention to ensure essential supplies reached civilians and to facilitate humanitarian relief.

Jihad Dawwas, 51, says he felt helpless as he could not do anything as his children had nowhere dry to sleep amid the rains.

Water poured into the tents at the displacement camp where he is sheltering, while strong winds blew away many of the surrounding tents. His children ended up sleeping while standing, he said, after rainwater soaked their mattresses and the plastic sheets covering their shelter.

“They slept standing up. By morning, some of my children had become ill because of the cold and the storm,” he told Al Jazeera.

Dawwas, who was displaced from northern Gaza, is sheltering with seven of his own children and three orphaned children of his brother. He said he had bought the family’s tent with his own money and had received no tent from any charity or aid initiative.

“A tent cannot replace a home, not even by one percent,” he said. “We are living in what is left of our lives.”

He said he had seen no caravans or temporary housing units arrive to help displaced families, despite the expectations raised by the ceasefire agreement.

“Our lives are a daily hell. We are completely forgotten. There is no fair distribution of aid, and no one is really asking about us,” Dawwas said.

He questioned why even basic shelter supplies had become so difficult to obtain.

“Do tents and tarpaulins really need all this pressure and effort just to become something we can ask for?” he asked. “They should provide us with tents and tarpaulins, and give us at least a dignified life.”
https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/.summary: More than 70,000 tents have been flooded since heavy rains began late on Friday. Hundreds of thousands of displaced Palestinians are sheltering in locations considered “highly vulnerable’ to more flooding. More than 90 percent of Palestinians have been displaced by the war that has attracted global condemnation.

https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/cisa-f.title: CISA Flags SonicWall SonicOS MFA Bypass Flaw Amid Reports of Possible Exploitation
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/cisa-f.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/cisa-f.text:
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has added a high-severity vulnerability impacting SonicWall SonicOS to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, following reports that it said may have been exploited in real-world attacks.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-19868 (CVSS score: 7.1 / 7.5), has been described as an authentication reinforcement vulnerability via alternate authentication methods.

"An authentication enforcement vulnerability in SonicOS SSL-VPN service may allow a user with valid credentials for an alternate authentication method to bypass SAML authentication controls. Successful exploitation may also bypass SAML-enforced multi-factor authentication (MFA)," SonicWall said in a Friday advisory.

The company also acknowledged that it "investigated a report indicating potential exploitation of this vulnerability," urging customers to update to the latest version as soon as possible. SonicWall did not disclose any additional specifics about the nature of the attack or who is behind the effort.

Also patched by SonicWall are a number of other high-severity flaws -

Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies are recommended to apply the patches by November 20, 2026, to secure their networks against the threat.

The development comes days after SonicWall detailed two unpatched vulnerabilities impacting end-of-life Global Management System (GMS) systems (CVE-2026-109593 and CVE-2026-109594), urging customers to upgrade to Network Security Manager (NSM).
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/cisa-f.summary: The vulnerability is described as an authentication reinforcement vulnerability. SonicWall SonicOS is the latest in a number of high-severity flaws. The company has urged customers to update to the latest version of its SonicWall system.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/q.title: 'I want to come home now': Teenager texted mother on night of her death
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/q.author: Talissa Siganto
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/q.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Krystle Monks, 19, died at a Bundamba home in February, 2023.  (Supplied)

Michael Kurt Pringle has pleaded not guilty to the murder of his partner, 19-year-old Krystle Monks.

Ms Monks died after after an alleged "violent assault" at Mr Pringle's Bundamba home in February 2023.

An Ipswich man accused of violently beating his partner before telling police she was critically injured by "misadventure" after jumping on the bed, has pleaded not guilty to her murder.

Michael Kurt Pringle is facing trial in the Supreme Court in Brisbane charged over the death of Krystle Monks.

A jury has heard the 19-year-old was taken to hospital in February 2023 and died the following day after her life support was withdrawn by family.

On Monday Crown prosecutor Nathan Crane told the jury it will be alleged her death was caused by a "protracted" and "violent assault" carried out by Mr Pringle at his Bundamba home.

"She sustained … blows to the head," he said.

"You can't see the traumatic brain injury that followed."

However, Mr Crane told the jury they will see evidence she allegedly suffered more than 60 "external injuries", and she was "peppered with bruising and abrasions".

"They are the markers of the violence that was perpetrated upon Krystle," he said.

The jury heard before Mr Pringle called emergency services to report his partner had fainted, he made three google searches, including "can people faint".

He told the Triple Zero (000) operator and later police, Ms Monks had been drinking and injured herself, the jury heard.

Mr Crane told the jury there will be evidence played to the court, in which Mr Pringle claims her death was the result of "misadventure".

"Mr Pringle says … Kyrstle Monks jumped on the bed, fell off the bed and hit her head on the dresser," he said

"That's the explanation ultimately."

Michael Pringle has been charged over the death of Ms Monks. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

The jury heard they will also be shown text messages between the pair earlier in the night, in which they were arguing about photographs of Ms Monks.

Mr Crane told the jury these messages demonstrated jealousy from Mr Pringle, and a "motive to be violent" towards her.

"You'll hear that Mr Pringle called her, within that half an hour on the text messages, a liar, a dog, a s**t, a rat, scum, and a c**t," he said.

Mr Crane told the jury it was "a relationship of animosity".

"You will see those words repeatedly in the course of this trial because those are the words he often used towards his partner over the preceding months."

The jury also heard on the same night she texted her mother to say, "I want to come home now".

This was after her mother had told her if she did not feel safe, she should reach out, the jury heard.

Several witnesses are expected to give evidence, which the jury heard will allegedly establish Mr Pringle had been physically violent to Ms Monks repeatedly throughout their short relationship.

The jury heard one woman set to testify did not know the couple but allegedly witnessed Mr Pringle punching Ms Monks while driving in his car, and she reported it to police.

Following this, the jury heard officers attended Mr Pringle's home and he denied assaulting her, but later messaged Ms Monks and said "apparently someone seen me hitting you lol".

Ms Monks co-workers and a neighbour of Mr Pringle's are also set to take the witness stand.

The trial is expected to run for two weeks.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/s.title: 150 years ago, a mishap in an SA paddock revolutionised farming
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/s.author: Isabella Kelly
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/s.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Brenda Bowman with Derek and Joy Birkin at the Ardrossan Heritage Museum. (ABC Rural: Isabella Kelly)

In 1876 two brothers showcased their stump-jump plough at a country show and solved one of the biggest farming challenges at the time.

The simple invention unlocked previously unviable farmland across the country.

The stump jump plough has been included in a five-coin set released by the Royal Australian Mint.

It has been 150 years since a mishap in a paddock led to a discovery that would forever change agriculture, but at the time the farmer-inventor was dismissed as a "fool and a lunatic".

Before 1876, one of the biggest challenges Mallee farmers faced was scrub stump.

Horse-drawn rollers and fire could flatten vegetation, but the stumps remained stubbornly in place, damaging the inflexible ploughs on the market.

Rollers were used to clear the hardy Mallee scrub. (Supplied: State Library of South Australia)

One day, Richard Smith, a blacksmith and farmer at Port Wakefield, was hard at work and broke part of his plough, according to Ardrossan Heritage Museum secretary Brenda Bowman.

"[He] realised through that accident that if the plough shear could move up and down, it could ride over obstacles," she said.

Richard and his brother, Clarence Smith, set about finessing a prototype that was to be unveiled at an exhibition at the Moonta Agricultural Show on November 6, 1876.

The first stump-jump plough was simple, but it would revolutionise Australian agriculture.

The museum contains many early designs of the plough. (ABC Rural: Isabella Kelly)

By attaching shears to the plough frame with a hinged joint and weight system, the plough could till soil without the scrub remnants being removed.

London-born Richard Bowyer Smith originated the stump-jump plough on the Yorke Peninsula. (Supplied: State Library of South Australia)

Despite addressing a common challenge, reactions to the invention were mixed.

"Some people thought it was a great idea and some people just thought it was lazy," said Ms Bowman, the widow of Clarence's great-grandson.

At the 1876 Moonta show, Richard Smith reportedly said: "I don't care what you say or think, I still firmly believe that my plough will open up a new agricultural era in South Australia."

Despite the scepticism the invention became commercially successful and in 1880 Clarence Smith opened a factory in Ardrossan.

The Clarence H. Smith plough factory employed up to 130 people at times, selling ploughs across the country and to New Zealand.

The factory opened by Clarence Smith traded until 1934. (ABC Rural: Isabella Kelly)

Testimonials in a factory catalogue show just how pleased farmers were with the tool — a Mr John Baker called it "the most perfect plough ever offered".

"Four horses worked it all the season comfortably, and ploughed 220 acres of very rough stump and stony land without bending or breaking anything," he wrote.

The plough remained popular until the Great Depression saw the Ardrossan factory close in 1934.

Though much of it was demolished, part of the building remains and is now home to the Ardrossan Heritage Museum.

The Ardrossan Heritage Museum is home to many early designs and catalogues from the Smith brothers. (ABC Rural: Isabella Kelly)

In an 1881 paper, the president of the Royal Agricultural and Horticultural Society of SA Sir Robert Ross credited the plough with a drastic increase in farmed land.

Before the invention, scrubland was regularly forfeited by purchasers who found it "almost impossible" to farm.

"In 1873, 4,826 acres were leased, and more than half forfeited: in 1874, 2,183 acres were taken up, and all forfeited," Sir Ross wrote.

Stump-jump ploughs at the Ardrossan factory, as seen in an early catalogue. (Supplied: PIRSA)

As the use of the stump-jump plough increased, so did the amount of land leased, and 285,670 acres were purchased in 1881 in what was "the largest sale that has ever taken place in the colony".

"Both the Government and the farmers of South Australia are considerably indebted to Mr R B Smith for his ingenuity and perseverance in forcing this valuable implement upon the public," Sir Ross wrote.

A sketch of the first single-furrow stump-jump plough by Richard Smith. (Supplied: State Library of South Australia)

A lapsed patent meant Richard Smith was not rewarded with riches for his invention, though in 1882 the state government awarded him £500 in recognition of the plough.

Richard and Clarence Smith ultimately had a falling out and Richard relocated to Western Australia.

The Royal Australian Mint has released a coin commemorating the plough. (ABC Rural: Isabella Kelly)

Though farming machinery looks a little different these days, the principle of the stump-jump plough remains, but with more hydraulics.

This year, the Smith brothers' stump-jump plough featured alongside the jaffle maker and the black box flight recorder in a coin collection chronicling five of Australia's most decorated inventions.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/w.title: Desperate Triple Zero calls played in Floreat double murder inquest
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/w.author: Lucy Murray
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/w.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Jennifer and Gretl Petelczyc were fatally shot in their home by a gunman who was searching for his ex-wife. (Supplied)

Chilling details of a series of desperate phone calls made in the final minutes of their lives by a teenager and her mother who were shot dead at their Perth home have been aired for the first time in a Perth court.

WARNING: This story contains details that may distress some readers.

Gretl Petelczyc, 18, and her 59-year-old mother Jennifer were killed by Mark Bombara at their home in the suburb of Floreat in May 2024, after he went to the house looking for his estranged wife Rowena.

An inquest into their deaths opened today and was played two Triple Zero calls made by Gretl, as Bombara — armed with two Glock pistols — threatened the mother and daughter in their home.

"There is a guy in my house with a gun," Gretl is heard to say in the first call, which was not answered by staff at the Police Assistance Centre for one minute and 20 seconds.

The call was disconnected, but contrary to official policy, police did not call back or dispatch officers to the scene, the Counsel Assisting the Coroner Rachael Young SC said in her opening address to the court.

The murders shocked the quiet Perth suburb of Floreat.  (ABC News: Julian Robins)

Meanwhile, Jennifer had called her best friend Rowena — Bombara's estranged wife — who heard Jennifer tell Bombara "she's not here, I told you she's not here", then "Mark, put down the gun".

Rowena, who was with her daughter Ariel at the time as they moved their belongings into their new apartment, also heard the call.

Gunshots were subsequently heard, and a woman was heard to say "please no, please Mark no, please leave my mum, no".

A second Triple Zero call from Gretl was replayed to the court, in which she whispers to the operator, "there is a guy with a gun in our house", before screams are heard along with a further gunshot.

The call is then disconnected.

Gretl had also messaged her sister Liesl, who was driving nearby with her boyfriend, asking her to call the police and telling her "my hands are tied" and "he has a gun to Jenny's".

In a fourth Triple Zero call, this one from Liesl, she tells the operator a man has a gun to her mother's head.

By this time multiple police vehicles had been dispatched to the home.

The first officers arrived at the home 11 minutes after the initial phone call by Gretl, and specialist police forced entry into the home at 4:46pm, 18 minutes after that call.

The officers discovered the bodies of Bombara and Jennifer Petelczyc.

Gretl was still showing signs of life and was rushed to Royal Perth Hospital, but died a short time later.

Bombara had two strokes that resulted in an acquired brain injury in the months before the double-murder suicide.

The inquest heard his daughter Candice describe his behaviour changes as "huge" and, that she had urged doctors not to discharge him from hospital in early May, about two weeks before the murders.

An internal investigation into the actions of WA Police officers in the weeks before Mark Bombara killed two women in the Perth suburb of Floreat finds eight officers did not perform their duty.

In a letter to the court, she and her siblings Isaac and Eden wrote the brain injury "led to behavioural changes" and their father "exhibited severe signs of depression and anxiety".

The family said they were "beyond disappointed" in the care he received at Sir Charles Gairdner Hospital, which they said had failed to provide a comprehensive mental health assessment, despite them requesting one before he was discharged.

A doctor performed an initial mental health assessment on May 7, in which Bombara denied he was having suicidal thoughts.

Candice told hospital staff she believed he was lying and asked for further assessments.

In the letter to the coroner, she said the hospital failed to inform the family Mark Bombara had an acquired brain injury.

Police at the site of the fatal shooting of Jennifer and Gretl Petelczyc in Floreat.  (ABC News: Julian Robins)

"A brain injury paired with significant mental health deterioration without proper treatment is clearly a recipe for disaster," the letter reads.

"Our hope is that this investigation identifies the shortcomings of the public health service and highlights the need for better resourcing and improved risk assessment systems."
