https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Hasina seeks new passport in clearest sign of Bangladesh return
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: Krishna N. Das
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
NEW DELHI – Ousted Bangladeshi Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina requested on Monday a new passport and identity card so she can return from self-imposed exile in India, according to a letter, her first such communication since fleeing in 2024.

The request marks the clearest step by Hasina to act on her plan to return to Bangladesh in December, more than two years after a deadly uprising ended her long rule, raising the prospect of fresh political and legal tensions in a country where her party is now banned.

She has said she plans to return to surrender before a court, and her aides said on Monday the date would be announced once various formalities were completed. Bangladesh’s war-crimes court sentenced her to death in November last year in her absence for ordering a deadly crackdown on the student-led uprising, though she has denied the charges from exile.

“In view of the reported revocation of her existing Bangladeshi passport and National Identity Card (NID) by the Interim Government and other authorities, I respectfully request that you take the necessary steps to issue a new Bangladeshi passport and National Identity Card for our client,” Hasina’s lawyers at London-based Matrix Chambers wrote to Preeti Rahman, acting high commissioner at Bangladesh’s embassy in Delhi.

The letter asked for the applications to be processed “expeditiously” on the basis of her Bangladeshi nationality and in accordance with “obligations arising under international human rights instruments.”

Rahman in Delhi and spokespeople for Prime Minister Tarique Rahman in Dhaka did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Hasina’s Awami League party was the country’s largest before it was banned following her fall. Many of her party colleagues have either been jailed or are in self-imposed exile in India or elsewhere.

Having ruled Bangladesh for 20 years as prime minister across multiple terms, Hasina still enjoys support among sections of the population, and a return could sharpen political divisions as the government in Dhaka seeks to restore stability after more than two years of upheaval.

On the other hand, it could improve Bangladesh’s strained ties with India, which deteriorated sharply after New Delhi gave her refuge.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.summary: Sheikh Hasina has requested a new passport and identity card so she can return from self-imposed exile in India. The request marks the clearest step by Hasina to act on her plan to return to Bangladesh in December. Hasina's Awami League party was the country's largest before it was banned following her fall.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.title: Mitsui Chemicals to take over chip linchpin JSR for $12 billion
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.text:
Mitsui Chemicals is buying JSR for ¥1.84 trillion ($12 billion) with support from state-backed Development Bank of Japan to strengthen its hold over a key chip materials linchpin.

Mitsui Chemicals and DBJ will acquire all shares of JSR from government-backed Japan Investment, the companies said in a filing Monday. DBJ will pay ¥200 billion in cash for a stake that will be converted to preferred shares without voting rights, it said.

The deal for JSR, one of the world’s leading makers of photoresists needed to make advanced chips, would further a government-backed effort to consolidate Japan’s fragmented semiconductor-materials industry. Japan is home to the world’s largest suppliers of silicon wafers and dominates several other critical chip materials, but many of its smaller suppliers remain vulnerable to foreign takeovers.

Mitsui Chemicals’ shares extended their decline to as much as 15% in Tokyo.

JIC took JSR private two years ago. JSR supplies light-sensitive materials used with ASML Holding’s extreme ultraviolet lithography machines to pattern fine circuits onto silicon wafers. Customers for JSR’s array of specialty chemicals include Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing, Intel and Samsung Electronics, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.

It was reported in September that JSR was weighing buyout proposals from Mitsui Chemicals and rival Mitsubishi Chemical Group.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.summary: Mitsui Chemicals and DBJ will acquire all shares of JSR from government-backed Japan Investment. The deal would further a government- backed effort to consolidate Japan’s fragmented semiconductor-materials industry.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq62.title: Inside the French drug gangs recruiting children to kill
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq62.text:
Warning: Strong language and descriptions of sexual violence

Although she had just bought hashish from a drug dealer, the woman decided to call the police.

It was because, along with the illegal drugs, she had been handed a note by the young seller during their brief meeting on a Marseille housing estate in 2022.

"We're being held captive and need help. We are 15-years-old," it read.

The teenage dealer, a French court heard earlier this year, was one of two boys being held by a gang which they had both initially approached looking for paid work - albeit illegal.

One boy had been tasked with handling money, the other worked streets around the Frais-Vallon estate. Soon though, bosses had accused them of being responsible for "shortfalls" in takings.

What followed were regular beatings, the court was told, and being forced to dance naked in front of a camera as a form of blackmail. One of the boys was also raped.

Hours after the woman was passed the note, the two teenagers had tried to escape from a second-storey window, injuring themselves in the process. One managed to get away, while the other was caught, beaten and stabbed, but survived.

Arrests were made. Photos on the phone of one of the boys' alleged torturers showed several other young men in a similarly distressed condition. Six men have since been handed hefty sentences for what happened to the two teenagers.

The boys' story highlights the grip that drug gangs hold over parts of France's second city.

While the blend of Mediterranean culture, street art and hip-hop scene has made Marseille a popular tourist destination - beyond the city centre, it is another story.

After months of trying, a BBC team managed to enter this dangerous world - centred on deprived streets and high-rise housing estates in the port city, which police do not enter lightly.

We found an environment where ruthless gangs lure vulnerable young people with promises of easy money, but end up trapping them in a world of drug dealing, brutality and exploitation.

We saw how gangs use social media to recruit hitmen and spoke to several young men caught up in the violence. From prison, one gang member accused of involvement in several murders explained how his "cold-bloodedness" had helped him rise through the ranks.

The city's most powerful gang, DZ Mafia, emerged victorious from a bloody turf war and is now one of the most feared criminal organisations in France.

DZ is the official internet country code for Algeria, where one of the gang's founders, a French-Algerian called Mehdi Laribi, was detained earlier this year under a French arrest warrant.

The criminal outfit rose to prominence in 2023, when it became the first French gang to capitalise on its notoriety by releasing video statements - using social media to market itself as a brand - says the head of the country's anti-drug trafficking unit, Dimitri Zoulas.

Its most recent statement came in July, when the mayor of a nearby town had to be placed in police protection, after intelligence suggested he was in danger of being targeted by the group.

In an online video, six masked men dressed in black stood behind a table - as one of them read a statement denying DZ Mafia's involvement.

France's expanding illegal drugs market - which has seen a surge in cocaine imports alongside high volumes of cannabis and synthetic drugs - has also helped the gang grow rapidly.

The number of cocaine users in France is expected soon to reach two million, says Zoulas, up from 600,000 in 2017. Drug smuggling across France generates €7bn (£5.9bn) a year, involving 200,000 people, he adds.

Many of those distributing the drugs are children and the authorities say the number of minors caught up in trafficking is increasing. During 2025, more than 10,000 children were involved in some way, according to official figures.

DZ Mafia is a prime example. To reach more customers, it needs more gang members - more children.

We have found it is now recruiting young people from across France - not just to sell drugs, but to carry out kidnap, torture and murder.

They are a generation seen as easy to corrupt, but also expendable, by the kingpins who typically control them from prison or overseas.

And, as police and judges warn, once these children enter Marseille's underworld, it is very hard to get them out.

Few know the human cost of Marseille's gangs like mother Karine Brouillard - who lives at the other end of France, almost as far from the Mediterranean coast as you can get.

Her son, Hugo, first ran away aged 15 - from his home in a village in the Nord department - after an argument with his family. He was picked up by police three days later, almost 1,000km (600 miles) away in Marseille, with money and cannabis on him. He was taken home.

But several years later, in 2023, Hugo planned to return south, telling his parents he had secured a holiday job at a restaurant near Marseille.

"He gave regular updates," Karine remembers. "He called me, everything was going well."

Three weeks later, a doctor called. Karine says she will never forget his words: "Your son arrived last night. He took a bullet to the head."

Police believe Hugo was brought for medical help from a gang-controlled area and suspect he was involved with one.

That area was Quartier Nord.

Our best way into Quartier Nord, where DZ Mafia wields power, is with the help of resident Fadella Ouidef, a 41-year-old mother-of-four who gives us a tour.

Thirty-seven seconds after entering one housing estate, we find ourselves cornered.

Car horns sound the moment Fadella's Peugeot passes a gang checkpoint - the teenagers manning the post immediately spot our camera. "Wait, stop filming," Fadella warns, as a grey 4x4 forces us to the side of the road.

"I'm making a report for my housing association," she tells the inquisitive driver. He eventually agrees to let us leave if we stop filming.

It is unnerving to see a non-police vehicle move so assertively and a relief to watch it leave.

"Lately, the gangs have been very aggressive," explains Fadella. "What we simply try to do is make sure our young people understand what's happening is wrong."

Fadella speaks to a wider fear among local families: that their children are enticed by huge sums of money to take a criminal path that robs them of their innocence.

Money is what led one young man to spend his teenage years with DZ Mafia.

In order for our interviewees to speak freely, or because of safety concerns, we have agreed to protect their identities.

Camil tells us he worked up the gang's ranks to "running security" in one area it controls.

The now 20-year-old, who claims to have left the group, is highly suspicious of our presence, but agrees to tell us how the gang recruits young members.

"They know how to get inside your head. Whatever you want, they give to you," he says. This can range from nice cars and spacious apartments, to drugs and prostitutes, he explains.

"You feel loyalty because of what they give you. You'll stay until the very end, until either death or prison."

Camil also gives a sobering assessment of what happens if the gang identifies a weakness in a recruit: "They'll exploit it. You're their bitch, it's over."

DZ Mafia member, Adam - not his real name - tells us he was part of a DZ Mafia hit squad when we speak to him in a Snapchat video call.

He is currently in prison awaiting trial, after being implicated in several murders.

"People noticed my determination, my cold-bloodedness and, without wanting to, I climbed up the ladder of the gang," says Adam. "It became my place, I had to roll with it."

During the chat, he agrees the killings he has been charged with were "quite shocking".

"Attempts in broad daylight, in traffic jams… it can range from going to hit a guy, slap him to taking him in front of his mother and burning him up in a car. I think I have good composure, I handle it fairly well."

We challenge Adam on whether he feels regret when carrying out such acts of brutality.

He says he is "feeling in-part guilty" but claims to have no regrets.

"If I hadn't done all of this, there are other people who would have done that in my place, and so on. I am just another brick in the wall," he says.

Like so many teenagers from Marseille, he knew large sums of money could be earned quickly in drug trafficking. Now in his twenties, he admits the environment he entered was a "trap".

At a so-called deal point in a social housing estate - sealed off and controlled by DZ Mafia - price lists for cocaine, hashish and marijuana are graffitied on a wall.

The estate acts as a natural fortress for drug dealers. With one major road in and out, they can control the flow of customers and see if the police are coming.

It is not uncommon for the sound of automatic gunfire to fill the night air in these areas.

After months of negotiations, a deal-point manager from a rival gang agrees to meet us where he works.

We enter the estate early in the morning, the birdsong and children walking to school providing a stark contrast to the industrial-scale criminal operation that takes place here.

"Joe" says he was making €3,000 (£2,500) a month when he was 13. Now he says that has risen to between €5,000 and €10,000 a month.

He seems to see his life path as pre-ordained, albeit a lucrative one.

We ask Joe if he thinks about the lives lost because of the violence carried out by his gang, but the 23-year-old has also long made peace with the pain and destruction drug trafficking can cause.

"It destroys people, but we all make our own choices," he shrugs.

The work that Joe's gang and DZ Mafia are doing represents a threat to national security, says Zoulas, of the anti-drug trafficking unit.

There are road accidents, as well as family violence, depressions, suicides and more than 700 overdoses each year, he says, "and it distorts the economy".

"We are heading towards a potential systemic breakdown of the criminal justice system."

Police have had success in Marseille and other cities against drug gangs.

Criminal operations are being frustrated, more kingpins arrested and drugs seized.

Since 2024, about 1,000 individuals associated with DZ Mafia have been arrested, and 600 incarcerated, police say.

But overall, it is a battle that is becoming more arduous, rather than easier.

As gangs seek to widen their operations, or replace members who have been arrested or killed, social media has become a potent recruitment tool - especially since the Covid pandemic, when many street-drug sales jumped online.

On social media, we found countless posts advertising jobs in Marseille for aspiring drivers, couriers and hitmen, often with glamourised AI-generated images.

Nets are also being cast wider, as it becomes harder to entice young people locally because they know more about what might happen to them.

The ads can reach teenagers in most corners of France - including Paris, Nantes and Lille - and serve as a powerful pull to Marseille, and the Quartier Nord, police say.

Online advertising has also changed the typical profile of someone who would join a gang's ranks, say law enforcement officials.

Now, it is often someone without a criminal past, but who has exploitable vulnerabilities, like having a difficult family life.

"These people are recruited by unscrupulous sponsors who send them into the lion's den," explains Thibaut Fontaine, the head of France's anti-organised-crime unit.

Their lack of criminal experience, he says, makes them easier to arrest quickly.

Karine still has no idea why her son, Hugo, was shot.

Asked what she would say to gang leaders recruiting children and young men in Marseille, she says: "They destroy families. Little sisters, little brothers, grandparents. But then, I don't think those people have a heart, really."

The restaurant where her son said he was going to work did exist, but staﬀ there told Karine they had never recruited anyone called Hugo.

The reason for his death almost certainly lies within Marseille's Quartier Nord.

Additional reporting by Marianne Baisnee, Lea Guedj and Paul Pradier
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq62.summary: Woman handed note by drug dealer saying she was being held captive by gang. She called police after she was handed the note by the dealer. DZ Mafia member Adam tells us he was part of a DZ hit squad when he was a teenager.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckj0.title: Pope delivers veiled rebuke of Milei's austerity measures
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckj0.text:
Pope Leo XIV has said Argentina's economy must benefit everyone including the poor, in a diplomatic but pointed critique of President Javier Milei's austerity measures.

The Pope was speaking as he arrived in Buenos Aires, the second stop on a 12-day tour of Latin America, only three weeks after having had surgery for lung cancer.

In response, right-wing leader Milei said his government was working to avoid "punishing the Argentines of tomorrow in order to benefit the Argentines of today".

This leg of the Pope's journey was expected be the most politically sensitive, with the president's agenda of slashing public spending having been denounced by the Catholic Church for hitting the poorest hardest.

"The economy must be at the service of the people, rather than people being at the service of the economy," Pope Leo said.

He stressed the plight of those who, "despite hard work, nonetheless struggle to meet their household's needs", and urged that "particular concern be shown for those affected by illness, dependency and disability" - a veiled reference to the government's controversial cuts to disability assistance.

In what appeared to be a rebuke of Milei's combative style and language, the Pope said strengthening democracy required a "willingness to listen" and the "careful use of words".

Milei had been particularly outspoken about Leo's predecessor Pope Francis, whom he called "evil on earth" and a "communist" for promoting a doctrine of social justice to help the poor.

On Sunday, however, Milei struck a conciliatory tone, calling Francis an "exceptional figure" and "undoubtedly the most important Argentine in history".

He was also keen to welcome the current Pope earlier, writing in a post on X that Argentina awaits "with immense joy".

Pope Leo urged Argentina to safeguard its democracy. "Those who exercise authority have a duty to act with prudence, to acknowledge the limits of the power entrusted to them, and to direct their decisions toward the good of the entire community," he said.

In his own address welcoming Leo to Argentina, Milei defended his libertarian policies, saying the rights to life, liberty and property are the backbone of Argentina's constitution and of Western democracies.

The Argentine leader, who has said he will seek re-election next year, is a strong supporter of US President Donald Trump, who has criticised Pope Leo for his opposition to the Iran war.

Pope Leo's trip to Argentina has been described as a homage to Francis, who did not return to his homeland during his own papacy.

The Vatican says no extraordinary measures are being taken in relation to the Pope's health, describing him as a "71-year-old who has undergone an operation" not someone with a "permanent medical condition".

Last month's operation to remove a tumour was successful and his doctors say the cancer has not spread.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckj0.summary: Pope Leo XIV says Argentina's economy must benefit everyone including the poor. He says the economy must be at the service of the people, rather than people being at the economy. Pope Leo is on a 12-day tour of Latin America, the second stop of his 12- day tour. He has had surgery for lung cancer

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckge.title: Jensen Huang: Silicon Valley superstar engulfed by personal scandal
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckge.text:
Jensen Huang is one of the technology industry's most high-profile figures.

He rose to prominence as the business he leads - artificial intelligence (AI) chip giant Nvidia - became one of the world's most valuable companies.

As the face of the AI boom, Huang also became close to Donald Trump as the president pushed for the US to keep its dominance of the technology over China.

The 63-year-old who was once lauded as the "Taylor Swift of tech" and referred to as "Daddy Huang" in Taiwan is now mired in scandal after an affair with a suspected Chinese spy.

Born in Taiwan in 1963, Huang was nine years old when his family moved to the West Coast of the US.

He graduated as an electrical engineer from Oregon State University, and then with a master's degree in the same field from Stanford University.

Huang then worked at US chip firm AMD before co-founding Nvidia.

He has an estimated fortune of $155bn, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index.

"Jensen Huang is a tech visionary of the likes of Steve Jobs," Stephen Witt, the author of Thinking Machine - a biography on Huang, tells the BBC, adding that he was responsible for creating AI hardware as we know it today.

Huang has a famously close relationship with Trump. At the recent AI summit at the White House, where 42 tech executives were present, the president was flanked by Elon Musk and Huang.

Trump said he had not spoken to the Nvidia boss since news of the investigation emerged.

"I just know he's a fine person, but you never know what's going on," Trump told reporters, adding that he had "done an amazing job for our country".

Huang has long found himself at the centre of US-China tensions. Trump has repeatedly said the two nations are in a race for dominance.

Trump has said "whoever wins AI wins", and the fear is that if China gains the upper hand in AI, it will supercharge the country's military and surveillance capabilities.

The US advantage is in large part because of US companies like Nvidia, working with producers like the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), which makes more than 90% of the world's most advanced chips.

Since 2022 the US has used various export controls to keep the top tech out of China, which it says helps retain America's competitive edge and protects its national security.

But it means companies like Nvidia have been largely locked out of the world's most lucrative market, with Jensen Huang once saying that Nvidia's share of the Chinese market had gone from around 95% to effectively zero. In recent years Huang has engaged in a flurry of shuttle diplomacy, dashing between Washington and Beijing, hoping to find a US-approved way back in, and shaping US policy on China along the way.

Sunday's revelations may explain why Huang has failed to bring home the biggest prize of all to Nvidia: the Trump administration's blessing to sell all but its most advanced chips to China.

Quarter after quarter of late, Nvidia has been locked out of that lucrative market. Despite his ostensible closeness to Trump, Huang has not managed to wrest this concession from the administration.

Huang founded Nvidia with fellow electrical engineers Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem in 1993.

The company was originally known for chips that process graphics, particularly for computer games.

Eventually it changed focus to AI, a field it now dominates.

"In 2012 these machine learning neural net researchers started to use it for that purpose and Jensen immediately recongnised that this was going to be a massive industry and the future of computing. He began to pour enormous amounts of resources into building what was essentially the AI hardware market," says Witt.

"Today when we think of that, we think of these giant data centres - none of that existed. There were no customers for the stuff he was building. In fact his first customer was Open AI at the time they had 30 people - he actually gave it to them, he donated it to them."

Nvidia is now worth some $4.5 trillion, making it one of the most valuable companies ever.

"The first real neural net of modern times on an Nvidia network was Alex Krizhevsky's Alexnet and they trained that on two Nvidia cards in Alex's bedroom. Now we do the same thing but we do it with 200,000 - 300,000 cards and instead of doing it in a bedroom we do it in a giant barn full of computers called a data centre," adds Witt.

"So when you think about a data centre buildout, when you hear the AI infrastructure buildout, Jensen runs a tollbooth. All of that goes through him. And it made his company at least temporarily, the most valuable company in the world."

Nvidia's board has announced a probe following reports by the New York Times that Huang had engaged in a romantic relationship with a woman believed by US intelligence to be a Chinese spy.

For now, though, Nvidia's board appears to have little appetite for removing Huang, saying in a statement on Sunday that they have "confidence in Jensen and his leadership team".

Sources tell the BBC his removal is unlikely because there is so much money at stake. There is also no clear successor to the 63-year old tech boss.

Huang met his wife Lori at Oregon State University, where she was also studying electrical engineering and was his lab partner.

They married in 1985, about eight years before he co-founded Nvidia, and have two children, Madison and Spencer.

He has credited Lori and Madison for making black leather jackets his signature style.

In 2007, the couple founded the Jen-Hsun and Lori Huang Foundation.

The charitable fund has seen its assets surge in recent years, driven by the soaring value of Nvidia shares, and is estimated to be worth more than $9bn.

Its donations include tens of millions of dollars to engineering programmes at Oregon State and Stanford University.

"Jensen in my conversations with him and in other conversations has gone to great lengths to present himself as a family man. That's very important to him," says Witt.

"He praises his wife, he talks about her in very glowing ways. Both of his children work for Nvidia. Spencer and Maddison. The fallout of this would be bad for anyone's family. But for someone who has gone to such great lengths to cultivate an image of being a family guy and who keeps his children very close, it is very bad."

Huang for his part released a statement which said, "I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry."

US officials had concluded that Alice Huang had been recruited to spy by China's top intelligence agency, the New York Times reports.

She was a top executive at Megaspeed, a data centre company based in Singapore. The firm had been suspected of helping divert Nvidia chips to China, a concern that Nvidia maintains was investigated and debunked.

Surveillance reportedly revealed communications between Alice Huang and an American citizen, who was subsequently identified as Jensen Huang through a process known as "unmasking".

It remains unclear what information Alice Huang – who is also known as Huang Le – allegedly passed to Beijing, how valuable it was, or when she is believed to have begun gathering intelligence.

Alice Huang did not respond to the paper's request for comment.

When the BBC asked Nvidia if the company was aware of intelligence concerns, the company said it was not.

"We trust that if we were the target of a genuine threat, the US government would have notified us," an Nvidia spokesperson told the BBC.

Additional reporting by Ayeshea Perera in Singapore and Helen Davidson in Sydney
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckge.summary: Nvidia co-founded Nvidia and founded Jen-Hsun and Lori Huang Foundation. Huang has said he was unfaithful to his wife and two children.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm5y.title: How yesterday's waste is becoming tomorrow's fashion
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm5y.text:
How many clothes, items of bedding and other fabric have you thrown away this year?

While resale sites are growing in popularity, in the UK we still bin about 711,000 tonnes of textiles annually – roughly the weight of seven US aircraft carriers.

The global fashion and textiles industry is one of the most wasteful, but recycling firms in Peterborough and Northamptonshire are using technology to change that.

They are gaining the attention of major brands but say they need laws, as well as consumers, to support them.

In a warehouse next to the A14 in Kettering, a mountain of crumpled fabric is slowly fed into a machine.

There are dressing gowns, duvets, branded banners and lanyards from events including the Commonwealth Games.

All are made from polyester – the world's most commonly used textile fibre – and all have been thrown away.

Traditionally they would be burned or buried in landfill but Project Re:Claim is trying to change that.

The partnership between The Salvation Army's trading arm (SATCoL) and Plan B Circular operates what they say is the first commercial-scale polyester textile-to-textile recycling facility in Europe – technology adapted from a bottle recycling plant.

The Salvation Army collects the items and those that cannot be reused in their current form are shredded and melted.

Impurities such as dead skin cells and hair are removed and polyester pellets (rPET) are produced which can be used to make new clothes.

"It's the future: using the clothing we have today to make the clothing that we need tomorrow," says Plan B Circular founder Tim Cross.

"We process 500kg of fabric an hour but we could easily scale up if there was demand.

"The problem is encouraging clothing manufacturers to change from using virgin polyester to recycled polyester from old textiles. And to design their new clothes to be easily recycled at their end of life."

"A polyester blazer doesn't need nylon buttons and labels. A sports top doesn't need metal zips. It can all be polyester."

That is important because the plant can only recycle items that are 100% polyester.

Most clothing "is a fibre mix like polyester-cotton, or often three or four different materials," says Majonne Frost, head of sustainability at SATCoL.

Researchers are trialling ways to separate these fibres, but doing it at scale remains difficult and costly, so most of those items are eventually destroyed.

Project Re:Claim says its rPET requires 89% less carbon to make than virgin polyester.

"We send the pellets back to China in what would otherwise be empty shipping containers, and it's spun back into yarn," Cross adds.

"We have the technology but we're way behind with legislation. It absolutely should be driving the way we design and make clothing."

EU rules are already changing and are forcing manufacturers to reduce the waste they produce, their environmental impact, and to make the industry circular.

It must ensure products are not only made from recycled content but are themselves recyclable at the end of their lives.

The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) says it is "funding the UK Textiles Pact, which is driving ambitious targets to cut waste and increase the life cycle of materials".

However, that scheme is voluntary.

In addition, Defra says "a taskforce of experts and businesses is looking at options to reduce waste in homes and businesses and will report back on next steps later this year".

Peterborough-based Gen Phoenix feels global consumer attitudes and legislation are beginning to drive change.

Every year it recycles thousands of tonnes of waste leather into new fabric which has been used by major brands, including Dr Martens, Nike and Coach.

It also specialises in train, bus and aviation seating.

"Jet2 was our first commercial customer, and now we're on one in every five commercial aircraft flying today," says chief executive John Kennedy.

"Our material has similar properties to traditional leather but with an 80% lower carbon footprint and it's lighter. Weight is important for airlines.

"We've saved more than 18,000 tonnes of material from landfill."

Leather is itself a waste product from the food industry, but still much is wasted that Gen Phoenix feels could be salvaged.

"If you think of an animal hide, it's the bits like the neck, the shoulders, the armpits, the belly – bits that don't make good finished leather," says Richard Peace, the company's senior director of research and technology.

The company ships in the waste as "wet blue" – the name given to hides partway through the leather process – from tanneries around the world.

It breaks the leather down into a fibre fluff, which is sprayed on to thin sheets of tissue paper.

The sheets are then sandwiched around a fabric – usually recycled polyester – before high-powered water jets bind all the fibres back together.

Called hydro-entanglement, it forms the new fabric without the need for resin binders, making the new product more easily recyclable.

"The importance of sustainability is seeing a groundswell, both in terms of legislation and consumer attitude - especially with Gen Z coming through," says Kennedy.

"Brands are definitely more invested and are being fairly quiet about the great work they're doing.

"We're continuing to innovate and expand, looking at recycling end process leather too.

"Peterborough is where we do all of our manufacturing and R&D (research and development), and while we may establish other sites, this is where the magic happens."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckvg.title: Charity wants bee, bird and butterfly population boost
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckvg.text:
A charity wants to raise £70,000 for a project aimed at boosting wildlife populations on farmland in the Thames Valley.

The Berkshire, Buckinghamshire and Oxfordshire Wildlife Trust (BBOWT) said the money would form part of its Nature Recovery Fund and would be used to tackle falling numbers of birds, bees and butterflies.

The trust said farmland bird populations had fallen by 63% since 1970, while half of the UK's 27 bumblebee species were in decline.

It said measures to help wildlife could include using fewer chemicals in farming to create healthier soil and less polluted waterways, as well as setting aside corners of grassland for animals.

BBOWT's chief executive Estelle Bailey said: "Farmland makes up 68% of our three counties, so to truly have an impact on nature's recovery, our work must expand far beyond our precious nature reserves."

In 2023, a report produced by government agencies, environmental groups and universities found one in six species in the UK were at risk of extinction.

Bailey added: "I want future generations to experience the joy of countryside filled with life - swallows darting above fields, butterflies and bumblebees feeding on abundant wildflowers, hedgerows alive with the sound of birdsong, and to eat locally grown food that supports a healthy, resilient landscape."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw98.title: Print commissioned by Nasa uncovered for exhibition
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw98.text:
A print by a Yorkshire artist commissioned by Nasa in the early days of space travel will go on show as part of a pop art exhibition.

Komtek I by Michael Fossick, who studied at Bradford School of Art, was created in 1962 to celebrate a Hong Kong company that produced microcomputers in the early days of space travel.

The print was part of a Nasa project to document the effort of sending the first humans to the moon and is on display as part of the Pop Art at Cartwright Hall exhibition.

The display tells the story of the British International Print Biennale, which took place at the Bradford gallery on 11 occasions between 1968 and 1990, and runs until March 2027.

While the exhibition also includes work by Andy Warhol and David Hockney, there is "definitely stuff that people won't have seen before", said curator Jill Iredale.

"It's a completely bizarre sort of connection somehow that an artist born in Sheffield that went to Bradford School of Art was somehow commissioned by Nasa," said Iredale.

"It was actually a screen print, but it was made from a very early computerised image," she said.

In March 1962, Nasa administrator James Webb awarded commissions to 38 artists, including Fossick, to document the space agency's achievements.

John H. Glenn became the first American to orbit the earth on 20 February 1962 and in the following decade Nasa's Mercury programme led to the Apollo missions, and eventually to Neil Armstrong setting foot on the moon in 1969.

Fossick chose to honour Komtek I, a microcomputer produced by Komtek Technologies Ltd in Hong Kong that was significant in the early years of the space programme.

He submitted the print to the First British International Print Biennale held at Cartwright Hall in 1968 where it won a prize.

Created by a group of local print makers and artists, at its height the British International Print Biennale included more than 500 works selected from more than 3,000 entries.

It received work by artists such as Andy Warhol, Roy Licthenstein and David Hockney, which remain in the gallery today.

Hockney was invited to be a judge on the first biennial in 1968 and created the poster for the show, which is on display in the exhibition.

Iredale said the pop art explosion in Bradford was a reaction to the seriousness of the World War Two and the boost in commercial print culture.

"Bradford had quite a strong, experimental kind of light, pretty kind of DIY aesthetic with artists and with the college as well," she explained.

"There was simply loads more young people around, post-baby boom, and an increase in opportunities for working-class youth."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm8e.title: Cancer survivor's battle for fertility funding
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm8e.text:
A woman from Lancashire who had stage four blood cancer said she is fighting for NHS-funded fertility preservation treatment.

Mollie Mulheron, 28, said she was unable to freeze her eggs before chemotherapy because her cancer was so aggressive she needed urgent treatment.

Although she has since recovered and is cancer-free, NHS Lancashire and South Cumbria Integrated Care Board said it would not fund egg freezing because she does not meet its eligibility criteria.

Mollie said: "It's clearly unfair because the funding is there before chemotherapy, so it doesn't make sense that it's not available now."

Mollie, who lives in Padiham, was travelling in the Galapagos Islands after university when she said she started to feel ill.

After travelling back home to get checked out, doctors found a melon-sized tumour, which was "crushing my heart and left lung," Mollie said.

It took approximately 800 hours of chemotherapy, over 150 days, for Mollie to be cancer-free.

"It was hell, but I did manage to beat it," said Mollie, who runs a language academy in Lancashire.

But because the cancer was originally so aggressive, she said she did not have time to freeze her eggs, something that is generally available through NHS funding.

This is because chemotherapy may impact fertility, and can permanently affect a person's ovaries and womb.

Mollie was being treated at St James Hospital in Leeds, where she was told she could access fertility protection after chemotherapy.

But, after moving to Padiham, she said she was told funding was not available.

"It does seem to be a postcode lottery that some places allow it and other postcodes don't at all," Mollie said.

Mollie has started an online petition calling for better protection of young cancer survivors' fertility and to address what she says is an NHS funding gap after chemotherapy.

Mollie said her ovarian reserve had more than halved in a year and she had been told she was likely to go through an early menopause.

She fears that without fertility preservation treatment she may not be able to have children in the future.

The 28-year-old said she was struggling with the prospect of losing that option, particularly as she did not want to feel pressured into starting a family immediately after recovering from cancer.

"I'd like to have some time after having cancer just to rebuild my life," she said.

Updated National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidance says healthcare professionals should discuss fertility preservation with people whose medical condition or treatment is likely to affect their fertility.

Mollie said the guidance was not mandatory and could be interpreted differently by local NHS bodies, creating inconsistencies in access to treatment.

She said the process had left her feeling frustrated and trapped in a cycle of uncertainty.

"It's just kind of going around in circles, it feels like, and it's just so unfair," she said.

A spokesperson for NHS Lancashire and South Cumbria Integrated Care Board said: "We are aware of the case and understand the patient's concerns, however, decisions such as this one are in line with the current eligibility criteria of the Assisted Conception policy for Lancashire and South Cumbria.

"Due to patient confidentiality, we are unable to comment on specific details of individual cases.

"Lancashire and South Cumbria ICB is currently working collaboratively with Greater Manchester and Cheshire and Merseyside ICBs to review a number of clinical commissioning policies, and assisted conception services have been identified as a priority, particularly in light of updated national guidance.

"The ICB would welcome any review of national policy that gives due consideration to the needs of all patients."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm8x.title: 'Painful condition meant I had to leave my job'
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm8x.text:
After years of suffering the pain of endometriosis, 21-year-old Charlotte Samphire was forced to leave her job because the symptoms were too severe to manage.

Now, the beauty therapist from East Yorkshire, along with Hull charity Hey Endo!, is hoping improvements will soon be made after a government report found the condition is having a significant impact on women's finances and careers.

"People need to know that women shouldn't have to choose between their careers and their health," she said.

Samphire, who has stage 4 endometriosis and has suffered years of debilitating pain since she was just 10 years old, said although her boss was understanding, she knows not everyone would be so lucky.

Endometriosis is a chronic condition in which cells that are similar to the lining of the womb grow in other parts of the body.

It can take an average of nine years to get a diagnosis from the onset of symptoms and it affects 1.5 million people in the UK.

The All-Party Parliamentary Group on Endometriosis recently published a report on the condition in the workplace, commissioned and funded by Endometriosis UK.

Kirsteen Sullivan MP, who is chairwoman of that group and also has endometriosis, said she wanted the government to introduce a national framework for women in the workplace.

"That framework should build on existing standards and the menopause action plans that were already introduced earlier this year," she said.

"I think that will provide support and guidance for employers so that they can better understand the support they should be providing to their employees, but also allow women living with the condition to better understand the kind of support they should receive."

She said the government should also review guidance around the Equality Act to ensure it better reflects fluctuating and chronic conditions.

Samphire said: "I worked in a salon and I loved working there, but I struggled to manage my endometriosis and I had to tell my employer that I couldn't fulfil my roles.

"Endometriosis changes women's lives every day, whether that's just being diagnosed or whether you've quit your job because you can't do it anymore, or whether it's taken over your mental health. It will do that to you.

"I believe the government should make it mandatory for employers to be educated on all conditions, whether they're visible or invisible, and the steps and support that they can take to help their employees.

"This could help so many women change their career paths, even change their lives."

Hey Endo! was co-founded by Helen Wilkinson, 34, and Ashleigh Hirst, 35. It became a registered charity in 2024 and now has more than 3,500 service users.

Last year, the charity launched a workplace Best Practice Charter in collaboration with the Hull and District Trades Union and Hull West and Haltemprice MP Emma Hardy.

Wilkinson said: "I went through 17 jobs in 14 years and a lot of it was due to sickness absence.

"I would either lose the job because I had too much time off or I would leave the job before they could sack me because I had too much time off."

She said some employers have been "absolutely brilliant" and tried to understand but in other workplaces the understanding simply wasn't there.

"Almost everybody who comes into our service from the beginning, within six months they're in a much better place with themselves," she said.

"They're a lot stronger and able to go out and advocate for themselves and they know their rights.

"For a lot of them, it's often a case of basic information that they weren't aware of, just directing them to things like the Equality Act and having a word with their occupational health team at work."

Hirst says her endometriosis symptoms started to appear around the age of 11. She describes her diagnosis, at the age of 25, as a "big wake-up call".

"I was just recently married but all of these symptoms came in a great big wave and just knocked me off my feet," she said.

"Being on the floor in pain and vomiting through the pain, I thought that was normal and I thought everyone went through it and I just kept it behind closed doors, but actually it's not normal."

Hirst says Hey Endo! would like the government to speak to local charities like theirs if a new national framework on endometriosis is developed.

"We have said for many years that there are so many women in the workplace who don't feel supported, who maybe feel like they have to change jobs and careers.

"It absolutely has to happen sooner rather than later."

A government spokesperson said: "For millions of women, endometriosis has a serious impact on their wellbeing, relationships and participation in the workforce.

"The government's Renewed Women's Health Strategy identifies endometriosis as a priority condition and states our commitment to improve the treatment and ongoing care for every woman affected."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmd6.title: How you can get council's £250 cost of living help
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmd6.text:
Applications for household grants of up to £250 are due to open for residents in part of Surrey.

Tandridge District Council is funding the scheme, which last ran in January, to support residents with the cost of living.

Applicants must live in the Tandridge district, be over 16 years old and be "experiencing financial hardship", the council says.

They must also prove they are struggling to pay for essential items for themselves or their dependants by submitting full bank statements for August, September and October.

Other evidence such as arrears letters and energy bills can be uploaded too.

Grants are available to households even if they receive support from elsewhere, such as Surrey County Council funds.

Tandridge District Council said it aimed to provide support to those who needed help the most.

Successful applicants will receive a one-off payment, with the soonest payment date at the end of November.

Households without children can apply for £150, while those with under 18s can apply for £250.

The scheme is worth a total of £150,000 and applications will be processed on a first come, first served basis, the council said.

Other authorities in the county offer their own cost of living support.

Residents can apply online or by phone from 10:00 GMT on 9 November.

People who apply by phone will have to take their bank statements to the council's offices in Oxted.

Applications close on 31 December at the latest.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm4g.title: Indoor soft play centres struggling to stay open
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm4g.text:
The owner of a soft play area in north Shropshire said it is in danger of closure as the hot summer has meant centres like hers have struggled to get people through the doors.

Jessica Harvey has run Funzone in Whitchurch for over a year, and said the industry is seasonal, with there being occasions when she was the only one at the centre all day.

"Over the summer, there has definitely been [times] where we probably had 10 to 15 people in all week, which just isn't sustainable", she said.

Funzone, which has existed as a soft play centre in Whitchurch for 17 years, was sold two years ago. But the company that bought it went into liquidation, meaning Harvey was able to buy the firm in October 2025.

She said her first hot summer has been extremely challenging.

"It has been a bit demoralising. We have tried so hard to bring things back, and obviously when you are investing heavily, but not only just investing, a lot of our time has gone into it too.

"I'm talking getting up at six o'clock in the morning, being there for four hours before opening, and then not leaving the place until 12 at night because you're painting or building."

Harvey added that she was able to make the money up by building a soft play trailer built for events, but said that with the weather getting colder, she would need people to start coming again.

"Eventually, if no one uses it and there was no money coming in, it's not a viable business, is it?" she said.

"So, you know, it would have to go. It [is a] kind of use it or lose it type situation."

Connor Galbraith and his wife Nicole opened Wacky Playland in Kidderminster nearly two years ago, leaving their jobs as an IT specialist and a chemist.

The pair posted to their social media pages to share the reality of what the cost of running the centre.

"Three months of usage of electricity cost us £9,756.42; building insurance per year, is £6,410.47. That's just the building paid for the landlord's insurance, not including our public liability, [or] employee liability insurance as well," Galbraith added.

"We have a service charge as well, every three months, that is £5,837.33.

"Some customers do not realise the prices behind it, they just see it as, 'oh it's a business'."

He added their aircon and the 5% VAT relief helped them keep their business going through the summer.

However, Galbraith said the business could still pay the bills but it was "really tight."

"If costs keep going higher and higher then it does kind of question where we can be because, I'm sure any business owner knows, that we have a lease as a 10-year lease and as goes up incrementally." Galbraith said.

"If, as years go by, our rent is going to go higher and if, in this world how it's looking things are going to get more expensive, then it kind of makes you scared, like where is it going to be."

Last month, the owners of The Kidz Barn, also in Kidderminster, announced their soft play centre would be closing its doors in January 2026, and would be put up for sale.

In a social media post, the centre said it "was not a decision that was made lightly."

"We weathered some incredibly difficult times. During COVID, there were moments when we genuinely didn't know if we would ever reopen our doors.

"Somehow, we got through those hardest months, and being able to welcome you all back was something we will never forget."

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/09/nx-s1-603.title: How a bank collapse left millions in limbo and toppled Paraguay's president
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/09/nx-s1-603.author: Charles Parkinson
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/09/nx-s1-603.text:
Protesters hold signs outside Congress in Asunción, Paraguay, on Friday, Nov. 6, 2026. The Senate impeached and removed President Santiago Peña over allegations linked to the collapse of Ueno Bank. Vice President Pedro Alliana was sworn in as his successor.

ASUNCIÓN, Paraguay — When Ueno Bank's services abruptly stopped working in the early hours of Tuesday morning, the consequences were immediate for the millions of Paraguayans who had come to depend on it for everyday transactions.

"People don't have any trust," said Elizabeth González, a 28-year-old barista at a café in downtown Asunción, a few blocks from Paraguay's Congress building, where protesters had begun gathering after the bank's collapse was announced Tuesday.

Earlier, one customer had walked into the café and insisted on paying in cash. He no longer trusted any bank.

"If Paraguayans themselves aren't confident right now, foreign investors will be less so," González said.

The collapse affected far more than the bank's shareholders. Ueno said it had 2.9 million customers — around 60% of Paraguay's adult population. The Central Bank said the bank had approximately 1.8 million depositors.

By Saturday, authorities said almost 1.2 million customers had received an advance payment under the state's deposit guarantee fund, but many were still waiting.

A shuttered Ueno Bank ATM in Asunción, Paraguay, after the bank's collapse left millions of customers unable to access their money and disrupted everyday transactions across the country.

It also led to the impeachment and removal of President Santiago Peña, a close ally of President Donald Trump, and exposed a power struggle inside within the ruling Colorado Party.

The anger was palpable outside Congress on Friday, where hundreds had gathered to protest not only their inability to access their money but also what they saw as a broader failure of accountability.

"I came not because it affects me personally, but because it affects all of Paraguay," said Elodia Saveredo, a 71-year-old housewife who sells her own handicrafts online.

Batarram Caballero, a 23-year-old fifth-year biochemistry student and president of the student center at the National University of Asunción, said classmates had money frozen that they needed to cover basic expenses.

"It wasn't a lot of money, perhaps, but it was money for their bus fare. It was money for their food," she said. "To hear that and not be able to do anything because I don't have the resources to help them is very discouraging."

Ueno Bank launched as a fintech in 2021 and began operating as a bank in November 2023. Its meteoric rise to become one of the country's most important financial institutions was driven by slick marketing and a digital model based around convenience and cashback deals; customers could open accounts on their phones and were offered incentives to process payments through the platform.

Caballero believes the crisis was foretold by an intense campaign in the days before accounts were frozen.

"They were bombarding us with messages telling us to put our money there," she said. "There were also rumors about what was already on the cards."

Demonstrators burn a flag depicting impeached Paraguayan President Santiago Peña during a protest over the banking crisis outside the National Congress in Asunción on Nov. 6, 2026.

The bank also held substantial public funds. The Social Security Institute, known as IPS, had around $355 million invested in Ueno, roughly 9% of its portfolio.

The sums involved have raised questions about how such a young bank came to hold so much public money.

Manuel Ferreira, an economist and former finance minister, told local outlet ABC Color that the collapse raised fundamental questions about how the bank managed its assets. He pointed out that, in a typical bank, shareholders provide only a small portion of the money behind its assets, while the bulk comes from customer deposits.

He also argued that marketing and discounts helped attract customers but did not create lasting assets. A bank's principal asset, he said, was its loan portfolio: money owed by borrowers.

But in the case of Ueno, many of those loans had gone to companies directly linked to the bank's controlling owners, Grupo Vásquez, including $146 million in loans made to just three companies. He described Ueno's promissory notes as being signed by the same people on both sides of some transactions.

The scandal hit Peña particularly hard because of his personal links to the bank's holding company, in which he held shares even after taking up the presidency. He also appointed Carlos Carvallo, who had led Ueno Bank, to head Paraguay's Central Bank in 2023.

In his asset declaration submitted weeks after taking up the presidency in 2023, Peña listed shares in Ueno Holding, then valued at around $845,000. Those shares represented around 1.6% of the company's paid-up capital when he later sold them in March 2025.

Paraguayan President Santiago Peña signs his resignation letter at the presidential residence in Asunción on Nov. 5, 2026, days after the Central Bank took over Ueno Bank amid a solvency crisis that left millions of customers unable to access their savings.

Prosecutors allege that, while president, he used his position to influence public agencies and state-owned entities to maintain deposits with the bank despite his connections to its parent group.

Peña resigned Thursday and was impeached and removed from office Friday. The following day, prosecutors charged him with breach of trust and administration for personal gain. He was ordered held in pretrial detention at a military facility pending the investigation. Peña has pleaded not guilty. Pedro Alliana, the country's vice president, has been sworn in as president to serve out the rest of Peña's term until August 2028.

Carvallo was also arrested and charged with breach of trust, administration for personal gain and producing false public documents. A judge ordered him held in pretrial detention at a police facility. Eight Ueno executives, including 36-year-old CEO Miguel Vásquez, were also arrested and charged.

The crisis has also put the spotlight on Horacio Cartes, a tobacco magnate and former president of Paraguay who wields considerable political and economic influence.

Cartes handpicked Peña, his former finance minister, to lead his Honor Colorado faction into the 2023 presidential election. But the relationship between the two men had become increasingly strained, apparently over Peña's efforts to establish his own power base within the party.

In September, senators aligned with Cartes sought information from the Central Bank about Ueno's transactions with related companies and its public-sector deposits.

After the bank collapsed, Cartes publicly distanced himself from Peña, releasing a public statement on Wednesday calling for an investigation and insisting there should be "no impunity for anyone." The following day, his faction backed Peña's impeachment.

The move was widely seen as a decisive withdrawal of political protection for Peña, and an opportunity for Cartes to reassert his influence.

Demonstrators burn Ueno Bank cards during a protest after Paraguay's central bank took over the bank amid a solvency crisis in Asunción, Paraguay, Nov. 5, 2026.

But for those gathered outside Congress protesting, the scandal was about more than a bank collapse. It was a reckoning with Paraguay's political establishment.

For Rodrigo Piatti, a 45-year-old activist with the anti-corruption campaign group Comisión Escrache Ciudadano, the scandal would only lead to real change if the political establishment, including Cartes, were challenged.

"Everything that's wrong with Paraguay… is Horacio Cartes and his line of succession," Piatti said. "[Paraguay needs] the opposition to take power. A real opposition to take power, and for all these criminals to be put in prison. That's the dream of all Paraguayans."

The crisis has also raised questions about Paraguay's image among foreign businesspeople. Eduardo López, a 35-year-old exporter whose company operates in Paraguay and the United States, said the scandal would only worsen the lack of confidence he had already seen among American business contacts.

"We are a serious Paraguayan company, but [American businesspeople] don't trust the Paraguayan government," he said. "It's a disaster."

Nearby, Lizza Lugo, a 22-year-old student leader at the National University, expressed frustration with the status quo and said she hoped voters would bring change in the 2028 presidential election.

"The laws apply differently to those who have money and those who don't. That is the reality in Paraguay," she said. "I do hope people don't have short memories, because they forget these things very quickly."

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.title: Ramla Ali wins first world titles at 36 with highly controversial split decision
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.author: Bryan Armen Graham
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.text:
British-Somali boxer claims first world titles in Texas

Kreps outlands Ali but loses disputed split decision

Baumgardner wins 135lb belt as Dubois feud heats up

British-Somali boxer Ramla Ali became a world champion for the first time at the age of 36 on Sunday night after winning a highly controversial 10-round split decision over former sparring partner Mikiah Kreps to claim the vacant WBO and IBF women’s junior featherweight titles in Arlington, Texas.

Ali, who grew up in east London after fleeing Somalia’s civil war with her family and went on to become the first boxer to represent the African country at the Olympics, completed her remarkable journey to the top of the 122lb division at College Park Center on her second attempt at a world championship – but only after a verdict rewarding her for a fight that appeared to be largely controlled by her opponent.

“I can’t put into words what this means to me and what this means to all of Somalia,” a visibly emotional Ali said in the immediate aftermath. “I’ve hopefully inspired so many young girls and boys out there to dream big and that’s all I’ve ever wanted to do.”

Ali (12-2, 3 KOs) took the upper hand early after scoring a knockdown in the third round when Kreps touched the canvas with her glove after taking a right hook flush to the chin.

But Kreps (11-1, 3 KOs) appeared galvanized by the setback, ramping up her volume and applying relentless pressure that disrupted Ali’s rhythm as the 30-year-old American took control of the exchanges and appeared to win the majority of the remaining rounds.

The ringside arbiters were sharply divided, with Ali prevailing by scores of 97-92 and 96-93 while the third judge favored Kreps 98-91. (The Guardian had it 97-92 for Kreps.)

Compubox’s punch statistics only cast further doubt on the decision. Kreps outlanded Ali by 115 blows to 78 overall, including a 91-70 edge in power shots, while connecting on the greater number of punches in eight of the 10 rounds. The New Yorker also threw 525 punches to Ali’s 346, maintaining a substantially higher work rate throughout the contest.

When the scores were announced, an overwhelmed Ali dropped to her knees and wept. She then spoke of her father who died six months ago, saying that her trainer had invoked his memory before the fight.

“When we were in the changing room, my coach said, because my dad passed away in May, ‘Do this for him,’” Ali said during an in-ring interview. “That’s where those emotions came out at the end, because I did it for my dad.”

Ali also paid tribute to Kreps, acknowledging her opponent’s industry and crowding tactics that had made the contest so difficult.

“Every time I went to the corner, I kept saying, ‘I’m so tired. I’m so tired,’ because your work rate was just next level,” she said.

Veteran promoter Lou DiBella, who has increasingly assumed the role of boxing’s unofficial ombudsman, was among those outraged by the verdict, calling for an investigation into the scoring.

“Mikiah Kreps won that fight and it wasn’t close. Stevie Wonder could see that,” DiBella wrote on social media. “Boxing can’t get out of its own way. I am appalled at that decision.”

Ali’s breakthrough came more than two years after her first crack at a world title ended in disappointment, when she lost a 10-round unanimous decision to Yamileth Mercado in a bid for the Mexican’s WBC junior featherweight strap. Her extraordinary life story is the subject of In the Shadows, a biopic starring Top Boy actor Jasmine Jobson that premiered last month.

In the main event, three-belt junior lightweight champion Alycia Baumgardner moved up to 135lb and added the IBF lightweight title with a commanding unanimous decision over Elif Nur Turhan. All three judges scored the fight a 100-90 whitewash for Baumgardner in a contest held under men’s championship rules with 10 rounds of three minutes each.

“What’s next is undisputed, like I did at 130,” Baumgardner said afterward, fixing her sights on a showdown with Britain’s Caroline Dubois, the WBC and WBO lightweight champion who took in Sunday’s fights from ringside.

The pair engaged in a heated ringside confrontation moments later, renewing a feud that has simmered for months. Dubois, 25, has repeatedly accused the American of avoiding her, while Baumgardner has maintained the Briton has yet to earn the right to share a ring with her.

Dubois is scheduled to face Stephanie Han in a 135lb title unification bout on 20 February at the Don Haskins Center in El Paso, Texas, with the WBA, WBC and WBO lightweight belts on the line. Should Dubois prevail, it would set the stage for a four-belt unification fight with Baumgardner for the undisputed 135lb title in what could be one of the biggest fights in women’s boxing in 2027.

Baumgardner’s and Ali’s bouts topped the seventh card staged by Most Valuable Promotions Women, the fledgling women’s boxing series launched by boxer-influencer Jake Paul in March alongside a three-year ESPN broadcast deal designed to give female fighters a regular platform on linear television.

Earlier on the program, Australia’s Skye Nicolson retained her WBC junior featherweight title with a unanimous decision over Japan’s Miyo Yoshida, winning by scores of 100-90, 99-91 and 98-92. Mexico’s Irma Garcia unified the IBF and WBA junior bantamweight titles with a unanimous verdict over Panama’s Nataly Delgado, with all three judges handing down scores of 97-92 after Garcia registered a sixth-round knockdown.

On the preliminary card, Brittany Sims and Shera Mae Patricio fought to a 10-round split draw in their contest for the vacant WBA regular bantamweight championship. One judge favored Sims 97-93, another had Patricio winning 100-90 and the third scored it 95-95, leaving the title unclaimed.
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.summary: Ramla Ali becomes world champion for the first time at the age of 36. Ali becomes first British-Somali boxer to represent the African country at the Olympics. Panama's Nataly Delgado wins WBA regular bantamweight title.

https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.title: Starwatch: Count these stars to find out how dark the sky is where you are
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.author: Stuart Clark
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.text:
Great Square of Pegasus’s four corners are widely visible, but its inner stars provide a useful indicator of darkness

This week, we are going to locate the Great Square of Pegasus and count stars to see how dark your sky is.

The chart shows the view looking south from London at 2000 GMT on 9 November. High in the sky is the Great Square of Pegasus, a distinctive pattern of four stars that marks the body of the mythical winged horse.

The four corner stars – Alpheratz, Scheat, Markab and Algenib – are bright enough to be visible even from suburban locations. The question is, how many stars can you see inside the square?

To do the experiment, find somewhere away from direct lighting and wait for at least 20 minutes to allow your eyes time to adjust to the darkness. No checking your phone to pass the time, as the bright screen will ruin your dark adaptation. Then look carefully inside the square and count every star that you can see with your naked eyes. Do not include the four corner stars.

If you can see just one star, your sky is relatively poor. Four stars indicate an average sky, while seven suggests good conditions. Count 13 and your sky is very good indeed. If you can see about 35, you are observing under an exceptionally dark sky.
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.summary: Great Square of Pegasus's four corners are widely visible, but its inner stars provide a useful indicator of darkness. This week we will count stars to see how dark your sky is.

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: Democrats to attend Cop31 climate talks boosted by midterms and eager to make up for Trump-era setbacks
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Oliver Milman
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
US government will have no official presence at UN’s annual climate summit, this year’s Cop31 held in Antalya, Turkey

T
he US will be absent from key UN climate talks that start on Monday, a further sign of Donald Trump’s scornful dismissal of the climate crisis. But Democrats’ crushing win in the US midterm elections has delivered a timely shot of optimism to countries now looking beyond the Trump era of climate obstruction.

For the second year in a row, there will be no official US government presence at the annual climate summit, this year known as Cop31 and held in Antalya, Turkey. While almost every other country in the world sends delegations to the talks, Trump has derided the climate crisis as a “hoax” and “bullshit” and triggered the withdrawal of the US from the entire international climate framework.

“This summit rejects reality by failing to acknowledge that extremist climate policies are destroying countries around the world,” a White House official said, confirming that the administration would not send anyone to Cop31.

The snub is so severe that about 20 members of the US Congress heading to the summit have been denied usual state department assistance, requiring them to turn to philanthropic funding for the trip. “I’m glad we found a way to get there, but it is insane,” said Sean Casten, a Democratic congressman who is attending Cop31. “We have a lot of rebuilding to do. It hinges on Congress to maintain diplomatic continuities at Cop and minimize the damage until adults are back in the White House.”

Trump’s active support of fossil fuels, evisceration of pollution limits and throttling of clean energy projects has caused the US to become an outlier among wealthy countries, a recent UN report found. While all the other 20 major economies reduced or slowed their carbon pollution last year, the US was a “major exception” by emitting an extra 133m tons of planet-heating gases from the burning of coal, oil and gas, the report states.

Despite the world rapidly surging past “safe” temperature thresholds because of such pollution, and escalating heatwaves, floods, droughts and other calamities, Trump has remained defiant. “If you don’t get away from this green scam, your country is going to fail,” the US president told other world leaders at the UN last year, adding that the climate crisis was “the greatest con job ever perpetrated on the world”.

But the Democrats’ stunning success in the midterms last week, wresting control from Trump’s Republicans in both the House of Representatives and the Senate, has buoyed delegates gathering in Antalya. While this will be the last Cop with the US as an official party, after Trump exited the UN framework, the midterms have raised international confidence of a looming return and new, post-Trump chapter.

“This marks the beginning of the end of the Trump era,” said Mohamed Adow, director of Power Shift Africa. “His grip on Congress has been broken and hopefully paves the way for a Democratic president in two years. For everyone fighting for a livable planet, this is a moment of renewed hope.”

Trump has done “enormous damage” to the climate but the midterms results, along with Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s recent electoral victory in Brazil, provides a major tonic, Adow said. “It opens the door to America returning to the climate fight with the seriousness its responsibility demands,” he said, adding that Cop31 would be the “perfect time to accelerate climate action and turn the tide on the Trump dark ages”.

US lawmakers arriving at Cop, all of them Democrats, are aware the world has long been subjected to wildly erratic US commitment to climate action, Casten acknowledged. “We go in with a fair amount of humility – as important as we are, the US has been an extremely unreliable partner on climate,” he said. “But going to Cop on the heels of these results feels a lot better. It can be a much more positive process now.”

Spanning two weeks of negotiations among 197 countries with an accompanying trade show-like jamboree of pavilions and side events interspersed by protests, the sprawling Cop process requires a sense of momentum. The electoral revolt in the US, the world’s largest historical emitter of greenhouse gases, should provide such a fillip, according to Susan Biniaz, a former longtime climate negotiator for the US at Cop.

“Much of the world is looking to the midterms for some kind of signal from the US electorate that they are unhappy with this administration,” Biniaz said. “This could elevate the mood. I don’t think the midterm elections will directly affect federal climate policy but they will help the spirit of the Cop.”

“There’s been a big shift since the midterms. I’m certainly more optimistic,” said Catherine McKenna, former environment minister of Canada. “Negotiations at Cop are important but it’s more important what happens at home and Trump has been incredibly disruptive. We will now have more Democrats acting on climate and talking about the solutions that will actually save people money.”

But what will a thumping Democratic majority in Congress be able to do on climate? Sweeping climate legislation, similar in scale to the Inflation Reduction Act signed by Joe Biden that was subsequently gutted by Republicans, is not likely given Trump’s veto power. Still, Democrats are exploring other avenues.

Investigative and subpoena powers will be used to probe parts of the administration, such as the Environmental Protection Agency, over staff cuts and what Democrats call the “unlawful” withholding of climate and clean energy spending. Trump’s attempt to pressure Europe into taking US gas will be scrutinized, as will the vulnerability of the insurance industry to the climate crisis and concerns over the US ceding clean tech industries to China.

Democrats will dominate the budget process and will likely reverse funding cuts to environmental programs and rein in datacenters, which have become highly contentious with the US public.

Some legislation, such as the speeding up of the permitting process to allow new clean energy production and transmission, may be possible with Republican support too. The midterms also delivered striking Democratic wins at the state level, bringing new governors to states such as Texas and Georgia, meaning widespread state-based action to shift away from fossil fuels will be possible.

Much of this will likely be framed as helping tackle the rising cost of living or government corruption, rather than the climate crisis itself. Some activists have criticized Democrats for so-called “climate hushing” even as most people in the US favor the end of the fossil fuel era, but Casten said emissions reductions will matter more to the new Congress than rhetoric.

“We are going to do everything – oversight, legislation and action through the courts,” he said. “There are things around the cost of gas, or housing and insurance that are climate conversations even if we don’t mention climate. It’s our job to understand how all those things are connected but we have to talk about climate change to people in a way that is salient to them. It’s not that we don’t want to talk about climate change at all.”

Regardless of how Democrats talk about the climate crisis, its effects are mounting. Scientists have warned, repeatedly, that sluggish progress in cutting emissions has left little time to avoid disastrous impacts.

The world is already set to overshoot the internationally agreed target of limiting the global temperature rise to 1.5C, locking in turmoil for people, wildlife and ecosystems around the world, and any lingering embrace of fossil fuels by major emitters like the US will only worsen this pain. When Democrats take over Congress in January, advocates will clamor for them to rapidly make up for lost time.

“They have to do more than hold the line – this was a sweeping mandate for change,” said Rachel Cleetus, program director with the climate program at the Union of Concerned Scientists. “The science is sobering. It’s not going to wait for the next election cycle. This is a reality that people are dealing with right now and responsible lawmakers have to recognize that. The world is eager for the US to step up.”
