https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-0.title: COP31 kicks off as planet faces imminent overshoot of 1.5°C climate target
https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-0.author: James Dinneen
https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-0.text:
Search author on:
                                    PubMed
                                         Google Scholar

Delegates arriving at the UN COP31 climate conference in Antalya for 12 days of talks.Credit: Sandro Basili/Shutterstock

The United Nations annual climate meeting starting today is the first to take place after confirmation that global warming will overshoot the headline limit of 1.5 °C. The aim of keeping warming within 1.5 °C above pre-industrial temperatures was set out in the 2015 Paris agreement.

As tens of thousands of delegates and observers arrive in Antalya, Turkey, for the COP31 meeting, some scientists and climate advocates say the 12-day event must discuss how to deal with the overshoot. Along with cutting emissions, this includes practical ways of removing massive volumes of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere.

The UN Environment Programme last month acknowledged that, under all plausible emissions trajectories, the world will surpass the 1.5 °C target agreed at COP21 in Paris. Its Limiting Overshoot report is the first UN report to state explicitly that overshoot is now inevitable. It also laid out how to bring temperatures back below the 1.5 °C target this century.

In addition to slashing emissions to near-zero levels, the report confirmed the need to remove hundreds of billions of tonnes of CO2 from the atmosphere this century, either using CO2 removal technologies or nature-based approaches such as reforestation. “[K]eeping 1.5 °C within reach requires climate policy to evolve to include the removal of already emitted [greenhouse gases],” the report states.

This idea to limit the “magnitude and the duration” of overshooting 1.5 °C is expected to shape discussion among parties at the COP meeting, says Clea Schumer, a research associate at the World Resources Institute, an environmental research and advocacy organization in Washington DC. Some language on limiting overshoot was included in the final decision of the COP30 summit last year in Belém, Brazil, but CO2 removal has mostly gone unmentioned.

Most governments “are happy that they finally don’t have to pretend any more that we will make it” to 1.5 °C, says Oliver Geden, a researcher at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs in Berlin. They now want to limit overshoot, “but how we actually do that, nobody is talking about”, he adds.

Steve Smith, a climate researcher at the University of Oxford, UK, agrees. CO2 removal has sparked controversy in the past over concerns that it might distract from the need to cut emissions. But it is possible that CO2 removal could move up the agenda amid discussions about the necessary return from overshoot, he says.

Environmental advocacy groups, such as New York-based Natural Resources Defense Council (NRDC), that had been skeptical of CO2 removal, have now changed their position. A report from the organisation in September called on environmentalists to support CO2 removal in the same way they supported renewable energy and electrification.

"It is now time to set the stage for another—an industry that removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere—to contribute to the fight for climate stability," the report says

However, so far, no country has included clearly quantified CO2 removal targets in climate commitments submitted to the UN, says Smith. Such targets would be necessary to achieve the large scales of CO2 removal that could bring warming back below 1.5 °C. “We really want governments to cut emissions and set out clear plans for scaling up CO2 removal," says Smith

Some scientists say the failure to cut emissions fast enough to avoid overshoot is a sign that there need to be reforms to COP meetings.

“We need to first recognize that global policy has failed. This is a moment of self-critique,” says Johan Rockström, a climate scientist at the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research in Germany.

Rockström leads a group of scientists advising a coalition of around 60 countries working in parallel to the COP. The coalition wants the world to move faster to transition away from fossil fuels, and met for the first time in April in Santa Marta, Colombia.

Rockström, together with other prominent climate scientists and diplomats, has argued for some years that the COP process needs reform. Ahead of COP31, he told Nature that a top priority should be to allow for decisions to be made by majority votes among parties. Currently, agreements must involve all countries coming to a consensus. In the past, this has meant that a small number of states can block decisions backed by the majority. “Overshoot gives even more impetus for the need for reform. It shows that we’ve not been able to make the progress that we need,” says Rockström.

However, that doesn’t mean COP meetings don’t still have an important role, say climate advocates. “COP gatherings have had a massive impact,” says Yamide Dagnet, a senior vice-president in Washington DC at the NRDC. “But their success has increasingly been measured in degrees averted,” she adds.

When the Paris agreement was signed in 2015, the world looked likely to reach around 4 °C of warming this century. Under current policies, the UN Emissions Gap report found that has declined to between 2.6 and 2.8 °C of warming this century, with a small chance of reaching significantly hotter temperatures.

Climate researchers say it is unrealistic to expect the COP meetings to shift the trajectory of the world’s countries on their own. “Action, in the end, has to be national,” says Ed Carr, senior scientist at the Boston, Massachusetts, office of the Stockholm Environment Institute, a non-profit research organization.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/t.author: Jano Gibson
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/t.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
State and Territory Government

Jeremy Rockliff (right) and Eric Abetz have both accepted the pay rise in full. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

Last year, Tasmanian Premier Jeremy Rockliff fought against a 22 per cent pay rise for parliamentarians and capped his own increase at 3 per cent.

But he has now confirmed that he and all other parliamentarians are receiving the full amount the Industrial Commission said they were entitled to after a seven-year pay freeze.

A health union has described the government's latest pay offer for nurses as unfair when compared with the increases given to parliamentarians.

All Tasmanian parliamentarians are now receiving the full 22 per cent pay rise they are entitled to, including the premier, who previously said it was "out of step with community expectations".

In June last year, the Tasmanian Industrial Commission determined that parliamentarians should get a 22 per cent pay rise after a seven-year pay freeze.

At the time, Jeremy Rockliff said on social media: "This is not on, and we will not be accepting it."

The Liberals then moved a motion in parliament to disallow the increase, but Labor and eight independents rejected it in the upper house in September last year.

In response, Mr Rockliff said he would accept only a 3 per cent pay rise for himself.

"I will personally be knocking it back," he said on social media in September last year.

"Three per cent, the same as what is being offered to our public workers, is fair and reasonable."

Jeremy Rockliff's Facebook post about the pay rise, from September 25, 2025. (Facebook: Jeremy Rockliff)

Several other Liberals also declared they would only take a 3 per cent rise, while most other parliamentarians accepted the full amount.

But today, Mr Rockliff said he and all other parliamentarians were now on the rate recommended by the commission.

"Tasmanians rightly did not expect one of the first actions of the new parliament was to be voting on a pay rise for MPs," he said in a statement.

"It was certainly not my focus and not the community's expectation.

"We tried to stop the pay rise. However, Labor voted for it.

"I did accept much less than recommended by the Industrial Commission for over a year.

"Now, as I understand it, all parliamentarians have been brought into line with the Industrial Commission's determination."

It means Mr Rockliff is now receiving $369,000 a year, a rise of almost $68,000 compared to what he was being paid before the commission's determination last year.

Ministers currently receive $291,597, while MPs get a base rate of $171,527, which is still the lowest rate in the country.

But the decision by Mr Rockliff and others to accept the higher rate comes at a time when the government is planning to slash 1,700 state servant roles by 2030 to rein in spending.

Eric Abetz says that "most people acknowledge my commitment to state service is not based on the pay". (ABC News: Madeleine Rojahn)

A health union has also questioned the fairness of offering nurses pay rises of 3 per cent, 2.75 per cent and 2.5 per cent over the next three years.

"[Treasurer] Eric Abetz last year took a 22.36 per cent pay rise," HACSU secretary Robbie Moore told a rally outside parliament yesterday, triggering boos from the crowd.

"Now you compare that to the offer that we've got for nurses … and literally going as low as 2.5 per cent, that's a pay cut [compared with inflation]."

In a statement, Mr Abetz, a former federal minister, explained why he had decided to take the 22 per cent pay rise.

"After our effort to disallow the pay rise was rejected by Labor and certain crossbench members, I, along with others, accepted the will of the parliament," he said.

"To seek to personalise this matter conveniently ignores that by serving in state parliament I forego my Commonwealth entitlement, which I have done for the past two years.

Bridget Archer, pictured with Jeremy Rockliff, says she has also accepted the full pay rise. (ABC News: Jonny McNee)

Health Minister Bridget Archer also confirmed she was now on the higher rate.

"I did not initially accept a 22 per cent pay rise. I accepted a 3 per cent pay rise for a year," Ms Archer said.

Ms Archer said the government was continuing to negotiate in "good faith" with health unions about the wage offer.

"We continue to be at the table," she said.

"I think those discussions have been constructive.

"And we look forward to delivering a fair and affordable pay rise for our nurses as soon as we possibly can."

One of Toby Greene's former teammates says he abandoned the Giants by joining Geelong. (Mark Metcalfe/AFL Photos/via Getty Images)

GWS defender Joe Fonti says former captain Toby Greene abandoned them by joining Geelong as a free agent.

Greene is one of a number of veteran players to have departed the Giants this summer, with Lachie Whitfield, Jesse Hogan, Jake Stringer and Kieren Briggs also gone.

The Giants are yet to nominate their next club captain after Greene's departure, with Tom Green and Connor Idun considered contenders for the role.

One of former GWS captain Toby Greene's ex-teammates has likened his move to Geelong as an abandonment.

The Giants' greatest player in their 15-year history, Greene left for the Cats in search of more family support for his young clan in his home state Victoria.

It was a sucker punch for the Giants, who had already parted ways with veteran forwards Jesse Hogan (Collingwood) and Jake Stringer (St Kilda).

The Giants' list overhaul did not end there, with star defender Lachie Whitfield (Carlton) and Kieren Briggs (Richmond) also leaving.

Toby Greene wasn't the only Giant to depart this summer, with veteran duo Jesse Hogan (left) and Jake Stringer (right) also joining rival clubs. (Getty Images: Steve Bell)

Young GWS defender Joe Fonti didn't waste time sugarcoating when asked about Greene's trade to the Cats.

"It's obviously hard when your captain abandons your side," Fonti said on Monday.

"I know Toby's a great, great fella, and he would have had his reasons.

"I suppose that sort of justifies it for him, so I can respect that.

"But it's not easy when your captain abandons you.

"It does sting a little bit, but yeah, onto bigger and better things, I guess."

The Giants at least received a vote of confidence in their mission from midfielder Tom Green.

Due to come off contract at the end of next season, vice-captain Green knocked back big money from Tasmania and instead added two more years to his deal at GWS.

The 25-year-old, who missed all of last season with an ACL tear, has long been touted as Greene's replacement as captain.

Last year's vice-captain, Connor Idun, has been touted as a potential captain of the Giants. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Brendon Thorne)

Star defender Connor Idun is also a ready-made leader for the Giants after serving as a vice-captain last season with Green.

"It's definitely really special that that's something that he's done and committed to the club," Fonti said of Green.

"He's one of our best leaders, really well-spoken and a great role model.

"To have him potentially step into that captaincy role would be really special.

"We've got a bunch of good leaders, so it could be anyone, but he's definitely one of them."

Joe Fonti (left) says GWS's young brass of players are ready to step up in the absence of the departed veterans. (AAP/Darren England)

The Giants have lost 1,088 games of experience during the trade period, but Fonti says the young group is ready to rise to the challenge.

Fonti, who has played 44 games across three seasons, will be looking to take up Whitfield's spot in defence.

"That's really cool and exciting that we've sort of got a young core coming through," Fonti said.

"A lot of what's coming from the media at the moment is that we're young and we potentially might struggle this year.

"But I don't see it in that way whatsoever. We play our best when our backs are against the wall."

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Gyan-tsuma: How one woman discovered her husband’s gambling addiction
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
It was her second marriage. She could not afford to fail again.

Mei Nanaumi, a woman in her 30s from Iwaki, Fukushima Prefecture, believed she had finally found a partner to spend the rest of her life with. Divorced and raising a child on her own, she had been welcomed warmly by her new husband’s family.

“They accepted me and my child with open arms,” Nanaumi recalled. “I thought I could get along with them well.” What she didn’t know about before remarrying, however, was her soon-to-be husband’s addiction to gambling.

In her late 20s, Nanaumi had been a single mother raising one child when an acquaintance introduced her to the man who would become her second husband. He struck her as kind and fond of children. They were attracted to each other, and it didn’t take long for them to consider marriage.

His parents were enthusiastic about the match, too, and arrangements proceeded smoothly. At one point, his family even told her that he could take her surname.

Soon after the wedding, Nanaumi happily discovered she was pregnant with her second child.

At the same time, she started to see a different side of her husband after they began living together.

He often came home late, saying he had to work overtime. But she respected him for being a hard worker. He was smart and did well at work, although she felt his pride could be a flaw.

She had never seen his pay slips. Not a single yen of his overtime earnings went toward their household expenses. His monthly mobile phone bill came to nearly ¥100,000. She wondered what he was spending the money on but could not bring herself to ask. Instead, she told herself that she needed to understand her husband’s devotion to work.

Then, about six months into their marriage, he suddenly disappeared, taking the bankbook of the account containing their living expenses.

Nanaumi could not reach him. Overwhelmed with worries over whether he had been involved in an accident or had become the victim of a crime, she contacted his parents.

To her surprise, their response was calm. “Leave it to us. Just wait,” they told her.

Nanaumi found their reaction puzzling, but decided to take it as their concern for her health as she was pregnant.

A few days later, his parents brought the husband home. The bank account, which had held about ¥500,000, was empty. Even worse, he had accumulated roughly ¥300,000 in debt.

His parents finally revealed that their son was prone to gambling but were quick to defend him, insisting that he was not addicted.

The husband offered his own version of explanation in a subdued voice. “I was trying so hard to become a good father that it became too much for me.”

Nanaumi was stunned. She had never imagined that marrying a woman who already had a child could put so much pressure on him. She could not abandon someone who, she believed, wanted to make her children happy. She swallowed her doubts and took responsibility for his debts. “I have to support him,” she recalled thinking.

Then, one day, while casually scrolling through social media, Nanaumi came across with messages with such terms as gyan-tsuma and gyan-mama — wives and mothers struggling with a partner’s gambling addiction. Nanaumi felt as if she were reading about herself.

She began posting her anxieties online, asking whether her husband might have been gambling while claiming to be working overtime. Messages of sympathy and encouragement poured in, and she found countless women online suffering through circumstances much like her own. For the first time, she felt she had found a place where she belonged.

Eventually, her husband’s behavior grew increasingly violent, perhaps because he could no longer gamble as freely as before.

It began with a coffee mug. He hurled it to the floor where it shattered, scattering coffee across the room. “You made me angry. This is all your fault,” he spat.

He continued to make unreasonable accusations that would tear down Nanaumi’s self-esteem. At times, he forced her to kneel on the floor and apologize with her forehead pressed to the ground. On one occasion, she was beaten in the face so hard that she suffered cuts inside of her mouth.

The shouting and crashing sounds were likely heard by neighbors. One day, a staff member from Iwaki city’s child consultation center came to Nanaumi’s door. The thought of asking for a help came across her mind, but she could not say the words and ultimately let go of the hand that had been extended to her.

Looking back, Nanaumi thinks she was made to believe that her husband’s violence was her fault. She now realizes that she had fallen into a pattern of codependency: finding her sense of self-worth by sacrificing herself for her partner.

The day before her younger child’s first birthday, her husband disappeared again.

When he returned, the more than ¥200,000 she had painstakingly saved for their two children was gone. Once again, he was brought back by his parents, this time with a written pledge. He promised never to gamble again and said he would seek treatment for gambling addiction.

But even when he claimed to be going to a medical institution, he would return home with an empty wallet. There was no sign of improvement.

As the cycle of gambling and violence continued, Nanaumi learned through a friend on social media about the municipal government’s consultation services for women. Specialists at the consultation office would provide support to women experiencing domestic violence, sexual violence, financial hardships and other difficulties.

Taking advantage of a moment when her husband was not watching, Nanaumi went to see a counselor at the office in Iwaki. “That is domestic violence,” the counselor told her immediately, advising her to escape before the children became victims, too.

But Nanaumi couldn’t take action, fearing that if her husband discovered her plans, he might beat her again and even hurt the children.

It was around the start of the COVID-19 pandemic’s spread in Japan that her husband vanished for the third time.

At one point in the past, he had said he was “no good” and that he was going to kill himself. However, a few days before he disappeared, he had brandished a kitchen knife and threatened her, saying, “I could kill you anytime.”

Nanaumi could not take it anymore, both physically and mentally.

A social media friend urged her to seize the opportunity to flee while her husband was gone. “This is your chance. You can get away,” the friend told her. The women’s counselor in Iwaki gave her the same advice.

This time, Nanaumi was quick to move. She found an affordable apartment that was available for immediate occupancy. She contacted her children’s daycare center and made it clear that staff should not hand her children over to her husband if he came to pick them up.

She also went to the nearest police station to report the domestic violence and obtained documentation of what she had suffered. Subsequently, a court issued a protection order.

Around the same time, she joined a mutual-support group for family members of people with gambling problems. Encouraged by others who understood her situation, she hired a lawyer to represent her in divorce mediation.

It took about a year to reach a settlement, but when it was over, she felt she had been given a second chance at life. “Many people helped me. They saved my life.”

Her former husband, apparently concerned about how the situation might affect his standing at work, told her he did not want custody of the children and had no intention of seeing them again.

He stopped paying child support after the second month. When Nanaumi contacted him about the payments, he responded with another threat, “I can come and kill you anytime.”

Even now, she lives with the fear that she could unexpectedly run into him, not knowing when or where it might happen.

However, she has no regrets about leaving him. In her 30s, she has begun a new life as a single mother of two.

For women who call themselves gyan-tsuma or gyan-mama — some of whom have become trapped in codependent relationships — Nanaumi has a message of encouragement.

“Take a moment to look around you,” she says. “Don’t be afraid to reach out and connect with others.”
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.summary: Mei Nanaumi, a woman in her 30s from Iwaki, Fukushima Prefecture, was shocked when her husband disappeared from her bankbook of their living expenses. She had never seen his pay slips, but he had accumulated roughly ¥300,000 in debt.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: G7 allies to assess impact of Trump’s midterm setback at Paris talks
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: John Irish
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
PARIS – A G7 foreign ministers gathering in Paris on Monday will provide the first opportunity for Washington’s allies to gauge whether a U.S. midterm defeat for President Donald Trump alters the administration’s approach to Ukraine, the Middle East and ties with its closest partners, four G7 diplomats said.

The diplomats signaled the Democrats’ gains could narrow the White House’s room for maneuver but warned against expecting a return to traditional U.S. multilateralism while foreign policy remains very much under Trump’s control.

The meeting, moved at short notice from Marseille to Paris for security reasons after weeks of protests across France, will see U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, viewed as a potential 2028 presidential contender, make his first appearance before allies since the elections.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: New Zealand’s Luxon on course for second term, but weaker hand in coalition
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
WELLINGTON – New Zealand Prime Minister Christopher Luxon is on course to hang on to power as the head of a coalition government with a razor-thin majority following Saturday’s election, but his National Party could lose control of key government ministries to right-wing partners.

Center-right National and the main opposition Labour Party both polled below 30% for the first time ever, losing votes to minor parties on the left, right and center — a trend that analysts said mirrored a global shift away from the political establishment.

Preliminary New Zealand Electoral Commission data shows Luxon’s three-party coalition could govern with a majority of just two seats. But that margin may disappear once overseas and other special votes — which make up a seventh of the total and typically skew left — are included during the final count on Nov. 27.

https://www.scmp.com/week-asia/health-en.title: A doctor was murdered in South Korea. 8 years on, ‘nothing has changed’
https://www.scmp.com/week-asia/health-en.author: SCMP’s Asia desk
https://www.scmp.com/week-asia/health-en.text:
With assaults hitting 1,200 a year, doctors want metal detectors and an end to rules requiring victims to press charges

The attack at Severance Hospital in Seoul last Wednesday left the victim, a psychiatry professor surnamed Kang, with a severe hand injury that required surgery and cuts to his face and head.

South Korea’s leading medical bodies have called for urgent new security measures inside hospitals in the wake of the incident, arguing that the current legal regime has failed to prevent violence against staff.

“The public can fully exercise its right to receive treatment only when the safety of medical staff is protected,” a representative from the Korean Medical Association (KMA) told a briefing on Thursday, according to sources cited by the Seoul Economic Daily.

“The government and the National Assembly must move beyond stopgap responses centred on after-the-fact punishment.”

The Korean Interns and Residents Association, the Korean Hospital Association and the Seoul Medical Association also issued statements calling for safer medical settings, according to the same newspaper.

The woman arrested in connection with last week’s attack, identified only as A, allegedly brought the kitchen knife she used into the hospital in a shopping bag.

A warrant to formally arrest her on suspicion of attempted murder was issued by the Seoul Western District Court on Saturday, Yonhap news agency reported.

Police had initially arrested her at the scene of the crime on charges of aggravated injury, the Seoul Economic Daily reported.

Sources told Yonhap that the woman, who is in her fifties, was not a patient waiting for psychiatric treatment. The agency reported that she “rambled” to journalists outside the court, accusing the hospital of failing to provide treatment in 2018 and causing her diabetes.

The KMA told local media that the woman’s specific condition had not been confirmed.

Police statistics cited by the Maeil Business newspaper show there were 9,061 violent crimes in South Korean medical institutions over the past five years, of which 5,897 were assaults.

The number of annual assaults rose last year, to around 1,200, after holding steady at around 1,100 a year since 2021.

One day after the Severance Hospital attack, Maeil Business reported that a man in his sixties wielded a weapon and threatened doctors and nurses at a clinic in Gapyeong county, Gyeonggi province.

The Lim Se-won Act, which introduced stiffer penalties for assaults on medical staff, followed the 2018 killing of Lim, a professor at Gangbuk Samsung Hospital, by a patient during a consultation.

“Years have passed since the Lim Se-won Act was implemented, but nothing has changed in essence,” Choi Joon-ho, chairman of the Korea Neuropsychiatric Association, told Maeil Business. “Recent events prove that the Lim Se-won Act is ineffective.”

Rules in force since 2020 require psychiatric institutions and hospitals with 100 or more beds to employ at least one dedicated security staff member and install emergency alarms that notify the police when triggered.

But KMA spokesman Kim Sung-keun told Seoul Economic Daily this was not enough, calling for the designation of high-risk zones and the use of metal detectors to keep out items such as knives.

He warned that repeated attacks would widen “the physical and psychological distance” between doctors and patients.

Maeil Business reported that doctors also want to scrap the rule that prevents assault charges from being brought without the victim’s consent. Medical staff, who must continue treating patients and run the risk of encountering their assailant again, often decline to press charges for fear of retaliation.

Alongside alarms, more guards and the provision of evacuation facilities, Choi told the newspaper that South Korea must consider scrapping this consent rule “to ensure the safety of medical staff”.

Of last year’s cases, 11 reportedly involved bodily harm to staff and another 11 involved property damage. In two of them, rescue operations were hampered by abusive language.

Another 15 cases were reported in the first five months of this year, the newspaper reported in July.

In one incident this May, a paramedic treating a collapsed man was punched and kicked more than 10 times and threatened with stabbing. A second paramedic who intervened was also attacked. The ambulance crew was out of action for about five hours, with four other teams sent to the site, the newspaper reported.

https://www.dw.com/en/us-president-donal.title: US President Donald Trump says deportation policy was 'too tough' for voters
https://www.dw.com/en/us-president-donal.text:
Trump said his deportation policy may be one of the reasons the Republicans lost so much ground in the midterm elections.

US President Donald Trump on Sunday said that his deportation policy for undocumented immigrants was "too tough" for voters and he can work with the Democrats in the new Congress to craft an immigration deal.

Speaking during his first major interview since his party lost control of the House and Senate in the midterm election, Trump said his deportation policy may have been part of the reason Republicans lost.

"I think it was too tough," Trump said. "I think it might be too tough, yeah. And a lot of people would say that it’s great. But a lot of people think it’s too tough."

In his interview to CBS that aired on Sunday, Trump said that he can find a way to work with the Democrats.

"The deal would be we would work something out. And I think it's something — I think that's something that's actually doable," he said in the interview.

Trump did not share the details of what the immigration deal would look like but shortly after the interview he appointed Stephen Miller, who designed the Trump administration's hardline deportation policy, as his chief of staff.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In his tenure, Trump's administration has aggressively pushed to deport millions of undocumented migrants which drew widespread criticism.

Trump said he was just joking about making Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC) boss Dana White his next White House press secretary.

"I was only kidding, but Dana loves the idea," Trump told reporters.

In a social media post Saturday, Trump implored White to accept his offer, writing, "Dana, please take the job!" and calling him a "violent fighter and warrior."

White is a long-time friend of Trump. He has maintained silence on Trump's remarks, saying that he would "have more to talk about" after meeting with Trump on Monday.

The position of the press secretary has been vacant since Katie Zacharia left on October 16 after less than a week on the job.

Trump on Sunday said that he will be meeting Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin ‌at an ⁠APEC ⁠leaders' summit in China next week to discuss ending the Iran war.

Before flying back to Washington from Florida, Trump while speaking to the media said: "One of the meetings, I think, will be with ‌President Putin and President Xi, and that'll be ‌interesting. ​We're talking a lot of things, including denuclearization, but we'll be talking a lot of things. We're trying to end the ​war in Iran."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Russia in October has said that this first of its kind trilateral meeting is "being prepared."

While Trump has mentioned denuclearization as the focus of the meeting, a Wall Street Journal report said that Putin wanted the three-way talks to broker a peace deal to end Russia's war in Ukraine.

In his interview with CBS Trump said that "I believe we're very close to ⁠making a ​deal" to end the Russia-Ukraine war that would result in a "little bit different shape Ukraine," without sharing any further details.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6y4.title: Krakow shooting suspect has died in hospital, police say
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6y4.text:
A gunman suspected of killing six people in Krakow has died in hospital, Polish police say.

The 24-year-old, who ministers said was apparently inspired by "far-right ideologies", was injured after opening fire in central Krakow, the second largest city in Poland, on Saturday.

Armed officers raced to the scene and engaged in a gunfight with the suspect, who was shot within three minutes of the attack beginning, preventing a further massacre, officials said.

Krakow police said the suspected gunman died early on Monday morning.

After the shooting, which began shortly before 15:00 local time (14:00 GMT) in Krakow's busy Main Market Square, police identified the attacker as a 24-year-old Polish man but did not confirm his name.

In the hours after the shooting, a minister has said early investigations indicate he was inspired by "far-right ideologies". The minister also described him as an "ultra-nationalist" without giving further details.

Six people - four women and two men - are confirmed to have been killed in the attack.

Contains disturbing scenes.

Four victims are Polish, while a British national and an Austrian woman were also killed.

Poland's Prime Minister Donald Tusk said three bodies - two women and one man - were found at the gunman's house when it was searched after the attack.

On Sunday, Polish police confirmed those three victims had been identified as the alleged gunman's 53-year-old father, 52-year-old mother and his sister, who was 21 years old.

Polish media has reported the suspect had a firearms permit and may have obtained the weapons from his family home.

Sixteen people, including five foreigners, two police officers and the attacker, were taken to hospital. The interior ministry later said they were from Austria, Britain, Germany, Portugal and Russia.

In the wake of the shooting, Poland declared the country would enter two days of national mourning.

After travelling to Krakow, Tusk said: "Until now in Poland we haven't had such drastic cases of terrorism...that's what we have to call this cruel attack on people's lives here in Krakow."

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he was "shocked and saddened by the appalling shooting in Kraków".

"My thoughts are with the families of those who have lost their lives, everyone injured and all those affected by this senseless violence. The United Kingdom stands in solidarity with the people of Poland," he added.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cj5y.title: 'My brother died, so I smashed up his TV'
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cj5y.text:
When Ellie Goudie's brother Ryan died aged 23, she could not bear the thought of anyone else having his belongings.

Instead, she paid to smash them to pieces.

Armed with a baseball bat in a Swindon rage room, Ellie destroyed some of the possessions Ryan had left behind, including his beloved television, saying it helped her cope with the pain of losing him.

"That was his. He can't have it any more, so no one should," she said.

For Ellie, the experience was about far more than breaking objects.

"I felt Ryan in here. He probably was doing it with me," she said. "I'm glad I've done it for him."

Ellie is one of a growing number of women turning to rage rooms, where customers pay to destroy household items with baseball bats and crowbars in a controlled environment.

Operators say many visitors are seeking an emotional release during some of the most difficult periods of their lives, including bereavement, trauma, relationship breakdowns and stress.

At The Rabbit Hole Rage Room in Swindon, owner Paul Bunney said about 70% of customers are women.

He said he sees a visible change in people after they come out of a session.

"Some people are quite reserved when they come in, and then when I go and speak to them after they have a big smile on their face." he said.

"They're hot, they're sweaty, and they've got rid of a lot of emotion."

Visitors travel from across the region to take out their rage on objects that were destined for landfill, like printers, crockery, hifi systems, kettles and old wine bottles.

Paul said materials are often separated and recycled afterwards.

For Ellie, the attraction was the sense of release she felt after months of grief.

"You're taking out your anger and you don't have to talk," she said.

"It takes away the emotion for the good hour or so you've got in here. And then you feel a relief when you come out

A similar story has emerged at another rage room in Bath.

Charlotte Bagnall, who runs Raging Bath, said what began as a fun attraction had developed into something much more meaningful.

"I think everyone at the moment needs release," she said.

"When you're here, you can just let go."

She said many customers arrive carrying emotional burdens they have struggled to process elsewhere.

"The people I've got to meet and the things they go through is fascinating, but also quite sad at times.

"To lighten that load they're carrying is huge."

Among them is Ceri Crannis, who booked sessions for her family after her daughter was stillborn.

She said the experience provided something she had struggled to find elsewhere.

"You don't get that release in therapy when you're talking," she said.

"There are some things that are just so deeply hidden that it comes out here, where loud music, smashing, breaking really does just hit the spot where nothing else has managed to do that before."

Ceri believes rage rooms can offer women a rare opportunity to express emotions that are often suppressed.

"Social norms are geared up that women are well behaved, they don't swear, you don't break anything."

Another rage room visitor, Sarah Bear, agreed.

"You can't shout and scream at the people in the world because actually those people have done nothing wrong, but you can take it out on stuff here that isn't going to hurt anyone," she said.

"So it's a really safe, controlled way to do it. And yeah, there might be some tears at the end of it, as, like, the relief washes over us, but it's worth it."

It's no surprise that rage rooms can offer an immediate feeling of relief, according to associate professor of psychology and inclusion at the University of Bristol, Dr Nilu Ahmed.

"It's hugely helpful in that moment.

"You've got a set amount of time so you know what you can do. You know that it's going to come to an end. So you're not going to go on a rampage and riot out in the streets. You know that it's going to be contained."

But Ahmed said it can't replace long term therapy.

"For deep rooted issues, it's going to come up again and again. And the question that I always talk about is where are those feelings being discussed?

"And if they are being taken into a rage room, what that is telling the individual or telling me as a professional, is that individual hasn't got a safe space to go and talk about that."

For Ellie, smashing Ryan's possessions did not take away the loss.

But she says it gave her an hour to channel her grief, remember her brother and leave feeling lighter than when she arrived.

Follow BBC Wiltshire on Facebook, X and Instagram. Send your story ideas to us on email or via WhatsApp on 0800 313 4630.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cj5y.summary: Raging rooms offer women a rare opportunity to express their emotions that are often suppressed. Many visitors are seeking an emotional release during some of the most difficult periods of their lives. The Rabbit Hole Rage Room in Swindon, Swindons, says 70% of customers are women.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck79.title: James Bond: What we know so far about the next 007 film
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck79.text:
When a bartender asked James Bond in 2006's Casino Royale whether he'd like his vodka martini shaken or stirred, the irritated spy replied: "Do I look like I give a damn?"

Such throwaway lines were a clever way of signalling to the audience that this was a new era for 007 - and that the film series launched in 1962 was being overhauled with the arrival of Daniel Craig.

Over the next few films, producers struck a balance between nodding to the past while also moving away from some of the cheesier elements of the series, no longer sticking rigidly to all of the tradition and tropes of Bond.

"Were you expecting an exploding pen?" Ben Whishaw's Q later asked the secret service agent in Skyfall. "We don't really go in for that anymore."

Two decades on from Craig's debut, the series is about to be rebooted once again, with a new actor and new creative team. It's an exciting time for Bond fans as they wait to see what shape the next era will take. Here's what we know so far.

After years of speculation, the wheels are firmly in motion and we expect to hear who the new James Bond actor is in November or December.

Speaking in August, producer Amy Pascal told Deadline: "I would say the end of the year is a good bet. We are being really, really methodical."

The final screen tests reportedly took place in late October, so, unless something unexpected happens, it should not take much longer for producers to make their decision and the actor to sign the contract.

After that, it's just a matter of how the announcement will be made. In an earlier era, Bond actors were revealed with a traditional photo call or press conference.

But now that the franchise is owned by Amazon MGM, some expect the company to make the announcement via its own Prime Video streaming service.

A handful of actors are thought to have made it to the final screen tests to take on Britain's biggest film role. The three frontrunners are thought to be:

Other actors in the frame include:

But remember, Craig was a surprise choice in 2005, so don't bet against a wildcard candidate whose name has not yet been widely reported.

The film is expected to go into production in 2027, before its release in 2028. No exact dates have been announced.

Film schedules can be notoriously fluid, but it's clear that development is well under way, with the director and writer already in place.

It will be the 26th film in the official film series, but the title has not yet been confirmed.

The movie will be directed by Denis Villeneuve, known for Prisoners, Sicario, Arrival, Blade Runner 2049 and the recent Dune trilogy starring Timothée Chalamet.

"Some of my earliest movie-going memories are connected to 007," the French-Canadian director said last year. "I grew up watching James Bond films with my father, ever since Dr. No with Sean Connery. I'm a die-hard Bond fan. To me, he's sacred territory."

He added: "I intend to honour the tradition and open the path for many new missions to come. This is a massive responsibility, but also, incredibly exciting for me and a huge honour."

Bond 26 will be written by Steven Knight, known for TV series such as Peaky Blinders and House of Guinness, and films including Burnt, Spencer, Locke and The Girl in the Spider's Web.

Knight has said it had always been on his "bucket list" to write a Bond film, adding that he felt he was "doing my duty for King and country" by joining the franchise.

He told the BBC he planned to "write the character, not the actor", adding: "The thing with Bond is it's its own universe and franchise. So there are certain rules.

"Obviously you have to move it along, but I love where it sits. I love that it's British. I love that it's not DC or Marvel... So I feel a responsibility to the text."

Only six actors have played James Bond. They are:

You might have noticed some overlap in the above dates.

That's because Connery returned to the lead role for 1971's Diamonds Are Forever, after Lazenby took his place for 1969's On Her Majesty's Secret Service.

Connery also later appeared in 1983's Never Say Never Again, a Bond film produced by a different studio and not part of the official film series.

If you discount the films not in the official series, there have been 25 Bond films in total. In order, they are:

With the change in ownership and a new creative team now in place, the new Bond film is likely to make a fresh start.

It would be difficult to continue the story chronologically given the ending of 2021's No Time To Die, but that still leaves producers with plenty of options.

A different version of James Bond, who exists in a different universe, would be easily pulled off in an era where audiences are used to major film franchises restarting in a different world or timeline.

Bond 26 could even be set in a significantly earlier era - an idea that gained more popularity after Tony Gilroy revealed he and fellow director Steven Soderbergh previously pitched a 1960s version of Bond.

Separately, actor Ralph Fiennes recently said he had once been in talks to play Bond, and had suggested producers make a "black and white and very sort of film noir-y" version set in the 1950s.

Neither idea materialised, but the suggestion went down well with some Bond fans, who noted a period piece would help make the film truer to Fleming's original character and books.

Exactly what shape the next film takes will become clear at a later stage. For now, fans are hoping that Christmas could be about to come early this year, as the world awaits the imminent announcement of the next actor to play 007.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck79.summary: The film is expected to go into production in 2027, before its release in 2028. The movie will be directed by Denis Villeneuve, known for Prisoners, Sicario, Arrival, Blade Runner 2049.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwzr.title: Maya Jama steps down as host of reality TV show Love Island
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwzr.text:
Presenter Maya Jama has announced she is stepping down as the host of reality TV show Love Island after three years.

The 32-year-old wrote on Instagram alongside a highlights reel of her on the programme that it was "time to throw myself into something new".

"While my own Love Island journey has come to an end, I wish the show and the team all the success in the world, I'll be cheering you lot on from the sidelines forever," the TV and radio presenter said.

Jama's announcement comes hot on the heels of an appearance as a contestant on Celebrity Traitors that won her praise and speculation in the Times that she could "get £1m per deal" thanks to her success.

Thanking fans and the production team on Love Island, she said she had an "unforgettable time" on the programme.

"I started hosting the show aged 28 and during the nine incredible series met the most wonderful humans along the way. I've loved every slow-mo walk, fire pit and live show.

But she added: "I've always believed that to truly grow, you have to take a leap every now and then."

Jama landed her biggest presenting role to date as the host of the reality TV show in 2023, taking over from Laura Whitmore.

The programme couples contestants together who then complete a range of tasks and keep swapping in the hope of meeting the love of their life.

An ITV spokesperson said: "Maya has been a fantastic and much loved host on Love Island - we thank her for everything she has brought to the show over the last three years and wish her every continued success."

Love Island is one of the most popular reality TV shows in the UK but the series has polarised viewers, with some arguing the show is misogynistic and raising concerns about the welfare of contestants.

Ofcom has previously received tens of thousands of complaints about Love Island including about alleged misogynistic and bullying behaviour by some contestants.

The watchdog has previously described the show as "emotionally charged" with "confrontational scenes" that can upset some viewers.

Jama first built her profile through radio including a role on Rinse FM, before landing a presenting role on BBC Radio 1 in 2018.

She went on to present a string of television programmes, including Channel 4's Stand Up To Cancer and ITV2's Don't Hate the Playaz, before taking over as host of BBC Three's Glow Up: Britain's Next Make-Up Star in 2021.

The presenter was recently watched by millions in the Celebrity Traitors final, and competed as a traitor alongside actor Richard E Grant, Youtuber King Kenny and comedian James Acaster during the series.

One commentator at the time said that, despite not winning the show, she had emerged as a winner of sorts as she was able to portray herself as "less like the presenter of Love Island and more like a genuinely versatile television star".

Her Celebrity Traitors appearance came after she made her acting debut in the second series of Guy Ritchie's Netflix drama The Gentlemen alongside Theo James and Kaya Scodelario.

Jama had auditioned for the cult Channel 4 series Skins, set in her hometown of Bristol, when she was 15, reaching the final stage for a role in the show that launched the careers of actors Daniel Kaluuya and Dev Patel.

She moved to London when she was 16 to pursue a career in the entertainment industry.

She began presenting a weekly music video countdown for production company JumpOff TV before joining MTV in 2014 as a presenter on The Wrap Up.

Jama became the youngest person to host the MOBO Awards, alongside Marvin Humes, in 2017.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwzr.summary: Maya Jama has announced she is stepping down as the host of Love Island. The 32-year-old said it was "time to throw myself into something new" She said she had an "unforgettable time" on the show. The TV and radio presenter said she would be cheering on from the sidelines forever.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckn9.title: 'Time is up': Minister warns media industry to take abuse seriously in wake of Brand case
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckn9.text:
Abuse in the media industry is probably still happening as organisations are not doing enough to protect women, the culture secretary has warned in the wake of Russell Brand's conviction.

Lisa Nandy told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme: "Time is up, it really is time for the media industry to take this seriously."

She added that since entering government, "many people" from within the industry had reached out to her "to allege that things have happened to them".

Brand is due to be sentenced on Monday after being convicted last week of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault, following allegations from multiple women spanning the decade between 1999 and 2009.

Nandy was asked whether she believed there was still exploitation and abuse within the media industry, following the Brand trial and cancellation of Channel 4 reality show Married at First Sight after the BBC revealed rape allegations.

She said: "I do not see that much has changed in terms of the way that institutions in the media industry and across public life, including politics, deal with women who very bravely come forward to allege abuse."

Nandy added that there was often no protection and a "very heavy cost" for women who speak up in industries such as media and politics, pointing to power imbalances and short-term contracts some staff members are given.

"Hand on heart, I can't say to you as the culture secretary that this is not happening today. In fact, if I had to wager, I would say it is," she said.

Nandy said many had come forward from within the industry, including from the BBC.

But she added that the BBC had been an "exemplar" in signing up to the industry body to protect whistleblowers - the Creative Industries Independent Standards Authority - and urged other organisations to follow suit.

A BBC spokesperson said the broadcaster "has made a significant commitment to improve its culture, processes and standards".

"Last year, following an independent culture review, we set out the behavioural expectations for everyone who works with or for the BBC and we were clear action would be taken if these were not met," the spokesperson added.

Starting his career as a stand-up comedian, Brand became a household name as a host of TV shows such as Big Brother's Big Mouth. He also had his own radio programmes on BBC Radio 2 and 6 Music.

During Brand's trial, he faced allegations from six women and was found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault. The women revealed how Brand used his fame to force them into sexual activity.

Following his conviction, a BBC spokesperson said there could be "no place for the abuse of power", adding: "Across the industry we must work together to ensure that anyone who suffers at someone else's hand feels able to report it, that their concerns are taken seriously and that they are listened to."

The corporation restated its apology to staff who felt they could not speak up with concerns about Brand's behaviour when he worked at the BBC between 2006 and 2008, because he was seen as "too influential".

Channel 4, which aired Big Brother and its spin-off programmes at the time Brand was a presenter, said it recognised the "profound impact of these crimes".
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckn9.summary: Lisa Nandy says it is time for the media industry to take abuse seriously. She says many people have reached out to her to allege things have happened to them. Nandy said there was often no protection and a "very heavy cost" for women who speak up in industries such as media and politics.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: Kraków shooting suspect who killed six has died, say police in Poland
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Staff and agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
Terrorism investigation was opened after a 24-year-old opened fire in a market square on the weekend

A gunman suspected of killing six people in a popular market square in Kraków has died in hospital, Polish police said early on Monday.

The suspect, a 24-year-old named in local media as Michal O who authorities say was probably inspired by far-right ideologies, had been wounded in a shootout with police and had been in critical condition in hospital.

“We would like to inform you that the perpetrator of the tragic events died in hospital early this morning,” Malopolska Policja wrote on X.

Polish prosecutors had opened a terrorism investigation after the man opened fire on Saturday afternoon, killing six including a Briton and injuring 17, in an attack that shocked a country that was considered safer than many of its European neighbours.

Karolina Galecka, an ⁠interior ministry spokeswoman, told radio TOK FM ​on ​Monday: “There ​were many different emblems on the perpetrator’s clothing that have been partially examined and interpreted.

“These patches were ​associated with various motifs that ​are currently ‌being analysed ​by ​specialists,” she added, declining to comment further as the investigation was ongoing.

Police confirmed on Sunday that three people found dead at the gunman’s home after the attack were his father, 53, mother, 52, and sister, 21.

Five of the wounded are foreign nationals from Britain, Austria, Germany, Portugal and Russia. Two police ⁠officers were also among the injured, one of whom was in a serious condition.

As two days of national mourning began, the national prosecutor’s office said on social media it had launched an investigation into “the killing of six people … using a firearm, and the attempted murder of many others, including police officers, this act constituting a terrorist offence”.

The rare mass shooting has deepened concern about extremism in Poland after several school stabbings in October that left one woman dead and which officials said were linked to extremist content online.

The interior minister, Marcin Kierwiński, said the suspect was fascinated with far-right ideologies and held “very radical” and “ultra-nationalistic” views.

The Kraków suspect drove into the city’s main square in the heart of the old town, which is usually packed with tourists, at top speed at about 3pm on Saturday. Wearing military-style fatigues and a bulletproof vest, he started shooting at random as he took what the Kraków police spokesperson Katarzyna Cisło described as a “wild ride” around the square.
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.summary: Suspect, 24, named in local media as Michal O, had been wounded in a shootout with police. He had been in critical condition in hospital after the attack on Saturday. Polish prosecutors had opened a terrorism investigation after the man opened fire on Saturday afternoon.

https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.title: Why we disrupted Annalena Baerbock’s award speech
https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.author: Ninian McGowan,Mohammad Haydar
https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.text:
When, in late August, the Dag Hammarskjold Foundation announced that former German Foreign Minister Annalena Baerbock was its 2026 medallist, we were stunned. The cognitive dissonance was striking, even if we had become used to this after years of unabashed hypocrisy within the world’s most powerful institutions.

According to the foundation’s homepage, the medal is given to a person who “contributes to a more just, peaceful and environmentally sustainable world through valuable achievements in politics or research”.

As this year’s medallist, Baerbock was invited to visit Uppsala University and deliver a lecture. Here was an event claiming to celebrate “compassion, humanism and commitment to international solidarity” while honouring the foreign minister of a government that approved 94 million euros ($102m) in arms exports to Israel in the span of three months in 2024.

The motivation provided for Baerbock’s selection as the 2026 Dag Hammarskjold medallist sounded like satire to us. She is described as a “strong proponent of a rules-based international order” even though her actions illustrate perfectly how she is the opposite of that.

As soon as Uppsala University started promoting the ceremony on campus, we decided to plan a protest. Baerbock needed to know that she was not welcome, that the university’s stance did not reflect the position of its students.

We entered the event split into groups and interrupted Baerbock’s seminar four times. She was increasingly frustrated with each interruption. She tried to respond to the argument of the first group with an incoherent ramble about an alleged misfired Palestinian rocket. But we were not arguing over a single rocket; we were criticising her unapologetic support for horrific violations of international law.

As foreign minister, Baerbock repeatedly expressed her strong support for the state of Israel as an occupying power, declaring that Israel’s security also is “in the interest of the German state”. As Germany’s foreign minister, she called it her responsibility to always defend Israel’s “security” – something she deemed “non-negotiable for Germany”.

She had no reservations about upholding Israeli claims that it had the right to target schools, hospitals and other civilian establishments because the alleged presence of resistance forces removed their protected status.

Baerbock has held these positions despite the International Court of Justice indicating provisional measures against Israel with the intention to encourage the international community to take action against the genocide in Gaza and despite the International Criminal Court issuing an arrest warrant for Israeli leaders on charges of war crimes and crimes against humanity. Instead, Baerbock chose to fuel the fire.

For all of these efforts, she was “rewarded” with the position of president of the United Nations General Assembly. Even in that role – in the heart of the institution that is supposed to uphold international law – she refused to call what is happening in Gaza a genocide. This is despite multiple reports, including by UN experts, that this is exactly what the mass killing is.

That Uppsala University co-organised Baerbock’s lecture is not surprising. The university continues to refuse to implement even the most modest of measures against an occupying power that openly commits genocide.

In 2022, the university administration showed no hesitation in ending collaboration with Russian institutions after the Russian invasion of Ukraine. Three years into the genocide in Gaza and the intensified ethnic cleansing of the occupied West Bank, it has taken no such action against Israeli institutions, despite repeated demands from students and faculty.

Yet we are grateful for this perfect opportunity to demonstrate why radical resistance is necessary. For many years, protests against the genocide in Palestine have obeyed the rules defined by those in power, without any effect. Palestinians have been killed while places of higher education refuse to take responsibility and diplomats utter nothing but hollow words.

If they will not listen to voices within their regulated framework, we see no choice but to disrupt their everyday efforts to hide their complicity.

We are criticised for our methods because they are “too much”. But for us, genocide is too much. Disagreeing politely and hearing out those who sell bombs to genocidal armies is what has brought us to this point of deadly inaction.

The views expressed in this article are the authors’ own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.
https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.summary: Annalena Baerbock was invited to visit Uppsala University to deliver a lecture. The university co-organised the lecture and was not welcome, says Al Jazeera. Baerbocks has held these positions despite the International Court of Justice indicating provisional measures against Israel

https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.title: What is next for Israel?
https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.author: Ilan Pappe
https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.text:
There are two ways to read the results of the Israeli elections. One way would be to see them as a defeat for the government of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. From holding a solid majority in the 120-member Knesset, the Netanyahu bloc has been reduced to a minority of 53 members. Anti-Netanyahu lawmakers, by contrast, hold 67 seats.

Had Israel been a democracy, we would have seen scenes of celebration similar to the ones we saw this year in Hungary, Brazil and Serbia, where political forces with undemocratic tendencies were defeated. But Israel is not a democracy, and Netanyahu was not necessarily defeated.

The second, more relevant way of reading the results of the Israeli election would necessitate accepting the apartheid nature of Israel and seeing the electoral arithmetic through that prism. In this case, Netanyahu won because he secured 53 seats in the Knesset – five more than the anti-Netanyahu Jewish bloc.

To form a government, a bloc needs to have the support of at least 61 members of the Knesset. The only way Netanyahu can do it is by enticing parties or lawmakers from the anti-Netanyahu bloc to join his bloc, as he has succeeded in doing many times in the past. Working with Palestinian parties, which secured 19 seats, is out of the question for him.

The obvious path for government formation for the anti-Netanyahu bloc would be to form a coalition – one that would include the two Palestinian parties. But to do so would mean to challenge Israeli apartheid. The main leaders of the Jewish anti-Netanyahu bloc, including Gadi Eisenkot, have promised not to do so under any circumstances.

There is another option: seeking the support of the religious Orthodox parties, which have so far been part of the Netanyahu bloc. To secure their backing, the anti-Netanyahu bloc would have to promise to exempt religious Orthodox youth from military service and guarantee funding for their learning centres.

However, Eisenkot’s main election promise was forcing young Haredi Jews into the army. So this is not a very likely scenario, but in politics, never say never.

There is also the option of a “unity government” led by some sort of rotation between the leading figures of the anti-Netanyahu bloc and Netanyahu. The problem here is that, according to a law passed a few years ago, as long as Netanyahu is still a defendant in an ongoing trial, he cannot serve as a minister; his coalition made sure that the legislation ridiculously would not apply to a prime minister.

Given that Netanyahu’s corruption trial is destined to go on for a very long time, the rotation would make it impossible for Netanyahu to be part of a government under Eisenkot as prime minister. That means he would demand to hold the rotating premiership first and leave open the option to collapse the government once his rotation is over.

Netanyahu has already done that before. In 2020, without any hesitation, he broke a rotation agreement with Benny Gantz, who had naively believed that after two years he would be the prime minister. This resulted in new elections, which Netanyahu won.

Finally, a very possible scenario is that neither of the two blocs would be able to form a government, which would mean new elections in six months. Netanyahu and his government would remain in office until the new polls, albeit with more limited authority.

This would give them the opportunity to reignite a war with Iran and Hezbollah and continue with their violent policies in the Gaza Strip and the West Bank in an attempt to attract more public support and win the elections.

This is the preferred option for Netanyahu because his relative defeat in the October 27 elections had a lot to do with the unprecedented galvanisation among the Palestinian voters in Israel and the more liberal Jewish Israelis living abroad who came back home in huge numbers to vote.

These possible scenarios tell only part of the story and are not enough to fully understand what the election results mean for Israel, the Palestinians and the region. Here are the more important conclusions one should draw from the results:

The first pertains to the future of the Palestinian citizens of Israel. They still could turn out to vote in large numbers if new elections are held soon. But if they are once more ignored and sidelined by the other political parties, they will never try it again.

In this case, it would be difficult for the leadership of this community to continue to delay a strategic decision: choosing which political space Palestinian citizens of Israel belong to – the Israeli or the Palestinian one?

Until today, they have given a chance to the Israeli political system despite its racism, apartheid tendencies and criminal policies towards Palestinians. Palestinian parties recommended Eisenkot for the premiership to President Isaac Herzog, who has now tasked him with forming a government.

If I can venture a prediction – and it is only a prediction – the anti-Netanyahu bloc would not engage meaningfully with the Palestinian parties. Its message, therefore, will be that the Palestinians of Israel are not legitimate players in the Israeli political field.

If I am wrong, this would be an incredible and transformative moment in the history of both Israel and Palestine, but there seems to be very little hope for such a development.

There are other lessons we can learn from where we are now with the knowledge that this is a very volatile moment in the history of Israel.

The first and most important one is that whoever forms the next government of Israel will continue the incremental genocide in Gaza, the intensified ethnic cleansing in the West Bank and the aggressive policies towards the region. These policies as before can only be stopped or tamed by the region and the international community sending a clear message to Israel that there will be a price tag attached to such policies.

The second lesson is that the Israeli Jewish society is as deeply divided as ever, to the point that it is impossible for it to maintain a stable political system, a thriving economy and a positive strategy towards the region and the world.

The third lesson is that Israel’s international isolation will increase as a result of this trajectory, including the continued dissociation from Zionism among young Jews around the world, including in the United States.

Finally and most importantly, this can have an impact on the global discussion about Zionism. The move by the Green Party in Britain to define Zionism as racism – despite being currently an exception and widely condemned – will gain validity with time.

These elections and future developments are making clear that Zionism in the current Israeli politics means the exclusion of Palestinian citizens of Israel from politics – first by ignoring them and quite possibly in the future by denying them the right to vote

Moreover, many in the international community will associate the term Zionism with a consensual Israeli policy of genocide, ethnic cleansing and apartheid.

The outlook in the short term is worrying. The overall message from the Israeli elections is that the future policies of the state will continue to threaten the lives of the Palestinians in occupied territory, Palestinian citizens of Israel, and the people of southern Lebanon and Syria. There will be more instability in the region.

In the long run, however, as bad as it is, the fundamental cracks in the Zionist project will widen, which might lead to its demise. One can only hope this will also lead to the beginning of a political reality that would benefit everyone who lives in historical Palestine and the region.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.title: How Israel’s separation wall compares with the Berlin Wall
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.author: Mohamed Hussein
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.text:
In the occupied West Bank, a barrier of concrete and fencing cuts Palestinians off from their land, their families and nearby towns.

Israel began building its separation wall in 2002. Planned to stretch 712km (442 miles), it runs deep inside Palestinian territory rather than along the boundary with Israel. In 2004, the International Court of Justice ruled it illegal.

Today’s date carries extra weight. Thirty-seven years ago on November 9, 1989, the Berlin Wall fell.

Built by East Germany in 1961 to stop its citizens fleeing to the West, it encircled West Berlin for 155km (96 miles), dividing the city and its people for 28 years.

Since 2003, Palestinians have marked the same date as an international day of action against Israel’s wall, which is more than four times as long and still being built. In urban areas, its concrete rises to about 9 metres (30ft), more than twice the height of Berlin’s.

But the wall is more than a physical structure. It operates alongside a wider network of checkpoints, roadblocks, gates and permits that restricts Palestinian movement across the occupied territory.

According to the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), about 456km (283 miles), or 64 percent, of the planned route had been built by April.

About 85 percent of it runs inside the West Bank rather than along the Green Line, the 1949 armistice line separating Israel from the West Bank. That route determines which communities, roads and farmland are cut off from their surroundings.

In some urban areas, the barrier is a concrete wall. Elsewhere, it is made up of fences, patrol roads, ditches and other security infrastructure.

For Palestinians, the comparison with Berlin carries a message. “It doesn’t matter how high the barriers will be, they will fall,” a Palestinian activist in Bir Nabala told Al Jazeera. “Like the Berlin Wall fell, the Palestinian wall will fall.”

The wall’s impact reaches far beyond the structure itself. Its route cuts Palestinian communities off from neighbouring towns, workplaces and farmland, disrupting livelihoods and everyday life.

More than 14,000 Palestinians live between the wall and the Green Line in an area known as the Seam Zone. To reach basic services, markets and relatives on the other side, they must pass through checkpoints.

Farmers are among the hardest hit. According to OCHA, about 150 Palestinian communities have land in this area. Reaching it depends on permits, prior coordination with Israeli authorities and access through designated agricultural gates.

There are about 62 such gates along the wall, and most stay closed for much of the year. During the 2025 olive harvest, 74 percent opened only on a limited number of days.

In Qalqiliya, the wall wraps around much of the city, cutting it off from nearby Palestinian communities and the land around it. Journeys to neighbouring towns that were once short can now mean passing through checkpoints or taking long detours.

The wall restricts more than movement. It reshapes how communities relate to their land and places that are part of their everyday lives.

The wall is only one part of a much wider network restricting Palestinian movement across the West Bank.

As of December, OCHA documented 925 checkpoints, road gates, earth mounds and other obstacles across the West Bank and occupied East Jerusalem. They restrict the movement of about 3.4 million Palestinians, often forcing long detours to reach work, school, hospitals and other services.

The network includes 89 permanently staffed checkpoints, 218 partial checkpoints, 232 road gates, 167 earth mounds, 114 linear closures and 105 roadblocks.

Checkpoints and road gates now make up nearly 60 percent of these obstacles, up from 15 percent two decades ago when temporary blockages, such as earth mounds and roadblocks, were far more common.

Crossing the wall itself requires permits. Of its 13 checkpoints, only three can be used by Palestinians with West Bank IDs and Israeli-issued permits to enter East Jerusalem and Israel. OCHA said these permits are hard to get and many have been revoked or suspended since the Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel and the start of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023.

The wall stretches for hundreds of kilometres, but its impact cannot be measured by distance alone. It is measured in the farmland farmers struggle to reach, the communities cut off from nearby towns and the checkpoints between people and the places they need to go.

In 2004, the International Court of Justice ruled it illegal. Since 2003, Palestinians have marked the same date as an international day of action against Israel’s wall.

https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.title: Lando Norris wins Sao Palo Grand Prix, but Mercedes seal constructors title
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.text:
Mercedes have secured ⁠⁠their ninth Formula One constructors world championship ⁠⁠and completed a title double in a wet Sao Paulo Grand Prix won by McLaren’s Lando Norris from pole position for the second year in a row.

The title, secured on Sunday, was the first team crown for Mercedes since 2021 and came a week after 20-year-old Italian Kimi Antonelli made headlines ⁠⁠as the youngest drivers champion with four races to spare.

Red Bull’s Max Verstappen finished second, putting on a masterclass from 21st on the grid due to engine penalties in a race that started and ended in the rain.

Teammate Isack Hadjar was third with George Russell fourth for Mercedes and Antonelli fifth with the fastest lap. After leading at the start, both made costly errors on an eventful afternoon.

Mercedes had needed to score only three points more than Ferrari to clinch the title, and the Italian team never threatened to prolong the fight on a treacherous track with Charles Leclerc eighth after a post-race penalty demoted him one place and Lewis Hamilton ninth in his 400th race.

“It was a very tough race, very, very tough,” Norris, the 2025 world champion, said of his 14th career win and 50th podium as well as his team’s first victory since August when ‌‌he won the Dutch Grand Prix.

“A lot of challenges today with the conditions and going onto slicks in the wet is always tough, especially when you are pushing for the lead and trying to catch up a little bit,” added the Briton, who lost out to Antonelli when the start lights went out.

“The main thing today was I kept it cool and didn’t make any mistakes and had the pace when I needed to. Nice to be back on the top step and what a place to do it as well.”

Norris took the chequered flag, waved by Brazilian football forward Neymar, 14.602 seconds clear of Driver of the Day Verstappen.

Mercedes, whose engines also power McLaren, have now equalled Williams’ nine constructors championships.

“It was a very strong beginning of the season, and that kind of got us ⁠⁠over the line,” team boss Toto Wolff said. “These last few races have been challenging at times. Today it was difficult, but overall, ⁠⁠I’m so proud of the organisation.”

McLaren’s Oscar Piastri was sixth with Racing Bulls’ Liam Lawson seventh after a fine race that saw the New Zealander start third and run in second place for the first five laps.

Nico Hulkenberg took the final point for Audi in a race of spins, slippery moments and changeable conditions.

Verstappen moved further ahead in the driver standings in the race for second place overall, now 17 points clear of Russell, who ⁠⁠moved up to third.
