Lando Norris won the Sao Paulo Grand Prix from pole position for the second year in a row. Red Bull’s Max Verstappen finished second, putting on a masterclass from 21st on the grid.

https://www.wired.com/story/welcome-to-w.title: Welcome to Weed Island
https://www.wired.com/story/welcome-to-w.author: Orlando Crowcroft
https://www.wired.com/story/welcome-to-w.text:
STEVEN TAN WALKS along a narrow concourse in the Northern Leaf greenhouse in St Lawrence, Jersey, reading aloud the strains of his cannabis plants: Pink Gasoline, Moon Beam Gelato, Carbon Fibre, Gorilla Kush. Rows of plants stretch off into the distance. To the untrained eye, they look largely the same, with their distinctive jagged-edged, multi-fingered leaf shape and sticky buds like tiny pinecones.

But Tan, the CEO and director of medical cannabis manufacturer Northern Leaf, knows them intimately. “These plants are all different,” he says, stopping next to a mature Carbon Fibre specimen. “Just like humans.”

Northern Leaf is one of the largest licensed medical marijuana producers in Europe. Its 100,000-square-foot growing facility is based in Jersey, the largest of the Channel Islands, located between England and France. Previously, this greenhouse was home to Jersey tomatoes, once a famed crop on the island that came close to extinction, thanks to growing fuel costs and cheaper competition from overseas. Now, it is fitted out with all of the technology required for cultivating cannabis that meets strict regulations for medical use, which include: automated irrigation, environmental monitoring, and air purification.

Despite being just 45 square miles in size, with a population of 100,000, Jersey—which lies 14 miles off the coast of the French mainland but is a British Crown Dependency—has emerged as an unlikely player in the medical cannabis industry. Although its total exports (over 9,200 kilograms in 2025) are small compared to UK growers, this represents an enormous amount per capita, and cannabis is fast becoming one of the island’s important new industries. Jersey’s chief minister, Lyndon Farnham, has previously said that he wants Jersey to be a “centre of excellence” for medical cannabis, and for cannabis production to become a mainstay of the island’s economy.

Jersey, a British Crown Dependency that sits between the UK and France, that has become an integral hub for the medical cannabis industry.

Currently, 90 percent of Jersey’s cannabis production comes from Northern Leaf. In 2025, the company exported £8.4 million ($11.3 million) worth of medical marijuana to markets including the UK and Germany (regulations mean it is only permitted to grow for export and cannot sell to customers in Jersey). Tan has much greater ambitions. He points to another famous Jersey export, Jersey Royal potatoes. “Jersey’s potato industry did £40 million in 2025,” he said. “I am already doing a quarter of the potato industry on 5 percent of the land. On 20 percent of the land, I could create an industry worth more than the potato industry. That is where it will get interesting.”

Born in Malaysia to a Chinese dad and Irish mother, Tan, 50, wanted to become a vet, but after graduating from university in 1998, ended up developing software for Citibank. He was making good money, but his heart wasn’t in finance. What really interested him was growing weed. “I loved the science of it, the genetics, the seeds, the smells,” Tan says.

The early 2000s were the perfect time for an inquisitive young business grad to get into the cannabis business. Across the world, governments were legalizing medical marijuana and moving towards decriminalization over draconian sentencing.

Tan began bouncing around jurisdictions that were relaxing laws on cannabis, working as a consultant in California, the Netherlands, and Canada. “I started to see these legal frameworks opening up. The minute they existed, I went there,” he says.

Jersey has a somewhat unique regulatory environment. As a Crown Dependency, it has close ties to Britain, but is not a part of the UK. Crucially, it is self-governing: It can make its own laws. Jersey’s main reputation today is as a tax haven, attracting some of the world’s wealthiest individuals and companies, thanks to its lack of capital gains tax and 0 percent corporation tax for most companies. Along its coastline, next to twee beachside cafes and Nazi bunkers (the Channel Islands were the only part of the British Isles to be occupied by Hitler’s forces in World War II), you can find offices of international banks and wealth management firms catering to the super rich.

Although traditionally culturally conservative, Jersey has become something of a trailblazer on cannabis. The island legalized medical cannabis in 2019. Today, five private clinics operate on the island. The latest figures suggest that 6 percent of the population is prescribed cannabis, compared to an estimated 0.4 percent in Germany and 0.1 percent in the UK. Upon legalization, the island’s chief minister, Lyndon Farnham, laid out ambitious plans for the island to become a hub of the medical cannabis trade, repurposing the horticultural facilities and know-how from its tomato-growing glory days for this new endeavor.

Tan joined Northern Leaf as CEO in 2024, when the company was in dire straits after a failed IPO. That year, it was valued at just £3.7 million, despite having spent as much as £30 million on its weed-growing facility.

Tan nevertheless saw a lot of potential, and over the last two years has seen capacity at the site increase from 25 percent to 75 percent. He believes the £8.4 million of product the company exported last year is just the beginning.

Northern Leaf's 100,000-square-foot growing facility. “On 20 percent of the land,” says CEO Steven Tan, “I could create an industry worth more than the potato industry. That is where it will get interesting.”

Sarah Clover, a barrister at Kings Chambers who works on cannabis licensing in Jersey, told WIRED the island’s advantage is hard to replicate. Growers are inspected by the UK Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA), which is known for enforcing rigorous standards on quality. “Anybody buying from Jersey knows that the stuff coming out of it is absolutely gold standard, because the MHRA says it is,” she says. Permits, however, are handled by a small team on the island: “You can make an application for a permit on a Monday and get it on a Tuesday.”

Many within the Jersey medicinal cannabis industry now want to go beyond growing the raw ingredient and package it for export as a final product on the island. Northern Leaf already has the facilities to do so, but Jersey law dictates it can only export bulk amounts of raw cannabis for other companies to process and pack for distribution and sale. The company is waiting to see if Jersey will change its law. “At the minute we’re kind of on this seesaw—which way will the island go?” Clover says. “It could really take off here. Jersey could be a life sciences hub, not just for cannabis but for all sorts of pharmaceuticals.”

But running a cannabis business on a small island poses challenges, and not everyone is enthused about the idea of expansion. Tan has faced off against residents every time that the facility has expanded production. Some locals have complained that they can smell cannabis from their balconies. Others have linked the growing industry to concerns over misuse of cannabis on the island, despite the fact that all of its product is exported. Cannabis is a “contributory factor” in 22 percent of admissions to the island’s acute mental health ward, according to Jersey’s health minister.

One patient, Michael, told WIRED that he was prescribed medical cannabis for 18 months after having tried two other prescribed medications for insomnia and anxiety. “The initial assessment was simple. I had a meeting with the cannabis doctor who was pretty evangelical about its medicinal properties. They check your medical history with your GP, and within 10 days you’re good to go,” he says.

Michael was prescribed 30 grams a month of “unbelievably good” cannabis and told that if he ran out he could back and ask for more. “I stopped because it was seriously affecting my mental health [and] I have since seen a psychiatric professional who said I should never have been prescribed it given my documented mental health history,” he says.

Illegal resale of medical cannabis is also an issue, with a rise in so-called “user-dealers,” who sell their excess medical marijuana to others. Jersey Police told WIRED this “undermines the legal framework and creates opportunities for criminal supply.”

Overall, however, cannabis-related offenses have dropped since Jersey legalized medical cannabis in 2019—from 216 in 2016 to just 12, as of July 2026.

Tan is circumspect about the challenges of operating on Jersey. “Culturally, the people here are harder to convince about cannabis,” he says. “It’s an older society.” But after 25 years working in the industry, he’s used to the pushback.

“It’s a normal challenge,” he says. “And I think when anyone sits down and meets me, they understand. This isn’t a bunch of stoners growing a bit of weed in a plastic greenhouse.”

Tan surveying Northern Leaf's crops.

While Jersey’s medical cannabis industry grows, some people on the island want to go further. In 2024, a vote to decriminalize recreational cannabis was defeated by a single vote in the island’s parliament. When it was brought back for another vote by the island’s then health minister, it was withdrawn before it could be debated. It is expected to be brought back before the parliament in the coming months.

Some individuals on the island have decided not to wait. By exploiting a loophole in current laws, they have made Jersey one of the only places in Europe outside of Amsterdam where THC products can be purchased and consumed legally.

One morning in February 2024, Gary Tucker arrived at work, his weed shop in St Helier, Jersey, to find a dozen customs officers and the local media waiting outside. It was a raid—and not his first. The officers emptied shelves and boxes into bin bags. “They were literally running their arms down the shelves and putting everything into bags. They took everything,” Tucker, a California native and former analyst in the US Army, told WIRED.

Tucker operates outside of Jersey’s medical cannabis industry. His shop, Bailiwick Botanicals, sells products that are clearly recreational: hash cakes, gummies, and other snacks, all infused with tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), the psychoactive ingredient in cannabis that gets you high and is heavily controlled.

He’s able to do this owing to a loophole in Jersey law which allows the sale of products containing CBD—another critical ingredient in cannabis, but one that doesn’t get you high. Jersey’s law says that the amount of THC in CBD products cannot exceed 3 percent of the weight of the CBD. So, if you want to sell products with high levels of THC, you just have to boost the CBD. “It’s just a math equation,” Tucker says.

Tucker admits it isn’t an ideal situation: studies suggest that ingesting high levels of CBD can cause liver damage. But he sees that as an issue with the regulation, not his solution. “I’m just following consumer demand,” he says.

Tucker is somewhat evangelical about the properties of cannabis. In his time as a weapons trainer for the military, he struggled with the mental health impacts of hearing that recruits he had trained had been killed in action. “I needed to step back from it. It started to really affect my mind,” Tucker says.

Veterans he knew were turning to cannabis, and Tucker began buying it on the black market. “It was the only thing that helped me,” he says. ”Cannabis gave me my life back.”

Tucker currently manufactures most of his products in the US before shipping them to Sark—a smaller Channel Island best known for having no cars and also its own government—and then to Jersey. New regulations in the US, however, mean Tucker may need to change his approach.

Tucker sees Jersey as a potential export hub for THC products to Europe. He believes Jersey’s budding weed industry should push beyond medical cannabis and into the recreational market. “This isn’t just a bunch of guys in a cellar somewhere. Not only does cannabis help people, but getting it to the shelf creates jobs. From the grower to the retailer. It permeates across all industries. We’re making cosmetics. We’re making gummies. We’re making drinks,” he says.

After the 2024 raid, Bailiwick Botanicals shut its doors for two weeks, and its full stock wasn’t returned until six months later. As of June 2026, Tucker and his team are selling THC-infused fudge, chocolate, and other sweets. His newest product, THC-infused coffee beans, is selling well. The police have stayed away.

In a written statement to WIRED, Jersey’s government said that the “possibility of abuse of our limits to get round the law in other jurisdictions is a matter of concern to the Government of Jersey and we are looking at ways to address it. Work is underway to consider whether Jersey’s existing legal exemptions for CBD products require amendment.”

“These plants are all different. Just like humans," says Tan.

For his part, Tan is reluctant to be drawn on his views on the so-called “rec” (recreational) market. For now, Jersey still has harsh sentencing rules on recreational cannabis use, with the penalties for possession and possession with intent to supply remaining up to five years and 14 years in jail, respectively. The proposed (and withdrawn) law to decriminalize cannabis notes that, the way the law is currently written, someone who rolled three joints and gave one to a friend would be guilty of supply and receive a criminal record. “Without change, people will continue receiving serious criminal records for small amounts … punishments [that] can result in additional harms greater than the drug itself,” it said.

While Jersey makes its own laws, however, it may not be able to completely legalize cannabis. Jersey is a signatory to the UN Convention on drugs control via the UK, and the UK Home Office would undoubtedly have a view if the island were to set itself up as an “Amsterdam on the Sea.” In 2022, an effort by the government of Bermuda (a British Overseas Territory) to legalize recreational cannabis was blocked after the UK withheld Royal Assent from the bill.

Back at the Northern Leaf warehouse in the Jersey parish of St Lawrence, Tan is flipping the lids off large boxes and rifling through clear plastic bags packed full of cannabis.

This is all weed that will not be sold, either because there were issues with production or the THC levels were too low. Instead, it is taken to a secure area of the facility where it is locked away in a reinforced armored vault. Specialist staff with bodycams take the bags to the island’s incinerator, where it is unceremoniously burned, as required by law.

Tan regularly makes a case to the government for changes to the law and support for the cannabis industry, such as an industrial energy tariff to help with spiraling energy costs.

He has claimed that Jersey could be home to “the Monsanto of cannabis,” alluding to the agricultural giant that was acquired by pharmaceutical company Bayer in 2018 for $66 billion. He’d like to get deeper into the genetics of cannabis, form a tissue-culture lab, and “bring out strains that nobody has ever seen.”

But speaking of himself, he references a different genre of business: He’s Willy Wonka, but for weed. Thirty years ago, when Tan quit corporate finance, his father warned him that he could make a lot more money if he stayed in banking. “And you know what, he was right,” he says. “But I would not have had nearly as much fun.”

The island's medical cannabis industry is one of the world's biggest growing industries. The government is considering whether its existing legal exemptions for CBD products require amendment.

https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/us-age.title: U.S. Agencies Warn Refrigeration Controller Attacks Could Cause Fires and Inventory Losses
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/us-age.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/us-age.text:
U.S. government agencies have warned that threat actors are actively targeting industrial refrigeration and cold-chain monitoring systems globally with an aim to cause service disruptions, fire hazards, and loss of inventory.

"The actors may exploit vulnerabilities or weaknesses in unpatched or internet-accessible controllers to remotely alter settings and force units into continuous heating and defrost cycles, which can cause widespread inventory loss and equipment hazards," according to a joint advisory.

According to the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), Health and Human Services (HHS), Department of Agriculture (USDA), and Department of Transportation (DOT), threat actors are likely to exploit authentication bypasses, arbitrary code injection, and weak configurations to gain access to these systems and cause the following effects -

In response to the threat, owners and operators are being urged to use strong authentication, keep systems updated, identify any systems that are accessible from the internet, isolate operational technology (OT) devices, change default passwords, retire and replace legacy devices, remove unnecessary remote access, and secure necessary remote access.

"Industrial refrigeration and cold-chain monitoring systems protect food, medicine, and other temperature-sensitive products, making them attractive targets for malicious cyber actors," said FBI Cyber Branch Operations Director Brett Leatherman.

"We are seeing these systems targeted across critical infrastructure sectors globally, putting inventory and equipment at risk."

In recent weeks, threat actors have targeted hundreds of supermarkets across Europe by exploiting weaknesses in internet-accessible refrigeration controllers to raise temperatures, in some cases to as high as 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit), or force cooling units into defrost mode, spoiling food and resulting in financial losses.

Targets of these attacks ranged from major supermarket chains to small grocers and butchers in Belgium, Estonia, Finland, France, Germany, Ireland, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal, Sweden, and the U.K.

Among those targeted was the French Blood Establishment, which confirmed that a cybersecurity incident affecting a refrigeration equipment provider had raised temperature and defrost settings to "extremely high levels" at three facilities used to store blood plasma. It's unclear who is behind the hacking spree.

Data from Censys shows that there are still hundreds of Danfoss StoreView instances exposed globally, with most of them located in France, although the number has dropped significantly from 3,004 to 708 between October 9 and November 5, 2026. The Copeland/Dixell XWEB exposure, likewise, has declined from 3,708 to 2,420.

The attack surface management platform described the refrigeration attacks across Europe as the latest addition to a list of other recent incidents targeting critical infrastructure, including gas station tank gauges, air raid systems, and water towers.

"North America accounts for roughly 38% of global ICS [industrial control systems] exposure," Censys said. "Asia's share grew from 22% in 2024 to 25% in 2026, while Europe's fell from 36.5% to 32%. However, these shifts have not produced an overall decline."

"While exposure numbers are high, they're hardly surprising: ICS exposure is a problem that's been reported on and warned about for years. It poses a critical risk to the public as gatekeepers to the world's critical infrastructure."

https://fortune.com/2026/11/09/ai-reboun.title: ‘AI rebounding’: Nearly 20% of U.S. workers replaced by AI are being asked back—now they’re demanding higher pay, job security and AI transparency
https://fortune.com/2026/11/09/ai-reboun.author: Joshua Hong
https://fortune.com/2026/11/09/ai-reboun.text:
Nearly one in five U.S. workers say they have experienced a workplace reversal that could signal a new trend in the labor force: their employer replaced them with AI, only to ask them to return later, according to new research from talent assessment firm SHL.

The phenomenon, which SHL calls “AI rebounding,” shows an early indication that some companies may be discovering the limitations of replacing human employees with AI.

“Organizations are making fast, sometimes myopic, decisions about their people based on an incomplete picture of what their employees can do with or without AI,” Lucy Beaumont, global senior vice president of product and design at SHL, said in a press release. “AI rebounding is what happens when a company automates a role before it has genuinely assessed the human capability inside it. The AI doesn’t deliver, the gap becomes obvious, and the business ends up rehiring the same experts they just let go of, at a far greater cost.”

The survey, conducted in June and July, found that 19.1% of American respondents said they had personally been replaced by AI and were subsequently asked to return to their jobs. Across both the U.S. and the U.K., the figure was 16%.

And among the returnees, 51% wanted a substantial pay increase before agreeing to return, SHL found. Additionally, 42% said they would require written guarantees about future job security, and 40% wanted transparency about how AI would be used in their positions.

Similarly, a Robert Half survey from July found that 32% of U.S. hiring managers whose organizations eliminated positions because of AI later had to reinstate the same or similar roles. Among that group, 40% said the positions required institutional knowledge or context that AI couldn’t replace. Another 39% cited relationship management, 39% pointed to increased business demand, and 38% said the positions required more human oversight and quality control than expected.

And some prominent companies have already encountered those limitations. Swedish buy-now, pay-later company Klarna began recruiting human customer service representatives after relying heavily on AI chatbots. CEO Sebastian Siemiatkowski acknowledged the company had gone too far in its reliance on automation, according to Bloomberg.

A Klarna spokesperson told Fortune human agents were needed “for complex, sensitive cases.” The company began directly hiring a “small number” of high-skilled humans into the customer service process to identify where the “human touch” can bring most value to customers.

Ford also hired and promoted 350 experienced engineers in June after AI-powered quality control tools failed to perform as expected. The automaker said AI had contributed to quality improvements but emphasized the importance of combining the tech with experienced engineering teams.

“These engineers carry the hard-earned wisdom of decades of design,” a Ford representative previously told Fortune. The company said AI is very important to quality gains, “and that, in tandem with deep technical expertise, is what’s needed.”

Despite the rise of AI rebounding, the number of companies that cited AI as a reason for workforce reductions has grown substantially.

According to outplacement firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas, employers cited AI in 121,401 announced job cuts through October, more than double the 54,836 announced layoff plans for all of 2025.

And younger workers are especially vulnerable to AI-led job displacement. A Stanford Digital Economy Lab study found that employment among workers aged 22 to 25 in occupations highly exposed to AI was 19% below where it would have been if it had grown at the same pace as employment among their less-exposed peers.

SHL’s research shows some promise for the younger workers, however. The firm found that younger workers were more likely to report experiencing the “AI rebounding.” Among respondents aged 18 to 24, 24% said they had personally been replaced by AI and later asked to return, compared to 19.1% of U.S. respondents overall.
https://fortune.com/2026/11/09/ai-reboun.summary: Nearly one in five U.S. workers say they have experienced a workplace reversal that could signal a new trend in the labor force. The phenomenon, which SHL calls “AI rebounding,’ shows an early indication that some companies may be discovering the limitations of replacing human employees with AI.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/c.title: Calls for data centre moratorium 'until we get the rules right'
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/c.author: Penny Travers and Annabel Whitehouse
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/c.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

By Annabel Whitehouse

The NEXTDC data centre in Bruce is one of more than a dozen facilities in the ACT.  (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

The Conservation Council is calling for a moratorium on any new data centres in the ACT, until industry-specific requirements are introduced.

The council says it is concerned about the impact new data centres are having on Canberra's water supply and electricity grid.

Both the federal and ACT governments are working on new rules and standards to govern the development of large-scale data centres.

The Conservation Council is calling for a moratorium on new and expanded data centre developments in the ACT, amid "increasing concerns" for the city's energy grid and water supplies.

There are currently fifteen data centres across the ACT, the first of which was built in 2007.

But Conservation Council ACT director Simon Copland is concerned about the "potential massive expansion" of data centres before proper checks and balances are put in place.

"This is a point of time, given the growth of AI, that we need to stop and have a conversation about this rather than rushing to approve everything," Conservation Council ACT director Simon Copland said.

Front of mind is a second CDC Data Centre in Beard, a suburb near Canberra Airport, which was conditionally approved in September.

The proposed $200 million centre is a three-storey building comprising of 12 data halls, and would be located next to another CDC data centre in the suburb.

CDC's first centre in Beard is expected to have a total capacity of 40 megawatts (MW). (ABC News: Harry Frost)

The application for the project was submitted a week before the ACT government promised to develop a data centre framework to "provide clear rules about where data centres can be located, the standards they must meet, and how proposals will be assessed".

But Mr Copland said there needed to be a halt on the development of data centres in Canberra until tougher regulations were in place, both locally and federally.

"We're seeing a potential massive expansion of this infrastructure and we're worried about the impact this is going to have on our energy system, on our water, on our biodiversity and on our community more broadly," he said.

Mr Copland said the first stage of the Beard development was expected to use 5 per cent of the ACT's peak energy, with the proposed second centre using "double that".

Canberra is proving an attractive location to build data centres.  (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Mr Copland said there was also community-wide concern about the impact data centres were having on Canberra's water supply.

"We know that climate forecasts suggest that the ACT is going to see reduced water flows through our major rivers," he said.

"And so we want to ensure that we actually have the water to be able to maintain these data centres into the future and it doesn't risk the health of our river system or the ability for Canberra to use water for other very important things.

"We're suggesting that [data centres] must operate in areas where there is a secure water supply, and we'd like to see the investment in technology such as closed-loop cooling, which uses less water, to ensure that we're not pulling off the water system consistently."

The Conservation Council is not alone in these concerns; the ACT Greens and other community groups have also called for a moratorium.

And Independent Senator for the ACT David Pocock called on the federal government to introduce a tax on data centres operators, along with stronger environmental protections, in June.

But Chief Minister Andrew Barr dismissed the idea in August, saying "the ACT already has rigorous planning, environmental, utility and regulatory requirements".

Federally, the government is also working on a new set of national standards and oversight for artificial intelligence, including forcing large-scale AI data centres to minimise water use and fund their own power supply.

Simon Copland says he wants a moratorium on additional data centres in the ACT until the government legislates standards for the industry.   (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Beyond the ACT, concerns around data centre locations and their demand on resources have led to protests in Australia and around the world.

Just this past weekend, community backlash saw plans for an AI data centre in Sydney's Cooks River scrapped; one planned for Lane Cove and another for Guildford were dropped in September.

But CDC chief executive Greg Boorer said over the past 20 years of operating in Canberra "nobody's ever complained about our facilities", adding that the company already uses closed-loop cooling.

He said Australia's planning rules had already helped the sector avoid becoming like the United States.

"I think it was always going to happen in the United States because they really prioritised speed and in some ways greed over doing the right thing, choosing the right locations, being a good community participant with regards to adding energy to the actual grid," he said.

Greg Boorer says data centres are not "horrible pieces of infrastructure" if built in the correct location.  (Harry Frost: ABC News)

"In Texas, for example, just a free for all, every man for themselves, dropping in literally gas jet engines next to residential locations."

However, Mr Boorer said it was time for the sector to be more proactive in its engagement with local communities.

Until recently, security concerns had led to a secretive approach to planning developments, but Mr Boorer said a lot had changed since they built their first centre in 2007.

"We actually have to do a better job," he said.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/q.author: Tom Hartley
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/q.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Traffic Offences

Demerit points being traded for cash appears to be a wider issue in Queensland. (AAP: Darren England)

The man who oversaw the rollout of Queensland's licensing and registration system in the 1990s says the government is staring at a "cybersecurity flaw" in the wake of revelations about demerit points being traded for cash.

The 7.30 investigation revealed widespread trading on black markets after a 27-year-old woman was charged with fraud. It's alleged she had accumulated 1,150 demerit points and more than $600,000 in fines.

Peter Grant is a veteran of the state's public service and oversaw its most complex IT systems as chief information officer; he says risks have changed dramatically since then.

"During the 90s, there was no social media. They didn't have to defend against this," Mr Grant told 7.30.

"[But] if you've got people who are manipulating your business processes to actually do fraudulent behaviour, you have a cybersecurity breach."

Mr Grant characterises the manipulation as a "cybersecurity breach" because, he says, it compromises the integrity of a government business process.

Peter Grant is Queensland's former chief information officer. (ABC News: Chris Gillette)

"These people are visible in the system over a long period of time — what we have here are people who are gaming the system, and they've created a cyber breach," Mr Grant said.

"The Queensland government has got to demonstrate that people can't get away with fraud and I would have thought that would have been a high-priority initiative.

"For the integrity of the system, this would start to get to the top of the list for me."

Dr Katie Williams, a former KPMG partner and senior lecturer in business information systems at the University of Queensland's Business School, says she would expect to see the government review its systems around control gaps and pain points.

Dr Katie Williams says the system needs to be strengthened. (ABC News: Chris Gillette)

"A system that is set up correctly in the first place and regularly monitored and capable of tweaking makes it harder for fraud to remain undetected," Dr Williams said.

"Based on what we're seeing in other parts of Australia, there's an opportunity to perhaps consider, at a really detailed level, the enabling legislation."

7.30 was told police have raised the detection issue with the agencies responsible for administering the system — Queensland's Revenue Office and Department of Transport and Main Roads — and remain frustrated by inaction.

When asked by 7.30 government agencies described their processes for detecting fraud as robust.

On Monday afternoon the Queensland Treasurer's Office told 7.30 in a statement:  "New measures have already been implemented and ...  we will continue to strengthen the system we inherited from the former government, if needed, to stamp out fraud."

The statement said those measures were implemented in late 2025 as part of a new fines and integrity framework.

Queensland Premier David Crisafulli told 7.30: "I think [the] loophole has been closed" but said if there are other loopholes "then of course we will look at it".

Queensland Premier David Crisafulli says no one can make a system "bulletproof". (AAP: Darren England)

A consequence of the 'cash for demerit points' schemes is that authorities have not been able to confirm how many drivers may have escaped licence suspensions through fraudulent demerit point transfers.

Revelations from the investigation have caused concerns for police, road safety and motorist advocacy groups, including RACQ.

"We don't know the size of the problem, but we should know the size of the problem in Queensland, and that is the key thing here," said Michael Kane, RACQ's executive manager of public policy.

"There's no point having stronger laws to make our roads safer if people simply can find a way around the consequences.

In New South Wales, similar abuses prompted a dedicated taskforce and proposed legislative changes supported by both major parties.

Camera-detected offences include mobile phone use, seatbelt offences, red light violations and speeding. (ABC News: Chris Gillette)

Launched in 2024, the Demerit Point Integrity Taskforce uncovered "extraordinary examples of misconduct", NSW opposition roads spokesman Mark Coure told parliament, including people accumulating hundreds — and in some cases more than 1,000 — demerit points while continuing to drive.

"If dangerous drivers are able to manipulate the system, avoid licence suspensions and continue offending with zero consequences, then the purpose of the demerit point scheme is fundamentally undermined," Mr Coure said.

"We saw examples of unverifiable foreign licence details being used repeatedly to avoid penalties. We saw evidence of advertisements on social media where individuals were offering to take demerit points for others in exchange for money."

The taskforce resulted in proposed reforms that would require passport details and the country of issue when an overseas licence holder is nominated as the responsible driver and introduce new offences relating to false disputes and fraudulent nominations.

NSW Minister for Roads, Jenny Aitchison, said the proposed legislation would crack down on international licences being nominated for fines.

Jenny Aitchison is NSW's Minister for Regional Transport and Roads. (ABC News: Romy Stephens)

"Revenue NSW systems are being integrated with Australian Border Force data to verify if a nominated overseas driver was actually in the country when an offence occurred," she said.

"The bill forces an individual who nominates an overseas driver for a demerit-carrying offence to provide the nominee's passport number and country of origin."

A spokesperson from Transport for NSW said its taskforce saw the licences of 50 repeat offenders suspended, and resulted in 190 vehicle registrations being cancelled.

The department told 7.30 that its proposed reforms are "designed to support a fair, consistent, and safety-focused licensing system in NSW".

But while those changes are being deliberated, it hasn't stopped other schemes from establishing.

Among the purported services 7.30 uncovered was a website bearing a striking resemblance to the official Service NSW portal. Its contact button redirected 7.30 to WhatsApp.

This website advertising a demerit point fraud scheme is based off the official Service NSW website. (ABC News: Christopher Gillette)

In messages, the person claiming to be offering the service said they had "certain access to live dummy accounts" registered under Service NSW, and knew "how to get it accepted straight away and keep it all automated."

When asked how much a $434 fine and 3 points would cost to wipe, the person said, "ill [sic] do it for $500 total if sorting it today … I just need penalty notice number, date of offence and full name it's in and it will take 3 minutes … you only pay after you can see it's sorted."

NSW Police said it is aware of "reports concerning websites and online services claiming to facilitate the removal of demerit points in exchange for payment".

"The NSW Police Force does not comment on specific investigations; however, any information alleging criminal conduct is assessed and investigated where appropriate."

"Demerit point fraud is a serious offence that undermines the integrity of the licensing system and road safety."

RACQ says Queensland authorities need to "get much tougher" and consider policy intervention, legislation intervention, and police action.

Michael Kane is the head of public policy at the Royal Automobile Club of Queensland (RACQ). (ABC News: Michael Lloyd)

Mr Kane told 7.30 the government needs to demonstrate that it understood the problem and was addressing it.

Griffith cybersecurity expert Dr David Tuffley says a taskforce could determine the number of people actively exploiting the state’s loopholes.

"That's going to take some courage from the government, to basically take a deep breath and run the query and just see how bad it is," he told 7.30.

Mr Crisafulli acknowledged the infringement and demerits scheme is "an important part of justice," but avoided answering if his government would commit to a review or taskforce.

"You will never make a system bulletproof, but you can make it better," he said.

"We will continue to do all we can to make sure we have systems that are strong.

"If people have done the wrong thing, then they should have to pay their dues."

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.title: Philippine economic slump worsens on Iran war, bad weather
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.text:
The Philippine economy unexpectedly slowed for a fifth straight quarter, raising questions about the central bank’s rate-hike cycle and heaping pressure on President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.

Gross domestic product expanded 2.1% in the three months to September from a year earlier, the statistics agency said Monday. That compares to 2.4% in the second quarter and was a full percentage point below the median estimate of 3.1% in a Bloomberg News survey.

Agricultural output fell 4.8% in the third quarter, and services growth continued to slow. Farm output was hurt as typhoons battered the climate-vulnerable nation, with El Nino further clouding the outlook.

The peso fell 0.3% and the benchmark stock index dropped as much as 0.7% after the data release, which underscores how deeply the nation is underperforming neighboring economies. Growth was less than half the pace seen in Indonesia or Malaysia, and less than a quarter that of Vietnam.

The data underscore the damage to the Philippines from the U.S.-Iran war, which has driven up crude oil prices and inflation, forcing the central bank to hike interest rates. The resulting higher cost of living and still-unresolved government corruption scandals have weakened consumer and business confidence.

High food and energy prices constrained consumer spending, a key economic driver which continued to post slower growth. Tighter financial conditions weighed on investments which remained in contraction. Cyclones and the monsoon disrupted farm production, which reduced rural incomes and added to supply pressures.

The data come days after the release of the latest inflation print showing an acceleration to 7.8% in October, the fastest pace in almost four years. That was expected to lead the central bank to continue raising rates following a jumbo 50-basis-point hike in October.

Economic Planning Secretary Arsenio Balisacan refrained from calling on the Bangko ng Sentral Pilipinas to pause its rate hikes, noting the central bank is trying to cool price gains.

“If the BSP actually succeeds in anchoring the inflation expectation back to the target, then that actually will impact positively consumption and investments,” he said at a briefing in Manila. “It’s not necessarily bad for growth.”

Still, he said achieving the 2026 growth target of 3.5% to 4.5% is “very challenging at this point given the current environment but we are hoping that the fourth-quarter performance will be better.”

The BSP now must weigh the weak economy against surging prices and support for the peso, which has dropped almost 7% to be Asia’s second-worst-performing currency this year. Inflation has remained well above the central bank’s 3% goal since March.

“While we think they should still deliver more jumbo hikes, they may opt for a smaller hike in December because of growth concerns,” said Bank of the Philippine Islands lead economist Emilio Neri Jr. A small hike could leave the peso under greater pressure, he added.

“This could also increase the possibility of inflation getting de-anchored,” Neri said. “Core inflation is just rising too fast.”

Marcos will also face pressure to act to support the economy, which is heavily dependent on imported energy from the Middle East.

Growth started to slow in the third quarter of last year. At that time, confidence began a lengthy slump after Marcos revealed corruption in government involving billions of pesos in flood-related infrastructure. The graft scandal is unresolved, while Vice President Sara Duterte, who denies wrongdoing, is on trial in the Senate over alleged unexplained wealth.

NEW YORK – Airlines are installing deluxe seats, enlisting Michelin-star chefs for luxury menu offerings and designing elite airport lounges as the industry bets its future on growing demand for premium travel.

The strategy is expected to accelerate the shrinking share of coach class on many flights, with airlines envisioning as much as 70% of passengers paying for enhanced options, if not first class or business class.

Airlines face significantly higher jet fuel costs due to the Iran war, but view such upselling as a profitable long-term bet.

https://www.scmp.com/tech/big-tech/artic.title: Can DeepSeek challenge OpenAI, Anthropic in AI agents as Harness adoption takes off?
https://www.scmp.com/tech/big-tech/artic.author: Minxiao Chang
https://www.scmp.com/tech/big-tech/artic.text:
Hangzhou-based start-up ramps up efforts to monetise its powerful foundation models as AI agent platform gains traction

Users of Harness through the company’s official application programming interface were consuming around 92 trillion tokens a day as of November 4, the Hangzhou-based start-up said. That is equivalent to about 1.1 billion tokens consumed per second.

A “harness” is the software infrastructure that turns a large language model into an AI agent that can autonomously execute tasks on behalf of users, rather than simply respond to prompts.

DeepSeek’s Harness went live on August 13, followed by a desktop app on September 29, allowing developers to run AI agents that can execute code and use external software to carry out tasks.

The company said the number of third-party plug-ins had grown to about 35,000 since launch, with around 60 per cent of active users having built or installed at least one.

“Our goal is for DeepSeek’s Harness to act as an operating system for the agent era,” said Cui Tianyi, a former Jane Street engineer who joined the Harness team in March, in a social media post on Sunday.

One community-built plug-in combines tools for reading, highlighting and translating academic papers, while allowing users to ask an AI agent questions about the material. Another shows developers what information an agent is using and how that changes throughout a conversation.

The company is increasingly turning its attention to monetising its powerful foundation models. It set up its first product division last month, led by Cui, Chinese media outlet The Paper reported.

https://www.dw.com/en/india-news-delhi-a.title: India news:  Delhi air quality level 'severe' after Diwali
https://www.dw.com/en/india-news-delhi-a.text:
Illegal fireworks during Diwali celebrations have impacted New Delhi's air quality level. DW has the latest.

Here is our rolling coverage from India on Monday, November 9:

Nineteen Indian seafarers who had been stranded in Yemen's Hodeidah and Sanaa for nearly two weeks have been evacuated, the Indian Embassy in Yemen said in a post on X late Sunday.

The embassy added that the sailors were in good health and on their way back to India.

A 2022 truce that had paused fighting in Yemen's longstanding conflict crumbled  in July, restarting fighting between the Houthi rebels and the Middle Eastern country's Saudi Arabia-backed government.

According to India's foreign ministry, 23 Indian nationals have been killed since the Middle East war began in February, with seafarers accounting for 15 deaths.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Residents of New Delhi and nearby areas have woken up breathing, or rather choking on, smoke and fine particulate matter, as revelers celebrating the Hindu festival of Diwali disregarded a firecracker ban, adding to the ongoing pollution crisis that grips the capital in the winter months.

Several parts of New Delhi and the surrounding satellite cities that make up the National Capital Region (NCR), have reported an Air Quality Index (AQI) in the "severe" category, posing significant health risks.

Skies over the capital which were lit up by fireworks on Sunday night are now blanketed with a  thick layer of toxic smog.

Air pollution in parts of Delhi-NCR dangerously surpassed the World Health Organization's (WHO)  recommended 24-hour average limit on Monday by over 50 times, reports said.

IQair, that cites data from a government monitoring station in the city, put the level of cancer-causing PM 2.5 microparticles at 879 micrograms per cubic meter in Delhi's central Mandir Marg area early on Monday, news agency AFP reported, which comes up  to nearly 59 times the WHO limit of 15 micrograms per cubic meter.

New Delhi is one of the world's most polluted capitals. The city has for many years witnessed a recurring winter smog fuelled by vehicular  emission, crop-residue fires in neighboring states and industrial activity.

Millions of people celebrate Diwali with fireworks in the smog season, releasing massive amounts of fine particles — PM2.5 and PM10 —  and soot in the already compromised air.

On Saturday, Delhi witnessed the worst air on Diwali eve in a decade.

Last month, India's top court had restricted conventional firecrackers, allowing only "green firecrackers" in three-hour timeframes on Saturday and Sunday. But the Supreme Court's ban failed to hold.

"Green firecrackers" are designed to produce lower air and noise pollution but still emit 65 to 70% of conventional firecracker pollution.

A series of winter pollution rules had also kicked in in New Delhi from November 1, including vehicle restrictions and construction bans.

Air pollution has been a Gordian knot for successive Delhi governments who blame each other for failing to tackle the issue.

But a long-term solution to curb New Delhi's air pollution crisis remains elusive.

This is Dharvi Vaid Dhulia,from DW's studio in New Delhi, bringing you our Monday digest of all the news, events and trends that are making a splash  in India.

The morning after Diwali  — the festival of lights — has left the Indian capital shrouded in toxic smog as people flouted a firecracker ban in large numbers, exacerbating the city's seasonal pollution conditions.

Several parts of New Delhi and its surrounding regions are choking with the Air Quality Index (AQI) in the "severe" range.

As I write this, I can still hear crackers going off intermittently well into the Monday morning — the popping sound making me check the AQI indicator on the air purifier next to me, every time.

In other news, 19 Indian seafarers stranded in Yemen's Hodeidah and Sanaa for the last two weeks have been evacuated and are on their way back to their home country.

Stay tuned as we bring you all this and more.

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.title: ‘It’s a feeling of being screwed over’: once-quiet village despairs over ‘monster’ warehouse
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.author: Josh Halliday North of England editor
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text:
Residents of Astley in Greater Manchester will tell public inquiry next week of ‘cacophony’ of noise causing sleep deprivation and depression

W
hen Stephen Retford retired from the police in 2006, he looked forward to a quiet life after nearly three decades catching villains. But now the former detective has landed another big case – one that is extremely close to home.

“It’s the total injustice of it,” the 70-year-old seethed, staring up at the 18-metre-high mega-warehouse that looms over the quiet village of Astley in Greater Manchester. Residents are up in arms about the “monster” construction, likening it to having a “cruise ship in our back garden”.

Andy Burnham expressed concern over the development weeks before he became prime minister, and Bev Craig, his successor as Greater Manchester mayor, said she too was concerned. “Old industry wouldn’t have got that close to your house,” she said. “So why is it that new industry can?”

This week, villagers will attempt to block plans by Whistl, the distribution firm that operates the warehouse, to use dozens of HGVs and trailers for its round-the-clock operation. In a two-day public inquiry, they will describe how the “cacophony” of noise is already driving some to sleep deprivation and depression.

“It’s had a profound impact on the neighbourhood,” said Retford, a burly man with a booming voice who after so many years in the police is not easily shaken. “The noise wakes you up at 2am and you can’t get back to sleep. We’ve not had a proper night’s sleep in well over a year. It’s a living hell.”

This once-quiet village is now on the frontline in a nationwide fightback against superstructures springing up everywhere from Devon to Cardiff and the Scottish Borders. Plans were announced last week for Britain’s largest datacentre at the site of the Drax power plant in North Yorkshire, and a further 315 “hyperscale” datacentres are queueing to connect to the National Grid.

Down the road from Retford’s house, a woman looked out of her daughter’s bedroom window at the Whistl warehouse just metres away. The woman, a police officer who does not want to be named, said her 10-year-old son, who is autistic, refused to play in the garden because of the “continuously whirring” noise of the conveyor belts. Her eight-year-old daughter has become too scared to play in her bedroom.

“As soon as she comes home from school, those blinds will be shut because she doesn’t want anyone to see in,” she said, pointing to a CCTV camera on the warehouse facing their home. “She hates it. She does get scared about it.”

Like many of their neighbours, the woman and her husband moved to Astley before plans had been submitted by a firm part-owned by Peel Group, one of Britain’s biggest landowners, run by the billionaire John Whittaker.

Back then, they were surrounded by farmland where lambs, cows and horses grazed. Now their view is a giant hunk of grey steel that was named the worst new building in the UK this year. “It was a lovely view, so secluded,” she said. “When we saw the structure of this, it was like: oh my God, what is this?”

As mayor, Burnham said earlier this year that the development had not been managed properly and that key things “should have been done differently”. Wigan council said it acted properly in approving the superstructure despite objections from the local MP and dozens of residents. However, the council’s leader, Labour’s Nazia Rehman, admitted last month that “some lessons have been learned” and said that in future “consultations [with residents] will be proactive”. Local leaders have scrapped plans for four other giant warehouses in response to the backlash.

Helen Halbous, who moved to the estate seven years ago, said: “It’s a feeling of being screwed over by Wigan council, having been born and brought up here. People who had a voice of power [in the council] either made this awful decision or they looked away and let it happen. It was a little mining village and now we’re this industrial centre. It’s so wrong.”

Halbous, 47, said she and her partner, Sami Halbous, now felt trapped in a house they once loved and they feared they would be unable to sell up. “A neighbour had their home valued and they lost 30%, and that’s if they can sell,” she said.

Residents felt hoodwinked about the size of the structure and its closeness to their homes, Halbous said. “The plan in 2019 was it was to be used for employment. It was never to have an 18-metre-high warehouse. Those permissions were changed [before 2024] and changed really quietly. We wouldn’t have bought here and let ourselves get trapped like this.”

PLP, the land owner, said the size and scale of the buildings had not changed since its planning application in 2023. It said earlier plans for smaller units, submitted in 2017 by Peel, one of its biggest shareholders, had since lapsed.

Wigan council said it recognised the “strength of feeling in the community and do not underestimate the impact residents tell us the development has had on them”. It said an independent review found its planning process was “legally sound” and followed national guidelines but there were “lessons around engagement and transparency”. It said: “We have acknowledged those findings and have taken steps to improve our approach.”

Whistl, which began operating at the site in July, has responded to the concerns by promising to use quieter vehicles and stopping their use outside between midnight and 6am. The firm said it took residents’ concerns seriously and was “committed to meeting its licensing responsibilities and being a good neighbour”. A Whistl spokesperson said the noise mitigation measures would remain in place and the overnight pause on activity in the yard would continue while all parties tried to “identify a sustainable, long-term solution”.

Retford became so fed up with the disturbance that he began overnight observations to track the big vehicles clanking around near his home. He commissioned independent acoustics experts to produce a sound report, convinced that the “cacophony of rolling thunder, a booming sound”, breached regulations.

A fightback fund launched by residents has so far raised £78,000, much of which will be spent on lawyers for next week’s public inquiry.

For Retford and his wife, Carole, 71, the impact has been huge. “Bloody hell, there’s not a lot of things I’ve not seen in my life,” he said. “I don’t get easily shocked and I’m not a flaky character, but this has had a profound effect on me. We’re not fuddy-duddies or nimbies. This is big business riding over the little people like us, saying ‘screw the lot of you’.”

Retford and his wife have spoken to their doctor about sleep deprivation. “It’s a torture for a very good reason, because it just drains you – and that is the effect it’s having on us,” he said.

Carole became close to tears. Staring up at the warehouse, she said: “It’s changed our lives. Your moods go up and down to being very depressed and very emotional about it because there’s no way out at the minute. People use the ‘depression’ word too lightly, but if you feel there’s no way out, it does get to you.”
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.summary: Residents of Astley in Greater Manchester will tell public inquiry next week of noise causing sleep deprivation. Residents will try to block plans by distribution firm that operates warehouse. Whistl has responded to the concerns by promising to use quieter vehicles.

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: Cop31 live: world leaders gather for crucial climate crisis talks
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Ajit Niranjan
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
Among the 70,000 registered attenders at today’s Cop will be civil society groups, Indigenous people from around the world, lawmakers from many countries, representatives of subnational governments, businesspeople and investors working on clean energy - and a number of fossil fuel lobbyists, whose repeated presence and influence at the annual “conference of the party” meetings of the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) has sparked protest.

Though Turkey is hosting, Australia will preside over the formal agenda of negotiations, under a compromise agreed last year when both countries bid for the right to hold the meeting.

Hello, and welcome to the live blog for Cop31, this year’s UN climate summit. I’m Ajit Niranjan, the European environment correspondent – I’ll be running the liveblog from Berlin over the next two weeks while my colleagues in Antalya, Turkey, bring us updates from where the action is. We’re looking forward to guiding you through a hectic fortnight of planetary significance.

More than 90 heads of state and government, along with ministers and senior officials from close to 190 countries, are expected to descend on Turkey’s coastal city of Antalya this week, for the latest round of UN climate talks. Against a backdrop of rapidly rising temperatures and extreme weather, supercharged by fossil fuels, and fractious geopolitics, made worse by soaring inflation owing to the Iran war, the fortnight-long meeting will focus on “implementation” of the world’s targets to cut greenhouse gas emissions and help those stricken by the climate crisis.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.title: Which countries and industries emit the most greenhouse gases?
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.author: Marium Ali,Hanna Duggal
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.text:
World leaders and delegates are gathering in Antalya, Turkiye, for COP31, the annual climate summit of the United Nations, which runs from November 9 to 20.

They meet as global emissions continue to climb. The world emitted 54.1 billion tonnes of greenhouse gases in 2025, 0.7 percent more than the year before and 68.5 percent more than in 1990, according to the latest figures from the European Commission’s Joint Research Centre (JRC) and the International Energy Agency (IEA).

Greenhouse gases, mainly carbon dioxide and methane, trap heat in the atmosphere, raising global temperatures and fuelling heatwaves, droughts, floods and other extreme weather conditions.

In this visual explainer, Al Jazeera breaks down which gases are warming the planet, which industries and countries emit the most, and how their emissions have changed over time.

Carbon dioxide (CO2) made up 73.8 percent of global greenhouse gas emissions in 2025. It is released mainly when fossil fuels such as coal, oil and gas are burned, while deforestation removes trees that would otherwise absorb it.

Methane (CH4) accounted for 17.6 percent of emissions that year, followed by nitrous oxide (N2O) at 5.3 percent and fluorinated gases (F-gases) at 3.3 percent.

Global CO2 emissions have risen by 76.3 percent since 1990, according to the JRC.

As these gases build up in the atmosphere, they trap more heat. In 2025, the heat stored in the world’s oceans reached its highest level on record, and the rate of ocean warming has increased sharply over the past two decades, according to the World Meteorological Organization (WMO).

Extreme weather has killed tens of thousands of people and forced millions from their homes in 2026, according to the WMO.

In Europe, heatwaves, droughts and wildfires between May and August caused more than 30,000 excess deaths, and 220,000 people were evacuated in France alone.

On August 26, a glacier collapse and the resulting flash flood in the Himalayas killed more than 1,500 people in Nepal along its border with China, while about 5,600 remain missing, according to the UN.

In June and July, Typhoon Bavi forced three million people to evacuate in China and killed 26 in the Philippines. Weeks later, severe Tropical Storm Maysak killed 171 people and caused more than $3bn in losses in China.

Earlier in the year, floods and windstorms across the western Mediterranean displaced more than 180,000 people in Morocco, while extreme cold and snow in North America killed 174 people.

The map below shows some of the most extreme weather events of 2026.

The world’s greenhouse gas emissions have more than doubled since 1970, rising from about 23 billion tonnes to 54.1 billion tonnes in 2025, according to the JRC.

The power industry, which generates electricity, is the largest source, producing nearly 30 percent of global emissions in 2025. Its emissions have roughly quadrupled since 1970, driven by soaring demand for electricity in fast-growing economies such as China and India.

Industry, including manufacturing and mining, is the second-largest source at 21 percent. This covers fuel burned in factories as well as gases released when producing cement, metals and chemicals. Industrial emissions climbed steeply in the 2000s as China’s manufacturing boomed.

Transport, including cars, shipping and aviation, is third at 16 percent.

Together, these three sectors produce about two-thirds of the world’s emissions. The rest comes from agriculture (12 percent), the extraction of coal, oil and gas (11 percent), buildings (6.6 percent) and waste (3.6 percent).

Global emissions have fallen only a handful of times since 1970, including in the early 1980s, after the 2008 financial crisis and during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020. Each time, they rebounded.

In 2025, the three largest emitters produced almost half of the world’s greenhouse gases. China emitted almost 16 billion tonnes (29.5 percent), the United States 6.02 billion tonnes (11.1 percent) and India 4.51 billion tonnes (8.3 percent).

The 27 countries of the European Union together accounted for 5.8 percent, followed by Russia (4.8 percent), Indonesia (2.5 percent), Brazil (2.4 percent) and Iran (2.1 percent).

International shipping and aviation, which fall outside any single country’s total, together produced 2.6 percent of global emissions, more than most countries.

It was not always this way. The Industrial Revolution of the 18th and 19th centuries drove up emissions first in the West, particularly in the United Kingdom and the US, as they built factories and moved to mass manufacturing. Global emissions then rose sharply after World War II and have more than doubled since 1970.

China’s emissions surged in the early 2000s as its economy boomed, and it overtook the US as the world’s largest emitter in the mid-2000s.

But measured over time, the picture changes. Since the mid-18th century, the US has produced 23.5 percent of all CO2 emissions, compared with 15.4 percent from China, according to the Global Carbon Budget.

In China, the power sector is the largest source, producing 42 percent of the country’s almost 16 billion tonnes of greenhouse gases. Industry accounts for 31 percent and fuel production for 9.5 percent.

In September 2025, Chinese President Xi Jinping, for the first time, pledged to cut the country’s greenhouse gas emissions by 7 to 10 percent from their peak by 2035.

In the US, transport is the largest source at 29 percent, mostly from cars and trucks. The power sector accounts for 26 percent and industry for 14 percent.

In India, which still relies heavily on coal for electricity, the power sector produces 35 percent of emissions, followed by industry at 24 percent and agriculture at 19 percent.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.title: Ousted PM Sheikh Hasina seeks passport in sign of Bangladesh return plan
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.text:
Bangladesh’s ousted Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina has requested a new passport and identity card to allow her to return from self-imposed exile in India.

The request is the clearest sign that Hasina, who has been living in India for two years, plans to make good on her promise that she would return to Bangladesh in December.

Hasina told the news agency Reuters that she intended to surrender before a court in Bangladesh, and her aides said on Monday the date would be announced once various formalities were completed.

Bangladesh’s war crimes court sentenced Hasina to death in absentia last November for ordering a deadly crackdown on student protests that swept the country in 2024. As many as 1,400 people may have been killed in those protests, according to United Nations estimates.

Hasina’s letter to the Bangladeshi government, cited by Reuters, asked that her request be processed “expeditiously” on the basis of her Bangladeshi nationality.

Hasina is the daughter of Bangladesh’s founder and first president, Sheikh Mujibur Rahman. She served as prime minister from 1996 to 2001, and again from 2009 to 2024.

As Bangladesh’s longest-ruling prime minister, Hasina’s return raises the prospect of renewed legal and political issues in the country of 127 million people.

She still enjoys support among sections of the population, and her return could impact the Bangladeshi government’s efforts to stabilise the country and its economy after two years of disruption.

However, her return to Bangladesh could smooth relations with India, which sharply deteriorated when the former prime minister fled there in 2024.

Hasina was ousted by a popular, student-led mass protest movement that broke out after the Supreme Court restored a job quota system that had prioritised the descendants of the country’s liberation activists.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.title: Who are the seafarers caught in the US-Israeli war on Iran?
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.author: Usaid Siddiqui
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.text:
Commercial vessels moving through the Strait of Hormuz and its surrounding waters have come under repeated attack since the United States and Israel launched their war on Iran nine months ago.

The conflict has transformed one of the world’s busiest shipping corridors into a dangerous passage for crews transporting oil, gas and other goods.

On Sunday, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said three “rogue oil tankers travelling an unauthorised route” in the strait were subject to “explosions and severe fires”.

The International Maritime Organization (IMO) has recorded the deaths of at least 25 seafarers since the war started on February 28. Many of those killed have been citizens of India, one of the world’s largest suppliers of merchant sailors.

“It is unacceptable that throughout this conflict seafarers have been placed in harm’s way,” the International Chamber of Shipping (ICS), a shipping trade association and advocacy group, told Al Jazeera.

“It is incumbent on all parties to take all necessary steps to safeguard the safety of seafarers who are simply going about their job and have found themselves, through no fault of their own, in a highly volatile situation,” an ICS spokesperson added.

The latest incidents have raised questions about the safety of civilian crews, their ability to refuse dangerous assignments and the protections available under international law.

The Strait of Hormuz is a crucial passage for international shipping, Before the war, roughly one-fifth of global oil consumption passed through the waterway, which connects the Gulf to the Arabian Sea.

Iran essentially closed the strait after the US-Israeli attacks began, warning that ships trying to sail through the waterway without authorisation could be targeted. Meanwhile, Washington has  imposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports.

Attacks on shipping have involved missiles, projectiles and naval mines that have damaged vessels, set them on fire or sunk them. According to the IMO, at least 129 incidents have been reported.

On Thursday, Iranian forces said five oil tankers and a tugboat caught fire in separate incidents in the strait.

Separately, a Marshall Islands-flagged tanker named Velos Sapphire suffered an explosion north of Qatar, killing one crew member.

October was particularly dangerous for commercial shipping with at least 31 vessels hit.

The victims are largely civilian merchant sailors working on oil tankers, cargo ships and other commercial vessels.

Many come from countries far removed from the conflict, including India, whose nationals have suffered particularly heavy losses, with at least 16 killed.

In June, three Indian sailors were killed in US strikes on commercial vessels near Oman, prompting New Delhi to summon a senior American diplomat.

On Tuesday, Gandhar Nahim Ajij from Gujarat died after the cargo vessel MSV Al Jusufi was struck off Oman. Thirteen other Indian crew members were rescued.

In October, 12 crew members were injured when the Panamanian-flagged tanker On Peace was struck near Oman. Eleven of those injured were Indian nationals.

People from other countries have also been among the dead. In September, two Filipino crew members were killed when the Saudi tanker Sidr was hit by projectiles near the Strait of Hormuz.

Iranian civilian maritime workers have also suffered casualties.

In May, the head of Iran’s merchant marine union said at least 44 Iranian seafarers had been killed and 29 injured since the start of the war.

Beyond the threat of death or injury, the war has also taken a toll on sailors’ mental health, according to the ICS spokesperson.

“Shipowners are working hard to ensure that impacted seafarers have access to mental health support services as well as increased access to calls with family and friends,” the spokesperson added.

About 6,000 seafarers remained stranded near the Strait of Hormuz in October, the IMO said in late August.

In March, an arrangement was negotiated between maritime unions and shipping companies through the International Bargaining Forum, under which seafarers could refuse to enter designated danger zones and receive company-funded repatriation and compensation equivalent to two months of basic wages.

At the same time, the International Transport Workers’ Federation said the agreement also provides for increased wages and twice the standard compensation for seafarers who die or suffer a disability.

However, those protections do not necessarily cover every seafarer. And seafarers in the Gulf also face grave mental suffering, maritime charities warned in May, saying many faced loneliness, anxiety and distress.

“As we have throughout the conflict, we strongly urge all ships operating in the region to conduct thorough risk assessments and to maintain vigilance in line with the latest BMP [best management practices] maritime security guidelines,” the ICS spokesperson said.

Under Article 38 of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, ships and aircraft “enjoy the right of transit passage”, a right that no country may suspend.

Article 17 also guarantees foreign vessels the “right of innocent passage” through another country’s territorial waters. Under Article 19, such passage is considered innocent provided it is not “prejudicial to the peace, good order or security of the coastal state”.

While the IMO in June sought arrangements to evacuate stranded sailors, efforts to establish safe passage have faced repeated obstacles as attacks in and around the Strait of Hormuz continue unabated.

Academic Abdul Khalique says while international law undoubtedly does apply, “its enforcement is the weak link.”

“The law is clear on the obligations. The gap is political will and practical enforcement,” Khalique, head of the Liverpool John Moores University Maritime Centre, told Al Jazeera.

“For seafarers themselves, legal protections matter most when paired with operational avoidance.”

The International Maritime Organization has recorded the deaths of at least 25 sailors. For seafarers themselves, legal protections matter most when paired with operational avoidance, says Al Jazeera

https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261.title: Poland braces for tense week after deadly shooting deepens political divisions
https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261.text:
Poland is facing a week of political tensions after the deadliest shooting in decades shattered residents' sense of security in the deeply divided nation.

The country had been spared from such attacks and was unaccustomed to everyday violence until Saturday, when a gunman opened fire at random in the historic market square of Krakow, the country's second city.

Six people, including two foreigners, were killed, and about 15 others were wounded, in Poland's worst fatal shooting since the end of communism in 1989.

READ MORE
Poland launches terrorism probe into mass shooting in Krakow

The gunman is suspected to have killed nine people in all after the bodies of three people – his parents and sister – were found at their home two hours' drive from Krakow. Police announced on Monday that the suspect had died in hospital.

Prosecutors on Sunday opened an investigation into an "act of terrorism" and Poland's interior minister has said the suspect was fascinated by "far-right ideologies", which has drawn the ire of the conservative and nationalist opposition.

The shooting comes as Poland – a nation deeply divided politically – prepares for a critical week.

On Tuesday, a high-stakes meeting of the Constitutional Tribunal is due to be held, a focal point in the ongoing battle between Donald Tusk's government and its opponents over judicial appointments.

READ MORE
Polish president holds crisis talks after dramatic court standoff

The right-wing opposition accuses the liberal, pro-European administration of undermining the constitutional order.

The governing coalition, for its part, maintains it is trying to correct "political" nominations to the court and reforms made by the nationalists, which it claims run counter to European democratic standards.

For several weeks, nationalist protesters have camped outside the court to "defend it" but the crisis escalated abruptly late last month.

Riot police moved in to block access and a judge newly appointed by the parliamentary majority said she was taking over in the interim – effectively suspending the incumbent, who is close to the right and to the nationalist head of state Karol Nawrocki.

After the Krakow shooting, the nationalist Law and Justice party (PiS), which was in power from 2015 to 2023, called off planned protests for Monday and Tuesday.

But they could resume later in the week.

Wednesday's Independence March is causing the greatest concern, however.

The annual event draws up to hundreds of thousands of right-wing supporters, from Catholic conservatives and white-supremacist fringe groups to antisemitic, pro-Russian far-right elements.

President Nawrocki has announced his attendance.

Some observers have described it as "high-risk", fearing that the crowd may deviate from its agreed route and head instead to the Constitutional Tribunal.

Prime Minister Tusk on Sunday dismissed rumours that the march could be stopped.

"No one intends to ban the Independence March," he wrote on X. "Speculation on this matter is nothing but disinformation."

To display this content from X (Twitter), you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.

But he urged participants to "refrain from aggression" and warned against taking part in counter-demonstrations.

His appeals may well go unheeded given the divisions in Polish politics, which are unfolding against the backdrop of a rising far-right movement.

"An extremely destructive polarisation which does not merely dismantle the state in an institutional sense but also divides society even more deeply on an emotional level," said leading writer Boguslaw Chrabota in the weekly Rzeczpospolita on Sunday.

Radicalisation of political discourse "gives rise to Polish Breiviks", he argued, referring to the Krakow shooting and Anders Breivik, who killed 77 people in Norway in 2011.

Political scientist Ewa Marciniak, from Warsaw University, suggested that the tragedy in Krakow could soon be exploited for political gain.

"Tragedies like the one in Krakow only serve to sharpen political divisions," she said.

"After a period of shared mourning comes the search for those responsible, all taking place in a political climate defined by deep-seated, mutual hostility among political leaders."

With parliamentary elections scheduled for autumn 2027, events such as the Krakow tragedy or the ongoing crisis surrounding the Constitutional Tribunal, are likely to be used "to deepen conflicts" and "draw the public into them", she added.
