BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Flower Gardens

Arum lilies, agapanthus and watsonias were included in the winning bouquet. (Supplied)

A bouquet of invasive weeds has taken out the top flower prize at an agricultural show in WA's South West.

The winner said she wanted to draw attention to some of the region's most problematic invasive plants.

Invasive plants are thriving in the region and people are encouraged to think carefully about what they put in their gardens.

A bouquet featuring some of the worst invasive weeds in Western Australia's South West has won a top award at the Margaret River Agricultural Show.

Nature Conservation Margaret River entered the unusual floral arrangement in a bid to raise awareness of the environmental damage caused by invasive weeds, including plants commonly found in home gardens.

The bouquet featured arum lilies, English ivy, watsonia, Flinders Range wattle, agapanthus, periwinkle and Victorian tea tree.

Margaret River Agricultural Show vice-president Julie Kirby said there had been a record-breaking 200 floral exhibits across several individual categories, including roses, wedding bouquets, mixed arrangements, floral art, and mixed weed arrangements.

Obelia Walker with winning bouquet of weeds. (Supplied)

Nature Conservation Margaret River's entry was awarded ribbons in the mixed weeds category and best overall exhibit.

"The best exhibit is one that really catches the judges' eyes," Ms Kirby said.

"We have trained and accredited judges from the Western Australian Horticultural Council and they thought that the overall design, the workmanship, and the colour harmony and the quality and the condition of this particular display was just so impressive.

"With the mixed weed arrangement you don't need to grow it yourself, you can go and collect it from bushland or the roadside, or wherever you've got weeds present and enter them."

She said the bouquet was disposed of safely to prevent the seeds from spreading.

"It was a beautiful and educational way to show how garden plants can escape to become bushland weeds," Ms Kirby said.

Nature Conservation Margaret River biodiversity officer Obelia Walker said the organisation saw the competition as an opportunity to draw attention to some of the region's most problematic invasive plants.

Obelia Walker didn't expect the top gong. (Supplied)

She said she was surprised to discover the arrangement had taken out the overall bouquet award.

"I didn't realise that I'd actually won the champion bouquet for the whole category," Ms Walker said.

She said the judges recognised the arrangement as a creative way to get the community thinking about the threat posed by invasive weeds.

"Weeds are sometimes a tricky one to get people to pay attention to," Ms Walker said.

"They really take over and smother all our lovely native plants.

"Arum lily, of course, can just become such a monoculture and a carpet, but the others can as well."

The arum lily, considered one of the most damaging weeds in the country, was banned from sale in WA more than 20 years ago, but the rogue garden plant's infestation of forests across WA's South West shows no sign of slowing.

Arum lilies are infesting Boranup Forest. (ABC South West WA: Georgia Loney)

More than 3,000 private landowners have requested help to eradicate the weed on their properties.

Ms Walker said invasive weeds often thrived because they had no natural predators encouraged gardeners to consider alternative plants rather than risk introducing invasive species into the environment.

The organisation hopes the unusual prize-winning bouquet will encourage people to look more closely at what they are planting in their backyards.

David Warner (left) says Usman Khawaja's (right) statements about the 2018 ball tampering incident are "100 per cent accurate". (Getty Image: Alex Davidson, ICC)

David Warner has backed Usman Khawaja's claims on the 2018 ball tampering scandal, saying the statements in his book, Sabr, are "100 per cent accurate".

Warner was suspended from domestic and international cricket as a result of the scandal and was also permanently barred from leadership positions.

Speaking for the first time in eight years on the saga, Warner emphatically backed Khawaja, his childhood friend.

"Uzzie, I throw my full support behind you. I thank you for everything you've done," he said in an Instagram statement.

"It's 100 per cent accurate, what you've said.

"Now everyone knows the truth, it's out there. People wanted to know it, you've come out and said it, and now people are saying, 'Why eight years on?' talking about selling a book.

"This is Usman's story. This is what Usman believes. Uzzie wrote down every single thing from that day on. Uzzie, thank you."

Warner slammed Cricket Australia's investigation into the ball-tampering claims.

"Now, this whole interview process was rushed and botched," he said.

"Uzzie was sitting next to Cameron Bancroft [in the dressing room]. Uzzie was not interviewed. How that is a thorough investigation? It baffles me.

"We're not here to point fingers and we're not opening old wounds.

"It's about accountability, transparency ensuring that the truth is properly examined, and perhaps it's time people stop scrutinising the person asking for accountability, and asking those responsible for the investigation to provide it.

"There [were] a lot of statements and inaccuracies over the last eight years that were out in the media by people and there were a lot of people who stayed silent."

Warner said his delayed response to Khawaja's claims being made public was down to explaining his involvement in the scandal to his daughters.

"The last couple of days, I've been talking to my daughters and that is why it's taken me a couple of days to get this out, because I've had to tell them exactly what had happened, especially my 12-year-old Ivy," he said.

"[She] wanted to know why we were holding her, why there were so many cameras and why we were all crying on TV.

"That was a hard thing to do, but one thing I did say is, 'Girls, tell the truth because lies will eventually get out.' It is a very tough time.

"This is for everyone in Australia. It has been the question that everyone is asking. Uzzie, you've said it how it is, it is 100 per cent accurate.

"It has been a tough time for my family, Steven [Smith] and Cameron [Bancroft] no doubt, but this is what needed to come out."

Warner is the first of the banned trio to speak publicly in the wake of Khawaja's comments being made public.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/q.title: Premier says tougher laws 'will be considered' after war memorials damaged
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/q.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

CCTV shows a car ramming a flagpole at the Hervey Bay RSL (Supplied)

Police are investigating two separate acts of vandalism at war memorial sites in Redlands and Hervey Bay.

A cenotaph in Cleveland was damaged while a man driving a ute repeatedly rammed a flagpole at the Hervey Bay RSL.

The acts of damage come just days ahead of Remembrance Day on November 11.

Police have charged one man and another is assisting with enquiries after two separate acts of vandalism at war memorial monuments in Cleveland and Hervey Bay.

The pillar of a 106-year-old war memorial cenotaph in Anzac Park at Cleveland, east of Brisbane, was found broken on Sunday morning.

Photos show the pillar which sat atop the memorial shattered on the ground below.

A war memorial in Anzac Park in Cleveland was damaged overnight between Saturday and Sunday. (Supplied: Redlands RSL Facebook)

At around midday on Monday a 20-year-old Cleveland man attended a police station and is currently assisting police with their enquiries.

Police said they are looking for three other people reported in the area at the time.

Meanwhile, sub-branch president of the Hervey Bay RSL, Brad Gray, came to work on Monday morning to find the club's flagpole damaged.

CCTV footage shows a black Nissan Navara driving into the pole three times just before 7am.

Police attended the scene a short time later and apprehended a 38-year-old man in the vehicle nearby.

The man has been charged with a range of offences including wilful damage, possessing a knife in a public place and drug charges.

The vehicle had a mattress placed over its bonnet and windscreen.

Both incidents occurred just days before Remembrance Day.

Queensland Premier and Minister for Veterans David Crisafulli said the damage done to the Cleveland memorial was "disgraceful".

"We will watch the outcome very closely if it progresses through court, and it tougher laws are needed, they will be considered."

Hervey Bay RSL president Brad Gray said the vandalism won't stop Remembrance Day events. (Supplied)

Mr Gray said the damage to the RSL's flagpole was not good timing.

"I've got no hope I get anybody in to repair ir before Remembrance Day. It'll have to be like that."

"I don't get what these people get out of desecrating a war memorial," he said.

He said there are no changes planned for Wednesday's Remembrance Day events.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/n.title: NT teen 'keyboard warrior' charged with terrorism offences seeks bail
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/n.author: Roxanne Fitzgerald
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/n.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

By Roxanne Fitzgerald

Lawyers for a teenager facing terrorism charges in the NT says the boy poses no threat to the community. (Unsplash: Gilles Lambert)

A 14-year-old boy facing terrorism charges in the NT has applied for bail.

His lawyer argues he is not a danger to the community and that prolonged incarceration will worsen his mental health issues.

The case was adjourned until Friday, when the judge will rule on whether to grant bail.

A Northern Territory teenager charged with terrorism offences was a "young man fantasising while he's hating the world" and a "keyboard warrior" who should be "treated, not penalised" in custody, a court has heard.

The 14-year-old — who cannot be identified for legal reasons — was arrested on October 28, after the Joint Counter Terrorism Team searched his home following a tip-off from a member of the public.

He stands charged with one count of collecting documents likely to facilitate terrorist acts, one count of possessing violent extremist material and one count of possessing or controlling firearms and explosives manufacture material.

The teenager faced the NT Youth Justice Court via video link today, with his family filling the gallery as his lawyer argued he should be granted bail to continue seeing a psychologist.

The 14-year-old's defence lawyer says he is "troubled" but "not indoctrinated". (Unsplash: Nic Chi)

Defence lawyer Ian Rowbottam told the court the teenager was allegedly found in possession of videos featuring white supremacist Brenton Tarrant, who killed 51 people at two New Zealand mosques in 2019, and of the 1999 Columbine High School shooting.

He is also alleged to have been in possession of The Anarchist Cookbook, which was first published in the 1970s and includes instructions on how to make explosives and illicit drugs.

The court heard police also allege the boy had a document on his computer associated with white nationalists preparing for political conflict titled "hell fighter training", and another file featuring the words "blood lust" in red font.

He is also alleged to have possessed instructions on making a 3D-printed, semi-automatic gun.

Mr Rowbottam acknowledged his client had "looked at" the material, but said he was in no way dangerous, arguing "there is a very big difference between a young man fantasising while he's hating the world" and actually carrying out acts of violence.

"Yes, he is troubled, no, he is not indoctrinated, and in my submission, the suggestion of him being a danger to anyone would [need to] rely on some assertion that he is somehow indoctrinated into the far-right ideas," he said.

Ian Rowbottam says the videos his client accessed are widely available online.  (Unsplash: Jay Wennington)

"There is, in my submission, no link between this young man and far-right ideas.

"He doesn't like the world, and that is a problem that needs to be dealt with [through] appropriate mental health professionals.

"Incarceration is not going to achieve that, it will make the situation worse."

Mr Rowbottam said his client had "no finances or ability" to obtain material to make a 3D-printed gun, instructions for which he argued were "widely available on the internet".

The NT Police Commissioner has raised the alarm about the growing issue of extremism and radicalisation.

He said while the Crown alleged the teen had a formula for gun powder, there was "no suggestion of him trying to purchase any of this".

Mr Rowbottam said he had himself watched the video of the New Zealand massacre shortly after it happened and said the Columbine shooting video was "easily available" online.

He said the videos were "available on the internet" and "you don't need to get on the dark web to find them".

Mr Rowbottam said while there was no doubt those attacks were carried out by extremists, he disagreed with the Commonwealth's position that the material in itself promoted an extremist ideology.

He said he understood "blood lust" was a "C-grade" film.

Mr Rowbottam argued there were exceptional circumstances justifying the teenager's release to his mother's home, including that his stepfather had recently died, and that he should be "treated, not penalised".

He proposed conditions including a curfew and no access to the internet.

"We say the distress from the passing of his stepfather has put him in a position of acting out," he said.

Australian Federal Police investigators say the boy and a teenage girl arrested on similar charges last week knew each other. (Supplied)

Mr Rowbottam said the teenager had been receiving treatment for mental health issues for the past year but since being taken into custody had only received one session with a psychologist, which his mother had paid for.

Prosecutors opposed bail, but Judge Thomasin Opie requested a report on whether the teenager could access specialist help in custody.

Judge Opie reserved her decision on bail and the boy is scheduled to return to court on Friday.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/culture/202.title: ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ makes monster debut at the box office
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/culture/202.author: Alyssa I. Smith
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/culture/202.text:
Godzilla is once again proving to be a formidable box-office force, with the latest installment in the long-running kaijū (monster) franchise setting records in Japan before making a powerful debut abroad.

“Godzilla Minus Zero,” directed by Takashi Yamazaki, opened in Japan on Nov. 3 — Japan’s designated “Godzilla Day” in honor of when the original “Godzilla” debuted in Japanese theaters in 1954 — earning ¥910 million ($5.75 million) and attracting more than 590,000 moviegoers on its first day.

According to the film’s official X account, the opening-day takings marked the highest single-day box office revenue for a live-action film in Japanese history. A subsequent post announced that domestic attendance had passed 1 million within four days of release.

The sequel to 2023’s “Godzilla Minus One” continued its strong run overseas, opening in 3,254 North American theaters on Friday and grossing $14.5 million on opening day, taking the top spot in the daily box-office rankings.

It went on to gross $31.6 million over its opening weekend, making it the biggest debut to date for distributor Gkids and the strongest opening for a live-action foreign-language film since 2004’s “Hero.”

“Godzilla Minus Zero” is the first Japanese feature shot for IMAX screens, and it has brought in $21.3 million worldwide through Sunday from IMAX screens alone.

It recently screened at the Tokyo International Film Festival, which wrapped on Wednesday, as the event’s centerpiece film.

Its predecessor, “Godzilla Minus One,” earned roughly $105.4 million worldwide and became the highest grossing Japanese-language live-action film ever released in North America. It also made history as the first Japanese film to win the Academy Award for best visual effects at the 96th Academy Awards in 2024.

“When we were making ‘Minus One,’ going overseas wasn’t even a consideration, and it ended up reaching so many people,” Yamazaki, who also handled the screenplay and visual effects for both films, told The Japan Times in a recent interview. “Making something rooted in home isn’t the opposite of making something for the world.

“If we tried to imitate Hollywood, there’d be no point. Not thinking about overseas audiences is, paradoxically, how we think about them. That’s the only way Japanese films can really travel.”

https://www.dw.com/en/germany-news-germa.title: Germany news: Germany marks fateful date of November 9
https://www.dw.com/en/germany-news-germa.text:
Germany is commemorating the Nazi-led November pogroms 88 years ago. Events are also being held to mark the anniversary of the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989. DW has more.

This is a roundup of the stories from and about Germanyhitting the headlines on Monday, November 9, 2026:

Commemorations are to be held nationwide to commemorate the Nazi pogroms of November 9-10, 1938, when mobs went on an antisemitic rampage, killing at least 91 Jewish people, ransacking Jewish businesses and burning down hundreds of synagogues.

President Frank-Walter Steinmeier is to attend events in the eastern city of Weimar, where he is due to lay a wreath and hold a speech at the memorial site established at the site of the former Nazi concentration camp of Buchenwald.

The Jüdische Gemeinde zu Berlin is to have all the names of Jewish Nazi victims read out over the day in commemoration of the pogroms.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz will be attending a ceremony marking the 20th anniversary of the Ohel Jakob Main Synagogue in Munich, which was opened 68 years to the day after the main synagogue in the city was destroyed in the pogroms.

The pogroms are sometimes known as "Reichskristallnacht" or "Night of Broken Glass," but this name has fallen out of favor as underplaying the horrors of what happened.

Guten Tag from DW's newsroom on the banks of the Rhine in Bonn!

November 9 is known as the "day of destiny" in Germany, a day that has in the past seen both horrific events and others that have shaped the country in a more positive way.

Into the first category come the November pogroms of 1938, in which the Nazi regime unleashed a wave of antisemitic violence that led to the deaths of dozens of Jewish people and the burning of hundreds of synagogues.

Events will be held nationwide to commemorate the 88th anniversary of the pogroms, including some in Weimar attended by German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz will also attend a ceremony marking the 20th anniversary of the Ohel Jakob Main Synagogue, which opened 68 years to the day after the destruction of Munich's main synagogue in the pogroms.

But November 9, 1989, also saw the opening of the Berlin Wall, when thousands of East Berliners unexpectedly crossed into the west of the city, an event that eventually led to the reunification of Germany.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6pv.title: Scientists predict 2026 hottest year on record as climate talks begin
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6pv.text:
The world is on course for its hottest year on record as the planet is hit with warming from climate change and El Niño, scientists have told BBC News.

The warning comes as world leaders and negotiators gather in Turkey on Monday for the opening of COP31, the latest UN climate summit.

Berkeley Earth, the independent US research group behind the forecast, said that even with two months of the year left it is 95% confident that 2026 will surpass the previous record set in 2024.

The impact of rising heat has been felt acutely in recent months by countries attending COP, with extensive wildfires across Europe and the sudden glacier collapse in Nepal which killed more than 1,000 people.

"We have had a run of record warm years," said Dr Robert Rohde, of Berkeley Earth. "That is what we expect as global warming progresses… glaciers collapsing, record-breaking heatwaves and droughts."

On Friday, the EU's Copernicus climate service confirmed that October was the hottest on record.

But Rohde warned this was just the start. "There is potential for much larger and much more dramatic changes down the line," he said.

The main driver of rising global temperatures has been the increasing concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere, largely caused by burning fossil fuels.

The UN's World Meteorological Organization (WMO) published its own report on Monday, and although more cautious than Berkeley, it has forecast that 2026 will be among the four warmest years on record.

It said that 2027 will provide no let-up, as an unusually powerful El Niño will continue into next year, pushing temperatures higher.

WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo said it "gives new meaning to the phrase off the charts".

The findings underline the challenge facing negotiators gathering in the seaside Turkish city of Antalya for COP31.

At previous meetings the focus has been on reducing emissions - tackling the cause of climate change. But now an increasing number of nations are facing the reality of having to do that alongside adapting to new weather extremes as the planet warms.

"No single COP is a silver bullet. No single conference can bridge the chasm between the science and reality," Simon Stiell, the UN's climate chief, is expected to tell governments on the opening morning.

But he will add "the urgency of this moment must drive us forward. Global heating is already costing the Earth."

Last month the UK defence secretary warned the public and businesses to think about how they would cope with increasing natural disasters, including stockpiling food.

Wes Streeting pointed to wildfires this summer and record heat, which the Met Office has said was made 130 times more likely by climate change, as well as increased risk of flooding this winter as a result of El Niño.

Stephen Belcher, chief scientist at the Met Office, told BBC's Panorama: "We're designed for a climate of the 20th century that we don't live in any longer, so it's going to change all aspects of our lives."

The additional greenhouse gases being added to the atmosphere have trapped additional heat and about 90% of that has been absorbed by the oceans.

That's where El Niño comes in, said Saulo. "It doesn't add new heat to the planet. It releases heat from the ocean, which is the warmest ever measured. There is simply more heat available to release."

This natural climate pattern is pushing global temperatures even higher.

The world is currently on track for 2.8C of warming above pre-industrial levels by the end of the century - all but guaranteed to exceed the goal of 1.5C set under the Paris Agreement to avoid the worst effects of climate change.

Countries will negotiate for two weeks with leaders, including Prime Minister Andy Burnham, attending the conference this week.

Previous climate summits have yielded new targets for countries to follow on cutting fossil fuels, increasing money for developing countries and protections for forests.

Although emissions continue to increase, countries have also made significant progress in increasing renewable energy capacity. The International Energy Agency has predicted growth in the next six years will be 57% greater than the previous period.

Stiell is also expected to say that expanding renewable energy was both a climate and economic solution for recent energy shocks. "Global renewables saved around half a trillion dollars last year."

The Turkish government says it wants discussions this year to focus on a new goal for electrification - moving energy systems away from fossil fuels towards electricity - and cutting waste levels.

But the discussion is likely to split countries.

Early drafts of the EU position seen by the BBC make clear they would only sign up to a goal on electrification if it did not allow countries to meet the target using gas.

"It is important that progress on electrification is underpinned by clean energy sources," it said in a memo to members.

But nations, such as Saudi Arabia and Russia, have previously pushed the interim use of gas as a "cleaner" fossil fuel alternative to coal.

Celeste Saulo of the WMO said she could not offer an explanation as to why countries have previously not reached agreement on certain issues, but said "what I see are the impacts of what this lack of consensus generates with more extreme events".

The BBC understands that the UK government is reluctant to set any new goals at COP31 and thinks the focus should be on achieving existing agreements.

However, in September the government was criticised by MPs on the International Development Committee for cutting its aid budget meaning it could not fulfil previous climate funding commitments.

Wealthier nations had agreed at previous COP meetings to triple the amount of money going to developing countries to help them adapt to climate change to at least $85bn (£63bn) by 2035.

The latest data from 2024 shows that countries have reached about a third of that figure, but the UN said this week that the current damage from climate change being experienced is "substantial" and much more money could be needed.

But many countries have redirected aid budgets towards defence spending and short-term financial relief for households as gas and oil prices spike following the Iran-US war.

Governments are also expected to use the forum to discuss global AI policy including the growing demand for energy and water resources from data centres underpinning the technology's rollout.

Additional reporting by Miho Tanaka.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Adam Gabbatt in New York
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Trump’s most controversial aide begins his first day as White House chief of staff

Stephen Miller, the influential architect of Donald Trump’s aggressive immigration crackdown, is due to start as White House chief of staff today. His promotion has horrified many, handing even more power to the president’s most controversial aide.

The 41-year-old has been with Trump since the beginning of the US president’s political career – serving as a speechwriter during his 2016 presidential campaign – and has long been seen as a hardliner on the right, serving as the driving force behind first-term Trump policies such as family separation at the US-Mexico border and the travel ban on people from many Muslim-majority countries.

Here is Miller in some of his own words:

“We are being conquered,” Miller told Fox News in 2023.

“This is a complete resettlement of America in real time. It took hundreds of years, going back long even before our founding, going back all the way to the earliest days of the colonies in America to slowly build everything that we have.

“And now we have millions of people coming in from different cultures and different ways of living and different belief systems. They’re going to take those belief systems with them to America.

“So, a generation from now, I am telling you … people will not know the country that they are living in. These consequences are permanent. Unless there’s massive large-scale deportations by the millions, it will be irrevocable.”

In an interview with CNN’s Wolf Blitzer in 2018, Miller was asked about Trump’s plan to abruptly pull troops out of Syria.

“Isis [Islamic State] has been defeated. But if Isis wants to retrench and regrow and reorganize, it’s going to be up to those countries to defeat their enemy.

“Wolf, when did the American people sign up to be in every war in every place on every side of every conflict all over planet Earth?”

Pretti, a 37-year-old intensive care nurse who was observing immigration officers in Minneapolis, was shot and killed by federal immigration agents in January.

In a post on X, Miller described Pretti as “a domestic terrorist”. In a separate post, responding to criticism of Pretti’s killing, Miller responded: “An assassin tried to murder federal agents and this is your response.”

His description is at odds with footage showing him being tackled and shot by border patrol officers.

“The United States is the power of NATO. For the United States to secure the arctic region, to protect and defend NATO and NATO interests, obviously, Greenland should be part of the United States.”

Asked by CNN host Jake Tapper if he would “take it off the table” that the US would use force to seize Greenland, Miller said: “The United States should have Greenland as part of the United States. There’s no need to even think or talk about this in the context that you’re asking, of a military operation. Nobody’s going to fight the US militarily over the future of Greenland.”

The US supreme court blocked Trump’s attempt to ban birthright citizenship – which asserts that nearly all people born on US soil are American citizens – in June, prompting Miller to claim the ruling was “a deep knife wound in the heart of the American republic”.

Miller told Fox News: “We have people from all over the world, from third-world nations, nations that on their own would have never invented the wheel, let alone modern technology, let alone medicine, let alone air travel. And they can just come into the country, have a baby at a hospital paid for by you and me, and then that baby is automatically a citizen? That baby can sit on a jury when he turns 18 and sit in judgment of you and sit in judgment of me and sit in judgment of our loved ones? Can decide who our mayors are? Our governors are? Our presidents are?”

Miller added: “If your ruling requires you to suicide your civilization, your reading of the Constitution is wrong.”

In January the US attacked Venezuela and captured its long-serving president Nicolás Maduro, with Trump hailing the attack – in which at least 40 people, including civilians and Venezuelan soldiers, died – as “an assault like people have not seen since world war two”.

Two weeks earlier Miller had posted on social media: “American sweat, ingenuity and toil created the oil industry in Venezuela. Its tyrannical expropriation was the largest recorded theft of American wealth and property. These pillaged assets were then used to fund terrorism and flood our streets with killers, mercenaries and drugs.”

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: ‘A new age of climate extremes’: Earth accumulating heat at accelerating rate
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Damien Gayle Environment correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
Increased heat will supercharge extreme weather events, warns UN agency as Cop31 climate summit begins

Heat is accumulating in Earth’s systems at an accelerating rate, the UN’s weather agency has reported as the Cop31 climate change summit begins in Turkey, with 2026 on track to be one of the four warmest years on record.

The imbalance between incoming energy from the sun and energy leaving Earth reached its highest level since monitoring began, the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) said in its State of the Global Climate update.

That imbalance and the accumulation of heat will supercharge extreme weather events such as heatwaves, droughts and tropical cyclones.

Around the world, the average surface temperature for January to September 2026 was about 1.47C above the preindustrial average, the agency said. Sea surface temperatures hit monthly records and sea level was the highest since records began. The ocean absorbs 90% of the excess heat trapped by greenhouse gases and 2026 is on track to be a 10th successive year of record ocean heat.

“We have entered a new age of climate extremes,” said António Guterres, the UN secretary general. “A supersized El Niño is colliding with a planet already superheated by manmade climate change. Climate records keep falling. The human costs keep rising. And those least responsible are suffering first and worst.”

Diplomats and world leaders are meeting on Monday in the Turkish resort city of Antalya for the 31st conference of the parties (Cop) to the UN framework convention on climate change. In 1992, when the convention was signed, the atmospheric concentration of carbon dioxide, the primary greenhouse gas, was 356.42 parts per million (ppm). In 2025 it was 426.8 ppm, the WMO said. Overall, since 1750, the onset of the Industrial Revolution, the concentration has increased 53%.

The WMO reported that ocean heat content estimates indicate Earth’s energy imbalance rose at a rate of 0.3W per sq metre each decade for the period 2001–2025, compared with 0.13W per sq metre between 1960 and 2025.

Accordingly, 2026 is on track to be one of the four warmest years on record globally, making 2023 to 2026 the four warmest years since records began.

The year started with La Niña conditions in the Pacific, which typically act as a brake on global temperatures, lowering the average by about 0.1-0.2C. A brewing El Niño, a phenomenon that warms global temperatures, and whose latest iteration is forecast to be stronger than any to have taken place in the past 1,000 years, makes it likely that the final mean temperature for 2026 will be higher than 1.47C above the pre-industrial average.

Heat in the upper 2,000 metres (6,500ft) of the ocean in 2025 was the highest in the observed record and was accelerating, the WMO said. “This warming is projected to continue, representing a change that is irreversible on centennial to millennial timescales,” according to the report.

At the poles, Antarctic sea ice reached its third-lowest annual maximum ever in 2026, while the Arctic maximum was the lowest or second lowest. Elsewhere in the cryosphere, glaciers lost more than 400 gigatonnes of mass. It was the fourth consecutive year in which all 19 glacierised regions around the world experienced mass loss, the WMO said.

Bill McGuire, a professor emeritus of geophysical and climate hazards at University College London, said there were “no surprises” from the report, “to the extent that every measure reported, whether it be global temperature, sea level rise or sea ice extent, points to the fact that we are in deep shit”.

He said: “Of most concern is the growing imbalance between the incoming energy from the sun and that leaving the planet. Increasing greenhouse gas concentrations in the atmosphere mean that while the heat coming in stays the same, that going out is steadily decreasing as our world hangs on to more and more of it.

“It is this growing imbalance – rather than just emissions – that most accurately tracks global heating and how quickly our planet will continue to heat up in the decades to come. This is because natural feedbacks are now coming into play that are driving up the temperature more rapidly than 20 years ago.

“The latest research suggests we will cross the 1.5C limit permanently in 2028, and with the planet now heating at an extraordinary rate of 0.4C a decade, we can expect to smash through 2C in the late 2030s.

“The widely publicised idea that we are still on track for 2.6-2.8C by the end of the century now seems wildly optimistic, if not downright impossible.”

https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.title: MotoGP: Bezzecchi denies Marquez world title as motorsport returns to Qatar
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.text:
Marc Marquez has been made to wait another two weeks to win his eighth MotoGP title after finishing behind Marco Bezzecchi at the Qatar Grand Prix in Lusail as motorsport returned to the country after a delay due to the United States-Israel war on Iran.

Ducati’s Marquez had a chance to retain his crown on Sunday after winning the sprint race but needed his closest rival, Jorge Martin, to finish without any points.

Pole-sitter Bezzecchi claimed his sixth GP win of the season to cut the gap separating him from Marquez to 74 points.

However, the Italian, who is third in the championship standings, essentially has no chance of winning his first world title because that gap is the same as the number of points that remain available.

Bezzecchi was undone on Saturday by crashing out of the sprint race when trying to overtake Marquez in a desperate attempt to put pressure on the Spaniard.

“It feels amazing,” Bezzecchi said after he bounced back to win on Sunday. “I’m very happy. It was the performance we deserved

“It’s been a fantastic weekend for us. I’ve been super quick and super comfortable on the bike.

“It’s a shame for yesterday, but it’s part of the game, and to bounce back like this makes everything even better.”

Martin couldn’t quite emulate his heroics from Saturday when he shot up from 11th on the grid to nearly overtake eventual winner Marquez before eventually finishing third.

But racing this weekend for the first time since suffering a broken right wrist, Martin was given a warm round of applause from his team after keeping the title race alive.

Martin, Bezzecchi’s teammate at Aprilia, finished seventh and is still in contention even though he is 60 points off the pace with two race weekends remaining.

But Marquez could claim a record-equalling eighth premier class title, one more than his great rival Valentino Rossi, if he finishes two points ahead of Martin in the Portimao sprint in two weeks.

“[My strategy] was just to try to manage the race for the first five laps,” Marquez said.

“I saw that in one part of the race, I was super fast, but I knew that riding on that riding style, I was eating the front tyre.

“Third position was [would have been] OK, but I saw that [Raul] Fernandez was struggling, so you never know. I attack and four points more.”

Fernandez finished third at Qatar’s MotoGP, which marked the return of major motorsport to the region for the first time since the war on Iran began.
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.summary: Marc Marquez finished behind Marco Bezzecchi at Qatar Grand Prix in Lusail. The Spaniard is now 74 points behind his closest rival Jorge Martin in the title race. Marquez could win his eighth MotoGP title if he finishes two points ahead of Martin in Portimao.

https://www.wired.com/story/bug-activist.title: Bikers and Bug-Lovers Join Forces to Fight a New Google Data Center
https://www.wired.com/story/bug-activist.author: Joel Khalili
https://www.wired.com/story/bug-activist.text:
ON WEDNESDAY AFTERNOON, Jamie Robins strolled up to the entrance of Google’s UK headquarters in Kings Cross, London. He brandished a letter containing details of a petition signed by almost 55,000 people, calling for Google to abandon plans to build a large new data center in Thurrock, 15 miles to the east of London.

Robins works for wildlife conservation trust Buglife, part of an unlikely alliance of special-interest groups trying to block the Thurrock development. Buglife and local wildlife groups fear for an endangered plant, rare bumblebee, and other invertebrates whose habitat they say will be destroyed. Nonprofit Foxglove says the data center will emit too much pollution. The Thurrock Hammers motorcycle club wants to return to racing on the site.

Members of the various groups joined Robins outside Google’s office last Wednesday, holding placards demanding the company “search elsewhere” for somewhere to put its facility.

Across the UK, companies like Google are preparing to build industrial-scale data centers, part of a scramble to meet the swelling demand for the compute needed to run artificial intelligence models and other digital services. The UK government is eager to encourage them, hoping to capture a share of the hundreds of billions of dollars flowing into the AI industry and minimize the country’s dependence on foreign partners for compute. But like in the US, people living near to the proposed developments are making their objections known and trying to gum up the works.

Google says its plans for the Thurrock site prioritize biodiversity and the reduction of emissions. “We share the concerns that Buglife and others have—and their expectation that this site should be developed sustainably,” Adam Elman, director of sustainability EMEA at Google, tells WIRED. But the situation in Thurrock underscores the level and breadth of resistance that data center developers face as the public mood towards them appears to sour. Though small, the demonstration outside Google was one of a number of anti-data center protests that took place across Europe last week. In Amsterdam, protesters scaled a crane at a Microsoft data center site and unfurled a “fuck AI” banner.

“There’s local campaign groups against data centers popping up every week,” says Robins. “People are angry about data centers turning up in their back gardens. They’re angry about data centers flouting local opinion—and about the impact it has on wildlife.”

The Thurrock site is located next to a fuel stop, where an arterial road meets the highway that encircles London. On the plot, the remnants of Arena Essex, a disused motorcycle racing stadium, border grassland scribbled with old footpaths, and a lake.

Google acquired the site through a subsidiary in 2023. In May last year, it applied for permission to build a data center campus there. When locals caught wind, they coordinated with national wildlife and environmental groups and began to kick up a fuss. Of the 1,000 responses submitted by members of the public to the planning authority, only one supported the project. (Thurrock Council says that many of the responses were submitted by people living outside the local area.)

The protest group argues that Google’s proposal fails to properly account for the negative effects of the data center development: the loss of the raceway sporting facility, the destruction of habitat for rare flora and fauna, and the up to 570,000 tonnes of emissions it could produce each year—which Foxglove claims cannot be accommodated under the UK government’s carbon budget.

“We’re an outlier. We object on different grounds. I think that’s why I think we’re quite useful to the whole campaign,” says Mark Sexton, director at the Thurrock Hammers motorcycle club. “The unlikely alliance has got some attention.”

Google says the objections are grounded in misconceptions about its plans. The company claims it will achieve a net gain in biodiversity by retaining habitat and transplanting endangered plants to another location; and that it will offset the emissions by financing new sources of renewable energy generation, with a view to becoming carbon-neutral by 2030. Google argues that razing the motorcycle stadium will not result in the loss of an invaluable community facility because the track has already been out of use for a number of years. “We want to be good neighbors,” says Elman. “We recognize the ecological value of these sites. Our goal is to minimize the impact as much as possible.”

Unconvinced by Google’s reassurances, the protesters intend to continue to fight the development—one small act of protest at a time. “Do I think we’ve got much hope? Not right now,” says Rob Pownall, founder of nonprofit Protect The Wild, who attended Wednesday’s demonstration. “But this is another chip off that massive ice block.”

There are some signs the grassroots anti-data center movement is starting to win concessions. In the US, some states have instituted permitting freezes and data center moratoria, and pro-data center candidates were roundly crushed in this week’s midterm elections. In the UK, Foxglove recently succeeded in a legal challenge that forced the government to withdraw planning permission for a data center to the west of London.

Thurrock Council tells WIRED it expects to rule on Google’s initial planning application early next year. After that, the company will need to come up with a more granular plan for developing the site, which will be subject to another lengthy vetting process. The protesters say they intend to make life hard for Google at every step.

“These planning campaigns can go on for years,” says Robins. “It’s a war of attrition.”
https://www.wired.com/story/bug-activist.summary: Google is planning to build a data center in Thurrock, 15 miles to the east of London. Buglife and local wildlife groups fear for an endangered plant, rare bumblebee, and other invertebrates whose habitat will be destroyed. Google says its plans for the Thurrock site prioritize biodiversity and the reduction of emissions.

https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/former.title: Former OpenAI Engineer Pleads Not Guilty to Planting Covert Device in Executive Meeting Room
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/former.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/former.text:
The OpenAI engineer who was arrested and charged last month for planting a covert audio recording device in the company's office has pleaded not guilty.

According to reports from Bloomberg and CNBC, Saudi national Abdulrahman Alfozan made an appearance in San Francisco federal court on Friday, where he entered the plea. His next hearing is scheduled for November 17, 2026.

If proven guilty, the 35-year-old faces a maximum of five years in prison and a $250,000 fine, followed by three years of supervised release. He has been held without bail since his arrest on October 9, 2026.

Late last month, a grand jury indicted Alfozan on a single count of interception of oral communications.

Prosecutors allege that the former OpenAI employee placed a "sophisticated recording device" in an executive OpenAI conference room in what has been described as an attempt to unlawfully record sensitive conversations.

He was arrested three days before he, along with his wife and son, were scheduled to fly from San Francisco to Riyadh on a one-way ticket.

"His wife and son, however, immediately left the United States without him," U.S. prosecutors said. "Rather than wait until the October 12 flight as booked, they initially planned to fly to Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, on October 11 on a one-way ticket booked and paid for by the Saudi government."

"That flight was canceled, however, when a member of the Saudi military booked and paid for yet another one-way ticket for the defendant's wife and son, this one business class to Doha, Qatar, on October 10, 2026. They did make that flight, departing San Francisco about 36 hours after the defendant was arrested."

In a subsequent court filing, it was alleged that Alfozan was in frequent contact with a member of the Saudi Royal Family via WhatsApp. He was also deemed a flight risk, with court documents claiming that the defendant took great pains to create bespoke, encrypted recording devices to record sensitive meetings involving senior OpenAI personnel and executives.

https://www.carbonbrief.org/qa-what-is-t.title: Q&A: What is the Belém-Antalya mechanism for a ‘just transition’?
https://www.carbonbrief.org/qa-what-is-t.author: Molly Lempriere
https://www.carbonbrief.org/qa-what-is-t.text:
One of the key expected outcomes from the upcoming COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, is the launch of a “just transition mechanism”.

This follows years of calls from civil society to support a “just transition” as countries shift towards low-emissions energy systems and away from fossil fuels.

At the COP30 UN climate talks last year in the Brazilian city of Belém parties agreed to establish a “mechanism” to support this goal, called the “Belém-Antalya mechanism” (BAM).

Groups that have championed the BAM want it to act as a central hub on just transitions, providing support for workers and communities around the world.

However, the details of exactly what the much-touted BAM will consist of remain vague, with developed and developing countries disagreeing about its functions and purpose.

Disagreements continued at the UN climate talks in Bonn in June 2026, including on the crucial question of how the BAM will be financed.

Here, Carbon Brief looks at where the idea for the BAM came from, how it could support just transitions and what to expect from COP31.

A “just transition” is the idea that workers and communities should be supported in the shift to a low-carbon economy. It is a central principle behind the idea of climate justice.

Often, the term refers to those linked to the fossil-fuel industry, but it can also refer to transitions taking place in agriculture, heavy industry and various other sectors.

The concept originated in the 1980s, when US labour unions forged alliances with environmental justice groups. It has since become a key part of international climate discussions.

The preamble to the 2015 Paris Agreement includes a commitment to “tak[e] into account the imperatives of a just transition of the workforce and the creation of decent work and quality jobs in accordance with nationally defined development priorities”.

Bert De Wel, policy officer at the International Trade Union Confederation (ITUC), tells Carbon Brief:

“The labour movement is very happy with the wide audience and broad political support that the concept has received since its inception in the 1980s. The inclusion in the Paris Agreement, with the reference to the creation of decent work and quality jobs was a milestone for the movement. While other demands have been added…we continue to stress the labour dimension as being central to the concept.”

Three years after the creation of the Paris Agreement, at COP24 in the former coal-mining city of Katowice, the Polish presidency highlighted the issue of just transitions.

The need for carbon-cutting policies to ensure “a just transition of the workforce” that creates “decent work and quality jobs” was included in the “Silesia declaration”, issued by the presidency during the first week of COP24.

While the declaration was only signed by 50 countries – roughly a quarter of the parties at the summit – it was still “noted” in the final COP text.

This helped to drive momentum behind the idea, culminating in formal agreement at COP27 in Egypt to launch a “work programme on just transition” (JTWP).

De Wel says the establishment of the JTWP was a “major step forward” that allowed parties to “speak about just transition in more concrete terms”.

In the years since, negotiators have worked to flesh out the JTWP, with disagreements between parties about what its purpose should be.

Broadly, developed countries would like it to focus on domestic workforces, while some nations want a more global outlook, including support for transitions in developing countries.

The JTWP has proved a challenging negotiating space, with talks at the COP29 summit in 2024 closing without an agreement, in what one observer dubbed a “betrayal”.

However, despite these frustrations, parties at COP30 in Brazil agreed to establish a new institutional mechanism on just transitions, which has become widely known as the BAM. The move was hailed as a “victory” by civil society.

In the run-up to COP30, civil society began to push for the establishment of an “institutional arrangement” that would move work under the JTWP from talk into action.

(This was originally called the “Belém action mechanism” by civil society groups, who subsequently updated this to the “Belém-Antalya mechanism” following the outcome at COP30. However, in the JTWP text agreed at COP30 it is only described as a “mechanism”, sometimes also referred to as the “just transition mechanism”.)

Anabella Rosemberg, senior advisor on just transition at NGO umbrella group Climate Action Network (CAN) International, tells Carbon Brief:

“The idea of the mechanism emerged from the collaboration of civil society, trade unions, feminist groups, youth and Indigenous peoples in the UNFCCC.

“It was clear that the kind of activities being run under the JTWP – two dialogues a year and one ministerial – would not support the delivery of just-transition strategies on the ground, so a new approach was developed to get words into action.”

Following the inception of the idea, civil society did “tonnes of stuff to boost it up the agenda”, Dr Leon Sealey-Huggins, a senior campaigner at the charity War on Want, tells Carbon Brief.

This ranged from presenting demands and proposals to different constituents, organising joint letters and writing policy papers, all the way through to designing logos, creating memes and even a song.

These efforts ultimately paid off: during the Bonn climate negotiations in June 2025, one draft text included the idea for a new institutional arrangement. One of the options in the draft text was for a “toolbox, guidance framework, global platform, technical assistance network [or] mechanism”.

This inclusion was broadly welcomed as a “big win” for civil society groups, although parties acknowledged that more needed to be done to flesh out the idea.

Going into COP30, civil society groups continued to push the idea of creating a BAM, with protests, banners and badges visible around the venue.

Early in negotiations, the G77 and China – a large coalition of developing countries at UN climate talks – put forward their own proposal for a just transition “mechanism”. This, they suggested, could provide technical assistance, support international cooperation and help to foster partnerships in an effort to address implementation gaps.

Their proposal faced initial pushback from developed-country parties including Norway, the UK and others, who opposed it due to concerns that it would duplicate existing systems and require additional funding.

Developed countries also opposed the use of the term “mechanism”, with the EU suggesting an “action plan” as a potential alternative. Nevertheless, the creation of a “mechanism” was included in the final draft text on the JTWP.

This text was formally approved during the COP30 closing plenary to extended applause from many in the hall.

In a statement at the time, Chiara Martinelli, director at CAN Europe, welcomed the decision:

“Delivering BAM was a major civil society win. It creates a coordinated institutional home to drive forward progress on the just transition.”

The decision to develop the mechanism included a request for parties to work over the subsequent year – through to COP31 – on a plan to get things started.

According to civil society, the BAM could help tackle the fractured just-transition landscape by centralising resources and helping to overcome a number of barriers.

Speaking to Carbon Brief, Rosemberg says the just-transition space “lacks coordination and the right kind of support and is quite disconnected from climate action imperatives”. She adds:

“The BAM can play a role in bringing those [people] trying to make just transition happen together, identify gaps and barriers, foster cooperation and accelerate support.”

Civil society has put forward a number of proposals likely to inform the structure of the BAM. Most consist of a mechanism with three parts, which would encompass and expand upon the work that is currently being carried out under the JTWP.

One proposal by a coalition of five NGOs suggests the mechanism is formed of a steering body, a “knowledge arm” and an “implementation arm”.

The steering body would coordinate the work of the two arms of the BAM, including deciding the topics that should be discussed under the ongoing JTWP, which will continue to feature in climate negotiations. They suggest the body would recommend topics that require negotiation when “gaps that require political guidance are identified”.

Their proposal is illustrated in the infographic below, showing the steering body acting as a central hub for work within the BAM.

The final part of the BAM, the “implementation arm”, would act as a hub to enable and coordinate technical, financial and knowledge-based assistance for those pursuing a just transition.

Rosemberg says the vision of civil society is for work to go “beyond negotiators’ dialogues”. She says the BAM could enable the organisation of a “matchmaking platform” to provide support faster, as well as dedicated groups to identify and mobilise financial resources. She adds:

“Finally, through bottom-up identification of barriers, the BAM can also allow a discussion on enabling just transition that is informed by practitioners. The BAM can show that implementation does not necessarily mean taking issues outside of the UNFCCC.”

A separate proposal for the structure of the BAM from the Global Campaign to Demand Climate Justice (DCJ) – a separate coalition of NGOs – similarly proposes three elements. These would be: coordination and coherence; knowledge generation; and international cooperation and support.

Sealey-Huggins, who is affiliated with DCJ, notes:

“If it works in practice, what we’ll see is a cascade of just-transition policies implemented across countries, across sectors in a unifying, transformational moment for justice-centered climate action, and that will be the key to unlocking the transition that’s been missing so far.”

Another proposal for the BAM comes from the Grantham Institute at the London School of Economics. It suggests the three functions of the mechanism should be capacity-building, technical assistance and knowledge-sharing, but it recommends a dual-arm structure comprising a policy arm and an operational arm.

De Wel tells Carbon Brief that while there is “rather broad consensus on the functions”, parties are pushing in “very different directions” on how the BAM will be set up.

Within UN climate negotiations, some parties have raised concerns about the potential cost of the mechanism.

The push to launch the BAM comes at a time when the UNFCCC itself is facing a funding gap, following the US withdrawal. Several other parties have also delayed or reduced their contributions, in response to changes in domestic priorities.

This has led to the UNFCCC cancelling events and not filling vacated positions, as the organisation struggles to carry out its existing functions.

As such, some parties have expressed hesitancy about creating another mechanism under the remit of the UNFCCC, which also requires funding. However, proponents of the BAM argue that the costs of running it would be minimal.

Rosemberg tells Carbon Brief that the BAM represents “an opportunity to streamline and make efficient use of public resources”. She adds:

“The mechanism does not necessarily require the creation of a costly new institution. Instead, it can leverage existing climate-finance channels and philanthropy.”

She adds that a “similar body” to the potential mechanism, the Climate Technology Centre and Network, costs less than $10m a year. Rosemberg notes that this is “not an impossible amount to be found if there is political will to make just transition happen”.

De Wel notes that the mechanism will build on existing work inside the UNFCCC and out, including the International Labour Organization’s “just transition policy gateway”. He further emphasises that “we’re clearly not asking for a new [just-transition] fund, we want all climate finance to be just-transition proof”.

Alongside highlighting the potential efficiencies of the BAM design, many have argued that the potential benefits are well worth the cost of the new mechanism, with Sealey-Huggins telling Carbon Brief:

“The cost to the [BAM] secretariat pales in comparison to the potential benefit of the action.”

Despite the “victory” in Belém of agreeing to set up the new just-transition mechanism, climate negotiations in Bonn in June 2026 quickly hit sticking points.

While Bonn did ultimately agree on a “skeleton” draft text to send forward for further negotiations at COP31, many details still need to be agreed in Antalya for the BAM to start functioning.

De Wel cautions that a “swift approval of the agenda of COP31 allowing parties to start the negotiations” is “crucial”. He adds:

“We can’t lose any time, there is so much work that needs to be done on [just transition]. Then we need a constructive approach by the major country blocs. If one of them starts playing tactical games, then it will be lost.”

In a submission to the UNFCCC earlier this year, CAN called for a series of measures to get the BAM up and running. This includes calling for a decision to be made on a first face-to-face meeting of a “just-transition committee” – a core part of the mechanism in the group’s proposal – to be held in April 2027.

Ahead of COP31, negotiating groups such as the Alliance of Small Island States (AOSIS), the least developed countries (LDCs) and the African group expressed support for the mechanism and called for it to be focused on implementation.

The EU also supported the launch of the mechanism, but along with other parties cautioned that it should be complementary to the JTWP.

While no submissions opposed the creation of the mechanism, groups such as LDCs called for a focus on “means of implementation” – commonly understood as finance – highlighting it is likely to continue to be a key point of discussion in the upcoming summit.

Sealey-Huggins tells Carbon Brief what his “pie in the sky best-case scenario vision” for the outcome at COP31 would look like. He continues:

“G77 and China make the case again that the mechanism must be equally resourced. It must be well-designed. It must include people’s participation. It must address the barriers to implementation of just transition. It must facilitate the means of implementation. It must ensure justice at the very heart of climate action.

“And then it’s agreed and it’s implemented immediately. So this work begins straight after Antalya to start forming committees and other bodies that can undertake the implementation.”

However, Rosemberg cautions that there is still a “question mark [remaining over] the level of ambition of the [COP31] presidencies, who need to move from simply talking about establishing any [just-transition] mechanism to engaging parties, so that we get a mechanism that is fit for purpose”.

US President Donald Trump said that his mass deportation of undocumented immigrants was "too tough", according to an excerpt of an interview with CBS aired Sunday.

Asked about his deportation policy, Trump told CBS' "60 Minutes": "I think it was too tough ... I think it might be too tough."

The excerpt was published by CBS on X ahead of a broadcast of the interview on network TV later Sunday. It was recorded after the Republican Party's heavy loss in midterm elections on Tuesday.

To display this content from X (Twitter), you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.

While Trump has won some domestic support for securing the US southern border, his administration's aggressive push to deport millions of undocumented migrants has drawn widespread criticism.

However, Trump on Friday appointed the architect of that hardline policy, Stephen Miller, as his chief of staff on Friday, signaling a bare-knuckle fightback after the Republican election loss.

Trump announces immigration hardliner Stephen Miller as new chief of staff

Miller has been synonymous with scenes of masked immigration agents committing violence after he backed federal agents who shot and killed two Americans early this year.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/w.author: Emma Wynne, Oliver Peterson, and Lucie Bell
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/w.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Consumer Protection

Burk Fuel has 14 outlets across Western Australia.  (ABC)

The WA Commissioner for Consumer Protection is taking Burk Fuel to court over allegations the octane rating of fuel at its service stations has been misrepresented.

The agency says samples tested between July 2025 and February 2026 came back as unleaded 91.

Burk Fuel has previously denied the allegations, saying it sources its fuel from supplier to many Perth service stations.

A chain of Perth petrol stations sold unleaded 91 fuel as  higher octane 95 and 98 fuel, WA's consumer watchdog has alleged, prompting it to begin a civil claim against the company in the Supreme Court for alleged breaches of the Australian Consumer Law.

Burk Fuel operates 14 outlets across Perth and regional WA.

In a statement released on Monday the Consumer Protection Agency said it had ordered independent testing on samples taken from several of its service stations between July 2025 and February this year.

"All of the samples came back as 91 fuel," Consumer Protection Commissioner Trish Blake told 102.5 ABC Perth.

Ms Blake said that would constitute a "massive breach of trust for the consumers" if the allegations were found to be true.

"Particularly for something like fuel, where you do not have the independent ability as a consumer to inspect the product and know if you're getting what you've paid for," she said.

"You have to be able to rely and trust on the trader."

Trish Blake says the agency will seek significant penalties if the allegations are upheld. (ABC News: Cason Ho)

When authorities announced the investigation in April this year, Burk Fuel strenuously denied the allegations, saying they used a reputable supplier and their fuel was regularly tested.

Unleaded 91 is regarded as the minimum standard for most petrol cars. Higher-octane 95 and 98 fuels are recommended or required for more high-performance vehicles.

Ms Blake said buying allegedly mislabelled fuel could have a significant impact on customers.

"It's a significant difference in value," she said.

"But also a lot of the high-performance cars only run well on the high-performance fuel.

"Some people will have been putting, in good faith, what they believe to be premium 98 unleaded fuel into their high-performance car."

Unleaded 91 is cheaper than higher-octane varieties of fuel. (ABC News: Abbey Haberecht)

Ms Blake said the agency would seek significant financial penalties if the allegations were proven true in court.

She said the agency had also sampled fuel from other traders in Western Australia.

"I was very pleased to find that all the other traders, all of their fuel samples came back exactly as they were being promoted to the consumer," Ms Blake said.

The investigation was sparked after a consumer contacted 102.5 ABC Perth, raising questions about fuel quality at Burk Fuel.

Ms Blake praised the person for coming forward.

"They're an absolute deadset legend in my book, because the more that we can help consumers to have trust in the economy and keep traders honest, the better it is for everyone," she said.

In a statement, Burk Fuel said it intended to defend the proceedings.

"Burk's operations continue to operate as normal. Burk will not be commenting further while the matter is before the court."

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/commentary/.title: Voters reset the debate on data centers and billionaires
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/commentary/.author: Dave Lee
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/commentary/.text:
For much of the past year, the debate among AI leaders has been whether to slow the pace of artificial-intelligence development. Last week, those outside of that select community finally had their say. Voters of all stripes chose to pull hard on the only lever available to them.

Building data centers in the U.S. just became even more difficult, but perhaps as important, voters issued a challenge to the AI billionaires behind them.

Victorious Democrats must now contend with the outcome while ensuring U.S. AI labs remain competitive on the global stage. In China, the bottleneck is in finding enough cutting-edge chips to fill its AI factories. In the U.S., the challenge is building enough factories to hold all of its chips. Which scarcity proves the greater handicap in the AI race remains to be seen.

Americans were compelled to the polls for many reasons, but scrutiny of data-center projects — and the rejection of tech money — was a recurring theme. Just after the polls closed, of the 41 data-center-related ballot measures tracked by Ballotpedia, all but one passed in favor of preventing, restricting or otherwise exerting additional controls on development.

In Texas, Elon Musk’s $224 million — part of his $474 million in spending on the midterms — ended up being more of a gift to the eventual Senate winner, James Talarico, who held it up as an example of the corrosive influence of Musk and Big Tech. The state’s next governor, Gina Hinojosa, the first Democrat to hold that position in more than three decades, promised a data-center moratorium. Data-center builders, Bloomberg News reported, are facing their “worst case scenario.” Or, in Musk’s words: “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now.”

He won’t need to put them there just yet. The midterm results do not grind data-center construction to a halt in the U.S. Musk’s SpaceX is on course to add 13 gigawatts of data-center capacity by the end of 2027, though it might be a challenge to power it. That buildout is more than Google added in data-center capacity from 1999 to the end of 2025, according to SemiAnalysis.

But this result will present an obstacle for further expansion plans across the industry, particularly those earmarked for 2028. There’s no point in sugarcoating it, said Yorkville Ives analyst Dan Ives. “Will these midterm elections slow the pace of the planned 800 to 1,000 data centers across the U.S. fueling the AI Revolution?” he asked in a note. “The answer in our view is a clear YES.”

Yet once the victory lap is over, Democrats must tread with caution. A vote against a data center is not necessarily one against AI in all its forms, and it certainly doesn’t signal opposition to economic growth of the kind AI is expected to bring. There is a risk that empty fields — projects that could have been — might come to symbolize Democrats squandering America’s leadership in AI. At the same time, a buzzing, humming data center in rural Ohio might become a monument to a broken promise.

The answer is to build data centers but on better terms. Before the midterms, AI lobbying efforts could in no small part be concentrated toward one man who asked little in return other than they refer to AI as “superintelligence,” stand behind him smiling for the cameras and quietly send along tens of millions of dollars for a new ballroom. With control of both chambers, Democrats can look to advance federal bills that ensure the cost burden of data-center construction does not land with a thump on consumers’ doormats.

And then there’s another part of the data-center equation that must not be overlooked — far bigger, I’d argue, than the debate over the construction projects themselves.

A good deal for Americans on data centers extends into broader protections from the effects of AI. They come in the form of massive funding for school programs, colleges, apprenticeships and the acquisition of new skills for all ages. They include a financial cushion for those for whom the change came too quickly and legislation to protect creative industries from obliteration. They guard against predatory advertising and dynamic-price gouging. They hold AI companies fully accountable for disgusting harms such as AI-generated child abuse imagery and so-called revenge porn. They give devastated families proper recourse when an AI fails to act when a user is in obvious emotional distress and in need of an intervention.

When an AI company rolls out its blueprints for a data center, these issues should be on the table as well. The conversation must become one and the same if the public is to be won over.

As Democrats attempt this, they will be wise to remember that people weren’t always so viscerally opposed to data centers. For decades, citizens happily benefited as these vast warehouses of humming server racks enabled them to watch Netflix, play online games, store a lifetime’s photos in the cloud, call a loved one in high-definition video across the world or do any number of things our digital revolution brought us.

Then, something changed fundamentally. Tech leaders went from exceedingly rich to unfathomably rich. Their platforms and money brought them unprecedented power, and they soon moved to wield and consolidate it. The AI boom brought these disparities into even sharper focus, coming as it did with the promises from AI luminaries that this exciting new technology would upend our individual livelihoods, shake the foundations of the global economy and perhaps wipe us out altogether. Citizens have been made to feel they have little choice. “You may or may not lose your job to AI,” Nvidia Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang once said. “But you will absolutely lose your job to someone who uses AI.”

But the public does, in fact, have a choice and it was made at the ballot box. The key takeaway for Huang — and Musk, Mark Zuckerberg, Sam Altman and Dario Amodei, et al — should be to understand that these votes were as much against them, the billionaire class of tech leaders who have so far failed to sell the American public on their vision, as they were against data centers.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/commentary/.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang says the public has a choice and it was made at the ballot box. The key takeaway for Huang is that the public does, in fact, have a choice.

https://www.scmp.com/news/world/article/.title: Cop31 leaders urge world to accelerate fight against global warming
https://www.scmp.com/news/world/article/.author: Reuters
https://www.scmp.com/news/world/article/.text:
UN summit opens in Turkey amid record heat, regional conflict and soaring power demand from AI

Leaders of ⁠the Cop31 climate summit urged the world to accelerate the fight against global warming as rising temperatures and an increasing number of climate-driven disasters threaten lives and the global economy, as the annual meeting began in Turkey on Monday.

The comments at the start of the two-week UN conference were an appeal to governments to focus on climate, even as other international crises from war to soaring inflation and the uncertainty of AI compete for their attention.

“The urgency of this moment must drive us ‌forward,” UN Climate Change Executive Secretary Simon Stiell said in prepared remarks for the opening of the event on Turkey’s Mediterranean coast, adding that progress so far was “nowhere near fast enough”.

A report by the United Nations Environment Programme published in October said the world was already set to overshoot 1.5 degrees Celsius of warming above pre-industrial times, the threshold set at the 2015 Paris climate summit to avoid the worst consequences of warming.

This year is on track to be one of the four hottest on record, driven by a powerful El Nino, a UN report showed on Monday. The year has also stood out with a series of extreme heatwaves across western Europe and a glacier collapse in Nepal that triggered a catastrophic flood killing more than 1,450 people, ⁠with thousands still missing.

Turkey’s Cop31 presidency has focused this year’s summit on a goal to electrify more than a third of the global economy by 2035, up from around a fifth today. ‌It is asking nations to sign onto a pledge supporting that target.

Theoretically, such a goal could help reduce planet-warming emissions by speeding the global shift away from fossil fuel-powered vehicles, furnaces, boilers, cooking stoves, and other greenhouse gas-emitting equipment.

“We want people to feel the results of climate talks in daily life: in buildings ‌that use less energy, in clean public transport, in energy they can afford and in new jobs,” Turkey’s Cop31 President Murat Kurum said in prepared remarks.

But climate ⁠advocates have criticised the pledge because it does ⁠not require the additional electricity to come from low-carbon sources, setting up an early fight over whether electrification alone should count as climate progress.

The Iran war has underscored the world’s attachment to fossil fuels, as has Russia’s invasion of ‌Ukraine and the ensuing sanctions on Moscow’s energy exports, though some say the wars have also shown the benefits of moving to renewables.

The Iran war, now in its ninth month, severely disrupted Middle East oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, lifting fuel prices ‌around ‌the globe and prompting a scramble for new supplies.

US President Donald Trump’s administration – which is shunning climate talks for the second year running – has encouraged policies maximising oil, gas, and coal production to address ‌the Mideast disruptions.

South Korea, India, Thailand and other Asian nations, meanwhile, have also increased their reliance on coal or taken steps to boost coal-fired power generation.

“A lot of people who previously might have ⁠been embarrassed to argue for continuing very high use of fossil fuel are now feeling empowered to make that case,” said John Holdren of Harvard University, who was a science adviser to Barack ⁠Obama when he was US president.

At the same time, the deployment of renewable energy has also risen, driven by surging exports of cheap clean tech from China, cheering advocates for ambitious climate action.

Stiell told the summit renewables were the clear answer to improving energy security.

“This year’s fossil fuel cost chaos has delivered a global shock wave, hitting households hard and ‌spreading inflation like a cancer,” he said.

“But the solutions ‌are clear,” he added, saying renewable energy installations had saved the global economy hundreds of billions of dollars.

The rapid roll-out of AI is also complicating talks, driving a surge in global power demand and contributing to rising greenhouse gas emissions.

Turkey will call on governments, businesses and other institutions at Cop31 to sign a pledge outlining principles to ensure AI is developed and deployed sustainably.

Chris Bowen, Australia’s president of Cop31 negotiations, said he hoped the conference would show the world that multilateralism works.

“Paris is working,” he said, referring to the landmark 2015 deal to limit global warming. “But we must move faster.”
