https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.title: CFMEU ‘enjoy a significant level of influence’ over Victorian government, Big Build royal commission hears
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.author: Nino Bucci and Jack Larkin
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text:
Inquiry into allegations of corruption begins block of hearings focused on 2022 level crossing removal project

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The royal commission into allegations of corruption on Victorian Big Build projects has heard a major construction company feared putting the Construction, Forestry and Maritime Employees Union (CFMEU) offside because of its close links to the Daniel Andrews Labor government.

The first block of hearings under the commission into the integrity of major public and civil infrastructure construction projects in Victoria will hear evidence about the union’s involvement in a level crossing removal project at Gap Road in Sunbury, north of Melbourne, in 2022.

The project involved the removal of a level crossing and the construction of a new rail bridge and underpass.

The counsel assisting the commission, Chris Young KC, said 20 witnesses have been compelled to appear during the November hearings.

But he warned that others were not complying with orders to produce documents to the commission, including using the excuse of “government policy” to delay their production. Failing to comply with such orders is a criminal offence.

“It is extremely concerning that some parties have not complied with the terms of those notices to produce,” Young said.

The hearings in November will focus on what government officials did during a June 2022 meeting in order to appease the union, who had forced work to stop on the Gap Road project.

Young showed the commission evidence that – in the years before the union interfered in the project – there was increasing awareness within the construction sector about the prospect of industrial action curtailing work, and the growing influence of the CFMEU.

He said that in 2017, one of the companies involved in the Gap Road project, John Holland, noted that the CFMEU was “proud of the fact that none of their site visits are code compliant”.

It also noted in an email the “significance of the CFMEU relationship with the Andrews government in Victoria, and the impact this is having, and will have in the future, in respect of client relationships with the Victorian government”.

Such was the extent of that relationship that John Holland officials suspected the CFMEU would have a “substantial amount of knowledge around proposed government tenders and input” in respect of the tender process.

“We are thus particularly mindful of the optics in our interactions with union stakeholders,” the 2017 email said.

Four years later, the construction company noted that “the CFMEU are emboldened by their success on major infrastructure projects,” and later in 2021, that they “enjoy a significant level of influence within the state government”.

“It is a level of influence not seen in previous years and is unlikely to diminish.”

Young told the hearing that four of the CFMEU officials who would later force work to stop at Gap Road had similarly interfered in the Metro Tunnel project.

He said the officials entered the Gap Road project’s eastern portal 29 times in January 2020, and were involved in activity considered to be unlawful, but nonetheless received attention from the government, who asked if the safety issues they raised were valid.

Young said that a “very high risk rating” was applied to the possibility of industrial action on Gap Road.

But he said that it was not until May 2022 where this risk escalated, and CFMEU officials more regularly appeared on site.

By early June, Neil Thompson, the health and safety manager for the Rail Network Alliance involved in the project, was calling police, desperate for their help in removing union officials who were stopping work including by sitting on barriers and refusing to move.

Young tendered internal notes taken on the union activity that showed there were references to the CFMEU officials warning workers “you guys better not turn up tonight otherwise we will smash you during the day” and “their life would be make very difficult for them personally” if they continued working on the project.

A recording of a phone call between Thompson and WorkSafe and a subsequent email showed that on 6 June – the day before a meeting that is central to the commission’s hearings – he was unclear about how to get work to continue on site.

He stressed the need for the union to be removed, given trains had been stopped on the line in order for a bridge to be built.

“We actually called Victoria police to escort themself off site. Victoria police said there was nothing they could do,” Thompson said in the call to WorkSafe.

“We’re going around in circles a bit because last week WorkSafe said there was nothing they could do.

Get the most important news as it breaks

after newsletter promotion

“We’re just having to put up with no work happening at the moment.”

The following day, Young said, there was a 13-minute meeting, followed by a subsequent meeting at the CFMEU, which resolved the issues.

Two CFMEU officials, Joe Myles and Paul Tzimas, attended the meeting, along with four officials from the project, he told the hearing.

Young said that while the commission had obtained significant documentation regarding the events leading up to the meeting, little was known about what occurred during it, and why it was significant, so the commission would be reliant on the memory witnesses had of conversations four years ago.

The key questions included what stopped the work, and whether those disruptions were used as leverage by the CFMEU, he said.

It remained unclear exactly how much the CFMEU disruption to works on the site had cost, nor what the cost was to end the disruption, Young said.

But the union interrupted work on the site for 36 hours – and traffic controllers employed after the disruption charged significantly more than those previously employed, documents in evidence before the commission show.

The hourly rate increased from about $45 to $88, or from $59 to $147 for penalty rates, the documents show.

This meant that, for example, one 10-and-a-half hour shift cost $609 under the previous firm, but $1225 for the same shift under the new firm, Young said.

The Major Transport Infrastructure Authority director general started considering the cost implications of a CFMEU campaign to increase the rates of traffic controllers about the same time the disruptions occurred on the Gap Road project.

A September briefing prepared for the then-minister for transport infrastructure, Jacinta Allan, estimated that the changes could cost the authority $60m-$78m for current projects, and well in excess of $400m for those projects in planning.

Earlier on Monday, the premier, Ben Carroll, said the royal commission was one “that Victoria needed and Victorians deserve”.

“I want every Victorian to get the answers they deserve,” Carroll said.

“This is a royal commission for Victoria. It’s a tough royal commission. It’s truly independent – [it has] the broadest terms of reference possible, a special prosecutor established as well. I said I’d do this in my first press conference and now it is up and running as it should be.”

Carroll confirmed legal representation for two former premiers, Jacinta Allan and Daniel Andrews, was “supported by the state” as has been the case at “other previous royal commissions”.

The opposition leader, Jess Wilson, said: “They’ve trashed the future of this state, and now Ben Carroll is allowing the taxpayer to foot the bill for them to be defended in the royal commission, it doesn’t pass the pub test.”

The hearing continues.

Benita Kolovos contributed reporting to this story
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.summary: The first block of hearings under the royal commission begins on November 15. The hearing will focus on what government officials did during a June 2022 meeting to appease the union. The company feared putting the Construction, Forestry and Maritime Employees Union offside because of its close links to the Daniel Andrews Labor government.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: ‘A global political awakening’: how gen Z protests are sweeping the world
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Ashifa Kassam and Lex McMenamin
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
From Serbia to Bangladesh and India to France, young people are pushing back against authoritarianism and reshaping political landscapes

In Brazil, they rallied online by the millions, sharing videos and spreading memes. In Serbia, they cycled across Europe and ran ultramarathons to make their voices heard.

Both movements burst into international public view last month as they became central during election campaigns to the pushback against authoritarianism. What they also offered, however, was a window into a wider phenomenon playing out across the globe, as youth-led movements reshape political landscapes.

“Gen Z is rising,” said Erica Chenoweth, a political scientist at Harvard Kennedy School. “It is abundantly clear that a significant proportion of gen Z is tired of sitting on the sidelines while their political systems fail them.”

Researchers have documented at least 25 protests around the world in which this age group – roughly those between the ages of 14 and 29 – has played a role.

From Bangladesh to Belgium and Italy to India, it seems gen Z, who account for about a third of the world’s population, have found their voice. “Gen Z may be experiencing a global political awakening,” Chenoweth wrote in a recent essay.

Their reasons for taking to the streets have varied widely, from protesting against corruption and an unequal playing field to calling for more investment in education, affordable housing and action on the climate crisis.

Many of the first protests to make waves were in Asia and Africa. In 2024, students in Dhaka, Bangladesh, made global headlines after they pulled off what was described as the world’s first successful gen Z-led revolution.

The protests began over a quota law but swiftly snowballed into a wider show of discontent against the increasingly autocratic rule of the prime minister, Sheikh Hasina. Two months later, Hasina resigned and fled the country by helicopter after being, as the Associated Press reported, “chased out by young protesters”.

Two years later and 4,000 miles away, students were at the helm of another revolution in Serbia, pushing back against a government that had steadily tightened its grip on the media and stuffed institutions with party loyalists.

Late last month, Serbia’s students’ movement was catapulted from the streets to the halls of power as they ousted Aleksandar Vučić in elections, bringing an end to his party’s 14 years in power.

Students and young people have long been at the forefront of the push for change, the analysts Cait Dallaire and Sebastian Dittgen wrote recently, citing the US civil rights movement and the 2011 Arab spring.

“What is unique about the current movement is the infrastructure of mobilisation: TikTok and X amplify and accelerate grievances; Discord servers and group chats enable decentralised planning; virtual private networks and mirrored content help organisers circumvent internet shutdowns,” they said.

It was this potent combination – young people in the streets and social media – that helped drive Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s comeback to win Brazil’s presidential election last month. After a bruising loss in the first round to the rightwing senator Flávio Bolsonaro, there was dismay in the country’s political left.

That was until students from the Fluminense Federal University mobilised in a pro-Lula march, setting off a wave of similar actions across the country. Soon after, the congressman and Lula ally André Janones, 42, created a WhatsApp channel called “Lula’s Army” that attracted millions of people looking to help boost pro-Lula content on social media.

On the night of his victory, Lula recognised their power. “I want to thank the generosity of Brazil’s young people who took to the streets to defend democracy,” he said.

Some politicians have sought to engage gen Z from the start. In the US, Zohran Mamdani’s campaign for New York mayor combined a canny use of social media with a legion of about 50,000 volunteers that had young people at its heart. The New York Times wrote that “volunteering for Mr Mamdani’s campaign became a salve” for young New Yorkers as the campaign became not just about “mobilising, but socialising”.

It was a nod to the global context in which many gen Zers have come of age; one riven by conflicts such as the Israel-Gaza war, the escalating climate crisis and the rise of nationalism, while the rules that have shaped the international order since the second world war are fraying.

In recent weeks, youth-led protests have begun to sweep Europe, from school students in France demanding better conditions in which to work to those in Spain who pitched tents to rally for affordable housing. In Germany, thousands of people took to the streets to protest against the cost of living and call for more investment in education, health and climate action in a movement organised by a group calling itself Gen Z regelt!, or Gen Z will sort this.

Sign up to This is Europe

The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment

after newsletter promotion

Analysts have been swift to point to the link between the protests. “The reasons are different, but they share the same spark: the breakdown of the social contract,” Arancha González, the dean of the Paris School of International Affairs, told the Italian newspaper Corriere della Sera. “In Europe, the idea that economies generate wellbeing and social equality has been shattered.”

A similar note of disillusionment threads through India’s Cockroach movement, which began as an online satire and has since swelled into a show of force against the strongman government of Narendra Modi. Fuelled by social media and rooted in democratic ideals, the power of the movement was laid bare this summer after Cockroach-led protests forced the resignation of the country’s education minister.

Equally visible is the pushback by India’s security forces against the movement, detaining thousands, unleashing teargas and beating people with lathis, or wooden clubs. Authorities went to extreme lengths in October to keep them from gathering in central Delhi, barricading roads and shutting down the internet and public transport.

It was a window into another facet that has defined youth-led protests, as research suggests they tend to be met with higher levels of repression, despite the fact that they are no more likely to use violence than others.

In France, lawyers and rights groups say several teenagers have suffered war-like injuries from police weapons. After the 2024 protests in Bangladesh, UN human rights experts said as many as 1,400 people had been killed, mostly by security forces, while thousands more suffered severe, often life-altering injuries.

In a recent analysis, Civicus, a non-profit that monitors global civic freedoms, said: “Because they question the distribution of economic and political power, gen Z-led protests have invariably been met with state violence,” linking the violence meted out to young protesters with their focus on systems and institutions that have long been generally accepted.

In Morocco, more than 2,000 people were charged and many received harsh prison sentences after a 2025 movement known as Gen Z 212 targeted officials over corruption, neglected public services and the lack of opportunities. Weeks later, in Mexico, youth-led protests over corruption and crime led to clashes with police in which dozens of people were arrested.

The outcomes of both of these movements show the varying success of gen Z protests. But at times, the foundations laid in one protest have given rise to others. In the US, much of today’s youth organising was shaped by the pro-Palestine student movement, in which there were thousands of arrests, expulsions and suspensions. Many schools instated anti-protest policies amid a broader rollback of educational freedom on campus.

Students, however, have continued to push for change. Last month hundreds in North Carolina marched in the heat to the polls after their historically Black university was denied a polling site, while thousands across the country have responded to the Cornell 7 case by skipping class, protesting and launching occupations.

As Chenoweth of the Harvard Kennedy School noted, the wave of recent youth-led protests may mark the beginning of a “profound generational transformation in world affairs” – one that could be capable of countering the global trend of democratic backsliding.

Ultimately, however, as Bilal Narjissi, a 17-year-old high school student in a suburb north of Paris recently told the Associated Press, the explosion of youth movements across Europe hints at a wider truth that has long been overlooked across the globe.

“We all agree on one point,” he said. “That young people are treated like children, far too much, and that they aren’t listened to enough.”

https://fortune.com/2026/11/09/sharebite.title: Sharebite has donated 18 million meals. Its CEO wants US employers to copy Brazil
https://fortune.com/2026/11/09/sharebite.author: Lara Murray-Sterzel
https://fortune.com/2026/11/09/sharebite.text:
Dilip Rao spent the 2026 midterm campaign listening for someone to talk about hunger. He says almost no one did.

“You read these stats about how 48 million Americans or 50 million Americans live in food-insecure households. That’s the reported number!” said Rao, CEO and co-founder of Sharebite, a New York–based employee meal-benefits platform. He argues the real figure is roughly three times higher.

“So you’re talking about close to 150 million people. Nearly half the country’s population is struggling; they’re living from paycheck-to-paycheck, and they don’t know where their next meals are coming from,” he said.

That number is Rao’s estimate. The official baseline is 47.9 million people who experienced food insecurity in 2024, according to Feeding America’s analysis of federal data. It may be the last reliable count for some time, because the USDA has stopped collecting the household survey behind it.

The pressure behind those numbers is showing up at work. Annual inflation reached 3.7% in September, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, and food prices are up 33% since 2019, per an Associated Press analysis of federal data cited by NPR. A Government Accountability Office report found that Uber, Lyft and DoorDash now lead major employers in workers receiving SNAP benefits, ahead of Walmart and McDonald’s.

Rao’s pitch is that companies can close part of that gap through something many already pay for: lunch. “We just have to start thinking about hunger, not only as a societal problem but more as an economic problem that businesses can help solve,” he said.

Founded in 2015, Sharebite is built for businesses, not consumers. Companies use it to manage employee food ordering, meal allowances, and catering for in-office, remote, and hybrid teams, setting stipends and spending limits from one dashboard instead of processing expense reports.

For every meal ordered on the platform, Sharebite donates an equivalent meal through nonprofit partners including Feeding America and City Harvest. The company says it has donated more than 18 million meals to date.

Its investors include Contour Venture Partners, Essential Capital, Lafayette Square, Liberty City Ventures, and Fiserv, the payments company on the 2026 Fortune 500. Sharebite raised a $39 million Series B round in 2022.

Rao, a former Credit Suisse investment banker, says the idea came from watching how other countries tackle food insecurity by “mobilizing private sectors to step in and help solve it.” He felt it was “high time for us to be able to implement something like that.”

He describes the company as his form of civic service, arguing that serving society, building a successful business, and drawing on the private sector are “all interwoven together.”

Rao’s favorite model is Brazil’s Workers’ Food Program, created in 1976. Companies that join receive tax incentives for feeding their employees, and the program now reaches about 22 million workers, according to Brazil’s Ministry of Labor and Employment.

“Meal benefits or meal vouchers are a standard practice in Brazil as a result,” Rao said.

He argues the U.S. should add food to the employer benefits framework that already covers health care and retirement, a change he says would support workers and stimulate small-business activity. Rao, who has written commentary for Fortune, made a similar case in a 2023 essay on hunger among American workers and again in a 2025 piece written as the record government shutdown ended.

The business argument rests partly on cost. Healthcare spending and lost productivity tied to poor diets and food insecurity exceed $1.1 trillion a year, according to a fact sheet from the Food is Medicine Institute at Tufts University.

Lunch has also become a lever in the return-to-office. Workers surveyed by Owl Labs said they would come back if employers covered commuting, childcare, and lunch and coffee, Fortune reported in 2023.

Rao says Sharebite’s job is aligning “a real business need with a much broader problem,” and credits his team with developing “solutions to solve those problems at that scale” as it works with larger customers.

Rao says demand is accelerating. “Last week was our best week ever in the company’s history. October was a record month for us. And it’s the same people who’ve been here for the last few years. Our headcount is small, but our business continues to grow,” he said.

He added that the business is more than 30 times larger than it was four-plus years ago.

After roughly a decade “building inside this category,” Rao doesn’t think the market has matured. In his view, it is “still at the early beginnings of this entire category.”
https://fortune.com/2026/11/09/sharebite.summary: Sharebite CEO says the real figure is roughly three times higher. The company is built for businesses, not consumers, not customers. It says it has donated more than 18 million meals to date.

At a political rally in Arizona in October, U.S. President Donald Trump joked that he “probably went a little too far” with the U.S.-Israeli military strikes against Iran that he initiated in February. The electoral catastrophe that unfolded for Republicans in the midterms a few weeks later made this abundantly clear.

During a midnight interview with Fox News at the end of election night on Nov. 3, when asked about what had hurt the GOP most at the polls, Trump conceded that “I think a part of it was Iran.” Setting aside equivocation the following day, Vice President J. D. Vance posted on X, “The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night. … And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.”

At a political rally in Arizona in October, U.S. President Donald Trump joked that he “probably went a little too far” with the U.S.-Israeli military strikes against Iran that he initiated in February. The electoral catastrophe that unfolded for Republicans in the midterms a few weeks later made this abundantly clear.

During a midnight interview with Fox News at the end of election night on Nov. 3, when asked about what had hurt the GOP most at the polls, Trump conceded that “I think a part of it was Iran.” Setting aside equivocation the following day, Vice President J. D. Vance posted on X, “The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night. … And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.”

Energy prices had soared, and voters noticed that they weren’t being put first, punishing the incumbent party for this betrayal. The president’s most consequential foreign-policy mistake has turned out to be launching a war against a major regional power in the Middle East with a surfeit of misplaced optimism and scant consideration of what might go wrong. The irony does not need much teasing out.

It is not as if the president was not warned. As the New York Times journalists Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan detail in their book Regime Change, U.S. intelligence was skeptical of key elements of the case for war that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu presented to Trump at the White House Situation Room on Feb. 11.

Seeing upsides everywhere he looked, the Israeli prime minister said that Iran’s ballistic missile program would be destroyed in a few weeks, that a weakened Iran would be unable to close the Strait of Hormuz, and that the risk to neighboring states was small. He also reported that Mossad intelligence suggested that an intense bombing campaign would destabilize the regime, allowing Iranian opposition forces to assume control.

The CIA’s director, John Ratcliffe, reported back to the president and his principal advisors the next day. Agency analysts believed that military action could take out Iran’s leadership and destroy its ability to threaten its neighbors. But Ratcliffe said that the suggestion that airstrikes would spark regime change was “farcical,” according to the Times reporters. Secretary of State Marco Rubio stepped in to paraphrase: “In other words, it’s bullshit.” Vance strongly agreed. The chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, Dan Caine, told Trump, “Sir, this is, in my experience, standard operating procedure for the Israelis. They oversell, and their plans are not always well-developed. They know they need us, and that’s why they’re hard-selling.” Warning lights were flashing everywhere.

Trump ultimately decided to authorize Operation Epic Fury on the basis that decapitating Iran’s leadership and striking decisively against its offensive capabilities was sufficient cause. It was a remarkable leap of faith for a man whose opposition to reckless foreign wars—Iraq, first and foremost—had helped him secure the Republican presidential nomination in 2016.

He restated this view in defeating President Joe Biden eight years later, too. At a campaign rally in Pennsylvania in October 2024, Trump said, “I will not send you to fight and die in a foolish, never-ending foreign war.” In launching war against Iran, Trump ignored private doubts expressed by his vice president, CIA director, secretary of state, and chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth was the only person to unequivocally back war with Iran (which places him in a precarious position now.)

The history of U.S. foreign policy is replete with examples of influential and well-placed advisors ignoring or marginalizing compelling intelligence that contradicted their plans for war or escalation. In the case of the wars in Iraq and Vietnam, they also happen to correspond with the worst foreign-policy mistakes in American history. And just like Trump’s war against Iran, these were conflicts of choice, not of necessity, to deploy Richard Haass’s helpful binary. The rationales undergirding each war were different, but a common theme is present across all—ill-advised certainty defeated counterevidence and caution.

Determined to locate evidence that connected Saddam Hussein with al Qaeda’s 9/11 attacks, former Deputy Secretary of Defense Paul Wolfowitz repeatedly instructed the CIA to investigate the link and repeatedly got the same reply: No such relationship existed between this secular leader and the radical Islamist terrorist group.

The undersecretary of defense for policy, Douglas Feith, set up an alternative intelligence-gathering outfit, the Policy Counter Terrorism Evaluation Group, in the Pentagon to locate what the CIA had supposedly missed. It found nothing, but this did not stop Vice President Dick Cheney from insisting repeatedly that Saddam’s Iraq was linked to the 9/11 attacks, bolstering public support for any invasion of Iraq.

Tulsi Gabbard has killed a key report for covering climate change.

In late 2001 and through 2002, George Tenet’s CIA was browbeaten and ultimately marginalized as it failed to locate the smoking-gun evidence—both on weapons of mass destruction and Iraqi links with al Qaeda—that Bush administration hawks insisted would be there if only the agency looked hard enough. The war was launched in March 2003. Though the initial military action was ruthlessly effective—as was the case with U.S.-Israeli action against Iran in February—what happened after Saddam’s fall was not.

The August 1964 Gulf of Tonkin Resolution, which gave U.S. President Lyndon B. Johnson congressional authorization to wage war against North Vietnam, was predicated on a North Vietnamese attack on two U.S. destroyers that never actually happened. As LBJ later told Undersecretary of State George Ball, “Hell, those damn, stupid sailors were just shooting at flying fish.”

The resolution gave the Johnson administration ample latitude to do as it saw fit in Vietnam—LBJ said it was like “grandmother’s nightshirt. It covers everything.” Just two senators—Democrat Ernest Gruening from Alaska and Republican Wayne Morse from Oregon—voted against, warning their colleagues that they were effectively signing an undated declaration of war. Both men lost their next elections, but history has treated them kindly.

As the war escalated, Walt Rostow, one of the conflict’s key architects, was constantly at odds with intelligence analysts on how it was progressing. As Johnson’s national security advisor from April 1966, Rostow was in a powerful position to present his own spin on the intelligence reports that he received. He would cherry-pick small sections of good news in larger intelligence reports counselling caution and present his own optimistic summary to Johnson. As historian Arthur Schlesinger Jr. later remarked, “Intelligent people in the State Department have told me that Walt would funnel in the stuff that sustained his own thesis.” Rostow’s relationship with Langley understandably soured. When forwarding some raw eyewitness testimony to LBJ in the fall of 1967, Rostow wrote, “This is what the bombing of Hanoi and Haiphong really looks like—with all due respect to intelligence analysts 10,000 miles away.”

Rostow was certain that the U.S. bombing campaign against North Vietnam that he helped devise was winning the war and discounted intelligence that challenged his take. It was almost an article of faith for him.

The architects of the war against Iran in February held similar overconfidence in bombing’s coerciveness in an incredibly complex theater of operation. Airpower is indeed a crucial military tool, but unrealistic political goals—forcing North Vietnam to give up on its war of unification or forcing regime change in Tehran—are rarely achieved from the skies. Ignoring the intelligence that points this out simply invites failure.

Wolfowitz and Rostow were ideologues who believed they had finessed fundamental truths about the wars they strategized that the intelligence community had missed or refused to see. Trump’s worldview is very different to these two defense intellectuals—a Cold War liberal and a neoconservative—with their Ph.D.s from Chicago and Yale and scholarly books and publications.

But the certainty that Wolfowitz and Rostow held in the efficacy of the wars that they pushed in Iraq and Vietnam is mirrored by the confidence with which Trump launched his Iran misadventure. Few things are as dangerous in foreign policy as a powerful individual with undue confidence in a bad idea. And like Rostow and Wolfowitz, who did not later question the soundness of the advice that they dispensed, the president is not naturally predisposed to critical self-reflection.

“I would have done it again,” the president told reporters recently. It will be interesting to see how this position holds up as Iran becomes a critical flash point in the 2028 Republican primaries.

Chris Fagan's former assistant Cameron Bruce (pictured) has been chosen as his successor to lead Brisbane. (Travis Hayto/AFL Photos via Getty Images)

Cameron Bruce has been appointed Brisbane's new senior coach following the departure of Chris Fagan.

Bruce has served as an assistant under Fagan for the last five seasons after leaving Carlton at the end of 2021.

Bruce is expected to be officially unveiled as Brisbane's coach on Tuesday.

Brisbane has chosen Cameron Bruce to be its new head coach after the departure of three-time premiership winner Chris Fagan.

The 47-year-old, who served as an assistant under Fagan for the last five seasons, beat out a strong collection of candidates including Nathan Buckley and Adam Simpson.

Bruce wins the Brisbane role having acquired more than a decade of AFL assistant coaching experience at three different clubs.

His coaching career began with Hawthorn, where he was an assistant under Alastair Clarkson for five seasons between 2013 and 2017, a period which yielded the club three premierships.

Bruce served as an assistant under Fagan for all three of Brisbane's premierships over the last three seasons. (James Wiltshire/AFL Photos via Getty Images)

Bruce then joined Carlton as an assistant under Brendon Bolton before departing at the end of 2021 following an extensive review into the underperforming club.

Bruce enjoyed a 13-year career as a player, making a combined 234 appearances for Melbourne and Hawthorn. He was a member of Melbourne's 2000 grand final side and was also a best and fairest winner for the Demons in 2008.

Fagan has joined Carlton as the club's new director of coaching after his exit from Brisbane following a decorated, decade-long stint.

Bruce is expected to be formally named Brisbane's senior coach on Tuesday.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Man arrested over operation of rogue cellular base station in Tokyo
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
A Chinese man has been arrested on suspicion of illegally operating a mobile phone base station without a license in busy entertainment districts in central Tokyo, the Metropolitan Police Department said.

Yu Hai, a 31-year-old Chinese national living in Tokyo’s Kita Ward, is alleged to have installed radio equipment in a vehicle and operated an unlicensed base station in Tokyo’s Ginza district on Saturday, the police said.

He has denied the allegations against him, reportedly telling investigators, “I’ve never used any radio equipment before. I don’t know anything about it.”

The police also referred him to prosecutors on suspicion of violating the radio law by interfering with important radio communications, saying he disrupted NTT Docomo’s mobile phone services.

This is believed to be the first case in Japan in which an individual has been arrested for interfering with mobile phone communications, according to the police.

Investigators said the suspect allegedly used specialized equipment installed in a vehicle to transmit radio signals that interfere or block normal mobile phone communications.

He then caused nearby smartphones to connect to an unlicensed base station that transmitted signals using the outdated second-generation (2G) mobile communication standard.

Taking advantage of weaker authentication mechanisms in 2G technology compared with current 4G and 5G standards, Yu is believed to have sent fraudulent text messages in Chinese through the Short Message Service (SMS).

The messages reportedly told recipients that payments using their credit cards had been temporarily suspended due to the risk of unauthorized use overseas. Recipients were then directed to websites where they were asked to enter their credit card details and other personal information.

The suspect is believed to have repeatedly carried out the operation in Tokyo’s Ginza, Shinjuku and Shibuya districts. The signals he allegedly transmitted reportedly caused as many as 10,000 smartphones a day to lose mobile service within a radius of at least 500 meters.

Since January last year, police have received inquiries from 18 people, including Chinese tourists, who lodged reports over suspected fraud. Their combined losses are estimated at about ¥4 million ($25,300). The police are investigating whether the operation involved an organized group.

In December 2024, NTT Docomo received reports from customers about communication disruptions. An investigation conducted the following month led the company to identify the suspect.

The Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications, which was notified of the findings, issued him a verbal warning. However, he allegedly continued the illegal activities.

The discovery of rogue base stations attracted attention on social media last year. The ministry issued a public warning in May last year, saying that the interference of mobile phone services had occurred due to what it suspected to have been the operation of unlicensed radio equipment.

Nobuo Suzuki, a professor at Kindai University well-versed in mobile networks, said dedicated software for building base stations can be downloaded by anyone from the internet.

Advances in radio equipment have also reduced the cost of setting up such stations compared with the past, Suzuki said, adding that this might have made them a tool for criminal activities.

Although operating an unlicensed base station requires specialized technical knowledge and remains difficult, advances in artificial intelligence may be making the process easier, he said.

In Thailand and Hong Kong, the media has reported the discovery of similar cases between last year and this year involving fraudulent SMS messages being sent through rogue base stations.

Japan has already discontinued services using the 2G mobile communication standard exploited in the case. Smartphone users are therefore advised to exercise caution if their devices suddenly display a 2G connection or lose mobile services.

Mobile carriers and other organizations are advising users who receive suspicious text messages not to open any links and to delete them immediately.

Some smartphone models allow users to disable connections to 2G networks.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/commentary/.title: South Korea’s military ambitions get a reality check
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/commentary/.author: Ruth Pollard
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/commentary/.text:
The deck is stacked against a significant shift in military control on the Korean Peninsula, yet that is exactly what South Korean President Lee Jae Myung is staking his leadership on. It’s the right idea, at the wrong time.

Seoul still relies on an American general to lead combined U.S.-South Korea military operations in wartime, one of the enduring legacies of the Korean War. Lee wants to put a South Korean in charge. Yet Seoul is having a difficult time with the second Trump administration — the two sides are divided over their trade agreement and Lee’s reluctance to get involved in the U.S. president’s war in Iran.

That acrimony is bleeding into all aspects of the relationship. Indeed, the U.S. Ambassador to South Korea, Michelle Steel, has described ties as being in a state of turbulence. So why is Lee pushing so hard now to speed up the timeline to take wartime operational control of the combined forces, when Washington has indicated 2029 is a possibility and the allies have yet to agree on a final date?
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/commentary/.summary: South Korean President Lee Jae Myung wants to put a South Korean in charge of the military. But Seoul is having a difficult time with the second Trump administration.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/commentary/.title: China’s hard power keeps undermining its soft power
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/commentary/.author: Waka Ikeda
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/commentary/.text:
Well, that didn’t take long. At the end of last month, Sanrio announced it was ending a merchandise collaboration with Japanese spy drama “Vivant” after Chinese state media accused the hit series of portraying China negatively.

Days earlier, CCTV and the Communist Party-run Global Times had attacked the show’s second season, in which a fictional Chinese intelligence agency, Xinxi, tortures members of Japan’s secret “Betsuhan” unit. The outlets called the scenes a distortion of history and an example of “China threat” messaging.

Then came the commercial fallout. On Oct. 28, Sanrio’s Chinese subsidiary canceled its Hello Kitty collaboration with the show and all related promotions, citing content inconsistent with the company’s corporate philosophy. Reuters reported that Sanrio also deeply apologized for the concern caused.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/commentary/.title: The rise of the global oligarchic world order
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/commentary/.author: David Lingelbach
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/commentary/.text:
BALTIMORE/BOGOTA – For most people, the word “oligarch” conjures images of Russian elites who amassed huge fortunes in the wake of the Soviet Union’s collapse or, more recently, the tech billionaires who filled the front row at U.S. President Donald Trump’s second inauguration. But oligarchs are global, systemic and increasingly entrenched. They are a defining feature of the emerging world order.

We define oligarchs as actors who accumulate and fuse substantial wealth and consequential power (a criterion that, unlike Aristotle’s, does not require rule for the rich as a class). Today, some oligarchs, like Trump, start with wealth, which they use to acquire power (and yet more wealth). Others use power to accumulate immense wealth, as Russian President Vladimir Putin has done over the last quarter-century. Still others, like Saudi Arabia’s Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (MBS) and Morocco’s King Mohammed VI, possess both from the start.

One need not be a billionaire to be an oligarch. We believe a net worth of $20 million, alongside evidence of wealth-power fusion, provides enough financial independence for an actor to build and exercise power without relying on others for the resources to do so. Applying this wealth threshold together with our wealth-power fusion criterion, we estimate that 59 heads of state or government today are oligarchs. Among them are leaders of eight of the world’s 20 largest economies (at purchasing-power parity, according to International Monetary Fund estimates for 2026).
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/commentary/.summary: Oligarchs are global, systemic and increasingly entrenched, says David Frum. They are a defining feature of the emerging world order, he says. One need not be a billionaire to be an oligarch, he adds.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Takaichi and LDP weigh disciplinary action for party members who abstained from food tax vote
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: Eric Johnston
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and the Liberal Democratic Party find themselves in a quandary about what to do with four LDP lawmakers who, in a surprise move, abstained from voting on the food consumption tax reduction bill, which passed the Lower House on Friday.

The party is expected to discipline the four over their actions. But it faces a dilemma, as an internal backlash could erupt if the punishment is seen as too strong or too weak.

The LDP leadership demanded that the four — former Prime Minister Shigeru Ishiba, Yuko Obuchi, Hajime Funada and Yoshihisa Furukawa — submit written statements Monday as to why they defied their own party over the bill to cut the tax from 8% to 1% for a two-year period starting next April by walking out before it was voted on.

“The consumption tax is intended to be fully allocated to social security expenses, such as medical care, nursing care, pensions and childcare, which are expected to increase exponentially,” Ishiba told reporters Monday after sending his statement to party headquarters.

All four expressed concerns while the bill was being debated in the Lower House about where the government would find the money to make up for the annual tax revenue shortfall of ¥5 trillion ($31.6 billion) the bill’s passage is expected to create and whether the measure would be effective.

“It’s extremely problematic to lose financial resources for (social security expenses) when we don’t have an alternative way to fund the shortfall,” said Ishiba.

With the LDP holding a two-thirds majority, the bill, a key goal of the Takaichi administration, easily cleared the Lower House Friday.

But Friday’s sudden rejection by the LDP Lower House lawmakers could complicate its passage in the opposition-controlled upper chamber. Opposition parties against the bill are sure to argue that even prominent LDP members are opposed.

LDP leaders are also concerned that Upper House party lawmakers who share similar concerns as Ishiba and the others may also rebel if the party doesn’t reprimand them.

“The bill needed to be voted in accordance with the party line. Party discipline is extremely important,” LDP policy chief Takayuki Kobayashi said on Friday.

Takaichi, meanwhile, refrained from commenting on the move by the four, telling reporters Friday that the actions were those of the individual lawmakers.

“We submitted this bill with confidence, and we will provide a solid explanation of its significance and effects,” Takaichi said.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.summary: Four LDP lawmakers abstained from voting on the food consumption tax reduction bill, which passed the Lower House on Friday. The party is expected to discipline the four over their actions. But it faces a dilemma, as an internal backlash could erupt if the punishment is seen as too strong or too weak.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Government betting on language app powered by anime and AI
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: Jessica Speed
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
Japan is betting it can turn pop-culture fans into fluent Japanese speakers with a potential AI-powered language-learning app through which users can practice conversations with popular characters.

The app, which is to be developed by the Japan Foundation (JF) at the request of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs following budget approval for the next fiscal year, is expected to be completed by fiscal 2028 and will primarily target young people overseas who are interested in anime and manga.

The app will use artificial intelligence to allow users to practice conversations with characters from popular anime and manga.

Previous apps and websites made by the foundation have relied on original characters because of copyright restrictions, but for this new venture, the JF plans to negotiate with rights holders to secure the use of well-known characters. It is also the first time the foundation has incorporated AI into its language-learning services.

Japan is increasingly seeking to strengthen its soft power diplomacy, aiming to turn growing international enthusiasm for its cultural exports into a broader base of fans of the country, particularly in emerging and developing economies across Africa and Central and South America, where it has yet to establish as strong a presence as it has in other markets.

A 2024 JF survey found that interest in anime, manga, J-pop and J-fashion was the most commonly cited motivation for studying Japanese, as reported by 61.3% of students at overseas Japanese-language education institutions.

The survey also found that the number of Japanese-language learners overseas reached a record 4 million, up 5.4% from the previous survey in 2021. Interest in studying and working in Japan also increased, with 37.3% citing studying in Japan and 36.4% pointing to future employment in the country as motivations.

The ministry has requested ¥1.83 billion ($11.6 million) for fiscal 2027 to support the overseas expansion of Japanese content. Other government initiatives aimed at strengthening Japan’s soft power include establishing networks between Japanese and local content industry professionals, promoting legitimate distribution channels to combat piracy, and supporting translators who help introduce Japanese works to overseas audiences.

The ministry hopes the app will also expand access to Japanese-language education in regions where schools and qualified teachers may be scarce, and provide a relatively low-cost alternative to establishing additional overseas teaching facilities.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.summary: The app will use artificial intelligence to allow users to practice conversations with popular characters. It is to be developed by the Japan Foundation (JF) at the request of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The app is expected to be completed by fiscal 2028 and will primarily target young people overseas who are interested in anime and manga.

https://www.dw.com/en/turkey-pushes-for-.title: Turkey pushes for transition at COP31 as coal burns
https://www.dw.com/en/turkey-pushes-for-.text:
The host of this year's UN climate summit remains heavily dependent on fossil fuels as it tries to inspire a global switch to clean energy.

As Turkey welcomes delegates to the 2026 UN climate talks in Antalya and pushes for cuts in global greenhouse gas emissions, it can point to surging renewable energy capacity at home.

The COP31 host has approved more than 33 gigawatts (GW) of battery storage projects since 2022 that can power over 27 million homes.

Among the largest battery project pipelines in Europe, this storage will complement fast-expanding wind and solar energy that today provides 22% of electricity in Turkey, up from 4.5% a decade ago.

Yet this clean energy upswing is a long way from compensating for an over-reliance on fossil fuels.

Turkey's coal-fired electricity generation increased by roughly one-third in the last decade, and in 2024 overtook Germany and Poland, which previously had the highest coal power capacity in Europe before it began to decline.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Turkey is among the few industrialized countries that is yet to commit to a phase-out date for coal — the fossil fuel with the highest planet-heating emissions.

Yet at the same time, "coal's position in the electricity market in Turkey is increasingly precarious," Efe Baysal, Turkey team lead at global environment network, 350.org, told DW.

He points to high local community opposition to coal projects on environmental grounds or due to lack of financial viability. According to German nonprofit climate campaigners, Beyond Fossil Fuels, some 97% of new coal projects have been cancelled in the last decade in Turkey, in what it calls "a global record."

"Turkey's coal project failure rate is the final nail in Europe's coal coffin," said Kasia Szeniawska of Beyond Fossil Fuels in a statement earlier this year. "Coal power is finished: it's financially risky, increases costs for billpayers, harms people's health, and sabotages climate goals."

But in June, Turkey announced plans to expand one of its largest coal plants and near double its capacity.

The move underlines Turkey's "conservative energy policy" and "highly insufficient" climate goals, said Umit Sahin, head of the climate change program at the Istanbul Policy Center, a global research institute.

Turkey's current climate target allows emissions to keep rising until 2038, meaning it will struggle to meet its plans to reach net zero by 2053, notes Climate Action Tracker, a climate research think tank.

Aside from climate concerns, Turkey's high dependence on imported fossil energy makes it extremely vulnerable to volatile global oil and gas markets. The nation currently imports 95% of its natural gas, 83% of crude oil and 60% of its coal – which together make up a "lion's share” of Turkey's energy capacity, said Baysal.

It is partly this dependence that has inspired Turkey's push for greater electrification at the COP31 climate conference.

In September, the country launched the "35x35" global electrification pledge, which aims to increase electrification of world economies from just over 20% today to 35% by 2035.

The goal is for electrification to replace fossil fuels, including in transport, buildings and industry, and preferably using clean energy, though this is not mandatory – heat pumps, for example, emit fewer greenhouse gases than gas boilers, even when the electricity is generated using fossil fuels.

The pledge complements existing UN climate goals of doubling energy efficiency and tripling renewables to keep temperature rise in line with the Paris climate agreement.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Turkey COP31 president Murat Kurum will promote the 35x35 pledge in Antalya on both climate and energy security grounds.

"[The war in the Gulf] has shown us, once again, that fossil fuels do not guarantee energy supply security," he said earlier this year at a UN climate meeting in Bonn, Germany. "Investment in alternative energy sources, in particular to support energy diversity, means stability, resilience and clean development."

But despite the rhetoric, Climate Action Tracker says that under Turkey's National Energy Plan, the COP31 host is only on track to electricify around 25% of total energy consumption by 2035.

Turkey is one of numerous Mediterranean countries facing extreme climate impacts like wildfires and record heat, in addition to recent severe and deadly flooding.

As it hosts this year's climate summit, the country has a great opportunity to hasten the energy transition, says Baysal, especially since it receives nearly double the annual sunlight of Germany.

Turkey is already starting to realize some of this potential, with one analysis showing the country produces more solar module manufacturing capacity than several major European countries combined.

Solar increased from around 0.1% of total installed electricity capacity in 2014 to almost 21% at the beginning of 2026, according to Turkey's resources and energy ministry.

The COP31 host can reduce its emissions 35% by 2035 if 10 GW of solar and wind is added each interim year — as opposed to the government's target of 8 GW — notes Umit Sahin. This goal will be helped by fast-expanding battery capacity, he said.

"But if you don't phase out coal, your emissions cannot go down," he added.

Meanwhile, the COP presidency could be a "turning point" and "a very important step for Turkey," Sahin told DW.

If the country wants to show climate leadership, and reduce energy dependency, it will need to embrace a "progressive climate policy" that promotes a full energy transition, he added.

Serdar Vardar and Jonathan Rampley-Sturgeon contributed reporting to this article.

Edited by: Tamsin Walker

The country is one of several countries that is heavily dependent on fossil fuels. The energy transition will need a full climate policy, says the COP31 host.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck0j.title: Trump says he was 'kidding' about Dana White press secretary offer
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck0j.text:
US President Donald Trump has said he "was kidding" about asking Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC) boss Dana White to be the White House press secretary.

Trump told the media on Sunday that White "loves the idea" but that the invitation was "just a little fun".

It comes after the president posted on his Truth Social platform on Saturday that he had offered White the role, asking him to take it while writing, "Dana will be a Press Secretary like none other."

White said later that day he was going to meet the president on Monday, but would not be drawn into whether or not he would take the vacant position.

On Sunday Trump told reporters White was visiting him on Monday for "other reasons".

"I think he's going to be in Washington. So he's going to come over and see me.

"I will tell you, I was only kidding. But Dana loves the idea. And there's only one Dana. He's great," the president said.

"But, it was it was just a little fun."

The press secretary role is yet to be filled after it became vacant in October when Katie Zacharia quit after less than five days in the job.

She took over from Karoline Leavitt, who was the youngest press secretary in US history and had held the role since Trump began his second term.

Trump's job offer came after a heavy loss in the midterm elections, where the Republican Party lost its majority in both houses of Congress.

In his Truth Social post on Saturday, he said he was "pleased to announce" that White "has been offered the job".

He said he had asked White to bring with him several current and former mixed martial arts fighters as "assistants".

"We need these people to defend us against the Lunatic Left," he wrote.

"Dana, please take the job!"

Asked about the Trump offer at a news conference on Saturday, the UFC chief executive said he had "lot of jobs already".

"I'm sure we'll have something to talk about after that," he said of their planned Monday meeting, but did not say whether or not he would take the job.

White leads UFC, and PowerSlap, a regulated slap-fighting promotion league, as well as recently launching promotion company Zuffa Boxing.

He is also a board member of Meta, the owner of Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp.

White appeared as a speaker in support of Trump's White House campaigns at the Republican National Conventions in 2016, 2020 and 2024.

He also appeared on stage for Trump's victory speech in the 2024 presidential election.

This summer, the UFC staged a cage match on the White House lawn.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm93.title: Nine foreigners caught allegedly trying to leave South Africa to fight in Ukraine
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm93.text:
Nine foreigners have been arrested in South Africa after they were caught allegedly trying to leave the country to fight in the war between Russia and the Ukraine, police say.

The group, aged between 20 and 26, were arrested in and around Johannesburg by a multidisciplinary team on Sunday evening.

They were caught as they were "preparing to board flights out of the country", authorities added, but their final destination is unclear.

The group is accused of contravening South Africa's laws, which outlaw mercenary activity without government permission.

Police said the group were arrested at South Africa's biggest airport, OR Tambo, and a hotel in Bruma, east of Johannesburg by a multidisciplinary team that involved Interpol.

The police statement added that the involvement of Interpol and other international law enforcement agencies indicated that the suspects had also allegedly violated laws in their respective home countries, prompting cooperation with South African authorities.

Authorities declined to disclose the group's nationalities but confirmed that none of them resided in South Africa.

They have also not said whether the group allegedly intended to fight for Russia or Ukraine nor provided details of the organisations allegedly involved in facilitating their travel.

Citizens of several African countries, including Kenya, Ghana and South Africa, have gone to fight for Russia in Ukraine - some they had been duped and had not realised where they were going.

A Ukrainian intelligence assessment estimated earlier this year that more than 1,700 people from 36 countries in Africa have been recruited to fight for Russia.

Kenya at the time estimated that 252 citizens had been illegally conscripted in Russia. In March, Foreign Minister Musalia Mudavadi visited Moscow to address the issue.

He said at the time that an agreement had been reached to stop recruiting Kenyan nationals.

In February, Ghana said that 55 of its citizens had been killed in the conflict, with 272 believed to have been lured to fight since the war started in 2022.

The same month, South Africa secured the return of 17 South Africans who were allegedly tricked into joining the war.

In December last year, South African authorities arrested five people, including a journalist, for allegedly recruiting people to join the war.

Ukraine has also been recruiting foreign nationals, including from Africa.

The nine arrested are expected to appear in court either later on Monday or Tuesday.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cv2d.title: At least 34 dead after Europe-bound migrant boat sinks off Senegal
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cv2d.text:
At least 34 people have died after a boat carrying migrants sank off the coast of Senegal, the Senegalese Press Agency (APS) reports, citing an official source.

The interior ministry said one person had been rescued, but the number of people still missing was yet to be established.

The small wooden boat capsized between the capital, Dakar and the northern city of Saint-Louis, as it headed towards Spain's Canary Islands.

Spanish migrant rights group Walking Borders recorded 635 deaths on the Atlantic route to the Canary Islands between January and May 2026, the highest toll among the routes it monitors.

Saliou Diouf, founder of Senegalese migrant aid group Boza Fii, told AFP that all the bodies recovered so far were Senegalese. The nationalities of other people on board was yet to be established, as search operations continued.

President Bassirou Diomaye Faye has expressed his condolences to the victims' families and urged Senegalese nationals not risk their lives on the dangerous sea crossings.

In a statement posted on X, he pledged to intensify efforts to dismantle the networks organising the journeys.

"We will relentlessly continue the fight against those who organise these crossings and the work that gives our young people reasons to hope here," he said.

The tragedy comes amid renewed concerns over the dangers facing migrant attempting to reach Europe by sea.

Walking Borders estimates that about 21 people died for every 100 who reached the Canary Islands during the period it monitored.

Senegalese authorities said they had intercepted another boat, on Friday, carrying 142 migrants attempting to reach Spain.

Those on board included 23 women, two babies and two other children. Police said the group comprised nationals of Senegal, Gambia, Guinea-Bissau, Guinea and Nigeria.

Meanwhile, a state of emergency was declared on the Spanish island of El Hierro on Saturday following a surge in migrant arrivals.

More than 3,300 people have reached the island in about 30 boats since the beginning of November, according to local authorities.

This amounts to almost a third of the population on the island, one of the main entry points into Europe for migrants arriving from West Africa.

Fernando Clavijo, president of the Canary Islands regional government, described the situation as "absolutely unsustainable," reports the Reuters news agency.

The route has grown in prominence amid tighter controls and increased cooperation between European countries and North African states, which may have diverted some journeys away from the central Mediterranean.

Limited employment opportunities, family pressures and established migration networks are among the factors driving people to leave Senegal, according to the International Organization for Migration (IOM).

For many young people, the prospect of finding work and earning more abroad remains a powerful incentive, despite the risks of crossing the Atlantic in overcrowded boat.

Nearly one in four young people in Senegal was unemployed in the second quarter of 2026, according to the country's statistics agency.

The figure highlights the challenge facing President Faye's government as it seeks to create jobs for a predominantly young population that overwhelmingly voted for him in the 2024 elections.

In a statement on Sunday, Senegal's interior ministry said it would continue efforts to combat people-smuggling networks, including by strengthening cooperation with neighbouring countries.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c65y.title: Thirteen migrants die after boat sinks off Crete
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c65y.text:
At least 13 people have died after a boat carrying migrants sank off the coast of the Greek island of Crete.

The coastguard said it had rescued 18 people, all of whom were Sudanese nationals. Four of the survivors were taken to hospital, including a toddler.

Authorities said it was not immediately clear what caused the deaths, but they believe the boat had been at sea for days and had struggled to reach shore due to strong winds.

Crete remains one of several key gateways for migrants attempting to reach Europe from the Middle East and North Africa, with more than 22,000 of the 86,400 sea arrivals so far this year landing in Crete alone.

One unnamed coastguard official who spoke to news agency Reuters on condition of anonymity said the survivors were "shivering from the cold".

The migrants' boat was spotted by a Moroccan-flagged container ship about 15 nautical miles (28km) off Crete's coast.

The Greek coastguard rescued another 187 people in three separate incidents off the coast of Greece on Monday.

More than 37,000 migrants have arrived in Greece so far this year, UN figures show, already surpassing the number who arrived in the entirety of 2025.

The Greek government has announced plans to deal with the influx, including opening a temporary housing complex near the Cretan capital, Heraklion.

Greece was at the heart of Europe's migration crisis in 2015-16, when nearly a million people arrived on its islands, mostly from Turkey.

Arrivals later fell as border controls tightened, but crossings from Libya have surged in recent years, particularly among people fleeing conflict in Sudan and seeking better economic opportunities from countries including Bangladesh.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqd0.title: Four killed in Gaza after sand embankment collapses onto tents, health ministry says
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqd0.text:
Three children and one woman were killed when a sand embankment collapsed onto tents in central Gaza following heavy rain, the Hamas-run health ministry says.

Five injured people were also reportedly rescued after the incident on Sunday night at a camp for displaced families south of Deir al-Balah.

Videos showed men using phone torches to search for survivors beneath boulders, sand and collapsed tents.

The Civil Defence service, which operates under the Hamas-run interior ministry, said the "humanitarian tragedy" should prompt urgent action by international organisations to provide safe shelters for displaced people and move tents away from sandy areas, slopes and locations at risk of collapse.

Torrential rain on Saturday reportedly flooded tens of thousands of tents across Gaza, leaving many Palestinians without a dry place to sleep.

The Civil Defence said water levels reached up to 1.5m (4.9ft) in some places and that its first responders were able to respond to only 10% of the 2,100 distress calls they received.

"Protecting the lives of displaced people is an urgent humanitarian responsibility. Their tents must not become death traps beneath sand and rainwater," it warned.

The Civil Defence initially reported on Sunday that three children and two women were killed when the sand embankment collapsed. But the health ministry said on Monday morning that only one woman was among the dead.

She was identified as Tahrir Nabhan, while the children were named as Mariam Nabhan and her brother Salah, and Habiba al-Zein.

Mustafa al-Masri told the BBC that he and other rescuers had used their bare hands to dig the victims and survivors out of the sand and rubble.

"It was extremely difficult. This mound was huge and wide. It collapsed onto the tent, and we didn't know what to do," he said.

"When we got here, we, along with the young men from the camp, pulled them out with our own hands. We pulled out the children and the woman."

"Their father arrived shouting, 'My children, my children, my children, my children.' We pulled his children out, put them in the ambulance, and took them to the hospital."

Masri added that he had been displaced from the northern town of Beit Hanoun but had stayed in central Gaza because there was "nowhere for me to return to".

"We went out looking around, searching through the open areas and hills, but I couldn't find any place other than this area that felt suitable for me."

The International Organization for Migration's regional crisis co-ordinator, Karl Baker, told the BBC from Gaza that the territory's 2.1 million population was confined to only 30% of its total area and that many people were "unfortunately living in areas which would not be normal if we were not in this time of conflict".

He said the UN agency and its partners were trying to make sure there were enough tents and tarpaulins, as well as improved drainage in camps, to help them get through the winter.

However, he warned that aid currently getting into Gaza was not sufficient to meet the demands of the population, describing it as "the very smallest of Band-Aids [plasters]".

"We need more support, in-kind donations. We need funding in order to help the communities to help themselves," he said. "We need a lot more to happen."

UN agencies have called on Israeli authorities to allow in the specialist equipment and materials required to improve living conditions for displaced families.

Cogat, the Israeli military body tasked with co-ordinating deliveries, said on Sunday that more than 91,000 tents, 12 vacuum trucks for waste removal, and fuel and engine oil for pumping facilities have been delivered since the start of the "Gaza Winterization Plan".

But it added that Israel would not permit the entry of equipment that could be used for military purposes by Hamas and other Palestinian armed groups.

An estimated 80% of all structures in Gaza have been destroyed or damaged during the war between Israel and Hamas, according to the UN.

More than 1.9 million people have been displaced, many of them multiple times, and 1.2 million of them are currently living in tents or makeshift shelters, it says.

The UN has warned that the humanitarian situation in Gaza remains dire despite the ceasefire agreed in October 2025, as Israeli air strikes and other attacks continue to hit populated areas, causing casualties and property damage and driving further displacement.

The Gaza war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.

Since then, more than 74,640 people have been killed in Gaza, according to the territory's health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.

Additional reporting by Malak Hassouneh

Five injured people reportedly rescued after incident on Sunday night at a camp for displaced families. Civil Defence says water levels reached up to 1.5m (4.9ft) in some places.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwrk.title: 'Devastating message' as ANC records worst-ever result in South Africa election
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwrk.text:
South Africa's ANC has recorded its worst-ever showing in local elections since Nelson Mandela led the country out of apartheid and into democracy more than 30 years ago, a result the party has called "catastrophic".

While it won the most votes of all parties in the country, the African National Congress won 31% of the overall vote, one third down from the 46% it gained in 2021, and a far cry from the 65% 20 years ago.

The story of its decline is also clear in the provinces and cities. The party won a majority in just one of the country's nine provinces, Limpopo. In 2021 it won six. It also won the most votes in just two of the eight cities, compared with six at the last local elections.

The Democratic Alliance (DA) came second in the overall vote with 25%, retaining majority control of the city of Cape Town. Former president Jacob Zuma's MK party came third overall with 10%, unseating the ANC as winner in the city of Durban, while the Economic Freedom Fighters (EFF), led by Julius Malema, once seen as a serious challenge to the ANC, came fourth with 6%.

"This has been a very catastrophic outcome for the ANC," said secretary-general Fikile Mbalula on Saturday. "We knew this disaster is coming, we're staring at it. As we got into elections, the cost of living of our people was too high. The middle class have turned on the ANC in big numbers."

Entering the count centre on Sunday nigh, South Africa's president and ANC leader Cyril Ramaphosa said: "We accept the will of the people however concerning it might be, we accept that this is how the people of South Africa in our towns, in our cities, in our metros have spoken - and this is their verdict, we accept it with humility. It is a decline that is concerning, that is how I characterise it."

It's a continuing decline for the ANC, which lost its parliamentary majority in the national elections in 2024 for the first time since the end of apartheid in 1994. It then had to form a coalition government with a raft of other parties in what is called the Government of National Unity (GNU).

While the Democratic Alliance made significant gains in the cities in these local elections, its overall vote share rose only marginally from 22% in 2021, and was below the 27% it gained in 2016.

Voter turnout was 52%, an increase from 46% in 2021, when elections were held during the Covid pandemic.

"This election is delivering a devastating message to the ANC," said political analyst Susan Booysen. "It's an ANC in decline at local municipal level, at the metropolitan level, and when the results are reflected provincially and nationally, we see severe declines in ANC levels of support all around."

The reason for that decline in support is largely due to poor service delivery and infrastructure across the country, from water and power to sanitation. "These are huge problems," says Booysen, "and have really been affecting the lives of ordinary people, in the suburbs, in the townships, and in very dramatic ways."

The big picture looks even more bleak for the ANC. The party will elect a new leader next year as Ramaphosa comes to end of his term. He is due to stay on as president of the country until the next national elections in 2029, but there are few candidates lined up to succeed him in either role.

"It is sort of the end of the liberation movement era in South Africa," said political analyst William Gumede, "and the dominance of the liberation movement since the end of apartheid. So the ANC is going to be a party that by 2029 could be the second biggest rather than the biggest party. It may actually spiral into a long period of just total infighting. This is a new era for South Africa's politics and also the ANC."

The elections also saw a significant shift in voting patterns, with the DA, traditionally known as the "white party" for attracting a largely white vote, gaining more black votes. "We're moving towards a post-racial voting pattern in South Africa," added Gumede.

South Africa now faces days of local coalition building, with the three metropolitan municipalities in the province of Gauteng, the country's powerhouse, under particular scrutiny. The ANC may even find itself shut out in the cities of Johannesburg and Pretoria.

"We are now in a coalition country," said Gumede. "Essentially, what the voters are saying is: 'Well, the ANC has dominated the last three decades, they didn't use their power to change the society for the good, so we don't want the dominant parties anymore, whether at national level, provincial level, or rather now at a local level. We actually want coalitions. We want people to work together.'"

Parties now have 14 days from the moment results were announced to negotiate coalitions.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwrk.summary: ANC has recorded its worst-ever showing in local elections since Nelson Mandela led the country out of apartheid. The party won the most votes of all parties in the country, but it lost 31% of the overall vote. The ANC lost its parliamentary majority in the national elections in 2024 for the first time since the end of apartheid

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6gq.title: Birds return to waterfowl park after oil vandalism
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6gq.text:
Resident birds have returned to Broughshane Waterfowl Park after an oil spill which caused the death of 13 of the flock.

The popular attraction in County Antrim was forced to close after a nearby home heating oil tank was vandalised, causing the oil spill into the pond.

In a post on social media, The Waterfowl Pond confirmed that work is still underway to address the oil contamination and that a number of pens remain out of bounds.

More than 20 birds were transported to the USPCA's headquarters for urgent specialist care following the incident.

The park, which was home to 120 birds, has since reopened.

Broughshane Environment Wildfowl and Wildlife Trust's chairman, Gary Hayward, said about 10-12 birds have returned including two black swans and Nēnēs.

Hayward said they are back safely in their pens and they are lucky to be healthy.

The Northern Ireland Environment Agency (NIEA) was first alerted to the incident on Thursday 22 October and have been involved in removing the oil waste.

The agency said the substance involved had been identified as home heating oil, or kerosene, and that the source had been traced to a nearby tank.

Hayward said that there is very little evidence of the oil left as the NIEA have removed the majority of it.

"They have made problems a lot less than they could have been," he told BBC News NI.

He said there is still some oil around the edges, and once the oil leaves the pens the birds will be moved back into them.

Siobhan Hawthorn, wildlife supervisor at the USPCA, has been a key part of the rescue operation.

She said that all of the birds needed bathed and treated due to the level of contamination they suffered.

The birds included geese, ducks and swans.

Unfortunately some had already ingested too much and died as a result.

The Waterfowl Pond offered thanks to the USPCA for looking after the birds.

"We are truly grateful for everything you have done."

It also paid tribute to the support received from the public.

"It's another positive step forward for our park, and we couldn't have got here without you."

The popular attraction was forced into closure after oil spill caused the death of 13 birds. The park, which was home to 120 birds, has since reopened
