https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6ly.title: What's your love language - and does it actually mean anything?
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6ly.text:
I'm "words of affirmation", and so is my husband. This is supposedly our shared love language.

But, while we do like receiving compliments, they make us both feel a bit awkward.

Despite this, our result was confidently defined when we took the original Love Languages Quiz online, a personality test published by US pastor Gary Chapman who first came up with the five types of expressing and receiving love in 1992.

I'm sceptical. Does the theory really know more about us than our own lived experience of a 10-year marriage?

The five love languages are: Quality Time, Acts of Service, Words of Affirmation, Receiving Gifts, and Physical Touch - and they feel more ubiquitous than ever.

Contestants on dating shows ask each other their love languages; "My love language is…" is a common prompt on dating apps.

According to the Love Languages website, my husband and I are just two out of more than 150 million people to have taken this particular quiz.

Even though we scored much lower on some of the other languages, they speak more directly to us.

For example I love spending "quality time" with my husband, and feel much more loved by him making lists of films to watch with me than when he pays me a compliment.

But where did the idea of these five neat categories come from? And are they relevant for modern dating and relationships?

Unlike other relationship theories - such as attachment theory - the concept of love languages doesn't have scientific origins.

Chapman said the theory came to him after observing couples during counselling sessions he held in his parish.

Counselling psychologist Dr Sarah Emmerson told the BBC that love languages are still mentioned regularly in her sessions.

"There's almost no-one out there who hasn't taken that quiz," she said. "[Couples] quite frequently bring that in and say, 'So my partner is Physical Touch and I'm Acts of Service, so this doesn't work'.

"Research has proven that there isn't a lot of validity to the idea that there are only five ways in which people show love, and that everybody fits neatly into these categories. But people still gravitate towards it, and we have to wonder why that might be."

For some, talking about love languages can simply be a useful introduction to thinking about how they communicate their needs to their partner.

Psychotherapist Georgina Sturmer said that it helps people think about "what you really like in a relationship, and what do other people really like" but points out it's "hugely limited" and risks "oversimplifying everything".

In recent years, many therapists have also warned that Chapman's examples refer too readily to scripture and unequal relationship dynamics.

In the Love Languages book Chapman describes counselling a woman, Ann, whose husband of 10 years is hostile and verbally abusive towards her, including frequently telling her he hates her.

His love language, Ann tells Chapman, is specifically sexual physical touch.

When Ann says she finds it "hard to be sexually responsive" to him, Chapman advises her that she should "rely heavily upon [her] faith in God" to make herself have sex with her husband more often.

This example also exposes another problem - that love languages can be used to coerce partners into showing or receiving love in a way they're not comfortable with.

"There's a risk if someone says, 'well my love language is receiving gifts, so you must give me gifts all the time, or my love language is physical touch, so you must be physically intimate with me all the time," Sturmer said.

The BBC has contacted the Love Languages team for comment.

So what can couples do if they want to understand each other, and themselves, better?

Listen to your partner: "Don't just wait until you can speak, but try to hear what they are saying and acknowledge their feelings," Dr Emmerson said.

Share how you feel using "I" statements, so you avoid blame: "If you reframe your words to lead with your own feelings, it helps you to express what's going on without leaving the other person feeling criticised," Sturmer explained.

Remember that disagreements are normal: "Healthy relationships often feature debate and disagreement," Sturmer said. "The challenge is not about avoiding rupture, it's about finding ways to repair it that can leave the relationship feeling stronger."

But, Dr Emmerson added, you should "pick the right time to talk about things that are difficult - not late at night, not when they've just come through the door".

Respond to bids for connection: Dr Emmerson said you should "try to be emotionally responsive to your partner when they are seeking connection" - even if they're doing so in subtle ways.

"This could be asking for a hug, or just telling you about something they just saw on their phone."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6ly.summary: Love languages are a form of expressing and receiving love. They are more ubiquitous than ever, and are used to coerce partners into showing or receiving love. Psychotherapist Georgina Sturmer says it helps people think about what they really like.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckx2.title: Senior doctors at Glasgow hospital in care delay warning
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckx2.text:
Senior emergency doctors at Scotland's biggest hospital have written to the healthcare watchdog to warn of harm to patients from delays to care.

The consultants also warned of uncontrollable system failure, in a letter sent to Healthcare Improvement Scotland (His) in July.

They said the situation in the emergency department at the Queen Elizabeth University Hospital (QEUH) in Glasgow had deteriorated since their last review, which was undertaken in 2024 and published a year later.

That report found that poor relationships between managers and consultants was likely to have had a detrimental impact on patient care.

The July letter said staff were being forced to step down patients from resuscitation areas and move people into corridors to address "sustained overcapacity".

They added that there was no effective strategy to address the problems, and said evidence now clearly linked overcrowding in accident and emergency areas to higher death rates.

A spokesperson for Health Improvement Scotland said it continued to "take the concerns raised by staff in the Queen Elizabeth University Hospital Emergency Department seriously."

The statement added: "As part of our ongoing follow-up work, we will be meeting frontline staff and reviewing progress against the recommendations from our previous review during November. We have also made Scottish government colleagues aware of the ongoing concerns and pressures that have been raised with us.

"It is for NHS Greater Glasgow and Clyde to implement the changes required and to address the issues identified. We expect the board to demonstrate progress in implementing the recommendations and responding to the concerns raised by staff.

"Given our ongoing review activity, it would not be appropriate to comment in detail on specific correspondence or to pre-empt our further findings from our follow up work."

The Scottish Liberal Democrats called on ministers to act on the letter.

Their health spokesman, Adam Harley MSP, said: "This letter is chilling. The Scottish government needs to wake up to the crisis at the QEUH and intervene.

"We cannot accept this constant crisis as the status quo.

"That patients who need resuscitation at one of our busiest hospitals cannot take their safety for granted shows an utter failure of accountability, and proves that our NHS is in dire need of rescue."

NHS Greater Glasgow and Clyde (NHSGGC) said they continued to address the issues raised in the letter.

A statement said a programme of improvement work was ongoing to deal with patient flow and numbers.

It said: "NHSGGC recognises that, despite the work to date, further support is required in the Queen Elizabeth University Hospital (QEUH). In recognising this, the continuation of our improvement work, including a refreshed whole system approach, is a priority .

"We recognise that some patients continue to wait too long within the emergency department, particularly when there are pressures on hospital capacity and delays in discharging patients who are clinically ready to leave, and improving this situation for both our patients and colleagues is really important to us."

The board said the department continued to be under pressure and patient safety remained their highest priority.

The Scottish government has been approached for comment.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckx2.summary: consultants warned of uncontrollable system failure in letter sent to Healthcare Improvement Scotland. They said situation in emergency department at Queen Elizabeth University Hospital in Glasgow had deteriorated. Report found poor relationships between managers and consultants likely to have detrimental impact on patient care.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmly.title: Psychiatric intensive care unit for women to open
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmly.text:
The first NHS intensive care unit for women with serious mental health needs in Kent and Medway is due to open.

Women in the region will have access to a dedicated NHS psychiatric intensive care unit for the first time, following a £4.63m investment by Kent and Medway Mental Health NHS Trust.

The 10-bed facility at Littlestone Lodge in Dartford will provide short-term, intensive care for women experiencing serious mental health difficulties who need extra support.

Dr Afifa Qazi, chief medical officer for the trust, said the opening was an important step forward and that until now women needing intensive care and support "have not been able to receive this specialist care from our team".

The unit is expected to provide around 2,500 bed days of care for women each year, and is due to welcome its first patient towards the end of November.

Qazi said: "This new service means we can now provide specialist, compassionate care at a particularly difficult time in their lives.

"Our team will take the time to get to know each woman, understand what matters to her and recognise her as a person, not just her mental health needs."

The trust said the unit would create a more joined-up pathway, helping women move smoothly between hospital wards and community services as their needs changed, with care planned around each woman's circumstances.

Two of the 10 beds will also be available to women referred by other NHS trusts, depending on individual needs.

The trust already provides intensive mental health care for men at Willow Suite, a 12-bed unit at Littlebrook Hospital. The new unit extends this specialist service to women.

People with personal experience of mental health services helped shape the unit, and its design also takes account of sensory needs, including those of women with autism and learning disabilities.

Jim Dickson, MP for Dartford, said women experiencing serious mental health difficulties deserved "care that treats them with dignity, compassion and an understanding of their individual needs".

"I'm pleased to see this new unit open in Dartford. It is an important investment in mental health services for women and their families across Kent and Medway," he said.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c933.title: Hut owner wins battle to keep living in off-grid home he built
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c933.text:
An off-grid hut that produces its own heating and electricity can continue to be the home of the man who built it, a council has decided.

Geoffrey Finnimore, a self-employed architectural designer, erected the structure in Glandwr, near Crymych, in 2020, but never told authorities or asked for permission.

Pembrokeshire council told him he must apply for retrospective permission for the home that is self-sufficient, and also collects rain water.

However, the local authority found that because it has now been occupied as a home for more than four years, it is immune from prosecution action.

"Without my home, which I created to solve my own problems and without state assistance, having to pay for other accommodation would be catastrophic for my finances and wellbeing," Finnimore said.

The council asked him to apply for a lawful development certificate for the property.

This is a formal legal document confirming the development is lawful.

But as he had lived there for more than four years, it meant he could not be prosecuted, so his application was accepted, the Local Democracy Reporting Service said.

Finnimore has been the principal custodian of 4.5 acres of land at Coed Troednoeth, Tir y Gafel since the previous owner left in 2018.

They had lived at the site in a campervan with a lean-to structure, according to the council.

But Finnimore described this as "less than adequate" for his health and wellbeing, so started developing the hut.

In a personal statement to the local authority, he confirmed he had lived at the site for more than 10 years, earns less than £10,000 a year as a self-employed worker, and provided evidence of his long-term residency.

He added: "This application has been sought by the council, and I have had to comply out of a position of vulnerability with respect to the prospect of enforcement against a building and living situation that has been demonstrated to be well-established and that I hold is deemed lawful.

"In the context of a housing and a cost-of-living crisis I have taken care of my own needs.

"So far as the council's responsibilities in that context goes, I see that as one less problem to solve.

"Conversely, I would consider a rejection of a well-justified application like this as a contribution that exacerbates these deep and present social concerns."

Council officers granted the certificate because they found, on the balance of probabilities, that Coed Troednoeth had existed and been occupied as a home for more than four years before the application, making it immune from enforcement action.

It added: "In June 2020, the land was purchased by Mr Finnimore and in November 2020, he began using the building as his principal dwelling, hence the justification to apply for a certificate of lawful use."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5n4.title: Man jailed over racist Badenoch death threats
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5n4.text:
A man has been jailed for sending the Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch emails threatening to shoot her dead.

Ex-teacher Kieran Kyle sent three emails on 2 May to the Tory party leader in which he made racist references and claimed to have been in the IRA, the court heard.

The 43-year-old, from Gillingham in Kent, pleaded guilty on 22 September at Westminster Magistrates' Court to two counts of sending communications of an indecent or offensive nature.

Kyle was sentenced to 20 weeks in prison at the same court on Monday.

In a victim impact statement read to the court, Badenoch and her husband Hamish said the "malicious communications and targeted harassment" not only had an effect on them, but also undermined "a healthy democracy".

In two of the emails, Kyle had made racist references and written: "I'm ex-IRA, so Bloody Sunday references from you are going to give you trouble," the court heard.

The messages were sent on the day Badenoch apologised for footage from Bloody Sunday being mistakenly used in a social media clip to criticise a parliamentary Bill on legacy issues in Northern Ireland.

The Tory leader had said she did not sign off the video and that it was sent out by "very young people".

The video criticising the Northern Ireland Troubles Bill, posted to her social media channels on 28 April, showed Badenoch saying the Labour legislation would "drag" Troubles veterans back to court.

Thirteen unarmed civilians were shot dead when members of the Army's Parachute Regiment opened fire on civil rights demonstrators in the Bogside area of Londonderry on 30 January 1972, a date that became known as Bloody Sunday.

The court heard Kyle had also sent an email to Badenoch's husband Hamish on 29 April, which used a racist term and said she had a "big mouth" and he should "put a leash on her".

Prosecutor Ben Holt said the North West Essex MP and her husband were left "distressed" and "upset", particularly by the "racist language and threats of violence used towards them".

He added Cheryl Bacon, head of Badenoch's parliamentary office, said the emails were "disgusting" and "distressing" to read.

Baiju Thittala, defending, told the court Kyle "did not know" who Badenoch was at the time of the offences, adding "he only realised later, once he had sent the emails".

Asked by the judge how Kyle, a former secondary school teacher, could not know who Badenoch was, Thittala said: "He just 'Googled' it and it came up as the opposition leader."

The judge said: "The first emails were sent to Mr Badenoch, so I don't think he did not appreciate who Mrs Badenoch was.

"So he clearly knew who Mrs Badenoch was because he researched her husband's details first."

The Badenochs said in their victim impact statement: "Our primary concern arising from this offence is not the personal impact on us, but the wider consequences that malicious communications and targeted harassment have on our democratic life.

"When individuals choose to intimidate, threaten, or aggressively target elected representatives or public figures, the harm extends far beyond any single person. It undermines a healthy democracy."

The continued: "Public service relies on people being willing to step forward, often at significant personal cost, to represent their communities and contribute to public life.

"Increasingly, however, those who do so face hostility, harassment, and attempts to silence or intimidate them."

The judge also handed Kyle a restraining order, meaning he cannot contact Badenoch, her husband or her parliamentary office for five years.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqzj.title: Find out who's in the running for this year's Booker Prize
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqzj.text:
Past Booker Prize winners Marlon James and Douglas Stuart are among the contenders to scoop the prestigious literary award this year, after a shortlist selection process that the judges described as "a tussle".

Jamaican writer James is nominated this year for his latest novel The Disappearers; while Scottish author Stuart is shortlisted for John of John.

This year's other contenders are award-winning US novelist Elizabeth Strout, and British authors M John Harrison, Luke Kennard and Rebecca Perry.

But seven books that appeared on the longlist in July were jettisoned, and Dame Mary Beard, who chaired the judging panel, said agreeing on the final six "has been, to put it mildly, hard work".

The winner will receive £50,000 and will be announced in London on Monday evening. The ceremony will be broadcast live on a special edition of BBC Radio 4's Front Row.

Scroll down to find out more about this year's nominees.

James previously won the Booker Prize in 2015 for A Brief History of Seven Killings, while Stuart won in 2020 for Shuggie Bain.

Praising this year's entries when announcing the shortlist in September, Dame Mary added: "English language fiction now is full of talent – talent old and talent new.

"It's full of wit, seriousness, pleasure, challenge, discomfort and real brilliance, and I think we should be rewarding our novelists a lot more than we do."

The other judges included former Booker Prize-shortlisted US novelist Patricia Lockwood, who said she discovered she was "bossier than I believed myself to be" when making the case for or against particular books in the judges' meetings.

"I was sort of standing up a lot and tossing books across the room and being really active. I was like, 'Wow, yeah, I didn't know I had it in me'."

Another judge, poet Raymond Antrobus, told reporters: "All of us individually had a different idea for a shortlist and then it was a tussle."

Lockwood jokingly added: "A tussle, yeah. We wrestled like pigs in the mud!"

Antrobus said the final choices are connected because they are books that "as well as having heart, also took risk".

"These books, we truly believe, cannot be replicated by artificial intelligence. These are very human books for the way they talk about and navigate a lived experience."

The judging line-up was completed by journalist, editor and critic Rebecca Liu and Pulp frontman Jarvis Cocker, who said being on the selection panel was "a bit like being in a band".

He said: "The way a band makes an appealing noise is by everybody combining, in a way, and if you don't like that then you have to go solo.

"You get something that you couldn't get [alone] and no-one's in control of it and you make a good noise together. So I hope that's what this shortlist is, a nice noise."

Cocker read some of the entries while on tour, and said he joined one judges' meeting online while wearing a dressing gown in a hotel room in Australia at 02:00 local time.

"When you're on tour, it's quite dull when you're travelling so it was quite good to have something to read," he said.

"I became known for being in those meetings wearing a towelling robe."

The End of Everything by M John Harrison

An unexplained catastrophe, and the arrival of mysterious alien beings, have turned British society upside down - and a man and his elderly aunt muddle through on the Kent coast. It's the author's first Booker nomination, and he'd be the oldest ever winner at 81.

The judges said: "The End of Everything can be read as a thriller, a mystery, a satire, a dystopia, a road novel, a work of realism. The landscape may be bleak, the catastrophe may be immersive, yet there still were moments we found ourselves laughing aloud."

The Disappearers by Marlon James

This epic, visceral story revolves around a violent attack on eight gay men who had gathered to rehearse a queer play in Kingston, Jamaica, in 1988, and its aftermath. The New York Times called it "a masterpiece, the novel of the decade and possibly of the century thus far".

The judges said: "A Jamaican epic from one of the most impactful Caribbean novelists today; readers will love the shifting register of the dialogue and poetic phrasings, often pierced through with sharp, double-edged humour."

Black Bag by Luke Kennard

An out-of work actor gets a new role - being locked in a black bag during psychology lectures for an entire term as a professor's experiment. The story unfolds into a humorous and poignant satire that makes sharp observations about the state of modern masculinity and creative life.

The judges said: "In a wonderfully quirky campus novel, Kennard combines an absurd experiment with a moving story about human frailty, passion, confusion and identity. There's something for everyone here."

May We Feed the King by Rebecca Perry

A modern-day museum curator is commissioned to recreate a past scene in a historic palace, and becomes immersed in the world of the young, reluctant king whose life she uncovers. It is the debut novel by Perry, who is also a poet and a former competitive trampolinist.

The judges said: "An affecting and lush jewel of a novel that moves between our present-day world to a medieval court and unsettles the idea that there's ever one universal historical truth."

The Things We Never Say by Elizabeth Strout

Strout, a former Pulitzer Prize winner and double Booker nominee, tells the story of a high school history teacher in his 50s who feels adrift in modern America. When a secret emerges, he must face big questions about his relationships and life choices.

The judges said: "A novel that engages with the deeply divisive politics of present-day America, without itself becoming divisive. This is the kind of book we need now: a calm antidote to contemporary events."

John of John by Douglas Stuart

The third novel by Stuart is about a fashion student who is drawn back to his home in a small, religious community in the Outer Hebrides in the mid-1990s. He and his father both nurse secrets. And both are called John.

The judges said: "A rich and moving novel about a father and son who live on a remote Scottish island in the 1990s, where small-town secrets and buried shame reverberate to surprising, devastating and even joyous effect."

Longlisted books that did not make the final cut included Emma Cline's Switzy, which had been seen by some as a frontrunner for the prize.

"Believe me, this is a nailed-on Booker winner," critic Giles Coren wrote in the Times this weekend.

"If this one doesn't win, I'll eat Mary Beard."

Dame Mary responded on Tuesday: "I know Giles Coren said he wants to eat me if Switzy isn't on the shortlist.

"Well, I'm going to get the cooker prepared and ask him how he wants me done."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqzj.summary: The winner will receive £50,000 and will be announced in London on Monday evening. The judges described the shortlist selection process as "a tussle" Elizabeth Strout Strout's John of John is a third novel by Douglas Stuart.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cxyv.title: 'I've got a band now' - Club anthem star Shygirl on why she's switching up her sound
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cxyv.text:
Hard-hitting beats, club anthems and unapologetically sexy lyrics are what Shygirl is known for.

But the singer and DJ - real name Blane Muise - has introduced a different sound for her second album, Swallow!, which dropped on Friday.

Shygirl hasn't totally left her electronic roots behind though.

You can still hear the sweat-soaked energy of Charli XCX's 365 remix and relentless pulse of 2024 hit mr useless on her latest record.

But there's also guitar strums, heartfelt songwriting and a dreamy haze, giving it an indie edge.

"I've learned over the 10 years I've been making music to have this confidence and to not be afraid of failure," she tells BBC Newsbeat.

"The big part of starting this record was wanting to have natural instrumentation and not feel like that was barred from me."

Shygirl puts the change down to a desire for a more "authentic" sound - a growing trend among British electronic artists who've been bringing a rockier influence to their music.

Asked why she took this musical direction, the 33-year-old says it was down to "the nostalgia of the indie sound".

"I felt the familiarity of that feeling, embracing the teenager within and the angst that I had and all the sounds that coloured that environment," she says.

Long-time producers Karma Kid and Casey MQ were "surprised" when Shygirl told them about her desire to work in more indie sounds, but she says the pair trusted her with the new direction.

Fans have been patiently waiting for something other than singles since her debut album Nymph was released in 2022.

The question now is whether they'll relate to this more rose-tinted version of Shygirl.

"It's not like I changed overnight," she insists. "In fact, it was because I was the girl I was in all the other songs that I became who I am now."

There are clear signs that Shygirl is entering a new chapter.

She cleared her Instagram feed before beginning the album rollout, and the artwork shows a bird hatching from an egg, symbolising rebirth.

But she points out the journey is an "evolution" rather than reinvention.

"I think it's less about moving away from me, but I would hate to repeat myself," she says.

"I would only wish to pick up the same tool if I felt like I had grown somewhat or had a renewed expertise for it."

That growth can be heard in tracks like Live the Life You Like - one of Shygirl's favourites on the album.

It features a gritty bassline and a manipulated riff that echoes a klaxon, which she describes as giving off "punk energy".

Leaning into that side of her sound has only made her more excited to take the record on a tour, starting with Europe in March.

"I've got a band now," she reveals with a grin. "I work with a drummer and a multi-instrumentalist and sometimes a bassist.

"It's just so fun to share the stage and be so inspired. We've rehearsed, but there's still so many moments for spontaneity and for us to look at each other and vibe."

Shygirl's the latest artist known for electronic music who's embraced a more organic sound.

Her close friend Charli XCX featured a rockier, guitar-driven style on her latest album Music, Fashion, Film.

One of the standout tracks on that album for Shygirl is SS26, because "her voice is so natural and exposed".

"You forget other people don't know that voice and they need to get to know that starting point to be able to appreciate everything else."

Shygirl believes that same stripped-back approach is shaping much of the current wave of British dance music, including her latest album.

"There's so many of us now, especially coming from the Brit pack, that are doing the same thing," she says.

Artists like PinkPantheress and Fred Again have also spoken about bringing indie influences into electronic music, something Shygirl says is "a reflection of what is going on in the world".

"I think there is a natural desire to have a sense of truth or something grounding," she says.

"And what is more grounding or more truthful than knowing exactly where a sound comes from."

So with artists borrowing more and more from across the musical spectrum, does genre still matter?

For Shygirl, it's less about what box listeners put her music in and more about whether it connects with them.

"Regardless if they like it or they hate it, I want someone to feel something. To be apathetic to my music would be the biggest insult to me."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cxyv.summary: Shygirl's second album, Swallow!, dropped on Friday. The 33-year-old singer and DJ has embraced a more organic sound. She says she wants to have a more authentic sound.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmwy.title: Ioan Gruffudd in AI warning after fan claimed they had been in year-long affair
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmwy.text:
Hollywood actor Ioan Gruffudd has warned fans of "explicit and disturbing" AI-generated content impersonating him online.

The 53-year-old star, from near Aberdare, Rhondda Cynon Taf, urged his followers not to send money to people using images and videos of his likeness, after the content was brought to his attention.

"A woman came to a convention I was recently attending and she was under the impression that she was in an extramarital relationship with me for over a year," he said in an Instagram post.

"She showed me hundreds of AI images and videos that someone claiming to be me had sent to her. The images were explicit and disturbing."

The actor said the woman had been targeted through a Facebook page dedicated to crime drama Elsbeth, in which Gruffudd played a musician named Angus.

Gruffudd, who rose to fame in the long-running Hornblower TV series, said a person behind the Facebook page had sent the woman "a cell number, and asked her to communicate via Telegram", an instant messaging app.

"'They began sending AI images and videos to 'prove' that it was me," Gruffudd added.

He said that if anyone believes they are speaking with him via social media pages that are not his official channels then "this is not me".

"I will never give out my cell number to anyone that I don't personally know.

"Please do not engage and never send money! I urge you to ignore and block all contact from anyone that claims to be me.

"Lastly, if you have been targeted by this person, please report them and their number to the police for investigation. I have done the same."

Gruffudd is not the only celebrity to speak out about misleading AI technology.

Other celebrities who have shared concerns include Scarlett Johansson, Tom Hanks, Sir Tom Jones and Martin Lewis.

In January, Sir Tom shared a similar warning after he became aware of a number of social media accounts attempting to scam fans.

In a post shared to Instagram, his management wrote: "Regrettably, it has come to our attention that there is a large number of fake online profiles impersonating Sir Tom Jones and/or his team, who are attempting to scam fans and members of the public.

"Please be aware that Sir Tom Jones only has access to his verified (blue tick) Facebook/Instagram/X/YouTube and TikTok accounts. Sir Tom does not communicate to individuals directly or personally via his social channels.

"If a fake profile tries to chat to you privately, report and block them. This will NOT be Sir Tom Jones or his team.

"It is sad and disheartening to hear of these scammers attempting to trap and abuse vulnerable people, so please be careful and stay safe online."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmwy.summary: Ioan Gruffudd warns fans of "explicit and disturbing" AI-generated content impersonating him online. Actor urges followers not to send money to people using images and videos of his likeness. Gruffuddle says he was targeted by a woman who showed him AI images and video.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crgq.title: Michael Ball's wedding surprise after radio proposal
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crgq.text:
A couple whose surprise radio proposal captured hearts across the country were given an unforgettable wedding gift when singer and broadcaster Michael Ball turned up to perform at their ceremony.

Dawn Lloyd was shocked when her partner of more than 25 years Dave proposed on BBC Radio 2's Love Songs with Michael Ball programme in the summer and was stunned all over again when the presenter appeared at the couple's wedding at Weston Hall, in Stafford, on Sunday.

"I had no inkling whatsoever that this was going to happen," she said. "I was blown away.

"I just can't believe Dave has surprised me like this a second time. I was fooled the first time and now he has got me again."

Ball appeared without warning during the ceremony and performed Love Changes Everything, leaving Dawn and the wedding guests stunned.

Dawn said the day had been "perfect", with Dave adding he was "grateful for what Michael has done for us as a couple and for all of the family and friends to enjoy it as well".

Dave and Dawn, from Cannock, won over listeners when Dave secretly teamed up with Ball to stage the proposal.

Dawn, believing she was taking part in a BBC tour, was welcomed into the studio by Ball, who pretended he was recording voiceovers, before Dave read out a love letter and proposed to the woman he had been with for 31 years.

During the broadcast, Dave revealed he had already booked the wedding at Weston Hall, choosing a date close to 11 November, the anniversary of the day they first got together.

Ball later said the proposal was "so moving" that "we thought we have to follow this through".

Weston Hall holds special significance for the couple and was where Dave first proposed in the late 1990s.

But Dawn, who was 19 at the time, was so overwhelmed that she laughed, and the engagement ring was later lost, meaning the engagement never officially stuck.

More than 25 years later, the couple, who now have three children, finally made it down the aisle at the venue where their story began.

The couple were shocked to be surprised when Ball appeared at their wedding on Sunday. Dawn Lloyd said she was shocked when she was stunned by the proposal.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c674.title: Mariah Carey set to headline 2027 music festival
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c674.text:
Best-selling female solo artist Mariah Carey has been announced as the third headliner for a music festival.

Live at Powderham organisers said the singer would bring her Firefly summer tour to Powderham Castle in Devon on 27 June 2027, alongside special guests Sugababes, with additional support from R&B group Eternal.

The All I Want For Christmas Is You and Love Takes Time singer has amassed more than 19 Billboard Hot 100 Number One singles – more than any solo artist in history.

She is due to be headlining the festival near Exeter alongside Shania Twain, who has been set to perform on 24 June 2027; and Alex Warren, performing on 26 June.

Her recent performances included appearing at the opening ceremony of the 2026 Winter Olympics in Italy.

Live at Powderham attracted more than 140,000 people over its four days in 2026, with headline performances from Lewis Capaldi, Alanis Morissette and Teddy Swims.

The festival's final headliner has yet to be announced.

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/09/nx-s1-603.title: British comedian Russell Brand sentenced to over 10 years for rape and sexual assault
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/09/nx-s1-603.author: Kate Bartlett
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/09/nx-s1-603.text:
This is a court artist sketch by Elizabeth Cook of Russell Brand in the dock at Southwark Crown Court, in London, Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026.

Russell Brand, the raunchy, irreverent British comedian who became a celebrity darling in the early 2000s, has been sentenced to over 10 years in prison after being found guilty on one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

"The total sentence is one of ten years, six months," said Judge Justice Bennathan on handing down the sentence at Southwark Crown Court in London on Monday.

Brand, 51, was a career chameleon who went from stand-up comic and MTV host to a political analyst esteemed by Britain's left, only to become a conspiracy theorist and Christian convert beloved by the U.S. right.

But critics of Brand said there was always a clear thread of misogyny running through his comedy routines, and that his mistreatment of women had been an open secret for decades.

Over the past four weeks, six women testified against the comedian in court in London, in a trial that garnered massive media attention.

A jury found Brand guilty last week on four of the seven counts against him. He was found guilty of raping a woman he'd met at one of his shows in 2009 and of sexually assaulting three women – at a bar, a radio station and a TV studio – between 2004 and 2009.

Brand denies all charges and said he never had non-consensual sex.

Before the judge handed down the statement, one of the women who brought the case against Brand gave a victim impact statement to the court. None of the women have been publicly named.

The prosecution read out an impact statement from the one complainant, who Brand was found guilty of anally raping at his home in 2009. In her statement she said: "It's something I carry with me every day and it often feels never-ending."

"I doubt my ability to make good decisions and no longer trust my instinct in the way I did," her statement said, adding that because of Brand's fame she didn't think she'd be believed if she reported him.

FILE - Russell Brand is seen on stage during a tribute for Amy Winehouse at the MTV Video Music Awards on Sunday Aug. 28, 2011, in Los Angeles.

Another complainant, who Brand was found guilty of sexually assaulting at a bar in 2004 when he grabbed her breasts, said the confusion of what she "should" or "could" do had stayed with her for over 20 years.

The complainant, who spoke in person from behind a curtain in the courtroom, said she felt "physically sick" seeing Brand in the press afterwards as his fame rose.

Another of Brand's victims, who he was found guilty of sexually assaulting in 2005, said the assault had "a lasting impact on her life" and that over the years "hearing his voice on television or seeing his image has made me jump."

A fourth woman, who Brand was found guilty of sexually assaulting when they worked together at a TV studio, said she was badly affected and afterwards felt her working environment was unsafe.

British media who were in the court for the sentencing – which like the trial was not televised – said Brand, who had spent the weekend in prison, was in the suit he was convicted in on Thursday and sat holding a set of white rosary beads as the victim statements were read. Brand's wife Laura, who had supported him throughout the case, was in court, as was his father.

After the victim statements, the defense and prosecution teams had the opportunity to make their last statements.

The prosecution called for a long sentence, saying there were aggravating circumstances in the anal rape case, such as Brand removing a condom. The defence meanwhile said Brand was "a fundamentally different person" from who he was at the time of the crimes.

After considering the victim impact statements and those by the defence and prosecution, the Judge handed down the sentence live on camera.

In his remarks, he said Brand had become "a sexual predator" and "paused to pay tribute to the determination and bravery" of the women who'd come forward.

He then ordered Brand to be taken down to the cells.

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/09/g-s1-1526.title: Congress is back after GOP's midterm defeat. And, Trump appoints new chief of staff
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/09/g-s1-1526.author: Brittney Melton
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/09/g-s1-1526.text:
Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

President Trump has appointed Stephen Miller as his new chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles. It's Trump's first major personnel change since the Republicans' defeat in the midterms. Miller, who was deputy chief of staff, has been key in shaping many of Trump's controversial policies, particularly on immigration. Voter data indicates that the Democrats gained support partly due to Trump's immigration enforcement.

White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles (R) waves while walking to board Air Force One with White House communications aide Danielle Alvarez (L) and White House Deputy Chief of Staff and Homeland Security Advisor Stephen Miller on October 23, 2026 at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland.

The 119th Congress is reaching its final weeks before a new Democrat-controlled House and Senate step in. Lawmakers' key agenda item is keeping the federal government open, as funding runs out on Dec. 11. They will likely use a short-term continuing resolution to extend funding, because they lack the time and political will to negotiate the typical 12 appropriations bills.

Massive artificial intelligence chip maker Nvidia is launching an internal investigation after reports that its CEO was involved in a close relationship with a woman accused of being a Chinese spy. The New York Times reported that a Chinese intelligence operation targeted Jensen Huang to send advanced Nvidia AI chips to China. NPR reached out to the Chinese Embassy in Washington, D.C., for comment but has not received a response. China denied the allegations on Monday in a press briefing.

Climate change is transforming the vibrant colors of nature, from Arctic landscapes to coral reefs. The effects of these color shifts are complex, and scientists are racing to understand them. Here's how climate change is altering the colors of the world:

A field of colorful wildflowers blankets the Atacama Desert in northern Chile, transforming the world's driest non-polar desert into a vibrant landscape during the rare flowering desert phenomenon, known locally as the Desierto Florido. This extraordinary event occurs when unusually heavy rainfall awakens seeds that have remained dormant beneath the desert soil for years, sometimes decades. Within weeks, thousands of flowers emerge, covering vast stretches of the desert in shades of pink, purple, yellow, and white. The blooms last only a few weeks before the flowers dry out and release their seeds, which remain in the soil until the next rainfall brings the desert back to life. Huasco, Chile, on Wednesday October 21, 2026. Tamara Merino for NPR.

The Atacama Desert in Chile has transformed into a vibrant patchwork of pinks, yellows, lilacs and purples, thanks to the El Niño super cycle. This floral bloom has been the largest and most colorful in at least 30 years. The phenomenon followed unprecedented rainfall that caused flash floods, damaging homes and forcing evacuations. The rain reached deep into the parched ground, awakening millions of dormant seeds, bulbs and tubers. Now, more than 200 species have burst into color, creating a breathtaking spectacle where every crevice is streaked with hues.

Comedian and actor Russell Brand leaves Southwark Crown Court in London, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026.

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/09/g-s1-1515.title: Why a South Korean city is turning to a U.S. college to outsmart AI?
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/09/g-s1-1515.author: Anthony Kuhn
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/09/g-s1-1515.text:
Student Ma Yeonwoo, center, raises his hand during a Great Books summer camp seminar about Mary Shelley's novel Frankenstein at the Toegye elementary school in the city of Chuncheon. Teacher Han Kyoung-min, to Ma's right, leads the discussion.

CHUNCHEON, South Korea — "Is the Frankenstein monster human?" a teacher asks students at the Toegye public elementary school in Chuncheon city, some 50 miles east of Seoul, as they discuss Mary Shelley's novel Frankenstein.

"I think we can call it a human being with no soul," ventures student Ma Yeonwoo.

The Toegye school has adopted the "Great Books" educational model used by St. John's College, whose main campus is in Annapolis, Md.

The class's discussion then shifts to whether artificial intelligence is human.

"No," Ma Yeonwoo responds, because humans created AI, and although it is intelligent, it "has no creativity."

In the "Great Books" model, teachers do not lecture, they only guide discussions. There are no majors or elective courses. Students do not seek answers from outside sources such as the internet and rely only on their readings, their own reasoning and class discussions with their peers.

That suits Ma Yeonwoo, who says he enjoys debating with his classmates.

"If only the teacher talks we can have one idea, but if we all debate together, like, we can get many ideas together," he says.

This nascent educational movement addresses several concerning trends. One is that international tests such as PISA have shown a post-COVID drop in South Korean reading skills, after decades in which South Korean and other East Asian students outperformed their American counterparts.

Another is South Korea's rapid adoption of AI in education. 51% of South Korean students say they use AI chatbots to study at least once a week, according to Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) figures. Students also face intense competition to pass college entrance exams, which piles pressure on them down to the pre-K school level and prompts many South Korean families to send their children to cram schools to gain a competitive edge, or to foreign schools to escape the system.

Incheon National University Professor Lee Yonghwa (center) guides a Great Books summer camp seminar at Chuncheon High School. Lee, a St. John's College graduate, established South Korea's first Great Books program at his university in 2019.

"We all feel that this system leaves students with no time to read and think," because they're too busy memorizing facts to pass tests," says Lee Yonghwa, a professor of English language and literature at Incheon National University, where he co-founded South Korea's first "Great Books" program in 2019.

But now, Lee laments, "Korean students are even losing their old capacity to memorize facts because they collect facts and ideas mainly from A.I."

And if they can't reason and think independently, he adds, they can't judge the quality of the results that AI generates for them.

The limitations of their educational system motivates many South Koreans to look for alternatives, from education overseas, to educational experiments at home.

"As someone who went through this system, I felt those limitations keenly," Chuncheon Mayor Yook Dong-han said in an interview at city hall. "When I became mayor, I wanted to introduce a different kind of education and a distinct educational philosophy to the city of Chuncheon."

Chuncheon draws visitors from neighboring Seoul to enjoy its mountains, lakes and rivers, and dakgalbi, a local dish of grilled or stir-fried marinated chicken.

Chuncheon's government established an academic partnership with St. John's College last year to promote the "Great Books" educational model.

There are now 120 college students and some 770 younger students taking the "Great Books" program in South Korea, and 40 teachers in training, according to Lee Yonghwa.

Although the program is still in its infancy, Yook says it represents a "small but revolutionary achievement — a breakthrough that challenges established practices," and generated interest among participating students that has exceeded his expectations.

South Korean students following the "Great Books" model read Aristotle, Shakespeare, Euclid, and Korean authors including Nobel laureate Han Kang.

Student Shin Donghyun reads from Martin Luther King, Jr's. Letter from a Birmingham Jail at a Great Books summer camp seminar at Chuncheon High School.

In one Chuncheon high school, students read Martin Luther King Jr.'s 1963 Letter from  Birmingham Jail.

They discuss King's ideas about what kind of laws are just and unjust, and which laws citizens should obey or disobey.

Lee Yonghwa says he's impressed that students connected King's letter to their own country, such as in 2024, when citizens and lawmakers defeated former President Yoon Suk Yeol's attempt to put South Korea under martial law.

That fits the purpose of the "Great Books" model, in which "each seminar table really becomes a miniature republic, where ideas clash but people cooperate," St. John's College President J. Walter Sterling wrote last year in an opinion essay.

Through civic participation and liberal education, he adds, "we quietly stitch the fabric of our democracy…before it unravels beyond repair."

NPR's Se Eun Gong contributed to this report in Chuncheon and Seoul.

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/09/nx-s1-603.title: Democrats won big on issues like immigration. But ICE still has the money
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/09/nx-s1-603.author: Jasmine Garsd
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/09/nx-s1-603.text:
Sergio Martínez-Beltrán

House Oversight and Government Reform Committee ranking member Robert Garcia, D-Calif., speaks in front of a picture of Teyana Gibson Brown, confronting federal agents as they raid her Minneapolis home on February 23, 2026 in Washington, DC.

In the days leading up to the midterm elections, hundreds of people left their "I voted" stickers on a memorial for Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a Houston man killed by federal immigration agents earlier this year.

"The fact that people were thinking of my dad and thinking of other immigrants — that just means the world to me," said Ronaldo Salgado, Salgado Araujo's son, told NPR.

Those votes resulted in a seismic political shift in Texas: for the first time, a Latina, Democrat Gina Hinojosa, will be governor. Texans also elected the state's first Democratic U.S. senator in nearly 40 years, and the Texas House of Representatives flipped.

"Unfortunately, Texas has become like the epicenter of ICE enforcement and like gross violence against immigrants," Ronaldo Salgado said. "Well, the voters have spoken — incoming lawmakers now have a duty to listen to us."

Immigration policy was one of the top issues on voters' minds this election, according to exit polling. Artemio Muñiz of the Texas Federation of Hispanic Republicans, told NPR "with these anti-immigrant-type policies, I think the Hispanic community got fed up."

That seems more true than ever in the counties along the U.S.-Mexico border, which flipped Democratic after supporting Trump in 2024.

"I think the message is clear from the Texas Hispanic community that the only acceptable or effective Hispanic outreach from the Republican Party in Texas is one that includes a reasonable solution for immigration," Muñiz said, suggesting the solution should include secured borders and a legal pathway for undocumented immigrants who have been in the U.S. for decades.

Voters wait in line to cast their ballot at the Manchaca Road Library on November 03, 2026 in Austin, Texas.

In Texas, Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa is facing calls to end the state's partnership with ICE.

"That's something that can happen on day one," said César Espinosa, the executive director of the Houston-based advocacy organization FIEL. He said his group would also like to see Hinojosa and the Texas legislature to push for driver licenses for undocumented immigrants. Already, Houston's mayor is reducing his police department's cooperation with ICE.

Nationwide, immigration advocates say they want to see ICE defunded, or severely restricted.

"We demand that the incoming Congress hold ICE accountable", says Murad Awawdeh of the New York Immigrant Coalition.

Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., who is set to become the next chair of the House oversight committee, had two words of advice for Republicans on Election Day: "Lawyer up."

Garcia has promised to look into several issues, including ICE accountability.

ICE is the highest funded federal law enforcement agency in the U.S. Congress essentially gave immigration enforcement a blank check in 2025 and in 2026 they awarded ICE and Customs and Border Patrol around $240 billion.

Federal agents walk near the scene where a man was shot by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer during an operation in the Bronx borough of New York on October 8, 2026, according to local media and police.

It's enough funds to run the mass deportation operation for the remainder of Trump's term.

Congress could claw back that money. And lawmakers are already eyeing more stringent oversight.

"We have to rein ICE in because its illegal, out-of-control activities (have) killed individuals … assaulted individuals … have incarcerated individuals," said Rep. Bennie Thompson, D-Miss., who is likely to chair the House Homeland Security Committee. "That system has to have accountability for the men and women who work in it."

He said he'd like to legally require policies, like requiring the use of body-worn cameras for federal immigration agents and banning them from wearing face coverings.

The major hurdle is President Trump: following the midterm election results the President said he would welcome the nickname "Mr. Veto."

Another possible indication of how the administration will be seeing immigration enforcement moving forward came Friday, a few days after the midterm elections. White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller was promoted to chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles. Miller's central project in government has been immigration control and mass deportations. Miller is considered the architect of the first Trump administration's child separation policy, and as NPR reported, was deeply involved in the project of turning large warehouses into immigration detention centers.

Naureen Shah at the ACLU says she thinks one of the most powerful things that could happen to change ICE behavior is Congressional oversight via subpoenas.

"ICE has to be afraid," she said. "They have to be afraid of losing their funding, they have to be afraid of being subpoenaed and asked extremely hard questions before a live audience of the American people."

The day after the Midterm elections, Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin posted a three-word tweet : "Deportations will continue."

Vice President JD Vance took to X to share his thoughts on the Republican Party's big loss. He said he believes it is due to voter's concerns over the economy, inflation and the war with Iran. He left immigration enforcement off that list.

He did, however, say he is open to changing enforcement tactics by focusing more on businesses that hire undocumented workers. But he said immigration amnesty is not the solution.

Shah of the ACLU says she believes ICE enforcement and the current state of the economy are inextricably linked. "What's really clear is that the stories of life becoming harder for everyday Americans are actually also stories about ICE's impact. People are afraid to take their kids to school, afraid to go to work. It impacts our schools, our teachers. It impacts the labor force when people aren't showing up for their jobs. So Democrats have an opportunity through their oversight device to tell a story about how to make everyday life more affordable for all Americans."

A security vehicle drives around the CoreCivic, Inc. California City Immigration Processing Center in the Kern County desert ahead of the facility reopening as a federal immigrant detention facility under contract with the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in California City, California on July 10, 2025.

The Trump administration has spent billions of dollars to expand ICE detention facilities — many of which have faced criticism and protest over dire conditions. There have been a record number of deaths in detention since the start of Trump's second term.

The day after mid-term election results the two major private detention center companies that contract for ICE, CoreCivic and the GEO Group , had their quarterly investor calls.

The main question asked by investors at the CoreCivic call was: how will the result of the midterms affect ICE operations?

CoreCivic President Lucibeth Mayberry optimistically, pointing out that "[ICE] have again began increasing enforcement activity. They have the secure funding to do so." But then she offered a word of advice to ICE about purchasing new detention centers: "we would urge the ICE administration to move quickly."

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/09/nx-s1-603.title: Nebraska rushed Medicaid work rules. Then a cancer patient was told he'd lost coverage
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/09/nx-s1-603.author: Rachana Pradhan
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/09/nx-s1-603.text:
Shortly after being diagnosed with kidney cancer, Eli McCreary of Omaha, Neb., was told by a hospital that he'd lost his Medicaid coverage.

Eli McCreary of Omaha, Neb., said he had recently been diagnosed with kidney cancer when he got a call from a local hospital run by CHI Health. He said he was informed that he wasn't insured anymore under Medicaid — and that the hospital would cancel his appointments unless he paid out-of-pocket.

McCreary, who was 64 at the time, said he phoned a call center for help. He said he was told his benefits under Medicaid, the government health program for people with low incomes or disabilities, now required that he have a job.

"You're required to do work to stay on," McCreary said a representative told him. "And you haven't fulfilled your work requirement."

Stay up to date with our Up First newsletter, sent every weekday morning.

For decades, McCreary said, he has battled drug addiction. A substance use treatment program discharged him in March, and in June he was diagnosed with cancer in his right kidney, according to documents reviewed by KFF Health News. He also has diabetes and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.

"I don't understand what job I can get," McCreary said. "I can't walk. I can hardly breathe. I can't move around. What job am I going to get?"

McCreary said he canceled a CT scan and other tests at the hospital, which is part of CommonSpirit Health, the nation's largest Catholic health system. He also delayed a cancer-related appointment with a physician who travels back and forth to Omaha. "I missed my window of opportunity with him for another month," he said.

Taylor Miller, a spokesperson for CHI Health, declined to answer questions about McCreary's experience. In an emailed statement, she said that "CHI Health is committed to helping patients understand their health care coverage and access to care, including available financial assistance resources."

Determined to be the first state to enforce Medicaid work requirements under President Trump's signature One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Nebraska launched the new rules May 1 — eight months before most states are set to do the same. With their newly elected majorities in Congress, Democrats have said they plan to repeal the changes to Medicaid in their first 100 hours in office in January. But it is unclear if they will be successful, because Trump could veto it.

Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen said in December that state officials "certainly appreciate President Trump and his whole administration for delivering this key reform." Pillen spoke alongside a videoed-in Mehmet Oz, the Trump administration official overseeing Medicare and Medicaid.

"We're excited to be able to be the first to make it happen," the Republican governor said.

Laura Strimple, a spokesperson for the governor, didn't respond to requests for comment. Jeff Powell, a spokesperson for Nebraska's Department of Health and Human Services, said its rollout "has been very successful." He pointed to state data showing 86% of affected applicants met the requirement or qualified for an exclusion and 93% of existing enrollees kept their coverage.

Health clinics and organizations advocating for poor and working-class Nebraskans say the rollout has been rife with problems — many due to poor training and inadequate staffing.

About 70,000 adult Medicaid recipients in Nebraska are subject to the work requirements. They must prove they're working or participating in a similar activity for 80 hours a month, unless they qualify for an exemption. State officials and consultants advising them have said the May 1 date was challenging to meet.

Eli McCreary of Omaha, Neb.

To deploy the law's Medicaid coverage restrictions, Nebraska budgeted millions of dollars for government contractors, according to state documents KFF Health News obtained via a public records request. Documents from Nebraska's health department outline $8.2 million in contractor costs to enact Medicaid changes, including work requirements and more frequent checks for whether people still qualify.

Nebraska operates the information technology system that determines who in the state qualifies for Medicaid, unlike most states, which outsource the work to companies under contracts often worth hundreds of millions of dollars. But Nebraska's health department nonetheless relies on the private sector to help administer its Medicaid program.

The $8.2 million in costs span two years. They stem from two companies that Nebraska uses to increase agency staffing: Public Consulting Group, based in Boston, and Atlanta-based Covendis, which supplies information technology staffers.

One of the companies has praised Nebraska's implementation of work requirements. A post on Public Consulting Group's website quotes senior consultant Latanya Michaux.

"I really cannot brag enough about how well Nebraska handled this requirement," Michaux said, crediting the firm's "incredible relationship" with the state.

Covendis executives did not respond to requests for comment. Powell said the health department "uses contracted staff when hiring a state employee is either uneconomical or impractical because of time constraints, or when the role requires highly specialized skill sets."

Advocates who work with Medicaid enrollees in Nebraska say that participants are confused and don't know whether the rules apply to them. These advocates say enrollees also have gotten inaccurate information. In December, Pillen said the state "won't be adding workforce" to implement the work requirements, a decision those advocates have criticized. Pillen in July also instituted a government-wide hiring freeze.

Nebraska listed at least half a dozen contractors costing more than $250,000 each, including one person whose compensation exceeds $1.8 million, the documents show. Nebraska submitted the records to federal Medicaid regulators as part of a routine process to secure federal money. Powell said the funding requests "may not reflect actual expenditures."

Sarah Maresh, a program director with the social justice advocacy nonprofit Nebraska Appleseed, said the amounts were "shocking."

"When you put in complicated policies like this, there are large corporations making money behind the scenes," Maresh said. "This just further confirms that it's happening in Nebraska quietly."

The Medicaid work requirements in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and other changes shepherded by Republicans will curtail insurance gains that came from the Affordable Care Act, also known as Obamacare. The GOP tax and spending law, which the Congressional Budget Office estimated would reduce federal Medicaid spending by more than $900 billion over a decade, adds reporting requirements and restrictions that make it harder for people to stay enrolled.

As of early July, most denials related to the work requirements among Nebraska adults applying for Medicaid were due to unsubmitted paperwork, according to internal documents from Nebraska's health department that KFF Health News obtained through a public records request. The state wrote this was "expected."

State data shows that average wait times at a Nebraska health department call center nearly doubled between May and July, going from about 13 minutes to 26 minutes, before declining in August. In interviews, advocates for Medicaid enrollees said they've encountered people who have waited on the phone for hours.

Nebraska received more than 101,000 calls in August, a 66% jump from May.

"If people are working, they just don't have time to be sitting on the phone to go through all of this stuff," said Kenny McMorris, CEO of the Charles Drew Health Center, a federally qualified health center in North Omaha. He said roughly half of Charles Drew's 13,385 patients are on Medicaid, and of those, 42% are subject to the work requirements.

"You can leverage the technology, but you still got to have people there to help," McMorris said.

Then there are experiences the official data may not catch, like what happened to McCreary — saddled with figuring out what happened with his Medicaid benefits amid a health crisis, and whether it was even true that he had to work to keep them.

McCreary had heard about the Medicaid work requirements but didn't know they might apply to him. Powell confirmed McCreary was eligible for Medicaid because of the ACA — putting him in the population subject to work requirements.

His ordeal underscores the fallout from being caught in confusing government systems and silos that aren't obvious to the public.

"This cancer ain't going to stop just because I ain't got insurance," he said. "It's going to keep working on me."

When he received the call from the hospital about his coverage, "I was really in despair," McCreary said. Eventually, he said, he called for help.

Nebraska's health department runs AccessNebraska, a call center for help with safety net benefits such as Medicaid and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, commonly known as food stamps. But the number McCreary recalls dialing ended up not being AccessNebraska — it was for a different call center, one for SNAP accounts that Nebraska outsources to a private company. Powell said the state has no record of McCreary calling the health department.

McCreary said the worker didn't have a good explanation for why the Medicaid work requirements would apply to him. Before his health deteriorated, McCreary worked as a driver for an asphalt services company. He said he worked "until I couldn't do the job anymore."

"I really had hoped to work longer," he said. "I kind of enjoyed that job."

Attorneys and policy professionals who work with people on Medicaid and other public benefit programs said that McCreary's substance use treatment, lasting four months starting in November 2025, and other health conditions should have exempted him.

The federal law outlines categories of exemptions, such as being too sick to work. People who are considered too ill include those who have a serious medical condition or a substance use disorder.

Nebraska's health department said it sent tens of thousands of letters, text messages and emails to inform enrollees about the new requirements. According to state documents, Nebraska said it would "implement enhancements" to its computer system and online portal, including allowing people to submit documents online and having "clear, plain-language" enrollee notices. McCreary, however, doesn't have an account on Nebraska Medicaid's online portal, preferring to handle things over the phone or in person.

He also said it's possible he missed letters from Nebraska Medicaid about his coverage.

"I don't know if it's my fault or not," McCreary said.

Shortly after being diagnosed with kidney cancer, Eli McCreary of Omaha, Nebraska, was told by a hospital that he'd lost his Medicaid coverage. He said he was later told that it was because he didn't fulfill a new work requirement that Nebraska instituted in May. (Chris Machian for KFF Health News)

The Cornhusker State's experience could be a harbinger of things to come. Next year, work requirements will apply to millions of adult Medicaid enrollees in more than 40 states.

The nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office has estimated the policy will lead to 5.3 million more people being uninsured in the U.S. by 2034.

The One Big Beautiful Bill Act's Medicaid changes are the most complicated in years — changes that government benefit experts say will strain and exacerbate long-standing problems with state technology systems for health benefits.

"It's already a shaky system, and now you've added more burdens on top of that," said Gelila Selassie, director of health advocacy for the nonprofit Justice in Aging.

Nebraska and federal officials, as well as consultants advising the state, detailed the difficulties and successes with the state's May 1 launch during an August panel discussion at a national conference in Oregon.

"They said, 'We're going to go live May 1.' To which CMS said, 'Oh, my God!'" Brent Weaver, an official who specializes in Medicaid IT at the U.S. Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, said about Nebraska.

Nebraska officials knew "they weren't as agile as they probably would have liked to have been," Weaver said, "but they didn't let that stop them."

"If they fail, we looked at it as a failure," he added in comments that broadly praised the state's approach.

CMS did not answer questions from KFF Health News about Nebraska's rollout and Weaver's remarks.

In Nebraska, a group of 60 people held hours-long meetings three days a week that were "very exhausting," Michaux, of Public Consulting Group, said during a different session at the conference.

"Our calendars were cleared, and that was the focus," Michaux said.

Because CMS had not yet issued regulations outlining key details such as how people could get exemptions — it would do so June 1 — Nebraska officials said they had to rely on the law's broad language to make initial decisions.

"We had to get comfortable being uncomfortable," Jacob Kawamoto, a deputy director at Nebraska's Medicaid division, said at the conference.

Public Consulting Group said it worked with the state to develop new guidance and "process guides" — materials for Nebraska eligibility workers with instructions on how to process Medicaid applications or renewals. Training materials for Nebraska caseworkers reviewed by KFF Health News refer to those guides.

"The training was very robust, and the process guides were very robust," Michaux said.

Maresh disagreed with that characterization. "There are gaps" in the state's training materials, she said, and caseworkers "are confused" about work requirements.

Public Consulting Group also helped the state institute changes to Nebraska's Medicaid IT system, according to the company. "We are preparing for future updates and enhancements," Michaux said.

In response to questions, Public Consulting Group spokesperson Alyssa Brown said the company "has supported Nebraska Medicaid via a broad range of consulting services since 2019, including work on federal and state compliance initiatives." She said Michaux "discussed" the process guides at the conference but Nebraska developed them. Similarly, Brown said the company did not develop training.

Federal taxpayers will largely bear the costs of implementing the One Big Beautiful Bill Act's Medicaid policies in Nebraska and elsewhere. Congress allocated $200 million in one-time funding to states. Under federal regulations, the U.S. government picks up most of the tab for state IT system changes, paying as much as 90% of the cost.

"Even though it was not so easy," Michaux said at the conference, "we definitely had fun standing up the Medicaid work requirement program."

Public Consulting Group's employees, Brown told KFF Health News, are "passionate about public service and helping our clients improve the lives of the people they serve."

As of August, roughly 1,100 Nebraskans had been denied benefits because of Medicaid work requirements. Most denials were because people did not respond to requests for information.

Nebraska's total Medicaid enrollment has declined by roughly 4,600 people since May, a drop of 1.4%, according to an August report.

As for McCreary, the Nebraska health department's Powell maintained he experienced "no lapses in coverage" and said he was disenrolled from Medicaid after turning 65. Despite what McCreary said he was told, Powell said Medicaid work requirements weren't the reason: He aged out of Medicaid and into Medicare before they could be applied to him.

Selassie, from the nonprofit Justice in Aging, said McCreary's care shouldn't have been disrupted.

McCreary is now enrolled in Medicare, and Medicaid covers some of his health costs. He was able to reschedule his canceled appointments.

"The cancer has grown so much," he said.

He had surgery in early November to remove his right kidney.

KFF Health News correspondent Samantha Liss contributed to this report.

KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF — the independent source for health policy research, polling, and journalism.

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/09/nx-s1-603.title: Democrats won big. Can they lower your grocery bill?
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/09/nx-s1-603.author: Joe Hernandez
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/09/nx-s1-603.text:
A supporter holds a sign during a campaign rally for Democratic Senate candidate Dr. Annie Andrews in Myrtle Beach, S.C., on Nov. 1. Andrews defeated her Republican opponent, Sen. Darline Graham.

It's been a feature of campaign ads and stump speeches for months: grocery prices are out of control.

Affordability concerns, including high food costs, were top of mind for voters heading into the midterms, as the Trump administration's tariffs and the war in Iran continued to drive up prices. That economic strain helped Democrats win control of both houses of Congress on Tuesday.

House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries said the incoming majority would make tackling high prices a priority come January. "It was a tremendous victory for the American people and a strong rebuke of MAGA extremism, which has made life more expensive for everyday Americans despite their promises to lower the high cost of living on day one," he told NPR on Friday.

The question is how Democrats will do that with President Trump still in the Oval Office, willing to wield his veto pen. Senate Democrats won't have a filibuster-proof majority, and Trump may have little appetite to roll back his signature tariffs or reverse course on the Iran war, two of the main causes of high food prices.

Lael Brainard, who leads a public policy group called The Kitchen Table Project, said Americans are nevertheless expecting relief from Washington — and quickly.

"They are feeling like they are getting squeezed by high prices that don't need to be that high," she said.

Despite the political hurdles, Democrats said they intend to move ahead with plans to cut grocery bills, including by rolling back Trump's tariffs. Those tariffs have not only raised the cost of certain foods and drinks imported to the U.S., but also created other pressures on the food industry by making it more expensive to import things like machine parts and packaging.

The Iran war has led to a surge in energy prices, which has made it more expensive to transport just about everything. Fertilizer costs also grew when the closure of the Strait of Hormuz cut off a significant portion of the global fertilizer trade.

But getting Trump to backtrack on tariffs or the Iran war — or his immigration crackdown, which has led to labor shortages on U.S. farms — could prove tricky for Democrats.

"I think the president would certainly want to find ways to reduce the cost of groceries. Democrats [also] see that in their interest," said Lehigh University political science professor Chris Borick. "The mechanisms, the tools, the levers that would be most readily available to do that — there's quite a bit of distance between the president and Democrats that'll be taking over both the House and the Senate."

Several incoming Democratic senators also floated other proposals during their campaigns that aim to make groceries more affordable.

James Talarico of Texas said he would push back against "attacks" on the federal food assistance programs WIC and SNAP, the latter of which is undergoing a major overhaul by the Trump administration and has seen a precipitous drop in participation since last summer. Kansas' Adam Hamilton announced his support for a national ban on "dynamic pricing" in grocery stores. And multiple candidates, including Roy Cooper of North Carolina, vowed to block food industry mergers they say would raise consumer prices.

Beyond the blue wave in Congress, Democrats also made gains in state capitals across the U.S. on Tuesday. At least 28 states will have Democratic governors beginning next year, and ten state legislative chambers flipped to Democrats, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures.

Incoming state governors have floated their own ideas for how to give residents relief in the grocery aisle.

Keisha Lance Bottoms proposed allowing municipalities in Georgia to suspend or fully eliminate their local sales tax on groceries, baby formula, diapers and more. Gina Hinojosa, the governor-elect of Texas, promised to outlaw "predatory surveillance pricing" and price gouging in grocery stores. In New Mexico, Deb Haaland said the state would explore a policy similar to one in Albuquerque that temporarily waives permitting fees for markets that sell healthy and affordable food in so-called "food deserts," the Albuquerque Journal reported.

However state and federal officials decide to go about lowering prices, Americans say they want to see cheaper groceries soon. According to a poll released by the Kitchen Table Project and Global Strategy Group in September, nearly half of respondents said their most important goal was seeing their grocery bills lowered within six months.
