https://www.npr.org/2026/11/09/nx-s1-598.title: On wild Cumberland Island, a land swap proposal stirs controversy
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/09/nx-s1-598.author: Debbie Elliott
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/09/nx-s1-598.text:
A wild horse grazes on whatever food it can find on Cumberland Island, Ga. on Oct 8, 2026. The National Park Service, which has managed the island since 1972, recently proposed a land swap with descendants of Thomas Carnegie, the wealthy Gilded Age industrialist who built homes on the island.

CUMBERLAND ISLAND, Ga.— Wild horses, feral hogs and deer roam free on this 18-mile barrier island, one of the largest and most ecologically diverse along the Atlantic coast. The landscape includes salt marshes, maritime forests, and an expansive stretch of pristine, untouched beach only accessible to the public by ferry.

Since 1972, the National Park Service has managed Cumberland Island National Seashore, including roughly 9,800 acres of wilderness designated by an act of Congress which stated that "the seashore shall be permanently preserved in its primitive state."

But there's more on this island than federally protected wilderness. Visitors also can find Native-American relics, remnants of Spanish missions, the ruins of ante-bellum plantations, and opulent homes built by the wealthy Gilded Age industrialist Thomas Carnegie and his wife Lucy, who had 9 children.

Descendants of the Carnegies still live or vacation here on private property, and the park service has proposed a land swap with them that would allow for new construction. That possibility is creating tension between the many stakeholders who all have differing views of what it means to preserve the island they hold dear.

Park superintendent Melissa Trenchik has been defending the plan, giving media tours to an area under a grove of huge live oak trees on Cumberland's west side, which overlooks an expansive salt marsh and Naval Submarine Base Kings Bay on the horizon.

It is currently parkland, which under the proposal would be handed over to two branches of Carnegie descendants for the construction of up to eight new private homes.

A portion of the maritime forest that's part of the proposed land swap.

"They obviously want to be with this incredible view," Trenchik told Georgia Public Broadcasting's Jillian Magtoto, as they stood on the edge of a maritime forest looking out over the Cumberland Sound.

The idea, Trenchik said, is to consolidate private ownership on the west side of the island, so the park can better interpret natural and cultural resources on the Atlantic beachside of Cumberland, including sensitive coastal and wilderness areas where the government could then prohibit development. The park service received more than 12,500 public comments on the proposal.

"Right now, if we do nothing, development is possible," she said of the private land the park service seeks to acquire.

Trenchik said the eight new "modest" homes would be subject to permanent conservation limits and could not exceed 35 feet in height. Critics, however, say the 15,000-square footage allowance, including driveway and outbuildings, is anything but modest.

"We're swapping for McMansions," said Joseph Manning, an attorney with Defenders of Wildlife, a Washington D.C. based conservation group fighting the deal.

The Greyfield Inn, which Carnegie family descendants own and operate as the island's only hotel.

Manning sees what's happening on Cumberland as the latest attempt by the Trump Administration to privatize public lands, pointing to other attention-grabbing headlines about a baseball park in Grand Teton, a land exchange in Yosemite, and repeated shrinkage of Bears Ears National Monument.

"Possibly the universal theme among all of these parks and refuges land exchanges that we're seeing is that they are not being done to expand public access," Manning said. "They're being done to benefit a particular special interest or just a handful of individuals or families, as is the case at Cumberland Island."

Barclay McFadden is a great-great-grandson of Thomas Carnegie, the brother of Pittsburgh steel magnate Andrew Carnegie.

"The hysteria about mansions and the Gilded Age and all that is so unfounded," McFadden said. "We love our island."

McFadden, who is involved in one of the land deals, said he's hurt by the way the debate over the land swap paints his family as modern-day robber barons without taking into account their history on the island.

"Five generations have been buried there. We have a family cemetery. It's still there. That's where I'll go," he said. "For our children and our grandchildren, it's a sacred place."

The land swap will allow them to build homes for those younger generations, McFadden said.

"We have been wonderful stewards of the island, and we have taken care of the island," he said, pointing out that his grandmother's generation had the opportunity to sell their property to developers in the 1970's. "They protected the island from turning into a golf course."

His cousin Jamie Ferguson, who is not directly involved in the current land swap proposal, said he trusts the Carnegie descendants' legacy of protecting what's special here. He jointly co-owns (with about 40 others) a Carnegie mansion here, now operated as a bed and breakfast – the Greyfield Inn.

Jamie Ferguson, a Carnegie descendent, stands inside the library at the Greyfield Inn, a former Carnegie mansion that he jointly co-owns (with about 40 others) and operates as a bed and breakfast.

Plum Orchard Mansion, which was donated to the National Park Service and is now featured on the once-daily "Lands and Legacies" tour of the island's public cultural sites and ruins.

"It's kind of like a live oak family tree - it's really widespread," said Ferguson, the family's unofficial historian. "The common thread we have though is this place."

He said his grandmother was adamant that the land remain in the family, even when other Carnegie descendants donated property to the National Park Service.

One advantage Ferguson sees to the land swap is greater visitor access to what he calls the "most important historical monument on Cumberland," a site known simply as The Chimneys. The remnants of about two dozen brick and tabby chimneys are lined up in rows under Spanish moss draped oak trees. It's where enslaved workers lived on an old sea island cotton plantation that pre-dated the Carnegies.

Ferguson points out the National Park Service is tasked with not just preserving the island's natural history, but also its cultural history.

A site known as "The Chimneys" contains the remnants of about two dozen brick and tabby chimneys lined up in rows under Spanish moss-draped oak trees. This is where enslaved people lived on an old sea island cotton plantation that pre-dated the Carnegies.

"Like it or not, we're part of that cultural history," said Ferguson. "And I don't mean that in a bad way. I mean, I believe that we're a part of that cultural history, and that comes with some responsibility too."

There are a few other private homes on Cumberland that are not owned by Carnegie descendants. Naturalist Carol Rucksdeschel lives in one of them. After living on the island for more than 50 years, she's still excited each day at what she discovers.

"God look at that - that's so beautiful," she said one recent day, spotting a pair of wood storks descending into the marsh grass.

At 85, Ruckdeschel still surveys Cumberland Island every Friday morning, combing the beaches looking for stranded sea turtles and new nests. The ecologist has emerged as one of the main voices opposing the land swap, which she worries is the "first nose under the tent" towards greater development on the island.

Naturalist Carol Rucksdechel lives in one of the few private homes on Cumberland not owned by Carnegie descendants. She has lived on the island for over 50 years.

At 85, Ruckdeschel still surveys Cumberland island every Friday morning, combing the beaches looking for stranded sea turtles and new nests.

"This plan to me is a real affront to the American people, but it's also an insult to the Park Service," Ruckdeschel said. "It's not what they're supposed to be doing. They're supposed to be protecting this place."

She's also not happy that the park service plans to double daily visitation to Cumberland, up to 700 visitors a day.

Ruckdeschel, who is involved with the conservation group Wild Cumberland, said she's friends with Carnegie descendants and acknowledges their love for the island. Still, she said, more homes and more people will disturb what the island should be – a pure primitive wilderness where nature overtakes what humans have left behind.

"It's stepping into its climax stage, which is terribly exciting," Ruckdeschel said of the rewilded maritime forest she's witnessed take over old plantation cotton fields.

A former cotton field where enslaved people worked is now an open field on Cumberland Island. Ruckdeschel believes the island should be a place where nature overtakes what humans have left behind.

"And that's what I would have loved to have seen the whole island do," she said. "And then people die out, places go back to nature and that's it."

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/09/nx-s1-603.title: Congress is coming back to Washington. Here's what to expect
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/09/nx-s1-603.author: Eric McDaniel
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/09/nx-s1-603.text:
Lawmakers are returning to Washington this week to finish up work before Democrats take control of the House and Senate in January.

It is the final hoorah for the 119th Congress. Republicans have just weeks left in control of the House of Republicans and the Senate. The main thing on the agenda: keeping the federal government open. Funding is set to run out on December 11, when a stop-gap measure passed about a month ahead of the midterms expires.

Any funding extension is all but certain to be done through another short-term bill, known as a continuing resolution. The typical government funding process — 12 carefully negotiated appropriations bills — would take time and political will that lawmakers currently lack.

Congress will also need to find a path forward on the National Defense Authorization Act, long considered a must-pass annual military funding package. This year, the bill is quagmired in the unforgiving politics of the Iran war. The conflict is opposed by a majority of Americans — something President Trump has acknowledged was a key force in driving his party out of power.

The House is also likely to vote on an impeachment effort targeting Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth. Introduced by Republican Thomas Massie of Kentucky, a key figure in forcing the administration's release of the Epstein files, the impeachment measure lists a number of charges, including that the administration failed to properly consult Congress on the military campaign.

Democrats are unlikely to be in a compromising mood on legislation, just weeks away from taking control of both chambers. That means continued work on big-ticket items like the Protect College Sports Act, meant to introduce new regulations around college athlete compensation, and a bipartisan energy permitting overhaul will likely wait until the new term.

With slim majorities in both chambers, they could also have to contend with some attendance problems after a demoralizing performance in last week's midterm elections. That further complicates passing legislation through chambers already governed by the thinnest of majorities.

Mike Ricci, a Republican strategist with the group Seven Letter and aide to former Speakers of the House John Boehner and Paul Ryan, told NPR that a number of forces could help draw reluctant lame duck legislators back to Washington, including winding down their offices, finding new work and attending the White House Christmas party.

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/09/nx-s1-601.title: Supreme Court weighs effort to shield federal law enforcement as ICE complaints rise
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/09/nx-s1-601.author: Carrie Johnson
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/09/nx-s1-601.text:
The Supreme Court is seen on Oct. 1 in Washington, D.C.

Five years ago, a gang riot broke out inside a federal prison in Hawaii.

Kekai Watanabe was beaten with a makeshift weapon known as a "lock in a sock."

When he complained about serious back pain, a nurse told him to "stop being a cry baby."

Seven months later, doctors diagnosed Watanabe with a fractured tail bone, and he sued the nurse for violating his Eighth Amendment right against cruel and unusual punishment.

On Monday, the Supreme Court will hear his case, which could determine whether federal law enforcement officers can be held to account when they violate constitutional rights. The claim by Watanabe, now 40, echoes far beyond the walls of prison — and into American streets where immigration officers have been accused of beating and running over migrants.

"What's at stake here is whether, basically, we as a country are going to hold federal law enforcement officers accountable when they violate clearly established constitutional rights," said Georgetown law professor Steve Vladeck, who filed a "friend of the court" brief in the case. "I mean, it really is, I think, that stark."

It's already difficult for these claims to proceed, because the court requires people to show the facts in their cases are identical to precedent. In the federal prisons, the landmark case dates to 1980. The prisoner in that lawsuit died from untreated asthma. The nurse's lawyers say Watanabe, the inmate from Hawaii, survived the gang attack in 2021, so his case is different enough that it should be dismissed.

Mary Hampton Mason worked at the Justice Department for nearly 35 years, in an office that evaluated these kinds of legal claims. Mason said rogue officers are rare, and problems are typically systemic.

"It's a result of agency culture, it's a result of training, it's a result of all sorts of things, but these failures are really institutional," Mason said.

The Supreme Court created a right to sue federal officers for wrongdoing in a 1971 case known as Bivens. But Mason said that precedent has been hollowed out for years, and the court should finally overrule it because it gives plaintiffs false hope.

"In fact in the last 20 years, I'm only aware of one Bivens case that has resulted in a judgment for the plaintiffs that … didn't get reversed on appeal, and that's in thousands and thousands and thousands of cases filed," she said.

But supporters of the prisoner say that number doesn't account for settlements or how these lawsuits can deter other bad behavior. If individual federal officers and agents can be on the hook financially, the argument goes, they could think twice before breaking the law.

"That's why damages are so important," said Gregory Cui, an attorney at the MacArthur Justice Center, a civil rights legal organization. "Because they're a way to try to fix things, to give a person the means to pay for medical care or rebuild their life."

In a "friend of the court" brief, Cui reported that the grievance process for people inside federal prison almost never works for inmates, who succeed just 1% of the time in changing things such as access to medical care or better conditions behind bars.

Cui and other legal experts said the Supreme Court agreed to hear this case at a time when abuses by federal immigration agents and others are in the spotlight. Now, they said, is the wrong time for the court to eliminate one of the few avenues of accountability for those errant officers.

"A world with no Bivens is a world in which federal law enforcement officers would enjoy absolute immunity, where no matter how egregious their conduct is, no one can hold them liable," said Vladeck, of Georgetown Law Center. "As alarming a prospect as that may have been five years ago, it should be an especially terrifying one today, and it ought to be one that even this Supreme Court is worried about endorsing."

Both sides agree Congress has the power to weigh in and give people whose rights have been violated by federal officers a clear way to sue. But so far lawmakers have not advanced legislation to hold those people to account.

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/09/nx-s1-602.title: U.N. climate talks begin today. Here are 3 things to know
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/09/nx-s1-602.author: Julia Simon
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/09/nx-s1-602.text:
This year's U.N. climate conference, known as COP31, takes place in Antalya, Turkey, from Nov. 9 -20.

For the next two weeks, country leaders will be in Antalya, Turkey, for the annual United Nations climate conference, called COP31. This year, the ongoing U.S.-Israeli war with Iran will loom over the negotiations. Now in its ninth month, the war has sparked a global energy crisis. The unprecedented closure of the Strait of Hormuz and spiking oil and natural gas prices have laid bare the fragility of relying on fossil fuels.

But this energy crisis – unlike the energy crisis in the 1970s and the one following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 – is different, says Kingsmill Bond, an analyst at the energy think tank Ember.

"This is the first time you've really had a global energy shock where you've got really cheap solutions to address it," Bond says.

Those solutions include solar panels, batteries and electric vehicles. In recent months, countries around the world have pivoted sharply towards these technologies. Many of them are produced in China and offer economic security, as well as reduced emissions.

The economic case for climate solution technologies will make it easier for countries to support them at the conference, Bond says. "There's much more opportunity, I think, for people to get behind change at COP."

Here are three things you need to know about this year's COP.

Climate technologies like solar, batteries and electric vehicles are also called electrification technologies. Bond says that's why some are calling this "the electrification COP."

"The big target that the COP is setting is for the world to increase the electrification rate from around 23% today to around 35% by 2035," Bond says. "So 35 by '35 is the mantra."

These electrification goals assume countries will grow their electricity mix with cleaner renewable energy. Energy experts say that is a reasonable assumption, because that's what has been happening in recent years. Large solar and wind projects provide more cost-competitive energy than natural gas and coal projects, according to financial services firm Lazard.

"Think about solar, wind," says Li Shuo,  director of the China Climate Hub at the Asia Society Policy Institute. "More green energy will help you decarbonize better and faster."

As the COP process enters its 31st year, many countries have argued that the U.N. process has not done enough to tackle the single biggest driver of climate change: burning fossil fuels.

Fossil fuel producers such as Saudi Arabia and Russia have consistently opposed having fossil fuel language in the text of final conference agreements.

In April, more than 50 countries came together to discuss ways to phase out oil, gas, and coal at the First International Conference to Transition Away from Fossil Fuels. Conference organizers told NPR the conference was a way to complement the U.N. process.

More than 25 of those nations are developing a legally binding treaty that would advance a phase-out of fossil fuels. Supporters of the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative hope more countries will join their cause at COP31.

The U.S. State Department told NPR in an email that the U.S. will not be sending a delegation to COP31. They also did not send anyone to last year's COP in Brazil.

The Trump administration has reversed action on climate progress, phasing out subsidies for electric vehicles, solar and wind, reducing regulations for greenhouse gases, and halting renewable energy projects.

Last year, some countries told NPR they were happy that the Trump administration was not at the climate talks. "Generally, it's a good thing they're not here because we have less recalcitrants to deal with," Ralph Regenvanu, minister of climate change of Vanuatu, told NPR then.

But some democratic lawmakers will be at COP31, including Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, a Democrat representing Rhode Island. Fresh off Democrats' midterm victory sweep, Whitehouse says he and the other lawmakers plan to keep the focus on fossil fuels and a potential carbon pricing mechanism.

" It cannot remain free for the fossil fuel industry to pollute if we want to have any chance of a pathway to climate safety," Whitehouse says.

Violent storms lash northern Iraq and parts of Iran, while Portugal faces strong winds and Japan braces for further snowfall

Deadly flash floods hit northern Iraq on Saturday as severe thunderstorms swept across the region, including in neighbouring Iran. The city of Erbil, in Iraq, was particularly badly hit, with extensive damage to homes and businesses. Streets were inundated as torrential rain fell over a short period.

Rainfall exceeded forecasts, with an estimated 80mm falling in the city, compared with expectations of 30mm. Two people were killed in the floods.

In Europe, Storm Bruna is forecast to bring strong winds to Portugal this week, particularly along the west coast. Gusts are expected to reach 50mph (80km/h), with heavy rain and thunderstorms also expected. The total rainfall could reach 200mm by the end of the week. The storm has already affected the Canary Islands, where Tenerife recorded a gust of 80mph on Saturday night.

Japan experienced a cold and snowy end to last week, with further snowfall expected in Hokkaido and parts of the mountains in the main island Honshu.

Temperatures in Japan are forecast to fall below the seasonal average early this week, with Sapporo, the capital of Hokkaido prefecture, expected to plunge to 10C below average. Maximum temperatures in the city are likely to be about 4-6C on Monday and Wednesday, while Tuesday’s high is forecast to be about 0C. Minimum temperatures could fall to -6C by Wednesday, and -8C in other western parts of Hokkaido on Tuesday.

Ski resorts are preparing for visitors after snowfall began on Friday. Total snowfall is expected to reach 30-50cm around Kiroro and Niesko, with about 20-30cm in Furano, Rusutsu and Sapporo.

Other resorts could receive up to 20cm of snow by Wednesday. Strong winds accompanied the snow on Friday and over the weekend, with gusts of about 75mph in Kiroko and Niesko.

During the strong El Niño, sea surface temperatures in the equatorial Pacific were about 3.5C above the climatological average at their peak in late October. As a result, Peru has been experiencing air temperatures 5-10C above the seasonal average. The unusually warm conditions expected to continue into next week.

https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.title: ‘Exceedingly heavy-handed’: ACT police criticised by magistrate for Tasering disabled Aboriginal woman
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.author: Nino Bucci Justice and courts reporter
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text:
Exclusive: Body-worn camera footage shows woman pulled off bench and a Taser activated despite ‘putting up no resistance’, magistrate says

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A magistrate has criticised “exceedingly heavy-handed” ACT police officers who Tasered an Aboriginal woman with an intellectual disability during a routine arrest.

The woman, named Emma, pleaded with officers not to use the stun gun on her and told them she was unarmed during the arrest at a Canberra bus stop in January.

Police were called because of reports Emma had a knife, but she was only found to have two pairs of scissors, one of which was broken, in a nearby backpack.

Guardian Australia is not using Emma’s full name at the request of her lawyer to protect her privacy.

The court was shown police body-worn footage of the arrest, in which she is seen raising her hands immediately after officers arrived and pointed a Taser towards her.

As she pushed back against an officer who was trying to handcuff her she was pulled to the ground.

While two officers held her down another placed a Taser against her back and activated it, in what is known as “drive stun” mode. Seven officers were present at the time.

The ACT magistrates court heard in September that officers also threatened to use OC spray against Emma after she appeared to self-harm by deliberately striking her head against a police van during the arrest.

A transcript of the hearing was released by the court to Guardian Australia in October.

Special magistrate Sean Richter, a former South Australian police officer, said he found the conduct of officers “incredibly” and “exceedingly” heavy-handed, and agreed that they were aware of who Emma was and her vulnerabilities before they arrested her.

“I sometimes wonder when we lost the ability to speak to people,” Richter said.

“She’s a woman that was putting up no resistance.

“She’s sitting on the bench with her arms in the air.”

Richter said Emma was involved in a motor vehicle accident when she was 12 and received a traumatic brain injury.

He said the ACT civil and administrative tribunal described her as having a mental impairment and a neurocognitive disorder, and said she had been placed on a psychiatric treatment order.

Emma was charged with multiple offences by police in relation to the incident, but all of them except possessing a knife without reasonable excuse were withdrawn by the prosecution. She pleaded guilty to that offence, which related to the scissors in her bag, and was convicted. Emma also faced Richter on other matters unrelated to the arrest.

“I was shown the video of her arrest on the charge of possess knife without reasonable excuse. I will say this; I consider that the actions of the police in that matter were unwarranted and heavy-handed,” Richter said.

“Here was a woman sitting on a park bench putting her arms in the air. She’s clearly known to the police because one of them names her.

“It’s blatantly apparent to anyone that deals with this woman that she has a significant cognitive disorder and should be treated as such. I find it amazing that in this day and age the police reacted in the way that they did.”

In a statement, ACT policing said it “notes the comments of Special Magistrate Richter in relation to the arrest of a woman in January 2026.

“As an associated civil claim is under way in relation to this matter, it would not be appropriate to provide further comment.”

Get the most important news as it breaks

after newsletter promotion

In that civil claim filed in July, Emma’s lawyer, Michael Lalor, accused one of the officers involved in the arrest of misfeasance in public office.

The officer is accused of making a series of misleading statements or omissions in police evidence that resulted in more serious charges being laid, and Emma spending 28 days in custody before bail was granted after her lawyers viewed the body-worn camera footage of the arrest.

The statement of claim alleges the misleading statements include that Emma ignored police commands, that she had “abruptly” bent down towards her bag, that she attempted to strike an officer multiple times in the face, and that she was Tasered because she engaged in a “high level of violence”.

Lalor also writes in the civil claim that it would be alleged police provided misleading statements regarding the witness who called officers saying they had seen a woman with a knife.

Police said that the civilian witness had “immediately feared for his safety and departed swiftly” after seeing Emma, but the statement of claim said police failed to make clear the man and his partner “were inside a moving vehicle with the doors locked at the relevant time”.

That witness also told police, according to the statement of claim, that “I wasn’t particularly scared, I was in a car with the doors locked, so I knew she couldn’t really stab me.”

Lalor is also alleging breaches of the Human Rights Act and exemplary damages for assault and battery.

Police have not yet been required to file a defence to the claim.

ACT police have come under repeated recent scrutiny for their use of force, particularly against Aboriginal people.

In August, the commonwealth and ACT ombudsman criticised police for failing to clearly define “racial profiling” after officers in Canberra pulled guns on an Indigenous teenager they mistook for a suspect in an aggravated burglary.

In June last year, the ACT ombudsman found that in about a third of cases it reviewed, unprofessional behaviour by officers such as impatience, aggression, foul and abusive language appeared to unnecessarily escalate situations.

This led to “use of force in circumstances where a more sensitive and trauma-informed approach to negotiation and de-escalation might have avoided the need to use force or as much force”.

As part of that investigation, the ombudsman recommended that police identify and implement measures to better equip its officers with a greater understanding of “mental illness and how it affects a person’s behaviour and ability to comply with directions”, but police did not accept the recommendation.

ACT ombudsman found unprofessional behaviour by officers appeared to unnecessarily escalate situations.

https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.title: There’s more than a whiff of politics to the sudden call to slash Labor’s green energy subsidies
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.author: Patrick Commins
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.text:
EVs and home batteries are in Treasury crosshairs despite a better economic case for scaling back nuclear-powered submarines and diesel fuel rebates for miners

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

As Jim Chalmers, the treasurer, comes under increasing pressure to fight inflation by slashing spending in the mid-year budget update, the drumbeat is loudest for cuts in one specific area: green energy subsidies for households.

Receiving the most focus is the cheaper home batteries program, which from July last year has offered a taxpayer-backed 30% rebate to households and businesses.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

The scheme has become a victim of its own success. Treasury officials originally estimated it would lead to a million new batteries by 2030 at a cost of $2.3bn. The latest estimate is more than triple that figure, and only after a tweak to the policy.

Also in the crosshairs is the 2022 electric vehicle subsidy, which exempts workers from fringe benefits tax when they lease an EV through their employer and has proved more popular – and expensive – than predicted.

Despite reports that Treasury is pushing for cuts to the home battery scheme, the argument has hardly been made.

There is more than a whiff of politics to the sudden and urgent need to do away with clean energy programs, against, say, scaling back billions of dollars in diesel fuel rebates for miners.

When budget experts are asked broader questions about the big pressures on the federal government’s finances, rarely do they cite handouts for home batteries or tax breaks for electric vehicles.

In a speech on Monday, Angus Taylor, the opposition leader, again promised to “abolish Labor’s ideological climate bureaucracy” as part of his promised $31bn of budget savings over four years.

Meanwhile, the Albanese government’s recent efforts to apply an income test to private healthcare rebates for over-65s was met with howls of protest from the Coalition.

As Stephen Bartos, an economics professor at the University of Canberra, says, in all this talk about cutting spending, “nobody is mentioning nuclear-powered submarines”.

Bartos, a former deputy secretary at the Department of Finance and New South Wales parliamentary budget officer, says if the challenge is to close the budget deficit, then green subsidies “shouldn’t be their first port of call”.

“Partly because it’s small beer compared to the big-ticket items like health, NDIS and defence. But also because there is a rationale for green subsidies, if a declining one.”

The national disability insurance scheme, for example, was expected to cost nearly $54bn in 2025–26, which has made reining in the cost of the scheme an existential question for the government’s fiscal plans. In 2023, the Parliamentary Budget Office estimated the total cost of acquiring nuclear-powered submarines under the Aukus agreement to be as much $368bn over the life of the program.

The federal fuel tax credit scheme, which mainly helps major global mining companies, costs about $11bn a year and is rising fast.

Bartos is critical of government tax breaks for electric vehicles, but says the case for public support for batteries is stronger.

“I would probably be looking at where the price signals encouraging adoption [of clean energy] are weakest, and that’s probably batteries. For EVs, people are shifting no matter what.”

The case for the cheaper batteries scheme has also been undermined by Treasury officials’ abject failure to predict how popular it would be. A month into the program and it was already obvious they had got it wrong, as the expected cost blew out towards $14bn.

Not only was our appetite for subsidised batteries way higher than official forecasts, the original design of the scheme made it more desirable to buy bigger, more expensive batteries.

Sign up to Breaking News Australia

Get the most important news as it breaks

after newsletter promotion

There has since been a tweak to the design to account for that second issue, which is how Treasury now predicts – for what it’s worth – that the program will cost $7.2bn.

These cost blowouts have amplified derision of the home batteries as “middle-class welfare” of the worst sort.

Alison Reeve, the director of the energy and climate change program at the Grattan Institute, understands the concerns, but says the evidence to back that claim “is pretty thin when you look at where the batteries are being installed”.

Notably, this is in homes across outer suburbia, such as western Sydney, and in regional areas. In other words, not in enclaves of the comfortably well-off.

Then there is the bigger-picture issue: that we risk sacrificing long-term clean energy goals in the name of short-term fiscal objectives.

“Batteries are going to be a big part of our energy future,” Reeve says. “We do need to do some stimulating of that industry until it can stand on its own two feet.”

Slashing support for batteries would damage the burgeoning web of small businesses, suppliers and tradies who have invested in servicing the infant batteries industry.

That’s not to say there are ways to improve the cost and benefits trade-off in the home batteries program. This could be by ensuring subsidised batteries deliver a community benefit by contributing to the power grid in times of need.

“We need to make sure we are maximising the public benefit, rather than just the private benefit,” Reeve says.

There are lessons in how Western Australia has designed its home batteries support scheme.

“If you look at the west coast, you couldn’t get the state subsidy unless you linked yourself up to a virtual power plan run by the network operator. That was in order to benefit the whole network,” she says.

“We also need a clear path out of the subsidy so it doesn’t grow uncontrollably.”

The drumbeat is loudest for cuts in one specific area: green energy subsidies. The most focus is the cheaper home batteries program, which has offered a 30% rebate to households and businesses.

Lawsuit filed last year against IBM, Atos and Leonardo after delays to delivery to troubled new system

The EU has filed a lawsuit against IBM and two other companies involved in its troubled border-management system, an internal document has revealed.

The bloc’s IT agency, EU-Lisa, filed a case last year against IBM, the French IT company Atos and Italian defence contractor Leonardo, the three members of a consortium to implement and maintain the EU’s entry/exit system, which was launched in October 2025.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

The rollout has faced significant difficulties: some passengers at peak times have missed their flights as a result of delays blamed on the new technology and a lack of staff at the border.

The agency’s decision to sue the companies was revealed in its latest annual accounts, which stated that “following the various delays in the delivery of the EES by a contracting consortium the agency activated the available contractual and legal remedies to protect its financial interest”.

Since its launch the system has been beset by problems. Airports have complained of malfunctioning EES kiosks to regular outages of the system, which have led to waiting times of three hours at peak periods.

EU-Lisa said a claim had been submitted on 22 December 2025 to a court in Estonia, where it has its headquarters.

The agency declined to comment on the details of the case, but said the proceedings concerned “the system’s development phase and have no impact on its current operation” adding that “EES is fully operational”.

The lawsuit was first reported by the Financial Times.

The European Commission said it was not a party to the case, while noting it concerned “delays in the delivery of the EES at the time of system development” and was “not related to the operation of the EES”.

The system increased security checks on passengers travelling into the EU from outside its border-free travel zone. Travellers’ faces have to be photographed and fingerprints scanned before they are allowed into the Schengen area, which comprises 25 of the 27 EU member states as well as Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway and Switzerland.

The checks apply to people who are not citizens of one of the 29 Schengen countries, Ireland or Cyprus.

The system is managed by EU-Lisa, the bloc’s agency for large-scale IT systems in the domain of justice and security.

The Guardian has contacted IBM and Leonardo. Atos declined to comment.

We are restarting our live coverage of European news after the mass shooting in Kraków, Poland’s second-largest city, over the weekend in which six people were killed.

In an update this morning, the authorities said the 24-year-old Polish attacker, who had been injured in a shootout with police, has died in hospital.

Polish prosecutors had opened a terrorism investigation after the man, from the town of ‌Ostrowiec Swietokrzyski in ‌southeastern Poland, opened fire on Kraków’s popular Main Market Square on Saturday afternoon, killing six people, including a Briton, and injuring 17 others.

On the first of two days of national mourning declared after the rare mass shooting, police confirmed yesterday that three people found dead at the gunman’s home after the attack were his father, 53, mother, 52, and sister, 21.

Five of the injured are foreign nationals from Britain, Austria, Germany, Portugal and Russia. Two police ⁠officers were also among the injured, one of whom was in a serious condition.

The interior minister, Marcin Kierwiński, said the suspect was fascinated with far-right ideologies and held “very radical” and “ultra-nationalistic” views.

But officials appeared to backtrack from these comments as nationalist opposition politicians questioned the grounds on which they were based.

“Until the matter is fully clarified and the authorities are in ‌possession of complete information, it is best to refrain from making comments, even if there are ​some initial indications,” government spokesperson Adam Szlapka told TVN24.

Meanwhile, the justice minister, Waldemar Zurek, said despite the attacker’s death, the investigation will continue, aiming to establish if he ⁠acted alone. Main Market Square reopened on Sunday evening after a security cordon was lifted.

In an earlier post, we mentioned that US-mediated peace talks between Russia and Ukraine are set to take place in the United Arab Emirates on Tuesday and Wednesday.

According to the Financial Times, the national security advisers of France, Germany and the UK and the chiefs of staff to the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, and Nato secretary-general, Mark Rutte, will take part in sections of the negotiations, despite the Kremlin insisting this morning that no European officials will be present.

The apparent European demand for at least some involvement in the discussions will stem from concerns that without their input Russia will leave with favourable terms.

The Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, has accused European governments of not knowing who speaks for them – but has conceded that security talks will require Europe’s involvement at some point.

After speaking with Von der Leyen, the Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a post on X this morning that they had “coordinated our positions regarding the meeting in Abu Dhabi”.

The British prime minister, Andy Burnham, says he wants the UK to move to a closer relationship with the EU after the next election and one option would be to join the single market. This would significantly boost trade with the EU, but it would involve Britain accepting free movement rules. Norway is in this position – not in the EU, but in the single market.

At one point before the 2016 Brexit referendum, even Nigel Farage would sometimes say that the Norway option would be a good choice for the UK. But today Burnham is being advised to think twice before copying Norway – by the Norwegian PM.

In an interview with Tim Ross from Politico, Jonas Gahr Støre pointed out that being in the single market but not in the EU means accepting regulations decided by others. He said:

After Brexit, British friends called me and said, tell us about the Norwegian way of doing it. And I said, if you left the EU because there was too much Brussels, don’t take the Norwegian version. Because here, you know, basically we are taking most of their decisions, we implement them.

Wearing military-style clothing and a bulletproof vest, the gunman drove at high speed into the square in the heart of the old town, which is usually packed with tourists, and started shooting at random in a “wild ride” around the square, the Kraków police spokesperson Katarzyna Cisło said.

The two injured police officers – Jakub Kulik, a former paratrooper and volunteer firefighter, and Artur Morański– were hailed as heroes for their rapid response and for preventing further casualties.

Greece receives a large number of undocumented migrants through the Mediterranean, often from nearby Turkey and countries in northern Africa.

Greece has been accused by human rights groups of forcibly returning migrants ⁠and ​asylum seekers on its sea and land borders, a ​practice it denies.

Many of the people making these dangerous journeys are trying to escape rapid climate change, famine, oppressive governments and war, and are often not eligible to apply for asylum from their home countries.

Ukraine has been targeting Russia’s oil industry, from pipelines ​and ports to refineries and tankers, in an effort to undermine ⁠Russia’s war economy.

The Kirishi refinery, about 800km (500 miles) from the Ukrainian border, has suffered several Ukrainian drone attacks ​this year.

The facility, one of the key suppliers of diesel to ​the domestic market and for export, is reported to produce more than 6% of Russia’s total refined oil.

We are restarting our live coverage of European news after the mass shooting in Kraków, Poland’s second-largest city, over the weekend in which six people were killed.

In an update this morning, the authorities said the 24-year-old Polish attacker, who had been injured in a shootout with police, has died in hospital.

Polish prosecutors had opened a terrorism investigation after the man, from the town of ‌Ostrowiec Swietokrzyski in ‌southeastern Poland, opened fire on Kraków’s popular Main Market Square on Saturday afternoon, killing six people, including a Briton, and injuring 17 others.

On the first of two days of national mourning declared after the rare mass shooting, police confirmed yesterday that three people found dead at the gunman’s home after the attack were his father, 53, mother, 52, and sister, 21.

Five of the injured are foreign nationals from Britain, Austria, Germany, Portugal and Russia. Two police ⁠officers were also among the injured, one of whom was in a serious condition.

The interior minister, Marcin Kierwiński, said the suspect was fascinated with far-right ideologies and held “very radical” and “ultra-nationalistic” views.

But officials appeared to backtrack from these comments as nationalist opposition politicians questioned the grounds on which they were based.

“Until the matter is fully clarified and the authorities are in ‌possession of complete information, it is best to refrain from making comments, even if there are ​some initial indications,” government spokesperson Adam Szlapka told TVN24.

Meanwhile, the justice minister, Waldemar Zurek, said despite the attacker’s death, the investigation will continue, aiming to establish if he ⁠acted alone. Main Market Square reopened on Sunday evening after a security cordon was lifted.

Stay with us for the latest developments on the police investigation and other news from around the continent.

Assault on Michel Zecler in 2020 is rare case of police brutality reaching court, at time of heightened tensions

Three French police officers have gone on trial over the beating of a black music producer who they say was not wearing a face mask during the Covid pandemic, in a rare case of police brutality reaching court.

The assault on Michel Zecler, now 47, triggered outrage in France over police violence, which victims and researchers say is systemic but authorities and law enforcement unions claim is limited to isolated cases.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

“I expect this trial to hold the police officers accountable,” Zecler told Agence France-Presse in a recent interview.

Campaigners and rights groups have said the case was further evidence of what they saw as the French police’s systemic racism, in a country where they said ethnic minorities received harsher treatment than white people.

Police brutality has been in the spotlight during the student-led protests in recent weeks, during which a 14-year-old lost most of his teeth when a police officer appeared to fire a grenade at him at close range.

Police stopped Zecler outside his Paris studio on 21 November 2020, accusing him of failing to wear a mandatory face mask and suspecting him of cannabis use.

They pushed him into the entrance of his office and violently beat him in an assault recorded by his studio’s security cameras.

Police officers Aurelien B, now aged 29, Pierre P, 37, and Philippe T face charges of intentional violence committed in a group, as well as forgery when they tried to cover up their actions in an official report. They face up to 15 years in jail.

The officers’ lawyers declined to comment before the trial, which started on Monday.

The producer sustained about 30 punches and truncheon blows to the face and body over a five-minute period, according to the investigation.

The medical report noted craniofacial trauma, a wound to the lip and scalp, and a complete rupture of his biceps tendon, leaving him unable to perform his job for 45 days.

France’s human rights ombudswoman has said police used “racist insults” during the assault, according to four witnesses. But the officers denied this and the alleged racism was not included in the indictment.

Zecler said they had used a racist slur against him. “I was insulted and I will repeat this at the hearing,” he said.

In their arrest report, the officers claimed the producer had hit them and tried to seize a truncheon, a version of events refuted by the camera footage that the French media website Loopsider released several days later.

Sign up to Headlines Europe

after newsletter promotion

“I don’t understand the hatred I saw in their eyes,” said Zecler, who has a titanium anchor in his left arm after the ruptured tendon and says he still suffers nightmares.

“If there hadn’t been cameras … their reports would have been enough to send me to prison,” he said.

Most cases of alleged police brutality in France are dealt with internally.

A French police officer is to be tried over shooting dead 17-year-old Nahel Merzouk at point-blank range in June 2023 outside Paris. Video footage also contradicted the police’s version of events in that incident, sparking nationwide protests.

Guilty verdicts in alleged police brutality cases are rare.

In 2024, a judge gave suspended jail sentences to three officers who inflicted irreversible rectal injuries on a black man, Théo Luhaka, during a stop-and-search in 2017.

Young men “perceived as Arab, black or from north Africa” are four times more likely to be stopped by police than the rest of the population, according to a report last year by France’s rights ombudswoman.

They are 12 times more likely to be subjected to more severe measures, including being frisked during checks, it said after a survey of more than 5,000 people.

Judge Bennathan asks Brand to stand up as he passes his sentence judgment.

He says the sentence for rape is nine years imprisonment.

The total sentence is 10 years, six months, with the sexual assault offences.

The judge gave prison sentences of nine months, 18 months, and eight months for those three offences.

Prosecutors had called for the judge to mete out a sentence of this severity, for a category one penalty which ranges from 10-15 years.

The judge had said he was “very conscious” that Brand’s imprisonment would “deprive your children of the presence of their father”.

That sad loss to them, however, is caused by your serious offending.

Brand’s lawyer Ian Winter KC earlier had strenuously made the case that a lengthy sentence would have a “catastrophic” impact on Brand’s wife and three children.

Brand was taken into custody immediately after a jury found him guilty last Thursday so has not had the opportunity to say goodbye in person to his family.

Judge Bennathan also commended the Met Police for “their hard work in gathering evidence and taking great care of all the women who testified.”

As I reported earlier, one of the victims said she had wanted to withdraw her case after the stress and pressure and public attention, but she persisted with the support of specialist police teams.

The Met Police have said they expect other women may come forward to report their experiences of abuse and assault.

Right before delivering his sentence decision, Judge Bennathan said:

Finally, before passing sentence, I pause to pay tribute to the determination and bravery of all the woman whose evidence I have been recounting.

I do not increase your punishment becauseof it but all those women had to face being confronted and being told they lied, or twisted the truth, and or they’d agreed to your sexual demands. That was all done because of you, and your instructions.

Officers have taken Brand out of the courtroom.

He has served a few days at HMP Wandsworth already, after being denied bail last Thursday following his conviction.

Brand must serve two-thirds of the 10-and-a-half years sentence before he will be eligible for parole, says the judge.

That means he will be behind bars for seven years.

He says the sentence for rape is nine years imprisonment.

The total sentence is 10 years, six months, with the sexual assault offences.

The judge gave prison sentences of nine months, 18 months, and eight months for those three offences.

Prosecutors had called for the judge to mete out a sentence of this severity, for a category one penalty which ranges from 10-15 years.

The judge says with the mitigating factors in play, he will reduce his sentence for Brand by a year.

He has not given the full sentence yet.

Judge Bennathan has repeatedly called Brand a sexual predator during his address so far.

He notes mitigating factors of no crimes having been reported in the past 17 years, and some evidence testifying to Brand’s character.

The judge, laying out the crimes, notes Brand’s “staggering arrogance” and how his entourage regularly indulged Brand’s actions.

Three of the four crimes took place in public settings, in front of other people – at a bar, radio station and a setting where an advert was being filmed. Others in the room laughed after the assaults, the women said.

These insults in front of an audience, said after the assault amount to an additional humiliation.

The whole episode reeks of casual disrespect, and your belief that fame meant you could act however you liked, when you liked, unhindered by the rules by which decent people live.

The judge is relaying the sexual assaults Brand committed against the women.

He starts with the attacks on one woman in a pub in London where Brand groped the breast of a fellow party attendee.

“The effect on her had her wandering the streets of London, phoning a friend in the middle of the night, tearful and distressed.”

He outlines another assault, where Brand, visiting a radio station with an entourage launched himself at a woman, groping and kissing her in front of her colleagues and his entourage.

He notes the attack’s impact on her, how it damaged relationships with her male colleagues.

“There was the added humiliation of you assaulting her in front of an audience and the laughter afterwards”.

Judge Bennathan starts with Brand’s climb to fame 20 years ago.

“About 20 years ago, Russell Brand, you were becoming famous. You were clever – and in many people’s eyes, funny and charismatic.

“You had also become a sexual predator,” he says.

“Your status protected you until 2023 when journalists published allegations” about his rapes and sexual abuse of women.

Such public reporting “empowered” other women to come forward to police, says Bennathan.

Judge Bennathan is about to begin his sentencing remarks, having considered the submissions from the prosecutor and Brand’s defence lawyer this morning.

A reminder that Russell Brand, once one of Britain’s most high-profile actor-comedians, was convicted last Thursday of raping one woman and sexually assaulting three others.

Good morning. Monday is often the busiest day of the week at Westminster but, with the Commons still enjoying a mini November recess, today is looking a bit quiet. Andy Burnham is on a visit to a hospital this morning and he wants to talk about a £40m programme in England to try to keep vulnerable patients out of hospital. The Department of Health and Social Care has the details here, and Andrew Gregory explains it all here.

But Burnham may find he ends up taking more questions from the media on another Guardian story, Kiran Stacey’s scoop about the government being on course to water down electric vehicle (EV) targets.

With Burnham attending the Cop climate crisis summit later this week, the revelations won’t boost Burnham’s credentials with environmentalists.

The final EV decision has not yet been taken, but the Greens are already outraged. These are from Zack Polanski, the Green party leader.

This week leaders meet for the UN climate summit.

The context? A summer of heat deaths. Scientists saying 2026 will be the hottest year ever.

Our Government’s contribution?

To bend over backwards to the car industry, and scrap plans for rapid electrification.

This Government is building up a shocking record of backsliding and bad decisions on climate issues.

At a time when we desperately need leadership, they bend to the will of polluters by slashing key rules and pushing ahead with fossil fuel extraction.

And this is from the former Green leader Caroline Lucas.

A truly terrible decision at a truly terrible time. The shift to electric vehicles is government’s single biggest decarbonisation policy. Cutting EV targets would send a message on eve of #COP31 that UK is no longer serious about #climate action.

Here is the agenda for the day.

Morning: Andy Burnham is visiting a hospital in Hertfordshire.

11.30am: Downing Street holds a lobby briefing.

I’m afraid we are no longer able to have comments open below the line every day on this blog. If you want to contact me, please email politics.live@theguardian.com. You can use this email to flag up corrections, comments for publication, questions or complaints.

The UK Sustainable Investment and Finance Association, which represents people in the finance sector committed to sustainable investment, has said that it will be “highly disappointing” if the government does water down its electric vehicle (EV) targets.

Commenting on our story today (see 9.26am), James Alexander, its CEO, said:

Rumours that the government is set to substantially slash the ZEV [zero emission vehicle] mandate will be highly disappointing to investors backing the rapid electrification of the UK’s road transport system.

The mandate has underpinned this flow of capital, as it has offered a clear sense of the size and trajectory of the future EV market.

But a third change to the framework in just three years could severely dent its credibility and put future allocation decisions at risk.

Andy Burnham has been criticised for hiring a controversial consultancy firm to help No 10 with work on his 10-year plan.

As the Sunday Times reported yesterday, the Boston Consulting Group (BCG), one of the world’s biggest consultancy firms, has been asked to contribute. James Purnell, Burnham’s chief of staff, worked for BCG briefly after standing down as an MP in 2010.

No 10 says the support it is getting from BCG is “limited, short-term and focused on specific specialist advice”, and it has been reported that just one consultant is involved.

But the appointment is controversial because consultants from the company worked on plans being drawn up by the Trump administration for the post-conflict reconstruction of Gaza. BCG said that that work was unauthorised, and that the two partners involved in the project – dismissed by critics as a blueprint for ethnic cleansing – were later “exited from the firm”.

Commenting on the story, Neil O’Brien, the Conservative’s policy renewal spokesperson, said:

Amazing that Burnham is so lacking in vision that he has to ask management consultants what his own vision is

Zack Polanski, the Green party leader, said in a statement:

Aside from an obvious point that you don’t appoint companies like the Boston Consulting Group if you have any actual intention of ending 40 years of neoliberalism, Trump’s ‘Gaza Riviera’ blueprint is clear ethnic cleansing and the idea that Andy Burnham has invited these people into the heart of Downing Street shows contempt for the victims of the genocide.

Andy Burnham has said that the bravery shown by Russell Brand’s accusers should hasten efforts to improve the support that rape and sexual assault victims get from the criminal justice system.

Acknowledging that more needed to be done, Burnham said:

I’ll be honest and say I don’t think you ever can do enough to get the right support in place for victims to give them the confidence to come forward, because we know that still isn’t there in the way that it should be.

But I have already taken a decision to make sure there are rape and serious sexual offence teams in every police force by the end of next year. It was going to be 2029, I brought it forward, and I lean back on my work as mayor of Greater Manchester in this regard. There is so much that needs to be done. We have to bring it forward.

Obviously today, everybody will be thinking about the women who had the courage to come forward. Their bravery will, I believe, change the system more broadly, and we will be relentless in making whatever improvements we can.

But there’s no complacency here. There’s a lot more that needs to change.

Andy Burnham has described reports that the government will water down its electric vehicle (EV) targets as “speculation”.

Asked about the story on a visit to a hospital in Watford, Burnham said:

The consultation on the mandate for zero emission vehicles concluded only a fortnight ago, so obviously that is being looked at now. The range of responses to the consultation … so these reports are just that: they’re reports, they’re speculation and no decision has been made at this point.

(In Westminster, when stories get described as “speculation”, that normally means that they are true – but that people just aren’t ready to say so yet.)

Downing Street has insisted that the government remains committed to the principle of the zero emission vehicle (ZEV) mandate – while not denying today’s Guardian report saying interim targets to achieve it are set to be watered down. (See 9.26am.)

Asked about the story at the daily lobby briefing, the PM’s spokesperson said:

The government is fully behind the zero emission vehicle mandate, and no decisions have been taken yet.

We’re sticking to our commitment, phasing out new cars that run only on petrol or diesel by 2030, every new car and van will be zero emission by 2035, and our legally binding net zero targets. None of that is changing.

The consultation is about getting the details right, so the switch works for drivers, for car makers and for the thousands of workers whose jobs depend on it.

As the Guardian reports, a key meeting on the ZEV mandate is scheduled to take place on Wednesday. But it has been reported that the decision may not be announced this week. Asked if the announcement might be delayed to avoid embarrassing Andy Burnham when he attends the Cop climate conference this week, the spokesperson just repeated the point about how no decisions have yet been taken.

Andy Burnham has a commanding lead over all the other main UK party leaders on polling on who would be the best PM, according to new figures from YouGov. In head to head polling, Burnham has a 12-point lead over Kemi Badenoch, and much bigger leads over Nigel Farage, Ed Davey and Zack Polanski.

Badenoch is ahead of all the other leaders apart from Burnham on this measure. Davey only beats Farage and Polanski. Polanski loses to all four other leaders featured in this polling, and Farage only beats one of them, Polanski, but only by a one-point margin.

As Dylan Difford reports in his write-up for YouGov, even Lib Dem and Green supporters think Burnham would be a better PM than Davey and Polanski respectively, by a significant margin. This was not the case when Keir Starmer was Labour leader and PM. Difford says:

Such is the scale of Burnham’s advantage over his fellow progressive leaders that those who backed the Greens in 2024 are divided 43% to 35% in his favour over whether he or Polanski would make the better PM, while 2024 Lib Dem voters actually back the Labour leader over Davey by a decisive margin of 58% to 17%.

In May, by contrast, Lib Dem voters favoured Davey over Starmer on this question by a 30 point margin (with Labour voters only favouring Starmer by 24 points), while Polanski’s lead among Green voters was 51 points.

This chart illustrates how polling on this measure has changed over the past year.

Last week Rupert Lowe, who leads Restore Britain, a small, far-right party that is even more hardline than Reform UK (the party Lowe represented when he became an MP in 2024), issued a statement saying the party would not accept any “foreign influence” in its affairs.

Lowe was referring in particular to engagement with lobbyists. But today the Financial Times is running a story pointing out that, in another respect, Lowe is the beneficiary of foreign influence to a very significant degree.

That is because his comments are getting a remarkable amount of attention on X, the social media platform owned by Elon Musk, who is a strong supporter of Lowe and his extremist, anti-migrant politics. In their story, Jim Pickard and Amy Borrett say that “only three world leaders have amassed more views on X than [Lowe] in the first 10 months of this year: Indian prime minister Narendra Modi, US president Donald Trump and Sanae Takaichi, the Japanese premier.”

While Lowe may be tempted to believe that his success on the platform is down to the wit and wisdom of his tweets, Pickard and Borrett point out that there is a simple explanation as to why his posts do so well. They report:

Some 43 per cent of Lowe’s 1.7bn views on X in the first 10 months of the year were from posts that were reposted or commented on by Musk.

Posts by Lowe that were quoted by Musk had almost 100 times the number of views of those where the X owner did not interact. Musk has 241m followers on X.

Being amplified to this extent by Musk does not just provide Restore Britain with useful publicity; as Michael Savage reported in a story over the summer, Lowe has also earned substantial sums from the platform because it pays people for content that goes viral.

In an interview with Sky News, Julia Lopez, who is serving as interim shadow business secretary while Claire Coutinho is on maternity leave, said that the Conservatives would like to get rid of the ZEV [zero emission vehicle] mandate entirely. She said that she did not think there was enough consumer demand for electric vehicles, and that there were not enough charging points.

But she still welcomed reports that Labour will weaken the EV targets. “If Labour wants to be pragmatic and change some of those targets, that’s good,” she said.

Karin Smyth, a health minister, was doing a media round for the government this morning. Asked about reports that EV targets are going to be cut, she just stressed that “on this particular issue, no decisions have been made”.

But the Green party is not minded to wait before speaking out. In addition to comments on social media from Zack Polanski and Caroline Lucas, the party has now issued a statement from the Green MP Siân Berry saying:

The switch to EVs has the potential to create greater emissions savings than any other energy transition policy, while providing drivers with vehicles that can be significantly cheaper to run.

Yet again, this Labour government is heading in the wrong direction. Instead of pandering to corporate lobbying and stalling on the phase out of petrol and diesel vehicles, they should be boosting EV uptake through vehicle scrappage schemes and cheaper, more abundant and more reliable public charging infrastructure.

Andy Burnham says he wants the UK to move to a closer relationship with the EU after the next election and one option would be to join the single market. This would significantly boost trade with the EU, but it would involve Britain accepting free movement rules. Norway is in this position – not in the EU, but in the single market.

At one point before the 2016 Brexit referendum, even Nigel Farage would sometimes say that the Norway option would be a good choice for the UK.

But today Burnham is being advised to think twice before copying Norway – by the Norwegian PM.

In an interview with Tim Ross from Politico, Jonas Gahr Støre pointed out that being in the single market but not in the EU means accepting regulations decided by others. He said:

After Brexit, British friends called me and said, tell us about the Norwegian way of doing it. And I said, if you left the EU because there was too much Brussels, don’t take the Norwegian version. Because here, you know, basically we are taking most of their decisions, we implement them.

The Tories have criticised the Scottish government for posting a message on its X social media account about a Sikh festival at 11am yesterday – as the nation was observing the two-minute silence for Remembrance Sunday. Harriet Cross, the shadow Scottish secretary, said:

It is hard to see their decision to post about a Sikh festival at precisely 11am, at the very moment that people across the country were observing a two-minute silence to honour our war dead, as a coincidence.

There is no reason why they couldn’t have recognised both - not least out of respect to the 83,000 Sikhs killed fighting in both World Wars.

This failure to mark Remembrance Sunday shows a total disregard for the sacrifice our soldiers made and continue to make in defence of our country.

At 11am yesterday John Swinney, the Scottish first minister, was with other leaders in Edinburgh laying a wreath at a remembrance ceremony.

Businesses which trade goods made with slave labour will have to withdraw them from sale, the government has said, revealing it will change the law to enforce the new ban. The Press Association reports:

Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, said he plans to introduce new legislation to introduce mandatory human rights due diligence for companies, which will require them to remove products made with forced labour and modern slavery.

He outlined the move in a letter to the Commons business committee, which has been calling for new business safeguards against modern slavery for nearly two years.

The new duty will apply to British businesses with a global turnover of more than £350m, and non-UK businesses with a UK-generated turnover of more than £350m.

Those who do not comply with the new duty may be forced to withdraw products from sale which have come from forced labour or modern slavery, Reynolds said.

The commitee has been calling for modern slavery protections to be strengthened since it heard evidence from Chinese-owned clothing company Shein in January 2025.

In that session, the firm repeatedly declined to confirm whether its products contained cotton sourced from China, including Xinjiang, where it is believed that the Uyghur minority are subject to forced labour.

Here is an article by Fiona Harvey and Jasper Jolly published last month on what the consequences would be if the government were to relax its EV targets, as the Guardian today reports now seems inevitable. (See 9.26am.)

And here is an extract.

The end goal of 2035 is likely to remain, but under a consultation that ended on Friday, the 2030 targets could be weakened to 70% or even as low as 50% of new cars. Taken with previous watering down of the policy to allow more sales of hybrid cars – which use both electric and combustion engines – that change would lead to emissions greater than burning all the gas in the Jackdaw field, according to the ECIU [Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit].

If the mandate were cut more drastically to require only 50% of sales to be EVs by 2030, this could mean an additional 147 megatonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent, which would equate to about 58% of the likely emissions from burning the oil produced by the Rosebank field.

Jess Ralston, an analyst at the ECIU, said weakening the target would not solve the problems for manufacturers, who are already facing intensified competition from China as increasing numbers of people opt for EVs. It would also not benefit the public because EVs can be £1,750 a year cheaper to run, and potentially more with oil prices rising.

And this is from the former Green leader Caroline Lucas.

A truly terrible decision at a truly terrible time. The shift to electric vehicles is government’s single biggest decarbonisation policy. Cutting EV targets would send a message on eve of #COP31 that UK is no longer serious about #climate action.

Here is the agenda for the day.

Morning: Andy Burnham is visiting a hospital in Hertfordshire.

11.30am: Downing Street holds a lobby briefing.

Troubled utility lobbies for deadline on part of the debt to be extended to March 2028

Thames Water has asked creditors for more time to pay back billions of pounds in debt, as the water company scrambles to keep itself afloat.

The UK’s largest water company said it had proposed an “interim” deal under which the deadline to pay off an unspecified portion of the £20bn of debt on its balance sheet would be extended from 2027 to March 2028.

The company, which serves 16 million customers across London and the Thames Valley, has been on the brink of collapse for several years after it became overwhelmed by debt. Its shareholders walked away in 2024, which in effect left the company under the control of its creditors, who are working out a deal to avoid bankruptcy.

The creditors gave Thames Water a separate £3bn lifeline in February last year to try to see it through negotiations on a deal to reduce its debts and inject more money. The creditors, collectively called the London & Valley Water company, are led by a group of US hedge funds, including Elliott Management and Silver Point Capital, and institutional investors, including BlackRock and M&G.

Last month, Thames Water asked creditors for a further £2.4bn emergency loan, as it warned it would be unable to reach a longer-term deal to sort out its debt before running out of cash by “the end of 2026 or the start of 2027”. The company on Monday said it had started the process of raising the first £600m of that funding.

The prime minister, Andy Burnham, faces a decision on whether to allow a takeover deal by the water company’s creditors, which would involve writing off fines and reducing the company’s environmental commitments. He is also considering whether to nationalise Thames Water or approve another form of state control.

Labour politicians and environmental campaigners have said Burham should instead put Thames Water into special administration, a form of temporary government control while a new buyer is sought.

On Monday, the Liberal Democrats called on Burnham to tell parliament what he is doing to fix the water industry if he does not publish a full plan by the end of the year.

https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.author: Gwyn Topham Transport correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.text:
Call for overhaul of manually operated level crossings after delivery worker was killed by passenger train in Kent

An Amazon delivery driver was killed by a train after he drove his van on to railway tracks at a manually operated level crossing, apparently without realising he needed to open the exit gate first, an official investigation has reported.

Safety inspectors said there was “an obvious risk of further tragedy”, with a second similar fatal event still being investigated, and called for an overhaul of this type of crossing.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

The van driver, Brandon Hatcher, 23, of Ashford, Kent, died at the Bax crossing near Teynham after being hit by a passenger train from Ramsgate to London in July last year.

While signs at the crossing told road users to check for a green light before opening both gates, and again before closing both gates, the Rail Accident Investigation Branch report found that the traffic light system “almost certainly led [the driver] to believe that it was safe to enter the crossing once the entry gate had been opened, despite the exit gate still being closed”.

Hatcher drove his van across most of the track and was parked when the lights turned red and alarms sounded to indicate an approaching train. He opened the exit gate but not sufficiently to pass at the first attempt, tried again and was returning to the door of his van when the Southeastern train, travelling at 90mph, came within view 300 metres away.

The train driver applied the emergency brake but could not avoid the fatal collision. Three train passengers reported minor injuries.

The signage had been redesigned in recent years but the RAIB found that it “did not sufficiently consider how diverse information sources may influence crossing user behaviour”.

It said the training and guidance provided to the delivery driver, who was self-employed but working on behalf of a logistics company, GG Logistix, delivering Amazon parcels, “had not prepared him to use the crossing safely”. It called for Network Rail and the Department for Transport (DfT) to review the design, laws and guidance around this type of level crossing to reduce the risk.

Another delivery driver was also killed when hit by a Northern train at a manual crossing in Lancashire in August. The circumstances of the death of Simon Gettings, 55, remain under investigation.

Andrew Hall, the chief inspector of rail accidents, said: “These deaths are a tragedy, but as a train can be derailed by striking a delivery van, both accidents could also have had serious consequences for the people on board.

“Private user worked crossings are a 19th-century concept operating in a 21st century world of more dense, faster rail services, more rural housing and abundant home deliveries. Most road users are unfamiliar with this type of crossing and with how to use them safely.”

He urged the rail industry and the DfT “to find effective ways to mitigate this obvious risk before there is further tragedy”.

The rail regulator, ORR, said it would “ensure lessons are learned and improvements made to protect crossing users, passengers and railway staff”.

David Davidson, the chief operating officer for South Eastern Railway, said: “Our thoughts remain with the family and loved ones of Brandon Hatcher who tragically lost his life following a collision with one of our trains.”

He said they would study the report’s recommendations closely, adding: “We have already made changes to the layout of the site and we have published a toolkit with guidance on this type of crossing for professional road drivers. We will continue working with the industry and all our partners to help prevent accidents like this from happening again.”
