Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.

Donald Trump said he thinks his administration was too aggressive on deportations and that he was open to an arrangement to allow some undocumented immigrants to remain in the US.

The president said, in his first major interview since his party lost control of the House and Senate in the midterm elections, that his deportation policy was part of the reason Republicans lost.

He told CBS’s ‘60 Minutes’ in an interview that aired on Sunday:

I think it might be too tough, yeah. And a lot of people would say that it’s great. But a lot of people think it’s too tough.

The president’s comments were an unusually frank acknowledgment that one of the defining policies of his second administration had become a political liability. But they were seemingly at odds with his decision on Friday to elevate Stephen Miller, the architect of his immigration crackdown, to White House chief of staff.

Trump said that he thinks he could reach an agreement with the new Democratic majority, adding:

We would work something out. And I think it’s something - I think that’s something that’s actually doable.

The president claimed that his policy “both helped and hurt”, since people gave him an “A+ for closing up the border” and “very high marks for getting the bad ones out”. But he admitted: “I get hurt because we also took people that had good jobs, that created one violation, or breaking of the law, and that was that they came into the country illegally.”

His comments come as his most controversial aide Miller was due today to start his new role as chief of staff. In a social media ‌post, Trump called Miller, 41, “one of ​my most trusted advisors” and praised the outgoing Susie Wiles for doing “an ⁠outstanding job”.

Read our full report here:

In other developments:

On the race among Republicans to succeed him for the 2028 presidential election, Trump hinted at staying neutral. Asked whether he’d endorse a potential successor, the president said “probably, not necessarily.” “We have a tremendous bench. I have so many people that I have great relationships with,” Trump said in his CBS interview.

Trump said on Sunday that he “was only kidding” when he announced a day earlier that he had offered the job of White House press secretary to Dana White, the chief executive of the Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC). Speaking to reporters on his way back the White House from his beach club in Florida, Trump explained the premise of his joke, that if the UFC boss, who is a devoted fan of the president, took over the briefing room, flanked by six fighters, reporters “wouldn’t mess around with him so much”.

Trump will meet with Qatar’s prime minister at ⁠the White House today, according to the White House schedule, as the ⁠conflict with ⁠Iran ​drags on and diplomatic efforts to end it face significant obstacles. Trump is due ⁠to meet with Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al-Thani, who also serves as Qatar’s foreign ⁠minister, in a closed-door meeting. Vice-president JD Vance ​is also scheduled to meet ‌with the ‌Qatari leader, according to a US official.

A US deportation flight of Iranian nationals bound for Iran by way of Pakistan was abruptly canceled Sunday morning, according to an attorney who spoke to some of the detainees slated for repatriation. At least eight Iranians were loaded onto a plane Sunday morning in Mesa, Arizona, for a deportation flight headed to the country of Georgia, then on to Pakistan, according to Ali Rahnama, an attorney with the Iranian American Legal Defense Fund who filed emergency motions on behalf of some of the Iranian detainees. The flight was canceled without explanation, he said.

We’re also bringing you the latest as we get the final US House race results – where currently Democrats have a 92-seat majority. There are 19 races that still have to be called, so as we get the latest result counts we’ll provide an update.

Democratic Congressman Hakeem Jeffries, currently the House minority leader who is poised to become new Speaker next year, told CBS News that the Trump administration will hold a closed-door congressional briefing today to discuss Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

Last week the Republican chairs of three key House committees also called on Huang to appear before lawmakers in a closed-door hearing on 18 November.

Nvidia announced it is launching an independent investigation following reports that Huang, its founder and CEO, had been the target of “a foreign intelligence effort”.

That effort, reports claim, led to Huang conducting a romantic relationship with a Chinese woman, Alice Huang, who was recruited to spy for China’s Ministry of State Security intelligence agency.

On Sunday Donald Trump said he had yet to speak with the Nvidia CEO. “I just know he’s a fine person, but you never know what is going on,” the president said of Huang. “I’m sure. I hope everything’s fine. He’s done such an incredible job, and so I would certainly hope he’s a fine person, in my opinion.”

We’re also keeping an eye on the latest results out of Mississippi, in the neck-and-neck US Senate race.

With 97% of the votes counted, Democrat Scott Colom is leading the Republican incumbent, Cindy Hyde-Smith by more than 2,500 votes. A reminder that election officials in the state can accept ballots until 10 November (five business days after election day) as long as they are postmarked by 3 November.

We’ll bring you the latest as we learn more.

Donald Trump is in Washington today. He’ll spend most of the day in closed door policy meetings. At 12pm ET he’ll welcome the Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani, the prime minister of Qatar, to the White House. That summit is closed to the press for the time being, but we’ll bring you the latest in case that opens up.

This meeting comes just days after Trump said that the US carried out out new “minor” strikes on Iran, targeting an Iranian air defense system, as a deal to end the conflict remains stalled.

On Sunday, the president told CNN that it is “highly unlikely” he will need to resume strikes as long as there is progress in negotiations over Tehran’s nuclear program and reopening the strait of Hormuz.

“The answer is highly unlikely it’s going to be necessary. They’re a failing nation. It just came out, you saw this year, 301% inflation. Highly unlikely it will be necessary. I would if necessary, but we hit them really hard. I hit them so hard. You don’t know how hard I hit them,” he said.

Don’t worry, cash-strapped Americans, “relief is on the way”, the senator Chuck Schumer promised last week in a press conference celebrating Democrats’ massive midterms win.

Winning candidates promised to cut food and healthcare costs, rein in corporations ripping off consumers and workers, curb billionaire power and make the world’s biggest economy better serve the working class.

There’s broad agreement on those lofty goals and on some short-term steps. But the big win is bringing decades-old battles to the fore, about how the US federal government should fund safety nets and check healthcare and food costs.

The “lame duck” period between an election and a new Congress’s swearing-in in early January is often a frenzy of behind-the-scenes battles and public posturing as corporate lobbyists, thinktanks, voter groups and big donors try to influence the agenda.

This time, it’s all that on steroids.

Already, JB Pritzker, the Illinois governor, has issued a 75-page list of 200 policy proposals for Congress’s “day one agenda”; Columbia professor Tim Wu is pushing an “affordability bill”; Texas’s new senator James Talarico is promising universal healthcare for all; there’s an 181-page investigation memo circulating; and moderate Democrats are arguing for more incremental steps.

Meanwhile, Trump’s power to veto bills means anything the president doesn’t like will need a clutch of Republicans to pass, making things more complicated. Expect a mix of affordability bills the president will back, like curbs on private equity and credit card interest rates, and ones he will veto, which Democrats will use for anti-Republican political messaging.

Public health leaders and politicians who made healthcare a central part of their platforms swept into office in the US midterm elections last week, setting the stage for national, state and local changes.

Voters, faced with an unprecedented rise in vaccine-preventable diseases such as measles, alongside devastating outbreaks of foodborne illnesses, chose national candidates who prioritized public health, healthcare affordability, reproductive health and the impeachment of Robert F Kennedy Jr, among other key issues.

“The American people are speaking out against President Trump and the policies that he’s been rolling out since the day he took office,” said Julie Scofield, a member of the coordinating committee at the grassroots organization Defend Public Health. “I think it’s a complete repudiation.”

Mallory Harris, a scientist in Austin, almost delayed having children because she was worried about accessing life-saving healthcare, such as vaccines and abortion, if she needed it. She had doctors check her immunity against viruses including measles, and sought assurances from her physicians that she would have access to appropriate care. Harris found out she was pregnant just as 2026 officially became the worst year for measles in the US since before she was born. Texas has no paid time off for maternity or paternity leave, but Harris and her husband will try to wait until the baby is six months old and can get the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) shot early before starting daycare.

Dealing with public health emergencies like these have been “a top issue” for her as a voter. After the election, “it suddenly became a lot less scary”, Harris said. “We’ve seen scientists and physicians getting elected in record numbers. We saw big shifts in places that have had measles outbreaks.”

Donald Trump will meet the prime minister of key mediator Qatar on Monday as efforts to end the Iran war ramp up ⁠following last week’s midterm elections, though ⁠senior US and Gulf officials cast ​doubt on the chances of an imminent deal.

With no victory in sight more than eight months into the conflict he launched alongside Israel on 28 February, Trump has played down the likelihood of major warfare ⁠restarting soon but remains unwilling to accept an existing Iranian truce plan.

Mutual attacks continue, with the US striking Iran’s Qeshm island overnight, according to Iranian state media, and Iran attacking tankers in the Gulf and strait of Hormuz this month, while its Yemeni ⁠Houthi allies have hit Saudi Arabia.

Speaking to reporters on his way back the White House from his beach club in Florida, Trump explained the premise of his joke, that if the UFC boss, who is a devoted fan of the president, took over the briefing room, flanked by six fighters, reporters “wouldn’t mess around with him so much”.

“So I was kidding, but I think Dana likes the idea, and he is a very capable guy,” Trump added. “Of course, I was kidding. And you could see that because I put all of the great fighters as his assistants, that they’re all going to come with him … It was just a little fun.”

Earlier on Sunday, the president shared an animated AI cartoon made by one of his supporters on social media, which showed UFC fighters beating up journalists and one, Josh Hokit, repeating the racist remark about Michelle Obama he made during the UFC event at the White House on Trump’s birthday in June.

The president said that his mock announcement that White would become his spokesperson, in a social media post on Saturday, “was an example of something where I was kidding, and then people said, ‘You know, that’s actually a pretty good idea’”.

Stephen Miller, the influential architect of Donald Trump’s aggressive immigration crackdown, is due to start as White House chief of staff today. His promotion has horrified many, handing even more power to the president’s most controversial aide.

The 41-year-old has been with Trump since the beginning of the US president’s political career – serving as a speechwriter during his 2016 presidential campaign – and has long been seen as a hardliner on the right, serving as the driving force behind first-term Trump policies such as family separation at the US-Mexico border and the travel ban on people from many Muslim-majority countries.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Richard Luscombe
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Former president’s new book Promise Me America provides an inside look at January 6, Covid-19 response and more

Joe Biden will undertake only limited promotion of his upcoming White House memoir because of advancing cancer, the former president said in a social media post on Sunday night.

His new book, Promise Me America, which will be published on 17 November, is Biden’s account of a one-term presidency that began in 2021 in the shadow of the insurrection at the US Capitol on 6 January 2021 by supporters of Donald Trump eager to overturn the outgoing Republican president’s defeat by his Democratic rival in the 2020 election.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

The deadly invasion of the Capitol as Congress was due to meet to certify Biden’s victory, after a rally near the White House where Trump urged his supporters to go to Congress and “fight” for him, remains a historic shame such that Biden in his book says of the current president that it “should follow him to his grave”.

In the post on X, Biden – who was diagnosed with an “aggressive” form of prostate cancer in May 2025, four months after leaving office – said the number of speaking engagements he can manage in support of his book’s publication will be limited.

“Some days are better than others,” he said. “It hasn’t stopped me. But sometimes it slows me down. What that means is, unfortunately, I won’t be able to do as many conversations about my book as I’d hoped.”

Instead, Biden said: “I’m hopeful the words on the page speak for themselves”. He said he and his wife, Jill, were touched and grateful for the support of the American people since his condition became known.

The memoir takes an extensive look at the deadly violence in Washington DC fomented by supporters of Trump, who was seeking to remain in office after his defeat by Biden in the 2020 presidential election.

“Donald Trump led an insurrection,” Biden wrote.

“The rioters weren’t ‘peaceful protesters’. They came armed to stop the official certification of a legitimate election.”

Noting that Trump later pardoned more than 1,500 of those convicted of offenses related to the January 6 riot, Biden said: “To this day, Trump and his supporters continue to preen and posture like they’re supporters of law enforcement.

“Here’s my view: You don’t get to turn a blind eye to cops being punched, speared, sprayed, and brutalized and call yourself a friend of law enforcement. What Trump did on January 6, 2021, should never be forgotten. It should follow him to his grave.”

Trump’s actions since he returned to office in January 2025 also come under Biden’s scrutiny, including the chaotic creation of the so-called “department of government efficiency” (Doge) that put hundreds of thousands of people out of work but failed to yield touted savings.

“All presidents must confront a feeling that their legacy is vulnerable to the pendulum of politics and the whims of their successors,” Biden wrote.

“In my case, that feeling was magnified by the dismissive and destructive nature of Donald Trump, who seemed unable to tolerate the idea that someone else’s accomplishments might be worth building on rather than tearing down.”

Biden, in the post, said the book explores “the challenges we faced, the decisions I made, and why I made them”, covering a pivotal period in US history including the Covid-19 pandemic, economic troubles and trying to restore alliances and relationships with allies frayed during Trump’s first term.

Biden said he realized as soon as Trump took office again, much of what he had worked to achieve was soon to be dismantled.

“Trump, he said, “took a wrecking ball to our traditions.” Biden previously published a memoir called Promise me, Dad, about the death of his elder son, Beau, from cancer.

The Associated Press contributed reporting

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.title: Black girls in LA keep seeing women around them getting killed. They’re driving change
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.author: Abené Clayton in Los Angeles with photographs by Julien James
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.text:
Black women and girls represent an outsized share of LA homicide victims – frustrated with police and legislators’ failures, they’re stepping up and speaking out to stop the violence

As a child, Tioni Theus was a ball of energy. After school she liked to play golf and dance. On weekends, she’d go to the movies and the mall with her older cousin. Driving back home at the end of the day to her family’s apartment in South Los Angeles, California, she’d ask: “What are we doing next?”

Everything changed when Tioni was 13. Her mother was hit by a car and critically injured, leaving her unable to take care of her daughter. While her mom recovered, Tioni lived with other family members. But the accident left Tioni angry, her older cousin Nafeesah Kincy said, and she struggled to understand that her life had permanently changed.

Tioni started talking to strangers online, Kincy noticed, and hung out with unfamiliar people, including older teen boys and young men. Then she left her family’s care and would bounce between random people’s houses, Kincy said, or spend nights with a boyfriend at a hotel. Each time she saw Tioni, Kincy would implore her to come back to her family.

Over the next two years, Tioni stopped going to school and became “lost in the streets”, said Kincy, who would take her cousin to get food, or meet at another family member’s house to drop off care packages with deodorant, clean underwear and tampons. Family members pleaded with Tioni to stay with one of them permanently.

“It was devastating because I couldn’t protect her,” she said. “We did everything we knew to do.”

Then, on 8 January 2021, Tioni’s body was found on a stretch of highway with a gunshot wound to her neck. She was 16. How she ended up there remains unknown.

Tioni’s killing shocked many in Los Angeles, but it outraged LA’s Black community. In the weeks following her death, there were repeated calls for a swift investigation, for compassion from local leaders, and tangible measures to curb the violence. Black women and girls make up about four percent of the population in the LA region, but represent an outsized share of female homicide victims.

Local and state leaders said they heard their calls. They put together a $115,000 reward for information, and the city commissioned a report to better understand why Black women are killed more often than women of other races. But five years later, there have not been any arrests for her killing, and families, community organizers and violence prevention workers say not enough has changed to prevent future deaths.

Families and organizers want local governments and police to be more outspoken about the harms Black women and teen girls face, to study the dynamics more deeply, to fund programs that address the intersection of domestic and community violence, and to make gender-based violence a key component of the region’s general violence prevention strategy.

“We are in a climate where Black women are the most unprotected species,” Kincy said. “We’re not looked at as human. Even our own men don’t feel the need to protect, and it’s scary, it’s sad and disheartening.”

At the same time, some of the root causes of this violence, including misogyny and long-held stereotypes about Black women and girls, can’t be legislated or policed away. So Black women in LA are doing it themselves, using taskforces, rallies, summer programs and podcasts to share their stories. Doing this, they say, can grow the number of people who are looking out for them – which is particularly important right now after the Trump administration cut millions in federal funds for gun violence prevention.

“It feels like people just don’t care,” said Ken’Niyia, 15. “It feels like Black women are not seen as something that should be protected.”

Ken’Niyia, a 15-year-old track-and-field athlete who sports two long french braids, lives in Inglewood, one of several Black- and brown-majority cities in LA county. Over the summer, she enrolled in a program that gave teen girls a place to connect with each other, share their experiences and learn about systemic racism, gender-based violence, rape culture, and the myriad ways generations of Black women have overcome them.

The program has given the girls the rare opportunity to talk about their shared experiences of feeling unsafe in their neighborhoods, and understanding the ways stereotypes about Black women and girls influence their lives, they said.

“We talk about things that are important to know when you’re a teen trying to navigate life,” said 17-year-old Laniyah. “It gives us Black girls a chance to be vulnerable with each other.”

The girls say they’re regularly followed by men in cars and on the streets while they walk home, to school or the store. They’ve witnessed shootings and lost loved ones to gunshot wounds. They’ve heard stories of girls their age being killed on the streets and in domestic violence incidents.

“Even if it’s not happening to me specifically, just to know that it is happening makes me feel unsure,” Ken’Niyia said.

In addition to not feeling safe, several of the girls said they felt left behind, or that the rest of the city was judging them. “It feels like anything that happens to us, Black women in Los Angeles, is our fault,” said Dalila, 17.

There have been several shootings outside Dalila’s home, including one two years ago, when her cousin was shot in the mouth. The cousin survived.

All of these girls live in the areas that have long seen an outsized share of the city’s violence and systemic neglect, where people live on meager incomes and access to grocery stores and thriving business corridors are scant.

Living here puts girls like Dalila at a higher risk of violence compared to their peers of other races and income brackets. And when they are harmed, Dalila said, they don’t get the same compassion white women do.

“People say, ‘She lived in South Central. She’s a product of her environment,’” she said.

The workshops the girls attended were organized by the Women’s Leadership Project (WLP), a nonprofit that offers mentorship to teen girls and queer youth and educates local high-schoolers on gender-based violence and the social issues that contribute to it.

Though the organization was founded 15 years before Tioni’s death, her short life has galvanized the group, said its director, Sikivu Hutchinson. “I don’t like to say [Tioni’s] a symbol, but she is unfortunately representative of so many things. It’s really just symptomatic of the lack of protection, lack of harm reduction, and the lack of prevention and care,” Hutchinson said.

WLP has been pressuring local officials to focus on the violence Black women and girls face in their schools, homes and neighborhoods. The group is calling for the creation of a youth center in Tioni’s name that would give young people in South Central a safe place to hang out, do homework, and take classes.

“In South Central, we see boarded-up buildings, vacant lots, pot shops and liquor stores, but no youth spaces. All of that is a symptom of the disinvestment in the so-called inner city,” Hutchinson said. “We want all of those resources and services in our community because of the high rates of harm and victimization that young people are experiencing.”

The city of Los Angeles and its police department have touted strong decline in overall homicides in recent years, but domestic violence killings, which overwhelmingly claim the lives of women, have remained a persistent issue. In 2022, LA recorded 392 homicides, according to LAPD’s annual homicide report, but by 2024 that number had declined to 284. The number of domestic killings remained consistent, though, with 32 murders in 2022 and 33 in 2024. Black women are disproportionately the victims of domestic homicides. Black women make up about 13.5% of the city’s female population, but a third of its female domestic homicide victims.

This trend also extends to the rest of the county. Black women had the highest homicide rate of any racial group in 2024, according to California department of health data. The only other demographics with high rates are Black and Latino men, who historically have made up most of the region’s homicide victims.

It’s not just LA. Black women across the US have long had a higher risk of being killed than women of other races, according to a 2024 analysis of homicide data by the Violence policy center. That year about 700 Black women and about 1500 white women were killed by men. Black women make up 13% of the US female population, white women make up 55%. Black women were most often killed with a gun, by a man they knew.

The city of LA says it’s working to address the high rates of violence by bolstering its response network for domestic violence victims, and by funding programs that can prevent gun violence in the neighborhoods where Black women and girls die most frequently.

The office of the mayor, Karen Bass, pointed to investments the city has made in its nearly 20-year-old gang reduction and youth development (GRYD) program, which operates programs throughout the city, including South Central. Though GRYD is mostly geared toward pulling Black and Latino men and teens out of the cycle of violence, staff also refers families to supportive programs. The program has helped bring down homicides in the city’s hardest-hit neighborhoods throughout South Central by almost 30% in 2025, the mayor’s office said.

California has tried to address the issue at a state level, when in 2023 lawmakers created the Ebony Alert, a first-in-the-nation emergency notification system specifically geared towards finding missing Black women and girls. Since the alert became law in 2024, it has been activated for 182 people. Of those, 175 have been found alive, one was found deceased, according to California highway patrol data.

Still, the racial and gender disparities in victims of violence remain.

Some cities and states have come up with frameworks to address the issue with more fervor. Minnesota created a taskforce made up of elected officials, nonprofit leaders and representatives from law enforcement agencies to specifically look into the killings and disappearances of Black women and girls. The group advises the state’s department of public safety on ways to reduce violence against them, and how to work with service providers to give tailored support to Black victims’ families and domestic violence survivors.

The Minnesota taskforce was in part created in memory of Brittany Clardy, an 18-year-old who was murdered in 2013. Clardy’s family reported her missing after she left to go to a nearby store but then stopped answering calls and texts. She was found dead in her car two weeks later.

The man who ultimately pleaded guilty to her murder was also convicted of murdering another woman, 24-year-old Klaressa Cook, who was found dead in the trunk of a car just months after Clardy.

In the years following Clardy’s killing, her sister, Lakeisha Lee, spoke in front of the state legislature and started a foundation to help support girls who are at risk of being sex-trafficked.

It’s not uncommon for these kinds of efforts to be spurred by people who’ve lost a mother, daughter or sister to violence, said Dr Brittany Lewis, founder and CEO of Research in Action.

“This happens because families endure going to committee hearings to convince people that the death of their family member matters,” she said. “And that what they need is much bigger than the band-aid solutions we’re producing.”

Not only do Black women and girls face disproportionate rates of violence, but when they’re killed, their cases are less likely to be solved. In 2022, the Los Angeles police department solved all killings of Black female victims. But the next year, that rate declined to 90%. In 2024, it plummeted to 67% and in 2025, at a time when the number of homicides in the city was plummeting, just half of the killings of Black women and girls were solved, according to the LAPD’s annual homicide reports.

Shalissa Collier, whose daughter Mikeona Johnson was found dead in the trunk of her car in Los Angeles in September 2020, was determined to beat this trend.

After Mikeona’s death, Collier learned that she had long been abused by a former partner and that her daughter had filed for three separate restraining orders against the man.

Collier says she brought these findings to Los Angeles police, but six months later they came to her home to tell her that the department didn’t have any leads and would be closing the case, Collier said. “LAPD pissed me off. I can’t even sugarcoat it,” she recalled.

Collier began organizing candlelight vigils and press conferences in front of the LA county’s district attorney’s office. She also spoke with independent journalists and on the podcast Misogynoir Murders, which highlights the stories of missing and murdered Black women.

In February 2024, the roommate of Johnson and her partner, Phillip Charles Howze, went to police with new information, and Howze was arrested. He was convicted of second-degree murder and sentenced to 15 years to life.

With her daughter’s killer sentenced, Collier in October was finally ready to bury her daughter’s ashes, and she held a burial ceremony.

“I felt like it would be fitting to do it, especially after he got his time. Now she can finally rest,” Collier said.

Misogynoir Murders started out as an attempt to center the stories of Black women and girls in the true-crime genre. Now, host Ronnetta Rideout says she sees it as a community service for the families that want to keep the stories of their daughters, sisters and mothers alive.

“[Black women] were still very underrepresented even in stories, even though we’re overrepresented in the actual data,” Rideout said.

LAPD declined to respond to questions about its initial decision to close Mikeona Johnson’s case. When asked about the department’s approach to solving the homicides of Black women and girls specifically, public information officer Jeff Lee said LAPD “takes all acts of violence seriously, and every homicide is thoroughly investigated. Detectives follow all available leads and work to identify those responsible, leaving no stone unturned in the pursuit of justice.”

He did not offer specifics on whether or not the recommendations from the 2023 city report have been implemented within the department.

California highway patrol said it is still actively investigating Tioni Theus’s murder.

While Tioni’s family awaits answers from law enforcement, they say members of the South Los Angeles community, too, have a role in preventing violence against Black women and girls, whether it’s reporting underage girls on sex-trafficking corridors to police or supportive services, calling out predators who are grooming teens online, or sharing information that can lead to an arrest.

“I feel like as a community we can’t be silent any more,” Kincy said. “We can’t wait for politicians, lawmakers or even the police. We have to stand up and make people accountable.”

Michael Dolphin, Tioni’s great-uncle, agreed. “This is not a white folks problem, it’s not an LAPD problem, it’s not a Mayor [Karen] Bass problem. It’s a community problem, because someone knows what happened,” he said.

He wants the city to pour resources into programs that can rehabilitate young people who have been repeatedly arrested or are currently incarcerated. These investments, he hopes, can stop teen boys from becoming violent.

“We need to figure out ways to catch these kids earlier,” he said. “We need to figure out how to get involved sooner and provide alternatives to hanging out on the street.”

Dolphin remembers his niece as a smart, loving teenager. He saw her often in the mornings, on her way to school, when she would come by to visit her great-grandmother, whom Dolphin was caring for. They would share breakfast and go over her homework together. “She liked her schoolwork,” he said. “And big mama’s house was a quiet, peaceful refuge for her.”

Kincy says she hopes that the story of her bubbly, sometimes clumsy teen cousin who walked on her tiptoes can lead to greater awareness around the increased risk of violence and exploitation Black teen girls and young women face and shed light on stories that received less news coverage than Tioni’s.

“When Tioni’s story hit, it resonated with people because it happened to their kid as well and they didn’t get the exposure,” Kincy said. “We can bring light to these stories through her.”

Jensen Huang reportedly had close relationship ‌with Chinese businesswoman accused of passing information to ‌Beijing. Plus, tennis legend Billie Jean King tells all

Don’t already get First Thing in your inbox? Sign up here

Good morning. Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, has been placed under “independent investigation” by the tech company after reports emerged he had been “the target of a foreign intelligence effort”, namely a close relationship ‌with a Chinese businesswoman who is accused of passing information to ‌Beijing. Nvidia stock is down 5% in pre-market trading as a result.

The company’s board said in a statement that while it had no reason to believe that either US national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, its inquiry would examine all available information. Republican lawmakers have expressed alarm, asking Huang to give the House foreign affairs and intelligence committees a closed-door briefing next week on Nvidia’s “security protocols against foreign adversary espionage”.

More than 90 heads of state and government, along with officials from close to 190 countries, are expected in Antalya this week for the latest round of UN climate talks. Against a backdrop of rapidly rising temperatures and extreme weather, with fractious geopolitics made worse by soaring inflation driven by the US-Israel war on Iran, the fortnight-long meeting will focus on “implementation” of the world’s targets to cut greenhouse gas emissions and help those stricken by the climate crisis.

Chris Bowen, Australia’s climate and energy minister and president of negotiations for Cop31, which his country is co-hosting with Turkey, told the Guardian: “We need a tangible outcome … that people can see is real. We need progress, it needs to be a step forward on previous Cops.”

The Guardian will have extensive coverage of the Cop31 conference, including a daily live blog, and these explainers on what is at stake and what the talks can achieve, and who the key players are. Find all of our Cop31 coverage here.

Donald Trump set the stage this weekend to push his administration further right, claiming the US took a “giant step back” after voters widely rejected his party. Despite Republicans losing both chambers of Congress in Tuesday’s midterms – with voters repudiating key policies from sweeping tariffs to the war with Iran – the administration appears set to double down.

Yet Trump struck a contradictory note on immigration. Speaking on Sunday, he admitted his deportation policy was “too tough” and politically damaging, offering to negotiate a deal with Democrats to let some undocumented immigrants remain. That olive branch, however, clashed directly with his decision to elevate Stephen Miller, the architect of the crackdown, to White House chief of staff.

What are Democrats planning to do with control of Congress? While party leaders say their exact strategy remains under discussion, all signs point to the Democrats embarking on aggressive campaigns of both investigating and lawmaking. “We made a promise to the country that we would fight for an affordable America, and we intend to keep it,” said Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to become speaker of the House.

Why are the midterms results a threat to Pete Hegseth? Jeffries said he strongly supports impeaching the defense secretary, saying Hegseth “has abused his power, undermined our national security, and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran. Pete Hegseth has got to go.” The departing Kentucky Republican representative Thomas Massie has moved to revive his impeachment effort against Hegseth.

A gunman suspected of killing six people and injuring 16 others in a market square in Kraków, Poland, has died in hospital, police said on Monday. The suspect, a 24-year-old who authorities said was probably inspired by far-right ideologies, had been in a critical condition after being wounded in a shootout with police. Polish prosecutors opened a terrorism investigation after the man opened fire on Saturday afternoon in an attack that shocked the country.

Israel’s former military chief Gadi Eisenkot has started the tough task of forming a government, reaching out to Benjamin Netanyahu’s allies and saying the long-serving prime minister had brought the country to a historic crisis. Eisenkot, 66, formally received a mandate from Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, who gave him 28 days to form a government despite his bloc lacking a majority.

Kyle Larson has joined Nascar’s all-time greats with his third Cup title in six years. The 34-year-old becomes the first repeat champion since 2010.

Donald Trump has said he was “only kidding” about making UFC’s Dana White his next press secretary.

Pope Leo has delivered a stinging critique of the Argentinian president Javier Milei’s austerity measures in a speech met with rapturous applause in Buenos Aires.

Godzilla Minus Zero has taken the US box office by storm in its opening weekend. The foreign-language film topped the box office in the US and Canada with $31.6m in takings.

A pianist for a Royal Caribbean cruise ship is expected to survive after two fishers discovered him treading water in the Pacific Ocean nearly 20 miles offshore. The unidentified man was taken to hospital after the rescue, according to the US Coast Guard, which is investigating how he went overboard. Authorities believe the man may have been in the ocean for approximately nine hours.

Lucy Knight interviews the tennis legend who is as competitive as ever in her ninth decade, and discusses sexuality, tenacity and what it was like to finally graduate from college this year.

In a war driven by drones and battlefield sensors, access to space is essential. After Starlink speed restrictions and Russian Oreshnik missile strikes, Kyiv is racing to develop its own space capabilities. Senior international correspondent Peter Beaumont reports.

Heat is accumulating in Earth’s systems at an accelerating rate, the UN’s weather agency has reported, with 2026 on track to be one of the four warmest years on record. The imbalance between incoming energy from the sun and energy leaving Earth reached its highest level since monitoring began, which will supercharge extreme weather events, such as heatwaves, droughts and tropical cyclones.

Nasa has launched a callout for a new generation of astronauts as it searches for explorers who could live and work on the moon. If you fancy it, applications are due by 3 December. Good luck!

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Parents and teachers decry Google pledge to yank Search if schools block AI: ‘This threat is nothing but extortion’
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Maya Yang
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Company says schools should control student AI use, but if they block its AI tools, they’ll lose access to search engine

Parents and teachers across the US are criticizing Google’s announcement that schools choosing to block AI tools could also lose access to Google Search.

Google announced last week a range of new AI tools for schools and classrooms, alongside options allowing teachers and administrators to restrict their use. The company said schools should have control over whether students use AI in the classroom, but that schools that choose to block Google’s AI tools will also lose access to its search engine.

“We believe schools should have control over AI in their classrooms and in providing administrators with controls to help them manage their approach,” said Chris Phillips, vice-president for education at Google. “After listening to schools, teachers, leading researchers, and policymakers, we are now updating our approach to controls for Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom, and Google Search. Access to these products will be entirely off for K-12 student accounts until school administrators explicitly turn them on.”

Parents and teachers across the country raised concerns to the Guardian about AI’s potential to weaken students’ critical-thinking skills and the growing influence of big tech in education.

Some called on schools to consider alternative search engines, while others argued that students should be taught how to use AI responsibly rather than prevented from accessing it altogether.

Jen Atay, a 51-year-old teacher in Hawaii, lambasted Google’s approach, saying: “When the software is free, you are the product, and it is inappropriate for Google to test or develop AI with minors. This should not be allowed at all.”

A 44-year-old father of two boys in Amissville, Virginia, said he worries that “AI will weaken people’s ability to think critically. I use AI in my work, but it would not be effective if I did not have well over a decade of experience under my belt. Even the best models are often flat-out wrong in their responses.”

“These tools are not something that should be introduced to children at such a young age. I’m hopeful that a Democratic Congress will force the adoption of legislation that will protect our schools from corporate malfeasance such as this. This threat from Google is nothing but extortion and it should be treated as such,” he added.

Similarly, Eyla Whitemoon, a mother and educator based in Kernville, California, said: “By infiltrating or ‘partnering’ with our institutions, Google and Meta et al, created a false dependency and our starved public education system happily merged with their ilk. And just like any good mob boss, drug dealer or capitalist minion, these companies got society hooked on their products and now are raising the cost of their supply … My heart aches for what our children won’t experience in a future where AI is in charge and the mega technoautocrats sit in their bunkers and hide.”

Meanwhile, a 64-year-old educator based in Ann Arbor, Michigan, said: “Thankfully, after having to revamp all teaching in response to AI, Gen Z has begun appreciating what they stand to lose on account of surrendering their cognitive skills to AI. There are alternative search engines to Google and those will now be what we turn to. Teachers and students alike detest the tech industry’s demand that we kiss their feet and give ourselves up to be their peons.”

Others questioned why schools should depend on Google at all.

An 84-year-old retiree and mother in Maryland, said: “Google decided to follow the evil path to riches. When they started, they were great. Today they are simply evil money grubbers … Schools should tell Google to go pound sand and simply have kids use DuckDuckGo or one of the other search engines … There is nothing Google offers that is not available from some other source.”

Rachel Dominguez, a 42-year-old parent in Minneapolis, Minnesota, also suggested that schools turn to academic databases instead of relying on Google Search.

“Seeing as how Google Search has turned into an AI slop-first service, maybe it’s better that the kids learn how to use databases such as Academic Search Premier, JSTOR, and arXiv. Most school districts have subscriptions to these services, and students learning to use them would be better prepared for college. A trip to the media center is not some abnormal chore … That is, if the librarian still has a job in the first place,” she said.

Not everyone believes blocking AI is the answer. Some argued that schools should focus on teaching students how to use the technology responsibly.

A 67-year-old emerging technology teacher in Texas said: “I do not blame Google. AI is not going away. I’ve been very frustrated this year trying to teach AI literacy with AI blocked. Schools need to teach how to properly use AI, not block it.”

A California resident echoed that view, arguing that schools could use Google’s AI tools to teach students to question the information they receive.

“Google Search has existed since the 90s and it’s crazy of them to completely remove it instead of just removing Gemini. That being said, I would like to see schools actually permit the use of Gemini and use it as an opportunity to show students how its sources aren’t always valid and you can’t trust everything an AI tells you,” they said.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: ‘A complete repudiation’: public health won big in US midterm elections
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Melody Schreiber
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Election wins of Annie Andrews, Abdul El-Sayed and more who ran on healthcare issues are viewed as sign of home as Trump administration unravels US health policy

Public health leaders and politicians who made healthcare a central part of their platforms swept into office in the US midterm elections last week, setting the stage for national, state and local changes.

Voters, faced with an unprecedented rise in vaccine-preventable diseases such as measles, alongside devastating outbreaks of foodborne illnesses, chose national candidates who prioritized public health, healthcare affordability, reproductive health and the impeachment of Robert F Kennedy Jr, among other key issues.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

“The American people are speaking out against President Trump and the policies that he’s been rolling out since the day he took office,” said Julie Scofield, a member of the coordinating committee at the grassroots organization Defend Public Health. “I think it’s a complete repudiation.”

Mallory Harris, a scientist in Austin, almost delayed having children because she was worried about accessing life-saving healthcare, such as vaccines and abortion, if she needed it. She had doctors check her immunity against viruses including measles, and sought assurances from her physicians that she would have access to appropriate care. Harris found out she was pregnant just as 2026 officially became the worst year for measles in the US since before she was born. Texas has no paid time off for maternity or paternity leave, but Harris and her husband will try to wait until the baby is six months old and can get the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) shot early before starting daycare.

Dealing with public health emergencies like these have been “a top issue” for her as a voter. After the election, “it suddenly became a lot less scary”, Harris said. “We’ve seen scientists and physicians getting elected in record numbers. We saw big shifts in places that have had measles outbreaks.”

Democrats flipped state houses and legislatures in several states, and these leadership changes will dramatically reshape actions on abortion, gender-affirming care, vaccines and more, experts say. Several of the candidates successfully argued that cuts to Medicaid, Affordable Care Act subsidies, and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (Snap) have wounded America, and rising prices – especially in healthcare – are a big concern.

In Texas, attorney general Ken Paxton investigated pediatricians for giving vaccines; sued providers, even in other states, for mailing abortion pills; and declared that gender-affirming care for minors qualifies as child abuse. His successor has already announced he will be dropping several lawsuits like these.

In Georgia, the home of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), Keisha Lance Bottoms is now the first Black woman ever elected governor of a US state. As the mayor of Atlanta, Bottoms clashed with Brian Kemp, Georgia’s Republican governor, on public health measures for the Covid pandemic. Jasmine Clark, a microbiologist also from Georgia, will serve in the US House. Jon Ossoff, who won re-election to the Senate, concluded his victory speech by guaranteeing “healthcare for every single American”.

Amy Acton, governor-elect of Ohio, and Abdul El-Sayed, senator-elect from Michigan, were public health leaders in the Covid response – which their opponents unsuccessfully tried to use against them.

Annie Andrews will be the first pediatrician in the US Senate, and she campaigned on impeaching Kennedy, who is the health and human services secretary, and pushed for improving vaccination rates after measles tore through her home state of South Carolina.

Richard Pan, a pediatrician who served as a state senator in California and will now serve in the US House, led the creation of a state law eliminating religious and personal exemptions to vaccination – and he sparred with Kennedy over the change. Kennedy later apologized for calling vaccines a “holocaust”.

Amish Shah, an emergency medicine doctor, flipped a US House seat in Arizona after campaigning on improving public health, among other issues. Adam Hamawy, a surgeon from New Jersey, won a US House seat by focusing in part on affordable healthcare.

“There were more candidates running in this midterm election from a public health perspective and background that made this part of their platforms and part of the issues they were talking about,” Scofield said. “I think that’s extraordinary.”

Voters in several states also rejected proposed restrictions on abortion, and Virginia passed a constitutional amendment to enshrine marriage equality and reproductive rights.

Several Democratic candidates faced anti-trans ads from their opponents.

“The results show that those ads backfired,” Scofield said. “Anti-trans attacks didn’t work.”

Candidates including Andrews and James Talarico in Texas changed their public support for gender-affirming care, which was disappointing to see, she said: “No doubt we have educating to do.” Organizations such as Defend Public Health will continue to “stand solidly and squarely behind our transgender community and full access to gender-affirming care”, she added. “That is just a non-starter for us.”

Anti-trans initiatives in states including Washington and Colorado appear to have passed, though Democratic leaders in those states have already begun questioning whether they are constitutional.

“It’s super important for people to remember that a lot of public health authority rests with the states,” Scofield said. While Congress plays an important role in setting policies and providing funding to state and local public health agencies, many public health decisions happen at the state and local level, she said.

On the federal level, it is likely Congress will take action around restoring cuts to Medicaid and Snap, addressing the premium tax credits, and making sure funds are deployed appropriately by agencies such as the CDC and the National Institutes of Health (NIH), Scofield said. Many of the administration’s actions on gutting research and dismantling agencies were illegal, acting outside of Congress, she said.

Trump administration officials including Jay Bhattacharya, head of the NIH, and Kennedy have frequently positioned themselves in opposition to what they describe as government overreach on Covid measures and vaccines.

“Voters were willing to turn out for candidates who supported public health,” Harris said. That goes “directly” against what these health officials appear to have interpreted as their mandate, she said. After the election, she added, “a lot of things are going to change quickly, and also there’s real damage that’s been done and real risk that remains.”

Tuesday’s results have reassured people like Harris who have had to confront more preventable disease outbreaks and more restrictions on abortion and other forms of healthcare than the US has had in decades.

“It has meant a lot to see people getting elected who have spoken about these fears and address them head on,” Harris said. “It’s really important to have leadership who cares about you and your family.”
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: Voters chose candidates who prioritized public health, healthcare affordability, reproductive health and the impeachment of Robert F Kennedy Jr. Many of the administration's actions on gutting research and dismantling agencies were illegal, says Scofield.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Economic relief is on the way, Democrats say. But what, how and when?
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Heather Timmons in Washington
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Winning candidates promised to cut costs, rein in corporations, curb billionaire power and improve the economy

Don’t worry, cash-strapped Americans, “relief is on the way”, the senator Chuck Schumer promised last week in a press conference celebrating Democrats’ massive midterms win.

Winning candidates promised to cut food and healthcare costs, rein in corporations ripping off consumers and workers, curb billionaire power and make the world’s biggest economy better serve the working class.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

There’s broad agreement on those lofty goals and on some short-term steps. But the big win is bringing decades-old battles to the fore, about how the US federal government should fund safety nets and check healthcare and food costs.

The “lame duck” period between an election and a new Congress’s swearing-in in early January is often a frenzy of behind-the-scenes battles and public posturing as corporate lobbyists, thinktanks, voter groups and big donors try to influence the agenda.

This time, it’s all that on steroids.

Already, JB Pritzker, the Illinois governor, has issued a 75-page list of 200 policy proposals for Congress’s “day one agenda”; Columbia professor Tim Wu is pushing an “affordability bill”; Texas’s new senator James Talarico is promising universal healthcare for all; there’s an 181-page investigation memo circulating; and moderate Democrats are arguing for more incremental steps.

Meanwhile, Trump’s power to veto bills means anything the president doesn’t like will need a clutch of Republicans to pass, making things more complicated. Expect a mix of affordability bills the president will back, like curbs on private equity and credit card interest rates, and ones he will veto, which Democrats will use for anti-Republican political messaging.

Most voters want Congress to protect social security, raise wages and lower the costs of basic necessities, healthcare and family care, a recent Equal Rights Advocates Action Fund survey found, echoing many others.

Their support for anyone in office is conditional.

“Everyone’s on notice now. This is probation and not a mandate,” Carrie Joy Grimes, the founder of WorkMoney, a non-profit that advocates for lower costs and higher wages for US workers, said of Tuesday’s election results. “People have not suddenly become Democrats. People are very clear that they want something different.”

Grimes said she’s telling the group’s millions of members: “It’s incumbent on everyday people to take what just happened and keep thumping on both parties.”

Here’s the concrete areas where Congress is planning to respond:

Schumer and other Democrats have pledged to end the Iran war, which has pushed up heating oil and other costs, and to end Trump’s tariffs, which cost the average household $1,110 this year.

They should move immediately, insists Chris Van Hollen, a Maryland senator who is exploring a 2028 presidential bid. “Democrats should not advance spending to continue to fund this war” by refusing to vote for a continuing resolution that expires in mid-December, he told the Lever. “The Vietnam war ended only when Congress defunded it,” he added.

The path for ending Trump’s tariffs is unclear; he and his cabinet have ignored links to high costs. But some congressional Republicans are now criticizing them, making the two-thirds majority needed to pass a bill without Trump a possibility.

Earlier this year, Democrats, including the Vermont senator Peter Welch, introduced a bill to end tariffs on Canadian goods that was blocked by Republicans. In the new Congress, it’s headed to the White House, Welch told CBC: “We can’t force the president to sign the legislation we put on his desk, but we can pass it in good faith.”

Democrats have promised to immediately roll back the cuts to subsidies in the Affordable Care Act and the work requirements to Medicaid that were part of the $1tn in Medicaid cuts in Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Passing those changes will have to be negotiated with Trump or Republicans, and could come as part of a bigger spending package.

Many Democrats, including Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed and South Carolina’s Annie Andrews, ran on pledges to upend an expensive, ineffective healthcare system that leaves millions with crushing medical debt and are pushing universal healthcare.

Again, the what and how are still unclear. New York’s Alexandria Ocasio Cortez will head a House “working group” on healthcare that will figure out what to do next, Jeffries said Wednesday in response to questions. “We’ll be having conversations as a House Democratic family,” he said.

On the Senate side, the Help committee (health, education, labor and pensions), chaired by Vermont’s Bernie Sanders, is expected to take a lead role. He’s already calling for a Medicare for All plan, and immediately for lowering the Medicare age to 55 and adding vision and dental care.

Expect revivals of the Patients Before Monopolies Act, a bipartisan bill that promises to break up big healthcare conglomerates, and bills to curb private equity’s healthcare acquisitions.

Republican states including Arkansas and Tennessee have already passed laws banning companies from owning pharmacies and pharmacy benefit managers. David Joyner, the CEO of CVS Health, said Wednesday that the monopolies bill was a reason the company decided to break up.

Voters are concerned about the high cost of living, but also about Trump administration corruption and foreign policy chaos, Democrats say. They hope to tie that all together.

Likely House leader Hakeem Jeffries set up five “affordability working groups” in 2026 on issues including grocery and gas prices and childcare. He’s asked House members to try to link every investigation they do back to one of these affordability issues.

Already, sitting Congress Democrats sent out “target” letters to oil companies, airlines, tech companies, banks, grocery stores and others asking about their practices that have made life more difficult or expensive for the American consumer. They’re making plans to grill CEOs in public hearings about algorithmic pricing, executive compensation and skyrocketing corporate profits, before introducing bills to change corporate behavior.

Democrats will scrutinize “the extent to which corporations engaged with the Trump administration”, said Ronak D Desai, who heads the congressional investigations practice for the global law firm Paul Hastings. They’ll be looking for evidence that companies helped Trump or his allies in unethical ways, and then seek to tie that to affordability, he said.

Many of these target letters are not yet public, but there are public clues as to how these links could work. Maryland’s Jamie Raskin last week asked the White House to provide details about tariff carveouts for Apple and other companies that gave Trump lavish gifts, for example.

The Trump administration has fired or pushed out hundreds of workers at agencies that regulate air, water and consumer safety.

Congress can’t order them to be reinstated, but it is likely to investigate the firings and their effects on consumers’ health, safety and pocketbooks in public hearings that put budget chief Russ Vought and other Trump officials in a spotlight.

Senator Elizabeth Warren, who will run the Senate banking committee in January, created the Consumer Finance Protection Bureau after the housing meltdown of 2008 to protect consumers from financial scams. The agency’s funding has been slashed, and orders punishing companies for mistreating consumers were scrapped.

“Congress will investigate both the Trump administration’s efforts to dismantle the CFPB and whether companies previously subject to enforcement were now the beneficiary of any sweetheart deal,” Desai predicted.

Right now, Congress should swing for the fences, some say. Democrats need to take on “the corporate power that has hollowed out the American dream”, said Joe Van Wye, senior adviser on public policy and legislation at Washington law firm Cuneo Gilbert Flannery and LaDuca.

“I don’t think nibbling around the edges, only passing bills Trump is going to pass, is going to cut it,” Van Wye said.
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: Democrats are trying to link every investigation they do back to one of these affordability issues. They're making plans to grill CEOs in public hearings about algorithmic pricing, executive compensation and skyrocketing corporate profits.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Time to fight back: five leading thinkers on what Democrats should do post-midterms
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Robert Reich, Wajahat Ali, Katie Phang, Judd Legum and Charles Blow
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Democrats have taken control of Congress in a sweeping blue wave – now the real work begins

Welcome to a special edition of How We Win, a Guardian opinion series with leading thinkers, offering bold ideas for America’s political future. Sign up here to receive future editions in your inbox.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

Democrats should use their mandate to be Democrats again. That means taking on concentrated wealth and economic power – the oligarchy – with a wealth tax on multimillionaires and billionaires. Campaign finance reforms to get big money out of our democracy. Labor law reforms to make it easier for workers to form unions and harder for employers to fire them for doing so. And tough new anti-monopoly laws to give government authority to bust up concentrations of economic power, especially in tech.

– Robert Reich, former US secretary of labor and a Guardian US columnist

The majority of voters repudiated the corrupt, racist Republican party that made life unaffordable and committed crimes with impunity. To keep people from their pitchforks, Democrats need to use this singular power for transformation, not restoration. Preach and practice affordability and accountability. (Talking to you, Hakeem Jeffries.)

We’re not going to just move forward, hold hands and get along. We have to vanquish the Maga spirit to ensure the ghost of the Confederacy can no longer haunt and terrorize our country.

First, Democrats should unleash hell in the name of justice. This means investigations of the Jeffrey Epstein class, Elon Musk, Pete Hegseth, Jared Kushner, Robert F Kennedy Jr and Stephen Miller. Second, Democrats must end the trade wars and the failed, disastrous war in Iran while not getting outflanked by Republicans in rejecting Israel’s interference in our politics. Restore Affordable Care Act subsidies and reverse the $1tn cuts to Medicaid. And how about Medicare for All?

– Wajahat Ali, editor of The Left Hook and co-host of The Democracy-ish Podcast

One of the most insidious aspects of Trump’s second term has been his aggressive destruction of the rule of law. Trump’s weaponization of the Department of Justice to instill fear in his political opponents has eroded the public’s trust in our system of justice.

With their clear mandate from voters, Democrats must immediately launch investigations into the actions of Trump’s former lawyer Alina Habba, former US attorney Lindsey Halligan, US attorney Jeanine Pirro and other US attorneys and federal prosecutors who furthered Trump’s intimidation campaign. US attorney general Todd Blanche, who allegedly quarterbacked several of these illegal and unethical prosecutions, should be investigated first.

After the 2021 attack on the Capitol, at least 20 million people tuned in to watch the first hearing of the January 6 select committee. Public hearings would allow Americans to witness the extent of these lawyers’ complicity in following the whims of the president to pursue vindictive indictments and prosecutions. The all-out assault on the rule of law by Trump and his justice department must be stopped. It should be a top priority for the Democrats as they begin the 120th Congress.

– Katie Phang, independent journalist, trial lawyer and political analyst

The most crucial issue for 2026 voters was not grocery prices, or the Iran war or immigration. It was corruption. And that’s exactly the issue Democrats should start on when they gain control of Congress in January.

Sign up to How We Win

Bernie Sanders, Robert Reich, Stacey Abrams, Mehdi Hasan, Paul Krugman and other bold thinkers on how to defeat Trumpism and build a better future. From our opinion desk.

after newsletter promotion

The first order of business should be to pass a law banning all members of Congress and the president from trading individual stocks. (Trump has made more than 25,000 individual stock trades since returning to the White House.) Such a bill should pass with overwhelming – and potentially veto-proof – bipartisan support. What better way for Democrats to begin their majority than to deliver real reform on an issue of importance to voters?

Next, subpoena Jared Kushner. Trump’s son-in-law is a top US negotiator on every key foreign policy issue while reportedly remaining on the dole of foreign governments. It’s one of the biggest corruption scandals in history. Kushner claims he is a volunteer, not a government official. That makes it difficult for him to assert executive privilege.

– Judd Legum, founder and author of Popular Information

First, I would caution Democrats not to consider this victory a mandate, but rather an assignment. Voters were repulsed by Trump and his actions, but they were not writing Democrats a blank check. They want accountability for corruption and affirmative action toward greater equality and economic relief.

However, the “blue wave” delivered neither a filibuster-proof nor a veto-proof majority in Congress. The goal now is to keep expectations aligned with actual opportunity and ability.

– Charles Blow, author, political analyst and contributing writer to the Guardian

Follow them on Substack and elsewhere: Stacey Abrams, Robert Reich, Paul Krugman, Naomi Klein, Mehdi Hasan, Bernie Sanders, Rebecca Solnit, Katie Phang, Judd Legum, Wajahat Ali, Margaret Sullivan, and Charles Blow.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Trump is humiliated and angry – and Europe is where he’s free to lash out | Nathalie Tocci
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Nathalie Tocci
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
The US president sees Europeans as the mirror image of his ‘woke’ domestic foes. They should brace for further betrayal this winter

E
uropeans have greeted the blue wave that crashed down on Donald Trump and his Republican party with jubilation and relief. Jubilation, because Trump’s second presidential administration has been the most destructive in the history of the transatlantic relationship. His disdain for Europe and his evident delight in attacking its governments – in particular that of Ukraine – have been hard to swallow.

Relief, because the midterm election results confirm that Europeans are not unique in being appalled by Trump’s actions: a large majority of Americans are too. I was in Washington immediately after the vote, and the mood was one of excitement and a newfound confidence. And like many Americans, in these results Europeans see hope that US democracy can be saved, American foreign policy moderated and the transatlantic partnership revived.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

They are both right and wrong. Despite recent backsliding, democracy is alive and kicking in the US. The Democratic party, which for a long time seemed stunned and paralysed by Trump’s return to the White House, is bubbling with fresh energy and ideas. Its claim to be a big tent is no longer an abstract ideal but a reality, with a remarkable array of diverse and charismatic figures shining through – from the Christian progressive James Talarico in Texas to the democratic socialist Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, who will be the first Muslim in the US Senate, and Georgia’s moderate Jon Ossoff.

The political power of a big tent is a lesson European liberals and progressives should heed, as many European countries head into crucial elections in the coming months facing strong headwinds from the far right.

The resounding defeat of Trump’s agenda – and in particular Americans’ stark rejection of the war on Iran, acknowledged explicitly by JD Vance and implicitly by Trump himself – could also lead Washington to soften its stance in the Middle East. Before the US midterms (and elections in Israel), the region had seemed set on a ladder of escalation; the Republicans’ drubbing could now force Trump to climb down. That will be good news if it happens. And European leaders, though largely sidelined, should do their utmost to encourage de-escalation by backing the diplomatic outreach of Gulf states such as Qatar.

But Europeans would be badly mistaken to think this mellowing will extend to US policy towards Europe and the war in Ukraine. Regarding Europe, the lesson Trump is likely to draw from the midterms is that his mistake – if he can bring himself to conceive of making any – was not being Trumpy enough, not lashing out hard enough at the continent’s liberal democracies.

After all, while Trump’s Maga base is sceptical of the Iran war, it applauds the normalisation of ties with Moscow and the withdrawal of support for Kyiv, and would be happy to see a more decisive US military disengagement from Europe. Trump’s decision to promote Stephen Miller to chief of staff points in that direction. While Miller has not played a prominent role on Ukraine so far, he is among the foremost proponents of the Maga worldview that might makes right. In the European context, this predatory approach often translates in the belief that Russia will (and therefore should) prevail. Over the past two years, Trump has humiliated and insulted Europeans, imposed punitive tariffs on them and threatened Greenland. In fairness, though, the US military disengagement from Europe and Nato has so far been limited.

Hemmed in on his Middle East adventurism, and having achieved most of what was within reach in Latin America – from the toppling of Venezuelan dictator Nicolás Maduro to a string of rightwing electoral victories across the region, blunted only by Lula’s unexpected comeback in Brazil – Trump is left with Europe to lash out at. It would be surprising if he didn’t. While little can be expected from the resumption of Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi, Europeans should brace for dirty tricks from the Trump-Putin-Xi Jinping trio, which may meet at the Apec summit in Shenzhen later this month, and from a Trump-hosted G20 in Miami in December. And it would be surprising not to see a further, uncoordinated US military pullback from Europe.

Trump and Maga have always seen Europe as the mirror image of their domestic foes: a bunch of presumptuous, woke, emasculated liberals. Now that those foes have made a comeback at home, Trump’s rancour towards Europe is likely to grow.

To imagine that the worst is over and that the transatlantic partnership will settle back to the good old days would be more than wrong. It would be delusional. The midterms may mark the beginning of the end for Trump, putting the US on track for a Democratic victory in the 2028 presidential election. But that road is long and strewn with obstacles. And even if a Democrat victory is achieved and the two sides of the Atlantic seek to pick up the pieces of their broken relationship, what they rebuild will look quite different. For a start, the US’s betrayal of Europe over the past two years can’t be quickly forgotten, but also the new class of Democrats emerging from this election lacks the commitment to Europe held by older generations.

Sign up to This is Europe

The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment

after newsletter promotion

The transatlantic relationship can and will be rebuilt. But it will be narrower, more interest-based and less sentimental. Europeans should not look to the US midterms for a past to be revived. The time for transatlantic nostalgia is over.

Nathalie Tocci is a professor of practice at the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies, Europe, and a senior fellow at Bocconi University’s Institute for European Policymaking
