https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Diversity, decency and a new south: who were the real winners in the US midterms? |
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Robert Reich
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Tuesday was a victory for equity and inclusivity and a rejection of hate and fear. The biggest losers? Megadonors and Super Pacs

R
ather than regurgitate the particular wins and losses that occurred on Tuesday, I thought it more useful, at this point, to look at the big picture and identify the largest overall winners and losers for the country as a whole.

Biggest winner: a diverse, equitable and inclusive America. It’s Donald Trump’s DEI nightmare. Georgia voters elected Keisha Lance Bottoms, the first Black female governor in the country. Texas chose Gina Hinojosa, the state’s first Latina governor and first Democratic governor in more than 30 years. California elected Xavier Becerra, the state’s first Latino governor. New Mexico chose Deb Haaland, the country’s first female Native American governor. Florida elected Byron Donalds, the first Black governor in Florida’s history (a Republican).

Not signed in before? Create a free account

For the US Senate, New Hampshire chose Chris Pappas, that chamber’s first out gay member. Minnesotans picked Peggy Flanagan, the first Native American woman elected to the Senate. Michiganders chose Abdul El-Sayed, the first Muslim elected to the Senate.

These are remarkable wins. Some are attributable to a surge in voting by Black people, many of whom were understandably incensed at efforts to push Black representatives out of Congress through overt racial gerrymandering. And by Latinos, enraged at ICE’s wanton arrests and detentions. Women upset by Republican efforts to outlaw abortion in their states. And LGBTQ+ people, angry about the blatant bigotry of Trump and his Republican enablers.

But many straight white men and women also disagree with Trump’s narrow definition of America. It turns out that the nation is far more diverse, equitable and inclusive than Trump or his Republican enablers want (or believe) it to be. They tried to make us fear and hate one another over our many differences. They indubitably failed.

Another winner: the new south. For as long as anyone can remember, the states that comprised the Old Confederacy have been regressive, conservative, intolerant and, at least since the Civil Rights Act of 1964, Republican.

No longer. On Tuesday, three of the four most populous southern states (Texas, North Carolina and Georgia) voted for Democrats up and down their tickets. Texas Democrats carried every statewide office from governor through lieutenant governor, attorney general, and even railroad commissioner. North Carolina and Georgia Democrats also scored stunning victories.

The biggest surprise was Annie Andrews’ win over Darline Graham in South Carolina’s Senate contest. As I write this, another possible gobsmacker: the Democrat Scott Colom may actually win the Mississippi Senate seat held by the Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith.

Even Democratic losers in the south came remarkably close to winning: the Democratic Senate candidate Jamie Davis was within a hair’s breadth of victory in Louisiana. Florida’s Angie Nixon almost won the Senate seat there.

What accounts for this new south? Partly a large and growing professional class (in metro Atlanta, North Carolina’s “research triangle”, and Houston, Dallas, Fort Worth and Austin) combined with an increasing flow of young workers and their families from other states, seeking more affordable housing. Add to this, an abundance of Latino and Asian immigrants. All told, the new south is more tolerant than the old. Much of it is also more more educated.

A third winner: decency. During the run-up to the 2026 midterms, American voters were inundated with Republican attack ads, inflamed rhetoric, and personal smears against Democratic rivals. Those efforts backfired. Americans soundly rejected the politics of hate and fear, and embraced common decency.

Trump, JD Vance and RFK Jr did their worst to fuel Islamophobia against Michigan’s Dr El-Sayed. Trump claimed if El-Sayed won, he’d “invite hordes of jihadis to our shores”. RFK Jr baselessly linked El-Sayed to the Muslim Brotherhood. Their fear-mongering obviously didn’t work.

Vance suggested that the Texas Democratic senatorial candidate James Talarico is gay. Another backfire.

Ohioans were so turned off by the Trump-endorsed billionaire Vivek Ramaswamy’s attack ad against his Democratic opponent Dr Amy Acton – using Acton’s mother, whom Acton hadn’t seen since she was 12, when her stepfather was accused of raping her – that the ad may have helped fuel Acton’s win, making her the first Democrat to win Ohio’s governorship since 2006. (Trump thought the ad was just fine, and Vance even blasted fellow Republicans who spoke out against the ad, calling their criticism “disgusting” and telling them to “stop whining” because “politics is a tough business.”)

Since Trump came on the scene, many Republicans have eagerly imitated his scurrilous character assaults. Such smears have become so common that we tend to forget that most Americans don’t particularly like this form of politics. They prefer Barack Obama’s tempered rhetoric and the late John McCain’s dignified and respectful way of disagreeing. Now, after the 2026 midterms, perhaps decency is back.

So who were the biggest losers? Besides Trump and his Republican sycophants, the biggest losers are the mega donors and Super Pacs that poured record amounts of money into failed Republican candidacies.

Top awards for strategic stupidity go to the crypto industry (which tried unsuccessfully to derail Democrat Sherrod Brown in Ohio); Aipac (which did everything it could to block El-Sayed and prevent any mention of Israel’s genocide in Gaza); the AI industry, which spent loads of cash trying but failing to allay voter’s concerns about datacenters; and Elon Musk, who sought, singlehandedly, to save Ken Paxton’s doomed Senate campaign in Texas.

Musk deserves his own special place in the loser’s circle. The richest person in the world became the poster child in the 2026 midterms for billionaire greed, legalized bribery, and corporate welfare. He sunk almost a half billion dollars into failed Republican campaigns, the most that any single human being has ever spent on elections – and for naught. After Tuesday’s blowout, shares in Musk’s SpaceX and Tesla dropped off a cliff.

Once they’re in control of Congress, Democrats will want to know what personal data and information Musk might have obtained when he ran his ill-fated “department of government efficiency”; what, exactly, happened with Ukraine’s Starlink access; and why the US government should continue to grant him an effective monopoly on satellites anyway rather than nationalize Starlink. To say Musk will be on the hot seat understates the temperature where he’ll be sitting.

In sum, considering the overall winners and losers from the 2026 midterms, I’d say America came out way ahead.

Robert Reich, a former US secretary of labor, is a professor of public policy emeritus at the University of California, Berkeley. He is a Guardian US columnist and his newsletter is at robertreich.substack.com. His new book, Coming Up Short: A Memoir of My America, is out now in the US and in the UK

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Anti-AI populism is the future of American politics | Garrison Lovely
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Garrison Lovely
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Democrats should drag Sam Altman, Dario Amodei and Elon Musk before the world and make them explain just what it is they’re trying to do and why

The AI industry had a bad night last week.

The Democrats’ sweeping midterms victory is a rebuke of Donald Trump, the industry’s most powerful champion.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

Almost everywhere they could, voters rejected datacenters: moratoriums and other restrictions passed in more than 30 localities across nine states. And, with wins in places such as Texas, Ohio and Georgia, an estimated 41% of planned datacenter capacity is in states with governors-elect backing moratoriums.

To be sure, the election results were not primarily about AI. In 2024, Trump ran on lowering prices and starting no new wars, then began a war that raised prices. While corruption, the cost of living, Iran and immigration were seen as more important to people’s votes in NBC exit polls, AI and datacenters were cited by 23% of voters as “crucial” in their decision, and Democrats won these voters 67% to 30%.

AI will become the defining political fight of the 2028 cycle. The future of US politics will belong to whoever voters believe will bring the industry to heel.

AI industrialists, in their telling, are racing to build job-destroying machines that might also destroy us. Anthropic’s CEO, Dario Amodei, writes that “AI isn’t a substitute for specific human jobs but rather a general labor substitute for humans”.

And OpenAI’s CEO, Sam Altman, infamously said, “AI will probably, most likely, sort of lead to the end of the world, but in the meantime there will be great companies.” They built their machines on “the largest theft of labor in human history”, as one Microsoft executive put it.

Could you script better villains?

And in recent years, no issue has grown more in salience than AI. Local organizing around the country drove an explosion of opposition to AI datacenters. Following a summer full of rogue AI hacking incidents and prominent warnings from AI developers, AI extinction fears have gone mainstream.

Hacks and cyber-attacks, driven by AI, have recently spiked and will get much worse. And all the backlash we’ve seen to date emerged in a period of 4% unemployment. As signs of widespread labor automation grow, we’ll find that we’re nowhere close to the ceiling of anti-AI sentiment.

The industry will be hard to tame, but the political upside of doing so is enormous – and it’s anyone’s game. When NBC asked which party would be better on AI, 30% of voters named Democrats and 27% named Republicans, with 43% saying neither. The savvier Republicans realize this and are already making the case for a post-midterm break with Silicon Valley.

Indeed, coziness with the industry trying to replace us with machines was a political liability for Republicans on Tuesday. Trump, following advice from billionaire venture capitalists like David Sacks and Marc Andreessen, has taken a “let it rip” approach to AI.

Tech executive donations got them prime seating in the Capitol rotunda during Trump’s inauguration, and no industry has donated more to his ballroom. This summer, the president declared in a social media post: “The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor.”

And at the industry’s behest, almost every House Republican voted for a provision in Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act to override state AI regulations with no federal replacement – an unprecedented move. (Senate Republicans wisely voted to strip the measure.)

All this and more was fodder for Democratic attack ads, with more than 130 federal and gubernatorial races mentioning tech accountability or AI (only two Democratic-aligned ads between 2020 and 2024 mentioned big tech).

To get more than a one-cycle bump, Democrats actually have to deliver on the accountability Republicans failed to provide. And Trump won’t be on the ticket in 2028, but the AI industry isn’t term-limited.

Whoever can most convincingly run against Altman, Amodei, Elon Musk, Jensen Huang and Mark Zuckerberg will gain far more politically than they’ll lose in foregone Super PAC contributions, the limits of which were also on display on Tuesday.

The only competitive race the main AI industry Super Pac spent big in resulted in a loss to Democrat Annie Andrews in South Carolina, who ran on “protecting kids, not big tech”. Musk’s record-breaking spending of nearly half a billion dollars flopped: Republicans lost every one of the five Senate races he spent the most on.

All this argues against a return to Democrats’ Obama-era chumminess with Silicon Valley. Tuesday night clearly demonstrated that economic populism is the most potent force in American politics – and it’s incompatible with a friendly relationship with corporations that have already grown far too powerful.

Thankfully, those worried about AI’s dangers have more – and more empowered – champions than ever. Democratic leadership and key incoming committee chairs have signaled that AI will be one of their top priorities. And the party’s left flank is going further.

A weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our lives

after newsletter promotion

Texas Democrat Greg Casar, a former labor organizer and the chair of the Congressional Progressive caucus, declared: “AI will be the number one issue in 2028.” Casar has co-sponsored a bill with the Vermont senator Bernie Sanders that would pause AI development until a federal cabinet-level agency is in place and ban artificial super-intelligence outright.

In his 60 Minutes interview, the Michigan senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed called for a “full-on pause” on frontier AI development and also said he was making AI his number one issue. In his victory speech, the senator-elect Troy Jackson of Maine said: “We are not that far from Terminator, and I don’t want to be ‘hasta la vista, baby.’”

Republican senators with competitive races or White House ambitions will want to differentiate themselves from their party, creating opportunities for Democrats to pick up the votes needed to get over the 60-vote filibuster threshold. And some Republicans, like Missouri’s Josh Hawley, have been leaders on drafting robust AI-regulation bills. Trump, as he’s reminded us, could always use his veto power, but he’s signaled a surprising openness to working with Democrats.

To mitigate the harms from AI and deliver on their affordability mandate, Democrats should pass popular pro-worker legislation and dare Trump to veto it. Some ideas: ban surveillance pricing and “bossware”, make it easier for workers to unionize (and organize across sectors), and create strict liability for AI developers.

Democrats need to get creative in shifting the incentive structures for companies from labor replacement to worker augmentation. Legislation should strengthen workers’ ability to make wage theft claims if their work is used to train AI models that lead to layoffs or reduction of hours.

And if the AI you develop and use does what would be criminal if a human did it, as AI agents from OpenAI and Anthropic have, you should be criminally liable.

I’ve previously argued here and in my new book, Obsolete, that we urgently need to stop the race to build universal labor-replacing machines (what the industry calls artificial general intelligence).

That requires more political will than we currently have. In my view, if the public really understood what the industry was trying to do, we would shut down further development immediately.

Congressional hearings can compel the sharing of important non-public information under oath. This summer, Casar asked AI companies difficult questions about the spate of criminal hacking incidents they have been responsible for but got incomplete and misleading answers in return.

Now, Democrats will be able to back future inquiries with subpoena power – something the senator Ed Markey reminded big tech executives of: “They are going to need to plant new forests for all of the subpoenas we’ll be printing.”

Congressional hearings can also create a spectacle around something that is technically public, but not widely known, like the industry’s holy grail. AI companies are explicitly planning to fully replace their researchers with AI systems that can train smarter generations, hoping to kick off an explosion in AI capabilities that results in systems that are superhuman at basically everything.

Seems risky? Don’t worry, they’re planning to fully automate AI safety research too. If you talk to the people leading this work, they’ll admit it’s a terrible plan – they just can’t think of a better one.

Democrats should drag Altman, Amodei and Musk before the world and make them explain just what it is they’re trying to do and why they’re doing it without our consent. It will also be a chance for Democrats to show whose interests they’ll put first: the public or the billionaires trying to replace us with machines.

Garrison Lovely is a freelance journalist and the author of Obsolete: The AI Industry’s Trillion-Dollar Race to Replace Us – And How to Stop It

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: We can’t just ‘move on’: Democrats must hold Trump accountable | Jan-Werner Müller
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Jan-Werner Müller
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
The new Congress cannot maintain the culture of political impunity that got us here in the first place

Fresh from an overwhelming victory, Democrats might quickly divide over what should be seen as unnecessary fracture.

Establishment figures demand a focus on “kitchen table issues”, while others insist that successful candidates did not just campaign on the cost of living, but managed to connect people’s daily struggles with the unprecedented corruption of the Trump administration.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

Indeed, Democrats have a mandate to enforce accountability. And it is imperative not to treat accountability as some kind of abstract moral question; even the most hard-headed politicians have to understand that the inability to deal with crimes and misdemeanors now will come back to haunt them – and, in fact, the nation as a whole.

Kamala Harris counseled that Democrats should concentrate on “commonsense legislation”, since the votes for impeachment simply are not there; Barack Obama has – as always – called for politicians to bring the country together.

As wise as this advice might sound, they would amount to continuing what the writer Richard Beck has called our “impunity culture”. Richard Nixon was forced to resign, but then promptly pardoned by his successor; Ronald Reagan’s Iran-Contra shenanigans never had any real consequences; after Abu Ghraib, Obama urged us to move on.

We moved on – and eventually found ourselves with Donald Trump, whose whole experience in life, business and politics has been one long morality tale about how elite figures get away with it. He has also made it a basic principle of his approach to governing that impunity can be exchanged for loyalty: after all, his underlings believe that he will pardon them before 20 January 2029.

What has happened more than once is likely to happen again. If Democrats do not find ways of holding Trumpists accountable, the message to present and future politicians will be: there are never consequences. This will also provide an incentive for those fearing the law to enter politics.

What’s more, the repercussions of impunity for Trumpists are not confined to the US: for any other government ever to trust an American administration again, there would have to be globally visible accountability, as well as a comprehensive cultural distancing from Trumpism.

Concretely: no triumphal arch or statues, golden or not, can remain standing; no foreign visitors should ever land at airports named after a president who both inspired and oversaw hitherto unknown levels of corruption (as well as cruelty).

And in the short run? Democrats can force both administration officials and associated oligarchs to testify under oath. Of particular interest would be figures who claim to be civilians, but de facto exercise state power: think Jared Kushner.

And, of course, Elon Musk. As the political scientist Dan Moynihan has pointed out, it is absurd that Elon Musk has appeared more often on Saturday Night Live than in front of Congress to talk about Doge; the country needs answers about what his vandals did in 2025, whether they stole and weaponized data, and how exactly his companies remain untangled with the American state – creating a kind of dependency on one person that, as Ukraine discovered already, is incompatible with any kind of responsible governance.

As in the last years of the first Trump administration, those called to testify might simply ignore the invitation to the Hill. Democrats can go to court, and they will win, but all that takes time.

The policy scholar Norm Ornstein has suggested the Capitol police should simply capture recalcitrant individuals and hold them at the Capitol. That is legally possible and even has precedents; but it is unlikely to happen (though it would also provide a symbolic closure of the period that began with Maga hordes assaulting Congress on 6 January 2021).

Direct legal consequences are also unlikely, as long as the Department of Justice sees itself as merely an extension of the president’s will. Many lawyers have left; the sycophants who replaced them are often unqualified, and, in any case, unwilling to do anything about rampant corruption and criminality.

That leaves impeachment. While the votes might not be there in the Senate, Democrats could start to go after the most egregious cabinet members – Hegseth and Robert F Kennedy Jr might compete for the top of the list.

Impeachment has a political purpose – it is meant to prevent further damage to the Republic – but it can also serve a pedagogical function. It shows citizens the evidence for crimes and misdemeanors, and that evidence, carefully assembled, can then eventually also be helpful to a Department of Justice that has regained its integrity.

If nothing else, the country, just like societies emerging from authoritarianism elsewhere in the world, will need a precise record of what happened, for a sense of closure, if nothing else.

Republicans will cry “weaponization” – again. But that simply shows that they are unwilling to entertain any limits on the behavior of their leader and what must be called his extended mafia state.

And, who knows, some Republican senators might jump ship when confronted with the question of whether they still support a secretary of defense, who has done enormous damage to US military power.

Self-declared moderates among the Democrats will say that precious political capital and public attention should not be squandered on issues which have no impact on people’s day-to-day lives.

But this profoundly underestimates citizens’ desire for justice; it also fails to see that, with a large majority in the House, one can do more than one thing. As Raphael Warnock keeps reminding his party, one can walk and chew gum at the same time.

Jan-Werner Müller is a Guardian US columnist and a professor of politics at Princeton University

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Today’s AI won’t achieve superintelligence. But catastrophic risk is real | Sunita Verma
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Sunita Verma
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
The same technical limits that prevent superintelligence make these systems dangerous. But we know how to regulate them

Many Silicon Valley leaders believe superintelligence is an imminent threat to society. The White House even published an accord about it. This isn’t enough.

Geoffrey Hinton, the godfather of AI, estimates the risk of human extinction is at least 10% within the next few decades. The Anthropic CEO, Dario Amodei, argued that unchecked AI “could outrun our ability to understand and control these systems”. In response, 1,300 leaders and employees from many leading AI companies signed a letter calling to “deliberately pace” development.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

Public unrest grew this summer after a series of cyberattacks by “rogue” OpenAI agents broke out of a contained environment and hacked the software company Hugging Face. Two months later, the Australian government disclosed another OpenAI agent attack had broken into the government’s health portal, stealing private health data.

To reassure the public, Jensen Huang, the chief executive of Nvidia, said on CBS that there was a “zero percent” chance AI could end humanity by 2030.

Huang is right to challenge the “doomsday narratives” about human extinction. But I believe there are real risks large language models (LLMs) pose, even if narratives of them scaling into superintelligent terminators are technically implausible.

I spent almost 20 years at Google building and working with AI and machine learning. I now lead technology development at Ironclad, helping businesses apply AI to manage their contracts.

From where I sit, even if LLMs will not scale to superintelligent machines, that does not mean this technology poses zero risk. The same technical limits preventing these machines from scaling to superintelligence make the risk of catastrophic outcomes very real.

According to OpenAI, a review of the Hugging Face attack found that the agents recognized their hack was “outside intended scope”. They pressed on anyway because they were following instructions with unintended consequences. This was likely caused by loose controls on their digital environments and very broad instructions to achieve their objectives.

These models are designed to minimize error by predicting the next piece of text during their pre-training. Models are then “tuned” to follow human instructions, getting better “rewards” the more closely they follow instructions.

How someone specifies the instructions to the model can “influence” the pathways the model will take to fulfill the instructions. That mathematical reward shapes how it solves problems.

Once it commits to an approach, it keeps refining step-by-step, with no built-in incentive to ask whether the whole direction has reached a dead end. If a hack is discovered, the machine is designed to exploit it, not explore an alternative approach.

While newer “reasoning” models will review their own steps, this isn’t the same as recognizing a flawed approach and abandoning it completely. Even Hinton has said that their main concern is “to achieve whatever goal you give them” – even if that means behaving dangerously.

That is an architectural design and limitation. Scaling these models will not give them the human propensity to pause, re-evaluate, and then try an alternative approach. An agent that excels in a trial has proved that it can execute code, not that it can judge.

The real world brings edge cases, ambiguous instructions, and endless ways to complete a task. Regulations change, software updates ship, and markets shift every day. Today’s models learn once up front and then stop. A system trained on yesterday’s conditions does not automatically understand today’s.

Even if every change could be recorded and fed to a model, it would need to learn and connect it to everything it already knows. Richard Sutton, a reinforcement learning pioneer, made a similar argument: the world is too big and changes too fast to be learned in advance.

Needing human judgment limits a large language model’s likelihood of significantly surpassing human intelligence. But that same ceiling does not contain its capabilities to solve difficult problems. Last month, OpenAI announced that a swarm of 10,000 concurrent agents collectively resolved a variant of the Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness problem, a major mathematical challenge, in 88 hours.

None of this diminishes what these models do well; I see the value of that daily. But it challenges the belief that scaling today’s architectures leads to superintelligence and questions whether that conversation is the dialogue worth having.

It’s important to note that no one yet fully understands, in rigorous mathematical terms, why today’s models behave the way they do, and the research that would explain it, known as interpretability, is still nascent.

Recognizing our limited understanding doesn’t excuse responsibility. It underscores why impartial governance is needed. How can we trust a company’s safety certification if it cannot explain how the technology works?

What we’ve seen is that this technology poses a societal risk, much like hazardous materials. Its misuse can cause catastrophic damage. And it’s not the materials or technology consciously determining the havoc they wreak, it’s their makers and handlers who do so intentionally or unintentionally.

There needs to be systems in place for governing these types of risks. For example, when a plane crashes, the National Transportation Safety Board, not the manufacturer or the airline, investigates, and its findings shape how every airline flies. The focus remains on the technology’s design, maintenance and procedure.

Instead of debating the possibility of superintelligence or malicious intent, we need to focus our discussion on the immediate shape of oversight for these models, perhaps by leveraging existing frameworks.

Sunita Verma is CTO of Ironclad and a former Google executive who spent her career building AI systems

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.title: Trump’s pathetic Dana White gambit could not mask his midterm humiliation | Howard Bryant
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.author: Howard Bryant
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.text:
Trump has long relied on sports to project strength and fuel his culture wars. But after a crushing midterm defeat, even his UFC ally cannot distract from the political fallout

I
n the wake of being destroyed in the midterm elections, it was only a matter of time before Donald Trump did something outrageous in an attempt to misdirect public attention away from his catastrophic losses. Before the midterms, published reports suggested the possibility of apocalypse, global or domestic – a nuclear strike on Iran, martial law to suspend last week’s, the invalidation of individual races, such as in Alaska – but Trump opted for banality over Armageddon, offering his vacant press secretary opening to Ultimate Fighting Championship CEO Dana White.

It was absurd, and widely posited that a confused Trump had erroneously conflated UFC’s White with the Dana White who made more sense, former Heritage Foundation staffer Dana White. Because the public reactions made him look even more lost, confirming the sentiments of recklessness and disorder, utter chaos and buffoonery that led to the Republicans being routed in the midterm elections, the president said his offer to White was all a joke. As a disciple of the notorious McCarthyite Roy Cohn, who taught Trump one of his main political pillars – never apologize or admit wrongdoing. Ever. – Trump should not, of course, be taken at his word.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

Either by mixing up the female PR professional Dana White with the UFC ringleader and having to backtrack regardless, Trump’s bluster has at last been pierced by last week’s mandate that a larger segment of the electorate is no longer charmed by his garrulousness, or energized by his ugly charisma. The downward spiral has begun. His press secretary job is vacant because his last choice, Katie Zacharia, lasted less than a week. Failure can only mean that Trump will intensify his worst instincts and play the hits that have always worked, in the arenas with the most eyeballs.

One of those arenas has always been sports, and thus it tracks that, joke or not, he would use White to wring another bit of life out of a news cycle. When Trump has needed headlines or kindling, he has turned to sports. He used the public’s always bizarre adulation and resentment toward Black athletes a decade ago by attacking Colin Kaepernick and the NFL, and sports has stood at the center of his culture wars ever since. He and his justice department have pivoted from the NFL to the NBA, waded into MLB by trying to turn Pride Night into an anti-Christian grievance. The WNBA now lives in his crosshairs.

Trump has always relied on sports to bail him out. In trying to appeal to the machismo of his base and give America’s 250th birthday a performative sheen of strength, Trump held a UFC cage match on the White House South Lawn earlier this June – an event that was highlighted by one of White’s fighters racially insulting former first lady Michelle Obama. Given the Black community’s animosity toward him but the number of high-profile Black athletes who support him – Lawrence Taylor, Mike Tyson, Darryl Strawberry, Herschel Walker, among many others – sports have provided a cover for his racism.

Trump relied on sports giving him the real-man boost and muscularity he always craves, but this time the gambit failed. The whole thing looked pathetic. He looked confused and like he did not know what he was talking about, and there was no way out. The professional White publicly announced she was not a candidate. Trump looked befuddled, and employed another of Cohn’s teachings – always stay on the offensive, and increase the attack – by telling reporters Sunday that UFC’s White “loved the idea”, and that “You wouldn’t mess around with him.”

None of it resonated. What did resonate was a tired America rejecting him in places Republicans had not lost in decades, and in one case, Kansas, in nearly a century. He and his party were repudiated so comprehensively that even to the people who used to laugh, the jokes aren’t funny anymore, and for once, even the distracting, celebrity power of sports couldn’t inflate what is a sagging tent.

Howard Bryant is the author of 11 books, including Full Dissidence: Notes from an Uneven Playing Field, and Kings and Pawns: Jackie Robinson and Paul Robeson in America. He also writes on Substack

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.title: Bears edge Bucs with game-winning field goal despite Caleb Williams’s sloppy night
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.author: Associated Press
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.text:
Chicago QB throws career-high four interceptions

Mayfield leads Tampa Bay rally that falls short

Caleb Williams and the Chicago Bears played one of their worst games of the season – and won.

That last part was the only thing that mattered to them Sunday night.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

Williams found Colston Loveland for a 38-yard reception that set up Cairo Santos’s 38-yard field goal as time expired, and the host Bears picked up a sloppy 27-24 victory over Baker Mayfield and the Tampa Bay Buccaneers at Soldier Field.

Chicago (7-2) committed five turnovers, including a career-high four interceptions by Williams. But he delivered after Mayfield rallied the Buccaneers in the final minutes.

“I don’t get gun shy. That’s not me. That’s not my identity,” Williams said. “And with that, I’m going to keep ripping it and keep ripping it.”

With Chicago facing a second-and-nine from their own 46 in the final minute, Williams passed to a wide-open Loveland at the Tampa Bay 35. The tight end ran down the sideline before he was pushed out of bounds at the 16.

After two kneel-downs by Williams, Santos delighted the crowd of 60,470 by drilling his second field goal of the night.

It was Chicago’s first win with five-plus turnovers since a 23-13 victory over the Minnesota Vikings on 3 December 2006.

“It’s hard to win with five turnovers and yet we found a way to do it,” Bears coach Ben Johnson said. “They know that we didn’t play as well as we’re capable of playing but I believe the best is yet to come in terms of our football in the back half of the season. So we’ll continue to build that as we go forward.”

Chicago had a 24-16 lead when Luther Burden fumbled on a helmet-to-helmet hit by Tampa Bay rookie Rueben Bain Jr. Bucs defensive back Ifeatu Melifonwu returned the ball to the Bears 17.

Bucky Irving had an 11-yard carry before going in from the 6 for his second touchdown of the game. Mayfield scrambled for the two-point conversion, tying it at 24 with 2:51 left. Mayfield was 18 for 32 for 243 yards and two interceptions. Irving finished with 97 yards on 20 carries.

Mayfield failed to complete a pass in Tampa Bay’s previous game, a 16-0 win over Atlanta in wet conditions. The Buccaneers (3-6) rushed for a franchise-record 324 yards in the victory over the Falcons, including 170 by Irving.

Williams was 22 for 37 for 279 yards and two touchdowns in Chicago’s fourth straight win. Burden had seven catches for 97 yards before he was shelved by a concussion. Jeffery Simmons had a sack in his first home game since he was acquired in a trade with Tennessee.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.title: Joe Burrow is reviving the Bengals and pulling away in the race for MVP
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.author: Doug Farrar
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.text:
The quarterback has led Cincinnati to four straight wins with stat lines that put him in the company of Tom Brady. At this rate, the trophy seems his to lose

A
t the end of the 2021 season, the Cincinnati Bengals came up three points short in Super Bowl LVI against the Los Angeles Rams. Near the end of the 2022 season, the Bengals came up three points short – a 23-20 score line again in the AFC championship game against the Kansas City Chiefs. But from 2023 through 2025, those Bengals had to walk the desert for a while. Between injuries to quarterback Joe Burrow, an offensive line that was problematic at best, and one of the NFL’s worst defenses from year to year, Cincinnati had a combined regular-season record of 24-27, and no playoff appearances.

Now, the new Bengals are 6-2 after their 34-17 shellacking of the Atlanta Falcons on Sunday at the Santiago Bernabéu stadium in Madrid. And Burrow is on a tear we’ve rarely seen from any quarterback. Over the last four weeks, his 16 touchdown passes is the most in a four-game span in Bengals history (which goes back to 1968). He is the second quarterback in pro football history with 16 or more passing touchdowns and two or more rushing touchdowns in any four-game span, putting him up with Tom Brady in 2007 – the season in which the New England Patriots’ offense scored 36.8 points per game, and Brady was at his best. Burrow has been pressured on just 30.2% of his dropbacks this season, as opposed to 33.8% in 2025 and 34.2% in 2024.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

When healthy, Burrow is as good as any quarterback you’ll see. At this moment, he’s better. Against a Falcons team ranked fifth in pass defense DVOA entering Sunday, Burrow completed 24 of 29 passes for 271 yards, three touchdowns, no interceptions and a passer rating of 140.1. The Falcons had no answers against Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins, Burrow’s dynamic receiver duo, and unlike in previous seasons, Cincinnati’s defense is prepared to … if not match the offense’s efforts, at least hold things up. The Bengals are average on defense, but when you have an offense like this, that’s good enough. The only time anyone was able to dim Burrow’s brightness was when the Bernabéu lights briefly went out in the fourth quarter.

Add in the fact that Cincinnati’s run game is nothing to write home about (their 3.87 yards per carry and minus-0.13 EPA per run are each among the league’s worst), and it’s clear that as much as any NFL player, Burrow will be required to take his team as far as they can go. That’s good news for the Bengals, because Burrow has traveled to the realms of the near-unstoppable.

Burrow has never won the NFL MVP award. (He came in fourth in both 2022 and 2024 when Patrick Mahomes and Josh Allen won it, respectively.) But at this rate, the trophy seems his to lose.

Since Burrow is the MVP of the season’s first half, how about Myles Garrett for Week 9? The Rams’ edge rusher had been out since Week 1 of the 2026 season with a knee injury, and in his return to action, per Pro Football Focus, he recorded three sacks, nine total pressures and a forced fumble in LA’s 20-13 win over the Washington Commanders. Garrett, of course, was supposed to be the centerpiece of the Rams’ dream team following a blockbuster trade with the Cleveland Browns, and his presence was desperately needed for a franchise that was just trying to get above .500 on the season. Garrett did his level best for the now 5-4 Rams, and it wasn’t just that the sacks happened, it was when they happened.

Garrett’s first sack came with 2:20 left in the first half and the Commanders up 10-3. That was the forced fumble, recovered by linebacker Omar Speights. That led to a Rams drive that ended with a field goal at the end of the half. The second and third sacks came in the fourth quarter as the Rams were trying to hold their 20-13 lead.

The Rams are no longer in that dream team conversation, but maybe they can at least ride the wave to a playoff berth. If Puka Nacua can stay healthy, that is. Nacua, the Rams’ top receiver, caught 14 passes on 19 targets for 150 yards and a touchdown in the win, but also suffered a knee injury that may keep him out for a while.

Nico Collins of the Houston Texans is easily one of the NFL’s best X-iso receivers, which means that he can line up against the opponent’s best cornerback in one-on-one situations, and what would usually be a 50-50 contested catch turns into 90-10 in Collins’ favor because of his skillset. Collins made that abundantly clear with 8:16 left in the third quarter of Houston’s 44-22 win over the beleaguered 0-8 Los Angeles Chargers.

In this case, cornerback Tarheeb Still was the unfortunate victim of Collins’ rare gifts. Texans quarterback CJ Stroud threw to Collins, but Still seemed to have this ball at least deflected, if not outright intercepted. Until Collins somehow one-handed the catch to Still’s right side, and that was that. Collins caught four passes on four targets for 55 yards and a touchdown, and the touchdown was certainly the catch of the day.

Runner-up: The corgi race during halftime of the Denver Broncos’ 26-21 win over the Carolina Panthers at Bank of America Stadium in Charlotte, North Carolina, took an interesting turn, as Lennox the Corgi went rogue from the vertical race path and decided instead to become a canine Barry Sanders. By our estimation, Lennox evaded seven attempted tackles, and even stopped to ask his pursuers at one point, “Are we playing or what?”

With such lateral juice, contact balance, and swagger, Lennox could have a bright future ahead of him.

86-2. With 26 seconds left in the first half of the New York Giants’ 19-11 win over the Philadelphia Eagles, Philly punter Braden Mann booted the ball from his own eight-yard line to the New York six-yard line. That was an 86-yard punt, which tied for the seventh-longest in pro football history.

However … with 6:53 left in the game, Mann fumbled the center snap, and had a punt of minus-two yards. It is, of course, the only time in a game that a punter had one punt of more than 80 yards and another with negative yardage. Mann also had punts of 63, 62, 60, 54, 44 and 17 yards, so you could say that he painted with every color in the palette.

The Kansas City Chiefs have kicker issues nobody would want, and they’re attempting to solve them in ways that nobody should want. Andy Reid’s team did beat the New York Jets 35-12 on Sunday, but kicker Harrison Butker’s woes continued. Since the start of the 2025 season, nobody has missed more kicks (field goals and points after touchdown) than Butker’s 17, and the additional spice to that story is of course Butker’s political beliefs. During a now-infamous commencement speech at Benedictine College in 2024, Butker went for Maga bingo, criticizing then-President Biden, the “tyranny” of diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI), Pride Month and women who wish to work outside the home.

Recently, the Chiefs signed another kicker to insulate themselves from Butker’s on-field mistakes – former Baltimore Raven Justin Tucker. Tucker was once one of the best kickers in the history of the game, but his talents fell off until he was released in May 2025. The obvious reason for Tucker’s release was the more than a dozen wellness and massage therapists who accused Tucker of inappropriate sexual behavior. Tucker never faced criminal charges for the allegations, which he denied, but the NFL slapped him with a 10-game suspension for violating the league’s personal conduct policy.

It is unknown as to why Reid and his staff would align themselves with two sub-par kickers with such pasts, but it is what it is. As for Butker’s future following a game in which he missed a 56-yard field goal attempt, and missed the 51-yard mulligan he got when the Jets were busted for defensive offside, Reid had this to say:

“I’m sure I’ll be asked about Butker. I’ll address that as we go throughout the week. I’ll look at everything, and no need to ask. That’ll be the answer that you get. I’m not making any decisions right now.”

All in all, a rough week for those who may share Butker’s beliefs.

The 6-2 Jacksonville Jaguars may well be the NFL’s most dangerous team right now. Last Thursday, they beat the Baltimore Ravens 33-10, and with that, they now lead the NFL in point differential (+108) and turnover differential (+9). And if Joe Burrow isn’t the NFL MVP front-runner right now, it’s only because Jags quarterback Trevor Lawrence is. Lawrence has completed 146 of 224 passes this season for 1,932 yards, 18 touchdowns, four interceptions, and a passer rating of 111.7 – the NFL’s best going into the Sunday slate. Jacksonville have more on the ball in their run game, and certainly on defense, than the Bengals do. They also have the NFL’s second-easiest schedule for the remainder of the season, behind only the Houston Texans.

If you’re looking for an NFC team with the momentum to meet the Jaguars in a hypothetical Super Bowl LXI matchup, train your eyes to the 6-3 Green Bay Packers. Matt LaFleur’s team completely leveled the defending AFC champion New England Patriots in a 45-27 result that was not as close as the score indicated. Packers quarterback Jordan Love, the NFL’s most fearless deep-ball thrower this season, completed 23 of 29 passes for 372 yards, three touchdowns, no interceptions and a passer rating of 153.2. Receivers Christian Watson and Matthew Golden each went over 160 yards on the day, and each had a receiving touchdown.

But the scary thing about these Packers is a Jonathan Gannon-led defense that is one of the NFL’s best, and that defense put Patriots quarterback Drake Maye in several vices. Maye was sacked four times and threw three interceptions. Like many quarterbacks, he found it rather difficult to navigate an opponent that presents every look you can imagine – and is preparing to get Micah Parsons back from injury for the second half of the season.

If there’s one thing that could stand in the Packers’ way, it’s that the NFC North is an absolute buzzsaw. Following the 7-2 Chicago Bears’ 27-24 win over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers on Sunday night, and before the 6-1 Minnesota Vikings’ Monday night tussle with the Buffalo Bills, the NFC North is on its way to the highest winning percentage for a single division in pro football history. The 2024 NFC North (45-23) holds the top mark at .662, but the current North division is on a different planet (25-8) at .758.

The Bears didn’t always make it easy on themselves – quarterback Caleb Williams ended three of four second-quarter drives with interceptions after throwing two touchdown passes in the first quarter – but the Bears’ defense, with new acquisition Jeffery Simmons, was a monster. Until, that is, the Bucs scored 11 unanswered points in the fourth quarter to tie the game at 24-24 with 2:56 left in regulation.

But the Bears rediscovered their equilibrium on the game’s final drive, especially when the Bucs uncharacteristically blew the coverage on Williams’ 38-yard pass to tight end Colston Loveland with 47 seconds left. That set up Cairo Santos’ 38-yard game-winning field goal as time expired.

It is highly unusual for Williams to throw twice as many interceptions (four) as touchdowns (two) in a game – in fact, the 2024 first overall pick had never thrown more than three picks in a game in his NFL career. But the fact that the Bears were able to win this one anyway speaks to their completeness as a team, and their overall resilience.

Who might be on the move before Tuesday’s NFL trade deadline at 4pm ET? We’ve already seen two major deals, with guard Quenton Nelson moving from the Indianapolis Colts to the Seattle Seahawks and defensive lineman, and the aforementioned Jeffery Simmons going from the Tennessee Titans to the Chicago Bears. The 2-7 Colts appear to be in fire-sale mode, with running back Jonathan Taylor and receiver Josh Downs among those who could find new homes. Also worth watching: Jacksonville Jaguars receiver Brian Thomas Jr, who has struggled to find his place in coach Liam Coen’s offense; Titans running back Tony Pollard; and Philadelphia Eagles cornerback Riq Woolen.

https://www.theguardian.com/stage/2026/n.title: ‘Thicky thicky dumb dumb’ satirist Cody Dahler on his viral videos: ‘my material is presented to me on a silver platter!’
https://www.theguardian.com/stage/2026/n.author: Interview by Liam Pape
https://www.theguardian.com/stage/2026/n.text:
The writer and podcaster on why politics is made to seem more complicated than it is and his mission to unpack world events for everyone

Why did you get into comedy?
My mum was a professional dancer and always encouraged me to perform. Given that I have zero rhythm, comedy was my other option. She wrote me a poem called Mrs Brown’s Moggy, about a cat that was often very soggy, for my school’s talent show. Because you can’t tell the difference between real and polite laughter at the age of six, I assumed I’d killed my first gig and convinced myself I was born to do nothing else.

Where do you find your material?
In a world where Robert Jenrick claims Nigel Farage has “probably done more than almost anybody to stand against racism”, the answer is that my material is presented to me on a silver platter each morning.

When did it click that you might be on to something with your “thicky thicky dumb dumb” videos?
When Donald Trump captured the Venezuelan president, Nicolás Maduro. Up until that point I was covering four or five stories in each video. But obviously Trumpty Dumpty’s top-class diplomacy meant that people only really wanted one story breaking down for them. That was the video that really exploded online. If you look closely at the picture of the blindfolded Maduro in that US military helicopter, you can see my career taking off with him.

What can readers expect from your new book?
An attempt to help them understand why everything is so crap, written in a way that won’t make them feel like a thicky thicky dumb dumb in front of all their mates. Partly because the book answers questions that my followers sent in to me. While researching it, I was pretty shocked by how inaccessible books about British politics were. Everything seemed to be Margaret Thatcher 1973-74: The Pre Policy Years and Governed! – A Battle for the Soul of Britain’s Fiscal Policy Within the Bank of England. No disrespect to the fiscal policy nerds but I’m pretty sure even they don’t want to read that. I know from doing political videos online how interested and engaged people are about politics – it’s just that nobody is talking about it using language they actually understand.

What’s a topic you’ve found particularly difficult to explain?
I genuinely believe that things are made to sound more complicated than they are to exclude people from engaging with politics. And often to get politicians off the hook for not knowing what the hell they’re doing. So basically, my big-headed answer is once I’d waded through the academic guff that’s used to make people feel cleverer than you, most things were actually very simple to explain.

You’ve got more than two million followers online. What’s one of the strangest fan encounters you’ve had?
At the live recording of my podcast, The Truth (In My Opinion), at the Bedford pub in Balham, an audience member called Bethany came up to me to say she’d travelled from Chicago that day specifically to see the show. Given that many of my north London friends thought south London was too far for them, I thought that was pretty amazing.

Any bugbears from the world of comedy?
Oh God, absolutely – but I’d like to keep my career for now, thank you very much!

Best advice you’ve ever been given?
Make your own stuff.

Worst advice you’ve ever been given?
Say yes to everything.

What’s next for you?
Frostbite. I’ve made the mistake of basing my entire brand around wearing shorts in all weathers. Now winter and El Niño are on the way …

The State of This! is published by Blink (£16.99). To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply

https://www.theguardian.com/games/2026/n.title: Crime pays: how Grand Theft Auto became a cultural colossus
https://www.theguardian.com/games/2026/n.author: Christian Donlan
https://www.theguardian.com/games/2026/n.text:
Ever since it crashed on to PC and consoles in the late 90s, GTA has been tearing up the game-making rulebook. We explore how its cultural references, rebel spirit and sprawling sense of freedom make it a definitive work of art

I
n the 00s, when the Grand Theft Auto developer Rockstar Games revealed a new project, video game writers from all over the UK would make the journey to the company’s office in London. They would be ushered one by one into a darkened room to sit facing an enormous TV. There would be a dish of sweets on a low bench in front of them but, in the reverential hush that descended, it was never entirely clear if it was acceptable to eat them.

After a few moments, the screen would come to life. Rockstar would sometimes begin its presentation not with footage from its new game, but clips from classic movies. This is the context of what we are making, Rockstar was saying, and that is where we belong.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

Yet, what’s interesting is that the studio’s ambitions were already straining against its cinematic influences. A cowboy adventure such as Red Dead Redemption might start with curated moments from spaghetti westerns – but the game itself would be eager to evoke everything from Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid to Warlock (the 1958 revisionist Old West novel by Oakley Hall) and the paintings of Frederic Remington.

Rockstar has since grown in stature so much that its newest game, Grand Theft Auto VI, had its first in-depth reveal in a Netflix special, with the added cachet of making Netflix’s own servers shudder a little on launch day.

So many video games deserve a place in the wider culture of the age from which they came. What are the 1980s without Pac-Man and Tetris? But with the release of Grand Theft Auto VI this November, Rockstar finds itself in unprecedented territory. The numbers alone are dizzying. Grand Theft Auto V, which launched in 2013, has sold more than 230m copies, and GTA VI is said to have cost more than $1bn to make.

This is surely the biggest video game release of all time – one that has sent rival games rushing to find other street dates, and sent ripples through the rest of the media (and beyond). That raises a few questions. How did Rockstar get to this point with a game that initially explored the simple pleasures of running people over? What are the cultural touchstones ensuring GTA continues to fascinate so many people, regardless of whether they’ve ever picked up a game controller? And when it comes to art, where does GTA belong?

The first Grand Theft Auto was made by the Scottish developer DMA Design in 1997. Players would race around a series of fake US cities, stealing cars and colliding with pedestrians. The action was viewed from a top-down perspective and the tone was high-spirited, befitting a design heavily inspired by the penny victories of pinball.

Speaking to the Guardian in 2015, Paul Farley, one of the game’s designers, explained that there was no budget for a fact-finding trip to the US, and there was only one PC with internet access in the whole studio. “We’d come in on a Monday and say: ‘What movies did you watch at the weekend? What music are you listening to?’” Nonetheless, what can now be seen as the GTA experience was already starting to form. Here was a game offering freedom, a heightened sense of place, and sharp stabs of dark humour. The cars that players could steal had names such as Impaler and Mundano, reminiscent of the Culprits, Autocrats and Fiascos parked outside hotels in Martin Amis’ novel Money. Amis was already a useful reference in broader ways, too. As one online commentator said, Amis deals in “great ugliness described with surprising beauty”. That certainly sounds like GTA.

Grand Theft Auto 2 offered a polite expansion on these central ideas, but by the time of Grand Theft Auto III in 2001, the series was evolving. GTA III was the first game in the series to offer players a 3D world to explore, which meant the skyscrapers of Liberty City, based on New York, now rose overhead, while the pedestrians wandering its streets looked recognisably human, and reacted with horror as you sent them scattering.

The game was a gigantic hit, in part because of its references to films such as Goodfellas, and its promise of placing players within their own Scorsese movie. But the real thrill came from being in a world that had been so richly observed. GTA III was overwhelming.

“It’s real simple,” says Christopher Byrd, a literary critic who writes for the New Yorker and the New York Review of Books, and covers games for the New York Times. “I’d never seen an urban landscape rendered like that in a game.”

GTA III’s approach, setting crime stories in a detailed open world in which the player could go wherever they wanted, came to define the series’ 3D games – as did the cinematic influences. Grand Theft Auto: Vice City took the action to Florida and was heavily inspired by Scarface and Miami Vice, while Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas, set in a faded, sun-lasered version of southern California, borrowed from hip-hop culture and movies such as Boyz n the Hood.

This ensured that when Grand Theft Auto IV took the action back to an ersatz New York, an increasingly thoughtful tone was not the surprise it once would have been. We weren’t playing pinball any more. The game now focused on the immigrant experience of an eastern European protagonist, approaching Liberty City with a weathered eye on the American dream. It was still a game that understood the subversive thrill of stealing cars and running people over, but it was as much a response to the “war on terror” as it was to the films of Michael Mann and his contemporaries.

By GTA V, the series had become something larger and stranger. GTA V has plenty of cinematic and even literary influences, ticking off everything from The Sopranos to the likes of The Serial, that glorious skewering of so-Cal obliviousness by Cyra McFadden. But by this point, these references to other media felt like a small part of the overall proposition. The simulation elements, which had been growing since players of the first GTA got into a car and changed the radio station, were now taking over.

The city of Los Santos had convincing traffic flows and a working fire department that would respond to any accidents you might cause on your road towards riches. Outside pulling off heists, players could make a fortune on the stock market or real estate. These things are all hustles, the game seemed to suggest, so why discriminate?

The sheer breadth of the games Rockstar was making by this point was intoxicating. Talking to Game Informer in 2009, writer and producer Lazlow Jones revealed that “one of the best quotes we saw was from a reviewer who stopped at the internet cafe and surfed the spoof internet we created. They said something like, ‘I’m trying to find the bottom of this thing, and I can’t.’”

But if you’re trying to understand the appeal of a series like GTA, the criminal element is still important. As Leslie Benzies, then head of Rockstar’s Edinburgh studio, told Digital Trends in 2012: “We do not sit down for design meetings and say, ‘Let’s make the most appallingly violent game possible.’” Instead, he explained, the team is drawn to worlds in which violence is everyday life. “People know that games are no longer all about eating dots or blowing up spaceships,” he said. “They can be dark and edgy and challenging.”

This approach will never go out of style. “We’re never not going to have crime,” says Geoff Manaugh, the creator of the “architectural conjecture” website BLDGBLOG, and the author of A Burglar’s Guide to the City, a wildly good read that explores the relationship between urbanism and crime. “The minute you have a rule, someone’s going to want to break the rule.”

Sign up to Pushing Buttons

Keza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gaming

after newsletter promotion

Put like that, perhaps games like GTA are perfect for exploring criminality. “I’m only using this as an analogy, but crimes [like bank robbery] are almost like an IQ test,” Manaugh says. “In the sense that you’re presenting people with things in front of them, and then you’re asking them to connect them in a way that results in this goal.” To Manaugh, these crimes are often real games. “You are playing by the rules in a different way, and you’re solving the puzzle differently. On that level, there’s no mystery to me why games and crimes go together.”

GTA V riffed on various real-world crimes, including the work of the Hole in the Ground Gang, who drilled into a Los Angeles bank vault in 1986 before escaping underground and have never been caught. But the lurid appeal of the outlaw life still can’t entirely explain the appeal of GTA. After all, games have been violent since people shot their first Space Invader.

“The [non-gaming] public imagines that these games are nonstop kinetic affairs in which you’re always doing something, robbing someone, getting in a fight,” Byrd says. “And people who spend a great deal of time with them know that often it’s the ‘downtime’ between missions: that’s what stays with you the most. It’s the aimless driving or seeing the mountaintop and going up there and watching the sun cycle for 45 minutes. There’s a possibility of dwelling in the world that I think is unique … the Grand Theft Auto games are so stuffed with incidental details and little pieces of gameplay that you can create for yourselves. You’re just enjoying the purposeless beauty of it all.”

This is territory that GTA has marked out for itself. “The closest phenomenological experience that we’ve had before as human beings … is that moment when you leave the movie theatre and the illusion is still in your head,” Byrd says. “You just saw Tom Cruise in a film, and when you’re walking out of that movie theatre, you’re walking … as though you have your own Tom Cruise swag going on. That’s now in video games, but it’s really only this one series that’s done this.”

Manaugh is not surprised that recent GTA games seem to be all but overwhelmed by their detailed simulations of the cities in which they are set. “There are just so many overlapping things to pay attention to if you go into a city,” he says. “They are just constantly laminating different types of opportunities [on] top one another … They’re lands of fecundity and promise.”

In other words, GTA may be making the case that the city is now an artistic form in its own right. For Byrd, this makes the most recent GTA games something broader than a video game that is influenced by cinema and pop culture. It puts him in mind of the gesamtkunstwerk beloved by Wagner: a work that combines a range of disparate art forms into a cohesive whole. “[GTA’s] more of a totalising artwork that is bringing everything together,” he says. “The music is as much of a pillar as the driving, the shooting, the conversations.” He goes on to cite an online post he read arguing that games like GTA are the cathedrals of the 21st century. “You have teams of the most talented people coming together to create this glorious work that we can all be appreciative of, in which people can find something of interest to them, whether or not they’re in the church of video games.”

Games such as GTA V belong in the context of those journalistic 19th-century novels by the likes of Zola and Thackeray that used the widest lens possible to capture a time and place. They’re the equivalent of Rockstar co-founder Dan Houser’s own favourite novel, Middlemarch. They’re the equivalent of Dickens opening Bleak House with that unimprovable one-word sentence: “London.”

Such a glittering constellation of influences helps explain why GTA VI seems to have something in it for almost everyone. It’s a satire, a toybox, a knockabout updating of Bonnie and Clyde and a surprisingly sincere love story about its two heroes, Lucia and Jason, who are trying to make a life for themselves in an unkind world. Alongside the usual run of cinematic references, GTA VI seems fixated on social media, perhaps a canny understanding that Hollywood’s biggest rivals are now TikTok and Instagram.

In the run up to its release, it is easy to focus on the game’s lavish variety, but to say that you can simply do a lot of things in GTA these days – sky-diving, off-road racing, manning your own taxi cab, annoying alligators – is increasingly missing the point. The point instead lies with the density of every frame: the fuzzy edges of exposed drywall in an apartment that has been hastily refitted as a drug den, the brisk splatter of blood that appears on paintwork when someone’s face collides with it. And it goes beyond these vivid details into the realms of things you may only vaguely be aware of. Fly over the mountains in GTA V and the game delivers turbulence in little bursts of haptic feedback through the controller. You may not even notice it, but afterwards you might notice its absence in other games. They don’t pull you into their worlds as convincingly.

But perhaps the defining characteristic of GTA is not its wealth of details, but the contradictions that these details inevitably allow to percolate – contradictions as deeply rooted as those of the country it explores. GTA is a satire of consumerism that has itself made billions of dollars. It’s an underdog story from a gigantic company that is now fighting its dismissed former staff in court. It’s about criminals who scare us, except for the odd ingenious bank robber who we might feel is sticking it to the man. And GTA VI aims to deliver a textured depiction of a modern relationship in a world where the restaurants have names like Effluvia. It’s a representation of the modern American landscape, from fast food to talk radio, that was masterminded by a studio based in Edinburgh.

Maybe these internal contradictions, and that clarifying distance, are what are truly vital about this game. “A lot of us are jaded by the pressure that digital life has exerted upon us,” Byrd says. “We’re jaded by AI slop and the fact that life feels artificial. There is some kind of great paradox that we shouldn’t try to necessarily explain away: this is the one piece of a truly grand simulated reality that many of us are really hankering for.”

Grand Theft Auto VI is released on 19 November

https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.title: Is it true that … dock leaves cure nettle stings?
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.author: Kate Lloyd
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.text:
It’s a time-honoured treatment and rubbing certainly helps, but other leaves could be just as good

I
f you’ve ever brushed against a stinging nettle, chances are someone told you to find a dock leaf. The wide green leaves of dock plants seem to grow conveniently nearby, and rubbing one on a sting is a time-honoured remedy. But does it actually work?

Probably not in any way that’s unique to the plant, says John Tregoning, a professor at Imperial College London and the author of Live Forever? A Curious Scientist’s Guide to Wellness, Ageing and Death.

When you brush against a nettle, tiny hairs on the plant can pierce the skin and release a mixture of chemicals, including histamine, acetylcholine and serotonin. These trigger burning, itching and redness.

Could dock leaves contain chemicals that counteract the sting, such as antihistamines? “Maybe, but probably not,” says Tregoning. There is little evidence that dock leaf sap contains substances capable of significantly relieving the reaction.

Sign up to Inside Saturday

The only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.

after newsletter promotion

So why do people swear by them? Rubbing a leaf against the skin may provide a competing sensation that temporarily distracts from the pain, says Tregoning. “There’s a limit to the number of sensations that the nerve cells can process, so if you overstimulate them with the rubbing there’s less feedback from the pain.”

The distraction of searching for the leaves may also help. “The short burst of pain is relieved in the time spent hunting for the dock leaves.” Tregoning suggests that applying the sap may also have a cooling or soothing effect. But none of these things are unique to dock leaves.

A small study compared dock leaves with lettuce leaves as a treatment for nettle stings in nine medical students. It found no meaningful difference between the two. Tregoning suspects that any perceived benefit is most likely to be a placebo effect.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: This grim story of marine park whales could yet have a positive outcome – if it teaches us to value other species | Elle Hunt
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Elle Hunt
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
There is no ‘saving’ these traumatised mammals from places like Marineland in Canada. Humans need to understand that our actions are not easily undone

Remember “Save the whales”? Now that was an environmental campaign everyone could get behind. Surely you don’t want whales to die!

It may have got the 1986 global ban on commercial whaling over the line, but in these sophisticated times that slogan seems woefully reductive, even naive. As Greenpeace warns on its website, 40 years later: “There is still more work to be done to save the whales.” Yes. You might say, surveying the state of our ocean ecosystems, there’s quite a bit.

Even saving the whales from captivity – broadly agreed to be the right thing to do ever since the Blackfish documentary, about Tilikum the orca at Seaworld in Florida – is far from an easy win. Over the past few months, I’ve been following the sorry saga of Marineland, Canada’s most famous marine park, known for its nostalgic advertising jingles as a “magical place” where “the fun never stops”.

Marineland closed to the public two years ago due to financial pressures and performing whales and dolphins falling out of favour as family-friendly fun. Public sentiment has steadily turned against cetaceans in captivity. By mid-2019, when Canada finally outlawed the keeping of dolphins and whales, Marineland had been embattled for decades over both the principle issue and persistent allegations of mistreatment (including from whistleblowing former employees).

The lengthy list of reported whale deaths on Marineland’s Wikipedia page, dating back to the 1992 fatality of an unnamed whale from drowning, makes for grim reading. The Canadian Press newspaper counted 21 deaths since 2019 alone. You might assume, then, that Marineland’s closure was a rare win for animal lovers, a cut-and-dried case of saving the whales – but for many of its former residents there has not been a happy ending.

Despite what Free Willy led us to believe, saving the whales is not simply a case of triumphantly releasing them into open waters. These animals – adapted to captivity, if not traumatised – aren’t capable of surviving in the wild, forcing a difficult choice: either organise their transfer to another marine park or put them down.

Even relocation can be traumatic for such complex, sensitive animals, as seems to have proved the case here: of the 30 whales and four dolphins that were moved from Marineland to aquariums in the US and Spain, seven (six beluga whales and one dolphin) have died in their new homes.

It’s not known whether this was a direct result of the move or underlying health conditions. Either way, experts say it is likely the animals were already under chronic stress – and also that relocation was really the only option possible. Doug Whiteside, the head vet at Calgary Zoo, told CBC News it was a “kind of Hail Mary effort … [to] provide a better life for these whales”. Now 20% of Marineland’s beluga whale population is dead and more are thought likely to follow, with whale welfare advocates on “death watch”.

What can we take from this grim ending? Well, first, that we were wrong to put these animals in tanks to begin with. To rework the Dogs Trust motto, a whale is for life. We might have finally woken up to the wrongs of keeping cetaceans in captivity for our entertainment, but the animals themselves do not just disappear once we’ve lost the desire to see them. There’s a tendency to imagine animal rights and welfare as a balance that – with a will and a way – we can eventually redress. For example, if animals are suffering in captivity, we just need to free them; if their habitat is being lost, we can always restore it.

Most of the time this is a comforting fallacy, overstating humans’ potential for impact when we’re doing the right thing and understating it when we’re not. The truth is, our activities and interference irrevocably change animal lives, typically for the worse. An orca such as Junior, for example – caught off the coast of Iceland in the mid-1980s then kept in a concrete pool at Marineland, indoors and alone – never had a chance of recovering the kind of life he might have lived had he remained in the wild with his pod. Keiko, the cetacean star of Free Willy and the first captive orca to be fully released into the wild, lasted only about 18 months.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

In these situations, trauma is surely not too strong a word and, in animals as in people, it is not easily undone. The Whale Sanctuary Project is most engaged with the work, developing a 100-acre marine sanctuary in Nova Scotia for formerly captive cetaceans that can serve as a model for future projects elsewhere. But even that project has realistic aims, setting out not to save the whales but to give them sanctuary and “a new life that makes up for as much as possible of what went before”.

As a mission statement, it is appropriately humble, aimed not at absolution but atonement. I’ve never forgotten what I was told by Signe Preuschoft, a primatologist who has dedicated her life to the painstaking work of teaching orphaned young orangutans how to survive in the wild. That kind of rehabilitation and reintegration won’t play a meaningful part in the species’ survival, and is arguably low-priority compared with conserving habitat and ecosystems.

But, Preuschoft argued, we owe it to the individuals whose lives have been so catastrophically derailed by our species. Our destruction of these animals’ ecosystems and environments means suffering, she said. “It means maiming, disease, living in fear, dying, seeing your children die.” We might not be in this awkward position – of attempting to save the whales from a multitude of threats of our own creation – if we had valued their lives to begin with. Even the survivors might be free from Marineland but they are not unscathed.

Elle Hunt is a freelance journalist

Newsflash: Nvidia’s shares have dropped sharply at the start of trading in New York, as Wall Street gives its verdict on the company’s spying scandal.

Shares in the chip maker fell by almost 7.5% as soon as the opening bell rang out, as investors respond to the news that CEO Jensen Huang has admitted having an extramarital affair – reportedly with a Chinese spy.

That knocked the shares down to $172.75 each, down from $186.64 on Friday night.

That, by my maths, wipes $335bn off Nvidia’s valuation, following the board’s decision to launch an independent investigation into whether Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.

It lowers the company’s value to around $4.16tn, down from $4.5tn on Friday night.

Nvidia are the top faller on the Dow Jones industrial average (DJIA) in early trading.

Despite the chip giant’s troubles, the DJIA has jumped by 661 points, or 1.3%, to 51,947 points in early trading.

Twenty three of the 30 stocks who make up the DJIA are in positive territory, with investors cheered by a 4.7% fall in the oil price today.

Jensen Huang’s personal fortune has taken a heavy hit too.

Nvidia’s CEO owns around 3.61% of the company’s stock. At the end of last week, that stake was worth $162bn.

But today’s share price tumble means its value has dropped to $150bn, after Huang admitted cheating on his wife.

This morning’s sell-off has pushed Nvidia’s shares down to a seven-month low.
