https://www.medscape.com/viewarticle/de-.title: De-escalation of Surgery Safe for Low-Risk Thyroid Cancer
https://www.medscape.com/viewarticle/de-.text:
PHILADELPHIA — Patients with low-risk differentiated thyroid cancer treated with the less invasive approach of thyroid lobectomy vs total thyroidectomy, as recommended in American Thyroid Association (ATA) de-escalation guidelines from 2015, show no significant increases in the risk for disease recurrence, new research found.

The guidelines recommended lobectomy instead of thyroidectomy for intrathyroidal, papillary, and follicular thyroid cancers 1-4 cm.

While some patients may indeed ultimately require thyroidectomy, benefits of the less invasive approach are important, first author Terrence Peng, MD, MPH, of UCLA General Surgery Residency, told Medscape Medical News.

These include reduced risks for nerve injury and hypoparathyroidism in addition to a reduced lifelong need for thyroid hormone replacement, said Peng, who presented the results of the study at ATA’s 2026 Meeting.

He added that “the findings align” with the updated 2025 ATA guidelines, which strongly recommend hemithyroidectomy (lobectomy) as an initial operation for unilateral, low-risk differentiated thyroid cancer no larger than 2 cm without extrathyroidal extension or lymph node spread, and which conditionally recommend lobectomy for tumors between 2 and 4 cm.

To further investigate treatment patterns and whether de-escalation was associated with an increased risk of thyroid cancer recurrence, Peng and colleagues evaluated data on hospitals in the California Cancer Registry between 1999 and 2021.

The extent of de-escalation of differentiated thyroid cancer treatment was stratified into tertiles of limited, moderate, and aggressive, based on the percentage of decrease in total thyroidectomy rates for intrathyroidal differentiated thyroid cancer (1-4 cm) before vs after the ATA guideline publication.

Patients with less than 2 years of follow-up were excluded.

Overall, 12,206 patients were treated between 1999 and 2015, and 5403 were treated from 2016 through 2021. The majority of cases, about 92%, were papillary thyroid cancer; about 89% were treated in high-volume hospitals.

The results showed that the rate of thyroid lobectomy increased from 31% pre-2015 to 41% in the post-2015 group among patients treated at centers described as having limited de-escalation patterns. This increase was from 30.7% to 41.3% in the moderate de-escalation group and from 32.3% to 61.9% in the aggressive group.

In addition, the use of radioactive iodine within 3 months of the initial surgery decreased from 57.1% to 25.4% in the limited de-escalation group, from 52.5% to 22.1% in the moderate group, and from 49.9% to 15.7% in the aggressive group.

With a mean follow-up of 55.3 months in the post-2015 cohort, the overall rate of structural thyroid cancer recurrence, defined as requiring reoperation more than 6 months after the index operation, or receiving radioactive iodine more than 1 year after the index operation was 1.9%, compared with 2.8% in the pre-2015 group, which had a mean follow-up of 123 months.

Overall, 84% of patients were disease-free in the pre-2015 group and 81% in the post-2015 group, with the highest rates of disease-free status (88%) observed in the post-2015 aggressive de-escalation tertile (P < .001 vs the limited and moderate tertile groups).

There were no significant differences between the groups in terms of overall mortality, with only two cancer-specific deaths reported over the study period.

Limitations of the study include that the researchers were unable to determine the rationale for the use of total thyroidectomy vs lobectomy, and the generalizability of the results outside of California are unclear, Peng noted.

While the study did not explore the reasons behind the variation between the centers’ tertiles of de-escalation, he underscored that “we should not simply assume these variations are uniformly owed to gaps in awareness.

“For example, there may be access-to-care nuances that influence providers’ decisions in that regard, though this would require further study to move beyond speculation,” he explained.

In the meantime, the findings should “help to ease the concerns of those who may be limited de-escalators due to being more risk averse regarding recurrence,” Peng said.

“I think it would be helpful to consistently communicate that, based on the available evidence, guideline-concordant surgical de-escalation remains appropriate for this population and is not associated with increased risk of recurrence.”

Commenting on the study, Debbie Chen, MD, a clinical assistant professor and health services researcher in the Division of Metabolism, Endocrinology, and Diabetes at the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor, said ,“[O]verall, the results are very fascinating, especially in terms of the different degrees of de-escalation without significant differences in terms of disease recurrence or thyroid cancer-specific deaths.”

In terms of caveats, she added, “I think the things that I'd be most curious about are the hospital-level factors and differences at the patient level.”

Chen echoed that generalizability of the findings remains a question, “especially in the context of 89% of centers being high-volume hospitals. I don't know that that is broadly applicable to the rest of America.”

In general, however, “I think evidence like this is reassuring and really does support the directionality of how the guidelines have [changed],” she said. “[The findings] give reassurance that we are heading in the right direction.”

Peng and Chen had no disclosures to report.

https://fortune.com/article/price-of-oil.author: Joseph Hostetler
https://fortune.com/article/price-of-oil.text:
At 7:15 a.m. Eastern Time on November 6, 2026, oil was priced at $102.05 per barrel with Brent serving as the benchmark (we’ll explain different benchmarks later in this article). That’s an increase of $2.53 compared with yesterday morning and around $38 higher than the price one year ago.

Check Out Our Daily Rates Reports

It’s impossible to forecast oil prices with detailed precision. Many different elements affect the market, but ultimately it boils down to supply and demand. When worries about economic recession, war, and other large-scale disruptions increase, oil’s path can shift fast.

Gas prices at the pump don’t only track crude oil. They also include what it takes to refine and move that fuel, the taxes layered on top, and the extra markup your local station adds to stay in business.

Since crude oil generally makes up a majority of the per-gallon cost, changes in its price have an outsized impact. When oil surges, gas prices typically rise in tandem. But when oil retreats, gas prices often lag on the way down, a trend sometimes described as “rockets and feathers.”

In case of emergency, the U.S. has a store of crude oil known as the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. Its primary purpose is energy security in case of disaster (think sanctions, severe storm damage, even war). But it can also go a long way toward softening crippling price hikes during supply shocks.

It’s not a long-term answer and is more meant to provide temporary relief, assisting consumers and keeping critical parts of the economy running, like key industries, emergency services, public transportation, etc.

Both oil and natural gas are key sources of the energy we use every day. Because of this, a big change in oil prices can affect natural gas. For example, if oil prices increase, some industries may swap natural gas for some segments of their operations where possible, which increases demand for natural gas.

To gauge oil’s performance, we often turn to two benchmarks:

Between these two, Brent better represents global oil performance because it prices much of the world’s traded crude. And, it’s often the best way to track historical oil performance. In fact, even the U.S. Energy Information Administration now uses Brent as its primary reference in its Annual Energy Outlook.

Looking at the Brent benchmark across several decades, oil has been anything but steady. It’s seen spikes due to factors such as wars and supply cuts, and it’s also seen crashes from global recessions and an oversupply (called a “glut”). For example:

All to say, oil’s historical performance has been anything but smooth. Again, it’s hugely affected by wars, recessions, OPEC whims, evolving energy initiatives and policies, and much more.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/06/elon-musk.title: ‘The nail that sticks out gets hammered first’: Elon Musk’s net worth falls $113 billion from Tesla and SpaceX drops
https://fortune.com/2026/11/06/elon-musk.author: Mia Osmonbekov
https://fortune.com/2026/11/06/elon-musk.text:
Wall Street had a historic moment the day after Democrats swept the midterms, with the Dow rising 3% on Wednesday, its best performance after a midterm in 44 years. But on Thursday, it erased those gains, dropping 2.9% as investors dumped AI-related stocks like AMD and Micron.

But for Elon Musk, who spent an estimated $427.5 million to $483 million on backing Republicans, the losses started on the same day as the rally, and then accelerated. Tesla shares fell by 3.3% and SpaceX shares fell by 3.8% on Wednesday’s market close, erasing tens of billions from Musk’s fortune as they also underperformed against the S&P 500’s 1.6% growth and stocks like Amazon and Apple, which jumped 6.1% and 5.3%, per Fortune’s analysis. He lost $33.5 billion of his paper wealth that day, and another $79.7 billion in Thursday’s selloff, bringing his two-day loss to about $113 billion as of market close on Nov. 5, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index.

In short, in 48 hours, Tesla and SpaceX went from having a combined market cap of about $3.5 trillion on Tuesday night, to a combined $3.04 trillion on Thursday night, wiping out about $456 billion in total. As of Thursday night, SpaceX’s market cap is $1.68 trillion, about 87% of what it was on midterms night, and Tesla’s market cap is $1.36 trillion, about 86% of its value from then.

Investors are worried the two companies and their founder will face increased scrutiny from the new Congress. Democrats have signaled they want to investigate Musk’s involvement with DOGE gutting federal agencies and his potential conflicts of interests, since SpaceX has earned billions from federal contracts. The incoming House Oversight Committee chair Rep. Robert Garcia has vowed to investigate “corporate corruption,” and his spokesperson told Politico on Oct. 20 that Musk’s role in DOGE “is something we plan to investigate.”

“The nail that sticks out gets hammered first, and Musk has certainly stuck out, especially in government, whether it be donations, the election, and any of the feathers he ruffled while he was at DOGE,” Keith Snyder, senior equity analyst at CFRA Research, told Fortune.

The scrutiny could extend to SpaceX’s satellite business, its most consistently profitable segment. Sen. Richard Blumenthal from Connecticut sent a letter to Musk asking about SpaceX’s contracts with the Department of Defense and its ability to restrict Starlink after reports circulated that Ukraine’s military lost access to Starlink without notice.

But Snyder said the brief SpaceX and Tesla selloff was investors having a “knee-jerk reaction” to the election and overestimating the impact Democrats can have on the companies. After all, President Donald Trump still has veto power over any major AI restrictions they can pass, and is still friendly toward Musk.

“Reining in AI has been a stated goal of theirs, but you have to remember Trump seems to still be backing Musk and has veto power,” Snyder said.

For investors hanging their hopes on a SpaceX and Tesla merger and worried about Democrats’ interference there, Snyder said that because the Federal Communications Commission has a Republican majority, he doesn’t expect major actions there except Democrats’ power to “dramatically slow things down.” Fortune has reported that the merger math doesn’t add up for SpaceX shareholders.

“There’s too many pieces that are already in place for Musk, for Tesla, for SpaceX that will allow him to continue without having to worry about any kind of Democratic action,” he said.

Some analysts take a more bearish stance. Dan Ives wrote in a note on Thursday that a Tesla SpaceX merger “faces a much tougher regulatory roadmap” because of Texas turning blue. This new political reality partially made possible by voters angry over data centers coincides with investors’ long-running concerns about the AI buildout being unsustainable. Snyder said that anxiety could’ve contributed to the SpaceX selloff, but that SpaceX has an advantage in already having broken ground on data centers.

On its Q3 earnings call before the midterms, Musk said he was confident the company can bring 10 gigawatts of compute online by 2027 on top of the 2.5 to 3 gigawatts SpaceX will have by the end of 2026, a total number that AI and semiconductor research firm SemiAnalysis quantified as equivalent to all of Google’s data center capacity from 1999 to 2026 in just one and a half years.

“Even if they’re able to achieve 25% to 50% of that goal, that would be incredible in terms of capacity build out,” Snyder said.

He said where he sees more risk for SpaceX and for AI in general is if there’s a Democrat win in the White House in two years, since for now there will be a political gridlock with a Republican president and a Democrat-controlled Congress.

“The fears to these AI companies are real now,” he said. “[Democrats’] agenda has clearly stated they want to rein in AI, and so, ‘27, ‘28 is gonna be a stalemate, but it then becomes what happens in ‘29.”

https://fortune.com/2026/11/09/jensen-hu.title: Jensen Huang’s $21 billion net worth at stake: CEO’s admission of affair with an alleged Chinese spy is ‘capping gains’ for Nvidia stock
https://fortune.com/2026/11/09/jensen-hu.author: Eleanor Pringle
https://fortune.com/2026/11/09/jensen-hu.text:
For the first time in a long time, Nvidia’s investors may be feeling a little cold about their investment’s performance.

Last week, the famed chipmaker and many of its peers in the wider AI and technology industry suffered an estimated $2.5 trillion rout as investors questioned the hurdles facing the sector. The issue is political: The midterms saw Democrats win the Senate, the House, and many statehouses, prompting the question of whether regulation will become more complex under a divided government.

But adding to Nvidia investors’ concerns is the admission of its CEO, Jensen Huang, that he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

Huang’s net worth, tied to the computer processor and AI company he co-founded, stood at just over $171 billion early last week. It dropped to $150.9 billion by Thursday, and briefly rebounded to $154.9 billion by Friday—the latest data point on Bloomberg’s Billionaires Index.

The trajectory follows the path of Nvidia’s share price, now down 18.6% in the past month.

But even as signs of a small reversal bloomed Friday, the weekend brought another blow. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry,” Huang said in a statement shared overnight.

“To my colleagues at NVIDIA … you deserve better from me. Leading NVIDIA is the privilege of my life. My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility,” he added, saying he would work to “earn back” the confidence of the board, partners and company shareholders.

The woman he had an affair with has been identified in a series of reports as a suspected Chinese spy. Nvidia’s board of directors confirmed in an accompanying statement overnight that it had launched an independent investigation “in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.”

The Chinese government has denied involvement in the alleged spy plot involving Huang, calling the debacle “nothing but smears.”

The board added that while it has no reason to believe sensitive national security or NVIDIA “secrets” were compromised, it will “examine all available information.”

Analysts are digesting the news this morning ahead of markets opening in New York. Equities in Asia rallied this morning, noted Deutsche Bank’s Jim Reid, “although concerns surrounding an internal investigation involving Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang are capping gains.”

“The company is down around -3.5% on platforms that provide weekend prices,” he added.

The importance of Nvidia among the companies at the forefront of AI development cannot be overstated. It is the premier supplier of chips to AI companies and one of the largest investors and guarantors of companies in the AI supply chain—to the tune of hundreds of billions.

Yet President Trump was unruffled when asked about one of the country’s most famous CEOs being potentially implicated in a national security threat.

“I have not spoken to [Huang] about it,” Trump told reporters last night. “I just know he’s a fine person, but you never know what is going on.”

Betting on the prediction market Kalshi had the odds of Huang leaving the company before July 27 at 25%. Professor Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, senior associate dean for leadership studies at the Yale School of Management, put the odds of his resignation at 50-50. Huang owns the largest single stake in Nvidia, and his children are among his employees. If he were to leave, there is no obvious successor.

Nvidia’s board said it has “confidence in Jensen and his leadership team.”

President Trump was also confident Huang would continue to lead the company, saying: “He’s done an amazing job for our country.”

https://fortune.com/2026/11/09/crypto-in.title: The crypto world braces for Liz Warren’s return. Has anything changed?
https://fortune.com/2026/11/09/crypto-in.author: Jeff John Roberts
https://fortune.com/2026/11/09/crypto-in.text:
She’s back. Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), the longtime scourge of the crypto industry, is poised to return as a political force in January. That’s when Warren is expected to take over as Chair of the powerful Senate Banking Committee—a role that is critical for steering financial legislation, and comes with broad subpoena and investigative power. This is not exactly good news for crypto firms, of course. The question, though, is whether—just maybe—Warren and the industry can lay aside old antagonisms in order to advance both consumer protection and financial innovation.

As background, the bad blood between Warren and the crypto industry stems from the Biden years. That’s when former Securities and Exchange Commission Chair Gary Gensler set out to basically extinguish the U.S. crypto industry with a spate of lawsuits and investigations. Among Washington D.C. insiders, many saw Warren and her staffers as the architects of Gensler’s campaign.

In response to that Biden-era legal onslaught, the crypto industry overcame its longtime disdain of Washington politics, and it waged a big-money campaign in 2024 to elect President Trump, and to drive critics from Congress. The campaign worked stunningly well. Crypto firms helped sweep Trump into office, leading to a hands-off regulatory environment that left Warren fuming ineffectively on the sidelines.

Now, the shoe is on the other foot again. Despite blowing around $170 million on campaign ads to boost Republican candidates in the midterms, the crypto industry had what one lobbyist described simply as an “awful night.” Not only did crypto firms fail to do anything to stop the Democrats’ blue wave, they made tactical choices that look downright foolish in hindsight. That includes spending over $63 million in a failed bid to defeat crypto skeptic Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio), who not only won his Senate race by a comfortable margin, but will likely become Chair of the Agriculture Committee, which oversees commodities regulation.

When they are wielding committee gavels next January (which is widely expected but not confirmed), don’t expect Warren and Brown to do the crypto industry any favors. But it doesn’t necessarily follow that we’ll see a return to the scorched earth tactics of the Biden years. Ron Hammond, Head of Policy at Wintermute, notes that a recent Time essay by Warren appeared to telegraph her agenda. The essay puts CEOs of various industries on notice and promises to target Trump family corruption, but makes no mention at all of crypto—potentially a sign the industry will not be an immediate target.

Hammond, who is deeply plugged into the D.C. crypto scene, also noted that the crypto firms that stand to lose the most from Warren’s return are those that are seeking out or have obtained banking charters. In this scenario, Warren may ally with traditional banks, which earlier this year helped smother the Clarity Act, in order to block or roll back those charters.

Warren and her allies will be unable to make any drastic moves, though, because the Trump-appointed heads of key financial agencies—including the SEC, CFTC, and OCC—will hold their positions until the end of his term. This means that, for the next year or two, we can expect moves by Warren that are symbolic in nature, but that point to where she and the Democratic Party are heading in 2028.

Politics is never static, and while it’s a safe bet that Warren is not going to become a Bitcoin HODLer, there is a world where the Senator becomes less antagonistic. As an olive branch, she could acknowledge the undeniable benefits of blockchain innovations like stablecoins, as well as the popularity of crypto among younger Americans.

As for the crypto industry, the midterm results delivered a long overdue lesson that politics in Washington D.C. is a long game and that, while trying to bludgeon critics with PAC money may feel satisfying, it’s not the most effective strategy. And while crypto CEOs will never see eye-to-eye with Liz Warren—their respective libertarian and progressive worldviews are simply too different—there is room to acknowledge her advocacy for consumers is sincere, even if it is at times misguided.

Maybe all of this is naive, but last week’s election results felt like a break from politics as usual. Voters appear exhausted by jerks on both the left and the right and, for now at least, moderation is the order of the day. How refreshing would it be if Liz Warren and the crypto industry came to recognize that too?

Jeff John Roberts

https://fortune.com/2026/11/09/hr-leader.title: HR leaders have a new nightmare: Job seekers asking ChatGPT what employees really think of their company
https://fortune.com/2026/11/09/hr-leader.author: Kristin Stoller
https://fortune.com/2026/11/09/hr-leader.text:
HR leaders have a new fear: Job candidates asking ChatGPT what their company is really like.

Some 70% of job seekers now use generative AI tools like Claude, ChatGPT, and Perplexity to research employers, new Indeed data shows. And when job seekers ask about company culture, roughly 40% of the sources cited come from Glassdoor and Indeed, not company career pages.

That creates a new challenge for HR. AI is helping shape candidates’ perceptions of employers using information companies don’t directly control. A polished career page may tell one story, while employee reviews tell another—and job seekers can ask a chatbot to piece it all together.

But AI isn’t uncovering anything that isn’t already online, says Taylor Meadows, principal advisor at Glassdoor. His advice is to feed the beast.

“Your employer brand exists whether you are participating in it or not,” Meadows says. He recommends starting with an AI audit, asking different LLMs, “What is it like to work at X company?” Then, “reverse engineer” the problems that surface.

Meadows also suggests publishing Q&As addressing real questions from employees and candidates on social media and third-party review sites. “Let that be the good, the bad, and the ugly,” he says. “It’s going to be an opportunity for you to talk about what’s going well, but then it’s going to also be an opportunity to exercise some humility.”

Companies should also create content that showcases what it’s like to work in different departments, since culture can vary by team. Encouraging employees to share authentic experiences helps, too, Meadows says.

Even offboarding matters. Departing employees may leave reviews that AI later surfaces, making their final impression of the company especially important.

“None of this is about perfection and none of this is about control,” Meadows says. “It’s just about informing and influencing.”

Kristin Stoller
Editorial Director, Fortune Live Media

This week, Sabrina Clark, chief people officer at leadership consultancy SYPartners, answers your burning workplace questions. Responses have been edited for length and clarity.

Q: A friend of mine received strong performance reviews from three previous managers at their company. Then they got a new manager who put them on a PIP (performance improvement plan). They could not switch back to working with one of their previous managers because they were on a PIP, and their new manager didn’t indicate when it would end.

Because a competing company was interested in this employee, they chose to leave and join that company, but is there anything they could have done if they wanted to stay at their previous employer?

A: I imagine your friend is pretty frustrated to have gone from being rated a strong performer to being put on a PIP. While the discrepancy might lie with their new manager, it’s also possible their previous managers avoided giving difficult feedback or that the demands of your friend’s new work environment exposed gaps in their skills.

Whatever the reason, I would have advised your friend to ask their new manager, “What would success look like, and when will we assess it?” A performance improvement plan should always specify what needs to improve and how progress will be assessed, and include a timeline with regular check-ins and a defined review date. It should also explain the possible outcomes: successful completion, an extension with a new review date, or termination. Your friend deserved to know where the finish line was.

Given the seemingly strained relationship with the new manager, your friend could also have involved an HR leader or the manager’s manager to help uncover why their reviews differed so much and to help decide what happens next.

Ultimately, your friend could have pressed for more clarity, but their employer owed them a clear and fair path forward.

https://fortune.com/article/the-ceo-job-.title: The CEO job is hard enough to land once. HP’s incoming chief has done it twice
https://fortune.com/article/the-ceo-job-.author: Ruth Umoh
https://fortune.com/article/the-ceo-job-.text:
Emma Walmsley is joining an exclusive club. When she takes over HP in January, the former GSK chief will become a two-time CEO of a major multinational, having crossed three industries to get there.

Her trajectory offers a revealing study in how executives build careers that make them attractive to boards across industries.

Walmsley spent 17 years at L’Oréal, holding management positions across four global cities before running its consumer products business in China. She joined GSK in 2010, became CEO of its consumer healthcare division in 2015, and took the top job in 2017, becoming the first woman to lead a major pharmaceutical company.

Over nearly nine years, she navigated activist pressure, the pandemic, and the separation of Haleon, GSK’s consumer healthcare company. She also faced investor criticism over GSK’s drug pipeline and shareholder returns. Since 2019, she has served on Microsoft’s board, gaining exposure to the technology industry and a company central to HP’s PC business.

Her appointment follows the departure of Enrique Lores, who rose from engineering intern to CEO during more than three decades at HP before leaving for PayPal in February. After nine months under interim chief Bruce Broussard, HP has chosen a leader whose career followed a strikingly different trajectory.

Her next assignment presents a different commercial challenge.

HP says it needs to unlock growth as AI transforms personal computing. Analysts see more immediate pressures. Rising memory-chip prices are squeezing manufacturers, PC demand faces uncertainty, and the printing business continues to contract.

Walmsley joins a prominent group of executives recruited for another turn in the corner office. Kraft Heinz appointed former Kellanova chief Steve Cahillane in 2026. Verizon tapped former PayPal CEO Dan Schulman in 2025. Starbucks recruited Chipotle chief Brian Niccol in 2024, while Papa John’s hired former Wendy’s CEO Todd Penegor the same year. Mary Dillon, who previously led U.S. Cellular and Ulta Beauty, became Foot Locker’s CEO in 2022.

Their appointments reflect the appeal of executives with established track records running large organizations, navigating competitive pressures, and leading corporate transformations.

According to Spencer Stuart, 21% of incoming S&P 1500 CEOs in 2024 had previously led a public company, up eight percentage points over three years.

But hiring repeat CEOs comes with a revealing complication. In a study of 855 S&P 500 CEOs, Spencer Stuart found that 70% of those who went on to lead another S&P 500 company delivered stronger market-adjusted shareholder returns in their first CEO role. Researchers warned that experienced CEOs can rely too heavily on familiar strategies.

For Walmsley, whose experience restructuring GSK helped establish her credentials, HP presents a test of how readily those skills transfer to a technology business confronting different competitive pressures.

Ruth Umoh

https://fortune.com/2026/11/09/bain-capi.title: Bain Capital’s Ajay Agarwal bet on robots when Silicon Valley wouldn’t. Now he sees a ‘golden era’ for physical AI
https://fortune.com/2026/11/09/bain-capi.author: Morgan Chittum
https://fortune.com/2026/11/09/bain-capi.text:
Morgan Chittum here. The point of venture capital? Get in early on the next big thing. But when one firm backs a buzzy startup, others often rush to follow. The more compelling—albeit riskier—story belongs to the contrarian: the investor willing to get there first and stand alone.

That’s the kind of bet Bain Capital Ventures’ Ajay Agarwal made more than two decades ago, backing a robotics startup that Silicon Valley investors had largely turned away. The company was Kiva Systems, which Amazon would later acquire for $775 million.

When Agarwal met Kiva cofounder Mick Mountz in 2004, the company had no revenue, no finished product, and no customers. At the time, software was a quicker, cheaper route to market. But Mountz’s pitch was simple: Instead of making warehouse workers walk the aisles to retrieve products, have robots bring the shelves to them. “Within five minutes of the meeting with Mick, I thought to myself, ‘This is the best meeting I’ve been in in 18 months,’” Agarwal told me. “I didn’t know anything about robotics or hardware, but he explained the problem in a way that you could explain it to your grandmother.”

Convincing Bain’s partners to invest, however, would take more work. “Their initial reaction, which I don’t blame them for, was ‘We don’t know anything about robots,’” Agarwal said.

Through Bain’s network, Agarwal connected Kiva’s team with Don Ralph, who ran North American e-commerce fulfillment for Staples, for additional due diligence. That one-hour meeting turned into three. The next day, Ralph called Agarwal: “I’ve been in this industry for 35 years. That was the single most compelling technology I’ve ever seen. You have to invest.”

Bain later led Kiva’s first funding round and Staples became its first customer. High-profile companies like Zappos, Gap, and Zara followed suit. Eight years later, Amazon bought it for $775 million. Bain told Fortune its initial investment in Kiva generated a 26.6-fold return.

Now, Agarwal sees an even bigger, wider opportunity. “We’re in the golden age of hardware and physical AI,” he said. That’s the technology that lets robots and other machines perceive and act in the real world.

This time, though, the rest of Silicon Valley has joined in.

Robotics and physical AI startups raised $27.6 billion in funding across 1,009 deals in 2025, more than double the previous year’s total, according to PitchBook figures. Among them is TerraFirma, a construction robotics company that Bain was the first to back in 2024. In July, the startup announced a $100 million Series A led by Kleiner Perkins, with Bain investing again.

What makes Agarwal think this momentum will last? For starters, the talent. TerraFirma’s founders, Noah Schochet and Noah McGuinness, came from SpaceX. Physical Intelligence, another leading robotics startup, was started by Berkeley roboticist Sergey Levine and ex-Google DeepMind researcher Karol Hausman.

“I think it’s a reaction a little bit to people feeling jaded by 20 years of workflow software,” Agarwal said. “People may be feeling like this is not ambitious enough. I want to do something bigger. I want to do something harder.”

The hardware is also cheaper. Many crucial components now cost a fraction of what they did years ago. Part of that comes down to scale: Smartphone and electric vehicle makers buy up cameras, sensors, and batteries in massive quantities, helping drive down the cost of parts that robots use as well. “That means the ROI that you can deliver is so much more compelling,” he said.

Finally, more advanced AI means machines have a better shot at handling real-world scenarios. “They can deal with situations they haven’t seen before,” Agarwal said. “They can adapt and adjust to the edge cases which inevitably happen in a physical environment.”

Twenty-two years ago, Agarwal had to convince his partners to take robots seriously. That’s no longer the hard part. It’s finding a bet the rest of Silicon Valley hasn’t already crowded into.

https://fortune.com/article/price-of-oil.title: Current price of oil as of November 9, 2026
https://fortune.com/article/price-of-oil.author: Joseph Hostetler
https://fortune.com/article/price-of-oil.text:
As of 7:30 a.m. Eastern Time today, oil sold for $97.65 per barrel (using Brent as the benchmark, which we’ll get into momentarily). That’s $2.66 lower than yesterday and approximately a $33.50 rise over the past year.

It’s impossible to predict the future of oil prices. Several factors determine the movement of oil, but it ultimately boils down to supply and demand. Again, when threats of economic downturn, war, etc. are high, the oil trajectory can turn rapidly.

When you pay for gas at the pump, you’re paying for more than just the crude oil itself; you’re also springing for links along the chain, such as the refineries and wholesalers—not to mention taxes and local gas station markups.

Still, the crude oil aspect affects the final price most dramatically, as it typically accounts for more than half the price per gallon. When oil prices spike, so do gas prices. And frustratingly, when oil prices drop, gas prices tend to take their time drifting down to the lower price (sometimes referred to as “rockets and feathers”).

In case of emergency, the U.S. has a store of crude oil known as the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. Its primary purpose is energy security in case of disaster (think sanctions, severe storm damage, even war). But it can also go a long way toward softening crippling price hikes during supply shocks.

It’s not a long-term answer—more of an immediate relief to assist the consumer and keep critical parts of the economy running, like key industries, emergency services, public transportation, etc.

Oil and natural gas are both major energy fuels. A big change in oil prices can affect natural gas by extension. For example, if oil prices increase, some industries may swap natural gas for some segments of their operations where possible—which increases demand for natural gas.

When examining oil’s performance, there are generally two major benchmarks:

Between the two, Brent better represents global oil performance because it prices much of the world’s traded crude. And, it’s often the best way to track historical oil performance. In fact, even the U.S. Energy Information Administration now uses Brent as its primary reference in its Annual Energy Outlook.

Looking at the Brent benchmark across several decades, oil has been anything but steady. It’s seen spikes due to factors such as wars and supply cuts, and it’s also seen crashes from global recessions and an oversupply (called a “glut”). For example:

All to say, oil’s historical performance has been anything but smooth. Again, it’s hugely affected by wars, recessions, OPEC whims, evolving energy initiatives and policies, and much more.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/09/vietnam-t.title: Vietnam’s $140 billion U.S. surplus isn’t driven by illegal transshipment, says ex-ambassador Marc Knapper
https://fortune.com/2026/11/09/vietnam-t.author: Jay Ganglani
https://fortune.com/2026/11/09/vietnam-t.text:
Only a “very small percentage” of Vietnam’s exports to the U.S. are illegally transshipped, Marc Knapper, the former U.S. ambassador to Vietnam, said on Nov. 3, as the Trump administration tries to apply the term to a wider set of supply chain activities.

“The term transshipment has come to mean different things to different people,” Knapper, who served as the U.S.’s top diplomat in Vietnam from 2022 to 2026, explained at the Fortune Southeast Asia 500 Summit in Ho Chi Minh City.

Illegal transshipment is the falsification of a good’s country of origin to evade tariffs. For example, a Vietnamese exporter that imports a finished product from China, labels its country of origin as Vietnam, and then exports it to the U.S., is conducting illegal transshipment. Such activity is “fraudulent,” Knapper said, adding that Vietnam has been “cracking down pretty hard” on it, working with counterpart customs agencies, including U.S. Customs and Border Protection.

However, elements of the Trump administration have offered a more expansive definition of transshipment that includes what Knapper called “broader supply chain activity…the kind of things that every country does, including the United States, which is [to] assemble things based on inputs from neighboring countries.” He added that “some have falsely labeled normal supply chain activities as transshipment.”

The Trump administration claims that this activity—shifting some parts of a Chinese supply chain overseas to take advantage of lower tariffs—hurts the U.S. economy and denies it tariff revenue. In August, the White House Office of Trade and Manufacturing Policy accused over 40 economies of running a “Great Transshipment Scam” with estimated federal revenue losses of $19 billion to $26 billion a year.

Vietnam’s goods trade surplus with the U.S. reached $140 billion in the first ten months of the year. Knapper pointed out this surplus grew “in spite of the tariffs imposed by the United States on Vietnam…American consumers, American manufacturers, love made in Vietnam.”

Under an initial trade agreement announced in July 2025, Vietnam accepted a 20% tariff on its regular exports to the U.S., and a 40% tariff on goods deemed to have been transshipped from China, though the deal didn’t specify how that would be calculated. (That deal is now in limbo following the U.S. Supreme Court’s decision in February deeming most of U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariffs to be unlawful).

Currently, the U.S. levies a 12.5% tariff on many Vietnamese goods, imposed after a Section 301 investigation alleged the country hadn’t done enough to combat forced labor.

Many companies have shifted parts of their supply chains out of China and into Southeast Asia in recent years in what’s become known as a “China plus one” strategy. Rising U.S. protectionism, increasing costs in China, and a greater push for supply-chain resilience are encouraging this shift.

Chinese companies are also eager to expand into the region, seeing it not just as manufacturing destination but also as a new consumer market. “They call it their chuhai strategy, which means getting out of China and doing business in Southeast Asia and Vietnam,” Yap Kwong Weng, CEO of Vietnam SuperPort, said. “The question is, can companies come into Vietnam now, seize the opportunity, and really gain a competitive advantage from it?

China-ASEAN trade exceeded $1 trillion for the first time in 2025, according to China’s State Council.

In August, Vietnam’s National Assembly approved an additional $3.3 billion for a railway linking the country to China. While the project has faced setbacks because of delays in land clearance, officials target completion by 2030.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/09/binances-.title: Binance’s new CFO inherits a test that goes beyond the balance sheet
https://fortune.com/2026/11/09/binances-.author: Sheryl Estrada
https://fortune.com/2026/11/09/binances-.text:
Good morning. Taking on a CFO role for the first time is no small feat. Doing it at Binance, the world’s largest digital currency exchange, in the aftermath of what has been described as the biggest heist in crypto history, is quite another.

Justin Yek, a former VP of finance at Airwallex, will become Binance’s new CFO, succeeding Kaiser Ng, who has held the position since 2022 and is stepping down to pursue a new venture, the company said on Saturday. Binance co-CEO Yi He said in a statement that a transition plan had been “implemented over the last half year.”

On Oct. 29, hackers drained an estimated $6.3 billion from the platform, Fortune’s Jeff John Roberts reported. Binance later said North Korean hackers orchestrated the attack, using social engineering and malicious software to compromise engineers and gain access to systems that enabled unauthorized withdrawals.

The damage was partly contained. Tether and Circle froze about $2.5 billion in stolen stablecoins. Binance says it has replenished 98% of the stolen coins through reserve funds and other sources, and that users won’t bear the losses. Read more here.

But, the incident brings questions that go beyond cybersecurity. How strong are Binance’s internal controls? And how can the exchange convince customers and regulators that their assets are safe?

Those are questions that will inevitably land on the new CFO’s desk.

Yek brings a résumé suited to a growing global fintech. At Airwallex, he progressed from head of strategic finance and corporate development to VP of finance, leading the company’s global finance team. Before that, he spent about nine years in investment banking at Citi and Morgan Stanley, working on more than $30 billion in equity, M&A and debt transactions, according to his LinkedIn profile.

That’s substantial experience in corporate finance and dealmaking. But the CFO title is new to Yek, and he lacks the crypto-exchange experience of Ng, who joined Binance from Kraken.

Cybersecurity is increasingly a finance issue, not just an IT concern. The financial consequences of a breach, including lost assets, customer remediation, regulatory scrutiny and reputational damage, can ultimately fall on the CFO. For example, Deloitte’s Q3 2026 CFO Signals survey found cybersecurity was the top external concern for finance chiefs, cited by 50%, ahead of the economy and inflation.

At Binance, Yek’s first test as CFO will be helping restore the trust that money alone can’t replace.

Sheryl Estrada
Sheryl.Estrada@fortune.com

Wehner joins Fireworks after 14 years at Meta, where he most recently served as chief strategy officer. He joined Meta, then called Facebook, in 2012 and was the company's CFO from 2014 to 2022. At Fireworks, he will be tasked with scaling the company's finances and operations. Founded in 2022 by former Meta and Google employees, Fireworks was valued at $17.5 billion in a Series D round in July.

David Gilbert was appointed interim CFO of TransUnion (NYSE: TRU), an information and insights company, effective Jan. 1, as part of a planned leadership transition. Current CFO Todd Cello will remain finance chief through Dec. 31, and will then serve as a full-time advisor through March 1. Gilbert brings more than three decades of TransUnion experience. He currently serves as SVP and International CFO. Gilbert joined TransUnion in 1991 and has held several senior roles across finance and operations. The company initiated a search for a permanent CFO.

Finance may not be the biggest employer of tech talent, but it's competing for that talent. Finance and insurance companies posted 17,790 tech job openings in October 2026, fifth among industries, according to CompTIA's latest Tech Jobs Report, which is based on Lightcast job-posting data.

Professional, scientific and technical services led by a wide margin with 83,514 postings, followed by manufacturing, administrative and support services, and information and media. Across all industries, active tech postings totaled about 630,000 in October, a slight increase from September.

Postings that mention AI skills "continue to rise," CompTIA said. The mix of roles is telling for finance teams. Demand grew for software developers and engineers (up 3,066 from September), systems engineers (up 3,434) and DevOps engineers (up 2,833). Postings for data analysts fell by 702. That suggests employers may be putting more money into building and running systems, including AI.

AI chip leader Nvidia's board has opened an independent investigation into reports that CEO Jensen Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence campaign, Fortune’s Jason Ma writes. A committee of independent directors, assisted by outside counsel, will oversee the inquiry.

Huang has acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife and apologized to his family and colleagues. Separately, reports citing U.S. intelligence assessments allege that he had a romantic relationship with Alice Huang, an executive at Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed. The two are not related, and U.S. intelligence reportedly suspects Alice Huang of gathering information for China.

In a statement, Nvidia's board said it "has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised," but that its inquiry "will examine all available information." Read more here.

"This is a black eye moment for Jensen and will spark multiple congressional inquiries at a minimum and will create an overhang on the stock for a myriad of reasons. The key question investors will be asking is: Will Jensen remain CEO of Nvidia?"

—Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co., wrote in a Sunday investor note.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/nvidia-j.title: Nvidia stock falls 5% as scrutiny turns to Jensen Huang’s affair with alleged Chinese spy
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/nvidia-j.author: April Roach
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/nvidia-j.text:
Nvidia’s board opened an independent investigation after reports that CEO Jensen Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence effort.

The stock fell on Monday as investors assessed leadership risk around Huang.

It marks a “black eye moment” for Huang, said Yorkville Ives & Co.’s Dan Ives.

Nvidia
 stock fell 5% on Monday after the tech giant launched an investigation into CEO Jensen Huang’s relationship with a businesswoman who intelligence agencies say is a Chinese spy.

U.S. intelligence agencies said Alice Huang, an executive at cloud company MegaSpeed, has been passing information to Beijing, according to reports in The New York Times and The Financial Times.

Nvidia said its board has launched an independent investigation following the reports that Huang was the target of a “foreign intelligence effort.”

Huang “fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it,” the company said in a Sunday statement.

The co-founder and CEO told staff in an email that he had “fallen short” of his responsibility to serve his colleagues, the board, partners and shareholders around the world.

“I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry,” Huang said in the email.

China’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said on Monday the “so-called Chinese spy narrative” was unsubstantiated, Reuters reported.

The probe has sparked questions about Huang’s future as CEO of the company.

But any talk of replacing Huang is “comedy,” Dan Ives, senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co., told CNBC’s “Squawk Box Europe.”

While the probe and affair is a “game changer” for the CEO and company, it doesn’t alter the view that Nvidia remains two to three years ahead of China in AI chips, Ives said.

“You’re talking about what I would view as a torchbearer — the leader of AI technology — not just in the U.S. but globally. So I think the fact that we’re in this situation, from an investor perspective, the clear worry is, does Jensen stay on as CEO? The Street would say probably likely, but given the board investigation, anything could happen, and that creates a huge uncertainty.”

Tech stocks took a hammering last week as investors reassessed the data center build-out after Democrats won control of Congress.

Asian tech stocks rose across the region on Monday, rebounding from Friday’s losses. Shares of U.S. chipmakers also climbed, with AMD
, Marvell
, Arm
, Intel
 and Qualcomm
 rising on Monday.

Joachim Klement, investment strategist at Panmure Liberum, said the impact is currently contained to Nvidia.

But if Huang’s position is “endangered,” then “Nvidia might cut back on supporting other companies, whether it’s in Asia or in the U.S., that might then spread a little bit more into the other semiconductor names,” he said.

U.S. President Donald Trump on Sunday praised Huang’s leadership but said he hadn’t spoken to the CEO about the investigation.

“I think he’s an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it. You have to hear it,” the president told reporters.

“He’s done an amazing job for our country,” Trump added.

Shaun Maguire, partner at Sequoia, also defended the tech giant CEO, saying in a post on X that Huang is “one of the greatest entrepreneurs of this generation.”

He added: “two mistakes don’t make a right, and I believe Jensen is irreplaceable for America’s AI leadership.”

SpaceX
 and Tesla
 CEO Elon Musk reshared Maguire’s post, adding that he agrees with the venture capitalist’s statements.

Nvidia reports third-quarter earnings on Nov. 17 and will hold a major conference in Washington, D.C., at the end of the month.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/home-lis.title: Home listings pile up in October, but sellers won't slash prices
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/home-lis.author: Diana Olick
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/home-lis.text:
Active inventory in October was up 7.4% year-over-year.

Newly pending home sales dropped 16.8% in October from the year before.

“November is shaping up to have an even larger contraction,” said Mischa Fisher, Zillow’s chief economist.

Homebuyers continue to retreat, but sellers are still digging in, refusing to cut prices or give up. As a result, September’s frozen housing market is now October’s frozen and increasingly bloated market.

Active inventory in October hit 183,500 homes, up 7.4% year-over-year, according to Realtor.com. That is the fastest annual growth in eight months. Active listings have been rising each month since February. This is despite the fact that new listings are actually falling, down 7.5% from October 2025.

The market has seen several years of extremely lean supply, driven by the homebuying frenzy during the first two years of the pandemic, when mortgage rates hit more than a dozen record lows. Now supply nationally is just 6.6% below typical pre-pandemic levels, the narrowest gap since the pandemic.

“The market is cooling on both sides, but in different ways. Buyers are stepping back as higher mortgage rates cut into their buying power, while sellers are listing less often without a broad increase in delistings or price cuts,” said Danielle Hale, chief economist at Realtor.com. “We’re seeing a pause in new supply, but owners who already have homes on the market appear to be largely unphased.”

Just over 20% of sellers cut prices in October, about the same as both September and October of last year. There was also no meaningful increase in delistings by sellers.

Mortgage rates came down a little bit in October month-to-month, but they are still over a full percentage point higher than a year ago. That continued to weigh on sales. Newly pending sales, representing signed contracts, not closings, dropped 16.8% in October year-over-year, according to Zillow. That was the biggest annual drop since August 2023 and slowest October since 2018.

While rates fell slightly, home prices continued to gain. Zillow estimated the monthly mortgage payment on the typical U.S. home was $2,004 in October, assuming a 20% down payment and excluding taxes and insurance. That is an increase of 12.8% from last year and 4.8% higher than in September, the biggest one-month jump in four years.

“November is shaping up to have an even larger contraction, but the silver lining is that next month is likely going to be the worst of it,” said Mischa Fisher, Zillow’s chief economist, in a release. “I expect the pace of the slowdown to ease into the new year. There are deals to be had for buyers able to brave the affordability headwinds in the coming months, and the continued inventory buildup means there is a lot of upside for sales into next year if we get rate relief.”

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/congress.title: Congress returns with government funding, Pete Hegseth and the debt limit on the agenda
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/congress.author: Justin Papp,Garrett Downs
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/congress.text:
Congress returns Monday and will need to quickly take up must-pass legislation to avert a potential government shutdown.

In addition to government funding, Congress needs to pass the National Defense Authorization Act and could take up permitting reform and measures related to congressional stock trading and name, image and likeness deals in college sports.

But the House and Senate will likely be limited in what they can accomplish in the waning post-election weeks: Democrats will have little incentive to compromise as they prepare to take control of Congress, and lawmaker attendance could be an issue.

The House and Senate are due to return to Washington on Monday with a crowded legislative agenda in the final weeks before the end of the 119th Congress.

Congress will need to act quickly to extend government funding, which expires Dec. 11. Lawmakers will need to pass the National Defense Authorization Act, and they may tackle ambitious proposals including a construction permitting package and a bill to regulate name, image and likeness rules in college sports.

The work will commence under a new dynamic. Republicans come back to the Capitol diminished after suffering substantial losses in this week’s midterms. Democrats swept to a commanding majority in the House with at least 255 seats in the 435-member chamber and could emerge with as many as 56 seats in the Senate.

With majorities in both chambers looming, Democrats will have little incentive to cut deals with their GOP counterparts.

The most pressing concern lawmakers will face when they return is funding the government. Current funding expires Dec. 11. Congress must pass another continuing resolution to retain current spending levels or a full-year suite of appropriations bills before then to avoid a government shutdown.

Appropriations bills and continuing resolutions require bipartisan majorities due to the Senate’s 60-vote filibuster threshold. Democrats are unlikely to negotiate a full year of government funding before the new Congress is sworn in, given that they will soon hold commanding majorities in both chambers and can use that to leverage concessions from the White House.

“This former preschool teacher is going to teach President Trump a simple lesson: The power of the purse belongs to CONGRESS!” Sen. Patty Murray, D-Wash., the presumptive chair of the Appropriations Committee, said in an X post Tuesday as election results rolled in. “It’s NOT Trump’s money. Taxpayer dollars belong to the American PEOPLE.”

Adding another wrinkle to the funding push is the electoral loss of Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, who chairs the Senate Appropriations Committee and is one of the “four corners” of spending talks. Collins lost reelection to Democrat Troy Jackson, ending a five-term career in the Senate.

Some lawmakers, including Sen. Kevin Cramer, R-N.D., have called for Congress to raise the debt limit before Republicans lose control.

In September, the federal debt hit $40 trillion for the first time, bumping up against the $41.1 trillion ceiling written into the GOP’s 2025 budget reconciliation law known as the “one big beautiful bill.”

The Bipartisan Policy Center, a nonprofit that tracks the debt limit, said Treasury is likely to hit its maximum borrowing capacity by mid-summer. The U.S. may no longer be able to meet all its obligations by November 2027, according to a Bank of America estimate from Nov. 6.

But Democrats may instead prefer to use the debt limit as a bargaining chip in the next Congress.

Republicans could theoretically raise the debt ceiling in a budget reconciliation package, as they did with their 2025 law. But cobbling together a post-election coalition to clear another reconciliation bill with exceptionally narrow margins would be difficult. Budget reconciliation, which allows party-line bills to skirt the filibuster in the Senate, requires near-total unity.

Congressional leadership, particularly on the Republican side, is likely to have difficulty with lawmaker attendance after dozens of members lost their seats in an electoral bloodbath. Leadership will also struggle to whip members into line, especially those who do not have another election to run.

Top senators on energy committees struck a deal on a permitting bill before the election. That accord to make construction easier could now be in jeopardy, though the Senate plans to hold a procedural vote to advance it Monday evening, according to a Senate aide familiar with the schedule. The person asked not to be named because the move has not been announced.

The resounding majorities Democrats won in both the House and Senate may give them incentive to torpedo the permitting deal in hopes of securing a better one later. The deal also may have been in trouble prior to the election, with top Democrats in the House not supporting the version their counterparts in the Senate accepted.

Politico reported Thursday that Democratic Minority Leader and likely next House Speaker Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., did not support the permitting deal.

Lawmakers have long sought, and failed to reach, a bipartisan, bicameral deal on permitting reform. Democrats want to speed up the buildout of clean energy. Republicans have long complained that the federal permitting process and environmental laws that comprise it stymie the U.S.’s ability to build critical infrastructure.

The House passed a version of the NDAA, which would authorize more than $1 trillion in defense spending, in July. But Senate Democrats blocked their chamber’s version of the bill that same month over concerns about the Iran war.

“Donald Trump is dragging America deeper into a war in Iran with no authorization, no plan, and no exit strategy. Democrats will not go along,” Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., said in a statement at the time.

The NDAA is typically seen as a must-pass, bipartisan bill.

The legislation as it stood in July also drew pushback from businesses over a provision that would restrict Pentagon contractors from executing stock buybacks and paying dividends unless they have the Defense Department’s approval.

A new wrinkle threatens to derail the NDAA process during the lame duck, however. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth faces a vote on articles of impeachment upon Congress’ return, and Democrats have already been highly skeptical of the Pentagon’s asks in this year’s budget as the expensive Iran war drags on.

Other priorities could also get floor time.

The Senate in September approved, in a bipartisan vote, a package that would establish federal rules for the ways in which college athletes are compensated. But that legislation has many opponents in the House, particularly among Democrats in the chamber, making its passage more complicated.

There’s also been a yearslong effort to ban members of Congress from owning or trading individual stocks.

In previous Congresses, the effort was stymied by leadership from both parties. And more recently, a bipartisan push to pass legislation was derailed after House Democrats demanded the ban also apply to the president.

One GOP-led proposal, called the Stop Insider Trading Act, passed the House with some bipartisan support in July, but met with Democratic opposition because it would apply only to Congress and would not require lawmakers to divest existing holdings.

Sen. Todd Young, R-Ind., called for action on the issue in an X post Thursday. Young is a co-sponsor of the Senate version of the Stop Insider Trading Act.

“We have a great opportunity in the lame duck session to restore a small amount of trust by banning Members of Congress from trading stocks. I’ve been talking about this for many months, and it should be a no-brainer,” Young said.

Democrats, however, are eager to claim a victory on congressional stock trading in the next Congress.

Jeffries, in a letter to fellow House members announcing his candidacy for speaker, listed it as a priority as part of Democrats’ anti-corruption agenda.

“We must root out corrupt price gouging, clean up the mess at the Supreme Court and ban Members of Congress from trading stocks. Accountability begins at home,” Jeffries wrote.
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/congress.summary: Congress returns to Washington on Monday with a crowded legislative agenda. Congress must pass the National Defense Authorization Act. The bill is typically seen as a must-pass, bipartisan bill.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/us-iran-.title: Rubio sees little hope of diplomatic breakthrough to Mideast deadlock amid 'outrageous' Iranian demands
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/us-iran-.author: Hugh Leask
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/us-iran-.text:
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said talks with Iran were not close to a breakthrough and called some Iranian demands “outrageous and ridiculous.”

Oil prices fell Monday after President Donald Trump said renewed strikes on Iran were “highly unlikely” if negotiations made progress.

Iran wants U.S. sanctions to be lifted before negotiations resume.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has accused Iran of “outrageous and ridiculous” demands as efforts to reach a lasting resolution in the Middle East war appeared stalled.

Speaking with reporters in Florida on Sunday evening before traveling to Paris for the G7 foreign ministers’ meeting, Rubio indicated the two sides remain far apart on negotiations, after Tehran proposed shortening the timetable for restarting talks from seven days to two.

Rubio said President Donald Trump would prefer to solve “this and every problem diplomatically,” but added that “sometimes that’s not possible, unfortunately.”

Energy prices moved lower on Monday morning after President Trump said Sunday that further strikes were “highly unlikely” if negotiations progressed toward a strong agreement.

Brent crude
, the international price benchmark, was down 0.75% at $97.58 per barrel by 5:25 a.m. ET. Meanwhile, U.S. West Texas Intermediate
 futures for December delivery were trading 0.42% lower at $90.45.

Trump said in a CNN interview prior to Rubio’s comments that a resumption of hostilities in the more than eight-month-long conflict was unlikely, provided that talks to constrain Iran’s nuclear ambitions and reopen the Strait of Hormuz can progress.

“I wouldn’t say we’re on the verge of a breakthrough,” Rubio said. “Right now, it hasn’t been very productive because the Iranian demands are simply not just unacceptable but, in some cases, outrageous and ridiculous and really not realistic.”

Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said Monday that Tehran wants U.S. sanctions lifted and the war ended on all fronts before negotiations begin.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/eli-lill.title: Eli Lilly’s Foundayo obesity pill eases sleep apnea in late-stage trial, paving way for approval
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/eli-lill.author: Annika Kim Constantino
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/eli-lill.text:
Eli Lilly said its new obesity pill, Foundayo, significantly reduced the severity of the most common sleep-related breathing disorder in a late-stage trial.

The drugmaker plans to file by the end of the year for U.S. approval of the daily pill for moderate-to-severe obstructive sleep apnea in adults with obesity or who are overweight.

The results make the pill one of several GLP-1 treatments to show promise in treating the condition.

Eli Lilly
 on Monday said its obesity pill Foundayo significantly reduced the severity of obstructive sleep apnea, the most common sleep-related breathing disorder, in patients with obesity, in a late-stage trial.

The drugmaker plans to file by the end of the year for U.S. approval of the daily pill for moderate-to-severe obstructive sleep apnea, or OSA, in adults with obesity or who are overweight. The results make the pill — which rolled out in the U.S. in April — one of several GLP-1 treatments to show promise in treating the condition.

OSA refers to interrupted breathing during sleep due to narrowed or blocked airways, which can cause drops in oxygen and increases in blood pressure that are associated with serious complications, such as hypertension, heart failure and stroke. The condition affects nearly 1 billion adults globally, including 80 million people ages 20 and over in the U.S., according to the National Council on Aging. Most have never been diagnosed, Lilly said in a release.

Lilly’s blockbuster weight loss injection Zepbound became the first medication to win U.S. approval for OSA in December 2024. Patients have limited treatment options outside of that drug and many use cumbersome machines that provide positive airway pressure, or PAP, to allow for normal breathing.

“Foundayo is already making a difference for people living with obesity, and with plans to submit these results to the FDA by the end of the year, we could have the opportunity to help people living with OSA,” Dr. Thomas Seck, senior vice president of product development of Lilly Cardiometabolic Health, said in a release.

The trial tested Foundayo in two independent studies, the first of which included 363 patients who were unable or unwilling to use PAP therapy. The second study included 349 people who were on PAP therapy for at least three months at the time of screening and continued that treatment during the trial.

Patients in both studies who took Foundayo started at a low dose and increased it gradually at four-week intervals to different maximum dosages.

Researchers specifically examined how much the pill reduced the so-called apnea-hypopnea index, or AHI, which records the number of times per hour a person’s breathing shows a restricted or completely blocked airway. The index is used to evaluate the severity of obstructive sleep apnea and the effectiveness of treatments for the condition.

People who took Foundayo and were not using PAP therapy had an average of 21.1 fewer AHI events per hour at 52 weeks, compared with an average reduction of 4.8 per hour for the placebo, according to the results.

Foundayo also met the trial’s second goal in that group, leading to an overall AHI reduction of 43.8% compared with a decrease of 6.3% for the placebo. Lilly said 31.5% of the participants in the Foundayo group met the criteria for remission or improvement to mild OSA.

Meanwhile, patients who were on both Foundayo and PAP therapy had an average of 18.3 fewer AHI events per hour at 52 weeks, compared with an average reduction of 5.5 per hour for the placebo.

Foundayo led to an overall AHI reduction of around 27.5% in that group, compared with a decrease of 3% for the placebo. The company said 19.6% of the participants on Foundayo and PAP therapy also met the criteria for remission or mild OSA.

Foundayo also reduced what’s known as the sleep apnea-specific hypoxic burden — a measure of how deeply and for how long oxygen levels fall during sleep. That metric fell by 55.9% in people not using PAP therapy and 45.8% in those using it.

Lilly said the pill also helped patients lose roughly 11% of their weight across groups at 52 weeks and helped to lower a marker of inflammation.

The company said the safety data and how well patients tolerated Foundayo were generally consistent with previous trials on the pill.

Around 12% of people on Foundayo who were not using PAP therapy discontinued due to side effects, compared to 3.8% with the placebo. Meanwhile, 6.8% of those on both Lilly’s pill and PAP discontinued the drug due to side effects, compared with 0.6% in the placebo group.

The most common side effects were gastrointestinal, including nausea, diarrhea, constipation and vomiting, and were generally mild to moderate in severity. That’s consistent with other GLP-1 medications.

The drugmaker plans to file by the end of the year for U.S. approval of the daily pill for moderate-to-severe obstructiveSleep apnea. The results make the pill one of several GLP-1 treatments

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/goodyear.title: Goodyear Tire CEO Mark Stewart steps down as company continues turnaround plan
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/goodyear.author: Catriona Marangi
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/goodyear.text:
Goodyear said CEO Mark Stewart is stepping down from the company effective immediately after serving in that role since January 2024.

The tire company appointed Roger Wood as interim CEO and president.

Goodyear faces continued challenges due to tariffs, higher raw material costs and increased competition from China.

Goodyear Tire & Rubber Co.
 announced Monday that CEO Mark Stewart would be stepping down from his role effective immediately.

Board member Roger Wood is taking over as interim CEO and president, Goodyear said.

The leadership change comes as the tire company is in the midst of a multiyear transformation plan.

Stewart was hired in January 2024 to lead the company, with the goal of revitalizing the legacy American business to make it more efficient and profitable.

The company has faced disappointing results thus far, reporting last week third-quarter results that saw net sales down 2.3% year over year and an adjusted net loss of $31 million. Goodyear failed to reach a 10% operating margin by the end of last year, which was a major goal of the turnaround plan.

Goodyear said it formed a special committee of the board earlier this year to conduct a “strategic review of the company’s businesses and operations focused on identifying opportunities to strengthen performance and drive shareholder value.”

It said Monday it will continue that work by evaluating strategic and operational initiatives that include further optimizing the company’s business mix and footprint, improving efficiency and investing in new products and capabilities that support long-term growth.

“Goodyear has made meaningful progress in becoming a more efficient and focused company, and the board believes this is the right moment to transition leadership to accelerate that progress and capture additional opportunity,” Goodyear Chair Joe Hinrichs said in a press release.

The company has faced headwinds from tariffs, higher raw material costs and increased competition from China.

Wood has been a member of the company’s board of directors since July 2023 and was previously the co-CEO of Tenneco as well as CEO of Dana Holding Corporation.

The company will start a search for a permanent replacement as part of its strategic review.

Shares of Goodyear were down roughly 4% in early trading Monday.
