Board member Roger Wood is taking over as interim CEO and president. The tire company has faced headwinds from tariffs, higher raw material costs and increased competition from China.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/restaura.title: Restaurant chains refocus on food quality to bring back diners
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/restaura.author: Amelia Lucas
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/restaura.text:
Restaurant chains like Chipotle Mexican Grill and Applebee’s are upgrading their core menu items to try to win back diners.

For some companies, like Wendy’s and Burger King, improved food is a key step in ambitious turnaround plans.

In 2009, Domino’s Pizza won over customers with an improved pizza recipe and ads that criticized its old version.

Juicier chicken tenders. Revamped sauces. Richer and creamier Frosties.

Across the restaurant industry, chains are turning their focus back to their food in the hopes that better quality will win back diners.

Over the last two years, consumers have dined out less frequently and grown pickier about where they choose to eat, based on data from Black Box Intelligence. In that time, “value” has been the buzzword du jour for restaurant executives, who have explained to analysts and investors that the word encompasses more than menu pricing alone.

Now, industry CEOs are turning to their corporate chefs to try to beat rivals on quality and taste, as they look to expand their definition of value. Discounts and one-off promotions can lift traffic for a time, but the actual product still matters for restaurants’ long-term growth, as well as franchisee profitability.

From Wendy’s
 to Chipotle Mexican Grill
, chief executives touted new or upcoming improvements to menu items on their quarterly earnings conference calls in recent weeks.

“We think the product’s improved and even better,” Chipotle CEO Scott Boatwright told analysts on the company’s call in late October, referring to the burrito chain’s brisket, which returned to menus for a limited time Thursday.

For some chains, better food is a key step in ambitious turnaround plans.

For example, “quality food at real value” is one pillar of Wendy’s five-part turnaround strategy that the chain unveiled on Thursday.

“We’re also rebuilding our food offerings and have begun testing improvements to quality and craveability of our core items, including thicker, crispier bacon, a richer and creamier Frosty, whole leaf lettuce on sandwiches and improved salads,” Wendy’s CEO Bob Wright told analysts on the call Thursday.

That same day, the company reported its seventh straight quarter of same-store sales declines and publicly rejected a $1.4 billion takeover bid led by Nelson Peltz’s Trian Partners. Wendy’s said the proposal did not take into account the potential value that its turnaround plan could unlock.

There is precedent to suggest that better-tasting food can contribute to higher sales.

In 2009, Domino’s Pizza
 changed its recipe, swapping out its sauce, adding garlic to its crust and switching to shredded mozzarella with a hint of provolone. Along with blunt commercials that compared its previous crust to cardboard and old sauce to ketchup, the changes helped to spur U.S. same-store sales growth of 9.9% the following year.

Now, some of the same team that led the Domino’s turnaround is copying the playbook at Burger King’s U.S. restaurants.

Part of the burger chain’s multiyear comeback plan has focused on revamping its core menu items. It started earlier this year with its flagship offering, the Whopper, which received a better bun and a new mayonnaise. And in September, it rolled out an overhaul of its nuggets, switching to 100% white meat, crispier breading and a more flavorful marinade. It also reformulated its sauces.

“We’ve tried to look at our biggest categories first,” Josh Kobza, CEO of Burger King parent Restaurant Brands International
, told CNBC. “We’ve also thought about the ones where the fixes are more straightforward and less operationally involved.”

Following the changes, Whopper sales were up by a double-digit percentage in the third quarter, Kobza said on the company’s earnings call in late October. And nugget sales climbed more than 35%. Burger King said its U.S. same-store sales jumped 8.4% in the quarter.

Like Domino’s, Burger King is highlighting diners’ past gripes with its Whoppers and nuggets in its ads, which star Burger King U.S. president and former Domino’s executive Tom Curtis.

Better-tasting food isn’t just for chains that are in trouble.

Even Chili’s, which has seen its same-store sales soar 52% over the past three years, is improving more of its existing menu options. After tackling its baby back ribs, burgers and nachos, it will turn next to salads and steaks, Brinker International
 CEO Kevin Hochman told CNBC.

“We’re going to be doing more dry aging of our beef to make it more tender, versus doing it in a plant,” he said. “It’s a little bit more expensive, but we think the taste is going to be a whole lot better.”

Chili’s rival Applebee’s launched a juicier chicken tender during its latest quarter, according to John Peyton, CEO of the chain’s parent company Dine Brands
. In 2027, Applebee’s plans to overhaul more of its protein options.

“We think proteins are, number one, our biggest opportunity,” Peyton told CNBC. “Number two, they’re a big focus of the way people are thinking about eating right now, leaning into proteins and a little bit less with the carbs.”

Chicken is also a focus for McDonald’s
, which is testing hand-breaded wings, strips and a sandwich in a handful of Chicago-area restaurants. It plans to expand the trial to more locations in the U.S. and Ireland in early 2027.

Moreover, McDonald’s is trying to improve its coffee, with fresher beans and upgraded equipment, executives said at the company’s investor day in September. Both chicken and coffee are fast-growing categories, offering more opportunities to lift sales than McDonald’s signature beef burgers.

While the burger giant isn’t in full turnaround mode like rivals Wendy’s and Burger King, its U.S. business has struggled in recent quarters after its value strategy didn’t gain the traction the company had hoped. In the third quarter, its U.S. same-store sales fell 0.2%.

In addition to menu tests, McDonald’s is also leaning into training to improve the quality and consistency of its core menu items. Starting in October, the company launched “Make It Golden,” a multiyear training program for corporate employees, restaurant workers and franchisees.

Ultimately, improved menu items mean little if the recipe changes aren’t well executed.
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/restaura.summary: In 2009, Domino's Pizza won over customers with an improved pizza recipe and ads that criticized its old version. Burger King rolled out an overhaul of its nuggets, switching to 100 U.S. same-store sales fell 0.2% in the third quarter.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/aca-stat.title: These states are offering extra ACA premium subsidies in 2027
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/aca-stat.author: Greg Iacurci
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/aca-stat.text:
About a dozen states are offering state-funded premium assistance to some ACA marketplace enrollees in 2027.

The programs are intended to soften the impact of enhanced federal premium tax credits that expired at the end of 2025.

Eligibility and subsidy amounts vary by state, and many programs focus on lower-income marketplace customers.

The states include California, Colorado, Connecticut, Maryland, Massachusetts, New Mexico, New Jersey, Rhode Island, Vermont, Virginia and Washington state.

Health care coverage in some states is going to get slightly more affordable in 2027.

At least 11 states are providing funding to Obamacare enrollees to reduce their monthly insurance premiums, which qualifying enrollees should see when they sign up for coverage this open enrollment season.

The move follows a lapse of enhanced federal premium subsidies in 2025 that drove up costs for millions of people who buy health plans on the Affordable Care Act marketplace. The states include California, Colorado, Connecticut, Maryland, Massachusetts, New Mexico, New Jersey, Rhode Island, Vermont, Virginia and Washington state.

Most of the states are continuing policies they put in place for 2026, in the aftermath of the loss of the federal subsidies. But Rhode Island and Virginia are debuting their respective programs for 2027, while other states like California expanded eligibility to additional consumers.

Health policy experts said the state funding could help prevent more consumers from dropping their insurance coverage, following a significant drop decline this year. It also comes amid a broader affordability crunch for U.S. households, which voters cited as a top issue in the recent midterm elections.

While enhanced federal premium subsidies lapsed at the end of 2025, there’s still a tranche of federal subsidies — known as premium tax credits — that remain in place. The funding offered by these 11 states comes on top of any federal subsidies consumers may receive.

The amount of financial assistance varies by state, and each state has different eligibility criteria. Many target their programs at lower-income consumers, experts said.

“This was an effort to make coverage more affordable again” for some people, said Louise Norris, a health policy analyst for insurance referral site healthinsurance.org. “It can certainly be significant if you qualify for the help your state provides.”

The states offering additional premium assistance operate state-based health insurance marketplaces rather than HealthCare.gov. They’re also largely Democratic-leaning states, health policy experts said.

Most offered premium assistance to state residents in 2026. However, Rhode Island and Virginia are new to the list for 2027.

In many of the states, officials said the move to offer state-funded premium assistance is a direct response to the lapse of enhanced ACA premium subsidies at the end of 2025.

After the lapse of the enhanced subsidies — which had been in effect since 2021 and helped push ACA enrollment to record highs — Obamacare premiums increased by an average of 58%, to $178 per month on average in 2026 from $113 per month the prior year, according to KFF, a nonpartisan health policy research group.

Democrats pushed to renew the enhanced premium subsidies — the crux of a government shutdown in 2025 that lasted more than a month — but the Republican-led Congress opted not to extend them.

ACA enrollment fell to 19.2 million as of February 2026, a 13% decline from 22.1 million in February 2025, according to figures published in June by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services.

Evidence suggests enrollment has fallen further since then, according to a KFF analysis.

Health policy experts largely attribute the decline to the expiration of enhanced subsidies, since the lapse pushed up costs for consumers.

“Where Congress has failed, Colorado is stepping up,” Gov. Jared Polis said in September in a press release discussing insurance premium assistance. “Despite the loss of the enhanced premium tax credits, we are doing everything we can to keep health insurance prices down so Coloradans can afford access to health care.”

Not all consumers enrolled in an ACA marketplace health plan will be eligible for their state’s financial assistance.

Of all the states, New Mexico is the only one that is fully replacing the enhanced federal premium subsidies for ACA enrollees in the state in 2027, extending a policy in place for 2026, according to health policy experts.

While ACA enrollment declined nationally in 2026, New Mexico was the only state to see an increase in its enrollment figures, growing 14% between 2025 and 2026, according to KFF.

Some states allocated more funding to their premium assistance programs for 2027 relative to 2026.

In California, for example, Gov. Gavin Newsom, a Democrat, and the California Legislature increased the amount of state funds available for the Covered California State Subsidy Program to $300 million in 2027 from $190 million in 2026, according to a press release on the state’s health insurance marketplace.

Californians with incomes up to 200% of the federal poverty level in 2027 — $31,920 for an individual or $66,000 for a family of four — will be eligible for a state premium subsidy. In 2026, those subsidies are available for households with incomes up to 165% of the federal poverty line.

As a result of the eligibility expansion, an additional 200,000 will be eligible for financial help who weren’t eligible in 2026, Covered California, the state marketplace, said in a press release.

Massachusetts also increased its investment in financial assistance for ACA enrollees to $620 million in 2027 from $600 million this year — the largest state investment in the country, state officials said in October.

The value of state assistance can be modest for some consumers, depending on factors like their income and monthly premiums, health policy experts said.

For example, in Washington state, ACA enrollees with an income up to 200% of the federal poverty line and who receive a federal subsidy can get a state-funded subsidy of up to $35 per month. Those with an income between 201% and 250% of the poverty line can get up to $20 per month.

That said, states that offer premium subsidies saw a lower decline in ACA marketplace enrollment than in states that didn’t offer any financial assistance, experts said.

“We saw that states in 2026 that did offer assistance had smaller declines in enrollment,” said Justin Lo, a senior researcher at KFF who specializes in the Affordable Care Act. “If the previous pattern continues, we will also see possibly better enrollment retention in states that are more generous with their subsidies.”

It’s not a guarantee states will be able to continue funding these subsidies into the future, experts said.

“Funding is obviously the crux of the issue,” said Norris, of healthinsurance.org. “Whether states will be able to continue to provide funding for these programs really depends on these states’ budgets.”
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/aca-stat.summary: The move follows a lapse of enhanced federal premium subsidies in 2025. The value of state assistance can be modest for some consumers, depending on factors like income and monthly premiums.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/coreweav.title: CoreWeave confronts 'doom cycle' narrative as neocloud credit risk overshadows growth
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/coreweav.author: Jordan Novet
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/coreweav.text:
Leading neoclouds CoreWeave and Nebius have both lost about half their value in the past month as they get set for earnings reports this week.

Yields on some CoreWeave bonds are trading above 16%.

Last week’s midterm elections, which produced sweeping victories for Democrats, added to uncertainty about the pace of the AI buildout.

After a tumultuous month for neoclouds that saw stock prices cut in half, investors are eager to hear how the leading companies in the space plan to navigate a tightening credit market and an unfavorable political environment.

CoreWeave
 is set to report quarterly results on Tuesday, followed by Nebius
 on Thursday. Both companies are reliant on debt to fund their purchases of cutting-edge artificial intelligence systems, but they’re confronting a skeptical base of lenders as the AI trade sours on Wall Street.

The neoclouds had a particularly rough day last Thursday, suffering dramatic drops and contributing to the Nasdaq’s steepest slump in 19 months. Leading chipmakers Nvidia
, Advanced Micro Devices
 and Micron
 also plummeted on concern that raging anti-AI sentiment would further complicate buildout plans.

Nvidia, a major investor in a number of neoclouds, including CoreWeave and Nebius, faces its own fresh turbulence after CEO Jensen Huang admitted Sunday that he’d had an extramarital affair with a business executive who intelligence agencies say is a Chinese spy. That news could add further volatility to an already nervous market.

Democrats last week won governors’ races in Georgia, Iowa, Nevada, Ohio and Texas, and voters rejected data centers in all but one of the 41 related measures on ballots across the country.

CoreWeave CEO Mike Intrator took to LinkedIn to try to temper investors’ fears.

“We currently don’t anticipate any impact to CoreWeave’s existing customer commitments or associated backlog as a result of shifts in the political landscape,” Intrator wrote.

But the market was unrelenting. Yields on some CoreWeave bonds maturing in 2031 jumped above 16%. The spread on its five-year credit default swaps, which are insurance against default, soared above 1,240 basis points, up 50% in the past month.

“I do agree completely that neoclouds in particular are going to be the most impacted,” Anastasia Amoroso, chief investment strategist at Partners Group, told CNBC’s “Closing Bell” on Friday. Unlike hyperscalers Amazon
 and Microsoft
, the top neoclouds are unprofitable and heavily dependent on a small number of customers.

IREN
, a smaller publicly traded neocloud, said in its earnings report late Thursday that about 48% of its backlog was tied to Microsoft. But the company provided some relief to the market after reporting that AI cloud revenue more than doubled from the prior period. IREN’s stock jumped 20% on Friday, recouping its losses from Thursday.

Daniel Roberts, co-CEO of IREN, told CNBC that there’s a “disconnect between what we’re seeing in public market and what we’re seeing at the customer level,” but he acknowledged the challenge posed by financial markets.

“Capital markets have become more selective in the last few weeks, and the questions have undoubtedly moved from how big the contract is to whether it can be delivered, financed, and run at a profit,” Roberts said on the earnings call. His company currently has $10 billion in debt.

At the end of June, CoreWeave was sitting on $5.5 billion in cash and $35 billion in debt. The company owed $1.3 billion at a 15% interest rate on a facility that comes due in March 2028, and had $3.2 billion in obligations on an August 2030 facility at an 11% rate, according to the latest earnings statement.

CoreWeave is unlikely to go bankrupt in the near future, and it has the funds to deliver on existing contracts, but growth over the next five years will require more capital, said Luke Yang, a Morningstar analyst covering CoreWeave.

“If they want to issue money through equities, the stock price is not working in their favor, because the stock has been beaten down,” Yang said. “So I also want to see how management talks about how to close this financing gap.”

Yang said he’s also paying attention to the broader neocloud market.

Nscale, based in the U.K., filed paperwork for an IPO in September but hasn’t published an updated prospectus since then. “I wouldn’t say it’s a good time for them to go public,” Yang said.

SB Energy, which filed at the beginning of September, is in a similar predicament, and Australian neocloud Firmus nixed plans for an IPO last month.

The uncertainty has not helped CoreWeave’s case, Intrator told employees in an October memo seen by CNBC.

“But these companies are trying to raise enormous amounts of capital without the execution, revenue, scale or software solutions that CoreWeave delivers to its customers,” he wrote.

Investors are still on watch. Paul Meeks, head of technology research at Freedom Capital Markets, told CNBC’s “Power Lunch” on Thursday that the narrative is “just so negative.”

“Unfortunately, it’s a self-fulfilling prophecy, a doom cycle, where if the creditors are worried about CoreWeave paying back their debts, then of course they have to borrow going forward to fund their AI infrastructure build at exorbitant rates,” he said.

CoreWeave generated $5 billion in revenue in 2025. Meeks estimates that number jumping to $42 billion in 2028, with an EBITDA (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization) margin that year of close to 70%.

“If they can get on that path and folks feel comfortable with that path, then they’ll feel more comfortable about the debts and CoreWeave’s financial wherewithal to pay those debts.”

For the most recent quarter, analysts expect revenue growth of about 160% from a year earlier to $3.55 billion, according to LSEG. Nebius is expected to report sixfold growth to about $908 million.

Meeks said he expects the market to get “some relief” from both earnings reports.

CoreWeave declined to comment. Nebius didn’t respond to a request for comment.

For Meeks, the key is getting capital markets back on board with the neoclouds’ growth story, and believing that profits are on the way.

“You can have a healthy bank, but if there’s a run on banks generally speaking then they could be in some trouble,” he said. “So I am not fool enough to downplay the credit risk.”

https://www.cnbc.com/make-it/2026/11/09/.title: Why tech workers are flocking to NYC
https://www.cnbc.com/make-it/2026/11/09/.author: Sophie Caldwell,Zachary Green
https://www.cnbc.com/make-it/2026/11/09/.text:
Erin Sullivan had only visited New York City once before she decided to take a job in the Big Apple.

But that visit made a strong impression: “Having the freedom of just hopping on the subway and getting anywhere was so magical for me,” she says. “I knew that I wanted to end back up” in the city.

After graduating from the University of Oklahoma in 2023 with a computer science degree, Sullivan, 25, landed a role as a software engineer at Bank of America in New York City.

She’s part of a growing contingent of tech workers who are drawn to the city.

The New York metro area is now home to the most tech workers in the country with 394,300 jobs, edging out the San Francisco Bay Area’s 375,730 jobs, according to an August report from CBRE, a real estate services and investment firm.

Between 2022 and 2025, New York’s pool of tech employees grew by over 30,000, while San Francisco’s shrank by nearly 24,000 workers.

In today’s tech talent market, “the Big Apple is on top,” says Lauren Crowley Corrinet, vice chairman at CBRE.

But a big part of New York’s tech hiring boom comes from outside the traditional tech sector, according to Julie Samuels, president and CEO of Tech:NYC, a nonprofit representing the city’s technology industry.

According to Tech:NYC’s data, just 35% of NYC’s tech employees work at tech companies and startups, while 64% are employed by non-tech companies like banks and media organizations, based on their report published in November 2026.

“When you think about industries like finance, like real estate — industries that have been in New York for a really long time — it has become increasingly clear that technology is driving their work as well,” Samuels says.

To keep up with artificial intelligence developments, “everyone is hiring” tech workers and consultants, she says: “All these traditional industries are thinking about how they can bring AI into the fold in their own work.”

And AI companies are expanding their reach in the city, too: OpenAI leased a 90,000-square-foot office in lower Manhattan, and Anthropic says it plans to double its New York workforce to 1,000 employees in 2026.

It’s no mystery why workers are drawn to New York City, according to Corrinet: “Everything’s here, and it’s just such a rich and engaging place for people to live.”

But New York’s high cost of living can pose a challenge even for tech workers “who make six figures right out of college,” according to Samuels. On the other hand, there are valid concerns that an influx of highly paid tech workers could worsen the affordability crisis for other New Yorkers, she says.

Her goal is to ensure that New York’s growing tech presence benefits all New Yorkers, not just those who work in the industry.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/novonesi.title: Could supplements be the next big opportunity in the GLP-1 weight-loss drug boom?
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/novonesi.author: Elsa Ohlen
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/novonesi.text:
GLP-1 medications and dietary supplements could play complementary roles in managing obesity and supporting longer-term health, Novonesis CEO Ester Baiget told CNBC on Monday.

“We have scientific evidence that [is] going to support the patients [on] GLP-1s feeling better, as a companion during the treatment,” Baiget said.

The lucrative weight-loss drugs market pioneered by Novo and U.S. rival Eli Lilly has had far-reaching consequences beyond health companies.

Supplements could be the next major sector to benefit from the weight-loss drug boom, Novonesis CEO told CNBC on Monday, as the biosolutions company explores whether microbiome products can help patients on popular GLP-1 medicines.

“We have scientific evidence that [is] going to support the patients [on] GLP-1s feeling better, as a companion during the treatment,” CEO Ester Baiget told “Squawk Box Europe,” referencing an ongoing study with Novo Nordisk
.

GLP-1 medications and dietary supplements, such as those being developed by Novonesis, could play complementary roles in managing obesity and supporting longer-term health, she argued.

While medications can help treat obesity, improving the gut microbiome through nutrition and scientifically backed supplements could support longer-term health, Baiget said.

The microbiome refers to the community of microorganisms, including bacteria, fungi and viruses, that live in or on different parts of the body, particularly in the gut.

Baiget also sees strong commercial demand for supplements with proven health benefits.

“We see that when we prove science with answers, there is a tremendous pull in the market,” she said. Novonesis is currently studying what Baiget referred to as “a unique cocktail” of pro-, pre- and post-biotics to support patients taking GLP-1s made by Wegovy and Ozempic maker Novo Nordisk.

The lucrative weight-loss drugs market pioneered by Novo Nordisk and U.S. rival Eli Lilly
 has had far-reaching consequences beyond health companies.

From consumer staples and food companies reassessing meal composition and sizes, to fashion companies seeing a boost from consumers buying new clothes after dropping sizes, drugs like Wegovy and Zepbound are widely considered to be reshaping consumer spending across industries.

According to a PwC survey of U.K. adults, about 70% of GLP-1 users are spending less on snacks, while 40% are spending more on vitamins and supplements. More than 80% of respondents who had now stopped taking the medicine said they maintained some of the dietary changes they adopted while on treatment.

Meanwhile, the global dietary supplements market was valued at an estimated $209.5 billion in 2025 and is projected to more than double to $431.7 billion by 2033, according to Grand View Research.

Growing health awareness is driving demand for supplements and functional foods and drinks containing ingredients such as vitamins and probiotics, as consumers seek benefits beyond basic nutrition, the market research firm found.

The global probiotic supplements market was estimated to be worth around $10.5 billion in 2025, growing to $17.5 billion by 2033.

Some research has linked GLP-1 treatment to insufficient protein intake and deficiencies in certain vitamins and minerals, but the extent to which the medications themselves are responsible remains unclear. The microbiome-based products being studied by Novonesis are different from protein and vitamin supplements, and any potential benefit for GLP-1 users has yet to be established.

For Novonesis, if benefits are scientifically proven, it could be a welcome boost to its human health business, which is currently under pressure.

Its human health business reported an 8% decline in organic sales in the third quarter, weighed down by weaker demand for probiotic supplements sold through offline channels in North America.

The company, formed through the merger of Novozymes and Chr. Hansen in 2024, is a leader in enzymes and microbial solutions used across industries such as food, agriculture, and healthcare. Its products are used in everything from dairy fermentation to dietary supplements.

The company holds nearly 50% of the enzymes and cultures market, compared with around 20% for rival International Flavors & Fragrances, according to Morningstar.

Novonesis gets about a third of total sales from the North American market, while Human Health accounts for about 11% of its total sales.

1. Anything less than a 10% decline today for Nvidia
 would be lucky given the dead-money nature of the stock. In the premarket, shares are off 6%. This was a tough stock to own even before we learned the board is investigating CEO Jensen Huang for an affair with an accused Chinese spy. The investigation should revolve around whether Jensen knowingly or unknowingly sent GPUs to China because of his relationship with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang. My weekend column for Club members.

2. Even with Nvidia’s decline, stock futures are green across the board this morning. Dow futures are leading the way, up over D00 points. We’re getting help from a more than 4% drop in Brent crude. The main question for this week: Can the artificial intelligence trade get its momentum back? This Nvidia story is a new wrinkle. CoreWeave
’s earnings report tomorrow night is hugely important too.

3. Wells Fargo lowered its price target on CoreWeave
 to $115 from $160 ahead of the quarter. But analysts kept their buy rating on the stock, calling CoreWeave the best company in the neocloud space. They expect CoreWeave’s revenue and compute capacity to come in better than expected. Funding needs to be a key focus for investors.

4. Fellow neocloud Iren
 had its price target at JPMorgan cut to $55 from $65. Kept its buy rating, though, with analysts seeing continued improvements into contract pricing. Why cut your price target then? Why not wait for the stock to rebound higher? I’ll be interviewing Iren CEO Daniel Roberts on “Mad Money” tonight. First time on.

5. Advanced Micro Devices
 was upgraded to buy from hold at Oppenheimer. Analysts raised their estimates for AMD and expect its data center business to accelerate materially into 2027. OpenAI and Meta are key customers. AMD shares have been crushed since their all-time closing high on Oct. 6, tumbling over 30% as the market turned against AI buildout winners. Oppenheimer’s price target of $600 is $49 below that record close.

6. Jefferies hiked its price target on Eli Lilly
 to $1,700 from $1,610 and kept its buy rating on the longtime Club stock. Analysts argued that Lilly’s international GLP-1 business is underappreciated by Wall Street and could represent roughly half of revenues long term. Upside surprises from the ex-U.S. business have been critical to the stock this year.

7. JPMorgan upgraded SAP
 to buy from hold and increased its price target. These were the companies that were thought to be overrun by AI, but it turns out they’re needed to integrate it. The analysts described it as going from “pilot to production.” While in different businesses, in enterprise software, we own Salesforce
, which is making it own push to help companies integrate AI.

8. Alphabet
 out and Meta Platforms
 in. JPMorgan made the swap on its analyst focus list, saying it could take time to improve search monetization, which was a ding on the Google parent’s most recent quarter. As for Meta, the analysts see continued strong revenue from AI-driven ads; also bullish on Muse. They kept buys on both Club stocks.

9. No iPhone Duo delays after all? JPMorgan said its product availability tracker shows Duo delivery dates on the Apple
 foldable “broadly unchanged.” Tracker shows lead times on iPhone 18 Pro Max “moderate sharply but remain modestly above the prior year.” Pro leads “near immediate.” The takeaway? JPMorgan sees Apple’s “revenue growth likely to benefit from customer preference for the higher-priced models.”

10. Very interesting call: KeyBanc raised its Ollie’s Bargain Outlet
 price target to $120 from $98. Kept buy. The analysts said Ollie’s stock valuation reflects concerns associated with transitory, weather-related challenges in the company’s fiscal second quarter. They believe Q3 is running ahead of Street expectations. Ollie’s is expected to report earnings next month.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/nvidia-j.title: Nvidia's CEO turmoil gives newly empowered Democrats fresh ammunition in pursuit of oversight
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/nvidia-j.author: Kif Leswing
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/nvidia-j.text:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy comes as the company is about to face heightened scrutiny in Washington, D.C.

Huang apologized in a letter to staffers for being “unfaithful to my wife,” and said the board is conducting an investigation “regarding the national security concerns” raised in reports.

Nvidia’s base of investors has already grown more skeptical due to fears that the AI buildout may slow.

Nvidia
 CEO Jensen Huang’s close ties to the U.S. government were already poised to loosen with Democrats winning control of Congress and promising far more oversight of AI development than what the chip giant has experienced under Republican leadership.

That was before Huang admitted on Sunday to having an extramarital affair with a businesswoman who intelligence agencies say is a Chinese spy. The woman, Alice Huang, is affiliated with an Nvidia customer called Megaspeed that’s been accused of helping restricted Chinese companies acquire Nvidia’s artificial intelligence chips.

Huang apologized to staffers in a note on Sunday for being “unfaithful to my wife,” and said the company’s board was investigating any related national security concerns. Nvidia’s board said it has “confidence in Jensen,” who co-founded the company in 1993 and has led it ever since, building a net worth of more than $150 billion in the process.

Even before last week’s midterm elections, which saw Democrats win sweeping majorities in the House and Senate, vocal party leaders wanted answers from Huang about China’s access to advanced Nvidia chips and his company’s lobbying for favorable legislation. Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts said days before the election, when the spy story was first surfacing, that “we must pass bipartisan legislation to keep our advanced AI technology out of China’s hands.” Months before that, in June, Huang declined an invitation from Warren to testify before the Senate Banking Committee.

With Democrats about to take the gavel, Delaware Sen. Chris Coons, who is in line to chair the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, wrote on X on Saturday that “Congress will investigate and get answers,” following the allegations that appeared in a New York Times report Friday.

It’s a sharp reversal for Huang, who gained first-name status with President Donald Trump and has been closely allied with the administration in trying to limit AI regulation. Nvidia shares plunged 12% in the two days after the election, pacing a drop in AI-related stocks, on fears that incoming lawmakers, at the federal and state levels, and a host of newly passed ballot measures will slow the buildout and halt the AI boom.

Huang is a singular voice in the AI industry, as his company’s technology is used to train nearly all major AI models. He’s also turned Nvidia into an essential source of financing for AI startups, and pulled together some of the biggest names on Wall Street into a group that announced plans in August to raise $500 billion for investing in the buildout.

At Nvidia, Huang is the sole public face of the company and has no clear second-in-command. He decides which projects are a strategic priority, and frequently sends short emails to individual engineers about details. Huang has said he has 60 direct reports and reviews every employee’s salary. Meanwhile, he packs his calendar with meetings with world leaders and CEOs, alongside keynote speeches at conferences and trade shows.

“Nvidia is not an ordinary company and Jensen is not an ordinary CEO; he IS Nvidia,” Bernstein analyst Stacy Rasgon wrote in a note on Sunday, adding that it’s not clear who would succeed him.

Patrick Moorhead, CEO at Moor Insights & Strategy, said in an email that “Jensen holding so much power is why Nvidia moves faster than anyone.”

Unlike many of his tech peers, Huang is not chairman of the board. Rather, he’s one of 11 board members, and there’s no designated chair.

One investor close to Huang told CNBC that, depending on what the board’s investigation finds, he could foresee Huang taking a leave of absence.

“Today’s news will not slow Nvidia,” a company spokesperson said in a statement. “Jensen is committed to continuing to lead Nvidia as CEO without interruption.”

But scrutiny of Nvidia is set to intensify on Wall Street and in Washington, where Huang’s level of influence is almost certain to change.

He has been a major advocate for more chip exports to China, arguing that it’s better for AI labs there to build on American technology than to encourage the development of domestic alternatives. Huang joined Trump on Air Force One in May on a China trip that’s now raised additional questions about what the administration and Huang knew about Chinese spying at the time.

One question Democrats are likely to probe is whether the Trump administration was aware of Huang’s relationship with the alleged Chinese spy, and whether the Nvidia CEO influenced American policy, said Sam Bresnick, a research fellow at the Center for Security and Emerging Technology.

“That is going to be very high up on the Democrats’ lists of people to investigate to try to figure out to what extent was the Trump administration aware of what was going on,” Bresnick said.

But pressure isn’t just coming from Democrats. House Republican leaders have already asked Huang for a closed-door briefing on Chinese spying issues later this month.

Trump has continued to back Huang, telling reporters on Sunday that he’s an “honorable guy” and has “done an amazing job for our country.”

“I think he probably has an excuse for it,” Trump said of the incident.

Amid all the noise about the election results and the spying revelations, Nvidia is facing a crucial stretch on the markets.

Neoclouds CoreWeave
 and Nebius
, which are both backed by Nvidia and are big buyers of its chips, are scheduled to report earnings this week after their stocks lost roughly half their value over the past month. Investors are particularly concerned about their hefty debt loads and how they’ll continue to fund their buildouts with interest rates rising and lenders turning skittish.

Nvidia has its own earnings report coming on Nov. 17, when Huang, assuming he sticks with the typical format, will face questions from analysts. And then there’s the Anthropic initial public offering, which is critical for Nvidia as it’s both an investor in the Claude creator and counts the AI lab as a significant customer.

A couple of weeks after earnings, Nvidia is hosting a large conference in Washington, D.C., where Huang is scheduled to give the keynote on Dec. 1.

Bullish investors and analysts can still point to the insatiable demand for Nvidia’s technology. The company recently projected 70% sales growth in its upcoming fiscal year. Analysts polled by FactSet expect nearly $694 billion in fiscal 2028 sales.

“We believe demand for the company’s products seems unlikely to be affected,” Rasgon wrote. “But it seems plausible to postulate increased risks (regulatory etc.) as AI buildouts become an increasingly political issue.”

— CNBC’s Seema Mody, Katie Tarasov, Ashley Capoot and MacKenzie Sigalos contributed reporting to this report.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/megaspee.title: What is Megaspeed? The Nvidia chip buyer in the spotlight after Jensen Huang’s affair
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/megaspee.author: Jenni Reid
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/megaspee.text:
Nvidia is investigating whether CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a woman intelligence agencies belive is a Chinese spy.

He has admitted to an affair, understood to be with an executive at Singapore-based cloud provider Megaspeed.

It has faced scrutiny over allegations that Nvidia chips it acquired were diverted to China. Megaspeed denies wrongdoing and says inspections found no violations.

Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed is in the international spotlight after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted to being unfaithful to his wife, following reports linking him to Megaspeed executive Alice Huang.

U.S. intelligence officials believe she is a Chinese intelligence asset, according to The New York Times.

While the Nvidia CEO — one of the world’s most prominent executives and a figurehead of the AI industry – did not name Megaspeed or Alice Huang in his statement, he acknowledged his infidelity and said Nvidia’s Board of Directors had begun an independent investigation “regarding the national security concerns raised in news reports.”

“I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America’s national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American,” he said.

Nvidia said in a statement it had “no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised,” but that its “Board’s inquiry will examine all available information.”

Tech darling Nvidia sells advanced AI and data center chips and has customers including Microsoft
, Amazon
, Google
, Meta
 and Oracle
. The explosion in AI adoption in recent years has fueled its stock and pushed it to a $5 trillion market cap earlier this year.

Megaspeed sells services to Asia Pacific-based companies that need large amounts of computing capacity, usually for AI projects, by selling access to computing resources hosted in data centers in Southeast Asia.

It advertises itself as a “core business partner” of Nvidia’s computing power cloud business in the region, allowing customers to rent computing power from Nvidia GPUs, or “graphics processing units” — specialized chips designed to do many calculations at the same time.

The service allows businesses to complete costly AI operations without buying and operating all the hardware themselves. It can also give customers remote access to computing power from advanced chips located outside China. U.S. controls restrict the export of some advanced chips to China, but remote access is a separate question.

Megaspeed, which has offices in Singapore and Indonesia, has previously faced media and government scrutiny over whether some of its GPUs have been redirected to China.

A report published by Bloomberg in December 2025 stated that the U.S. government was investigating Megaspeed’s ownership structure and whether it had smuggled Nvidia chips to China.

A response to the article published on Megaspeed’s website said it contained “misleading information and incorrect insinuations.” It added that inspections by the Bureau of Industry and Security of the U.S. Commerce Department, the Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry of Malaysia, and Nvidia had found “no evidence of any violations concerning the illicit transfer of chips or any illegal activities.”

Businesswoman Alice Huang is an “executive” at Megaspeed and a “publicly reported Chinese intelligence asset,” according to a House Select Committee on China statement on Nov. 5. Committee heads have requested Jensen Huang’s attendance at a Nov. 18 briefing to establish “the extent to which U.S. national security has been placed at risk” after reports raised “significant national security concerns regarding [China’s] access to sensitive U.S. technology and information.”

According to New York Times reporting this month, Alice Huang is a Chinese citizen who speaks good English and is well-connected among high-ranking chip industry executives.

The Times reported on Friday that a memo was distributed among policymakers in the Trump administration last spring identifying a Chinese businesswoman with a close relationship to Jensen Huang as passing information about U.S. AI chips to Beijing’s top spy agency and seeking policy influence.

Bloomberg reports that Alice Huang also goes by Huang Le and helped set Megaspeed up in 2023, shortly after the U.S. issued its first chip export bans targeting China during the Biden administration. The sanctions are an attempt to curb Chinese breakthroughs in artificial intelligence, especially in military applications, via U.S.-made technology.

Bloomberg previously listed her as one of the people collaborating with a Singapore police investigation into the company’s activities in relation to China. Singapore’s government has said it had not investigated Alice Huang’s alleged intelligence ties or her relationship with Jensen Huang.

CNBC has contacted Megaspeed for comment.

The reports about the relationship prompted renewed scrutiny of Jensen Huang’s past comments on engaging with the Chinese market. He told CNBC’s Arjun Kharpal on Oct. 22: “No market is closed forever, and China wants foreign companies to invest in China, just as Germany wants foreign companies and countries to invest in Germany.”

“And so the market has to be open and it has to be welcoming. There’s no reason to believe that market is going to be closed to the best competitors in the world, and Nvidia is surely the best in the world at doing what we do.”

Correction: This article has been corrected to change an instance of an incorrect spelling of Jensen Huang’s name.

https://insideclimatenews.org/news/09112.title: Fallout From the Flames
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/09112.author: By Kiley Price, Keerti Gopal, Nina Dietz
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/09112.text:
An inside look at top climate news, delivered every two weeks.

Welcome to Inside Climate, a podcast from the staff of Inside Climate News. Powerful wildfires upended life for residents in Maui, Hawaiʻi, in 2023. In early 2025, the Eaton and Palisades fires caused similar devastation in greater Los Angeles. Years have passed since the fires were contained but researchers are still trying to understand the lasting effects of these disasters. Co-host Kiley Price discusses those efforts with Inside Climate News reporter Keerti Gopal, who has chronicled the recovery in Maui, and contributor Nina Dietz, who has covered the health impacts of the fires in Los Angeles.

Listen and subscribe on YouTube, Spotify, Apple Podcasts, Amazon Music, and iHeart.

It’s been three years since high winds spread multiple wildfires across Maui and eviscerated the town of Lahaina.

KEERTI GOPAL: The Maui wildfires were the deadliest fires that the U.S. has seen in more than a century.

Since then, researchers have been closely following thousands of survivors, trying to understand the fire’s lingering effects on human health.

KEERTI GOPAL: They’re finding elevated levels of these metals in survivors’ urine months after the fires.

MEDICAL WORKER: You’re gonna take a huge inhale.

KEERTI GOPAL: Some of these metals are linked to elevated cancer risks.

Meanwhile, Los Angeles is on a similar recovery path to Maui, due to the deadly Palisades and Eaton fires that covered portions of Los Angeles in ash almost two years ago.

NINA DIETZ: There’s this huge issue of contaminated homes. They have things like lead and cadmium, and in some cases, even cyanide and arsenic in crawl spaces.

As large, urban wildfires burn more synthetic materials, researchers are racing to better understand health impacts.

NINA DIETZ: A few scientists have actually brought up 9/11. There’s this real concern that we’re going to see this major cancer cohort that we do not have the capabilities to deal with and that could have been prevented.

That’s coming up on Inside Climate.

Welcome to Inside Climate. I’m your host, Kiley Price.

On Aug. 8, 2023 a red flag alert was issued by the National Weather Service in Honolulu, warning of “high fire danger with rapid spread.” That same day, fires tore across parts of Maui and leveled thousands of structures on the island’s western shore.

The flames have been extinguished, but the fire continues to leave its mark on thousands of survivors who have struggled to rebuild their lives. Many battle insurance companies over homes and hospital bills. Others endure lingering health issues, but can’t afford to seek medical care.

A multi-year research project spearheaded by the University of Hawaiʻi aims to chronicle the health impacts of the fire. Its early findings indicate that urban wildfires could have far more damaging impacts than previously known.

Meanwhile, a couple of scientists who studied the Maui aftermath have since relocated to California to conduct similar analyses following the Los Angeles wildfires of 2025. Both places have struggled to maintain funding for research as the Trump administration reshapes FEMA and other agencies that have historically supported disaster recovery and response.

We’ll speak to ICN reporter Keerti Gopal, who traveled to Maui earlier this year to follow the researchers studying and addressing survivor health and raising funds to expand the study.

And then we’ll talk to contributor Nina Dietz, who has been reporting on the health risks of the LA wildfires as part of ICN’s “After the Fires” series, supported by the Pulitzer Center.

Keerti, thanks so much for coming on the show today.

Thank you for having me.

Keerti covers the intersections of climate change, public health and environmental justice at Inside Climate News. She’s a National Geographic Explorer and has received several fellowships from Fulbright, the Solutions Journalism Network and the National Press Foundation.

So you traveled to Hawaiʻi a few months ago to report on the aftermath of the devastating Maui wildfires, which broke out in August 2023. That wildfire killed more than 100 people and destroyed more than 2,200 buildings, costing around $5.5 billion in damages. How are things looking three years later?

Recovery is definitely moving forward, but there’s still a lot of work to be done and it’s going pretty slowly in some ways. As of October, according to the county, there are about 300 single-family homes that have been completed and another 300 homes in multifamily units. And that’s part of only about 30 structures. Overall, that’s about 330 buildings out of 2,200 that were destroyed, like you said. And more than 12,000 people were also displaced in these fires. So there’s a lot of people that are still living in temporary housing.

So how have the wildfires and this recovery process itself affected people’s health?

Yeah, so I went to Maui to write about the Maui Wildfire Exposure Study, which is a multi-year research effort from the University of Hawaiʻi, and they’re really looking to chronicle both the short- and long-term health impacts of the fires. In the past three years, they’ve had more than 2,500 participants in the study, and they’re looking at a range of kind of dimensions of health. So they’re looking at lung function, metabolic health, mental health. They’re looking at cancer risks and environmental exposures, things like heavy metals in survivors’ urine.

They’ve found so far that the health impacts are ongoing. So there have been widespread mental health impacts, including high levels of depression, anxiety and PTSD. And they’ve also found that those are really closely related to things like housing instability and lack of employment. And they’ve also found things like breathing troubles with survivors and links between elevated levels of heavy metals, some metals that were found in the burn zone ash as well, and links between that and impaired lung function in survivors.

So food insecurity and declining levels of social support are also two things that are persistent issues three years on. And they’ve found that in children there are some pretty concerning results with ongoing emotional stress and trauma and some issues with blood pressure and lung health that you wouldn’t be expecting to see in young kids.

Yeah, and you kind of touched on this, but this is an interesting place for a fire to happen because it’s partially urban. How is that different from a forest wildfire? And can you explain to me how and why Maui wildfire victims were exposed to those heavy metals that you mentioned?

Yeah, so the Maui wildfires were the deadliest fires that the U.S. has seen in more than a century. And when a wildfire burns through an urban environment where people are living, it’s burning up all of the chemicals that are part of our daily lives. So things like cars, homes, electronics, other synthetic materials that we have in our homes, and that brings a lot of unique health concerns that you might not see in a forest fire that’s burning through organic materials, so like a forest, trees, things like that, not the kind of man-made synthetic types of things that we have in our urban environments, which can contain chemicals, contain toxins. And in urban environments, fires can also kind of dislodge some of the contamination that might be existing in a soil from another era of a place. So on Maui, they’re continuing to research this, and it’s actually really difficult to pinpoint the source of some of the heavy metals that you’re mentioning. So they’re finding these elevated levels of these metals in survivor’s urine months after the fires. And right now they’re trying to understand better, like, where those could be coming from. Some of those sources might predate the fires. They’re looking into, kind of, the history of agriculture and industry and plantations on Maui to try to see what connections there might be there.

And what health impacts might those specifically have?

So some of these metals are linked to elevated cancer risks and widespread health risks. And specifically in this study, they found an association—so they’re not necessarily able to say causal yet—but they found an association between elevated levels of some of these metals and lower lung function, so trouble breathing. And that’s months after the fires happen. So it’s really kind of underscoring the need for continued monitoring and the fact that these fires can have an impact on people’s bodies long after the smoke is gone.

Right. ’Cause in the context of fire and recovery, three years is not that long, right?

Absolutely. Something this study has really underscored that is broadly applicable to disasters is how long the aftermath is, both for people’s like literal recovery, rebuilding, getting home and also health and mental health and ongoing trauma. So, yeah, the researchers are hoping to keep this study going for several more years. And it’s something that’s a conversation in the post-disaster research space, is that we need to be doing these kind of longitudinal studies looking long term at these health impacts, because you can’t know right after the fires what the long-term health impacts are gonna be.

It makes sense that researchers would want to study survivors and understand these health impacts, but how does this project differ from other response efforts?

This is a really unique study. It’s called the Maui Wildfire Exposure Study. It’s also known as MauiWES for short. And it’s kind of unique because they’re combining research with interventions. And they’re working to kind of get participants connected with things like therapy, food assistance, in some cases, like cash support, healthcare providers, in some cases even health insurance, and so they’re really hoping that this could potentially become the new norm for post-disaster research. And I’ve spoken with a lot of post-disaster researchers in other parts of the country about this study. And there’s a broad consensus, it seems like, that this is a really unique and kind of remarkable study. Some participants even said that the study saved their lives.

Wow, can you tell me more about that?

There’s one participant who I met, her name is Amy Jackson, and she came into MauiWES about a year after the fires. And she had such a low hemoglobin count that it wasn’t even registering on MauiWES’s system. And so the team immediately was like, “You need to go see your doctor.” She went to urgent care, they sent her to the hospital, and at the hospital she had to get a blood transfusion because her hemoglobin was so low, and the doctors told her that, you know, she was in critical condition. So she really sees MauiWES as having saved her life. And she actually was a trauma nurse, and she said that she, like, never really goes in to get medical care typically, and she had only signed up for the study because she wanted to get the $100 cash incentive that they were giving out to give her daughter for her birthday. So she herself was like, “I would never have gone in to see a doctor if it wasn’t for this study.” And that was something that I heard a lot because, you know, there is a provider shortage on Maui and it is kind of difficult to see specialists. It can also be difficult to see primary care providers. And so when MauiWES did their kind of first round of testing, about six to 12 months after the fires, that was a lot of people’s first time ever seeing a health care provider since the fires, which is pretty intense considering what people had been going through.

Can you tell me more about this provider shortage?

Yeah, so that’s something that affects across the state of Hawaiʻi, and it’s particularly severe on Maui. Maui is a relatively rural island, so they have kind of like a more rural healthcare infrastructure, and it’s been a challenge to get physicians to come to and stay in Hawaiʻi. So that’s something the state is dealing with. There’s a shortage in primary care providers across the board, and then there’s also a real shortage in specialists.

I think this is probably at odds with how a lot of people who are not from Hawaiʻi might understand what Maui looks like. Can you talk to me about what the full time population is on Maui?

Maui overall is really diverse, and Lahaina in particular, which is where the fires hit hardest, is a really diverse community. So before the fires, from census data, about a third of Lahaina residents are immigrants, and Maui also has a really strong Filipino population, partially because of the plantation history of the island.

And something that the researchers mentioned was that for some of the immigrant population, and particularly undocumented immigrants, that kind of access to healthcare was even more of a challenge and even more of a concern. There was one participant who I met who is undocumented and she came into the study with kind of persistent symptoms of, like, bronchitis and pneumonia. She’d had them for months, she hadn’t seen a doctor. And she was showing kind of signs of a potentially serious lung infection. And some of the physicians who were volunteering with MauiWES were really concerned and they said she needed medical attention. But she didn’t have insurance and she was also one of the 10 percent of study participants who had lost their jobs in the fire, so she didn’t really have options. And this was a pretty unique situation where the study actually was able to partner up with this local community organization called Roots Reborn that works with immigrants on Maui. And they worked with Kaiser Permanente, a private insurance company, to get her charitable insurance and then she was actually able to get surgery that she needed. And that has happened through MauiWES and their partnership with Roots Reborn. They’ve done that for hundreds of people, getting them get connected with health insurance.

There’s been a lot of reporting about challenges to post disaster recovery and funding under the Trump administration as it aims to reshape FEMA and other related agencies. Has that impacted MauiWES at all or the broader wildfire recovery?

Yeah, it’s definitely a big conversation in the wildfire recovery and post disaster recovery space. Something that has been an ongoing challenge for MauiWES is funding and keeping the study funded. Partially because they are trying to do this as a long-term effort, and it’s expensive to keep that up. So when they first started, they kind of like hit the ground running after the fires, trying to get testing up as quickly as they could, and they did that with kind of early charitable funding from some organizations and companies on Maui. And then they got some funding from the state. And then about a year after the fires, they got funding from the NIH, National Institutes of Health. But that support kind of came into question after Donald Trump took office because he was slashing a lot of the programs focused on diversity and health outcomes, and their funding was from the Minority Health Disparities Program. And so they weren’t really sure what that was going to look like going forward.

Where do things stand now? Is this study going to continue?

Yes, so it’s a happy ending. They actually ended up getting their federal funding through. And that came through this summer and in the fall. And they also got another $2 million from the county, Maui County, and that one’s really focused on kind of expanding the initiative to other more remote corners of the island and kind of places that are impacted by those healthcare shortages we were talking about.

When you’ve spoken to the researchers, how are they talking about some of the lessons learned from their experiences and passing it on to other communities, places like California, which is no stranger to fires, and other places around the country?

Yeah, that’s been really striking. Something that’s been coming up a lot is that climate change is bringing more of these intense and severe disasters with more frequency. I mean, Hawaiʻi this summer alone has been kind of hit with back to back storms. There’s been a lot of damages and just a lot of kind of like very little time to recover in between these storms.

Building that resilience and trying to figure out how do we respond to disasters better and more quickly and more holistically is super important right now. And so they’ve been talking to researchers in Utah after the fires there. They were talking to researchers across the country and in particular, in Los Angeles and Southern California. There’s a big health study effort that’s happening right now following the fires there in 2025. And they’ve been partnering really closely with MauiWES and kind of talking about how do we incorporate a lot of the same kind of holistic structures and things like that into that study there.

Keerti, I think this is the perfect place to pause because we’re going to speak with Nina Dietz, who has been doing related reporting on the Palisades and Altadena wildfires that happened in 2025. Thank you so much for sharing about your reporting.

Awesome. Thank you for having me.

Nina, it’s great to have you join the show given all the extensive reporting you’ve done at Inside Climate News on the series “After the Fires,” which examines the health risks following the LA wildfires. Welcome.

Thanks. And thanks for having me here to talk about this series.

Yeah, Nina is a contributor at Inside Climate News and frequently writes about climate, environmental health and accessibility in the environmental context as a freelance journalist. Her work has appeared in Sierra Magazine, Wired and Science Friday, among others.

Nina, we just heard from Keerti Gopal about the health impacts victims of the Maui wildfires are experiencing, but they are in year three of their recovery. You’ve been documenting the health impacts of the wildfires in Los Angeles, which took place in January 2025. The Eaton and Palisades fires burned through more than 38,000 acres, destroyed more than 16,000 structures and killed 31 people. They also displaced 205,000 people.

Where do things currently stand with recovery efforts in the Palisades and Altadena?

So the recovery’s been pretty slow. More than 70 percent of survivors are still displaced and there’s this huge issue of contaminated homes. A lot of the homes that were left standing were at first assumed to be safe, but we’ve learned that they are pretty toxic. They have things like lead and cadmium and in some cases, even cyanide and arsenic in crawl spaces, just soaked into the paint. And the cleanup itself has had a number of issues because the Army Corps of Engineers and EPA declined to do post-remediation soil testing. So though it had been cleaned up, it’s not really clear to what standard.

Yeah, and as I mentioned, we just spoke about the Maui wildfires. You’ve been following researchers studying fire impacts in the spring of 2025 in LA. Have any of their efforts mirrored what happened in Maui or diverged?

One of the saving graces in the case of the LA wildfires, if such a thing can be said to exist, is that this occurred in a state that has a very robust university system where there are a lot of interlinked universities, where as soon as it became clear that the government was not going to be stepping in to do the testing, the UC system and individual scientists just sort of jumped in, as well as the Harvard T.H. Chan School, who’s also done a lot of work in Maui. So I think some of the same scientists who actually spent several months out in Maui afterward were ones I  interviewed for my initial story.

Yeah, you, you mentioned some federal involvement right after the fires, but why isn’t the Army Corps collecting soil samples? And have the cleanup efforts been satisfactory in LA?

It comes down to some rather bureaucratic bid issues. They couldn’t get a contract or bid that was within their budget. Part of that has to do with the scale of the wildfires, and another part of that has to do with how underfunded the post-disaster branch of these major agencies is. So I would not be surprised if this is not the last time we see this happening.

Yeah, we heard from Keerti that Maui victims had elevated levels of heavy metals in their samplings. Did researchers discover similar findings with LA victims of the fire?

They found a lot of high levels of lead. There was, some of that testing is still ongoing, and some of it has yet to be released. Of what’s been released, some of it has to do with the firefighters themselves, where they actually took samples before the fire season and samples again right after the LA fires, and they found really elevated levels of inflammation proteins in the blood and inflammatory markers.

And what might that indicate?

It can indicate a variety of things, but in this instance it indicates probably that something has done some damage somewhere in the body, or that the immune system is noticing something that it does not like in the body. The immune system is sort of the bouncers of the body. And that works really well if you’ve got a virus or bacterial infection, but if you have tiny particles that are really embedded in your cells, it can actually become a problem because the body’s attempts to get it out can actually cause more damage.

Was there anything else the researchers discovered with exposures to heavy metals?

So the toxic metals actually showed up in these really ultrafine particles known as nanoparticles that are under one micron. They’re small enough to reach the heart, the lungs, and like I said, really embed themselves in your cells. UCLA’s Candace Tsai says there’s no safe exposure level for these particles. They really just embed themselves all over your body. And they can end up in your brain, which is particularly terrifying to me.

Are researchers finding that various air, water or soil tests and results for certain hazards are within the range that the EPA deems safe?

So the academic community has known for a long time that the EPA limits are too high. A lot of them are based on OSHA limits, which are set based on occupational exposure, which assumes either a certain level of PPE or eight hours a day of exposure, and it’s not at all expected for kids. So there’s particular compounds, especially lead, lithium and barium, that people are particularly concerned about in this instance. But the rulemaking is very slow, and the Trump administration is actually currently walking things back instead of making things stricter. So while on paper things might look OK—which isn’t the rule across the board, but in some instances things do look OK on paper—that doesn’t mean that they’re safe for human health.

We heard of funding issues that threaten to end Maui’s health impact study. Have LA researchers faced similar issues in regards to funding or any setbacks to their research due to state or the federal government?

So the fires happened at a really bad moment in terms of funding. It was just before Trump’s inauguration. There sort of seemed to be a very big show being made of trying to do the clean cleanup quickly without really funding the studies to make sure it was done thoroughly. That got even worse when the Trump administration and UCLA were at loggerheads, and the administration decided to freeze all federal funding. It really disrupted a lot of studies. I know that one lab actually tried to buy the equipment that they would need and the reagents that they would need for the year, and tried to plan ahead before their funding was frozen.

People have said that the LA fires burn materials that have stark similarities to substances that caught fire in the aftermath of 9/11. What have researchers said about concerns they have comparing those two events?

So a few scientists have actually brought up 9/11, especially from the fine particulate asbestos standpoint. But one scientist in particular pointed to research suggesting that the exposure might be similar to what we saw after the World Trade Center collapse. People living nearby during cleanup later had elevated cancer mortality due to the exposures of the burning urban structures that released heavy metals, asbestos and synthetic carcinogens. There’s a very similar concern for the workers who were doing the cleanup and the people who were working on the pile after 9/11, and there’s this real concern that we’re going to see maybe 10 years out, this major cancer cohort and this major COPD cohort that we do not have the capabilities to deal with it, and that could have been prevented.

LA is obviously a big place, but research has shown that the impacts of a wildfire can expand far beyond the burn zone and can sometimes be invisible to the eye. Do you feel like people understand the risks that they’ve been exposed to across LA?

I feel like that varies. The Palisades actually were relatively, I mean it’s hard to say lucky, but the people around that area weren’t exposed nearly as badly because the Santa Anas were blowing the debris and the dust straight out over the Pacific. But the Eaton fire was on the eastern edge of the city, so it had a whole city to blow over before it reached the Pacific. We’re not quite sure how far away this damage extends, or what the long-term outcomes will be, but we can definitely say that it is probably not just within the burn scar. That being said, people who were instructed, like right after the fires, that all they needed to do was go back to their homes if they were still standing and vacuum up and wipe down walls and things like that, we now know that that was not the correct thing to do. Things were really driven into the homes by 100 mile per hour winds in such a way that they were really heavily contaminated. And that it’s very hard to actually get all of that unless you’re taking a house apart and down to the studs or you have some experienced professional remediation.

So people might have thought that their homes were clean and they weren’t. You mentioned that some LA researchers have previously studied the Maui wildfires. What can California learn from Hawaiʻi, which is further along in its process in some ways?

I will say that there’s a same sort of toxic fingerprints in certain areas. And the need to approach it with care and clean things correctly has become clear that it’s running parallel in both places. I will also say that much like in Maui, in LA, there are also undocumented immigrants and children that are at higher risk of health issues and a lack of medical care and funding is impacting both. Scientists sampling in the field have also noted that many of the workers on the cleanup did not speak English in LA. I believe the same was noted in Maui in some areas and that they often didn’t have PPE. And even when they did, they did not necessarily know what the dangers they were trying to protect themselves from were. It was not explained to them in their language. So there is a significant concern for their health in the long term.

Nina, thank you so much for all of this in-depth reporting. We’ll look for more of it as the second anniversary of the fires approaches this January.

Sounds good. Thank you for having me.

As people look to repair and rebuild after a disaster, a number of scams have further complicated those efforts. Dozens of individuals who lost their homes in the 2023 Maui wildfire have contacted state and local officials reporting serious problems with contractors. No criminal charges have been filed against contractors, for now.

To avoid becoming a victim of construction scams, experts recommend hiring licensed contractors, consulting a lawyer before signing a contract and withholding payment until any outstanding issues are resolved.

California has several laws that protect consumers from contractor and home improvement fraud. But in the wake of the Eaton fire that destroyed the community of Altadena, many residents have encountered predatory developers that are buying up property and making it harder for locals to rebuild.

To prevent further expansion by developers, this fall California Gov. Gavin Newsom signed the “Keep Altadena Land in Altadena Hands Act.” The law will limit the number of controversial high-density developments in two Altadena ZIP codes.

While the law will help limit future developments, it won’t have much impact on the 60 new housing proposals that have already been approved and represent between 200 and 300 new structures in Altadena.

https://insideclimatenews.org/news/09112.title: Chesapeake Bay’s Osprey Population Is Falling. Is Its Food Supply a Factor?
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/09112.author: By Aman Azhar, Johnny Sturgeon
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/09112.text:
For 20 years, Roberta Kellam, a retired lawyer and longtime birder, has watched ospreys return to their nests and raise chicks from her home on Nassawadox Creek, on Virginia’s Eastern Shore.

She’s been monitoring around two dozen nests near her house. Kellam has also surveyed osprey populations with Bryan Watts, a longtime researcher at William & Mary’s Center for Conservation Biology and logs her observations on Osprey Watch, a citizen-science project the center runs.

Nassawadox Creek drains into the Chesapeake Bay, the nation’s largest estuary and home to the world’s largest breeding population of ospreys. The birds typically return from their wintering grounds in late February and early March to rebuild nests and raise chicks.

But about eight years ago, the situation turned from joy to dread.
