Thus far, the global response to the African threat has largely focused on military operations, especially in the Sahel. But to truly address the phenomenon, outside powers and world leaders will need to understand the underlying forces that have led to this proliferation of extremist groups. Above all, they will need to find new ways to help African countries address the erosion of state institutions and governance that has made terrorism endemic across the continent.

Africa’s entanglement with terrorist and jihadi groups is hardly new. Al-Qaeda’s 1998 attacks on U.S. embassies in Dar-es-Salaam and Nairobi were planned from Sudan, where Osama bin Laden had been based between 1991 and 1996. After 9/11, security experts viewed those attacks as a crucial precursor that should have set off alarm bells. Then, in the early years of the twenty-first century, local African groups coalesced into al-Shabab, based in Somalia, which also began to pursue transnational terrorism as an affiliate of al-Qaeda. Later, al-Qaeda in the Islamic Maghreb formed a major foothold in Mali. These developments prompted a number of Western-led antiterrorism campaigns, often supported by African forces. Most notable were the military interventions in the Sahel led by the French and other Western special forces and the initial U.S.-supported intervention force in Somalia, the so-called Somali Warlord Alliance.

But these counterterrorism operations did little to stop extremist activity in Africa. In the 2010s, countries in and close to the Sahel began to transition from being breeding grounds of terrorism to becoming the focus of terrorist attacks. Over the past few years, these countries have not only continued to be the places where terrorist groups can organize, radicalize their adherents, and spread violent extremist ideology; they also now bear the brunt of terrorist attacks and killings and the instability and breakdown in security that go with them. Worse, this activity has spread to new areas of the continent, such as Benin, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and Mozambique, where there had not been jihadis previously. In these countries, terrorist groups have capitalized on long-standing popular grievances spurred by government neglect, exclusion, and poverty. The jihadi expansion has been led by new local groups with connections to al-Qaeda and its branch JNIM in the Sahel region of West Africa and to ISIS affiliates in central Africa, whose major motivations include generating wealth from illegal mining, smuggling, and transnational organized crime.

What the outside world has often failed to recognize—both in the earlier and more recent phases of extremism—are the underlying factors that have made so many African countries prone to this activity. In nearly every case, fragile or collapsing state institutions have been crucial enablers: states’ inability to ensure the welfare and security of their citizens, to exercise sovereign authority over the length and breadth of their territory, and to alleviate the widespread poverty, unemployment, and disease that have created openings for extremism. In many countries, these factors have been exacerbated by large numbers of internally displaced persons and refugees, a lack of social infrastructure, and perennial violent conflict.

The unique characteristics of African demography have added to the challenge. In contrast to the aging populations of most other regions of the world, people under the age of 30 make up nearly 70 percent of Africa’s population and are also most affected by state failure. Large numbers of young people are not in school—more than 270 million African children in 2026, accounting for more than 40 percent of the global total. Nigeria alone has nearly 20 million youth out of school, the highest of any country in the world. At the same time, youth unemployment has remained persistently high: the continental average is 18 percent, but in some countries, such as Djibouti, where mass employment opportunities are limited and young people generally lack the requisite education for skilled employment in the logistics and transport sector that dominates the economy, youth unemployment may reach more than 75 percent. Disaffected young Africans constitute a huge reservoir of potential recruits for extremist groups, which have grown commensurately: according to recent estimates, al-Shabab has more than 15,000 fighters and JNIM has around 6,000.

But state complicity also plays a role. It is now well documented that political leaders have been building ties to bandit and terrorism groups to secure and consolidate their power. For example, the emergence of Boko Haram and various other militant outfits in Nigeria has been abetted by state governors and influential politicians employing them to intimidate opponents during elections. It is worth noting, as well, that elites in Muslim-dominated northern Nigeria initially opposed the U.S. designation of Boko Haram as a terrorist group—based on the assumption that the group was defending the interests of mainstream Muslims and northerners. This kind of support helped legitimize the group and enabled it to extend its control beyond the northeast of the country. The adoption of sharia law in the early years of the twenty-first century by 12 predominantly Muslim states in northern Nigeria also helped incubate Boko Haram. In this sense, Nigeria followed the path of Sudan, whose long history of Islamic fundamentalism and practice of sharia law made it a safe haven for bin Laden as he began to build his ideology of global terrorism.

Yet another contributing factor has been climate change and natural resource wars. Many of these countries have difficult desert geographies and have been beset with growing food insecurity and conflicts over diminishing resources. The result has been the emergence of so-called ungoverned territories within a number of African countries—areas characterized by power vacuums, porous borders, and illicit mining of critical minerals and other natural resources by terrorist groups, bandits, and criminal gangs. Often in these places, parallel state structures have been established by nonstate actors—not only to provide public goods, including safety, protection, and social services but also to challenge state legitimacy through sectarian uprisings and war. As these extremist nonstate groups seek to root their ideologies in ethnic, religious, and communal identities, territorial control has become central to their goals. This is especially true of jihadi groups such as al-Shabab, Boko Haram, JNIM, and ISIS affiliates, which aim to create caliphates, although none has thus far demonstrated the capacity to take over an entire state.

Although the domestic sources of African terrorism are important, external factors and global interconnections have been even more crucial to its spread. Take the continent’s jihadi and radical Islamist movements, which have for decades been inspired and supported from outside. For example, the 1979 Iranian Revolution spurred the rise of Shiite movements among Muslim youths across Africa. The Iranian government actively supported the movements by sponsoring the establishment of schools and mosques, offering scholarships for students to study in Iran, and creating training and indoctrination programs. Today, Ibrahim al-Zakzaky’s radical Islamic Movement of Nigeria, whose goal is to overthrow the secular government and establish Islamic law, remains one of the more resilient Iranian affiliates in Africa and has training camps in northwestern Nigeria that are linked to Iran and Lebanon’s Hezbollah.

In the 1990s, the exploits of the Taliban in Afghanistan inspired young Muslim radicals in northern Nigeria, where the forerunners of Boko Haram initially called themselves the Taliban. In turn, terrorism researchers have identified Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and other Middle Eastern powers as funders of Salafi extremism, which espouses the violent imposition of Islamic law on everyone, including fellow Muslims. Such is the success of these efforts that many African terrorist groups today consider themselves part of the global network of Salafist jihadism.

Among the most important external forces driving African terrorism are porous borders and the free flows of weapons, drugs, money, and human trafficking into and out of the continent. These flows have facilitated the integration of African groups into transnational terror networks. Al-Shabab was one of the earliest examples of this phenomenon: the group was founded by Somali supporters of the Afghan mujahideen in the late 1980s. Later, it became an affiliate of al-Qaeda, pledging allegiance to the group in 2012.

Other African groups followed a similar trajectory. Al-Qaeda’s African affiliates have grown to include Ansaru, a splinter faction of Boko Haram operating in northern Nigeria, as well as al-Qaeda in the Islamic Maghreb, which is based in Algeria. ISIS has added a panoply of African groups to its own network, such as Islamic State Sahel Province in Burkina Faso, Mali, and Niger, and Islamic State West Africa Province, which is active in the Lake Chad Basin. And it has developed ties with Islamic State Central Africa Province, which also operates in parts of Mozambique and the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda; and Islamic State in Somalia, which is a rival of al-Shabab. Meanwhile, al-Shabab has cultivated links to the Houthis in Yemen, a development that has heightened the potential for transnational terrorism to become enmeshed in the struggle for control of the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden between Egypt, Ethiopia, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey following conflicts and closures in the Strait of Hormuz.

These transnational affiliations have offered African groups many advantages, bringing new sources of funding, new weapons (including drones), and training in suicide bombing and IEDs, as well as indoctrination, foreign fighters, intelligence, and logistics. In return, African terrorist groups have helped their international affiliates by engaging in sea piracy and smuggling, human trafficking and migrant smuggling, money laundering, kidnapping for ransom, robbery, livestock rustling, drug trafficking, and illegal mining. African groups use many of these activities, as well as illegally taxing the areas under their control, to raise illicit funds for their international affiliates.

In addition, African jihadis provide personnel for international operations—al-Shabab members have been involved in terrorist training operations in the Philippines—and safe havens for fugitive terrorists. During the decades of the post-9/11 war on terrorism, there was a steady influx to Africa of foreign terrorists, fighters, and instructors who were fleeing Iran, Iraq, Syria and other parts of the Middle East. Others came from North Africa, especially following the civil war in Libya and unrest in Algeria. These foreign extremists brought with them massive amounts of weapons and helped turn Africa into a center of terrorist activity. As the epicenter of global terrorism today, Africa now houses numerous al-Qaeda and ISIS operatives, a fact that increases the risk that Africa-based groups may be planning operations beyond the continent.

In theory, international engagement in African security should help contain the rising terrorism threat. But the record thus far is not promising. During the war on terrorism, the United States, the EU, the United Nations, and international security organizations provided support for numerous counterterrorism campaigns on the continent. These efforts included backing the G5 Sahel—a counterterrorism initiative by Burkina Faso, Chad, Mali, Mauritania, and Niger—as well as support for regional counterterrorism initiatives, including in Mozambique and Somalia, as well as the Multinational Joint Task Force, which aimed to combat terrorism in the Lake Chad region. Most of these efforts failed or were not sustained long enough to change the trajectory, and the worsening security situations that they left in their wake fueled anti-Western sentiment. And now, with Russia and China pursuing interests of their own in many parts of Africa, involvement by outside powers is often driven by a desire for strategic minerals and a quest for geopolitical influence, interventions that have only further encouraged terrorist activity.

In the Sahel, the withdrawal of U.S. and French forces between 2022 and early 2025 created power and security vacuums. Russia has quickly exploited the situation, using bilateral defense pacts and mercenary and Africa Corps forces to gain access to minerals and natural resources that France had previously controlled. Indeed, in many parts of Africa, global competition for critical minerals has become a new driver in the spread of terrorism. In the Manono district of Congo, for instance, American, Australian, and Chinese firms are enmeshed in long-running disputes over lithium deposits, which has made counterterrorism operations in the same area more difficult: the various international players no longer want to coordinate on counterterrorism and terrorist groups are using external rivalries to strengthen their own operations. A similar scenario is playing out in other resource-rich areas.

It is now urgent that leading world powers adopt a different approach. A first step is to recognize the problem for what it is. Jihadi terrorism today is not a local or regional problem afflicting a handful of African countries; it is a worldwide threat. It can be effectively tackled only through concerted and sustained international action. Although internationally-backed counterterrorism efforts by the African Union and other regional forces are more needed than ever, the new scramble for resources has become an obstacle to international collaboration in Africa. In this regard, it will be crucial to embrace the common protocols and regulatory frameworks for critical minerals and other resources being developed by the AU and other regional African organizations—which seek to reduce the scope for illicit activities and ensure that that the countries benefit more from the resources through more inclusive and accountable governance structures.

Most important, outside powers need to engage with the root causes that have made the continent so prone to terrorist activity, even when it has been effectively countered elsewhere in the world. As the former UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon said in 2015, “Good governance is what will kill terrorism.” Northern Ireland after the Good Friday Agreement—whose institutional reforms such as power sharing, human rights protections, and community policing proved to be more effective than military operations—is a case in point; so is the 2016 peace agreement between the Colombian government and the FARC, which included governance reforms in previously neglected parts of the country as part of its stabilization measures.

The United States as well as governments in Europe and international bodies need to shift their focus from military operations to addressing the actual social and economic sources of state fragility that have made so many African countries fertile ground for conflict and extremist violence. This would of course involve strengthening state capacities, and it would require regional efforts as well as more targeted development assistance. None of it will be easy, but doing nothing would be far worse. Unless African countries and their international partners can begin to address the underlying dynamics that are driving Africa’s transnational terrorism problem, it is unlikely to stay in Africa for much longer.

https://www.foreignaffairs.com/taiwan/re.author: Rebecca Lissner, Mira Rapp-Hooper
https://www.foreignaffairs.com/taiwan/re.text:
REBECCA LISSNER is Senior Fellow for U.S. Foreign Policy and Director of the Future of American Strategy Initiative at the Council on Foreign Relations. She served as Deputy Assistant to the President and Principal Deputy National Security Adviser to the Vice President during the Biden administration.

MIRA RAPP-HOOPER is a Visiting Senior Fellow at the Brookings Institution. She was Special Assistant to the President and Senior Director for East Asia and Oceania and Director for Indo-Pacific Strategy at the U.S. National Security Council during the Biden administration.

Why the Risk of a Crisis Is Growing

Rebecca Lissner and Mira Rapp-Hooper

Just a few years ago, U.S. President Joe Biden caused a stir when he confirmed publicly that his administration would defend Taiwan if the island were attacked by China—a divergence from the traditional U.S. policy of strategic ambiguity, in which Washington does not commit to taking any particular action. In May, U.S. President Donald Trump made waves for taking a different position. In a television interview, he described Taiwan as “a very good negotiating chip” in dealings with Beijing and mused that the island was close to China but far from the United States, implying that U.S. interests in Taiwan were negligible. In doing so, Trump seemed to confirm something many Asia watchers had feared: that this U.S. president would be willing to loosen the United States’ commitment to Taiwan to bolster his relationship with Chinese leader Xi Jinping.

A few days later, Secretary of State Marco Rubio told the Senate Foreign Relations Committee that there had been no change in U.S. policy toward Taiwan. But Trump’s words were alarming nonetheless—in part because they reflect a shift in Washington that goes beyond the Oval Office. Since 2025, politicians from both parties have been shying away from affirming the United States’ long-standing support for Taiwan. Meanwhile, China is developing new strategies to coerce Taiwan without going to war, and Beijing will be increasingly tempted to use them if it judges that the U.S. commitment to Taiwan is waning among both politicians and the public.

Yet that would be a grave miscalculation on China’s part. In fact, the United States’ interests in Taiwan are growing, not diminishing. Whatever the nature of Washington’s rhetoric right now, the United States would have to respond to any action by Beijing that threatened those interests, and both countries would then face a great-power crisis. To defuse this dangerous situation, American leaders must update the United States’ Taiwan strategy to reflect a new reality—and they should begin immediately.

Taiwan’s unique international status has long made U.S. policy complex. The Republic of China, now known as Taiwan, was a World War II ally of the United States. When the People’s Republic of China was founded on the mainland, in 1949, the Republic of China’s president, Chiang Kai-shek, decamped to Taiwan, and the United States maintained formal diplomatic ties with Chiang’s government, not the People’s Republic of China. In 1954, as the Cold War crested in the Pacific, the United States concluded a formal mutual defense treaty with Taiwan, in part to forestall increasingly aggressive artillery barrages from the mainland. Nearly 20 years later, however, when U.S. President Richard Nixon and his national security adviser, Henry Kissinger, began to engineer a diplomatic opening to the government in Beijing, they knew it would cost Taiwan.

In part because they understood that building diplomatic ties with Beijing would be painful for Taiwan and cause controversy in Congress, where Taipei had many boosters, Nixon and Kissinger slow-walked the process. So did Nixon’s successor, President Gerald Ford. It finally fell to President Jimmy Carter to make the change. On January 1, 1979, the United States ended its alliance with Taiwan and recognized the mainland government as “the sole legal Government of China.” Congress was irate. Lawmakers from both parties quickly drafted the 1979 Taiwan Relations Act, which remains in force. The law requires Washington to provide Taipei with defensive arms, creating the trappings of an alliance with Taiwan despite the relationship’s unofficial status. In 1982, the Reagan administration made an additional set of commitments to Taiwan, known as the Six Assurances. These include an affirmation that Washington does not endorse Beijing’s sovereignty claims over Taiwan and a promise that the United States would not use arms sales to Taiwan as a bargaining chip.

In the 50 years since, U.S. Taiwan policy has been remarkably successful. Through its partnership and arms sales, the United States has helped underwrite peace and stability in the Taiwan Strait, and Taiwan has thrived as a democracy and an economy, even as Washington has maintained a relationship with Beijing. But U.S. commitments to Taiwan have lately come under increasing strain. China has proceeded with a massive military buildup designed to give Beijing the option to take Taiwan by force; used coercive economic tactics, launched cyberattacks, and interfered in elections to put pressure on Taipei; and run frequent army and coast guard exercises to demonstrate its ability to strangle the island. All of this has stoked concerns across the Pacific that the United States’ long-standing partnership might not be enough to keep the peace in the Taiwan Strait.

The fear that China could attempt to retake Taiwan by force, possibly during Xi’s tenure, has grown in recent years. Analysts have frequently cited 2027 as the beginning of the window of maximum danger, based on a 2021 statement made by Philip Davidson, the former commander of U.S. Indo-Pacific Command, about when the People’s Liberation Army might be prepared for an invasion. But this timeline was never hard and fast, and Xi’s recent purge of more than 100 officers has likely delayed the military’s readiness. U.S. intelligence assessments do not anticipate an invasion of Taiwan next year, and most scholars believe the Chinese government would consider such a move as a last resort only if unification could not be accomplished by other means.

The primary danger now is that Xi will escalate a pressure campaign designed to coerce Taiwan into negotiating a change in its status. Since 2025, China’s leaders have used their diplomatic channels to the Trump administration, including Xi’s direct line to Trump, to insist on American concessions on Taiwan in exchange for progress in trade talks. In May, China secured a pause on a planned $14 billion U.S. arms sale and other defense funding for Taiwan. Beijing may hope that additional incremental moves will further weaken Taiwanese confidence in the United States and that such actions will be difficult for Trump or a future U.S. president to reverse.

China is also clearly planning for more dramatic forms of coercion. It has a few options: since 2022, China’s military has practiced blockades of Taiwan, and its coast guard has simulated a quarantine of the island’s major ports. Beijing could also use customs enforcement or other administrative measures to attempt to assert its jurisdiction over Taiwan while minimizing the likelihood that the United States would intervene to stop it. If Taiwanese President Lai Ching-te, who favors Taiwanese independence but has not pursued it in office, is reelected in 2028 and Chinese leaders believe that the path to a peaceful unification is closing, Xi may consider using these tools against the island in late 2028 or early 2029, before a new U.S. administration takes office. Given Trump’s alienation of U.S. allies in Asia and Europe and Washington’s limited means to respond to a maritime quarantine, Beijing might hope to get away with such a large-scale coercion campaign without inviting serious pushback.

Taiwan’s growing strategic importance makes Beijing’s development of new coercive options more concerning. Washington is no longer maintaining a partnership with Taipei because of a historical commitment or, as Beijing would have the world believe, to needle China. The artificial intelligence boom has put Taiwan at the center of the global economy. Taiwan is a critical supplier for the U.S. tech industry, and the United States recognizes that it cannot be a leader in AI without Taiwan.

The scale of the United States’ economic dependence on Taiwan is revealing. Taiwan is the country’s fifth-largest trading partner; a Chinese blockade of the island would imperil more than $250 billion in trade and could shave more than three percent off U.S. GDP in a year, according to a Bloomberg report. As much as 97 percent of the global supply of the high-end logic chips used in smartphones and other advanced electronics are produced or packaged in Taiwan. Losing access to Taiwanese chips could reduce advanced electronics production globally by 60 percent, with factories forced to rely on their chip inventories. The United States’ auto and medical device industries could deplete their inventories in a matter of weeks. The U.S. firms Amazon, Apple, and Nvidia are among the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company’s ten largest customers, which together represent more than $14 trillion in market capitalization. With AI growth buoying the U.S. stock market and the broader economy, a crisis in Taiwan would trigger a crash—potentially one similar in scale to the stock market crash at the start of the COVID-19 pandemic.

The economic effects of a Chinese effort to squeeze Taiwan would not be limited to the United States. The research firm Rhodium Group has conservatively estimated that a yearlong blockade of the island could cost the global economy between $2 trillion and $3 trillion. A full-scale war would be far worse; Bloomberg has estimated that it would cause $10 trillion in economic losses and a global recession. It is therefore increasingly likely that the United States would be forced to act if Taiwan’s supply chains were put in jeopardy. The cost of standing aside would simply be too high.

Yet just when the United States needs to be doing all it can to prevent a crisis, Washington’s support for Taiwan appears to be wobbling. Trump’s musings about Taiwan’s geographical distance from the United States and his use of arms sales as a bargaining chip are the headline examples, but they are not the only indicators of a shaky U.S. commitment. Policy analysts have argued that the United States should change its position to definitively oppose Taiwanese independence or even withdraw U.S. forces from the military bases in Japan and the Philippines that are closest to Taiwan.

Public opinion in the United States is shifting, too. Americans’ feelings toward China have warmed considerably over the past two years, according to a July 2026 Chicago Council on Global Affairs survey. A majority, 57 percent, support friendly cooperation and engagement with China, whereas 40 percent support an active effort to limit the growth of China’s power. The share of Americans who see China’s territorial ambitions as “a critical threat” has decreased by more than ten percentage points since 2022, and those who favor the use of U.S. troops if China invaded Taiwan has fallen from 52 percent to just 38 percent.

In part, the declining support for defending Taiwan reflects Americans’ growing wariness of instability and conflict. A sense that the world was descending into chaos helped fuel Trump’s 2024 campaign; as president, Trump has heightened that sense by taking assertive military action in places such as Iran and Venezuela. Americans are now suffering the economic consequences of nine months of war in the Middle East, further deepening antiwar sentiment, as the midterm election results vividly demonstrate. Candidates for office used to clamor to sound tough on China, but many now blanch at the idea of suggesting that the U.S. military should defend Taiwan against a Chinese invasion, calculating that this is not the time to be seen as a hawk.

Of course, public attitudes can change quickly during a crisis. If China actually committed aggression against Taiwan, Americans could become more supportive of a strong U.S. response. And if the early stages of a conflict saw American casualties or a Chinese attack on U.S. critical infrastructure, the U.S. public could very well rally around the flag and demand a muscular intervention.

For now, however, China may believe that the United States’ will and ability to fight are both diminishing. The war with Iran has substantially reduced U.S. military readiness for a Taiwan contingency. The United States has used up much of its missile defense stock, including roughly two-thirds of its Patriot interceptor inventory, which was already depleted by U.S. aid to Ukraine, and as much as 80 percent of THAAD interceptors against Iranian drones and missiles. Even before the Iran war, analysts had warned that the U.S. military could run out of long-range, precision-guided munitions in a fight over Taiwan; now, the munitions shortfalls have become perilously acute. The war has also drawn military assets away from the Indo-Pacific. In August, Washington moved its last aircraft carrier in Asia, the USS George Washington, out of the region. It has also relocated missile defense systems to the Middle East, including Patriot and THAAD systems that had been deployed in South Korea.

The result is an increased risk of dangerous miscalculation. Should Chinese leaders assess that the United States’ commitment to Taiwan is wavering in both political parties and that the country is ill prepared for a fight, they might conclude that they have an opportunity to pressure Taiwan without inviting an American response. Yet because the United States has a greater interest in Taiwan today than at any point in history, Beijing’s bet could turn out to be wrong. China could announce a maritime quarantine of Taiwan or another coercive measure only to have the United States intervene, potentially prompting a great-power standoff.

Avoiding such a showdown will require American leaders to recommit to deterrence. First, Washington needs to update the way it communicates its positions. In their public remarks, policymakers should clearly state that the U.S. economy’s dependence on Taiwanese exports makes peace and stability across the Taiwan Strait a vital interest of the United States. American political leaders should emphasize to Beijing that the United States has an obligation to prevent a crisis that would tank the U.S. stock market, cut critical supply chains, and fell many American industries.

Clarifying U.S. interests would not impugn 50 years of careful diplomacy with China, nor would it require any change to U.S. policy as established by the Taiwan Relations Act, the Six Assurances, or the series of joint U.S.-Chinese statements, made between 1972 and 1982, known as the Three Communiqués. The updated statements, rather, would convey to Chinese leaders that certain changes to the cross-strait status quo would be unacceptable to the United States, even if Taiwan were to acquiesce to those changes under pressure. Washington would support a peaceful unification, for example, only if the process guaranteed the security of critical supply chains.

Once the United States makes its interests clear, it will also have to back up its statements with a new playbook to deter Chinese actions that fall below the military threshold. Beijing may already be in the early stages of imposing a quarantine on the island. Washington should not tolerate additional measures that interfere with commerce and maritime traffic in and out of Taiwan. To deter China from taking such steps, the next U.S. Congress should use legislation to clarify its wholesale, bipartisan opposition to Chinese blockades, quarantines, and other restrictions. Even if the White House continued to take a softer position, this would send a message to Beijing that other political actors might force the president’s hand. Congress should also press the administration to prepare punitive diplomatic and financial measures for use in the event of an escalating Chinese quarantine of Taiwan. By planning these reprisals well ahead of any coercive action, Washington would signal that a maritime pressure campaign would entail clear costs for Beijing and carry dangerous escalation risks.

The United States should strengthen military deterrence, too. The next Congress must pressure the Trump administration to release the stalled $14 billion package of arms sales to Taiwan, as well as other security assistance the administration is slow-rolling. Congress has a legal obligation to do so under the Taiwan Relations Act. Pausing security aid violates U.S. policy, and allowing the Trump team to make this concession in its likely quixotic pursuit of rapprochement with Xi only weakens Washington’s hand.

Washington does not have to—and shouldn’t—take these steps alone. U.S. allies such as Germany, Japan, and South Korea would suffer nearly as much as the United States if China were to take control of Taiwan’s semiconductor industry. These countries have an interest in working quietly together to deter and develop joint responses to Chinese coercion while also collaborating to diversify their chip supply chains and make them more resilient. In the United States, this work does not have to wait for a new presidential administration. Congress can send delegations and use other diplomatic opportunities to start developing plans with parliamentary counterparts abroad.

As the 2028 U.S. presidential election approaches, moreover, candidates from both parties should speak clearly about the country’s strong economic interests in Taiwan and about their commitment to deterrence. This does not require embracing bellicose positions, but presidential candidates do need to state firmly that any move by Beijing to choke off vital supply chains would harm U.S. interests and demand an American response. Consistent messaging would also signal to China’s leaders that they should not expect a future administration to be bound by Trump’s policy concessions—and signal to allies that come 2029, the United States will again be a reliable partner in standing up to China’s economic aggression.

The United States needs to update its Taiwan policy, but ceding ground as Trump has done only makes the cross-strait balance less stable. Unlike other Cold War–era policies, the importance of preventing Chinese aggression against Taiwan has become more—not less—vital with the passage of time. U.S. interests in Taiwan are plainer and easier to explain than they have ever been. Only by stating those interests clearly and backing up the words with actions can the United States continue to avert a crisis or conflict that would be devastating for all.

https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261.text:
British comedian and actor Russell Brand was sentenced Monday to 10 years and six months in prison for raping one woman and sexually assaulting three others.

Judge Joel Bennathan told Brand that he showed a “casual and arrogant disregard” for any woman to say no to him during sentencing remarks that put the crimes in the context of his rise to stardom.

READ MORE
British comedian Russell Brand found guilty of rape, sexual assault

“About 20 years ago, Russell Brand, you were becoming famous,” Bennathan said. “You were clever – and in many people’s eyes, funny and charismatic. You had also become a sexual predator.”

The 51-year-old actor-comedian – known for outrageous stand-up routines and behaviour on television and radio broadcasts, along with drug and alcohol battles – had asserted he was innocent and all his encounters were consensual.

But a jury of eight men and four women found him guilty of attacking four of six accusers on allegations dating back to 2004. He was cleared of two counts of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault.

https://www.france24.com/en/environment/.title: COP31: Betting on electricity to break the climate deadlock
https://www.france24.com/en/environment/.author: Cyrielle CABOT
https://www.france24.com/en/environment/.text:
After biodiversity comes climate. Starting Monday, countries from around the world will gather in Antalya, Turkey, for the 31st Conference of the Parties on climate (COP31).

This year, the major climate negotiations open on a particularly bleak backdrop, amid a tense geopolitical context and following a summer marked by a series of disasters. The goal set in 2015 by the Paris Climate Agreement to limit global warming to +1.5°C now seems impossible to reach. The world is heading towards a 2.8°C rise in temperature by 2100 if nothing changes, and a 2.6°C rise if the international community continues its current efforts, the UN warned once again in its latest annual report published on October 21.

READ MORE
Turkey to push for 'electrification' drive at COP31 as climate threats mount

But, paradoxically, this global context is precisely what gives climate advocates a reason for hope.

“This COP is the first since the situation in the Strait of Hormuz plunged the world into an unprecedented energy crisis,” said Gaïa Febvre, head of international policy at the French climate advocacy group Réseau action climat (RAC). “Everywhere, leaders and citizens alike have seen hydrocarbon prices skyrocket, and there has been a growing awareness of our dependence on fossil fuels.”

To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.

One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.

At recent COPs, states failed to target the main culprits of global warming: fossil fuels – gas, coal and oil. While in 2023, during COP28 in Dubai, participants had painstakingly managed to agree on the need to start a “transition away from fossil fuels”, debates on implemention hit a brick wall and COP30 concluded without any mention of the issue in the final text.

“This new summit appears as a perfect opportunity to emphasise the necessity to step away from fossil fuels and accelerate the green transition with the development of renewable energies,” Febvre said. “There is an alignment between issues of energy sovereignty and climate ambitions.”

Seeking to capitalise on this “momentum”, Australia and Turkey – which are co-chairing COP31 – have decided to bring an alternative to the forefront: electricity. During preparatory discussions in Bonn, Germany, back in June, they proposed setting a target for 35 percent of final energy consumption to come from electricity by 2035. The project is titled “35-35”.

WATCH MORE
Countries turn to coal to avoid shipping disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz

“This is the most important pillar in reducing emissions – you need to increase electrification in cities, in manufacturing, in [all aspects of life], and will serve us in the bigger picture, the bigger targets [of the Paris agreement],” said Murat Kurum, Turkey’s Minister of the Environment.

“No one can sanction the sun, no one can blockade the wind,” Australia’s Minister for climate change and energy Chris Bowen said. “Solar energy has to travel 150 million kilometres to Earth, but it does not have to travel 150 kilometres of the Strait of Hormuz,” he added in a direct reference to the blockade of the main transit route for hydrocarbons from the Middle East to the rest of the world.

To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.

One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.

Electrification is expected to be on the COP30 agenda starting Tuesday, a day dedicated to energy. The conference presidency is expected to call on countries to voluntarily commit to the 35-35 target. Several countries – including EU members – have already indicated that they would answer favourably.

This should be a first symbolic step before serious discussions start.

“Turkey is also pushing for this issue to be debated as part of the official negotiations and thus be included in the final COP agreement,” Febvre said.

Countries will then need to find a common objective, as the final text needs a consensus in order to be adopted.

“In recent years, electricity has already been accounting for an increasingly large share of the global energy mix,” said Gareth Redmond-King, head of international programme at the UK-based non-profit Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit.

By the end of 2024, it accounted for 23 percent of final energy consumption, according to data from the International Energy Agency.

“At the national level, some countries are ahead of the curve,” Redmond-King said. “Japan, for example, has already reached 35 percent of its energy from electricity. China is approaching 30 percent. The EU and the US are in line with the global average at respectively 23 and 22 percent.”

READ MORE
UN nature summit approves two key agreements after marathon negotiations

In France – which has just announced a substantial electrification plan – electricity accounts for about 27 percent of final energy consumption.

Given these figures, is the goal of 35 percent by 2035 achievable? And can it really make a difference for the climate?

According to an analysis from the Climate Action Tracker, if current policies remain unchanged,  electricity’s share of energy consumption would reach 28 percent by 2035, with the transportation sector lagging far behind.

“It would require political will and investment from governments, but this goal seems achievable,” said Redmond-King. “Driven by China, in particular, electrification technologies have really taken off in recent years. We’ve seen this, for example, with the widespread adoption of electric cars and heat pumps … And more and more industries are making the shift, attracted by energy that is becoming increasingly cheaper compared to fossil fuels.”

“But for this energy transition to be fair, the most developed countries will have to agree to support countries in the Global South. And the private sector will also have to agree to get involved,” said Febvre.

As for the impact on the fight against climate change, it will depend on the actual ambition of states, insisted the two experts, who will be keeping a close eye on the negotiations in Antalya.

To begin with, “35 percent of electrification is interesting, but it must be a floor, not a ceiling,”said Febvre.

Above all, the source of that electricity will need to be looked at: renewable energy, nuclear power or fossil fuels? Febvre expects a “battle of words” behind the scenes at the COP.

“When drafting the agreement, we’ll have to see if countries can reach a consensus among advocates of ‘clean’ energy – that is, renewables and nuclear power – those pushing for ‘green’ energy using only renewables, and those who also want to maintain fossil fuels,” she said.

In other words, “electrification must go hand in hand with decarbonisation,” Redmond-King summarised.

However, India – as well as much of the African continent and oil-producing countries – would surely reject any mention of “clean” or “green” electricity. On the other hand, the EU is likely to push for electricity to come primarily from decarbonised energy sources, including nuclear power.

READ MORE
France and Germany agree to ease EU car emissions rules in new deal

For now, the text proposed by the Turkish presidency calls for increasing “electricity’s share of total final energy consumption... in line with pathways consistent with keeping 1.5°C alive and complementary to efforts to expand renewable energy and improve energy efficiency.”

Therefore, nothing explicitly states that the electricity must come from sources that do not emit greenhouse gases. The text can be understood as a call to expand electrification as a whole, while also making efforts to develop renewable energy.

This is exactly Turkey’s model. According to the global energy think-tank Ember, 43 percent of Turkey’s electricity came from clean sources in 2025, including 22 percent from wind and solar power and 16 percent from hydropower, a record figure. But in parallel, the country has continued to build new coal-fired power plants and has not set a formal target for phasing out fossil fuels. The two co-presidents of COP31 are, in fact, historically linked by a coal agreement.

Beyond electricity sources, the challenge will also revolve around the amount of energy produced, Febvre said. In 2025, for the first time, renewable energy sources generated more electricity than coal. But in parallel, fossil fuels also increased.

This is due to energy demand continuously rising, whether it’s to power air conditioners or heaters during extreme weather events, or the data centres essential to the development of artificial intelligence.

READ MORE
Pacific leaders urge climate action as UN pre-COP talks open in Fiji

“Amid all this, we also have to adopt a real energy conservation plan,” said Febvre. “It’s no longer a matter of adding this energy to our current resources, but of permanently replacing fossil fuels.”

The debate is therefore shaping up to be heated. Even if COP31 were to produce an ambitious commitment to electrification, the hardest part would still lie ahead.

“We’ll have to take action to make the plan a reality,” Febvre said. “But this will have to be done fairly, taking into account local realities and the challenges faced by different countries.”

https://www.france24.com/en/france/20261.title: French PM brings forward 1.6% increase in minimum wage in bid to calm protests
https://www.france24.com/en/france/20261.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/france/20261.text:
French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said on Monday he was bringing forward a planned hike in the minimum wage to December from January, as he sought to defuse a cost-of-living crisis that has sparked some of France's worst civil unrest in years.

The government has faced a series of demonstrations in recent weeks which started over underfunded schools but have morphed into broader protests, including riots in major cities on October 17 that caught security forces off guard.

READ MORE
'Deeply regressive': How the French government plans to make protesters pay for riots and looting

France's national minimum wage would normally be raised on January 1 to reflect inflation, but instead the government will raise it by 1.6% in December, Labour Minister Jean-Pierre Farandou told a press conference.

The increase will bring the monthly minimum wage to a net €1,502 ($1,676), up €24 from the current level, where it has been since June, when it was raised by €35 to reflect higher inflation.

The government is concerned about mounting social tensions five months before a presidential election in which far-right leader Marine Le Pen is the frontrunner in the polls.

To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.

One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.

The hike falls short of union demands, with the CFDT, France's largest union, calling for a €100 increase, while the left-wing CGT union is demanding a 10% rise, equivalent to around €150 a month.

"This is the second-biggest increase in 20 years, so it should not be held in contempt," Lecornu told journalists after meeting with unions and employers' federations.

CFDT head Marylise Léon said the increase was "insufficient" after the meeting, while CGT head Sophie Binet described it as "crumbs" and added: "We didn't come here to beg for alms." Binet also called for new protests on November 17.

France combines one of Europe's highest minimum wages with one of the largest shares of workers paid at or near that level.

The minimum wage amounted to 67% of average earnings in 2024, while 12.7% of employees were paid at or near the minimum wage, compared with 8% in Germany and 3.5% in the Netherlands, according to Eurostat data.

Changes to the minimum wage, which in France usually is automatically increased in line with inflation in January and sometimes midyear, therefore have a particularly broad impact on labour costs and are a politically sensitive subject.

The government is eager to find ways to ease public anger but it has little room for manoeuvre because of its mounting debt burden.

Protests erupted in high schools in September but have since spiralled into a broader outpouring of anger over living costs, public services and political stagnation.

READ MORE
French presidential election: How far-left Mélenchon became a Gen Z favourite

The unrest comes five months before France's presidential election. Opinion polls currently suggest far-right candidate Marine Le Pen will face hard-left rival Jean-Luc Mélenchon in a run-off.

French President Emmanuel Macron, who is coming to the end of his second term and whose approval ratings have hit a record low in opinion polls, is barred from running again.

(FRANCE 24 with Reuters)

https://www.france24.com/en/tv-shows/pre.title: New James Bond actor expected 'within weeks' as 'unexpected' frontrunners emerge
https://www.france24.com/en/tv-shows/pre.author: Elitsa GADEVA
https://www.france24.com/en/tv-shows/pre.text:
Novaya Gazeta's front-page headline reads: "What will we leave behind?" Moscow has classed the independent paper as a "foreign agent", a label used to stifle dissent and media that don't obey the Kremlin. They received the label back in September, so what followed didn't come as a surprise. In late October, the team received an eviction notice – they have to be gone by November 10 and evict the office that many journalists have called home for decades. Banks also blocked readers' donations, leaving the editorial team without a single source of income. The Times says that Novaya Gazeta was "the last free newspaper in Russia. Now Putin has come for it". The paper writes that for more than 30 years, the Russian paper "has fearlessly defended human rights in Russia". It says that its closure is "widely seen as revenge for its criticism of the invasion of Ukraine". Dmitry Muratov, Novaya Gazeta's co-founder, spoke to the paper. He said that this is the culmination of a long and violent journey that started in 1993, when Mikhail Gorbachev donated money from his Nobel Peace Prize to help establish the paper. El País condemns the closure of Novaya Gazeta, which it describes as a symbol of "great Russian journalism". Its final issue comes after three decades of exposing war crimes, political assassinations and high-level corruption.

Also in Russia, a new data leak from the state statistics agency reveals some numbers about the war in Ukraine, The Moscow Times reports. The leaked figures say that more than 450,000 Russians have been killed in the war in Ukraine. Russia hasn't officially disclosed its battlefield losses since September 2022. But if this number is correct, it would make the war the fourth most common cause of death in the country since 2022 and the deadliest conflict since World War II.

Next: NASA is expanding its Artemis programme. The Guardian reports that it now wants to send a new generation of astronauts to live and work on the Moon. NASA says the successful candidates would help "shape humanity's future in space". If you're interested, the application deadline is December 3. Applicants must be US citizens and have a master's degree in a related field, such as science or mathematics, or training as a pilot. They must also have three years of "related professional experience". This is all happening as the space agency is currently building a base on the Moon and is planning the first crewed missions to Mars.

Finally, who will be the next James Bond? MovieWeb says Robert Pattinson will play the iconic British spy. But according to OK! Magazine, there are three frontrunners: Jack Lowden, Jacob Elordi and Callum Turner. Nothing has been officially confirmed yet, but the winner could be revealed "within weeks".

You can catch our press review every morning on France 24 at 7:20am and 9:20am (Paris time), from Monday to Friday.

https://www.france24.com/en/france/20261.title: Judo star Teddy Riner announces bid for French presidency
https://www.france24.com/en/france/20261.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/france/20261.text:
France's five-time Olympic judo champion Teddy Riner announced on Monday that he would run in the country's high-stakes presidential election next year.

"My name is Teddy Riner and today, I am telling you face to face: I am a candidate in the 2027 presidential election," the 37-year-old athlete said in the surprise announcement on social media.

To display this content from X (Twitter), you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.

Riner said in an interview with Le Parisien newspaper published Monday that he is positioning himself as “neither right-wing nor left-wing” and hopes to become a “president who brings people together".

Asked whether his bid should be taken seriously, Riner said “what would be irresponsible would be to remain silent and stand by as a spectator to what is happening in our country, and what has been happening for several years now".

Riner, among France's best-known sports figures, enters the race with far-right presidential candidate Marine Le Pen leading in the polls to replace centrist President Emmanuel Macron next year.

Protest marches have been drawing huge crowds for weeks in Paris and elsewhere across France as demonstrators demand higher wages and back the country’s student protest movement, piling fresh pressure on the beleaguered government.

Riner said he is aware of the social tensions running through the country and that he can’t accept young people and older generations saying they are struggling to imagine a future for themselves.

“I hear the anger, which some people echo in their rhetoric with a great deal of negativity, coming from people who no longer have any ambition or the desire to think big,” Riner said. “Yet France is a great country. It has allowed me to become the person I am today and given me the opportunity to dream big. Today, that is precisely what is missing. There is no longer that ambition, no longer that hope.”

Riner said in September that wants to end his stellar career with a fourth individual Olympic gold medal at the Los Angeles Games in 2028. Asked by Le Parisien if his presidential bid means he is giving up on the Olympics, the 2.04-meter (6-foot-8) heavyweight said no.

“Not if my duties as president allow it and the French people give me their blessing,” the 11-time world champion said.

French authorities in September said they investigated online racial abuse aimed at Riner after he expressed concern about the rise of the far right. In an interview with French sports television show Stade 2, Riner said he was “freaked out” by the rise of extremism. Asked if he meant “on both sides” – meaning the far left and far right – Riner replied “the far right".

According to polls, the nationalist Marine Le Pen is the front-runner ahead of hard-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon.

“The country is experiencing deep divisions right now, let’s not kid ourselves,” Riner said. “And in the face of that, I don’t see a single candidate putting forward a credible and fair vision capable of bringing the French people together rather than dividing them. There is no one today offering genuine, sincere hope. It’s always one side against another. I’m running for president to show that we can get France back on its feet. We are capable of achieving great things together.”

Asked about what would be his first initiative on the international stage if he is elected, Riner said he wants to make sure France works well with its allies and commands greater respect.

“A lot of people around me have been talking about my first handshake with Donald Trump,” he said, laughing. “We’ll see who has the firmer handshake.”

Riner has won five Olympic gold medals in judo. He won the heavyweight division at the 2012, 2016 and 2024 Olympics and mixed team golds at the 2020 and 2024 Games.

Riner has also won 11 world titles.

Another French star judoka, David Douillet, was elected to the French parliament in 2009 and served as sports minister from September 2011 to May 2012.

(FRANCE 24 with AP and AFP)

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/r.title: Breaking: Russell Brand jailed for more than 10 years for rape and sexual assault
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/r.author: Mazoe Ford
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/r.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

British actor and comedian Russell Brand has been sentenced in London after being found guilty of rape and three counts of sexual assault. (Reuters: Hannah McKay)

British actor and comedian Russell Brand has been jailed for 10 years and six months for rape and sexual assault.

Judge Joel Bennathan said that as Brand was becoming famous he was "clever and, in many people's eyes, funny and charismatic" but he had also "become a sexual predator".

He added that Brand's celebrity status "protected" him until 2023, when journalists collected and published allegations about him that then "empowered a number of women to come forward and tell their stories".

After a four-week trial at London's Southwark Crown Court, Brand, who targeted four women between 2004 and 2009, was last week found guilty of the four charges, and acquitted of a further two counts of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault.

The 51-year-old had pleaded not guilty to all charges and claimed he never engaged in any non-consensual sexual activity.

A prison van carrying Brand arrives at Southwark Crown Court on the day of his sentencing. (Reuters: Corey Rudy)

When the sentence was read out Brand stood still and showed no emotion.

The comedian's wife Laura, who was sitting in the public gallery with a security guard and friend, closed her eyes and put her head down.

As Brand was led away by court officers, he mouthed to his wife "I'll be ok".

Brand was one of the UK's most high-profile comedians, presenters and actors during the 2000s.

During sentencing, Russell Brand was referred to as a "sexual predator". (Reuters: Toby Melville)

The rape conviction relates to a fan who was 21 years old when Brand raped her at his North London home in 2009.

They met after he picked her out of the crowd in the foyer following one of his live comedy shows at the Hammersmith Apollo.

During the trial, the woman told the court that what started as consensual sex, then changed suddenly into an activity she did not consent to.

She said she begged him to stop but he did not.

The three sexual assault convictions relate to one woman a bar in 2004, a woman at radio station around the same time, and a woman he was working on a project with for Channel 4 in 2009.

By law in the UK, the women who made complaints about the comedian are all granted lifelong anonymity by the court.

After deliberating for eight and a half hours, a jury found Brand guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault. (Elizabeth Cook via AP)

Judge Bennathan said he wanted to "pay tribute to the determination and bravery" of all the women who evidence during the trial.

"Whatever women wear, wherever they go, indeed whatever they drink, they retain the right to say no and to demand justice from the criminal courts when sexual predators like you, Russell Brand, act without their consent," Judge Bennathan said.

Before Judge Joel Bennathan handed down his sentence in London, he considered victim impact statements from some of the women.

Ms C, who was groped by Brand at a London bar, attended court in person reading out her statement from behind a screen so she could only be seen by the judge.

"That undeserved feeling of shame and what if I'd done this or done that has been carried around inside me for over 20 years," she told the court.

"For many years as his star was rising it was impossible to escape seeing him all over the media, being celebrated for his disgusting behaviour against women like it was all a joke.

She said during the trial she felt her character was "being torn apart on social media by people believing all of us women were making it up".

"There’s been accusations and death threats from manic supporters of him on social media," she said.

Crown Prosecutor Reil Karmy-Jones KC read out statements sent in by three of the other women, including the woman who was raped by Brand and referred to as Ms E.

"The consequences of what happened have affected almost every aspect of my life," Ms E wrote in her statement.

"Even now, I continue to experience anxiety, difficulties with trust, reduced confidence and the lasting effects of trauma.

The judge also listened to arguments about sentence severity from both the prosecution and defence.

Brand's barrister Ian Winter KC told the court his client had abused the influence and power that came with fame, but was a "fundamentally different person today and has been for a very long time".

He asked the judge to consider that the rape was a "short" and "momentary" failure to respect her consent.

The comedian's wife Laura was sitting in the public gallery while her husband was sentenced.

He said the case was having a devastating impact on Brand's family.

"Words are totally inadequate to convey the total devastation that [Brand's wife Laura] is experiencing," he said.

“They are wrestling with how to explain to a child, who’s just turned 10, what has just happened here."

He also told the court of Brand was a person of "positive, good character" who did a lot of charity work and had helped a number of alcoholics recover from their addictions.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/s.title: The sales tactics to be on alert for this Black Friday
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/s.author: Jessica Irvine
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/s.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Retail Industry

Retailers are being warned not to use dodgy sales tactics this Black Friday. (ABC News: Daniel Irvine)

Bogus "countdown timers", false "storewide" discount claims and misleading price comparisons are all in the regulator's sights ahead of this year's Black Friday sales season.

Americans are yet to defrost their turkeys, but some Australian retailers have already launched their post-Thanksgiving sales as cash-strapped shoppers try to nab a bargain before Christmas.

It has prompted a warning from the consumer watchdog about a proliferation of illegal marketing tactics.

The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) has expanded its annual "sweep" of Black Friday advertisements from retailer websites to also include social media posts and marketing emails.

"Consumers should be aware that a 'sale' sign doesn't always mean it's a good deal," warns ACCC deputy chair Catriona Lowe.

"We know some businesses use tactics to mislead consumers into thinking they are getting a bargain even when they are not."

Six Australian retailers, including Michael Hill and MyHouse, have been fined a collective $217,800 by the ACCC over the past two years for misleading advertising during the Black Friday sales.

This year, the consumer watchdog is urging cash-strapped Australian shoppers to be on the lookout for the following four misleading sales tactics.

The ACCC fined jewellery retailer Michael Hill $19,800 last year for advertising a Black Friday "Member Event 25% off Sitewide" sale online, when, in fact, not all the products on its website were part of the sale and discounted.

A Michael Hill advertisement for a member sale. (Supplied: ACCC)

MyHouse was also fined $19,800 after the ACCC found the homewares retailer's Black Friday advertising of "Up to 60% Off Sitewide" was misleading as it didn't apply to all products and the asterisk referring to "terms and conditions" was not prominent enough.

MyHouse was fined by the ACCC. (Supplied: ACCC)

Websites displaying countdown timers or "time-limited" offers are also under the microscope.

Such timers are misleading and deceptive to consumers if the advertised offers extend beyond the stated end date.

Furniture retailer James Lane was fined $19,800 for advertising that claimed its Black Friday sale last year would end on December 3.

James Lane's sale extended beyond the advertised end date. (Supplied)

An ACCC investigation found the retailer had, in fact, decided in advance of launching its campaign that the sale would last beyond the advertised end date, which it did, for one week.

Trampoline and children's outdoor playset retailer Vuly paid penalties of $39,600 for two separate instances where it used a bogus countdown timer.

Its online Click Frenzy countdown timer advertised — to the exact second — when an "up to 30% off" sale would end. At that time, however, the clock simply reset to a new and boosted sale offer of "up to 45% off".

Vuly's countdown clock went down to the second. (Supplied: ACCC)

"Retailers risk ACCC enforcement action if they misrepresent the size, scope or duration of their sales," Ms Lowe said.

Shoppers should also be alert to other pressure-selling tactics, including misleading testimonials and messages designed to create a sense of scarcity, such as warnings about low stock availability, the ACCC said.

The deputy CEO of the Consumer Policy Research Centre (CPRC), Chandni Gupta, said "scarcity cues" could include notifications such as "10 people are looking at this product right now".

Retailers may also use warnings that stock is low — for example, "only 1 item left!" — when, in fact, new stock may be arriving the next day.

A percentage discount can make us feel like we’ve scored a bargain but "doesn’t actually tell us whether the final price is good".

"There is an imbalance of power as there is no way for a consumer to confirm whether the urgency is real or not," she said.

She urged shoppers to be wary of pressure sales tactics this Black Friday season.

"If the deal looks too good to be true, it probably is," Ms Gupta cautioned

Retailers use sales countdown clocks on their social media, emails, and websites to create urgency. (ABC News: Hanan Dervisevic)

Finally, the ACCC is warning consumers to be sceptical of advertisements offering large percentage discounts, such as 50 per cent or more off.

If the product has not actually been sold at the higher price before the sale, the discount is unlawful under Australian Consumer Law.

Electronics retailer digiDirect recently amassed fines totalling $99,000 across five instances where it mislead consumers with the discounts it displayed across a range of products.

Despite claiming "price slashed" and the use of strike-through price discounting, an ACCC investigation found digiDirect rarely sold the products at the higher price.

One example was a mini wireless keyboard, advertised as on sale for $149, down from $229.

Misleading price comparisons are a regulatory focus this year. (Supplied: ACCC)

Misleading "was/now" discount advertising has been in the regulator's sights this year, including the recent ACCC case against grocery giant Coles for its "Down Down" discounts.

"Consumers continue to look for the best prices and may delay major purchases until Black Friday and Cyber Monday in anticipation of good value and legitimate discounts," Ms Lowe said.

The warning comes as the ACCC is being urged to act against retailers abusing consumer protection laws.

"I think it is vital that the ACCC takes strong enforcement action against retailers who mislead and rip off people," said Meg Dalling from the Consumer Action Law Centre.

CPRC's Ms Gupta said new laws against "unfair trading" coming into effect next July should help to protect consumers from "dark patterns" in advertising tactics, including bogus countdown timers and low-stock notifications.

Dodgy sales tactics to look out for this Black Friday

"Our research has shown 83 per cent Australians have had a negative experience with these dark pattern sales tactics," she said.

"People have lost money. They felt pressure to make a purchase that they otherwise wouldn't, or they paid more than they would have otherwise due to these tactics."

Separately, the ACCC has urged shoppers to be wary of fake online shop fronts replicating the websites of legitimate retailers during the Black Friday sales period, cautioning shoppers to double-check the credentials of any site they visit, which can include making sure the web address starts with "https://" and shows a locked padlock symbol.

If shoppers spot an advertisement they think is misleading or deceptive, they can report it to the ACCC via the Report a consumer issue page.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/k.title: Gunman dies in hospital after killing six and injuring 15 in Krakow shooting
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/k.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Poland's interior minister, Marcin Kierwiński, said the suspect held "very radical" and "ultra-nationalistic" views. (Reuters: Jakub Porzycki)

The gunman who killed six people and injured 15 others in central Krakow has died in hospital.

Polish prosecutors said the mass shooting is being treated as an act "constituting a terrorist offence".

The Polish government has vowed to review the requirements and regulations governing gun permits.

A gunman who killed six people and injured 15 others in a mass shooting in central Krakow, Poland, has died in hospital.

The man was shot by police officers and arrested minutes after he opened fire on people from his car in Krakow's historic main square on Saturday, local time.

Polish prosecutors said on Sunday the attack is being treated as an act "constituting a terrorist offence".

The square reopened on Sunday evening, with mourners gathering to lay flowers and candles in honour of the victims. (Reuters: Jakub Porzycki)

The government had said the assailant, identified as Michal O, a 24-year-old from the town of Ostrowiec Swietokrzyski in south-eastern Poland, may have been inspired by far-right ideology, without providing further details.

The incident sparked a bitter political dispute over his motives, with Poland's nationalist opposition criticising the government's statement about far-right ideology.

Law & Justice party leader Jaroslaw Kaczynski said the claims were a "blatant lie".

Polish prosecutors say the shooting is being treated as an act "constituting a terrorist offence". (Reuters: Jakub Porzyck)

On Monday, government officials appeared to walk back from the initial comments.

Four women and two men are dead, 15 others are injured and the gunman is in hospital after a shooting in a market square in the Polish city of Krakow.

"Until the matter is fully clarified and the authorities are in possession of complete information, it is best to refrain from making comments, even if there are some initial indications," government spokesperson Adam Szlapka told local news.

Justice Minister Waldemar Zurek said on Monday that despite the death of the shooter, the investigation would continue, aiming to establish whether he acted alone or was inspired by any group.

"Evidence is being collected, but I will not show or disclose it. I ask for restraint," Mr Zurek told Radio Zet.

An interior ministry spokesperson said earlier on Monday there were many different emblems on the perpetrator's clothing that had already been partially examined and interpreted.

Four women and two men were killed in the shooting. Three of the women and one of the men were Polish, according to Malopolska regional governor Krzysztof Jan Klęczar.

A man from the United Kingdom and a woman from Austria were also among the dead, authorities said.

The bodies of the shooter's father, mother and sister were found in their family home on Saturday, and officials said they were also likely killed by Michal O.

About 411,000 people hold gun permits in Poland, which has a population of 37 million. (Agencja Wyborcza: Jakub Włodek via Reuters)

A video posted on social media showed a police officer repeatedly shooting the attacker, who was lying on the street. The officer later slowly collapsed to the ground.

Of the 15 injured in the attack, 14 remain in hospital in a stable condition.

A police officer who assisted in apprehending the shooter remains in a serious condition, according to Krakow Province Governor Krzysztof Kleczar.

The Polish government will review regulations on requirements for people with gun permits following the tragedy, Mr Zurek said.

Both the shooter and his father had gun permits, and several firearms were found in the family apartment and the assailant's car, prosecutors said.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/d.title: WA Aboriginal affairs minister visits Pilbara amid child welfare crisis
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/d.author: Kimberley Putland, Amy Rossbach, Alistair Bates, and Keane Bourke
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-09/d.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Indigenous Peoples

Don Punch has been facing mounting calls to resign. (ABC Pilbara: Kimberley Putland)

Don Punch has visited South Hedland amid mounting criticism of his response to systemic child protection failures.

The town was thrust into the spotlight after reports of children living in squalid conditions.

WA Premier Roger Cook says he is proud of the work Mr Punch has done as the Aboriginal affairs minister.

Western Australia's Minister for Aboriginal Affairs Don Punch has slammed the politicisation of child protection failures in the state's north and rejected calls for his resignation during a visit to South Hedland.

The town has been subject to intense attention in recent months after evidence of systemic child protection failings emerged.

Facing questions about his role in the crisis, Mr Punch said he was "lobbying for better outcomes for Aboriginal people" and had travelled to South Hedland after receiving a letter from Nyamal-Pitjikarli elder Doris Eaton.

"Aboriginal issues and Aboriginal people are beyond politics," Mr Punch said.

Media and politicians have swarmed South Hedland in recent months. (ABC News: Andrew Seabourne)

Last month the WA government announced it would hold a coronial inquest in the 2022 murders of three Aboriginal children in nearby Port Hedland, which had been the subject of a lengthy campaign by their grandmother, Dorothy Papertalk.

The case received fresh scrutiny as media reports revealed further allegations of neglect and triggered visits from senior politicians, including the premier, but not the Aboriginal affairs minister.

A coronial inquest is announced into the deaths of three children killed by their mother in Port Hedland in 2022.

Mr Punch has faced severe public backlash for ruling out a trip to the Pilbara unless he was specifically asked by elders.

Multiple local elders, including Ms Eaton, told the ABC that Mr Punch should not need an invitation.

In South Hedland today, Mr Punch walked back statements he made about the Aboriginal affairs portfolio only being about native title and heritage protection.

"My job is to go out and listen to Aboriginal people, Aboriginal elders, talk with communities and understand the issues that they're facing," he said.

Mr Punch's visit came as the opposition launched a petition calling for his sacking from the portfolio.

It has been signed by Robert Isaacs, who has spent decades working to improve the lives of First Nations people.

Don Punch met with Kariyarra elder Pat Mason and other elders. (ABC Pilabara: Kimberley Putland)

He said he was motivated by watching decades of Aboriginal affairs ministers who "really haven't performed the work that Aboriginal people expected".

"I want parliament now — the state parliament in WA — to look at appointing an Aboriginal commissioner that reports directly to the parliament," Dr Isaacs said.

"So every member of parliament is getting the metrics across, they're understanding about where this funding is going, billions of dollars, about policies, about directions of programs."

That would replace what he described as a largely powerless portfolio and address concerns about too many people speaking on behalf of Aboriginal Australians, which he said he'd had a "gutful" of.

Don Punch says his political opponents are exploiting the situation. (ABC Pilbara: Kimberley Putland)

Mr Punch said he suspected Mr Isaacs was prompted by WA Liberal Leader Basil Zempilas.

"He is making a football of Aboriginal people to simply score his own political goals and it's appalling behaviour," Mr Punch said.

Kariyarra elder Patricia Mason was one of the elders who met with Mr Punch during his visit.

"I think Punch just wants it to go away," she said.

"They're about a quick fix, and a quick fix leaves us in a crisis."

Ms Mason said constantly engaging with politicians and the media was taking a toll.

"I'm feeling mentally and physically drained," she said.

Premier Roger Cook said his party would not consider the parliamentary petition under any circumstance.

"Don's doing a great job. He's working well with the community and we're really proud of his work," he said.

Basil Zempilas rubbished the premier's comments about the monister's performance. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

Mr Zempilas hit back at the premier's defence of the minister.

"Has he not read or heard any of the comments from the Aboriginal elders form the Hedland region who are so exasperated by Don Punch's actions?" he said.

Mr Punch has pledged to return to South Hedland in the next couple of months.
