First of all, I’m so glad you’re bringing this up because we literally, over the past three years, have been dealing with exactly this. Because believe it or not, and it’s so bizarre to think about, none of us right now has a right to our own voice or likeness under federal law. Most of us don’t even have it under state law. State law, which is called the right of publicity, usually only applies to advertising or endorsements. I couldn’t take your face and put it on a Wheaties box without asking you because I’m selling it and making money, and I’d be using your popularity to do so. Those are very limited rights. Now we’re in the world of deep fakes where everybody can do anything, make you say or do something you never said, you never did, and that you might not approve of — and we don’t have a basic right to ourselves under the law.

It seems so weird in a country that was founded on individual liberty and individual rights that we wouldn’t have an individual right to ourselves. So we had to sort of start from scratch. And what we did was get together with YouTube in the very beginning. These things, even if they’re not created by the platforms, the avenue to the fan is through the platform. And everybody’s not going to bring a lawsuit against everybody in order to get this stuff down when it’s proliferating as fast as it is. So the question was, what responsibility does or can the platform have to give a very simple takedown mechanism that anybody could use? Because this is your face, it’s your right. It’s not like the record company owns the right to your face, or the movie company. You own the right to your face.

So if you don’t like the fact that somebody used your face or your voice in a way you didn’t like, you should be able to very quickly say, “That’s me, I can prove it’s me, and I don’t want it up there.” And the platform should want to do something to protect the integrity of the platform without liability.

Can I just stop you? This is why it’s a nightmare hypothetical, right? A longstanding trope at The Verge started by our former colleague, Sarah Jeong, is that copyright law is the only functional law on the internet. The only way you actually really want to regulate the internet is to take things down. That is the thing that people want to accomplish. The First Amendment basically prohibits the government from creating some mechanism to take things down, except in the case of copyright law, where we have the Digital Millennium Copyright Act. There’s a huge notice-and-takedown regime in that law, and it is frequently abused on all of these platforms to get things taken down.

The purpose of that law has been stretched beyond recognition. If you issue a YouTube strike to a YouTuber on that platform, all hell breaks loose. That is an act of war because unless you’re doing it for the right purpose, they know you’re doing it to harass them.

This is a lot, right? You’re describing a new notice-and-takedown regime that isn’t based in the law. It’s based on some private company’s understanding of what a likeness is. And there are all kinds of reasons that I might want to publish a video of Donald Trump. There are all kinds of reasons that I might want to publish a video of Drake that have nothing to do with using his likeness for commercial purposes. And granting those people the ability to take things down is the same problem without, I don’t know, a federal fair use regime or some other… How do you balance that?

Great. So this is why it took three years, and it’s still going on, because what you’re saying is, first of all, you need to learn from the experience with the DMCA. It is the precedent we have, and there are obviously problems on both sides. You need to learn from those. The second is you need to create a new intellectual property right, in this case, much closer to trademark than to copyright, but still an intellectual property right, because that is, as you said, sort of the functional way of balancing that against the First Amendment. If you have an intellectual property right, you are allowed to remove it despite somebody’s other free speech rights. In this case, there’s a weird analysis of, do you have a free speech right to control how your voice is used? So it’s like free speech versus free speech.

What we did was, besides getting together with many First Amendment law scholars and trying to hammer this out, which was a fascinating learning process, by the way... I feel like I got to go back to law school and listen to these brilliant constitutional scholars talk about the tension between the First Amendment and intellectual property rights. What you have to do, if you’re going to create a takedown regime, is put in hurdles on both sides. You have to put in hurdles on the “I’m telling you to take it down” side. And there are lots of things we’ve learned from the past, like: Are we going to force a, in this case, First Amendment review before you can send the notice? What’s the punishment if you send a false notice? Is that punishment high enough to deter false notices? Then on the back end, you have to have a counter notice, right? And then how do you make sure that that works well and that it’s not too low a hurdle, but a little bit of a hurdle because you want to have balance on both sides?

And then finally you have this middle area where there’s going to be a decision about whether or not it’s a parody, for example, which many are, and the First Amendment trumps copyright when it comes to a parody. What if it’s news? And what is news anymore? What is bona fide news versus some of the stuff I’m getting when I’m scrolling? We then created this middle period where a temporary restraining order, a very quick legal action, could take place and a judge could actually decide the constitutional question — because nobody wants the platforms deciding constitutional questions. The people on both sides are like regular people. They’re not going to be making ultimate determinations. So that’s ultimately what we came down to in the NO FAKES Act, which is the name of the federal bill that’s now being pushed. And whether the balance there is perfect or not yet, I don’t know, but I do know that we learned a lot of lessons from the DMCA.

I think everybody is very aware that the First Amendment defenses are really paramount in any kind of regime like this, and that overprotecting on either side… If you overprotect on the First Amendment side, then this also applies to a girl who’s bullied in high school and some kid takes her face and sticks it on a body that’s not hers. You don’t want that staying up when it shouldn’t. On the other hand, I have the right to use your face for certain things because that’s my free speech, and it’s really funny, or I’m making a point about underlying character or something like that. So, long answer: there’s no perfect response, but this time we had OpenAI at the table, we had YouTube at the table, we had people from Public Knowledge at the table who bring a different perspective than we would bring. We ultimately got to a place where I don’t think folks are thrilled on all sides of it, but I think they think it’s progress.

It’s something. I will grant you that it’s something. It’s better than what we have now, but it’s fundamentally the creation of a new intellectual property right.

And there’s some balance there that almost certainly will track the same balance that copyright law and music have undergone over the past hundred years.

The initial debates about copyright law and music were about player pianos. We’ve built huge institutions to manage these rights.

I said I was going to talk about Google a lot, and the tension inside of Google when it comes to this is the next sort of nightmare law school hypothetical for you. Google has two conceptions of itself. YouTube describes itself as a licensing regime. There’s a lot of content on YouTube; the creators make it, and Google takes a license to it. Whether or not any creator ever gets to negotiate that license is of secondary concern. There’s a lot of music on YouTube, and the industry had to fight its way into licensing on YouTube. Music is existential for YouTube, and the industry knows it has that power. There’s a real back and forth. Maybe the only industry that has true negotiating power with YouTube is the music industry. And you can see this play out over and over and over again.

On the other side of the house, Google Search is a huge business; they will describe it to you as a fair use regime. We’re going to ingest all the photos in the world and let you search them; that’s fair use, and we’re going to litigate our way through that. We’re going to ingest all the books in the world for Google Books; that’s fair use, and we’re going to litigate that. And they have done that over and over and over again.

You can work with the people at YouTube. They’re very reasonable. Neal Mohan is a smart guy. He understands that he needs music on that platform to survive, and he will build you the tools that you’re asking for, and he has. And then the people running Google are like, “We’re just going to eat everything, and training an AI model is fair use.” And just in that one company, they are totally at odds with each other. They’re going to kill each other somehow. How do you make sense of that?

What’s so fascinating to me about YouTube is that it is the first real lesson in the arc of the DMCA. It’s where I think a technology-based company realized that even if you win the fight on intellectual property rights, if you don’t have a partnership through a license in the actual market where fans are, you are not going to have the service that fans really want. And so it was the first time that everybody realized that you can win the case but lose the business. Music is such a driver of YouTube, and I think this applies to AI too. Having pristine copies that fans really want, and then having marketing partnerships and partnerships with people who invest in and partner with creators, is what matters. Those creators have a better sense of how to create the bond between that particular artist that they’ve been living with and sort of building a brand around. They understand that, versus sitting in a cubicle in a tech company and trying to decide how to connect the fan with the artist in the best way, that the former piece is irreplaceable.

And I think YouTube realized that and developed Content ID even though they technically won in court and didn’t have to, so to speak. Now, the partnership is so ingrained that there’s a dependency, or a codependency, and that’s how it’s supposed to work. It also works because of this concept in copyright law called substitution. If what you’re creating substitutes for something else, it’s probably not fair use. That’s what we’re arguing in our case against Suno. You’re basically creating music that is competing on the same platform right next to human-made music; you can click on either one, and you’re paying the same subscription fee. And so you’re affecting the economic pool, and you’re effectively substituting in the marketplace.

This is the fourth factor of the fair use regime.

This is the fourth factor of fair use, which courts say is the most important: are you affecting the potential market for the underlying work? And if you are, that’s sort of problem number one. Google, unlike in the YouTube case under the DMCA, the case that they won in the Supreme Court was about creating an index. And the idea is if you click on it, it could lead you to the work that you might then buy. The search result doesn’t substitute for the work, but it could lead you to the work, which at the end of the day may not have the same economic consequence. It could even have a positive economic consequence. At least they would argue that.

So there’s this weird thing: Google won its case, and YouTube won its case, but YouTube formed a partnership despite the win because that’s the best fan experience. And Google didn’t because it wasn’t as related to the fan experience. The fan experience was potentially pointed to by their activity. So that’s my weird law school take on the two cases.

If you’re running Google, if you’re in charge of Google Gemini, you need all of the data in the world. That is just how it works. To make the models better and to win against OpenAI, you need more data, and all of those companies just took it. I do not think Google came to you and said, “Can we license all the music in your database even though we already have a license on YouTube?” In fact, they just scraped YouTube.

I don’t think creators have woken up to the fact that they’ve given a lot of economic value to Google and its models. The other AI companies also scraped YouTube, and Google can’t yell at them because then they will have to reveal that they scraped YouTube, and this is about as tense a fight in the AI industry as there is.

You’re going to come to Google at some point, and you’re going to say, “No, you got to pay us for that training.” I know you’re suing Suno, but that feels like a little test balloon for the people with the real money. At some point they’re going to say, “No, this training was fair use.” We’re watching this dynamic play out in dozens of these cases across the industry. How do you make sense of that? Where you’re going to say, “You’re going to kill us. If the AI models flood YouTube with fake music, you’re actually going to kill the supply of the data that you need.”

So there’s the legal side and the business side. On the legal side, obviously we’re bringing this as a precedent-setting case to show that it is not fair use to train on music. And whatever exemption you want to think of, it’s hard for us to imagine how it applies. I don’t think national security is at risk because you have to copy Drake. I don’t think that there’s-

No, we’re putting it into policy. Everything is an arc, as you know, but in the beginning of a disruption, you try to put into policy the basic rights that are going to allow the creators to control their creation, to charge what they want for their creation, and to develop the licensing deals that they feel they want to develop. The streaming revolution allows “exploitation,” not in the negative sense, but in the positive sense. It allows it to last forever. That’s why you have all these new investors coming into the music community because it’s a little bit more like a commodity now. That’s why Goldman Sachs is buying catalogs. That’s why all of these new companies are coming in, and they’re buying catalogs of music because music’s evergreen. It’s water. People are going to love it forever.

And as an artist, you now have an opportunity you never had in the past. I just want to hit pause here and say that the baby punk rocker in me is... We could do another full hour on artists who now have the opportunity to sell their catalog to Goldman Sachs. It’s another hour. I know it’s there.

Listen, we are all 20-something at some time, and then we’re 50-something at another time. Everybody wants to take care of their grandkids at some point.

But this is an opportunity that they have now that they didn’t have before. And so I think that this disruption… I think there’s more skin in the game for the actual creator than there was in the past when the revenue was more bifurcated or trifurcated. Nobody on the creative side of the equation thinks that it’s right that Suno will be making all the money from all of the music that has been created in the past, and that substitutional effect is going to deprive the artist or any of their partners.

If the artist is in the middle of the sun and you’ve got all the folks around them from performing rights organizations, to record companies, to publishers, to managers, to producers, to agents, et cetera, they’re all sort of partners in a piece of that larger puzzle. There are other outcomes here. I think it’s Warner that’s partnered with Suno; they made a model on Warner’s music so they don’t run into these issues. Your solution there, at least as I understand this conversation, is labeling. You’re going to put labels on the AI stuff so the fans can make a market decision, and the bet is the fans will choose humans. Is there another solution to the glut of supply?

I’m not privy to the licensing agreements that exist with Suno or any other AI company because I represent competitors, so they would never tell me. But I would imagine that it’s about dilution: where you don’t want to put artists’ music at risk on streaming platforms, because 90 percent of what they’re competing with is AI slop, if I could use that term. The licensing agreement gives you the leverage and the ability, if your rights are secured, to say, “I’m not going to let you download all this stuff.”

I mean, it’s rumored that in the Udio agreement, a walled garden had to be built so that fans could make music within the network on their own Spotify-like app. It wouldn’t discourage them from also having Spotify or Apple; it increases the revenue for everybody, but we’re not going to allow you to download from this platform and dilute that platform.

I don’t know if that’ll work. That seems to be one model. It could be that the terms with Suno had a limit on it or considered supply. I’m not a business person; I’m a policy person. But I think that there are plenty of ways, if the rights are secured, that through licensing arrangements and agreements, creators could then have the leverage to affect the supply so as not to cannibalize the work that they have on other platforms.

Well, I think the policy problem of supply is that it will affect the business somehow. We should talk about Spotify for a minute. It’s amazing that we haven’t spent more time talking about Spotify.

I think the model companies are not going to listen. You can see what they are doing. They are gluttonous for data, and they think that they can outrun the consequences. We’ll see what happens there. Spotify is not training a model. Spotify is just distributing music. That’s the thing that they’re doing; they’re a pure-play business in that way, and they have a lot of incentives for AI music to replace the music they have to otherwise pay for on that platform. They have a lot of incentives for white noise and fake streams in history to do these things, and they’ve gotten in trouble for some of it. This is a real thing that happens on this platform. Are they going to participate in a labeling scheme and say, “This is AI music?”

I think so, because as much as they have an economic incentive to lower their costs, their biggest economic incentive is to keep fans paying $9.99, $12.99, $15.99 per month. And so if fans feel duped, if you are putting —

Is that proven out in the market? I’m actually very curious about this.

You’re saying there’s AI slop on Spotify now, or when you search for Taylor Swift, you get a bunch of weird Taylor Swift soundalikes, which is an experience everyone has on Spotify. It hasn’t churned those fans yet. There’s not some exodus to Tidal or Apple Music. Spotify is still dominant in its way.

Right. I think they’re walking down the road slowly, probably a little too slowly. I’m trying to see if they can do just enough to keep those two things in balance. Right now, for example, Spotify is saying, “We will only disclose or label a recording as AI in the credits.” Well, how many people look at the credits? I wish more people looked at the credits; they would discover producers and songwriters and other awesome folks who have contributed to the recording — but they don’t.

They need to do it at the track level. They’re not there yet. But they are disclosing AI personas that are made, because that’s sort of the highest on the dupe scale. And then under that, they’re looking at the fact that 90 percent of the recordings available on Spotify get 10 percent of the revenue, and 10 percent of the content gets 90 percent of the revenue. It’s because most of what’s on there gets less than 10 listens, or less than a hundred listens, and all of this slop is just going on, which means storage costs and all sorts of other things that they have to think about.

So I think that they will go as far down the road as fans will demand, as their users will demand. I think we’ll get to a point where people get these recommendations in their algorithm. “If you like this song, you’ll also like this one.” And when you listen to it, it turns out it was AI, you didn’t know it was AI, and you’ll feel deceived. That’s when they’ve got a giant problem because they’re responsible for that recommendation. They’re the ones that fed that to you. And we do have lots of consumer research out there showing that subscribers, just like all consumers, want to feel like nobody’s pulling the wool over their eyes.

But is there an actual market pressure? I can think of all kinds of times fans have revolted against Spotify. I love the band Stars, and every now and again they’ll tweet, “We didn’t make any money on this song on Spotify.” And everyone tweets at Spotify, and they’re mad. Spotify’s not paying artists any more money. Is there an actual market pressure that will make this labeling happen, or is it policy pressure?

It’s both. It’s a combination, because there are already laws in other countries that are mandating labels. And once a market like the EU or the US — that’s such a big market — or the UK or China, once they demand labeling on a global system, it’s actually cheaper to do it all around the world than it is to just geo-block it in one country.

This is the California car emission model of regulation, right?

It’s amazing what California can do because these companies are headquartered there. I mean not Spotify, but Apple and Google and others. And so the transparency law in California is the reason why Suno has to, as of August, put a watermark saying, “This is AI-generated” that’s machine-readable. One state, but they’re doing it all over the world because that’s what… So it’s a combination of policy, which obviously we are very directly engaged in, and competition. I predict that what Apple decides to do that is more fan-friendly will drive Spotify, and vice versa.

There’s not that much churn between them, but if there’s some sort of perception that you’re being more subscriber-friendly than somebody else, that tends to drive results. It does the same on the privacy issue, for example, where there’s no law on it, but now companies are competing to say, “We’re the private browser. Apple, we protect your privacy.”

One company says that. Let me ask you this. I’ve only got a few minutes left, and I want to take one turn at the end to talk about how you measure for platinum certification, because that’s also up in the air.

But let me just ask you one more question here on labeling. We have spent a lot of time at The Verge covering labels for images and media. There are all these standards that exist. I have one poor reporter, her name is Jess Weatherbed, and she has been forced to learn everything about the C2PA standard and content, SynthID, and all these things.

I’m so sorry. It’s really important, though.

They’re very important, and we spend a lot of time covering them because they have to work. And they have to work in a number of different places in the chain, right? They have to work in the camera, in Photoshop, on Twitter, and everyone has to agree. If Elon Musk does not want SynthID to show up on his platform, it doesn’t matter if it worked in the camera. This is a big chain.

It seems harder in music, much harder because a bunch of bedroom DJs are probably not going to participate in your technical scheme for labeling when they upload to DistroKid. An artist getting a beat from a producer over iMessage — who knows if that metadata will survive. You might have to watermark the sound files themselves in some deep intrinsic way, and that can get you into all kinds of trouble because now you’re screwing with the audio files at the software level and artists don’t like that. How do you make labeling work at all?

Yeah, you’re hitting on our daily meetings. So I mean, there are the international organizations like DDEX, for example, that can help align fields and stuff like that. C2PA, which can give you a model for provenance. But at the end of the day, it has to be the platforms and the distributors that are willing to do it. Because when it comes to generative AI, the record labels are not tagging and putting generative AI up on Spotify. That’s out of the DIY world.

That’s somebody going to a music generator, downloading it, and putting it up through DistroKid. So your gateway is DistroKid, TuneCore. It’s the distributors. Are they using AI detection technology to determine that it’s fully generated? You might not be able to use AI detection technology to say your song is five percent of this or use it for attribution yet, but you can definitely use it to say this is fully generated AI. And if so, are they willing to tag it so that it works with Apple and Spotify’s platform?

Then, on the platforms themselves, this is sort of like the parental advisory program; it might be voluntary, and everybody might have a little bit of a different way of implementing it, but fans are pretty clear. When something’s labeled as parental advisory, which probably just draws more young people to listen to it —

But when it’s labeled as parental advisory, people kind of get it. They know. It’s become sort of a culturally known thing. I think labeling for fully generated AI can definitely get there, but the distributors have to be willing to play. It can’t just be the platforms because if it doesn’t go downstream, they’re going to go in different directions. And already, Deezer’s going in one direction, Apple’s going in another direction, Spotify’s going in another direction. To me, the fully generated problem, which is a DIY problem, is a distributor problem. And we have to provide incentives to the distributors to get them to take responsibility and play ball.

Do you think that technology exists to support the policy there? You need a technology that can detect AI-generated media. I’m not sure that any of that exists or works well.

I think it exists and works well for fully generated AI music. We also do a lot of testing at the RIAA. That’s another thing that our tech team does. And then we disclose the results back to the folks who gave it to us. We won’t disclose it to anybody else, but if you want to know what our test says about your technology, we’ll tell you.

And I think when it comes to fully generated AI, there’s plenty of detection technologies out there that do a really good job. Once you get below that, time will make it better. So I don’t know that we could get into a lot of gradations right now. Deezer, very successfully, on a platform level, uses AI detection technology and then labels what it detects as fully generated AI, and it’s got a very low false positive rate.

I want to end by talking about the certifications for platinum records and so on. It’s an important part of what you do. All the artists want their little records on their wall. It’s amazing that it’s still records. One of our jokes at The Verge is also that no one knows how to count anything, that Nielsen ratings — I should probably disclose, we are now part of the company that owns Luminate, which powers the Billboard charts.

The Billboard charts and their methodology are always in flux. Actually, I think as of this year, they’re in a fight with YouTube. YouTube does not want to be counted on the Billboard charts because some methodologies are... Counting is very political.

You literally give awards for counting to a big number. That is in flux as artists gain more attention on TikTok. And I have probably heard that whole Nicole Kidman song, in fragments on TikTok. I’ve never listened to the whole thing all the way through, and I’m certainly never going to buy a copy of it. Again, all in flux, and then somewhere in there is a bunch of AI remixes, and now I’ve listened to “Pop Star” by Drake 10,000 times because Darth Vader is singing it to me.

How are you thinking about that methodology, as to who’s creating what? AI is in the mix, and we’re listening to more and more fragments to discover songs on social platforms than anything else.

I swear to God, you are in my daily meetings.

Can I just tell you? I’m happy to hear that. I drive The Verge team crazy because I’m like, the music industry is the future always. And they’re like, no one wants to listen to that. So thank you for indulging me. I appreciate you.

I mean, you have your finger on the pulse. This is exactly the type of stuff we’re thinking of. So right now we’re still in the world of 1500 streams equaling one unit, and what used to be the sale of a CD. Now it’s obviously singles-based more than albums-based, although we still do certify albums. And if you look at the chart eligibility program that is now being implemented outside of Billboard and OCC, in other places of the world, they have made rules to say, unless it’s substantially human, we are not going to allow it to be eligible for the chart because you’re literally taking the place of a human artist on number 49. Billboard, so far, will allow it, but they’ll label it.

We haven’t, because we certify albums that were released by record companies. We have yet to run into the issue of the AI slop or the machine-created piece. But as we get more into assistive AI, as creators start to use AI more, and you look at the chart eligibility of substantially human, does a stream as part of that 1500 mean that it still has to be a human stream? Yes, I’m sure that we will come down on that side.

But what does substantially human mean? I think over time that might change. It might be different three years from now than it is today. But at the core, it’s got to be in the control of the creator. And some people would argue that putting nine words into a music generator is an act of creation.

Oh, they will. They’re going to. Yeah.

And that they are a creator, and therefore it’s the same thing. It’s not the same thing. Not saying that craft doesn’t change over time, and that in songwriting it’s also different than in producing and creating a recording. Using AI in the songwriting process may look very different than it does in the recording process, so we have to think about that too. But as far as gold and platinum go, we are still in the reliably safe zone of being able to know with a great deal of certainty exactly what we’re doing. I think the evolution over time is going to be in how creators use AI more than it will need to be in something that’s fully machine-readable or machine-created.

Well, Mitch, you’ve given us so much time. As you can tell, I’ve thoroughly enjoyed this conversation. I could keep going for hours and hours now.

Me too. I mean, honestly, this has been awesome. You freaked me out a little bit because you... It’s so great to see, though, because the stuff that you’re focused on is exactly what we are trying to grapple with every single day. And I think where we’ve come to is that we can’t pretend that there are easy answers. We can’t just react sort of in a knee-jerk way. We’ve got to try to figure out a path forward that’s going to allow the industry to change and grow. This industry’s adapted more times than any other industry in the history of our country. I mean, nobody goes from wax cylinders to AI in a hundred years. Can you imagine asking Boeing to make cars? So, a very adaptable industry.

I agree with you that we’re ahead of the game and that we are the future. We’re sort of living it. And the lessons that we learned from the music industry, we can apply to a lot of other things. So this has been awesome.

Thank you so much for being on Decoder. Really appreciate it.

You got it. Take care.

https://www.theverge.com/tech/1029676/me.author: David Pierce
https://www.theverge.com/tech/1029676/me.text:
The company is betting that the future of blogging looks a lot like group chats.

The company is betting that the future of blogging looks a lot like group chats.

For the first time ever, Medium is becoming more than just a blogging platform. The company is launching a new app, called TK, that combines note taking and journaling with something resembling a private social network. The app is meant to get you writing more, and help you share that writing with friends and fans. And it’s part of a much bigger idea about blogging, and a much broader thesis about the state of the internet.

“I don’t think we’ve actually had a launch of anything important since 2017,” Medium CEO Tony Stubblebine tells me over Zoom, a few days ahead of the company’s biggest launch in apparently almost a decade. That was when Medium’s then-CEO, Ev Williams, decided to quit chasing ad dollars and become a subscription business. “It’s clear that the broken system is ad-driven media on the internet,” Williams wrote at the time. “It simply doesn’t serve people. In fact, it’s not designed to.” Medium began charging for access to most content. “We got out of the attention economy,” Stubblebine says now.

The trend Williams saw back then, though, has only accelerated and metastasized. AI companies are hoovering up any content they can get their hands on, legality be damned; search engines and chatbots are sending less and less traffic back to the web. Medium, like most websites on the internet, relies on Google for a huge portion of its traffic — in the time of Google Zero, that’s an existential risk. “When Google started taking away all the traffic,” Stubblebine says, “what I told them is that this hurts us, but it also hurts you, because I’ll just tell you what my product roadmap is going to do: I’m going to switch to private blogging… We’re just going to take everything underground.”

https://www.theverge.com/21570161/holida.title: Here are the shipping and return policies for all the big-name retailers
https://www.theverge.com/21570161/holida.author: Sheena Vasani
https://www.theverge.com/21570161/holida.text:
We’ve read the fine print and rounded up the policies for each major retailer to make things simpler.

We’ve read the fine print and rounded up the policies for each major retailer to make things simpler.

If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

With the holidays quickly approaching, everyone will soon be on the hunt for gifts and the fastest way to get them. Thankfully, many retailers offer generous shipping policies, with some even providing free two-day shipping or same-day delivery if you’re willing to pay a little extra. And just in case the gift you choose isn’t quite right, many retailers offer extended return policies so your giftee can get something more to their liking.

For your convenience, we’ve compiled the current shipping and return policies for all the big-name retailers, from Amazon to Walmart. A few already have holiday policies in place, but we’ll be keeping tabs on them and updating our list accordingly. Hopefully, knowing more about how much leeway you have to make a return will help lessen that inevitable holiday angst (fingers crossed).

Shipping: Same-day delivery is not available on Thanksgiving, Christmas, or New Year’s (it’s also limited on Black Friday). However, Prime members get free same-day delivery on qualifying orders in qualifying ZIP codes provided they meet the “minimum qualifying dollar threshold” (which varies by location) of eligible items in their cart. One-Day and Two-Day Delivery with no minimum purchase amount required is also available to Prime members for qualifying products. Non-Prime buyers will find shipping options on the order page of each specific product.

Returns: As part of its holiday promotional period, Amazon says most items purchased between November 1st and December 31st can be returned until January 31st, 2027. Apple products, however, must be returned by January 15th, 2027. Note that this policy applies to both Prime and non-Prime buyers.

Shipping: Apple has yet to provide details on its holiday shipping policy; however, last year, it offered free delivery of in-stock items that hadn’t been engraved by Christmas Eve if you ordered before 9PM ET on December 21st. Apple also offers free next-day or two-hour delivery from local stores in most metro areas for an additional fee, or you can opt to pick up purchases yourself by visiting your local Apple Store.

Returns: Apple is offering an extended return period for online orders received between November 6th and December 25th, allowing you to return items until January 8th, 2027. Purchases made after December 25th are generally subject to the usual terms and conditions, and must be returned within 14 calendar days of your initial purchase date.

Shipping: Target offers free two-day shipping on many orders if you spend $35 or more or use your Target Circle Card. Same-day delivery costs $9.99 per order, but it’s included with a Target Circle 360 membership ($10.99 a month / $99 a year). Your mileage may vary for same-day delivery availability based on the item and your location.

Returns: Target offers an extended return policy for electronics and entertainment items purchased between November 1st and December 24th, allowing you to return them until January 24th, 2027. Mobile phones and Apple products (including Beats products) purchased during the same window must be returned by January 8th, 2027. Target’s standard return policy applies for most other items, with a generous 90-day window for third-party products and up to a year for Target-branded products with a receipt.

Shipping: Walmart’s holiday shipping policy doesn’t currently mention a deadline for delivery by Christmas, but it does break down the available fulfillment options. Walmart provides free next-day delivery in eligible ZIP codes, free two-day delivery, and free standard shipping for eligible orders of $35 or more. Walmart Plus subscribers also receive free next-day and two-day shipping with no order minimum. Some orders and ZIP codes may also qualify for same-day delivery, if you’re willing to pay an additional fee.

Returns: Most items purchased between October 1st and December 31st may be returned until January 31st, 2027. Some exceptions, like smartphones, may apply.

Shipping: B&H Photo offers free two-day and next-day shipping on select items. Most other products qualify for free standard shipping (one to seven business days), and free expedited shipping (one to two business days) is generally available for items over $49.

Returns: B&H Photo allows returns within 30 days of the delivery date, provided the items are in new condition and still housed in their original packaging. For the holidays, most items purchased between November 1st and January 1st can be returned until February 1st, 2027.

Shipping: Best Buy is offering free next-day and two-day shipping on qualifying orders for My Best Buy Plus and My Best Buy Total members. Non-members, meanwhile, can get free next-day shipping on qualifying orders totaling $35 or more. Same-day delivery is also available on select items, seven days a week, and you can check your eligibility by entering your ZIP code in Best Buy’s online portal.

Returns: Best Buy offers a 15-day return window for most products, while “activatable” items like smartphones and wearables, which come with a third-party contract, must be returned within 14 days. My Best Buy Plus and My Best Buy Total members have up to 60 days to make returns, though the 14-day limit still applies to activatable products.

For the holidays, Best Buy has an extended return window, which allows most products purchased between October 30th and December 31st to be returned until January 15th, 2027. The exceptions above surrounding activatable devices still apply, and holiday decorations are also limited to 15 days regardless of their purchase date.

Shipping: At Costco, shipping fees vary by product and shipping method, although shipping is often free. The wholesale retailer also offers a variety of delivery options, including “white glove” service for larger appliances. Same-day delivery is also available on some items via Costco’s partnership with Instacart.

Returns: Costco generally has an open return policy, except for electronics such as TVs and computers, which have a 90-day return window. Other exceptions are listed on its return page.

Shipping: GameStop currently offers free shipping only to GameStop Pro members on orders of $54 or more. It also offers same-day delivery in certain locations if you order from your local store at least three hours before the store closes.

Returns: GameStop hasn’t listed its holiday return policy yet, but you can return products within 15 days, provided the packages are unopened and you have the receipt. Pro members, meanwhile, get 30 days.

Shipping: Most Dell products include free standard shipping (no minimum purchase required). The delivery window can vary based on your order, but Dell also offers expedited and express shipping options, along with a delivery date estimate based on the ZIP code you provide at checkout. Orders placed by December 23rd with qualifying express delivery windows are expected to arrive before December 25th; Dell’s 2026 Holiday Shipping and Delivery Schedule outlines additional shipping times based on which speed you choose.

Returns: Under Dell’s extended return policy, you can return purchases made between November 1st and December 29th until January 15th, 2027.

Shipping: DJI offers free shipping on purchases of $200 or more. Otherwise, shipping fees are specified on the order form. Shipment times can vary for each product depending on availability.

Returns: DJI offers returns within 14 days of receiving the purchase, provided the item remains in like-new condition or suffers from a manufacturing defect.

Shipping: All standard orders qualify for free shipping with no minimum. Just note that this applies to the lowest-cost shipping available, which may not be the fastest.

Returns: Google hasn’t announced any special holiday return policies yet. For now, all purchases are covered by the standard terms and conditions, which let you return most items within 15 days of receiving them. Nest Thermostats and Verizon contract phones, however, come with an extended 30-day return window.

Shipping: For many items, standard shipping is free and arrives within three to six days. HP also offers expedited and priority shipping options for an additional fee. The company will not ship or deliver items on Christmas, Thanksgiving, or New Year’s Day.

Returns: You can return most items purchased from HP’s website within 30 days of delivery. There are exceptions, though, and select items may be subject to a restocking fee of up to 15 percent.

Shipping: Most products sold through the online Microsoft Store include free two- or three-day shipping, with express shipping available for an additional fee.

Returns: You can return most physical products purchased online for free through January 31, 2027, as long as they’re in like-new condition. The item must be in its original packaging, with all parts, manuals, and other accessories included. Items exempt from this policy include digital gift cards, gift cards for services and subscriptions, and select hardware, such as the ROG Xbox Ally and Ally X, Surface for Business devices, and HoloLens.

Shipping: Many of Newegg’s items come with free shipping and are delivered within one to five business days; for details, check the individual product page.

Returns: Qualifying items purchased between November 1st and December 31st can be returned or replaced until January 31st, 2027.

Shipping: According to the Sam’s Club FAQ, shipping costs for most items vary based on the item’s size, weight, shipping method, and delivery address. Plus Members get free shipping on many online items, and same-day delivery or curbside pickup is available for free if you’re a Plus member ($120 a year) and place a qualifying order totaling $50 or more by 1PM local time. Club members ($60 a year) can pay $12 for same-day or next-day shipping, or get free curbside pickup.

Returns: Sam’s Club does not have a specified return period; however, some products may have specific return periods stated. For example, electronics and major appliances have a 90-day return window, while phones are subject to a 14-day return policy.

Shipping: Sonos offers free shipping on all products, with in-stock items typically shipping the same day if purchased by 11AM local time. You can also pay extra for two-day or express shipping.

Returns: Sonos offers a 30-day return policy and even provides free return shipping. However, you must have bought the product directly from Sonos, and you must initiate the return within 30 days of receiving your purchase. The product must also include the original packaging and be in new or as-new condition to be eligible.

Update, November 9th: Updated to reflect shipping deadlines and return policies for the 2026 holiday season.

https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/bitter.title: Bitter Hackers Deploy New PapRAT Backdoor in Cyberespionage Campaign Targeting South Asia
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/bitter.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/bitter.text:
The South Asian cyber espionage group known as Bitter (aka APT-C-08, APT-Q-37, Hazy Tiger, Orange Yali, T-APT-17, and TA397) has been observed targeting South Asian organizations with a previously unreported remote access trojan called PapRAT.

"PapRAT has both C++ and Rust implementations," Fortinet FortiGuard Labs researcher Cara Lin said. "Its capabilities include command execution, file uploads and downloads, file deletion, directory and drive enumeration, and screenshot capture. The Rust variant adds PowerShell execution and other commands."

The campaign is notable for making use of three different infection chains -

The living-off-the-land (LotL) approach is designed to execute commands from a remote server ("goodnfortunes[.]com"), allowing it to collect directory and task lists, directory information from Desktop, Documents, and Downloads, installed antivirus product data, and mounted drives.

The harvested reconnaissance information is saved as "abc.pdf" and exfiltrated back to the C2 server via a curl command, after which the staged file is deleted from the host.

A second version of the script has been found to retrieve a file called "talk.log" from "techtalkhelp[.]com." The payload contains a Base64-encoded script to obtain additional instructions from the same server and execute them as PowerShell commands.

"This staging model gives the attacker operational flexibility, while the commands are updated server-side without pushing a new binary, avoiding PE drops and process injection that some security appliances could easily detect," Fortinet said.

The PapRAT malware delivered via the MSI installer in the second attack chain is designed for remote control. It supports eight commands -

A Rust version of the malware incorporates three more commands -

A notable aspect of the third attack chain is that it combines the salient aspects of the first two sequences by using a script to download an MSI installer via curl. Like before, the MSI installer serves as a conduit for PapRAT, which then proceeds to drop WmRAT, a malware previously identified as used by Bitter.

The findings indicate that the threat actor continues to refine its custom arsenal to establish and maintain access to targeted systems.

"These changes underscore the importance of monitoring malicious behavior across scripting tools, scheduled tasks, and installer activity alongside detecting known malware signatures," Fortinet said. "Organizations should treat unexpected LNK files, URL shortcuts, disk images, and MSI packages with caution, particularly when delivered through unsolicited messages."

PapRAT malware is designed to execute commands from a remote server. The PapRat malware is also designed to collect directory and task lists, directory information from Desktop, Documents, and Downloads.

https://www.darkreading.com/cybersecurit.author: Arielle Waldman
https://www.darkreading.com/cybersecurit.text:
Cybersecurity In-Depth: Feature articles on security strategy, latest trends, and people to know.

New guidance provides a basic framework for less-technical solo business owners, but it may miss the mark on how to secure technology that requires no human oversight.

Threat actors always target the path of least resistance, and for years that's been small-to-medium sized businesses (SMBs). Now, new guidance from the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) aims to help companies with possibly even fewer resources: "solopreneurs."

For solo business owners, incidents can be a dealbreaker, with some shuttering completely following an attack. But risks also extend through the supply chain, as threat actors exploit vulnerabilities as a backdoor to hit larger enterprises.

NIST has published the Cybersecurity White Paper 50 (CSWP), a series of recommendations on how to curb cyber risks for a population that makes up 81.9% of all U.S. businesses.

The agency is trying to offset challenges with guidance for password hygiene, ransomware threats, and adhering to regulations requirements— areas where solopreneurs typically lack the time, money, or people to build out a security program on their own.

Related:Incidents Move Too Fast for Pen & Paper

NIST said the guide translates its Cybersecurity Framework into lay language for non-employer firms. But with 33 pages to work through, is it worth the investment?

Most of the practical core is within reach for solopreneurs, says Martin Zugec, technical solutions director at Bitdefender. People just need to scroll to the short list on Page Two which calls for phishing-resistant multifactor authentication (MFA), a password manager, a standard (non-admin) account for daily work, automatic updates, and tested backups with one copy kept offline.

"None of that needs a security background, and you can do it in an afternoon," Zugec tells Dark Reading.

Compared to other NIST technical publications, Zugec says the CSWP is much easier to digest. Like NIST advertised, the language is plain and every action comes with a reason, a first step, and a note on what changes as businesses grow, he adds.

NIST outlined how businesses can respond to growing contractual agreements and an increasing number of suppliers and third parties as they expand operations and it becomes even more crucial to know third-parties’ cyber postures. That means staying current with regulations and establishing a formal process to manage risks that relationships could introduce.

While Bryson Byrd, cybersecurity advisor at Huntress, applauded NIST for the guidance, he says it still reads like it was written for practitioners. Terms like “least privilege,” “risk register,” and “data sensitivity classification” aren't the language of someone running a bakery or a consulting practice, he adds.

Related:Behind the Scenes of How Operation Blackout Went Down

"For too long, solopreneurs have been an afterthought in cybersecurity guidance," Byrd tells Dark Reading. "The intent is right, but the closer guidance like this gets to the language of everyday business owners, the more likely it is to actually get implemented."

But it's not just the language, Byrd says. It also assumes the owner knows how to turn on logging, review account sessions, and work though a separate spreadsheet of worksheets. And he points to a recommendation on obtaining legal counsel's input before notifying customers following an incident as an extra cost that often is not in the budget.

The guidance doesn’t appear to take into consideration that "nobody goes into business to build the most secure company that exists," he adds, but to build something over time. Every hour a solopreneur spends on asset inventories, backup testing, tabletop exercises, and compliance tracking is an hour taken away from running the business, which is the priority.

"Asking a single person to do all of this is extraordinarily cumbersome and, quite frankly, unrealistic," Byrd explains.

Byrd observes gaps in the guidance in places "we see hurt small businesses in the real world." The first is domain registrar, which is important to address, since attackers regularly go after small business domains to launch impersonation attacks and siphon money from customers and partners. Control of the domain means threat actors assume control over email and the business's website too.

Related:Why CTF Competitions May Be More Important Than Ever

"Locking down the registrar account with multi-factor authentication, enabling registrar lock, and turning on auto-renewal should be part of any baseline for a solopreneur," Byrd recommends.

The second gap he addresses is email authentication. The three core protocols — Sender Policy Framework, DomainKeys Identified Mail, and Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance — are becoming more important to protect a business from being impersonated and to ensure its legitimate email is delivered, adds Byrd.

The third and perhaps most impactful for a business of one is what happens when the owner is unavailable for an extended period of time due to an illness, family matter, or simply to take a well-deserved vacation.

Ransomware groups target businesses during off-hours, weekends, and holidays. If something does happen that demands an immediate response, it's essential for someone to be there. It could mean the difference between an incident and a breach.

"A break-glass plan that gives a trusted person or partner emergency access to critical accounts is still needed, and it belongs in any cybersecurity plan for a solopreneur," he advises.

Previously, SMBs and self-employers adopted the mindset that they were too small to be considered a target. That has since been disproven tenfold and is only growing worse.

Advancements in autonomous tools and artificial intelligence (AI) have lowered the barrier to entry and the cost of attacks, letting threat actors target that population at scale. They realized they had a choice: go after large enterprises with strong defenses for one big payout, or target thousands of small shops with weak security that are far more likely to pay up.

As the struggles evolved, so must the guidance. Daniel Eliot, lead for small business engagement at NIST, says this paper comes nearly 10 years after its predecessor, NISTIR 7621 rev.1.

A lot has changed in 10 years and after the initial call for comments, "that feedback was instrumental in moving the project forward."

AI is forcing a lot of security guidance to be updated and making that guidance easier to write, Zugec notes. He noticed new additions in CSWP included a section on AI and a warning that AI makes phishing more convincing.

NIST urged businesses to take a second or third look at any message that asks people to click a link, download a file, transfer funds, or log into an account.

But contrary to popular belief, AI hasn't brought any new or novel attacks, observes Zugec. It is changing who runs businesses and what they rely on to operate.

Solopreneurs are using AI assistants to read their mailboxes, run commands, write code, and use accounts under the owner's identity, he explains. While it enables one person to do the work of a small team, it also expands the attack surface.

"Many solopreneurs will use agentic AI to grow faster than their security does," he says. "The guide gives no advice on what these agents should be allowed to reach, or on securing the code they write."

The biggest gap Zugec found in the guide is "AI that acts." NIST treats AI as something passive that businesses need to inventory and review outputs for, but agentic AI has increasingly removed humans from the equation.

As agentic AI enables more people to run a business alone, the security of those businesses matters more than ever, Zugec warns. That will warrant outside help, as people increasingly turn to vibe coding to build applications on their own. He urges solopreneurs to have their code reviewed by someone with coding and security experience before anything ships.

If anything is public-facing, that means an attacker can reach it and it needs to be protected.

"AI is good at producing software that works, but not necessarily software with a small attack surface," he says. "The guide doesn't cover this, yet it's often the first risk solopreneurs run into."

Zugec spotted other weaknesses too. For example, NIST pushed for continuous updates, but a solopreneur can’t realistically track every legal and contractual security requirement, negotiate security terms with a cloud provider, or monitor their systems around the clock.

Secondly, it never ranks tasks, which makes prioritization difficult for a one-person team. For example, it opens with governance, the least actionable task, while MFA and backup advice only starts on Page 14. It also fails to cover two common attack routes: ClickFix, which tricks people into pasting a command themselves, and a malware that steals their logged-in session, which bypasses MF

"It lists around 25 actions and says outright that it isn't a checklist, so a busy owner has to decide what comes first," Zugec says. The guide also sets its scope by headcount, which is problematic. Technically the headcount would be one, but risk follows what information businesses hold and who targets them.

It's not just about size, it's about what's exposed. Risk heavily varies between someone who sells candles on Etsy as a side gig versus someone in the finance industry trading billions in cryptocurrency.

"A solo crypto operator or a consultant with client secrets needs far more than the guide’s baseline," Zugec says.

https://www.newscientist.com/article/259.title: Is Schrödinger’s cat both dead and alive? No, it’s just haunted by its past
https://www.newscientist.com/article/259.author: Karmela Padavic-Callaghan
https://www.newscientist.com/article/259.text:
Today, for breakfast, I had a smoothie. This isn’t unusual: I drink the same smoothie every weekday morning. At some point in the past, I discovered I particularly liked it and made it a habit. It is a simple example of something that makes intuitive sense – that our past experiences determine our present actions, and they, in turn, determine our future trajectories.

But what if I told you that the past never actually existed? Or, at least, that it doesn’t matter? It sounds left field, but I would only be channelling an assumption that lurks within many laws of physics largely unchallenged: that the present moment is all we need to know about to predict the future. Without making this assumption, the amount of information you need to predict the future is at risk of dramatically blowing up, rapidly making it impractical to say anything at all.

Or so we thought. Now, there’s a move afoot to reclaim the past for physics. Its proponents think that could resolve long-standing questions at the core of quantum theory, such as why it is so weird as it is, but equally not as weird as it could be – and, along the way, clarify the true nature of time itself. “I think it’s a big deal. I think it will be a big thing for the foundations of physics,” says quantum information researcher Jacob Biamonte at École de Technologie Supérieure in Montreal.

To begin to understand how physics cancelled the past, imagine a game of marbles. To predict where any marble will be in a second’s time, all we need to know is its current position, speed and direction of travel, all effectively ignorant of the marble’s deep past. We then roll the relevant physical laws – in this case, Isaac Newton’s laws of motion – forward into the future. We don’t need to know anything about the collisions that brought the marble to its present position – luckily, as calculating the myriad past possibilities might rapidly overwhelm our computational ability.

https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-0.author: Wenhuan Xu
https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-0.text:
Wenhuan Xu is a postdoctoral researcher at Simon Fraser University in Vancouver, Canada, working on global change and environmental health.

Search author on:
                                    PubMed
                                         Google Scholar

Around the globe, less than one-third of postdoctoral-level job listings provided a salary range, whereas nearly half asked for collaboration experience.Credit: vicky_81/iStock via Getty

I did not start reading postdoctoral-researcher job adverts because I wanted to analyse academic-labour hiring practices. I started because I needed a job.

As my postdoc in forestry at Simon Fraser University in Vancouver, Canada, neared its end in October, I found myself looking for another position. Some evenings, I would sit with too many browser tabs open: one job in the United Kingdom, one in Canada, another in Germany, all of which promised exciting science. I was looking for a project that matched my training, a laboratory group whose work I admired and a city that I could imagine living in.

But after a while, I began to see a pattern. The adverts were often clear about what institutions wanted from me, but remarkably vague about what they were offering in return. This was never just a professional puzzle. My wife and I have four children, so salary, contract length, relocation costs, visa issues and childcare are not abstract details — they determine whether a move is even possible.

A 60-minute guide to landing your next job in science

To better understand this imbalance, I started systematically collecting data from the ads. In 2024–26, I compiled 7,846 research-job adverts from seven international job boards (LinkedIn, jobs.ac.uk, Times Higher Education Unijobs, Nature Careers, EURAXESS, Science Careers and EuroScienceJobs). From those data, I identified 2,896 postdoc-equivalent listings across 53 countries. What had felt personal looked different at scale. (Nature’s Career columns are editorially independent of the Nature Careers jobs board.)

Around half of those nearly 3,000 listings were in Europe and roughly one-quarter were in North America. Asia, Africa and Oceania represented much smaller shares of the postdoc pie. I also scanned each ad for seven practical terms: salary range, contract length, pension, health insurance, visa support, parental leave and relocation assistance. The amount of information that each region was willing to share with applicants differed starkly (see ‘Says little, asks a lot’). Ads from Oceania disclosed these details most often. European ads, despite dominating the job boards, revealed much less on average. Ads from Asia and Africa divulged the least.

That does not mean postdocs are necessarily better supported in one region than another. It means that the information available at the point of application is systematically uneven. For someone considering an international move, that matters. My family and I were genuinely weighing up different futures: returning to Asia (I am from China and have been in Canada since 2018), moving to Europe or staying in North America. When a listing omitted salary or contract length, I was not just missing data — I was lacking the information needed to assess rent, childcare, immigration and whether a move was truly practical. In my own job search, this was immensely frustrating.

For each serious opportunity, I made a one-page comparison sheet. I began with the advertised salary and contract length, then checked the university’s published pay scale and, if I could find it, the relevant collective agreement between the institution and a union. Housing needed a more-local comparison than a city-wide average: I first looked at whether the university offered accommodation for staff or postdocs, then compared its price and availability with rentals close to campus and in nearby non-university neighbourhoods.

If NASA ever hopes to build a permanent moon base for astronauts, let alone aim for Mars, the U.S. space agency is going to need a whole lot of space travelers. And now, you have a chance to be one of them.

NASA on Saturday (Nov. 7) put out the call for a new class of astronaut candidates who think they have the "right stuff" to fly, live and work in space. Those astronaut hopefuls have until Dec. 3 to apply (the application website is here), with NASA planning to make its final selections in late 2027.

"This is an extraordinary time to join NASA's astronaut corps," the space agency's chief, Jared Isaacman, said in an announcement, which was made during NASA's "Max Power" air show at Kennedy Space Center (KSC) in Florida. "The people we select could walk on the moon, live and work at the Moon Base, and help pioneer the systems and operations that will ultimately carry crews to Mars."

It's been two years since NASA last sought applications for astronauts. In 2024, more than 8,000 people applied, though only 10 — five men and five women — made the cut. They're in the middle of a two-year training program right now.

This new 2027 astronaut group will be the 25th astronaut class in NASA history. Its announcement comes the same year that NASA returned astronauts to the moon for the first time since the Apollo era with the Artemis II moon flyby. Four more astronauts will test Artemis moon landers in Earth orbit on the Artemis III mission in 2027.

NASA currently has 32 active astronauts in its spaceflying corps. The agency has recruited 370 people to fly in space since 1959, when the first seven Mercury astronauts were selected and unveiled to the world.

"There is a lot to be done in order to get all of these new vehicles and the new suits and everything as we continue to work towards the moon, build a base there, stay permanently, and then eventually onto Mars," NASA astronaut Nichole Stilwell, class of 2021, told Space.com in an interview at KSC during the Max Power event. "And so we just don't have enough people, and we're looking for more."

If you're interested in applying to be a NASA astronaut, you should take a look at the requirements first.

NASA's core guidelines require applicants to be U.S. citizens and have a master's degree in a STEM field like "engineering, biological science, physical science, or computer science from an accredited institution," the space agency said in a statement. You'll also need at least three years of experience in your related field.

Don't have a master's degree? Here's three other ways NASA might consider your application, according to the agency's advisory:

If you're a medical doctor and are considering applying to be an astronaut, your residency training can be counted toward your professional experience, but only if it is completed by July 2027, NASA said.

If you want to be a pilot astronaut for NASA, you'll need some serious flight hours under your belt. Here's a rundown of some ways to meet that requirement:

"For those who apply, becoming a NASA astronaut is more than a career opportunity,” said NASA chief astronaut Scott Tingle, who also chairs the Astronaut Selection Board at the agency's Johnson Space Center (JSC) in Houston. "It is a chance to join a legacy of explorers who have pushed the boundaries of discovery and play a role in the missions that will shape humanity’s future in space."

Once NASA selects its 2027 astronaut class, the new recruits can expect to begin a two-year training program based out of JSC, which is home to the agency's astronaut corp and Mission Control.

“The window is open. The mission is waiting.," NASA Deputy Administrator Matt Anderson said in a statement. "And the only thing missing from the greatest adventure humanity has ever embarked upon is you."

Space.com Content Manager Chelsea Gohd contributed to this report from NASA's Max Power event at the Kennedy Space Center in Cape Canaveral, Florida.

https://www.statnews.com/2026/11/09/glp-.author: Elaine Chen
https://www.statnews.com/2026/11/09/glp-.text:
The Food and Drug Administration on Monday warned that GLP-1 drugs carry a potential risk for a rare but serious eye condition and required pharma companies to inform patients and doctors of the risk.

The condition, called non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, or NAION, is sometimes referred to as an “eye stroke” and is caused by insufficient blood flow to the optic nerve. It typically causes sudden vision loss and, in severe cases, can lead to blindness. There are currently no proven treatments for the condition.

GLP-1 drugs such as Novo Nordisk’s Ozempic and Wegovy and Eli Lilly’s Mounjaro and Zepbound have exploded in popularity for their potent weight loss effects, but as with any drugs that are given to large populations, side effects can show up in real-world use that weren’t observed in clinical trials.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/trump-el.title: Trump questions midterm election results, revives voting-machine conspiracy
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/trump-el.author: Dan Mangan
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/trump-el.text:
President Donald Trump questioned the legitimacy of the midterm election results, resurrecting his pattern of raising doubts about electoral losses for himself and other Republicans.

Trump’s social media post raising questions about the election came six days after his fellow Republicans suffered historic defeats at the polls nationwide, including in several GOP strongholds like Texas and South Carolina.

Democrats regained majority control in the Senate and Congress in the elections.

“Does anybody really believe that this ‘Election’ was honest,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.

President Donald Trump on Monday questioned the legitimacy of the midterm election results, resurrecting his pattern of raising doubts about electoral losses for himself and other Republicans.

Trump’s social media post raising questions about the election came six days after his fellow Republicans suffered historic defeats at the polls nationwide, including in several GOP strongholds like Texas and South Carolina.

“Does anybody really believe that this ‘Election’ was honest,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.

“How could the Polls be so wrong??? Some early voting ‘dumps’ were so large that it was impossible to win, no matter how many people went to vote,” the president said. “It’s all about the machines, which are far more important than the voter!”

Trump’s post was a sharp pivot from what has been a somewhat conciliatory tone after last Tuesday’s thumping of Republican candidates.

“I’ll get along probably with the Democrats unless they want to be destructive,” Trump said a day after the election.

After his electoral loss to former President Joe Biden in 2020, Trump argued, without evidence, that he only lost as a result of widespread ballot fraud.

Trump’s claims, which were joined by dozens of unsuccessful court cases challenging election procedures, culminated in the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the U.S. Capitol by a mob of his supporters after he spoke at a rally outside the White House.

The riot disrupted a joint session of Congress for hours. Later that day, Congress confirmed Biden’s election by the Electoral College.

Critics of Trump’s conspiracy theories about elections have noted that he lost the 2020 race when he was president, but won the 2024 presidential election, when Biden was in the White House.

They also noted that in the past week, Republicans had control of states that saw major Democratic wins that few analysts would have predicted a year ago, including Texas, Kansas, South Carolina, and Iowa.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/honda-to.title: Honda to invest $3 billion in new vehicle assembly plant in Ohio
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/honda-to.author: Michael Wayland
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/honda-to.text:
Honda Motor plans to invest $3 billion to build a new assembly plant near its current facilities in Marysville, Ohio.

The automaker said the plant will focus on hybrid vehicles and is expected to begin production in 2029.

The auto industry has been trying to localize more production amid President Donald Trump’s tariffs and inflated logistics costs that have cut into profits.

MARYSVILLE, Ohio — Honda Motor
 plans to invest $3 billion to build a new assembly plant in Ohio, the automaker announced Monday.

Honda said the new plant, which is near its other facilities in Marysville, Ohio, is expected to begin production in 2029, have a capacity for 240,000 vehicles annually and create more than 2,000 jobs. The facility is expected to focus on hybrid vehicles, which have been growing in popularity in the U.S., but Honda said it will be capable of making traditional gas-powered vehicles and electric vehicles as well.

The plant is expected increase Honda’s light-duty vehicle capacity to 1.3 million units annually in the U.S. It currently has 12 manufacturing plants in United States, eight of which produce engines or automobiles. It’s the company’s first new mass production U.S. vehicle assembly plant since it opened a facility in Indiana in 2008.

The auto industry has been trying to localize more production amid President Donald Trump’s tariffs and inflated logistics costs that have cut into profits.

Honda’s plans for a new plant come roughly two weeks after Volkswagen-owned luxury brand Audi announced it would invest more than $4 billion in its first U.S. manufacturing facility in Georgia.

Detroit automakers General Motors
 and Ford Motor
 plus international automakers Toyota Motor
 and Hyundai Motor also recently said they will spend billions of dollars on new or updated U.S. facilities.

Honda’s announcement comes after the automaker in May indefinitely suspended an $11 billion investment plan to produce all-electric vehicles and batteries in Canada. It also canceled three planned EVs for the U.S. market.

The new Ohio plant is expected to notably boost Honda’s U.S. production and American-produced sales. Honda said nearly all of its vehicles sold in the U.S., including its Acura luxury brand, were produced in North America, including more than 60% in the U.S.

American Honda Motor Co. executive Jennifer Thomas recently emphasized the Japanese automaker’s commitment to the U.S. and need for additional capacity.

“In order to be competitive in this market, you’re going to need to build products here,” Thomas, senior vice president of corporate affairs, said Oct. 27 in Detroit. “We are focused on trying to maximize the existing capacity that we have, but we are at capacity, and so we’re exploring all options.”

Thomas also warned the automotive industry faces a “catastrophic” scenario if the U.S. and Canada cannot reach a new trade deal by the end of this year, when Trump has threatened to double tariffs on Canadian vehicles and parts from 25% to 50% on Jan. 1 if the two countries don’t reach a deal.

Honda said it has built more than 33 million vehicles and more than 39 million engines in the U.S. since it started auto production in the U.S. in 1982.

The Japanese automaker currently has more than 30,000 employees in the U.S.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/weekend-.title: Weekend trading of Nvidia scandal shines light on new financial products
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/weekend-.author: Oliver Renick
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/weekend-.text:
Perpetual futures emerge as first input for Nvidia investors over the weekend.

Prediction markets and premarket options trading offer glimpse of growing need for more market access.

Perpetual futures on Nvidia started moving lower Sunday as news of the Huang scandal broke.

As news of a potential scandal surrounding Nvidia
 CEO Jensen Huang began to trickle out on Sunday, investors faced a simple question: what could it mean for the stock?

One answer could be found in an obscure but growing corner of the markets: perpetual futures.

On Sunday at 3 p.m. ET, well before pre-market equity trading had started, a number of traders began placing bearish bets on Nvidia perpetual futures. Specifically, perpetuals on Nvidia traded first, with Hyperliquid’s xyz contract slipping to as low as $180.15 on $200 million of volume by 3:30 p.m. E.T. Both equity shares and perps on Nvidia fell below $178 overnight. It traded 7% lower on Monday.

Sunday’s trading shines a light on a product that is increasingly filling a market void when traditional markets are off-line.

In their simplest form, perpetual futures are highly leveraged bets that never expire. They can track almost any asset class and trade around the clock, seven days a week.

“Perps have filled a significant gap or void in the market,” said Rich Repetto, a former exchange analyst and market structure expert.  “They provide access as well as price discovery to markets when there otherwise would be a vacuum.”

When Iran launched a drone attack against Israel on Saturday, April 13 in 2024, traditional markets were completely closed, and crypto native exchanges that offered perpetual futures were the only global proxy for real time market sentiment in oil and the S&P 500. As that conflict escalated, perpetuals — or perps as they are called — became a go to for many traders looking for inputs over the weekend.

“It should be very clear at this point that news doesn’t stop when the market is closed,” said David Schamis, CEO of Hyperliquid Strategies (PURR)
, the publicly-traded treasury company investing in HYPE tokens that power the de-entralized exchange. ” Investors want deep liquidity and price discovery when it is needed, not just nine-to-five.”

Perps weren’t the only new, exotic product to see increased volume over the weekend. Prediction contracts tied to Huang’s potential exit also saw a spike in activity. Specifically, a Kalshi contract asking when Jensen Huang might leave as Nvidia CEO, which was listed just days before the bombshell reports, saw over $105,000 traded on Sunday.

And pre-market trading in options on Nvidia – which began trading just weeks ago – saw $15 million in options premium traded in Nvidia across about 40,000 contracts. A little over half the contracts were puts, with just under $10 million of premium tied to puts, SpotGamma data show.

The emergence of new products highlight the growing need for more information as traditional financial exchanges extend market hours trading.

“When the markets close, we lose real-time feedback,” said Options Action contributor, Mike Khouw. “Futures, prediction markets and expanded afterhours trading helps fill that gap.”

Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.
