https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261.title: Spain's right holds poll lead over Sanchez's Socialists ahead of November 29 snap election
https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261.text:
Spain's conservative People's Party (PP) would beat Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez's Socialists but require the far-right Vox to secure a parliamentary majority, according to the latest polls in the run-up to a general election on November 29.

The electoral campaign starting in four days is expected to be dominated by issues such as housing, immigration and corruption – as wells as reverberations from last month's deadly train crash that triggered the resignation of Transport Minister Oscar Puente.

READ MORE
'Desolation, despair': Spain begins three days of mourning after deadly train crash

A SocioMetrica poll published by El Español newspaper projected around 200 seats in the 350-seat lower house for the PP and Vox combined. The Socialists would secure 108 seats – two more than in the previous survey.

The poll, which is based on 5,460 online interviews and factors in 3 percentage points in margin for error, showed a net transfer of 832,000 voters from the left to the right.

A survey by polling institute 40dB for El Pais showed the gap between the PP and the Socialists narrowing to two percentage points, but the combined right-wing bloc still achieving a working majority of around 190 seats.

A Sigma Dos poll published by El Mundo also pointed to the Socialists recovering some ground lost after the train crash and now likely to win 105 seats, but far behind the 199 seats for the PP and Vox.

An IMOP poll for El Confidencial focused on vote transfers rather than seat projections, pointing to a drop in voter loyalty for the Socialists and a rise for the PP – the latter largely at the expense of Vox supporters.

Sanchez, who has been in power since 2018, called a snap election on October 5 after right-wing parties voted down emergency legislation aimed at tackling the country's housing crisis.

https://www.france24.com/en/france/20261.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/france/20261.text:
A covert Russian network sought to exploit ​last month's riots in France by using social media to blame the unrest on uncontrolled immigration and portray the government as having lost control, according to an internal EU assessment seen by Reuters.

A separate internal assessment – compiled by France's foreign ministry and also seen by Reuters – found that social media accounts linked to Israel and to the US MAGA movement also pushed "hostile narratives" around ​the riots, linking them ‌to radical Islamism and migration.

Taken together, the assessments offer insight into how external actors have been trying to use France's domestic turmoil for their ⁠own political ends, according to analysis by European disinformation specialists.

The European Union analysis found that a covert Russian network known as "Operation Overload" spread videos impersonating Western media outlets to target French audiences – some falsely claiming migrants had raped protesters or terrorist attacks were imminent.

The Russian foreign ‌ministry did not respond to a request for comment. In August, ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova rejected allegations by a French state watchdog agency of spreading ⁠disinformation about France's 2027 elections and said they would "not be the last concoction which the authorities will use to manipulate public opinion".

Rioting erupted in cities across France last month as demonstrations against rising living costs and declining public services spiralled out of control in some of the worst violence the country had witnessed for ​decades.

The EU analysis, which covers the period from October 7 to 21, found that Russia sought to "depict the French leadership as weak and increasingly ‌authoritarian".

“Such events offer opportunities to undermine national governments, fuel fear and division, and shape public perceptions ahead of elections,” said the restricted-circulation EU document, prepared by disinformation experts in the bloc's diplomatic service.

It found no evidence that Moscow or other actors had instigated or escalated the protests, describing the activity as "the opportunistic exploitation of unrest".

The French foreign ministry's ‌assessment found that the 10 most-viewed X posts on the unrest from "pro-Russian spheres" had 2.8 million views from October 16 to 18. But those figures were dwarfed by the views achieved by X posts on the riots from accounts linked to the MAGA movement and to ​Israeli officials and influencers.

The 10 most-viewed X posts on France's unrest by MAGA-linked officials, media outlets and influencers received more than 49 million views from October 16 to 18, according to the French ministry report.

The 10 most-viewed posts from Israeli officials, government accounts, media outlets and influencers had more than 35 million views in the same period, the French ​report said.

Elina Treyger, a senior political scientist at the RAND Corporation think tank, said such campaigns wage a slow-burning "narrative competition" that over time ​can shape how Western democracies are seen in Europe and beyond. Treyger said they feed an anti-immigrant backlash that is pushing European voters ​toward political extremes.

Reuters was not able to independently verify assertions made in either the French or the EU report.

Asked for comment, French officials referred Reuters to remarks by President Emmanuel Macron, who said on October 21 there had been no visible foreign interference behind ​the protests but there had been "foreign manipulation of information".

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s office and the Israeli foreign ministry did not respond to requests for comment.

The EU report said "Operation Overload" – active since September 2023 – has targeted Western "public figures, institutions, and media outlets" to "discredit these entities and their support for Ukraine while promoting content aligned with Russian interests."

Its activity "also intended to undermine European support to Ukraine by claiming that European governments prioritise Ukraine over domestic issues," the report said.

The Institute for Strategic Dialogue, a Britain-based think tank, said in a report last year that ⁠Operation Overload was "a persistent and high-volume Russian information operation. It impersonates trusted sources to sow discord, confusion and distrust."

"The operation creates and posts videos that appear to be news reports, uses AI to clone experts’ voices, forges newspaper headlines, and ⁠manipulates images," the institute said – adding that ​it "pivots from country to country to exploit crises and debates."

France's disinformation watchdog Viginum published a detailed report on Overload and similar Russian operations in 2024. French officials have said they resurface during protests, elections or other opportunities to discredit France.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/c.title: COP31 summit targets major electrification push as 1.5C goal slips away
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/c.author: Laura Tingle
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/c.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Climate Change

Global temperatures will rise beyond the 1.5 degrees above pre-industrial level that was the target of the Paris Agreement. (Reuters: Wolfgang Rattay)

The COP31 climate summit, being jointly hosted by Türkiye and Australia, has conceded that the Earth will warm by more than 1.5 degrees.

Nations will push for greater electrification of energy and for less reliance on fossil fuels.

But both Australia and Türkiye are being criticised for their reliance on polluting energy sources.

A pledge to have 35 per cent of the world powered by electricity by 2035 is the central aim of UN climate talks in Türkiye this week, as the international summit concedes for the first time that global temperatures will rise more than 1.5 degrees Celcius above pre-industrial levels.

Australia and Türkiye are joint presidents of this year's UN meeting on climate change.

Climate change minister Chris Bowen told the opening session of the conference that it was meeting "at a moment of consequence, whether it be glacial collapse in Nepal, heat deaths in Europe, or an intensifying El Niño" .

"Climate change is here. It is not a forecast. It is not a prediction. It is the lived reality for billions of people."

Chris Bowen says despite missing the 1.5-degree target, global cooperation is working limit the impact of climate change. (Reuters: Ritzau Scanpix/Liselotte Sabroe)

But discussion of what to do to reduce the burning of fossil fuels that has fuelled so much of that change is the elephant in the room at this year's meeting — not formally on the agenda, despite UN Climate Change Executive Secretary Simon Stiell telling the conference that "this year's fossil fuel cost chaos has delivered a global shock-wave, hitting households hard and spreading inflation like a cancer".

"The fall-out has been severe, both economically and politically, as we've just seen", in reference to the turmoil of the Iran War, and subsequent elections around the world.

As United Nations climate talks commence in Türkiye, Australia's position as a climate leader will be tested.

As a major fossil fuel exporter, Australia has already come under intense criticism — particularly from Pacific nations — because it has allowed coal mining to expand and the North West Shelf gas project to be extended.

Türkiye's promotion of the push for faster electrification also comes against the backdrop of its own heavy reliance on fossil fuel generated electricity

It is Europe's largest coal power generator, with around 55 per cent of its electricity generated by coal and natural gas.

But the 35 per cent voluntary target remains relatively unambitious.

According to the International Energy Agency, electricity-generated power currently accounts for a 23 per cent share, and is forecast to rise to 30 per cent by 2035 as a result of existing policies already on track.

The international pledge at the climate talks held in Paris in 2015 was to limit the long term rise in global temperatures to 1.5 degrees per cent above pre-industrial levels.

Just eleven years later, Antalya is the first meeting to concede that won't happen.

This year's summit will urge countries to pledge greater electrification of their energy generation. (Reuters: Mohammed Aty)

Mr Bowen struck an optimistic note, saying that before Paris "the world was heading for warming approaching 4 degrees".

"Today, projections are closer to 2.6 degrees".

Türkiye and Australia say the Antalya meeting will focus mostly on trying to implement measures already agreed to, rather than set ambitious new targets.

Much of the focus will be on increasing finance support to poorer countries to adapt their energy systems and to offset the impacts of climate change.

This will include measures to slash methane emissions, particularly in the oil, gas and waste sectors.

Climate Council member and economist Nicki Hutley, who is attending the Antalya meeting said a global push to electrification "is exactly what Australian households need from this summit".

"We import most of our refined fuel, so conflicts overseas land at Australian bowsers fast, but sun and wind can't be blockaded or embargoed."

"What's missing is a clear commitment to move the world away from coal, oil and gas. Electrification only delivers lower bills and real security if we stop tying ourselves to volatile fossil fuel markets."

https://www.dw.com/en/ice-hockey-norway-.title: Ice hockey: Norway says it's been kicked out of World Juniors in favor of Russia
https://www.dw.com/en/ice-hockey-norway-.text:
The wrangling over Russia's return to international ice hockey continues, with Norway saying it has been kicked out of the next major tournament – to accommodate Russia. Switzerland has joined a "boycott."

With just weeks to go until the start of the 2027 World Junior Championship, it remains unclear who will be the 10th (of 10) participant. This comes after the Norwegian Ice Hockey Association (NIHF) said that the International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) had informed it that it had been removed from the tournament so that Russia could take part.

The move, which has yet to be publicly announced by the IIHF, comes in apparent response to last month's Court of Arbitration (CAS) ruling, which ordered it to allow Russia to return to international play. The World Juniors is the first tournament affected by the CAS decision. The IIHF barred Russia and Belarus from international play shortly after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

In a statement issued on Saturday, the IIHF said it was "taking the necessary steps required by the CAS ruling and reviewing what conditions would need to be met to safeguard our Championships, protect the organization's financial stability and secure the long-term future of international ice hockey."

As of Monday, the IIHF website still listed Norway as one of the participants in the World Juniors, which is to be hosted by Edmonton and Red Deer, Alberta beginning on December 26. Still, Swiss Ice Hockey responded to Norway's statement, saying it's team would not face Russia at the World Juniors – as would be the case if it replaces Norway in the schedule.

However, it is far from certain that Russia will actually be able to ice a team in the tournament, as just last week, the Canadian prime minister ruled out the possibility.

"While Russia and Belarus are supporting this illegal, unjustified ​war in Ukraine, as long as that's going on, there will be none of those athletes competing for their countries in Canada," Mark Carney said.

"So, ​if you're asking specifically about the World Juniors, the Russians will not be there."

How this circle could be squared is unclear. Carney's pledge, coupled with the stated refusal by Finland, Sweden, Switzerland and others to face Russia in an international tournament, appears to have given the NIHF hope that its team could still play in the upcoming World Juniors. Several long-time corporate sponsors have also threatened to pull out if Russia is allowed to compete.

"This makes us hope that the last word has not been said about our participation in Canada in December," NIHF General Secretary Petter Salsten said.

"The Norwegian Ice Hockey Association is awaiting further information from the IIHF in the coming days."

Meanwhile, the German Ice Hockey Association (DEB) is still in discussions with the government in Berlin and the IIHF about how to proceed – or not – with hosting the Men's Ice Hockey World Championship next May.

"We intend to host the World Championship in Germany next year, and I am very optimistic that we will succeed in doing so," DEB chairman Frank H. Lutz told German broadcaster MagentaSport on Saturday.

While he acknowledged the IIHF's CAS-ordered requirement to include Russia and reiterated the DEB's rejection of the court ruling, he provided no indication as to how this obstacle could be overcome.

Lutz, who said he would be in Berlin for more consultations this week, had previously said handing back Germany's hosting rights was a possibility – if only as a last resort.

On Friday, government spokesman Stefan Kornelius said Berlin supports the DEB's efforts to find a solution.

"However, given the boycotts that would follow Russia's readmission, that would effectively be impossible. For this reason, we intend to explore — through dialogue — how we can still ensure the tournament takes place."

Asked at the same press conference whether Germany could issue visas to a Russian team for the tournament, a Foreign Ministry spokesman indicated that this would be difficult under restrictions currently in place.

"At a time when Russia is waging a war of aggression against Ukraine, there can be no 'normalcy' — and we will certainly not pretend that there is," said spokesperson Martin Giese.

However, he did not categorically rule out the possibility.

It has been suggested that government officials could be choosing their words carefully out of concern for Munich's chances as it bids to host the Summer Olympics in 2036, 2040, or 2044.

The International Olympic Committee (IOC) recently lifted its sanctions on Russian athletes and suspension of the Russian National Olympic Committee – opening the door for their return to competition, despite the ongoing war in Ukraine.

The thinking goes that the IOC would expect national Olympic committees who are bidding to host an Olympic Games – like the German Olympic Sports Confederation (DOSB) – to follow its lead.

Asked whether the debate over Russia's possible involvement in a hockey tournament could affect Munich's chances, government spokesman Kornelius said he didn't wish to "speculate on implications."

Still, with the IOC set to decide in the next few weeks whether Munich advances to the next stage of the process, one has to think that the issue could hardly have come up at a more inopportune time for the DOSB.

https://www.dw.com/en/fake-news-in-afric.title: Fake news in Africa: In an age of disinformation, who decides what's true?
https://www.dw.com/en/fake-news-in-afric.text:
From Ghana to Mozambique, the fight against fake news keeps gaining momentum. But combating disinformation also requires safeguards for free speech, leaving some governments in an inconvenient position.

Misinformation poses a threat to democracy worldwide: An exaggerated WhatsApp message, a manipulated TikTok video or an apparent breaking news alert on Facebook can all misguide people in Africa and beyond — particularly in the run-up to elections.

As artificial intelligence is making it increasingly easy to manipulate images, voices and videos, more and more countries are trying to equip their populations with skills to identify and counter fake news.

But are these efforts really about raising awareness, or are certain governments using this fight to control public opinion, silence dissident voices and misguide the populace — from both within and outside of these respective nations?

Journalism lecturer Dani Madrid-Morales at the University of Sheffield believes that African governments must significantly step up their efforts to combat sources of disinformation and misinformation.

He told DW that "there are very few countries — if any — that are actually doing a good job" to beat the influence of fake news.

Meanwhile, he also points out that there also are civil society initiatives in various African nations which help inform people about the dangers of such false narratives.

For instance in South Africa, organizations like Africa Check and Media Monitoring Africa work together to highlight the impact of fake news on elections. Similar coalitions also exist in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and Senegal.

However, these initiative mostly focus on fighting disinformation during election periods; the rest of the time, they typically lack funding and sustained engagement with civil society to continue to make a change.

There also are deliberate efforts by certain governments not to battle fake news; some let it happen while others engage in deliberately spreading this.

Madrid-Morales distinguishes between three types of disinformation within this context: There are scams and similar schemes, which some governments, he says, fail to sufficiently fight, leaving people susceptible to financial losses.

He adds that there also are certain foreign influence operations trying to impact public opinion from outside a country and, in many instances, outside of the continent.

Finally, there are political disinformation campaings which originate from within a country, he explains.

"Governments are particularly interested in the third category," says Madrid-Morales, adding that this is particularly prevalent in the Sahel region.

He highlights how in nations like Burkina Faso and Mali, military governments have shut down media outlets, prosecuted journalists and expelled foreign correspondents to silence free speech.

In his view, these junta governments are primarily concerned with preventing negative or false information about themselves from circulating.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Foreign powers meanwhile also appear to play a considerable role in shaping public opinion across the continent.

Afrobarometer, a pan-African research network, examined the influence of international actors in terms of their influence over the continent.

The study found that over 60% of respondents viewed China's political and economic influence positively; this was followed by 52% for the United States.

Both countries have no past colonial history in Africa, although they are now vying for economic gains while focusing on infrastructure projects — partly to maintain this largely benevolent perception.

However, perceptions of other former colonial powers varied notabbly depending on factors such as the impact of past injustices: For example, in French-speaking countries, only 34% of respondents viewed France's ongoing influence positively.

Komi Amewonou from Afrobarometer  meanwhile told DW that such attitudes are not necessarily the result of targeted propaganda campaigns but rather of African governments letting negative perceptions simpy run their course.

In some countries, there are media development project trying to educate people and animate them to think for themselves.

Ghana, the NGO Penplusbytes runs the "Caravan of Hope" — a project supported German development agency GIZ and the by DW Akademie.

This mobile campaign brings media literacy training to rural communities through theater, role-playing exercises, public discussions and videos in local languages. The initiative has managed to reach 3,000 people in five districts to date.

The campaign also involves trusted community figures, as studies show that locals mostly trust people they know personally — particularly traditional village leaders and community representatives.

Rebecca Avusu from Penplusbytes, who helped develop the project, told DW that "information must be verified before people believe it or pass it on. This is particularly important for those without smartphones or with limited formal education."

Initiatives in South Africa take a similar approach: The country is home to Africa Check — one of the continent's best-known fact-checking initiatives.

The organization visits schools and teaches classes how to identify manipulated images, verify sources and deal with misinformation circulating in WhatsApp groups.

However, Madrid-Morales says that there can be a downside to such media literacy programs as well; pointing to research conducted in South Africa, he highlights that while some young people do become more discerning consumers of information, others eventually lose trust in almost every source, resulting in a complete lack of knowledge about important developments.

In other parts of the continent, there's greater resistance against such media literacy initiaves — chiefly by their own governments.

In 2026, the International Media and Information Literacy Institute (IMILI) was opened in the Nigerian capital Abuja under the auspices of UNESCO, with a mission is to promote research, training and international cooperation in media literacy initiatives.

The government has said that it aims to play a leading international role in Africa in the fight against fake news; however, civil rights groups say the state often blurs the line between genuinely battling disinformation and silencing public dissent in the country.

In Kenya, there are similar concerns: The Media Council of Kenya has the role of supporting journalists and fact-checking initiatives.

However, it's scope of operations is limited, as the organization abides by the country's laws to remain in operation — in particular legislation supposedly designed to target the spreading of false information.

Conversely, these laws have come under increased scrutiny, as they can also be abused the silence views against the government.

Madrid-Morales says that in such contexts, there need to be independent oversight bodies to ensure that people do not refrain from expressing themselves publicly for fear of reprisal.

Meanwhile in Mozambique, the media institute MISA has also launched a series of fact-checking initiatives such as MISACheck. The program is designed to train young journalists and social activists in fact-checking techniques.

Olivia Massango, the vice-president of MISA, says however that the efforts of such civil society groups may seem like a drop in the ocean.

Massango is particularly critical of how state authorities deal with misinformation: "When something becomes inconvenient, the government ... invokes public interest, but ultimately often ends up protecting only what suits it, or what it finds troubling," she told DW.

As an example, she cites an internet blackout justified on the grounds of protecting public safety.

"Combating disinformation must not mean criminalizing opinions, criticism or journalistic work," she warns.

More and more African nations meanwhile are turning to Europe in hopes of adopting mechanisms to fight fake news.

Morocco and Senegal are among the examples where proposed legislation is inspired by EU standards. Madrid-Morales however stresses that while following strong EU legislation in the battle against disinformation, there also need to be independent oversight and enforcement mechanisms to make them work.

In the cases of Senegal and Morocco, these are yet to be established.

Rebecca Avusu is also concerned about such efforts maintaining loopholes to suit governments is and as needed: "We do not want laws designed to combat disinformation to become instruments for silencing people who question government decisions or express legitimate opinions," Avusu warns.

https://www.dw.com/en/turkey-workers-kil.title: Turkey: Workers killed in Izmir steel plant blast
https://www.dw.com/en/turkey-workers-kil.text:
At least 10 workers lost their lives in an explosion at a steel factory in Izmir, with the Turkish authorities warning more people are trapped under the debris.

An explosion and fire at a factory in western Turkey left 10 workers dead, while rescuers searched for four more believed to be trapped under the debris.

The blast took place at the HABAS steel plant in Aliaga, in the port city of Izmir. The city's governor Suleyman Elban told reporters that 15 people were injured, two of them critically, and that further search and rescue efforts were underway.

The plant's production line was in the middle of a shift change rather than active production, according to the governor. Only some 200 workers were present instead of the expected 300.

An earlier statement from the governor's office said that the blast happened around noon (09:00 GMT) when an overhead crane toppled into a furnace during the casting of liquid steel. It also said that the authorities were investigating the incident.

Mayor Cemil Tugay wrote on X that the initial fire following the blast had been extinguished, but the exact number of dead and injured would become clear only after the debris had been cleared.

Interior Minister Mustafa Ciftci, announced that those injured in the incident have been taken to hospital and their condition is being closely monitored.

Minister of Justice Akın Gürlek announced four public prosecutors have been assigned to the case.

Eyewitness Nuri Ali Ulker described the blast as "very intense."

"The ground shook," he was quoted as saying by the state-run Anadolu news agency.

Another witness, Deniz Ulker, told the agency that the explosion "felt like the earth's crust was shifting beneath us. I thought it was an earthquake."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The HABAS plant was established in 1987 and can produce 4.5 million tons of steel annually, according to the company's website.

Turkey's leftist opposition party TIP lashed out at the government saying that the blast has once again laid bare how occupational health and safety are completely disregarded in the country.

The described the incident as "workplace homicide."

In an online post, TIP leader Erkan Bas said that "[t]he regime of bosses has declared war on the workers."

Union leader Basaran Aksu said that "the massacre calls for the resignation of the minister of labor."

He warned that "workers' blood" was being shed for profit.

According to the Health and Safety Labor Watch, an independent NGO in Turkey, there were 226 workplace deaths reported across the country in September this year.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmz7.title: Action on energy costs is my overriding aim, says Fahnbulleh
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmz7.text:
The energy secretary has stressed that affordability is her "overriding objective", as she said reducing bills would be key to maintaining public support for climate action.

Speaking to BBC Panorama, Miatta Fahnbulleh insisted that the government's drive for cleaner power would help to cut energy bills in the long term.

But she conceded that the push to reduce carbon emissions was currently "under pressure" amid discontent at rising prices in recent years.

It comes as ministers grapple with how to respond to a predicted surge in energy prices in January, expected to mark the biggest rise in bills for four years.

Labour has faced extra political pressure over its climate ambitions since coming to power, as Reform UK rose in opinion polls and the Conservatives under Kemi Badenoch disowned their previous ambition of reaching net zero by 2050.

Both opposition parties have taken particular aim at public subsidy schemes designed to boost renewable sources of electricity generation, arguing that the drive for cleaner energy has driven up costs for consumers.

UK households currently pay one of the highest rates for electricity in Europe.

Bills have increased due to subsidies but also because of the high price of gas (a fossil fuel) driven up by international conflicts.

Asked during her Panorama interview what her main task was, Fahnbulleh replied: "With the cost of living biting, affordability is my overriding objective, without a doubt."

In the interview, which was recorded last week, and aired on Monday night, she argued that Labour's push for greener electricity was "one of our routes to delivering affordability".

"The drive to clean power is about decoupling our dependence on global fossil fuel markets," she added. "Ultimately if we have homegrown renewables, nuclear, that's the way in which we will drive bills in the long term."

However, she conceded that struggles over energy affordability were part of the reason the consensus on climate action was "under pressure".

"People want to blame net zero for that. Now, I don't believe that's the case.

"But I'm very clear that part of the way in which we build and maintain public consent is that we've got to show that this transition, which we have to do on climate grounds, is good for people's pockets."

The UK had a record number of heatwaves this summer and suffered successive damaging wildfires, which the Met Office has said was made 130 times more likely by climate change.

Just last month, whilst hosting the UK's first summit on wildfires, Andy Burnham acknowledged that as a result of climate change "the summer we've just had is likely to be a more regular situation going forward".

But he has also vowed to lead a "cost of living government" and reindustralise the economy.

This has prompted some in Westminster to speculate that he could demote climate action to help reduce energy costs in the short-term.

His government has dismayed some green activists by diverting funding from the energy department to help meet defence funding targets, including money previously earmarked for energy efficiency schemes.

Last month the government approved drilling at the Jackdaw gas field which also prompted criticism from some campaigners, although ministers have sought to argue it will minimise imports of higher emission fuels.

A decision is yet to be taken on whether production can begin at Rosebank, the UK's largest known untapped oil field, located off the coast of Shetland.

Speaking to Panorama, Fahnbulleh insisted reducing carbon emissions "absolutely is a priority", pointing to this summer's droughts as evidence of the need to tackle global warming.

However, she conceded that Labour's target for 95% of electricity generated in Britain to come from clean power sources by 2030 was a "stretch".

On Monday, it was reported that the government is considering weakening the electric vehicle mandate requiring car manufacturers to phase out production of petrol and diesel cars by 2035.

This could prove a blow to not only the country's climate targets but the UK's claim to be providing leadership on the issues just as ministers head to Turkey for COP31, the UN's climate summit.

But she admits that the push to reduce carbon emissions is currently "under pressure" Comes as ministers grapple with how to respond to predicted surge in energy prices in January.

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/09/nx-s1-602.title: Palantir hires a former Democratic senator as it faces scrutiny in new Congress
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/09/nx-s1-602.author: Luke Garrett
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/09/nx-s1-602.text:
Sen. Jon Tester, D-Mont., speaks during a hearing on Capitol Hill in Washington, on May 2, 2023.

Tech companies are expecting a wave of scrutiny from Democrats for the industry's ties with the Trump administration when they take over Congress in January. In anticipation, many are hiring former Democratic lawmakers and aides to make their case to the incoming House and Senate majorities.

Among the latest to make that move is Palantir, which has hired former Sen. Jon Tester, a colorful Montana Democrat who's also an organic farmer.

"My agreement with Palantir is advisory in nature, it is not lobbying," Tester, who lost reelection to the Senate in 2024, told NPR in an interview.

The secretive American software and artificial intelligence company has drawn the ire of Democrats in Congress during President Trump's second term. Palantir — named by billionaire founder Peter Theil after the mythical "seeing stone" from J.R.R. Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings — has been accused of abetting mass surveillance on Americans and immigrants.

"Perception is reality in Washington, D.C. and in politics in general," said Tester. "But the fact is, I think Palantir has got a good story to tell, and they need to tell it. And hopefully folks will be receptive to it."

Palantir has long denied claims it aids mass surveillance on the American public — saying it doesn't gather or manipulate data at all, but instead creates tools for government agencies and private companies to organize and optimize their own information. The company has said it is committed to "protecting privacy and upholding liberal democratic values."

Earlier this year, while in the minority, Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Ore., along with 30 other Democratic lawmakers demanded answers about Palantir's contracts with the Department of Homeland Security and whether its tools are part of efforts by the federal government to surveil Americans. Palantir denied the accusation and said it is "neither conducting nor enabling mass surveillance of American citizens," but Wyden wasn't fully satisfied with its response, according to his Senate office.

"Senator Wyden has a number of questions about Palantir's work to facilitate the Trump-Vance abuse of government data that he intends to ask again as chairman of the Finance Committee," Wyden's staff wrote in a statement to NPR. "If Palantir is not responsive next year, compulsory processes will be on the table."

It's not a coincidence that tech companies are turning to Democrats to help burnish their reputation, said Aya Ibrahim, a senior fellow at the AI Now Institute and a former State Department official.

"I think at the end of the day, these companies have an inordinate amount of money and they will try and put it wherever they can in order to stave off any real accountability," Ibrahim said.

During Trump's second term, Palantir's CEO and co-founder Alex Karp — a self-described liberal — has been highly critical of Democrats on issues like immigration and AI.

"I would say to my Democratic friends, also of which I still have, I hope many," Karp said in an interview with Axios in 2025 specifically referencing his support for much more restrictive immigration policies. "You have to grow a spine because a lot of these people actually agree with me in private."

During his 18 years in the Senate, Tester was an outspoken critic of the PATRIOT Act that passed shortly after the 9/11 attacks that expanded the Justice Department's surveillance powers. When asked whether his concerns over government surveillance remain and whether he has the same concerns with his new employer, Tester said Palantir is different and that the company doesn't build "big databases" or trade in private data.

"I wanted to do away with the Patriot Act because it was about privacy," Tester said. "It was about making sure that I am not being watched by anybody, including Big Brother. And by the way, I've talked to many people within Palantir. They believe the same way I do. This is an organization that believes in privacy."

Last year, over a dozen former Palantir employees criticized the company over its $30 million contract with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement to create a tool that provides "near real-time visibility" into the movement of migrants. The former employees argued the company violated its own code of conduct by working with the Trump administration on such products.

Valued at over $350 billion, Palantir currently holds $2 billion worth of federal contracts, according to government records. The lion's share are with the Departments of Defense, Homeland Security and State — but the software firm also works with the Departments of Agriculture, Veterans Affairs and Health and Human Services.

Tester said he'll be focused on the government services side of Palantir's work.

The former Montana senator called the midterm election results a blue "tidal wave" after two years of a Congress that gave him "great disappointment."

"It is going to make a difference as far as the policies that are being advocated for," Tester said of the upcoming Congress. "I don't think you're going to see the kind of aggressive tactics that were taken forth by ICE moving forward."

NPR does not offer or accept money for coverage or interviews.
Anyone who makes such an offer or request is not an NPR employee and does not represent NPR.
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/09/nx-s1-602.summary: Tech companies are expecting a wave of scrutiny from Democrats for their ties with the Trump administration. Palantir has been accused of abetting mass surveillance on Americans and immigrants. The secretive American software and artificial intelligence company has drawn the ire of Democrats in Congress during President Trump's second term.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: Judo star Teddy Riner announces plan to run in France’s presidential election
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Ashifa Kassam
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
Five-times Olympic champion says he is neither leftwing nor rightwing but would seek to ‘bring people together’

The French judo star and five-times Olympic gold medallist Teddy Riner has announced plans to run in next year’s presidential election, describing himself as someone neither leftwing nor rightwing but who would seek to “bring people together”.

With more than five months before the April-May ballot to replace Emmanuel Macron, the race has been shaping up to be a showdown between political extremes. Polls point to a hollowing out of the political centre, suggesting that the anti-immigrant National Rally leader Marine Le Pen could be the frontrunner, with the radical-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon trailing behind.

Riner joins a crowded field of candidates, with analysts describing him as a long shot, given his lack of experience and no party backing.

On Monday, he sought to position himself as someone who would unite people and bring “common sense, steadfastness, justice” to France.

“I know what people are going to say about me: ‘He’s crazy. He’s not from the establishment. He doesn’t have the codes. He’s never done politics,’” Riner said in a video posted on social media.

He listed the issues facing the country, from soaring debt to the rising cost of groceries and the precarious futures faced by those who don’t have the right network, family name or skin colour. “If refusing to bow my head and refusing the chaos makes me crazy, then yes, I’m completely crazy,” he said.

The announcement comes about six weeks after Riner, who has often been voted France’s most popular sportsperson, faced a wave of racist abuse and online harassment after telling a TV sports show he felt “anxiety” about the rise of the far right in France.

It also comes as the country has been rocked by protests over the cost of living, heightening the ongoing protests by schoolchildren over crumbling and crowded classrooms.

Riner, 37, who was born in the French Caribbean territory of Guadeloupe and grew up in Paris, cited his years of throwing and pinning down judo opponents to make the case for being elected president. “Fighting has always been part of me. I know what it’s like to fight, fall and always get up,” he said. “France does not need a professional politician who recites lessons and quarrels all day long.”

In an interview with the newspaper Le Parisien published on Monday, he described his views as neither rightwing nor leftwing.

Instead Riner, one of France’s most recognisable and popular athletes, pointed to broader issues. “The country is experiencing deep divisions right now, let’s not kid ourselves,” he said. “And in the face of that, I don’t see a single candidate putting forward a credible and fair vision capable of bringing French people together rather than dividing them. There is no one today offering genuine, sincere hope. It’s always one side against another.”

As Riner prepared to attempt to gather 500 sponsorship signatures from elected officials, as required by French law, he said some of his motivation to run came from those young and old who were finding it difficult to envision a future for themselves.

“I hear the anger, which some people echo in their rhetoric with a great deal of negativity, coming from people who no longer have any ambition or the desire to think big,” he said. “Yet France is a great country. It allowed me to become the person I am today and gave me the opportunity to dream big. Today, that is precisely what is missing. There is no longer that ambition, no longer that hope.”

If elected, he said he was hoping to strike a balance between both careers so he would be able to compete in the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.

He wouldn’t be the first judoka to embrace French politics: David Douillet was elected to the French parliament in 2009, years after his retirement from judo, later serving as the sports minister from September 2011 to May 2012.

Dani Podgoretskaya, an analyst at Eurasia Group, said there was little chance Riner would be seen as a serious contender.

“The French take the presidential election very seriously, given how much power the office holds. He has no experience in elected office, no party and no detailed programme yet,” she told Agence France-Presse. “While I still find it possible that we may yet see a providential figure emerge who unites the anti-populist vote, I doubt that Riner is that figure.”

When asked about his priorities on the world stage, Riner seized on the moment to crack a joke about potentially meeting the US president. “A lot of people around me have been talking about my first handshake with Donald Trump,” he said. With a laugh, he added: “We’ll see who has the firmer handshake.”

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.title: ‘Black English’ and ‘Asian English’ should be census options, MPs say
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.author: Jessica Elgot Deputy political editor
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text:
Exclusive: Cross-party call for ethnicity options to be broadened beyond ‘English’ being only within ‘White’ category

Britons should be able to define themselves as both Black and English, according to senior MPs who are calling to broaden the range of ethnicity options in the census.

The cross-party push is a riposte to Reform UK politicians who have claimed that people from minority ethnic backgrounds cannot have English ethnic identity.

The Liberal Democrat president, Josh Babarinde, is launching the drive, with backing from the former deputy prime minister David Lammy, the former foreign secretary James Cleverly and other prominent MPs including the Conservative Mark Pritchard and the Lib Dem chair of the health select committee, Layla Moran.

The MPs say the current definition of Englishness on the census means 60% of England’s World Cup squad would not technically be classified as English on the census.

“I’m a proud Englishman and Englishness is about more than the colour of your skin,” Babarinde said. “Most people in this country already agree that you don’t have to be White to be English. Just look at the England football team. But our census hasn’t properly caught up.”

MPs backing a bill proposing the change have been highly critical of comments from the Reform UK MP Suella Braverman – a former Conservative home secretary – in which she said she did not consider herself ethnically English because of her south Asian heritage.

Braverman said she did not take “a ‘laissez-faire, anything-goes’ attitude to ethnicity, citizenship and identity … I take the conservative approach. Englishness is an ethnicity. There have been English people for centuries and we need to recognise this more if we are to start taking a more muscular approach to citizenship and nationality. And no, it’s not racist to say this.”

Those remarks are part of the motivation for some MPs to seek a change to the next census to ensure that Englishness is not categorised separately to ethnicity. In England, the ethnic group question offers “English” only within the “White” category, although about 11% of UK-born population in England and Wales (about 5 million people) are from a minority ethnic background.

But Asian, Black, mixed and other respondents can describe themselves as British, for example “Asian or Asian British”, but have no option to describe themselves as English.

This stands in contrast to the census in Scotland and Wales, which offers options such as “Scottish Asian”, and “Black Welsh”.

Sign up to Breaking News UK

Sign up for the Breaking News UK email to get newsletter alerts direct to your inbox

after newsletter promotion

MPs will give their backing to a 10-minute rule bill on Tuesday tabled by Babarinde. The short bills rarely become law but are used by MPs as devices to raise particular matters of policy. The bill would require the ethnic group question in future censuses in England to give respondents in every category the option to identify as English.

The bill also has backing from Conservative MP Ben Obese-Jecty, Labour’s Adam Jogee and and the Lib Dems’ Munira Wilson.

“This bill is about standing up to those want to gatekeep Englishness exclusively for White people and standing up to those who seek to divide us over who counts as English. This is about bringing people together around our shared Englishness,” Babarinde said.

Braverman’s comments have drawn criticism even within Reform UK. The party’s chair, Zia Yusuf, distanced himself from her view, saying: “I’m a Chelsea fan and in my view Ashley Cole is the best English fullback in history, and I won’t take any other position. So in my view, Ashley Cole is English. The argument that he’s not English doesn’t hold water with me.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Dolores Huerta obituary
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Michael Carlson
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
American activist and trade unionist who fought for the rights of farm workers

Although she was never the president of the United Farm Workers union, Dolores Huerta, who has died aged 96, was one of the most significant American trade union leaders of the 20th century. Her battle cry, “Sí, se puede!”, coined in the midst of tensions with police in Arizona in the 1970s, was adapted to the English “Yes, we can” and became Barack Obama’s slogan during his successful campaign for the US presidency in 2008.

While the UFW leader Cesar Chavez was the public face of the union as its president, Huerta was the organiser who helped break the resistance of California’s grape growers by building bridges to secondary boycotts by unions packing and transporting grapes, and by organising boycotts of national supermarket chains such as A&P and Finast, who sold them. “To take on agriculture, which to this day is still a powerhouse, that took a lot of guts,” her son Emilio said.

It sometimes also took a lot of restraint. When a New York Times investigation of Chavez’s life revealed that the union leader had sexually abused women and girls, Huerta revealed that she had been raped by Chavez. She had previously “felt pressured” to have sex with him while on a working trip in 1960; the rape occurred in his car parked in a grape field in 1966. Both times she became pregnant (she gave these children up, to be raised by others). She also detailed a brutal working culture within the UFW, which she attributed to “machismo”. She explained keeping her secret for so long because “building the movement and securing farm workers’ rights was my life’s work”.

It was also in her blood. She was born in Dawson, New Mexico, where her father, Juan Fernández, was a coal miner and United Mine Workers activist. He was driven out of town for these activities, and became a beet picker, but returned and in 1938 was elected, as a “fiery union leader”, to the state legislature. By this time her mother, Alicia (nee Chavez), had divorced him, and moved the family to Stockton, California, where her father, Herculano, helped her raise the children while she worked in a cannery and as a waitress. She opened her own restaurant in 1941, and in 1942 bought a hotel from a Japanese-American family forced to move to a “relocation centre” during the second world war.

Dolores graduated from Stockton high school, where she faced de facto segregation by race and class. She married her high-school sweetheart, Ralph Head, in 1948. After their divorce in 1951, she studied part-time while raising a family, and received a teaching qualification from Stockton College (now San Joaquin Delta College) in 1953. Discouraged by the poverty of her students, she left teaching in 1955, and joined the activist Fred Ross’s grassroots civil rights group, Community Service Organisation (CSO), where she met Chavez. That year she married Ventura Huerta.

In 1958 she helped organise what became the Agricultural Workers Organising Committee (AWOC), which was affiliated to America’s national trade union congress, the AFL-CIO. In 1962, she, Chavez and Gilbert Padilla started the National Farm Workers Association (NFWA). In 1965, they joined Filipino workers during the grape strike in Delano, north-west of Bakersfield, and the AWOC and NFWA became the United Farm Workers, with Chavez as president and Huerta as vice-president, by which point she had separated from Ventura and was living with Chavez’s family.

The Delano strike propelled Chavez and the UFW into national prominence, especially when, while campaigning for president in 1968, Robert F Kennedy symbolically broke bread with Chavez to end the union leader’s hunger strike. Huerta would later be on the platform and receive thanks from Kennedy at the Ambassador hotel in Los Angeles just moments before the candidate was assassinated.

Eventually, the successes of the UFW led to the California Agricultural Labor Relations Act, signed into law by Governor Jerry Brown in 1975. By that time, Dolores had divorced Huerta, and was living with Chavez’s brother Richard, her partner until his death in 2011. She continued to serve as the UFW’s chief negotiator, though her positions sometimes changed ahead of the union’s, and Chavez’s. The UFW originally opposed relaxing controls on immigration from south of the border, as illegal workers were used as a strike-breaking tool by big farmers. Huerta moved towards assisting immigrants to settle and work legally before it became union policy.

Similarly, although she was attracted early to feminism, meeting Gloria Steinem and founding the Coalition of Labor Union Women, she and the union originally dismissed feminism as being “middle class”, their position focusing on liberation in work, not on sexual liberation outside traditional female roles. However, in a 1976 interview with Steinem’s MS magazine Huerta spoke of feminism helping her to deal with the cultural guilt she felt over her two divorces.

Huerta used her growing profile to campaign on a wider range of social issues. Her awareness, going back to her CSO days, that the roots of workers’ strength lay in overcoming poverty and lack of education led to her protesting over other issues. She was arrested a reported 22 times, and in 1988, demonstrating at an appearance of George W Bush in San Francisco’s Union Square, she was nearly killed by police who broke several of her ribs and ruptured her spleen. After recovering, she took a leave of absence from the UFW, donated her $825,000 settlement from the city to women’s causes and campaigned for the Feminist Majority Foundation. Just before Chavez died in 1993, he apologised to Huerta for treating her and other women in the union “differently”, and she returned to the UFW, primarily as a campaigner.

In 1999 she stepped down from the UFW board, and in 2002 she founded the Dolores Huerta Foundation, whose aim was to encourage community democracy through “United Neighbours” groups, again an echo of her early days with the CSO. “I want to give our children an inheritance of justice,” she said. “That is the greatest gift I think any of us could have.”

She accepted the presidential medal of freedom from Obama in 2012, and in 2018 Jerry Brown signed a bill making 10 April Dolores Huerta Day in California. She received numerous honours, including the Eleanor Roosevelt Foundation’s human rights award, and has been the subject of two documentaries, Dolores (2017) and Seeds of Change (2025), and an opera, Dolores, which debuted in 2025. Rosario Dawson portrayed her in Diego Luna’s 2014 film Cesar Chavez.

https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/1.title: Nvidia shares slump amid investigation into CEO Jensen Huang
https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/1.text:
Nvidia stock tumbled in early trading after the company launched an internal investigation into whether CEO Jensen Huang had been targeted by a Chinese intelligence operation.

News of the probe into the California-based semiconductor giant sent its stock tumbling over 4 percent as United States financial markets opened for the week, while tech stocks and wider indexes rose.

The probe comes amid reports that Huang developed a close personal relationship with a Chinese business executive of a Nvidia partner company who allegedly passed information to Beijing. In a letter to employees, Huang admitted to not being faithful to his wife, but did not elaborate on the details of the relationship.

“NVIDIA’s Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation. I support the investigation and will cooperate fully,” Huang said in the letter.

On Sunday, the firm announced the investigation. “The Board prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders,” the company said in a statement.

“While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board’s inquiry will examine all available information.”

The investigation puts Huang’s future in the spotlight at a company with a market capitalisation of $4.5 trillion. Huang is Nvidia’s fifth-largest shareholder, owning 3.6 percent of the company, according to LSEG data. However, Nvidia’s co-founder does not have majority voting control, unlike executives at other companies in the sector, such as Meta and SpaceX.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq was not affected by Nvidia’s downturn on Monday, with the index up 2.7 percent in early trading. Microsoft rose 2.2 percent, with chip maker AMD trading up over 10 percent on a new deal with Google and a stock analyst’s upgrade. Digital and e-commerce giant Amazon rose 3.8 percent.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 1.7 percent, and the S&P 500 rose 2.1 percent.

Analysts are sceptical that the controversy surrounding Huang will lead to him stepping down.

“Founder-led companies outperform because one person carries the vision,” Michael Monaghan, portfolio manager of Founders 100 ETF, told Al Jazeera.

“Based on the current information, I would see that as highly improbable [that he is removed].”

This is not the first investigation into Huang’s relationships in recent months. In October, The New York Times reported that the CEO had a relationship with the alleged China operative, Alice Huang, a former executive at the Singapore-based company Megaspeed. The two Huangs are not related.

Megaspeed, a data centre and cloud computing company, described itself as “a core business partner of NVIDIA’s computing power cloud business in the Asia-Pacific region” on its website.

US authorities investigated and concluded that Alice Huang was a Chinese intelligence asset, although the Chinese government pushed back against those allegations.

“The so-called Chinese spy narrative is purely a groundless accusation, slander, and a smear,” Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters in Beijing.

The developments come amid a rough week for artificial intelligence (AI) investors on Wall Street. After markets settled following definitive results in the US midterm elections, candidates who ran on anti-AI platforms won overwhelmingly, giving Democrats, who are more critical of the AI industry than their Republican colleagues, control of both the House and the Senate in the new Congress.

Additionally, all but one of the data centre ballot measures seeking to restrict construction of new facilities across the US passed, sending shares of major AI firms tumbling on Thursday before they rose again on Friday.

“Jensen has two sets of enemies in Washington: China hawks who want the export door shut, and the crowd trying to stop the data centre buildout. The longer this drags, the stronger they get,” Monaghan told Al Jazeera.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.title: More than 50,000 displaced by deadly Ethiopia border clashes
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.text:
Moyale, Kenya – When Hawa Hassan fled her home in Ethiopia’s Moyale area, she left almost everything behind. Her house was burned during the violence, she said. But one memory has stayed with her: a 13-year-old girl shot while sitting near a wall.

Hassan said the girl had not touched a flag, a detail she raised while describing tensions over flag displays in the disputed border area. Her account of the killing could not be independently verified.

The journey into Kenya was brutal. Hassan told Al Jazeera that some women gave birth while fleeing, and that families arrived without food, cooking utensils or bedding. Newborn babies were sleeping on bare floors. Diarrhoea was spreading, while families feared malaria as mosquitoes multiplied.

For many, crossing the border has meant escaping gunfire only to face another struggle: finding food and shelter. The arrivals are also stretching Kenyan communities. Families that opened their homes are sharing scarce supplies, even as some worry the violence could reach their own neighbourhoods.

A government-led assessment conducted on October 29 and 30 estimated that 35,950 people had been displaced as of October 24. About 25,000 were staying with host families and nearly 11,000 in temporary displacement sites.

The number has since risen. During a meeting, Kenya Red Cross regional head Malik Adan said the number of people displaced by the conflict had increased from an estimated 36,000 to more than 50,000. The figure includes people living in temporary settlements as well as those staying with relatives and host families.

The overall number of displaced people has yet to be independently established, and no final figure has been confirmed.

The assessment covered 758 households and involved government authorities, United Nations agencies, the Kenya Red Cross and other humanitarian organisations. The figures reflect different reporting periods.

The fighting is rooted in a long-standing dispute over land and administrative control between Ethiopia’s Oromia and Somali regional administrations. Tensions escalated around October 18 over the raising of the Somali regional flag in the disputed Moyale area, reflecting competing claims over territory and authority.

For those arriving in Kenya, the politics are secondary to the immediate question of where they will sleep and what they will feed their children.

Mwasaru Mercy, Kenya’s acting commissioner for refugee affairs, told Al Jazeera that a multi-agency government team had been deployed to Moyale. The Department of Refugee Services is coordinating with local authorities and the UN High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR).

But gunfire could still be heard, Mercy said, raising fears of further displacement. Many arrivals need food, shelter, bedding and mosquito nets.

“There are no contingency food stocks specifically for this incident because it happened abruptly,” Mercy said.

Authorities are trying to mobilise humanitarian organisations and donors. A refugee camp has not been established because the security situation must improve first. The government is working with UNHCR to register arrivals and assess their needs.

Those affected include Ethiopians fleeing violence, traders, and Kenyans forced from their homes by stray ammunition, Mercy said.

Fatima Mohammed Cole, UNHCR’s representative in Kenya, said many arrivals were women and children. Families are spread across several locations, including six sites hosting Ethiopians. They need shelter, food and healthcare, while crowded conditions raise concerns about the spread of disease.

Cole said gunfire was still being heard in Moyale and appealed for a ceasefire that would allow families to return home.

The response is also under way inside Ethiopia. The Ethiopian Red Cross Society said it had provided emergency shelter and household items worth about 30 million Ethiopian birr ($182,970) to 1,000 households displaced from Moyale town and surrounding areas.

The supplies included 2,000 tarpaulins, blankets and sleeping mats, as well as dignity kits, jerrycans, kitchen sets, soap and solar lamps. Distribution was under way, the organisation said. The operation is separate from assistance in Kenya.

In Kenya, residents who initially opened their doors are finding it harder to keep going.

Abdi Maalim, a member of the Moyale Cross-Border Peace Committee, told Al Jazeera that some Kenyan families had moved further inland after bullets and heavy weapons landed close to their homes. He called for more border patrols to prevent armed groups from crossing into Kenya.

Families that once cooked for five or six people are now feeding 20 or 30.

Moyale’s role as a trading point between Kenya and Ethiopia has added to the strain. Maalim said trucks carrying goods between Mombasa and Addis Ababa had been stranded near the border for almost two weeks. Kenyan trucks were also stuck in Ethiopia, and businesses in Moyale had slowed sharply.

Bank closures have disrupted the circulation of the Ethiopian birr. Traders reported price rises of about 20 percent as supplies became harder to move.

Security analyst Dr Abdiwahab Sheikh Abdisamad told Al Jazeera that the clashes had grown beyond a local dispute over territory, exposing deeper ethnic divisions and political competition between Ethiopia’s regional administrations.

He said perceptions of Oromo expansionism and allegations of federal government support for Oromia’s regional leadership risked deepening mistrust. He warned that armed fighters crossing the border, stray bullets and further displacement made this a Kenyan security concern as well as a refugee emergency.

Kenya’s Inspector General of Police, Douglas Kanja, said additional officers would be deployed along the border to strengthen security. During a visit to Moyale on November 5, he said Kenya was engaging Ethiopia’s federal government to help end the conflict.

Kanja said about 10,000 people were staying in temporary shelters and public institutions, while others had been taken in by host families. He said one Kenyan had died after being hit by a stray bullet, while a police report indicated that an Ethiopian man had also died from gunshot wounds sustained in Kenya.

The 10,000 figure refers to people in temporary shelters and public institutions, not the total number displaced. It is not directly comparable with the Red Cross estimate of more than 50,000, which includes people staying with host families.

Hassan wants to return home, but only when it is safe. Until then, she and thousands of others depend on host communities and humanitarian agencies. The longer the fighting continues, the harder it will be for those communities to keep absorbing the cost.

Maalim said residents had already stretched their resources to accommodate the new arrivals.

“Previously, we were supplying this town alone. Now we are literally taking care of two towns together,” he told Al Jazeera.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.summary: Tensions escalated over the raising of the Somali regional flag in the disputed Moyale area. 10,000 people are staying in temporary shelters and public institutions.

https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/09/medium.title: Medium’s new TK app brings AI assistance directly into the writing process
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/09/medium.author: Sarah Perez
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/09/medium.text:
Online publishing platform Medium on Monday launched a new app, called TK, which aims to bring AI technology deeper into the writing process. The idea behind TK is to make it easier to turn ideas into written words by incorporating an AI assistant into the editor itself, allowing users to ask for help by typing “@TK” followed by their request or prompt.

In publishing and journalism, the term “TK” serves as a placeholder used to mark where missing information can be added later. The “TK” stands for “to come,” but uses a “K” instead of “C” as there are few English words where the “tk” letter combination exists, making it stand out more easily in written text where it could be caught by proofreaders.

In Medium’s app, TK takes on a new role as it tries to help users fill in the blanks.

The company suggests the AI assistant could help answer questions that you might normally have to switch to another tab to quickly look up, like how many days are in a particular month. The app could also pull in bits of writing you had previously saved to the app when you were still fleshing out your ideas.

In addition, Medium says TK will ship with particular skills for editorial feedback, headline feedback, and others that could match your draft to the style guide for Medium publications.

Medium’s move to embrace AI in the early stages of writing could prove controversial at a time when the publishing and literary worlds have been reckoning with the role that artificial intelligence has played in the creation of new long-form prose. Multiple authors have lost book deals over suspicions that they used AI technology to help them write, while other literary awards have come under scrutiny after winners were suspected of writing with AI assistance.

While writers have long used automated tools for proofreading and light grammatical edits, there is growing concern across the publishing industry that an AI assistant’s editorial “suggestions” can become the writing itself, instead of being reflective of the thoughts in the writer’s own mind.

But because AI models were trained on human writing, there are also questions around the reliability of AI detection tools in terms of their ability to properly determine when something was written with AI, rather than with its assistance, versus not at all.

TK leans into this debate, taking the side that these nuances will ultimately no longer matter in the end. Instead, the company celebrates what AI can bring to the world of writing, saying that “artificial intelligence makes writing more important, not less,” and proclaiming that “AI is a technology that has the power to amplify human intelligence and it uses the written word as a foundation.”

Still, Medium concedes that AI does raise the possibility of low-quality content and blurring the line between what’s human-written versus AI-written. To address these concerns, TK allows authors to publish notes that transparently explain how AI was used in their writing.

“This is a start of what we believe is required to publish in the AI era, which is to make the provenance of writing clear, transparent, and inspectable, right down to the prompting and source material,” Medium explained in a blog post about the launch.

In addition to writing assistance, TK will help users remember and organize what they had previously written and suggest writing prompts. The app can also optionally connect to your own AI agent through TK’s MCP server or Claude skill, so the app can better understand your projects, your positions, and other ideas that could be stored in your agent’s memory.

Meanwhile, the new app incorporates human feedback in a social layer, the company says, allowing writers to share their early drafts with others and get feedback.

At launch, TK is available on the web, but a desktop app is on the roadmap, Medium says. The app can import and export Markdown, but it’s not a Markdown app itself. The writing in TK is also not encrypted, as the app is designed for collaboration, but users will be able to set access control permissions on their work.

Medium, which is profitable, says TK will be a free tool for those with a Medium account.
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/09/medium.summary: Medium launched a new app called TK on Monday to help writers fill in their ideas. The app uses an AI assistant to help users fill in the blanks of writing. The company says the app will be free and available on the web, but a desktop app is on the roadmap.

Sony is also renaming this particular Portal from PlayStation Portal Remote Player to PlayStation Portal Player. The name change, combined with extra internal storage, seems to suggest that this particular model might get access to streaming apps.

The existing PlayStation Portal doesn’t support streaming apps like YouTube, Disney Plus, or Netflix, and is primarily designed to stream PS5 games from a console or the cloud. The PlayStation Portal isn’t powerful enough to play PlayStation games locally, but extra storage could also let you sync media for offline playback.

This Japan-only PlayStation Portal is launching on December 10th, priced at 39,980 yen (around $253).
