https://arstechnica.com/space/2026/11/sp.title: SpaceX now fundamentally an "infrastructure company," senior official says
https://arstechnica.com/space/2026/11/sp.author: Eric Berger
https://arstechnica.com/space/2026/11/sp.text:
“Grok analyzing the same video is 99.9 percent perfect.”

For a long time, SpaceX has been synonymous with the development of newer, larger, and ever-more-reusable rockets. But that began to change over the last decade with the introduction of Starlink, and the change has accelerated during the last 18 months as the company has pivoted to data and artificial intelligence.

At last week’s UP.Summit conference in Florida, the vice president of launch at SpaceX, Kiko Dontchev, offered some of the most revealing comments to date about the company’s changing focus, how it is embracing AI, and why the Falcon 9 rocket—which has dominated global launch for a decade and remains the world’s preeminent launch vehicle—is firmly on the road to retirement.

“In the last couple years, when I talk about SpaceX, yes, we are a rocket company, but fundamentally we are an infrastructure company at this point,” Dontchev said. “We’re building infrastructure on the ground and low Earth orbit, soon on the Moon, and obviously eventually Mars.”

Earlier this year, SpaceX acquired one of founder Elon Musk’s other companies, xAI. SpaceX engineers were already using xAI’s tools, Dontchev said, but in recent months, employees have really started to figure out how artificial intelligence can speed up their work.

“What’s happened at SpaceX is we’ve really gone through a huge acceleration of adoption,” Dontchev said. “Even just a year ago, we weren’t adopting it that quickly, but really starting this year, we started to adopt it extremely rapidly. And the acceleration we have seen in our ability to do engineering is unlike anything I’ve ever seen at the company in my 16 years.”

Tasks that would take SpaceX employees hours to days now take seconds to minutes, he said. And it’s not just the engineers. Dontchev said the work of identifying foreign object debris, or FOD, in aerospace parts has been largely automated using the AI assistant Grok. This debris can cause catastrophic damage to engines and other spacecraft components.

“We’ve automated being able to detect FOD,” he said. “We’ll have an inspector go in and borescope a tube, and we find that humans are about 94 percent perfect (at) finding a piece of it. Grok analyzing the same video is 99.9 percent perfect.”

SpaceX has also automated visual inspections of other hardware it produces, such as Starlink customer terminals, due to similar gains in accuracy. Dontchev said AI is now being used at every level of the company’s operations.

“We’ve truly started to integrate it to where every single person, including the technicians and the technician leaders, are starting to use it in their day-to-day, and it’s completely leveled the playing field and accelerated people’s growth,” he said.

Since SpaceX’s founding in 2002, a community of spaceflight enthusiasts gravitated to the company because of Musk’s vision for humanity becoming a multiplanetary species, beginning with the settlement of Mars. But concern has grown in this group that SpaceX is drifting away from that vision. Musk has recently made a hard pivot toward the deployment of orbital data centers, envisioning hundreds of thousands of solar-powered satellites providing computing services to users on Earth. Musk has largely stopped talking about sending humans to Mars, except in passing.

Dontchev insisted that human settlement and Mars remain part of the core of SpaceX’s aspirations.

“We have come to understand that this tool is critical to us accelerating our pace of innovation,” he said of artificial intelligence. “Without AI, I think we still would have gotten to the Moon. I think we still get to Mars with SI. We’re going to get there so much faster.”

Dontchev arrived at SpaceX just before the company flew its first Falcon 9 rocket in mid-2010. But because the company was never able to solve second-stage reuse, SpaceX needs to move on, he said.

“Falcon 9, I love that rocket to heart,” he said. “I’ve launched many of them, all of them, in fact. But it’s still not fully reusable. We still throw that second stage away every single flight. Starship—we’re going to catch both the first stage and the second stage.”

For 100 launches a year, it is possible to fly a partially reusable rocket, he said. But for a company that aspires to launch thousands of rockets a year, and eventually maybe even 10,000, the cost and time lost in manufacturing a new second stage for every launch is simply not sustainable.

It is also significant that Dontchev spoke less about Starship’s payload capacity and more about its productivity per launch. The first orbital Starship launch, in late September, carried larger Starlink V3 satellites. And in the aggregate, this single mission carried 10 times the bandwidth of the Starlink payload launched by a Falcon 9.

Flying Starship from Florida, he said, will further improve capacity compared to Texas launches. Launching from Florida offers more favorable trajectories to certain orbits, potentially allowing Starship to carry more satellites without expending propellant on dogleg maneuvers. Dontchev said a single Florida Starship launch will be able to carry up to 20 times the bandwidth of a single Falcon 9.

To that end, the pad infrastructure for Starship’s first launch tower at Kennedy Space Center’s Launch Complex 39A is nearly finished. The company is also developing two additional pads in Florida.

“Pad 39A is effectively complete,” he said. “We’re going to transport boosters and ships over barge here to the Cape. We’re hoping to actually do the first transports this year in December, and then maybe even fly by the end of the year.”

Starship is clearly being optimized to serve SpaceX’s launch needs. But what about commercial launch customers that have relied on Falcon 9 rockets over the last decade?

During his remarks, Dontchev did not address widespread concerns in the US commercial space industry and beyond that SpaceX has not moved to replace the Falcon 9’s lost capacity with Starship. For now, multiple sources have indicated, SpaceX is holding Starship launches in the coming years for its own needs, and potentially those of NASA and other government customers.
https://arstechnica.com/space/2026/11/sp.summary: SpaceX vice president Kiko Dontchev says company is embracing artificial intelligence. Dontcheng says company has been using AI tools for years, but has been moving rapidly.

https://arstechnica.com/tech-policy/2026.title: Nvidia CEO's affair becomes a national security problem
https://arstechnica.com/tech-policy/2026.author: Demetri Sevastopulo, Financial Times
https://arstechnica.com/tech-policy/2026.text:
Nvidia is probing whether Chinese intelligence targeted its CEO through an affair.

Nvidia’s chief executive Jensen Huang has admitted having an affair two days after the FT reported his alleged romantic relationship with a woman the US intelligence community believes was working as a spy for China.

Huang revealed the affair in an internal message to employees on Sunday that was obtained by the FT.

“I owe my family and all of you an apology,” Huang said in the message. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”

In a separate statement, Nvidia said its board would open an independent investigation “in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.”

Huang said he would fully cooperate. “My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust,” he said. “I have fallen short of that responsibility. I am fully committed to Nvidia and will work to earn back your confidence.”

The FT reported on Friday that the US believed Huang had a romantic relationship with a Chinese woman who was recruited to spy for China’s Ministry of State Security intelligence agency.

American officials this year wrote a memo, based on information from US intelligence, which said the Nvidia boss had been romantically involved with Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based customer of the chipmaker, according to people familiar with the document.

The affair is a damaging blow to the Nvidia chief, who in recent years has become the face of the AI boom, one of the technology’s loudest champions, and transformed the Silicon Valley group into the first $5 trillion company.

It also comes at a critical juncture for the wider AI sector, which faces a deepening political backlash in the US and growing investor concern over whether the hundreds of billions of dollars spent on infrastructure will pay off.

Nvidia’s Frankfurt-listed shares were down more than 6 percent in early trading on Monday.

Huang’s admission of an affair comes after Nvidia previously dismissed suggestions of an improper relationship with Alice Huang, saying the interactions were “nothing unusual or unexpected” when dealing with an Nvidia customer.

The American government memo, which said US intelligence believed the Megaspeed executive had been recruited by the MSS, was drafted just before President Donald Trump traveled to Beijing for a summit with Xi Jinping.

Jensen Huang has developed a close relationship with Trump, which has frustrated US national security officials who believe he is too willing to sell advanced chips to China that could harm American security.

Asked about Huang on Sunday, Trump told reporters he had done an “amazing job” for the US. Asked if he regretted not acting on the intelligence about the affair, Trump said: “No, I don’t think so. I think he’s an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it. You have to hear it.”

“I have not spoken to him about it. I just know he’s a fine person, but you never know what is going on,” Trump added.

After broadly staying out of politics, Huang started to build relations with Trump after the president called him out of the blue on his birthday.

He quickly became one of Trump’s favorite executives, accompanying him on state visits, including to China earlier this year and the UK last year.

Huang has repeatedly lobbied Trump to adopt a more permissive approach to shipping Nvidia’s AI chips to China, after the company was entirely cut off from the critical market by new export controls in 2025.

The resulting deal—with Trump permitting the export of Nvidia’s older-generation H200 chips to China, with the US government taking a cut of sales—had a minimal impact on the Silicon Valley company’s sales, as Beijing pushed back against its technology. But it further angered China hawks in the US administration.

The US government had already been investigating Megaspeed over concerns that it was smuggling Nvidia chips into China.

Nvidia on Sunday said a committee of independent directors, helped by external lawyers, would oversee the investigation.

“The board prioritizes US national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of Nvidia and its shareholders,” the company said. “While the board has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the board’s inquiry will examine all available information.”

Huang, who co-founded Nvidia as a video-game graphics card company in 1993, is one of the longest-serving founder-CEOs in Silicon Valley. More than most technology groups, Nvidia’s success is tethered to that of its CEO.

Huang leads a close and loyal core team of about half a dozen executives, acting as its chief salesman on the international stage while directly managing dozens of direct reports who keep the company running.

He has credited this “flat” organizational structure for the speed at which the company operates, helping it to stay ahead of rivals in the AI chip market and increasing its market valuation from roughly $1 trillion in 2023 to $4.5 trillion today.

Elon Musk, a close ally of Huang, was among the first to offer support, agreeing with a social media post that he was “one of the greatest entrepreneurs of this generation” and “irreplaceable for America’s AI leadership.”

But John Moolenaar, the Republican head of the House China committee who, with other lawmakers, has requested Huang to testify before Congress, said: “It is vital that Jensen Huang address our national security concerns in Congress related to China’s access to sensitive technology and information.”

https://arstechnica.com/cars/2026/11/f1-.title: F1 in Brazil: You’ve got to keep your tires alive
https://arstechnica.com/cars/2026/11/f1-.author: Jonathan M. Gitlin
https://arstechnica.com/cars/2026/11/f1-.text:
A topsy-turvy grid and intermittent rain resulted in a very entertaining race.

In sports, a “dead rubber” is a match that takes place after the outcome of the series or championship has already been decided. The people in charge hate this*—if you wrap up a title two-thirds of the way through a season, the viewers evaporate, as there’s nothing left at stake. But anyone who decided to skip this year’s Brazilian Grand Prix this past weekend missed one of the year’s most entertaining races, as a combination of a mixed-up starting order, some very fast drivers at the back, and a wet track that dried and then saw rain again resulted in action aplenty.

A peculiarity of F1 is that even if you manage to win a championship, there’s no guarantee you’ll be in a position to defend it. Take McLaren’s Lando Norris, who took the crown in 2025 after a nail-biting fight with his teammate Oscar Piastri and Red Bull’s Max Verstappen. Sadly for Lando, McLaren did not start this year in a position to win races, and even with several upgrades, the team has produced a car that is still very tricky to drive. But this weekend in Brazil, Norris demonstrated the form that earned him the number 1.

Rain on Saturday during qualifying helped jumble the usual running order. It was heavy enough that drivers used the wet weather tire with deep treads, which usually generates so much spray that visibility disappears and running has to be suspended. But with fewer cars on track in the later knockout qualifying sessions, this was not a problem for once. More disruption came from grid penalties for Verstappen and Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton, both of whom needed to use extra power unit components outside of the season’s allowance.

Norris claimed pole, with this year’s new champion, Kimi Antonelli, alongside in his Mercedes. Row two was filled with the unusual sight of Liam Lawson’s Racing Bull and Nico Hulkenberg’s Audi, followed by Red Bull’s Isack Hadjar and Oliver Bearman’s Haas. Next was George Russell in the other Mercedes, then the even more unusual sight of Fernando Alonso’s Aston Martin, normally found much farther back. One could say the same about William’s Alex Albon, who qualified ninth ahead of the second McLaren of Oscar Piastri.

It looked like it was going wrong for Norris right from the start of the race. Antonelli made a better start and passed him into turn 1. Lawson followed through into second place at the next corner. But Norris kept his head down, and by lap six, he was past the Racing Bull, with about five seconds to make up on Antonelli.

Well-timed pit stops saw Norris switch to the right tires at the right time, and he made none of his rivals’ mistakes, even when the rain returned in the final few laps—at least until the podium ceremony, when he tried to fizz his champagne bottle but instead shattered it.

Keeping one’s tires in the right operating window was vitally important in Brazil, but more than a few struggled with it. The Mercedes duo appeared to struggle to generate sufficient tire temperatures, and their cars looked difficult to handle, prompting plenty of complaints from both Russell and Antonelli to the garage. Russell had been progressing well and ran in the top three early in the race but spun after leaving the pit lane for his first stop, ending up facing the wrong way.

A few laps later, Antonelli spun his own car from the lead, this time going into turn 1, letting Norris back into first. Antonelli then did it again four laps later, ending fourth. Eventually, the Mercedes finished with Russell in fourth and Antonelli in fifth. But the team sealed its Constructors’ Championship, so there was still plenty of celebrating despite the relatively mediocre results (by Mercedes’ high standards).

It’s worth watching the in-car footage from the first couple of laps from both Hamilton and Verstappen, who lined up 20th and 21st out of 22 cars. By the end of lap 1, Hamilton was already in ninth and making things look easy—then again, Brazil was his 400th F1 race start, and he has won more than a quarter of them.

But within four laps, his charge had been blunted. Getting his rear tires up to temperature was key to making up so much ground, but with the track drying, the intermediate tires everyone started the race on had a finite life. With his used up, Hamilton started sliding back down the order. On two occasions, he ended up racing his teammate Charles Leclerc, who started mid-pack with his own penalty.

Unlike in Mexico, Italy, or Holland, the two red cars were able to play nice with each other. But neither managed their tires well, and the best they could do on the road was seventh (Leclerc) and ninth (Hamilton), which became eighth for Leclerc after he was given a five-second penalty for rejoining the track unsafely after running off track while battling Lawson.

Verstappen’s first lap wasn’t quite as good as Hamilton’s—the Red Bull was also never entirely within its setup window all weekend. But taking longer to turn on the rear tires probably contributed to their longevity. While Hamilton’s charge through the pack was blunted, Verstappen was in ninth place by lap 4. By lap 24, he was in second, having taken advantage of Antonelli’s second spin. Verstappen would eventually finish the day in second, 14 seconds off Norris.

F1 takes a weekend off next week, then returns for the night race in Las Vegas.

*Perhaps the prime example of this is NASCAR, which switched to a fairly incomprehensible playoff series it has continued to tweak for years in an effort to prevent anyone from winning the big cup until the last race of the year.

https://www.healio.com/news/neurology/20.title: Inducing torpor could provide brain benefits after stroke
https://www.healio.com/news/neurology/20.author: Shawn Arrajj
https://www.healio.com/news/neurology/20.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

SAN DIEGO — Inducing torpor to put the body into a hypothermic state could have neuroprotective benefits after a stroke, according to research presented at the American Neurological Association’s 151st annual meeting.

Physicians have known hypothermia to be neuroprotective following a neurological injury, but delivering therapeutic hypothermia to patients with stroke has been challenging, Eric Landsness, MD, PhD, associate professor of neurology at Washington University School of Medicine, told attendees.

“My lab started asking a different question: Instead of forcing the body to get cool to protect the brain, can we harness the brain’s internal endogenous neural circuitry to induce a hypothermic, hypometabolic, neuroprotective state?” Landsness said.

Inducing hypothermia typically involves a physician lowering a patient’s body temperature using controlled cooling methods.

However, doing so can be counterproductive for patients who have experienced a stroke, Landsness noted. When the body is cooled externally, the brain attempts to maintain temperature through processes such as shivering, which increases metabolic rate.

Torpor is a naturally coordinated state controlled by specific neural circuits in the preoptic area of the brain, Landsness said. Researchers in 2020 discovered that genetically activating these neurons can cause a drop in body temperature that lasts for roughly 72 hours.

In the current study, Landsness and colleagues used a preclinical model stroke called transient little cerebral artery inclusion in animal models. After expressing the cells in the neurons, they induced a 30-minute stroke and tracked neurological function, body temperature and infarct volume.

According to Landsness, activating the cells led to a drop in body temperature that lasted for about 48 hours. On motor tests taken 72 hours after the torpor, models showed almost no behavioral deficits compared to baseline, as well as a greater than 50% reduction in infarct volume.

“With identifying a genetically defined neuro population, we can induce a profound hypothermic, hypometabolic state that is not just a slowing of general metabolism but a rapid reorganization,” Landsness said. “When we apply this technique to a stroke model, we see a profound reduction in ischemic injury and neuroprotection.”

In a follow-up study, Landsness and colleagues determined the drop in temperature was necessary for the neuroprotection, and not simply activating the neurons.

Using whole brain metabolomics, the researchers are now seeking to identify the key metabolic pathways associated with the neuroprotective event.

“Ongoing work is asking whether this is possible in non-human primates,” Landsness said. “We have proof of principle that this thermoregulation circuit can potentially be accessed noninvasively. But the next question is still very much open.”

Landsness E, et al. Inducing a torpor-like state through targeted preoptic circuit activation protects the brain after stroke. Presented at American Neurological Association Conference; Oct. 17-20, 2026; San Diego.

Disclosures: Landsness reports no relevant financial disclosures.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/09/kiley-pul.title: Meet the 23-year-old college dropout already making six figures as Walmart’s youngest U.S. store manager
https://fortune.com/2026/11/09/kiley-pul.author: Preston Fore
https://fortune.com/2026/11/09/kiley-pul.text:
Kiley Pulley is already living a version of the Gen Z dream. At 23, she earns more than six figures, has bought her first home, and is planning a wedding she hopes to pay for without taking on debt. But she isn’t an AI startup founder or an heir to a family fortune—she’s built her career at Walmart and is now the youngest U.S. store manager.

Pulley first joined Walmart at 16 as a part-time cashier, following in the footsteps of her mother and sister, who also worked for the retail giant. At the time, she was simply a high school student looking to earn some extra spending money.

Her climb up the ranks began two years later, when she was promoted to Academy Trainer, a role responsible for training and developing new employees. But the Arizona native had just started her first semester at Grand Canyon University and initially wasn’t interested in turning her part-time job into a career. Six months later, however, she accepted a promotion to Team Lead—a move that changed how she viewed her future at Walmart.

“When I got Team Lead, it really stuck with me that Walmart is something I can make a career out of and something I want to continue to grow in,” Pulley told the Phoenix Business Journal. “That’s when I started applying for salary positions.”

By 19, she became an operations manager, and two years later, Pulley became store manager, making her the youngest person to hold the position at any U.S. Walmart store. Now 23, she still holds that distinction, leading a Neighborhood Market outside Phoenix.

Pulley told Business Insider that her approach to career growth was relatively simple: show up every day ready to learn something new—and make herself available for opportunities beyond her job description.

She regularly participated in calls with Walmart leaders, including monthly discussions with her market manager, and became involved in succession planning. As she moved into the operations manager role, she also took on projects across her market to prepare herself for the next step.

Pulley even volunteered to cover for store managers on their days off to gain the experience that was needed to be promoted. Ultimately, that willingness to seek out additional responsibility helped her build relationships with senior leaders and develop the skills needed to advance.

“Kiley has embodied ambition, dedication and perseverance since I first met her six years ago as an hourly associate,” Ray Shouse, Walmart’s Phoenix market manager, told the PBJ. “Throughout her career, she has consistently sought out mentors and development opportunities to strengthen her leadership.”

But her ambitions haven’t stopped with store manager, either. Pulley is back in school with the help of Walmart’s tuition-assistance program and hopes to be promoted to a market manager by 27 or 28—and eventually a regional executive vice president.

As Pulley continues climbing Walmart’s ranks, she’s following a path that has taken others to the top of the Bentonville, Arkansas-based retailer.

Walmart CEO John Furner started out as a part-time hourly associate in the company’s garden center in 1993. He eventually worked his way up to store manager before moving into merchandising roles across Walmart and Sam’s Club.

One of the most important qualities any leader can have, he’s said, is ability to embrace change.

“As long as I’ve been in retail—it’s officially 33 years—it’s always been changing,” Furner said in an interview with Fast Company earlier this year. “Getting comfortable with change in a world that continues to change, I think, is a really great trait for any leader.”

Furner’s predecessor, Doug McMillon, also worked his way up from an entry-level position, starting as a warehouse associate unloading trucks before serving as CEO from February 2014 to January 2026. Like Pulley, he said one of his secrets to climbing the ladder was volunteering for work that was on the horizon for his next promotion.

“One of the reasons that I got the opportunities that I got was that I would raise my hand when my boss was out of town and he or she was visiting stores or something,” he recalled in a 2024 interview with Stratechery.

“I then put myself in an environment where I became a low-risk promotion because people had already seen me do the job,” McMillon added.
https://fortune.com/2026/11/09/kiley-pul.summary: Kiley Pulley is the youngest U.S. store manager at Walmart. She first joined Walmart at 16 as a part-time cashier and became an operations manager at 19. She is now the youngest person to hold the position at any U.s. Walmart store.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/09/publisher.title: Exclusive: Publisher Spines raises $64 million in new funding to accelerate effort to automate book publishing with AI
https://fortune.com/2026/11/09/publisher.author: Jeremy Kahn
https://fortune.com/2026/11/09/publisher.text:
Spines, a startup that uses AI to help authors publish their books, including using AI agents to edit manuscripts, design covers, translate text, market the published book, and manage their social media campaigns, has secured $64 million in new capital, the company said Monday.

The company, which has offices in Israel and New York, is what is known as a “hybrid publisher.” Hybrid publishers largely work with authors who are unable to obtain a traditional publishing deal from a commercial publishing house or who wish to retain more control and receive a larger royalty split than an author typically would get with a traditional publishing house. As with self-publishing, authors pay hybrid publishers an upfront fee to publish their book. Hybrid publishers also take a cut of an author’s sales as royalties. But hybrid publishers provide a greater level of service and support to authors than is the case with self-publishing.

The funding package for Spines includes a $29 million Series A-1 equity round led by Zeev Ventures, with participation from Aleph, NordStar, M-Fund, LionTree, and angel investor Dan Senor. Spines is also receiving $35 million in what it calls “a non-dilutive growth financing facility” from Twelve, a credit-focused investment management firm.

The company declined to disclose its valuation after the funding.

Spines is also announcing that its new AI-powered services have helped it hit a $50 million annual revenue run rate, representing 400% year-over-year growth. The company has published more than 8,000 authors to date, accounting for some 12,000 titles, founder and CEO Yehuda Niv told Fortune. He said roughly 400 new writers sign up for Spines’ service each month.

About 15 years ago, while partway through a master’s degree in electronic engineering, Niv published a book of his own and concluded that “the publishing process is completely broken.” That bad experience motivated Niv to get into publishing himself. He bootstrapped Niv Publishing, which he says became Israel’s largest publishing house, putting out about 1,200 titles a year. Roughly six years ago, he said, he realized that AI would eventually “make every [traditional] publishing company on the planet irrelevant.”

In response, in 2021 Niv founded Spines, which describes itself as an “operating system for authors.” Writers upload a finished manuscript, and specialized agents handle editing, proofreading, formatting, cover design, metadata, ebook and print-on-demand files, and distribution to more than 100 channels, including Amazon, Barnes & Noble, and Baker & Taylor. Authors can produce an audiobook with a synthetic narrator or a clone of their own voice, and translate the book—and that audiobook—into other languages. Spines currently offers seven target languages and plans to reach 20 within six months. After publication, the platform tracks royalties and runs marketing campaigns.

Niv argues the agents can do some jobs better than the freelancers authors typically hire. Of the roughly 10,000 authors he published in Israel, he said, every one had the same problem: “The cover designer didn’t have time to read my book.” Spines’ cover agent reads the manuscript, researches which retail categories give the book its best shot, which designs work best in those categories, and designs the cover to match those metrics.

AI agents accelerate the time it takes to get from manuscript to having a book in stores, a process that in traditional publishing takes many months to more than a year, bringing it down to just weeks.

Spines’ publishing packages start at about $3,000 and run to $20,000 for a premium tier that publishes a book in three languages, each with an audiobook; most authors pick a mid-tier bundle costing $5,000 to $7,000, Niv said. Spines recently changed its royalty split so that authors keep 80% of net royalties, up from 70%. The company reports royalties monthly, rather than the twice-yearly or annual statements common in the industry, and is working toward weekly and eventually real-time reporting, Niv said.

Niv said that Spines only publishes books “100% written by humans” and that it uses software to try to weed out AI-generated manuscripts. “We are not here to replace [authors] with AI,” he said, insisting that Spines exists to “empower” human writers.

Still, some aspects of Spines’ use of AI may raise copyright issues, particularly around AI-designed book covers. U.S. courts and the Copyright Office have held that images made entirely by AI can’t be copyrighted. Niv said Spines licenses the image-generation tools it uses and passes a license on to authors. He argued that is often a broader license than what authors get from human illustrators, who usually keep the copyright and license the image only for the book cover.

Spines has roughly 350 employees, Niv said, adding that only about 50 work in R&D; most of the rest handle customer success and support, helping authors with decisions that he says software can’t make for them. “Our AI agent designed for you three amazing covers, but eventually you have to choose one,” he said. “For an author, that’s an emotional decision.” Spines’ human marketing experts are there to help.

For now Spines sells its platform directly to authors who don’t have a traditional publisher. But Niv said the company is in early talks with one of the Big Five U.S. publishers about a partnership in which Spines and its AI agents would be used to help run that publishing house’s services.

“Spines has all the ingredients to become the category leader in the next generation of publishing,” Oren Zeev, the founding partner of Zeev Ventures, said in a statement.

Niv said Spines will use the debt facility to fund growth and the equity to build out its product and expand beyond the U.S. into other English-speaking markets, including the U.K., Canada, and Australia. He said he is aiming for 200% to 300% annual growth. Most of the company’s staff work in Eastern Europe, the U.S., and Latin America, but R&D and management are based in Herzliya, Israel.
https://fortune.com/2026/11/09/publisher.summary: Hybrid Zeev Ventures is based in Herzliya, Israel, and is based on its headquarters in Herzlya. It is aiming for 200% to 300% annual growth, says founder.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/p.title: Pope draws record Buenos Aires crowd after rebuking Milei over austerity
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/p.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Pope Leo's Mass at the Monumento de los Espanoles drew more than 2.5 million people. (Reuters: Pedro Lazaro Fernandez)

Roughly 2.5 million people have attended a Mass on the streets of Buenos Aires with Pope Leo XIV.

The pontiff is conducting a tour of South America, where he previously spent decades as a missionary.

During his visit in Argentina, he appeared to criticise the economic policies of Javier Milei's government.

Buenos Aires officials said approximately 2.5 million worshippers have turned out for a vast public Mass by Pope Leo XIV, with pilgrims travelling from across Argentina and camping overnight to get a glimpse of the pontiff.

The event came as the Catholic leader gave a pointed criticism of the country's populist president, Javier Milei, rebuking his government's economic policies.

The gathering is tipped to be among the largest of Leo's 12-day Latin American tour. Crowds chanted "Ole, ole, ole, Leon, Leon" and waved yellow-and-white Vatican flags as they waited.

Some faithful travelled more than 1,000 kilometres to attend, while others kept vigil through the night along the capital's broad avenues.

As part of his South American tour, Pope Leo is making the first papal visit to Argentina since 1987. (Reuters: Martin Cossarini)

Giant screens carried images of the pope's journey through the city as folk musicians performed and pilgrims sheltered from the spring sun under umbrellas.

"It's going to be unforgettable. It's going to be one of a kind," said health worker Marta Calderon, who camped out overnight to see Leo on the second leg of his Latin American tour.

Leo said in his sermon how happy he was to see Catholics in a region that has long been a stronghold for the Church but where it has been losing ground recently to fast-growing evangelical denominations.

Earlier, the Chicago-born pope visited the Pequeno Cottolengo, a home for abandoned people with disabilities in the Buenos Aires suburb of Claypole.

"It fills my heart with joy to celebrate … with you," said the pope.

"My visit to this land of Argentina has allowed me to see on your faces the enthusiasm of your faith."

Addressing residents, staff and volunteers, Leo said disabled people were "not a burden on society" but "a blessing."

"A nation's progress is also measured by how it welcomes all people with disabilities and particular needs," he said.

His remarks touched on a sensitive issue in Argentina, where disability organisations and Church leaders have voiced concern over measures affecting assistance programs under President Javier Milei's austerity drive.

A day earlier, the pontiff urged Argentinians to safeguard democracy and called on the Milei government to not punish the poor through harsh austerity measures.

The pope appears to be critical of the policies of Argentina's President Javier Milei. (Reuters: Yara Nardi)

Mr Milei has been criticised within the country for subsidy cuts, public sector lay-offs and reducing welfare such as disability benefits.

He has also been accused of undermining Argentina's democracy through divisive rhetoric and attacks on the press.

"Efforts should be made to promote whatever creates opportunities, stimulates private initiative and ensures that economic growth also benefits those who are disadvantaged," Leo said, in a line that drew strong applause.

The total cost of the October 11 attacks could add up to tens of millions of euros nationwide, one French supermarket owner estimated

French officials suspect ⁠that Iranian state-backed hackers were behind the ⁠cyberattacks that knocked out commercial refrigerators and freezers across ⁠France last month, two people familiar with the matter said on Monday.

That would make the hacks among the most disruptive cyberattacks of the war with Iran that began in February, a conflict that has been marked by scattered incidents of alleged cyber disruption. These have included disruptions to the Los Angeles transit system in March, to US water treatment plants in July and to ships ‌bound for the United States in August.

The French foreign ministry and the Paris prosecutor’s office did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Iran’s mission to the United Nations did not return messages seeking comment. Iran routinely denies carrying out malicious cyber operations.

https://www.dw.com/en/russia-independent.title: Russia: Independent Novaya Gazeta shuts its Moscow newsroom
https://www.dw.com/en/russia-independent.text:
The investigative newspaper is closing its doors after Russian authorities labeled it a "foreign agent" and ordered it vacate its Moscow premises.

The Novaya Gazeta newspaper closed its Moscow office on Monday, saying it was not able to continue reporting amid a campaign of state pressure in Russia.

The investigative outlet, co-founded by late USSR chief Mikhail Gorbachev, had long been a thorn in the Kremlin's side. In recent years, it ran into increasing roadblocks amid its critical coverage of the Russian invasion of Ukraine.

It was branded a "foreign agent," a Soviet-era term resuscitated by President Vladimir Putin's administration, with officials ordering it to vacate its Moscow offices.

Russian banks were also forbidden from processing donations from readers and supporters. The paper had been heavily dependent on this income stream after moving wholly into online publishing, with the transition taking place shortly after the invasion of Ukraine. Russian authorities introduced new wartime censorship rules in the wake of the full-scale invasion.

2021 Nobel Peace Prize-winning founding editor Dmitry Muratov issued an appeal for free speech in wartime Russia as journalists gathered in the Novaya Gazeta offices to witness its closure.

"Those in our country who advocate for peace have been denied the right to read what they choose, as we see happening today," he said. "We are currently at a point where the section of the Russian constitution that guarantees political and civil rights has ceased to function."

Russia's government meanwhile sought to play down the significance of the closure, with Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov saying it was part of a "rotational process" in a fiercely competitive media landscape.

Novaya Gazeta was a flagship for post-Soviet democratic Russia and the era of "glasnost" or openness, also launched by Mikhail Gorbachev. The reformist Soviet leader used some of the prize fund for his 1990 Nobel Peace Prize as seed money for the publication.

The paper has built a reputation for fearless reporting, which has also put it in the crosshairs of Russia's wealthy and powerful. Six of its journalists were murdered since the paper was launched in 1993.

They included Anna Politkovskaya, who spent years investigating allegations of abuses by Russia's military during its campaigns in Chechnya. An early critic of Putin, she was found dead in her apartment bloc on the president's birthday in 2006.

Images published in Russian media on Monday showed the paper's editor-in-chief, Sergei Sokolov, taking down photographs of Polikovskaya and other reporters murdered in what's thought to be retribution for their work.

Last month, when first announcing that the paper would close, Sokolov said the outlet had "been killed." The paper was shutting down after "the Russian authorities — the Russian special services — have forced the editorial team to end its work," he said.

Muratov called for a ceasefire in Ukraine and urged foreign observers to remember the strength of dissent that endured in Russia, even if it was being pushed underground by censorship laws and other repression or intimidation.

"We canot blame the citizens themselves for this," Muratov said, "especially the wonderful, truly remarkable younger generation."

"I urge you to distinguish between the Russian authorities and the Russian people,"  he added.

Muratov also called for the release of around 4,000 people he termed political prisoners in Russia.

Novaya Gazeta's leadership has not made it entirely clear whether its closing down in Moscow marks a defeinitive end to the outlet's reporting, or whether they might perhaps seek to regroup and begin operating in some form from outisde Russia, as several other publications including DW have been forced to in recent years.

One of its journalists, Irina Vorobyova, said that the paper's spirit would survive like a "good virus" and would "continue in everyone that was part of it."

https://www.dw.com/en/india-s-demonetiza.title: India’s demonetization: 10 years on, promises remain unfulfilled
https://www.dw.com/en/india-s-demonetiza.text:
A decade after the 2016 currency ban, its impact on India's economy and the fight against black money remains contested.

On November 8, 2016, Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced in a televised address to the nation that he was withdrawing all 500- and 1,000-rupee banknotes from circulation at midnight.

The surprise move invalidated 86.9% of the value of currency in circulation in a single stroke.

Modi asked Indians to make a "grand sacrifice for cleansing our country."

He promised that the hardship would help eliminate black money, corruption, counterfeit currency and terrorist financing. The exercise was presented as a major step towards a cleaner and more transparent economy.

Millions of Indians rushed to banks to exchange their savings. Long queues formed outside banks and ATMs, with people waiting for hours, sometimes without knowing when they would get their money.

Workers missed wages, small businesses struggled to pay employees and families found it difficult to buy everyday essentials. Reports of people dying during the cash crisis added to the distress.

"I still remember my domestic help's father," businessman Prakash Patra from Jaipur city told DW. "He panicked, collapsed, and passed away right there, standing in a long queue just trying to exchange his family's life savings. It wasn't just cash that was lost in those lines. It was human lives."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

For India's most vulnerable, particularly rural women and people without bank accounts, the sudden cash shortage made savings difficult to access. Money set aside for family weddings, medical emergencies and basic survival was suddenly compromised.

Joe Athialy, executive director of the Centre for Financial Accountability, a financial watchdog, says the impact fell disproportionately on the poor and the informal economy.

"Demonetization destroyed livelihoods, disrupted small businesses and pushed millions into deeper economic insecurity. The poor and those dependent on the informal sector bore the greatest cost," Athialy told DW.

Arun Kumar, former professor of economics at Jawaharlal Nehru University and author of "The Black Economy in India," shared a similar assessment. The government wrongly assumed that illicit wealth was primarily held in cash, he said.

"And it penalized the cash-dependent informal sector while leaving the real engines of the black economy untouched," Kumar told DW.

The first major setback came in 2018, when the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) reported that 99.3% of the demonetized currency had returned to the banking system.

Only a small fraction of the withdrawn money had failed to come back, undermining the expectation that large amounts of undeclared cash would be extinguished.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

A decade later, there is little evidence that demonetization made a significant dent in black money or corruption. Economists have long pointed out that much illicit wealth in India is held in property, gold and other assets rather than cash.

Some supporters of the policy argued that forcing cash into the banking system would help formalize the economy and widen the tax base. But the extent to which these changes could be attributed to the currency withdrawal remains contested.

Lekha Chakraborty, a professor at the National Institute of Public Finance and Policy, said research after the exercise pointed to limited success in achieving its stated objectives.

She draws on studies that examined both the immediate economic shock and its longer-term effects.

"The research points to modest gains against demonetization's primary objectives, alongside temporary but real economic costs. The impact was particularly severe in the informal sector, where cash remains central to everyday transactions," Chakraborty told DW.

"The economic shock was real, even if much of it faded over time. But there is little to suggest that demonetization produced a lasting change in the way black wealth is generated or concealed."

Athialy argues that the policy was based on a flawed understanding of how illicit wealth is held in India.

"Cash is only an insignificant part of the black economy. Much of India's unaccounted wealth is held in assets such as real estate and in tax havens, not currency," he said.

He also questions the absence of accountability for the disruption and its institutional consequences.

"Nobody has been held accountable for the economic disruption or the undermining of institutions such as the RBI."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Digital payments have expanded rapidly since 2016. The Unified Payments Interface (UPI), launched in August that year, has become a major part of India's retail payment system today.

In 2025-26, UPI processed 241.6 billion transactions, worth 314.2 trillion rupees (approximately €2.95 trillion), according to the RBI.

Yet the growth of digital payments has not reduced the amount of physical currency in circulation.

RBI data show that the value of banknotes in circulation stood at 43.15 trillion rupees (about €405 billion) on October 23, 2026, compared with 17.97 trillion rupees (€169 billion) in November 2016.

The figures show that Indians are increasingly using digital platforms for everyday payments, but cash remains firmly in circulation.

Chakraborty cautions against attributing the growth of digital payments to demonetization. "Digital payments largely continued a trend that was already under way before the currency ban," she said.

A decade after the unprecedented move, the gap between the government's promises and what demonetization ultimately delivered remains central to its legacy.
https://www.dw.com/en/india-s-demonetiza.summary: India's prime minister withdrew all 500- and 1,000-rupee banknotes from circulation at midnight in November 2016. The move invalidated 86.9% of the value of currency in circulation in a single stroke. The impact fell disproportionately on the poor and the informal economy.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmg4.title: France accuses Iran of supermarket fridge hacking
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmg4.text:
France has accused Iran of being behind cyber-attacks that raised the temperatures of supermarket fridges and freezers.

Speaking at a news conference, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said the attack was carried out by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) of Iran.

He said the attack was "unprecedented in both its scale and its level of aggression", adding that the country would "implement sanctions at the European level against all those responsible for this attack."

The cyber-attack last month saw fridges and freezers in hundreds of supermarkets across France heated up, which spoilt fresh and frozen food estimated to be worth millions of euros.

Then last week, dozens of supermarkets across seven other European countries were also impacted by a cyber-attack that targeted fridges and freezers. It is not known if the instances are linked.

Iran is yet to respond to Barrot's allegations.

Separately on Monday, the Paris prosecutor said an investigation had been opened into the head of an offensive cyber unit associated with Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) as well as his two deputies.

Laure Beccuau named the unit as Shahid Kaveh, which she said had an affiliation with the electronic and cyber centre of the IRGC.

On 11 October, hackers gained control of the software that regulates the temperatures of the refrigeration units used in many of France's supermarkets.

More than 100 of Coopérative U's supermarkets were hit, as well as 180 stores from Intermarché and its Netto brand. In some stores, temperatures of the fridges reportedly rose to 50C (120F) overnight.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck79.title: Trump questions midterm elections integrity after previously accepting results
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck79.text:
US President Donald Trump has questioned the legitimacy of the midterm election results in which Republicans suffered sweeping losses - days after saying he would accept the outcome.

"Does anybody really believe that this 'Election' was honest. How could the Polls be so wrong?" Trump wrote on Truth Social on Monday.

This appeared to contradict what he told the New York Times on election night that he was "absolutely willing" to accept the results.

Democrats retook both chambers of Congress in last week's elections. State and local officials across the US said voting had been mostly problem-free.

Some key races, including Senate contests in Alaska and Mississippi, have yet to be called.

In the Truth Social post, Trump made vague claims about polling, voting "dumps", and "machines" without providing specific evidence of error or wrongdoing.

He has previously attempted to cast doubts on the integrity of elections he has lost, although he himself was not on the ballot in the midterms.

"We would have won easily if I was on the ballot," Trump told CBS News, the BBC's US partner, after it was confirmed his party had lost both the Senate and the House.

As it stands, Democrats have won 54 US Senate seats and 254 US House seats, giving them comfortable majorities in both chambers even as counting continues in some races.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck79.summary: Trump questioned the legitimacy of the midterm election results in which Republicans lost both the Senate and the House. He wrote on Truth Social on Monday that he was "absolutely willing" to accept the results. Trump has previously attempted to cast doubts on the integrity of elections he has lost.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw1l.title: Poundland unable to buy new stock as fears over collapse grow
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw1l.text:
Poundland is unable to buy new stock to fill its shelves after being blocked by its owners from accessing cash in its bank accounts.

The discount chain is on the brink of collapse with one insider describing it as "running on fumes". It has until Thursday to secure a rescue deal

About £50m has been frozen by its American owner Gordon Brothers, the BBC understands, meaning its 600 shops are running out of stock.

Pressure is building on Gordon Brothers, which bought Poundland for £1 last June, after the owner rejected a takeover bid that could have saved the thousands of jobs currently at risk. Gordon Brothers has been approached for comment.

Poundland has filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators, which protects it from its creditors until Thursday.

Access to funds was limited because of a tension between Gordon Brothers' dual role as both creditor and shareholder, a source said, but added they expected a relaxation of funds in the next two days.

Last week, Poundland boss Barry Williams told staff like-for-like sales, which exclude new store openings, were up 11.4% last week, which included Halloween, but said this was £1.5m ahead of budget.

He said the business made a profit of £18.1m in the year to September, which was a "strong recovery" from the previous year where the business made losses of £68m.

The latest annual accounts have yet to be audited.

However, Gordon Brothers has painted a different picture of the business, saying the chain remains "challenged and vulnerable to any potential downturn in future trading".

It said it had provided significant funding to support the company's ability to trade since it acquired the business.

It has also made £18m, from a combination of debt interest payments and other fees and charges.

On Wednesday, executives from Gordon Brothers will appear before the Business Select Committee with MPs probing whether they are genuinely pursuing a solvent rescue of the business, which has 11,000 employees, and whether every realistic step is being taken to protect jobs and stores.

The session is being held in private given commercially sensitive discussions are still under way with bidders.

On Thursday, the 10-day moratorium to protect Poundland from its creditors expires, but if there is a prospect of a solvent deal, the deadline could be extended.

If not, Poundland is set to collapse into administration and could be broken up.

A source familiar with the sales process said London-based Xyra Group was making "significant progress" in its last minute bid to buy Poundland and could now be the front runner.

An extension of Thursday's deadline now seems an increasingly likely scenario. But such a case would be difficult to put forward if Gordon Brothers continues to block funding.

One observer remarked "if Gordon Brothers is going in front of that committee, you don't want to be giving the message we're pulling up the drawbridge".

Even if a deal is agreed to sell the business as a whole, there is no guarantee a new owner would not reduce the number of stores, but suppliers to Poundland would prefer that outcome to hundreds of sites being sold off to other retailers.

There has been interest from the likes of Poundstretcher, Tesco and B&M in picking up stores which could mean continuing employment for many workers.

The central issue is whether a piecemeal sale would protect more jobs than a buyer willing to keep Poundland trading as a national chain.

French foreign minister vows European sanctions against Tehran over ‘unprecedented’ hacks last month

Europe live – latest updates

France has said Iran’s Revolutionary Guards were behind “unprecedented” cyber-attacks on supermarket fridges in the country last month, vowing European sanctions against Tehran.

“I can confirm that this attack was carried out by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps of the Islamic Republic of Iran,” the French foreign minister, Jean-Noël Barrot, said on Monday of the hacks on 11 and 12 October.

“This attack is unprecedented in both its scale and its level of aggression,” he said, adding, “We will implement sanctions at the European level against all those responsible for this attack.”

Iran’s mission to the United Nations did not return messages seeking comment. Iran routinely denies carrying out malicious cyber operations.

The October hacks were followed this month by a second wave of hacking ‌that hit more than 100 establishments across Europe and even affected refrigerators used by French blood banks, prompting employees to move some of the blood to other cold storage units.

The seemingly straightforward nature of the refrigerator hacks – and their repetition ​across multiple countries – prompted speculation about who might be responsible amid ongoing concerns over Russia’s suspected sabotage campaign in Europe, the war between the US and Iran and the global rise of AI-powered cyberattacks.

https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.title: Labour’s Brexit red lines ready for ‘dignified retirement’, says their co-author
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.author: Jessica Elgot Deputy political editor
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.text:
Exclusive: MP Chris Ward believes ditching pledges and forming closer ties with EU would protect it from global threats

One of the architects of Keir Stamer’s Brexit red lines has called for Andy Burnham to abandon them at the next election, saying a new relationship with the EU would protect the UK from global threats.

The call is the latest voice from a prominent figure in Starmer’s administration for a faster transition to a far closer European relationship, after the former chancellor Rachel Reeves said it was right for Burnham to consider rejoining.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

Chris Ward, one of Starmer’s closest confidants in politics and one of the ministers who worked on the EU reset, said that it was the security relationship that meant a change was now imperative.

The Labour MP for Brighton Kemptown and Peacehaven said it was now time to give a “a dignified retirement” to the red lines, which rule out rejoining the EU, the single market, the customs union and restoring freedom of movement.

Ward also suggested there was little compelling argument for rejoining the single market without full EU membership, saying he had “never understood the argument for the latter without the former”.

But he said the main reason for abandoning the red lines was that the UK “could no longer rely on the Americans” which was a major geopolitical shift that merited an entire reappraisal of Britain’s diplomatic relationships. “That question was unthinkable in 2016, but it is unavoidable in 2026,” he wrote in an article for the Guardian.

Ward, who was Starmer’s chief adviser as shadow Brexit secretary and who co-authored the red lines in Labour’s manifesto in 2024, said that they had now outlived their usefulness and should no longer be part of Labour’s future thinking.

He remains close to the former prime minister and said that the drive to renew the relationship with the EU may prove the defining political moment of this autumn.

He said the party had agreed upon the red lines in the manifesto because they were “designed precisely to close down the debate and to narrow the target that Brexit had become for Labour”.

“I still believe that strategically this was the right course for Labour, and the reset deal that – touch wood – will get over the line at next month’s UK-EU summit will demonstrate that real benefits can be delivered within those red lines, whether cheaper prices for businesses, a youth mobility scheme or the return of the Erasmus+ scheme.

“By the next general election, however, those red lines will have served their purpose. They should be given a well-earned and dignified retirement. Frankly, they no longer speak to the world as it is in 2026, let alone as it may be over the years to come.”

Ward said it was well known that rejoining the EU or single market would have economic benefits but said supporters of rejoining should make a different argument.

“Pinning the case for a new relationship on old arguments risks both the same result and missing what’s really changed,” he wrote.

“Instead, its the huge geopolitical shifts and, above all, the new security and cyber threats the UK and Europe now face day in, day out that demand we now reassess the depth and nature of relationship.”

Sign up for the Breaking News UK email to get newsletter alerts direct to your inbox

after newsletter promotion

He said Starmer had twice had to scramble alliances together – on Ukraine and on the strait of Hormuz – because “we could no longer rely on the Americans”.

“It would now be brave in the extreme to continue to pin our future security – and that of Europe – on the outcome of US elections, or the false hope that whoever is in the White House we can still bank on the US as we did in 2016, let alone 1945.”

Ward said there should be public debate on whether the UK should formally rejoin or seek a form of associate membership like Canada.

But he said the prime minister will “need to be clear as to why now is the right time to reopen the Brexit debate, what we are seeking, and why it is so important to our national interest. A re-run of the tired arguments of 2016 won’t do that. Defending red lines designed for 2020 won’t do that either. But appreciating the urgent strategic challenges of the decades to come just might.”

Burnham will attend the European Political Community summit in Dublin on Thursday, expected to be used to see Labour’s reset deal over the line and to meet many European leaders for the first time.

Burnham will also meet European leaders on the sidelines to set out his ambitions for further integration after he announced his intention to seek a closer and more permanent relationship – including potentially rejoining the bloc.

At a Brexit reset meeting on 20 November in Brussels, the UK will sign new agreements on agriculture and food, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme.

The prime minister is then expected to give a speech after the summit on options for the future relationship. Burnham has said previously an option to rejoin the single market could be offered in a Labour manifesto but fully rejoining would need a referendum.

Elon Musk and other finance moguls defend Jensen Huang after he admitted to the affair in an email to employees

Nvidia’s board needs to do some succession planning – sharpish

Donald Trump, Elon Musk and prominent finance moguls have expressed their support for embattled Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, as the head of the world’s most valuable chip company faces an internal investigation over a romantic relationship with an alleged Chinese spy.

“I have not ​spoken to him about it,” Trump told reporters on Sunday. “I just know he’s a fine person, but you never know what is going on. I’m sure, I hope everything’s fine. He’s done such an incredible job”.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

“I think he’s an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it,” Trump later added, saying he believed that Huang would and should stay on as CEO.

Huang’s defenders framed his affair as a personal lapse in judgment rather than evidence of treachery against the United States, which has imposed strict limits on what chips Nvidia can sell to China.

Huang, who has been married to his wife, Lori, since 1985, admitted in an email to employees on Sunday that he had an affair and that he would cooperate with an internal investigation. Nvidia’s board of directors put out a statement the same day that the company was launching a probe regarding reports that Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort.

The chip mogul is alleged to have had a relationship with Alice Huang, a businesswoman that US intelligence services suspect of spying for the Chinese government, according to The New York Times. Trump was reportedly briefed on the relationship last year, the Times reported, but took no action. Alice Huang and Jensen Huang are unrelated, with the latter being one of the world’s richest men and CEO of Nvidia, worth more than $4tn, for the past 33 years.

US intelligence agencies believe Alice Huang, acting on behalf of Beijing, pushed Jensen Huang to lobby Trump for relaxed export controls on Nvidia’s sales in China, which he has done multiple times publicly. Nvidia said in a statement that neither trade secrets nor US national security had been compromised.

The affair and alleged intelligence operation involving Huang could have far reaching implications for Nvidia and the tech industry, which are already enduring a period of high market volatility. Huang’s leadership of Nvidia, which is deeply financially intertwined with other leading tech companies like OpenAI, has long been viewed as crucial to the company’s success and stability.

As news of the scandal broke over the weekend, Musk and prominent investors shared their support of Huang. Musk posted “I agree” in response to prominent venture capitalist Shaun Maguire’s defense of Huang. Maguire argued the Nvidia CEO “did something incredibly dumb” but that he is “one of the greatest entrepreneurs of this generation”.

“Two mistakes don’t make a right, and I believe Jensen is irreplaceable for America’s AI leadership,” Maguire posted. He stated the Nvidia CEO “did something incredibly dumb” but that he is “one of the greatest entrepreneurs of this generation”.

“Let’s also not nuke our AI industry because China ran a successful intel op,” Maguire added in a separate post.

Bill Ackman, the US hedge fund manager and pro-Trump billionaire, meanwhile, suggested that Huang is “human” and deserves public support over the affair.

“He is an incredible human. Even incredible humans make mistakes,” Ackman posted. “He takes full responsibility as he should. We should all support him and his family. Onward.”

Ackman followed up with another post later clarifying that he wasn’t suggesting Huang “gets a free pass” but that he was “hoping for a simple affair, not a risk to our national security”.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Elon Musk and the tech bros banked on Trump and lost. Humbled, humiliated: what will they do next? | Jonathan Liew
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Jonathan Liew
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Democrats won seats on anti-datacentre tickets and Musk wasted nearly half a billion dollars. Big tech may be losing its grip, but it won’t go quietly

P
hotos That Precede Unfortunate Events: a couple of months back, Donald Trump hosted some of the world’s most powerful tech executives at the White House for a “Super Intelligence luncheon”, which by coincidence is also how my mum described her tuna sandwiches in a forlorn attempt to get me to eat them. Sitting either side of the president were Elon Musk, making a rare offline appearance in daylight hours, and Jensen Huang, the Nvidia chief executive carving out a precious slot in what we now know was an extremely busy schedule.

Over a delicious meal of microchips and rare-earth metals, the billionaires sketched out a utopian future of an AI industry unencumbered by regulation or safeguards, powered by their heroic strongman leader, a political genius effortlessly able to impose his will upon an entire nation. And perhaps it should have been apparent even at the time that these (mostly) men were putting their faith in a guy who had recently been defeated by pond algae. But as the drinks and the good times flowed, it was still possible to believe that the sun would never set on the thousand-year American superintelligence empire.

And so, while we’re all learning lessons from the resounding defeat delivered to Trumpism last week, might we start with a modest and sober reassessment of the Silicon Valley oligarch class? For years, we have been told that these are some of humanity’s greatest seers and visionaries, the Leonardos and Einsteins of the 21st century, the people best placed to plot a course for our species, despite for the most part not being able to smile without looking as though they were undergoing a juice enema.

As it turned out, this small band of brilliant clairvoyants somehow failed to anticipate the possibility that the deeply unpopular man they were clasping in a tender embrace would be subjected to an absolute democracy-mogging in just a few weeks, throwing their altruistic wet dreams into chaos. After all, last week’s midterms were not simply a rebuke to one man or one party, but to an entire ideology. Across the US, voters took their revenge not just on big tech, but on the politicians who had enabled it.

In Texas, Gina Hinojosa beat the Republican incumbent, Greg Abbott, by promising an immediate moratorium on datacentre development, and despite being outspent almost eight to one, in large part by big tech donors desperate to preserve their tax breaks. In Ohio, the Democratic challenger Sherrod Brown described his opponent, Jon Husted, as “the face of datacentres”, a visually horrifying concept. In total, 46 of the 47 ballot measures relating to datacentres were defeated. By Thursday morning, the markets had responded with a devastating sell-off of tech stocks, the repercussions of which are still shaking out as you read this.

Should we read anything into the fact that the biggest progressive landslide in 52 years, catalysed by a concerted mobilisation of Black, Latino and young voters, was sufficient to send the financial markets into existential panic? Anyone able to join the dots for us there? Is it relevant that the São Paulo stock exchange plunged about 14% after Lula da Silva’s shock election victory in Brazil last month? Just what is it about the popular repudiation of hard-right autocrats that appears to spook the pillars of capitalism so much?

For the time being, big tech does not appear to be as politically polarising in Britain as it is in the US. This is largely because much of the recent acceleration has occurred under a Labour administration, in particular under the late lamented Keir Starmer, a prime minister who in retrospect may actually have been a semi-sentient chatbot all along. “We will test and understand AI before we regulate it,” Starmer once said, which he appears to have done by plugging it directly into his own mouth for two years. But this is an issue that will continue to rise in democratic salience, in part because it relies on the undemocratic manufacture of consent, an inexorable march deliberately designed to circumvent scrutiny.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Take the UK government’s AI growth zones, designed to supercharge datacentre development by taking decisions on nationally significant infrastructure projects (NSIP) away from local councils. A recent report by Spotlight on Corruption found that over two years, ministers met only two community groups and no environmental organisations while developing the policy, while at the same time ministers and senior civil servants were hired to 38 roles at AI companies. Naturally, you are likely to hear very little opposition to any of this, either from the billionaire-owned press or the official opposition; indeed, Kemi Badenoch is perhaps the only major party leader you can imagine typing “what do I think of AI” into an AI prompt.

You will occasionally hear the assumption, made on both sides of the Atlantic and often on the flimsiest of evidence, that voters are increasingly fed up with democracy. But what if we’re getting this the wrong way round? What if, in fact, it is those who are supposed to be upholding democracy – the politicians and media and captains of industry, all slowly stewing in X-brained algorithmic talking points – who are beginning to tire of it? While Musk spends enormous chunks of his fortune trying (and failing) to tip the electoral scales in favour of the hard right, Reform UK rakes in £72m in donations from two cryptocurrency billionaires. Bonus question: do we think the brave men and women out there on the tech frontier will respond to democratic setbacks by demanding more democratic accountability, or less?

And, of course, in these febrile and fragile times you have to take your wins wherever you get them. But as any ChatGPT user will tell you, making bold claims on the basis of a bare minimum of data is always an exercise fraught with risk. Saying no once will never be enough. In a note to investors last week, Goldman Sachs wrote: “We expect the datacentre issue to somewhat fade in importance and any moratoria on datacentre development to be short-lived.” You can decide for yourself what it means by that.

Jonathan Liew is a Guardian columnist

https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.author: Andrew Gregory Health editor
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.text:
Some patients with autoimmune condition, taking part in trial, have been able to return to work and resume hobbies

Doctors have made a potentially significant breakthrough in the hunt for a treatment for stiff person syndrome, the autoimmune condition which affects the singer Céline Dion.

Stiff person syndrome (SPS) is a rare disease that attacks the central nervous system and can cause devastating rigidity throughout the body and painful muscle spasms. Despite decades of research, there is no cure.

Now a team of neurologists in the US trialling a novel form of immunotherapy have reported “exciting” and “very encouraging” results: the treatment has prompted dramatic improvements in people living with SPS.

Patients who previously needed help with basic daily tasks and struggled to walk have regained their ability to take part in everyday life, with some even returning to work and resuming hobbies, according to doctors at the Mayo Clinic.

The novel treatment, CAR-T cell therapy, is already used to treat cancer, and reprogrammes a patient’s immune cells to help fight disease. During the study, SPS patients’ own T cells, a type of immune cell, were extracted and engineered to wipe out disease-causing cells.

Neurologists said the results, published in medical journal Jama Neurology, were particularly exciting because patients had been able to return to activities they feared they would never be able to return to.

Dr Anastasia Zekeridou, a neurologist and researcher at Mayo Clinic in Rochester, said: “What was most striking was the degree of improvement we saw in some patients.

“With existing treatments, we may be able to improve symptoms, but we very rarely see patients return to their previous level of function. These early results are very encouraging, and the key question now is whether those improvements will be sustained over time.”

Jonathan Walden, one of the patients in the trial, had reached the point where walking and basic daily tasks required help from his family. But after CAR-T, he has returned to work.

“I can go to work every single day. I can do everything I did before. I go hunting; I can go fishing,” he said. “I have not had one episode since receiving treatment.”

Shari St Germain, another patient, had been suffering severe leg cramps and difficulty walking, and later even muscle rigidity and falls. But following CAR-T, she experienced major improvements. Every day feels “better and better”, she said.

“After the treatment, I got up one day and I’m like ‘I’m feeling really good’, and I went to walk on the treadmill,” she said. “My husband comes running in because I’m crying and he’s like ‘Are you OK?’ And I’m like ‘I just walked for seven minutes on the treadmill’.”

Dr Sean Pittock, chair of the department of neurology at Mayo Clinic, said: “CAR-T therapy has already transformed the treatment of some cancers, and we are now beginning to see its potential in autoimmune neurologic diseases.

“The results in stiff person syndrome offer tremendous hope, not only for people living with this disease but potentially for patients with other immune-mediated neurologic conditions where effective treatment options remain limited.

“There is still much we need to learn, but this opens an exciting new avenue for the field.”

Dion announced she had been diagnosed with SPS in December 2022. In an Instagram video, she told fans the condition had affected “every aspect of my daily life”, including harming her voice.

Yasmin Sheikh, head of policy and public affairs at Anthony Nolan, a blood cancer charity not involved with the trial, said: “This research is an exciting development, providing more evidence that CAR-T cell therapies could have applications beyond blood cancer and offer new hope to people living with other conditions, including SPS.”
