https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.title: Can you solve it? The multi-choice maths quiz taking over the world
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.author: Alex Bellos
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.text:
This Kangaroo is jumping!

There is nothing in education quite like the Kangaroo. A multiple-choice maths challenge sat by more than seven million children in around 120 countries, from Afghanistan to Zimbabwe, it is arguably the world’s most widely-taken primary and secondary school test.

Today’s puzzle is taken from the 2024 Kangaroo. But before we get there, some background.

The first Kangaroo was held in France in 1991. It was inspired by an Australian maths challenge that has been running since the 1970s, hence the name. Other European countries soon came on board and, since around 2000, so did the rest of the world. The country with highest participation is Brazil (1.8 million pupils), followed by Germany (900,000), France and Poland (both 300,000).

The purpose of the Kangaroo is to promote the enjoyment of mathematics. The questions vary in style every year, and are designed to test problem-solving skills and clear thinking.

“We want to share our passion for the beauty of mathematics with everyone,” said Meike Akveld, a Swiss mathematician who is president of the Association Kangourou Sans Frontières (AKSF). “I like to think of the Kangaroo as the sports day of mathematics. It is for everyone, at all levels.”

The Kangaroo is divided into six age levels: lower and upper primary; lower, middle and upper secondary; and sixth form. The questions are set by the AKSF and distributed by national associations, who decide how many questions to use for each level and how long pupils are allowed. Usually, the papers are sat on the third Thursday in March, and last around an hour.

Today’s problem was the final question in the 2024 sixth form paper, making it the hardest question that year. Not many children would be expected to get it right. But it is certainly within the capabilities of a top GCSE student.

A four digit number abcd satisfies the equation abcd = aa + bb + cc + dd.

[Note: abcd means that the first digit is a, the second is b, the third is c and the fourth is d. It does not mean a x b x c x d. The numbers a, b, c and d do not have to be different.]

As an extra, what are b, c and d?

I’ll be back at 5pm UK with the solution.

PLEASE NO SPOILERS. Please discuss marsupials, mass-participation mathematics and multiple choice.

The Kangaroo currently has a relatively small reach in the UK, with only about 21,000 Brits taking part this year, about the same numbers as in Mexico and Serbia. One explanation for this low number is that we already have a well-established system of national mathematical challenges, run by the UK Mathematics Trust (UKMT). The UKMT now incorpoates three levels of Kangaroo within its ecosystem, however, and participation is likely to grow.

The movement is also being helped by the Kangaroo Maths Trust, a UK-based charity established earlier this year with the financial support of algorithmic trading fund XTX Markets.

Indeed, the Kangaroos are bounding out in all directions. This year the AKSF launched the first Kangaroo Open, for adults, and next year will run a Kangaroo for children under 6. You’re never too young for multi-choice maths!

For more information about entering the Kangaroo in the UK, contact the UKMT. For all other countries, find your national Kangaroo association here.

You can read previous Kangaroos in the World Olympiads Bank, an archive of almost 100,000 problems from international competitions in maths, physics, chemistry, biology informatics and astronomy. In the Kangaroo section, the levels are Pre-Ecolier (lower primary), Ecolier (upper primary), Benjamin (lower secondary), Cadet (middle secondary), Junior (upper secondary), Student (sixth form). The archive was created by Sokratis Romanidis.

I’ve been setting a puzzle here on alternate Mondays since 2015. I’m always on the look-out for great puzzles. If you would like to suggest one, email me.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: I wrote Labour’s Brexit red lines. This is why it’s time to scrap them | Chris Ward
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Chris Ward
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
The world has moved on since 2020 – in uncertain times, closer ties to Europe are the best way to peace and security

Chris Ward is Labour MP for Brighton Kemptown and Peacehaven

I
f offering the public some “breathing space” in the cost of living crisis was the mantra of last month’s budget, the political space it created to revisit our relationship with the European Union may prove more defining.

I’ve spent what feels like much of the past decade immersed in the Brexit debate – first as an adviser, then helping to craft the red lines that shaped Labour’s 2024 manifesto, and latterly as a Cabinet Office minister working on the EU-reset. In truth, the discussions we have had as a country and within my party on this issue have not really moved on since the moment we left on 31 January 2020.

There’s good reason for this. The red lines we drew up in the aftermath of the Labour leadership contest in 2020 – ruling out rejoining the EU, the single market, the customs union or restoring freedom of movement – were designed precisely to close down the debate and to narrow the target that Brexit had become for Labour. They enabled us to fight the 2024 election on a manifesto that was both pro-EU, by advocating a closer relationship, but also clearly stopping short of anything that looked like rejoining the bloc or relitigating the 2016 referendum. Schrödinger’s Brexit.

I still believe that strategically this was the right course for Labour, and the reset deal that – touch wood – will get over the line at this month’s UK-EU summit will demonstrate that real benefits can be delivered within those red lines, whether cheaper prices for businesses, a youth mobility scheme or the return of the Erasmus+ scheme.

By the next general election, however, those red lines will have served their purpose. They should be given a well-earned and dignified retirement. Frankly, they no longer speak to the world as it is in 2026, let alone as it may be over the years to come.

The major reason for this is not, in my view, an economic one. The economic case for rejoining either the EU or the single market (I personally have never understood the argument for the latter without the former) is basically the same as it was in 2016: that it will boost GDP, raise living standards, go some way to heal our public finances, and open access for British businesses to a market of 500 million people. All that comes, of course, with accepting freedom of movement and the other rules of the club. So far, so 2016. But pinning the case for a new relationship on old arguments risks both the same result and missing what has really changed.

Instead, it’s the huge geopolitical shifts and, above all, the new security and cyber threats the UK and Europe now face day in, day out, that demand we now reassess the depth and nature of that relationship. We should be in no doubt that – whether from Russia, China, Iran or elsewhere – these are of a different order and immediacy to in 2016. At the same time, the reliability of the US as our primary security partner can no longer be taken for granted. Donald Trump’s second term – which saw a British prime minister forced to twice scramble “coalitions of the willing” precisely because we could no longer rely on the Americans – should be seen as confirmation of this, not an aberration. It would now be brave in the extreme to continue to pin our future security – and that of Europe – on the outcome of US elections, or the false hope that, whoever is in the White House, we can still bank on the US as we did in 2016, let alone 1945.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

And so it is this question – how to ensure peace and prosperity in a time of growing global threats and US retrenchment – that should drive our foreign policy, our geostrategic choices and our domestic priorities for the years to come. That question was unthinkable in 2016, but it is unavoidable in 2026. It, of course, demands much greater urgency in increasing domestic defence spending, but it should also drive our future discussions with the EU.

The minimum we should now seek with the EU is a deep and enduring defence and trade partnership – pooling and rebuilding our defence and security might, and aligning our economic interests where possible.

Our primary goal should be to ensure that we are, together, better able to protect ourselves, and less dependent on a volatile US. Mark Carney’s push by Canada for “associate membership” and “the deepest possible partnership short of accession” with the EU stems from precisely this realisation. The very least Britain should now seek is a future relationship with the EU that is as ambitious.

Whether, ultimately, that deep security and economic partnership can only be achieved through formally rejoining the EU or through an associate deal should, of course, be part of the debate that has now been opened. But to fully capitalise on the political space we now have, we need to be clear as to why now is the right time to reopen the Brexit debate, what we are seeking, and why it is so important to our national interest. A re-run of the tired arguments of 2016 won’t do that. Defending red lines designed for 2020 won’t do that either. But appreciating the urgent strategic challenges of the decades to come just might.

Chris Ward is Labour MP for Brighton Kemptown and Peacehaven

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: Hometown glory? Norwegian library unveils £100k history book donated by Erling Haaland
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Miranda Bryant Nordic correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
Rare 16th-century edition of Viking royal sagas given to Bryne by Manchester City footballer and his father

At his local library in the southern Norwegian town of Bryne, the father of superstar striker Erling Haaland made a confession. “Sometimes my son and I are a little impulsive,” Alf Inge Haaland, known as Alfie, told the assembled crowd on Monday morning.

The spontaneous act in question was the purchase of the only surviving privately owned edition of a 1594 book, Snorre Sturlasons Kongesagaer (Snorre Sturlason’s Royal Sagas). The auction purchase for 1.3m Norwegian kroner (£103,000) was Norway’s most expensive ever book sale.

The Haalands then shocked and delighted their local librarian last December with the information that they planned to donate the exceptionally rare book to them so that it could go on permanent display in their home town.

The book was on Monday unveiled to an audience of excited schoolchildren at the Time library in Bryne. Many of the children are in the midst of a reading frenzy in the hope of winning a competition to see Haaland and his teammates play a match at the national stadium in Oslo.

“It’s a cool book with a lot of history,” the Manchester City and Norway striker’s father told the children. He also led a rendition of the Norwegian football team’s trademark Viking row with a drum.

His son, who could not be there in person, was shown in a video interview in which he talked about his interest in Vikings from a young age. Despite not being a big reader, he said that he did read a lot to his one-year-old son.

Snorri’s royal sagas chronicle the history of the Old Norse Viking and medieval kings of Norway, regarded by many Norwegians as a key document of national identity. The stories, about kings, queens, farmers and warriors, were first told orally and then written down by the Icelander Snorri Sturlason in the mid-13th century.

The book is the first printed edition of the sagas in Danish-Norwegian – Norway was under Danish rule between 1536 and 1814 – translated from the original Old Norse. At the time, there were no printing presses in Norway, so the edition was printed in Copenhagen and based on the translation of Mattis Størssøn.

The national librarian of Norway, Åse Wetås, said there were no known copies of the book like it. “It is a very special book for everybody in Norway.”

While they have three other copies at the National Library of Norway, none of them are complete. “This is a complete and very beautiful copy of this book from 1594,” she said. “There are some other copies, a few, but we don’t know any of them to be in this good condition. So it is a gem really. A very special gem.”

The book will be on public view in a display case at the library in Bryne and a digitised version of the full text is also available with explanatory notes.

Wetås said the gift was unlike anything she had ever come across and was especially important at a time when reading, writing and democracy were in crisis. “I think that’s the most important and long-lasting part of this: promoting reading, knowing your own history, promoting reliable sources.”

Haaland mania hit fever pitch in Bryne over the summer, when the 26-year-old Norwegian, who was born in Leeds where his father played for Leeds United, led his team to the World Cup quarter-finals. Their record-breaking run inspired visitors from across Norway and the world to visit the town in which he grew up and trained. As well as providing Bryne with yet another Haaland tourist attraction, the gift of the Royal Sagas book has further deepened his relationship with his home town.

Andreas Vollsund, the town’s mayor and Haaland’s former schoolteacher, said Haaland had always been a star in Bryne, but this latest move with the book and reading competition was “next level”. “We now see how good a person Erling is, to do this for his home town. He doesn’t need to do this, he wants to do this.”

Anne Tjørhom Frick, the library director at Time, said she was elated to have the book in Bryne. “It is quite surreal really that someone from a municipality of 20,000 can make such an impact on people worldwide, but also that he remembers where he came from,” she said. “We have had people come here all summer saying: ‘Where is the book?’ But now it is finally here.”

The Haalands’ reading competition, which will measure time spent reading through November and January, had inspired avid participation by the local schoolchildren, she said. On Tuesdays, when school closes at 1pm, she said pupils arrived 15 minutes later to start reading and did not leave until closing time at 6pm. Many of them, she said, “read in almost complete silence, only getting up to go to the bathroom or pick a book”.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.title: France accuses Iran of cyberattack on supermarket fridges
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.text:
France has opened an investigation and accused Iran of being behind recent cyberattacks targeting refrigeration units in supermarkets.

French authorities said on Monday that it is probing a cyber unit affiliated with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps over the attacks, which caused fires and food waste.

Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said that the Iranian ambassador had been summoned and that sanctions would be brought against Iran at a “European level”.

The Paris prosecutor’s ⁠office said ⁠it has requested international arrest warrants against ⁠the leader ⁠of Shahid Kaveh, ⁠an offensive cyber unit affiliated with the Revolutionary ‌Guards, and his two ‌deputies.

“I can confirm that this attack was carried out by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps of the Islamic Republic of Iran,” Barrot said of the cyberattacks on French supermarkets that occurred October 11 and 12.

“This attack is unprecedented in both its scale and its level of aggression,” he said. “We will implement sanctions at the European level against all those responsible for this attack.”

Authorities say hackers gained internet access to the refrigeration systems and remotely cranked up temperatures to 50C during the night when shops were closed.

Millions of euros worth of food was spoiled, according to retailers. In some cases, the raised temperatures sparked fires or melted equipment.

French supermarket groups E-Leclerc, Intermarche, Carrefour, Monoprix and Cooperative U were all hit.

At least 300 of Intermarche’s stores and its Netto brand were affected. Cooperative U said more than 100 of its supermarkets were targeted, while Carrefour said 80 supermarkets were affected and Monoprix reported that about 5 percent of its roughly 490 stores were hit.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.title: Israel’s Shin Bet finds no evidence of foreign election meddling: Report
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.text:
Israel’s Shin Bet has failed to find evidence of foreign interference in last month’s elections, despite claims from the domestic security agency’s chief, David Zini, and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the newspaper Haaretz has reported.

Two senior Israeli law enforcement officials said that the investigation, which is still ongoing, has found no evidence that several hundred thousand shekels had been transferred from the Palestinian Authority (PA) to Arab-led parties in Israel, Haaretz reported on Monday.

There were no transfers from Qatar or any other Arab country being investigated. That’s despite allegations from Netanyahu’s party, Likud, that money had been transferred to boost turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel, without the party providing any tangible evidence to support its claims.

The allegations continue a long-running anti-Qatar campaign in Israel that predates the election. Haaretz has previously reported that a secret campaign involving Israeli influence expets and political advisers targeted Qatar in the weeks after the Hamas-led October 7, 2023 attacks.

Qatar has denied all the allegations of interference, and called them unsubstantiated.

The latest claims from Zini and Netanyahu intensified in the wake of the strong electoral performance by the parties, led by Palestinian citizens of Israel, in the October 27 elections. Their 19 seats, confirmed by Israel’s election authorities, mean that Jewish parties opposed to Netanyahu have enough seats in parliament to force the prime minister out, if they are willing to work with the Arab-led parties.

Israeli President Isaac Herzog has tasked opposition politician Gadi Eisenkot with making the first attempt to form a government, possibly spelling the end of Netanyahu’s time as prime minister.

“[It is] certainly not a security matter, and it is highly doubtful that it is even a criminal one,” one of the officials quoted by Haaretz said.

“All there is is intelligence information without any real substantiation,” another quote attributed to one of the officials said.

Dozens of people have been questioned, but no evidence has so far been found of money being transferred. Haaretz also found that major fuel companies in Israel found no unusual activity involving fuel cards, undermining the allegation that Arab voters had been bribed with fuel cards in exchange for their votes.

Zini, who was selected by Netanyahu to lead Shin Bet last year and is regarded as an ally of the Israeli leader, has sought to investigate several leading politicians who are Palestinian citizens of Israel.

Netanyahu also questioned why Ahmad Tibi, a leading Arab politician in Israel, visited Qatar a few days ahead of the election.

Tibi explained that his trip to Doha was to appear on Al Jazeera.

Qatar has denied the unsubstantiated allegations of interference or funding of any activities aimed at influencing the Israeli election results.

“We reject the accusations made by certain Israeli politicians and their contacts in the media, who have launched yet another disinformation campaign aiming to drag Qatar into Israeli political disputes following this week’s elections,” Qatar’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesman Majed al-Ansari said in a social media post on October 29.

Israel’s attorney general Gali Baharav-Miara said on Sunday that she had seen no evidence from the investigation of anything that would have influenced the election results “or substantiate a claim of influence that could lead to a change in the election results”.

Israeli police and Shin Bet are expected to submit their assessments to Baharav-Miara in the next few days, the report said.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.summary: Israel's Shin Bet has failed to find evidence of foreign interference in last month's elections. No evidence of money being transferred from Palestinian Authority to Arab-led parties in Israel, Haaretz reports. Qatar has denied all the allegations of interference, and called them unsubstantiated.

https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/09/uber-l.title: Uber launches parking service following SpotHero acquisition, with an eye on robotaxis
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/09/uber-l.author: Kirsten Korosec
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/09/uber-l.text:
Uber on Monday said it is launching a new service that lets customers reserve and pay for parking in major U.S. cities, about nine months after the ride-hailing company acquired parking app SpotHero.

The acquisition, announced back in February, gives Uber access to a network of 13,000 garages, lots and valet services across more than 400 cities, the company said. And while Uber’s initial plans will focus on human drivers, the company also plans to leverage these parking spots to help the dozens of autonomous vehicle companies it has partnered with.

Uber said the parking spots could be used as staging and waiting locations for autonomous vehicles to help reduce congestion and deadheading, which refers to the miles a vehicle travels without a paying passenger or cargo on board.

For now, the company plans to focus on commuters driving their own vehicles. Uber said it will initially launch in 15 U.S. cities, including Atlanta, Austin, Boston, Chicago, Dallas, Denver, Los Angeles, Miami, Nashville, New York City, Philadelphia, San Diego, San Francisco, Seattle and Washington, DC.

Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi indicated earlier this month that the company wants the app to be more relevant to commuters.

“Commute is one of our largest categories,” he said during Uber’s third-quarter earnings call. “And to be able to offer commuters an Uber to work, a pass to avoid surge, and parking if they want it when they want to drive is a great example of us building out our inventory of services to the commuter who is a top customer for us.”

The parking service is the latest in a series of efforts at Uber to build an ecosystem of products that keep customers engaged with its app for everything from hailing a ride and ordering food and groceries, to packing delivery, renting cars, booking hotels, and connecting users with public transit and robotaxis.

Uber’s membership program, called Uber One, is a key part of that strategy. Uber One attracts subscribers by offering rewards and credits, perks that have helped the program grow to more than 55 million members as of September 30. For instance, Uber is offering members a chance to earn 10% back in credits on eligible parking reservations. Those credits can later be used for rides and Uber Eats orders.

Uber Parking can be accessed directly on the app’s homescreen. Users can enter their destination, select the date and time they need parking, and then review options on an interactive map. Users can filter the results to find self-parking, valet, garages, or surface lots. All pricing is shown upfront.

Once a user has found a parking spot, they can book after entering details about their vehicle, and use the payment method in their Uber wallet. Once they arrive at the parking spot, users will either scan a unique QR code or gain entry through license plate recognition. Uber said users will be able to cancel their bookings for free until the start time.
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/09/uber-l.summary: Uber says it is launching a new service that lets customers reserve and pay for parking in major U.S. cities. The service is the latest in a series of efforts at Uber to build an ecosystem of products that keep customers engaged with its app.

https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/09/anthro.title: Anthropic joins AI’s natural gas frenzy, buys $3.4B worth of turbines
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/09/anthro.author: Tim De Chant
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/09/anthro.text:
AI’s power crunch has become so acute that Anthropic, a company that has generally avoided buying physical infrastructure, is spending $3.4 billion on natural gas turbines.

The AI company, which is planning to go public this year, is buying Caterpillar generators that equipment supplier OnePWR had originally ordered, according to a Financial Times report. The generators are capable of producing up to 1.7 gigawatts of electricity.

Historically, Anthropic has preferred to rent rather than buy. The company disclosed in its S-1 filing in May that it is paying SpaceX subsidiary xAI $1.25 billion per month through May 2029 to use xAI’s computing power.

“We expect to enter into additional similar services contracts,” Anthropic stated in the filing, meaning more deals to rent computing power.

But as demand for compute ramps up, the market for power has also grown increasingly uncertain, which may have forced its hand. The backlog for natural gas turbines stretches into the early 2030s, and queues to connect to the electrical grid can be just as long.

Anthropic’s purchase looks like a last resort.

According to the report, OnePWR ordered the turbines a couple years ago, but couldn’t find financing to complete the purchase. Anthropic had planned to buy them from OnePWR but instead went directly to Caterpillar, the manufacturer.

It’s not clear why OnePWR was unable to secure financing despite Anthropic’s apparent interest as a customer. Whatever the case, Anthropic likely wanted to keep the generating capacity to itself rather than give a competitor an opportunity to snap it up.

AI companies have been ramping up their purchases of natural gas equipment and supplies in recent years. Google, Amazon, Microsoft, and Meta have all announced plans to build massive natural gas power plants to power their data centers on site, rather than drawing from the public grid.

The binge has given a second wind to fracking, the drilling method used to extract natural gas from underground rock. And if the buildout proceeds as planned, U.S. data centers alone could consume more natural gas than Germany and Japan combined by 2035. The reliance on natural gas also exposes hyperscalers to price fluctuations. One analyst expects that prices could more than triple by the end of the decade in some markets. If that happens, Anthropic might have a serious case of buyer’s remorse.
https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/09/anthro.summary: AI company Anthropic is spending $3.4 billion on natural gas turbines. The company is paying SpaceX subsidiary xAI $1.25 billion per month through May 2029 to use xAI’s computing power.

https://www.theverge.com/transportation/.author: Andrew J. Hawkins
https://www.theverge.com/transportation/.text:
Powered by its SpotHero acquisition, Uber’s new parking reservation tool is a play for commuter loyalty — and a staging ground for its robotaxi future.

Powered by its SpotHero acquisition, Uber’s new parking reservation tool is a play for commuter loyalty — and a staging ground for its robotaxi future.

Uber announced the launch of Uber Parking, a native in-app reservation feature that allows drivers to find, book, and pay for garage and lot spaces ahead of time. The new feature is a result of Uber’s recent acquisition of SpotHero, integrating a network of over 13,000 facilities across more than 400 cities into the company’s platform.

The new feature works by tapping the new “Parking” icon in the Uber app to view an interactive map with upfront prices and arrival times. You can filter spots by self-park or valet, outdoor lot or garage, and whether staff are on-site. The app will prompt you to enter your vehicle details and license plate, after which can enter certain lots using a QR code on your phone or through an automatic license plate scan. If your plans change, you can extend your time directly in the app or cancel for free right up until your reservation starts.

Uber One subscribers can earn 10 percent back on parking reservations as account credits within 24 hours. These credits can then be spent on rides or Uber Eats deliveries. Uber says that its subscription service has grown to more than 55 million members across 47 countries as of late 2026.

Uber Parking is launching in 15 initial markets, including Chicago, NYC, Boston, San Francisco, Los Angeles, Washington D.C., Atlanta, Austin, Dallas, Denver, Miami, Nashville, Philadelphia, San Diego, and Seattle — eventually rolling out to SpotHero’s existing 400-city footprint.

The move also ties directly into Uber’s wider bet on robotaxis, working with over 30 autonomous vehicle partners across multiple cities. In the long run, these 13,000-plus parking facilities won’t just hold commuter cars — Uber plans to turn them into urban holding pens and waiting areas for driverless robotaxis.

Stashing autonomous fleets off the street when demand dips helps keep empty cars from aimlessly circling city blocks, cutting down on traffic, emissions, and wear on the vehicles, Uber says. Ultimately, it shows that the company is thinking bigger than just ride-hailing and delivery — it wants to control the city’s physical roads and parking spaces, regardless of whether the person traveling is driving their own car, riding in the backseat, or letting a computer take the wheel.

By getting into parking, Uber is also tacitly admitting that its earlier mission to end personal car ownership and driver’s licenses didn’t succeed. But there is a loyalty-retaining strategy at play here, too, with Uber intent on keeping its customers operating within in its own platform ecosystem, whether they’re hailing a ride or driving their own car.

https://www.technologyreview.com/2026/11.title: Nancy Pelosi’s replacement is ready to regulate AI
https://www.technologyreview.com/2026/11.author: Grace Huckins
https://www.technologyreview.com/2026/11.text:
Scott Wiener has made AI regulation a cornerstone of his political career. Now he’s headed to Congress.

As a California state senator, Scott Wiener authored legislation aimed at curbing the risks of advanced AI. Now, after winning a tight congressional race for former Speaker of the House Nancy Pelosi’s open San Francisco seat, he could play a key role in setting federal AI policy.

I spoke with Wiener on Friday, only a few hours after he had been declared the victor. But he was already thinking about AI risk. The previous day, the AI nonprofit METR had released a report that had been widely interpreted as evidence that Anthropic had achieved recursive self-improvement, a phenomenon in which AI meaningfully contributes to its own advancement and AI progress potentially spins out of control.

“It’s very concerning,” Wiener said, citing the report as evidence that we are quickly running out of time to regulate AI. “It was my hope that Congress would take decisive action before [the end of] this year,” he said. “That does not appear to be happening.”

Wiener has been increasingly focused on AI in recent years, and he’s made many of the AI safety movement’s concerns his own: During our 20-minute conversation, he used the phrase “recursive self-improvement” half a dozen times, for example.“We need to slow this down,” he says. “Because it’s moving very quickly, and we could sleepwalk into a disaster.”

Wiener has already had real influence on AI policy. SB 1047, a bill that he authored in 2024, was set to become the first real piece of frontier AI legislation in the country before it was vetoed by California governor Gavin Newsom; he then sponsored SB 53, a lighter-touch bill that Newsom signed. Both bills have inspired proposed federal legislation.

Wiener’s congressional campaign received over $3 million from Public First Action, a nonprofit in favor of AI regulation that receives substantial funding from Anthropic. That contribution led opponents to criticize him for being too close to the AI industry, but Wiener says that couldn’t be further from the truth.

“Public First supported me because I was the first lawmaker in the country to introduce AI regulation and the first to pass it and get it implemented,” he wrote in a message after our interview. “The attacks on me for [Public First’s] support were shockingly cynical—literally attacking a candidate who actually regulated AI over Big Tech’s objection and falsely claiming the candidate is somehow too close to Big Tech.”

Wiener says that if Congress forms a select committee on artificial intelligence—something that Democrats have discussed since September—he’d be eager to serve. And he’s enthusiastic about many of the policy ideas floating around Congress. “I think it’s really important to have a strong, empowered, nimble federal regulator,” he says, noting that Representative Ro Khanna, a fellow Democrat from California, has proposed legislation to establish such a regulator.

He also highlights the importance of whistleblower protections, testing and auditing requirements, and a kill switch requirement, and he wants to see Congress leverage its oversight powers to hold the AI labs to account. “This is about the future of humanity, and we want to make sure that the public has a say and that the public knows what's going on,” he says.

And as a longtime state legislator, he is opposed to broad federal preemption of state AI laws, which some of the proposed federal legislation would require. “States are, as Brandeis says, laboratories,” he notes. “You want the states to be able to continue to be nimble in ways that Congress sometimes is not.”

Above all, Wiener says, he wants Congress to pass policies with real teeth. “It’s critically important that when Congress acts, that we do so in a way that is truly meaningful and that meets the moment,” he says. That means taking seriously the possibility of AI catastrophe, something he discusses in the sort of language typically used by AI safety experts. “We’re in a moment that is very dangerous in terms of the risk of loss of control over AI,” he told me. “We need to deal with recursive self-improvement. Once you’re in that realm, that really is potentially a recipe for total loss of control.”

He’ll have some allies in the fight against catastrophic AI risk. Senator Bernie Sanders, for instance, has met with many of the AI safety movement’s most influential figures and has spoken repeatedly about AI and existential risk. But there’s still a large gap between Wiener’s Bay Area, AGI-pilled perspective and the national mood on AI, which is anchored by opposition to data centers. The fact that voters approved 40 out of 41 anti-data-center ballot measures on Tuesday might seem to be a good sign for Wiener and others who support AI regulation, but Wiener says he sees this movement as far more tied to local concerns than to bigger questions about AI risk.

“Peoople who are really opposed to where AI is going—this is an area where they can actually do something about it,” he says. “But the data center revolt—to me, I think it’s more so that people are upset that there could be something like this in their community, with all the impacts near people’s homes, driving up electric bills and using water. I think that’s the bigger issue for most people, from what I can tell.”

Wiener describes himself as only “cautiously optimistic” about Congress’s ability to rein in AI, given its poor track record on regulating the tech industry. He also has concerns about the ability to get legislation past President Donald Trump, who called concerns about catastrophic AI risk a “hoax” in September and has demonstrated a stark unwillingness to collaborate with China, something that Wiener sees as essential to preventing the worst consequences of AI.

But he says Trump’s unpredictability provides  some measure of hope, though it’s a fraught kind of hope. “So far what we’ve seen are some problematic things, but not complete disasters,” Wiener says. “I hope that it doesn’t take a disaster to spur the president into acting. And I hope if that’s what it does take—which, like I said, I hope it doesn’t—but if it does, I hope it’s as small as possible.”

Ten years after AlphaGo’s match against Go champion Lee Sedol, today’s AI still isn’t tapping into the machinery that made that win possible.

https://www.zdnet.com/innovation/samsung.author: Maria Diaz

Innovation

Artificial Intelligence

Galaxy device owners who are heavy AI users would likely start paying for some features they've long enjoyed for free.

November 9, 2026, 11:55 am ET

Samsung is reportedly planning a shift from free unlimited Galaxy AI tools to a tiered subscription plan. This would be a major adjustment for Galaxy device owners who are heavy AI users, as they’d likely have to pay for some features they’ve long enjoyed for free.

Also: 7 Samsung Galaxy settings I always change

Tools like Photo Assist, Now Brief, and Creative Studio will still remain free, according to reports — they just won’t offer unlimited usage. Once the allotted number of free credits runs out, Samsung plans to introduce either standalone packages to top up AI credits or a monthly or annual subscription for users to continue using these features.

No free usage limit has been specified for users, but the highest-tiered subscription claims to offer usage limits four times higher than the free plan. A subscription would also give users access to exclusive features, presumably high-compute and newer processes.

The Galaxy AI Premium subscription would start at $4.99 per month or $47.99 per year, and reports indicate it would go up from there.

Samsung is planning to roll out a paid subscription model for the Galaxy S27 series, according to code references in 2027 Samsung devices. The company is reportedly planning to expand the plan to older devices through One UI updates, including S24 series models and newer devices, as well as Fold and Flip series phones.

https://www.darkreading.com/cybersecurit.author: Kristina Beek
https://www.darkreading.com/cybersecurit.text:
As AI accelerates change across the enterprise, PwC's James Shira explains why security teams must rethink their approach to risk and adapt their strategies.

James Shira, global CISO and CIO of PwC, has spent more than two decades navigating the evolution of cybersecurity, from its early days as a largely technical function to its continuously growing role in corporate agendas and spending. Shira's path into the industry was, as he puts it, as "consistent and inconsistent as the paths people follow." Originally considering a career in law, Shira decided to pivot, more seriously considering pursuing cybersecurity through independent study, and then formal education. Today, he oversees both technology and security at one of the world's largest professional services firms, giving him a broad perspective on the challenges facing security leaders.

In this episode of Heard It From a CISO with Dark Reading associate editor Kristina Beek, Shira discusses the skills and experience needed to build a career in cybersecurity, including the value of industry certifications, higher education, and on-the-job experience. He also examines the qualities that distinguish effective security teams, the challenges of balancing the CISO and CIO roles, and how security leaders can establish credibility with corporate boards. For Shira, successful leadership comes down to more than technical expertise. It involves building trust, communicating complex issues clearly, and creating an environment where employees can develop.

Related:NIST: Solo Shouldn't Mean Less Secure

Shira also shares his thoughts on the topic on everyone's minds: artificial intelligence. He warns that that rapid adoption is expanding attack surfaces, adding pressure on security teams, but also notes that AI technology will add opportunities for professionals seeking roles in the field. As for what’s ahead, Shira expects significant societal and industry change and shares that this rate of change is likely to be the new standard — it’s best if everyone is prepared to go along for the ride.

This is part of Dark Reading's ongoing Heard It From a CISO video series, which features frank, exclusive conversations with cybersecurity leaders in the trenches. Check out the entire series here.

This transcript has been edited for clarity and length by Informa TechTarget's internal AI assistant. For the full experience, please watch the video.

James Shira: I think there's a lot of strength in diversity of experience and perspective, and so we try to embrace that. I like people who are self-confident and have their own point of view. It makes for mutual learning and some intense debates at times. But I think that makes for better decisions.

Related:UK Wades Into Tech Sovereignty Amid AI Policy Changes

Dark Reading’s Kristina Beek: Hi, everyone. My name is Kristina Beek. I'm an associate editor at Dark Reading, and I'm here for another episode of Heard It From a CISO. Today, I'm joined by James Shira. Thank you so much for joining us. I would love it if you could introduce yourself and talk about your background and your current role as CISO at PwC.

James Shira: Sure. It's great to be with you today. My name is James. I am the global CISO and CIO for PwC. I've been involved in what we used to call IT security since 1999. I became a CISO in the early 2000s, I think 2000 or 2001, really based on an opportunity and happenstance. I've been involved in the community since that time, now 25 or 26 years. For the last eight years, I've also been operating as our global CIO.

DR’s Kristina Beek: Love to hear that. How did you first get involved specifically in cybersecurity, technology, or security in general? I know there are a lot of different ways people get involved. Some people study computer science, and some come from very alternative backgrounds. What does your path look like?

James Shira: I think my path is probably as consistent and inconsistent as the paths people follow. I was planning on getting a degree to become a lawyer, actually. Then, being a blue-collar kid, I realized I couldn't afford law school. After two years, I needed to make a change, so I redirected toward business and information systems. That was my undergraduate background.

Related:UK Warns Its Critical Infrastructure Faces Grave Risk

When I graduated in 1998, there was a bit of a mini-recession, what we often refer to as the dot-com crash. At the time, I used to read the physical Wall Street Journal pretty religiously, and there was a lot of discussion about security. We didn't call it cyber then. I figured this was a space that needed leaders and leadership. I was very interested in working toward and building an executive career path, and I wasn't sure — probably like a lot of college graduates — how to go from having no experience to having an opportunity to be in a role like the ones I'm privileged to have today.

I really started by researching, reading, learning, and studying, a lot of self-directed study, including some computer science-based material. I also did a program at Columbia that's now a master's program, which was very helpful to me. I was one of the first students when we started. The idea was like an MBA for technologists, and I'm proud to say it's now a Master of Science degree. I had the opportunity to be a student mentor there for a long time. It was really on a whim that I thought this space was going to be incredibly interesting, and it's proven to be.

DR’s Kristina Beek: That brings me to my next question: What would you recommend to somebody who wants to go into cybersecurity today? In general, what would your advice be? What insights could you provide in terms of what would be best to study? Should they prioritize certifications or a four-year education? There are a lot of different ways to go into cybersecurity today.

James Shira: For sure. I think the four-year education discussion we're all having right now is really relevant. I have younger kids, so I've got some time before they get there. I think it's a really relevant conversation because of the cost. Having worked my way through college and taken out loans at the time, those loan amounts look really small compared with what people are confronted with today. I think it's a very fair question and debate that people should have.

I'm a big proponent of certification on our security team. We really encourage people to do it, and we sponsor some of them. I'm not going to name them because we'd be here for a long time, but I think it's a very smart strategy.

The way I describe it to our folks is that I talk about the concepts of internal equity and external equity. Your internal equity when you come out of college is zero. You're new; you're coming into the industry. You build that up over time with your employer. Obviously, you want to pick the right place to work, as best you can. In the early days, experience in and of itself is the value you're pursuing.

The second piece, external equity, is something you can drive as hard as you want. As a young person without a lot of experience, you can pursue certifications. Some require years of work, but there's a lot out there. The most successful people I've had the privilege to mentor start out with a high degree of emphasis on certifications. Then, after five to seven years of experience, they make a choice about whether they're going to pursue a management track or a higher-end technical director or subject-matter-expert track.

On your question about a four-year education versus certifications, my personal view is that if you want to be in a role similar to mine, or the same as mine, you're going to want that four-year degree. You may even want a master's eventually. If that's your intended path, I would encourage you, notwithstanding the loans, to complete your undergraduate degree. There are a lot of great schools with programs that can be helpful. If you look at that and say to yourself, 'That's a significant debt burden, and I don't think it makes sense. I'm not sure I want to pursue being an executive,' then I think you should do the certifications and work on getting as much experience as you can.

DR’s Kristina Beek: That's great insight. You talked about building equity and how, when you're fresh out of college, that really depends on your employer and the company you choose to work for. Moving back to PwC, what interested you in the company? Why did you choose to work there, and what has it been like being CISO?

James Shira: When I was coming out of Zurich Financial Services, now Zurich Insurance Group — which was also a great time in my career — I was interested in finding the right CISO challenge at a similar or bigger scale. What interested me about PwC at that time was that it was a 160-plus-year-old institution. I had never worked in professional services; I had only worked in financial services. So a different industry interested me.

I think the organization's values here at PwC were very consistent with mine, and it's been a privilege to be here. It sounds clichéd, but it's really a great place. The quality of people, on average, in my experience, has been really high. People have a desire to do the right thing, and as a CISO, that's incredibly helpful. A lot of our security strategy is culturally centered on employee behavior and training, so those things were very consistent and have been very helpful.

I know some CISOs drive programs through cultures that are less amenable. This culture was incredibly amenable to moving its security program to the next level. Nobody's program is perfect, but that was helpful. Lastly, I had the opportunity to bring a lot of my colleagues with me. I have the privilege of sitting in these roles, but it's not something I did on my own. It's something we've done collectively as a team. Given the scale of the mission here, I had the opportunity to bring some colleagues from my previous employer over, and it's been awesome to see their careers flourish here as well. In short, it's a great place to work.

DR’s Kristina Beek: That brings me to a follow-up question. When it comes to a team, whether it's business-oriented or security-focused, what makes a great team? What kinds of people are you looking for, whether in terms of personality or skills?

James Shira: I'm going to answer your question in reverse order. The people I like to work with don't come in a common package. I think there's a lot of strength in diversity of experience and perspective, and so we try to embrace that. I like people who are self-confident and have their own point of view. It makes for mutual learning and some intense debates at times, but I think that makes for better decisions.

The people I'm looking for don't have to have gone to a specific school. They don't necessarily need a traditional profile, but they definitely need to be self-confident and self-directed. I talk to the team a lot about emotional resiliency. I think it's a really important concept in the security industry because, when I got started, security was past the mailroom, past the bathrooms, in the basement somewhere, and rarely in the boardroom. Now, people coming into the field wouldn't even recognize that, because security is such a central, strategically critical issue for companies. I need that confidence in our employees so that, when they become the leaders they can be, they can flourish based on that confidence. It's hard to build a great team without that.

The second piece I think is incredibly important is transparency. It's something I work diligently to practice when I'm speaking in front of the thousands of colleagues I have the privilege of leading: being as brutally transparent as possible about whatever we're trying to do. It's uncomfortable at times, and it can be challenging to answer the questions you get, but I think it provokes the kind of cultural engagement that makes for a great team.

The one thing I'll say lastly is that I don't think mediocrity, as a rule, fits in high-performing teams. You have to embrace your high performers, try to elevate and promote them, and create an environment where they can be as self-directed and successful as they can be.

DR’s Kristina Beek: Absolutely. When you were answering that, one of the things you talked about was how the CISO role and cybersecurity in general are now in the boardroom. I see a lot of articles about how to communicate with C-suite members as a CISO, how to deal with friction, and how to get your board to believe you. What would you say about communicating your needs as a CISO to the rest of the board? Do you encounter friction in your experience, and how do you deal with that?

James Shira: I think it's a great question. I'm going to offer a point of view. I'll start by saying I've gotten it wrong. I don't have all the answers, but I've learned through mistakes and by having great mentors.

I think credibility with a board starts, frankly, through delivery. The first thing you have to do is build a track record as best you can. That might sound counterintuitive: don't I need the board's buy-in before I deliver? Somewhat, but I think conversations with our various boards here, and the conversations I've had previously, show that over time, through delivery of the program and driving the change you're advocating for, you can build a lot of credibility.

The second of my three points is that you have to find your own authentic voice. Personally, I'm not a natural. I kind of joke with the team at times that I'm a radio guy, not a TV guy, and I've had to work at being a TV guy. You have to find your own authenticity through your own style. A lot of times, those of us who get the privilege of being in these C-level jobs receive a lot of advice and pressure about how to present and who to be. I would encourage people listening to find their own style and approach that works best for them. Obviously, measure it against how effective it is, but embrace the style that's authentic to you. For me, I just try to be myself with our board.

The last thing I'd say, and I think it's maybe the most important point, is that you have to bring the expertise to the board, not try to drag the board to your expertise. In our domain, don't underestimate how intimidating it can be for the people listening. It's security. They see the headlines. Maybe an issue has occurred in that business. As board members, they feel responsible for providing oversight over management, and they're under tremendous pressure to do so. Don't underestimate that.

If you come at them with a high degree of expertise, terms, acronyms, and things they don't understand, I've found that doesn't work. That would be one of the mistakes I've made in the past. What's worked well for me is not to dumb it down, but to simplify it. If you have enough mastery of a topic, you can describe it in a way that doesn't make the other person feel intimidated and helps them say, 'Okay, I get that.' One suggestion I would offer is to use storytelling. That's what I've done, and it has worked well for me.

DR’s Kristina Beek: While you're obviously CISO, you're also CIO, so you have two perspectives. What is it like balancing the responsibilities of both roles?

James Shira: The good news is that, over the last eight years I've had the privilege of being in these roles, there's been a tremendous amount of harmonization between the technology transformation of large enterprises and the need to get the cyber piece right. Therefore, unlike when I started, when security was past the mailroom and in the basement, it's now such a primary issue for organizations that it's really on the CIO's agenda. I think having both of those skill sets is a very critical thing in this day and age.

The one difference I'd acknowledge for the audience, because otherwise anybody watching would think I missed it, is that at times the CIO role can be inherently more political than the CISO role. Let me explain briefly. As a CISO, you objectively know what good looks like: don't have a breach, don't have an incident, improve your audit posture, drive good risk management, and so on. What good looks like in the CIO world can sometimes be less black and white and more gray. It can change in a way that a traditional CISO might find challenging to navigate.

I, for one, never anticipated the amount of passion and energy that debating different HR or finance platforms might bring. I've learned how to spend a lot of time with CFOs and COOs in our businesses. That's made me not only better professionally, but also more sympathetic to the issues they have, especially in some of the smaller businesses where a decision we might make from a CIO perspective has a significant material impact on their cost basis. There are differences, but in summary, it's a very complementary experience for me. The biggest challenge is time management and moving time between the different things.

DR’s Kristina Beek: Absolutely. AI is, of course, always part of the conversation. It's changing how attackers work, and it's also changing how organizations operate. What do you see as the biggest cybersecurity opportunity or risk associated with AI right now?

James Shira: I think the most important issue with AI, straight down the middle, is how it changes, evolves, and increases an organization's attack surface. The second issue is the rate of change it brings: how fast it moves and how fast systems have to move. Those are the two dynamics.

What happens to the size of your attack surface? AI can really explode it. At the same time, AI puts pressure on the pace of change across the whole security function. For us specifically, that means dealing with the amount of patching, vulnerability management, inbound requests, and client requests. You have to manage those two dynamics.

On the technology front, in my career — which some people in this audience might think is long, while others might think it's not that long yet — I've never seen anything move as fast. In a short period of time, we've gone from a nascent technology that we're all excited about to actually operationalizing it. At least in my career, I haven't seen anything cross that divide so quickly. Therefore, I think it's ultimately the biggest change-management exercise, maybe ever. That's really where leaders need to center and focus their time.

DR’s Kristina Beek: A lot of people are coming out of college or going into college with the expectation of going into cybersecurity or computer science. AI is changing the field very rapidly. A lot of people are scared that they may not even have a job or that there may not be a place for them in this field. What would you say to that, with the rise of AI?

James Shira: I understand where people get that. I understand how people get that. I think it's understandable, but I think it's wrong. The amount of change across society and industries is significant. It's very difficult for me to chart a course in my head for what isn't going to change. Therefore, I think the opportunity for young professionals is to be the change agents — to deliver the change.

I think one thing we don't always do well for our young professionals, but need to, is tell them the truth about the adversity of change management. It's hard. It's hard, and it's going to be hard for them. Do I think AI is a job-elimination technology? I don't. But I understand and respect how people might reach that conclusion.

If you're doing highly repetitive, data-centric activities, that's not, frankly, what you go to college for. Some of us had to do that coming out of college, earning our stripes, but that's not generally what you go to college for. That probably gets changed a lot by AI. Of course. I don't think it's a displacement strategy.

DR’s Kristina Beek: Going back to what you said about how AI is changing things so rapidly, what do you think cybersecurity leaders will spend the most time thinking about three to five years from now? I know that's hard because things are changing so quickly, but what do you see for the future?

James Shira: I think the constants I would expect not to go away are the rate of change, the pace, and the pressure. Therefore, I think you have to find consistency in process and strategic principles, meaning how you manage your strategy shouldn't change. You should find the things in executing the strategy and operationalizing it that don't need to change, because so much around you will be changing.

In our history, and in at least my part of the 20-year history of IT security and cybersecurity, when there's been a technical change — think cloud, client-server, mobile, or whatever — we've effectively changed every aspect of how we implemented security controls. I'm hoping and working diligently to avoid repeating that pattern in the AI space because I think it just adds too much volume to an already high-intensity, high-volume situation.

Three to five years from now, I'm hoping AI can be a much more consistent enabler of delivering secure outcomes, but we're still learning how to fully operationalize it. Then there's the issue of token costs, which we're not going to get into today, but that has a high degree of relationship to driving the overall security budget, which we're figuring out as we go.

Secondly, I don't think most companies will have enough money to build a security program the way we've historically done it, at the size and scale that AI could imply would be required. Third, I think organizations are going to have to shrink their digital footprint as they transform. The good news is that — obviously, hope is not a strategy — AI will hopefully allow us to interact with our systems of state much more efficiently than building applications as the recurring front door to all of our systems, as we've done for the last 10 or 20 years. That ought to have a great benefit in reducing the attack surface, too. I think that's what companies need to do, and I think that's what will look so different in three to five years.

Lastly, I'd say I'm expecting significant societal and industry change, especially in a five-year window. I'm not sure I'm going to have a robot at home, but maybe some of us will. I think physical AI is going to place a significant premium on investment capacity, both on the hardware side and on the adoption and implementation side.

There are Orwellian views of that, where you could see the doom and gloom. I think there's also a tremendous opportunity. Some countries are not having the birth rates we need. Frankly, there isn't enough reproduction to maintain the numbers of people in society. So robots in some places in the world are going to be incredibly helpful in allowing us to deliver the things people need in society.

But I'm excited by it. I'll summarize by saying I think the big fundamental choice you have to make every morning when you wake up is to embrace the change, both in yourself and in how you do the job, because the change is almost— I joked with a colleague the other day, and she's a really capable runner while I am not, that this is kind of like being on the treadmill at the speed Annie would go at, not the speed James would go at. Some days I feel like I'm hanging in there, and other days I feel like I'm about to fall off the back of the treadmill. I think everybody just needs to say that's part of this.

DR’s Kristina Beek: Absolutely. That's great to hear. Normally, I end these interviews by asking what the future of cybersecurity looks like to you, but we've already touched on that. So I'd rather end with a different question: You've spent a lot of time in tech and security and have seen how it's evolved. What has been the most rewarding part of that work, and what do you think will continue to challenge or motivate you, especially in a field where the risks are sometimes really high?

James Shira: Sure. It's an easy answer for me: it's the people part. It's the team. Every success I've had the privilege of being part of is not a James thing. I had a role, sure, but it's a team thing.

When you see someone — we have a number of people in our organization who started as interns at my previous employer. One colleague started as an intern and is now an executive. Another colleague, Annie, whom I mentioned, is now a partner. Those are the things that lift me back up when I have a bad day, which happens. It's when we see people building and shining in their own way, self-actualizing. That's pretty cool, and I think that's the right way things should work.

Look, it doesn't always work that way. There are probably people on the team who don't feel they got a fair chance, or who feel something didn't go perfectly. That's the challenge of working in teams of people, because people — me, you, all of us — are not perfect.

But the best days for me are when I see colleagues rise, shine, and do great things, and even leave the organization and go do great things somewhere else. That's pretty awesome. I think that's our opportunity with AI and security. We have to embrace it, try to see the positive in it, and grow through it.

DR’s Kristina Beek:Absolutely. I so enjoyed this conversation. Thank you so much for joining me today.

James Shira:Me too. Thanks for your time.

Associate Editor, Dark Reading

Kristina Beek is associate editor at Dark Reading, where she covers a wide range of cybersecurity topics and spearheads video-related content, where she contributes both content and production skills to Dark Reading's expanding video coverage. She is the creator and host of the Heard It From a CISO video series, where she interviews CISOs, directors, and other industry strategists to provide insights into the ever-evolving cybersecurity landscape. In addition to her editorial work, Kristina manages Dark Reading's social media channels (including social video), and has held numerous roles within Dark Reading over the years, including copy editor and breaking news reporter, before transitioning her focus to multimedia journalism.

Kristina graduated from North Carolina State University in 2021 with a degree in Political Science, concentrating in law and justice, and a minor in English. During her time at NC State, she honed her writing skills by contributing opinion pieces to the university's newspaper, as well as writing fiction, poetry, and short essays. Upon graduating, she began her career as a content editor, focusing on higher education topics before joining Dark Reading in December of 2022.

Currently based in Washington D.C., you can find Kristina reading, taking walks in Georgetown, trying all the restaurants she can, and taking pictures of all the dogs she sees.

A single gene on the X chromosome may help explain why autism is less common in women and girls. The gene, ZFX, has powerful effects on a set of genes that contribute to the risk of autism, and is expressed more in women than in men.

“It’s about the fact that ZFX has a relationship with these other autism-associated genes,” says Rebecca Andersen, a neurogeneticist at Boston Children’s Hospital in Massachusetts. CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. — NASA has officially launched the Moon Base Student Challenge, asking students to help build humanity's future on the moon. And there's $1 million in prizes up for grabs for the winners.

To build and sustain a base on the moon, NASA will have to solve a myriad of problems. And they're looking to the next generation for help, the space agency's chief Jared Isaacman said Sunday (Nov. 8).

"We are inviting students from across the country to help solve some of the problems that stand between humanity and a permanent presence on another world," Isaacman said. "We're putting 1 million in prizes together to support the best ideas and recognize the teams behind them."

Isaacman made this announcement wearing his blue flight suit from the rocket garden at NASA's Kennedy Space Center Visitor Center amidst the agency's MAX POWER air show event. Just the day before, he flew fighter jets in that suit and even jumped out of a plane, skydiving into the event. Soon after this announcement, he was flying another fighter plane above the crowd.

The audience for this announcement was filled with students of all ages. Some young children wearing costume spacesuits squeezed as close as they could to the front of the room while teenagers considering their futures listened intently. It was clear that Isaacman's presence and words were landing with this group.

But what moon base challenges does NASA want to see these students tackle? In short, all of them.

"The moon base will allow us to conduct groundbreaking science, test new technologies, and prepare again for where we inevitably go next, which is the red planet," he said. "But before any of that can happen, we have an awful lot of problems that need to be solved."

"We need ways to generate power through the long lunar night. We need to protect our astronauts from that incredibly harsh and dangerous and demanding environment on the surface. We need to move people and equipment around on the surface and support human life three days away from Earth," Isaacman said, illustrating just a few of the big issues that present with the concept of a moon base.

This challenge is open to high school and post-secondary students based in the U.S. For participating students, they will form teams that will work on an idea from one of six different technical topics related to creating and running a moon base. These six topics include power systems, habitats, communications, mobility, life support and astronaut safety.

This will be what Isaacman described as a "multi-phase competition that mirrors how ideas are developed actually in the aerospace industry."

"Teams will first submit concepts, then they're going to refine them, and finalists will have the opportunity to present their solutions directly to NASA leaders and stakeholders," he further explained.

"The prize money is great for sure, but the the real opportunity is to work on problems NASA is actively trying to solve right now, so students don't need to wait to graduation to contribute to that effort," Isaacman added.

Right now, NASA has a long road ahead of them before a moon base is actually built. In mid-2027, the agency is planning to launch its Artemis III mission which will see a crew of four astronauts practice rendezvous maneuvers with two different lunar landers. If all goes to plan, this will be followed by Artemis IV landing humans on the moon's surface for the first time since the final Apollo mission in 1972.

The agency is making these big steps forward to not just a crewed return to the moon, but a sustained, long-term return to the moon. However, knowing that a fully-fledged moon base is still firmly in the future, they are banking on the ingenuity, creativity and passion of

If you're a student or know a student interested in participating in this challenge, you can find more information on NASA's website here. Interested students can register until Jan. 25, 2027.

https://www.space.com/entertainment/spac.author: Sergio Pereira
https://www.space.com/entertainment/spac.text:
The first trailer for Other World: A Stranger Things Adventure doesn't show much, but there are enough clues for fans to figure out what it's about here.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

So, you thought "Stranger Things" was done and dusted after all that Conformity Gate nonsense? No way! Netflix's sci-fi sensation returns in the live-action prequel series "Other Worlds: A Stranger Things Adventure."

Created by the Duffer Brothers and Kate Trefry, with the episodes set to be directed by Joe Wright ("Darkest Hour", "Black Mirror"), this new show isn't set in Hawkins or the electric '80s. No, this time around, the action takes place in Marion, Nevada, in 1955, and you know what else is located in Nevada, right? Area 51.

The teaser trailer certainly teases the possibility of a trip to the world's most paradoxically famous secret military base, showcasing a bike and radio resting outside of a fence with a sign that clearly says it's a restricted area (in any TV show or film, that's actually an invitation to see what's on the other side). Of course, the tease doesn't end there, as the thunder booms in the sky and there's a visual hint of a wormhole.

No story details about "Other Worlds: A Stranger Things Adventure" have been released to date, but there are some clues out there for all the Internet sleuths.

Trefrey wrote the Henry Creel-focused "Stranger Things: The First Shadow" play, while Matt Duffer explained to Variety how a spin-off show would tackle the rock that Henry found in the briefcase in "Stranger Things." So, yes, expect this to be a Henry-centric affair and the start of his long, hard road to hell and becoming Vecna.

What'll be interesting, though, is to see how the show ties into the history of Area 51. After all, it was on April 12, 1955, that CIA officer Richard Bissell discovered the site, while the "Other Worlds" trailer has the date of April 19th clearly marked onscreen, so the timelines align nicely here.

"Stranger Things" has never been shy of tying itself to real-world science and historical events, so it'll be fascinating to see how the show explores Area 51 as a concept and the secrets everybody believes are hidden there.

Was it really a site to test highly advanced weapons and aircraft, or was E.T.'s cousin held hostage there until he revealed Colonel Sanders' 11 herbs and spices? Who knows, with all this renewed excitement around this mysterious military facility, we might get another "Storm Area 51" event to enjoy and laugh at all over again.

Regardless, more "Stranger Things" is welcome news, and since it's presumably about one of the show's best characters, Henry Creel, it only adds another layer to his already intriguing lore. If we can't have an origin story about Hopper's incredible and envious moustache, this is the next best thing.

"Other Worlds: A Stranger Things Adventure" arrives on Netflix in 2028.

CHICAGO — If one word could describe research presented at this year’s American Heart Association scientific sessions, it might be “neutral.”

The meeting began with two blockbuster disappointments, hinted at in top-line results released weeks or months ago but detailed with unvarnished specificity Saturday morning. The ZEUS trial targeting inflammation showed no difference between the treatment and placebo arms. The HORIZON trial taking aim at lipoprotein(a) also revealed nearly identical results, whether participants were on or off the drug.

In other words, neutral.

Annette Young is pleased to welcome Renaud Foucart, Senior Lecturer at the Department of Economics ECARES at Lancaster University. France's 1.6% minimum-wage increase, in response to the countrywide protests, may offer a temporary reprieve from social unrest, but it does little to resolve the deeper political and institutional crisis confronting the country. https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-10/i.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

The attacks affected supermarket fridges in multiple countries, prompting stores to pull produce from shelves. (Reuters: Stephanie Lecocq)

France's Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot says the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corp is behind the recent "unprecedented" cyber attacks on supermarket fridges.

Mr Barrot is vowing he will press for Europe-wide sanctions against Iran in response.

The attacks, which saw the temperatures of fridges turned up remotely, caused many supermarkets in multiple European countries to close.

France has summoned Iran's ambassador and vowed consequences after officially naming the country's Islamic Revoluntionary Guards Corps (IRGC) as responsible for cyberattacks which crippled supermarket fridges across Europe.

The attacks saw the temperatures of fridges remotely turned up, forcing stock to be pulled from shelves and many supermarkets to close.

On Monday evening, local time, France's Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot became the first European leader to place blame for the fridge cyber attacks on the IRGC

"I can confirm that this attack was carried out by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps of the Islamic Republic of Iran," Mr Barrot said of the cyber attacks on French supermarkets that occurred October 11 and 12.

"This attack is unprecedented in both its scale and its level of aggression.

Fridges in multiple European countries were affected by the hacks in mid-October and last week. (Reuters: Stephane Mahe)

French prosecutors also announced they would open a probe into an alleged Iranian cyber unit responsible for last month's attacks, which saw hundreds of supermarkets affected.

"A judicial investigation has been opened against the head of the Iranian group Shahid Kaveh, an offensive cyber unit affiliated with the Electronic and Cyber Center of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC-CEC), against his two deputies, and against any other individuals who may be identified," Paris prosecutor Laure Beccuau said in a statement.

Neither Mr Barrot nor prosecutors said whether a second spate of fridge cyberattacks last week were connected.

Those more recent attacks came in the same week that dozens of European flights were subjected to bomb hoaxes. No country has so far been blamed.

Suspicion for both the fridge cyber-campaign and the bomb hoaxes had fallen on either Iran or Russia, with the latter also alleged to be waging a so-called "hybrid war" across Europe on allies of Ukraine.
