https://www.japantimes.co.jp/life/2026/1.author: Alex K.t. Martin
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/life/2026/1.text:
On a drizzly Thursday morning on the Yanaka Ginza shopping street in Tokyo’s Taito Ward, Claudio Braghetta is doing a little window shopping. The Swiss traveler arrived in Japan a week ago and has already visited Nagoya, Sendai and Nikko, Tochigi Prefecture. He heads home Saturday.

“I notice there aren’t many trash cans in Japan, in Switzerland there are public trash cans along the streets,” he says. “It’s great that in Japan, the cities are still clean even without them.”

Braghetta says he has been carrying a plastic bag with him while traveling  to collect his garbage, and uses convenience store bins to dispose of waste from items he has purchased there.

“I try to respect local customs whenever I travel abroad,” he says.

Braghetta’s experience reflects what can be a significant frustration for many tourists to Japan. In a survey conducted between November 2025 and January 2026, the Japan Tourism Agency asked 4,110 foreign visitors departing Japan about difficulties they encountered during their trips. A lack of public trash cans topped the list, cited by 17.2% of respondents.

Apart from convenience stores and train stations, options are limited. Even the shōtengai (shopping streets) in Tokyo’s neighborhoods often have no public waste receptacles, despite the many shops selling takeout food to the steady stream of locals and tourists passing through each day.

There are several reasons for the shortage. The 1995 Tokyo subway sarin gas attack, carried out by the Aum Shinrikyo doomsday cult, and subsequent counterterrorism measures prompted the removal of waste bins from many public spaces. Tokyo Metro, for example, removed bins from all its stations in January 2022, citing security concerns.

Local authorities have also cited overflowing receptacles, illegal dumping of household waste and the cost of collection and maintenance as reasons for removing public bins. Osaka, for example, began phasing out the roughly 5,000 trash bins once located at major intersections and other public spaces in fiscal 2009 and has since removed them all.

“Installing trash bins does not necessarily mean the rubbish will disappear; in some places, the bins simply become piled high with garbage,” Tokyo Gov. Yuriko Koike told a news conference on Nov. 28, 2025. She suggested that Japan should encourage foreign visitors to carry their trash home, while noting that installing and maintaining bins, collecting waste and sorting it all entail costs.

Japan had long promoted the principles of reduce, reuse and recycle, as well as the idea of mottainai, or avoiding waste, Koike said, suggesting that the country’s approach to trash disposal could serve as a positive example to the world.

With public bins scarce, finding somewhere to dispose of empty cans and bento boxes remains a challenge. Technology may offer some solutions.

SmaGO, a solar-powered smart trash can developed in the United States and distributed in Japan by Forcetec, is one such solution. First installed in Tokyo’s upscale Omotesando shopping district in 2022, the units compact rubbish every five minutes automatically, giving them about five times the capacity of conventional trash cans. The company says roughly 650 units are now operating nationwide across about 80 locations, including 118 at Tokyo Dome.

“There are many places that recognize the need for trash bins but hesitate to install them because they’re worried the bins will overflow or because of the labor required to collect the rubbish,” says Rina Ogata, a spokesperson for Forcetec.

“You can install SmaGO and reduce the frequency of rubbish collection. The communications function also allows operators to check online how full each bin is, so they can make collections more efficiently before the bins reach capacity.”

Ogata says the company has adapted its approach to Japan’s local waste-disposal habits. Because people often discard plastic bottles with their caps still on, the bottles are harder to compress. Instead, the company uses bins that do not compact waste for plastic bottles, cans and glass bottles. These bins also have a communications function that allows operators to monitor how full they are remotely.

Forcetec does not disclose the price of its SmaGO bins, but the technology comes at a cost. Most are purchased outright, Ogata says, with various subsidies helping to offset the expense.

In Tokyo, for example, city grants can cover a substantial portion of the purchase price, while corporate sponsorship is helping fund operating costs at installations in Omotesando. In Kyoto, known for its efforts to preserve its historic streetscape, companies have donated smart bins to the city through a corporate hometown tax program that allows businesses to support local projects while receiving tax benefits.

Meanwhile, JR East is testing a mobile trash bin in the form of an autonomous robot developed by California-based Cartken for indoor and outdoor use. The railway operator began trialing the device in the concourse of Shinjuku Station, one of the world’s busiest railway stations, on Sept. 8.

Trash bins at major stations need to be emptied frequently, placing a considerable burden on cleaning staff. The trial aims to explore ways to reduce the workload involved in waste collection without inconveniencing passengers.

The robot uses sensors and a preloaded map to navigate its surroundings and can also be monitored and controlled remotely. Its 40-liter bin has sensors that track how full it is, allowing the robot to stop before it reaches capacity.

“When operating in crowded areas, it’s essential to plan routes carefully to ensure the robot does not move against the flow of pedestrian traffic,” says Rina Mitomo, a spokesperson for JR East.

The trial also found that having the robot move at a relatively slow speed allows it to shorten its safety distance — the distance at which it automatically applies the brakes to avoid getting too close to passengers — enabling it to move more smoothly, Mitomo says.

Based on the results so far, the team has found that the robot can navigate the station relatively easily outside peak commuting hours. Although it is too early to draw conclusions from the survey of passenger acceptance, Mitomo says the initial feedback has been more positive than anticipated.

Beyond waste collection, JR East sees potential for the robots to provide other services, including sharing train operation updates, directing passengers to station facilities, displaying advertisements and selling products. Will commuters soon get used to seeing trash bins on the move? Much will depend on how smoothly the robots can navigate the crowds.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/life/2026/1.summary: Japan has long promoted the principles of reduce, reuse and recycle. JR East says the robot can navigate the station relatively easily outside peak commuting hours.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckzd.title: Russell Brand sentenced to 10-and-a-half years in prison for rape and sexual assault
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckzd.text:
Russell Brand has been sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison, after being convicted of rape and sexual assault.

In his sentencing remarks, Judge Joel Bennathan, described Brand as a "sexual predator" and criticised his "staggering arrogance".

Brand was sentenced to nine years for rape, with an additional 18 months, nine months and eight months for three counts of sexual assault.

He will serve two thirds of his sentence in prison before being released on licence, and will be liable to be recalled to custody if he breaches its terms, the judge said.

Brand will serve the sentences for the three counts of sexual assault concurrently, adding 18 months to his nine years for rape.

The disgraced entertainer was found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault, involving four women between 2004 and 2009.

The few days Brand has already spent in prison since Thursday will count towards his sentence, the judge said.

The guidelines state offenders jailed for four years or more for some serious violent or sexual offences will be released at the two thirds point. In Brand's case that would be seven years.

Once released, he is likely to spend the rest of his sentence on licence and will have to abide by specific rules such as wearing a tag. His sentence will not be included in the early release scheme. Sex offenders, along with murderers, are exempt from the scheme.

In his sentencing remarks, the judge paid tribute to the bravery of the women who gave evidence during the trial.

The judge also commended the Met Police for their "hard work in gathering evidence and taking great care with all women who testified".

Brand did not react in the dock as he was sentenced. Before being taken down to the cells, he mouthed "I love you" to his wife Laura Brand, who was in the court.

In total, Brand was sentenced to:

In further remarks, the judge said Brand's status protected him until 2023, when journalists from the Sunday Times, the Times and Channel 4's Dispatches outlined a series of misconduct allegations, leading to women making complaints to police.

He said Brand harboured a "casual arrogant disregard to any woman's right to say no to you", while his fame meant he believed "you could act when you liked and how you liked".

The judge said the evidence in the case also showed that Brand's entourage during the peak of his celebrity had "indulged your dreadful behaviour".

The former actor and comedian's wife Laura Brand was seated just a few feet away from the former comedian in the glass-walled dock as he was being sentenced.

Earlier, as he arrived in the dock on Monday morning, Brand mouthed to his wife: "It'll be okay, I don't know how, but it will", and he was seen praying and making a cross sign with his hand as the victim statements were read out.

Before Brand's sentencing, the court heard victim impact statements from the women he had been accused of assaulting.

One of the women, who spoke from behind a screen, said she had been in "shock and turmoil for years".

"I was extremely upset and traumatised," she said. "I didn't have any respect for myself. I was thinking I was damaged goods - scared of giving off signals that could be taken the wrong way."

She added: "I just want to say - a leopard may change its spots but it's still a leopard."

After the sentencing, one of Brand's victims said: "I am eternally grateful to the police and prosecution team for their support and for allowing my voice to be heard. I finally feel believed."

Another victim said: "I am grateful to the support from the Independent Sexual Violence Advisor (IVSA), the police team who from the start took my testimony seriously and the prosecution team who have been with me throughout this process."

She added: "I do not believe that I could have come this far without them."

After the sentencing hearing, Detective Superintendent Andy Furphy said: "Today's sentence marks a significant milestone in our investigation and means Russell Brand has been held accountable for his crimes.

"My thoughts today are with the women who came forward and made this investigation possible."

He added: "I hope today's outcome provides some measure of closure and allows them to continue rebuilding their lives."

The verdicts were delivered on Thursday following a four-week trial at Southwark Crown Court in London.

Brand was found not guilty of two counts of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault.

He will automatically have to sign the Sex Offences' Register as part of his sentence because of the crimes he committed.

David Roberts, senior crown prosecutor for the Crown Prosecution Service, said: "We want to thank all the women who were at the heart of this case.

"They did not know each other, and each has carried what happened to them for almost two decades."

He added: "Today's sentence cannot undo the harm the victims have lived with, but we hope it brings them some measure of justice."

One of the women, who spoke from behind a screen, said she had been in "shock and turmoil for years" in her victim impact statement.

"I was extremely upset and traumatised," she said. "I didn't have any respect for myself. I was thinking I was damaged goods - scared of giving off signals that could be taken the wrong way."

She added: "I just want to say - a leopard may change its spots but it's still a leopard."

The prosecution later read a statement from another victim who was sexually assaulted by Brand in 2005.

"Russell Brand has managed to move on," the woman said in the statement. "This has had a lasting impact on my life. I recognise this now.

"However, over the years, hearing his voice on television or seeing his image has made me jump. I had a strong adverse reaction hearing his voice."

She added: "Russell Brand is a sexual predator who has no remorse... I just hope he is not allowed to hurt any more women."

The prosecution also read a statement from the woman Brand was found to have raped about how she felt after the assault.

"I felt anxious, humiliated and overwhelmed," she said. "I struggled to sleep and eat, I struggled to cope with my emotions, I had to take time away from my work," she said.

She continued: "I had to live with my parents, I sought help and support... I am living with trauma, something I carry every day.

"My confidence and self esteem have been badly affected. I no longer trust my instincts."

The woman said one of the worst parts of what happened was her fear that she might have contracted HIV. She also said she was in considerable pain after the assault.

Another woman, who was sexually assaulted while working on a Channel 4 project with Brand in 2009, said in a statement that she was "really upset" afterwards.

"I felt I lost my trust in people, I felt my working environment wasn't safe," she said. "I felt powerless in that moment and it had a knock-on effect on my confidence."

At the sentencing hearing, Brand's barrister Ian Winter KC put forward six character references, including one from Georgina Baillie, the granddaughter of the late actor Andrew Sachs.

Baillie was thrust into the spotlight in 2008 when Brand and Jonathan Ross left offensive messages about her on her grandfather's answering machine during a Radio 2 broadcast.

Winter said Georgina Baillie "was an alcoholic and now has been sober for six years because Mr Brand both persuaded her, then paid for her to go through rehabilitation".

Baillie, an actor and artist, had a relationship with Brand in the mid 2000s.

The defence barrister noted Baillie was the person "at the eye of the Sachsgate storm" for which Brand "was rightly, and he accepted, rightly pilloried for, for what he said was a disgraceful prank on live radio".

Winter also told the court that the former entertainer's wife Laura Brand, who gave evidence in her husband's defence during the trial, was experienceing "total devastation" at the verdicts.

He said Mr and Mrs Brand were "currently wrestling with how to exactly explain to a child who's just turned 10 what has happened here".

"It brings home the consequences of this conduct to totally innocent people who have been caught up in it," he said.

Sentencing Brand, the judge said: "I am very conscious that your imprisonment will deprive your children of the presence of their father.

"That sad loss to them, however, is caused by your serious offending."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckzd.summary: Russell Brand sentenced to life in prison for rape and sexual assault of two women. Judge Joel Bennathan described Brand as a "sexual predator" Brand will serve two thirds of his sentence in prison before being released on licence.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Only known handwritten final draft of MLK Jr’s I Have A Dream speech to be auctioned
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Anna Betts
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
The document is expected to fetch more than $10m and the proceeds will be donated to several charities

The likely only surviving handwritten final full draft of Martin Luther King Jr’s historic 1963 I Have a Dream speech is set to be auctioned in New York City in January, with proceeds benefiting several charities, including the King Center in Atlanta, Georgia.

Auction house Christie’s has announced that the document is expected to fetch more than $10m, and that the pages will be displayed publicly at the auction house from 15 to 21 January, before being offered in a single-lot sale.

Described as “the only known handwritten final draft of the speech”, the auction house said that the document was rediscovered in 2024 in a desk drawer belonging to a former aide of King’s, Edward T Clayton, by his widow, Xernona.

She had originally found it in the late 1990s but did not know then that it was the only known final draft, and put it back in the drawer, until 2024, when she rediscovered the document and experts established that it is unique, Christie’s added.

According to the auction house, King completed the draft of the speech in the early hours of 28 August 1963, at the Willard hotel in Washington DC.

“Focused on limiting his remarks to five minutes, and considering both word choice and flow, Dr King wrote the final draft of the speech in blue ink across seven yellow legal pad pages after days of discussions with many advisers – including trusted speech writer Edward T Clayton,” Christie’s said.

Just hours after the ink dried that day, King delivered the pivotal speech in Washington DC with his towering rhetoric during the height of the civil rights struggle for racial equality in the US.

“The stirring words that he delivered that afternoon have come to be regarded as the most important speech of the 20th Century, and one of the most important speeches in American history,” the release said.

Christie’s said the pages contain edits and crossings-out and “offer a rare glimpse at Dr King’s writing process”.

Notably, this original draft does not include the words “I have a dream”, as King “famously added” those words “spontaneously while delivering his speech on the day of the [civil rights] march”, Christie’s said.

“This is a treasure of American history,” said Peter Klarnet, Christie’s manuscripts specialist. “It gives you chills to look at it. Reading along, you’re there in the moment with Dr King, watching him compose it and making edits in real time. It captures a moment that literally changed the course of our nation and makes it very real and very human.”

King’s son, Martin Luther King III, said in a statement that it is “poetic that the past will protect the future”.
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: The likely only surviving handwritten final draft of Martin Luther King Jr’s historic 1963 I Have a Dream speech is set to be auctioned in New York City in January. The document is expected to fetch more than $10m and the proceeds will be donated to several charities.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.title: College Football Playoff will double in size to 24 teams starting next year
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.author: Associated Press
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.text:
Power Four conference title games to be eliminated

Five teams will auto-qualify with rest picked by panel

The College Football Playoff will double in size to 24 teams beginning next year, bringing an end to a three-decade era of conference title games that used to be among the marquee events of the season.

College leaders announced the new format Monday, after ESPN agreed to rework its contract to add the 11 new games. Terms were not announced, though ESPN said it was a deal for five years and an additional $1.7bn, on top of the $7.8bn contract that runs through the 2031 season.

The revenue generated from the new games will presumably make up for the estimated $345m the Power Four conference title games were worth. ESPN would then not be on the hook for $140m of the extra money due to cancellation of the title games, the network reported.

The new format will have five automatic qualifiers – the champions of the Power Four leagues and the best-ranked team in the smaller Group of Six conferences – with the other 19 teams being chosen by a selection panel. Notre Dame does not receive any guarantees, the way it does this year if it’s ranked in the top 12 for what will be the final year of the 12-team postseason.

The top eight seeds will receive first-round byes in the new format and the playoff will start on the second weekend in December, with the first two rounds of games on campus. The traditional Army-Navy game will be played on the first weekend in December, which used to be reserved for conference title games.

Both the SEC and the Big Ten, whose approval was needed to adopt this change, and their Power Four brethren – the Big 12 and the ACC – are banking that most of the additional spots will go to their members so some of the second-tier teams have new motivation to keep spending big in an era of NIL and $50m football rosters.

“Opening the playoff to more programs, more student-athletes and more fanbases across the country is great for college football,” said Mississippi State president Mark Keenum, who is chair of the CFP board. “We look forward to seeing this expanded format come to life next season.”

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: Nvidia’s board needs to do some succession planning – sharpish | Nils Pratley
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Nils Pratley
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
The chipmaker faces business risks and political scrutiny due to its over-reliance on founder and CEO Jensen Huang

Why is Nvidia’s Jensen Huang at the centre of a US-China row?

T
oo big – and too well-connected – to sack? One doesn’t have to be overly cynical to think Jensen Huang, the Nvidia boss, starts with one huge advantage as the chipmaker’s board starts its independent investigation into the alleged honeytrap spy scandal. The world of US big tech is not, to put it mildly, strong on checks and balances on a founder’s power.

Huang does not enjoy the supercharged voting rights that are par for the course elsewhere – his shareholding is a plain vanilla 3.6%. On the other hand, Nvidia’s board does not appear to have spent much time worrying about succession planning and “key person risk” or other standard concerns of corporate governance wonks outside the US.

There isn’t even a Nvidia board member with the title of chair. Instead, a “lead director” is “designated annually by a majority of the independent directors”, which sounds like a formula for ensuring the attention remains wholly focused on Huang, the sole executive member.

It’s the American way, of course: the cult of the superstar founder or chief executive runs deep and there is a fair argument that such set-ups encourage adventurous risk-taking in pursuit of grand corporate visions. But such governance arrangements look unsuited to situations where the behaviour of the boss is under scrutiny and the role of the board itself is being examined.

The investigation will examine whether Huang “has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort” but the independent directors stressed there is now “no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised.”

OK, but legitimate questions don’t end there. Did Huang break Nvidia’s internal code of conduct? Did he mislead the board about his relationship with Alice Huang (no relation), the alleged Chinese spy? Was the board aware of US intelligence reports that Ms Huang had been hired by China’s ministry of state security to spy on the Nvidia boss, as reported by the New York Times? What security precautions were in place? Other boards in other countries might have insisted on suspending the boss until all the facts are in.

In the meantime, the defence of Huang from elsewhere has begun. “An honourable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it,” said Donald Trump. “Jensen is irreplaceable for America’s AI leadership,” opined Shaun Maguire, a partner at Sequoia Capital, the powerful Silicon Valley investor. Yes, there is little doubt the US tech and political establishment would like this saga to end up in a series of bland conclusions about an everyday infidelity.

Nvidia’s board, however, would be wise not to rely on the “irreplaceable” consensus holding, or the political heat going away. This affair will be trawled over by newly empowered Democrats in Congress because it touches on how forcefully – or not – the administration has been enforcing its own national security restrictions on chip sales to China. This process will go on for months. Huang’s personal relationship with Trump will come under the spotlight like never before.

Sign up to Business Today

after newsletter promotion

Will the Nvidia boss, even if he is cleared by the board’s investigation, still look so all-conquering by the end? His lobbying clout in Washington will be diminished. And Nvidia’s shareholders, if they’re doing the job properly, will surely insist on far greater visibility on where the company’s chips end up.

There may come a point where it is in Nvidia’s own interests to move on from the Jensen Huang era. The 63-year-old deserves all his accolades for spotting the enormous AI opportunity for the GPU chips that originated in the world of video games. The rise of Nvidia has been extraordinary. But over-reliance on one individual is also a business risk. Time for some overdue succession planning – it may be needed.

The chipmaker faces business risks and political scrutiny due to its over-reliance on founder and CEO Jensen Huang. The world of US big tech is not, to put it mildly, strong on checks and balances on a founder’s power.

https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.title: Did you solve it? The multi-choice maths quiz taking over the world
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.author: Alex Bellos
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.text:
The answer to today’s Kangaroo puzzle

Earlier today I set you the following problem from the international maths Kangaroo, a multiple choice challenge taken by more than seven million children every year. (For more details about this extraordinary event see the original story.)

Here is is again with the solution.

A four digit number abcd satisfies the equation abcd = aa + bb + cc + dd.

[Note: abcd means that the first digit is a, the second is b, the third is c and the fourth is d. It does not mean a x b x c x d. The numbers a, b, c and d do not have to be different.]

As an extra, what are b, c and d?

Let’s first list the values of xx for x = 1 to 6.

11 = 1, 22 = 4, 33 = 27, 44 = 256, 55 = 3125, 66 > 9999.

I didn’t calculate the exact value of 66, because as soon as I realised it was greater than a four digit number I knew I had an upper bound for the values of a, b, c and d. They must all be less than 6.

One of the digits must be 5, because if all the digits were 4 or below, the only way for aa + bb + cc + dd to have four digits would be 44 + 44 + 44 + 44 = 1024, which does not satisfy the equation.

So, how many of the digits are 5? Let’s go through the cases

All of them. Thus abcd = 5555 ≠ 4 x 3125. So this is not a solution.

Three. Thus abcd = (3x 3125) + (either 1, 4, 27 or 256)

= 9375 + (either 1, 4, 27 or 256)

This means that a = 9. But a ≠ 9 so this is not a solution either.

Two. Thus abcd = 6250 +(two of either 1, 4, 27 or 256). Again, this is not a solution since if it was, a = 6, which we know is false.

So, only one of a, b, c and d is 5.

We now know that abcd = 3125 + (some combinaton of three from 1, 4, 27 and 256). Thus abcd < 4000. So a = 3.

We now have the answer to the multiple choice question, but let’s try and find b, c and d. One of them is 5. So we have

abcd = 27 + 3125 + (two from 1, 4, 27 and 256)

abcd = 3152 + (two from 1, 4, 27 and 256.)

It cannot be the case that both remaining digits are 4, because if they were abcd = 3152 + 256+256 = 3664, and no 6s are allowed.

Imagine that one digit is 4, which would mean that abcd = 3408 + 1, 4 or 27, i.e abcd = 3409, 3412, or 3435.

We can eliminate 3409 because it has a 9, and 3412 because it doesn’t have a 5. The answer is 3435 = 33 + 44 + 33 + 55.

To make sure there are no other solutions, let’s see what happens when abcd = 3152 + two from 1, 4 and 27. The possibilities are 3154, 3157, 3180, 3160, 3183, 3206. Only the first one is potentially ok, since it has all digits less than 6, but the number does not satisfy the equation in the question.

I hope you enjoyed today’s puzzle. I’ll be back in two weeks.

For more information about entering the Kangaroo in the UK, contact the UKMT. For all other countries, find your national Kangaroo association here.

You can read previous Kangaroos in the World Olympiads Bank, an archive of almost 100,000 problems from international competitions in maths, physics, chemistry, biology informatics and astronomy. In the Kangaroo section, the levels are Pre-Ecolier (lower primary), Ecolier (upper primary), Benjamin (lower secondary), Cadet (middle secondary), Junior (upper secondary), Student (sixth form). The archive was created by Sokratis Romanidis.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.title: France accelerates minimum wage hike in bid to quell protest
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.text:
The French government has announced it will move a planned rise in the minimum wage forward by a month as it seeks to quell mass protests over the cost of living.

French ⁠Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu announced on Monday that the 1.6 percent increase in the minimum wage, originally planned for the start of 2027, will now take effect from December 1, 2026.

The move comes amid weeks of student-led demonstrations that started with calls for greater investment for the country’s underfunded schools but have morphed into broader protests and serious unrest – part of a wave across Europe.

The minimum monthly wage in France currently stands at 1,477.93 euros ($1,656); the increase raises it by 24 euros ($27) to 1,502 euros ($1,683).

“Regarding the SMIC [minimum wage], we have decided two things: to bring forward the increase to 1 December as opposed to 1 January, and to raise this increase to 1.6 per cent,” said Labour Minister Jean-Pierre Farandou at a press conference.

This increase represents “the second-largest rise in 20 years; it should not be underestimated”, Lecornu told reporters, stressing that this boost is “not merely symbolic”.

“This increase has been carefully planned to ensure it does not lead to job losses,” the PM said.

The last rise came in June, when inflation levels triggered a 35-euro ($39) hike.

Despite the accelerated increases, the minimum wage still falls short of union demands. The CFDT, France’s largest union, has called for a 100-euro ($112) increase, while the left-wing CGT union is demanding a 10 percent rise, equivalent to around 150 euros ($168) a month.

CFDT head Marylise Leon said the increase was “insufficient”. ⁠CGT head Sophie Binet described it as “crumbs”.

The government is concerned about mounting social tensions five months before presidential elections.

Far-right leader Marine Le Pen is the frontrunner in the polls. Far-left candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon of the France Unbowed party, who has been accused of encouraging the unrest, unveiled his programme on Saturday to some 17,000 supporters.

He pledged to boost the economy by capitalising on consumer spending and “through billions [of euros] that already exist”, adding that these savings “must be channelled towards our country’s environmental and social needs”.

After taking over DC Studios in 2022, James Gunn and Peter Safran are going to be replaced by a former Marvel exec.

Soon, James Gunn and Peter Safran will no longer head up Skydance’s DC Studios. After taking the helm of DC Studios as co-CEOs in 2022, Gunn and Safran are being replaced by former Marvel SVP of Production and Development Jeremy Latcham, Deadline reports.

However, Gunn and Safran will “continue to produce on various DC projects” and are still working on the Superman followup Man of Tomorrow, Deadline says. Gunn also posted on Instagram that he and Safran have “just been engaged on another DC project which I’m writing.” In his Instagram post, Gunn said that his time at DC Studios has been “trying, to say the least. I dislike the at-times corporate nature of the job (thanks to Peter for taking the brunt of that).”

The change in leadership follows the recent closure of the megamerger between Paramount and Warner Bros., which resulted in the combined Skydance company that’s led by CEO David Ellison. Latcham takes over DC Studios on December 1st and will report to Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein, the co-chairs of Skydance Motion Picture Group.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/09/what-is-n.title: Meet Jensen Huang’s son-in-law, a former pro skier and the Nvidia CEO’s ‘consigliere’ who could play a massive role in the company’s succession plan
https://fortune.com/2026/11/09/what-is-n.author: Sasha Rogelberg
https://fortune.com/2026/11/09/what-is-n.text:
In January, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was asked how he’s managed to lead the company since its 1993 founding.

“The secret for being CEO for this long is, one, don’t get fired, and, two, don’t get bored,” he said at an event in Las Vegas. “I don’t know which one comes first. How long [will I continue as CEO]? For as long as I deserve it.”

Ten months later, Huang is putting that adage to the test: Over the weekend, he admitted to having an affair with a business executive suspected by U.S. intelligence of acting as an operative for the Chinese government. China’s foreign ministry denied the allegation.

As Huang faces increased scrutiny after he admitted to the affair with an alleged spy, he now faces questions about whether he can continue on as the company’s top brass.

Nvidia has since launched an independent investigation into its CEO and his romantic relationship with suspected spy Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed International. Megaspeed is a data center and cloud computing company and one of Asia’s largest buyers of Nvidia chips. Nvidia’s board said Sunday that it has no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised.

“I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry,” Huang said in a statement on Sunday.

“Today’s news will not slow Nvidia. Jensen is committed to continuing to lead Nvidia as CEO without interruption,” a company spokesperson told Fortune in a statement.

The probe has reinvigorated investors’ concerns about the need to construct a succession plan, which, notably, Huang and Nvidia have not publicly shared. As of Monday morning, Nvidia stock is down more than 6%. Bernstein analysts, in a note published on Sunday, noted it would be unclear who could or would fill Huang’s shoes because the identity of his company is so inextricably linked to his own.

“Nvidia is not an ordinary company and Jensen is not an ordinary CEO,” they wrote. “He IS Nvidia, clearly sets the long term strategy and direction, and (with supposedly 60 direct reports) pulls most of the company’s strings himself.”

Huang’s two children, Madison and Spencer Huang, both have roles in the company, but Huang’s son-in-law Nico Caprez, Nvidia’s 35-year-old vice president of global AI infrastructure growth, could be among the next in line to lead the AI juggernaut.

“I do imagine Huang is kind of preparing [Madison] and Nico for that next step,” one Nvidia employee who works with Caprez, told The Information last month.

Caprez is a former alpine skier representing Switzerland who began his career as a Boston Consulting Group consultant. He graduated with an MBA from the London Business School in 2021, where he met Madison Huang. The two married this September.

While Madison serves as a senior director of physical AI and robotics product marketing, and Spencer is a director of robotics product management, Caprez rose through the ranks at Nvidia to lead global AI infrastructure growth in less than three years, starting as a corporate development manager in February 2024 before becoming the director of global AI infrastructure enablement for Nvidia’s cloud partners about a year ago.

The young executive was part of deal-making efforts to raise $500 billion with six major asset managers including Apollo Global Management and Blackstone, to finance Nvidia chips for data centers in August. Caprez also reportedly assisted in Nvidia’s efforts to take minority stakes in two data center developers as part of its AI infrastructure buildout.

Senior leadership has extolled Caprez’s value both within the company and to the CEO more specifically. Vladimir Troy, Nvidia’s vice president of AI infrastructure who works alongside Caprez, said “Nico is very important.” A cloud executive who also met with Caprez called him “Jensen’s consigliere” in an interview with The Information.

Huang, however, has been mum on who will lead the company in its next era, whenever that may be. In an interview with Bloomberg last month, the CEO shied away from speculation his daughter would one day replace him at Nvidia’s helm.

“I don’t hope the job on her, and the reason for that is because if that’s their aspiration, Spencer of Madison’s, they have to go earn it, and it’s really, really hard work,” he said. “For many people, they can focus on their job and their families. When you’re the CEO of the company, you have to focus on, of course, your family. But I’ve got a whole bunch of other families I’m caring for. I’m responsible for an entire industry, and so I think the pressure of being the CEO is high.”

Huang’s newly precarious spot at the top of his company has some worries not just about who one day replaces him, but whether anyone really can.

“The so-called ‘key-man risk’ looms large here, and it’s doubtful markets have adequately priced it in,” economist Mohamed A. El-Erian wrote in a post on X. “This will not be easy for the board to navigate.”

Daniel Newman, CEO of global technology research firm the Futurum Group, said that what’s made Huang so difficult to replace is that the company has been built around his leadership style, which leans autocratic.

“He really drives everything that happens. He has a team of lieutenants that are in charge of making sure that what he asks becomes gospel, that it’s executed ferociously, maniacally,” Newman told Fortune. “The market has built such admiration and confidence for him that he’s become a Jobs or a Musk type of figure at Nvidia, where there just isn’t really any thought of it not being a founder-led company.”

Whenever Nvidia transitions to new leadership, it will likely see a shift in strategy, moving slightly away from the rapid clip of innovation Huang has pushed, to becoming an “execution machine” that has solidified backend and supply chain uncertainties to deliver efficiently to partners, Newman added. Changes in the company focus also mean that even if there’s one CEO, there will likely be a leadership team, not a single figure, making Nvidia’s biggest decisions.

“It’s very improbable that they’re going to find one person that’s going to fill all the gaps,” Newman said.

https://fortune.com/2026/11/09/new-york-.title: New York’s graying workforce: Residents over 65 are holding onto jobs longer and driving healthcare to become one of the ‘fastest-growing’ sectors
https://fortune.com/2026/11/09/new-york-.author: Emma Burleigh
https://fortune.com/2026/11/09/new-york-.text:
Workers from across the country have long flocked to New York to chase dream jobs and lock down six-figure salaries—but now the opportunity landscape has changed. Professionals have to compete for a limited number of roles, and baby boomers are holding on tight to jobs that might otherwise be up for grabs.

A new report from New York Gov. Kathy Hochul’s office reveals that the state continues to struggle with strained hiring and cautious business expansion in an uncertain economy. Total statewide employment is estimated to grow only 0.2% in 2026 and 0.3% in 2027, after rising 1% the year before. Hiring will remain sluggish through next year, the report forecasts, and workforce growth will be subdued because of New York’s shrinking, graying population.

“The growth of the State’s labor supply will be limited due to constraints in population growth and the aging workforce,” the report notes. “These trends will likely restrict employment growth, but unemployment rates should remain stable.”

Currently, 19.3% of New York’s population is 65 and older—up from 15% a decade ago—according to Hochul’s mid-year report. These baby boomers are intensifying the need for social and healthcare services, in-demand industries that have been battling severe labor shortages across the country. On top of that, America’s oldest working cohort is delaying retirement to make ends meet; a 2022 study from New York’s Office of Budget Policy and Analysis found that residents aged 65 and up were the only group that showed significant labor growth over the 10 years. Older Americans are driving demand for workers in certain industries while potentially delaying the vacancies younger professionals would compete to fill.

“Demographic shifts are driving demand for health care and social assistance, making this the

fastest growing sector in the labor market,” the recent report explains. “Anticipated shifts in Federal healthcare funding raise concerns about the sector’s ability to sustain employment growth. Meanwhile, job growth in leisure and hospitality, manufacturing, and construction is expected to remain weak due to high interest rates and a slowing economy.”

Now, New York is struggling to expand its pool of available workers even as businesses pull back on hiring. The state’s workforce was 1% smaller in 2021 than it was a decade earlier, compared to a nationwide increase of 5.1% during the same period, according to the 2022 report. And the combination of a shrinking labor pool and an increasingly older workforce isn’t unique to New York; across the U.S., baby boomers are staying on the job well past traditional retirement age, reshaping what it means to leave the workforce for good.

The number of those who are working past 65 has quadrupled in the U.S. since the 1980s, according to 2023 analysis from Pew Research Center, with around a fifth of the older generation holding down their jobs.

Beyond using employer-provided healthcare for as long as possible and keeping their schedules full, Americans are working longer because they worry their savings could run dry. Over two in five retired Americans, about 20 million people, worry their funds won’t support their ideal retirement lifestyle, according to a 2025 survey from investment banking firm D.A. Davidson. Now, Americans plan to work for four years longer than they’d wish to keep their heads above water amid a high cost-of-living and surging healthcare expenses, according to 2026 research from Economist Enterprise.

“I think that the days of retirement being a one-time, one-way exit and then you’re done are over,” Elizabeth White, author of 55, Underemployed, told Fortune in 2024.

For some who have already called it quits on their careers, that fear has already become a reality. Nearly 20% of American retirees are “struggling” or “living the nightmare,” according to a 2025 study from Schroders. Meanwhile, only 5% said they were “living the dream.” Now, the price of clocking out for good is in the millions.

When BlackRock, the world’s largest asset management firm, surveyed U.S. voters earlier this year on how much they think they’d need to retire comfortably, the average response landed around $2.1 million. And Larry Fink, the company’s CEO, said that “almost no one” is close to reaching that goal; BlackRock’s study found that 62% of respondents had less than $150,000 saved for retirement—about 7% of the $2.1 million they think they’d need to stop working. Fink also pointed out that the U.S.’s climbing senior care costs and lack of preparedness for rising life expectancy is exacerbating America’s retirement savings problem.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/boeing-l.title: Boeing to cut 5% of commercial airplane workforce as production increase is slower than expected
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/boeing-l.author: Leslie Josephs
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/09/boeing-l.text:
Boeing said it plans to cut 5% of its commercial airplane workforce through a combination of attrition and layoffs.

The plane maker is still working to stabilize production rates of its popular 737 Max planes.

Boeing’s head of its commercial aircraft unit, Stephanie Pope, said in a memo that adjusting the production schedule “puts us in an overstaffed position.”

Boeing
 said Monday that it plans to cut 5% of its commercial airplane workforce as its production ramp-up is moving at a slower pace than the company expected.

The cuts will be through a combination of attrition and layoffs, Stephanie Pope, head of the commercial aircraft unit, said in a memo to staff.

Pope reiterated that the company is still working to stabilize production rates of its popular 737 Max planes.

“Adjusting our production schedules and reducing aircraft output puts us in an overstaffed position,” she said in the note. “Unfortunately, that means we need to align our staffing levels to our revised business plan, resulting in a reduction of approximately 5% through a combination of attrition and involuntary layoffs, with notifications beginning in December.”

Boeing CEO Kelly Ortberg said late last month that the plane manufacturer doesn’t expect to significantly ramp up output of its best-selling 737 Max aircraft until the second half of 2027, which is longer than the company had been expecting.

Boeing is targeting a production rate of 52 planes a month in the second half of 2027. It has been manufacturing about 47 of its 737 Max planes a month.

Hakeem Jeffries, who is set to be speaker of the house, announced this weekend that he would vote in favor of a resolution to impeach Hegseth. The Defense Secretary is one of the most controversial figures in President Donald Trump’s cabinet, and has purged the Pentagon of many top officials widely perceived as highly effective. He has repeatedly made provocative culture-war comments that have little to do with national security. And most damaging to his reputation, Hegseth has become the face of the war in Iran.

No matter how unpopular the U.S. military operations have been, Hegseth has stood behind the president. He has defended the pledge to eliminate Iran’s nuclear program and to establish a stronger foothold in the region, even as voters, including those in red states, flocked to the polls to express their disapproval of the administration’s foreign policy.

He has defended the pledge to eliminate Iran’s nuclear program and to establish a stronger foothold in the region, even as voters, including those in red states, flocked to the polls to express their disapproval of the administration’s foreign policy.

What happens next remains to be seen. Some Republicans privately hope Hegseth will resign, either voluntarily or under pressure, so that Trump can replace him with someone who has a more favorable public presence and clearer strategy for bringing U.S. involvement in the war to an end. Most Democrats are wary about initiating impeachment proceedings against Trump, given that he has only two years left in office and has historically benefited politically when under attack. Hegseth, however, remains a possible target for impeachment. Pursuing him, potentially with some Republican support, would allow Democrats to demonstrate that they are serious about holding the administration accountable.

Twenty years ago, Defense Secretary Donald Rumsfeld lost his job after becoming the face of an unpopular war. The question now is whether Hegseth will meet the same fate.

When President George W. Bush announced his nomination of Rumsfeld to be secretary of defense on Dec. 28, 2000, following a highly divisive election recount, most experts considered Rumsfeld one of the most qualified people for the job. A Navy veteran of the 1950s, he had served in the U.S. House of Representatives from 1963 to 1969. He then left legislative politics to become President Richard Nixon’s director of the Office of Economic Opportunity, and later counselor to the president and director of the Cost of Living Council. In 1973, Nixon named him U.S. ambassador to NATO. After Nixon resigned in disgrace over the Watergate scandal in August 1974, President Gerald Ford appointed Rumsfeld as White House chief of staff, and in 1975, Ford nominated him as secretary of defense, a post he held until President Jimmy Carter took office in 1977. Rumsfeld then spent many years working in the private sector while remaining involved in politics as a champion of neoconservatism.

His nomination as was greeted as a sign that the new President Bush would surround himself with a team of seasoned experts. After 9/11, Rumsfeld, who had a close and long-standing relationship with Vice President Dick Cheney, emerged as an important voice within the administration, helping to develop and implement a counterterrorism strategy intended to prevent comparable attacks on U.S. soil. In October and November 2001, the success of the military operations against the Taliban regime in Afghanistan was praised as evidence of his strategic prowess. The same was true in 2003, when the United States went to war with Iraq and Baghdad fell within weeks. On May 1, Bush declared an end to major combat operations beneath a “Mission Accomplished” banner, and in December, U.S. forces captured Iraqi leader Saddam Hussein.

Beneath those successes, however, things were already going wrong for Rumsfeld and for the war. The first major trouble came when looting broke out across Baghdad in April 2003, including at the Iraq Museum and the National Library and Archives. It soon became clear that the Pentagon had done little planning for the aftermath of Hussein’s downfall. “Stuff happens,” Rumsfeld told reporters, brushing off their questions about the looting. Meanwhile, the U.S. military failed to find stockpiles of weapons of mass destruction, which had been the main justification for the war.

By the 2006 midterms, the Iraq War was deeply unpopular. Large numbers of U.S. ground troops were still struggling to establish political stability and contain sectarian violence, and they were suffering heavy casualties. The 2003 decision to disband the Iraqi army proved enormously costly, and in April 2004, a weeknight 60 Minutes broadcast had revealed widespread abuse of detainees of Abu Ghraib prison. Although the story was initially framed as the work of a few rogue soldiers, it soon became clear that the abuses were connected to Pentagon policies authorizing harsh interrogation methods. Rumsfeld privately offered to resign several times, but Bush refused to accept.

There had also been scattered calls from Congress to force the issue. In May 2004, New York Rep. Charles Rangel introduced eight articles of impeachment against Rumsfeld in response to the revelations of Abu Ghraib.

After their tours of duty, many soldiers returned with post-traumatic stress disorder and could not get the support they needed to transition back to civilian life. Democrats made the war a central theme of the 2006 campaign, presenting it as evidence of Republican misrule: Bush’s deeply flawed and unnecessary decision to go to war with Iraq in the first place, made with strong congressional Republican support, compounded by the failure to plan for what would happen once the government collapsed. In September 2006, Republicans were able to block a vote on a nonbinding statement from Senate Democrats expressing a “sense of the Senate” that Bush replace Rumsfeld. “To fight a war on terror,” New York Sen. Charles Schumer said during the floor debate, “you need to be both strong and smart. And with Secretary Rumsfeld in this administration, you do see a great deal of strength but you don’t see enough on the smarts.” Behind the scenes, White House chief of staff Andrew Card lobbied the president, unsuccessfully, to replace Rumsfeld, too.

Rumsfeld himself was an issue. His approval ratings, which had stood at 71 percent in 2003, had fallen to 44 percent in Gallup polling by January 2006. That spring, in what Time called “The Revolt of the Generals,” six retired generals called for Rumsfeld to resign. “When I introduce the Secretary of Defense to my troops, I’m going to be a loyal subordinate,” Army Major General John Batiste told the magazine. “But it was boiling inside me. Every time I looked at him, I was thinking about … that s___ war plan, I was thinking about Abu Ghraib, and I was thinking about the challenges I had every day trying to rebuild the Iraqi military that he disbanded.”

The defense secretary puts stunts over substance. The U.S. should send him on permanent leave.

One lawmaker lays out the case for indicting the defense secretary.

The secretary of defense is now the most influential senior official in the Trump administration.

Still, Bush stood by his man. Responding to critical editorials and calls for Rumsfeld’s resignation, Bush told the press on April 18: “Don Rumsfeld is doing a fine job. He’s not only transforming the military, he’s fighting a war on terror. … I hear the voices, and I read the front page, and I know the speculation. But I’m the decider, and I decide what’s best. And what’s best is for Don Rumsfeld to remain as the secretary of defense.” Whenever the issue came up in conversations with the White House, Robert Draper wrote in his 2007 book, Dead Certain, Bush doubled down. “The moment someone would say ‘Fire Donald Rumsfeld,’ Donald Rumsfeld would get a new lease on life,” said a White House aide.

The criticism did not abate. On Sept. 25, 2006, six weeks before the election, Batiste and two other retired generals told the Senate Democratic Policy Committee that Rumsfeld was unable to handle the job. On Saturday, Nov. 6, the newspapers associated with the Military Times Media Group published an editorial titled “Time for Rumsfeld to Go.”

Although Bush had publicly defended Rumsfeld into the final days of the campaign, the outcome made continued support all but impossible. A number of issues drove the election, including corruption, the cost of living, and healthcare, but opposition to the Iraq War was chief among them. Democrats won control of the House and Senate.

The president realized that he needed to change course. According to Rumsfeld, Cheney had given him advanced warning that Bush planned to finally accept his resignation. On Nov. 8, Bush announced that he was nominating Robert Gates as the new secretary of defense. “America is safer and the world is more secure because of the service and the leadership of Donald Rumsfeld,” Bush said. The decision was a blow to Cheney, who counted on Rumsfeld as an ally, and a victory for the foreign policy realists who served under President George H.W. Bush.

The leadership shake-up paved the way for a basic shift in strategy, announced in January 2007: from a U.S. mission focused on fighting insurgents and handing security over to newly constituted Iraqi forces, to a so-called surge of additional troops whose mission was to protect the Iraqi population and win their support against the insurgency.

Many Republicans privately expressed regret that Bush had not made the decision earlier, which might have given the GOP a fighting chance to hold its majorities. As New York Times reporter Adam Nagourney put it, then-Rep. Rahm Emanuel, an Illinois Democrat, “gave private thanks that the president had not robbed the Democrats of a potent issue by firing Rumsfeld before the campaign was engaged.”

The war in Iran is not nearly as large as the Iraq War, and there is no ground war, but Trump’s policies have proven to be extraordinarily unpopular from the start, and as prices rise, the war has only become more controversial. There is little love for Hegseth, even among Republicans. Not only does he embody much of what critics think is wrong with Trump 2.0, but because he is not the president, Republicans feel freer to attack him.

Rumsfeld’s resignation offers a template for today’s Republicans who are angry about what has happened in Trump’s second term, and it could be that Hegseth will now go. But even if he leaves—or if Congress forces him out—it is unlikely to bring a fundamental change in policy. The Trump White House has centralized power in the president himself, so he will remain the source of policy decisions and the focus of attacks. Despite Democratic victories in last week’s midterms, Trump is unlikely to change course. It would take budgetary and investigative pressure from Congress to make that change.
